title: Home "Treat" Home
text:
Think of a bird choosing each small piece of its nest. The bird chooses carefully. Each piece has an important property to help make the nest just what the bird needs. If we took the nest apart, another bird could take those pieces and make a different nest.

Using pieces to create one whole object is something we can see in the world around us. Builders use different materials to build our homes, schools, and roads. Each material they use has important properties that make the whole project better.

Scientists and inventors do the same thing. They combine different materials with unique properties to create something new. This is how we get new medicines, phones, and other new technology.

Another example is recipes. Cooks combine separate ingredients to make a new food. The same ingredients can be used in different recipes. Cooks choose ingredients that have the kind of properties they need to make their recipe work. They might need a certain ingredient that is sweet or salty. They may need something that is liquid, or that will add a certain texture. The most important thing is getting all the ingredients to work together to make something extra “tweet.”

Reflect and Connect

What are other situations where it is important for someone to choose materials carefully? Explain how properties of matter are important then.

title: We the People Face Challenges
text:
After the Constitutional Convention, George Washington of Virginia was unanimously elected the president of the United States. The first Congress met and began the business of governing. There were many challenges facing the new federal government. Some of those challenges were because of new laws. Some challenges were inherited from the old system.

One challenge inherited from the old system was the debt created from the war. The cost of keeping an army supplied during the Revolutionary War had added up. Under the Articles of Confederation, the individual states were responsible for paying off this debt. However, the Confederation Congress did not have the power to collect tax money. The new federal government, however, had a taxation system in place. The new secretary of the treasury, Alexander Hamilton, created a plan. To give the new government a positive financial system, he suggested that the war debt be paid in full. After much debate, he persuaded the federal government to pay off the debt. To pay the debt, the Bank of the United States was established, and a system of currency, or money, was created that is still in place today. To strengthen the United States, Hamilton proposed that the United States promote manufacturing. He also advocated that the country limit its trade dependency on manufactured goods from Europe.

Another challenge the new government faced was how to balance the demands of manufacturing and agriculture. Manufacturing favored the northern states but diminished the agricultural plantation system of the southern states. Thomas Jefferson, in contrast, promoted policies that favored agriculture and the southern states. Hamilton and Jefferson’s opinions created two different ways of thinking that eventually led to two political parties. The two parties were the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans. Hamilton led the Federalists. Jefferson led the Democratic Republicans.

By 1798, Washington had retired as president. John Adams, a Federalist, was the second president. Thomas Jefferson, a Democratic Republican, was vice president. The two parties had such differing opinions on every topic that there was constant conflict in the government. The Federalists accused the opposing views of the other party as being disloyal to the Constitution.

Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts. These Acts targeted immigration and immigrants living in the United States. The Acts also made it a crime for American citizens to “print, utter, or publish ... any false, scandalous, and malicious [hostile] writing” about the federal government. These legal actions were a direct challenge to the First Amendment, especially freedom of speech and the press. Many newspapers who supported Jefferson’s political party were arrested and shut down for printing material that opposed the Federalists.

John Adams ran for re-election in 1800 against Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr. Jefferson and Burr received the majority of votes in a tie. As directed in the Constitution, the election went to the House of Representatives to break the tie. After weeks of discussion and voting, with a tie occurring each time, Alexander Hamilton stepped up to endorse Thomas Jefferson over his friend, Aaron Burr. This swayed enough House members to vote for Jefferson as president. Burr conceded defeat and became vice president. The first peaceful transfer of power occurred after a very tense election process. Burr’s peaceful concession strengthened the Constitution and the new country.

The Alien and Sedition Acts were repealed, or not renewed. President Jefferson began his administration by looking to give more power to the states. However, as time passed, an opportunity would come that made Jefferson stretch the authority of the presidency. He made the largest land purchase in the history of the United States.

title: Change Over Time In Alabama
text:
1900

Alabama’s total population was listed in the census as 1,828,697.

The five leading industries in the state were:

iron and steel

lumber and timber products

cotton goods

foundry products (for producing steel)

steam railroad construction and repair

1909

Cotton was one of the most important industries for the economy of Alabama. It was critical both to agriculture and manufacturing. Sixty percent of the crop value in the state was from cotton alone.

1910

The census showed the population topped two million for the first time in state history at 2,138,093.

Impacting Historical Event

the Great Depression

1931

Nearly half of the state’s workforce worked in agriculture. The other half were in timber and steel production.

1935

The cotton industry remained strong in Alabama. Other industries were hurt by the Great Depression. Workers outside of agriculture lost their jobs in large numbers.

Impacting Historical Event

World War II

1942

Business in Alabama grew rapidly after the start of World War II. Cotton production and the demand for steel to help the war effort led the increases. Many Alabamians found new jobs in industries that supported the military.

Impacting Historical Event

Cold War

1950

Alabama’s census showed a population of over three million for the first time at 3,061,743.

1956

Electronic machines were first used in businesses to help manage operations. This was the early start of the electronics boom in Alabama.

1966

Alabama's largest industries, steel and paper, change to automobiles and high-tech. The state economy saw massive growth as a result.

1987

Alabama’s population pushed over four million.

1993

Mercedes-Benz announced a plan to build a large vehicle plant in Alabama. The state provided incentives like tax breaks and financial assistance to build the facility. These incentives helped bring the automaker to the state.

1998

During the year, Alabama exports grew by a massive 25 percent. The increase was due, in part, to Mercedes-Benz M-class exports.

1999

American Honda Motor Corp. announced a plan to build a $400 million facility in Lincoln, located in Talladega County.

2000 and beyond

Since the rise of the auto industry in Alabama, Toyota, Hyundai, and Polaris have each built manufacturing plants in the state. The aerospace industry has also grown with the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville. Recently, U.S. Space Command was relocated to Huntsville. The number of beverage plants throughout the state has increased. Alabama is now home to over 780 bioscience research and development companies. They specialize in things like medicine, medical equipment, and new healthcare procedures.

Alabama’s total population was listed in the 2020 census as 5,024,279.

Current top five industries in Alabama:

aerospace and aviation

bioscience

agriculture

beverage production

automotive

title: Changes to Cities in Alabama
text:
In the 20th century, the population of Alabama changed. In earlier times, Alabama was very rural and had an agriculturally based economy. As the century moved on, there was a shift, with more people in Alabama moving into cities. Places like Birmingham, Mobile, Tuscaloosa, and Huntsville increased in population. This increase was due to growing industries like bioscience, aerospace, and the automotive industry. For the first time in the 20th century, the state began to identify as more urban and suburban. People moved away from places like the Black Belt Region. As a result, the legacy of the plantation economy was left behind.

Population as of 2020

Birmingham: 210,928

The city has seen manufacturing of metals decline since 2000. However, metal manufacture and distribution still represent both the legacy and current economy of Birmingham.

Huntsville: 199,845

The city is home to the growing bioscience industry in the state of Alabama. It is also home to military installations. The Redstone Arsenal and the NASA Marshall Space Flight Center are located here. The city is also the headquarters of the United States Space Command.

Mobile: 189,994

The Port of Mobile is the largest port in the state of Alabama. It contributes greatly to the population of the city. In recent years, Mobile has seen a small decline in population. However, the port itself has seen great growth. In 2021, the port set a record for the most containers processed in its history.

Tuscaloosa: 100,633

The city is home to a Mercedes-Benz Auto manufacturing plant. The state’s largest university, the University of Alabama, is located here. Tuscaloosa has grown rapidly in the 20th century, from just 5,000 residents in 1900 to its present size.

title: Changing Demographics in Alabama
text:
Census

Alabama’s demographics have changed. People have moved in and out of Alabama. The differences in data between the 2010 and 2020 censuses show how Alabama demographics have changed.

Immigration

Immigrants come from all over the world and settle in the United States. Sometimes, people come for job opportunities or for family. These reasons are called “pull factors.” Other times, people come because of problems in their home countries. These problems are things like war, violence, or natural disasters. We call these “push factors.” Just like the rest of the United States, Alabama has a diverse immigrant population.

In 2018, 162,567 immigrants claimed Alabama as their home.

Mexico, China, India, Guatemala, and Germany were the top origins of immigrants to Alabama.

In 2018, 166,266 people in Alabama were born in the United States and had at least one immigrant parent.

Migration

Migration happens when people move within a country or region. Sometimes, individuals will migrate from one state to another. Other times, they may move from one city to another in the same state. Alabama has seen people migrate into the state as well as migrate away. Take a look at the map and see how many people have come to or left from around the state. People also migrate for a variety of reasons. What are the push and pull factors for Alabama?

title: Changes to Roads in Alabama
text:
Roads are used as a method of transportation in Alabama just as they were in the 19th century. As the roads in the United States grew, however, the roads in Alabama did as well. The reasons for this growth came from the changes in major industries, technology and the need for access to the Port of Mobile. As a result, transportation in Alabama changed and adapted throughout the state.

In the 19th century, roads were primarily used by people for walking and carts. As Alabama moved into the early 20th century, people began to drive automobiles on roads. They would use these roads for the movement of goods and services. They also used the roads to access places like the Port of Mobile. Road access to the port was important. Goods coming into the port needed to be moved off of ships and brought to cities further inland. Roads like the Old Federal Road were built and used in the 19th century. In the 20th century, improved paved roads like interstate highways were being used.

In the later 20th century, the interstate system grew so that Alabama’s largest cities could be accessed more quickly and easily than ever before. Compare the maps of the current interstate system and the 19th century road system in Alabama. What similarities and differences do you see?

title: Changes to Natural Environments in Alabama
text:
Plantations slowly phased out of the economy during the Reconstruction Era. The state of Alabama saw an increase in “second forests.” These forests reclaimed former open plantation lands. Second forests were one factor in growing the timber industry in Alabama. Second forests are an example of how changes in natural environments can spark development in new industries.

Today, Alabama still has mild winters and warm, humid summers. Tornadoes and hurricanes are a hazard to the state. The Dixie Tornado Outbreak in 2011 set a record for the most tornadoes in a single day. Hurricanes that reach Alabama and make landfall can leave catastrophe in their wakes. In 2004, Hurricane Ivan changed the economy and impacted tourism in Alabama. Federal and state governments have worked to develop national and state parks for preservation and protection.

National Monuments and Preserves

Little River Canyon National Preserve

Little River is unique because it flows for most of its length atop Lookout Mountain in northeast Alabama. Natural resources and culture come together in this area. They tell the unique story of this special place in the southern Appalachians.

Russell Cave National Monument

Russell Cave is an archaeological site with one of the most complete records of prehistoric cultures in the Southeast. In the 1950s, archaeologists uncovered a large quantity of artifacts. The artifacts represented over 10,000 years of use in a single place.

State Parks

There are over 20 state parks in Alabama. Each state park is unique and has a special story to tell. Cathedral Caverns State Park is a massive cathedral-like cave that was purchased by the state in 1987. Gulf State Park has over two miles of protected beaches along the coast. Bladon Springs State Park was originally a spa. People came for the mineral springs on the property. No matter where you go in the state, you are bound to find a unique state park to fulfill your curiosity.

title: The Supreme Court
text:
Established by the United States Constitution, the Supreme Court began to take shape with the passage of the Judiciary Act of 1789. At this time, a position on the Court was not seen as glamorous. The networks of courts under the Supreme Court required the Justices (members of the Court) to visit frequently. This required days of travel in poor conditions.

At first, the Justices would not stay in the Court for their life appointments as suggested in the Constitution. This changed when outgoing president John Adams appointed John Marshall as Chief Justice in 1800. John Marshall served as Chief Justice for 34 years until 1834. Several of his fellow Justices served for more than 20 years.

As the country grew and the government implemented the Constitution, there were many judicial reviews conducted by the Supreme Court. The justices reviewed the laws to determine if they were in agreement with the Constitution. When a law was not in line with the rights of the people as outlined in the Constitution, the law was labeled as unconstitutional. It was no longer considered a law. When a law was “upheld” by the Supreme Court, it meant it supported the rights protected in the Constitution and was considered law.

These reviews provided a check and balance of power designed by the Founding Fathers.

title: Foreign Policy
text:
It is important for nations to get along with each other for many reasons. Foreign policy is the government’s guidelines for business with other countries. Some countries wanted to be friends with the new United States. Others wanted to challenge the new government.

The continued rivalry of the governments in Europe caused concern in America. The British were still occupying areas of Canada. France had colonies in the Caribbean. Spain had colonies in Mexico and the southwest territory of North America. These colonies were gaining independence. The United States was concerned that the other European governments would try to restore the colonies.

President James Monroe issued a foreign policy order in 1823 known as the Monroe Doctrine.

“The American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for colonization by any European powers.”

This policy described that any attempt by a European power to exert its influence in the Western Hemisphere would, from then on, be seen by the United States as a threat to its security.

The Monroe Doctrine is still a part of U.S. foreign policy today.

title: University of Alabama Research on COVID-19
text: There is a growing bioscience industry in the State of Alabama. These research facilities were positioned to assist in research during the pandemic caused by the COVID-19 virus. Research institutions in Alabama played a large role in the research of the virus. Many helped develop vaccines. In 2020, the University of Alabama School of Medicine published crucial research and conducted clinical trials. The Alabama Vaccine Research Clinic also has a major role in the testing and development of vaccines. This research has helped the CDC (Center for Disease Control) in the United States. It has also helped the WHO (World Health Organization) in Geneva, Switzerland.

title: Phenomenon Introduction
text:
Bed in Summer

by Robert Louis Stevenson

In winter I get up at night

And dress by yellow candle-light

In summer, quite the other way,

I have to go to bed by day.

I have to go to bed and see

The birds still hopping on the tree,

Or hear the grown-up people’s feet

Still going past me in the street.

And does it not seem hard to you,

When all the sky is clear and blue,

And I should like so much to play,

To have to go to bed by day?

title: Bedtime Poetry
text:
The Pleasant Dark

by Annette Wynne

The pleasant dark that comes at night

Is just as friendly as the light,

Dark wraps a curtain over all --

The trees, the houses, far and tall;

The pleasant dark comes down to bless

The world with mother-tenderness.

She folds her children in her arms

And keeps them safe from loud alarms;

The far green hills where children play

Are hidden till the brand-new day.

For hills and eyelids know what’s best --

That darkness-time is time for rest.

The pleasant dark that comes at night

Is just as friendly as the light.

Behind Each Star

by Annette Wynne

Behind each star a small dream hides

But will not show its head,

Unless you’re very, very good --

And fast asleep in bed.

title: Alabama and the Civil War
text:
The Excitement of War

The fall of 1860 and early winter of 1861 were a time of both tension and excitement for citizens of Alabama. Anticipating a possible war, Governor Moore ordered militiamen to take Fort Morgan and Fort Gaines at Mobile Bay. They also took the arsenal north of Mobile.

On April 12, 1861, Confederates fired on Fort Sumter and a series of events followed. The Civil War began with excitement. Many young men from Alabama wanted to prove their bravery and ability to fight. They rushed to enlist in the Confederate army. For some, the greatest worry was that the war would be over before they could make their way to the front lines.

Most of these young men did not know that the war would take four years and change life in the South forever.

Economy of the Civil War

One of the ways in which economics impacted Alabama during the Civil War was the lack of industry. The land was so good that people had been able to make a much better living by growing cotton and other crops. Therefore, weapons, ammunition, railroad tracks, and train cars were only some of the items that were in short supply. In a war, supplies and soldiers are both needed.

Alabamian Bravery at Gettysburg

When it came to soldiers, Alabama had no shortages.

The Confederate soldiers from Alabama joined the Army of Northern Virginia for the planned invasion of the north in Pennsylvania. Union and Confederate troops clashed in a town called Gettysburg. Many consider the battle of Gettysburg to be a turning point of the war. For three hot July days, the armies fought. On July 2, 1863, the regiments from Alabama advanced on the Union Army at the high ground called Little Round Top. The 20th Maine Infantry held a position there. The 15th Alabama Infantry of Law’s Brigade attempted to dislodge the Union 20th Maine Infantry.

The Alabamians went up the steep slopes, facing deadly fire, three times. They were repulsed all three times. Little Round Top was a key location for victory. The Alabamian brigades were honored for their courage and their determination even in defeat.

The Battle of Mobile Bay

One of the most significant battles fought in Alabama was the Battle of Mobile Bay. Union Rear Admiral David Farragut ordered the attack on Mobile Bay at dawn on Aug. 5, 1864. The battle did not begin well for Farragut. One of his new ironclad ships hit a mine in the water, killing about 150 men.

The Union had a large enough fleet that even with the navy and three forts fighting for Alabama, eventually the Confederate fleet was destroyed. The last ship in the Alabamian navy was the CSS Tennessee, led by Admiral Franklin Buchanan. This ship took on the entire Union fleet by itself. This last ship fought until it was disabled and forced to surrender in spite of impossible odds.

title: The Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole Tribes in the 21st Century
text:
The United States is still home to many Native American tribes today. Some tribes have remained intact and still inhabit their ancestral homelands. Others have formed new tribes and adopted new names. The Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole are just a few of the many Native American tribes that continue to preserve their cultures, traditions, and beliefs.

Choctaw

The Choctaw Tribe traditionally lived in Alabama and Mississippi. Thousands of members of the tribe were forced to relocate to present-day Oklahoma as a result of the Indian Removal Act. Today, three Choctaw tribes are federally recognized by the United States government. Federally recognized tribes have an official relationship with the U.S. government. They have certain rights, responsibilities, and powers. They have access to certain benefits, services, and protections from the U.S. government.

The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma is the largest federally recognized Choctaw tribe. This tribe has over 200,000 registered members. Many members of the tribe live on the Choctaw Nation’s reservation, which covers about 11,000 square miles of southeastern Oklahoma. A reservation is an area of land designated to a tribe or tribes by the United States government. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma has its own constitution, which outlines the structure of the government and the rights and responsibilities of the members of the tribe. The tribe is governed by a tribal council. The tribal council is led by a chief. Tribal chiefs are elected by the members of the tribe and serve for a term of four years.

The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma preserves its cultural traditions and customs. Members of the tribe continue to use centuries-old techniques to make pottery, baskets, and beadwork. Traditional tribal dances still play an important role in the community. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma has a group dedicated to preserving the traditional dances of the tribe. They wear traditional dance regalia, (clothing and ornaments worn for a specific purpose or occasion) and participate in outreach programs to teach others about the tribe.

The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians has over 11,000 members. Most of the members of the tribe live on the tribal reservation, located in central Mississippi. The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians received federal recognition in 1945. The tribe is governed by a tribal chief. The tribal chief works with members of the tribal council to pass and enforce laws. Laws and government organization are outlined in the tribal constitution.

Traditional cultural customs and practices continue to play a large role in tribal life. The Choctaw language is still taught in schools on the reservation. It is widely spoken in public and private life, in stores, restaurants, community offices, and homes. Visitors can view Choctaw artifacts and learn about the history of the tribe at the Chahta Immi Cultural Center, located in Philadelphia, Mississippi.

The smallest federally recognized Choctaw tribe is the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians. Currently, the tribe has 327 members. As a federally recognized tribe, the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians has its own reservation. The tribe controls 64 acres of land in Trout, Louisiana. Like the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians, the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians is governed by a chief and tribal council.

Members of the tribe work diligently to teach younger generations and members of the community about the tribe's history. Native speakers teach traditional language classes to other members of the tribe. Each year, the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians host PowWow in the Pines. A powwow is a cultural event where tribal members gather together to perform traditional songs and dances. It is also a meeting place, where people can display and purchase art, jewelry, pottery, and many other items. Powwows are often open to the public and are a wonderful way for people to learn about the customs and history of different tribes.

Chickasaw

The Chickasaw Nation of Oklahoma is one of the largest federally recognized tribes in the United States. As of 2019, the Chickasaw Nation of Oklahoma included more than 70,000 members. The tribal reservation is located in southwestern Oklahoma and encompasses 7,648 square miles of land.

The government of the tribe is modeled after the federal government of the United States. The tribe is governed by an elected governor, lieutenant governor, tribal council, and justices of the tribal supreme court. Each member of the tribal council serves in a specific office to aid the governor and members of the tribe in the areas of business, commerce, health, education, family services, and culture.

The Chickasaw Nation works hard to preserve its history and teach others about the tribe’s culture, traditions, and beliefs. Visitors can learn more about the traditional customs of the tribe at the Chikasha Inchokka' Traditional Village. The Chikasha Inchokka' Traditional Village includes reconstructed Chicksaw homes. Visitors can also experience cultural demonstrations, such as storytelling, cooking, dancing, and sports. The Chickasaw reservation is also home to the Center for Study of Chickasaw History and Culture, the Chikasha Poya Exhibit Center, and the Itti' Anonka' Nannakat Oktani (Spirit Forest) exhibit, where visitors can experience the wonders of the natural world and learn about the tribe’s connection to their environment.

Creek

The Muscogee (Creek) Nation is one of the two federally recognized Creek tribes in the United States. It is the largest of the Creek tribes, with more than 86,000 members. The government of the tribe is divided into three branches: executive, legislative, and judicial. The executive branch is led by the principal and second chiefs. The tribal chiefs work with members of the tribal council, who make up the legislative branch, to make decisions and manage the affairs of the tribe. The judicial branch consists of district courts, the tribal supreme court, and the office of the Attorney General. Judicial leaders work together to enforce the laws of the tribe and protect its citizens.

Members of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation participate in many programs and events to promote their culture and preserve the tribe’s history. The Mvskoke Language Program teaches members of the tribe to read, write, and speak Mvskoke. Every year, the Muscogee (Creek) Nation hosts the Muscogee Nation Festival in Okmulgee, Oklahoma. This three-day event is a celebration of Muscogee culture. The festival includes cultural exhibits, parades, sports tournaments, concerts, rides, and Muscogee arts and crafts.

The Poarch Band of Creek Indians is the second federally recognized Creek tribe in the United States. It is the only federally recognized tribe in the state of Alabama. The tribe includes about 3,000 members. The government of the Poarch Band of Creek Indians is very similar to the government of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The executive branch is led by the tribal chair, who is responsible for management of all tribal organizations and activities. The legislative branch is made up of nine members who serve on the tribal council. The tribal council works closely with the tribal chair to make decisions for the tribe. The judicial branch is made up of the tribal supreme court and local courts.

Seminole

The people of the Seminole Tribe of Florida are often referred to as the “unconquered people” because they refused to leave their home and resisted forced removal for hundreds of years. Approximately 3,000 members of the tribe live in Florida today on six different Seminole reservations. They engage in many economic activities, including tourism, agriculture, and cattle ranching.

Members of the tribe work hard to preserve their tribal customs and traditions. They share these customs and traditions with one another and other people in the state. The Seminole Tribe of Florida is a federally recognized tribe and has its own tribal government. The tribe is governed by a tribal council and board of directors. These groups work together to uphold the laws and regulations created by the Seminole Constitution.

The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma is the largest of the federally recognized Seminole tribes. There are almost 19,000 members of the tribe today. More than half of the members of the tribe live in Oklahoma. Several members of the tribe live on the Seminole Nation reservation, which covers 633 square miles of land in central Oklahoma.

Like other federally recognized tribes, the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma has its own government. The tribe is led by the chief and assistant chief. These elected officials work with elected representatives and members of various committees to ensure the welfare and safety of all members of the tribe. They also deal with all cultural, financial, educational, and health-related matters of the tribe.

Members of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma are determined to preserve their culture and traditions. The Seminole Nation Language Program runs an extensive language program to teach members of the tribe and community the language of their ancestors. The Historic Preservation Office works with local and state officials to teach people about the rich history of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma.

title: Early 19th Century Alabama
text:
Alabama Land Fever

In just 10 years, between 1810 and 1820, the population of Alabama grew by 1,000 percent! By 1820, nearly 200,000 people lived in Alabama. They all came to find land. In the East, the fields had been farmed until they were worn out. The economy (resources and trade) in the East was not doing well. Loads of people came to Alabama by wagon or flatboat. Others came by walking, with all their belongings strapped to their backs. Most of the newcomers were poor farmers. Alabama held a lot of promise. It had big rivers that allowed people to ship things from place to place.

Learning on the Frontier

In frontier Alabama, children often went to school inside the forts where they lived. They only learned the basic things: reading, writing, and math. In some places, children did not have ink and paper. They wrote on smooth boards, using ink made out of fluids from animals.

Slavery in the South

When settlers moved south to Alabama, so did the practice of slavery. Slavery went on for many years in the South. Enslaved African Americans were forced to work hard in the hot sun. They farmed corn, cotton, and tobacco. This practice was mostly for wealthy plantation owners who could afford it. Many men who were free but poor had much smaller farms.

Building a Cabin

Most farmers on the frontier lived in log cabins. When a new cabin was needed, everyone in the settlement turned out to help. The men cut down trees and trimmed off the limbs with sharp axes. Then, they cut the trees into logs of the same length. After that, they cut deep notches in either end of each log. That way, it would fit snugly on top of the log underneath it. Roofs were made from shorter trees and cut into boards. Sometimes, the builders hammered wood pegs into the roof to secure it. Other times, they just lifted a bunch of heavy rocks onto the roof. Children helped too. They mixed up batches of sticks, small rocks, and mud to fill the spaces between the logs. That kept the rain and wind out.

Religion in the Old South

There was plenty of religion in the frontier South. The Catholic Church had come with the original French settlers. In the 1800s, Protestant churches came into the state. The first Methodist preacher was Lorenzo Dow. Dow and other ministers rode throughout the countryside, preaching outdoors. They were called circuit riders. They became so popular that many people built small parson rooms onto their houses for traveling preachers to stay in. They would even leave the door open, just in case a preacher wandered in after the family had gone to bed. Preachers helped establish some of Alabama's first schools.

title: Steamboats in 19th Century Alabama
text:
The geography of Alabama shaped its population and economy. The Mississippi Territory, which included Mississippi and Alabama, was created in 1798. Then, in 1803, the Louisiana Purchase added even more land to the United States. Settlers from the East wanted to move farther west.

Alabama did not have a good road system. However, Alabama has many rivers. Those rivers provided waterways for people to travel west from Georgia and South Carolina.

As people moved west, cities grew along the rivers. Cities provided goods and services, making it even easier for more people to move west. As agriculture developed, farmers needed a way to transport their goods. Even into the 19th century, road systems had not developed. Using wagons with horses or oxen to carry goods did not work. Again, the rivers were the solution.

Keelboats are boats with flat bottoms. They aren’t always fast, but they are good for carrying heavy cargo. In the early 1800s, keelboats became common in Alabama to carry cargo along the rivers to cities and ports. At the ports, goods could be loaded onto ships.

In 1807, Robert Fulton made the first steamboat that was reliable and affordable. Soon, many packet boats, or steamboats that were designed to carry cargo, were common in Alabama.

Steamboats were a good way to carry cargo, but they had some dangers. American Indians sometimes attacked boats. The Poarch Creek and other tribes were not happy that so many settlers were coming into their ancestral lands. Some of them retaliated.

Boiler explosions were another danger. A boiler is a metal container for a fire that heats water into steam. The steam powers the machines that move the boat. Steam is very powerful. If the pressure of the boiler grows too high, the whole boiler can explode.

A third danger was the captains of the boats themselves. Steamboats were a fast mode of transportation for the 19th century. Sometimes steamboat captains could not resist racing their boats. This was not a safe practice, and sometimes it led to accidents.

In spite of these dangers, steamboats were an effective way of moving goods. As technology developed, steamboats got some competition. Railroads took a lot of work to build, but they began to compete with steamboats as early as the 1830s. In about 1830, there were only 23 miles of tracks in the United States. It was not nearly enough to move goods and people around a state, let alone a whole country. However, the amount of tracks grew every year. By 1880, there were about 93,000 miles of track in the United States.

The competition between trains and boats would create tension during the 19th century.

title: Agriculture in Early Alabama
text:
Hernando de Soto first explored the Alabama area in 1539. He met American Indian tribes that were skilled at raising corn. As de Soto traveled through Alabama, he introduced pigs, horses, and cattle to the area.

In the early 1700s, the French settled the area around the Mobile River. They tried to start plantations using the labor of enslaved people. However, their plans did not work. They said that though the soil was fertile, the land was unhealthy to humans during the growing season. They tried raising cattle instead. This was more successful. They started importing cattle from other areas, such as Mexico and Cuba.

When the British took over the area, they gave out land grants. A head of a household would receive 100 acres, plus 50 acres for each additional member of the household. Veterans of the French and Indian War would receive even more land. Not a lot of people wanted the land at first. Many wanted to be merchants. Those who did want land wanted it to be near water sources. After a while, landowners developed large plantations along Alabama’s rivers.

Colonies in the West Indies usually bought their timber from New England. However, the Revolutionary War cut off their access to it. Demand for timber from Alabama’s Wiregrass region grew. The area had forests of pine, white oak, and cypress.

title: Farms in Early Alabama
text:
As the soil in the original Southern states started wearing out, settlers migrated, or moved, to Alabama.

In northern Alabama, the land was good for growing crops. However, it needed to be cleared of trees and other plants, so farming was still hard work. There was little time for anything but growing enough crops to survive. Men, women, and children worked in the fields. They built hasty log cabins with either split logs or dirt for floors. The family would sleep in the cabin's attic.

Farmers made their living by growing corn, sugarcane, and vegetables. They also raised cattle, poultry, sheep, and hogs. Hogs were popular because pork was easy to preserve, or save, to eat later. Farmers also grew cotton as a cash crop.

Early in Alabama’s settlement, farmers actually ignored what became known as the Black Belt. This area stretched across the middle of Alabama. The Black Belt had very fertile soil. However, it was difficult to plow, and there was not much water. Later, deep wells were drilled and heavy plows began tilling the soil. The Black Belt then became the perfect place to grow cotton.

The Piney Woods and Wiregrass regions are in southern Alabama. They have sandy soil and swampy land. This land wasn’t good for growing crops, but it was very good for raising cattle. Farmers would let their cows wander to find shelter and food and then gather them for market.

title: Plantations in Early Alabama
text:
Plantations were a big business because they were big farms with hundreds of acres of land. They grew cash crops, such as cotton, sugarcane, and tobacco. In Alabama, the largest crop was cotton. An invention called the cotton gin made it much faster to remove the seeds from cotton. It made cotton less expensive to process and worth more money.

At first, plantations used mostly indentured servants. Indentured servants were poor Europeans who wanted to come to America but had no money to travel. Wealthy landowners paid for their trip. In return, the indentured servants agreed to work without pay for a specific period of time. They were given food and lodging. Their daily lives were difficult, with limited freedom.

Labor on plantations shifted to almost all enslaved workers in the 19th century. Plantation owners relied on the free labor of the enslaved Africans who were forced to come to America. From sunrise to sunset, enslavers made the enslaved people work the fields. Some enslaved people, especially women, did domestic work, such as laundry, cooking, and caring for the plantation owner’s children. Often, enslaved people were separated from their own children. They had no freedom. An overseer would be in charge of them.

Plantation owners and their families lived in the main house. Their children would usually have private tutors since schools were not easy to get to. The kitchen would often be in a small structure near the main house. It was usually made of bricks so that it wouldn’t burn down. This kept the main house safer and cooler.

Other buildings surrounded the main house. Some were living quarters for the servants. At most plantations, small cabins were the homes of the enslaved people. The cabins had only one or two rooms and a few pieces of furniture.

Plantations had to be self-sufficient since they were often far from towns and stores. They had buildings for all the things they needed on a daily basis. There were sheds for storing crops, a smokehouse for storing meats, and barns for livestock.

title: Urban Life in Early Alabama
text:
Most of early Alabama was rural. It was made up largely of farms and plantations. As cotton became more profitable, Alabama formed some urban areas (cities). An urban area in early Alabama might seem small to us today. For example, St. Stephens, Alabama’s first capital, had only 40 houses in it. When Cahaba became the capital, it had only 1,000 people living in the city.

Living in an urban area was more complex than living in a rural area. People in urban areas had to live and interact with many people of many different classes. They also needed goods that only artisans and craftsmen could make.

There were social classes in most urban areas. These classes included the gentry, middle class, farmers, indentured servants, and enslaved people.

The gentry was the highest and the smallest class. They controlled much of the money. Some were merchants or financiers (people in charge of money). Others were government officials and plantation owners. The men ran the government, the banks, the stores, and the plantations. The women ran the households and became involved with local organizations. Their children received the best education.

The middle class consisted of craftspeople and artisans. Coopers made barrels and buckets. Tanners turned animal hides into leather. Leather was used to create things like shoes, boots, and saddles. A silversmith might then create silver buckles to go on the leather shoes or decorate the saddles. The same silversmith would also create teapots, tableware, jewelry, and other household items. As the necessities of urban life became more complex, more artisans had to work together to create goods.

Teenage boys would often apprentice to one of these craftsmen. They would work for the craftsman and learn how to do that job well. The apprentice was not paid for his work. However, he was given a place to stay, food, and the clothing he needed. An apprenticeship lasted anywhere from four to seven years. When he completed his training, the apprentice would receive a set of tools and open his own business. Sometimes girls became apprentices, but this was rare. A female apprentice would usually work for a seamstress, dressmaker, or maybe a tailor.

Farmers lived most of their lives in rural areas, raising crops and livestock. They came to urban areas only to sell their products and purchase things they could not make themselves. Though farmers were essential to the workings of cities, they rarely visited the cities.

Indentured servants and enslaved African Americans also lived in urban areas, though not nearly as many as lived in Alabama’s rural areas.
