title: The Great Depression
text:
Black Tuesday, Oct. 29, 1929, was the end of a successful and hopeful time in the United States. During the 1920s, millions of people bought shares of stock, or partial ownership of companies. Stock prices continued to rise. People borrowed more and more money from banks to buy more shares. On Black Tuesday, the prices of stocks fell sharply and the shares were worth nothing. Many people lost everything they owned that day. The stock market crashed and the U.S. economy crashed along with it.

The Great Depression

The stock market crash was only the beginning of tough times for the country. Many banks lost money, too. People worried that their money in the bank might not be safe. They rushed to the banks to withdraw their funds. When banks were out of money, they closed their doors. Some of the banks began to go out of business completely. People who had deposited money in the banks were out of luck. There was no money left.

Many banks tried to get some of the money back that they had let people borrow. They began to ask people to immediately pay back their loans. Sometimes, the banks took people’s homes and farms when their loans weren’t paid.

Businesses were also affected by the economic downturn. Some businesses lost most of their money in the stock market crash. Many of them had to cut back employees’ hours, reduce their pay, or terminate employment altogether. Other businesses lost everything and were forced to close. This caused massive unemployment throughout the country.

Farmers in America had already been suffering economically since the end of World War I. During the war years, Europe needed food and was willing to pay high prices for it. Farmers were making profits and many of them wanted to expand their farms and buy new equipment. The farmers borrowed money from banks to help pay for the land and machinery. When the war ended, the supply of crops far outweighed the demand for them. This caused the price of crops to drop. Farmers could not pay back the money they had borrowed from the banks. Many farmers lost their land and the unpaid loans contributed to the failure of some of the banks by 1929.

Within a few years, millions of Americans were out of work. Some of these people traveled on railroads from town to town looking for new jobs. Farmers who had lost their land traveled all over the country to find work on other people’s farms. Some businesses had more than 1,000 people apply for a single job opening.

Worldwide Effects

Although the Great Depression started in the United States, it quickly became a worldwide problem. After World War I, the United States helped many European countries pay their debts. When the American economy failed, there was no money to send to foreign countries. As a result, the western European countries fell into a period of economic depression, too. Great Britain and Germany were hit the hardest.

The Great Depression lasted for more than a decade. Unfortunately, it took another great war to bring prosperity back to the world.

title: Credit and Consumerism
text:
Personal incomes for many people increased in the 1920s and manufactured goods became more affordable and readily available. However, for consumers who wanted to purchase items such as cars or washing machines, the prices were often still out of reach. Manufacturers began to use the concept of extended credit to make it possible for more people to purchase their products. Under this new system, consumers purchased goods on installment plans. They would be able to obtain goods immediately and pay for them in regular payments over time. They would make these payments until the purchase price, plus interest, was paid in full.

Banks also began extending the country’s first home mortgages. The bank loaned a buyer the money needed to purchase a home. The bank held the deed or mortgage of the home until the buyer paid off the loan. Of course, interest was added for using the bank’s money.

Previous eras had emphasized financial thrift and saving money. The new generation of the 20s emphasized borrowing and spending. A quickly increasing number of people were accumulating debt. This was not a problem as long as business boomed and people were employed. However, with the stock market crash of 1929, these conditions changed in America and around the world. Jobs disappeared, unpaid debts were demanded of consumers, and many people were left in deep financial trouble.

title: Take a Closer Look (Including Reading Passages)
text:
The Ordinance of Secession was created in January 1861. It was the official document telling the United States that Alabama was no longer a part of the Union. Even though the document is not very long, it is packed with important ideas. Taking a closer look at the text can make some of those ideas clear.

The title of the document is "An Ordinance to dissolve the union between the State of Alabama and the other States united under the compact styled 'The Constitution of the United States of America.'" What does the word “dissolve” mean to you? What do you think it means in this context?

The constitutional convention adopted the Articles of Confederation in 1777. According to the title, what was the author's purpose in writing the Ordinance of Secession in 1861?

Take a closer look at Paragraph 1. How do the authors of the ordinance feel about Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin?

Paragraph 1

Whereas, the election of Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin to the offices of president and vice-president of the United States of America, by a sectional party, avowedly hostile to the domestic institutions and to the peace and security of the people of the State of Alabama, preceded by many and dangerous infractions of the constitution of the United States by many of the States and people of the Northern section, is a political wrong of so insulting and menacing a character as to justify the people of the State of Alabama in the adoption of prompt and decided measures for their future peace and security, therefore:

How would you summarize paragraph 2 in your own words? Why is "withdraw" an important word in this paragraph?

Paragraph 2

Be it declared and ordained by the people of the State of Alabama, in Convention assembled, That the State of Alabama now withdraws, and is hereby withdrawn from the Union known as "the United States of America," and henceforth ceases to be one of said United States, and is, and of right ought to be a Sovereign and Independent State.

Paragraph 3 talks about power. According to this ordinance, is power going to the national government or to the state governments?

Paragraph 3

Sec 2. Be it further declared and ordained by the people of the State of Alabama in Convention assembled, That all powers over the Territory of said State, and over the people thereof, heretofore delegated to the Government of the United States of America, be and they are hereby withdrawn from said Government, and are hereby resumed and vested in the people of the State of Alabama.

In paragraphs 4 and 5, the state of Alabama is setting a date to meet with some other states. Based on evidence from the article, what do you think Alabama wants to meet about?

Paragraph 4

And as it is the desire and purpose of the people of Alabama to meet the slaveholding States of the South, who may approve such purpose, in order to frame a provisional as well as permanent Government upon the principles of the Constitution of the United States,

Paragraph 5

Be it resolved by the people of Alabama in Convention assembled, That the people of the States of Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Missouri, be and are hereby invited to meet the people of the State of Alabama, by their Delegates, in Convention, on the 4th day of February, A.D., 1861, at the city of Montgomery, in the State of Alabama, for the purpose of consulting with each other as to the most effectual mode of securing concerted and harmonious action in whatever measures may be deemed most desirable for our common peace and security.

The Civil War started on April 12, 1861. How far apart were the Ordinance of Secession and the beginning of the Civil War?

title: Location
text:
Maps are geographic representations of places. We use these representations to acquire, process, and report information from a spatial perspective. Maps help us to know where something is located. Location allows us to describe where a place is. We describe places with both relative and absolute location. The relative location of a place tells us where a place is relative to, or compared to, something else. When we are describing the relative location of a place, we use words such as "by," "near," "above," or "below." If your friend tells you that their house is “down the street and across from the supermarket,” they are using relative location.

A place's absolute location is its exact location. Absolute location is more helpful when you're trying to find an unfamiliar place. Absolute location in a city could be an address. A grid line system, called longitude and latitude, is also used to find a place's absolute location. Cartographers use these lines to divide a map into small squares. These squares make finding a location easier. The squares form a grid. A coordinate grid uses letters and numbers to label the grid lines. Vertical lines of longitude go around the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole. Lines of longitude show how far east or west places are from the Prime Meridian. We call these lines meridians. Horizontal lines of latitude show how far north and south places are from the Equator.

title: Equator and Latitude
text:
We divide up the world for mapping purposes. Imagine a horizontal line that runs around the middle of the world. Cartographers draw this imaginary line on many of the maps they make. They call this line the Equator. The Equator divides the Earth into hemispheres. A hemisphere is a division on Earth between north and south or east and west.

The Northern Hemisphere includes all of the land and oceans that are north of the Equator. The Southern Hemisphere includes everything to the south. The Equator crosses parts of South America, Asia, and Africa. Horizontal lines of latitude run east and west around the Earth. These lines show how far from the Equator places are. We call these latitude lines parallels.

title: Prime Meridian and Longitude
text:
Cartographers draw lines on a map from the North Pole to the South Pole. This helps us be more specific in our mapping. One of these lines, the Prime Meridian, divides the world in half vertically. These halves are called the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere.

Absolute location uses latitude and longitude lines to pinpoint where something is located. These lines are measured in degrees. Each degree is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute has 60 seconds. The Earth is divided into 24 different time zones. The reason for this division is because the Earth rotates on its axis once a day. A time zone is one of the ways that the world is divided and is based on what time it is in a given location. The starting point for these time zones is the Prime Meridian in Greenwich, also called Greenwich Mean Time. Theoretically, every 15 degrees east or west of Greenwich means one hour more or less. In practice, however, time zones do not go through the middle of countries. Larger countries have multiple time zones. For convenience, time zone boundaries often follow political boundaries instead of longitude lines.

The International Date Line is another imaginary line on Earth's surface. It defines the boundary between one day and the next. The International Date Line is located halfway around the world from the Prime Meridian.

title: The Battle of Fort McHenry
text:
In August 1814, the British controlled Chesapeake Bay. That same year, they invaded the new American capital, Washington, D.C. They burned the Capitol building and the White House. First Lady Dolly Madison managed to save the portrait of George Washington and a few other items before leaving. The destruction of Washington, D.C., lasted 26 hours.

Following the attack on the nation’s capital, British naval forces entered Baltimore Harbor to attack Fort McHenry. That night, Francis Scott Key, an American lawyer, was helping to negotiate a prisoner's release. He watched the battle from a British warship. The British bombarded the fort with cannons throughout the night. The American flag over Fort McHenry never fell, though. This signaled an American victory. Key was so inspired watching the battle that he wrote his thoughts as he watched the flag.

“Oh, say can you see by the dawn's early light

What so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming?

Whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight,

O'er the ramparts we watched were so gallantly streaming?

And the rocket's red glare, the bombs bursting in air,

Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there.

Oh, say does that star-spangled banner yet wave

O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave?”

Key’s words would later be set to music and become the national anthem of the United States in 1931.

title: Osceola and the Seminole Nation
text:
Florida was a new territory to the United States after an agreement with Spain in 1821. The Seminole Nation was living in Florida. American settlers wanted the land in Florida so they could build their own communities. Before Andrew Jackson became president, he was a general in the U.S. Army. His troops went into Florida to seize land for the American settlers. Jackson became the military governor of Florida. Later, as president, he continued to push out the Seminole for the benefit of American settlers.

The United States government made a treaty with a few Seminole chiefs in 1832. The Treaty of Payne’s Landing promised the Seminole people lands west of the Mississippi River if they agreed to leave Florida. Many Seminole volunteered to move. Some decided to remain and defend their claim to the land.

In 1835, the U.S. Army arrived to enforce removal. Osceola was a leader of the remaining Seminole tribe. Osceola inspired the Seminole to resist the army. The Seminole knew the terrain and hid in the thick Everglades after surprising the army patrols. Osceola led the bands of Seminole warriors for seven years.

In 1842, the U.S. Army tricked and arrested Osceola. They offered a flag of truce, meaning a ceasefire or break in fighting. When Osceola met to talk about the truce, he was arrested. He was transported and put in prison in Fort Moultrie in South Carolina. Osceola died of malaria within three months of his arrest.

Some of the Seminole Nation hid in the Everglades, where their descendants still live today. The remaining members of the Seminole moved west of the Mississippi.

title: Sequoyah
text:
Sequoyah was a Cherokee leader and silversmith. He was also known as George Gist or George Guess. It is not known for sure when he was born. Historians think he was born in 1776. He was raised by a single mother and worked in her trading post.

Sequoyah was in the U.S. Army in the War of 1812. He was quick to learn many things. He was amazed by how people could look at symbols on a piece of paper and get information. The Cherokee only had a spoken language. The English had a spoken and written language. The English had an alphabet for the sounds of their words. Sequoyah wanted this for the Cherokee people.

By 1821, Sequoyah had designed and created a syllabary, or symbols for the sounds and syllables in the Cherokee language. He taught his people to read and write the Cherokee language.

The Cherokee created newspapers to share information. The newspapers were printed in Cherokee and English, and because of this, ideas were exchanged easily. The oral histories of families and the nation were highly valued. These stories were written into books for all to share.

Sequoyah changed the world of the Cherokee by teaching others to learn to read.

title: Separate But Equal
text:
In 1896, the U.S. Supreme Court decided that racial segregation, or the separation of white Americans and Black Americans in public facilities, was constitutional. The idea of “separate but equal” accommodations was upheld by the Supreme Court case Plessy v. Ferguson. The requirement was that the separate facilities had to be of equal quality. However, when it came to education, there was rarely any equality.

When the Civil War ended and Reconstruction began, separate schools were slowly established for African Americans. All schools and their funding were under the control of elected government leaders who were not African American. School boards did not give African American schools enough funding, materials, or staff. Schools for African American students were housed in older, run-down buildings, and they had fewer, older books. African American teachers were paid less than white teachers.

For decades after the Civil War ended, many African Americans continued to live in poverty. Entire families worked to make enough money to meet their basic needs. Many children had to work beside their parents to maintain their crops. This resulted in many African American children not being able to attend school for long periods of time, if at all. By the mid-1930s, only 14 percent of African American children between 15 and 19 years old were enrolled in public high schools in southern states. The schools that did exist offered core subjects with no educational material or equipment and no courses in music or art.

During this time, many people, Black and white, were working to make things better for African American children. In the 1930s, a businessman named Julius Rosenwald established a fund to improve the education of southern African Americans by building schools in rural areas. Septima Clark, an African American teacher, created Citizenship Schools in 1957. These schools helped African Americans learn to read so they could qualify to vote. Laws at that time in many southern cities required voters to be able to read.

Charles Cobb was another civil rights activist with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee in 1964. He helped establish more than 40 Freedom Schools that were organized to achieve social, political, and economic equality. The schools educated students in strategies to make social change.

Efforts to change laws and provide equal opportunities for all students regardless of race continued. In 1954, a landmark Supreme Court case, Brown v. Board of Education, resulted in a ruling that would lead to the desegregation of schools. It would take many years to desegregate schools because the decision faced defiance in many communities. How could desegregation be enforced? Enforcement would have to come from the executive branch of the federal government.

title: Civil Disobedience: Rosa Parks and the Greensboro Sit-In
text:
A department store seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, named Rosa Parks boarded a bus after work in December 1955. Public buses at that time had clearly marked seating for white people and African American passengers. Public bus drivers were authorized to enforce segregation laws on the bus. Parks took a seat in the African American section and settled in for the ride home. As passengers continued to board, the designated section for whites filled to capacity. The bus driver, James Blake, instructed Parks and three other African American passengers to give their seats to white passengers. Parks refused and was arrested for refusing the orders of the bus driver. Parks went peacefully with the arresting officers. This was an act of civil disobedience.

Civil disobedience is the active refusal of a citizen to obey certain laws, demands, orders, or commands of a legal authority. The citizen accepts the consequences of the arrest. Civil disobedience is used to call attention to a law that many feel is unjust. In reaction to Rosa Parks's arrest, African Americans in Montgomery boycotted the city bus system. Led by a minister named Martin Luther King Jr., people refused to ride the bus for over a year.

Inspired by Rosa Parks’s simple act of rebellion against segregation, more civil rights leaders emerged. Civil rights leaders decided that something had to be done about the unfair treatment and segregation. They came up with a plan to have “sit-ins” at public places. This was nonviolent and a peaceful means of protesting.

In 1960, four African American college students left their college, North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, and headed to a lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina. No one paid attention to the young men as they entered the store. It was open to customers of all races. The lunch counter in the store, however, was for white customers only. The four students sat down at the lunch counter and asked the server to take their order. The server reminded them that the lunch counter was segregated, so African Americans were not allowed to eat there. The students were asked to leave, but they silently remained where they were.

When the store closed for the evening, the Greensboro students left peacefully. The following day, the group of four students brought more people to sit at the lunch counter. The sit-in lasted for many days. Both African Americans and white people participated. Many people supported the sit-in, while others believed the students were trying to cause trouble. Some people even taunted and harassed them. In other cities across the South, thousands of people held the same types of demonstrations.

The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was an organization that helped people learn peaceful ways to protest. In order to keep all of their protests nonviolent, SNCC created a set of rules for those who wanted to participate. They were instructed to follow these instructions exactly:

Do Not:

1. Strike back nor curse if abused.

2. Laugh out.

3. Hold conversations with the floor walker [store supervisor].

4. Leave your seat until your leader has given you permission to do so.

5. Block entrances to stores outside nor the aisles inside.

Do:

1. Show yourself friendly and courteous at all times.

2. Sit straight; always face the counter.

3. Report all serious incidents to your leader.

4. Refer information seekers to your leader in a polite manner.

5. Remember the teachings of Jesus Christ, Mahatma Gandhi, and Martin Luther King, Jr. Love and nonviolence is the way.

These examples illustrate the force for change that can come from standing up (or sitting in) against injustice.

title: Civil Rights Activists
text:
Freedom Riders

The first group of Freedom Riders was organized in 1947 in Washington, D.C. To test a decision by the U.S. Supreme Court. This decision said that segregation in interstate travel was unconstitutional. African American and white people boarded buses together to ride through the South. As they traveled, they tested each city’s compliance with the law.

The Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) revived the Freedom Riders initiative in 1961. They wanted to test another Supreme Court decision from 1960 that said segregation at bus terminals between states was also unconstitutional. This time, women were included among the riders. African American and white freedom riders began their trip in Washington, D.C. They planned to travel to New Orleans and stop at bus terminals along the way. African American riders would try to use white-only restrooms, lunch counters, and waiting areas.

The ride was uneventful through Virginia and North Carolina. When the riders reached Rock Hill, South Carolina, three riders (two African Americans and one white man) entered a whites-only waiting room. They were violently attacked by white people waiting in the terminal.

As the ride continued, the group split into two buses. Both buses were attacked by angry mobs in Alabama. In fact, a member of the mob threw a bomb into one of the buses. The Freedom Riders all escaped the burning bus, but then they were attacked by the mob.

Photographs of the burning bus were printed in newspapers and broadcast on television. The nation's attention was drawn to the Freedom Riders. Hundreds of new Freedom Riders joined the cause. Pressure from the government and the shocked public resulted in federal regulations being respected. There were no more segregated facilities in bus terminals.

Ruby Bridges

Ruby Bridges was born in Mississippi in 1954. When she was only six years old, she was integrated into an all-white school in New Orleans. Ruby and other black children had to take a test to determine if they would be allowed to attend all-white schools. Ruby passed the test, so she headed off to first grade. The New Orleans school board delayed Ruby’s entry into the white school until November. Four federal marshals were sent to the school to escort Ruby.

When Ruby tried to go to class, an angry mob tried to keep her out. The marshals had to walk in front of and behind her to protect her. People were yelling and throwing things at her. Ruby was brave. When Ruby finally got inside, she had her own room and teacher because none of the white parents would allow their children to be in the school with Ruby. A woman named Barbara Henry from Boston was the only person who wanted to be her teacher.

Today, Ruby Bridges says that she had no idea why people hated each other when she was six. She did not understand the concepts of racism and civil rights at the time. She didn't understand what desegregation was. She just wanted to go to school. Ruby Bridges still fights for civil rights so that no one will ever again have to go through what she did.

title: The Chicano Rights Movement
text:
The Civil Rights Movement is often only associated with African Americans. However, the Civil Rights leaders intended to include all Americans of color struggling for equality. These leaders influenced Hispanic Americans to organize their own movements for fairness and equal rights. Marches were held in Philadelphia, Chicago, New York City, and Puerto Rico. In the American Southwest, the Mexican-American struggle became known as the Chicano Civil Rights Movement.

In the Chicano Civil Rights Movement, Hispanic Americans faced many issues. For example, Puerto Ricans were American citizens but weren't treated as such. Puerto Rico is an unincorporated American territory. Many Puerto Ricans who migrated to the mainland ended up in low-paying jobs and poor living conditions.

Many Mexican Americans lived in rural areas and made a living as farmers and migrant workers. César Chávez was born in 1927 on his family’s farm near Yuma, Arizona. He became an important leader among migrant workers, and a farmers union called the United Farm Workers or UFW.

Working under the UFW, Chávez organized boycotts and strikes against fruit and vegetable growers. The growers refused to give farm workers fair pay, reasonable working hours, and safe places to live. Chávez asked all strikers to take a pledge of nonviolence. Chávez led a march of workers 300 miles to the state capital in Sacramento. The nonviolent approach to conflict gained great support from other unions, social groups, and political activists.

Hispanic Americans faced racism in nearly every aspect of their lives. The environment and occupations available to them differed from opportunities for non-Hispanic Americans. Growing movements like the Chicano Civil Rights Movement helped minority voices to be heard in the struggle against prejudice and injustice. Many continue working to make minority voices heard for the issues involving Hispanic American rights that still remain unresolved today.

title: The Native American Rights Movement
text:
In the 1950s and 1960s, the people who lived on Native American reservations lived in poverty. Their families had been forcibly moved there by the federal government. Healthcare was difficult to get or did not exist. The death rate of Native Americans living on reservations was over 30 percent higher than it was in the whole U.S. population. Half a million Native Americans lived in unsanitary, run-down dwellings. Few were able to get an education, and employment opportunities were very limited. In the 1950s, the U.S. government tried to take over reservations without tribal consent and move the tribes into urban areas.

Facing bigotry, challenges to their sovereignty, and continued racism from the federal government, Native Americans created organizations to fight for their civil rights. The first intertribal association, called the National Congress of American Indians, formed in the 1940s. The best-known organization of Native Americans began in 1966. It was called the American Indian Movement. This organization led Native Americans in an automobile caravan from California to Washington, D.C. to draw the government’s attention to the injustices many Native Americans faced. They called the caravan the “Trail of Broken Treaties.”

Native Americans finally began seeing the results of their protests with the Indian Education Act of 1972. This act gave Native American parents more control over their children’s education. The Child Welfare Act also gave tribes control of custody decisions that involved Native American children. Several important Supreme Court cases supported the rights of Native American tribes to govern themselves and retain fishing and hunting rights. In 1980, several tribes sued the government to recover land that had been illegally taken from them. The government paid the tribes millions of dollars in restitution.

The problems facing Native Americans have not all been solved yet. Advocating and protecting the rights of people is ongoing for each generation.

title: Gender, Relationships, and Civil Rights
text:
Societies, cultures, and countries have held different views throughout history about people who are LGBTQ+. Many of those viewpoints have also changed over time. When Early European settlers arrived in what is now the United States, they made laws against those not conforming to traditional norms. Same-gender relationships remained illegal in some states until 2003. Other laws have prevented people who are LGBTQ+ from exercising other rights, like getting married or having access to healthcare.

Several laws have changed because of the work of human rights activists. For example, on June 28, 1969, New York City police raided an LGBTQ+ club called the Stonewall Inn. When community members saw how roughly police treated the people at the Stonewall Inn, they began protesting. The protest turned into a riot. The Stonewall Riot, or Stonewall Uprising, lasted six days and involved hundreds of people. Although people had long been advocating for these rights in the United States, the Stonewall Riot sparked new resolve in the pursuit of equal rights.

Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera were two activists who participated in the Stonewall Riot. In the following years, they advocated for the entire community's rights, especially transgender people. They founded STAR House, a shelter for homeless LGBTQ+ youth.

Many other activists have petitioned the United States government to give this community equal rights. Today, activists continue the work of Johnson, Rivera, and other figures of the LGBTQ+ rights movement.

title: The Women’s Rights Movement
text:
In 1848, around 300 people gathered at the Seneca Falls Convention in New York. Some historians consider this important meeting to be the beginning of the women’s rights movement in the United States. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was one of the attendees of the conference. She was an outspoken supporter of women’s right to vote in federal elections, known as suffrage. It was a radical idea at the time, but Stanton was determined. She and other important figures, like Susan B. Anthony and New Jersey native Alice Paul, continued to advocate for women’s suffrage. Women finally gained the right to vote in 1919, more than 60 years after the meeting in Seneca Falls. Many other people contributed to the cause, including Mary McLeod Bethune. Bethune championed the right of Black women to vote and participate in democracy.

Suffrage was only one piece of the women’s rights movement. During World War II, men left their jobs to join the military. Women took up the roles, becoming part of the workforce. Prior to WWII, women were mostly expected to stay at home, caring for children, cooking, and caring for the house. Many women enjoyed the opportunity to do other challenging jobs. However, when soldiers returned to the United States after the war, women were expected to leave their jobs. This led to a new wave of campaigning for women’s rights. Women sought an equal right to employment, as well as changes that made it easier for people with children to work. Their work caused more changes in laws and protections. One change was the Civil Right Act of 1964, which made it illegal for employers to discriminate based on race, sex, color, religion, or national origin.

Throughout the following decades, women’s rights activists continued to petition the government to give women equal rights and freedoms. They continue to address issues such as equal pay and protection against violence and sexual harassment.

title: Education and Culture
text:
With more schools springing up throughout Alabama after Reconstruction, there was a great need for more teachers. So, normal schools (schools to train teachers) were built. The first normal school in Alabama (and in the South) was the State Normal School College. Located in Florence, it opened in 1872 and later became the University of North Alabama. Other normal schools were built in Jacksonville, Livingston, Troy, Huntsville, and Marion.

Two African American normal colleges were established in December 1875. They were located in Huntsville and Marion. The college in Marion was later moved to Montgomery and is now Alabama State University. The Huntsville Normal and Industrial School became Alabama Agricultural and Mechanical School.

Land Grant Colleges

Alabama lawmakers saw the need for farmers and engineers to learn the latest farming techniques. In 1872, they founded the state’s first Agricultural and Mechanical College in Auburn. This school was a land grant college. It was built on land granted by the federal government and was funded (paid for) by a state tax on fertilizer. Students focused on learning about agriculture and mechanical arts in addition to traditional subjects such as mathematics, English, and history. It later became Auburn University. Today, there are many land grant colleges (colleges built on land granted by the federal government) across the nation.

1. Booker T. Washington

Booker T. Washington was an African American man who was known throughout the country as a leader in education and civil rights. After being freed from slavery, his family moved to West Virginia. His stepfather worked in a salt mine there, and Washington got a job packing salt into barrels. When a new school for African Americans opened in town, Washington talked his parents into letting him attend the school. He went to work very early in the morning, attended school for a while, and then returned to work in the afternoon. He later attended Hampton College in Virginia, where he graduated at the head of his class. After teaching for a few years, Washington was asked to open a new college for African Americans in Alabama. The school, Tuskegee Institute, opened in a small building with only 40 students at first. In addition to their regular studies, Washington taught the students how to make bricks, which they used to build more buildings. He also taught them how to clear land, raise and harvest crops, and sell the produce. The profits were used to build more buildings. Washington became famous for his hard work and his new educational idea: learning by doing.

2. Margaret Murray Washington

Margaret Murray Washington was the first president of the National Federation of Colored Women’s Clubs. She is most well-known, however, for founding country schools, teaching women how to live and take care of their homes, and working to improve prisons. She also started the Mount Meigs School for Boys and an industrial school for girls. Margaret was married to Booker T. Washington. She worked hard to help him make his dream of creating a great educational institution come true. Talk about a very busy woman!

3. Pattie Ruffner Jacobs

By 1900, women in some states were given the right to vote. Here in Alabama, however, women were not allowed to vote. Many men felt that if women were allowed to vote, they would neglect their responsibilities at home. Pattie Ruffner Jacobs disagreed and began the Birmingham Equal Suffrage (right to vote) Association in 1911. She was also president of the National American Women’s Suffrage Association. She led women from all across the country in making speeches, writing articles, and marching in parades to push for the right to vote. It wasn’t until 1920, however, that all women were finally allowed to vote.

title: Alabama’s Role in Space Technology
text:
Aerospace is the part of technology and industry that focuses on aviation and space flight. Alabama has huge investments in and history with aerospace. In 1960, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) program began the Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. Redstone Arsenal is a plant that was used for rocket engine development during World War II. Huntsville, Alabama’s first capital city, was known for its large homes and its strong cotton industry. The establishment of the MSFC brought many scientists, engineers, and researchers to town. In 1960, when the Marshall Space Flight Center was established, there was growing interest in the science field and more than 100 German-born scientists became U.S. citizens to join the race to space. In 1961, the Mercury-Redstone vehicle that sent Alan B. Shepard into space was tested at Marshall Space Flight Center. MSFC took the lead in the industry. MSFC scientists were commissioned to build the Saturn V rocket. The Saturn V Rocket would launch astronauts to the moon. These efforts brought great results when Neil Armstrong walked on the moon in 1969. Redstone technology was responsible for making both the Saturn V rocket booster and the lunar rover products possible.

The impact of NASA and the surge of scientists, researchers, and engineers to Huntsville shaped the cultural and intellectual climate. Many entrepreneurs, scientists, researchers, and engineers were drawn to the area to be a part of space technological advancement. The 1960s and 1970s were a time known for the arms race between Russia and the United States. Many missiles were developed at Redstone. NASA decided to branch beyond rocket propulsion in the 1970s and 80s and created additional programs to train, like Space Camp, a program originally started to encourage 4th-6th grade students to pursue careers in the math, science, and technology fields. MSFC has also been a part of developing the International Space Station and launching the Hubble Space Telescope. The U.S. Space & Rocket Center and NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center keep Huntsville as a leader in American rocket and space development.

title: Technology Timeline
text:
Technology is always innovating (improving and changing). Over time, new inventions, new research, and great ideas improve technology. Today, new technology, like artificial intelligence, virtual and augmented reality, and quantum computing, are all being invented, improved, and innovated. Numberless technologies have been created, but here are some origins of common technologies we use every day.

1802: Refrigiratory: Thomas Moore created an icebox. The refrigiratory helped preserve dairy products during transport.

1834: Refrigerator: Jacob Perkins invented the world’s first vapor-compression refrigeration system.

1844: Telegraph: Samuel F.B. Morse invented the telegraph. The Telegraph is a communication system that transmits coded information over a distance.

1876: Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone. Bell made the first phone call to Thomas Watson and said “Mr. Watson, come here – I want to see you.”

1876: Refrigeration: Carl von Linde patented his process to liquefy gas, a part of basic refrigeration technology.

1886: Automobile: Carl Benz patented the world’s first three-wheeled automobile.

1895: Radio: Guglielmo Marconi developed the idea of the wireless telegraph, or radio. He sent wireless Morse code messages over four miles. Marconi applied for and obtained the world’s first patent for wireless telegraphy in England.

1900s: World Wireless System: Nikola Tesla experimented with the idea of building a system to connect the world wirelessly.

1913: Electric Refrigerator: Fred W. Wolf created an electric refrigerator that wasn’t successful and invented ice cube trays.

1927: Monitor Top Refrigerator: General Electric’s model was widely used.

1927: Television: The first electronic television was designed by Philo Taylor Farnsworth. It was popularized in the 1950s when the black and white home television set was created.

1957: Space Technology: On October 4, 1957, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (U.S.S.R.) sent an artificial satellite called Sputnik into space to orbit the Earth. This marks the beginning of space technology.

1960: Internet: J.C.R. Licklider created and spread the idea of the “Intergalactic Network” of computers. Computer scientists created “packet switching,” which allowed for transmitting electronic data and is a foundational technology of the internet.

1990: World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web. This is the most common way of accessing data online through websites and hyperlinks.

title: Mae Jemison
text:
Mae Jemison was born in Decatur in 1956. Her mother worked as an elementary school teacher and her father was a maintenance worker. She had two older siblings. Jemison was always interested in learning about science and astronomy (learning about stars). When she was three, her family moved to Chicago, where her uncle introduced her to the world of science. She went to college at Stanford and Cornell and earned degrees in chemical engineering and African American studies. She later received a doctorate of medicine. In 1983, Jemison worked as a doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia. She helped provide medical care, create an educational curriculum, and train others about health for two years. Jemison moved back to the United States in 1985 and worked as a general practitioner. The next year, Jemison applied to NASA’s astronaut program and was selected to be one of the 15 candidates. Jemison became the first African American woman in the NASA astronaut training program.

Jemison also became the first astronaut to be a Science Mission Specialist. In 1992, Jemison became the first African American Woman in outer space when she served as a mission specialist alongside Jan Davis, another native Alabama astronaut, aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavor. Jemison logged 190 hours, 30 minutes, and 23 seconds during the Endeavor mission to space.

title: HudsonAlpha
text:
Innovation is an integral part of Alabama history. HudsonAlpha is a nonprofit institute that focuses on biotechnology. Founded in Huntsville, Alabama, in 2008, HudsonAlpha is an institute that has dedicated its work to genomic sciences and biotechnology. Genomics is the study of genes and how genes interact. A genome is an organism’s full set of DNA. Biotechnology is technology focused on biology. In biotechnological studies, biological processes are studied to learn how they can be used for other purposes including industrial needs. One major focus of biotechnology is the study of manipulating the genetics of microorganisms. This type of study can assist with producing antibiotics, hormones, and other sciences that improve human health and wellness. When HudsonAlpha opened in Alabama, it earned national recognition as a global leader in genetics and genomic technology. Jobs, research opportunities, educational advancement, and opportunities to innovate are all outcomes of the addition of HudsonAlpha to Alabama’s innovative history.

The research done at HudsonAlpha has created discoveries that benefit many areas of medicine and science. HudsonAlpha has made discoveries for conditions like childhood genetic disorders, cancer, lupus, and multiple sclerosis. Studies also innovate research that helps with genomic techniques in plant life. One of the main goals of HudsonAlpha is to make discoveries that will improve health and create processes, research, and innovation that contribute to a more sustainable (maintainable) world.

title: Space Command Headquarters
text: The United States Department of Defense has a program called Space Command. The U.S. Space Command is responsible for all military options involving space. It is responsible for preparing military operations that will take place in space. The Air Force, Army, Navy, and Marine Corps all contribute to the service needed by Space Command (SPACECOM). Space Command was set up in Colorado Springs in 1985 and merged with the U.S. Strategic Command in 2002. In January 2021, it was announced that headquarters, or the center for operations of a program, for Space Command will move from Colorado to Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. The move to Redstone Arsenal will bring with it 1,400 personnel and the opportunity for more economic, industrial, and scientific growth in Alabama.

title: Automotive Industry of Alabama
text:
Alabama is a central hub for manufacturing and production of automobiles. In 1997, Vance, Alabama, produced the first M-Class in the Mercedes-Benz production line. Alabama is now a leader in the auto industry across the nation. There are assembly plants for Mercedes-Benz, Honda, Hyundai, Mazda, and Toyota in Alabama. Almost one million cars and trucks are produced by Alabama automakers each year. Nearly 1.5 million auto engines were produced in Alabama in 2020. In Tuscaloosa and Calhoun, expansions for the International Automotive Components Group are investing roughly $55 million. Many other new projects, as well as expansions of existing projects, contribute to the growing and thriving auto sector in Alabama.

Alabama ranks third in the nation in terms of dollars exported due to auto production. By 1991, Alabama had grown automotive manufacturing and production from 15 to 86 companies. International and national companies rely on the Alabama auto sector. A company called International Diesel selected Huntsville, Alabama, as a location to create new V-6 and V-8 diesel engines in 1999. In 2000, Mercedes-Benz expanded its production in Alabama by $600 million, and in 2020, invested an additional $1 billion to begin expanding plants, built a battery factory, and began production of the electric passenger cars. The auto industry creates jobs, provides elite training, and partners with 24 local two-year colleges to offer apprenticeships and customized education programs.

Safety concerns were addressed when Cadillac added windshield wipers on its 1922 cars and when Nils Bohlin developed seatbelts in 1959 Volvo cars. title: Who Were Abolitionists?
text:
There were many people in America who opposed the enslavement of people. Most of the northern states had abolished, or legally ended, slavery by the early 1800s. However, slavery remained legal in all of the southern states.

There were many people who opposed abolition. They believed people from Africa were not equal to people from Europe. They believed in keeping people enslaved. The pro-slavery group had authority in making laws. Laws were made and enforced to keep African people enslaved.

A religious group in Pennsylvania was very active in protesting the laws that kept slavery legal. The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) was this group. They believe in peace and equality of all people. The Quakers worked to end slavery and free all people. This was called abolition. They even petitioned Congress to end slavery in 1790. One Quaker minister, Lucretia Mott, began to boycott items produced by the labor of enslaved people. She also worked to set up anti-slavery societies. Many women worked to gain rights for all people, including women.

Philadelphia became home to the abolitionist movement. People organized and raised awareness of abolition with print, speeches, and actions.

William Lloyd Garrison started an anti-slavery newspaper called the Liberator. He published his beliefs about equality. He wanted African Americans to be granted every liberty and right promised to white Americans. In over 30 years, he never missed printing a weekly issue. He also helped organize the Anti-Slavery Society. He became a strong spokesperson for abolition.

Other abolitionists were African Americans who had escaped slavery. People like Sojourner Truth, Frederick Douglass, and William Wells Brown gave speeches to large audiences about their lives and experiences. This endangered them because they were exposing their status as runaways. They could have been captured and returned to their former lives. Douglass and Brown, along with other escaped enslaved people, wrote in newspapers and books to reach more people. The opposition to their work was often violent. People smashed their printing presses and burned their books.

The Free Soil political party did not believe in freeing enslaved people. However, they did believe that any new territory or state should be a free state with no legal slavery. The Free Soil members were elected to Congress. These members helped make compromises and negotiated new laws in Washington, D.C., to end the growth of slavery. However, laws for enslaving people were still legal.

When people disobey a law, there are consequences. Knowingly going against a law in protest is called civil disobedience. The abolitionist movement practiced civil disobedience. Breaking the law can have dangerous consequences. Law-abiding people willingly broke the law to help enslaved men, women, and children to escape to freedom.

title: Firing on Fort Sumter
text:
The Union army had troops, supplies, and forts located in every state. The new Confederate States of America took command of the Union forts and supplies located in their states. The Union troops were allowed to leave peacefully with their possessions. Many officers and soldiers resigned from the Union Army to join the Confederate Army.

Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie were Union locations in the harbor in Charleston, South Carolina. Fort Sumter was built on an island in the center of the harbor in 1820. It was built to defend the busy harbor from outside attack. Forty-one years later, Fort Sumter was not completely built and only had a few military supplies. Fort Moultrie was well supplied with military equipment.

Major Robert Anderson was the Union commander at Forts Moultrie and Sumter. After South Carolina seceded in December 1861, he knew the South Carolina government wanted him to surrender the forts. As an officer in the U.S. Army, he could not do that. Anderson also knew the Confederates would not accept that answer without a fight. Anderson quietly moved the 80 men in his command at night to Fort Sumter on Dec. 20, 1861.

New Confederate general P. G. T. Beauregard was in command of the new military in Charleston, South Carolina. Beauregard had been a student of Anderson’s at the military academy West Point. Beauregard demanded the surrender of Fort Sumter from his former teacher. Anderson refused.

For months, the men at Fort Sumter waited. They were low on supplies. Efforts by the federal government to get them supplied were turned away by the Confederate forces. On April 12, 1861, the waiting was over. Anderson received this message:

Sir: By authority of Brig. General Beauregard Commanding the Provisional Forces of the Confederate States we have the honor to notify you that he will open the fire of his Batteries on Fort Sumter in one hour from this time.

The Confederate forces under the command of General P. G. T. Beauregard opened cannon fire on the island fort. For 34 hours, the bombardment continued. Major Anderson agreed to evacuation terms. On April 15, 1861, the American flag was lowered and the Union troops at Fort Sumter left.

The Civil War began with the lowering of the American flag, signaling the surrender of the Union fort to the new Confederate States of America. Lincoln’s words from 1858 rang through their minds: "A house divided against itself cannot stand."
