title: Technology and Transportation
text:
In the 19th century, America was expanding. People from the eastern states were eager to claim the land in the West. People were on the move. Movement of people brings about the exchange of ideas. It also creates the demand for better technology to make that movement easier. Once in a new place, people still have wants and needs. Communities create markets. New markets increase demand for products. Demand for products increases the need for transportation. Increased transportation keeps people in communities more connected. This growth cycle was happening in America from 1800 to 1860.

Canals

Waterways in America were the highways for moving people and goods. New York City merchants wanted goods from the western frontier. Connecting the Hudson River to Lake Erie became a goal for the state of New York. The Erie Canal was the first publicly funded project. A canal is a large channel dug in the earth that is filled with water for boats to use. The New York government used tax money to pay workers to dig the canal. From 1817 to 1825, thousands of workers used shovels and carts to dig 363 miles of canal. From Albany, New York, to Buffalo, New York, the canal was the longest human-made waterway in North America. Use of the canal for transporting goods to market made New York City the nation's busiest harbor.

Steam Engines

Science advanced in the 1800s to control steam pressure. This was used to make wheels rotate. The steam was created by burning coal under a boiler of water. The water was heated to boiling, which created steam. The steam pressure was then used to move mechanical parts.

The steam engine was invented in England. Americans imported the first steam engine from England in 1829. This triggered a new industry. Entrepreneurs began experimenting with how the steam engine could be used to make work easier. Many new jobs were created because of the steam engine.

The steam engine was used to create better transportation on water and on land. When this engine was put into a boat, a boat could move through the water without depending on the wind or currents. Boats could travel up to five miles per hour. The steam locomotive could move more cargo and do it faster than horses or oxen could. Transporting goods and people became faster. The dependability of the machines led to predictable schedules for getting goods to market. The northern states used this new technology to increase manufacturing.

The Cotton Gin

Eli Whitney invented a machine that simplified the work of removing cotton seeds from harvested cotton. The southern plantations grew cotton using the work of enslaved people. One enslaved worker could only remove seeds from about one pound of cotton a day. At this speed, farmers did not make much money from cotton. Then Whitney built the cotton gin. The gin was a large wooden box with a crank on the side. The machine could separate the seeds from cotton quickly. It could process 50 pounds of cotton a day. This meant more cotton could be grown, harvested, and sold. The cotton industry expanded. Plantations grew. The new territories in the west could grow cotton. With the rise in cotton production, more workers were needed. Therefore, the need for enslaved people to work the plantations grew.

The southern states were invested in agriculture and the plantation system of using enslaved people for labor. The economic growth in both regions would be a cause of conflict over the first 50 years of the 1800s.

title: Henry Clay and the American System
text:
The War of 1812 created debt for the United States government. There was no plan on how to pay this debt. Henry Clay of Kentucky created a plan. He saw an opportunity to reshape and strengthen the economy in the United States. Clay called the plan the American System.

Clay’s plan involved setting a tariff on imported goods. This would make imported goods more expensive than local goods. The second part of Clay’s plan was to establish a Bank of the United States. The bank would set the currency, or system of money, to be used in the country. Prior to 1820, the United States did not print much money or make coins.

The final part of Clay’s American System was connecting the nation through transportation. Clay wanted to grow the economy by promoting trade within the country. He didn’t want to export all goods overseas. The United States needed a fast, efficient network to move goods. Small dirt roads made for horses and buggies weren’t enough. Clay proposed a network system of canals, railroads, and new, larger roads. He planned to pay for this system with the new tariff and a sale of public lands for settlement in the west.

Not everyone liked Clay’s American System. People in the southern states felt the tariff was unfair for them to pay. The tariff would impact their cotton sales outside the country. The South already had rivers to transport their goods. Southerners didn’t want to pay for canals and roads in the North. Clay’s vision did much to create a national network and helped establish the nation’s economy as both industrial and agricultural. The American System plan was a step to greater federal power over the states.

title: John Deere and the Steel-Tipped Plow
text:
Farming the prairie was tougher than anyone expected. To prepare a field for planting, farmers used a plow, a tool with a blade that turns the soil over and creates rows for planting. Plows were pulled by horses or oxen. They had blades made of cast-iron. The iron plows did not work well on the prairie, though. The iron couldn’t cut through the tangled roots of the prairie grass. The sticky prairie soil clumped up and stuck to the iron plow blades like glue. Farmers had to stop every few minutes to clear their plows of the sticky mess.

Farmers on the prairie struggled with this problem for years. Then, a blacksmith named John Deere solved the problem. John Deere was from Vermont, but he was unsuccessful setting up a business there. Like so many others, he saw moving west as an opportunity to start fresh. He settled in Grand Detour, about 100 miles outside of Chicago, Illinois. One day, he was sharpening blades at a sawmill. There, he found a broken steel saw blade. The blade had been polished smooth after passing through so much lumber. It reminded Deere of other work he’d done polishing steel tines on a hayfork. Polishing that steel hayfork made it pass through the soil easily to gather more hay. He wondered if polished steel on a plow blade might do the same thing. He designed a large plow with steel on it and called it a “grasshopper plow.” He sold this first steel-bladed plow to a local farmer in 1838. That farmer told his friends how well it worked cutting through the grass and sticky soil. By 1855, Deere’s factory was filling orders for 10,000 plows a year. John Deere’s invention made farming the prairie possible.

title: A Public Education for All
text:
During the Civil War, public education in Alabama stopped almost entirely. Teachers who didn’t support the Confederacy were fired. Other teachers left to fight in the war. In addition, most textbooks had come from the north, so it was difficult to find school books.

After the war ended, public education started again. The Republican government believed that education was important. They wanted everyone to learn to read. Government officials voted to raise property taxes to pay for increased education. Some money came from state funds. Other help came from the Freedmen’s Bureau. By 1870, tens of thousands of African Americans were in school.

Schools continued to remain segregated, however. Black students and white students were taught mostly in separate schools. In addition, political and racial problems continued. As the government switched back and forth between Republicans and Democrats, support for public education changed as well. It was also hard to find teachers. In some areas, schools were burned, and teachers and students were threatened.

It became very hard for the government to pay for two different education systems: one for white students and one for Black students. In addition, the school systems were unequal. Wealthier, larger schools had more money and better teachers while smaller schools in rural areas had little support.

title: Alabama Economics in the 1800s
text:
The economy of Alabama was very specialized in the early 19th century. Specialization is a term used to describe a focus on a single product or industry for income. During and after the Civil War, Alabama began to diversify, or vary the products and industries it was part of. This helped Alabama move past an agriculturally centered economy to the diverse economy we see in Alabama today.

Plantation Agriculture

Plantation agriculture was a form of large-scale farming that was typically seen in the Deep South. Plantations came in all sizes. Some were small, while a few in Alabama had over 1,000 or more acres of land, about the same size as 750 football fields! Plantations typically produced just one or two crops that were seen as “cash crops” and were sold for profit. In 19th century Alabama, the primary cash crop was cotton. Once grown, cotton was processed in textile factories in Alabama and around the world.

Plantations thrived in the South because of the enslaved individuals who worked for plantation owners. Most plantations forced work on 20-50 individuals, while on larger plantations in Alabama, 250 or more people could have been forced into slavery. In Alabama, most plantations were located in the Black Belt Region of the state. This is where the soil was best-suited for growing crops like cotton because of the rich, black soil that was found throughout the region. After slavery had been abolished, those formerly enslaved people needed to turn to other methods of work for survival. While some left Alabama entirely, others began tenant farming. These people rented land to live on from a plantation owner. Their debt would be paid either by working on the plantation or by selling crops they grew themselves. Sharecroppers also did farming work to survive. In this case, they would work the plantation and in exchange, they would receive a portion of that cash crop they could sell themselves. Alabama’s entire economy relied on tenant farming and sharecropping systems both before and after the Civil War to survive.

Ordnance, Ships, and Munitions

Alabama played a large role in supporting the Civil War. For instance, the Selma Ordnance and Naval Foundry and the Selma Arsenal and Gun Works were leading manufacturing centers for the South. They produced materials like guns, cannons, and ammunition for the Confederate military. The city of Selma was located in an ideal location because it was close to the Alabama River. This provided access to both the Port of Mobile and the capital, Montgomery. Alabama also served as a major shipbuilding center for the Confederacy, with operations centered in Montgomery, Mobile, and Selma.

Iron and Steel Industry

The iron and steel industry grew rapidly in the state of Alabama after the Civil War. The center of this growth was the city of Birmingham. The area around the city was rich with iron ore, extending at least 25 miles from the factory site all the way to Red Mountain, a ridge on the southern side of Birmingham. To the north were deposits of coal, perfect for heating the furnaces to smelt the ore. Smelting is a process of heating, melting, and removing the metal from the ore itself.

title: The Cost of the Civil War
text:
Any time groups of people engage in war, there are costs. Costs can be economic, structural, political, and emotional. The Civil War is known as America's bloodiest conflict. There were many casualties. Casualties are soldiers who die or become injured or sick. Casualties can also include people captured as prisoners of war or those who go missing in action. During the Civil War, about 1.5 million casualties were reported. About 35,000 of the 122,000 Alabamians who served in the war died.

Combat is the time when soldiers are fighting. Despite much combat in the Civil War, the greatest danger to soldiers was actually disease. Medicine at the time of the Civil War was far less advanced than it is today, and many injured or sick soldiers died because of the lack of adequate medical care and treatment for their injuries. A modern-day view of the casualties of war may include psychological effects, but these were not considered or counted in the casualties in the Civil War, and likely, those suffering from them also did not receive care.

Economically and politically, the Civil War was also costly. The financial cost of the Civil War is estimated to be about $5.2 billion. In order to pay for the war, the government decided to create the Legal Tender Act and the National Bank Act. The Legal Tender Act allowed the government to print dollar bills and sell bonds to raise money. The National Bank Act allowed the government to create a national banking system and a national system of money. The national banking system was used to loan the government money to pay for the war. Political changes rocked many Alabama citizens as industries changed and previously enslaved workers were freed and needed work. The economic recovery was slow and would take a lot of hard work and many years.

title: Military Law
text:
In 1861, Alabama had seceded (withdrawn) from the Union. When six of the seceded states met in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1861, they established a unified government: the Confederate States of America, or the Confederacy. These states attempted to form their own nation and contributed to fighting in the Civil War.

In 1865, when Confederate commander Robert E. Lee surrendered Confederate forces to the Union army at Appomattox, Virginia, life for the people in seceded states would change. Many people in Alabama were upset that their main sources of income, plantations, were being disrupted because people who had been enslaved were no longer an option for free labor. Refusal of the state legislature to ratify the 14th Amendment (which granted citizenship to people who were formerly enslaved) resulted in Alabama being placed under military rule. Military rule is when the military holds power over the people in hopes of securing consent from those being governed.

title: A New Constitution (1868)
text: In February 1868, the Reconstruction Constitution was ratified. This was the first proposed constitution in Alabama to be voted on by the people. This was the first Alabama constitution to guarantee rights to all citizens. The new constitution was Alabama’s most progressive (favoring reform) constitution at the time. It protected the property rights of married women, protected suffrage for African Americans, and broadened the voting rights of poor white individuals. The constitution also encouraged industrial development by creating a bureau and a public board of education that offered provisions for financial support to public education.

title: Readmission to the Union
text: The newly drafted Alabama Constitution was approved by the U.S. Congress in June 1868. In order for Southern states to regain admittance to the Union, the Southern states were required to draft new constitutions, guaranteeing the right to vote to all men. In 1866, Congress had passed the 14th Amendment. This extended rights for every individual and banned states from violating the rights of any person. On July 13, 1868, the Alabama Legislature ratified the 14th Amendment, and Alabama was readmitted to the Union the very same day. By 1868, six states had gained readmittance, and by 1870, all states were readmitted after abiding by the terms set forth by the federal government.

title: Scarcity in Alabama
text:
In Alabama at the close of the Civil War, goods and services were scarce. Scarcity means there is not enough of something, which makes it difficult to find and purchase. Scarcity usually makes prices go up. When goods and services become scarce, families have to choose carefully what they will buy and what they will sacrifice. They have to decide what they need most. Sometimes scarcity can be a big problem. If food or water is scarce, it is hard for people to survive and meet their needs.

The population in Alabama decreased during the Civil War because individuals died in the war efforts. There were also many individuals who were injured during the fighting and were not able to work. Many goods and services relied on having people do the work or make products. Because of the high emphasis on agricultural work in Alabama and because of the end of slavery, there were agricultural shortages, which meant food shortages. Additionally, there was no federal currency in the South at this time. The South had exchanged all currency with Confederate-minted currency, which was worthless after the war. Plus, hard currency (gold, silver) had been shipped to partners overseas to pay the war debt. The lack of actual money to use to purchase goods made it difficult to pay workers, buy goods, or purchase services.

Today, communities work together to try and avoid scarcity. One way that communities do this is by evaluating needs and wants and working together to create goods and services that help people meet their needs and wants.

title: Transportation
text:
As the state evolved, so did its transportation systems. At the same time, transportation evolution drove a lot of change in Alabama. During the Civil War, railroads were a primary source of transportation for supplies and men. Both the North and South needed railroads to move their supplies and people. In an attempt to take the lead during the war, Union raiders destroyed some Southern railroads by pulling up ties and burning crossties. Many other railroad lines were destroyed by overuse and lack of maintenance.

Although transportation suffered because of the Civil War, as Alabama settled into a new way of life post-Civil War, there were many improvements to modes of transportation. Railway systems improved, and by 1900, there were more than 4,000 miles of working tracks.

title: Needs and Wants of a Community
text:
Just like individuals, groups of people have needs and wants. Goods and services help to fulfill those needs and wants. Goods are items that people buy, like food, clothing, furniture, and toys. A service is work that a person does for someone else. Examples of services include teaching, fixing a car, or delivering a package.

Many goods and services are provided by businesses. A business employs workers, also known as laborers, who do the physical work of producing goods or performing a service. In exchange for their work, the business pays the laborers money. The workers can then use the money to pay for the needs and wants of their household.

A household is a group of people who live in the same home. Households come in many shapes and sizes, but most have similar needs. The people in a household need shelter, food, water, a way to stay warm, and medicine to help them stay well. Their wants may differ, and so might their resources to meet those needs and wants. People within a household might also be able to provide different services for the group. A household member might be able to cut hair or fix appliances. That can help a household save money for other needs and wants.

Communities provide some important services for households, such as distributing water and electricity. Communities have needs and wants, too. Local, state, and federal governments examine a community’s needs and the possible resources available to meet those needs. Community members can share their opinions. They can attend community meetings, give demonstrations, write articles for the newspaper, and display signs to express their opinions. When all the opinions are heard, government leaders decide how to best meet their community’s needs. Sometimes, they must reach a compromise to reach a positive outcome. In a compromise, everyone gives something up to create a solution that helps the most people.

Needs and wants can change due to personal, environmental, and economic events. If someone loses their job, they may not have money to spend on wants. Basic human needs like food, water, shelter, and clothing become the main priority. Resources can become scarce, or not available, after a natural disaster or in times of war. It can be difficult for people to meet their basic needs. Businesses, households, and communities must work together to share resources and help each other.

title: How Water Spider Shared Fire
text:
How Water Spider Shared Fire

When the animals first lived on the Earth, fire came down from the world above. It hit some trees on a small island. The animals saw the fire. They all wanted it to cook their food and to keep warm. There was a problem. How could they get the fire?

"I know I can get fire," said Raven. Raven was strong and smart, so everyone thought this was a good idea.

As Raven flew over the fire, the heat came up and burned him. "Ouch!" said Raven. The fire turned his feathers black. Raven could not get the fire. More animals tried, but no one could get the fire.

At last, the tiny water spider said that she would try. Everyone laughed. "You are too small," they said.

"I will try anyway," said Water Spider. But she did not hurry like the others had. Instead, she took the red clay from the earth and made a bowl. She put the bowl on her back and slowly crossed the water to the island.

She carefully put one coal from the fire into her bowl and took tiny, careful steps back across the water. She shared the fire with everyone. The animals respected Water Spider because she was smart to get the fire and kind to share it.

Adapted from the Cherokee story

title: The Fight for Equal Rights
text:
According to Amendments Thirteen, Fourteen, and Fifteen of the U. S. Constitution, all citizens are guaranteed the same civil rights. These amendments were added to the constitution after the Civil War. However, it would take many years, many court battles, and many sacrifices before all people in Alabama were considered "equal and not separate."

A few weeks ago, you learned about the Jim Crow laws, which grew out of the Black Codes in Southern states. They remained in force until 1964 and required racial segregation (separation of people according to race) of African Americans in all public facilities. The laws required that public schools be segregated and that most public places, including restaurants, trains and buses, have separate facilities for whites and African Americans. It forced African Americans to accept less than white Americans, because the facilities for them were often inferior to white facilities.

During the first half of the 20th century, African Americans yearned for the day when their children could attend good schools with new equipment and textbooks. They wanted to take their children to the city parks and swimming pools and to the corner store for ice cream sodas. They wanted better jobs and homes with indoor plumbing. They wanted the same opportunities and the same rights as white citizens.

African American community leaders encouraged their fellow citizens to be proud of their achievements and of how far they had come. They dreamed of a better future, too, and they talked about how to bring about change. Soon they realized that more could be done if they organized and worked together in groups.

The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), a group that had been formed in 1909 to work for the rights of African Americans in the United States, held a meeting in Montgomery in 1947. The purpose of the meeting was to recruit members in Alabama who would dedicate themselves to the fight for civil rights.

Among the people who attended the meeting that day were Rosa Parks, Johnnie Carr, and E.D. Nixon, courageous people who you will read about in this week's lesson. You will also learn about Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Governor George Wallace (who tried to keep segregation in Alabama), and Clifford and Virginia Durr, a white couple who fought alongside African Americans in the Civil Rights Movement.

title: Montgomery Is the Place for You
text:
If you are looking for a place that will take you back to the time of some important events in our nation's history, then Montgomery, Alabama, is just the place for you. There are several historical sites in downtown Montgomery that honor the courage and sacrifices of those who fought for civil rights for all Americans.

The Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church is where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. first preached his message of peace and brotherhood among all people. You will see the pulpit where King gave his inspiring speeches, the office where he planned the bus boycott, and a huge mural that was painted to honor his life and work. Nearby is the Dexter Avenue Parsonage Museum, the King family's home while he was pastor of the church. Inside you will see actual furnishings used by the family. At the Rosa Parks Library and Museum, you can watch a reenactment of the events that led to the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

The Alabama Department of Archives and History is also in Montgomery. An archive is a place like a library, where historical documents are kept. It is the oldest state-funded archives in the United States. Built in 1940, it has several galleries and exhibits that celebrate our state's history, as well as a great place for kids called "Grandma's Attic." The African American Center at Alabama State University offers you the opportunity to see civil rights exhibits and hear the stories of those who took part in the Civil Rights Movement. The Civil Rights Memorial is a beautiful monument designed by Maya Lin. It honors those who gave their lives in the fight for equal rights.

Don't forget to stop by the Alabama State Capitol. Here you will see where Jefferson Davis took his oath of office as president of the Confederate States of America. You will also see what many parts of the capitol looked like during the Civil War. Oh, and don't forget to visit the gift shop called Goat Hill. If you are interested in planning a family field trip to our beautiful state capital, you can find resources online to plan your trip.

title: The Civil Rights Movement
text:
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

The effort to get equal rights for people of all races is sometimes called the Civil Rights Movement. The person most famous for increasing civil rights for African Americans and others was Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Martin didn't start out as "Dr. King, the famous civil rights leader." His interest in civil rights began when he was a young boy, traveling on a train with his family. They were having dinner when someone came and pulled a curtain down between his family and the others on the train. The white people wanted to be separated from African Americans. This separation of races, or segregation, happened all over the country and not just in the South. Discrimination means treating people unfairly because of their race, gender, or abilities. It meant that African Americans were not allowed to eat at the same restaurants, drink from the same water fountains, go to the same schools, or do anything that would bring them into close association with white people.

Young King felt insulted that day on the train, and he eventually dedicated his life to pulling down the "curtains" between his race and the rest of the country. He was most famous for his belief in nonviolent resistance. He taught his followers not to fight back when they were attacked by police or mobs. This policy worked well for the civil rights cause. Television allowed the world to watch as the police set mean dogs on King's followers or washed them all the way down city streets with fire hoses. Television also reported the bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in 1963, which tragically took the lives of four young African American schoolgirls who were attending Sunday School there, and the brutal murder of a young African American boy who was riding down the street on a bicycle with his brother. Despite these terrible acts, King's followers continued to gather together in huge crowds to peacefully protest against unfair segregation and discrimination laws. When the protesters refused to fight back, people all over the world began to speak out in favor of the Civil Rights Movement.

From 1955 to 1968, King's efforts changed the laws of our country, giving equal rights to all races. In 1964, he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at age 35. The next year, King organized a march from Selma to Montgomery, a distance of about 50 miles. The march began on March 7, but because the organizers had not received official permission for the march, the people were stopped by state troopers. More than 50 people were injured that day. King and his followers didn't give up, however. They got permission for another march two weeks later. President Lyndon Johnson even sent federal troops to protect the protesters. Only 300 people walked all the way from Selma to Montgomery, but more than 25,000 people joined them on Dexter Avenue as they marched to the state capitol. Sadly, in 1968, an angry escaped convict killed King. This brave, peace-loving man changed our world forever.

E.D. Nixon

E.D. Nixon was an American civil rights leader who is remembered by many as the "Father of the Civil Rights Movement." He was president of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP when Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on the bus. He and the Durrs, a white couple, put up the money to get Rosa out of jail. Afterwards, he helped Martin Luther King Jr. organize the Montgomery Bus Boycott. For 13 months, thousands of African Americans in Montgomery rode bicycles and horses, formed carpools, or walked to work instead of riding city buses. Finally, a decision by the Supreme Court forced the Montgomery Bus Company to accept integration and the boycott came to an end. Nixon and King also created the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA). He continued his fight for civil rights into the 1960s.

Johnnie Carr

Johnnie Carr was a young girl when she met her friend, Rosa Parks, at Montgomery Industrial School. When she grew up, Carr cleaned and cooked for white families. Later, she took a job selling insurance, where she met her husband, Arlam Carr. The Carrs started working with the NAACP, where they met E.D. Nixon and helped with the Montgomery Bus Boycott. Carr also joined the Montgomery Improvement Association, where she met and worked with King. She later served as president of that organization for many years.

For her tireless efforts, self-sacrifice, and outstanding contributions to the fight for civil rights for all Americans, Carr was awarded the Roosevelt Freedom Medal. In 2004, she received the Rosa Parks Woman of Courage Award. At the awards ceremony, as Carr was being introduced to the audience, the speaker said, "She shows what one person can do when she knows she is right and needs no reassurance of the justness of her cause."

title: Rosa Parks: A Profile in Courage
text:
"I didn't get on the bus to get arrested. I got on the bus to go home," said Rosa Parks. She was 42 years old in 1955, and on Dec. 1 of that year, she kicked off a revolution that spread throughout the South and beyond. She didn't fire a shot or run for office or speak before Congress on that day. No, the revolution began when she simply refused to get up from her seat on the bus when a white man wanted to sit down. In those days, it was illegal for African Americans to sit while white passengers stood up.

"Well, I'm going to have you arrested!" said an angry bus driver.

"You go on and do so," said Rosa. It was that simple. Soon, in the face of great danger, African Americans in Alabama boycotted (refused to use) the buses all together, and a wave of protest spread through the South. It wasn't long before segregation laws in the South were declared unconstitutional. Rosa Parks has been called "the torchbearer" by some, but what does she think of herself? "I would like to be known as a person who is concerned about freedom and equality and justice and prosperity for all people," she said.

Virginia and Clifford Durr, who were white, moved to Alabama and worked alongside African Americans in the fight for civil rights. Because of their beliefs and their involvement in the Civil Rights Movement, they lost friends and fell out of favor with many in the white community.

In December 1955, the Durrs and E.D. Nixon bailed Rosa out of jail when she was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a city bus. Many years later, upon hearing that Virginia had passed away, Rosa stated that Virginia's "upbringing of privilege did not prohibit her from wanting equality for all people ... I will miss her." Clifford, a lawyer, is remembered by many for his courage and his commitment to doing what was right and fighting what he believed to be wrong, no matter the consequences.

When Rosa died in October 2005, her casket was placed in the U.S. Capitol for two days so people could pay their respects to her. Rosa became the first woman to receive this honor.

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
Goods weren't the only things introduced to Europe and the Americas during the Columbian Exchange.

Beliefs

The Indigenous peoples of the Americas had very different beliefs than Europeans. A shared belief among tribes was that everything in their environment was alive and treated with respect. The Europeans did not have the same beliefs as Indigenous peoples. These differences in beliefs would lead to future conflict between them.

Europeans thought it was their duty to change the native peoples to be like Europeans, including converting them to Christianity. Many beliefs, practices, and even places for natives were destroyed by Europeans, because they did not agree with them. Native peoples resisted and often fought back, leading to wars with Europeans in New England.

Slavery

As Europeans began to colonize the Americas more, the market for free labor increased. European slave traders from Portugal, France, England, and the Netherlands bought men, women, and children from West Africa. The slave traders packed their ships with the people from West Africa and made the dangerous journey across the Atlantic Ocean. Many Africans died before they reached the Americas.

Wealthy businessmen took advantage of the slave market to increase their wealth. Crops like sugarcane, tobacco, and cotton were all grown and required a great amount of work. The farms where enslaved people worked were called plantations. Enslaved people lived very difficult lives. Many were abused and separated from their families. They had no freedom and lived in very bad conditions. Enslaved people would work 16 hours a day doing hard labor for no money. They were considered property. Enslaved people were bought by plantation owners as soon as they were brought to America. The majority of enslaved people were Africans. A small number of Indigenous people were enslaved.

Disease

Europeans brought many diseases to the Americas. These diseases include smallpox, measles, and influenza. These diseases were very deadly for native people. Native peoples had no immunity to these diseases, and they spread very quickly and easily in their communities. Millions of American Indians died from these diseases. These diseases were still affecting tribes in the late 1800s.

title: Inquiry
text:
This week, you are going to engage in an inquiry about New Jersey problem solvers.

What is inquiry?

Inquiry is a way to engage in investigation or research. We use the inquiry process in our daily lives when we encounter a problem or have a question that we want to answer. Asking questions is the basis of inquiry. The inquiry process looks like this:

title: Compelling and Supporting Questions
text:
A compelling question is a question that is interesting and important to you. It is not a question that can be answered simply or with a “yes” or a “no.” It is a question that usually has a variety of answers. For example, which compelling question is better?

Which president held office the longest?

What makes a good president?

Supporting questions help clarify the compelling question. They are smaller and simpler questions. These questions help to focus the research process. They also help to define words and break down large concepts. If our compelling question is “What makes a good president?” our supporting questions could be:

What is the job of a president?

What types of problems does the president deal with?

What are some examples of how past presidents have dealt with problems?

The compelling question that we are going to be answering this week is: What characteristics have New Jersey’s problem solvers shown?

title: Make a Claim
text: To help guide research and properly answer the compelling question, we make a claim. In science, this first claim is called a hypothesis. In social studies, our first claim is going to be our best guess, using our background knowledge. As we research, we will need to refine our claim based on the evidence that we find. It is good when claims change, because it means we are thinking through our evidence and considering what our research means for our compelling question. This process is called reflection. To reflect means to think a lot about something. It is important to reflect on your research and claim.

title: Our Class Inquiry
text:
Now it’s time to practice!

Supporting Question: What is problem-solving?

New Jersey experiences challenges, just like any organization. If a problem happens frequently or over a long period of time, it needs to be solved. When creating a solution, it is important to think through all possibilities and listen to everyone’s ideas. This helps problem solvers find the best solution. Every citizen in a community can be involved in solving problems. There have been many New Jersey residents throughout history who have seen problems and created solutions. Following generations have benefitted from these people’s dedication and creativity.

title: Justice William J. Brennan Jr.
text:
Supporting Question: Who has been a problem solver in New Jersey?

William J. Brennan Jr. was born in Newark, New Jersey. His parents were Irish immigrants. He attended Harvard Law School and practiced law in New Jersey. During World War II, Brennan served the army as a lawyer. After, Brennan went back to private practice and became a judge. Dwight D. Eisenhower nominated Brennan to the Supreme Court in 1956. Brennan served as Supreme Court justice from 1957 to 1990.

Supporting Question: What kinds of problems did Justice Brennan face?

As a Supreme Court Justice, Brennan encountered many problems. When a court case comes to the Supreme Court, it means someone is appealing to change previous verdicts, or decisions made by another judge. Often Brennan’s cases dealt with protecting the rights guaranteed to citizens by the Constitution. Some of Brennan’s most influential cases on the Supreme Court dealt with the First Amendment.

Supporting Question: What kinds of solutions did Brennan come up with?

Brennan defended the freedom of the press in 1964 with the court case New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. In this case, the New York Times, a newspaper, had made a claim that the city of Birmingham, Alabama, was treating civil rights demonstrators with violence. The city commissioner sued the New York Times, saying that the paper had printed some small factual errors, so they owed the city commissioner money. Alabama courts agreed and told the newspaper that they had to pay the city commissioner $500,000. However, the commissioner did not dispute that the city had been violent toward civil rights activists. Brennan stated that if the press was not allowed to publicly debate important issues because they had to worry about small errors, it would be a denial of freedom of the press, a right guaranteed in the First Amendment.

Supporting Question: What problem-solving characteristics did Brennan display while on the Supreme Court?

In order to be a problem solver, Brennan had to exercise many different character traits. Being a judge requires empathy, or the ability to understand and share another person's feelings. Being a judge also requires civility, which is the ability to speak and listen with the intent to understand all sides of an issue. With civility, Brennan could ensure that the judgments could be correct and fair.

Claim: The most important characteristic of New Jersey’s problem solvers, like Justice William J. Brennan, is the ability to listen.

text:
This photograph shows a 10 year old girl named Lalar Blanton. She is looking out the window with her back to the spinning machines. She had been working for more than a year already when this photograph was taken. This is an example of a primary source because it shows a real working child who was photographed as a way to raise awareness about child labor.

People have been gathering together records and information for a long time. Having lots of information in one place makes it easier to find answers. That is part of what makes the internet so useful. This is a drawing of the Library of Congress from 1853. Many, many pieces of information, photos, videos, artifacts, books, and other resources can be found through the Library of Congress.

History tells about what happened in other times and places. This image shows drawings of plants for fortifications in Florida during 1779-1815.

Many stories and myths build up around actual history. There are many stories about George Washington's teeth, for instance. One of the most well-known stories says that he had wooden teeth. In fact, he had a variety of different dentures made from different materials (including human teeth). This is an image from around 1910-1915 titled G. Washington's Teeth.

The home-washing invention turned clothes washing from a service to a good. People used to pay others to do the washing (a service), but now most people do their own washing using a washing machine (a good). This is an advertisement from 1869 for a home washing invention.

This photo from 1942 shows people crowding around an ice cream truck to get a treat. The people who made the ice cream are the producers, the people who are selling the ice cream are the sellers, and the people buying the ice cream are the buyers.

title: Week 17 Primary Sources
text: There are many groups who have contributed to the culture of the United States. One great example is the Harlem Renaissance. During the 1920s and 1930s, many African Americans moved from the South to cities in the North. As they created communities, they produced art, music, poetry, and more, which still influences the United States today. This is a portrait of Langston Hughes, a famous African American poet during the Harlem Renaissance.

Even though this dollar bill printed by the Merchant's Bank of Trenton in 1861 is no longer valid currency in the United States, it still looks familiar because of the image of Abraham Lincoln and other aspects of its design. Many countries, including Canada and Mexico, use images of noteworthy people on their money.

text: This 1829 map accomplishes a lot by having color coding, explanatory notes, a scale, labeling, and extra diagrams.

title: Week 2 Primary Sources
text:
Because of its location, Florida gets extreme weather, including hurricanes. This photograph shows cars sunken in floodwaters by Hurrican Jeanne in 1980.

The name of this 1763 Florida map is "A New and Accurate Map of East and West Florida, Drawn from the best Authorities." It has many details to demonstrate the physical features of the land.

title: Week 3 Primary Sources
text: This is a 1950s map of the area around Two Egg. It was created before Interstate 10 was built.

title: Week 4 Primary Sources
text:
This photograph shows Ethel Peterson, a 27-year-old expert lift-truck operator at the Paraffine Company in Emeryville, California. Driving a lift-truck like this requires very specific skills.

This photograph from 1941 shows a picker in Maryland filling a basket with tomatoes. He was paid one cent for each basket he filled in addition to his daily wage.

There are different ways to earn money, and unfortunately, employers can find ways to avoid paying a fair or living wage to their employees. This is the cover for a book written in 1913 to help women protect themselves against being underpaid.

A common way for people to earn interest during the world wars was to let the government borrow their money by purchasing war bonds. This is an advertisement for buying war bonds during World War I.

One way that people make money is by renting their property to other people. This is a sign from 1940 advertising apartments near the waterfront. What would it be like to have rent be only a dollar a day?

Another way people make money is by owning a business. This is a picture of a family-owned poultry business from 1994.

Starting a business can be risky. These children are already in business as vegetable sellers in 1909, working to get their wares to market each day.

Part of having a job in the United States is paying taxes on that income. It's not just recommended, either. If someone doesn't properly pay their taxes, that is considered a crime. Here is a notice issued by the New York City Police Department for a man named Dutch Schultz, who violated federal tax income law.

title: Week 5 Primary Sources
text:
This is an advertisement from 1878 for 22 different products. Economic wants are part of finding ways to be satisfied with life. Once basic needs are met, fulfilling wants can sometimes lead to enjoyment or waste.

Many inventions are driven by trying to let people have more of what they want. In this case, people want to have clean clothes with less work: and so the home washing machine and wringer was invented. Those who bought this labor-saving device exchanged money for less time doing the washing.

Something advertisements do is try to sell people an idea of what life would be like if they bought this product. In this advertisement, there is a high standard of elegance that is being marketed to viewers.

During the Civil War, money was scarce for many people. This advertisement from 1861 is showing just what can be bought for various amounts. When winter is coming, people need warm clothing more than they need to buy something they want for other reasons.

This is a detail from an advertisement from 1855 promising to sell at the "lowest possible price." Sellers often use promises such as these to bring in more customers, especially those with limited income.

Budgets have long been promoted as a good way to manage expenses and money generally. This is an image from 1940, showing a bank book and a budget book.

This advertisement from 1916 is marketing by showing consumers how much it would cost for various holiday activities.

title: Week 6 Primary Sources
text:
During the world wars, people were advised to use their savings to buy war bonds. This would bring them interest on their saved money, which would help them later. This 1915 advertisement is specifically directed at women, telling them to "make every penny do the work of two" by putting their "savings in the war loan."

Buy an ice cream now or save the money to buy a war bond later. With money, there is always a trade-off. This photo from 1942 shows people crowding around an ice cream truck to get a treat.

To be thrifty means that a person knows how to make their money go as far as possible. This detail from an advertisement in 1931 talks about ways that married women were cutting back costs during the Depression.

Part of the way a bank works is by having people let them use their money. Encouraging people to put their savings in a bank (rather than in their houses) means the bank has access to that money and can use it to make more money. Some banks have even sought out particular groups. This is a picture in an interior shot of the Seaman's Bank for Savings in New York City in 1943.

When people bought war bonds during the world wars, they did it in part to be patriotic and help during the war, but also because they would get their money back with interest (all the money they had spent, plus extra) when they redeemed the bond later. This is an advertisement for war bonds from 1919.

This 1877 print says: "Credit, don't ask it, it isn't square." Because buying on credit is like using the idea of future money, it is a riskier way of making purchases, especially because there will also be interest when it is time to pay.

Investing money is a way to grow savings over time, but only if the investment is safe. This shows investors drowning in the "seas" of Wall Street and Speculation. The title of this 1901 lithograph is "Investors beware!"

This shows a pair of lithographs from 1849, showing how investors feel when their stocks are going up or going down. Stocks are a way to increase future income if the stocks do well.

When parents encourage their children to save money, they often do so by giving them a piggy bank, a ceramic vessel with a slit in the top where coins and folded bills can be put in. This shows a black piggy bank from North Carolina's Lexington Barbecue Festival.

title: Week 7 Primary Sources
text:
The thing about accidents is that they happen when least expected. This is a newspaper clipping from an article about the Monongah Mine Disaster of 1907. In the course of their normal workday, many workmen were killed or trapped in the mine when there was an explosion. It is still considered the worst mining disaster in history.

Life isn't always simple. Sometimes, looking into the past can expose pain and hurt and resentment. This is an image of a family tree diagram from 1888. The Library of Congress has an article talking about how genealogy researchers encounter lots of unexpected emotions as they help people learn more about their family roots.

Disasters happen and continue to happen. Preparing for possible emergencies can help when things go wrong. This is a newspaper clipping about a three-day blizzard in March 1888 that happened from Delaware to Montreal. It was so intense that it has been named "The Great Blizzard of 1888."

Life can be dangerous. A common form of risk for many, many years was traveling by sea. This shows an illustration of a shipwreck from the late 1800s.

title: Week 8 Primary Sources
text:
This is the first page of a timeline that shows the events and factors that led to a statewide teacher strike in 1968 in Florida.

The state of Florida has a constitution, but so does the Seminole Tribe of Florida. Here is the cover page of their constitution and bylaws that were ratified in 1957.

title: Week 9 Primary Sources
text:
This is a page from a 1922 book called Fundamental Facts for New Citizens. On page 29, it begins laying out the branches of government., starting with Congress.

Local and state governments work together, and they also work with the federal government. At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Law Library of Congress had a team of writers create a report on the federal, state, and local government responses to COVID-19. This is the cover page.

title: Primary Sources
text:
One of the ways that people change how governments work is by bringing awareness to problems. Ida Tarbell became famous for her writing as an investigative journalist exposing hidden issues. This is an advertisement for her exposé of Standard Oil.

Often, the way things get done is because people simply decide to do them. Volunteering time, effort, money, and resources is a way to get things to happen. Here is an image of Tallahassee American Red Cross volunteers making ditty bags for servicemen overseas.

Once representatives have been elected, they meet together to work out what should be done to help the city, state, or country to run well and to represent their consituents. Here is a photograph of the Florida House of Representatives in session in 1978.

title: Week 11 Primary Sources
text: This is Billy Bowlegs III, who was a Seminole tribal historian.

title: Week 12 Primary Sources
text:
This drawing from 1591 shows the native people living their lives as the French explorers' ships enter the waterways of Florida.

This illustration shows the moment when Hernando De Soto, with his soldiers, sailors, and priests, landed in Florida.

title: Week 13 Primary Sources
text:
Primary sources can tell a lot about what happened in the past through the viewpoint of the person who created the artifact being examined. This is a piece from the journal of Thomas Sidney Jesup during the Second Seminole War. He is writing from his own perspective about the war.

This is a map showing the lands given up by the native tribes of Florida as the European settlers took over.

title: Week 14 Primary Sources
text:
St. Augustine is known for being the oldest permanent settlement in the United States. Here is the oldest school house in St. Augustine. It is located in St. Johns County.

This is a detail of a map showing the area around St. Augustine. On the map, there is a marking for Fuerte Negro, also known as Fort Mose.

This map from the end of the 16th century shows the extent of Spanish Florida, which went from the Chesapeake Bay all the way to what is now New Mexico.

Florida had many Spanish missions. This image shows a detail from a map of a Spanish Mission south of Florida drawn in 1755 that shows how the missions were designed to create a contained community.

title: Week 15 Primary Sources
text:
Different countries staked claims of the land now called Florida. Among them were the French. This is a map by a French mapmaker, Jacques Le Moyne de Morgue. His maps had tremendous influence in shaping how Europe viewed the Americas. On this map, he identifies about 50 Native American communities.

The Louisiana Purchase was a big deal. As a result of this purchase and the following Adams-Onis Treaty, Florida became a U.S. territory. This shows a map of Florida just a few years after the treaty.

title: Week 16 Primary Sources
text:
This is the final page of the Treaty of Moultie Creek. This treaty was part of the Seminole Wars, and it effectively forced the Seminoles to move to a reservation. These are the signatures on this page: William P. Duval, James Gadsden, Bernard Segui, Neamathla, John Blunt, Tuski Hajo, Mulatto King, Emathlocha, and Econchictimico.

This image shows the Seminoles being deported from Florida.

title: Week 17 Primary Sources
text: This is a sketch of a steamboat piston by John Fitch. The steamboat would do much to help with the advancement of settling Florida because of its many waterways, low-lying land, and swamps.

title: Week 18 Primary Sources
text: This is a photograph titled "Pioneers traveling through prairie land—Orange County, Florida."

title: Week 20 Primary Sources
text: During the Civil War, Florida's troops were often on the move. This photograph shows a camp of the Confederate soldiers near Pensacola in 1861.

title: Week 21 Primary Sources
text:
Reconstruction didn't fix all the problems it was meant to fix. This is an illustration from a newspaper showing Andrew Johnson holding a leaking kettle labeled “The Reconstructed South” toward a woman representing liberty and a baby representing the 14th Amendment. The tea kettle isn't very good at holding water, let alone making tea.

Florida's economic boom was like the clouds parting and letting the sun through. With the railway and steamboat companies extending travel, settlement, and business opportunity, the future was looking bright.

Lue Gim Gong developed frost-resistant citrus fruits and other plants that helped save the citrus industry in Florida. This picture shows him inspecting oranges.

title: Week 23 Primary Sources
text: This is a still from a film taken of the U.S. cavalry unloading ambulance supplies from a freight train in Tampa, Florida, during the Spanish-American War.

title: Week 24 Primary Sources
text:
Florida drew many immigrants, among them sponge divers from Greece.

Charles Ringling of the Ringling Brothers and the Barnum & Bailey Circus bought a lot of land in Sarasota Floirda. He became a businessman and investor and helped shape Florida. This is a picture of a poster of him with his brothers.

title: Week 25 Primary Sources
text: During the land boom in Florida, there were many marketing campaigns designed to bring more and more people to settle in Florida's cities.

title: Week 26 Primary Sources
text: This is a picture of a migrant worker's shack during the Great Depression. It is made of tin and burlap. It was photographed by a canal near Belle Glade, Florida.

title: Week 27 Primary Sources
text: This is a telegram declaring the need for people in Jacksonville to turn out the lights of their amusement concessions because it was likely that the submarine that destroyed two U.S. ships was guided by those very lights.

title: Week 28 Primary Sources
text: These three preachers (J. Metz Rollins, Edwin F. Norwood Sr., and C.K. Steele) arranged a boycott for Tallahassee city buses because of the segregated seating.

title: Week 29 Primary Sources
text:
Because of its location, Florida became the stage for the United States in the international scene and in space as the Space Race got underway. This is a picture of a booklet advertising Rocket City in 1962, showing how Florida was seeing itself in relation not only to the United States but to the world and beyond.

This is a still from a short film about the early space program and the economic impact it had on counties near Cape Canaveral. It also shows footage of the Gemini launch.

title: Week 30 Primary Sources
text: Tourism has been a part of Florida from nearly the beginning. This is a panel from a brochure made for the World's Fair in 1933-1934, promoting Florida and all that the state had to offer, including a message from the governor and locations of the exhibits about Florida.

title: Week 31 Primary Sources
text: Immigrants have helped Florida grow into what it is today. Some of these immigrants are refugees who risk everything to escape to a hope-for freedom. This is an image from a newspaper in 1964, showing how Cuban refugees made an escape boat out of a trailer.

title: Week 1 Primary Sources
text: This picture is part of an advertising campaign for the Victory Corps. It shows a student at Polytechnic High School in Los Angeles, California, learning to use a sextant to determine longitude and latitude. Those who were trained could become technicians for the U.S. military.

title: Week 2 Primary Sources
text: This is an interesting piece of history from 1965 showing notes on a page of coordinates for places in South American and North America.

title: Week 3 Primary Sources
text:
This is a striking early map of North America showing the physical features by means of bold lines called hachures, which give an idea of the steepness of an incline through their thickness and density.

This is a map made by the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency). It shows clear borders for the United States.

This is another map created by the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency). It showcases each state and its capital, including spaces for Alaska, Hawaii, and Washington, D.C.

This 1851 map of native lands is an interesting demonstration of where the mapmaker decided to put detail and where things were more conceptual than literal.

This map uses strong color-coding as well as a coordinate grid to lay out the colonies and territories of the time. There is also an indication of mountains with small hump marks. This map looks very different from maps of this part of the country today.

Because most of the mounds were lost as settlers built buildings and started farms, this map is a unique record.

title: Week 4 Primary Sources
text:
This shows the process the process of analyzing primary sources: Observe, reflect, and question.

This is a fragment of the earliest draft of the Declaration of Independence. It shows how Jefferson reworked his ideas.

When events happen in daily life, people experience them and write about them. These are actual newspaper clippings from a strike. These are primary sources because they were written when it happened.

During the meetings to create the Constitution, Thomas Jefferson created a table to keep track of the tally of state ratifications for the proposed amendments. On this table, there are twelve amendments proposed, but only ten made it into the Bill of Rights.

Today, most people have a camera in their pockets that lets them make an instant record of something that is happening. During the Civil War, photographers would travel with their own wagon so they could develop their film and take pictures of what was happening.

The U.S. Constitution and the Florida Constitution share structural similarities. They both have a preamble, articles, and amendments. Some of the wording in the Florida Constitution also reflects wording in the U.S. Constitution. This shows the preamble and first five sections of Florida's 1885 Constitution.

There are many symbols of the United States, one of the largest being the Statue of Liberty. This photograph shows construction of the statue with the left hand and head of Lady Liberty in the background, almost like a giant.

Right from the start, the Constitution needed to be amended. This is a printing of the first proposed amendments to the Constitution. Not all of them made it into the Bill of Rights, but that was a good start.

text:

Going from the Articles of Confederation to the Constitution was risky. It could undo everything that the U.S. had fought for in the Revolutionary War if it destabilized the new country. When the Constitution was ratified at last, there was relief as well as celebration. Here you can see an announcement and schedule for a parade in New York to celebrate the impending ratification of the Constitution.

The Bill of Rights was rejected before it was accepted and included to limit the reach and power of national government over its citizens. Here is a page of James Madison's notes about the debates at the Constitutional Convention about the Bill of Rights.

Finding the right balance in the government so the courts could work effectively at interpreting law and settling conflicts was a process. Here is a letter from Washington addressed to the Supreme Court at the time.

Josiah Thomas Walls was the first African American to represent Florida in Congress starting in 1871. He was also the only Black person to represent Florida until the early 1990s.

The Federalist and the Anti-Federalists pulled issues back and forth between state and national governments. This satirical engraving was created to point out issues with Connecticut specifically, but the struggle applied to the nation as a whole.

text: Maintaining and preserving the government takes work. title: The Polar Climate
text:
Areas near the North and South Poles of the Earth have polar climates. Polar climates are very cold. Temperatures rarely reach above 50 degrees Fahrenheit in the summer! Cold temperatures make polar climates dry. Since cold air can't hold much moisture, there aren't many clouds. Some polar areas receive very little rain or snow. During the winter, polar regions received little sunlight. In the summer, some days have 24 hours of sunlight. The most famous polar animal is the polar bear. Polar bears live in the Northern Hemisphere. They have adapted to the polar climate. Polar bears have black skin. Their fur is actually clear, which allows the sun to reach their skin. Their skin absorbs the sun's heat, keeping them warm. Polar bears are huge animals and fantastic swimmers. Their large size gives them the ability to hunt large prey in their environment.

title: The Tropical Climate
text:
Tropical climates are found close to the Equator, or the middle latitude of the Earth. They are hot and humid. Because they are near the Equator, tropical areas receive lots of sun for a large part of the day. If you visit a tropical climate, you shouldn’t forget your umbrella. There are no dry or rainy seasons in tropical climates. The high rainfall in tropical climates is spread through all parts of the year. Tropical climates have thousands of different species of plants and animals. One plant you might know is the banana plant. Bananas grow well in the humid heat of the tropical climate. An animal that lives in the tropical environment is the sloth. Sloths spend their days in the canopies of tropical rainforests in Central and South America. Being so high up keeps them safe from predators. It also keeps them close to the food they love: leaves that other animals can't reach. Their extra-long arms help them hang easily on the branches.

title: The Continental Climate
text:
Continental climates are found in the inner parts of a continent. These areas are far away from the ocean. In the United States, for example, the Midwestern states have this climate. This climate does not have a high yearly rainfall or snowfall. Continental climates do not have high humidity. Continental climates have large temperature differences between winter and summer. The summers are very hot, and the winters are very cold. Many plants in these climates change with the different seasons. Maple trees grow new leaves in the spring. When the weather turns cold and the days have less sunlight in the autumn, maple trees lose their leaves. Many animals living in continental climates change their behavior with the seasons too. Black bears eat heavily during the summer months. They build up their weight and energy stores. When it gets cold, they hibernate. They spend most of their time during the winter months sleeping and staying out of the cold.

text:
Temperate climates sit between tropical and polar regions. They are mild climates. Temperate climates rarely change in temperature during the year. They are usually warm year-round. Temperate climates are ideal for farming. The soil in temperate climates is rich in nutrients. They have a good amount of rainfall. They offer good soil and predictable weather. In some climates, it is common that farmers can plant for only one or two seasons during the year. Farmers in temperate climates, however, can grow crops during almost every season of the year. text:

Dry climates can be hard places for plants or animals to live due to the lack of water. Those that do live in dry climates have adapted to the climate to survive. For example, coyotes live in the desert, which is a type of dry climate. Their fur is a mix of tan and gray, which helps them camouflage with the sand and rocks. Coyotes burrow into the ground during the day. They hunt at night when it is cooler. The saguaro cactus has shallow and long root systems. These help the cactus to soak in as much water as possible. This type of adaptation allows the saguaro cactus to grow in a dry climate.
