The seven articles lay out the three branches of government and the rules for each branch. The 27 amendments guarantee the rights of the people. The amendments have been added as the nation has grown. The amendments give clarity and specific rules to the government.

Article 1: The Legislative Branch

“All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”

Section 1 grants Congress the power to make laws in two organized parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Section 2: The House of Representatives is defined. The election of members is every two years. Each member must be at least 25 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least seven years.

The number of representatives will be determined by the population “of free persons, including those bound to Service for a term of years [indentured] and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of other persons.” The country will be counted every 10 years in a census. If there is a vacancy from any state, the executive branch will call for an election. The House of Representatives will have the sole power of impeachment (to challenge and investigate a member of government).

Section 3: The Senate is defined. Each state will have two elected senators to Congress for a six-year term. Each senator must be at least 30 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least nine years. The vice president of the executive branch will be president of the Senate. The vice president may only vote to break a tie. The Senate will also elect a president to serve in the absence of the vice president. The Senate will have the sole power to try all impeachments. Impeachment will not extend to more than a removal from office in the government.

Section 4: Congress will meet at least once every year on the first Monday in December.

The remaining six sections define the rules and responsibilities of each group in the system of checks and balances. They help to keep power distributed across the branches of government. There are clear directions on what Congress is forbidden to do. Only Congress can raise and spend money. Congress is responsible for the Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, and Coast Guard. The representatives of the people are in charge of the military. The final section closes with powers forbidden to the states.

Article 2: The Executive Branch

“The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America. He shall hold his Office during the Term of four Years, and, together with the Vice President, chosen for the same Term.”

Section 1: A person who is a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for 14 years can work for the executive office. Once elected, the president shall take the following oath or affirmation: "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the Office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my Ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States."

Section 2: Sets up the president as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. It further defines the powers within the office for hiring people for government posts with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Section 3: The president is required to give information on the state of the Union to Congress.

Section 4: "The President, Vice President, and all civil Officers of the United States shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors."

Article 3: The Judicial Branch

“The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.”

As established under Article 2, the president will nominate a judge for the judicial branch. The nominee must then be confirmed through the Senate.

Section 2: The office of the judiciary will extend to all cases of law arising under the Constitution. It also covers the laws of the United States and all controversies between the state, citizens and states, and citizens and citizens.

Section 3: Treason against the United States is defined. Treason is giving aid and comfort to enemies or waging war against the United States.

title: Relations of the States to Each Other
text:
“The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.”

Article 4 establishes relations between the states. It also defines the state's relations with the federal government.

Section 1: All legal documents in one state must be accepted by the other states.

Section 2: Criminals must be returned to their state of citizenship by state law enforcement agencies. Any person held to service or labor who escapes to another state will be delivered to the person who claims their labor.

Section 3: Admission of new states to the Union is held in Congress. Congress can change any state boundaries when deemed necessary. State constitutions are to be a representative democracy like the federal government. The states will be protected by the national government against invasion or violence within the state.

title: Amending the Constitution
text:
“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution.”

Article 5: Unique to the United States government, this article defines the process for changing the Constitution. Other governments have to create an entirely new government or Constitution. This was usually done through much conflict.

Any amendments to the Constitution must have the people involved in writing, reviewing, and ratification. Since 1789, 33 amendments have been introduced over the years, but only 27 have been ratified.

One amendment that failed to be ratified was the “Titles of nobility.” This amendment would have taken U.S. citizenship from any American who accepted a title of nobility from a foreign country.

The last amendment that was introduced was in 1985. The District of Columbia would have been treated as a state. The ratification period ended without the required votes for passage.

title: Ratification Process
text:
The final article of the Constitution defines the process for ratification.

Nine of the 13 states had to vote to approve the Constitution to create the new government. Each state held conventions where each part of the document was discussed. The Federalists and Anti-Federalists practiced civil discourse. Civil discourse is when each side tries to persuade people to their views and beliefs in a respectful and open manner. There was concern about the absence of a bill of rights to protect individual rights. Compromises and promises were made to get the Constitution ratified by nine states.

The states and the dates of ratification are listed here, in order of ratification:

Delaware: Dec. 7, 1787

Pennsylvania: Dec. 12, 1787

New Jersey: Dec. 18, 1787

Georgia: Jan. 2, 1788

Connecticut: Jan. 9, 1788

Massachusetts: Feb. 6, 1788

Maryland: April 28, 1788

South Carolina: May 23, 1788

New Hampshire: June 21, 1788

title: The Bill of Rights
text:
The Constitution, ratified by the states in 1789, gives the framework and rules for each branch of the United States government. Each of the articles gives the rules and regulations for the functions of each branch. The Constitution defines what the government can do.

The Constitution did not give protection to the individual rights of the people. Those sentences were defined in the Declaration of Independence as "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." The Constitution did not fully explain what the government could not do.

Many delegates wanted a list of protections for the people. The Federalists did not want a list. The delegates at the convention compromised. If the states would ratify the Constitution, a list of rights would be the first action of the new government. In the First Congress of the new government, James Madison, a representative from Virginia, introduced 12 possible amendments to the Constitution. Ten of the proposed amendments became the “Bill of Rights.” The Bill of Rights was ratified on Dec. 15, 1791.

The Bill of Rights states that Congress cannot make any laws that take away a citizen’s rights. It also gives specific rules for what actions the government has to take to protect the rights of the people. The Supreme Court is the branch of government that uses the Bill of Rights and the other amendments to determine the constitutionality of a law. Constitutionality refers to how aligned a law is to the Constitution. When the law is not in line with the rights of the people in the Constitution, the law is “struck down.” This means it's no longer a law. When a law is “upheld” by the Supreme Court, it means it is still a law. This process is called judicial review. The Supreme Court serves as part of the checks and balances between the branches of government.

The Declaration of Independence defines the principles and ideals of freedom and liberty. It is the Constitution and the Bill of Rights that set up how a government could be made to protect these principles and ideas. These three documents have become the foundation of the United States government. The history of the United States is the story of ensuring liberty and freedom for its citizens.

title: The Supreme Law of the Land
text:
Article 6: This article provided for the peaceful transfer of power from the Articles of Confederation to the new federal government.

The new government honored all debts and contracts made by the Confederation Congress. This also established the Constitution as the “Supreme Law of the Land.” No state law could go against the Constitution. This article established the strong federal government wanted by the Federalists. There were still many parts of the country that supported states' rights. All disagreements went to the Supreme Court to be resolved.

The Senators and Representatives ... and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.

title: Government in the United States
text:
The purpose of government is to provide safety and security for those in the community from threats outside of the community, maintain justice and order within the community, and help the members of the community meet their wants and needs. The government of the United States is a constitutional republic.

A constitutional republic is a form of government based on a written document that determines the power and functions of an elected representational government. The written law of the Constitution is enforced by representatives chosen by the people. At every level, the people's consent is what gives the government power to act. This is known as popular sovereignty. A constitutional republic must balance individual rights with the common good. Effective leaders work to meet the needs of citizens and protect their rights.

According to one of the Founders, John Adams, “Government is instituted for the common good … not for profit, honor, or private interest of any one man, family, or class of men.” The common good is when people think about what is best for everyone. It refers to decisions that benefit most members of a community. Our government supports the common good through laws. If citizens work together toward the common good, freedom and self-government can be successful. Everyone in the community benefits.

Another important facet of the United States government is rule of law. John Adams stated that “the rule of law means a government of laws and not of men.” Rule of law is based on fairness, equality, and justice. It means that the government is accountable to the law. The government can only use its power as defined by laws. There are four important guidelines for the rule of law:

Laws have to be adopted and approved through government processes.

Laws have to be clear, and everyone needs to know about them.

Laws are applied equally to all citizens.

When there are disputes about the law, individuals will have representatives who are neutral to deliver the best outcome.

The primary governing body in the United States is the federal government. The power of the federal government is limited by the Constitution, but it has the power to:

print money

declare war

build the military

make treaties (agreements with foreign countries)

make and enforce laws for doing business between the states and foreign nations

make laws to enforce the Constitution.

title: Three Branches of Government
text:
To keep any one person or group from having too much power, the Constitution divides the government into three branches. We call this a system of checks and balances. Each branch was designed to address specific issues and concerns. Each branch has its own structure, processes, and leaders. These leaders use different processes as checks to protect individual liberties. Individual liberties are rights that the government cannot take away. For example, the president may veto legislation passed by Congress. A veto stops a bill from becoming a law. Congress also has checks on the president. For example, the Senate must confirm executive appointments. The courts can check Congress by declaring laws unconstitutional. This basic structure of the national government is also used to guide the development of state and local governments.

The three branches of government are the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The executive branch of government enforces our country’s laws. It is also in charge of the military. The head of the executive branch is the president of the United States. The president is chosen by voters. The president and vice president are elected together for four years. They may serve two terms, for a total of eight years. The president chooses members of the cabinet to advise him or her. Cabinet members are often experts in their fields. They help run the executive branch by leading departments. For example, the Department of Defense is in charge of the military. At the state level, the executive branch includes the governor, departments, and agencies that enforce state laws.

The legislative branch makes the laws and sets taxes. Congress is the legislative branch of our government. It is divided into two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. Two senators are elected from each state. A state’s number of representatives depends on how many people live there. Larger states send more representatives. Smaller states send fewer. Today, there are 100 senators in the Senate and 435 representatives in the House. All of them were elected by the people of their states.

The judicial branch interprets the laws, or decides what they mean. It also determines whether the laws follow the Constitution. The judicial branch is headed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court is made up of judges called justices. They are chosen by the president and voted on by senators. State supreme courts are similar to the U.S. Supreme Court. They decide whether laws go against their state’s constitution. The judicial branch also includes other federal courts and local courts. Local courts decide whether someone is guilty of a crime. The judicial system’s role is to make sure the law is followed and all citizens’ rights are protected.

title: Checks and Balances
text:
The writers of the U.S. Constitution wanted to limit the power of government so that the United States would be strong and endure. Articles I, II, and III of the Constitution separate the government into three branches.

This ensures that branches of government share power equally. In order for these branches to work together, the Founders created a system of checks and balances. This means that each branch of the government has to be in agreement with the other two.

Each branch has the power to stop certain actions of another branch. This happens if a branch believes those actions are unconstitutional or not in the best interest of the country. The system of checks and balances helps make sure that no branch of government becomes more powerful than the others.

Congress can pass a law, but the president must approve it. Congress can also override the president's decision to veto, or reject, a law. The Supreme Court has the power to strike down a law that has been approved by both Congress and the president if it believes the law is unconstitutional. The president appoints justices to the Supreme Court, but Congress must approve the choices. Because of this system of checks and balances, U.S. citizens can be sure their rights are always protected.

title: The Supreme Court
text:
The Supreme Court is the top court in the United States. It was established by the Judiciary Act of 1789. The United States Supreme Court is the highest authority in the judicial branch of the federal government. The role of the Supreme Court is to interpret laws and determine how those laws apply to court cases. The Supreme Court must also decide if laws and decisions made at a local, state, and national level are constitutional.

Nine judges, called justices, serve on the Supreme Court. Justices are not elected. Instead, the U.S. president nominates justices. Then, the Senate votes on whether the nominees can serve on the Supreme Court. The court is led by the chief justice of the United States. Supreme Court justices serve lifetime appointments. As of June 2022, 116 justices have served on the Supreme Court since 1789.

title: The Senate and House of Representatives
text:
The legislative branch is composed of the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives. These chambers make up the U.S. Congress. The Senate and House of Representatives were established by Article I of the Constitution. The purpose of the Senate and House of Representatives is to make and pass laws.

The Constitution stipulates that two senators should represent each state in the Union. To serve in the Senate, officials must meet certain qualifications, including:

must be at least 30 years old

must be a citizen of the United States for a minimum of nine years

must be a resident of the state they wish to represent

If a candidate meets all of these qualifications, then they are eligible to run for the U.S. Senate. Senators are directly elected by the people of each state. The term of office for a senator is six years. The vice president of the United States serves as the president of the Senate.

The number of members of the House of Representatives is determined by the population of a state. States with larger populations have more members that represent their state while states with smaller populations do not have as many representatives. To serve as a member of the House of Representatives, a candidate must:

be at least 25 years old

be a citizen of the United States for a minimum of seven years

inhabit the state they represent

Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms of office.

title: Democratic Principles
text:
Americans have different customs, traditions, and ethnic origins. Americans are united by the principles of a constitutional republic. The Constitution states that citizens need to respect individual rights and freedoms. Authority from the people limits the actions of the government, which protects their rights of liberty and freedom. By creating and enforcing laws, citizens can ensure their rights are protected. Respecting the rights of others means that everyone is treated equally. The principles of fairness, equality, and justice have influenced new laws and policies over time at the local, state, and national levels of government.

Fairness, equality, and justice are principles that have influenced government and laws. Fairness is a fundamental American value. Fairness is about making sure that everyone has what they need to be successful. Our government supports fairness by making laws to keep things fair for everyone. All people should be treated equally.

Equality means that all people are treated the same, regardless of who they are. Our government provides services and protection to all citizens. Justice means that people behave in a way that is fair, equal, and balanced for everyone. Fairness, equality, and justice are democratic values. These values guide our government. They protect the rights of citizens.

Another democratic principle that guides the American political system is majority rule. Majority rule refers to a system in which more than half of those participating in the decision-making process determines the outcome. Majority rule works in tandem with minority rule. Minority rule provides opportunities that a member is entitled to have, or to receive from others within the limits of the law, even though they may not be part of the controlling group. Organizing government in this manner ensures that all people are given a voice in government decisions.

title: Conflict Resolution and Problem-Solving
text:
We can overcome conflict by engaging in civil discourse. Civil discourse helps people live peacefully together and define a problem in a respectful way. You practice civil discourse when you talk in appropriate ways with other people to build understanding. Although there are people with different opinions in a debate, civil discourse reminds us to treat others with respect. As American citizens, we have the right to free speech. This means we can express ourselves freely. However, we also have a responsibility to be polite and listen to others when they are speaking. Civil discourse allows for both of these things to happen.

People can overcome conflict by taking steps to solve a problem:

Engage in civil discourse by stating the problem.

Identify the cause of the problem.

Suggest solutions for the problem.

Attempt to solve the problem.

Reach out to experts to brainstorm possible solutions. Some experts may include teachers, parents, and community helpers.

title: Governments of American Indians
text:
One of the defining principles of government in the United States is the division of power between multiple branches and levels of government. There are many levels of government in the United States, including tribal, state, and local governments.

There are approximately 5 million people in the United States who are of Native American descent. These people belong to hundreds of tribes across the country. Many Native American nations in the United States have their own tribal governments. This means they have their own sovereignty. Sovereignty is an inherent right to self-govern. Tribal governments within the United States follow laws created by the federal government and the U.S. Constitution. However, when Native Americans are on tribal lands, they are subject to the laws of their tribal nation.

The federal government has a duty to protect the rights of Native American tribes. Tribes are often called "nations within a nation." Tribes can receive federal designation from the United States government. Federally recognized tribes have an official relationship with the U.S. government. They have certain rights, responsibilities, and powers. They are able to access some benefits, services, and protections from the U.S. government.

There are 574 federally recognized tribes in the United States. Members of these tribes are the descendants of the ancient tribes that have lived in North America for thousands of years. Each of the federally recognized tribes of the United States has its own reservation. A reservation is an area of land designated to a tribe or tribes by the United States government.

Tribes that are not federally recognized could be one day. They can petition the Bureau of Indian Affairs to receive federal recognition. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is a government agency that establishes which tribes are federally recognized and which are not.

The largest federally recognized tribe in the United States is the Cherokee tribe. The Cherokee tribe, whose central tribal government is located in Oklahoma, is made up of over 800,000 members. The Navajo tribe is the second-largest federally recognized tribe in the United States, with over 300,000 members. The smallest federally recognized tribe in the United States is the Augustine Band of Cahuilla Indians. Located in southern California, the Augustine Band of Cahuilla Indians tribe includes 3,000 registered members.

Tribal governments are led by Native American chiefs. Tribal councils make laws for their tribal nations. They write their own constitutions and have their own court systems. Tribal governments tax their people, too. They use the money to pay for police officers, education, and healthcare for the people. They also decide how to spend money on roads, public water, and electricity.

title: State Government
text:
Each of our 50 states has a state government. State governments are modeled after the federal government and consist of an executive, legislative, and judicial branch. All state governments are led by the executive branch. The executive branch is responsible for signing bills into law, appointing judges, proposing the state budget, organization of the state militia, and overseeing all agencies that work within the government.

The executive branch is led by the governor of the state. The governor is elected by the people. Of the 50 states in the country, 28 states limit a governor’s term in office to two consecutive, or back-to-back, terms. Thirteen states do not have a term limit for the governor, while the remaining states have varying term limits.

Most states also have a lieutenant governor, a secretary of state, and an attorney general. These make up the executive branch and are elected by the people and serve varying terms. The lieutenant governor assists the governor in matters of state and fulfills the responsibilities of the governor if they are unable to do so. The secretary of state is responsible for elections, record keeping, and safeguarding the state archives. The attorney general is the head of law enforcement for the state.

The legislative branch is responsible for creating state laws. All states, except for Nebraska, have a legislative branch made up of two houses. This is known as a bicameral legislature. Nebraska has a unicameral legislature. This means that the legislative branch of Nebraska has only one house. The larger of the two houses is often called the House of Representatives, but it is also called the House of Delegates or the State Assembly. The smaller of the two houses is called the Senate.

The state’s judicial branch is led by the state supreme court. State supreme courts are responsible for correcting or definitively ruling on decisions that have been made in lower courts. The justices ensure that the correct procedures were followed. If problems or disagreements cannot be resolved within the state, cases can be taken to the U.S. Supreme Court.

title: State Constitutions
text:
Just like the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions guarantee and protect citizens' basic rights. State constitutions list the rules for state government. They also explain how a state can make laws. State constitutions describe how the state government divides and shares power with counties and cities.

State constitutions can change over time. These changes are called amendments. Lawmakers and voters can work together to amend the existing state constitution to meet the needs of citizens. To amend means to change or add to. Citizens can vote to amend their state constitution.

title: Local Government
text:
A local government is a government that serves the people of a town, city, or county. There are several types of local government structures in the United States. The most common types of local government structures are county governments, municipal governments, and special districts.

County governments are responsible for assisting the state government in meeting the needs of those who live within the county’s boundaries. County governments are run by a board of supervisors. Members of the board of supervisors are elected by the people who live in their county. County governments are usually responsible for keeping records. This means that counties keep track of births, deaths, marriages, and business licenses. County governments are also in charge of voting, vehicle registration, and collecting taxes on land and property. Many counties also offer health and welfare services, like nursing care, immunization, and child care classes. Some counties also run the public library system.

Municipal governments are responsible for the health, welfare, and safety of people in a town, city, village, or borough. Municipal governments are run by elected officials, including a mayor or city manager, city council, or board of directors. These local leaders help make good decisions for the people who live in a city or town.

Special districts are created by a state to serve a specific purpose. Special districts usually serve a single purpose. School districts are a type of special district. School districts are responsible for the education of the students who live within the district. School districts are run by a school superintendent, along with a board of education. A school superintendent is a professional teacher or school administrator who is hired to lead the school district. The superintendent works with the school board to make decisions about how the schools in the district should run.

title: American Indian, State, and Local Courts
text:
The purpose of local, state, and tribal courts is to interpret laws and settle conflicts. How does the court system work? First, citizens bring their problems to state trial courts. Members of Native American tribes often bring their issues and legal matters to tribal courts first. State trial courts are located in the county you live in. Tribal courts are located on Native American reservations. The judges in the trial and tribal courts listen to the problem, or case, and both sides of the story. They think about the evidence that each side presented and then make a decision based on what they heard. Judges' decisions solve conflicts and provide consequences for those people who break the law.

If a person does not agree with the trial or tribal court's decision, they can file an appeal. This appeal goes to the Court of Appeals at the state level. Sometimes, the Court of Appeals keeps the trial court's decision. Other times, they overturn the original outcome. If a person is still unhappy after the Court of Appeals' decision, they can apply to take their case to the state supreme court.

State supreme courts vary in the number of judges, or justices, that they have. They make decisions on cases and solve problems that people bring before them. The state supreme courts take cases that have first gone through the trial courts and Court of Appeals. Justices decide cases in two ways: by opinion or by order. In both types of cases, the judges must meet to analyze the case and determine the verdict.

If a case cannot be resolved by the state courts, it can be elevated to the Supreme Court of the United States. The U.S. Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It upholds and interprets the laws of the Constitution. It also ensures that the rights of all Americans are protected. Currently, the Supreme Court is made up of nine judges. Supreme Court justices work together to determine the outcome of important court cases. The Supreme Court reviews thousands of cases each year.

title: Becoming a Citizen
text:
A citizen is an official member of a country, state, or community. If you were born in the United States, you are a U.S. citizen. If your parents are citizens, you can become a citizen no matter where you were born. People who are born outside of the United States can choose to become a citizen. If you choose to become a citizen of the United States, the government requires specific things that must be done.

To become a citizen, you must be at least 18 years old and have lived in the United States for at least five years. You must be loyal and willing to pledge allegiance to the United States. To pledge allegiance means to take an oath of loyalty.

You must have a basic understanding of U.S. history, government, and the Constitution. In addition, you must be able to speak, read, and write English.

The process of becoming a citizen has three different steps. First, you must file an application. This includes being fingerprinted, taking photographs, and providing legal documents. Applicants must also pay a fee to submit their documents. The next step is to take the naturalization exam. This exam has two parts. It has an English test and a U.S. history and government exam.

The last step is to appear in court. You must go before a judge and ask to become a U.S. citizen. The judge listens to your reasons for wanting to become a citizen. Then, the judge will make a final decision. Once you are made a citizen, you have all the rights and duties of any other U.S. citizen.

title: Rights of Citizens
text:
People have many different rights. These include unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights. Rights have different functions. Unalienable rights, also called natural rights, are rights that people are born with and cannot be taken away. The Declaration of Independence defines these rights as the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

Civil rights protect people from the actions of government, organizations, or other people. The United States government, organizations, and other people cannot prohibit the rights of citizens to:

vote

a fair trial by jury

government services

due process of the law (legal actions or proceedings that must be followed)

serve in the military

serve in public office

equality through the law

assemble or petition the government

freedom of speech

freedom of religion

freedom of the press

Political rights allow people to participate freely in government. People can protect their civil rights through political rights. These rights are defined in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights at the federal level. They are defined at the state level in state constitutions. Examples of political rights include:

voting

serving on a jury

holding political office

attending a protest

petitioning the government through action and/or speech

supporting a social or political issue

expressing an idea in speech and the press

joining a political party

equal access to public services

Economic rights are financial choices and privileges that individuals may select without government interference. These rights enable people to make use of civil and political rights. Economic rights include the right to:

own property

change employment

operate a business

join a labor union

access polling places

meet basic wants and needs

multiple economic opportunities

not being required to pay fees and taxes based on race, gender, ethnicity, religion, or sexual orientation

title: Americans with Disabilities Act
text:
One law that protects the unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights of people living in the United States is the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Congress passed the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990. Its purpose is to “prohibit discrimination against people with disabilities in several areas, including employment, transportation, public accommodations, communications and access to state and local government programs and services.”

The Americans with Disabilities Act is divided into five titles, or sections. Each title has a specific purpose.

Title I: Protects against discrimination in the workplace and ensures that people with disabilities receive appropriate accommodations in their workplace

Title II: Ensures access to services, facilities, and transportation provided by local and state governments

Title III: Prohibits discrimination in public places and requires that people with disabilities receive appropriate access to facilities

Title IV: Requires telecommunications companies to provide equal services to people with disabilities

Title V: Defines various types of disabilities and prevents retaliation by employers, organizations, other people, etc. against individuals who enforce their rights under the act

By protecting unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights, governments can ensure that all citizens have the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. These rights also ensure that governments cannot interfere with the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

title: Being a Global Citizen
text:
The world is divided into many nations. Each nation has its own governments, languages, customs, and laws. The fundamental rights of the individual and the common good of the world depend upon all citizens exercising their civic responsibilities. Citizens can exercise civic responsibility at the community, state, national, and global levels. You are a citizen of many communities. You are a member of a family, classroom, school, community, state, and nation. In addition to this, you are also a member of a global community. You are a global citizen!

One way you can be a responsible global citizen is to respect other people’s rights, culture, language, customs, and laws. Just like you, people around the world have the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. We call these universal human rights. This means that all people should be treated fairly and have the opportunity to meet their needs. It is important that we respect others, even if we don’t always understand or agree with them. Across global communities, governments and citizens alike have a responsibility to protect human rights and to treat others fairly. It is important that people from all groups and cultures collaborate to find solutions to our global challenges.

In an interconnected world, it is important to consider different cultural perspectives before proposing solutions to local, state, national, and global challenges. As an active global citizen, you can research global events to find opportunities where you can make a difference. For example, you can collect needed items for victims of natural disasters around the globe. You can also spread awareness of environmental issues that impact the world.

As a citizen of many communities, you can choose to make a difference. Here's the process you should follow:

Identify a global problem.

Learn more about the problem.

Identify possible solutions to the problem and locate people or organizations that are willing to help.

Create a plan to implement the solution.

Involve other people from your community to help solve the problem.

title: Historical Thinking
text:
History is not just a clear timeline of events from one period to the next. Many events in history can occur at the same time. Events can also occur within the same time period. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technology change over time. Historians analyze how things remain the same as well as how things change throughout history. Historians examine patterns to understand how things change in a historical context.

To understand patterns in history, historians often ask the following questions:

What changes have happened?

What has stayed the same?

Who benefited from changes?

Who did not benefit from changes?

When we apply historical thinking to an event, we think outside of our own experience. We try to imagine what things would have been like in a different time period. This helps us think about multiple perspectives. It also creates empathy, or a feeling of caring, about people and events of the past.

title: Analytical Thinking
text:
Historians examine cause and effect to understand an event. A cause is an event that makes or causes something else to happen. An effect is the result, consequence, or outcome of what happened. Historians study both causes and effects of events to create a complete picture of the time and place of the event in context. Historians use analytical thinking when they examine cause and effect.

Analytical thinking also occurs when historians look at an event, focusing on the individual parts and how they contribute to the whole event. For example, historians can analyze the westward expansion of the United States during the 1800s by researching the effects of the Louisiana Purchase. The map of the Louisiana Purchase shows the geographic region that represented the United States before and after the purchase. We can analyze the effect of expansion that resulted from the Louisiana Purchase.

title: Critical Thinking
text:
Critical thinking involves labeling and identifying people, objects, and events based on their characteristics. Comparing is examining two or more events, people, places, or ideas to identify how they are the same. Contrasting is examining events, people, places, or ideas to see how they are different. Historians often compare and contrast historical events, people, places, and ideas. Historians do this to deepen their understanding and identify patterns.

Historians use different sources to compare and contrast. Historians also compare and contrast multiple perspectives of the same event. Being able to compare and contrast historical events also allows historians to compare and contrast past events to current events. This can deepen their understanding of history. It can also provide a more accurate view of history.

title: Chronological Thinking
text:
Time can be measured in many ways, using various tools. Historians use many tools to study the past. One of the easiest tools to measure the passage of time is a calendar. A calendar shows the days of the week and months of the year. It can help us track events in our lives and when they happened. Time can be represented in days, months, years, decades, and centuries. These words help us understand when things happened.

To determine historical context and organize their thinking, historians use timelines. A timeline is a list of events in chronological order, or in the order that they happened. A traditional timeline starts with the earliest event that is being studied. Traditional timelines are often represented horizontally and are read from left to right, but they can also be represented vertically.

Historians also use timelines that begin with the most recent event being studied and work their way backward. These are often referred to as backward timelines. Backward timelines are often represented vertically and are read from top to bottom, but can also be represented horizontally.

When historians use chronological thinking, they study the passage of time and label it. Many events in history can occur around the same time. The tools and items people used in the past become artifacts we can study. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technologies change over time. Artifacts help us understand how people’s lives have changed over time. Historians analyze artifacts and timelines to see how much things have changed throughout history. They examine patterns to understand how and why things happened. This allows them to provide context for an event or a person’s life. Historians also ask questions when examining sources to determine historical context, including:

Where did the source come from?

Who is the author?

Who created it?

When was it created?

Why was it created?

How was it created?

title: Changing the World
text:
One of the major themes of history that historians, archeologists, and other scholars study is how things change over time. They used artifacts, primary sources, and other pieces of evidence to study the way life has changed. People, families, communities, states, and countries experience many changes over time. The food people eat, the way people make a living, and the resources they use all change. Homes, transportation, and products change. Traditions, cultural customs, and beliefs also change.

For thousands of years, people relied on the natural resources in their environment to survive. They hunted, fished, and gathered food from their environment. They built shelters and homes from the available resources around them. Clothing, jewelry, and shoes were made from plant materials and animal furs and hides. They crafted tools from animal bones, stones, shells, and other natural resources. People began to create permanent settlements. They built cities, cultivated and harvested crops, and established trade networks.

Over time, many people began to explore areas of the world that were unknown to them. New forms of transportation and technology made travel easier. Explorers established extensive trade routes that spanned oceans and continents. The discovery of new resources led to more goods in markets. Goods became more readily available. People began to look for new ways to make people’s lives easier. They invented new forms of technology to make transportation, medicine, education, entertainment, and all areas of life safer, more affordable, and better. One thing that has changed greatly over time is the use of energy and its production.

Energy and people’s uses of energy have changed dramatically throughout history. Over time, sources of energy have changed. Thousands of years ago, people relied solely on the environment for energy. They used the sun and moon to find their way while they traveled. They used fire to warm their homes and cook their food. As people gained access to new resources, they began to search for new forms of energy. Scientific advancement has led to the forms of energy we now enjoy today.
