title: The Business of Energy
text:
Lighting the night created opportunities for entrepreneurs. An entrepreneur is a person who organizes and operates a business. Lighting the night created opportunities for many businesses.

Candles

Candlestick makers found opportunities to make more candles. Candle making was a long process of dipping a wick into liquid wax. The wax would harden. The candle would be dipped again and again. Candles got used up quickly. People needed many candles in a week to illuminate the night.

Oil

Edwin Drake drilled into the earth and discovered oil in 1859. Drake proved getting oil was possible. He sparked additional drilling. The nation’s fuel and energy source changed quickly. Oil has to be processed. With oil, we make products like kerosene, gasoline, and lamp oil. Drilling for oil opened many new opportunities for entrepreneurs.

Electricity

Electricity has been studied for centuries. Benjamin Franklin conducted experiments with lightning. Franklin’s experiments were published in 1751. Franklin developed the terms we use today in learning about electricity. Michael Faraday discovered that electricity could be produced by a motor. Faraday built a motor, generator, and transformers. Many of these things could create electricity safely. Thomas Edison invented the light bulb. Edison found a way to use electricity to create light inside a glass bulb. The light bulb was safer than candles because it had no open flame. Nikola Tesla designed the way to get electricity safely across long distances. Tesla teamed up with George Westinghouse to build the first electric power plant generator. Electricity was created by a generator. The generator was powered by moving water, burning coal or oil. Wires were put on towers from power plants. Wires strung from tower to tower moved electricity safely to homes and businesses. Homes were wired for electricity from the towers. Edison’s light bulbs were now paired with Tesla’s electric current. In 1893, the Chicago World's Fair became the first public place to be illuminated at night by electricity.

title: Energy Sources Evolve
text:
The Nuclear Age

During the 1960s, nuclear power plants were built. Nuclear energy is created when atoms are split in a reactor. The energy is then made into electricity. The electricity is then delivered through the wiring system created by Tesla and Westinghouse. Nuclear power can be dangerous if the nuclear reactor is damaged. Such damage would affect millions of people over thousands of miles.

Wind and Solar

Today, many entrepreneurs are using motors to create electricity. The motors are powered by the wind, using wind turbines. The wind turns propeller-like blades that spin the motor to create electricity. Energy from the sun is also being used to create electricity with solar panels. Private individuals can have wind and solar power on their land. The energy created can be used by the individual or in small family communities. There are laws and regulations in place to protect consumers when buying energy.

Fiber Optics

Thin strands of glass can be used to transport light pulses across distances. The strands are bundled together to look like wire. Fiber optics technology provides homes and businesses with internet, phone, and television services.

title: The History of Electricity at the White House
text:
The White House was originally constructed in 1792 to serve as the home of the president of the United States. The White House has gone through extensive changes during its over 200-year history. One of the greatest changes was the energy source that powered one of the most important buildings in the United States. The first sources of energy used in the White House were candles and eventually oil lamps. That all changed with the introduction of electricity in 1891.

Sept. 14, 1891: Electricity was first installed in the White House. At this time, many people were afraid that they would be electrocuted by the electric surge of energy running through their homes and businesses. President Benjamin Harrison and his wife, Caroline, were no exception. They feared that they would be electrocuted by this new source of energy and refused to touch the light switches themselves.

1926: During the presidency of Calvin Coolidge, the first electric refrigerator was installed in the White House.

1933: Air conditioning was installed in the private rooms of the White House during Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s first term in office.

1948-1952: The White House underwent a major renovation. New electrical systems were installed throughout, and updated fixtures and features were added.

1979: Energy production moved toward conservation with the installation of solar panels on the roof of the west wing. The solar panels were installed to heat the water in the White House staff cafeteria and dining area.

1993: Upon moving into the White House, President Bill Clinton attempted to conserve energy through various projects. Energy-efficient windows were installed; a new air conditioning system replaced the old, ineffective system; and all the light bulbs were replaced with energy-efficient bulbs.

2003: Toward the end of his first term in office, President George W. Bush installed the first solar electric system in the White House, which included 167 solar panels on the roof of the maintenance facility to power the building. Solar systems were also installed to heat the water for the White House pool and spa.

2008: The famous lantern on the White House portico was updated and new light-emitting diode (LED) lights were installed. LED light bulbs use 75 percent less energy and last 25 times longer than incandescent light bulbs.

2014: Solar panels were installed on the main building of the White House during President Barack Obama’s second term in office, providing 6.3 kilowatts of solar energy. This is enough energy to power a 2,000 square-foot home.

title: Conflict and Cooperation Over Time
text:
The history of the United States features many examples of conflict and cooperation. There have been conflicts in which people have fought over land, resources, ideas, and more. Just as often, there have been instances of cooperation in which people worked together to accomplish great things. Many conflicts have led to hardship and suffering but also to the creation of great things. Cooperation has created new movements and ideas while allowing people to accomplish things they could not have on their own.

In American history, conflict has occurred when groups of people find themselves with wants or needs in opposition to other groups. As communication between people and groups decreases, the likelihood of conflict increases. Sometimes, people have disagreed over who should be in charge or what kind of government to have. When this happens, we have seen events like the American Revolution. The colonists disagreed with the British government’s rule, so they fought to establish their own country. The violence of the American Revolution led to the creation of a new country. Other conflicts have been more destructive. The American Civil War, a conflict between the North and the South, was the deadliest American war in history.

Cooperation between people has been common throughout American history as well. People have worked together to overcome difficult times or accomplish new feats. The American Revolution is an example of conflict and cooperation. The 13 Colonies came together to resist British rule, even though they had different ideas about what the future country should look like. They identified a common cause and compromised with one another to accomplish their goal of independence. The creation of governments is a major example of cooperation. Each state has its own constitution, and each one was created by people working together to craft a document that met the desires of many different groups.

The presidency of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, also known as FDR, lasted from 1933 to 1945. It was an important time in American history. It featured serious domestic and international issues that created conflict and cooperation. Economic issues, social injustices, and wars all happened while FDR was president. These difficult times created conflict, but people met those conflicts with cooperation in an effort to solve them. The Great Depression saw massive unemployment. Many people lost their jobs and could not find new ones. World War II was the largest single military conflict in history. Along with these major historical events, social and racial conflicts occurred between people in the United States. As conflict created difficulties and struggles, people cooperated in efforts to solve these problems and create a better country and world.

title: Domestic Instability
text:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt faced domestic issues that caused conflict in the United States during his presidency. Domestic problems occur within a country, and the ones Roosevelt faced mainly affected Americans during this time. The biggest domestic challenge during his presidency was the Great Depression. This was a devastating economic collapse that created major domestic issues and led to conflicts and cooperation over potential solutions.

Beginning in the late 1920s, before Roosevelt became president, the U.S. economy suffered major problems. Many people lost massive amounts of money when the stock market crashed on Oct. 29, 1929. These economic problems led to people spending less money. With people spending less, companies began losing money and cutting jobs, putting many people out of work. With the unemployment rate climbing, fewer people had money to spend, which caused companies to make even less money and cut more jobs. These events led to the Great Depression.

By the time Roosevelt became president, around 13 million people were out of work, and banks were no longer operating. During the Great Depression, thousands of Americans rushed to take their money out of the banks. When the banks did not have enough money on hand to give to their customers, they had to close. The people who were unable to get their money back lost that money. Roosevelt was responsible for leading a country where one in every four workers had no job and many people had recently lost their life savings in the “run on the banks.”

Some of the major political conflicts Roosevelt faced came from his effort to solve the economic issues of the Great Depression. Labor organizations made up of worker groups had certain needs and demands. Business owners and other capitalists had different desires. Political opponents thought Roosevelt’s solutions were straying too far away from the ideals of capitalism. Others thought his solutions did not go far enough to help people who needed help most.

Other domestic issues impacted the country during Roosevelt’s presidency. The country was seeing more immigrants arriving from different countries. New groups of people arriving in the United States found a country struggling with racial and social issues. As president, Roosevelt was the leader of the entire country, and he was faced with uniting an increasingly diverse population. He faced conflict from different groups based on decisions he made in an effort to solve or help reduce racial and social issues. Various racial and social groups benefited from policies Roosevelt created, even as other groups suffered.

title: Ethnic and Racial Relations
text:
During the early 1900s, racial and ethnic conflict grew in the United States. During the early years of the century, immigration to the United States increased. More people from other countries were arriving, looking for new opportunities. These immigrants were changing the demographics of the country. In addition to these new citizens, there was a large Black population still struggling against mistreatment and a lack of equality and opportunities. As the 1900s progressed, conflict continued around racial and ethnic relations in the United States.

Roosevelt faced many of these ethnic and racial issues during his presidency. In an effort to identify and address issues specific to Black Americans, he created what was known as the “Black Cabinet.” A president’s cabinet is a group of people who advise the president and lead various governmental departments. Roosevelt’s “Black Cabinet” was a group of African American leaders who were brought together to advocate for the needs of Black people in the country. This group included important figures like Mary McLeod Bethune and other African American government officials.

When the government passed policies and made efforts to try and help people recover from the Great Depression, the “Black Cabinet” advocated for assistance to be given to the African American community as well. Before this, African Americans were often intentionally or accidentally excluded from benefiting from these programs. They also lacked access to educational opportunities and voting. In addition to these issues, segregation was still enforced in many parts of the country, which legally excluded African Americans from certain public and private places.

Through the efforts of Black Cabinet members, government employment programs that helped people get work were opened to African Americans when they might otherwise have been excluded. Despite some successes, Black Cabinet members faced conflict when attempting to accomplish their goals. Exclusion and inequality continued for African Americans in the United States.

Another racial and ethinc issue arose for Roosevelt during the days and months following the Japanese attack on American naval and air bases in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. This attack brought the United States into World War II. During the wave of immigration in the 1900s, thousands of Japanese citizens came to the United States, with many earning citizenship or having children who became citizens.

Although there was no evidence that people of Japanese descent were untrustworthy, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 3066, an order that forced the removal of people of Japanese descent from Pacific Coast states like California, Oregon, and Washington. It did not matter if they were born in Japan or the United States or whether they were citizens or not. The U.S. Army set up camps in remote western states like Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming. Over 120,000 people were held against their will in these camps.

title: Labor Relations
text:
The economic damage caused by the Great Depression hurt workers especially hard. Unemployment was common throughout the country. Roosevelt became president in 1933, when the unemployment rate was around 25 percent. One-fourth of all workers could not get a job. Companies were not making money and could not afford to hire more workers. Roosevelt faced major pressure to solve these issues. His priority in the first 100 days of his presidency was to help ease the labor problems in the United States.

President Roosevelt encountered many issues involving relations between workers and business owners during the early years of his presidency. This conflict made it difficult for the country to overcome the economic issues of the Great Depression. In 1935, Roosevelt and Senator Robert Wagner convinced Congress to pass the National Labor Relations Act. It provided workers with the ability to more easily create and join unions. This helped them fight for better pay and working conditions. With these improvements in their workplaces, productivity increased, which helped ease the economic difficulties of the time.

Roosevelt also created new government programs to help put people back to work. If companies could not hire new workers, he decided that the government could and should. He created government organizations like the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) and the Works Progress Administration (WPA) that hired people who were out of work. The CCC hired young, unmarried men for construction and conservation projects around the country. The WPA was a similar program that also included projects for professionals like writers, architects, musicians, and others. Many of the projects completed by the CCC and WPA still exist.

During the early 1900s, women and African Americans in the United States were often excluded from employment opportunities because of gender and race. Women were expected to stay home and take care of the household. African Americans were generally forced to accept hard jobs that offered low pay for long hours. Both groups were also usually paid less for doing the same jobs. These gender and racial standards were harder to overcome during the Great Depression when there were even fewer jobs.

Women and African Americans were the first people to lose their jobs and the last people to be considered for job openings. During World War II, this changed. As the country geared up for war, many men left the workforce and joined the armed forces. Because women and African Americans were generally excluded from military service, they instead filled the open jobs left by the men who went to war.

title: Military Conflicts
text:
During the early years of Franklin Roosevelt’s presidency, conflict began brewing in different parts of the world. In Europe, German leader Adolf Hitler began growing his power and influence while strengthening his military. European leaders became concerned that he might be preparing to start a war. Japan invaded China and began expanding into other parts of Asia. While this was happening, Roosevelt faced pressure in the United States to maintain an isolationist policy, remaining neutral in these growing conflicts. Most Americans wanted to stay out of international conflicts that did not directly involve them.

When Germany invaded Poland in 1939, the United States did not declare war like many European countries did. A conflict in Europe did not threaten Americans directly, and Roosevelt was not willing to enter a war that a majority of Americans did not support. American military leaders were also hesitant to get involved in the war. Even though he could not send troops to fight, Roosevelt found other ways to support American allies like England and France.

In 1940, he created the Lend-Lease Program, which provided weapons and other supplies to the British and other countries like the Soviet Union in their conflict against the increasingly successful German military. The program allowed the United States to lend and lease military supplies to the British military. In this way, Roosevelt could help America’s allies without sending troops to fight in a war the American people and military leaders did not support. This example of cooperation provided the Allied countries with around $50 billion worth of supplies and helped them keep Germany from conquering all of Europe.

While Roosevelt supported America’s allies in Europe, Japan continued to expand and conquer more territory in the Pacific. On Dec. 7, 1941, Japanese military forces launched a surprise attack on the U.S. Naval Base in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The base was home to the U.S. Pacific Fleet, a formidable force of battleships, aircraft carriers, and other naval ships. The Japanese Navy wanted to take out as much of the fleet as it could. The Japanese knew that if the American Navy continued to expand in the Pacific, Japan would eventually end up in conflict with the United States. The attack on Pearl Harbor was their attempt to win the fight before it began.

While they were able to damage or destroy many of the battleships, they did not completely destroy the fleet. The aircraft carriers were out to sea during the attack. The Japanese attack was not completely successful and had the additional consequence of uniting the American people. Before the attack, Americans generally wanted to stay out of the conflict. After the attack, they rallied together in the effort to win the war against Japan and its allies, Germany and Italy.

Fighting a war in two different regions of the world required Americans to sacrifice and collaborate. Immediately, men began volunteering for military service. The U.S. military needed people, and the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor motivated many people to enlist. As these men left for war, factories had to find new workers to replace them. The factories were needed to produce weapons, aircraft, and other supplies needed to fight a war. Women, African Americans, and members of other minority groups gained opportunities for work that they had been excluded from before. The Bracero Program is one example of an exception made to support the war effort.

Americans also supported the war in other ways. They purchased war bonds with money that went directly to the war effort. At the end of the war, they would get their money back. Purchasing a war bond showed optimism. War bonds would not be worth much if the Allies lost the war. The war effort required the use of vast amounts of resources. Americans were forced to ration the goods they used. Rubber, sugar, metal, and a variety of other things were needed to provide troops with food to eat and weapons to fight with. Using less food and donating supplies was a sacrifice Americans made to support the war effort.

By the end of the war, women and other minority groups were contributing to the military as well. Women joined auxiliary and volunteer corps, where they served as nurses and noncombat pilots, among other positions. While segregation was still enforced in the military, there were several military units composed of minorities. Tank and fighter squadrons made up of African American military members fought in the war. A unit of Japanese Americans served, even as their relatives were placed in internment camps during the war. Despite all the conflict both within the United States and internationally, World War II encouraged collaboration among Americans, even as they struggled against ideas of gender and racial roles in American society.

title: Immigration
text:
In the early 1900s, the United States saw a major growth in people moving to the country from other places. Not only did the total number of people coming into the country increase at this time, the immigration became more diverse. In the earliest years of the United States, immigration was dominated by western and northern Europeans. By the early 1900s, more southern and eastern Europeans began moving to the United States, as well as immigrants from countries in Latin America and Asia.

By the time Franklin Roosevelt became president, the United States had begun to restrict immigration, allowing fewer people to come to the United States to live. Despite this decrease, immigration created various points of conflict in the country, especially as the Great Depression and World War II brought on significant economic pressures. Beginning a new life in a new nation is not an easy thing to do. Immigrants encountered many difficulties, and conflicts arose as the country worked to incorporate these new and growing populations.

Some groups suffered direct consequences of Roosevelt’s immigration restrictions. Jewish people in Germany were persecuted and discriminated against by Adolf Hitler and the German government. Increased violence against Jewish people in Germany convinced thousands of German Jews to seek safety in the United States by immigrating. Most of these people were denied the ability to immigrate because of Roosevelt’s restrictive immigration policies.

Other groups that had immigrated in larger numbers before the limits on immigration struggled during the Roosevelt administration. With work difficult to come by, many people resented immigrants who were able to find jobs. Prejudice sprang up against immigrants from Asia and Latin American countries. Immigrant workers suffered abuse and violence at the hands of Americans who saw them as a threat to their own economic success during the Great Depression.

As difficult as it was to find a job during the Great Depression, it was equally difficult to find workers during World War II in the United States. As an example of cooperation between nations, the United States and Mexico created the Bracero Program in 1942. During the war, there was a severe lack of agricultural workers. For a country at war, growing food was essential. Although the United States maintained a restrictive immigration policy, the Bracero Program allowed Mexican workers to enter the United States on a short-term basis to work in the agricultural industry, filling the need for farm workers.

title: People Can Make a Difference
text:
When studying history, it can be easy to get caught up in the major historical actions and movements and think that they were destined to happen the way they did. It’s easy to believe individuals were simply swept along as these events occurred the way they were meant to. Likewise, it can feel like current events are so big that any one person or group of people has no power to change things. However, if we look closer, we can see many examples of people making a difference and changing the course of history.

People from all backgrounds, races, ethnicities, and genders have left their mark on history and made a difference in the world. They have done it with their intellectual abilities. They have done it with their physical skills. They have done it with their artistic gifts. They have influenced politics, science, athletics, and so much more. Everywhere we look in history, we can find individuals and groups who have made a difference in the world through their actions, ideas, or words. Some people had an impact on a larger scale, like their country or even the entire world. Many others influenced and improved their specific discipline or local community.

If we think carefully, anyone could come up with some examples of people who made a difference. There are many famous historical figures who might come to mind. Famous U.S. presidents, like George Washington or Abraham Lincoln, might be included. Both men made important contributions to making the United States the country it is today. Scientists like Albert Einstein are famous for making great strides in our understanding of the universe. Prominent athletes like Jackie Robinson made impacts that went far beyond fields and stadiums. Brave individuals like Amelia Earhart took on amazing challenges to show the world what was possible.

It can be easy to forget that many, many people throughout history have made a difference, even if we’ve never heard their names. The articles this week will share the stories of some important people and groups who made a difference in history and society. Some names will be more well-known than others. However, each one made a significant contribution to the world we live in today.

title: Week 29 Essential Question
text: How can people and groups make a difference in their communities, state, and the United States?

title: Katherine Johnson
text:
Katherine Johnson was born in 1918 in West Virginia. She displayed a natural ability with numbers and skipped ahead to high school several years early. After graduating from college with a degree in mathematics and French, she began teaching. In Virginia, where she was teaching, schools were still segregated, with white and Black students attending separate schools. As a Black woman, Johnson taught at an all-Black public school.

In 1952, Johnson decided on a career change and moved with her family to Newport News, Virginia, to work at the organization that would eventually be known as the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA. She used her natural talent and mathematics education to work on analyzing flight test and crash data. This experience made her the perfect person to work on the mission to send the first American into space. Her work with flight data gave her excellent training for calculating flight trajectories.

Her most famous contribution came when computers were completing the final calculations for the first manned flight. Astronaut John Glenn, aware of Johnson’s abilities, asked NASA to have her check the calculations by hand. When she confirmed they were accurate, John Glenn gave the go-ahead and became the first American to go into space. Johnson’s work was integral in making sure the mission was successful.

title: Jim Thorpe
text:
Jim Thorpe was born in Oklahoma in 1887 and was a member of the Sac and Fox Indian Nation. The tribe had been forced from their traditional home in the western Great Lakes region to Oklahoma. Thorpe’s athletic excellence was discovered during his time at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, a government school for American Indians. Hiking, hunting, roping, and his physically challenging childhood in Oklahoma prepared him to excel in the field of sports.

His abilities caught the attention of the school’s coach, Glenn “Pop” Warner, who recruited Thorpe to the track and field team. Thorpe eventually participated in just about every athletic event his school competed in, even ballroom dancing. The small school was able to compete with much larger colleges, partly due to Thorpe’s influence. It wasn’t until his athletic abilities earned him a spot on the 1912 United States Olympic team that the rest of the world would learn of his talent.

Jim Thorpe competed in two events: the pentathlon and the decathlon. Each of these events actually consists of multiple competitions. The pentathlon has five, while the decathlon has ten. Thorpe won both events and set Olympic records for time, distance, and points that would not be broken for decades. After the Olympics, Jim Thorpe competed as a professional football player, eventually serving as the first president of the National Football League (NFL) when it formed in 1920.

title: Ellen Ochoa
text:
Ellen Ochoa was born in California in 1958, where she grew up with an interest in math, science, and music. Her love of music almost led her to pursue it in her education. Instead, she chose science as her field of study and earned degrees in physics and engineering. She earned her PhD in electrical engineering at Stanford and decided that she wanted to follow in the footsteps of another famous woman, Sally Ride, and become an astronaut.

After graduation, Ochoa worked at Sandia National Laboratory in Albuquerque, New Mexico. She worked on optical systems that are designed to observe objects and analyze them, like specialized cameras. During her time at Sandia, she invented several new optical devices, which went on to improve NASA’s ability to collect optical data. This work and her brilliance in the fields of math, science, and computers led NASA to admit her as an astronaut in 1990.

Ellen Ochoa spent almost 1,000 hours in space as the first Hispanic female astronaut. After four missions to space, she continued to work at NASA, eventually serving as the director of the Johnson Space Center. She has earned many awards and accolades for her work. Today, she continues to advocate for space exploration and science education.

title: Norman Borlaug
text:
Norman Borlaug was born near Cresco, Iowa, in 1914 to a family of farmers. Growing up on a farm in a rural part of the country gave Borlaug a start in his career. He studied forestry at the University of Minnesota while working for the U.S. Forest Service. Following his work there, he returned to the University of Minnesota to earn a master's degree and a doctorate in plant pathology.

He used his knowledge and education to work on developing new wheat plants. He was able to develop a version of wheat that had several advantages over previous versions. His wheat was more resistant to disease, which meant that more of the crop would survive to produce food. His wheat also yielded more wheat per acre. By this time in the 1960s, it was obvious to him that his new wheat plant had a chance to help ease world hunger.

Borlaug traveled the world, sharing and spreading his new wheat plant. People in countries throughout South America, Africa, and Asia were able to plant this wheat, which provided them with more food. For his contribution to helping ease world hunger, Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. He continued in his work, identifying new dangers to wheat production worldwide and offering solutions until he died in 2009.

title: The Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASPS)
text:
During World War II, the United States struggled to find enough men to do all of the jobs needed to fight the war. Women were not allowed to serve as soldiers and sailors. By 1942, the U.S. military realized that if women could serve in noncombat positions, it would free up more men to go fight. To take advantage of this, a woman named Nancy Harkness Love created the Women’s Auxiliary Ferrying Squadron (WAFS) with 25 women. Their job was to fly airplanes from the factories where they were built to training bases in the U.S. This allowed the men who were doing this job to transfer and serve as combat pilots.

At that time, many people believed that women were not able to physically pilot military aircraft. The women of the WAFS began to disprove that belief. Eventually, the U.S. Army Air Corps allowed famous female pilot Jackie Cochran to create the Women’s Flying Training Detachment (WFTD) to provide flight training and practice to female pilots. In 1943, the WAFS and the WFTD merged into the Women Airforce Service Pilots, and the women who flew were known as WASPs. Over 1,000 women eventually served as WASPs, proving that women were capable pilots and could provide valuable contributions to the war effort.

title: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP)
text:
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) is a civil rights organization that was founded in 1909. The goal of the organization is to promote racial equality and ensure that laws guaranteeing equality are protected and enforced. In the early 1900s, racial discrimination and violence against minorities were widespread in the United States. The creation of the NAACP was a direct result of the race riot in Springfield, Illinois, the previous year.

The NAACP went to work, fighting racial inequality in the United States. NAACP members worked toward this goal in a variety of ways. They fought unjust laws in the court system. They peacefully protested inequality and brought attention to these issues. They worked with politicians, convincing them to pass civil rights legislation, and solved problems of racial inequality through legal processes. The NAACP had several important historical figures as founding members, including W.E.B. du Bois, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, and Jane Addams.

Founded in New York City, the NAACP had over 300 branches around the country by 1919. Through the 1900s, the NAACP helped win major civil rights battles. They fought to end segregation and were instrumental in legally ending the practice of segregated facilities and organizations. Many members faced violence for their actions. Despite this, the NAACP and its members contributed to many great strides the country took toward racial equality. The organization and its members continue these efforts today.

title: Fred Korematsu
text:
Fred Korematsu was 23 years old when Executive Order 9066 was signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Japanese Americans were to be incarcerated in guarded concentration camps. Korematsu refused to go. He was arrested and convicted for this action. Korematsu was forced to live at the Tanforan “Assembly Center” in California. This was a former horse racing track that was converted to housing for Japanese Americans. Korematsu and his family were then forced to move to Topaz, Utah.

Korematsu and others believed the incarcerations were unconstitutional. He appealed his case through the court system to the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. In 1944, the Supreme Court ruled that the incarceration of Japanese Americans during the war was justified as a “military necessity.”

In 1980, President Jimmy Carter appointed a special commission to review the facts of incarceration for Japanese Americans. This commission concluded the decision to forcibly relocate American citizens occurred because of prejudice, fear, and poor political leadership. It was discovered that evidence supporting freedom for Japanese Americans was not presented to the courts.

In 1983, Korematsu’s conviction was overturned. The government offered Korematsu a pardon. Korematsu responded that he was not interested in a pardon from the government. He believed the government should be seeking a pardon from him and the others who were wronged.

title: Immigrants
text:
The United States has a long history of immigration. People from around the world came to take advantage of the opportunities our country provided. Immigrant communities developed across the country. As people from other countries and cultures arrived in the United States, they contributed to the success of their immigrant communities, as well as to the country.

Immigrants have historically come to the U.S. for better opportunities in education and work. Many have successfully obtained a higher education or found success in a field of work they might not have had the opportunity to pursue in their home country.

Immigrant communities have also contributed to the growth of the country. During the late 1800s, immigrants from China, Ireland, and other countries were the main workers for the Transcontinental Railroad. This was the first railroad to cross the entire country. The completion of this railroad allowed goods and people to make the trip from coast to coast faster than ever, which improved the economy of the country.

American culture has been influenced by immigrants as well. Many musical composers and artists during the 1900s were immigrants or children of immigrants. Irving Berlin, born in Russia, wrote “God Bless America,” among many other well-known songs. Immigrants have shared their unique perspectives through song, dance, theater, art, music, movies, and more, all of which have influenced American culture.

title: César Chávez
text:
César Chávez was born in Arizona in 1927. His grandfather came to the United States from Mexico where his parents owned a small grocery store and ranch. Times were hard for his family. They lost their business and moved to California to find work. They became migrant farm workers. These types of workers travel from farm to farm, working in the fields. Chávez was only 11 years old at the time.

Life as a migrant farm worker was difficult. Living conditions were poor. Many people lived together in small, dirty shacks without clean water or electricity. Money was limited, and jobs were hard to find.

When he got older, Chávez began working for the rights of migrant workers. In 1962, he helped form the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA). This group later became United Farm Workers in 1966.

United Farm Workers (UFW) was a union (a group formed to protect workers' rights). It worked to get better pay and safer working conditions for migrant workers. Chávez’s motto was “Sí, se puede,” which means, "Yes, it can be done." The UFW organized migrant workers and took their demands to the people who owned large farms and ranches. Chávez organized strikes, or "huelgas," against owners if they refused to meet workers' demands. A strike is when workers refuse to work until they receive more money, better working conditions, or both. From 1965 to 1970, the UFW asked Americans to boycott, or refuse to buy, California lettuce and grapes until growers started treating the workers better. Chávez said, "We are not slaves and we are not animals. And we are not alone."

César Chávez practiced civic virtues by working to improve conditions for thousands of migrant workers throughout the United States. He made great progress, and the fight for better treatment of migrant workers continues today.

title: Larry Itliong
text:
Farmers in America have always hired immigrants to work for them. During and after World War II, immigrants came to the west coast of the United States looking for jobs. Many found jobs but were treated badly. Living conditions were poor, and pay was low.

During the 1960s, farm workers demanded better treatment. One was a Filipino named Larry Itliong. He was one of the first to make a plan for forcing farm owners to change their ways. Itliong led the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee (AWOC). He was such a good leader that he was asked by union leaders to go to Delano, California, to go on strike for better pay. A strike is when workers refuse to work until their demands are met.

There were two main groups of farm workers in Delano: the Filipinos and the Mexicans. At first, the Mexican workers ignored the strike. That was good news for the farm owners. The Mexicans kept working, so they didn’t need the Filipinos. The strike was no good. Seeking support, Larry Itliong asked César Chávez, leader of the Mexican workers and the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA), to join the strike. The Filipinos and Mexicans joined together and refused to work until the owners promised to pay them more. AWOC and NFWA merged together to form the United Farm Workers (UFW). The strike lasted for five years, and although Chávez gained national attention for the strike, Itliong faded into the background and was largely forgotten.

Today, we remember him as someone who was hardworking, brave, and a good leader. His contributions to the Delano Grape Strike helped change the lives of thousands of agricultural workers.

title: Milton Hershey
text:
Milton Hershey first discovered that he had a passion for making candy at the age of 14 in 1872. He apprenticed under a master confectioner for four years in Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

In 1876, when he was just 18 years old, Hershey set out on his own and opened his first candy business in Philadelphia. Unfortunately, despite his training and passion, this first business venture ended in bankruptcy.

Six years later in 1882, Hershey traveled to Denver, Colorado, and learned how to make caramels using milk. With this recipe, he eventually returned to his hometown and started the Lancaster Caramel Company.

In 1893, Hershey attended the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, Illinois. There, people from all over the world came together to exhibit new inventions, art, food, machines, and more. Hershey was particularly interested in machinery from Germany that was used for manufacturing chocolate. Hershey decided to purchase the equipment and then began experimenting with recipes to find a good, affordable recipe for milk chocolate.

By 1900, Hershey had created a chocolate recipe he knew he could sell. He sold the Lancaster Caramel Company and used the money to build a factory that could mass-produce milk chocolate candy. Before this, milk chocolate was considered a luxury, but with Hershey’s recipe and factory, he made it affordable for the common person.

Milton Hershey never forgot the difficult years of his youth. He and his wife, Kitty, never had children of their own, so they founded the Milton Hershey School. The school offered free housing, clothing, meals, medical and dental care, and recreational activities. They gave millions of dollars to this and to many other worthy causes over the years.

title: Booker T. Washington
text:
Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia in 1856. He learned how to read in his spare time. At age 16, he walked 500 miles to Hampton Normal Agricultural Institute in Virginia and convinced the headmaster to let him work as a janitor to help pay his tuition. Washington worked and studied diligently to become an educator and leader. The president of the Hampton Institute recommended that the school hire Washington to be a teacher.

Then, around 1881, Washington was offered the opportunity to be the principal of a new school for African Americans: The Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Tuskegee, Alabama. Washington accepted the role, where he continued to work until the day he died. Washington began teaching students at the institute before any campus buildings were even built. The construction of the first buildings was done by Washington and his students. The school continued to grow.

He designed the class courses and hired a staff of skilled educators, including the famous George Washington Carver, who did important work in botany and farming technology. Booker T. Washington believed education was a key to advancement for African Americans in the South. He said, “I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome.”

title: Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton
text:
Women didn’t always have the equal rights they enjoy today. Two women that played a major role in getting equal rights for women were Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton was born in Johnstown, New York, in 1815. She got the best education for females at that time. After meeting Lucretia Mott, the leading American female abolitionist, Stanton began studying women’s rights. In 1848, Stanton and several others organized the world’s first women’s rights convention.

Susan B. Anthony grew up in a politically active family. She began the fight for women’s rights while speaking out against alcohol. She realized no one would take women seriously in politics if they couldn’t even vote. She began working to convince others to support women’s right to vote.

In 1851, Elizabeth Cady Stanton met Susan B. Anthony. The two shared a common dedication to women’s freedom from unfair rules. Together, Stanton and Anthony formed the National Women’s Loyal League. In 1869, they started the National Woman Suffrage Association. Their work helped bring about the 19th Amendment, which wasn’t passed until many years after their deaths. In 1872, Anthony voted in the presidential election illegally. She was arrested and fined $100.

Stanton continued her work on behalf of women’s suffrage until her death in 1902. When Anthony died in 1906, women still could not vote. It wasn’t until 1920 that the 19th Amendment was passed, giving women the right to vote. In recognition of Anthony’s hard work, the United States Treasury Department put Susan B. Anthony’s portrait on one-dollar coins in 1979, making her the first woman to be honored in such a way.

title: Harvey Milk
text:
Harvey Milk was born in New York in 1930 to Jewish parents on Long Island. Milk grew up in a time when members of the LGBTQ+ community were persecuted and didn’t have many rights. Because of this, Milk spent most of his early life concealing his sexual orientation. He was known to be a charismatic class clown and was well-liked by his peers and friends.

In the 1960s, Milk made his way to San Francisco, where he became immersed in the gay community there. In the 1970s, Milk opened a small camera shop in the heart of San Francisco’s gay community. Milk disliked the taxes being imposed on small business owners, so he ran for a seat on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1973 to try and make positive changes for the community.

After several years of trying and failing to win a seat on the board, Milk was finally elected in 1977. Milk was one of the first openly gay elected officials in the United States. He worked tirelessly to fight for the rights of all people in San Francisco. Milk fought against state legislation that prevented gay men and lesbians from teaching in California schools. He spoke out against discrimination and wanted laws that would protect housing and child care for all groups of people.

In 1978, Milk was assassinated for being gay and being a supporter of gay rights. Harvey was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009 more than 30 years after his death.

title: Eleanor Roosevelt
text:
Anna Eleanor Roosevelt was born on Oct. 11, 1884, in New York. Even though her parents were very rich, she had a pretty unhappy childhood. Roosevelt was shy and very awkward when she was younger. Sadly, both her mother and father died while she was still a child.

After her mother died, Eleanor was sent to live with her grandmother. Roosevelt was educated by private tutors growing up. When she was 15 years old, she went to a boarding school in England. A boarding school is a school that you live at during the school year. The school helped Roosevelt to grow into a strong, confident, and caring woman. She returned to New York City at age 18, where she became actively involved in social reform. In 1905, she married Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who was her fifth cousin. That means they weren’t closely related at all. (You probably don’t even know who your fifth cousins are.) Franklin and Eleanor had six children. Franklin went on to become the president of the United States in 1933, and Eleanor became the first lady of the United States.

Eleanor Roosevelt used her place in society to do good for people in need. She taught at a private school for girls, and she co-founded a nonprofit furniture factory in Hyde Park, New York. She also worked hard for human rights for all people. In 1946, Roosevelt was named chairwoman for the United Nations Commission on Human Rights.

Roosevelt became known throughout the world as a person who understood and wanted to help ordinary people. She was even called “First Lady of the World” because she helped people in every country. Eleanor Roosevelt was a woman who brought people together and encouraged them to make their dreams come true.

title: Zitkala-Sa
text:
Zitkala-Sa (Red Bird) was born into the Yankton Dakota Sioux tribe on the Yankton Indian Reservation in South Dakota. While she was still a child, Quaker missionaries visited the reservation and took Zitkala-Sa and several other children to be educated at White’s Indiana Manual Labor Institute. Zitkala-sa was pleased to learn how to read and write and play the violin, but her education came at a great price. Her name was changed to Gertrude Simmons, she was required to pray as a Quaker, and she was forced to cut her long hair, all of which were intended to strip her of her heritage and make her conform to the standards of white society.

By the time she returned to live with her mother on the reservation, she was 12 years old. However, her time at the institute had changed her so much that she no longer felt she fit in with her own people anymore. Three years later, when she was 15, she returned to the institute, hoping to further her education.

In 1899, she took a job as a music teacher at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania. To recruit more students for the school, Zitkala-Sa was sent back to her home on the reservation. To her dismay, she found her home and her people in poverty, and white people had encroached onto reservation lands.

Zitkala-Sa decided to speak out against the conditions her people were living in. She wrote articles and spoke out to dispel false rumors and stereotypes about her people. Many white people believed that American Indians should be assimilated into white society. This meant that they wanted American Indians to forsake their way of life and live, dress, talk, eat, learn, and worship like white people did.

Zitkala-Sa wrote articles about the loss of identity that American Indian children experienced by going to boarding schools and accomplished many things for American Indians over the course of her life. She collaborated with a professor from Brigham Young University to write the first-ever American Indian opera. She lectured all across the country about preserving American Indian heritage and identity. She became very politically active and helped establish multiple foundations for American Indian rights and women’s rights. She advocated for giving American citizenship and the right to vote to American Indians. Her work helped lead to the government passing the 1924 Indian Citizenship Act, which granted citizenship to American Indians and the right to vote in the United States. Her work also helped lead to the passage of the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which gave American Indian nations more power to govern themselves.

Until her death in 1936, Zitkala-Sa continued to work hard to improve education, healthcare, legal rights, and the preservation of culture and identity for American Indians across the nation.

title: Symbols and Landmarks
text:
The United States is rich with national landmarks and symbols. A landmark is an object or feature that is easily recognized that identifies a place. For example, the White House is a landmark of Washington, D.C. A symbol is a visual representation of important ideas, beliefs, traditions, and events, such as the Great Seal of the United States. Each symbol and landmark represents pivotal moments in U.S. history.

Over time, these symbols have taken on new meanings. They have changed to reflect the climate of American society. However, many of our important symbols continue to represent the ideas of freedom, democracy, independence, and citizens’ rights. These symbols do not belong to one person. They belong to all Americans and are on display for visitors to view.

The United States has many well-known and widely recognized American symbols. These include the U.S. Capitol Building, the national anthem, the Washington Monument, the Statue of Liberty, Mount Rushmore, the Great Seal of the United States, the White House, the Liberty Bell, and Independence Hall. Each symbol has a unique history and an important place in American culture.

title: U.S. Capitol Building
text:
On Sept. 18, 1793, a great ceremony was held in which George Washington laid the cornerstone of a very important building. This occasion marked the beginning of the construction of the United States Capitol Building.

Located in Washington, D.C., the Capitol Building looks very similar to the White House. However, it is a completely different building. Construction on the Capitol began in 1793, and it wasn’t officially completed until 1826.

The U.S. Congress met at the Capitol Building for the first time in 1800, even though it was still under construction at the time. Today, the Capitol is where our national government’s Senate and House of Representatives meet to discuss our nation’s laws and policies and work to make our country what it is today. With expansions and additions to the building since 1826, the Capitol Building now has over 600 rooms and covers over one million square feet of ground.

The U.S. Capitol is one of the most important buildings in the world. It has been home to the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives for almost two centuries. Since the cornerstone was first laid, it has been built, burned, rebuilt, remodeled, expanded, and restored. In a way, the Capitol’s survival reflects the determination and resilience of the American people. The Capitol is now a monument to the American people and our government.

title: National Anthem
text:
A national anthem is a song that represents a country and its values. It often tells a story about an event in the country's history. It often honors the courage of those who helped create the country or praises those who have protected the country in war. The national anthem of the United States is "The Star-Spangled Banner." It was written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812.

Key never intended to write the national anthem. He wasn't a poet, musician, or author by profession. However, his powerful words are a reminder of the strength and perseverance of the people of the United States. When the War of 1812 began, Key lived in Washington, D.C., and worked as a lawyer. He strongly opposed U.S. involvement in the war.

From the ship Tonnant, Key witnessed the bombardment of Fort McHenry. He feared the British would capture the important military post. The British attacked the fort and the American soldiers inside with heavy cannon fire for 25 hours. Key watched the battle and was convinced that the Americans would surrender the fort.

On the morning of Sept. 14, 1814, Key was amazed to see the American flag still flying over the fort. Key was inspired by the events he witnessed. Before he returned to shore, he composed several verses of a poem on the back of a letter he carried with him. He titled his poem “Defense of Fort M’Henry.” Key gave the poem to his brother-in-law, Joseph Nicholson, who was a commander of militia at Fort McHenry. Nicholson reprinted the poem and distributed it to the soldiers. Within weeks, the poem was featured in newspapers across the country and inspired American patriotism.

Key died in 1843, but his memory lives on. Statues and monuments were erected in his honor in towns all over the United States. His famous words were set to the tune “To Anacreon in Heaven,” and the poem was renamed “The Star-Spangled Banner.” In 1931, the song officially became the national anthem of the United States.

title: Washington Monument
text:
Many statues have been built in the United States to honor George Washington. However, the Washington Monument, in Washington, D.C., is perhaps the most well-known. The American people loved and revered George Washington during his lifetime. Some people wanted to build a monument to honor his service to our country in both the military and government. However, work didn’t begin on a monument until 47 years after his death. In 1836, a committee was formed, and a competition was held to choose a design for the monument. It wasn’t until 1848 that a design was chosen and the cornerstone for the monument was finally laid.

The Washington Monument took 36 years to complete because money to pay for it ran out and the Civil War disrupted its construction. Today, the point where construction was interrupted can be seen by the change of color of the stone in the obelisk. Completed in 1884, the Washington Monument stands at 555 feet, 5 1/8 inches tall, making it the tallest building in the world at the time.

Today, the Washington Monument, like its namesake, stands in no one’s shadow. It stands as a reminder of our country’s first president. Washington’s wise leadership and fierce devotion to the United States forever set the standard for all the presidents who followed him.

title: Statue of Liberty
text:
The Statue of Liberty has stood in New York Harbor since 1886. It has been a symbol of hope and peace for millions of new Americans. The Statue of Liberty was a gift of friendship from the people of France to the United States. It was created to honor American freedom and democracy. Edouard de Laboulaye, a French politician, came up with the idea for the statue. French sculptor Auguste Bartholdi was fascinated with the idea and agreed to design the statue. He traveled to the United States to gain support for the statue and determine where it would be located. He decided that the best place for the statue would be Bedloe’s Island, located in New York Harbor.

Upon his return to France, Bartholdi hired structural engineer Gustave Eiffel, the designer of the Eiffel Tower. Bartholdi wanted Eiffel to help him create the immense statue. The two men finished the project in Paris. It was officially given to the American people there on July 4, 1884. The statue was then broken into 350 separate pieces and shipped across the ocean to America in 214 crates.

The United States was excited about the statue, but there was a problem. There weren't enough funds available to create a pedestal, or base, for the statue to stand on. Joseph Pulitzer, a famous newspaper owner in New York City, published an article in his newspaper. It encouraged Americans to donate funds for the project. People from all over the country wanted to help, and they donated the necessary funds to complete the project. The Statue of Liberty was assembled on Bedloe’s Island and was officially dedicated on Oct. 28, 1886.

Between 1892 and 1924, about 22 million immigrants entered the United States on ships landing in New York Harbor. Each of these immigrants was greeted by the Statue of Liberty. The statue soon became a symbol of freedom, not just for new immigrants, but for all Americans. Details on the statue serve as symbols of freedom. Lady Liberty holds a stone tablet in one hand inscribed with the date of American independence from Great Britain: July 4, 1776. In her other hand, she holds a torch to light a path to freedom.

title: The Great Seal of the United States
text:
The Great Seal of the United States was designed by Secretary of the Continental Congress Charles Thomson. The seal was approved in 1782 and is a symbol of freedom.

The central figure of the Great Seal is the bald eagle. The bald eagle holds several items in its beak and talons that symbolize American beliefs. In its beak, the bald eagle holds a ribbon. The ribbon has the saying “E pluribus unum,” which means, "From many, one." It serves as a reminder that the United States is a unified country.

In one of the eagle’s talons is an olive branch that contains 13 olives and 13 leaves. This symbolizes America's willingness to seek peace within the country and internationally. In the other talon, the bald eagle grasps a bundle of 13 arrows. This demonstrates that the United States will defend liberty and freedom when necessary.

The eagle’s head is turned in the same direction as the olive branch to show that the United States will always look for a peaceful solution to conflicts. On the Great Seal, there is also a shield with 13 stripes. Above the eagle is a cloud with 13 stars. The number 13 was used in all of these items to represent the original 13 colonies at the time the Great Seal was created.

title: The White House
text:
The White House is the home of the president of the United States. It is located at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. The Oval Office, where the president conducts meetings and some business, is in the White House. George Washington chose the site for the White House in 1791. Even though he chose the site for the building, Washington never actually lived in the White House. It took eight years to build, and John Adams and his wife, Abigail, were the first to move into it in 1800.

In 1812, a war broke out between the United States and England. British soldiers marched on Washington, D.C. They set fire to the White House in 1814. It had to be rebuilt, and several U.S. presidents have made additions and renovations to the White House over the years.

Every U.S. president since John Adams has lived in the White House during their presidency. It is more than just the president’s house, however. The White House is used to entertain leaders and special guests from the U.S. and foreign countries. Special parties and events are hosted on the grounds. It is also a museum of American history. You can even take tours of parts of the White House. Inside the house and on the grounds, there are six levels, 132 rooms, a single-lane bowling alley, a movie theater, a swimming pool, a tennis court, a running track, and more.

The White House has become an important symbol of America and our government. Some people even refer to the executive branch of our government as “The White House.”

title: The Liberty Bell
text:
Located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the Liberty Bell serves as a symbol of American independence. The original Liberty Bell was known as the State House Bell. It was created by the Whitechapel Foundry of London, England, in 1751. The Pennsylvania Assembly ordered the bell to commemorate the 50th anniversary of William Penn’s Charter of Privileges. This charter served as Pennsylvania’s first constitution. The bell was inscribed with a verse from the Bible. It reads, "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof."

When the bell arrived in Philadelphia, it was placed in the Pennsylvania State House. The Pennsylvania State House is now known as Liberty Hall. When the Pennsylvania Assembly tested the bell, it cracked and required immediate repair. Philadelphia blacksmiths John Pass and John Stow melted down the original bell to create a new one. At first, the bell did not serve as a symbol of liberty and independence. It was used to signal meetings and call the citizens of Philadelphia together for important announcements. Benjamin Franklin mentioned the bell in a letter to a friend. Franklin said, “Adieu, the Bell rings, and I must go among the Grave ones and talk Politicks."

Today, the most noticeable feature of the bell is the large crack located on the front. Historians are unsure when the crack first appeared in the recast bell, but it is believed that the bell cracked after years of heavy use. In 1846, metal workers repaired the bell by widening the existing crack to prevent it from spreading as well as to restore the bell’s tone. However, the repair was unsuccessful, and a second, smaller crack developed shortly after. Because of this, the bell was damaged beyond repair and never rang again.

The Liberty Bell was not given its current name until 1835. The inscription inspired many citizens to fight for liberty and protect the rights of all people prior to the Civil War. Abolitionists, people who disagreed with and spoke out against slavery, adopted the Liberty Bell as a symbol of their movement. In the late 1800s, the Liberty Bell toured the United States. Many people visited towns and cities near their homes to get a glimpse of the famous bell. The Liberty Bell continues to serve as a reminder of independence and freedom for all.

title: Crazy Horse
text:
Crazy Horse, also known as Tasunke Witko, was an Oglala Sioux chief born in what is now South Dakota around 1842. By the time he was a teenager, Crazy Horse was a skilled and well-known warrior among the Lakota people. As settlers continued to move west, the lives of American Indians, including Crazy Horse, drastically changed.

During the 1860s, Crazy Horse participated in several battles against the U.S. Army to deter pioneers from settling on American Indian lands. These conflicts ended with the signing of the Second Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868. This treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation, which included the Black Hills of South Dakota. Crazy Horse and his people lived in the Black Hills, but they did not trust the terms of the treaty.

In 1874, gold was discovered in the Black Hills. Gold seekers traveled through Sioux lands and began prospecting for gold. Sioux leaders, including Crazy Horse, were angry at the U.S. government for violating the Second Treaty of Laramie. From 1876-1877, Crazy Horse fought many battles during the Great Sioux War. On June 25, 1876, Crazy Horse and his warriors, along with members of the Arapaho, Lakota, Cheyenne, and Hunkpapa bands, defeated U.S. Army forces under the command of General George Armstrong Custer.

In January 1877, Crazy Horse fought his last major battle at Wolf Mountain in the Montana territory. Chief Crazy Horse and hundreds of his followers surrendered at the Red Cloud Agency near Fort Robinson, Nebraska. On Sept. 5, 1877, as Crazy Horse was being led into a jail cell, he was killed by a soldier.

In 1939, Oglala Lakota chief Henry Standing Bear asked Korczak Ziolkowski, a sculptor who worked on Mount Rushmore, to create a monument to Crazy Horse in the Black Hills. Construction began in 1948. Ziolkowski worked on the project until his death in 1982. Although the monument remains unfinished, Ziolkowski’s family has continued to raise funds and work on its construction. When completed, the monument will depict Crazy Horse on horseback. It will stand at over 563 feet high and 641 feet long!

title: Independence Hall
text:
Many historians consider Independence Hall the “birthplace of the United States.” Independence Hall is located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Independence Hall was originally called the Pennsylvania State House and was built in 1732 to house Pennsylvania’s colonial government.

In 1775, the Pennsylvania legislature loaned the Assembly Room of the Pennsylvania State House to members of the Second Continental Congress. Delegates continued to meet at the Pennsylvania State House during the American Revolution. The Constitutional Convention was also held in the Assembly Room of the Pennsylvania State House from May to September 1787. Many of the nation’s most important documents were drafted, presented, and ratified in the Assembly Room. These documents included the Olive Branch Petition, the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, the Bill of Rights, and the Constitution.

The Pennsylvania State House made a transition over the years from a government building to a national landmark. The Assembly Room was first referred to as the “hall of Independence” in 1824, and many years later, the entire building came to be known as “Independence Hall.” Independence Hall also housed the Liberty Bell for over 200 years.

Today, Independence Hall attracts thousands of visitors each year and serves as a symbol of American independence and government.

title: Celebrations and Remembrance in the United States
text:
How can someone learn about a country’s history? One way is to learn about its patriotic holidays and celebrations. Celebrations are when people mark or remember certain events, often with parties or special traditions. Celebrations also highlight people, events, or ideas that are important to a culture. They help connect individuals to their culture wherever they are in the world. Celebrations help to bring people in a community together. This creates a sense of belonging for the members of the community.

The United States has identified days of the year that have special meaning to people who contributed to the history of the country. The government recognizes certain days of celebration. Some of the days honor people who have held public office, served in the military, died in military service, or contributed to building the nation. Each of these days is a time to remember and reflect on the work of many, as America strives to be a country of freedom and liberty.

title: Week 31 Essential Question

title: Independence Day
text:
Independence Day is an entirely American holiday that commemorates one of the most important events in the nation’s history: the adoption of the Declaration of Independence. In the summer of 1776, representatives of the American colonies met to discuss issues that they had with King George III and the British Parliament. After many attempts to compromise with the king, the Continental Congress voted to declare independence from England and form their own country.

A committee of five delegates drafted a document listing the grievances, or issues, they had with the British government. The delegates officially adopted this document, called the Declaration of Independence, on July 4, 1776. The Declaration of Independence served as the foundation for other government documents, including the United States Constitution. Philadelphians had an unofficial celebration of the first Independence Day on the one-year anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration of Independence.

Observing Independence Day became a common holiday in the United States following the War of 1812. In 1870, Congress passed a law designating July 4th as Independence Day. From the very beginning, people celebrated Independence Day by gathering together, holding parades, and celebrating independence. Today, fireworks, American flags, and festivals fill towns across the country to celebrate Independence Day.

title: Veterans Day
text:
When World War I ended, many countries who were involved in the war, including the United States, looked for ways to honor the men and women who served in the armed forces. In 1919, President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed that Nov. 11 would be designated Armistice Day to honor the veterans of World War I. In 1938, Armistice Day officially became a national holiday in the United States.

Unfortunately, the United States has been in more wars since then, including World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, and others. Following World War II, Congress changed the name of the holiday to Veterans Day. This is to honor all veterans of all wars. Americans continue to fight in wars to help other countries and to preserve the rights and freedoms of American citizens. Americans remember and honor all veterans of the armed forces, including the United States Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, and Coast Guard, every year on Veterans Day.

title: Labor Day
text:
Labor Day sounds like a day when everyone would go to work, but it actually means quite the opposite. Labor Day is a holiday that was created for working people to take a day off. Historians are not certain who actually came up with the idea for Labor Day. Some believe that it was Peter McGuire. He was the first secretary of the American Federation of Labor. Others say the idea belonged to Matthew Maguire. He was the secretary of the Central Labor Union.

New York’s Central Labor Union chose to make the idea a reality by organizing the first Labor Day on Sept. 5, 1882, in New York City. The holiday was created to honor American workers who used their strength and skills to make life better for the entire country. The first Labor Day was celebrated with a parade, speeches, and a picnic for workers and their families. In 1894, Labor Day became a national holiday. People now celebrate it on the first Monday in September to honor workers.

title: Memorial Day
text:
Memorial Day is observed each year on the last Monday in May. This day is set aside to honor the nation's armed services personnel who were killed in wartime. Originally called Decoration Day, the first national Memorial Day celebration was observed on May 30, 1868, to honor Union and Confederate soldiers who died during the Civil War. The celebration took place at Arlington National Cemetery where many Civil War soldiers are buried. Observers decorated the graves of the soldiers with flowers, flags, and other mementos to honor their sacrifice.

By the end of the 1800s, the name of this celebration changed from Decoration Day to Memorial Day. Many states and towns held ceremonies and parades to honor service members who fought at home and abroad. In 1971, Congress declared that Memorial Day would be a national holiday and would be celebrated on the last Monday of May. Today, Memorial Day is traditionally a day of parades, ceremonies, and speeches.

title: Presidents' Day
text:
Presidents’ Day is a holiday that commemorates the hard work and dedication of U.S. presidents. Presidents’ Day is celebrated between Abraham Lincoln and George Washington’s birthdays. This holiday was originally intended to celebrate Washington’s life and accomplishments. Washington’s birthday was celebrated in the United States even while he was still alive. In January 1878, a bill was signed into law to make Washington’s birthday a national holiday.

In 1968, Congress passed the Uniform Monday Holiday Act, which moved the celebration and national observance of Washington's birthday to the third Monday of February. In the 1980s, the name of the holiday shifted to Presidents’ Day to include other U.S. presidents, including Abraham Lincoln, whose birthday was Feb. 12. Today, people across the United States celebrate Presidents’ Day with parades, festivals, and reading of George Washington’s “Farewell Address.”

title: Thanksgiving
text:
One of the oldest holidays that is still celebrated in the United States is Thanksgiving. The first Thanksgiving was celebrated by the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony in the fall of 1621. During the Pilgrims’ first winter in Plymouth, nearly half of the original 102 colonists died. By the spring of 1621, only five adult women, 35 men, and 17 children (ages five to 17) remained. To avoid starvation the next winter, the Pilgrims made a treaty with the Wampanoag for land and food. Part of the treaty included learning about farming from their new neighbors.

The Wampanoag taught and advised the colonists. The Pilgrims knew how to work hard and were good students. They followed the advice of the Wampanoag. This led to a good harvest and preparation for the coming winter. For three days, the Pilgrims and Wampanoag feasted to celebrate and give thanks for their plentiful harvest.

Thanksgiving was observed throughout areas of New England for many years following the first Thanksgiving celebration at Plymouth. In 1789, President George Washington declared that Americans should observe a day of thanks on Thursday, Nov. 26, but Thanksgiving only continued to be observed annually in New England.

Thanksgiving became a national holiday through the efforts of Sarah Josepha Hale. Hale was the editor of a magazine in Boston, Massachusetts. In 1827, she began to publish articles about the need for a national day of thanksgiving. She wrote letters to state governors, national senators, and presidents for 36 years explaining the need for a national day of thanksgiving. After 36 years, President Abraham Lincoln granted Hale’s wish. He proclaimed that Thanksgiving Day would be nationally observed on the fourth Thursday of November every year.

Today, Thanksgiving is observed by millions of Americans. People gather together with family and friends to reflect upon the things they are thankful for.

title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
text:
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born on Jan. 15, 1929. In 1954, he became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. There, he began organizing and working for civil rights. King soon became recognized nationally as a leader of the Civil Rights Movement. He continued his efforts for equality by writing numerous articles and leading peaceful protests and marches. King gave countless speeches, including his famous “I Have a Dream” speech during the historic March on Washington in 1963. On Oct. 14, 1964, King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. On April 4, 1968, he was in Memphis, Tennessee, preparing to lead another protest when he was assassinated.

On Nov. 2, 1983, President Ronald Reagan signed Public Law 98–144. This bill created a national holiday to honor King’s memory and legacy. Martin Luther King Jr. Day is observed on the third Monday of January each year to commemorate his birthday. The first observance of the holiday took place on Jan. 20, 1986.
