title: Tools to Help You Take Your First Steps in Your Inquiry Journey
text:
Your Observations, Feelings, and Thoughts

Nothing is more powerful than what you see or feel. You can start your inquiry journey by reflecting on your own observations, feelings, and thoughts. Look around your home, school, or neighborhood. Ask yourself questions to start your inquiry. What are you passionate about? When you are passionate about something, you are very interested in it and connected to it. Are you an animal lover, or do you care a lot about the environment? Is there a problem you see but nobody else does?

Local News

It's important to be aware of events that are happening in your community. Local news covers important stories that affect where you live. Local news outlets, such as newspapers and television programs, discuss positive and negative events that occur in your community. Talking to your family and teachers about the local news can help you understand what is happening and determine problems that you can help solve.

Internet Research

Conducting a simple search on the internet can help you see problems beyond your community. This includes the state, national, and international level. Talk to your family and teachers about safe ways to search the internet in order to find credible information.

Library of Congress

Did you know our country has its own library? It is called the Library of Congress. The Library of Congress has various collections of newspapers, books, documents, photographs, music, and many other types of sources created in our nation’s history. Many of their collections are available on the internet and are readily accessible to researchers of all ages.

Practice will always make perfect when it comes to inquiry. Looking at historical events or ideas helps you understand how you can use inquiry to help your community today.

title: Analyzing Primary Sources
text:
Analyzing primary sources helps us understand events, people, and places during a specific time period. California changed dramatically after gold was discovered there in 1848. Thousands of people flocked to California, hoping to strike it rich. Some were successful, but many people did not achieve the success they desired. Examine the primary sources from the California Gold Rush, then answer the analysis questions.

The following source is an excerpt from “Captain Sutter’s Account of the First Discovery of the Gold, 1854.” Captain John Sutter was a German immigrant who settled in California in 1838. Gold was discovered at his lumber mill in 1848, which prompted the start of the California Gold Rush.

“You should know that the mere appearance of Mr. Marshall at that moment in the Fort was quite enough to surprise me, as he had but two days before left the place to make some alterations in a mill for sawing pine planks, which he had just run up for me, some miles higher up the Americanos. When he had recovered himself a little, he told me that, however great my surprise might be at his unexpected reappearance, it would be much greater when I heard the intelligence he had come to bring me. ‘Intelligence,’ he added, ‘which if properly profited by, would put both of us in possession of unheard-of-wealth; millions and millions of dollars, in fact.’

I frankly own, when I heard this that I thought something had touched Marshall’s brain when suddenly all my misgivings were put at an end by his flinging on the table a handful of scales of pure virgin gold. I was fairly thunderstruck and asked him to explain what all this meant.…

We agreed not to mention the circumstance to anyone and arranged to set off early the next day for the mill. On our arrival, just before sundown, we poked the sand about in various places, and before long succeeded in collecting between us more than an ounce of gold, mixed up with a good deal of sand. I stayed at Mr. Marshall’s that night, and the next day we proceeded some little distance up the south Fork, and found that gold existed along the whole course … I myself, with nothing more than a small knife, picked out from a dry gorge, a little way up the mountain, a solid lump of gold which weighed nearly an ounce and a half.”

Who created this primary source?

When was the source created?

What does this source tell us about life in California during the Gold Rush?

The following source is an excerpt from a letter written by Augustin Hibbard to his brother on Sept. 4, 1850.

“After looking about a few days (which is here called prospecting) we commenced digging for gold, and we soon found that, although, in imagination it might be agreeable work, yet in reality, it was the most laborious and in the majority of cases the most unsatisfactory that men could be engaged in...

Not one in 500 make $50000 a year. And not more than one in a hundred, that makes more than his expenses. We were fortunate enough however to fall in with a party of men who had found very good diggings, they took us to the place and were very kind in giving us all necessary instructions. At first we could only make from 3 to $5.00 a day which would hardly board us but in a short time we improved so that we could make from 12 to 16 dollars a day...

After working about a month I was taken sick with the fever & ague. It was then & not until then that I realized what I had sacrificed in coming here. Instead of the soft couch, with the hand of affection to arrange the pillow for my burning head, it was a blanket or two spread upon the ground & the hands of strangers that ministered to my wants. Often in my troubled dreams was I at home receiving all those attentions which I so much needed and awoke to find myself alone in the tent burning with fever, parched with thirst and no one to give me a drink or to relieve me in any way. The poorest kind of medical attendance was all that could be procured…”

When was the source created?

title: The Lens of Crosscutting Concepts
text: The big ideas of science are called crosscutting concepts. Imagine looking through special lenses. These lenses only let you see the world in big ideas. You might only see patterns in the grass or sky. You might see how each part of plants or animals make up their whole. Scientists view phenomena through crosscutting concepts. It helps them see what’s happening in different ways. This week, you’ll be looking at many phenomena. You will view each through the lenses of different crosscutting concepts. Each will help you see what’s happening in a different way.

title: Patterns
text:
Patterns are all around us. A pattern is repeated information that predicts future information. Scientists and engineers look for patterns. Patterns help them make predictions about future behavior. Patterns in nature can be observed. Patterns made by humans can also be observed. Scientists study patterns made by nature and humans. A model can be used to represent patterns. A model is a visual or 3-D representation and is usually smaller than the original.

From what you have seen, draw a model for how you think this pattern would continue.

title: Cause and Effect
text:
Scientists often wonder why things happen. They also try to see or predict what happens because something else happened. When one event leads to another this is called cause and effect. A cause is the first thing that happens in a situation. An effect is what happens because of the cause. For example, Natalia forgot to water her plant (cause). This caused the plant to wilt or droop (effect). These two events are connected. When two people, things, or ideas are connected, they create a relationship.

Look at the image of the angled icicles through the lens of cause and effect. Answer the questions in the printable, “Cause and Effect Questions.”

title: Systems and System Models
text:
In science, it's important to see how different things work together. When this happens, all the parts work together to do something. This is known as a system. You can see systems all around you. There are systems in plants, space, and even the weather!

Scientists want to know how things work together in a system. To do this, they can create models of a system. Models are visual or 3-D representations.

title: Structure and Function
text:
Sometimes we see things in nature or things that are made by humans. You can see how these things are built. How something looks, its shape, or how it is built is called its structure. Everything in nature or that has been built has something it is meant to do. This is known as function. The structure of something will affect its function. Think of the structure of a swing set. It has large, stable, metal beams that go into the ground. It has strong chains attached to a seat. Its function is to have a solid base. This keeps the people who use the swing set safe.

title: Energy and Matter
text:
Everything on Earth is made up of materials. This material is called matter. Matter is anything that has weight and takes up space. Chairs are made of matter. So is water! Objects made of matter can be broken into smaller pieces. These pieces can be put back together to make the same thing. They can also make different things. Or these pieces can be put with more matter to make bigger things. Breaking matter into smaller pieces and rebuilding changes the matter. Matter needs energy to change. Energy is the ability to do work or create change. Heat is energy. Sound and light are energy too. Energy and matter can change, but never be destroyed. Scientists and engineers study energy and the way it affects matter.

title: Stability and Change
text:
Many things around us are always becoming different. This is known as change. Other things stay the same. When something works well and is not likely to change, it is called stability. Scientists and engineers observe things through the lens of change and stability. Changes can happen slowly or quickly. Scientists pay attention to things that may look stable but are really changing slowly. For example, you may not notice your body growing. That's because the change is slow. Scientists observe phenomena through change and stability. This helps them explain some of the reasons for changes. This can lead to new discoveries. It can also be the way to find solutions to problems.

title: Patterns
text:

When we find similarities and differences in nature, it can help to sort and arrange things into categories. Using patterns of change helps make predictions about future events. These help us understand if changes will happen quickly or slowly, based on what they’ve done in the past. Patterns made by humans can also be observed. title: Cause and Effect
text: After scientists find patterns, they often look for why the pattern happened in the first place. Every action in nature will have a consequence. When an event leads to another, it is called cause and effect. Looking at a phenomenon through cause and effect means to discover what happened and why. A cause is the first thing that happens. An effect is what happens because of the cause. For example, Natalia forgot to water her plant (cause). This caused the plant to wilt or droop (effect). Scientists also try to see or predict effects because of another event. When one thing leads to another, it creates a cause-and-effect relationship or a causal relationship. Sometimes, scientists have to determine if one event is actually causing a phenomenon or if they just happen to occur at the same time.

title: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity
text:
Have you ever seen a smaller version of a car, a large building, or the solar system? When we talk about different-sized objects and their relationship to other objects, we are talking about scale. Scale is an object’s size in relation to other objects. Objects in nature can range in size from very small to very large. Scale also refers to the time it takes to do something. Scale of time can be from short to long.

Look at the image of the two cats. One looks a little different. This is because one part of the cat’s body is larger than it should be. The size of a part or number when compared to other parts or a whole is known as proportion. Proportion in nature is important. The amount in chemistry helps create new products and medicine. Proportion of objects in nature helps things work properly. Proportions in your life may be the amount of time you spend on homework compared to spending time with your family.

Have you ever heard someone say, “It rained a lot last night”? To someone who lives in the desert, any rain probably feels like a lot. To someone who lives where it rains almost every day, “a lot” probably means hours and hours of rain. “A lot” does not have a specific amount. An exact or measured amount is known as quantity. title: Sacagawea
text:
Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman. She was an interpreter and guide for the Lewis and Clark expedition. At age 12, Sacagawea was captured and enslaved by an enemy tribe. She was then sold to a French Canadian fur trader named Toussaint Charbonneau. Lewis and Clark hired Charbonneau as an interpreter for their expedition. Sacagawea was brought on the trip as an interpreter because she spoke Shoshone. However, Sacagawea was never paid for her work. Sacagawea played an important role on the expedition. In addition to interpreting, she was very good at finding edible plants and herbs. This skill helped the explorers during their travels.

On May 14, 1805, the expedition boat she was in tipped over and filled with water. Supplies and documents fell into the water. Sacagawea stayed calm. She saved the supplies and documents from being lost to the river. About a week later, Lewis and Clark showed their appreciation by naming a part of the Musselshell River after her.

title: Louisiana: Past and Present
text:
At the time French settlers came in the 1700s, many indigenous cultures lived in Louisiana. The Louisiana Purchase altered the shape of our nation and the lives of Louisiana’s native people. Some tribes left or were forced to move to different lands. Some tribes stayed, and people with ancestry from these cultures still live in Louisiana today. The Chitimacha are the only native people to still live on a section of their original homeland. Today, many different groups of people live in Louisiana. Some things have changed as groups have moved in or out of Louisiana. Other things have stayed the same.

Life in Louisiana today is both similar to and different from life in the past.

Lands and Home

Louisiana's original inhabitants were close to nature. They relied on it and respected it. Mountains formed natural borders. Rivers provided food and trade routes. Families lived in houses made of wood, grasses, and reeds.

Food

While the men hunted, the women grew and gathered food. Their main crops were corn and potatoes. A tribe's territory often shaped its traditions. Those who lived along the rivers or coast could fish or catch alligators. Those that lived in wooded areas hunted for deer and bear.

Clothing

Hunting was an important source of food, but also provided clothing, tools, and jewelry. The women made clothes from animal skins. They also used cloth, feathers, and bark.

Recreation

Indigenous communities of the past played games and went to sporting events. Wrestling, racing, and archery were popular sports. Music and dancing were central to these events.

Celebrations

Many tribes had a celebration in the early part of November to honor the dead with dance, song, and food. Families gathered in the cemetery to visit graves and then returned home to a great feast.

title: Louisiana: Many Cultures
text: Louisiana's culture is unique. The music has different rhythms and beats. There are many lively festivals. The food is known for its spicy taste. The buildings were made with influences from around the world. Why is our culture so special? There's a good reason. It has been shaped by many different cultures that have mixed together right here in Louisiana. When the Louisiana Purchase was made, new land was added to our country. This land was different from much of the other land. People of Indigenous, European, African, and Latin American descent made a unique and mixed culture. This culture added diversity to the United States.

title: Mardi Gras
text:
Mardi Gras is a holiday that can be traced back thousands of years to ancient Roman festivals. It started in North America in 1699 when French explorers camped and held a small celebration not far from the future site of New Orleans. Over time, people have added unique traditions that have helped shape the holiday into what it is today.

Mardi Gras is celebrated with music, parades, events, and activities throughout Louisiana. North Louisiana is known for a parade featuring a royal court of pets. A tradition popular in southwest Louisiana involves dressing in colorful costumes and begging for ingredients to make gumbo. For the final ingredient, runners chase after a live chicken. King Cake, a braided pastry decorated in gold, purple, and green is one of the most popular treats of the Mardi Gras season.

title: Patterns
text:
Patterns are all around us. A pattern is repeated information that predicts future information. Scientists and engineers look for patterns by finding similarities and differences. When we find similarities and differences in nature, it can help to sort and arrange things into categories, or classify them. Patterns of change that stay the same create a consistent pattern. A consistent pattern helps make predictions about future events. They help us understand if changes will happen quickly or slowly, based on what they’ve done in the past. When you observe how quickly or slowly something changes, this is its rate of change. Patterns made by humans can also be observed in these ways. Scientists study patterns made by nature and humans.

title: Concept Correction
text: When we look at an object, we often think its appearance tells us what it is. Do you ever look at an ice cube and think that it is just ice? It can be hard to describe it in other ways. That makes it easy to believe that the different states of matter are all different substances. We would think ice is ice, and water is water. We would think there is no link between the two objects. This is not true, though. Why would we think this? Many who believe this will base their idea on what the two objects look like. Ice is a great example. We never call ice “frozen water.” We call it "ice." Really, ice is just water that has gotten so cold that it froze into a piece of ice! This is why knowing the states of matter is important. Water freezes into a chunk of ice, and when it melts again, we have water! The substance itself did not change. Its appearance changed. So, ice and water are not different substances.

title: Cause and Effect
text:
After scientists find patterns, they often look for why the pattern happened in the first place. Every action in nature will have a consequence. When one event leads to another, it is called cause and effect. Looking at a phenomenon through cause and effect means to discover what happened and why. A cause is the first thing that happens in a situation. An effect is what happens because of the cause. We describe the back and forth of cause and effect as a relationship, or a cause-and-effect relationship. For example, Natalia forgot to water her plant (cause). This caused the plant to wilt or droop (effect). Scientists also try to predict future outcomes based on past events. If a series of past events shows that one thing generally leads to another, this creates a cause-and-effect relationship. Cause-and-effect relationships can be used to observe, test, and explain phenomena. Sometimes scientists have to determine if one event is actually causing a phenomenon or if they just happened to occur at the same time.

Everything around you on Earth is made up of matter. Matter is anything that has weight and takes up space. It is the word we use for the stuff that makes up our world. title: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity
text:
Read the article. Then answer the questions in the Scale, Proportion, Quantity Worksheet.

A favorite hobby of some people is creating smaller models of cars or buildings. These are known as scale models. Scale describes an object's size in relation to other objects. Objects in nature can be very small or very large. One common way you've probably seen this in school is through a scale model of the universe. The universe is huge! Look at the image of the two cats. One looks a little different. This is because one part of the cat’s body is larger than normal. When the size of a part or number is compared to other parts or a whole, it is known as proportion. Proportion in nature is important. The proportion of objects in nature compared to other things helps things work properly. One example of proportion in your life may be the amount of time you portion to homework versus spending time with your family.

Have you ever heard someone say, “It rained a lot last night”? To someone who lives in the desert, any rain probably feels like a lot. To someone where it rains almost every day, “a lot” probably means hours and hours of rain. “A lot” does not have a specific amount. An exact or measured amount is known as quantity. Scientists and engineers always define quantity in their work. They will often ask questions related to quantity. How much water is on Earth? How big was the earthquake? How many stars are in the galaxy? Scientists can answer all of these questions because they have tools to measure different quantities for weight, time, and temperature.

Systems and System Models

In science, it's important to see how different things work together. When this happens, all the parts work together to achieve something. This is known as a system. You can see systems all around you. There are systems in plants, bicycles, bodies, space, and even the weather! You can describe each system by naming the parts. The parts of a system that interact are known as components. When components act or influence each other it is known as an interaction. For example, the chain, brakes, wheels, and seat are all components that work together to help a bike function. Sometimes a system can function on its own with its own components, but also helps a bigger system function. This is called a subsystem. For example, your bones can help you run to the playground. The digestive system helps carry nutrients to make your bones strong. Each of these are subsystems within the system of the body. To help scientists see how each component or subsystem works together, they create a visual or 3-D representation, typically on a smaller scale than the original, called a model.

title: Structure and Function
text:
Read the article. Then answer the questions in the Structure and Function Worksheet.

When you see something in nature or made by humans, you can observe how it is built. How something looks, its shape, or how it is built is called its structure. Everything in nature or that has been built has a purpose. This is known as its function. Sometimes function also refers to how an object works. The structure of something will affect its function. Think of the structure of a swing set. A swing set's function is to support people as they swing back and forth. To fit this function, it needs a solid base. It has large, stable, metal beams that go into the ground. This part or structure that acts as a support, base, or foundation is known as a substructure. Sometimes substructures can be observed, like the poles. Other times they are not observable, like the roots of a tree, but they still provide support. Roots, for example, keep the tree upright. Similarly, the poles of a swing set keep the people who use the swing set safe. But imagine if the strong chains attached to the seat were broken. The swing set would no longer function, and playtime would be over until the structure was fixed.

Many things in the world around us are always changing. Other things stay the same. When something works well and is not likely to change, it is called stability. Over time, systems can appear stable, but may eventually change. For example, a volcano may appear to be dormant, but over time may eventually become active and erupt! title: Specialization in Louisiana
text:
Customers in over 190 countries and territories buy Louisiana-made goods and services. What do they buy? Soybeans, wheat, corn, and sugarcane are some of the state’s main crops. The fishing industry in Louisiana provides shrimp, oysters, and other seafood.

Tree farming is a big part of Louisiana’s current economy. Wood gathered from local tree farms is sold as lumber and turned into wood pulp. Wood pulp is used to make all kinds of paper and tissue. Louisiana specializes in oil and coal. Much of the petroleum oil is turned into chemicals. Coal is used to provide energy. Louisiana also produces and sells liquid natural gas.

The state of Louisiana also provides many services. Tourism is one of the biggest. People come for Mardi Gras events, jazz music, historical sites, and Cajun and Creole cooking. The city of New Orleans is visited by millions of tourists each year.

title: Physical Characteristics
text:
The theme of place refers to how we describe a location. The physical characteristics of a place are part of its natural environment. What is the landscape like? Are there unique landforms or bodies of water? What are the common plants and animals? What are the weather patterns? What are the natural resources?

Landscapes, plants, climate, and animals are physical characteristics. These things give a location its unique appearance and meaning. Places on Earth are different because of their different physical characteristics.

title: Climate
text: Climate is a physical characteristic. Climate is the weather pattern that develops in a place over many years. The weather can change in just a few hours. The climate takes hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years to change. Climate includes the average temperature, precipitation (rain, snow, sleet), and wind in the area. People make decisions about food, clothing, and shelter based on the climate. We use climate maps to learn about what different places are like. We can learn about different climate zones around the world.

title: The First Census: 1790
text:
A government based on representation has to have an accurate count of its population. To determine the members in the House of Representatives, a census would be required. Article 2 of the U.S. Constitution requires a complete count of the population every 10 years. Aug. 2, 1790 was the first census day. Under the direction of Thomas Jefferson, the then-secretary of state, the census was taken in the original 13 states. They also included the districts of Kentucky, Maine, Vermont, and the Southwest Territory (Tennessee).

The 1790 census wanted the following information:

Name of the head of the family

Number of free white males 16 years old or older

Number of free white males younger than 16 years old

Number of free white females

Number of all other free persons

Number of enslaved persons

The census determined that there were four million people in the country in 1790. This census gives us a glimpse at the families and settlements of the new nation. The census records are available today through the United States Census Bureau.

title: Parts of a Primary Source
text:
You can identify a primary source by thinking like a historian. Primary sources have parts that will help you identify them. Ask important questions like a historian would. The answers will help you know if you can trust your source.

title: Where to Find Sources
text: Historians do research to know if they can trust a source. They look closely at artifacts and photos to make sure they are real. They read documents to make sure they tell the truth. You can read and look at sources, too. Libraries and museums hold many trusted sources of information.

title: Validity of a Source
text: It is important to know whether information is a fact or an opinion. A fact is information that can be proven and is true for everyone. Opinions are people’s ideas and beliefs about something or someone. They are often based on people’s preferences and experiences. Opinions should not be used to replace facts. However, it is helpful to look at as many sources as possible. Looking at things from multiple perspectives can help us have a deeper understanding of the past.

title: Chronological Thinking
text: Chronological thinking can help us understand the past. Chronological means things are listed in the order they happened. When we think about events chronologically, we think about what came first and what came next. We can keep track of events by using a timeline. A calendar is a useful timeline. It shows the days of the week and months of the year in order.

title: Timelines
text: A timeline shows events and dates in order. A timeline is divided into sections. Timelines show change over time. The space between events means that time has passed between the events. A timeline might show events that happened a long time ago. A timeline might show events that happened last week. You can create a timeline whenever you want to see events in order.

title: I Belong to a Community
text: A community is a group of people who live in the same place or have something in common. People from many places can join together in a community. One community you are a part of is your family or household. A household includes everyone who lives in the same home. You are also part of a classroom community. Your school community includes the teachers and other students at your school. You are part of a local community, too. Your local community includes your neighborhood, city, or town.

title: What Is Our Responsibility?
text: As a member of a community, you have responsibilities. One way to show you are a good member of your community is to respect others. You can take care of others in the community. You can obey the community’s rules.

title: Being Responsible at Home
text: You have responsibilities in your family or household community. You can be responsible by taking care of your things. You can help complete chores. You can show you are responsible by taking care of people who live with you.

title: Classroom Responsibilities
text: You have responsibilities in your classroom. You can show you are responsible by keeping classroom rules. You have the responsibility to work hard and learn. When you behave responsibly, you make it easier for other students to be successful, too.

text:

title: Rules
text:
Rules are instructions that tell people what they can and can’t do. Rules help protect our rights. They help us know how people should act in our communities. They tell us how to treat each other with respect. Rules help us live together peacefully and fairly.

We can make choices about our actions. We can choose to follow the rules. We can choose to act in a way that shows respect. If we choose not to follow the rules, we face consequences.

title: Rules at School
text: Rules at school are important. They help us show respect. Many rules are posted where everyone can see them. The principal and teachers make some of the rules. State leaders also make rules. School rules help us work together. We follow the rules when we show respect for our teachers and treat others fairly. Rules also teach us to treat school property with care. We follow school rules when we treat library books respectfully.

title: The Bill of Rights
text:
The Bill of Rights is the first 10 amendments to the Constitution. It was created to limit how the government can control our lives. It ensures the basic rights of the people. It explains our rights as citizens.

You have rights in school because of the Bill of Rights. You have the right to free speech. This means you can say what you think. It is important to be respectful when you say what you think.

You have the right to be treated fairly, no matter what you look like or where you are from.

title: Patriotism
text: Patriotism is a feeling of love for your country. Citizens feel patriotic for many reasons. We feel patriotic because of the freedoms we enjoy. We can feel patriotic when we think about people who protect our freedoms. We can feel patriotic because of the beauty of our country. Symbols of the United States make us feel patriotic. When we say the Pledge of Allegiance or sing the national anthem, we can feel patriotic.

title: The National Anthem
text: A national anthem is the official song of a country. It represents the country’s values. The U.S. national anthem was written by Francis Scott Key. He wrote it during the War of 1812. He was on a ship in the harbor. He saw a British ship that was attacking Fort McHenry in Maryland. Key was worried about the Americans in the fort. In the morning, he could still see the American flag flying. He was very glad. The experience inspired him to write the “The Star-Spangled Banner.” It was made the official national anthem in 1931. We sing this song to show patriotism for the United States.

title: Patriotic Songs
text: We sing other songs to show how we feel about the United States. “America the Beautiful” is a song about how beautiful the country is.

title: Globes
text: The world is a big place. You would have to travel 25,000 miles to go all the way around the middle of the Earth. However, you don’t have to travel at all to see what the Earth looks like. Globes are 3D models of the Earth. They show the shape of our planet. You can see where water and land are located. Globes show us the big picture.

title: Maps
text: Maps are flat drawings of places around the world. We can learn a lot by studying maps. Maps can show us towns, states, countries, and continents. They can help us find where a place is located. We can use maps to get from one place to another. A map can help us find the direction we need to travel. Maps also show us the distance between places.

title: Reading Maps
text: Map tools help us read and understand maps. Maps usually include a title, a legend, and a compass rose. Many also include labels and a scale.

title: Scale
text: Distance is how far one place is from another place. A scale is a map tool that shows distance. The scale measurement represents a real distance. For example, one inch on a map might represent 800 miles on the Earth.

title: Physical Maps
text: A physical map shows the location of natural features. Physical maps help us find rivers, oceans, and other bodies of water. They also show landforms. Landforms include mountains, plains, and more.

title: Work
text:
Work helps communities grow. Work is an activity that makes a good or provides a service. It can be physical or mental. Baking and firefighting are physical work. Writing and doing math are mental work.

A job is work we do to earn money. Income is the money a person earns for doing their job. People use income to pay for their needs and wants.

title: Spending
text: Spending means using money to pay for goods or services. Spending your money carefully takes thought. There are many choices to make. People must choose where to spend their money. They also must choose how much they are willing to pay. The goods and services we need and want do not always cost the same. For example, not all shoes cost the same amount. Responsible people make wise decisions about spending their money.

title: Saving
text: Saving is keeping some of your money for the future. When you save money, you must decide where to keep it safe. Many people save money in a bank or credit union. This helps them to save up for something expensive. For example, people might save money for a vacation, house, or car. Sometimes we only need to save for a short amount of time. You can save money at home in a piggy bank, wallet, or safe. This works to save for less expensive things, like a new toy or shirt.

title: Banks, Credit Unions, and Credit Cards
text:
Many people save their money in a bank or credit union. You can set up a checking or savings account, where you can store your money. Banks can also help you invest your money.

People can ask for a loan from a bank. A loan is money a bank gives to someone so they can pay for something expensive. When someone takes a loan, they agree to pay the money back to the bank. They also pay interest on the loan. Interest is extra money we pay back over time in order to use money now.

Many banks and other companies give people credit cards. Credit cards are small pieces of plastic. They let you buy something now and pay for it later. People who have credit cards agree to pay the money back each month. They also pay interest if they don’t pay the full amount they owe every month.

title: Water, Water Everywhere: Part Two
text:
“Water, water, every where,

Nor any drop to drink.”

-Samuel Taylor Coleridge, “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”

The poem quoted here is about a sailor who is lost at sea. Water surrounds him, yet there is not a drop to drink. Why is this the case? After all, Earth is known as the blue planet. Water is everywhere, and all living things need water. But nearly 97 percent of Earth’s water is salt water, mainly from oceans. Because of its high salt content, humans cannot use it for drinking or watering crops. That leaves only three percent of water on Earth that is fresh, and even then, not all of the three percent is available for us to drink or use. Nearly 99 percent of fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps (69 percent) or deep below the surface in groundwater (30 percent). Obtaining this fresh water and transporting it all around the world is extremely difficult.

Innovations in engineering have led to the creation of dams and reservoirs to stockpile the fresh water that comes from lakes, rivers, and groundwater. Dams divert freshwater sources, such as lakes and rivers, and gather them into central locations for future use. Additionally, humans have created wells to access deep, natural collections of groundwater, known as aquifers. Laws have been put in place to regulate or protect water sources across the United States. Despite this legal protection, water from open sources can contain harmful elements, like parasites or bacteria. Water treatment plants filter and clean water for humans to use for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, and agriculture. During hot summer months, reservoirs provide water to populations experiencing drought. Still, 884 million people across the globe don’t have basic services for drinking water. This is why water is so precious.

title: What Is an Inquiry?
text:
An inquiry is a way to investigate a problem or ask for more information. The process involves asking questions, thinking about evidence, and completing tasks.

Questions begin our inquiry. We need to ask the right questions to focus our inquiry.

Evidence is the facts we see that help us find answers to our questions. We research to find evidence and think about how it relates to our questions.

Tasks are the things you do. A task might be something you create. It could be an experiment. It might be research, using the questions you asked. It might be presenting information about your research. Your task may be something your teacher asks you to do or something you think of all by yourself!

What do I want to know about this?

3. Search for answers and experiment.

4. Interpret the information.

How does this information relate to my compelling question?

Which parts help answer my question?

What parts do not support my question?

title: Primary and Secondary Sources
text:
Historians use different sources to find out about people, places, and events in the past. There are two main types of sources.

Primary sources are created by people who saw or experienced something themselves. They are usually created around the time of the event. They can include photographs, diaries, drawings, maps, and letters.

Secondary sources are made by people who did not see or experience events themselves. They are usually created by people who have studied primary sources. Secondary sources include textbooks, magazine articles, book reviews, encyclopedias, and documentaries.

A story you write about your own vacation is a primary source. You were there and experienced the vacation. Someone can interview you and write about your vacation, too. Their story is a secondary source.

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
The people of the Americas met their wants and needs using resources from the land around them. They had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had government and religion. They fed their families by hunting animals and gathering berries, nuts, and fruits. They cultivated crops of corn, squash, beans, tomatoes, potatoes, and some grains. They created tools from the resources around them. They traveled by walking or using boats on the waterways.

The Europeans used natural resources to create manufactured goods. Like American Indians, they also had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had government and religion. They fed their families by farming and going to markets. The Europeans domesticated animals to keep on their farms. This meant they didn’t have to hunt for food. They had horses to help with the work on the farm and at the market. They cultivated grain crops of wheat, oats, and barley. The Europeans developed different modes of transportation. They used wagons and carts on land and ships on the sea. They manufactured goods out of metal and wood. They used many of their resources to help them explore new places across the ocean.

When these two societies met, there were intentional and unintentional consequences. The two groups traded ideas for the design of tools and transportation. The Europeans brought domesticated animals, pigs, chickens, and horses with them on their ships. The people of the Americas gave them plants, food, and precious metals. Sign language and gestures were used to help the two cultures communicate with each other.

Tolerance of differences between the two cultures could have expanded the positive exchanges. However, the Europeans were not tolerant of the differences they encountered. They believed the peoples of the Americas were inferior because their ways were different. Intolerance caused conflict and the captivity and deaths of many Indigenous American people.

The introduction of domesticated animals in the Americas caused imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation had nothing to eat.

The horse was a new animal to the Americas. The horse quickly became popular to help the people of the Americas in their everyday lives. They used horses for transportation and work. Horses became a valuable trade resource. The horses quickly multiplied. Descendents of these horses are still found on the east coast and the western lands of the United States.

The most deadly exchange was unintentional. The Europeans brought disease with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. The people of the Americas had never been exposed to such deadly germs. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of disease were easily transported by unsuspecting people. Historians estimate that disease killed 90 percent of the native population within 150 years.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
In 1494, one man who had sailed across the Atlantic Ocean returned home with all sorts of wild stories. He described the new world he had seen, full of strange plants, animals, and foods. He talked about the people he had met there. This man was not Christopher Columbus or a member of his crew. He was a Taíno from the Bahamas whom Columbus had captured and taken back to Spain. We don’t know his real name, but Columbus gave him the name Diego Colón.

After returning home, Colón told his friends and family about Spain. He described “the great cities and fortresses and churches” and “the people and horses and animals.” He saw strange “lands and food ... and bullfighting.” All were new to him, just like Native Peoples and their homelands were new to Europeans. As people traveled between the continents, they were exchanging ideas about technology, religion, and ways of life.

As European explorers reached different parts of North America, people from different groups, like the Iroquois and Patuxet, were brought across the ocean and saw Europe. People in the Americas and in Europe were not just curious about each other. As soon as they met, many saw new opportunities to meet their economic wants and needs. The people on the two sides of the Atlantic quickly exchanged goods, people, plants, animals, and diseases.

This exchange between the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia is called the Columbian Exchange. It is named after Christopher Columbus. The Columbian Exchange had a huge impact on life for people all around the world. Without it, Italy would never have invented pizza, and Ireland would never have grown potatoes. American Indians would never have ridden on horseback.

Animals like horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs changed economic life in the Americas. Farm animals became new food sources. Horses changed the way tribes like the Sioux and the Comanche hunted and traveled. Riding horses was a much faster form of transportation than following bison herds on foot.

European settlers also brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, bananas, and even honeybees with them. Columbus brought sugarcane to Hispaniola in 1493. Sugarcane grew well in the Americas and sold well in Europe.

Many plants from the Americas also had a big impact on Europe, Africa, and Asia. For example, American plants like potatoes, tomatoes, and corn changed how people ate. On both sides of the Atlantic, new plants on farms and in settlements often spread and changed even what grew in the wild. The world was truly never the same because of the Columbian Exchange.

title: Piracy and Privateers
text:
Kings and queens in Europe weren’t just excited about explorers heading out to the Americas. They were excited about explorers coming back. Their return meant new foods, goods, and gold. The more land their country claimed, the more resources could be brought to market. The countries in Europe wanted the goods from the Americas.

Spain sent explorers first. Once the Spanish started to conquer land and peoples, they set up regular trade routes for their ships. The ships followed known routes. It wouldn’t take long for others to identify the ships and steal their cargo. Other Europeans began arming ships with cannons and their crews with weapons. Pirates threatened these ships full of goods on their way back to Spain and stole their cargo.

Someone who attacks and robs a ship at sea is called a pirate. Pirates became a threat to merchant ships traveling between Europe and the Americas. The small islands in the Caribbean became the ideal place to hide stolen goods. The pirates became skilled at stealing cargo. The pirates of the Caribbean were ruthless in the pursuit of treasure and goods. Pirates were pursued by government authorities. When caught, they were punished with death.

There was rivalry and competition between the governments in Europe over the resources in the Americas. Due to this competition, monarchs saw an opportunity to use pirates. Pirates already had ships out on the sea and were fighting with their rival countries. The monarchs of England, France, the Netherlands, and Spain began granting a special license to certain sea captains and their crews. Their job was to attack ships that belonged to enemy countries. That special license was called a letter of marque. A letter of marque made a pirate a privateer. Unlike pirates, privateers were protected from punishment. They could legally sell captured goods. Privateers would raid ships in the name of their country, then split the profits with the monarch. Privateering also helped spread that government’s influence.

title: Demand in Europe
text:
Spain sent explorers across the Atlantic to open trade with India and earn money. Finding the Americas instead had an even bigger effect on Europe’s economy. As new goods came back from the Americas, people rushed to buy them.

At first, most things brought back from the Americas were luxury goods for the rich. Europeans brought back gold and silver. Wealthy buyers in Europe also liked fur from American animals. American crops like tobacco also became popular. Many people wanted to try the new goods, and as a result, prices grew high. Sugarcane, originally from Asia, was introduced in the hot climate of the Caribbean, where it grew very well. People in Europe were willing to pay high prices for sugar. High demand made sugarcane producers in the Americas want to increase their supply.

Some American crops were only popular with certain people or in certain places. Wealthy Europeans did not like potatoes at first. However, potatoes were a good food because they had a lot of calories and grew underground. This kept them from being destroyed by bad weather. Slowly, potatoes spread to many countries. Potatoes never had high prices like sugar. As people learned how to prepare and cook them for meals, they increased in production.

Europeans did not make corn a popular purchase. Many Europeans used corn as an ingredient in other dishes and used it to feed animals. Corn was accepted in Asia and Africa as an import from Europe.

The demand for different American goods in Europe had an impact on life in the Americas. The way land was divided, the way people worked, and even ideas about who had rights would all be influenced by economic demand in European countries.

title: Religious Conflict
text:
In the 16th century, there was conflict in Europe about religion. The conflict was about who was the authority for Christianity and the leader of the Roman Catholic Church. The Catholic Church was the only Christian denomination in Europe at this time. The Catholic Church was organized with a central leader: the pope. The pope was the religious leader for all Christians. All governments that were Christian in belief obeyed the directions of the pope. This made the pope higher in authority than the monarchs.

The king of England, Henry VIII, did not think anyone should have greater authority in England than the king. If the pope could tell the king what to do, then who was really the authority in England? This line of thinking led others to question who was the leader of the Christian church: the pope, the king, or the people?

The Catholic Church had rituals and rules of worship for people to follow. Many people began to think some of these were unnecessary and even wrong. They wanted the Catholic Church to be reformed. Some people began to turn to new beliefs and practices. They protested the Catholic Church. They became known as Protestants.

The pope wanted everyone to be Catholic. Many Catholic monarchs believed like the pope. The Catholic monarchs made laws to force their people to be Catholic. Those who disobeyed were persecuted.

Like the Catholic monarchs, Protestant monarchs also made laws to force people to be Protestant. Those who disobeyed were persecuted. The persecution between Catholics and Protestants increased the religious competition and rivalry between the countries of Europe.

title: Sugar Production and the Slave Trade
text:
In the 1400s, Europe traded with Asia for sugar. People loved the taste of sugar and paid high prices for it. Sugar is produced from sugarcane. Sugarcane needs a warm environment to grow. It also needs lots of rain or good irrigation. Europe did not have the right climate to grow sugar, so they had to trade for it.

When European explorers came to the Americas, they found a warm, wet climate where sugar could grow. Sugarcane grew especially well on islands in the Caribbean Sea. European colonists realized sugar could become a cash crop. A cash crop is a crop people grow to sell and make money. This led to large areas of land being used to grow only one kind of cash crop. These large farms became known as plantations.

It took hard work to grow and harvest sugarcane. Sugarcane doesn’t produce seeds. Someone had to cut hard stalks into pieces by hand and then plant them. It was also difficult to get soft sugar out of the tough stalks. As plantation owners earned more money from sugar, they looked for ways to get cheap labor to plant, harvest, and process the sugar. They began enslaving native people of those lands, taking away their freedom and forcing them to do the work. When many died from European diseases or risked punishment to escape, plantation owners turned to the slave trade from Africa. Men, women, and children were kidnapped in Africa and taken to the Caribbean and South America. Enslaved Africans were sold to plantation owners and forced to work in harsh conditions without pay or freedom. In Europe, sugar became easier to buy as the supply increased. European plantation owners became very wealthy at the expense of enslaved people.

title: African Enslavement
text:
Prince Henry the Navigator was a Portuguese duke. Although he was called the Navigator, he never went to sea. Prince Henry did control a large amount of money for an organization called the “Order of Christ.” This organization brought navigators and geographers together. They would plan expeditions to unexplored regions along the Atlantic coast south of Portugal. They hired a sea captain named Bartolomeu Perestrello and his ship for their expeditions.

The early voyages sent Perestrello to the mid-Atlantic islands, such as Madeira and the Azores. These explorations were followed by routes along the west coast of Africa.

As a result of their exploration, the Portuguese began to colonize new areas. Beginning in 1445, the Azores rapidly filled with colonists. They developed a rich sugar-producing colony. The sugar was exported to European markets. The Portuguese also established trading posts along the west coast of Africa.

These trading posts were to trade Portuguese goods to traders in Africa. The Africans traded a product in high demand by the Portuguese. This “product” was people. Men, women, and children were captured by the African traders and sold to the Portuguese as enslaved people. The enslaved captives were taken to sugar plantations on the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores. Many enslaved people were also taken to Spain and Portugal. By the mid-1550s, 10 percent of Portugal’s population was enslaved men, women, and children from Africa.

Exploration of the Americas created a new market where traders could sell enslaved Africans. The first recorded ship carrying 200 enslaved African people sailed to the Caribbean in 1525. Sold into a lifetime of enslavement, they worked on sugar plantations. This early trade by Portuguese ships began the long, tragic system of bringing enslaved people across the Atlantic.

title: Europe Before Westward Exploration
text:
In the 1400s, the whole world was on the move. Empires were growing in the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe. Rich empires served as patrons, meaning they could pay people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and exchanges of ideas through trade routes. A trade route is an area used by merchants for economic purposes.

In the Americas, new empires were rising. Near the Great Lakes, the Iroquois Confederacy was gaining more control over trade. Trade was expanding throughout the area, including what is now Mexico and South America. In Central America, the Aztec Empire was expanding. Aztec rulers were patrons of many great poets. In South America, the Inca Empire was expanding. Inca rulers were patrons of inventors who developed new technologies for farming, medicine, and bridge building. The empire used this new knowledge to increase trade and exchange ideas.

Across the Atlantic Ocean, in Africa, the Songhai Empire was growing. Trade across the Sahara in salt and gold made the empire wealthy. Songhai leaders became patrons for education. Under the Songhai, thousands of scholars and students gathered to study at the famous libraries in the city of Timbuktu.

In the 1400s, most of the world’s population lived in Asia. China and India had the world’s largest economies. Spices, silks, gold, and other goods were traded all the way to Europe. In the 1400s, the Ottoman Empire was rising between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans soon gained control of trade connections between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans were responsible for stopping trade to Europe.

For merchants in Europe, losing control of trade with Asia was hard. The countries of Portugal and Spain, however, saw an opportunity. These countries looked for new routes across the sea to Asia. Patrons from Portugal hoped to make money from trade in Africa and find a way to sail around Africa to Asia.

By 1490, Ferdinand and Isabella were the king and queen of Spain. Spain had just ended a religious war persecuting non-Christians called the Spanish Reconquista. They had taken property from Jews and Muslims in Spain, which made them rich enough to be important patrons. Ferdinand and Isabella wanted new trade routes and income. They just needed the right idea to pay for and the right person to try it.

An entrepreneur named Christopher Columbus had an unusual idea. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean and reach India that way. Columbus was looking for a patron. Columbus went to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand in Spain. Isabella and Ferdinand agreed to be patrons for Columbus. They paid for three ships Columbus could use. They also paid for the tools and crew needed for the voyage. Columbus made an agreement with Ferdinand and Isabella. The agreement described what both Spain and Columbus would receive if his journey was successful. This agreement clarified that Spain and Columbus would share the profits from any cargo he brought back.

Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. His journey would launch the biggest changes in government, knowledge, and trade the world had ever seen.

title: Age of Encounters
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa. Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He believed he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.”

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures and became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they learned on the voyage, other explorers followed.

Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim.

Explorers share information that helps others explore. Columbus opened a new door of adventure. Many followed and shared their new knowledge.

1. Christopher Columbus

Spain paid Christopher Columbus to sail across the Atlantic in 1492. Columbus hoped to reach India by sailing west. Instead, his ships landed in the Caribbean. There, Columbus met the Taíno people. Columbus’s voyage increased Europe’s interest in exploration and led to many other voyages and colonies.

2. John Cabot

Learning from Columbus, John Cabot became interested in finding a shorter route across the ocean. England sponsored Cabot to sail through the North Atlantic in 1497. Cabot thought he had landed in Asia, but it was actually what is now Canada. His voyage proved a northern route to the Americas could work. He met the Eastern Woodland Native Americans.

3. Pedro Álvares Cabral

In 1500, Portugal paid for Pedro Cabral to take 13 ships to India for trade. Cabral’s plan was to sail around Africa, but on the way, his ships sailed far into the Atlantic. This misdirection caused Cabral to land on the coast of South America. He met the Tupiniquim people.

4. Jacques Cartier

France hoped to find a northwest passage to reach the Pacific Ocean through North America. In 1534, France paid for Jacques Cartier to search. Cartier sailed up rivers in what is now Canada. He didn’t find a route to the Pacific, but he did meet the Mi’kmaq people and the powerful Iroquois Confederacy. Cartier’s trips started French trade in North America.

5. Francisco Vásquez de Coronado

Starting in Mexico in 1540, Coronado led an expedition for Spain in search of the Seven Cities of Cibola, which were said to be full of amazing wealth just waiting to be taken. Along the way, the expedition discovered the Grand Canyon and found many Native American villages, but there was no gold in any of them. Coronado passed through Arizona and New Mexico, crossed west Texas and the Oklahoma panhandle, and then entered Kansas around what is now Liberal. His trek took him through what is now Plains, Meade, Fowler, Minneola, and Dodge City.

title: The Tools of Discovery
text:
Hundreds of years ago, explorers traveled the oceans. How did they know where they were? Advances in technology, mathematics, and measurement in the 1400s made long-distance navigation possible. One good example of the methods they used comes from Columbus, who was one of the first navigators to keep detailed accounts of his voyage.

Some tools that Columbus used helped with celestial navigation, or using the sun, moon, and stars to find location. Sailors used an instrument called an astrolabe that they would point to the sky. Using the sun during the daytime and the North Star at night, sailors would point the indicator on the astrolabe at their chosen celestial object, then read a dial to determine their latitude. Another tool explorers used was the quadrant. A quadrant was used to determine altitude, the height of a fixed point above sea level.

These tools led to advances in map-making, or cartography. The original purpose of maps wasn’t to be accurate in size or proportion. Instead, they showed who had control of the land. Once maps showed more exact distances and details, they were easier to follow. The invention of printing also made maps easier to obtain.

Even the new ships Columbus sailed on aided in exploration. The caravel, a ship with broad bows and beams, was smaller, lighter, and easier to navigate than older boats. Their lighter weight and smaller design also made them faster. Most ships only had one kind of sail, but caravels were equipped to use both. With both square and triangular sails, caravels could sail into the wind. It also allowed them to sail both along shorelines and in open water. Though they were small, they had thick planking and could carry a lot of goods or people.

title: Exploration: Then and Now
text:
Does exploration change the world?

Questions are at the heart of every explorer and adventurer. Questions that explorers ask include: What if? What about? Why not? Where does this go? How does this work? The purpose of asking questions is to find answers. This was true for people of ancient times, and it is true today.

Why do people explore and search for answers? The reasons vary for each person. For some people, the reason is to simply find answers to their questions. Others are driven by a desire for glory or recognition. There are others who simply want to get paid for finding the answer. During the Age of Exploration, many Europeans explored the Americas to find resources and claim new land. More resources and land meant more money. Still, others are motivated in search of something new. For example, many scientists explore to find new medicines and treatments to help people who are sick. There are many reasons people explore.

What makes a good explorer? Explorers have to be persistent, accurate, curious, and patient. Explorers are also good at problem-solving, looking for patterns, planning, making models, and taking risks.

You are an explorer every day when you explore something you don’t know. The same characteristics explorers had in the past are necessary when you set out to learn something new today.

Be an explorer every day. Ask questions, find answers, and share so that others can learn.
