title: Trade, Taxes, and Scarcity
text:
Trade is one way people meet their wants and needs. Trade with others creates a trade network. In Europe, there was a trade network between Europe and the Indies. The “Indies” was what Europe called Asia in the 1400s. The trade network covered a route known as the Silk Road. This trade route was used for centuries.

Caravans were groups of traders that traveled together. Caravans brought spices, tea, silk, and other goods from the Indies to sell to the people of Europe. The caravans traveled through many countries to reach Europe. Each country traded with the caravans. Goods that come into a country for sale are called imports. Goods made in a country and sent to another country for sale are called exports.

Spices were not a natural resource in Europe. The supply of spices imported to Europe depended on the caravans on the Silk Road. In the 1490s, the supply of spices and other goods from Asia was stopped. The Ottoman Empire controlled a large section of the Silk Road. The Ottomans put high taxes on the goods coming into their country. This made the goods very expensive. Many traders could not afford to pay the taxes to the Ottomans. Therefore, the goods did not move on to Europe.

When the demand for a good such as spices is high but the supply is low, there is scarcity. The monarchs of Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella, wanted spices and goods from Asia to be in the markets in Spain. They were not able to export any Spanish goods or import goods from the Indies. The Ottomans were blocking the land route. Another route to the Indies was needed. If Ferdinand and Isabella could meet the high demand for Asian goods, they could sell for a great profit. Spain could become very wealthy.

This is the reason Columbus came to Spain. He had the idea of sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach the Indies. The new technology for navigation on the seas made this a reasonable plan. Ferdinand and Isabella became the patrons of Columbus. They took a financial risk on Columbus, hoping he would reach the Indies and return with spices. Columbus returned to Spain with a cargo of goods far greater than spices. The risk Ferdinand and Isabella took paid off greatly. The trade that began in 1492 between Spain and the Americas is called the Columbian Exchange. This exchange would have an impact on both worlds.

title: African Culture Before Enslavement
text:
In Africa, three powerful empires reigned in the Sahara in the centuries before the age of encounters. What made these kingdoms so wealthy? Gold. What kept them strong? Religion, trade, and warring with rivals.

The Ghana Empire was rich for hundreds of years before it fell in the 1200s. There were many gold mines in the area. Ghana’s merchants had so much gold that even their animals wore it as a decoration!

Ghana was controlled by kings who listened to the arguments of their people and passed judgement. Not only were they powerful in their communities, but they were also powerful in the trade between nations.

Arabs came from the West with salt to trade for gold, ivory, and enslaved people. Ghana’s kings charged taxes as traders entered and left the country. The wealth of Ghana grew.

But competition for the gold trade was high. After the Ghana empire lost power, the Mali empire took over. Mali was in power from 1220 until about 1500. Trade continued to prosper under Mali leadership.

One of the Mali emipire’s leaders, Mansa Kankan Musa, was a devout follower of Islam. His religious beliefs helped unite the country. He built Timbuktu as a place of learning. Islam was taught to the people.

After Musa’s death, people argued for control of Mali. Rebellion led to collapse, and another empire rose to power.

The Songhai empire began to grow in the 1300s. It grew until it touched the Atlantic Ocean. Gao was the capital and a great marketplace. One leader of the Songhai, Sonni Ali, built a powerful army. He was known as the “Master of the Water” because he used the waterways to attack enemies. He took control of major trade routes and more wealth flowed into the city. The Songhai empire’s leaders also helped support scholars and students until the empire was defeated in battle and collapsed in 1591.

title: Archaeology: How Do We Know?
text:
There is no cell phone footage. There are no documentaries. There's not even a photograph to prove that native people had been living in the Americas for thousands of years before European explorers arrived.

How do we know that people were here for so long? How do we know anything about their lives?

People leave clues that help us understand them long after they are gone. Sometimes, ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind innovations we still use today. Some of these include crops, like corn, and medicines. People left behind objects they made, too. We call these archaeological evidence.

An archaeologist studies things left behind by people who lived a long time ago. Some objects, called artifacts, get covered by earth or water for thousands of years. Many become fragile. To avoid damaging them, archaeologists rarely use their hands to observe artifacts. Instead, they use dry brushes and other tools to clean them. This helps make sure that they won’t remove things like leftover paint and food from the artifacts. For example, stone tools that archaeologists find can reveal traces of foods that native peoples ate.

Archaeologists often recognize patterns. They may see differences between earlier objects and later, more advanced ones. They may find evidence of trade by tracking the movement of similar artifacts. For example, Knife River flint comes from what is now North Dakota. Artifacts made from this flint have been found throughout the western United States. They have also shown up as far east as Ohio and Pennsylvania. This evidence suggests that native Peoples traded the flint all across the country.

But archaeologists don’t only study objects. At archaeological sites, or places where there is evidence of past human activity, they also study structures and human-made features. Structures like native Peoples’ homes can suggest whether a certain group had more of a close-knit community or a complex, sprawling society. Features like fireplaces or storage pits can also help scientists imagine what daily life in ancient cultures was like.

Archaeologists study these artifacts carefully. It’s important to show respect to people from the past and their descendants. Sometimes when archaeologists dig, they unearth sensitive things. They may find places where people are buried. Some people think burials should be examined for evidence. Others think they should be left alone. New technology has helped archaeologists with this problem. Today, they can often scan areas without digging. Not having to dig allows them to show more respect for burial places.

When combined with other forms of evidence, artifacts can tell a story.

One of the oldest archaeological sites we know of in North America was found in Cactus Hill, Virginia. Here, archaeologists found evidence of a people known to have lived about 14,000 years ago.

As archaeologists dug deeper, layer by layer, into the earth of Cactus Hill, other artifacts were uncovered. These pointed to another group of people, dating back around 18,000 years. What piece of evidence suggested that a different group of American Indians had lived there? The tools were not the same as the ones found in the earth above them. That means that 4,000 years earlier, people camped and cooked and fished in the same place as those who came after them.

Archaeology has proven that the early peoples who lived in the Americas were skilled. They built complex societies, traded goods with other ancient peoples, and had vibrant, sophisticated societies in America for thousands of years.

title: Trade, Barter, and Money
text:
How people use resources to meet their wants and needs is the basis for economics. There are goods and services needed or wanted in a community. Meeting the wants and needs of the community is considered a trade network.

The Native Americans had resources they used to meet their wants and needs. We see this in how the homes and shelters of the tribes varied depending on what natural resources were around them in the environment. Tribes on the coast did not have the same resources as the people of the Great Plains. The same is true about their daily lives and their art. To meet their wants and needs, people would trade.

One tribe might have a good year farming and raising maize. Another tribe’s crops might be destroyed in a weather disaster. The extra maize of the first tribe would be needed in the second tribe. To acquire the maize, the second tribe would offer the first tribe another resource they had plenty of, such as furs or carved utensils.

Sometimes a tribe would send representatives out to communicate and make connections with other tribes. Sometimes the traders were welcomed with music and celebration. A market would be opened for goods to be shown and opportunities for families to make a trade on their own. This is called bartering. Each trader had to negotiate for a satisfactory trade. The trade would depend on how much one of the traders wanted or needed the goods or service. If every family had sufficient furs for the winter, they wouldn’t look to trade for furs. However, if there was scarcity of items, trade values would go up in those goods, and more goods would be required to make a satisfactory deal.

Tribes in the local region would offer common items for trade. What was common in one geographic region could be highly valued in different geographic regions. Coastal tribes found dentalium seashells common. However, inland tribes who had never been to the ocean found seashells a high-value trade item.

Bartering still occurs today. Any time you trade a good like an apple for another good, such as a string cheese, that is bartering.

title: Trade Goods
text:
Two thousand years ago, there was a great city of people located in what is now Ohio and Illinois. Modern scientists have studied the remains of the city. The artifacts tell us that Hopewell was a huge metropolis of people, religions, entertainment, and trade. The variety of trade goods was extensive and came from all over the continent. There, archaeologists have recovered ocean shells from the Gulf of Mexico. There is evidence of pigments, which were minerals and soil from the southwest used in paints. The paints were used on pottery, hides, and body decorations.

There was also evidence of mica. Mica is a mineral that is reflective and can be cut into thin sheets. Mica crystals are also used in paints, pottery, and decoration. The Appalachian Mountains on the east coast of North America have deposits of mica.

The Appalachian Mountains in Pennsylvania and New York also have large pockets of limestone. Limestone is easily ground down and can be white in color. The white powder of limestone was used in the production of a variety of goods. Limestone can be easily obtained from open pits on the sides of the mountains.

Chunks of green copper ore and creations from copper were also discovered in the Hopewell city. Copper ore is found in the west, near present-day Utah.

Ornaments, jewelry, utensils, and everyday items were also found in the archaeological digs of Hopewell. These items provide evidence to the modern world that a vibrant and extensive trade network was in place in the Americas by the time of the Hopewell city.

title: King George III, Parliament, and Taxes
text:
During the colonial period in America, the kings of Great Britain created the colonies through charters. The charters guaranteed certain things to both the colonists and Great Britain. The colonists were granted the rights of British citizens. Great Britain was assured that the government of each colony could not go against the laws of Great Britain. The charters set the expectations for how the colonists and the government of Great Britain would interact with one another.

However, the government of Great Britain was more than just the king. There was also Parliament to deal with. Parliament is a representative branch of the British government that makes the laws. Parliament works with the monarch (the king or queen) to govern Great Britain. The prime minister is the leader of Parliament and works closely with the monarch. Parliament and the monarchy work to take action and make laws. Parliament also creates and collects taxes to pay for government expenses.

The colonists often interacted with Parliament, especially when it came time for taxes to be collected. Only people living in Great Britain got to vote in the elections choosing members of Parliament. The colonists were subject to the laws and taxes Parliament created, but they did not get to vote.

Sometimes, the colonists tried to go around Parliament and appeal directly to King George III. King George III had his own struggles maintaining his authority with Parliament. If he sided too much with Parliament against the colonists, he was seen as weak. If he sided too much with the colonists against Parliament, he would not get enough taxes collected. It was a difficult balance of power to maintain.

This balancing act got even harder in 1763, the year the French and Indian War ended. Parliament looked at the cost of the war. They realized they didn’t have enough money in the treasury to pay the expenses from the war. Parliament had been putting money in the treasury with taxes and tariffs from trade with the colonies, but they needed more money. Raising taxes, creating new taxes, and collecting the taxes was the only way they could do this. Parliament decided that the colonists would have to pay the debt of the war. The colonists didn’t pay much in taxes compared to the people living in England at that time.

While in America during the French and Indian War, British Army officers got to know the colonists and their businesses. These British soldiers, called Regulars, lived in the colonies to protect citizens and help regulate Parliament’s taxes. The officers noticed that the colonists were not paying their taxes and shared this with Parliament. Many colonial merchants would not pay the taxes at the seaport (harbor) on goods coming in from Great Britain. Some colonists would smuggle goods into their warehouses. They bribed tax collectors to look the other way. A great deal of money was not being paid in taxes and therefore not going into the treasury of Great Britain. Parliament decided this could not continue. Over the next few years, Parliament created acts (laws) to get the needed taxes. The colonists were angry with the taxes and the laws.

title: The Acts of Parliament and Colonial Responses
text:
From 1764 to 1770, Parliament and the colonists had interactions that created various levels of conflict. Parliament felt it was within its right to tax the colonists based on the cost of keeping them safe during the French and Indian War. The colonists felt differently. Some colonists felt they should pay the various taxes. Others felt that the taxes and Parliament’s actions weren’t fair. Many colonists did not believe that Parliament treated the colonists as British citizens.

The charters of the colonies were important in providing colonists with the rights of British citizens. However, the colonies had no one to represent them in Parliament.

The prime minister and members of Parliament argued that the colonies had representative government in each colony. They argued that this meant the rights of colonists were being fulfilled. This became the dividing principle. Colonists wanted to have direct representation where decisions were made and taxes were created and levied. The members of Parliament claimed the colonies did not need representation in Parliament. Parliament represented all British citizens.

“No taxation without representation!” became the repetitive answer from the colonists to each of Parliament’s actions. Communication between all the groups (Parliament, King George, colonial legislatures, and the people) began openly. As the decade and actions of Parliament continued, communication from all parties broke down. This began a cycle of communication and conflict. As communication decreased, conflict increased.

1763

Act: Proclamation of 1763: Restricts settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.

Response: Colonists who fought in French and Indian War for lands are angered.

1764

Act: The American Duties Act: Allows the Royal Navy to board and inspect any ship in American waters.

Response: Raises concerns about the lessening of colonists’ rights.

April 5, 1764

Act: Sugar Act 1764, or American Revenue Act 1764: Makes trading for molasses and sugar more difficult. Taxes are also placed on several foreign goods.

Response: First colonial disagreement with Parliament published.

1765

Act: Stamp Act: A tax on all paper documents. First internal tax placed directly on American colonists by Parliament.

Response: Massachusetts urges colonies to boycott British goods.

March 24, 1765

Act: Quartering Act: Forces colonial authorities to provide food and lodging for British troops.

Response: Sons of Liberty organize.

December 1767

Act: New York Assembly suspended for protesting the Quartering Act.

Response: Tensions increase between colonists and Great Britain.

June-July 1767

Act: Townshend Revenue Acts: New York Restraining Act, Customs Service Reform and Townshend Duty Act. Tax placed on paint, paper, glass, lead, and tea imported into the colonies.

Response: Colonists begin boycotting British goods.

July 1768

Act: Massachusetts Assembly suspended for refusing to cancel boycotts.

Response: Unrest and mob violence break out.

1769

Act: Virginia House of Burgesses closed as punishment for Virginia Resolves opposing British policy.

Response: Boycotts spread to more colonies.

March 5, 1770

Act: Boston Massacre: Colonist civilians shot and killed by British soldiers.

Response: Colonists are outraged.

title: The Boston Massacre
text:
The streets of Boston were filled with soldiers in 1770. After passing the Townshend Acts of 1767, which placed new taxes on the colonists, Parliament sent troops to the colonies to make sure these new rules were followed. Four thousand troops arrived in 1768 to police the 20,000 residents of Boston. Over the next two years, these British Regulars lived in people's private homes and public buildings. They were even taking extra jobs around the town that could have been given to unemployed colonists. Tensions and hostilities grew between the colonists and soldiers until, one night, everything finally erupted.

It was the evening of March 5, 1770. A single guard, Private Hugh White, was on duty at the customs house on King Street. A verbal confrontation occurred between Private White and a Boston resident. Quickly, a crowd assembled and began pelting White with whatever they could get hold of: stones, oyster shells, ice, and chunks of coal. In all the turmoil, people began to toll the bells of the city’s churches. This was the usual signal for summoning help in fighting fires. More people gathered at the scene.

Captain Thomas Preston led seven soldiers to the customs house, rushing in to relieve Private White. They were greeted by a large and taunting crowd of civilians. The mob dared the soldiers to fire at them, knowing that the soldiers couldn’t. They were not allowed to fire their weapons within the city without first having permission from government authority. The taunting grew louder as more people gathered. The church bells continued to ring. Everywhere, voices loudly asked about the fire.

Private Hugh Montgomery fell to the ground. As he regained his footing, a voice yelled, “Fire!”

So, the soldiers fired.

Five civilians died as a result of the incident; three died on the scene, and two died later.

Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson rushed to the scene. Civilian leaders of Boston pressured him to remove the soldiers from the city to prevent further violence.

Hutchinson assured the leaders, “The law shall have its course. I will live and die by the law.”

Corporal William Wemms, James Hartigan, William McCauley, Matthew Kilroy, William Warren, John Carrol, Hugh Montgomery, Hugh White, and Captain Preston were arrested and held for trial.

The British soldiers were tried before the highest court in Massachusetts. As English subjects, they had a right to a fair trial by jury and competent defense counsel. Loyalists, or those loyal to England, wanted the soldiers to be freed. Patriots, or those who wanted independence, wanted the soldiers found guilty but also wanted to show that Boston would give them a fair trial.

There were two separate Boston Massacre trials, one for the captain and one for the soldiers he commanded. The lawyer for the defense of the soldiers was John Adams. John Adams was the cousin of Samuel Adams, who was the founder of the Sons of Liberty. Preston and six of his men were found not guilty; two others were found guilty.

The victims of the massacre—Crispus Attucks, Samuel Gray, James Caldwell, Samuel Maverick, and Patrick Carr— were buried at Granary Burying Ground in Boston. A combined funeral for those who died was held a few days later. The procession was said to have been joined by 10,000 people.

The years that followed the massacre, from 1770 to 1772, passed quietly, without any major confrontations between the British and the colonists. However, the Sons of Liberty used the event to turn public opinion further against the British. Paul Revere called it “The Bloody Massacre Perpetrated in Kings Street in Boston.” He created an engraving (picture) of the event to use as propaganda against the British government.

title: Crispus Attucks
text:
Crispus Attucks was known as a hero who stood up for and died defending his freedom and rights. For many years, Attucks was enslaved. At age 27, he ran away from his enslaver, William Brown, and became a merchant seaman.

Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty called on sailors and dock workers. They asked them to support the resistance to British military at the seaport. Attucks and his fellow workers did just that on the night of the Boston Massacre on March 5, 1770. Attucks was frustrated with the British Regulars taking jobs from colonists who wanted to work. He was at a local pub with other sailors when one of the Regulars came in and asked for work. Attucks and others chased the soldier out of the pub.

Later that same night, Attucks was killed in the Boston Massacre. Attucks was on King Street in Boston, near the customs house, when the Boston Massacre happened. When shots were fired by the soldiers, Attucks was the first to fall.

title: The Mason-Dixon Line
text: The Mason-Dixon Line was measured in 1763–1770. The original colonial charters from the king were used to settle a disagreement between Pennsylvania Colony and Maryland Colony. Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon were hired to map out the Mason-Dixon Line. They were two of the most respected English surveyors. A surveyor is a person who examines land and makes maps of it. The line settled the dispute and would play a role later on in our country. It was later used for dividing the North and South in the 1800s. It was a human-made line that marked the boundary between slave-holding states and states where slavery was illegal.

title: Types of Sources
text:
Historians study many types of sources to unlock the mysteries of the past. Written sources are the most common type of sources used by historians. These sources provide written evidence about specific events, time periods, and people throughout history. Written sources include books, newspaper articles, journals, letters, and important documents.

Historians also use visual sources. These include maps, photographs, paintings, and videos. Historians use these sources to study events and learn more about the past. Additionally, they analyze oral histories to learn more about events and people. Oral histories are interviews, recorded on audio or video, with someone who experienced an event in the past.

Historians use artifacts to understand the past. Artifacts are human-made objects that help us learn about past civilizations and how they developed. They can also be ordinary objects used in the past by people working or interacting with others. Artifacts help us understand what people’s lives were like. Artifacts can include tools, pottery, artwork, clothing, and jewelry. Historians work with archaeologists to determine the purpose of different artifacts. Archaeologists are scientists who excavate and study items left behind by people throughout history.

title: Primary Sources
text:
Primary sources are created by people who saw or experienced something. Primary sources are usually created around the time of an important historical event. They include historical and legal documents. They also include books, newspaper articles, letters, diaries, photographs, maps, drawings, and census data.

Something is a primary source only if it was created by someone who was present at an event or lived during the time period you are studying. Interviewing a parent, grandparent, or teacher about their own life can be a primary source. Analyzing and studying primary sources helps us make connections between past, present, and future events.

title: Secondary Sources
text: Secondary sources are made by people who didn't see or experience the event. These are usually created by people who have studied primary sources and then provide their interpretation. Secondary sources are textbooks, biographies, magazine articles, book reviews, encyclopedias, and documentaries. If you write a story about your vacation, it is a primary source. You were there and experienced the vacation. If someone interviews you and writes about your vacation, their story is a secondary source.

title: Multiple Perspectives
text:
When we see or read something, it's important to identify if it is fact or opinion. A fact is something that can be proven true through evidence. An opinion is a statement that expresses someone’s feelings or beliefs.

Everyone brings a unique perspective. Experiences and events may be interpreted differently by people with different cultural or individual perspectives. It's important to understand the perspectives of others. When we look at multiple perspectives, we can have a deeper understanding of what happened in the past. This helps us create the most accurate analysis of people and events in history.

When we study historical sources, it's important to be aware of multiple perspectives. Historians look for bias in sources. Bias means favoring one belief or opinion over others. Historians look for bias to separate the true meaning of the information from the author’s perspective.

title: How Do We Examine Sources?
text: Historians analyze sources to answer questions about the past. When we analyze something, it means that we study it carefully. To analyze sources, we investigate them. We want to know about the author or creator, the purpose, and the format. This will help us to be confident in the source.

title: Analyzing Primary Sources
text:
The Industrial Revolution was a time of great change throughout the world. The Industrial Revolution introduced assembly lines and machines that made production easier. It began in England around 1760 and spread to the United States in the early 1800s. During this time, many people went from living and working on farms to living in cities and working in factories. Men, women, and children worked in factories to support their families. How did life change for people during the Industrial Revolution? How were their lives different from people’s lives today? Analyze the primary sources below to find evidence about life during the Industrial Revolution.

Life of Men During the Industrial Revolution

Many men looked for new economic opportunities during the Industrial Revolution. They moved from rural farm areas to urban cities to work in factories. Those who found work felt lucky to have a job. What evidence can you gather from the photograph about the lives of industrial workers? What were their working conditions like?

Life of Women During the Industrial Revolution

The following source is an excerpt from Loom and Spindle: Life Among the Early Mill Girls (1898), the autobiography of Harriet Hanson Robinson. She was a female textile mill worker in Lowell, Massachusetts, from 1834 to 1848. Harriet worked in the Lowell mills from the age of nine until she turned 23.

What can you learn about the lives of women during the Industrial Revolution from this source? What was factory work like? Do you think the workers were happy?

The early mill girls were of different ages. Some were not over ten years old; a few were in middle life, but the majority were between the ages of sixteen and twenty five. The very young girls were called "doffers." They "doffed," or took off, the full bobbins from the spinning frames, and replaced them with empty ones. These mites [young girls] worked about fifteen minutes every hour and the rest of the time was their own.

When the overseer was kind they were allowed to read, knit, or go outside the mill­yard to play. They were paid two dollars a week. The working hours of all the girls extended from five o'clock in the morning until seven in the evening, with one half ­hour each, for breakfast and dinner. Even the doffers were forced to be on duty nearly fourteen hours a day.

The most prevailing incentive to labor was to secure the means of education for some male member of the family. To make a gentleman of a brother or a son, to give him a college education, was the dominant thought in the minds of a great many of the better class of mill girls. I have known more than one to give every cent of her wages, month after month, to her brother, that he might get the education necessary to enter some profession. I have known a mother to work years in this way for her boy. I have known women to educate young men by their earnings, who were not sons or relatives. There are many men now living who were helped to an education by the wages of the early mill girls.

Life of Children During the Industrial Revolution

Examine the primary source. What do you notice about the children in the photograph? What do you think their lives were like?

How are people’s lives different today? Think about your life and the life of your family. Compare it to the evidence you collected from the primary source documents. Write a paragraph discussing how your life is different from the lives of people who lived and worked during the Industrial Revolution.

title: What Is an Inquiry?
text:
To solve a mystery, good detectives ask questions and search for evidence. This is known as an inquiry. An inquiry is a way to investigate a problem or to ask for more information. A successful inquiry requires three steps:

Asking questions

To begin the inquiry process, you must start by asking questions. In order for an inquiry to be successful, you have to ask specific questions throughout the process. By asking questions, you can develop your claim. A claim is a statement you make about what you believe can be supported with evidence.

Processing evidence

The next step is to collect and process evidence. Evidence is information gathered from sources to answer inquiry questions. The more evidence you gather, the stronger your claims will be.

Completing tasks to help solve the mystery

The final step to complete an inquiry is to create a final product that connects the inquiry questions to the evidence. This could be something you create or present after completing your research.

title: Week 1 Essential Question
text: How does the inquiry process help with learning?

title: Types of Questions
text:
Asking questions is the first step in an inquiry. There are many types of questions you can ask throughout the inquiry process.

Compelling Questions

The word compelling refers to something that sparks your interest and is exciting. Answering a compelling question requires deep thinking. There could be multiple answers to the same question. The answer you come up with depends on the evidence you find in your research. An example of a compelling question is: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone?

Supporting Questions

A supporting question gives you the information that you need to answer the compelling question. While a compelling question might have different answers depending on your research, a supporting question usually has only one answer. These answers give you the evidence you need to solve the mystery!

Each type of question is important and is needed for a strong inquiry.

Compelling Question: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone? To support your compelling question, you could ask:

What is the Bill of Rights?

What are rights?

What rights does this document protect?

Why was this document created?

Each type of question is important and is needed for a strong inquiry.

title: The Lenses of Social Studies
text:
Problems and questions that are compelling are usually big. This means it is necessary to investigate them through the lenses of different professionals in the field.

Thinking like a …

Historian

A historian researches and studies the past. They make claims to help us understand how people used to think and live.

Geographer

A geographer thinks about people and how they live and work in their environment. They make claims that help people build communities and use resources.

Political Scientist

Political scientists think about how government works. They help community leaders make laws for their people.

Social Scientist

Social scientists study the whole person: academic, social, emotional, physical, and mental. They analyze the effects that behaviors and emotions have on people or groups of people.

Economist

An economist thinks about money and finance. They look at money and production in a community. They make claims about the economy to help people make financial choices.

title: What Makes You Think That?
text:
During the inquiry process, we make claims about compelling questions. Your job is to research information and provide evidence to support your claim. Evidence can change our thinking and beliefs about a topic or idea. This is known as the reflection process.

To reflect on an idea means to think deeply about it and decide if it is still the best solution. The most successful thinkers are people who know how to reflect and change their thinking as needed. You can use the following sentence starters to build a claim for the compelling question: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone?

Make a claim!

I think _______ because ________.

Then think about the evidence!

I know this because …

According to the author …

In the picture, we can see …

From what I read in the text, we can see …

The most important evidence I found was …

If you were to make an initial claim on the example compelling question, what would it be and why?

title: Finding a Problem to Solve
text:
People often face many problems that need to be solved. Think about the compelling question that we have developed: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone?

Before the American Revolution, the British Parliament passed the Quartering Act. This act required colonists to house British soldiers in their homes or provide barracks for them at their own expense. To ensure this would not be a problem in the future, Congress included the Third Amendment in the Bill of Rights. The Third Amendment states that "No Soldier shall, in time of peace be quartered in any house, without the consent of the Owner, nor in time of war, but in a manner to be prescribed by law."

What steps can you take to answer the question and solve the problem?

Problem-Solving Steps:

What was your claim and why did you make it?

This is where we can look at the evidence and think about who needs help.

Ask yourself: What has to happen for the problem to be solved?

Think back to our lenses of social studies. Ask the questions that a historian, economist, geographer, or political scientist may ask. You may find a few possible solutions there! Write down three of those possible solutions.

Think about the hardest parts of each solution. Write those down.

Ask yourself: Who needs to be involved? Who has the power to change the problem?

Think about what you are good at and what may be difficult for you. Which solution makes the most sense for YOU?

Once you have looked at different solutions, pick one and try out your inquiry!

Ask yourself the compelling question again, and determine how you can solve the problem!

title: Diving Deeper: Thinking About Point of View
text:
Your personal history is different from everyone else's. This means you think about problems in ways that are unique to you. This can influence your point of view on different topics.

When you make a claim about a problem or question, you make it based on your point of view. This is also called perspective. Your perspective is extremely important. It helps you think about inquiry, define problems, and develop solutions to these problems.

Your perspective can be different from others. It is also important to think about other people's perspectives. Their insight might be different from yours, but it may help solve problems more efficiently.

title: Responding to a Compelling Question
text:
The inquiry process has several steps. You must determine the problem, search for evidence, and make connections to draw a conclusion. Finally, this will help you answer your compelling question.

Your compelling question will determine the information you need to look for. For example, let's say you want to answer the compelling question: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone? You should first search for sources that provide information about the creation of the Bill of Rights. Then, look for changes that have been made to the document and its impact on American citizens today.

Once you have determined what you are looking for, you can identify sources that will help you answer the compelling question. The most important thing to consider when answering a compelling question is how you use your sources. The sources you use can determine your answer to your compelling question.

title: Week 3 Essential Question
text: How does analyzing primary and secondary sources help us learn?

title: Research Skills
text:
There are several things to consider when conducting research. When examining sources, you should ask yourself: Is it credible? Credible means that you can trust the information from the source.

To determine if a source is credible, you should look at the author, or creator of the source. A credible author is an expert on the subject they are writing about. You should also determine the date when the source was created. Older sources may include information that is out-of-date or has been proven incorrect by later research.

When researching, you should ask yourself: Does the information seem to be accurate? What is the purpose of the information? Does it seem to have a specific tone? How is the information presented? Are there grammatical errors in the writing?

title: Evaluating Evidence
text:
Once you have analyzed your sources, it is time to evaluate them. To evaluate means to determine which information is most useful to you. When you evaluate sources in an inquiry, it means you determine the information that is most useful in answering the compelling question.

To begin this process, you should review all of the information you gathered from your research. This information is your evidence. Evidence is information or data that supports an argument. Evidence from your sources should be ranked by which pieces are most helpful in proving your point.

Then, make sure you are using credible sources. Once you have determined their credibility, you can use corroboration. Corroboration means finding evidence from multiple sources to support your claim. If you are able to provide corroboration with your sources, you strengthen your argument!

title: Analyzing Sources
text:
Once you have found and determined whether your sources are credible, you will analyze your evidence. Your analysis will look different based on the sources you use. Primary sources are firsthand accounts of events, people, and places. Secondary sources are described by someone who didn't witness the event or didn't live during the period of time they are writing about. There are different steps you can follow to analyze sources effectively.

Analyze

To analyze a text source, you can do a close reading. Close reading is thinking about what you are reading. During a close read, you can annotate the text, or take notes, to understand the text better. You should also pay close attention to the sequence of the text. Sequence is the order of ideas in the text. Knowing the order of thoughts and events is important because it will help you understand how the author came to their conclusion. This will aid you in developing your own conclusions about an idea or topic.

Determine Context

Examining context assists researchers when analyzing different types of sources. Context identifies the things that influence what is in the source and how it is presented. When analyzing the context of a source, the first two things to look for are when and where the source was produced.

Next, you should determine why the source was made. Sources can be created to promote different ideas, explain information, or express the author's opinions. The final thing to consider when analyzing context is to make connections between the time when the sources were created and events happening during that time. This can aid in your understanding of ideas and information in sources.

title: Constructing an Argument
text:
Once you have identified your compelling question, conducted research, analyzed your sources, and evaluated your evidence, it's time to construct your argument. An argument is also called a thesis.

A thesis states your argument and what you are trying to prove. To create a thesis statement, you should use your compelling question and evidence. To create a thesis statement:

Use the compelling question to create a stem for your thesis.

Examine your evidence and create a broad concept that you can add to your thesis stem. You can expand your explanation through additional paragraphs or presentations.

title: Justify Your Claim
text: Justifying your claim requires a careful presentation of your argument and evidence. You must present your argument first and then provide evidence to support it. When presenting your information, you should include your thesis statement and the evidence that supports it. Make sure you follow the rules of writing when constructing your argument.

title: Looking Back at Your Inquiry
text:
Let’s think about the compelling question again: Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone?

Now, it’s time to review your steps:

What is your claim?

Determine the lens of social studies you wish to use in order to answer the compelling question. What lens did you choose?

As a researcher, you gathered and evaluated evidence. What evidence did you look at? What information did you find?

You reflected on your claim. Did your claim stay the same, or did it change?

Finally, think about what it means to make a difference. Why is that so important to your problem?

After all of that thinking, now we look at the final step. This step is taking action and communicating your conclusions.

Now that you’ve learned about a problem, you know why it is important, and you have an idea of what to do about it. Let’s put a plan into action!

title: Week 4 Essential Question
text: Why should information be shared with others?

title: Diving Deeper: What Does It Mean to Have Empathy?
text:
People can have different perspectives and points of view about the same problem. It's important to respect other people's perspectives and points of view. This is called empathy. Empathy is the ability to understand and share somebody else's feelings. A good example would be to think about a problem that is not your own and ask, "How does that make them feel?" This helps you to understand the problem from their perspective.

One of the fundamental rights protected by the Bill of Rights is freedom of speech. Citizens have the right to express their opinion. However, does that give us the right to say whatever we want without consequences?

Pretend that one of your classmates is being made fun of for the clothes they wear. This is a problem we can solve using empathy. An empathy map helps us understand how empathy impacts a problem.

See:

student sitting alone at lunch

student visibly upset and frustrated with the situation

students laughing at a classmate

Hear:

classmates saying hurtful things to another student

student asking classmates to stop making fun of them

Think and Feel:

How can I help this student?

Why are others making fun of them?

I don’t want to be made fun of.

It is not okay to say whatever you want to someone.

Say and Do:

I want to help.

Talk to the student to understand their situation.

Discuss the problem with an adult.

Pains:

You could be the only one who wants to help.

The student may not want your help.

Others may not believe you.

Gains:

You could gain a new friend.

You could build a better classroom community.

You can help others express their feelings and opinions in a better way.

title: Applying Inquiry to a Problem
text:
What does taking action look like? You can take action in many different ways. You could write or create a letter, website, poster, art project, or article to discuss and solve the problem. You could also lead a project, volunteer, or develop a business idea to resolve the issue. The possibilities are endless!

Creating something takes a lot of skill. Think about your talents and the ways you can persuade others to help you develop a solution. To be persuasive means to be able to change somebody’s thinking and ideas to align with your own. If you care a lot about an issue, you may need to persuade people to care about it as much as you do. To do this, you must present the evidence you gathered and explain its importance!

To connect your ideas with a solution, you must consider three important factors:

What?

So what?

Now what?

What?

What is it that you are trying to do? Explain your project in detail with everything that you learned. Include all of the evidence you found.

So what?

You’ll need to answer the question “Why should people care?” Use your evidence to help people understand why your project matters. What are your long-term goals, and what do you want to achieve?

Now what?

Explain the action steps you need to take and how your project will benefit others. Should other people help your cause? What do you need to solve the problem? This is where you detail everything that you need for success. Don’t be afraid to ask your teachers or family for help!

title: Making a Difference
text:
Dylan Mahalingam

Dylan Mahalingam is a child welfare and environmental rights activist. He encourages young people to get involved and make a difference in their communities. When he was nine years old, Dylan cofounded Lil’ MDGs. It is an organization that helps children use the internet and social media in a positive way.

Dylan’s efforts have encouraged over three million children to improve the rights of individuals around the world. His organization continues to work with 24,000 volunteers per year from 41 countries. Dylan also serves as a youth speaker for the United Nations.

Malala Yousafzai

Malala Yousafzai was born and raised in Pakistan. In 2009, when Malala was 12 years old, the Taliban invaded the region of Pakistan where she lived. The Taliban are a religious extremist group who want to force their radical views onto other people. They believe that women should not receive an education. Malala disagreed. When the Taliban came into her city and forbade girls from attending school, she spoke up and campaigned for girls’ education. This put her in danger, but she continued to fight for the rights of all children. At the age of 14, Malala was shot by a member of the Taliban and almost died.

In 2013, she published her first book, called I Am Malala. The book chronicles her struggles and her fight for equal rights. On Oct. 10, 2014, Malala was made a corecipient of the Nobel Peace Prize for her dedication to education rights. In 2017, the United Nations named her the youngest ever official Messenger of Peace.

title: Tools to Help You Take Your First Steps in Your Inquiry Journey
text:
Your Observations, Feelings, and Thoughts

Nothing is more powerful than what you see or feel. You can start your inquiry journey by reflecting on your own observations, feelings, and thoughts. Look around your home, school, or neighborhood. Ask yourself questions to start your inquiry. What are you passionate about? When you are passionate about something, you are very interested in it and connected to it. Are you an animal lover, or do you care a lot about the environment? Is there a problem you see but nobody else does?

Local News

It's important to be aware of events that are happening in your community. Local news covers important stories that affect where you live. Local news outlets, such as newspapers and television programs, discuss positive and negative events that occur in your community. Talking to your family and teachers about the local news can help you understand what is happening and determine problems that you can help solve.

Internet Research

Conducting a simple search on the internet can help you see problems beyond your community. This includes the state, national, and international level. Talk to your family and teachers about safe ways to search the internet in order to find credible information.

Library of Congress

Did you know our country has its own library? It is called the Library of Congress. The Library of Congress has various collections of newspapers, books, documents, photographs, music, and many other types of sources created in our nation’s history. Many of their collections are available on the internet and are readily accessible to researchers of all ages.

Practice will always make perfect when it comes to inquiry. Looking at historical events or ideas helps you understand how you can use inquiry to help your community today.

title: Writing to Communicate Persuasively
text:
You can use the RAFT technique to help you understand and analyze the evidence you collected during your research.

Role of the Writer: Who is the writer? Why are they writing?

Audience: Who is the author writing to?

Format: In what format is the author writing? Is it a letter? A poem? A speech? Is it informational?

Topic: What problem is the author addressing? What change does the author want to happen?

title: Can You Persuade Me?
text:
Persuading a person to change their thinking is not an easy task. We need evidence and facts to support the claim we are trying to make. This is why it's so important to look at as much evidence as we can and ask good questions. There are many ways to persuade an audience.

Two common ways are persuading with reason or with emotion. Either way, the goal is to create a call to action for people to help us change a problem using your solution. A call to action means getting people to act in a way that we need them to so a problem can be solved.

Reason

“Just the facts, please” is a phrase we might often hear. It relates to facts the reader should know when it comes to understanding a problem we're trying to solve. A writer needs to give reasons and present the facts when writing to persuade readers. This is known as persuasion through reason. Reason means to use evidence to change someone’s mind and call them to action. Think about how you will use facts to persuade your audience.

Emotion

This form of persuasion relies on how you feel about a problem or letting someone else know how it affects you personally. This reaches out to a person’s empathy to persuade them to change their mind. Remember, empathy is connecting with another person's thinking and feelings. These emotions could show how a problem makes you or someone else feel. Will you persuade your audience through emotion or through reason?

The complexity of your problem will help you decide what the best way is to persuade your audience and support your claim. No matter how you persuade your audience, it's still important to consider all the evidence. That way, your claim is supported with facts and evidence.

title: The Inquiry Process
text:
Use the compelling question "Does the Bill of Rights protect everyone?" or create one of your own. Follow the inquiry process.

Ask a compelling question.

What do I want to know about this?

What do I already know? / What evidence do I already have?

What else do I need to find out?

Make a claim.

What is a possible answer?

What supporting question will help me focus my research?

Search for answers. / Experiment.

What kinds of resources will help me find answers?

Where can I find the resources?

How do I know the information is credible?

title: Essential Question
text: What does it mean to interpret information?

title: Where Can I Find Information?
text:
News

The news delivers information about your world. Local news stories tell you about your local community. The news also addresses events that happen in your state, your country, and places around the world. Reporters are people who write and talk about the news.

Libraries

Libraries are places that contain books, magazines, newspapers, and sometimes videos and music. Most schools and communities have a library. They are great places to do research. Librarians are people who work at libraries. They can teach you how to do research.

Internet Research

The internet has a lot of information. Not all of the information on the internet is accurate. It is important to analyze the information you find online. It is also important to learn how to stay safe on the internet. A librarian, teacher, parent, or other trusted adult can help you.

title: What Is an Inquiry?
text:
To solve a mystery, good detectives ask questions and search for evidence. This is known as an inquiry. An inquiry is a way to investigate a problem or to ask for more information. A successful inquiry requires three steps:

Asking questions

Processing evidence

Completing tasks to help solve the mystery

To begin the inquiry process, you must start by asking questions. In order for an inquiry to be successful, you have to ask specific questions throughout the process. By asking questions, you can develop your claim. A claim is a statement you make about what you believe can be supported with evidence.

The next step is to collect and process evidence. Evidence is information gathered from sources to answer inquiry questions. The more evidence you gather, the stronger your claims will be.

The final step to complete an inquiry is to create a final product that connects the inquiry questions to the evidence. This could be something you create or research you present.

title: Week 1 Essential Question
text: How does questioning help you learn?

title: Types of Questions
text:
Asking questions is the first step in an inquiry. There are many types of questions you can ask throughout the inquiry process.

Compelling Questions

The word compelling refers to something that sparks your interest and is exciting. Answering a compelling question requires deep thinking. There could be multiple answers to the same question. The answer you come up with depends on the evidence you find in your research. An example of a compelling question is: What causes people to change where they live?

Supporting Questions

A supporting question gives you the information that you need to answer the compelling question. While a compelling question might have different answers depending on your research, a supporting question usually has only one answer. These answers give you the evidence you need to solve the mystery!

Each type of question is important and is needed for a strong inquiry.

Compelling Question: What causes people to change where they live? To support your compelling question, you could ask:

What factors influence settlement?

What causes people to move from one place to another?

Does the environment play a role in the way people live?

title: How Can the Lenses of Social Studies Help Us Think About Inquiry?
text:

A political scientist may think ...

How do changes in their physical environment impact them physically and emotionally?

title: What Makes You Think That?
text:
During the inquiry process, we make claims about compelling questions. Your job is to research information and provide evidence to support your claim. Evidence can change our thinking and beliefs about a topic or idea. This is known as the reflection process.

To reflect on an idea means to think deeply about it and decide if it is still the best solution. The most successful thinkers are people who know how to reflect and change their thinking as needed. You can use the following sentence starters to build a claim for the compelling question "What causes people to change where they live?"

Make a claim!

I think _________ because __________.

And then think about the evidence!

I know this because ... According to the author … In the picture, we can see … From what I read in the text, we can see … The most important evidence I found was …

If you were to make an initial claim on the example compelling question, what would it be and why?

title: Diving Deeper: Thinking About Point of View
text:
Your personal history is different from everyone else's. This means you think about problems in ways that are unique to you. This can influence your point of view on different topics.

When you make a claim about a problem or question, you make it based on your point of view. This is also called perspective. Your perspective is extremely important. It helps you think about inquiry, define problems, and develop solutions to these problems.

Your perspective can be different from others. It is also important to think about other people's perspectives. Their insight might be different from yours, but it may help solve problems more efficiently.

title: Types of Sources
text:
Historians study many types of sources to unlock the mysteries of the past. Written sources are the most common type of sources used by historians. These sources provide written evidence about specific events, time periods, and people throughout history. Written sources include books, newspaper articles, journals, letters, and important documents.

Historians also use visual sources. These include maps, photographs, paintings, and videos. Historians use these sources to study events and learn more about the past. Additionally, they analyze oral histories to learn more about events and people. Oral histories are interviews, recorded on audio or video, with someone who experienced an event in the past.

Historians use artifacts to understand the past. Artifacts are man-made objects that help us learn about past civilizations and how they developed. They can also be ordinary objects used in the past by people working or interacting with others. Artifacts help us understand what people’s lives were like. Artifacts can include tools, pottery, artwork, clothing, and jewelry. Historians work with archaeologists to determine the purpose of different artifacts. Archaeologists are scientists who excavate and study items left behind by people throughout history.

title: Primary Sources
text:
Primary sources are created by people who saw or experienced something. Primary sources are usually created around the time of an important historical event. They include historical and legal documents. They also include books, newspaper articles, letters, diaries, photographs, maps, drawings, and census data.

Something is a primary source only if it was created by someone who was present at an event or lived during the time period you are studying. Interviewing a parent, grandparent, or teacher about their own life can be a primary source. Analyzing and studying primary sources helps us make connections between past, present, and future events.

title: Multiple Perspectives
text:
When we see or read something, it's important to identify if it is fact or opinion. A fact is something that can be proven true through evidence. An opinion is a statement that expresses someone’s feelings or beliefs.

Everyone brings a unique perspective. Experiences and events may be interpreted differently by people with different cultural or individual perspectives. It's important to understand the perspectives of others. When we look at multiple perspectives, we can have a deeper understanding of what happened in the past. This helps us create the most accurate analysis of people and events in history.

When we study historical sources, it's important to be aware of multiple perspectives. Historians look for bias in sources. Bias means favoring one belief or opinion over others. Historians look for bias to separate the true meaning of the information from the author’s perspective.

title: Secondary Sources
text: Secondary sources are made by people who didn't see or experience the event. These are usually created by people who have studied primary sources and then provide their interpretation. Secondary sources are textbooks, biographies, magazine articles, book reviews, encyclopedias, and documentaries. If you write a story about your vacation, it is a primary source. You were there and experienced the vacation. If someone interviews you and writes about your vacation, their story is a secondary source.

title: How Do We Examine Sources?
text: Historians analyze sources to answer questions about the past. When we analyze something, it means that we study it carefully. To analyze sources, we investigate them. We want to know about the author or creator, the purpose, and the format. This will help us to be confident in the source.

title: Responding to a Compelling Question
text:
The inquiry process has several steps. You must determine the problem, search for evidence, and make connections to draw a conclusion. Finally, this will help you answer your compelling question.

Your compelling question will determine the information you need to look for. For example, let's say you want to answer the compelling question: What causes people to change where they live? You should first search for sources that provide information about how different groups of people live. Then, you can search for information about how people modify, adapt to, and depend on their environment.

Once you have determined what you are looking for, you can identify sources that will help you answer the compelling question. The most important thing to consider when answering a compelling question is how you use your sources. The sources you use can determine your answer to your compelling question.

title: Research Skills
text:
There are several things to consider when conducting research. When examining sources, you should ask yourself, “Is it credible?” Credible means that you can trust the information from the source.

To determine if a source is credible, you should look at the author, or creator of the source. A credible author is an expert on the subject they are writing about. You should also determine the date when the source was created. Older sources may include information that is out-of-date or has been proven incorrect by later research.

When researching, you should ask yourself: Does the information seem to be accurate? What is the purpose of the information? Does it seem to have a specific tone? How is the information presented? Are there grammatical errors in the writing?

title: Energy Case Files
text: With a partner, discuss what Miguel wants to investigate. What is the purpose of his experiments?

title: Evaluating Evidence
text:
Once you have analyzed your sources, it is time to evaluate them. To evaluate means to determine which information is most useful to you. When you evaluate sources in an inquiry, it means you determine the information that is most useful in answering the compelling question.

To begin this process, you should review all of the information you gathered from your research. This information is your evidence. Evidence is information or data that supports an argument. Evidence from your sources should be ranked by which pieces are most helpful in proving your point.

Then, make sure you are using credible sources. Once you have determined their credibility, you can use corroboration. Corroboration means finding evidence from multiple sources to support your claim. If you are able to provide corroboration with your sources, you strengthen your argument!

title: Analyzing Sources
text:
Once you have found and determined whether your sources are credible, you will analyze your evidence. Your analysis will look different based on the sources you use. Primary sources are firsthand accounts of events, people, and places. Secondary sources are described by someone who didn't witness the event or didn't live during the period of time they are writing about. There are different steps you can follow to analyze sources effectively.

Analyze

To analyze a text source, you can do a close reading. Close reading is thinking about what you are reading. During a close read, you can annotate the text, or take notes, to understand the text better. You should also pay close attention to the sequence of the text. Sequence is the order of ideas in the text. Knowing the order of thoughts and events is important because it will help you understand how the author came to their conclusion. This will aid you in developing your own conclusions about an idea or topic.

Determine Context

Examining context assists researchers when analyzing different types of sources. Context identifies the things that influence what is in the source and how it is presented. When analyzing the context of a source, the first two things to look for are when and where the source was produced.

Next, you should determine why the source was made. Sources can be created to promote different ideas, explain information, or express the author's opinions. The final thing to consider when analyzing context is to make connections between the time in which the sources were created and events happening during that time. This can aid in your understanding of ideas and information in sources.

title: Constructing an Argument
text:
Once you have identified your compelling question, conducted research, analyzed your sources, and evaluated your evidence, it's time to construct your argument. An argument is also called a thesis.

A thesis states your argument and what you are trying to prove. To create a thesis statement, you should use your compelling question and evidence.

To create a thesis statement:

Use the compelling question to create a stem for your thesis.

Examine your evidence and create a broad concept that you can add to your thesis stem. You can expand your explanation through additional paragraphs or presentations.

title: Justify Your Claim
text: Justifying your claim requires a careful presentation of your argument and evidence. You must present your argument first and then provide evidence to support it. When presenting your information, you should include your thesis statement and the evidence that supports it. Make sure you follow the rules of writing when constructing your argument.

Collisions and Energy Transfer

Electricity and Electric Currents

Have you ever wondered how a tablet works? Or how flipping a switch can cause the lights to turn on? Electricity is energy that moves in electric currents. Electric currents are the flow of electricity from one place to another. Electricity can be found in nature, such as in lightning. The electric currents, or moving energy, are seen as a lightning bolt traveling through the sky. When electricity strikes an object, it can transfer energy and produce heat and sound energy.

Electricity can also be found in everyday items, where it can be controlled. Some everyday items that use electricity are lights, fans, stereo systems, toasters, refrigerators, and so on. Electricity always needs a source. In some everyday items, such as a tablet, the source may be a battery. In other items, such as a lamp, the source may be an outlet on the wall. Once electricity has a source, electric currents can carry electricity (or energy) along a path and transfer energy to the device. Electric currents can transfer energy from one device to another and create light, heat, sound, or motion! In your tablet, electric currents carry energy from the battery along a path until it reaches your screen and produces light. If the path becomes broken, electric currents cannot transfer energy from the source to the device.

Motion can create electric currents. Have you ever seen a wind turbine? When wind blows a wind turbine, the motion of the blade produces electricity. Another example is when water flows through a dam. The water turns the blades of a water turbine. The motion of the blades produces electricity.

title: Juneteenth
text: The Emancipation Proclamation declared that on January 1, 1863 all enslaved people would be free. News of the proclamation was slow to reach many parts of Texas. In other places, the news was hidden by slaveholders to preserve slavery. Two and a half years later, on June 19,1865, federal troops arrived in Galveston, Texas. African Americans celebrated when they heard the news that the Civil War had ended and that enslaved people were now free. Juneteenth is a short way of saying "June nineteenth." In 2021 it became an official national holiday. It is a day for African Americans to celebrate not only their freedom, but their history, culture and achievements. It is a day for all Americans to commit to the work of equality, and justice.

title: Thanksgiving
text:
Thanksgiving today is very different from what happened in the Plymouth Colony in the fall of 1621. The Pilgrims’ first year was very difficult. Only half of the colonists who arrived on the Mayflower made it through the winter. The Wampanoag Indians had helped them adapt and survive. To celebrate their first harvest, the Pilgrims held a feast. They had no oven and the sugar supply was almost gone, so there were no pies. Potatoes were not even grown in North America until at least 50 years later. The men probably did catch and cook wild turkeys.

The Wampanoag, who were invited to the feast, had also experienced a difficult year. They had lost many of their people because of disease. The Wampanoag were welcomed in the village, and so was the deer they brought to the feast. For three days, they shared in a celebration to give thanks.

title: Record Keeping in North America
text:
Many North American Indian tribes didn't have a written alphabet or use a written system of language. However, this doesn't mean that they did not keep records of important events and experiences. Native American tribes often used the resources from their environment to record information. One example is called petroglyphs. A petroglyph is a picture carved into rock. Petroglyphs represent important cultural beliefs, tribal stories, and significant events. Tribes living in the United States today consider petroglyphs sacred. They often gather around petroglyphs for celebrations and ceremonies.

Some Native American tribes used wampum as a form of record keeping. Wampum are small cylinder-shaped beads made from shells. They were strung together and worn as jewelry and belts. They were used to record important events, including treaties between tribes. The color and pattern of the beads represented different words and ideas. When woven together, the beads created a complete story or summary of the event.

title: The Medieval to the Early Modern Period
text:
In the fourth grade, you learned about ancient and classical civilizations. Building on that foundation, this year we will learn about medieval and early modern civilizations. This era spanned hundreds of years, from about 500 to 1500 C.E.

We will explore civilizations throughout the world, but mostly those in four major areas: Europe, Africa, Western Asia, and the Americas. During this period, these places were home to various civilizations like the Mali Empire, the Aztec, and the Inca. This era also included important historical events like the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Age of Exploration, and the European colonization of the Americas. The people who lived in these civilizations were developing more complex economic, political, and social systems. As these systems became more complex, global interactions increased. With new connections came new experiences and ideas, which created many transformations or changes.

Learning about this much history can be overwhelming. To help overcome this, we will focus on these areas of study: geography, economics, politics, and religion. Focusing on these areas will help us find connections between these different places and people. This study will help us understand some of the foundational changes that happened to create the modern era.
