title: Southwest Asia and North Africa
text:
In the year 395 C.E., the Roman Empire was split into two halves, the Western Roman Empire and the Eastern Roman Empire. The Eastern Roman Empire was also called the Byzantine Empire. The capital of the Roman Empire was moved from Rome to Constantinople around 330 C.E. Around the year 500 C.E., the Byzantine Empire encompassed much of the Mediterranean world. It even controlled the Western Roman Empire. However, the Byzantine Empire would lose the Western Roman Empire and its total area would also grow and shrink many times.

The Sasanian Empire occupied the area known by modern historians as the cradle of civilization, or the land of Mesopotamia. This area is considered to be the birthplace of writing and the code of law. Civilizations had fought for control of this area for centuries. The Roman Empire had been fighting with the Parthian Empire since 54

B.C.E. and the Eastern Roman Empire (the Byzantine Empire) continued to fight with the Sasanian Empire until 629 C.E.. The continual fighting between these empires would weaken them enough to give way to the rise of a new power, the Islamic Caliphates.

title: Europe
text:
In the year 330 C.E., the capital of the Roman Empire shifted from Rome to Constantinople. This shift moved the balance of political power out of Western Europe into the Byzantine Empire. Western European countries that had been once dominated by the Roman Empire, were now controlled by smaller, more regionalized authorities. The Western Roman Empire was conquered by a group called the Ostrogoths in the 500s. However, another power had taken hold in Western Europe, the Christian Church.

Christianity is a religion that worships Jesus of Nazareth. Christianity had become the official religion of the Roman Empire when Constantine I converted to the religion in the 300s. The highest office in the Christian Church is a bishop, and the Bishop of Rome is considered the rightful successor of Saint Peter, the chosen leader of Christianity after Jesus’ death and resurrection. The Bishop of Rome, also called the Pope, held a lot of influence in Western and Eastern Europe. There were other bishops in the Christian Church from many different cities, including a bishop in Constantinople. Bishops often had differing opinions about Christian doctrine and church authority. These differences of opinions were sometimes resolved, but would eventually lead to a schism, or a split in the Christian Church.

title: Treatment of Diverse Groups in the Colonies
text:
As the colonies grew, they attracted people from all over Europe. Early colonists sailed from England, Ireland, and Scotland. Over time, more traveled from the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Sweden. Thousands of immigrants journeyed to the Americas seeking new opportunities. People came from diverse cultures with different backgrounds and belief systems. Jewish people settled mainly in port cities like New Amsterdam (now, New York City) or Newport, Rhode Island. They were especially attracted to colonies founded on religious freedom. Some colonies, like Georgia, had charters that promised religious liberty to all people. Not all migrants were welcomed into the colonies or treated fairly, though. The poor and the powerless were often mistreated in the colonies, just as they had been in England.

Women were expected to follow strict guidelines of behavior. These guidelines restricted women to certain roles. They were expected to perform household chores like cooking, cleaning, and laundry. Women could wash other people’s laundry to earn money or food. They could also be midwives, who deliver babies, because these jobs were considered suitable for women. Women couldn’t have any rights unless they were married or had a male guardian.

A lot of people died of disease or starvation in the early colonies. Parents lost children, and children lost parents. Orphaned children often became servants for other families so they could survive. They had few rights until they married.

Most colonists didn’t trust people who were not residents. The law was not kind to a person without a home. Strangers were treated with suspicion. A person who could not pay their way or was deep in debt would be imprisoned until the debt could be paid.

English colonial leaders never accepted American Indians as citizens in their towns. American Indians were not seen as equals to white European settlers. Some were even enslaved by the colonists.

Most African Americans in the colonies were enslaved people. A few were born free, bought their freedom, or were set free by their enslavers. African Americans were rarely accepted by white colonists.

title: West Africa
text: West Africa was not a part of a written historical tradition, but an oral history tradition. Oral history is when important events are told from person to person and generation to generation, but are not written down. According to archaeology and oral history, West Africa was not a unified political kingdom around 500 C.E. West Africa consisted of smaller political groups, like tribes. West Africa was also a region rich in natural resources. Gold, ivory, and agricultural products were all located in the rich river valleys of West Africa, particularly along the Niger River. These goods were traded across the Sahara for centuries by a group of traders called the Berbers. The Berbers were a large ethnic and language group that lived in Northern Africa. They traded Mediterranean goods like horses, copper, and salt with West Africans for their gold and other resources. The Saharan trade lasted even as empires in Europe, Asia, and North Africa rose and fell. This trade and these desirable resources would lead to the rise of West African empires in the medieval and early modern era.

title: Americas
text:
Indigneous people lived across North, Central, and South America. Distinct cultures developed in each of these three regions. In North America, the Mississippian culture developed along the Mississippi River. One of the most distinctive features of the Mississippian culture was mound building. This culture continued into the era following 500 C.E.

In Central America, the Maya culture, which began in the 200s C.E., thrived until the sixteenth century. Another important city in Mesoamerica was Teotihuacán, which reached its peak around 500 C.E. The people of this city built three major pyramids and its pottery was traded all over Central America. Teotihuacán’s religion and architecture were so influential in Central America that the Toltec (400 years later) and Aztec people (a century later) adopted them.

Finally, in South America, many Andean cultures rose and fell in the coastal and mountain regions of the Andes Mountains. The Moche and Chimú lived on the coastal plains of Peru and built large adobe temples and other structures. The two greatest temples of the Moche were the temple of the sun and the temple of the moon. Both sun and moon were worshiped by the Moche as gods. The end of Chimú culture would come in the 1400s when the Inca would set out to conquer almost all the coastal areas of western South America.

title: Periods in History
text:
Calendars help people organize information in chronological order. Throughout history, different groups have created different calendars, each based on significant events. The Egyptians based their calendars on the lives of each pharaoh; a new calendar began every time a new pharaoh took the throne. The Islamic calendar is based on the year Muhammad migrated from Mecca to Medina. There are all kinds of calendars used across the world, the Hebrew calendar, Hindu calendars, Chinese calendars, and many more. Today, most of the world uses the Gregorian calendar for convenience. The Gregorian calendar is based on the birth of Jesus of Nazareth. The year 0 on the Gregorian calendar is the year Jesus is estimated to have been born. Anything before that date is labeled with a B.C., or B.C.E. For example, the Great Pyramid of Egypt was built in 3000 B.C.E. Anything after 0 is labeled with either A.D. or C.E. For example, the Chinese invented gunpowder and fireworks around 700 C.E.

In order to help organize the study of history, historians have split the Gregorian calendar even further by dividing the history of the world into time periods. This year, we will be studying the Middle Ages and the Early Modern Period. These time periods fit roughly between the years 500 C.E. and 1500 C.E. However, historical events and people’s lives don’t fit between nice, round numbers, so some of the events that we discuss happened in the years before 500 and extended into the years after 1500.

Prehistory (up to 600 B.C.E.)

Classical or Ancient History (600 B.C.E.–500 C.E.)

Medieval or Middle Ages (500 C.E.–1500 C.E.)

Early Modern (1500 C.E.–1750 C.E.)

Modern (1750 C.E.–present)

title: Sectionalism and Religious Conflict
text:
As more people came from England to North America, tensions increased between the colonies. Colonists came from different backgrounds. Some had different beliefs. Others developed different beliefs. How did this difference in beliefs affect life in the colonies?

Puritans came to New England for the freedom to practice their religion. In 1636, Puritan authorities banished Roger Williams because he said they should not punish people who disagreed with the Puritan religion. In 1637, Anne Hutchinson was also banished for disagreeing with Puritan leaders about religion.

Williams, Hutchinson, and others bought land from a Native American tribe, the Narragansett, and established a new colony, which later became Rhode Island. Just as the Puritans had left England to find religious freedom, Williams and Hutchinson had left Puritan Massachusetts to find that same freedom.

Other people tried to find ways to allow many beliefs in one colony. George Calvert was a British noble with the title Lord Baltimore. Calvert was Catholic. At the time, Catholics were persecuted in England and unwelcome in most colonies. So, the Calvert family left England and established Maryland, a Southern Colony. The Calverts welcomed other Christians, but those who came felt Catholics were preferred for jobs in leadership. Soon, there was fighting over religion in Maryland.

Like Catholics, Quakers were persecuted in England and unwelcome in most colonies. In the 1600s, William Penn, who worshipped as a Quaker, left England and established a new colony called Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania created an early constitution called the Charter of Privileges. Among other things, the charter guaranteed religious freedom and promoted tolerance. Tolerance was an important value in Quaker society.

Step by step, colonies offered more religious freedom. It wasn’t easy, but they began an experiment in independence that would change the world.

title: Did You Know: Engineering Design - Trash to Treasure
text:
When we think of the word "flexible," we often think of a gymnast who can bend and do flips. We do not always think of objects as being flexible. Can they be? Objects do not bend over backward or do handsprings. Since objects don't move like that, people might think that objects aren’t flexible. This is because we don’t test the flexibility of most objects. We often think objects are what they look like. However, materials used to make different objects can bend or shape around things. That ability is called flexibility.

Let’s use the example of a rope. A rope is a long, sturdy object. If we loop it around a tree branch, we can make a rope swing. We could use the rope to play a game, like tug-of-war. We can wrap a rope around a skateboard to pull our friend down the block. We could even use rope to tie a boat to the dock so the boat does not float away.

The rope is flexible, so it can be rolled, looped, or tied. This ability allows the rope to have many uses. We could not use a rock to make a rope swing. It would not work because the rock is not flexible. It just sits there! We have to look at all properties of an object to determine what it might be used for.

title: Did You Know: Home "Tweet" Home
text:
Have you ever looked at a house and thought that it was just one big box? Does it look like the wood came in a house shape? It is easy to believe. It seems like a house is all one big thing. But that’s not true. Many steps and many pieces are used to create a house.

First, someone chops down some trees. Then, people load all the cut trees on a truck. They drive those trees to a big machine that cuts and shapes them. The trees become rectangular wood pieces. Many things could be made from that set of wooden boards. People take the trees apart. They change the shape of the trees. Then they assemble these shapes into a whole new object.

We start with trees in a forest and end with a new house, a new school, or even a new treehouse. In the same way, concrete is mixed and shaped into blocks. Those blocks are put on top of each other. These small pieces can make something huge. It depends on how people use the small pieces and arrange them.

title: Think Like a Historian
text: Historians find, select, analyze, and evaluate sources. This helps them understand the past. We can also think like a historian. We can ask questions, such as: What happened? When did it happen? Who was involved? How and why did it happen? Historians use different forms of evidence, such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs, to find the answers to their questions. We call these sources.

title: Primary Sources
text: Historians use different sources to find out about people, places, and events in the past. There are two main types of sources. They are called primary sources and secondary sources. Primary sources are created by people who saw or experienced something themselves. These sources are usually created around the time of the event. They can include things like photographs, diaries, drawings, maps, and letters.

title: Secondary Sources
text: Secondary sources are made by people who did not see or experience events themselves. They are usually created by people who have studied primary sources. Secondary sources are things like textbooks, magazine articles, and book reviews. They are also encyclopedias and documentaries. If you write a story about your vacation, your story is a primary source. You were there and experienced the vacation. If someone interviews you and writes about your vacation, their story is a secondary source.

title: Past, Present, Future
text: History tells the story of people and events that happened in the past. The things we did yesterday are in the past. The things we are doing today are in the present. The things we do tomorrow and as we grow up are in the future.

These words are year, decade, score, and century. These words help us understand when something happened. They help us know when something was created.

How many days are in this month?

How many months are in a year?

title: Being Responsible at School
text: As a member of the school community, you follow the school's rules. You take good care of library books. You also take care of the equipment you use at recess.

title: Your Local Community
text: You live in a city or town. You obey the laws of your local community. You do so by picking up trash and recycling. When you ride your bicycle safely, you are obeying the laws of your community.

title: Rules in the Classroom
text: Rules in the classroom are often made by the students and teachers. Rules help us have order. They help us avoid conflict. Rules help us know the fair way to treat each other so that we can learn. Some rules might include how we take care of our belongings. One school rule could be that we raise our hands to speak. What are some of the rules in your classroom? Following the rules in our classroom shows respect for our classmates.

title: Rules at Home
text: Usually, families have rules at home. These rules are created for your protection and well-being. Rules help our homes run smoothly. Some rules at home could be telling the truth or listening to others. Maybe you have chores, or a time you have to go to bed. Following the rules at home helps us work together happily. It also helps us be safe.

title: Laws
text: Laws are rules written and approved by people in authority. Laws have consequences. Laws apply to everyone. Laws are created by community, state, and national governments. Laws protect the rights of people. They help resolve conflicts and promote the common good.

title: Laws in the City
text: Cities and towns have laws. Laws are made to help the city run well. They also keep people safe. For example, most cities have laws about not littering. These laws keep our cities clean and orderly. Some cities have leash laws for dogs. These are safety laws. Other cities require helmets when you ride your bike. When you ride your bicycle safely, you are obeying the laws of your city. When you don't obey the law, you might get a ticket.

title: Laws of the Country
text: The Constitution is the law of the United States. Laws make the country strong. Laws must agree with the Constitution. Every community has laws. If someone chooses not to obey the laws, there are consequences. A consequence is something that happens after making a choice and taking action. Consequences can be positive or negative. There are people in the community who help us obey the laws. Parents help us obey the rules at home. Teachers help us obey the rules in the classroom. The principal is responsible for helping us obey the school rules. The police are responsible for helping us obey the laws of our community.

title: Important Documents
text: One purpose of the government is to create laws. These laws are written down and displayed in documents. The United States has important documents. They include the Constitution, the Declaration of Independence, and the Bill of Rights. These documents outline our rights and responsibilities as citizens. Laws, treaties, and trade agreements are also considered important national documents.

title: The Declaration of Independence
text: The Declaration of Independence explains the rights of people. It says people have the right to "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." These rights are very important. The writers of the Declaration believed governments should protect these rights. The Declaration of Independence declared that Great Britain was violating those rights. It officially broke our ties with Great Britain. This began the creation of our nation.

title: The Constitution
text:
The Constitution of the United States is the country's law. It protects our natural rights. It defines our civil rights.

The Constitution has three parts. The preamble explains the purpose of the document.

The Articles explain how the government should be run. They define the power of the government. The Articles ensure that no branch has too much power. The Constitution checks the balance of power. It helps the power remain with the people.

The Amendments are changes made after the Constitution was written.

title: Amendments
text: Changes to the Constitution are called amendments. Amendments are additions designed to make a document better. The first 10 amendments are known as the Bill of Rights. They are not the only amendments that have been made over the years. Amendments made slavery illegal. Amendments gave women the right to vote. Amendments established the voting age as 18. Today, there are 27 amendments to the Constitution.

title: The American Flag
text: The American flag is a symbol of freedom. The flag has 13 stripes. There are seven red stripes and six white stripes. The stripes represent the first 13 states in the United States. The flag has 50 stars. There is one star for each state. The stripes on the flag are all the same width. The flag is a patriotic symbol of America.

title: Flag Day
text: We celebrate our flag on June 14. We call this Flag Day. Flying a flag on Flag Day is a way to show that you honor your country. The flag helps to remind us that we are all part of a community.

title: Pledge of Allegiance
text: Francis Bellamy wrote the Pledge of Allegiance. He hoped that the pledge would be used by citizens. The word pledge means we are making a promise. The word allegiance means loyalty. We show loyalty and patriotism by learning the words and meaning of the Pledge of Allegiance.

title: Legend/Key
text: A map’s legend explains the symbols and colors on the map. Some maps call this a key.

title: Title
text: Many maps have a title. The title tells us what the map is about.

title: Compass Rose
text:
The compass rose is a symbol. It shows directions. The four main directions are called cardinal directions. They are north, south, east, and west.

There are other directions in between these directions. They are called intermediate directions. For example, northeast is between north and east. Southwest is between south and west.

title: Political Maps
text: There are different kinds of maps. Political maps show us how places are divided. They show the borders that governments make. These border lines divide cities, states, and countries.

title: Technology in Geography
text:
Technology has helped us create new types of maps. Satellites take pictures of the Earth. These pictures from space help us create better maps.

Radar images help weather forecasters track the weather. Radar images help us know if it will be rainy or sunny. Weather forecasters use this information to create weather forecast maps.

GPS Technology in our phones allows us to type in directions and follow a digital map.

title: Donating
text: Donating is giving part of what you have to others. Donations can be money, resources, or time. Many people donate resources such as food and clothing. People donate extra food to a food bank for those who need it. Others donate money to people and organizations that solve community problems. You can also donate your time by serving others. When you volunteer to clean a park, you are donating time.

title: Creating a Budget
text: We can set goals for spending, saving, donating, or investing our money. When we plan how we spend and earn money, we call that a budget. Setting goals and creating a budget helps people pay for things they need and want. Budgets change as wants and needs change. Earning, saving, and spending are parts of a budget. It is important that when people are creating a budget they set short-term and long-term goals. This helps people make decisions between wants and needs.

title: Types of Questions
text:
Asking questions is the basis of inquiry.

The big question that guides inquiry is called a compelling question. Compelling questions should be interesting, like a mystery you want to solve. They should be important to you or your community. They don't have simple answers. Compelling questions make you think. An example of a compelling question is: What makes a good president?

Supporting questions help make the compelling question clearer. These questions look at a smaller part of the compelling question. They help give focus or action to the compelling questions. Supporting questions could be: What is the job of a president? What type of problems does the president deal with? What are some examples of how past presidents have dealt with problems?

Both types of questions help create a strong inquiry.

title: Make a Claim
text:
When we answer a compelling question, we make a claim. A claim is a statement about what we believe. Our claims should be supported with evidence. They can be written or spoken.

Sometimes, as we research, we see evidence that changes our original ideas. It is okay to change our claim as we find out more information. This process of change happens through reflection. To reflect means to think a lot about something. It is important to reflect on your research and claim. This will help you decide if your claim is still accurate or the best solution.

Make an initial claim about our compelling question, "What makes a good president?" Use the following sentence starters to build your claim.

title: Different Lenses
text:
Compelling questions are often very big. It helps us to think about them in different ways.

For example, historians look at the past to see how people solved problems. They look at different periods of time. They think about how past events have shaped the present.

Historians ask:

What happened?

When did it happen?

Why did it happen?

How did things change?

What did we learn from it?

Geographers study the interaction between people and the environment. Knowing how people and the environment impact a problem is important.

Geographers ask:

Where is it?

How do we use or interact with it?

Why is it important to us?

Political scientists study how a government works. They help community leaders make laws for their people.

Political scientists ask:

How will laws help our community?

Who has the power to create a law?

How are laws enforced?

Social scientists study the whole person: academic, social, emotional, physical, and mental. They analyze the effects behaviors and emotions have on people or groups of people.

Social scientists ask:

How did that event or action impact people?

What are the consequences of these actions or events?

How can I see this from a different perspective?

What are the facts, and what is my interpretation of the situation?

What is in my control, and what is not in my control?

Economists think about resources, money, and finance. They look at the production of goods and services in a community. They look at available resources and how they can help fix a problem.

Economists ask:

What resources are in our community?

How do people make money?

Why do people use different products?

What businesses are needed in our community?

title: Thinking Like a Historian
text: Historians identify, select, analyze, and evaluate sources to understand the past. When we think like a historian, we ask questions such as: What happened? When did it happen? Who was involved? How and why did it happen? Historians use different forms of evidence, such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs, to find the answers to their questions.

title: Types of Sources
text: Primary or secondary sources?

title: How Do We Examine Sources?
text:
Historians analyze sources to answer questions about the past. When we analyze something, it means that we study it carefully. To analyze sources, we investigate them. We want to know about the author or creator, the purpose, and the format. We want to be confident in the source.

Author/Creator

Who is the author or who made the source?

What was their role in the event or situation?

Are they a primary source or a secondary source?

Purpose

When was the source created?

Why was the source made?

Was the source made around the time of the event or much later?

Is the source trying to persuade, inform, or entertain?

Format

How was the source created?

What was it made of?

title: Multiple Perspectives
text: Everyone is different and has a unique perspective, or way of seeing things. Experiences and events may be interpreted differently by people. People have different cultural or individual perspectives. It is important to understand the perspectives of others. When we look at multiple perspectives, we can have a deeper understanding of what happened in the past. This helps us create the most accurate analysis of the people and events of history.

title: Life for Children in the 1920s
text:
What was life like for children 100 years ago? Think like a historian. Look at some primary source images and see what you can discover.

Look at the images of schools. What can you discover about school in the 1920s?

In the 1920s, not all children went to school. There were no laws that said children had to go to school. In fact, many young children worked to help their families.

Some worked in cotton mills. These were big factories that made fabric from cotton. Many young children worked in these factories.

What do you notice about the children in the photos?

title: Interpreting Information
text:
Once you have found the information, you need to interpret it, or decide what it means. We do this by analyzing, evaluating, and connecting.

Analyzing

When we analyze a source, we do close reading. Close reading means focusing on the important details in the text. This helps you to create annotations. Annotations are responses to different parts of what you read. It can be a statement, question, reaction, or connection you make from the reading.

It is also important to pay attention to sequence. Sequence is how ideas or events follow each other. Knowing the sequence helps you understand how the author came to their conclusion. This can help you decide if you agree with them or not.

Another important thing to consider is context. Context is information that affects how a source is presented. Context involves when, where, and why the source was created. It also includes the person or group who created it. Historical context is the events or trends that were happening when the source was made. It helps you understand what people thought was important during that time. When you analyze the context of a source, first look at when and where the source was made. Next, determine why the source was made. Analyzing a source helps us determine if it is reliable, or something you can trust.

Evaluating

To evaluate is to determine which information is most useful to you. In inquiry, it means choosing reliable information that best answers the compelling question.

This process begins with a review of the information from your sources. The information is organized based on how well it answers your question. This information is then called evidence. Evidence is information or data that supports a claim.

Connecting

You also need to search for connections in your evidence. How you use your sources is very important when answering a compelling question. Look for patterns or things your sources have in common. When your sources have things in common and directly relate to the compelling question, you include them in your answer.

title: Presenting Your Information
text:
After you have analyzed and evaluated your sources, you have to organize and explain your conclusions. We do this by creating a main idea and adding supporting details to back up our idea.

The main idea is the answer to your compelling question. You can use the compelling question to create your main idea. If your compelling question is “Can kids make a difference in their community?” then you have two choices.

1. Kids can make a difference in their community.

2. Kids can't make a difference in their community.

Then you add evidence that supports your main idea.

1. Kids can make a difference in their community because children help their families.

2. Kids can make a difference in their community by working with volunteer organizations.

You need to present your main idea and supporting evidence carefully to justify your claim. Your main idea comes first. Your evidence comes after that.

Our example compelling question is “Can kids make a difference in our community?” Our main idea is “Kids can make a difference.” We can then add evidence that kids can help their families. We can also explain that kids can volunteer in the community.

The order for presenting our information is: the main idea, first piece of evidence, second piece of evidence.

title: Government: What Is It, and What Does It Do?
text:
We need rules in school. Rules help us work together in an orderly way. They keep us safe and help us manage problems. Our communities need the same things. Governments were created to perform these functions or tasks. A government is a group of citizens who lead a community. Governments serve the needs of the people in a community. Governments create laws, which help provide order. They protect people and their property.

The United States government provides safety and security for the people of the country. It also maintains justice and order. It protects people and their property. The government also provides services.

title: The Government Creates Laws
text:
A primary focus of all governments should be to promote the common good. The common good means working to create laws and rules that benefit everyone.

The United States government makes laws and rules that guarantee and protect the rights of people. For example, it is against the law to steal. This law protects people’s property. Laws and rules also provide safety and security. For example, it is against the law to injure another person on purpose. This law keeps people safe. Laws in the United States say people are to be treated equally. The government is responsible for making sure all people are treated fairly under these laws. For example, it is against the law to treat a person unfairly because of the color of their skin. This law helps everyone to be treated equally.

Holding people and the government responsible for their actions is important.

title: The Government Establishes Order
text: The laws the government creates help us work together in an orderly way. Imagine if there were no traffic laws. How would we drive on the roads? Laws help establish the way that we do things in our community. In the United States, everyone has to obey the same laws. The laws apply to everyone equally. The laws have to be written down.

title: The Government Provides Security
text: A function of government is to help its citizens feel safe. Governments create laws that protect people and their property. They also provide services to help do this. Fire departments are government services. If your house catches fire, the fire department will help you. The police help provide security. The military is a part of our government. It protects our whole country.

title: The Government Provides Services
text:
The United States government creates services for the public. Government services help provide order and keep us safe. They create opportunities in the community for work. These services support our health. Governments use tax money to provide these services. There are many examples of government services.

Schools: Governments use tax money to help provide schools with buildings, classroom furniture, and playground equipment.

Public Libraries: Governments pay for libraries. Libraries provide books and research services. They also provide educational and entertainment resources.

Recreation: Governments provide places of recreation. They provide public parks, playgrounds, and sports fields.

Fire Department: The fire department is an important government service that protects communities. Firefighters protect life, property, and the environment.

Police: The police department helps fight crime. Sometimes, police officers patrol neighborhoods. They make sure drivers are obeying traffic laws.

Public Sanitation: The government cleans and maintains roads. This government service keeps us safe. Trash pick-up and street sweeping are government cleaning services. Governments pay to help keep our public places clean.

title: Past, Present, Future
text:
History tells the story of people and events that happened in the past. The things we did before are in the past. The things we are doing now are called the present. The things we will do later are called the future.

Chronological means that we put events in the order they happened. We do this by thinking about what came first, then next, and so on.

Look at the list of items, and think about your day today. Which events have happened or will happen to you today? Organize the events into the correct chronological order for you. What other events could you add?

Get up

Travel to school

Do homework

Have breakfast

Have lunch

Have dinner

Brush your teeth

Get dressed

Play with friends

Line up for something

Listen to your teacher

Read Studies Weekly

Watch a movie

Go to bed

title: How Do We Keep Track of Time?
text:
One way to keep track of chronological events is using a calendar. A calendar shows the days of the week and months of the year. It can help us track the events of our lives and when they happened.

Time can be represented in days, months, years, decades, and centuries. These words help us understand when things happened.

A timeline is a list of events in chronological order. It starts with the earliest event and ends with the most recent event. Timelines can show change over time. A timeline might show events that happened a long time ago. A timeline might show events that happened last week.

When historians use timelines, they measure the time and label it. They often think about what was happening in the world at that same time. This allows them to provide context for a historical event or person.

title: Historical Analysis
text: Many events in history can occur around the same period. The tools and items people used in the past become artifacts we can study. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technology change over time. Artifacts help us understand how people’s lives have changed over time. Historians analyze how much things have changed throughout history. They examine patterns to understand how and why things happened.

title: Cause and Effect
text: As historians examine patterns, they are often looking for cause-and-effect relationships. A cause is the reason something happened. An effect is the result of what happened. Look at this sentence: “It started raining as we were walking home, and we got really wet.” The effect, or what happened, is that we got wet. The cause, or reason, for getting wet is that it started raining while we were walking home.

title: Critical Thinking
text: Critical thinking is a clear and organized way of making connections. Critical thinking helps historians examine cause-and-effect relationships. Studying how individual parts contribute to a whole is also critical thinking. For example, the Civil War involved many people and battles. Historians look at how all the different people and battles affected the whole war. Critical thinking helps people to create a complete and accurate picture of events.

title: What Is Transportation?
text: Transportation is how a person or a thing gets from one place to another. Movement has always been important for people to meet their wants and needs. People have consistently looked for better and more convenient ways to travel. Better ways of transportation increased interdependence and economic growth. A key piece of technology for transportation is the wheel. This simple shape has had many innovations over the years. The wheel is attached in different ways to a box to carry goods or people. Yet the wheel is still round and is important for travel.

title: Moving People on Land
text:
Prior to the 20th century, moving people around a town or city was done with carriages or coaches. They were nicely constructed boxes with cushioned seats and four wheels. The carriage was pulled by one or two horses. For longer distances, the coach was built. It was bigger and more sturdy. A larger team of horses pulled a coach.

Innovators took the design of the box on four wheels, added a motor, and created an automobile. Automobiles became more comfortable for people to use. The motors became more powerful and increased the automobile's speed. Speed was important to move people quickly from one place to another.

To move more people the same distance within a city, the box and wheels became longer and wider. It was a form of transportation called a bus.

Roads and highways were built as automobiles and buses improved, speed increased, and trade expanded. Greater use of highways changed the landscape. The engines from the automobiles and buses caused air pollution.

title: Transportation on Land
text:
A covered wagon was four feet wide and nine feet long. The wagon was used for carrying possessions, not for people to ride in. A full wagon needed 4-6 horses to pull it. Two oxen could also be used. The wheels were made from wood with an iron rim. There were no roads, just open ground. The rough travel often broke the wheels.

Trucks evolved from wagons. Trucks came in all shapes and sizes and had motors. However, they all had four wheels. If heavier loads were needed, additional wheels were added to help move the trucks. The wheels were covered with a thick rubber tire. The tire made riding in the truck much easier. Tires also helped protect the load from damage. Trucks with 18 wheels use highways today to transport the heavy loads they carry.

The railroad was developed to move more products over greater distances. A train has an engine that pulls many attached cars, or boxes on wheels. The wheels on the train were made to sit on rails of steel. One train can move tons of goods and thousands of products across the country.

A trolley was designed from a train. A trolley is designed to move people. The wheels of the trolley are on a track of two steel rails. A trolley car can transport 35 people at one time.

title: Transportation on Water
text:
Water has been used as highways for moving people and goods for thousands of years. The early designs for water transport were canoes. Canoes could go long distances on rivers and streams.

A ferry is a flat platform that carries cars and wagons across the river when there is no bridge. There were many ferries before bridges and highways were built.

Ships were created to carry large cargo across the ocean. At first, ships used sails to catch the wind and move it through the water. Innovators changed the design of the ship to move easily through the ocean waves. A clipper ship carried goods and passengers faster than ever before.

Over time, motors were attached to the ship. A motor could move the ship though the water without needing the wind. Ocean travel became faster and more dependable. Today, there are ships that are so big they are like floating cities.

title: Transportation in Air
text:
The Wright brothers flew the first airplane in 1903. They designed the plane by studying birds in flight. Scientists had done many studies on air currents and wind. By using science, air travel was possible. An airplane uses air to move but still has wheels to help it move on the ground. Airplanes are used to move people and things across continents and oceans.

Air transportation is not just for airplanes. Today, there are drones that are used for delivering products to consumers. These small robotic vehicles have four propellers that use data input from computers to move.

title: Technology Influences Transportation
text:
The articles this week have been about transportation. As transportation across the country has grown, it has left its mark on towns, cities, and the land. There are interstate highways with many lanes to allow for speedy long-distance travel. There are bridges, tunnels, and parking lots across the land. Small roads connect rural towns and neighborhoods.

What transportation is in your community? What is the same across each type of transportation? Innovation and technology are the things that have improved transportation. Innovation and technology are going to impact transportation in the future. The wheel is the basic design for ground movement. What wheel innovations do you think we will see in the future? How will we use the wheel? Will we need the wheel at all?

title: Design Transportation
text: Design a means of transportation to move people or goods. It can be on the ground, water, or in the air.

title: What's the Next Step?
text: After analyzing and evaluating our sources, we need to act. We do that by sharing our conclusions and taking informed action. We can use the things we have learned to make a plan and take action to solve the problem.

title: Why Should I Take Action?
text:
Empathy is the ability to understand and be sensitive to the feelings of somebody else. It’s trying to look at a situation through another person’s eyes. Having empathy often motivates us to help other people.

Pretend you have a lot of litter around your school and playground. You might not think it is a problem. How would your principal feel? What about your classmate who tripped over some litter and hurt themselves?

An empathy map helps us understand how another person sees a situation. Let’s use the litter example. How might our school custodian feel about all of that litter?

See: What does your custodian see?

Garbage in the school and playground

Unwanted animals entering the playground

Unsafe corridors or play areas

Hear: What might your custodian hear?

Parents complaining and sad

The principal telling the custodian this is a problem

People asking him to fix this

Think and Feel: What might your custodian think and feel about it?

Angry or sad that the kids don’t care

Tired because it’s a lot of work to clear up

Frustrated because it seems like his job is never done

Say and Do: What might your custodian say and/or do about it?

Yell at kids who drop trash because he’s frustrated

Pick up the trash

Ask kids to pick up the trash

title: Making a Difference
text:
When we take action, we are making a difference. We are helping others and making our world a better place to live in.

Mikaila Ulmer

When Mikaila Ulmer was only four years old, she learned about how important honey bees are for our environment. Not only do they make great honey, they also help plants grow by spreading pollen from plant to plant. Mikaila entered a local business competition. She started a lemonade stand using a family recipe that used local honey to make it sweet. Some of the money she makes goes to help save honey bees. Her honey-sweetened lemonade is even sold in some grocery stores!

Ryan Hickman

Before Ryan was four years old, he saw a big problem. He saw lots of trash getting into the oceans. Since he really cared about the environment, he decided to do something about it. Ryan was able to start a business called Ryan’s Recycling. Since starting his business in 2012, he has recycled over 800,000 cans and bottles. He even sells t-shirts and donates the money to help the Pacific Marine Mammal Center in California. Ryan says “I love recycling because it helps keep trash from getting into the ocean near where we live, and that helps the animals in the ocean.”

title: What Does Taking Action Look Like?
text:
Taking action could be a lot of different things. It could be something you create, like a letter, web page, poster, art project, or article. It could also be volunteering or coming up with a new business idea. Maybe it's organizing a group of people to help with a project.

Creating action takes a lot of work. You may need to persuade others that your opinion is right. To persuade means to help somebody change their ideas or actions. If you care a lot about the environment, you may need to persuade people to care about it as much as you do. That means using the evidence you gathered to explain why they should care.

title: How Do I Persuade Others?
text:
What?

What is it that you are trying to do? Explain your project in detail. Include everything that you learned. Include the evidence you found.

So what?

You need to explain why people should care. Use your evidence to help people understand why your project matters. Show how your project will benefit others. What goals do you have, and what do you want to achieve?

Now what?

What do people need to do to solve the problem? This is where you detail everything that you need for success. Explain the action steps people need to take. Don’t be afraid to ask teachers or family members for help!

title: Engage in Your Own Inquiry
text:
With everything you have learned, you can see that engaging in your own inquiry is a lot of work. Let’s work through your problem and inquiry together!

Follow the steps to help organize your thinking.

title: Ask a Compelling Question
text:
What do I want to know about? Or, what problem do I want to solve? What do I already know about it? What evidence do I already have? What else do I need to find out?

Write your compelling question.

What are some possible supporting questions?

title: Make a Claim
text:
What is your initial claim for your compelling question? Or, what is a possible solution to the problem?

______________________________________________________________________

Why do you think that?

______________________________________________________________________

title: Search for Answers
text:
What kind of resources will help you find answers?

Where can you find the resources? Make a list of places you will look to find answers.

_____________________________________________________________________________

Explain how you will decide if your sources are credible.

_____________________________________________________________________________

title: Interpret the Information
text:
What sources did you find? How does your information relate to your compelling question? Which parts help answer your question? What parts do not support your question? Does it create other questions?

Review your claim again. Has it changed now that you have researched?

Do you see any possible solutions?

title: Present Your Conclusions
text:
What is the answer to your compelling question? Does it support your hypothesis or not? Summarize the information. How will you present your conclusion?

What is the main idea? What is the supporting evidence?

_____________________________________________________________________________

If your compelling question is a problem, what solution do you recommend? Write it down!

_____________________________________________________________________________

Develop a plan. (What? So what? Now what?) Be sure to include how you will persuade people in your plan!

title: I Am a Member of a Community
text: A community is a group of people who share a similar space while living, working, or playing together. People from many places come together in a community. You are a member of a community. One community you are a part of is your family or household. Your household includes the people who live together in your house. You are also a part of a school community. Your school community includes the other students and the teachers in your school. You are also a member of a local community: your neighborhood, city, or town.

title: Why Do People Form Communities?
text:
People live in communities for many reasons. Communities help provide material well-being for their citizens. This means people in communities work together to help meet their needs. They share resources and help each other succeed. They work to provide good education and transportation for their members.

People in communities also need safety and security. They create governments to help provide law and order. Many early communities in America formed so their members could practice their religion without fear.

title: Laws and Security
text:
One of the reasons people live in communities is for security. In the past, communities worked together to protect their resources from others. They had town councils and employed sheriffs to help provide order.

Today, rules and laws create order and protect people’s rights and property. We have the government, police, and military to provide order. Rules and laws also help to solve problems.

Laws are formal rules that apply to everyone in the community. Our government leaders help make laws to benefit our communities. In many communities, people vote on rules and laws.

title: Religious Freedom
text: In the past, some people were not free to worship as they liked. Some were punished for practicing their faith. Early American settlers created communities where they could practice their religion freely. The Constitution of the United States guarantees citizens religious freedom. We have people of all faiths in our communities today.

title: Communities Work Together to Improve
text: Community members work together to meet each other’s needs. Meeting needs is one of the reasons early communities were formed. In the past, a whole community might work on a neighbor’s farm. Then, they would help another neighbor build a barn. It takes everyone working together to meet community needs. It is important that all members actively participate in making a community better. Good community members participate by following the rules and laws of the community. They also respect other members of the community. They volunteer and help others. This helps make the community a safe and happy place to live.

title: Communities Change Over Time
text:
The needs of most communities change over time. The big cities we know today began as small towns. When a community grows, its needs change. The community then adapts to meet the new needs. Larger cities need more buildings, roads, and power to run. Responsible community leaders and members work hard to meet needs and improve their communities.

People change as we grow, too. Last year, you were part of a second grade community. This year, you will be part of the third grade community. As you grow and learn new things, you can help to make your community better.

title: The Founding of Jamestown
text:
In North America, Spanish settlements were in Florida. The Spanish wanted to stay close to the Caribbean, where they had colonies. The French claimed the north in Newfoundland, Canada. The French were establishing a strong fur trade with the Native Americans in the Canadian region. Neither the French nor the Spanish wanted the eastern coastline of America. The English gladly placed a claim.

The English government had sponsored many exploration expeditions to America. All land that was mapped and claimed by an English explorer was the property of the English monarch. No recognition was given to the Native Americans who already lived there. The monarch kept the land as a royal domain or granted it by charter (legal document) in large or small blocks to privileged companies or persons.

In 1607, the Virginia Company gained a charter for an area in America called Virginia. King James I signed the charter and gave permission for this company of investors to create a settlement (colony). The boundaries of the Virginia Company’s charter went north to present-day New York, south to present-day South Carolina, and west to the sea. The goal of the charter was to bring wealth to the king and company and spread Christianity to the Native Americans living in that area. The charter gave 20 percent of all gold and silver found in the territory to King James. It also granted all colonists the rights of Englishmen. This meant the laws in England would become the laws of Jamestown. The colonists were also bound to only trade with England. This new settlement would be called Jamestown in honor of the king.

In May 1607, three ships arrived at the southern end of Chesapeake Bay. One hundred and four men and teenagers became the second English colony in America. Years earlier, English colonists at a colony called Roanoke had disappeared without a trace. That colony was farther south than Jamestown. The men knew uncertainty was waiting in the new colony of Jamestown. Perhaps wealth beyond belief would be there.

The place chosen for the fort and houses was on an island. This island was an inlet at the mouth of a freshwater river that met the Atlantic Ocean. The salt water from the ocean mixed with the fresh water from the river to create a brackish, unusable water supply. The island was also surrounded by wetlands. Wetlands do not provide good living conditions.

The Powhatan Confederacy that lived nearby had villages away from the coast. Fresh water, forests, fields, and fish were all available to them.

The men and boys of Jamestown had nothing but hard work ahead of them. They had let tall tales of unbelievable wealth influence their attitude toward work. The majority of the colonists wanted to look for gold before building shelter and getting a food supply. Very few were interested in having a government to help solve and prevent problems in the settlement. Few of them were interested in building a relationship with the Powhatan Confederacy. None realized that half of them would not be alive the following year.

title: Essential Question
text: Why was tobacco grown on large plantations? What type of workforce was required?

title: Werowocomoco
text:
More than 400 years before European settlers arrived, the most significant city of what is now Virginia was Werowocomoco, the seat of power of the Powhatan. Werowocomoco was located across the York River from Jamestown, which was seated on what the English named the James River. The powerful Chief Powhatan lived there with his wives and children. Pocahontas was one of his children. Powhatan was chief of more than 30 tribes. His chiefdom included around 15,000 people! He was able to speak with a wide variety of groups. This enabled him to remain in power for a long time. Not all of the nearby tribes were led by Powhatan, but much of the surrounding area was inhabited by tribes that were. To pay tribute to Powhatan, tribes under his leadership would send food and goods. These were redistributed and used in ceremonial displays. The tributes were also used for rewards and trade.

Werowocomoco was the cultural and religious center for the Powhatan. They had hunted and fished in the area for thousands of years. Since Werowocomoco was located in Purtan Bay and surrounded by water, fishing was a common and important way to obtain food in their hunter-gatherer society. However, fish were not the only food staple. The Powhatan people ate a wide variety of vegetables, meats, and fruits. Their dinner might have included foods such as squirrel or raccoon. Other foods they ate included scallops, raspberries, and corn.

There is evidence that Native Americans had already been living in Virginia as far back as 15,000 years before European settlers arrived. They had homes and families there. Powhatan longhouses were called yi-hakan, which is pronounced “yee-ha-cahn.” The houses were engineered and built with sturdiness in mind. The foundations of their homes often included saplings set equal distances apart, bent over, and then lashed together. Bark or grass mats were then used as a secondary covering. The Powhatan had nomadic ancestors. They followed herds of animals and did not have a permanent home. By the time the European settlers arrived, however, they had been cultivating the land and farming for long enough that they didn't need to move their houses around. These houses were sturdy and simple. Usually, the more power and wealth an individual had, the longer and larger their home was.

An Englishman named John White came to Virginia in 1585 as part of an expedition to establish the English colony of Roanoke. The colony failed, but while White was there, he observed life in surrounding Powhatan villages. He painted watercolor pictures of what he saw. His pictures showed well-planned, organized villages. Longhouses were built in the centers of the villages. They were surrounded by farmland with growing crops. Some pictures showed a large circular area surrounded by tall poles or markers with carvings of faces. Villagers were shown actively moving around this circle in a game, dance, or ceremony. White also created portraits of individuals he met in the villages that provide rich details of their appearances.

Today, there are no remnants of any Powhatan buildings above ground. Werowocomoco was left behind in 1609, just two years after the arrival of the English to Jamestown. The Powhatan sometimes traded food with the colonists and maintained a peaceful relationship with them. At the same time, there was resistance to the English settlers who moved into their territory. The Powhatan fought to protect and keep their land. In time, the English settlers became too numerous and powerful to resist. The Powhatan eventually moved farther inland and would continue to be pushed farther from the coast with each conflict.

title: Survival in Jamestown
text:
The first colonists in Jamestown had heard rumors about gold lying on the ground waiting to be gathered. This temptation was hard to resist. The reality was that life in Virginia was harsh and cruel. Most of these men were adventurers and gentlemen. They did not know how to farm or hunt. Fortunately, practical men of the Virginia Company, such as Captain John Smith and some of the crew, knew about survival. However, a few men could not do the work of 100.

The men in Jamestown were relying on supply ships being sent on a regular basis. Instead of making or looking for food, they spent their time looking for riches. They also thought they could get food from the Powhatan through trade or force. They did not plant enough crops. They did not protect their food storage from rats and other animals.

By 1609, supply ships had come twice with supplies but also more settlers to feed. This temporarily helped the colony. Smith had been trusted by the Powhatan and had helped maintain trade. However, he was injured in an accident and had to return to England.

The Powhatan stopped trading food. They saw weakness in the English and wanted to use it against them to take their land back. When Jamestown sent hunting parties out, the Powhatan made sure the hunters did not return.

Jamestown needed food to get through the winter. The Virginia Company stocked a fleet of ships to send to Jamestown. However, the fleet encountered a hurricane in the Carribean and was scattered and damaged. Without the supplies, the colonists became desperate. Hunger and disease changed what people did to survive. There is evidence of betrayal, fighting, and death within the colony. Many people starved to death.

The effort to establish a permanent English colony in America came at a high cost to human life. In December 1609, there were 220 colonists in Jamestown. By spring, there were 60. This winter of 1609–1610 became known as the “Starving Time.”

title: To Work or Not to Work
text:
Life in Virginia posed many threats to Jamestown Colony’s survival. These dangers ranged from the climate to exposure to the raw wilderness to Native Peoples fighting for their land. Through a series of events, Captain John Smith became Jamestown’s political leader as well as its military leader.

Smith was a professional soldier, and the people of the Virginia Company felt he would be a big help. He had discipline and experience in directing men. Smith directed the construction of a fort for protection. He planned and ordered work teams to farm, fish, and hunt. Recognizing the dangers of the brackish water, Smith also ordered a freshwater well to be dug. This saved many lives by providing good water.

When Smith made contact with the Powhatan Confederacy, he traded for supplies for the colonists. If negotiations failed, he resorted to stealing food from the Powhatan storage areas. Smith also posted guards at the colonist's food storage area and enforced rationing. Smith ordered, “He who does not work, shall not eat.”

Smith became president of the council when he was the only surviving member of the original council appointed by the company. However, many thought he took his authority too far. The men of Jamestown were not soldiers. Many of the colonists resented his strict form of leadership.

However, Jamestown survived under Smith's leadership until an accidental injury forced Smith to return to England in 1608.

title: Populating Jamestown
text:
Jamestown was founded by the Virginia Company. Everything in the settlement was owned by the Virginia Company. The tools, equipment, and buildings belonged to the company. The company controlled the government. The board of directors in London appointed the governing council. The council then controlled the work schedule of the men. Work meant profit for the company.

The men and boys in Jamestown didn't feel very invested in their future. After seven years of working for the Virginia Company, the men could own their own land. Until then, there was little incentive to put much energy into the work. Jamestown was a workspace, not a community. Only men were allowed to be members of the company, so no families were in Jamestown.

For years, the colony had little growth in population or in profit. In 1609, John Rolfe was a new colonist to Jamestown. Rolfe transformed the profits of the Virginia Company with the introduction of one crop: tobacco.

Tobacco brought in a good profit for Jamestown. The large fields of tobacco needed large growing space and intensive physical labor. Jamestown had lots of land, but it didn’t have many people.

In 1618, Rolfe was key in getting the Virginia Company to change the rules for Jamestown to allow families. Families brought different craftsmen and merchants to the town. There was a need for new trade goods. More people brought more trade.

The charter changed. It gave property rights for individuals, not the company. The need for labor in the tobacco fields was critical. The Virginia Company offered 50 acres of land to any man willing to commit to starting a business and raising a family in Jamestown. They paid passage for any women who wanted to emigrate and marry a man in Jamestown. Rolfe married Pocohantas and started a family. Many other men found brides and started families. The population increased. Jamestown became a community rather than a workspace.

title: Types of Government in Jamestown
text:
Government in Jamestown Colony went through several different phases.

The charter for the Virginia Company guaranteed colonists the rights of Englishmen. This included the right to a representative government. However, Jamestown was owned by a company. This company chose seven men to act as the governing council in Jamestown.

This first government was set up to manage company workers. The seven council members made the rules. When authority rests with a small group, like in early Jamestown, the government is called an oligarchy.

In 1608, Captain John Smith was chosen to be president of the council. He was the only surviving member of the original council. Smith relied on strict military rules and consequences. He had all the authority. The men had none. This kind of military rule can be called a junta.

When Captain Smith returned to England, the Virginia Company appointed Sir Thomas West, 12th Baron De La Warr, as governor. He arrived in June 1610. He had no governing experience. He did not involve the colonists in any decision-making. De La Warr returned to England and left his deputy governor in charge. The colonists resisted many of the governor’s orders. Because the governor had the sole authority, resistance was met with severe punishment.

By 1619, the Virginia Company in London had renegotiated the terms of the charter with King James I. In this revised charter, a new form of government emerged. White men who owned property chose representatives to make laws for them in assembly meetings. They met in the town hall on a regular basis. This became the House of Burgesses. The rule of law was established. Every person became equally accountable in court. This type of government is called a representative democracy.

title: Tobacco
text:
Tobacco seeds are tiny. One seed is smaller than the head of a pin. The plant, however, can grow to be as tall as a man, and the leaves can be two feet wide.

In colonial times, tobacco needed two cleared fields to grow successfully. The first field was where the seeds were sown and grown into sprouted plants. When they were big enough, they were transplanted to the second field.

Each tobacco plant was moved to a mound of dirt. The mounds were knee-high and three or four feet apart. An experienced planter could make 500 mounds in a day. It was hard, dirty, tiring work.

Once the plants were healthy and growing, they had to be checked by someone every day. The soil was turned, all of the weeds were pulled, the tops of the plants were trimmed off, and shoots were removed so only a few leaves remained. These leaves received all the sun’s energy and nutrition from the soil so they could grow large. Destructive worms had to be picked off of the leaves by hand.

When the tobacco was ready, the mature leaves were cut, stacked, and hung up in bunches to dry and cure. Cured leaves were twisted into a rope and wound into balls that could weigh as much as 100 pounds. Finally, the tobacco was packed into barrels to be sent to England.

The process would begin again the next year. From January through November, tobacco required attention from many people. This is why it was called a labor-intensive crop. Virginia’s brand of tobacco was very popular in England. It became very profitable, and large farms called plantations developed. These plantations required more and more laborers to produce the crops.

title: Slavery in Jamestown
text:
By 1614, tobacco was a cash crop for the Virginia Company. The company needed to attract more people to settle and grow tobacco. They began the “Headright System” in 1618. Each man received 50 acres of land as personal property. Landowners claimed another 50 acres for each person they were responsible for. These could be family, indentured servants, or workers.

In August 1619, a ship came to Virginia with a cargo of 20 people from Africa. These people had been captured in Angola, an area in West Africa. They were sold to the Portuguese and then stolen by Dutch privateers.

Under the headright system, the landowners would get an additional 50 acres of land for every person they became responsible for. It didn't take long for landowners to start enslaving people rather than paying for indentured servants.

The plantation owners registered each enslaved person at the land register office. This new workforce would work the tobacco fields the landowners had just gained. More labor to cultivate the tobacco meant a bigger harvest. A bigger harvest meant greater profit for the owner. Cultivating tobacco was labor-intensive and required a lot of workers to grow it. This was the beginning of the slave trade in the American colonies.

title: Welcome to School
text: School is a fun place to learn. School is a fun place to play. School is a place where we make new friends.

title: I Am a Member of a Community
text: A community is a group of people. Communities live and learn in the same place. There are many kinds of communities.

title: Communities
text: You are a member of a family community. You are a member of a classroom and school community. You are a member of a local community.

title: Responsibilities
text: You are a member of many communities. You have responsibilities. You can be honest. You can make good choices.

title: Family Community
text: You are a member of a family. You can help your family. You can be kind to your family.

title: Classroom Community
text: You are a member of your class. You have friends in your class. Friends share. Friends play together.

title: School Community
text: Your class is part of the school. You have responsibilities at school. You can follow the rules. You can respect others.

title: Local Community
