title: Surface Water
text: Water is an important resource. There are many places where water can be found on Earth. Rain and snow are part of the water cycle found on Earth. Snow and rain come from moisture in the form of clouds. The clouds make water droplets. Eventually, the droplets become so heavy that they fall to the earth. When the water meets the earth, it can take different paths. Some water runs off the surface to form streams, creeks, rivers, and oceans. This is called surface water.

title: Groundwater
text: Some water soaks into the ground. This water becomes known as groundwater. The water collects in spaces between the soil and the rocks. This is the water that feeds the roots of plants on the earth's surface. Groundwater is accessed by drilling or digging wells deep into the ground. The image of a wishing well is an example of the access to a groundwater well. Sometimes groundwater naturally comes to the earth's surface in springs or lakes.

title: Drought
text: People use surface water and groundwater to meet their wants and needs. If there isn't much snow or rain, the groundwater can be diminished. This means it is used up and not replaced. If groundwater decreases over a period of time, it is called a drought. Droughts can last for months or even years.

title: Too Much Water
text:
Sometimes there can be too much water at one time in an area. This can happen because of heavy moisture in the clouds and little movement over land. If there is too much rain, the soil can’t absorb the water quickly. The surface water collects and has nowhere to go. The water stays on the surface and creates a flood.

A flood can be created when the groundwater is soaked to its maximum. Without a place to go, the water stays on the surface. Surface water collects in streams and rivers. The streams and rivers overflow their banks until the surface water and groundwater equalize.

This type of flood can damage resources and communities. People build dams on the waterways to help control this type of flood.

The dams hold the water in a reservoir, which is a large lake. The water is then used by the community. The reservoir helps meet the needs and wants of humans. It can be used for irrigation in agriculture. It can also be used in the production of goods.

The flow of the water through the dam can create energy, called hydroelectricity. This electricity is used by many communities. Hydroelectricity is a benefit of controlling the flow of water.

title: Important Documents of the United States
text:
Ideas, promises, and directions are written down for many reasons. Something in writing can be looked at many times. Writing can be shared with many people. The same ideas, promises, and directions are then known by many people. When a person signs a document, it shows that they agreed with what was written.

We find important documents on a local, state, and national level. On a national level, important documents include the Constitution of the United States, the Declaration of Independence, and the Bill of Rights. Laws, treaties, and trade agreements are also considered important national documents. These documents outline our rights and responsibilities as citizens.

title: The Declaration of Independence
text:
The Declaration of Independence is an important document in the United States. This document was written by Thomas Jefferson in 1776. It established the United States as an independent nation away from Great Britain. This meant the United States would have their own government.

The Declaration of Independence explains the purpose of government. A government is meant to protect “life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.” The new United States government would be founded on these principles.

title: The Constitution of the United States
text:
The Constitution of the United States was written to create the government that is described in the Declaration of Independence. Written in 1787, the Constitution sets the way the government functions. The Constitution gives directions on what the government can and cannot do in the United States.

Men got together in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to create the new government. The government is based on the people having the rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It is the people who give their consent, or agreement, to be governed. The way they are governed is described in the Constitution. The people elect representatives to make decisions for the common good.

Representing the people is an important democratic principle. President Abraham Lincoln said the United States is a “government of the people, by the people, for the people.”

The Constitution is divided into three parts.

Part 1: The Preamble
The Preamble explains the purpose of the document.

Part 2: The Articles
There are seven Articles that explain how the government should be run. They define the power of the government. The Articles ensure that no branch has too much power. The Constitution checks the balance of power. It helps the power remain with the people.

Part 3: The Amendments
The Amendments are changes made after the Constitution was written. The first 10 amendments are called the Bill of Rights.

title: The Amendments
text:
Changes to the Constitution are called amendments. Today, there are 27 amendments to the Constitution of the United States.

The first 10 amendments are known as the Bill of Rights. They are not the only amendments that have been made over the years. Among other things, amendments have made slavery illegal, given women the right to vote, and established the voting age as 18.

Congress sets up the process for states to ratify, or approve, an amendment. Three-fourths of the states must pass it. The system of checks and balances helps make sure all voices are heard. Citizens can voice their ideas about amendments to their elected officials. This gives the people a voice in the government.

title: The Bill of Rights
text: Part of the U.S. Constitution is a section known as the Bill of Rights. The Declaration of Independence spoke of the liberty and freedom of people. The Bill of Rights lists things the government is not allowed to do. This protects the liberty and freedom of the people. The Bill of Rights also explains how the government is to act in protecting the people’s liberty and freedom.

title: A Constitutional Republic
text: The government of the United States is a constitutional republic. This type of government has a written constitution. The Constitution determines what the government can and can’t do. Adult citizens vote for people to represent them in the government. These representatives make decisions according to the law. They are called public officials. When people vote, they agree to abide by the decisions of their representatives. To abide by a decision means to accept and follow it. The power of the government comes from the consent of the people.

title: The Constitution Guides the Government
text: The United States Constitution is the law of the land. It shows how the government must work. The Constitution says there must be three branches of government. These three branches are called the executive, judicial, and legislative branches. The branches share power. This way, no branch of government has too much power. This is called the separation of powers. The separation of powers creates a system of checks and balances in the government.

title: The Executive Branch
text:
Laws don’t work when nobody follows them. The executive branch makes sure that people follow the law. The head of the executive branch is the president. The president chooses people to help run the nation. The president is also the leader of the military.

The president has veto power. A veto means saying “no” to a bill. A bill is a plan for a law.

title: The Legislative Branch
text:
The Senate and the House of Representatives are the legislative branch. They make the laws. Together, they are called Congress. Congress proposes bills and votes them into laws.

Two senators are elected from each state. There are 50 states. How many senators are there, total? The House of Representatives has more representatives. States with more people have more representatives. Senators and representatives are elected by the people of their state.

The legislative branch also approves how tax money is spent. They vote on which programs and projects the government can spend money on.

title: The Judicial Branch
text: The judicial branch interprets the laws. They decide what the laws mean. They also decide if the laws follow the Constitution. The judicial branch is made up of judges and courts. The Supreme Court is the highest court in the land. The Supreme Court is made up of leaders called justices. They are chosen by the president and approved by senators. They work in the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C.

title: National Responsibilities and Laws
text:
The United States has national, tribal, state, and local governments. The national government makes laws for the whole country. They have responsibilities. Some of the responsibilities are:

Building and controlling the military

Creating federal courts

Creating post offices and stamps

Enforcing the Constitution

Making laws that protect safety

Making trade agreements

Printing money

We pay taxes to the government. The government uses the money from taxes to meet these responsibilities.

title: Levels of Government
text: In the United States, we have a national government that leads the whole country. We have tribal nations that have their own governments. We have state governments that lead each state. We also have local governments that lead our counties, cities, and towns.

title: State Government
text:
State government is like the national government. It has three branches. Each state has its own constitution, too. The state constitution is the law of the state.

The governor is the head of the executive branch. The governor signs bills into law. The governor also enforces those laws. Usually, the governor appoints state officials. In addition, the governor is the commander-in-chief of the state’s National Guard.

States also have a legislative branch. They make the laws of the state. Citizens who live in the state elect state senators and representatives. The number of state senators and representatives is different for each state.

The judicial branch includes the state’s courts and judges. Every state has at least one supreme court. The state supreme court interprets the state’s laws. It is the highest authority of the state judicial branch.

State governments collect taxes from the citizens. This money is used to build roads, hospitals, and schools. It may also be used to pay state police officers, school officials, and other state workers.

title: Local Government
text:
Local governments run cities and towns. Local governments might look different depending on the community. Some have three branches, like the national government. The executive branch of a city or town might be headed by an elected mayor. It might also be led by a city council. Some communities have a city manager who helps the mayor. Sometimes, the city council is the legislative branch of the local government. They make laws. Local governments usually have a judicial branch, too. It is made up of local courts and judges.

Local governments also have the authority to collect taxes. They use tax money to meet the needs of the community. They provide services like police protection, ambulance service, and garbage pickup. They also provide traffic lights and signs and public parks.

title: Tribal Government
text:
The federal government recognizes some tribal nations as sovereign nations. Sovereign nations have their own governments. Some also have their own constitutions. However, laws passed by Congress can still affect them. Tribal members are often invited to join local, state, and national groups. In these groups, they can help make sure laws are fair to their tribes.

Many tribal governments have three branches of government. The executive branch is headed by a governor, president, or chief. The legislative branch is often a tribal council. Tribal nations have their own courts and police. The courts are the judicial branch. The police help enforce the law.

title: Continental Congress
text:
The Continental Congress gathered once again in the summer of 1775. It was only weeks after the battles in Lexington and Concord. They didn’t know if the British military might enter the Pennsylvania State House and arrest each man for treason. They were preparing for war.

John Hancock was elected the president of Congress to keep the order of business and assign committees.

June 17, 1775, saw the first major action of the war. Inexperienced colonial soldiers held off hardened British veterans for more than two hours at Breed's Hill. Although eventually forced to abandon their position, including the high ground of Bunker Hill, the Patriots showed that they were not intimidated by the British Army. The Continental Congress responded by appointing George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.

Next, they drafted the Olive Branch Petition as a last appeal to King George III to avoid going to war with Britain. In the petition, the colonists pledged their loyalty to the king and claimed their rights as British citizens. Congress approved the petition on July 5, 1775, and sent it to the king. It was not well-received. The king responded by declaring that the colonies were in a state of rebellion.

British authority crumbled in the colonies. The Continental Congress took over as the national government.

The next order of business for Congress was to create a navy. Congress planned for aggressive action against British ships stocked with ammunition. It authorized the building of four armed ships and created rules for a navy. On Dec. 22, Congress named Esek Hopkins commodore of the new American Navy. Soon after, Congress authorized privateering and issued rules for dealing with enemy vessels and plunder.

In response to Congress, the British Parliament banned trade with the colonies and authorized the seizure of colonial vessels on Dec. 23. These actions weakened the influence of those members in Congress who wanted to work things out with Parliament and King George. Congress moved to support independence.

On April 6, 1776, Congress responded to Parliament's actions by opening American ports to all foreign ships except British vessels.

At the same time, reports came in from an American agent in London. This agent, Arthur Lee, also supported the revolutionary cause. Lee reported that France was interested in assisting the colonies in their fight against Great Britain.

In May 1776, Congress learned that the king had negotiated treaties with German states to hire mercenaries to fight in America against the colonists. This showed them that the king was preparing for a fight.

The pressure was growing for Congress. The British government refused to listen to or work with them. On June 8, 1776, Virginian Richard Henry Lee offered a resolution from the Virginia House of Burgesses stating that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.” John Hancock appointed a committee of five men to draft a document of independence.

Then, on June 28, 1776, the Committee of Five presented their draft of a declaration of independence to send to King George. The members of Congress edited and revised the wording. The delegates then sent messengers back to their home colonies to ask for advice. They needed to know how their colonies wanted them to vote on declaring independence.

title: Responsibilities of Citizens
text:
The United States government was created for the people and relies on them to succeed. People can make a difference in their communities by participating in the government and being engaged citizens. Being an engaged citizen includes voting, obeying laws, paying taxes, and being involved in local, state, and national governments.

Being an engaged citizen also means working for the common good. This means working for things that help everyone in a community and not just yourself. To promote the common good, citizens can participate in a variety of activities, including volunteering and donating their time and funds to a cause. You can help your community by working to preserve its history. You can engage in service projects to help others, such as organizing a fundraiser for those in need, participating in community clean-up events, and supporting recycling initiatives.

Engaged citizens also respect and protect the rights of others. They contribute to their community’s economic development. They respectfully hold leaders to their word. They stay informed about issues, share their opinions, and get involved in creating solutions. People can also contact leaders at the local, state, and federal levels by writing letters, making phone calls, and sending emails to express their concerns and opinions. This allows them to have a voice in decisions that improve their community. Citizens can also become involved in their community by running for political office.

title: Voting and Elections
text:
Voting is a formal process in which a group of people make a choice. This helps leaders make decisions for a community. An important part of voting is being informed about current issues and the people who are running for public office.

Voter guides provide background information on the candidates and ballot measures. These guides list the candidates running in each race and offer details on each one’s experience and goals. You can also be informed by listening to speeches, reading the news, and learning how each candidate feels about important issues. Good voters gather information from reliable sources. They use this information to inform their opinions.

To vote, citizens must first register as a legal voter in their state. Citizens must be at least 18 years old and live in the community where they are voting. All citizens can vote. This is a right and a responsibility of being a citizen. Many people throughout history have made many sacrifices so that all citizens can vote, regardless of gender, race, or economic status.

During elections, citizens find out the voting location in their community. A voting location is also known as a polling place. This might be at a school or community building in their neighborhood. There, they vote on issues and candidates. At the polling place, citizens have to prove their identity because they can only vote one time per election. How you submit your vote differs by location. You might vote using a computer or a paper ballot.

Most national elections take place every two years, on even-numbered years, but presidential elections occur every four years. They are always on the second Tuesday in November. State and local elections can occur at other times throughout the year. This includes primary and special elections. The right to vote is a privilege and a responsibility of all citizens.

title: Being Informed
text:
As engaged citizens, it is our responsibility to learn about what is happening in our community, state, nation, and world. This means understanding social, political, cultural, and environmental issues. There are different ways to stay informed. One way is to read and watch the news. There are different news sources available today. You can read newspapers and magazines.

The best way to stay informed is to research a topic. You can investigate issues to learn more about them. You can explore many sources and opinions to better understand the issues. Staying informed also means choosing news sources carefully. Make sure to choose sources that are credible, or reliable. That way, you know the information is correct. You can also talk to an expert in the field to help you understand a topic more clearly.

Staying informed is a very important responsibility for all citizens, especially when it comes to voting. Citizens must be informed of the opinions of candidates and how they will address community issues. Then, citizens can make the best decision when voting in local, state, or national elections.

title: Serving on a Jury
text:
One responsibility U.S. citizens have is to serve on a jury when called. Juries are important because they help decide if someone who has been accused of a crime is guilty of breaking the law. This is an important part of our country’s legal system. It can only work properly if responsible citizens participate in the process. People who are at least 18 years old are sometimes called to jury duty. A jury is a group of 6–12 people chosen to help decide a court case. In the United States, you are guaranteed a “jury of your peers.” This means that the jury will be made up of citizens just like you.

If you are selected to serve on a jury, you will participate in hearing the court case. Sometimes, this might only be a few days, but in some rare instances, cases can go on for months. After everyone has heard both sides of the issue, the jury deliberates, or discusses what they saw and heard, to make a decision. Jury members should use reason and logic when making their decision. In a criminal court, a jury must reach a unanimous decision. This means that all jurors agree on the verdict, or outcome. Juries must deliberate until they reach a unanimous decision. If they can’t, the case may have to start all over with another trial and a different jury. It is very important to take being on a jury very seriously.

title: Volunteering
text:
Responsible citizens who want to give back to their community, state, country, or the world can volunteer, or donate their time, to help others. Many people volunteer because they want to help others in need. There are many ways you can volunteer in your community. Food banks collect canned goods or deliver food to people in need. Other programs teach people to read. Some volunteers even build homes for the needy.

There are many volunteer organizations that help people across the United States. Many of these organizations have a rich history that stretches back for hundreds of years. One of the first volunteer organizations in the United States was a volunteer fire department organized by Benjamin Franklin. Volunteer fire departments are still a common fixture in communities across the nation.

In 1881, the American Red Cross was established by Clara Barton. Barton served as a nurse during the Civil War and witnessed firsthand the impact the war had on soldiers and civilians. She campaigned for many years for an American branch of the European-based Red Cross to be established in the United States. Today, the American Red Cross helps more than 200 million people each year at home and worldwide.

title: Public Service
text:
Another way that citizens can participate in their community and solve community problems is through public service. Public service is when people perform activities to make their community a better place. Any citizen can perform public service, regardless of their job. Public service can also include serving in government offices, elected positions, and the military. There are many ways that citizens can engage in public service. This can include attending a local public meeting, joining a neighborhood association, or volunteering with a community organization.

There are a lot of public services that are provided to citizens in a community. These often include police and fire departments, public transportation, sanitation services, public libraries, healthcare, and public education. That means your teacher is performing a public service!

title: Working to Solve Problems
text:
Issues in a community can impact the daily lives of citizens. Common community issues in many areas of the United States include transportation, water quality, access to clean water, funding education, and rising taxes. Citizens can work with their local, state, and federal leaders to solve problems that impact their community by attending meetings and contacting their representatives to make sure their opinions and ideas are heard.

One way that we can solve problems is by engaging in civil discourse. Civil discourse helps people have conversations about their community in a way that is respectful of other people’s opinions and points of view. You practice civil discourse when you talk in appropriate ways with other people to build understanding about an issue or problem. Although there are people with different opinions, practicing civil discourse reminds us to treat others with respect.

Steps that people can use to work together to solve problems in their community:

State the problem in a way that everyone can understand.

Identify potential causes for the problem.

Reach out to experts to brainstorm possible solutions. Some experts may include teachers, parents, and community helpers.

Suggest solutions to address the problem and create a plan.

Attempt to solve the problem.

Reflect on the plan and make changes if needed.

Through practicing civil discourse and community problem-solving, citizens and elected leaders can work together to overcome issues in their community, state, and country.

title: Pontiac
text:
Pontiac was a Native American chief of the Ottawa tribe. Ottawa comes from the Algonquin word "Adawe" meaning "to trade.” Their name originates from their role as traders even before they met the French. Pontiac saw how trading with the Europeans made his people dependent on European goods. He urged his people to go back to the Ottawa heritage of living off the land.

When the French left after the French and Indian War, Pontiac knew his people had lost their protection against the British. He worried that the Ottawa would lose their culture and their land to these enemies.

Pontiac spoke to the Wyandot, Shawnee, Seneca, and other Native American nations. He said they should unite against the British. Many listened. Warfare began, and many died fighting for western lands. This three-year war was known as “Pontiac's Rebellion.”

In the end, the Native Americans couldn’t win against the British military. There were no weapons or ammunition coming from their French allies. Pontiac negotiated with the British to bring no more conflict to the frontier. Pontiac spent the remainder of his life with his family near the Maumee River in what became Indiana and Ohio.

title: The Cost of Keeping an Army in North America
text:
Keeping an army of soldiers supplied for fighting in a war costs money. Each soldier was supplied with a musket, a bayonet and ammunition, a knapsack, a bedroll, and a canvas tent. New, bright red uniforms were given to the soldiers every year. By the end of the year, their old uniforms would be worn out.

Each week, food was purchased in the colonies, but it wasn’t the best quality. The British government didn’t expect the best for their men. The flour had chunks of the wheat and stem left in it. Three pounds of salted meat plus a pound of dried fish provided protein for the week. Soldiers would often combine their food to create soups or stews.

A letter from Lieutenant Robert Callender in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, to the governor in November 1756 tells a story of disappointment:

The men are allowed only one pound of beef per day, which is a half pound less than their former allowance, wherewith they are very much dissatisfied.

Britain had already spent a lot of money on wars and was in debt. The cost of fighting another war on a separate continent forced Britain to borrow even more money. The French and Indian War lasted seven years. Imagine how much money it would take to keep an army and navy supplied for that long!

title: Thomas Hutchinson
text:
Thomas Hutchinson was a descendant of Anne Hutchinson. His great-great-grandmother was banished from Massachusetts Bay Colony because she had different opinions about religion than the majority of the community. Anne Hutchinson helped establish Rhode Island Colony with Roger Williams. Rhode Island became a thriving colony. Rhode Island was known as a colony for religious freedom.

Thomas Hutchinson’s father was a wealthy merchant. His family was active in political, military, and charity events in the Boston area. As a member of the government, Thomas’s father set expectations for his sons to be educated and active. This heritage and support from his family influenced Thomas to be in service to others.

In 1750, Thomas Hutchinson had a Harvard education and smart business sense. He was elected to the representative government in Massachusetts and quickly learned to serve his community. He became a favorite of the royal governor. He was offered many offices including being a judge in many courts. He had no formal training as a lawyer, which made him unpopular with men who had training and practiced the law.

Hutchinson’s position in the courts gave him the opportunity to know many colonial leaders and royal officials. He was given the position of representing the royal governor of Massachusetts at the Albany Conference. He worked well with Pennsylvanian Benjamin Franklin. They found they had much in common. He coauthored the Albany Plan and tried to get the other colonies to endorse and accept it. He could see the benefits of having a central focus of government. The colonies were growing rapidly, and there were many dangers from many fronts that a central government could address. He worked hard to get the colonies to accept the Albany Plan but with no success.

title: Contributions of Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a self-made, rich man by the age of 44. He had a successful print shop that published a newspaper called The Pennsylvania Gazette. Twice a week, the paper published news, letters, and opinions from the public. Franklin used the Gazette to publish his scientific findings and his political opinions on events in the colonies.

Franklin’s experiments with electricity and his various inventions made him well-known, even in England. He had started a lending library from his print shop in Philadelphia. Libraries were a new idea and borrowing books caught on to promote learning. Many people wanted to meet and talk with him.

In 1750, he let his family run the printing business and devoted himself to science and public service. Franklin believed the colonies should cooperate more closely with each other. To support this goal, he created a famous snake cartoon titled “Join or Die.” The snake was cut into pieces and labeled with the initials of each colony. It was first printed on May 9, 1754, in The Pennsylvania Gazette.

In 1754, Franklin was appointed to represent Pennsylvania at the Albany Conference. It was there that he met Thomas Hutchinson and other colonial leaders. They shared ideas and created a plan to build a better government.

When he returned to Philadelphia, he built a network of reporters to bring him news from every colony for his newspaper. He began writing letters back and forth with colonial leaders and merchants from Massachusetts to Georgia. This became the start of a colonial mail system. Franklin’s public service to his colony and country was just beginning.

title: The British Army and Colonial Militia
text:
The purpose of an army in Europe in the 1700s was to be a fighting force for the king. The king paid for the soldiers and their equipment with taxes collected and put in the treasury. The British army included soldiers who were trained and disciplined for a harsh life. Punishments for breaking rules in the army were severe. Soldiers served in the army for a period of years.

A British officer was usually a man from higher society. He was awarded the rank. He did not earn the rank through his actions or education. They had little experience in being in the army or being a leader.

In contrast, the colonial militia was a temporary army. The men came together as needed to protect the town from outside threats. They did not train together. They brought their own equipment. Every man in the colony was a member of the militia. The officers were elected by the men of the town. Enlistment in the militia was short-term for a month or so. This way, the men could care for their crops, businesses, and families.

In the French and Indian War, the colonial militia served with the professional British Army. The British officers thought the discipline and training of the militia was a joke. The colonial militia officers tried to assist the British officers in knowing the geography and the non-traditional fighting tactics of the American Indians. The professional officers did not listen. They treated the militia with disrespect. The British officers did not trust the militia in encounters with the enemy. Such a gap between the army and the militia created problems. Each group made fun of the other for their actions and behaviors.

The British soldiers created a song to make fun of the militia. The men of the militia took the song and turned it into a great symbol of the American spirit. “Yankee Doodle” remains in our songbooks today.

title: Respect for the Land
text:
Native American tribes have a deep respect and connection to nature. They feel connected to the land. It played a vital role in their sacred beliefs and everyday life. They cared for the land and used resources wisely. They believed that if they took care of the Earth, the Earth would take care of them. Many tribes use the same name to describe the Earth, “Mother Earth.”

Native Americans did not believe in individual land ownership. The land was used by tribes and belonged to the tribe. Products from the land were communal and shared among the bands that lived there. Because tribes relied so much on the land for their resources, they needed lots of land to get those resources. Tribes would cover millions of acres to get food, fuel, water, and other resources. A certain area may be used for several years. Then the tribe would leave so the area could replenish itself. Eventually, the tribe would come back to that area when it was ready.

title: Models of the World
text:
Maps and other models of the Earth are integral to the study of world geography. A globe is a model of the Earth. Globes show us where water, land, and countries are located. Globes are useful when you need to see the Earth in a more accurate, spherical shape.

Maps are geographic representations of drawings of places around the world. They show where places are located and how to get there. Maps help us find the direction we need to travel. They can show large areas, like continents, or small areas, like cities. Maps can show elevation, which means height above sea level. They can show the population, or how many people live in a place. They can also show the climate or the weather over a long period of time.

The person who creates a map is called a cartographer. A cartographer has a point of view and decides what to include on a map. There are map tools that we use to help us when using maps and globes. Map tools include the title, legend, compass rose, cardinal directions, and scale. The map’s title helps us know the map's purpose and the kind of information we will examine on the map. The map’s legend or key explains what the symbols and colors on the map represent. Maps have a compass rose. The compass rose is a symbol that shows the cardinal directions: north, south, east, and west. The compass rose can also show the intermediate directions: northwest, northeast, southwest, and southeast. Distance is how far it is from one place to another. You can tell the distance on a map by looking at the scale.

title: Equator and Latitude
text: We divide up the world for mapping purposes. Imagine a horizontal line that runs around the middle of the world. Cartographers draw this line on many of the maps they make. They call this line the Equator. The Equator divides the Earth into hemispheres. A hemisphere is a division on Earth between north and south or east and west. The Northern Hemisphere includes all of the land and oceans north of the Equator. The Southern Hemisphere includes everything to the south. Many maps have lines running east to west, or side to side. These lines are called lines of latitude, or parallels, because they are parallel to the Equator. They mark distances in degrees. The Equator is zero. The lines of latitude north of the Equator are all named north (N) latitude. They go all the way up to the North Pole, which is 90 degrees N latitude. All of the lines south of the Equator are named south (S) latitude. They go all the way down to the South Pole, which is 90 degrees S latitude. Another reason that these lines are called parallels is that the distance between a line of latitude and another (either north or south) always stays the same, all the way around the Earth.

title: Prime Meridian and Longitude
text: On some maps, you will see lines that run north to south, or up and down. These lines are called meridians, or lines of longitude. They are different from the parallels because they are not the same distance apart but instead get closer and closer until they come together at the north and south poles. Look on a globe and find the poles. See how the lines of longitude come together? The middle line, or the line that is zero, divides the world in half and is called the Prime Meridian. These halves are called the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere. Since a globe has 360 degrees, each half of the Earth is divided into 180 degrees. Everything west of the Prime Meridian to 180 degrees (or halfway around the Earth) is the Western Hemisphere. These lines are named west (W) longitude. Everything east of the Prime Meridian to 180 degrees (or halfway around the Earth) is the Eastern Hemisphere, and the lines are named east (E) longitude. Latitude and longitude lines are used to create a coordinate grid on the map. A coordinate grid has numbers and letters along the margins of the map. These coordinates help you pinpoint a place’s exact location on a map.

title: Geographic Characteristics
text: Geography is the study of places. It explores the different features of environments around the world, including physical and human characteristics. Physical characteristics are part of the natural environment. These might include forests, mountains, oceans, and rivers. Landforms, bodies of water, climate, soils, biomes, natural vegetation, and animal life are all part of a place’s physical characteristics. Human characteristics are the changes people make to their environment, as well as the ways they adapt to their surroundings. They are a result of people’s ideas, choices, and actions as they interact with the world around them. Geography helps people understand the relationship between humans and the environment in which they live. People adapt to or make changes to their surroundings. They add bridges and roads to the landscape. They build homes, factories, and other buildings. They create borders around towns, counties, states, and countries. They draw upon natural resources. Humans have quite an impact on the environment around them. The physical environment has an impact on humans as well. Geography affects culture. The place a person lives can affect the type of house they live in, the clothing they wear, the activities they do, the food they eat, and even the jobs they engage in.

title: Geography’s Role in History
text:
Geography is the study of how people interact with their environment. This is not a one-way relationship. People don’t just change their environment to meet their needs; the physical characteristics of a place also influence the choices that people are able to make about where they choose to live. This two-way relationship has influenced the history of the world in many different ways. Here are some examples of how humans used their environment and how the physical environment influenced the choices people made.

Throughout history, most civilizations developed near river valleys. The Tigris, Euphrates, Indus, Nile, and Mississippi Rivers were all sites for civilization growth. Why? Rivers offer a constant source of water, which is necessary for human survival and crop growth. Most of these rivers were navigable as well. Navigable rivers are rivers that can be used to transport things because they are deep enough for boats without a lot of dangers. People built boats and used the rivers for trade and travel.

The Roman Empire occupied the land surrounding the Mediterranean Sea but never stretched much beyond it. Why? The Romans used the Mediterranean for travel. Areas that were not accessible by water were difficult for the Roman military to conquer. Natural borders, like the Arabian and Sahara deserts, were difficult, even impossible, for a large army to cross. Using the maps, can you think of more ways that humans interacted with the environment? How did physical geography dictate human choices?

title: Concept Correction
text: Have you ever grown a garden before? Gardens take work. You need to plant seeds in a sunny spot. You have to water the seeds each day. Then, right before your eyes, new plants will grow! That must mean every plant needs lots of daily sunlight and water, right? This is not true! So why would we think this? It is easy to believe this because we have seen it happen. We can see that if a plant in a sunny spot gets watered daily, it grows. It may even sprout some beautiful flowers. Is this true for all plants, though? Think about plants in Alaska. Sometimes it can be dark in Alaska for up to 22 hours a day. What about plants in a desert? Sometimes a plant might go days or months without any water. Plants in those environments have to be able to survive without daily sunlight or water. Dandelions in Alaska open to soak up as much sunlight as possible during the short time there is light. In the desert, a cactus will store water to use for long periods when there is no water. In areas where sunlight and water are not always available, plants adapt to their surroundings. Plants store the resources to survive.

title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
text:
Government action and decisions are put into effect by creating a bill that can become a law. A bill is a draft of a law presented to a legislature. There’s a special process that every citizen should know in order to be informed, active participants in the processes of government.

Every bill starts with an idea. Citizens can contact their elected representatives to propose an idea for a law that will make their community, state, or country a better place. Then, the representative can write a bill based on the proposal of the groups of citizens they represent. Once legislators write the bill, they must present it to the house in which they are a member. For example, a senator would present the bill to the Senate, and a representative would present the bill to the House of Representatives.

The bill needs approval from both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The bill goes to the executive branch if it is approved. In the federal government, the executive branch is the President of the United States. The governor is the executive branch in your state. If the executive branch agrees with the bill, it is signed into law. The executive branch can veto, or say no, to the bill if they don't agree. If that happens, the bill goes back to Congress.

A bill becomes a law with public opinion as part of the entire process. If representatives are responsive to the common good of the people they have been elected to serve, they can be continually elected to Congress. If representatives are not responsive, at every election, the people have the opportunity to elect someone else who will better represent them.

title: Taxes and Tyranny
text:
Colonists in America and the British Parliament were in a constant struggle over taxes in the 1770s. The Townshend Acts, passed in 1767, put taxes on many household items, such as paint, glass, and tea. Colonists didn’t want to pay taxes on items sold by the British. They decided to boycott them, or refuse to buy them. The boycott of British goods by the colonists ended up being very effective. The Townshend Acts were repealed, or reversed, in 1773. Parliament still insisted they had the privilege of taxing the colonies, though. To make this point, Parliament passed the Tea Act and continued to tax tea for the colonists.

The boycott of British goods hurt the profits of many companies. One company, the East India Company, had influence with the British government. The company’s directors convinced Parliament to help them out with the Tea Tax of 1773. This act taxed tea but also supported the East India Company. Parliament and the king said that the East India Company was the only company that could import tea to the colonies. This created a monopoly, meaning no one else was selling the same product.

Before the Tea Act was passed, tea was imported to America by individual merchants. Chests of tea were auctioned to merchants in London. The auctions were open to all businessmen, who bought the tea at competitive prices. The merchants paid the tax and included the tax in the price they charged for the tea.

The Tea Act took away all competitive buying from merchants. It meant that all the profits made from the tea would be given to the East India Company and their chosen agents in the colonies.

Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Charleston were selected as places for the delivery of the tea. The royal governors of the colonies selected the agents who would purchase and resell the tea. Governors selected friends and men loyal to the king to be tea agents. Colonists were angry. They saw this tax as a way for people loyal to the king to get rich and make the colonists pay for it.

The ships with the cargo of tea chests were scheduled to arrive in the colonies in November 1773. Everyone was making plans: Parliament, the East India Company, tea agents, and the Sons of Liberty. A tea storm was brewing.

title: Tea and the Culture of Tea
text:
American colonists loved to drink tea. It was part of their culture and lifestyle. A visitor to Boston in 1740 noted, “The ladies here visit, drink tea, and indulge every little piece of gentility … with as good grace as the finest ladies in London.”

Tea was the center of a colonial family’s day. It was served morning, noon, and night from a variety of teapots. There were inexpensive ceramic teapots that were made in the colonies. There were also fine silver teapots made by master craftsmen, like Paul Revere. Teacups were small and had no handles, unlike what we think of teacups today.

Although tea was grown in Asia, colonists got their tea only from British companies. The East India Company had a fleet of ships bringing tea to all parts of the world. Tea was sold in shops for three shillings a pound ($.75 in today’s money). Many types of black and green teas were available.

Governor Thomas Hutchinson of Boston knew how important tea was to the people. He wrote in a letter in September 1771 that in Boston and Charleston, “the consumption may be estimated at 19,200 chests per [year], or upwards of six million pounds.” That is a lot of tea, and a lot of money, too!

title: The Tea Parties
text:
Boston wasn’t the only city to have a tea party. Several other cities in the colonies protested the tax on tea in a similar manner. Let’s take a look at the Boston Tea Party and a few others.

December 16, 1773 Boston, MA

The ships Beaver, Dartmouth, and Eleanor were in Boston Harbor from late November to the middle of December 1773. The colonists, led by the Sons of Liberty, wanted the ships to return to England. They refused the unloading of the ships’ cargo of tea. Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson refused to let the ships return to England. On Dec. 16, 1773, 340 chests of tea were dumped into Boston Harbor by the Sons of Liberty.

December 22, 1773 Charleston, SC

Captain Alexander Curling of the ship London brought a cargo of tea to port in Charleston. Those responsible for receiving the delivery refused it. On December 22, a week after the Boston Tea Party, a committee of colonists told Curling to return the tea to England. The captain refused. The customs collector then had the 257 tea chests seized for unpaid import taxes. The tea was unloaded and stored away.

December 25, 1773 Philadelphia, PA

On Christmas Day, 1773, the British ship Polly was carrying 698 cases of tea. It landed at Chester, Pennsylvania, and its captain, Samuel Ayres, was escorted into the city. There, he was met by a committee of men representing a mass meeting of roughly 8,000 citizens. They told him to return the tea to England. They threatened Ayres and anyone who tried to bring the ship into Philadelphia or attempted to accept the shipment. The Polly sailed away without putting into port.

April 18, 1774 New York City, NY

The Nancy, commanded by Captain Benjamin Lockyer, dropped anchor at Sandy Hook, New York. Its cargo consisted of 698 chests of tea. The consignees sent a note to Lockyer, saying they would not accept the tea because it would “expose so considerable a property to inevitable destruction.” They advised Lockyer to return to England. Some of the Sons of Liberty escorted Lockyer into New York City, where he agreed to return to England with the tea.

April 22, 1774 New York City, NY

The ship London (which had been in Charleston, South Carolina, in December) arrived in New York under the command of Captain Chambers. Although Chambers protested that he had no tea aboard, the Sons of Liberty had received word that he was smuggling 18 chests of tea. Chambers was taken into custody, and members of the Sons of Liberty searched the ship. They discovered the tea chests, broke them open, and dumped the tea into the river. They then brought the broken chests back to the city, where they were used to light bonfires in the streets. Chambers was threatened with his life, but he managed to escape back to England on the ship Nancy with Captain Lockyer.

October 25, 1774 Edenton, NC

A British newspaper reported that “many ladies of this Province [North Carolina] have determined to give a memorable proof of their patriotism.” These women had resolved not to drink any more tea or use any British cloth to protest taxation without representation. The step was a momentous one for colonists because drinking tea was an English tradition that defined social gatherings. Giving up tea, which was a part of everyday life, showed just how angry they were with the English government. This event became known as the Edenton Tea Party.

title: Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty
text:
Samuel Adams was a Boston businessman and an outspoken critic of the British government. He organized a group of citizens to form the “Sons of Liberty.” This group’s purpose was to protest the actions of Parliament.

Samuel Adams recruited men who were angry with the king and Parliament for denying them their right of representation in government. Those who supported this protest against Parliament were called Patriots.

The Sons of Liberty met at a certain place called the Liberty Tree. They wanted to protest and intimidate Loyalists, or those who supported the king and Parliament. They would resort to violence to push the British government to the will of the colonial citizens. They were known to tar and feather tax collectors and other royal representatives. They looted Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson’s home and threatened his family. Most of the wealthy men in the colonies were Loyalists. They were British citizens who had benefited from their connections with the British government.

Samuel Adams attended the colonial legislature meetings. He supported the formal actions of the colonial government. He headed the Massachusetts Committee of Correspondence. These committees were set up to communicate with each colony and coordinate protests and boycotts. Samuel Adams tried to be a diplomat in the legislature to Parliament. He also believed that the Sons of Liberty needed to take action to protect the rights of the colonists.

title: John Hancock
text:
John Hancock was a wealthy man in the 1760s. He was from Massachusetts, and his family had money. Hancock may have been the richest man in New England when he inherited a shipping fortune.

Because he was a rich and outspoken leader in the Sons of Liberty, the British colonial officials were suspicious of Hancock. He frequently voiced his opinions against British policies in public meetings. This made him a focus of British investigations for anything they could think of. The investigations led the British to seize Hancock’s ship, Liberty. This caused the Sons of Liberty to start a riot. The ship was eventually released.

Hancock also had a role in the Boston Tea Party. Although Hancock wasn’t on a ship tossing tea overboard, he was at a meeting. He riled up the crowd with a famous statement: “Let every man do what is right in his own eyes.”

title: Thomas Hutchinson
text:
Governor Thomas Hutchinson of Massachusetts was born in America. He was a judge in the courts and was known to be fair in his rulings. He spent time with leaders of the Sons of Liberty, discussing liberty and rights of Parliament. These men of Boston were his friends.

As time went on, Hutchinson stayed loyal to the British government. An angry mob stirred by the Sons of Liberty destroyed his home in 1765 for his support of the Stamp Act. In 1770, he helped disperse the crowd after the Boston Massacre. By 1773, on a December night in Boston Harbor, the choices of Thomas Hutchinson had severe consequences. He chose to not send the ships with the tea back to London. The tea was destroyed. His family was in danger, and his career was over. Hutchinson sailed to England, never to return to America. He was replaced by General Thomas Gage. Boston was now under military rule.

title: Benjamin Franklin Goes to England
text:
In 1762, King George III appointed Benjamin Franklin’s son William to be the royal governor of New Jersey. Benjamin went to London. He was there to represent the Pennsylvania Assembly to the king and Parliament. Benjamin talked with government leaders. He supported the colonies. Letters between father and son demonstrate their support for each other and their king.

Benjamin returned to Philadelphia in 1775. His beliefs about the king and Parliament were starting to change. Benjamin and William began to disagree on political matters. As Benjamin became more of a Patriot, William continued to be a Loyalist. Father and son quit talking to each other. The disagreements between Parliament and the colonies divided neighbors, friends, and families.

title: The Powder Alarms and the Minutemen
text:
Since the French and Indian War, supplies such as gunpowder, ammunition, cannons, and muskets had been paid for with tax money from the colonists. However, these colonial supplies were stored with the British army supplies at storage places called powder houses.

Conflict increased between the colonists and the British. Several colonial governments were shut down by the king. British regulars were in every city. Because of this, the Patriots began slowly moving ammunition and powder from the powder houses to their own storage places. Eventually, the British noticed the supplies were gone.

Massachusetts was under a military government in 1774 as part of the Intolerable Acts. The royal governor, General Thomas Gage, was given orders by King George to stop colonial resistance and defiance. General Gage was told about the Patriots gathering and stockpiling ammunition and powder. He decided to secretly send troops to the powder houses and bring everything to Boston.

The British regulars were sent secretly to Charlestown, Massachusetts, in August 1774. They took the supplies from the powder house and returned to Boston. This did not go unnoticed by the Sons of Liberty. Rumors and fear went through the towns about the British going through towns and taking the gunpowder. An alarm system was put in place by the Patriots in case the British moved again to take stores of gunpowder. The men who answered the alarm would be known as Minutemen. They would be ready to meet the British regulars in a minute.

title: The Daughters of Liberty
text:
The men of the colonies had organized into a secret group of activists called the “Sons of Liberty.” These patriots had their wives and daughters support them in their protests and political opinions. The women who supported these patriots were called the “Daughters of Liberty.” The Daughters of Liberty were not formally organized. They acted as informal and knowledgeable support for their husbands, sons, and neighbors. During that time period, this was the way women could demonstrate their beliefs and political views.

On March 4, 1766, in Providence, Rhode Island, 18 Daughters of Liberty assembled at the home of Dr. Ephraim Bowen for a “spinning bee.” They spun cloth, ate dinner — with no tea — and declared the Acts of Parliament to the colonies to be unconstitutional.

Spinning bees were held in every colony. The ladies were working together to support the boycott of British goods. Through hard work, watching their money, and boycotting, the women could demonstrate they cared about constitutional rights.

title: What is Inquiry?
text:
To solve a mystery, good detectives ask questions and search for evidence. This is known as an inquiry. An inquiry is a way to investigate a problem or to ask for more information. A successful inquiry requires three steps:

1. Asking questions

To begin the inquiry process, you must start by asking questions. In order for an inquiry to be successful, you have to ask specific questions throughout the process. By asking questions, you can develop your claim. A claim is a statement you make about what you believe can be supported with evidence.

2. Processing evidence

The next step is to collect and process evidence. Evidence is information gathered from sources to answer inquiry questions. The more evidence you gather, the stronger your claims will be.

3. Applying inquiry to a problem

The final step to complete an inquiry is to create a final product that connects the inquiry questions to the evidence. This could be something you create or research you present.

title: Viewpoints and Perspectives
text:
As students of history, how can we learn about individuals and important details without losing sight of the larger systems and patterns that have shaped our world? We begin by asking questions. We can ask questions and develop claims about the geography, history, economy, and civics of societies we want to learn more about. Historians use primary and secondary sources to investigate various time periods or groups of people. Using these sources, we can study and interpret evidence to support our claims.

When using sources, it is also important to take perspective into account. Events that take place throughout history are often recorded by different people and usually have a variety of perspectives. For example, those who conquered a civilization typically have a viewpoint that differs from those who were conquered. As students of history this year, we can analyze perspectives about events, people, and ideas in both primary and secondary sources. By using the evidence from those sources, we can interpret history and be able to answer questions about major changes that occurred around the globe between 500 and 1500 C.E.

title: Analyze and Evaluate Evidence
text:
Your compelling question will determine the information you need to look for. Once you have determined what you are looking for, you can identify sources that will help you answer the compelling question. The most important thing to consider when answering a compelling question is how you use your sources. The sources you use can determine your answer to your compelling question.

There are several things to consider when conducting research. When examining sources, you should ask yourself, “Is it credible?” Credible means that you can trust the information from the source.

When researching, you should ask yourself:

Does the information seem to be accurate?

What is the purpose of the information?

Does it seem to have a specific tone?

How is the information presented?

Are there grammatical errors in the writing?

Once you have found and determined if your sources are credible, then you will analyze, or review, your evidence. To evaluate means to determine which information is most useful to you. When you evaluate sources in an inquiry, it means you determine the information that is most useful in answering the compelling question.

title: Counterclaims
text:
A claim is something you believe to be true. It is based on things you know and things you learn while investigating. A counterclaim is a claim or argument that goes against your claim. As a student of history, you should learn to recognize and make both claims and counterclaims. Using multiple sources from a variety of perspectives will help you accomplish this. Researching counterclaims can help you think more deeply about the things you are studying and learning. When you write a counterclaim, you think about multiple points of view or perspectives, which you can then use to strengthen your claim. Both claims and counterclaims should be researched and supported by evidence.

Here is an example of a claim and counterclaim:

Claim: People change where they live when they find better work in other locations.

Counterclaim: While it is true that people move for work, they can also move to a new place because the conditions of their home are no longer desirable. For example, people move away from droughts or famines.

title: Lexington and Concord
text:
After the powder alarm of 1774, tensions were high in Massachusetts. The Patriots and the British Regulars continued to clash. Then, in February 1775, General Thomas Gage and the British Regulars became the government and law enforcers in the colony.

By April 18, 1775, the Patriot militia in the town of Concord, Massachusetts, had gathered a large supply of munitions. Eighteen miles away in Boston, General Gage was informed of this supply.

General Gage gave these orders to Colonel Francis Smith:

...you will March with a Corps of Grenadiers and Light Infantry, put under your Command, with the utmost expedition and secrecy to Concord, where you will seize and destroy all Artillery, Ammunition, Provisions, Tents, Small Arms, and all Military Stores whatever. But you will take care that the Soldiers do not plunder the Inhabitants, or hurt private property … A small party of Horseback is ordered out to stop all advice of your March getting to Concord before you.

The Sons of Liberty heard about the orders. Patriots Paul Revere and William Dawes spent the night riding the 18 miles to Lexington and Concord, giving the alarm: “The Regulars are out.” The Minutemen answered the alarm.

British Colonel Francis Smith and the British Regulars arrived in Lexington early in the morning on their way to Concord.

Patriot Elijah Saunderson arrived at the same time. He wrote:

I was on Lexington Common ... and saw a large body of Regular troops advancing toward Lexington Company, many of whom were then dispersing [leaving]. I heard one of the Regulars, whom I took to be an officer, say, ‘... We will have them,' and immediately the Regulars shouted aloud, run and fired upon the Lexington Company, which did not fire a gun before the Regulars discharged on them; Eight of the Lexington Company were killed while they were dispersing, and at a considerable distance from each other, and many wounded, and altho’ a spectator, I narrowly escaped with my life.

British Regular Edward T. Gould was in the ranks of Colonel Smith in Lexington that day. He wrote:

On our arrival at that place, we saw a body of [colonial] troops armed, to the number of about sixty or seventy men; on our approach, they dispersed, and soon after firing began, but which party fired first, I cannot exactly say, as our troops rushed on shouting, ... which was continued by our troops so long as any of the [colonials] were to be seen.

Major John Pitcairn was the British officer at Lexington. He reported:

...when I arrived at the end of the village, I observed drawn up on the Green River near 200 rebels; ... they began to file off towards some stone walls ... the light Infantry ran after them. I instantly called to the soldiers not to fire ... and after several repetitions of those positive orders to the men, not to fire, ... some of the rebels who had jumped over the wall fired four or five shots at the soldiers, which wounded a man and my horse ... several shots were fired from a meeting house on our left. Upon this, without any order or regularity, the Light Infantry began a scattered fire and continued in that situation for some time, contrary to repeated orders ...

The British troops continued to Concord. The British soldiers went into every home, looting and looking for the supplies. The Patriot militia was waiting for them by the North Bridge on the road out of town. The British Regulars fired their weapons into the militia on the other side of the bridge. The Patriots returned fire, killing three British soldiers. As the British left Concord to return to Boston, the Patriot militia had grown to include over 2,000 men. They followed the British, firing on them from houses, stone walls, and trees. The British returned fire when they could, killing a total of 95 Patriots. The British had killed or wounded 273 people by the time they reached Boston.

The actions at Lexington and Concord in April of 1775 set off a chain of events that changed the world. These actions became known as “the shot heard ‘round the world.”

title: "Common Sense" and Thomas Paine
text:
Thomas Paine was born in England and lived there until 1774. In England, he met Benjamin Franklin, who persuaded Paine to come to the colonies. Paine came to America and found the colonies in great unrest. Seeing the struggle between the colonies and Parliament, Paine sympathized with the colonists. He immediately became a Patriot. Paine was an excellent writer, so he decided to write about the situation in the colonies.

In 1775, Paine wrote his most famous pamphlet, or booklet, called Common Sense. In the pamphlet, Paine encouraged American independence from Britain. This was an idea that hadn’t been widely talked about yet among the colonists. For the most part, they still considered themselves to be British, just treated unfairly. Paine’s words changed that view. He wrote differently than the Enlightenment thinkers that many of the colonial leaders were reading. Paine wrote to the common people. Though he wasn’t religious, Paine knew many of his readers were. He used words from the Bible and religious language to persuade people. Paine said the colonies were required to declare independence because the British government was corrupt.

Common Sense was published in January of 1776. It was before people were busy planting crops in the spring, a time many were staying indoors to be warm. It was a good time to read. Thousands of colonists read his pamphlet to themselves, aloud to one another over tea, and even at taverns and other meeting places. Many colonists loved what Paine said, and they asked for more and more printed copies. The pamphlet became America’s first bestseller. Of course, there were Loyalists who strongly disagreed with him. They said Paine’s writing was just misleading information to promote his political cause. However, Paine continued to write passionately against British policies even though the king and his Loyalists hated it. He felt strongly that things in the world needed to change. As he wrote in Common Sense, he believed, “The cause of America is in great measure the cause of all mankind.”

title: State Constitutions and Their Charters
text:
As the Second Continental Congress discussed how to deal with Great Britain, they examined the idea of independence. Congress saw that independence could result in confusion and chaos. The governments in the colonies were all following the laws of Great Britain. If they declared independence, they would no longer be part of Great Britain. So whose law would be in effect? Would there be any laws or courts? What money would they use? Would they still pay taxes? To whom? How would the army be supported? These and many other questions needed to have answers before independence was possible.

Congress realized that the framework for government was in place. Each colony had a government established through its colonial charter. Each had legislatures made up of elected representatives of the people. These groups chose the delegates to the Continental Congress. Congress recommended that each colony use its charter to form a constitution, which would be in place if there was a vote for independence. This is exactly what each colonial legislature did. Charters became state constitutions. If independence came, the colonies were prepared to become states with the stroke of a pen.

title: Committee of Five
text:
The Second Continental Congress adopted Richard Henry Lee’s resolution that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states.” Many delegates felt that to break away from Great Britain, they needed to give good reasons for it. They needed a document to present to the king and the world. They decided a committee would draft a declaration. Then the delegates would vote on it.

On Tuesday, June 11, 1776, the Congress “Resolved, That the committee, for preparing the declaration, consist of five ...” These five were two New England men, John Adams of Massachusetts and Roger Sherman of Connecticut; two from the Middle Colonies, Benjamin Franklin of Pennsylvania and Robert R. Livingston of New York; and one southerner, Thomas Jefferson of Virginia.

The committee decided Thomas Jefferson would write the narrative of the declaration. Then, they worked together to edit and revise it before presenting it to Congress on June 28, 1776.

title: General George Washington
text:
George Washington arrived in Philadelphia as a plantation gentleman and delegate from Virginia. Washington was known for his good judgment, honest character, and expertise as a businessman. He also served in the Virginia House of Burgesses. He was unanimously voted to lead the revolutionary army.

Washington was selected over other candidates such as John Hancock. Washington brought a number of talents to his position as Commander of the Continental Army.

Washington’s experiences in the French and Indian War were important. He had learned many important British military practices. He studied British army manuals. He also witnessed firsthand how vulnerable British formations could be in rough, forested land. He knew the British military officers personally. This knowledge would be used to the Patriot advantage. He also believed in the authority of the people to be in representational government.

Washington left for Massachusetts within days of receiving his commission. He assumed command of the Continental Army in Cambridge, Massachusetts on July 3, 1775.

title: Thomas Jefferson, the Author
text:
Thomas Jefferson was respected in Congress and was a great writer. Because of this, he was persuaded to write the draft of the Declaration of Independence. Jefferson had 17 days to produce the document and reportedly wrote a draft in just a few days.

Jefferson was well-educated and came from a wealthy family. He came to Philadelphia in 1776 with experience in drafting constitutions. He was the author of the new Virginia Constitution, which had been based in the Virginia colonial charter. He was a member of Virginia's legislature. His first political writing was the directions for Virginia’s delegation to the First Continental Congress. Writing for the House of Burgesses had given Jefferson experience in working with a committee. This had also given him the chance to study and think about the principles and ideals of liberty and freedom the Patriots were fighting for and understand why they mattered.

title: The Ragtag Revolutionaries
text:
Over 1,000 colonial militiamen assembled on Bunker Hill above the city of Boston in June 1775. None of them were professional soldiers. They were farmers, shopkeepers, craftsmen, businessmen, and dock workers. Still, they assembled to fight the British Army that occupied the city of Boston. They brought their own muskets and gun powder. They had no uniforms, just the clothes they were wearing. They used the ammunition and weapons that had been hidden in nearby towns. On the other hand, the 2,200 British Regulars were well equipped and well trained. On June 17, the British attacked the colonial forces. At the end of the day, 400 colonial soldiers were killed or wounded. The British suffered over 1,000 casualties. It was the first battle of the American Revolution.

The colonial army would continue to grow. Their need for equipment and supplies would also continue to grow. How was a Congress of men in Philadelphia going to fund an army? Many expenses were left to each individual colony to pay. A lot of the men had to pay for their own things. They also pooled their resources for tents, camp equipment, and food. This disorganized, diverse group of men was called a “ragtag” army.

The men of Congress also looked to an expert in financial matters: Haym Salomon. Salomon was a Jewish immigrant from Poland who came to New York City in 1772. He became a successful financial broker, or someone who arranges business transactions. Salomon agreed with the Patriots and joined the Sons of Liberty. The British army arrested him as a spy. In jail, he became an interpreter for German soldiers who had been hired to fight with the British army. Secretly, he encouraged many to desert. He was supposed to be executed, but he escaped. He set up his business in Philadelphia.

Salomon could see that the Continental Congress was struggling to get money to support the war. Salomon began raising money. He helped Robert Morris, the superintendent of finance, get loans from France and other countries. He often made personal loans to the government and to American leaders like James Madison, Thomas Jefferson, and James Monroe. When George Washington needed money for the army, he said, “Send for Haym Salomon.” Salomon’s clear thinking, generosity, and dedication provided the financing needed to create a professional army from a ragtag group of colonial men.

title: What Does Revolution Mean?
text:
The atmosphere in the American Colonies was different from that of Great Britain and other parts of Europe. During the time the colonies had been founded, the colonists from Europe abandoned the social attitudes of class. In America, each person worked and created their own lives. Each colony had a government that heard colonists’ ideas and acted on them. King George III and Parliament did not represent their interests. The colonists had no representation in the government of Great Britain. King George and Parliament demanded obedience from the colonists with no thought to the consequences for the people themselves. The leaders of the colonial governments called this lack of care, tight control, and the demands of the government on the people tyranny. Forcibly changing this type of government to another, better government is called revolution.

There were many new ideas in the world at that time about what a government should be and how it should benefit the people. In Europe, a group of men called “Enlightenment thinkers” shared their new ideas of government.

One of these thinkers was John Locke. He argued that people were born with natural rights, such as life, liberty, and property. These natural rights could never be taken away or even given up by individuals. He believed that governments acted only to enforce and protect the natural rights of the people. If a sovereign, or supreme ruler, violated these rights, the people had the right to revolt and establish a new government.

Another Enlightenment thinker was Jean-Jacques Rousseau. He argued that the government’s role was to protect everyone's life, liberty, and property. The people themselves should be sovereign.

The delegates in the Continental Congress studied the ideas of Locke and Rousseau. They discussed and explored the revolutionary ideas of both of these thinkers. The delegates knew the government of Great Britain was not what they wanted. Perhaps these great thinkers could help them carry out a revolution in changing their government.

title: History of Dogs
text:
There are multiple theories about the origin, or start, of dogs. Some believe that wolves started to spend enough time with humans that they became their pets. These wolves were more gentle than other wolves. Over time, humans began to choose specific traits of their dogs that they liked. They bred those dogs to get more puppies with those specific traits. This is called selective breeding. In ancient Egypt, dogs were bred for hunting and guarding. In China, dogs were bred to look like lions. Dachshunds were bred in Germany to hunt badgers. Miniature dachshunds were bred to hunt smaller animals. Enough people began to breed dogs for specific traits that dogs started to all look very different. These differences are called variation. Variation in dogs is the reason they don’t all look like wolves.

Phenomenon Explanation: In your own words, explain how dachshunds can be related to wolves. Use evidence you have collected this week to support your ideas. Be sure to include the words “inherit” and “trait” in your explanation.

title: Orange Tree Orchard
text:
Sarah loves to make orange juice. She decides she wants to plant an orange orchard in her backyard so she always has oranges available. To begin her orchard, she takes three seeds from an especially sweet orange and plants them in her yard. Trees take a few years to get big enough to grow fruit. A few years later, three beautiful orange trees are thriving in her backyard orchard. She decides to finally taste the oranges she has grown. She takes one orange from each tree. She expects them all to taste just like the orange she took the seeds from to grow the trees. Sarah is surprised to discover that that isn’t quite true. The fruit from the first tree tastes just like the original orange. The fruit from the second tree is bitter. The orange rind is a little bit lighter in color. The fruit from the third tree is much sweeter than the original.

What happened? Can you explain why the fruit from these trees taste different than their parent? Use evidence to support your claim.
