title: Changing Nebraska: Physical and Human Characteristics
text:
Geography is the study of Earth and its people. The study of the Earth’s physical characteristics, or its natural environment, focuses on such things as forests, mountains, oceans, rivers, vegetation, and animal life. When we study the influence of people on geography, we study human characteristics. This study includes the interactions people have with an area’s physical characteristics. Human characteristics include things like political boundaries of states and cities, bridges, and homes.

The physical and human characteristics of a place do not stay the same over time. Many factors cause changes. For example, people may move to an area because of its physical characteristics, such as its access to water and resources. Once there, the people will adapt the area’s physical characteristics to their needs. They will build structures, such as homes and bridges, and create services, such as police stations and hospitals. They will create human characteristics.

But the physical characteristics of the area might change. For example, if there was a drought, the water supply might not be able to support farmland any more. This change might cause many people to leave, and then the hospital might not have enough employees.

Changes happen frequently in the physical and human characteristics of an area. This cause-and-effect relationship has influenced the physical and human environment of Nebraska throughout its history.

title: kelli-test
text:
Cameron has a regular bedtime routine that he follows every night. He brushes his teeth, puts on his pajamas, and lets out his dog, Luna. Then he climbs into bed. One night as he was waiting for Luna to come back inside, he noticed the moon. It was shining brightly in the sky. It was a big, white circle that seemed to illuminate the whole yard. He wondered, "Why haven't I noticed the light of the moon before?"

Weeks went by, and Cameron watched the moon. He noticed that the moon looked like it was getting smaller. In fact, there were a few days when there was no moon at all! Cameron decided to start a journal. As part of his bedtime routine, he wrote in his notebook. He wrote information that he observed about the moon. Cameron wrote down the date and a description of the moon. He also sketched what the moon looked like.

After two months, Cameron was amazed at what he recorded in his Moon Journal. It took about 28 days to go through the sequence of moon phases. He noticed that the phases could begin and end on any day of the week. New phases did not always begin on the first of the month. When the moon seemed to disappear as a new moon, it would slowly appear larger until it was a full moon, and then slowly get smaller until it seemed to vanish again! This pattern happens over and over!

Now, when Cameron lets his dog out, he already knows what kind of moon to expect. His Moon Journal has made him feel like a real astronomer.

title: Changes for Plants and Animals
text:
The most dominant physical feature in Nebraska is its plains. Nebraska is part of the Great Plains, a region in the United States that covers much of the Midwest and extends north into Canada. The main native vegetation in the Great Plains is grass. However, it is quite rare to see the plains' grasses today. Most of the areas where these grasses once grew have been replaced by agricultural fields of corn, wheat, or other crops. Trees also grow more abundantly in Nebraska today. This is because of human efforts to plant more trees. In fact, it was a Nebraska City resident named J. Sterling Morton who proposed a tree-planting holiday called Arbor Day. Arbor Day was first celebrated in 1872 in Nebraska and is now celebrated nationwide.

Some animals native to the Plains region of Nebraska are the American bison, prairie dogs, and the American antelope. Historically, the most important of these animals was the American bison. The Native Americans who lived in and around Nebraska were nomadic groups that followed bison herds and used them for food and other materials. As pioneers came into eastern Nebraska, they saw bison for the first time. They were amazed to see so many. One pioneer wrote, "I could stand on my wagon and see more than 10,000 buffalo [bison] ... The plain was perfectly black with them on both sides of the river." Today, you won’t see 10,000 bison roaming the plains of Nebraska because they were hunted to near-extinction in the 19th century. However, you might see hundreds of cattle. Cattle thrive in Nebraska for the same reasons the bison did: its open, smooth landscape and good grasses.

title: Natural Disasters
text:
Many natural events can cause changes to the physical and human environment. The places people choose to live have built-in dangers in their environments. For instance, some parts of the world have fault lines, which can lead to earthquakes. Other regions experience erosion, which can lead to flooding. Some have volcanoes or avalanches. These are all examples of how the physical environment can affect people, human-made structures, wildlife, and the land.

Not all natural disasters are likely to happen in Nebraska. For example, avalanches and volcanoes can’t happen in Nebraska because there aren’t any mountains to create avalanches, and there aren’t any volcanoes to erupt. Some of the most common hazardous events that happen in the state are severe storms, such as thunderstorms, dust storms, and blizzards. Nebraska also has floods and tornadoes.

Nebraska’s thunderstorms can bring lightning strikes and hail. These can damage property, start fires, and even injure people. Dust storms occur when there isn’t enough precipitation and the wind carries the dry dirt around. These storms limit people’s ability to see and can hurt animals that live outside. Blizzards are snow storms with high winds of at least 35 miles an hour. Blizzards limit people’s vision, restrict travel, and freeze animals and crops. Storms can also cause floods in Nebraska, especially in areas with rivers and lakes. Tornadoes are wind funnels that can form at the base of a thunderstorm. As the funnel spins, it is capable of great destruction. All these storms and disasters can arise unexpectedly.

title: Mapping Tornadoes
text:
Nebraska is located in Tornado Alley, an area in the central United States where the most tornadoes occur. Nebraska has been the site of many tornadoes throughout its history. A tornado’s damage intensity is measured on the Fujita Scale. The scale was invented in 1971 and modified in 2007. It ranks a tornado’s damage on a scale of 0–5 and estimates the wind speed of the storm based on the damage that occurs. Wind speeds of an F0 tornado range from 40–72 miles an hour, while wind speeds of an F5 tornado range from 260–300 miles per hour.

The Omaha Tornado on March 23, 1913: At least seven tornadoes started in Sarpy County on this day, but one of them moved northeast through Ralston and grew to a quarter-mile wide before it moved across Omaha. The tornado then continued southeast of Harrison County, Iowa.

Grand Island Tornado Outbreak 1980: The tornados developed just northwest of Grand Island and moved south-southeast. Seven tornadoes developed and tore through Grand Island. The most destructive of these were rated F3 and F4.

The Hallam Tornado of May 22, 2004: Two tornadoes hit southeast Nebraska on this day. The largest storm traveled northeast from Daykin, through Hallam, and stopped just southwest of Palmyra. At the peak of its destruction, the tornado was an F4.

However, there are warning systems and plans used to help keep people safe during these natural disasters.

title: Railroads Changed Over Time
text:
The invention of the steam engine paved the way for the railroad. Most inventions are created to solve a problem. The steam-powered locomotive was created to help transport heavy mining materials from one place to another. The first railways were created in England for the coal mining industry. Locomotive and railway technology came to the United States in the early 1800s.

The first railroads in the U.S. were built in the industrial northeast, in places like Boston and Baltimore. These cities did not have easy access to rivers that could connect them to the interior of the United States. The railroad solved this problem. After railroads were built, cities on the East Coast were now connected to cities across the country, all the way to the Mississippi River.

Most Americans agreed it would be great to have a railroad that stretched from the East Coast to the West Coast, but deciding what route the railroad should take wasn't easy. Finally, it was decided the railroad should follow the old Platte River Road, and President Abraham Lincoln decided that the western track would begin in Omaha, Nebraska.

The job was enormous and very expensive, but railroad workers were able to complete the track in record time. The Union Pacific (from Nebraska, building west) was racing the Central Pacific (from Sacramento, California, building east). Both sides worked very hard, and the entire job was finished in about six years. Omaha became the headquarters of the Union Pacific Railroad, and the population of the city doubled in just one year. This is just one way the railroad brought big changes to Nebraska.

title: Highways Changed Over Time
text:
Nebraska has always been an important part of cross-continental travel. Lewis and Clark came through Nebraska while mapping the newly purchased Louisiana Territory. The Pony Express made its way from east to west through Nebraska. Pioneers passed through Nebraska on the Oregon Trail, the Mormon Trail, and on their way to California. Nebraska was the starting point for building the Transcontinental Railroad. Nebraska was a crossroads and would continue to be so as technology evolved.

In the early 1900s, the automobile was becoming more widespread. In 1912, a group of automobile manufacturers proposed a cross-continental highway that would stretch from New York City to San Francisco. It was built through 13 states, including Nebraska. It was called the Lincoln Highway and was formally dedicated in 1913. When the highway was built, new businesses were needed to accommodate travelers, such as gas stations, hotels, campgrounds, and restaurants. The grazing lands and habitats of Nebraska’s native animals were reduced around the highway. Decades later, portions of the Lincoln Highway were used to create a more extensive highway system that included I-80 and U.S. Route 30. A piece of the Lincoln Highway, paved in brick, is still preserved outside of Omaha. Today, Nebraska has over 9,000 miles of roads and highways.

title: How Reservations Have Changed Over Time
text:
Nebraska is home to many Native American tribes. Most of the Native Americans who live in Nebraska today were forced to leave their original homelands. The process of moving to the Nebraska region happened over the course of a few centuries but intensified in the 1830s. These migrations were caused by conflict with other tribes and governments and through both consensual and forced treaties with the U.S. government.

The Omaha originally lived in the Ohio River Valley but moved to the Missouri River Valley in the late 1600s. Their reservation was established in Nebraska in 1854. The Omaha gave some of their land to the Winnebago.

The Winnebago were native to Wisconsin and Illinois but were forced to leave and eventually settled in Nebraska. They were given land by the Omaha.

The Sac and Fox were from the St. Lawrence valleys and Great Lakes regions but were forced to leave those areas after conflict. The Sac and Fox are also called the Sac and Meskwaki Nation. They now live in Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, and Oklahoma.

The Ponca were once a part of the Omaha tribe, but at the beginning of the 1800s, they separated themselves from the Omaha. They have a separate reservation from the Omaha tribe.

The Santee Sioux, or the Eastern Dakota, are a band of the larger Dakota tribe. In the 1600s, the Santee Sioux lived around the Great Lakes. Because of war in the 1700s, they moved to Minnesota. In the 1800s, after making a treaty with the U.S. government, they moved to a reservation in Nebraska.

The Iowa or Ioway tribe was the tribe that the state of Iowa was named after. They had lived in Missouri but were forced to migrate due to conflict and the encroaching presence of settlers.

title: Crossing the Delaware
text:
It was December 1776, the first holiday season in the new United States. The 2,400 soldiers of the Continental Army under General George Washington were camped in Pennsylvania beside the Delaware River, west of Trenton, New Jersey. Trenton was the base for 1,400 Hessian soldiers. The Hessians were the flank (guard) for the British Army at Princeton, New Jersey. General Washington and his staff knew that if they could defeat the Hessians, they could move on and capture the British at Princeton.

Thomas Paine had just published a book to inspire the new country. “These are the times that try men’s souls.... Tyranny ... is not easily conquered ... the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph.” The words helped General Washington come up with a plan.

The Continental Commander knew that Germans celebrated the Christmas season. The Germans would be off guard. The colonial army could catch them by surprise. The weather for Dec. 25, 1776, was a snowstorm. This was another reason the Hessians would be off guard. There was just one difficulty: How could they move 2,400 soldiers and their equipment across a river and still take the enemy by surprise?

The men moved after sunset. Cargo boats were gathered up and down the river to ferry the men across. Men would go first to help unload the equipment on the New Jersey side when it arrived. General Washington would be in one of the first boats with the men from Virginia and his old friend, Captain Adam Stephen. He would supervise from the New Jersey shore.

The river had large chunks of ice that could hit and damage the wooden boats. The men had long poles to push the ice away. The weather was getting colder. The wind was increasing. Snow turned into freezing rain and sleet. The poorly dressed soldiers kept going. The wind began howling, which picked up the water and splashed it on the men in the boats. They were already soaked from the freezing rain. Still, they kept going back and forth across the river until 10 hours later, at 4 a.m., when the last boat landed.

Meanwhile, General Washington was concerned that the Hessians would have been warned. Spies were everywhere. There was actually a spy in the general’s camp. He didn’t know who, but he knew there was a spy. Did the spy tell the Hessians about the Continental Army’s plan? Would they be waiting for them? Washington remembered Thomas Paine's words: “These are the times that try men’s souls.... Tyranny ... is not easily conquered ... the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph.”

Washington assembled the men in their units and started the 10-mile march to Trenton on the ice-covered ground. The ice on the ground broke as the men marched. The sharp edges cut through the thin shoes of the soldiers. They kept going. The weather had not quit. It rained harder, with small ice pellets mixed into the rain. They kept going.

At about daybreak, the Continental Army arrived. The cannons were in place on the high ground, looking into Trenton. The attack began. The Hessians were surprised! They were not ready. Hessian drummers were frantically calling the Hessians to assemble and attack. Washington’s army blocked every attempted attack by the Hessians. Within 60 minutes, the fighting was over. The Hessians surrendered. Trenton was now in the hands of General Washington and the Continental Army. General Washington knew the meaning of Thomas Paine’s words “the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph.”

title: Military Encounters
text:
No one is quite sure which side fired that first “shot heard ‘round the world” on April 19, 1775. After the fateful battles at Lexington and Concord, both sides knew they couldn’t back down. The war had begun. There were many battles in the American Revolutionary War. The following were major turning points for the outcome of the war.

Battle of Bunker Hill

On June 16, 1776, the Americans entered the Charleston Peninsula, occupied Bunker Hill, and then moved on to Breed’s Hill. General Gage and his men decided to take the hills by force. The Patriots held off the first two waves of attack, then ran out of ammunition. The British sent a third attack and took over the hill.

Trenton and Princeton

On Dec. 25, 1776, Washington’s men crossed the ice-packed Delaware River. They marched to Trenton and then surrounded and attacked the Hessian army. Many Hessians joined the Patriots rather than be taken prisoner. A few days later, Washington’s men marched quietly into Princeton, a neighboring city. After a short fight against General Cornwallis, Princeton was also under Washington’s control.

Victory at Saratoga

The British had planned to quickly defeat the colonists by cutting off New England from the Southern Colonies. But the British plan didn’t work out. Washington’s army moved north and met General Burgoyne’s troops at Saratoga, New York. The Patriot forces surrounded the British, and Burgoyne surrendered on Oct. 17, 1777. This victory helped persuade the French to join the Patriot cause.

Battle of Kings Mountain

In September 1780, the British Major Patrick Ferguson challenged the South Carolina Patriot militias to give up their weapons. The rebel Patriots instead joined together to attack Ferguson’s Loyalists. Ferguson retreated, but the Patriots caught up with him at Kings Mountain, near the border of South Carolina. Ferguson was shot and killed. The Loyalists surrendered to the Patriots. This Patriot victory made Cornwallis’s army unable to invade North Carolina. He had to retreat farther back into South Carolina.

Yorktown: The End Is in Sight

British General Cornwallis took his army to Yorktown, Virginia, in 1781. He hoped to find fresh supplies and more soldiers, but it was too late. French ships had arrived to trap Cornwallis in Yorktown. Patriot soldiers and the French navy surrounded his army. Cornwallis surrendered on Oct. 19, 1781. His defeat meant that the entire British Army was beaten.

title: Valley Forge, Morristown, and Harsh Winters
text:
In the winter of 1777-1778, General Washington camped with the 12,000 men of the Continental Army at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania. The winter weather was unpredictable with rain, snow, sleet, cold, and freezing temperatures. Most had no shoes, and their clothes were old and torn. There was not enough food to feed the men. They were sick and hungry. Many soldiers deserted. Many more stayed and endured the trials in support of their leader and the war they were fighting.

The British Army occupied nearby Philadelphia that winter. They quartered their men in public housing and private homes at the expense of the citizens.

Washington spent much of his time writing to Congress demanding more supplies for his men. If the nation lost the army, the nation and independence would be lost. Washington said of these loyal troops:

"To see the men without clothes ... without blankets to lie upon, without shoes ... without a house or hut to cover them until those could be built, and submitting without a murmur, is a proof of patience and obedience which ... can scarcely be paralleled."

The men spent their days training to be soldiers. Baron Friedrich von Steuben, a military officer from the European country of Prussia (today’s Germany and Poland), provided training. As the drillmaster of Valley Forge, he taught them military skills. They learned to follow orders from an officer. They learned how to move together quickly as a fighting unit.

There would be more winters ahead for the Continental Army. In 1780, while the soldiers camped at Morristown, New Jersey, the weather was far more severe. The rivers were frozen 18 feet deep. Major General John Kalb wrote in his diary on Feb. 12, 1780:

"Those who have only been at Valley Forge or Middlebrook during the last two winters, but have not tasted the cruelty of this one [1780] know not what it is to suffer."

Historians tend to focus on Valley Forge more than Morristown. The reason for this is not because of the severity and suffering. It is because the men who survived Valley Forge became a well-disciplined army. It was an army ready to fight the professional British Army and win.

title: Hessians
text: One of the grievances in the Declaration of Independence was that King George III was “transporting large Armies of Foreign Mercenaries” to do his work. This refers to the German-speaking Hessians. Sometimes countries didn’t have enough soldiers to make a full army. The British Army was especially spread thin with its large empire reaching all over the globe. Because of this, sometimes, much smaller German-speaking countries offered their armies in exchange for payment. King George paid the small country of Hesse-Cassel to send their trained professional army (Hessians) to fight for Great Britain in America. A mercenary is a professional soldier hired to serve in a foreign army. The Hessians were mercenaries. Hessians participated in every major battle of the war. Some of the Hessians started to side with the Americans and deserted the British Army as the war went on. Many chose to stay in America after the war was over. The American Revolutionary War ended the mercenary practice for Hessian soldiers.

title: Marquis de Lafayette
text:
The cause of American revolution and independence gained attention and admiration from around the world. A young nobleman from France named Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was inspired by the Patriots. He volunteered to come and fight with them. Lafayette grew up in a wealthy family with a long tradition of military service. He wanted to make a name for himself in this Revolutionary War. Defying the direct orders of King Louis XVI of France, he crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1777. He was determined to assist the rebellious Americans. Upon arrival in the new country, he became friends with many Patriot leaders and statesmen. Although still a teenager who spoke little English and lacked any battle experience, Lafayette convinced the Continental Army to commission him as a major general on July 31, 1777. He refused to accept payment for his service in the army. He was daring and bold in battle, and those who fought under his leadership were very loyal to him. James Armistead, an enslaved man who joined to fight with the Patriots, so admired Lafayette after working closely with him that he took his last name. Lafayette joined Washington at Valley Forge and stayed in his command throughout the entire war.

In 1779, Lafayette returned to France and to the court of King Louis XVI. The king listened to Lafayette, and this time, he agreed with him about the American cause. The British and French had been rivals for centuries. The French king saw an opportunity to strengthen the opponent of Great Britain. He agreed to send support to the Americans. The French alliance gave the Americans funding, supplies, and military support. Lafayette returned to America with the money, supplies, and troops the Continental Army so desperately needed. He led both American and French troops through several important battles, all the way through the Siege of Yorktown.

title: The End of the War
text:
There were many factors that ultimately led to the end of the American Revolution. The United States formed several key alliances with several powerful European nations. The rising cost of the war heavily impacted the British government. This led to a major decline in the British war effort in North America.

In May 1781, General Charles Cornwallis led 7,000 British troops out of North Carolina and retreated to Yorktown, Virginia. Yorktown was on the coast and could be attacked by French ships. The British set up their defenses and waited for reinforcements. French ships moved toward Yorktown through the Chesapeake Bay, blocking British supply lines.

George Washington sent 4,500 troops, led by Marquis de Lafayette, to Yorktown. They would prevent the British Army from leaving. Washington sent other troops to join the French fleet in the Chesapeake Bay. Washington arrived in Yorktown on Sept. 28, 1781, and besieged the city for 11 days. Unable to defend the city, Cornwallis surrendered on Oct. 19, 1781.

Cornwallis’s surrender and the American victory at Yorktown did not bring an end to the fighting in North America, however. The fight to control the continent continued between American and British forces and their allies through the end of 1782.

Jan. 2: British forces defeat American militiamen near Charleston, South Carolina.

Jan. 19 to Feb. 13: French forces capture British-held St. Kitts in the Caribbean Sea.

March 8 and 9: American militiamen attack a group of Native Americans they believed were allies of the British near Gnadenhutten in present-day Ohio.

April 8: Battle of Delaware Bay. American naval vessels are attacked by three British ships but fought back, resulting in an American victory.

May 8: American and Spanish forces capture Nassau, Bahamas, a strategic port and major center of trade, from the British.

July 11: The remaining British soldiers and Loyalists evacuate Savannah, Georgia.

July 13: British forces and members of the Seneca tribe attack Hannahstown, Pennsylvania. The townspeople retreat to the fort, but the attacking force burns homes, farms, and other buildings in the town. Michael Huffnagle, a member of the town, records the event in a letter to American General William Irvine, stating that, “Such wanton destruction I have never beheld, burning and destroying as they went. The People of this Place behaved brave; retired to the Fort, left all of their prey to the Enemy, and with twenty men only and nine guns in good order, we stood the attack ‘til dark.”

Aug. 19: Battle of Blue Licks. British rangers and their Native American allies ambush members of the Kentucky militia, killing 64 Americans. Frontiersman and explorer Daniel Boone is present at the battle. He records the event in a letter to the governor of Virginia:

We discovered the enemy lying in wait for us. On this discovery we formed our columns into one single line, and marched up in their front within about forty yards before there was a gun fired … The inhabitants of this county are very much alarmed at the thoughts of the Indians bringing another campaign into our country this Fall. If this should be the case, it will break up these settlements. I hope therefore your Excellency will take the matter into your consideration, and send us some relief as quick as possible…

Aug. 27: The Battle of Combahee River. British sailors and soldiers sail up the Combahee River in South Carolina to capture supplies from American farmers in the area. The Americans drive the British out of the area but suffer heavy losses. Colonel John Laurens, one of the heroes of Yorktown, is one of the many American soldiers killed during this conflict.

Nov. 10: Battle of Piqua. American General George Rogers Clark raids villages of the Shawnee, allies of the British, near Chillicothe, in present-day Ohio. Clark also destroys the British trading post, Loramie's Store.

Dec. 14: The remaining British soldiers and Loyalists evacuate Charleston, South Carolina.

title: Treaty of Paris, 1783
text:
The last major battle of the American Revolution was fought in 1781. The Americans and French forced British Army General Cornwallis to surrender at Yorktown. After years of fighting, the British decided that the war was too expensive to continue. Although the battles were over, British forces remained in the U.S. They were still stationed around Charleston, South Carolina. The powerful main army was still in New York. While neither side took any decisive action, it took another two years for all the issues to be resolved. At last, both sides agreed to meet and discuss terms for a treaty to end the war. The king sent representatives from Great Britain. The United States was represented by Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay. They met in Paris, France, near the end of 1782. They spent 10 months working out the details of the Treaty of Paris. The treaty set out conditions that each side agreed to follow:

Britain would recognize the United States of America as an independent nation.

Britain ceded (gave up) its territory east of the Mississippi River. This doubled the size of the new country.

Florida would be ceded to Spain.

The United States was granted fishing rights off of the British-Canadian coast. This was a very valuable fishing region.

The Mississippi River was opened to navigation, or travel, by both U.S. and British citizens.

Issues of American debt owed to British creditors were resolved.

Many colonists had remained loyal to the king during the war. The treaty guaranteed that they would be treated fairly. The property that had been taken from them during the war would be restored to them.

Great Britain knew the value of continued trade with the new United States, so they were very agreeable in the process of creating the treaty. The Treaty of Paris was signed on Sept. 3, 1783. The British signed a separate peace treaty with France and Spain, officially ending the Revolutionary War.

title: Washington Resigns His Commission
text:
Only once before in history had a victorious general stepped away and resigned his commission. Cincinnatus, an ancient Roman patriot, quietly returned to his farm after his victories in war. This was more than 2,000 years before the American Revolution. It was extremely rare for a military leader to walk away from such power and authority. Most would have remained in their position and used their power in the military to rule. However, George Washington knew that he and his army fought for freedom from this kind of military rule. He knew that for the Revolution to be complete, he had to step away from power. On Dec. 23, 1783, he reported to the Continental Congress:

Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of Action; and bidding an Affectional farewell to the August body under whose orders I have so long acted, I here offer my Commission, and take my leave of all the employments of public life.

Washington’s action impressed even his enemies. King George III was reported to have said that Washington’s resignation would “place him in a light the most distinguished of any man living.” The king went so far as to say that he “thought him [Washington] the greatest character of the age.”

There is a painting titled General George Washington Resigning His Commission by John Trumbull. It is on display in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. This painting depicts the scene on Dec. 23, 1783, in the Maryland State House in Annapolis. There, George Washington resigned his commission as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. This voluntary action was significant for establishing civilian authority over the military. This was a fundamental principle of American democracy. The artist, John Trumbull, considered Washington's resignation to be “one of the highest moral lessons ever given to the world.”

title: Fate of the Loyalists
text:
Not all American colonists supported the cause for independence. Historians estimate that about 500,000, or 20 percent of all colonists, remained loyal to the British government. Loyalists faced a very different fate than the colonists who supported independence. Between 60,000 and 80,000 Loyalists left the American colonies during or after the American Revolution. They primarily settled in Great Britain, Canada, the Caribbean, and even Spanish Florida.

Many Loyalists stayed and faced significant hardships. Thousands of Loyalists who remained in the new United States had their property vandalized or destroyed. Those who lost their property during the war often did not regain it after the war. Some Loyalists were able to recover their property but were forced to pay additional taxes to reclaim it. Others faced public humiliation, ridicule, and violence.

Life for most Loyalists was very difficult following the war. Many Loyalists recorded their experiences in letters and other publications during and after the war. Judge Samuel Curwen, who was born in Massachusetts, spent nine years in exile for remaining loyal to the British government. During his exile, he wrote in a letter to a friend:

I abandoned my dwelling, friends, and means of life, which you know I possessed in no small degree and might have retained on the comparative trifling condition of insults, reproaches, and perhaps a dress of tar and feathers; an alternative I now see much to be preferred to the distresses of mind I am daily suffering.

In 1786, merchant James Clarke, who went into exile following the war, wrote, "My Attachment to our native Country is so fervent and sincere that I could freely give up my Life, and Ten Thousand more if I possess them, could I restore dear Rhode Island to its former happy, happy Situation."

title: Families Torn Apart
text:
The American Revolution had a profound impact on Patriots, Loyalists, and thousands of other colonists in the new American nation. Families were often at odds with one another and had differing opinions over American independence. Many families were torn apart because of these differing opinions.

Benjamin Franklin and his son William were an example of how differing opinions tore families apart during the American Revolution. Benjamin Franklin was an early supporter of American independence. He was a member of the Continental Congress and helped draft the Declaration of Independence. He also served as an ambassador to France and played a vital role in forming an alliance with the French government. Franklin was a Patriot, but his son had a very different opinion.

In 1762, King George III appointed William Franklin, Benjamin Franklin’s son, the Royal Governor of New Jersey. He worked closely with the British Parliament and was a loyal supporter of the king. When tensions began to rise between the colonists and the British government, William opposed the actions of the colonists. Benjamin Franklin was convinced that he could change his son’s mind, but William refused to abandon his allegiance to Great Britain. The relationship between Benjamin and William Franklin never recovered. William left the colonies in 1777, and the two only exchanged a few letters following the Revolution before they cut all ties with one another.

The Franklins were not the only family torn apart by the American Revolution. The Flucker family of Massachusetts was also a casualty of divided loyalties. The Fluckers were a wealthy and well-known family from Massachusetts. Thomas Flucker served as the Secretary of Massachusetts and worked closely with British colonial leaders. In 1774, Lucy Flucker, the daughter of Thomas and his wife Hannah, disobeyed her family’s wishes and married Henry Knox, a book shop owner from Boston.

The Fluckers remained loyal to the British government, while Henry and Lucy Knox joined the Patriot cause. Henry Knox joined the Continental Army and quickly rose through the ranks. He was promoted to the rank of brigadier general by 1777. The Flucker family left Boston and settled in England in 1775. The relationship between Lucy Knox and her family remained strained, and they never fully reconciled, even after the war ended.

title: Dissent Among the Colonies
text:
Following the American Revolution, the colonies disagreed on how best to move forward as a nation. There were many issues that needed to be addressed by the new country. What shape would the new government take? What powers would it have, and which powers would the states keep? What kind of economic policies would the country pursue and put in place?

The main problem was that any attempt to entrust a central government with power meant that individual states would have to give up power. This is something they did not want to do. Larger colonies like Virginia and New York would lose the ability to govern themselves and give up some of their independence to a new U.S. government. Taxes imposed on the new states by the government caused disagreements and rebellion in certain states as they opposed what they saw as government overreach.

Individual colonies borrowed money during the war, and each one owed a different amount to various countries following the war. Northern colonies supported Alexander Hamilton’s idea to have the new national government take on all debts taken out by the colonies during the war. Southern colonies, which generally owed less money following the war, did not want the central government to have to pay back money their colonies did not borrow. Ultimately, the U.S. government took on all colonial debts, which gave the newly formed states a clean economic slate.

title: Shays' Rebellion
text:
Though the end of the American Revolution meant that the United States would be a country free from British rule, that did not mean that the new nation was free from problems. Waging a war was very expensive, and the new American government faced many economic challenges.

One of these challenges was how to pay veterans who fought either in the Continental Army or one of the state militias. These veterans received very little to no pay for their service, and many had to go into debt to provide for their families. When it came time to pay those debts, they were unable to do so. In spite of this, the state government demanded payment, even though they were not paying the veterans their pensions.

One person facing this struggle was Daniel Shays, a former captain in the Continental Army. Shays was a farmer, and when he and other veterans began losing their land to debt collectors, tensions boiled over. In August 1786, the Massachusetts state government refused to help Shays or any other war veterans. Between August and December 1786, Shays and his followers, called “Regulators,” led many protests against debt collectors taking veterans’ lands.

On Jan. 25, 1787, Shays and 1,500 Regulators approached the federal armory in Springfield, Massachusetts. Their intent was to take control of the building to force the government to listen to their concerns. There were 1,200 Massachusetts militiamen guarding the armory. Confrontation between the two groups increased from shouting to the firing of weapons. Four of the Regulators were killed and 20 more were wounded.

This event contributed to the current government realizing that the Articles of Confederation did not protect the liberties of the people. A delegation of representatives from each state convened in Philadelphia to discuss changes in the current government. The Philadelphia Convention of 1787 was created for the United States government to be stronger and better able to address the economic and political needs of the people.

title: The Articles of Confederation
text:
With independence from Great Britain came a new government for the new nation. The Continental Congress had been the governing body during the war. When forming a government, Congress looked at a confederation organization.

Many of the delegates had worked with the Iroquois Confederation over the years. The words of Canasatego, leader of the Onondaga Nation, were wise. “... We heartily recommend Union and a Good Agreement between you our Brethren. Our wise Forefathers established Union and Amity [friendship] between the Five Nations; this has made us formidable [mighty], this has given us great weight and Authority with our Neighboring Nations. We are a Powerful confederacy, and by your observing the same Methods our wise Forefathers have taken, you will acquire fresh Strength and Power."

Strength and power were what the members of Congress wanted in a government for the new nation. Congress created the Articles of Confederation to provide the written rules for how the states' "league of friendship" would be organized. The Articles of Confederation gave rules for what actions Congress could take to govern the country.

The new government was fearful of a monarchy, where authority is centered on one person. The Iroquois Confederacy model spread authority over the members. The Articles had no strong central leader. Congress was the governing body. A new leader for congress was elected by the members every year. Congress elected John Hanson to lead the Confederation Congress. Each state had equal voting in Congress. Each state had one vote. Nine of the 13 states had to agree to pass any laws.

Each representative was fearful of taxation. “No taxation without representation” guided the laws in the new government. Each state would set their own taxes. Taxation would be based on the land value in each state. This reflected their value in owning land. These values would be determined by each state. The state legislatures would determine how much of the collected taxes would be sent to Congress for national use. Congress was given no authority to levy or collect taxes.

Each state had the authority to regulate trade and taxes on imports and exports. There were no consistent fees charged in the seaports to foreign countries. This created competition and trade imbalance between states and foreign markets. States even charged taxes for merchandise from other states.

Each state would create its own judicial system to enforce state laws. Congress would regulate themselves over the laws they would create.

Each state raised their own militia for defense. During the war for independence, there was a national army in service to Congress. Congress held debt for the war. Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress had to request money from the states to pay these debts.

Over the next few years, the operation of government under the Articles of Confederation proved to be ineffective. With power divided over many, there was confusion, competition, and conflict.

Congress recognized the government needed to be changed. Throughout history, governments in need of change resorted to power struggles, betrayals, raising armies, and war. The United States had just gone through such violence. Would such a change of government mean war?

In the history of the world, something very different happened. A current government organized a constitutional convention to change itself. States sent representatives to sit together, talk, and change the government with debate, compromise, and the people voting for acceptance. No violence. Government changed with the stroke of a pen. It was revolutionary.

title: Essential Question
text: How did the Constitutional Convention attempt to balance the interests of all of the states?

title: Conflict and Compromise at the Convention
text:
One of the greatest challenges faced at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 was dividing the power between state and federal government. Some delegates wanted a strong central government that had more power over the people and states. They were called Federalists. Other delegates favored a weaker federal government that gave more power to the states and the people. They were called Anti-Federalists. Both sides wrote essays that argued their points. These became known as the Federalist Papers and Anti-Federalist Papers. During the convention, several plans were presented to help balance the power of the new government.

The Virginia Plan

James Madison, a delegate from Virginia, presented the Virginia Plan. This plan gave Congress more power over the states and also provided for an executive branch of national government. This branch would carry out the laws passed by Congress. The plan also included a judicial branch to interpret, or explain, the laws. However, negotiations began to get sticky when the smaller states learned that states with larger populations would have more representatives in Congress than the smaller states.

The New Jersey Plan

William Paterson, a delegate from New Jersey, proposed a different plan. The New Jersey Plan said that each state, no matter its size, would have the same number of representatives in Congress. The large states didn’t agree with this idea. They felt that because they had more people, they should also have more say in running the nation.

The Great Compromise

Roger Sherman of Connecticut came up with an idea that bridged ideas from both plans. He proposed that Congress be made up of two parts, called houses. In the Senate, each state would have two senators, giving both large states and small states equal power. In the House of Representatives, the number of representatives would be determined by population. The larger the state, the more representatives it would have. Both sides agreed to the Great Compromise.

Slavery

The economy of the South relied on enslaved people to keep farms and plantations running. Many delegates of the North wanted to outlaw the slave trade, but delegates of the South disagreed. A compromise was finally reached. The slave trade would be allowed to go on for another 20 years and then be outlawed in 1808.

The North and South also disagreed over how to count the enslaved people when figuring out the population of each state. Population determined how many representatives each state had in Congress and affected collecting taxes. Finally, the Three-Fifths Compromise was agreed upon. Three out of every five, or three-fifths, of the enslaved people would be counted in the population. This ensured that state populations wouldn’t be too high in slave states. From their perspective, the issue of slavery was considered solved, at least for the time being.

Status of Native American Nations

During the Articles of Confederation, each state interacted with various Native American nations. Some states treated the Native Americans fairly. Other states did not. James Madison proposed that Congress be given the power to manage all interactions with the Native Americans, whether they lived within the boundaries of a state or not. This would bring consistency to actions for all tribal nations through the federal government. The final wording of the Constitution said that Congress had power “to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes.”

Individual Rights

Some delegates wanted to add a bill of rights to the Constitution to protect important individual rights. Others felt that since most states had their own bills of rights, this was unnecessary. Thirty-nine of the 55 delegates signed their names to the Constitution without a formal bill of rights on Sept. 17, 1787. Failing to add a bill of rights would prove to be a mistake that had to be corrected in the near future.

title: George Washington
text:
George Washington is often called the Father of Our Country. He was an active member of his community and nation. He served as the leader of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. He inspired the colonial soldiers to be brave and have faith in themselves. Washington led the new United States to victory over Great Britain. People trusted him and believed in him as a leader. He believed that governments should listen to the opinions of the people. Washington served bravely in the war with the other Patriots. Following the Revolutionary War, he left the army and returned to his farm in Virginia to live as a normal citizen.

In 1787, Washington was elected as chairman of the Constitutional Convention. He believed that the new nation could not and would not survive without a strong central government, national freedoms, and the protection of individual liberties. He worked with the other members of the convention to create a document that reflected their ideas for a new government. He believed so strongly in the principles and values outlined in the new Constitution that he was willing to sign it.

In 1789, George Washington became the first president of the United States. Washington tried to get the country's finances in order with the help of Alexander Hamilton, the new secretary of the treasury. He appointed Henry Knox his secretary of war. Knox advised the president on military matters and on relations with American Indians. He worked to create strong alliances with foreign nations. During his first term, Washington toured the United States and learned that most Americans supported their new government leaders. He hoped that the new United States would expand its territory west of the Mississippi River during his presidency.

He served two terms as president and refused to run for a third because he believed that one man should not hold that much power for that long. He set the standards for those that followed in his footsteps. Today, you can find his portrait on the dollar bill and quarter.

title: Alexander Hamilton
text:
At the age of 16, Alexander Hamilton enrolled at King’s College in New York. In 1774, he wrote an article that supported American independence. He then left King’s College to join the Revolutionary War. His bravery and courageous actions caught the eye of George Washington. He served as Washington’s right-hand man for the remainder of the war. After the war, Hamilton returned to his studies and became a lawyer.

In 1787, he was elected as a New York delegate for the Constitutional Convention. Hamilton did everything he could to make the Constitution become the supreme law of the land. He believed in the principles outlined in the Constitution and was willing to sign the important document. He helped write the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution and the new United States Government. In 1789, he became George Washington’s secretary of the treasury. As secretary of the treasury, he established the money system we still use today.

In 1795, he returned to New York to practice law. He also founded the Bank of New York, which is still in existence today. Today, you can see Hamilton on the 10-dollar bill.

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a talented inventor, scientist, diplomat, and writer. He was highly respected and admired in colonial America. Before working to create the new United States, he owned a newspaper company in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Franklin also served as a member of the Pennsylvania Assembly. He worked to make sure the colonists were treated fairly and had the same rights as all British citizens.

In 1775, he served as a representative of Pennsylvania at the Second Continental Congress. Benjamin Franklin brought consensus and compromise as he helped Thomas Jefferson write the Declaration of Independence.

During the Revolutionary War, he worked tirelessly as an ambassador in France. In 1785, he returned to the United States to serve his country. He served as a member of the Constitutional Convention in 1787. Franklin provided his wisdom and expertise to settle arguments and create compromise among the delegates. His ideas for government were the model for the House of Representatives and the Senate. He signed the Constitution in 1787. Benjamin Franklin signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

title: George Mason
text:
George Mason was a neighbor and friend of George Washington. Although he preferred life in Virginia to politics, Mason made very important contributions to our government. While at the Constitutional Convention, he faithfully attended sessions and spoke up on every topic of importance.

In the 1770s, before he attended the Second Continental Congress, Mason wrote the Virginia Declaration of Rights. This document described the rights of people. It influenced the content of the Declaration of Independence.

When the Constitution was being written, Mason was concerned that a list of guaranteed rights was not included in the new document. Mason was an Anti-Federalist. He was worried about the new government having too much power over the states. When the delegates voted to accept the new Constitution without a bill of rights, Mason refused to sign. He argued that the states should not ratify the new document unless amendments were included to protect individual rights. After ratification, a bill of rights based on the one suggested by Mason was added to the Constitution, protecting the rights of all Americans. This is the same Bill of Rights we have today.

title: Elbridge Gerry
text:
Elbridge Gerry came from a large Massachusetts family of 11 children. He grew up watching his father serve as an important leader in the community. As a young man, Gerry attended Harvard University. The more he learned, the more he felt that the colonists were justified in resisting unfair rules placed upon them by the British government. Gerry served in several local government positions after graduating. He was chosen to serve as a delegate of Massachusetts at the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

As an Anti-Federalist, Gerry was concerned about the proposed document of the Constitution. He saw several issues that he believed would make the federal government too powerful. He refused to sign the document unless several amendments were added. These amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

After the Constitution was ratified, Gerry was elected to serve in the House of Representatives in the new Congress. He later went on to serve as vice president to James Madison from 1812 until his death in 1814.

title: James Madison
text:
James Madison is known as the “Father of the Constitution.” Many of the ideas in the Constitution were Madison’s original ideas about the rights and freedoms that individuals should have. Our rights and responsibilities are defined and protected in the Constitution, thanks, in large part, to Madison. He was a very active delegate at the Constitutional Convention. He took notes, kept records, and made more than 150 speeches. When the Constitution was complete, James Madison knew it would take hard work to convince all the states to ratify it. He worked with John Jay and Alexander Hamilton to write the Federalist Papers, which were a series of essays that supported the new government. Madison wrote 29 of the 85 essays. Virginia was one of the last states to ratify the Constitution, and James Madison’s essays helped get the final votes.

Madison and the other Federalists worked hard to maintain the system of checks and balances among the three branches of government and protect the rights of citizens. In 1789, he was elected to the Virginia Assembly and worked to create religious freedom in his home state. He served as secretary of state during Thomas Jefferson’s presidency. In 1808, he was elected as the fourth president of the United States.

title: Thomas Jefferson
text:
Thomas Jefferson studied many subjects, including science, architecture, law, music, history, languages, astronomy, and mathematics. He believed that everyone was entitled to an education and that everyone had the ability to learn. Jefferson was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence. He was one of the first Americans to express the idea that all people are born with certain rights that should never be taken away. He felt that the only way to achieve this goal was to create a new, independent nation. His ideas of “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” would later influence the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.

During the American Revolution, he served as the governor of Virginia. He worked to create an alliance with France. He also worked very closely with fellow Founder James Madison to create religious freedom and equality in Virginia. Following the American Revolution, he served as the ambassador to France. He helped establish a trading relationship between the two countries.

Although he was not present at the Constitutional Convention, he believed very strongly in the Constitution. He agreed that any power not given to the federal government belonged to the states or to the people. He returned to the United States to serve as George Washington’s first secretary of state. He served as John Adams's vice president until he was elected president of the United States in 1800.

During his presidency, the United States more than doubled in size through the Louisiana Purchase. He also worked very hard to keep the United States from war with France and England. Following his presidency, he founded the University of Virginia and sold his personal book collection. This later became the Library of Congress.

title: Roger Sherman
text:
Roger Sherman signed the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, and the United States Constitution. Sherman was on the Committee of Five to write the Declaration of Independence. He was on the committee to write the Articles of Confederation. At the Constitutional Convention in 1787, he introduced the idea of a bicameral legislature, where states have representation based on population and a national senate where each state has two senators.

Sherman was known to be hardworking, dedicated to service, and extremely sensible. He was a self-taught surveyor, lawyer, and merchant. He served in the Connecticut House of Representatives and the General Assembly.

At the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, Connecticut was considered a middle-sized state: smaller than Virginia, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania, but larger than Delaware or Rhode Island. Sherman was vocal in protecting states’ rights over the federal government. Sherman supported Alexander Hamilton’s proposal of having the federal government pay the state debts for the revolution. One of his greatest contributions was the introduction of the compromise for a bicameral legislature.

Thomas Jefferson described Sherman as: “a man who never said a foolish thing in his life.” John Adams called him a best friend and “one of the strongest pillars of the revolution.”

Sherman served in the new House of Representatives and then the Senate until his death in 1793.

Roger Sherman once said: “When you are in the minority, talk; when you are in the majority, vote."

title: Let's Write
text: How did farming practices of the 1910s-1920s help cause the Dust Bowl? What were the results? Write a paragraph to explain the causes and effects of the Dust Bowl. Be sure to use details and evidence from the text.

title: William Paterson
text:
William Paterson was born in Ireland and immigrated to Pennsylvania with his parents in 1745. Paterson attended Princeton College and knew many of the other Princeton alumni, including Aaron Burr and James Madison. Paterson became a lawyer in New Jersey. He was selected to be a delegate to the first Congress of New Jersey. He helped write the New Jersey constitution. He became attorney general for the new state. His energy and commitment to law earned him the opportunity to represent New Jersey at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787.

Paterson opposed representation according to the population of the state. Being from the smaller state of New Jersey, Paterson feared there would be too much control from the larger states. He proposed that each state have only one vote. A unicameral legislature would be an equalizer for small states and large states. His proposal was incorporated into Roger Sherman’s Great Compromise of a bicameral legislature. A house of representatives and a senate was adopted by the convention.

As a Federalist, Paterson helped ratify the Constitution and went on to serve in the Senate. Paterson was the first senator to resign from office to become the governor of New Jersey. By 1793, Washington asked him to serve on the Supreme Court of the United States. He resigned the governorship to become an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court from 1793 to 1806.

Paterson supported the rule of law, which means no person is above the consequences of the law. He worked to help establish John Marshall as the chief justice of the Supreme Court. John Marshall’s work as chief justice elevated the independence of the Supreme Court to be a great part of the checks and balances system of the Constitution.

Paterson was active on the court until his death in 1806.
