What do you think the relationship between earthquakes and volcanoes is?

The Ring of Fire

One of the first signs of a potential volcanic eruption is an earthquake. An earthquake is a sudden and violent shaking of the earth. One place where scientists can see evidence of the connection between earthquakes and volcanoes is the Ring of Fire. The Ring of Fire is a region in the Pacific Ocean that experiences a lot of geological activity. In fact, about 75 percent of Earth’s volcanoes and 90 percent of Earth’s earthquakes happen in the Ring of Fire.

There are more than 450 volcanoes along the Ring of Fire. Follow the path of volcanoes with your finger. Start from the southern tip of South America, and go north, along the western coast of North America. Cross the Bering Strait from Alaska to Asia, then head south through Japan and the Philippines. Finally, round the eastern coast of Australia in the Pacific Ocean.

This area is caused by the Earth being made of large pieces that fit together like a puzzle. The land deep beneath the Pacific Ocean is one of these pieces. And that piece is moving! Its movement allows magma to rise up through the surface of the Earth, creating volcanoes. When this piece of Earth gets caught on the edges of other pieces, it releases motion energy: in other words, earthquakes!

Reflect and Connect

Sit still. Can you feel yourself moving? Believe it or not, the land you are on is slowly drifting. All the continents drift. Even the land deep below the ocean is moving. The Earth’s outermost layer of rock, or its crust, is made of large pieces. These pieces are floating on magma. When the pieces move, they can move toward, away from, or slide past other pieces. Different types of movements create different landforms. After millions of years, this slow movement has created big effects. We can see the effects in the patterns of where Earth’s features have formed.

First, areas of Earth where two pieces pull away from each other are usually under the ocean. This results in a long, thin opening, where magma then seeps up from deep within the Earth and fills in the opening. This creates ocean ridges. It can also form seamounts. If this happens on land, it forms large mountain ranges along continental boundaries or in the middle of continents, like the Himalayas in Asia.

Pieces of the Earth can also slide past each other. As they do, a huge amount of energy is built up. Every so often, this energy is released on Earth's surface as an earthquake. This type of movement often happens along the Pacific coast of the United States, and, therefore, we see fairly frequent earthquakes occurring in California. Patterns of Earth’s major landforms are caused by the pattern of Earth’s pieces.

title: Homes in Nebraska
text:
What’s the best way to build a house? It depends on what kind of lifestyle you live and what resources are nearby.

For centuries, the Native Americans who lived in the Great Plains area, including Nebraska, lived two lifestyles: agricultural and hunter-gatherer. The tribes who lived as agriculturalists (farmers) didn’t move around much. They usually built earth lodges to live in.

Earth lodges were built from a few supporting logs attached to beams on top. Then, smaller logs would branch out from them like a sun’s rays. All of it was covered with thick layers of sod (dirt) and grass. A hole would be left in the top to allow smoke from the cooking fire to escape. Earth lodges used the materials on the Great Plains to make a house that could stay warm during the cold, windy winters. Dozens of people would live in an earth lodge. Since earth lodges needed logs, they had to be built close to wooded areas.

The Native Americans who lived a hunter-gatherer lifestyle had to move around a lot. Their houses needed to go with them, so they often lived in tepees. Tepees were made of tall, thin logs set up vertically and leaned against each other. Animal hides were attached to the logs to make a large, conical (cone-shaped) shelter.

When settlers came to Nebraska, they were surprised that there were no trees to build with. They had to build small shacks or dugouts in a hillside. Some made bricks from river clay and stacked them to make walls. Soldiers at Sidney Barracks, Nebraska, built their walls using lime grout, a type of concrete made of sand, water, and a chemical called lime.

When the railroad came to Nebraska, people started importing lumber for their houses. Sometimes they would even order house kits that came with everything to build a house. They started building the kinds of houses they were used to back home.

With the transportation network we have today, most buildings and houses are made from materials that aren’t native to the region they are built in.

title: Water Resources in Nebraska
text:
Nebraska is one of the top-producing agricultural states in the nation. That is because farmers and scientists have learned how to find, use, and maintain Nebraska’s water resources.

For centuries, Native Americans grew crops such as maize (corn), beans, sunflower seeds, and squash in the Nebraska area. They also hunted bison and other game to eat. They practiced intercropping, which is planting different crops together. For example, they planted beans among the corn because beans return nitrogen to the soil, and corn needs nitrogen to grow.

For a long time, only farmers who lived near rivers could irrigate their crops. Irrigation means moving water to a farm instead of depending only on rain. Early in the 1900s, reservoirs, diversion dams, and distribution canals helped get water to more farms. But irrigation came to many more farmers when the Ogallala Aquifer was discovered.

The Ogallala Aquifer is a huge collection of underground water in the High Plains area. It covers about 174,000 square miles. Electric pumps can lift water from the aquifer and irrigate crops just about anywhere in Nebraska. More than 4.7 million acres of corn are irrigated in our state using nearly 200,000 wells.

Scientists and farmers have found ways to use less water. For example, farmers no longer till the soil each year. This keeps water from evaporating from the soil. They also plant crops that need less water. They use irrigation systems that apply water as close to the ground as possible so that less water evaporates.

title: Shelterbelts in Nebraska
text:
Many settlers who farmed Nebraska in the 1800s used farming methods from the eastern part of the United States or from the country they immigrated from. However, the environment in Nebraska was much different from those places.

The winds that sweep across the Great Plains can blow the topsoil away if it isn’t held down by plants. The wind also increases evaporation from soil and crops. This is a problem especially in western Nebraska where there isn’t much rainfall.

Most settlers didn’t take these things into account. The consequences became apparent in the 1930s when the Dust Bowl was reported in newspapers. The Dust Bowl was an area where drought, wind, and inappropriate farming practices combined to cause severe soil erosion. Winds would kick up “black blizzards” of topsoil being blown away. Soon the area could not be farmed.

The Dust Bowl was not in Nebraska, but a lot of soil erosion was taking place here, too. One important method used to stop continuing erosion is trees.

Shelterbelts are rows of trees planted close together. They provide shelter from the wind. Fields with shelterbelts have less erosion, need less water, and produce 12-15 percent more crops. Some early settlers planted shelterbelts to protect their livestock from the freezing windchill and to keep their homes warmer. Shelterbelts also provide spaces for wildlife to live, wood for fuel, and lumber for building.

In 1935, the U.S. Forest Service started the biggest tree-planting effort ever. Over eight years, workers planted 222 million tree seedlings in the Great Plains area. They made more than 18,500 miles of shelterbelts. The shelterbelts were often 16 rows deep and a mile long. Today, more than 20 million trees and shrubs are planted each year in the Great Plains to prevent soil erosion and increase crop productivity.

title: Water in Nebraska
text:
Rivers

The two most important rivers in Nebraska are the Missouri River and the Platte River.

But maybe we should say that they are the three most important rivers, because the Platte River starts as two rivers. They are called the North and South Platte Rivers. They start in the mountains of northern Colorado, follow their own paths through Colorado and Wyoming, and then come into Nebraska. They finally unite at the city of North Platte in central Nebraska. From there, they become a braided river which is a river with lots of small islands in it. Eventually, the Platte River empties into the Missouri River. This river provides irrigation water and hydroelectric power to Nebraska and is used to transport freight. The Platte River is a major river, but it isn’t very deep. Settlers could never use this river to transport freight. But they did use the river as a guide for several hundred miles of the California, Oregon, and Mormon Trails.

Reservoirs

The largest lakes in Nebraska are actually reservoirs. Reservoirs are human-made lakes. Lake McConaughy is the largest reservoir in Nebraska. It was formed by Kingsley Dam on the Platte River. The dam was made to provide hydroelectric power. The second largest reservoir is Lewis and Clark Lake. Part of this lake is in South Dakota. The lake is created by Gavins Point Dam from the Missouri River.

Sandhills Lakes

In the Sandhills Region of Nebraska are hundreds of small, natural lakes. Most are between two feet and four feet deep. These lakes are mostly made from the Ogallala Aquifer. The aquifer is a huge collection of underground water beneath the sandhills. The water seeps up from the aquifer, making these small lakes. During dry seasons, some of the lakes can disappear and turn into wetlands. Hundreds of thousands of migratory birds stop to rest in the Sandhills lakes during their migration.

Stock ponds

Stock ponds are like human-made Sandhills lakes. A stock pond may be built by a farmer who digs a large hole in the ground with excavating equipment. If the hole is deep enough, it will reach the groundwater and the water will fill the hole. A stock pond can also be made by blocking a stream to make a pond. Stock ponds are used to water livestock and stock fish.

Ground Water

When water soaks into the ground it becomes known as groundwater. The water collects in spaces between the soil and the rocks. This is the water that feeds the roots of plants and trees on the Earth's surface. Groundwater is accessed by drilling or digging wells deep into the ground. Sometimes groundwater naturally comes to the Earth's surface in springs or lakes.

title: Arbor Day
text:
Julius Sterling Morton was a newspaper editor and politician who loved trees. Morton grew up in Michigan, where there were many trees. When he was 22, he married Caroline Joy French. It was October of 1854. The day the couple married, they left Michigan and headed for the Nebraska Territory.

Michigan and the Nebraska Territory were very different. While Michigan was thick with trees, Nebraska was not. Some called this area a desert. The Mortons bought more than 150 acres of land in Nebraska City. Morton was offered a job as editor of the local newspaper. On their land, Morton and his wife built their home. They farmed the land. They raised cattle, chickens, and pigs. They planted trees. Their orchard included apple trees, cherry trees, and peach trees.

Nebraska might be called “The Great American Desert,” but Morton believed differently. He proved this by growing a variety of trees on his property. Some were saplings he and his wife moved from other places. Other trees were bought from the east and planted. These new trees thrived in the Nebraska soil.

Smart agriculture was important to Morton. He believed there were better ways to farm the land. He was a part of a gardening organization called the Horticultural Society.

When Morton became the president of the State Board of Agriculture, he came up with a great idea. What if there was a contest to see who could plant the most trees? On April 10, 1872, one million trees were planted in Nebraska. One million trees in just one day! This day is considered to be the first Arbor Day. Today, it is celebrated on Morton’s birthday, April 22. On the last Friday of April, if weather permits, people plant trees all over the world.

title: Regions, Resources, and Rivers Activity
text:
Nebraska is divided into six regions. Most regions are divided using common geographic characteristics. Each area has its own unique physical geography, climate, vegetation, and natural resources.

Nebraska's most important natural resource is not something we can dig out of the ground; instead, it is what lies under our feet: the land itself! Nearly all of the land in Nebraska is used for farming or ranching. This means that another important resource for the state is water. Without waterways and aquifers, farming and ranching would be impossible.

Some of the minerals found in Nebraska include sand, gravel, clay, oil, and natural gas. The large sand and gravel deposits found in different parts of our state are used for building roads and making cement. Clay is used to make bricks and tile. Oil and gas are found primarily in the southern panhandle and southwestern part of the state.

Directions: Using the resources map and the legend, write down the natural resources found in each region of Nebraska. Don’t forget to include water if the region has a river in it.

title: Week 12 Inquiry Question
text: What is the connection between resources and where people live?

title: Welcome to Pennsylvania!
text:
The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is a historically rich state. It is full of natural resources, waterways, and wildlife. The state is known for its beautiful and diverse geography.

The Appalachian Mountains run through the middle of the state. Over 250 million years ago, the Appalachian Mountains were formed. Minerals, ore, coal, gas, and oil were trapped within the mountain range. Over thousands of years, the mountains have worn down because of the weathering effects of rain, snow, and wind. The large mountain range varies in height over the state. This causes the many waterways to flow in different directions to reach the ocean. The waterways are home to many fish and amphibians. The state has over 83,000 miles of rivers, creeks, and streams. The amount of water available helps trees grow tall and strong. Thick, dense forests cover over 60 percent of the state. The plants in the forests provide food for large and small animals. Pennsylvania is divided into five geographic regions, or areas that have similar physical features. The Atlantic Coastal Plain is located in the southeastern corner of the state. It borders the Delaware River. It is home to the city of Philadelphia. The Piedmont region of Pennsylvania is also in the state's southeastern corner. The Piedmont has rolling hills and soil that is high in nutrients to help plants grow.

The Appalachian Mountains are in the Ridge and Valley region of the state. This area runs from the south-central border to the northeast. The Ridge and Valley region divides the state and has made travel challenging for centuries.

Pennsylvania's largest region is the Allegheny Plateau. This region is in the state's northern and southern sections. The Allegheny Plateau has gentle hills and soil mixed with large rocks and stones from retreating glaciers from millions of years ago. Mount Davis is part of the Allegheny Plateau. Located in Somerset County, it is the tallest point in Pennsylvania. It rises over 3,000 feet to the Appalachian Basin.

Pennsylvania's smallest region is the Lake Erie Plain. This is located along the northeast on the shoreline of Lake Erie. The soil and climate in this region provide for a variety of plants that are not seen in other areas of the state.

title: What’s in a Name?
text: The English colony of Pennsylvania was created in 1681. King Charles II gave land in America to William Penn. The king owed the Penn family a debt. A debt is something owed to another person. The charter or legal papers that gave Penn the governing power of the colony was signed on March 4, 1681. King Charles II named the colony after Penn’s father. He also used sylvania, the Latin word for “wooded land.” The name “Pennsylvania'' was written in the charter.

title: The Natural Resources of Pennsylvania
text:
Mineral Deposits (Coal & Limestone)

Pennsylvania’s mountains contain many valuable mineral resources. The two most important of these are coal and limestone. Coal was made millions of years ago by decaying or dead trees and plants. Heat and pressure from the mountains being formed made the plant material a solid rock-like material.

There are two types of coal in Pennsylvania. Anthracite coal is also called "hard coal". The coal is a shiny black color. When burned, anthracite coal provides a high temperature fire. Bituminous coal or "soft coal" is the most abundant kind found in the state. It can be black or brown in coloring. When burned, bituminous coal can provide heat, but not as high as anthracite coal. Coal can be found in the Ridge and Valley region and the Allegheny Plateau region of the state.

Limestone is another mineral found in the Ridge and Valley region. Limestone was formed from water and tiny pieces of rock being pressed together millions of years ago. There are minerals in the limestone that help plants like rhododendron and mountain laurel grow. The limestone can also be a filter to remove pollutants in water and air.

Trees (Forests)

Pennsylvania is home to over 180 different types of trees. Trees that grow in Pennsylvania generally fall into two categories: coniferous or deciduous. Coniferous trees stay green all year. The branches of pine trees are covered with flat green leaves called “needles.” The many branches of pine trees can create a shelter and protection for animals. Wood from pine trees isn’t strong. It can’t hold weight over periods of time. Softwood burns fast and has a sticky pitch or sap in the wood. The white pine tree grows taller than all other coniferous trees. It towers at 50 to 80 feet high. The Eastern Hemlock grows easily in Pennsylvania.

Deciduous trees lose their leaves every fall and grow again in the spring. The cold winters and warm summers help deciduous trees grow. The wood in the tree is dense and strong. It is called hardwood. Hardwood burns evenly and slow. It creates a warm temperature over a long period of time. The branches and limbs from hardwoods can support heavy weight. Hardwood trees include black cherry, red and white oak, hickory, maple, ash, and walnut. In autumn, the leaves of these trees change from green to bright colors of red, yellow, orange, and brown.

Rivers and Streams

Rivers, streams, runs, and creeks are all names for types of waterways in Pennsylvania. The small runs and creeks join to make a stream. Streams join to become rivers. Rivers join to become bigger rivers that flow to the ocean. The Allegheny River joins the Monongahela River. They form the great Ohio River. The Ohio River flows into the Mississippi in the middle of the continent. The Juniata and West Branch form the Susquehanna. The Susquehanna flows into Chesapeake Bay. The Susquehanna River is considered a shallow river. Shallow means something is not very deep. Large stone boulders can be seen in the water. On the eastern border, the Delaware River flows south. It meets the Atlantic Ocean. The Delaware River is deep. This makes for easy water transportation. The streams provide water for each living animal in the forests. Large and small animals of the forest depend on the water. Plant life thrives when there is abundant water.

The fresh water courses in Pennsylvania have been used as a way to travel. However, the same waterways are an obstacle, or blocker, for land travel. Pennsylvania has over 83,000 miles of waterways. After days of rain, the waterways are filled, and flooding can occur. In years of drought, or less rain, the small runs and creeks dry up. This lack of water creates a hardship for the entire system of life that depends on the water. Whether in drought or flood, the waterways provide for the living things within Pennsylvania.

title: Birds
text:
Over 300 types of birds make Pennsylvania their home. The ruffed grouse is the official state bird. The grouse is a large bird that lives in the Allegheny Plateau region's forests. It prefers the thick vegetation of rhododendron and mountain laurel. A ruffed grouse has also been called a partridge. Grouse don’t fly great distances. They are considered a “ground” bird, like pheasants and turkeys.

Smaller birds in the Ridge and Valley region eat seeds and berries. Larger birds that hunt other animals for food are called raptors. Pennsylvania has several raptor species. These include eagles, owls, falcons, and hawks. They make homes in the tall white pines and oak trees. Some even make homes in tall buildings in cities.

Crows, ravens, and smaller birds also live in Pennsylvania. They live around the farms in the Piedmont region. They thrive on the crops in the fields.

title: Elk
text:
Elk are a large member of the deer family. They need a large range or area to live. Their diet includes flowering plants, grasses, twigs, and bushes. These plants are all found in the Allegheny Plateau. The Native Americans in western Pennsylvania called the elk "wapitis." Elk were a source of food. Their furs were used to create bedding and clothes. The wapitis were hunted to extinction by the late 1800s.

In the 1920s, elk were relocated to Pennsylvania from Yellowstone National Park. The Pennsylvania Game Commission was committed to successfully bringing a herd to the state. The Commission wanted them in Elk, Potter, Clinton, Cameron, and Clearfield counties.

Today, the elk herd is thriving. The elk are seen in dense woods and open fields near the Bennet Branch of the Sinnemahoning Creek.

title: Beaver
text:
The waterways in Pennsylvania are home to an engineering animal: the beaver. Beavers need a source of water all year. They can be clever animals. Beavers are able to modify their habitat to meet their needs. A colony of beavers can move into a stream area and quickly build a dam. The dam backs up the water to create a pond. The flooding causes new vegetation to grow. Large hardwood trees don't grow well in a flooded area. However, soft wood willows, birch, and aspens can grow on the edge of the pond. Water lilies and cattails provide food for the colony. Fish, geese, ducks, and osprey all benefit from a beaver pond too.

The beaver's fur is very thick in the winter. Its thick fur helps to protect the beaver from the cold. People found the fur to be valuable. It was useful for clothing and other items. The value of the fur and the great number of beavers in Pennsylvania caused conflict between Native Americans and European colonizers. The beaver was hunted until the population was dangerously low. Today, the beaver population is healthy. The animal is protected by strict laws. The laws have helped the beaver population flourish.

title: Fish
text: Pennsylvania is home to some of the best trout fishing in the world. In 1970, the brook trout was officially named the state fish. You can also find bass, catfish, pike, bluegill, yellow perch, and more in the waterways of Pennsylvania. To support the fishing hobby, there are 15 fish hatcheries in the state. A hatchery is a place where fish are grown to be released into the wild. It is estimated that around 2 million people per year go fishing in Pennsylvania. The hatcheries help Pennsylvania’s economy and tourism. Hatcheries create jobs, tourist destinations, and bring thousands of people to Pennsylvania each year.

title: Pennsylvania Watersheds
text:
In Pennsylvania, there are about 85,000 miles of rivers and streams. The only state that has more is Alaska. All rivers and streams flow to the ocean. When the water in one area flows toward another body of water, it is called a watershed. Watersheds are created based on the shape of the land. A watershed can control the quality of water that flows through the region. A polluted area in any one of the regions will contaminate others down stream. Pennsylvania has six different watersheds (see map). All of these watersheds eventually flow into the Atlantic Ocean.

Waterways and watersheds are important for many reasons. Without them, we would not have the habitats, transportation, or technology that we have today. They also provide drinking water, which makes it very important to keep our waterways clean.

Name of Watershed

Interesting Facts

Potomac

Located in south-central Pennsylvania. Provides water to Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland, and Washington, D.C.

Genesee

Most of this watershed is in New York. Only a very small part is located in Pennsylvania. The water flows north to Lake Ontario.

Ohio

Located in western Pennsylvania and is considered a national watershed. It is the largest tributary to the Mississippi River and consists of 14 states.

Lake Erie

Found in the northwest corner of Pennsylvania. This watershed is part of the Great Lakes basin.

Delaware

The Delaware River creates the border between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The eastern part of Pennsylvania is included in this watershed.

Susquehanna

This watershed includes almost half of Pennsylvania. This basin is very prone to flooding. It eventually flows into the Chesapeake Bay.

Mining means digging into the ground to get useful minerals. A mineral is a natural resource that forms inside the earth’s crust. There are many kinds of minerals. Some examples are iron, coal, and salt. Diamonds and gold are minerals, too. Miners dig tunnels or pits into the earth so they can reach the minerals. Then, they use machines and tools to take the minerals out of the ground. People in other industries can use the minerals to make things. More than 60 minerals are used to make a computer. Minerals can also become part of airplanes, jewelry, vitamins, and much more.

title: What Is Grief?
text: Grief is when you feel very sad about losing something. You might feel grief if a pet dies or if you move to a new town. You miss something that you loved. Everyone feels grief in different ways.

title: The Five Parts of Grief
text:
There are five parts of grief that people can go through. These parts help you work through your feelings so you can feel better. These are things you might think or feel as you go through grief:

Denial: “This isn’t real.”

Anger: “This isn’t fair.”

Bargaining: “I will fix this.”

Depression: “I am so sad. I want to be alone.”

Acceptance: “This is going to be okay.”

title: Talk It Out
text:
It is important to talk about your grief. It's okay if you don’t know exactly what to say. There are no right or wrong words for your grief. The important thing is to start talking. As you talk, you can learn things about your feelings. Spending time talking with friends and family is also good. It can help you remember happy moments.

Who do you like to talk to when you feel sad?

title: Learn to Listen
text:
Your friend might feel grief. Let them know you will listen if they want to talk. Listening can help people know that you care.

Helpful things to say:

“I know I can’t fix it, but I will listen.”

“Can I sit with you? We don’t have to talk.”

Things to avoid:

Telling them what to do

Talking about negative feelings or memories

Interrupting them

title: Sympathy and Grief
text:
Natalia’s friend just broke his arm. Natalia has never had a broken arm. But she feels bad that Nick is in pain. Natalia feels sympathy for Nick. She makes him a card. Here are some ways you can show sympathy to others:

Make a card or draw a picture for them.

Offer to help them do a task.

Make time to listen to them.

Ask how you can help.

title: About Your Body
text:
Your body is amazing! It does so many things without you even thinking about it. Think about when you take a bite of food. Do you have to tell your mouth how many times to chew? Or how the food should travel through your esophagus when you swallow? Do you have to tell your pancreas, liver, and intestines how to break down your food? No! Your body does all of that automatically and more!

How many body parts can you name? Label as many as you can!

title: Keeping Your Body Clean
text:
Keep your body clean. When you keep your body clean, you are protecting your body from germs that can spread communicable (spreadable) diseases, like colds and flus. Having good hygiene can help kill bacteria and viruses. Bacteria and viruses can make you sick or smell unpleasant.

Here are a few ways you can keep your body healthy and clean:

Wash your hands.

Wear clean clothes.

Bathe or shower every day.

Brush your teeth twice a day and go to the dentist regularly.

These things are especially important as your body grows and matures. Can you think of anything else you can do to keep your body clean?

title: Health Through Movement
text:
Guess how many minutes of physical activity your body needs each day? ________ min.

It is best if you get at least 60 minutes of movement each day. 60 minutes is one hour. That may sound like a lot. But think about all the activities you love. Write down your three favorite types. Maybe it is dancing, jump roping, soccer, or even playing tag.

______________________________________________

______________________________________________

Your daily physical activity can be fun! And you can spread it throughout the day. You might get some of your movement in during recess or before school. Then get the rest of your movement after school with family or friends. Physical activity gives you more energy, strengthens your immune system, and gives you the chance to spend time with people.

title: Health Through Food
text:
Did you know that what you put in your body matters? Things you eat affect how your body feels and works. Look at these different types of foods and what they all do for your body:

Nutrients

Foods

Benefits

Beans, meat, eggs

Helps build and repair muscles and bones

Carbohydrates

Bread, crackers

Gives your body and brain energy

Balances blood sugar, helps protect you from diseases

Vitamins

Fruits and vegetables

Gives you healthy eyes, skin, and bones

Nuts and seeds, fish, dark leafy green vegetables

Helps your digestion and hydration

Water

Keeps you hydrated

Not getting enough of healthy foods can affect your health and keep your body from working properly. When you are missing one of these food groups, you may feel sluggish or get sick more easily.

title: Making a Healthy Environment
text:
Did you know that your environment affects your health? Your environment is what surrounds you. It includes the people and things around you. Having a clean, safe environment can help you be healthy. Keeping your environment clean can stop germs from spreading and help keep you healthy. You can keep your home, classroom, and community clean by recycling and picking up trash.

Draw a picture of what a healthy environment looks like to you.

title: Respecting Differences
text:
Did you know that there are over a million kinds of animals in the world? There are tigers, anteaters, and flamingos, to name a few. Can you think of three other animals?

1.

2.

3.

Every animal is different, but every animal is important in a different way. Each type of animal helps the world in a unique way. Every person is different too. Each individual has important things to add to the world. No person is better than another. It is important to be respectful toward individuals who are similar to and different from you. Race, religion, abilities, and sexual orientation or gender identity are things that make people different from each other. People even grow at different times and different rates. Diversity makes the world interesting and beautiful. Draw a picture that represents what diversity means to you.

title: Respectful Behaviors
text:
Etiquette is one way to show respect for others. You can demonstrate etiquette through your actions. Here are some ways you can show proper etiquette in different situations:

Clap at the end of a performance or game.

Is “booing” respectful? Why or why not? _________

Be a good sport whether you win or lose.

How can you be a good sport when you win? _______________________________________

How can you be a good sport when you lose? ______________________________________

Accept someone’s boundaries, including their standards/rules like their curfew or things they choose not to do because of their beliefs.

Use respectful language. This can include not swearing and not calling people names.

Include people who are different from you. You can invite someone with different abilities to play a game with you. You can invite someone who looks or thinks differently from you to be on your team.

title: Standing Up to Disrespect
text: You can choose to be respectful at all times. But you cannot choose when other people show respect. There will be times when people around you are not respectful. You can choose how to react. Teasing or bullying are examples of disrespect. You can respectfully stand up to unkindness and encourage your peers to be respectful. You can show respect when you stand up to others by using assertive but calm language. Avoiding violence is an important part of resolving conflict with respect.

title: Respectful Reactions
text:
Raquel asked her mom, “I know I should respect others, but what do I do if someone is mean to me? Do I have to be respectful then?”

Have you ever had a question like Raquel’s? It can be hard to treat someone with respect when they are unkind to you. But you are in charge of your words and actions. You get to choose how to react to someone’s unkindness. Let’s think about an example.

Someone pushes you down. Should you go and push them down too? When someone is unkind or disrespectful to you, you can choose to handle the conflict with respect. Instead of pushing them down, you can use your words and say, “Please do not push me down.” You can also ask an adult for help.

title: How Does Respect Make You Feel?
text:
The way you treat others can affect how you feel inside. If you are unkind to someone, you may feel guilty or sad afterward. You will never feel bad about treating someone with kindness and respect. You can be respectful and assertive. Write about how you feel when you choose to be respectful:

When you are respectful to others, they will be more likely to be respectful to you. Write about how you feel when other people treat you with respect:

title: Geography Impacts Location for Armies
text:
The battle of Gettysburg was a turning point in the American Civil War. It became a symbol of care and respect for those who fought. The physical features of Gettysburg attracted both armies there. The hills, woods, streams, and granite boulders created a marketplace for the town. Those same features created a bloody battlefield where two armies clashed for three days of intense fighting that would be remembered throughout American history.

By 1863, the farmland of northern Virginia had been destroyed. The many battles fought there during the American Civil War had laid waste to the landscape. Crops were not planted. Orchards were not harvested. Meanwhile, soldiers from all over the Confederacy joined the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia. Companies of soldiers from Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, and Arkansas arrived under General Robert E. Lee’s command. Lee, however, was desperate for supplies.

Lee knew about the richness of Pennsylvania farms. They had been untouched by the war. If the army marched there, he knew they could take what they needed.

There were other benefits to invading Pennsylvania. Capturing a northern city would be a victory for the Confederate States of America (CSA). Holding a position in Pennsylvania would endanger the safety of Baltimore, Maryland, and Washington, D.C., as well. Entering Pennsylvania was a big risk. Regardless, Lee turned the Confederate Army north to invade the state.

Lee used the physical features of the Blue Ridge Mountains to his advantage. Staying on the west side of the Appalachian Mountains, the Army of northern Virginia moved northward from Winchester, Virginia. The mountains shielded the 75,000-man army from being seen by the Union Army, just on the other side of the Appalachians.

The Union Army was 90,000-men strong. Major General George Meade wanted to keep the Union Army east of the Appalachians. With the army positioned there, they could help protect Washington, D.C. Meade knew Lee’s men were moving north. However, he didn’t know where they were going. The Union Army moved north to pursue, or follow, the Confederate Army.

When the Confederate Army entered Pennsylvania, they arrived at Chambersburg in the Cumberland Valley. Parts of the army continued to move north and east. They went to occupy Camp Hill and York, Pennsylvania. The CSA army confiscated, or took, supplies as they went through the farms of Adams and York counties. Small companies of the Confederate Army used the roads to easily move about the Pennsylvania countryside.

Twelve roadways converged, or met, in Gettysburg, Adams County. Gettysburg is in the valley between two ridges of the Allegheny Mountains. Seminary Ridge is to the west. It was named for the Lutheran college for ministers that was located nearby. To the east, about three miles from Gettysburg is Cemetery Ridge, named for the nearby cemetery.

The ridges run north to south. They are covered in patches of woods, fields, and farmland. Large granite boulders stick out of the ridges and fields. Streams run down the ridges to create wetlands and rivers. Culp's Hill, named for a local farm, is next to Cemetery Ridge. To the south of Cemetery Ridge are the small tree-covered mountains known as Big Round Top and Little Round Top. The town and farms can be seen from Little Round Top.

The Confederate Army camped on Seminary Ridge. The Union Army chose Cemetery Ridge. They camped from Culp's Hill to Little Round Top. The two armies met in a battle on July 1, 1863. Each tried to use the physical features to their advantage. The battle finally ended on July 3.

title: The Weikert Family Farm
text:
The Jakob Weikert family lived on Taneytown Road. Their farm was south of Gettysburg. It sat in the shadow of Little Round Top. They had lived there for 23 years. The farm was productive and peaceful until July 1863. During the Battle of Gettysburg, the Weikert farm became a field hospital. Wounded soldiers were brought there for medical assistance.

Many other barns, churches, and homes were used to help wounded soldiers. Thousands of soldiers were cared for by the citizens of Gettysburg. The people provided food, water, and bandages. They continued to care for soldiers and their families for months after the battle was over.

title: Firsthand Accounts from Gettysburg
text:
The 2,400 residents of Gettysburg knew the threat of invasion from the Confederate Army was possible. Like many others, they had family members in the military. They read about the war in newspapers and letters. Jennie McCreary was 17 at the time of the battle of Gettysburg. She wrote a letter to her sister Julia. "We never expected a battle,” she wrote. "[An] artillery duel or something of that kind might occur. But nothing more."

Like Julia, many other residents of Gettysburg wrote letters and kept record of the events. Because of their writings, we have firsthand accounts of what the battle was like.

June 30
On June 30, the Federal Cavalry arrived. Daniel Skelly recorded the events of that evening. “[The] people of Gettysburg settled down in their houses with a sense of security they had not enjoyed for days and with little thought of what the morrow had in store for them."

The people of Gettysburg saw soldiers from the Confederate Army too. Sarah Broadhead also wrote in her diary on June 30: "[This] morning the Rebels came to the top of the hill overlooking the town on the Chambersburg Pike and looked over our place. It begins to look as though we will have a battle soon and we are in great fear."

July 1
The next day, on July 1, the battle began. Amelia Harmon was with her aunt. During the battle, a party of Union soldiers took over their home. Harmon wrote that “the crack of rifles, the hurried orders, and outside the mingled roar of heavy musketry, galloping horses, yelling troops and the occasional boom of cannon“ was heard.

Fifteen-year-old Albertus McCreary kept record of what he saw and heard during the battle too. “It was about noon … the street was full of Union soldiers, running and pushing each other, sweaty and black from powder and dust," he wrote. "They called to us for water. We got great buckets of water and tin dippers and supplied them as fast as we could from the porch at the side of the house off the main street.… We were so busy that we did not notice how close the fighting was. Half a block away was hand to hand combat.... We kept right on distributing water until an officer rode his horse up on the pavement ... and said 'All you good people go down in your cellars or you will all be killed.'”

July 2
By July 2, the armies had positioned themselves on each side of the town. Soldiers from each army had sought refuge in private homes. Some were seeking medical help. Others were looking to gain a better fighting position.

To the south of town, the battle was waged in wheat fields, orchards, and along Little Round Top. Tillie Pierce, 15, recorded what she saw. “Toward the middle of the afternoon heavy cannonading began on the two Round Tops just back of the house. This was so terrible and severe that it was with great difficulty we could hear ourselves speak. It began very unexpectedly; so much so, that we were all terror-stricken, and hardly knew what to do.”

July 3
On July 3, the morning began with 230 cannons firing from both armies. Sarah Broadhead said it was a roar “as if heaven and earth were crashing together.” By afternoon, 12,000 Confederate soldiers marched across the rolling fields. They moved from Seminary Ridge to an area on Cemetery Ridge. This march was known as “Pickett’s Charge.” It was the last effort of the Confederate Army to gain control of Gettysburg. By 4:00 p.m., the fighting came to an end.

July 4
In the evening and during the night, the townspeople heard wagons and artillery rolling. There were muffled sounds of men moving. On July 4, a great thunderstorm lasted most of the day. General Lee and the Confederate army began retreating south to Virginia. The line of soldiers, supplies, and wagons was 17 miles long.

General Meade organized the remaining Union Army. They marched south too, following the Confederates. A news reporter for the Philadelphia Age described Gettysburg: “The ground was tramped into a bog, and was covered with every conceivable thing ... everything used in war or by soldiers was scattered around in plenty. The grain and grass which once grew there, was almost ground to a jelly.”

Annie Young wrote to her cousin: "If the Rebels are going to invade your state, as they have this, I would advise you to pack up and go as far north as you can.”

title: Dedication of the Cemetery
text:
After the battle, Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin visited Gettysburg. He met with David Wills. Wills was a political figure who lived in the center of town. Gettysburg needed aid. Wills knew Curtin had the authority to provide help. Curtin dispatched state militia to assist in the clean-up.

Wills and others decided to create a large cemetery. The soldiers who had died during the battle were buried there. They chose to build it on Cemetery Ridge. They named it the Soldiers’ National Cemetery. More than 3,600 Union soldiers were buried there. They all received military honors.

A dedication ceremony was held for the cemetery. It took place on November 19, 1863. It included a parade of dignitaries, or important individuals. There were speeches and music as well.

President Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication. His speech became known as the Gettysburg Address. Lincoln spoke about the war, the cemetery, and the families that were affected. His remarks helped create a sense of reverence, or deep respect, for the battle of Gettysburg.

Today, the Soldiers’ National Cemetery is called the Gettysburg National Cemetery. It is cared for by the federal government. Visitors can still travel there. The monuments and graves serve as a reminder about the people who were laid to rest there.

title: Elizabeth Thorn
text: Elizabeth Thorn was a German immigrant. She was living in Gettysburg during the battle. She was the caretaker of the Evergreen Cemetery. Thorn’s husband was enlisted in the Union Army. During the war, Thorn was left to care for the family. She was also left to take care of the cemetery alone. She was responsible for burying the dead in the community. Thorn was a compassionate person. She took her responsibilities seriously. In July 1863, Thorn buried 91 soldiers and one citizen of Gettysburg.

title: Matilda “Tillie” Pierce
text:
Matilda "Tillie" Pierce was born in Gettysburg in 1848. Pierce was just 15 years old during the Battle of Gettysburg. On the second day of the battle, Pierce carried water to the Union soldiers who passed by her house on Baltimore Street. Her neighbor, Henrietta Shriver, was the daughter of Jakob Weikert. She invited Pierce to come to her father's farm near Little Round Top. Schriver wanted to protect Pierce from the fighting in the town.

Pierce later wrote a firsthand account of all she saw in July 1863. Her account was published as a book. The book is called At Gettysburg: Or What a Girl Saw and Heard at the Battle. It still serves as a primary source for historians today.

title: Mary Virginia “Jennie” Wade
text:
Born in Gettysburg in 1843, Mary Virginia "Jennie" Wade was making biscuits to feed the Union soldiers. A stray bullet entered her house and took her life. Wade was the only recorded civilian death during the Battle of Gettysburg. She was just 20 years old.

Tillie Pierce saw Wade shouting in the streets just a few days before her death. Confederate soldiers attempted to take her young nephew, Sam, as a prisoner of war. However, the soldiers did not keep Wade’s nephew and returned him to the family.

After her death, many Union soldiers remembered Wade as the young woman who gave them water and biscuits during the Battle of Gettysburg. She was buried in the Evergreen Cemetery, where Peter and Elizabeth Thorn were caretakers.

title: Monuments Tell a Story
text:
Veterans of the Battle of Gettysburg wanted to honor the events. They wanted their families to know what happened. They wanted their comrades, or fellow soldiers, to remember too. In 1867, a marble stand was placed in the Soldiers’ National Cemetery. It was put there by the 1st Minnesota Infantry Regiment. Other regiments began placing monuments and statues on the battlefield.

The Pennsylvania state government created a Gettysburg Battlefield Memorial Association (GBMA). They were put in charge of organizing the many monuments from veterans. The GBMA had strict rules for placement of regiment markers. They also published an official history of the battle. They wanted it to be remembered accurately.

The state of Pennsylvania created the largest monument on the battlefield. It's located on Cemetery Ridge. The Pennsylvania Monument is made of granite. It includes an observation deck on the roof. The deck offers a clear view of the fields, hills, and town. Sixty tablets surround the monument. The tablets have the names of each soldier who was enlisted in a Pennsylvania regiment on July 1, 1863. More than 34,000 Pennsylvanians participated in the battle.

There are different styles of monuments throughout the battlefield. The monuments include details of the military units and officers. They also provide information about actions during the battle. There are statues of soldiers and military equipment. Many symbols can be found in the memorial, including eagles, stars, and flags.

Today, there are over 13,000 monuments at the Gettysburg National Battlefield. It also includes monuments to honor soldiers from the Confederate Army. The Confederate monuments were placed later, during the 20th century.

In Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address, he made it clear why it was important to remember the battle. He said:

We are met on a great battlefield.... We have come to dedicate a portion of that field as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live. It is altogether fitting and proper that we should do this. But, in a larger sense, we can not dedicate ... this ground. The brave men, living and dead, who struggled here have consecrated (to make something sacred) it.… The world will little note nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.

The monuments continue to remind visitors of what happened. They are the physical representation of Lincoln's words. The stories from that day continue to be told. As long as visitors continue to learn, the stories will not be forgotten.

title: How Can People Make a Difference?
text: There are many ways to make a difference. Authors inform and entertain us. Musicians and artists create beauty and enjoyment. Scientists work to improve our lives and discover new things. Educators teach us and help our minds grow. Humanitarians work to help people who need support. Activists strive to make sure people have rights and opportunities. There are heroes in every field who use their talents, knowledge, and passion to help their communities.

title: Asking Questions
text:
Scientists and engineers use special skills. These are known as science and engineering practices. The practices help them find answers to their questions.

Asking Questions About a Phenomenon

Scientists and engineers study phenomena. A phenomenon is an event that can be seen. More than one phenomenon is called phenomena.

Scientists and engineers study events. It helps them understand more about the world around them. They ask questions when they see something they do not understand.

They may ask why, how, when, or where something happens. They may ask questions about what can cause something else to happen.

Questioning Rules:

Ask as many questions as you can.

Do not stop to discuss, judge, or answer the questions.

Circle your best question.

Write your questions about the phenomenon.

[WRITING SPACE]

Claims and Investigations

Questions can have many answers. Scientists and engineers can use those answers to make a claim. They say what they believe or think is true. Scientists and engineers use skills to help them know which claim is correct.

Questions and claims help scientists and engineers plan an investigation. They study the event to find an answer to their questions. This helps them get more information. They use their senses to make observations. What they see helps answer questions. Answers help them learn more about the world.

Make a claim about how different drinks might affect teeth.

title: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information
text:
Scientists and engineers don’t just gather information from investigations. They also get information from the media. This might be text from books, the internet, videos, news articles, and more. What do scientists and engineers do with what they read and learn? They evaluate it. They decide if the information is good or not. Then they share the information with others.

As you read like a scientist, you should take notes about what you read. This helps you to remember what you read and learned. Use the ideas in the Annotating Text Poster to help you annotate this text.

"Sweet Tooth" by dentist Dr. Lauren Weekly

Before a child is even born, they have teeth. Teeth break through the gums and start to show when a baby is about 6 to 12 months old. When a child is about five or six years old, the teeth are pushed out by the permanent teeth. By the age of 12 or 13, most people have a full set of permanent teeth. These teeth have to last a lifetime. It is important to protect the teeth. Daily care of the teeth can protect them.

Sometimes we eat and drink things with sugar in it. Sugary drinks, like soda and juice, have sugar in them. Sugar is food to the bacteria already living in your mouth. Too much bacteria can lead to tooth decay. This happens when plaque from bacteria builds up. Plaque is a clear film that sticks to your teeth. Plaque can eat away the enamel, or outside, of your tooth. Sometimes, a hole can develop in a tooth. This is called a cavity. It is when a tooth decays, or breaks down. A dentist can repair the hole by filling it.

You can remove plaque and prevent cavities. Brush your teeth after eating or at least twice a day. It is especially important to brush before bedtime. Use floss to clean the space between your teeth. Use toothpaste with fluoride to help prevent plaque and cavities.

text:
What Is an Explanation?

When a scientist or engineer begins to explore a phenomenon, they may have an idea what is happening. They try to explain by writing an explanation. This gives the reason for their thinking.

Write an explanation of the phenomenon using the facts you learned this week.

[Writing lines]

What Is an Argument

Scientists' or engineers' explanations can be different. They come up with arguments for their explanations. An argument is a written claim. It is backed up by evidence and reasoning. They include evidence so others understand a person’s claim. Evidence is information that supports a claim. It proves the claim is correct. An argument also includes reasoning. Reasoning tells “how” or “why” the evidence supports the claim.

Models

Scientists and engineers often use models. Models help show their thinking. They are used to support their claim and evidence. A model is a visual or 3-D representation. Models are often smaller than the original. Models can be a drawing, picture, or an object.

Scientists use models to help explain the world. Models can show large or small things. Engineers use models to make designs. They build models to make sure everything will work.

A model can help you remember what you observe. A model can help you understand something. A model can help you explain something. A model can support a claim or argument.

title: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information
text:
Scientists and engineers don’t just gather information from investigations; they also get information from reliable media. Media information could include text from books, the internet, videos, news articles, and more. If the media is reliable, it can be trusted. It is from a good source. If you were reading an article about sugar’s effect on teeth written by a dentist, that would be reliable. If the article was written by a candy maker, it may not be reliable. What do scientists and engineers do with what they read and learn? They evaluate it. They decide if the information is good or not. Then they communicate the information to others.

Annotating Text: As you read like a scientist, you should annotate, or take notes, about what you read. This helps you to remember what you read and learned. Use the ideas in the Annotating Text Poster to help you annotate this text.

Sweet Tooth by dentist Dr. Lauren Weekly

Before a child is even born, they have teeth. Teeth break through the gums and start to show when a baby is about 6 to 12 months old. When a child is about five or six years old, the teeth start to fall out, because they are being pushed out by the permanent tooth behind it. By the age of 12 or 13, most people have a full set of permanent teeth. These teeth have to last a lifetime. It is important to protect the teeth. Daily care of the teeth can protect them.

Sometimes we eat and drink things with sugar in it. Sugary drinks, like soda and juice, have sugar in them. Sugar is food to the bacteria already living in your mouth. Too much bacteria can lead to tooth decay. This happens when plaque from bacteria builds up. Plaque is a clear film that sticks to your teeth. Plaque can eat away the enamel, or outside, of your tooth. Sometimes, a hole can develop in a tooth. This is called a cavity. It is when a tooth decays, or breaks down. A dentist can repair the hole by filling it.

You can remove plaque and prevent cavities. Brush your teeth after eating, or at least twice a day. It is especially important to brush before bedtime. Use floss to clean the space between your teeth. Use toothpaste with fluoride to help prevent plaque and cavities.

Your question will help you write the investigation purpose, or the reason you are doing the investigation. Why are you doing the investigation? What do you want to find out? Write the investigation purpose.

Investigation Purpose:

Now that you know the investigation purpose, you can plan your investigation. An investigation should have fair tests where one variable is changed and all other variables are controlled. For the egg "teeth" experiment, the variable that should change is the type of beverage. All other variables should be controlled. Make sure everything about your investigation is the same except for the beverages you use. In the sugar experiment, the controlled variables are the mystery substance and the water, and the changing variable is the sugar. Write the steps you will do in your investigation and the materials you will need.

Steps:

Materials:

Before you conduct your investigation, predict what the outcome of your investigation will be.

Now, follow your plan. Conduct your investigation. Do trials, or tests, with the eggs and beverages. Record your data in your scientific notebook. As you work, you may need to revise your steps.

My Data:

The last part of an investigation is to answer your question! Write the answer to your question.

title: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information
text:
Scientists and engineers don’t just gather information from investigations; they also get information from reliable media. Media information could include text from books, the internet, videos, news articles, and more. If the media is reliable, it can be trusted. What do scientists and engineers do with what they read and learn? They evaluate it. They determine if the information they gathered is free from errors and can be used. Then they communicate the information to others.

Annotating Text: As you read like a scientist, you should take notes about what you read. This helps you to remember what you read and learned. Use the Annotation Strategies to help you annotate this text.

Sweet Tooth by dentist Dr. Lauren Weekly, DDS

Before a child is even born, they have teeth. Teeth start to show when a baby is about 6 to 12 months old. Then, when a child is about five or six years old, the teeth start to fall out, because they are being pushed out by the permanent teeth behind them. By the age of 12 or 13, most people have a full set of permanent teeth. It is important to protect the teeth. Daily care of the teeth can protect them.

Sometimes we eat and drink things with sugar in them. Drinks like soda and juice have sugar in them. Sugar gives the bacteria in your mouth food. Too much bacteria can lead to tooth decay. Tooth decay is when a tooth breaks down. This happens when plaque builds up. Plaque is a clear film that sticks to your teeth. Acids in your mouth can eat away at the enamel, or the outside of your tooth. Sometimes, a hole can develop in a tooth when it decays. This is called a cavity. A dentist uses X-rays to see holes in the tooth and can repair the tooth.

You can remove plaque and prevent cavities. Brush your teeth after eating or at least twice a day. It is especially important to brush before bedtime. Brush your teeth up and down in a circular motion. Use floss to clean the spaces between your teeth. Use toothpaste with fluoride to help prevent plaque and cavities.

Evaluate

Evaluate the text. Think about who wrote the text. Is the information good? What did you learn?

Communicate

Tell a classmate what you learned from the article and your evaluation of the information. Record what your classmate communicated to you.

title: Explanations, Arguments, and Models
text:
What Is an Explanation?

When a scientist or engineer begins to explore a phenomenon, they may have an idea or belief about how or why the phenomenon is happening. They try to explain the phenomenon by writing an explanation. An explanation is a statement that explains their thinking about a phenomenon using the facts they know.

Write an explanation of the phenomenon using the facts you learned this week.

What Is an Argument?

Scientist’s and engineer’s explanations of a phenomenon can be different. Scientists and engineers come up with arguments for their explanations. An argument is a written claim that is backed up by evidence and reasoning. Evidence is information that supports a claim. It proves the claim is correct. Along with a claim and evidence, an argument includes reasoning. Reasoning tells “how” or “why” the evidence supports the claim.

Models

When scientists and engineers present an argument, they often use models to help show their thinking and support their claim and evidence. A model is a visual or 3D representation, typically on a smaller scale than the original. It can be a drawing, a picture, or even an object like a toy! Models can help you learn about the real thing.

Scientists use models to help explain the world. Models can show large or small things. They can show things from long ago. Engineers use models to make designs. They build models to make sure everything will work properly. They also use models to improve their designs.

You can make a model to help you remember what you observe. A model can help you understand something. A model can help you explain something. A model can support a claim or argument. For example, you could draw a model to explain what you saw and understood. You could use data as a model to show evidence from an observation.

Create an Argument

Create an argument using the Create an Argument worksheet. Base your argument on your explanation of the phenomenon.

title: Change in the 1800s for Native Americans
text:
Europeans started coming to North America in the 1500s. Before that time, only Native Americans lived in the land we now know as the United States. Native Americans lived in tribes, or groups of people who spoke the same language and had the same ancestors. Sometimes different tribes helped each other, but sometimes they didn’t get along.

Tribes of Indigenous peoples had learned to use the plants and animals around them as food and resources. There were many types of land in the United States. Some areas were covered in forests, other areas were deserts, and still other areas had mountains. In Nebraska, on the Great Plains, the land was covered mostly by grasses and shrubs.

The arrival of Europeans caused great changes to Native American ways of life. White settlers started living on the same land where Native Americans were already living. Sometimes the settlers and the Native Americans helped each other, but often they fought over the land. Over time, many thousands of Europeans came to North America. The white settlers outnumbered the Native Americans and forced them to move. The more land the settlers took, the farther the Native Americans had to move.

When a tribe was forced to move away, it was often moved onto the land of another tribe. This caused conflict between tribes. Moving to new land also forced various tribes to learn new ways of finding food and shelter. This could be very hard and dangerous.

Europeans brought diseases that had never existed in North and South America before. Some of these diseases, such as smallpox and measles, were deadly. Native Americans had no natural immunity to these diseases. Many of them died.

Europeans also brought tools and weapons that were new to Native Americans and changed the ways they lived. Metal tools, such as knives and awls, made it easier for Native Americans to make clothing and shelter. Native Americans learned how to make kettles for cooking. They also bought guns from Europeans. Guns helped them to hunt. In Nebraska, guns made it easier for Native Americans to hunt bison.

White settlers had many more guns than Native Americans had. This gave the settlers a big advantage in battles between settlers and Native Americans.

To understand Native American life in Nebraska today, we need to know how Native American life changed in the 1800s.

title: The Winnebagos Are Forced to Leave Wisconsin
text:
When the Winnebago tribe first met white settlers, the Winnebagos were living in what is now Wisconsin. In 1820, settlers forced the Winnebagos to move west. Then, more settlers arrived, wanting more land. They forced the Winnebagos to move again.

Every few years, the Winnebagos had to move. First, they moved to what is now Iowa, then to Minnesota, then to South Dakota, and finally to Nebraska. Many times during this period, U.S. Army soldiers arrested Winnebago tribe members and forced them to move, sometimes by train or boat, and sometimes by walking.

On the Winnebagos’ original land in Wisconsin, there were forests and lakes. The Winnebagos gathered berries for food. They also hunted animals and caught fish. When they were forced to leave Wisconsin, they were moved to the Great Plains, where there are no forests. They suddenly had to learn new skills for finding food and building shelter.

Some of the Winnebagos refused to leave Wisconsin. Some of them hid from the soldiers. Many of the Winnebagos who had come to Nebraska returned to their homelands in Wisconsin because there was not enough food and shelter in Nebraska.

Not all the settlers wanted the Winnebagos to leave Wisconsin. Many settlers wanted to be good neighbors to the Winnebagos. They helped the Winnebagos buy land in Wisconsin. Some newspapers reported about how the Winnebagos were being mistreated. Some lawyers and politicians defended the Winnebagos in courts and in the legislature. The last time Winnebagos were forced to leave Wisconsin was in 1874.

Many Winnebagos have stayed in Wisconsin. The Wisconsin Winnebagos officially became a separate tribe in 1881. Now they are known as the Ho-Chunk Nation.

A reservation for the Winnebagos in Nebraska and Iowa was created in 1865. A reservation is land that is set aside for a Native American tribe. Reservations were made as a way to force Native Americans to stay in one place. Today, Native Americans are not forced to stay on reservations. However, many Native Americans still live on reservations so they can preserve their communities and traditions. The Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska lives on the Winnebago Reservation today.

title: The Ponca Trail of Tears
text:
The Ponca tribe was a small tribe that lived on the Great Plains. When they first met European traders, the Poncas lived on the Niobrara River in what we now call Nebraska. In the 1800s, when settlers came, the Poncas were forced to move.

In 1858 and 1865, the federal government made treaties with the Poncas. A treaty is a promise of peace between two groups of people. After every treaty, the government broke its promises to respect the Poncas’ right to the land. The government took more and more land away from the Poncas.

In 1875, the federal government decided to force the Poncas to move all the way from Nebraska to the Indian Territory, which was in the state we now know as Oklahoma. Soldiers from the U.S. Army forced the Ponca to walk to the Indian Territory, 600 miles away. About 500 Poncas started the journey on May 16, 1877. Almost from the beginning of the trip, the weather was bad. There were heavy spring rains, and the trails were muddy. The summer became very hot. Many Poncas became sick.

Because of the Poncas’ suffering during this journey, it became known as the Ponca Trail of Tears. Nine members of the tribe died during the 54 days of the trip. Today, the trail is marked to help us remember the Ponca Trail of Tears. In Neligh, Nebraska, a headstone marks the grave of White Buffalo Girl, a child who died on the journey. The Ponca chief’s name was Standing Bear. His daughter, named Prairie Flower, also died on the Ponca Trail of Tears. She is buried near Milford, Nebraska.

title: Chief Standing Bear
text:
The Poncas finally arrived in the Indian Territory at the end of their Trail of Tears. For almost two years, Chief Standing Bear lived in the Indian Territory with his people. During this time, many members of the tribe died because of sickness. There was also not enough food for everyone. Chief Standing Bear’s son, Bear Shield, became very sick. Bear Shield knew he would die. He asked Standing Bear to bury his body in the place where he was born, in Nebraska.

The federal government had told the Poncas that they could not leave the Indian Territory. However, Chief Standing Bear decided to honor his son’s wishes and bury him in Nebraska. He and a few other Poncas carried Bear Shield’s body back to Nebraska. They walked 600 miles in the cold winter of 1879.

Soon after Chief Standing Bear arrived in Nebraska, the federal government arrested him and the other Poncas who were with him because they did not have permission to leave Indian Territory. They were put in jail.

Some of the people in Nebraska did not like seeing the Poncas treated badly. One of them was General George Crook, the army officer who had been ordered to arrest the Poncas. There were also newspaper editors and lawyers who wanted to help Chief Standing Bear. The lawyers filed a lawsuit against the government. If the Poncas won their lawsuit, the government would have to release them from jail.

In court, the government said that Native Americans were not people with legal rights. The government said that the Poncas did not even have the right to sue the government.

Chief Standing Bear asked the judge to let him speak. Standing Bear gave a beautiful speech to show that he and his people should have the same rights as everyone else. He raised his right hand and showed it to everyone in the courtroom. He held his hand still for a long time. Then he said, “That hand is not the color of yours, but if I pierce it, I shall feel pain. If you pierce your hand, you also feel pain. The blood that will flow from mine will be of the same color as yours. I am a man. The same God made us both.”

The judge decided that the Poncas had the right to sue the government. The judge freed the Poncas from jail. It was the first time that Native Americans’ rights were protected.

We remember Chief Standing Bear as a great leader who helped Native Americans receive their legal rights.

title: The Santee People Come to Nebraska
text:
The Santee Sioux (also called the Santee Dakota) are a group of Native Americans who live on a reservation in northeastern Nebraska. They suffered many things on their journey to Nebraska.

The Santees lived in Minnesota early in the 1800s. When settlers came to Minnesota, the Dakota were forced to live on smaller and smaller reservations of land. Eventually, they had only some land along the Minnesota River. Their traditional way of finding food was hunting. But their patch of land had become too small for hunting. They had to start farming instead.

In 1861 and 1862, the Dakota farms did not produce enough food. There was also a very hard winter. The Dakotas needed help to survive. However, the federal government would not pay the Dakota the money the government owed them. A war broke out between the Dakotas and the government in 1862. Many people were killed on both sides. The Dakotas lost the war.

After the war, most of the Dakotas were forced to leave Minnesota. They were spread across many areas, including North Dakota, South Dakota, and Canada. Some of the Dakotas were packed into crowded, dirty boats and taken to a place in South Dakota called Crow Creek. Many of them died during the journey. When they arrived at Crow Creek, there was not enough food. Many people starved to death. The rest survived only by hunting, though there were few animals.

In 1866, the Dakota families in Crow Creek moved to Nebraska. This is how the Santee Sioux Reservation came to be. The Santees have worked to make their home in Nebraska a beautiful place. They also remember their Dakota brothers and sisters who live in other places. They still remember the homes they were forced to leave.

title: Native American Boarding Schools
text:
A boarding school is a school where the students live all the time. A boarding school has classrooms, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens, and dining rooms. Students leave their families to live at a boarding school.

In the 1870s, white Americans started boarding schools for Native American children. Some people thought that Native Americans had bad traditions. They wanted to teach Native American children to be more like white people. The government took thousands of Native American children away from their families and sent the children to boarding schools.

There was one Native American boarding school in Nebraska. It was in Genoa, Nebraska. It was open from 1884 to 1934.

At Native American boarding schools, the children learned how to do jobs. Some students had good experiences there. However, they were not allowed to speak their Native languages or wear their Native clothes and hair styles. They were not allowed to live according to their Native religions. They could not learn about Native traditions. They had to do hard work. Many children died from diseases or abuse in the boarding schools.

Native American boarding schools started to change in the 1960s. Instead of forcing students to forget about their heritage, the schools started to help students learn about their peoples’ cultures and languages. There are not very many Native American boarding schools left today. The Native American boarding schools that still exist give students a good education and help preserve Native cultures.
