title: Geography of the Ancient Near East
text:
The Ancient Near East was a large and diverse region, located where the continents of Europe, Africa, and Asia join. Mesopotamia was bordered by mountains in the north and east. The rugged Zagros Mountains were hot and dry in the summer and cold in the winter. The region is also full of gentle hills and flat plains. To the south are the Syrian and Arabian deserts.

Surrounding the region are the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian/Arabian Gulf. In ancient writings, the Mediterranean is referred to as "the upper sea," and the gulf is called "the lower sea." In the Black Sea, the bottom layers of water do not mix with the upper layers. This means that deep down, there is no oxygen, and marine life cannot survive. It also means that ancient artifacts like wood, fabric, and bones are preserved because they can not be broken down by oxygen.

The Sumerians began their civilization between the Tigris and the Euphrates rivers. This land is now eastern Syria, southeastern Türkiye, and most of Iraq. The two great rivers start in the Taurus Mountains and are fed by the melting winter snow. The Tigris runs close to the Zagros Mountains. Smaller rivers and streams flow down into it and cause flooding in the spring. Both rivers flow southeast and run parallel to each other through green valleys, flat plains, and deserts. After traveling over a thousand miles, they join together and empty into the Persian Gulf. These rivers were the center of life and culture in ancient Mesopotamia.

title: The Fertile Crescent
text:
Although much of Mesopotamia was dry desert land, it snowed every year in the mountains. When the snow melted, the rivers often flooded. As the waters drained, silt was left behind. Silt is very fine sand or soil that is carried along by a river. It stays moist and has good air circulation. It also contains nutrients and minerals that help plants grow.

The yearly flooding of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers created a large region of rich soil in the shape of a crescent. A crescent is a curved shape that is wider in the middle than on the ends, like the moon when it is less than half of a circle. In fact, the area is often called the Fertile Crescent because of its rich and fertile soil, spread in a curved shape. Fertile means land that plants grow well in.

The Fertile Crescent ran from the top of the Persian Gulf, north along the Tigris and Euphrates valleys. It then turned south, along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, and ran through the Nile Valley in Egypt. Many different groups of people fought to control it over the years. The Sumerians, Babylonians, Chaldeans, Akkadians, and Assyrians all made Mesopotamia their home at different times in history.

title: The Importance of Water
text:
Water has played a critical role in history. Civilizations need water to survive and grow. Many early settlements began near lakes, oceans, and rivers to take advantage of the water. Almost every major ancient city was built near a river. Rivers provided water for drinking and washing. Rivers also provided fish and water birds for food. People used water for growing crops and for transportation.

The Tigris and Euphrates rivers were very important in Mesopotamia. The land between the two rivers was wet and full of marshes. The land surrounding Mesopotamia was made up of deserts and mountains. The climate was extremely hot and dry. Without the water from these two rivers, the civilization would not have been able to grow and thrive. The rich plant life also allowed many animals to live in this area.

The Sumerians developed a system of irrigation that helped them become some of the world’s first successful farmers. This allowed them to grow enough food to feed everyone. The Sumerians also learned to use the mud along the riverbanks to make things. Workers began to “specialize” in pottery and build brick homes. Remember that a stable food supply, permanent settlements, and job specialization are three important characteristics of a civilization.

The two rivers also provided water routes to other areas of the world. The Sumerians became successful trade merchants. People traveled in and out of the area. This began a natural exchange of ideas, practices, and inventions. As a result, the Sumerian culture began to spread and influence other areas of the world.

title: Advances in Agriculture
text:
As the people of Sumer settled in the Fertile Crescent, they changed from being hunter-gatherers to being farmers. Soon they started to rely on irrigation instead of rainfall to grow their crops. This change was part of the Agricultural Revolution.

The Sumerians began looking for ways to control the rivers that flooded in the spring and dried up in the summer. They invented a system with brick walls and dams that led the floodwaters into reservoirs. Reservoirs are human-made pools or lakes where water can be stored until it is needed. In the dry summer months, the Sumerians directed the water from the reservoirs into canals and ditches that carried it to the fields.

The use of irrigation resulted in more stable sources of food. The main crop in Sumer was barley. However, they grew many other foods, including wheat, beans, onions, melons, lettuce, cucumbers, apples, grapes, plums, apricots, pistachios, and a variety of herbs and spices.

The Sumerians also began domesticating animals. They raised goats, sheep, pigs, cattle, ducks, and even pigeons. In addition to eating the animals, Sumerians made cheese and other dairy products from animal milk. The people didn’t stop hunting entirely. Gazelle, deer, and waterfowl were commonly hunted in the area. More than 50 varieties of fish could be caught in the nearby waters.

title: Timelines
text:
Events in Order

Timelines help us to see a series of events in chronological order. Chronological means things are presented or described in the order in which they happened. A timeline starts at the date of the first event and goes forward by making leaps in time. For example, if you made a timeline of your life, it would start when you were born. Next, it might show the date you got your first tooth or took your first steps. It would continue with other important dates and events and end with where you are now. What you include on a timeline depends on what you want to show. Usually, it's the most important events that happened during a period of time.

Recording Time

Timelines can deal with history that happened hundreds and thousands of years ago. A man named Dionysius Exiguus came up with a way of recording time. His system divided events into two sections. He labeled anything that happened “Before Christ” as B.C. This section counts the years backward on the timeline from the year Jesus Christ was likely born. He labeled everything occurring after that as A.D. (“anno domini,” meaning “in the year of our Lord.”) This section counts the years going forward. Today, many people use the terms B.C.E. (Before Common Era) and C.E. (Common Era) instead. Can you think of a reason why?

Circa

As you research, you might notice that different sources use slightly different dates. This is because it is difficult to be exact about things that happened so long ago. Ancient civilizations overlapped as they developed all around the world. Not everyone agrees on the precise times for each period or event. Not everyone agrees on how old certain sources and artifacts are. New technologies are constantly being developed that help us study and date the past more accurately. Sometimes dates on a timeline will have a "c." before the number. This is an abbreviation of the Latin word circa, meaning “around” or “approximately.” This is used to show that we don’t know exactly when something happened.

Tools

Many scientists use timelines. Historians use them to divide the past into historical eras and periods. Archaeologists use them to place artifacts within a certain time period. Astronomers might use a timeline to predict when a comet’s path will pass by Earth. Timelines and time periods are tools that help historians compare events and developments in history and understand changes over time. Remember that historical timelines don’t work like our calendars today. They're not real to the history itself or to the people who lived through that history. No one in ancient Mesopotamia ever got up in the morning and said, "Today is the first day of 2300 B.C.E.”

title: Dividing Up Time
text:
We often divide time into chunks related to certain events or movements that were happening. We call them ages or eras. The Stone Age is a period of time when weapons and tools were often made of stone. The period of history that we will study this year is often called the Ancient Era. Dividing history into ages or eras helps us understand what was happening at certain points in time. It helps us see what life was like then.

Time is also divided into centuries. A century is equal to 100 years. We live in the 21st century. When we say “21st century,'' we are referring to the period of 100 years from 2001 to 2100 C.E. It is also called the 2000s. When we say "20th century," we are referring to the 1900s. It can be a bit confusing. That’s because, according to the calendar we use, the first century C.E. included the years 1-100 (there was no year zero), and the second century C.E. included the years 101-200.

title: Volunteering
text:
Responsible citizens who want to give back to their community, state, country, or the world can volunteer, or donate their time, to help others. Many people volunteer because they want to help others in need. There are many ways you can volunteer in your community. Food banks collect canned goods or deliver food to people in need. Other programs teach people to read. Some volunteers even build homes for the needy.

Volunteer organizations have also been created to protect animals, natural resources, and the environment around the world. There are hundreds of environmental organizations that work tirelessly to preserve Nebraska's natural wonders and creatures that call the state home.

title: Public Service
text:
Another way that citizens can participate in their community and solve community problems is through public service. Public service is when people perform activities to make their community a better place. Any citizen can perform public service, regardless of their job. Public service can also include serving in government offices, elected positions, and in the military. There are many ways that citizens of Nebraska can engage in public service. This can include attending a local public meeting, joining a neighborhood association, or volunteering with a community organization.

There are a lot of public services that are provided to citizens in a community. These often include police and fire departments, public transportation, sanitation services, public libraries, healthcare, and public education. That means your teacher is performing a public service!

title: Responsibilities of Citizens
text:
The United States government was created for the people and relies on them to succeed. People can make a difference in their communities by participating in the government and being engaged citizens. Being an engaged citizen includes voting, obeying laws, paying taxes, and being involved in local, state, and national governments.

Being an engaged citizen also means working for the common good. This means working for things that help everyone in a community and not just yourself. To promote the common good, citizens can participate in a variety of activities, including volunteering and donating their time and funds to a cause. You can help your community by working to preserve its history. You can engage in service projects to help others, such as organizing a fundraiser for those in need, participating in community clean-up events, and supporting recycling initiatives.

Engaged citizens also respect and protect the rights of others. They contribute to their community's economic development. They respectfully hold leaders to their word. They stay informed about issues, share their opinions, and get involved in creating solutions. People can also contact leaders at the local, state, and federal levels by writing letters, making phone calls, and sending emails to express their concerns and opinions. This allows them to have a voice in decisions that improve their community. Citizens can also become involved in their community by running for political office.

title: Many Nations
text:
Before European contact, North America was home to thousands of Native American tribes. A tribe is a name for a group of families and communities that have a common language, religion, and government. Languages, beliefs, and governments could have had differences within the same region.

Each tribe has its own myths about creation. For example, the Natchez believe they came from the sun. The Cherokee believe water is spiritually important. Native Peoples also spoke many different languages, not just one. Some believe there might have been between 250 and 500 languages in North America at the time of contact with Europeans. When one group of people met another, they might have used hand gestures to communicate.

Each individual tribe used its region’s resources to meet its wants and needs. Some tribes planted crops. Some followed migratory animals that they hunted for food and supplies. Native peoples fished, gathered berries, hunted, and made good use of the resources around them. Although many of the same resources were used within the same region, no two tribes looked exactly the same. Some tribes used trees and woven grasses to make long, rectangular dwellings. Others within the same region made dome-shaped houses out of the same materials.

Each tribe put its distinct mark on the appearances of its families and communities. The members of some tribes wore their hair long and made their clothing out of animal skins. Others made clothing from plant fibers. Visually, each tribe’s appearance made them distinct and recognizable to both friend and foe, even within the same region.

The natural resources of a region influenced the economic and cultural customs of the tribes that lived there. Animals of each region were used in tribal stories and beliefs. For example, alligators were prominent in the Everglades of the Southeastern region. However, other areas of the Southeastern region did not have alligators at all. The Calusa tribe revered the alligator in the Southeast, but the Cherokee, who did not live near alligators, revered the owl. This reverence was based on the environment and the available resources of each region.

As you learn about the tribes of North America this week, you may find that there are many commonalities between them. As you study, remember each tribe is unique and has its own history, traditions, and customs. Further analysis will help you to learn about the distinct culture and individuality of each tribe.

title: Governments of Native Peoples of North America
text:
Native Peoples had organized communities. Women played many different roles within the tribes. Some tribes had women in their government as leaders and advisors. In other tribes, women supported family and community survival. Some native peoples lived in small, independent groups. Other tribes formed large confederacies.

The smallest native political unit was the individual. Individuals had complete freedom to make their own decisions. Next was the band or village. A band was a group of people of the same tribe who were closely connected, often by family ties. They might fish, hunt, and grow food together. There were leaders for different duties. Bands had one chief for war and another leader during peacetime.

Clans were larger groups of distant relatives. The clan elders were chosen to make decisions for the group. Clans were often shared by many tribes. Bands or clans joined together to form tribes. A tribe was a group of people connected by a common language, beliefs, land, and culture. Tribes didn’t always have just one specific leader. They worked together to make major decisions, like going to war, choosing who to trade with, or choosing how to use natural resources.

A chiefdom was a group of tribes under one leader, or chief. For the Haudenosaunee, or the Iroquois, a woman might not be the chief of her tribe, but women helped make decisions about who their chief should be. The chief’s authority often stayed in the same family. Tribes like the Iroquois and Najavo believed authority was passed down through the matriarchal line. That means the power was passed through the mother’s line. Other cultures were patriarchal, or passed authority down through the father’s side of the family. For most tribes, if a chief wasn’t doing well for their people, that chief would be removed. In some groups, women made the decision to change the chief.

Some tribes joined together to form confederacies. Hundreds of years ago, the Mohawk, Onondaga, Cayuga, Oneida, and Seneca fought with one another. To end the wars, a prophet called the Great Peacemaker, an Iroquois woman named Jikonhsaseh, and Chief Hiawatha all convinced the tribes to unite. The Iroquois created a constitution, called the Great Law of Peace. This agreement included a balance of power between bigger and smaller groups, a two-branch legislature, procedures for passing laws, and more.

As the Cherokee were being pushed west, groups of Cherokee women asked the leaders of their tribes to not give the land away. No matter the structure, the purpose of having a government was the same: to provide safety and security for those in the community. How each group’s government achieved this varied. Some restricted freedoms and liberties, while others ensured them to provide safety and security. Both American Indian men and women worked together to provide safety and security for their people.

A government also provides justice and maintains order within the community and helps the members of the community meet their wants and needs. Each tribe chose leaders in different ways, and leadership varied between men and women. Leaders were chosen based on age, wisdom, leadership skills, or heredity. Each tribe chose the best leader to ensure the safety of the community. Authority was distributed across the community. A chief had authority over more people than a band leader. In a confederacy, the leaders had authority over a great number of people from many communities or nations. Women worked right alongside men. The goal was to provide safety, justice, and welfare for the people.

title: Customs and Traditions of Native Peoples
text:
The native tribes of North America have many different cultures and traditions. Each tribal group has its own beliefs, rituals, and traditions. Tribes have marriage ceremonies, funerals, and rites of passage for youth. Tribal culture includes language, storytelling, the arts, celebrations, food, and clothing. Many traditions are connected with the land the tribes call home. This connection to their homeland is similar for many tribes.

Language

Before the arrival of Europeans in North America, there were hundreds of different native languages spoken by millions of Native Peoples. Some languages were spoken within a very small area, while others were spoken by large numbers of people across the continent. Many native languages are still spoken today. However, many languages have also become extinct after the European colonization of North America. Today, many tribes are trying to bring back their original languages.

Storytelling and the Arts

The arts and storytelling are a large part of the culture of Native Peoples. Native Peoples living in North America did not use an alphabet to communicate, but they did have symbols that were part of stories. These symbols were placed on important, ceremonial items or painted on rocks. Native Peoples mainly used the spoken word to communicate and to preserve their history and traditions. Many stories explained their beliefs and the creation of the world. Some stories represented actual events that happened in the tribe’s past. Some represented relationships between families and their ancestors. Other stories are more like religious stories for the tribes. These stories have lessons on how to be a good person and treat everything with respect. Elders often taught these stories to children. Animals, birds, and the environment were often part of these important stories, creating a special bond to the land.

Throughout North America, Native Peoples made beautiful pieces of art from the natural materials around them. They used things like shells, porcupine quills, and feathers for decoration. Jade, turquoise, and other stones were used to create their art. They crafted jewelry and other items from silver, turquoise, and gold. Some cultures were known for creating elaborate sculptures out of stone, wood, and other materials. Many tribes wove baskets and made pottery. However, not all of the things made by Native Peoples were simply art. Many items were used in ceremonies and considered very sacred. These sacred items are only used for special occasions, like funerals. Early Indigenous art continues to influence artists, and many tribes continue to create art in the same way as their ancestors.

Ceremonies and Celebrations

Ceremonies and celebrations were often held to honor ancestors and celebrate the natural elements. Many holidays honor the sun, rain, and harvest. Dancing, singing, and praying are very important in ceremonies. Many ceremonies are performed to help people who are sick. Some ceremonies are held to celebrate when a child becomes an adult. When warriors came back from battle, special ceremonies were performed to help them not be angry. There were celebrations for a good harvest, giving thanks for the food. When a young hunter killed their first deer or bison, a special feast would be held to honor the animal and the new hunter.

Food

Native Peoples across North America relied on the land for food. Tribes hunted, gathered, and farmed for food. Many of the foods they ate were based on the seasons. Seasonal crops and hunting patterns played a huge role in community activities. Members of each tribe worked together to provide food for the community. Many of the foods that we enjoy today can be traced back to the crops grown by Native Peoples. These include corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, wild rice, squash, and beans.

Clothing

Before European exploration, tribes used natural resources from the land to create clothing. Their clothing represented the natural environment in which they lived. Clothing was practical and reflected the climate where people lived. Native Peoples used animal products, such as fur, feathers, bones, teeth, and claws, to make clothing and jewelry. They also used plants like tree bark and various grasses to make woven fabrics. They wore different forms of clothing for different purposes. Many tribes wore decorative headdresses, masks, and clothing for special ceremonies and celebrations.

title: Unique Emotions
text:
Every person is different. Every person has a different culture and family experience. Think about your culture. Think about your emotions. How does your culture and family affect your feelings? Identifying emotions involves paying attention to what you are feeling and who you are. Your emotions and experiences are uniquely yours.

Identifying your emotions also means being able to label what you are feeling. Understanding your culture and emotions helps you become self-aware. Giving yourself permission to experience a feeling is the first step to understanding and managing your emotions.

Some emotions can be complex. Your self-awareness helps you understand your emotions better. Many times, people feel more than one emotion at a time. Pay attention to your thoughts and feelings. Think about how you are unique.

title: Explore Emotional Vocabulary
text:
There are different words used to communicate what you are feeling. Your culture, family, or friends use unique words to describe different emotions. What words or images do you use to say you are happy? Do you use emojis or hand gestures? Different cultures might use different words, images, or hand gestures. How are your words similar to or different from your friend? How many different ways do your classmates say "happy"?

Selecting the right vocabulary words to describe your feelings will help you be able to communicate what you feel. Learning about cultural differences can be exciting and help you when it comes to communicating emotions.

title: Communicate Consistently
text:
Communicating emotions to others can help you process, or figure out, how you are feeling. It can also help others better understand how you are feeling. Communicating how you are feeling to others will help you be more kind and understanding. It will also help you establish healthy boundaries, or limits. If you feel exhausted, you can tell someone you need to rest. If you feel overwhelmed, you can ask for help. Everyone has the right to set healthy personal boundaries.

Nonverbal communication is when you communicate through your body language and facial expressions. Verbal communication is talking or signing. When you add verbal communication to nonverbal communication, it becomes easier to share your feelings with others. Communicating your feelings by using your words and body language will help you bridge cultural gaps in communication.

title: Recognize the Emotions of Others
text:
Recognizing emotions in others is similar to identifying emotions in yourself. When you know how others are feeling, you can show empathy. Empathy means understanding someone else’s feelings. You can think of a time that you felt a similar emotion to understand someone better. Showing empathy helps you create strong friendships. When you show empathy, others learn that you will be kind and understanding, especially when they feel sad or upset.

You can consider a person's culture and experience when you watch for emotional cues in others. You can also 1) observe, 2) infer, and 3) ask questions. And of course, always show respect. You can think about how your culture and experiences impact your view of the situation.

title: Choosing What to Do With Your Emotions
text: After you identify, label, and communicate how you feel to others, you are ready to start regulating your emotions. When you feel mad, what do you want to do? When you feel happy, what do you want to do? People can express emotions in many different ways. Regulating your emotions is all about choosing how and when you show your emotions. Some responses show respect for yourself and others. Some do not. Regulating your emotions involves finding appropriate ways to show how you are feeling. These ways should not cause harm to you or to others.

title: Navigate Challenges
text:
Managing your emotions can feel like a challenge at times. It is important to keep in mind that different situations require different emotions. Friendship usually involves emotions like happiness, joy, and excitement. Sometimes, you and a friend disagree, so it might involve feeling hurt, sad, or disappointed too. Affection for someone can feel exciting and happy or confusing and overwhelming. People show affection in different ways. One person might give a high five, another might write a kind letter. There are many appropriate ways to show all emotions. Think, does this emotion help or hurt me? Does it help or hurt the other person? If the answer is that it does not cause harm to you or someone else, chances are it is appropriate. Do your best to communicate your feelings honestly and with respect.

Communicating about your emotions through times of change can be very helpful to help you understand your feelings. Don’t be afraid to talk to a parent, guardian, or other trusted adult about physical or emotional changes you experience.

title: Respond to the Emotions of Others
text:
Have you ever heard that a smile is contagious? Why do you think that is? Has your mood ever been affected by the people around you? Often, our emotional state can be impacted by those we are with.

Co-regulating your emotions means managing your own emotions while recognizing emotions in others. It effectively means displaying empathy and seeking to understand others. It helps you feel less stressed and more connected to others. For example, when you are watching an event with your friends and everyone is laughing, you might enjoy it more than watching alone.

title: Record Keeping in North America
text: Many native tribes of North America didn’t have a written alphabet or use a written system of language. However, this doesn’t mean that they did not keep records of important events and experiences. One example of tribal record keeping are called petroglyphs. A petroglyph is a picture carved into rock. Petroglyphs represent important cultural beliefs, tribal stories, and significant events. Tribes living in the United States today consider petroglyphs sacred. They often gather around petroglyphs for celebrations and ceremonies.

title: Respect for the Land
text: Native Peoples have a deep respect for and connection to nature. They feel connected to the land. It plays a vital role in their sacred beliefs and everyday life. They care for the land and use resources wisely. They believe that if they take care of the Earth, the Earth will take care of them. Many tribes use the same name to describe the Earth: “Mother Earth.” Before European contact, Indigenous peoples did not believe in individual land ownership. The land was used by tribes and belonged to entire tribes. Products from the land were communal and shared among the bands that lived there. Because tribes relied so much on the land for their resources, they needed lots of land to get those resources. Tribes covered millions of acres to get food, fuel, water, and other resources. A certain area would have been used for several years. Then, the tribe would leave so the area could replenish itself. Eventually, the tribe would come back to that area when it was ready to be used again.

title: Innovations
text:
Tools

Native Peoples created and used many tools before Europeans arrived in North America. Various tools were used for hunting, fishing, farming, and everyday tasks. Tools were made from stone, wood, animal bones, antlers, and shells. They created drills and chisels to build homes, canoes, and weapons. Sewing needles were made from animal bone. People used them to sew clothing, shoes, and fishing nets. Many tribes also had specific tools for grinding corn, nuts, and other plants for eating and medicinal purposes.

Agriculture

Native farmers studied wild plants and learned which foods would grow well in certain areas. They also learned how to create new plants from old ones. Great Lakes peoples cultivated wild rice. The Iroquois grew crops in small mounds called “milpas” to prevent soil erosion. Tribes of the Northeast used fish to fertilize their crops. This allowed them to grow in sandy soil. Many native cultures created irrigation systems to water their crops. They built canals, pipelines, reservoirs, and dams to bring water from distant sources to their farms.

Medicine

Native Peoples found many ways to use plants as medicine. They knew which plants and herbs would cure common ailments, such as fever, pain, burns, and wounds. Black willow bark was brewed into a tea and consumed to prevent pain. Sage was used to treat stomach issues and skin rashes. Some tribes used milkweed plants to treat sore throats and prevent coughing.

Transportation

Before the arrival of Europeans, waterways were an important mode of transportation for Native Peoples and goods. Native Peoples have used canoes for thousands of years. Their invention made transportation, trading, and fishing much easier along waterways. Tribes used materials from the environment they lived in to make canoes.

Bark canoes were very popular because they were lightweight. They could also be made from materials in forested areas. Sometimes, people used animal skins to wrap around the stick frames of their canoes. In the northeastern United States, birch bark was very popular.

Canoes were also made by digging out the inside of large logs. This was long, hard work. The final canoe, called a dugout, was very heavy. Native Peoples of the Pacific Coast made dugout canoes from cedar. Cedar is wood that naturally resists water and rot. Some groups burned out the inside of a cedar log, then used sharp-edged rocks or shells to scrape out the burned parts.

Another interesting canoe was made with planks that were carefully split from a log and sewn together with strands of animal hide. The cracks between the planks were filled with a substance like tar, made from plant materials and mud. A swift canoe could take travelers 150 miles or more after a long, hard day of paddling.

title: Essential Question
text: How were the different groups of Native Peoples in North America organized based on their government and culture?

title: Essential Question
text: What were the motivations for Europeans to explore the Western Hemisphere?

title: Europe before Westward Expansion
text:
In the 1400s, the whole world was on the move. In the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, empires were growing. Rich empires served as patrons, meaning they could pay people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and exchanges of ideas through trade routes. A trade route is an area used by merchants for economic purposes.

In the Americas, new empires were rising. Near the Great Lakes, the Iroquois Confederacy was gaining more control over trade. Trade was expanding throughout the continent, including what is now Mexico and South America. In Central America, rulers of the Aztec Empire were patrons for many great poets. In South America, rulers of the Inca Empire were patrons for inventors who developed new technologies for farming, medicine, and bridge building. The Inca Empire used this new knowledge to increase trade and exchange ideas.

Across the Atlantic Ocean in Africa, trade across the Sahara in salt and gold made the Songhai Empire wealthy. Songhai leaders became patrons for education. Under the Songhai, thousands of scholars and students gathered to study at the famous mosques, libraries, and universities in the city of Timbuktu.

In the 1400s, most of the world’s people lived in Asia. China and India had the world’s largest economies because of trade. Spices, silks, gold, and other goods were traded all the way to Europe. However, at the same time, the Ottoman Empire was rising between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans soon gained control of trade connections between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans were responsible for stopping trade to Europe.

For merchants in Europe, losing access to trade with Asia was hard. The countries of Portugal and Spain, however, saw an opportunity. These countries looked for new routes across the sea to Asia. Patrons from Portugal hoped to make money from trade in Africa and find a way to sail around Africa to Asia. By 1490, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella were on the throne of Spain. Spain had just ended a religious war persecuting non-Christians. They had taken property from Jews and Muslims in Spain, which made them rich enough to be important patrons. Ferdinand and Isabella wanted new trade routes and income. They just needed the right idea to pay for and the right person to try it.

A man named Christopher Columbus approached Isabella and Ferdinand. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean and reach India that way. Columbus wanted the king and queen to be his patrons. Isabella and Ferdinand agreed to be patrons for Columbus. They paid for three ships Columbus could use, as well as the tools and crew needed for the voyage. Columbus made an agreement with Ferdinand and Isabella. The agreement described what both Spain and Columbus would receive if his journey was successful. This agreement clarified that Spain and Columbus would share the profits from any cargo he brought back. Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. His journey would launch the biggest changes in government, knowledge, and trade the world had ever seen.

title: Motives and Movement
text:
Why did people want to explore the seas? Why did people want to colonize new lands? Many had different reasons for what they did. Many wanted to find a safer route for trade between Europe and Asia. In addition to finding a safer trade route, many European countries wanted more from their voyages. Each voyage was funded for a specific purpose. Those purposes are often referred to as the three Gs: Gold, God, and Glory.

Gold

Many explorers were seeking riches for themselves and their country. They searched for gold and other precious metals that they could send back to Europe. These precious materials would be turned into coins, jewelry, and many other fine objects.

God

Religion was very important to many countries. Some explorers wanted to bring their beliefs to the people of the Americas. Many Portuguese and Spanish explorers wanted to spread the beliefs of Christianity and convert native peoples to their religion.

Glory

Europe is made up of many countries. These countries competed to claim land in the Americas. It was a race for explorers and settlers from each country to start colonies. Many explorers hoped to gain fame across the globe for their courageous actions and daring expeditions.

Together, these motivations gave rise to the Age of Exploration.

title: Age of Encounters in Western Hemisphere
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration for many years. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa.

Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He believed he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the Taíno people he met “Indians.” It wouldn’t be until 1503 when an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci would discover that the land Europeans were exploring was really another continent. People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim.

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures and became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they had learned on their voyage, other explorers followed. Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia.

John Cabot

Learning from Columbus, John Cabot became interested in finding a shorter route across the ocean. England sponsored Cabot’s journey to sail through the North Atlantic in 1497. When he reached land, Cabot thought he had landed in Asia, but it was actually what is now Canada. His voyage proved a northern route to the Americas could work. While in Canada, he met the Eastern Woodland Native People.

Pedro Álvares Cabral

In 1500, Portugal sponsored Pedro Cabral to take 13 ships to India for trade. Cabral’s plan was to sail around Africa, but on the way, his ships sailed far into the Atlantic. This misdirection caused Cabral to land on the coast of South America. There, he met the Tupiniquim people.

Jacques Cartier

France hoped to find a northwest passage to reach the Pacific Ocean through North America. In 1534, France sent Jacques Cartier to go find one. Cartier sailed up rivers in what is now Canada. He didn’t find a route to the Pacific, but he did meet the Mi’kmaq people and the powerful Iroquois Confederacy. Cartier’s trips started French trade in North America.

Francisco Vásquez de Coronado

Starting in Mexico in 1540, Coronado led an expedition for Spain in search of the Seven Cities of Cibola, which were said to be full of amazing wealth just waiting to be taken. Along the way, the expedition discovered the Grand Canyon and found many Native People villages, but there was no gold in any of them. Coronado passed through Arizona, New Mexico, crossed west Texas and the Oklahoma panhandle, and then entered Kansas around what is now Liberal. His trek took him through what are now the cities of Plains, Meade, Fowler, Minneola, and Dodge City.

Francisco Pizarro

Setting sail for Spain, Pizarro first traveled to the Americas just 10 years after Columbus’s voyage. Inspired by stories of great wealth, Pizarro traveled south along the coast in search of wealthy civilizations. He then traveled to a part of South America known to the Spanish as “Peru.” There, he encountered the Inca Empire. Pizarro decided he wanted to take possession of their wealth. Before Pizarro launched an attack, he had to sail all the way back to Spain to get the support of Emperor Charles V. When he returned to Peru, the Inca were in the midst of a civil war. Pizarro’s entrance coincided with a recent victory by a leader named Atahualpa. Pizarro set a trap and quickly took over Atahualpa’s forces. Pizarro then took over the capital of Cusco in 1533, ending the Inca Empire.

Hernán Cortés

Hernán Cortés was one of the most famous Spanish conquistadors, or Spanish soldiers who explored and conquered lands around the world. He conquered what is now central and southern Mexico. He encountered the Aztec Empire in 1519. The Aztec king was Moctezuma II. His people were very friendly to Cortés and his men because they believed Cortés to be one of their gods, Quetzalcoatl. The Aztecs submitted to almost everything Cortés wanted. Cortés captured Moctezuma and forcibly took over the Aztec Empire. His military victories led to 300 years of Spanish domination of Mexico and Central America.

title: Trade, Taxes, and Scarcity
text:
Trade is one way people meet their wants and needs. Trade with others creates a trade network. In Europe, there was a trade network between Europe and the Indies. The “Indies” was what Europe called Asia in the 1400s. The trade network covered a route known as the Silk Road. This trade route was used for centuries. Caravans were groups of traders that traveled together. Caravans brought spices, tea, silk, and other goods from the Indies to sell to the people of Europe. The Caravans traveled through many countries to reach Europe. Each country traded with the caravans.

Spices were not a natural resource in Europe. The supply of spices imported to Europe depended on the caravans on the Silk Road. In the 1490s, the supply of spices and other goods from Asia was stopped by the Ottoman Empire. The Ottoman Empire controlled a large section of the Silk Road. The Ottomans put high taxes on the goods coming into their country. This made the goods very expensive. Many traders could not afford to pay the taxes to the Ottomans. Therefore, the goods did not move on to Europe.

The monarchs of Spain, Ferdinand and Isabella, wanted spices and goods from Asia to be in the markets in Spain. With the Ottomans blocking the land route, they were not able to export any Spanish goods or import goods from the Indies. Another route to the Indies was needed. If Ferdinand and Isabella could meet the high demand for Asian goods, they could sell those goods for a great profit.

This was the reason Columbus came to Spain. He had the idea of sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach the Indies. The new technology for navigation on the seas made this a reasonable plan. Ferdinand and Isabella became the patrons of Columbus. They took a financial risk on Columbus, hoping he would reach the Indies and return with spices. Columbus returned to Spain with a cargo of goods far greater than spices. The risk Ferdinand and Isabella took paid off greatly. The trade that began in 1492 between Spain and the Americas is called the Columbian Exchange. This exchange had a large impact on both sides of the Atlantic.

title: Communicating Emotions
text:
When you feel emotions, you can choose how you respond to those emotions. You can bottle them up and choose not to acknowledge or share them. You can also let emotions out by communicating them to others. Analyze the difference between these two types of responses.

When you communicate your emotions with someone you trust, it can reduce your stress and take the weight of your emotions off your shoulders. Feeling too many emotions can be overwhelming. Think about a young child who gets angry. They usually communicate their frustration by yelling, screaming, crying, or even throwing things. They throw tantrums. Now that you are older, you have the words to communicate your feelings in a more mature and effective way. You can communicate your emotions by writing in a journal, talking with someone you trust, or even experiencing the emotions through music or art. Which response do you think will be most helpful to you?

title: Self-Regulating Emotions
text:
You can regulate your own emotions. It is important that you recognize how you feel and allow yourself to feel your emotions. Self-regulating means remaining in control of your response to your emotions. It is okay to feel anger and frustration, but it is never appropriate to harm yourself or others emotionally or physically. It is not appropriate to destroy or vandalize property when you are angry. When you feel anger, you can demonstrate self-control. Practicing deep breathing, writing in a journal, exercising, and creating are all positive ways to release frustration or other strong emotions. Self-regulating can help reduce health risks to yourself and to others.

What can help you self-regulate your emotions?

title: Managing Big Emotions
text:
Emotions can be hard to handle. At times, they can be powerful and feel extreme. You can use strategies to calm down, be present, and stay mindful.

Here are a few activities that can help you when your emotions are overwhelming or feel out of your control:

deep breathing

meditation

yoga

exercise

journaling

drawing

music

Most importantly, you can ask for help.

When should you ask for help?

Who can you turn to for help?

You can ask for help at any point when you feel alone or anxious about your big emotions. Turning to a trusted adult for help is ideal. In some cases, a counselor or therapist can provide helpful information. You should ask for help immediately if you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself or someone else in any way.

title: Everyone Has Feelings
text: Everyone feels emotions. Your friends, your siblings, and even your parents and teachers have emotions. How can you tell what other people are feeling? You can pay attention to people’s words, facial expressions, body language, and actions. People may tell you exactly how they are feeling. When that happens, you should be a good listener. Tell an adult immediately if someone tells you they are thinking about hurting themselves or someone else. Body language can tell you a lot about how someone is feeling. Are they standing tall and confidently or are they looking at the ground? Are they smiling or are they uninterested and alone? Pay attention to people’s actions. If someone asks you if they can play with you, it may be because they feel alone. Everyone is different in how they show their emotions. No matter what emotions another person is feeling, you can be kind and supportive by being a good listener and respecting the personal boundaries of others. You can also set healthy boundaries that help you take care of your own emotions too.

title: Responding to the Emotions of Others
text:
Emotions can be contagious. Have you ever been around someone who is always smiling? Is it easy to be sad around that person? Have you ever been around someone who is always grumpy? How do you feel when you are with them? Everyone around you is feeling emotions that can affect you, but you get to choose how you respond.

When your friend is happy and excited, you can choose to let those feelings rub off on you; you can choose to be happy for your friend and share those positive emotions. When someone is always complaining and negative, you can choose not to join. Instead, you can keep a positive perspective.

When others feel sad or angry, you can simply be empathetic, supportive, and respectful. Soak up other people’s positive emotions, not the negative emotions. It is important to be a good friend, but you are not responsible for other people’s feelings. If someone’s negativity is rubbing off on you, you can talk to them about it, or you can choose to spend a little less time with them. This is called setting boundaries. Setting boundaries helps you maintain privacy and safety.

title: The Plague
text:
In 1346, a strange sickness began making its way west from Central Asia. The Black Death, which earned its name from the black patches that appeared on its victims, ravaged its way across the world. Commonly called the plague, the Black Death spread fast and killed quickly.

There were three types of the plague a person could get sick with: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic. The bubonic strain was the most common and could be identified by the swollen lumps that appeared in the neck, armpits, and other areas of the body. About 80 percent of those infected with bubonic plague died. Pneumonic plague attacked the lungs, causing a very bad cough that killed about 95 percent of those infected with it. Septicemic plague infected the bloodstream and killed 100 percent of those who contracted it.

The disease changed Europe dramatically. Medical traditions were called into question. Doctors in the 14th century believed that studying ancient scholars like Hippocrates and Aristotle would offer solutions. When this failed to make any difference, many began to believe that old remedies couldn’t solve new problems. So, traditions changed. Medical texts became available in common languages, not just Latin. More scholars and doctors were able to study and contribute new knowledge of their own. Medicine began to become a profession of continual learning.

Church authority was also shaken by the plague. Members of the clergy died from the plague just as quickly and easily as anyone else. Parishioners began to question the church’s authority. Church leaders claimed that those who died of the plague were guilty of sin, only to die themselves of the disease. The lavish lifestyles of some of the clergy were called into question.

Jews were persecuted because of the plague. Some members of the Catholic Church spread rumors that Jews were responsible for the plague. They claimed that Jews had conspired against Christians by poisoning well water. Jewish communities were threatened by mobs. Many Jews fled persecution and made their way to places like Poland and other countries in Eastern Europe.

Between 1346 and 1353, an estimated 75 million people across Europe, Africa, and Asia were killed by the Black Death. Figures are hard to determine for many reasons. However, it is estimated that between 30 and 60 percent of the entire European population died of the plague.

So many peasants, or serfs, died that crops were left in the fields, and livestock desperately needed tending. The peasants who survived the plague realized that their labor was more valuable now. Feudalism had kept peasants poor and tied to their lords’ lands for hundreds of years. Serfs began demanding better conditions and wages to work the land instead of paying their rent with labor. Some noble landowners refused, while others agreed to the serfs’ new terms for the sake of bringing in much-needed crops. Peasants were no longer tied to the land and could move to different places. Those who started earning wages could afford to purchase better clothing, housing, and even luxury items that had been unobtainable before. The feudal system was crumbling, and there was no going back.

title: How the Plague Spread
text:
Where the Black Death originated is debated. Many scholars and historians believe it first broke out somewhere in Central Asia. One theory is that the disease originated in China and was carried west along the Silk Road. In the Mediterranean, sailors and dock workers could have become infected and spread the disease as they sailed to other areas.

Another theory claims the plague was used as biological warfare. Troops of the Mongol Empire laid siege to an Italian-held city on the Black Sea. The Mongol troops were infected with the plague and used the disease to infect the city. Residents fled by ship, taking the disease with them to port cities in the Mediterranean. From there, the disease would have spread quickly from port to port. Wherever it started, records show that by 1348, the plague was rapidly spreading across Europe, the Middle East, and northern Africa.

People didn’t understand how diseases spread in the 14th century. Some believed that bad smells in the air, or “miasmas,” caused illness. Others believed that illness was the will of God. Diseases were often blamed on witchcraft, poison, or groups of people. People didn’t know about germs and bacteria. Today, we bathe and wash our hands with clean water and soap. In the medieval period, soap was a luxury, and clean water wasn’t available to most people.

Those who contracted pneumonic plague, which infected the lungs, developed a terrible cough. Coughing spread plague bacteria into the air, infecting those who breathed it in. People who cared for the sick or who buried the dead often became infected.

Along with poor hygiene, rats were one of the main ways the plague spread. Fleas carrying the plague bacteria would feed on rats, catching a ride as the rats moved to new places. Rats onboard ships were common. Rats got into people’s homes, and sailors frequently shared their sleeping quarters with ship rats. Fleas need a live host, and when the rat carrying them died, the fleas would jump to the nearest warm body to feed. One flea bite was all it took for people to become infected with the plague.

The disease’s rapid spread was due to large numbers of ships traveling farther and faster than ever before. These ships helped spread the disease with every stop they made. It wasn’t until the 19th century that the bacteria of the plague, yersinia pestis, and the flea-infested rats being its primary carriers were discovered.

title: The Significance of the Hundred Years’ War
text:
The Hundred Years’ War was the name given to a series of conflicts between England and France that lasted for 116 years. It started with a disagreement between King Edward III of England and King Philip VI of France.

When Edward III became king of England in 1327, he inherited the Duchy of Aquitaine. The duchy was a province that included nearly half of France’s land at that time. This inheritance gave England control of land from the north of England all the way down to the south of France.

Because of the feudal system, Aquitaine was still subject to the French king. This meant the French king had a legal right to take back the land. Philip VI took back more and more land from Edward III. This continued until the English crown went from controlling almost half of France to only having authority over the Duchy of Gascony, a small province in the southwest of France.

Philip VI made an alliance with Scotland to take away Gascony from England. Edward III saw this as an insult and a threat. Gascony was an important trade partner to England. So, Edward III invaded France to regain his lost lands. Despite years of success in taking back French lands, by the end of Edward III’s reign, England once again only had control of Gascony.

After Edward III’s death, the English throne went to his grandson, Richard II. Richard was an ineffective leader and was dethroned by his cousin, Henry Bolingbroke. He became King Henry IV. He spent most of his reign defending his position as king.

Henry IV’s son, Henry V, inherited the English throne and began fighting France again. He won numerous battles. King Charles VI of France was forced to sign the Treaty of Troyes in 1420. The terms included in the treaty were that Henry V would marry Princess Catherine of Valois, Charles VI’s daughter, and he and his heirs would be next in line for the French throne. The peace did not last.

In 1428, a peasant girl named Joan of Arc went to Orléans, where she led the French to victory in battle against the English. She inspired the French and led them to victory in several other battles. However, she was captured by the English in 1430. She was tried as a heretic and killed.

The English were struggling to maintain control of France, and funds for the war were running low. In 1445, Henry VI (the son of Henry V) married a French princess, Margaret of Anjou, and paid for the marriage by giving the French provinces of Maine and Anjou back to France. In return, Henry VI believed that Charles VII would provide proposals of peace that would end war between France and England. This did not happen. In 1450, the French drove English forces out of France for the last time. After the English had been expelled, France and its duchies eventually became a united country.

title: Henry V
text:
Henry V is remembered as one of the greatest warrior kings of England. Although he eventually became king of England, Henry was not in line for the throne when he was born. After King Edward III’s death, Edward’s grandson, Richard II, became king at age 11. Richard was an inexperienced and ineffective leader.

In 1397, Richard II attended a tournament. There, two knights were settling a disagreement by fighting. Richard II stopped the fight and banished them both. One of these men was a cousin of King Richard II named Henry Bolingbroke. This was Henry V’s father. Two years after his banishment, Boliginbroke returned to England, imprisoned Richard II, and took the throne for himself as King Henry IV. Richard died during his imprisonment, and because Henry IV had taken the throne rather than been born to it, he spent most of his reign defending his position as king.

During his father’s banishment, Henry V was mentored by Sir Henry “Hotspur” Percy, who taught him about warfare and fighting. After Henry IV took the throne, Henry “Hotspur” Percy and a faction of Welshmen rebelled against him. Henry V fought beside his father against his old mentor when he was just 16 years old. Henry V proved himself a capable leader by leading part of the army in the battle. He was wounded but recovered and went on to become England’s next king.

Because of his mother, Henry V was a direct grandson of the previous French king. This meant he had a claim to the French throne. In order to solidify his claim, Henry V decided to invade France and resume the Hundred Years’ War.

At the Battle of Agincourt, Henry V led approximately 8,000 English soldiers to victory against 15,000 French troops. After this victory, he captured several other cities and regions in northern France, including the cities of Rouen and Normandy.

After a long campaign, the French king finally signed the Treaty of Troyes, which stated that Henry V and his heirs would inherit the French throne after the French king, Charles VI, died. Another term of the treaty was that Henry V would marry Princess Catherine of Valois, one of Charles VI’s daughters. This ensured that Henry V’s children would be direct descendants of the French king and give them a legitimate claim to both the English and French thrones.

In addition to securing control of the French throne, Henry V followed the example of his great-grandfather, Edward III, by speaking and writing in English, solidifying English as the common language of England. Today, English remains the official language of England.

title: Joan of Arc
text:
Joan of Arc was born in Domrémy, France, in 1412. While a young teen, Joan said she had visions of saints. She explained that these saints told her to help save France from the English. The French had been fighting the English for nearly 100 years, and France was losing. Joan went before Charles VII at his court in Chinon to tell him about her mission. Charles VII was skeptical about her claims. To make sure she was not a witch trying to deceive him, he had her examined by several members of the clergy, who proclaimed her a good Christian woman. Charles VII was convinced her mission was from God. He had steel plate armor made for Joan, which she wore into battle. She also had a special sword with five crosses on it.

Joan of Arc led thousands of French troops into battle. She carried a flag into battle that displayed religious pictures. She directed attacks and encouraged the soldiers to win. Her efforts led to a French victory over the English in Orléans. She went on to lead and inspire the French to win several other battles. This helped turn the tide of the Hundred Years’ War for the French. English soldiers called longbowmen had devastated French troops, but Joan of Arc showed the French that victory against the English was possible.

The English eventually captured Joan and put her on trial in Rouen. They accused her of heresy, or making false religious claims. The most serious charge against Joan was that she falsely claimed direct inspiration from God. The Catholic Church decreed that this was not possible. Joan of Arc also wore men’s clothes, which many thought was a crime against God. Authorities also accused her of practicing witchcraft. They found Joan guilty of heresy and killed her in 1431. In 1920, the Catholic Church made Joan a saint.

title: The Plague in Their Own Words
text:
The following excerpts come from accounts written by people who were alive when the Black Death swept through Europe.

… It began with swellings … in both men and women, some of which were as big as apples and some of which were shaped like eggs, some were small and others were large … [and] within a short while would appear over the entire body in various spots; the disease at this point began to take on the qualities of a deadly sickness, and the body would be covered with dark and livid spots …

… huge numbers of men and women abandoned their rightful city, their rightful homes, their relatives and their parents and their things, and sought out the countryside …

Wherefore they banded together, and dissociating themselves from all others, formed communities in houses where there were no sick, and lived a separate and secluded life, which they regulated with the utmost care, avoiding every kind of luxury, but eating and drinking moderately of the most delicate viands and the finest wines, holding converse with none but one another, lest tidings of sickness or death should reach them, and diverting their minds with music and such other delights as they could devise.

… Very few were ever cured…

Such was the multitude… brought to the churches every day and almost every hour that there was not enough consecrated ground to give them burial, especially since they wanted to bury each person in the family grave, according to the old custom…

—Giovanni Boccaccio (1313-1375)

Our early hopes are buried with our friends. The year 1348 has left us solitary and bereaved; and has taken from us what all the wealth of Ormus and of Ind could never replace. Such final losses are irreparable, and the wounds inflicted by death can never be healed. There is but one source of consolation; we shall soon follow those who have gone before. How long we must wait we know not. But this we do know, it cannot be for long; and the delay, however short, will not be without its trials.

—Francis Petrarch (1304-1374)

Death went from one end of the earth to the other, on that side and this side of the sea ... In some lands everyone died so that no one was left. Ships were also found on the sea laden with wares; the crew had all died and no one guided the ship. The Bishop of Marseilles and priests and monks and more than half of all the people there died with them. In other kingdoms and cities so many people perished that it would be horrible to describe … And from what this epidemic came, all wise teachers and physicians could only say that it was God's will.

—Jacob von Königshofen (1346-1420)

Then the bishop of Lincoln gave general power to all and every priest to hear confessions, and absolve with full and entire authority except in matters of debt …

—Henry Knighton (b. Unknown - d. circa 1396)

title: Building My Confidence
text:
Sometimes confidence takes time to build. Here are a few things you can do to increase your confidence:

Don’t compare yourself to others. Everyone has different strengths.

Use positive self-talk. The words you say to yourself are very important. Choosing to say and think kind things about yourself can boost your confidence.

Try new things. When you do this, you can learn new skills. Developing talents is a great way to increase your confidence.

title: Using Confidence to Stand Up for Myself
text:
When you are confident, you can stand up for yourself. You can say what you want and need. You are important, and your wants and needs matter. Use your confidence to …

Make positive health choices for yourself.

Speak up for yourself when you need help.

Stand up for your beliefs and standards.

Refuse drugs, alcohol, and tobacco.

Be assertive and respectful when resolving conflict.

title: Using Confidence to Stand Up for Others
text: Your confidence can also help people around you. You can use it for good. Confidence can help you stand up to bullies or teasing. It can give you the power to treat others with kindness and respect, even when they are different from you. You can be confident in the moral qualities that are unique to you. You can be confident in the choices you make about what is right and wrong. This is your character.

title: Confidence Through Failures
text: Everyone has strengths and weaknesses. No one is good at everything. People make mistakes every day. Did you know you can be confident even after making a mistake? Even when you fail, you can use your confidence to help you try again. You can be confident that you can do hard things and continue to develop your strengths.

title: Conservation and Preservation
text:
Conservation and preservation are two ways of protecting the environment. They are also the ways that humans interact with the environment. Conservation and preservation also find ways to support the animals in the environment to meet their needs and protect their environment.

Conservation means using resources wisely. When we conserve, we don’t use too much of something. We don’t make the environment dirty. We save the resources we need to keep using.

Preservation means keeping the environment just the way it started. We preserve the environment to enjoy its beauty. We don’t use it for other purposes.

One example in Louisiana is the Louisiana Wildlife Habitat and Natural Heritage Trust Fund. Their goal is to conserve the natural areas for wildlife and to restore and preserve the wetland areas along the coast. Conservation and preservation are both important. Preservation and conservation groups monitor how the land and the Earth’s resources are used. They also help us find ways to enjoy the Earth’s beauty by preserving the natural areas that are special to different regions.

title: Week 24 Framing Question
text: What can you do to conserve and preserve your environment?

title: Do Your Best!
text: You can have confidence even when you are not good at something. You can have confidence in your effort. Effort is how much you try. Working hard and giving your best effort in everything you do will help you feel more confident. You can do anything you put your mind to.

title: George Washington Carver
text: George Washington Carver was a great American scientist. He became a professor at Tuskegee University where he studied plants and soil. His work helped conserve our natural resources. He showed farmers how they could feed their hogs acorns and use the local soil from the swamps to fertilize their land. He showed farmers how to grow more crops on their land. He called this crop rotation. Carver showed how to take care of the soil so it stays productive for farming. His method of crop rotation helped farmers both conserve and preserve their soil. His biggest success in this area was using peanuts as a rotating crop. Farmers started using the rotation method and soon there was an abundance of peanuts. Carver created over 300 different products that could be made from peanuts. This helped the farmer to continue earning money from their crops. Thanks to Carver, we have more food and a better environment.

title: Theodore Roosevelt
text:
Theodore Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909. Roosevelt loved spending time outdoors. He loved to go camping and hunting. He wanted to make sure that everyone could enjoy the Earth’s resources. Roosevelt created national forests, monuments, parks, and wildlife refuges. He helped protect the wild animals that lived in these places. In 1869, he saw the bison herds become smaller and smaller. The construction of the transcontinental railroad, increased western settlement, and overhunting of the bison contributed to the shrinking of their population from several millions in the wild, to only around 300.

"The conservation of natural resources is the fundamental problem. Unless we solve that problem it will avail us little to solve all others."

—Address to the Deep Waterway Convention, Memphis, TN, October 4, 1907

Roosevelt created 5 national parks and 150 national forests. National parks and state parks are places that protect certain areas of land or places in our country. These parks are very beautiful places. They have some of the most amazing landscapes in the world. Roosevelt wanted to preserve them for everyone to enjoy. Yellowstone National Park was the first national park. There are many other national parks. These are in places like the Grand Canyon, Niagara Falls, Monument Valley, and the Great Smoky Mountains.

title: Week 14 Framing Question
text: How do the characteristics of a region shape its culture?

title: Northeast: Physical Characteristics
text:
There are 11 states in the Northeast Region of the United States. Many of the states have beaches along the Atlantic Ocean. There are also rivers, lakes, streams, waterfalls, and mountains in the region.

The Northeast has a natural landmark called Niagara Falls. The falls are located on the border of Canada and New York. The falls on the American side are the oldest state park in our country. Scientists estimate that 45 million gallons of water pour over the 167-foot waterfall every minute!

The Northeast has a temperate climate in its northern part. Winters are long and cold with ice storms and snowstorms. The southern part of the region is milder. It has cool winters and hot summers.

Vegetation in the Northeast includes different species of large trees. There are also fungi, mosses, and ferns. The states closest to Canada have maple trees, too.

Animals that thrive in the Northeast include black bears, red foxes, white-tailed deer, and chipmunks.

title: Southeast: Physical Characteristics
text:
The Southeast Region has 12 states. The region has beaches on the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. Freshwater sources in this region include lakes and rivers. The Appalachian and the Blue Ridge Mountains are some of the landforms. There are also barrier islands, swamps, and wetlands.

A special physical feature of the Southeast is the Smoky Mountains, or the Smokies. The Smoky Mountains stretch across North Carolina and Tennessee. They’re named for the blue mist that always seems to hover around the peaks and valleys.

The climate of the Southeast Region is tropical. Summers are long, hot, and humid. Thunderstorms and hurricanes are frequent. The region has many National Forests. It is a good region for trees.

Animals in the Southeast include snakes, crocodiles, and alligators. There are also black bears, panthers, and even flying squirrels.

title: Week 15 Framing Question
text: How is your region different from other regions?

title: Midwest: Human Characteristics
text:
The population of the Midwest is about 68 million. The Chippewa, Lakota, and Blackfoot were some of the Indigenous peoples living in this region before Europeans arrived.

The Midwest is known for some of the finest architecture in the United States. The designs often show us the European countries the designers came from. Missouri is home to the Gateway Arch. The Arch is the tallest man-made monument in the United States. It is over 630 feet tall.

Since the land is fertile, there is a lot of farming in the region. People grow wheat, soybeans, and corn. Others raise hogs and dairy cows. It is one of the most important areas of agricultural production in the world. There are also many manufacturing industries. A lot of vehicles and machines are made there.

title: Southwest: Physical Characteristics
text:
The Southwest has four states. The Gulf of Mexico and 10 rivers are the region’s main bodies of water. There are also a few lakes. Landforms there include high mountains, plateaus, valleys, and seven barrier islands.

The region is home to the Grand Canyon and Monument Valley. The Grand Canyon is considered one of the seven natural wonders of the world. The canyon is one of the greatest examples of water erosion in the world. Monument Valley is located on the Arizona-Utah state line. It is a collection of tall sandstone formations. These monuments can often be seen in western movies.

There are both dry and tropical areas in the region. Rainfall is mostly seasonal. In summer, only the tropical areas receive rainfall. Other areas get most of their rainfall in winter.

Blue palo verde, Texas ebony, Arizona cypress, and white oak trees grow in the region. Cotton, lettuce, melons, and grapefruit also do well there.

Swift foxes, black-tailed prairie dogs, and Texas horned lizards are some of the animals found in the Southwest.

title: The West: Physical Characteristics
text:
Eight states make up the West Region of the United States. The Pacific Ocean gives the region many islands and coastlines. The region also has many rivers and waterfalls. There are lakes, hot springs, and geysers, too. The West is home to mountain ranges, valleys, and canyons. One of these mountain ranges is the Rocky Mountains. This mountain range stretches from Canada to New Mexico. It is a rich habitat for all kinds of animals and plants.

The West is also home to Yellowstone National Park. The park has active volcano activity, making it home to famous geysers and hot springs. The most famous geyser is called Old Faithful.

It has dry, temperate, and tropical climate areas. The dry areas have Joshua trees and cacti. The temperate areas have redwood, Douglas fir, and different kinds of juniper trees. Coconuts, pineapples, and sugarcane grow in the region’s tropical areas.

Animals in the region include elk, wolves, and bighorn sheep. There are also bison, rattlesnakes, and horned lizards. There is a lot of marine life, too.

title: The Kingdom of Mali
text:
The Mali Empire was founded around the year 1245 C.E. by Sundiata Keita after it won its independence from the kingdom of Sosso. The king of Sosso placed trade restrictions on the region that would later become Mali. Angered by this, the Malinke tribe, led by Sundiata Keita, rebelled and fought against Sosso. The Malinke people, allied with other tribes and leaders of the region, defeated the Sosso, and captured the former capital of Ghana. Sundiata Keita became the high king of the land. He named this new empire Mali. The Mali Empire included parts of what are now Mali, Mauritania, Senegal, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

Islam was brought to West Africa by Arab traders before Mali became an empire. Records from travelers like Ibn Battuta show that Sundiata Keita converted to Islam and that his son was one of the first Mali kings to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. Contemporary accounts of Mali show that Islam did not replace previous cultures or native religious practices, but Islam was absorbed into them. This gave Mali a unique cultural and religious identity, different from other Islamic African countries.

Once it was freed from Sosso control, access to trans-Saharan trade routes were opened up to the Mali Empire. Mali’s location lay right in the middle of multiple trade routes. Because of this, Mali had a triple income. (1) Trade goods coming into Mali were taxed, (2) trade goods were bought and then sold at higher prices, and (3) Mali had control of the regions with rich gold deposits. Mali grew in wealth and power to the point that a full-time standing military was created to collect taxes at the borders and patrol trade routes to keep travelers safe from bandits and thieves.

In addition to its economic success, Mali also became a world-famous center for Islamic learning and study. Scholars from all over Africa and the Middle East traveled to Mali to study at its universities and mosques. This further enriched Mali’s already diverse and unique culture.

At the height of this historic empire, Mali stood as the largest and one of the richest empires in West Africa. Unfortunately, despite Mali’s great wealth and power, the unclear rules of royal succession led to disputes and civil war, which led to its decline and eventual fall.

title: Entrepreneurs
text:
An entrepreneur is someone who decides to create or run their own business. They are inventive or imaginative people. They have a vision about something new they can offer their community. Entrepreneurs begin with an idea for a business. It takes courage to start a new business and invest money for an idea you believe in. Half of all new businesses fail within the first five years. Entrepreneurs must be knowledgeable about their goods and services to succeed. They have to come up with a great idea and use all their resources wisely. They have to work very hard to be successful.

Robert “Bob” Lewis Evans was a successful entrepreneur and restaurateur from Ohio. Evans operated his own farm in Rio Grande, Ohio, where he specialized in making sausage. He opened The Sausage Shop, a restaurant that served the sausage and other pork products he made, in 1962. After much success, Evans opened his second restaurant in Chillicothe, Ohio in 1968. Over the next 50 years, Evans’ restaurant empire expanded to hundreds of locations in 18 states. Evans remained an active member of his community and supported education endeavors for students in Ohio until his death in 2007.
