title: What Is Empathy?
text: Have you ever heard the word "empathy"? Empathy means understanding someone’s feelings. It means sharing emotions with others. Empathy is something you can feel toward yourself and toward other people. When you experience something, you learn to recognize the same emotions in others. You can feel empathy for someone who is going through something you’ve experienced. You can imagine what the other person sees, thinks, and feels. Showing empathy for others demonstrates that you care about them. Can you think of a time that you have felt empathy for someone?

title: How Can I Show Empathy?
text: You can show empathy the same way you show affection or friendship. How do you show affection to people you love? You can serve them, give them gifts, or speak kindly to them. How do you treat your friends? You listen to them, ask about them, and spend time with them. Those are also all ways you can show empathy. You can show empathy by spending time with someone going through a challenge. You can be a good listener. You can give them something that made you feel better when you experienced the same thing.

title: How Can I Build Empathy?
text:
It can take time and practice to build empathy. Here are some things you can do to build empathy skills:

Be open to experiencing new things. When you have more experiences, you can relate to more people.

Get to know people. It can be hard to have empathy for someone you don’t know. It is amazing how your emotions shift once you know someone’s story.

Imagine yourself in someone’s situation. Ask yourself: “How would I feel?”

The most important way to build empathy is to care about others. When you care for others, you want to understand how they feel.

title: Listen to Others
text: You can build empathy for others by listening to them. What makes a good listener? A good listener tries to understand. They ask questions. They show that they are listening with their eyes and body language. When you listen to understand what someone is feeling, you can feel empathy toward them. The more you listen, the more empathy you can build.

title: My Morals
text: Lying is wrong. Being honest is right. How can you know if something is right or wrong? You can use your moral identity. Moral identity is your sense of right and wrong. It will tell you if your actions are good or bad. When you make a choice, pay attention to how it makes you feel. Think about how it makes others feel. If you make a choice that makes you feel worse, it was probably wrong. If you make a choice that hurts other people, it is wrong. If you make a choice that makes you and others feel better, it is probably right. Showing empathy can help others feel connected when they are going through a challenge. Empathy can strengthen friendships.

title: What About Bullying?
text: Bullying is when a person purposely does things that harm or intimidate others. Bullying can be a big problem. Sometimes people make mistakes with how they treat others. Sometimes people choose to be a bully. Empathy can prevent or solve bullying situations. You can choose to show empathy even when others do not. If you see bullying behaviors, you can show empathy for the victim. You can also show empathy for the bully. Remember to learn the story of others. Usually, when a person feels connected and understood, they choose to treat others with respect. You can choose to be understanding and kind. You can stand up for people who are bullied. You can be an example of kindness and respect.

title: Empathy for Yourself
text:
Everyone makes mistakes. Everyone needs empathy. Empathy helps people feel connected. When you or a friend make a mistake, you can use empathy to help resolve the problem. You can show yourself empathy the same way you show empathy to others.

Be a good listener: self-reflect.

Speak kindly: think kind thoughts.

Be understanding and patient.

When you show empathy for yourself, you take care of your emotional well-being.

title: Writing the Declaration of Independence
text:
The colonies were ready to become an independent nation. They decided to hold elections for representatives to attend the Continental Congress. The Continental Congress was a group of men who became the government during the revolution. One of the members, Richard Henry Lee, brought the idea to the congress that a committee should be formed. The goal of this committee would be to create a document. The purpose of this document would be to tell King George III that the colonies were free and independent from his rule.

Five men were appointed to this committee. They were John Adams, Roger Sherman, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston, and Thomas Jefferson. Their job was to create the Declaration of Independence.

The committee created several drafts of the declaration before the 13 Colonies approved the final draft. On July 4, 1776, the Declaration of Independence was ratified. To ratify is to make something official, usually by voting. The Declaration of Independence became an official document of the 13 Colonies. John Hancock was the president of the Continental Congress. He and the other 55 members signed the Declaration of Independence.

title: Essential Question
text: How did geography, climate, and proximity to water affect the lives of the Native Peoples of Ohio?

title: Prehistoric Cultures of Ohio
text:
For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of American Indians came from Siberia across a land bridge known as the Bering Strait to America about 12,000 years ago.

In recent years, however, archaeologists have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land-bridge travelers. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people came by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups represent the Native Peoples’ earliest ancestors.

Paleo-Indians

The Paleo-Indians were nomadic, meaning they traveled from place to place looking for food. They hunted large animals, such as mammoths, ground sloths, bison, caribou, and others. They traveled in small bands of 20 to 50 people. They built simple shelters using sticks, branches, and animal skins. They also looked for natural shelters like caves. The Paleo-Indians also ate roots, plants, seeds, and possibly even insects. They used animal skins for clothing and shelter.

Paleo-Indian tribes settled in Ohio’s Cuyahoga Valley between 13,000 and 7000 B.C.E. Their primary source of food and resources was the herds of caribou that lived in the valley. Archaeologists have discovered many examples of stone tools and weapons they used, particularly arrowheads and spear points.

The oldest known group of Paleo-Indians to inhabit present-day Ohio were the Clovis people. Historians and archeologists estimate that the Clovis people lived in Ohio between 9,500 and 8,000 B.C.E. The Clovis people were known for the spear points they carved from stone, such as flint and obsidian. Archeologists have found Clovis spear points across North America, including several sites in central Ohio.

Archaic Indians

The Archaic peoples lived in Ohio’s valleys and forests from 8000 B.C.E to 500 B.C.E. The Archaic peoples were similar to the Paleo-Indians who came before them. They were primarily nomadic. They hunted, fished, and gathered food. They made tools, including arrowheads, spear points, and axes from flint and granite that they mined from Ohio’s rich mineral deposits. They used materials that were not used by the Paleo-Indians to make tools. Later, they invented a spear-thrower called an atlatl. This was used to throw a spear farther and faster than just by hand.

Toward the end of the Archaic period, various bands of Archaic peoples began to create permanent settlements in Ohio to take advantage of the area's rich resources. The Archaic peoples of Ohio also began to trade with other Archaic tribes for resources. One group, known as the Glacial Kame people, traded for sea shells and copper, which were used in important ceremonies.

Early Woodland Cultures

The Woodland period lasted from about 800 B.C.E. to 1200 C.E. During the Woodland period, the Indigenous peoples of Ohio formed larger tribes than those of the Archaic peoples. They began to create more permanent settlements and engaged in widespread agriculture. Early Woodland cultures of Ohio grew different types of grasses, sunflowers, squash, and later, corn. They continued to hunt, fish, and gather for food. Hunting became easier with the introduction of the bow and arrow.

Many of the early Woodland tribes, including the Adena and Hopewell cultures, built large mounds in their villages. The earthen mounds were used for burials, ceremonies, and as gathering places for tribes. Historians and archeologists estimate that there are about 10,000 mounds in Ohio.

Fort Ancient Peoples

The Fort Ancient culture, also known as the Late Prehistoric people, flourished in Ohio from 1000 to 1650 C.E. The Fort Ancient peoples lived in the central and southern parts of the state. Fort Ancient peoples lived in larger villages. They constructed permanent homes around a plaza where people could meet. They grew much of their food, but they also hunted in Ohio’s abundant forests. Archeologists have also found evidence that the Fort Ancient peoples also raised turkeys for food.

Evidence suggests that the Fort Ancient people constructed one of the most well-known mounds in North America. Serpent Mound is located in present-day Adams County, Ohio. A smaller mound was originally constructed by the Adena people about 2,000 years ago but was repaired and enlarged by the Fort Ancient people around 1100 C.E. The mound is over 1,300 feet long and is 20 to 25 feet wide. Archaeologists believe that the mound was constructed to honor the snake, which was an important animal in many native cultures.

title: Historic Native American Tribes of Ohio
text:
Native Peoples have lived in Ohio for thousands of years, starting with the Paleo-Indians. The descendants of the prehistoric peoples of Ohio formed various tribes with similar languages, cultures, and governments. Each tribe relied on the natural resources of Ohio to survive. The forests provided trees to build homes and canoes. Many animals inhabited the dense Ohio forests and were a source of nutrition and resources.

The river valleys provided fertile soil for growing crops. The extensive waterways of the Ohio region allowed tribes to travel and tap into the resources found in lakes and rivers. Through the forests, waterways, and valleys, the tribes created a vast network of trails to cross the territory and engage in trade. The tribes created vibrant societies in the Ohio wilderness long before European settlers came to the area. These Native American groups, which include the Delaware, Miami, Ottawa, Seneca, Shawnee, and Wyandot, are known as the historic American Indians of Ohio.

title: The Delaware
text:
The Delaware tribe, also known as the Lenape or Lenni Lenape, originally lived along the Delaware River in present-day New Jersey. The tribe migrated to Ohio in the mid-1700s. The Delaware relied heavily on the natural environment to meet their needs. Like many other Woodland societies, the Delaware divided work responsibilities between men and women. Men hunted in the forests and fished seasonally. Women farmed and prepared food for the tribe. They grew corn, beans, squash, and tobacco. The women also picked berries and nuts that grew in the area. Wild strawberries, blueberries, cranberries, walnuts, and chestnuts all grew in the area.

The Delaware had a matrilineal kinship system. This meant that a person’s family line was traced through their mother's line. Newlywed couples were expected to live with the bride’s family. Inheritances were passed from the mother to her children, instead of from the father to his children. In fact, the authority of a Delaware sachem, or chief, passed matrilineally. The sachem was always male, but the role would pass to his sister’s sons or the closest male relative of the matrilineal clan. There were three matrilineal clans, or family groups, in Delaware society: the Turtle clan, the Wolf clan, and the Turkey clan. People’s clan membership was determined by their mother’s family line. The head sachem was always from the Turtle clan.

title: The Miami
text:
The Miami people migrated to Ohio’s Maumee and Wabash River valleys in the early 1700s. Corn was an important part of the Miami diet. They also grew beans, pumpkins, melons, and squash. All members of the tribe were involved in growing and harvesting crops. Women planted the crops, while the men harvested the crops and cleared the fields for planting. Men hunted for game, and the women were responsible for processing the meat for food and hides for clothing.

The Miami lived in smaller camps during the winter months. When they returned to their primary villages, the tribe held large feasts and celebrations. Tribal celebrations included singing, dancing, and games. The largest celebration was held to celebrate the end of winter and the tribe’s plentiful supply of furs and maple sugar.

The Miami tribe was divided into six bands, or small family groups that consisted of 10 to 50 members. Each band had its own chief. Members of each band lived in different villages. Each village had its own chief that answered to the band chief. Villages would elect delegates to represent them when all of the bands met together. The delegates represented the interests of their band and brought important matters to the tribal council, which made decisions for all of the bands of the Miami.

title: The Ottawa
text:
The name “Ottawa” comes from the Algonquin word “Adawe” meaning “to trade.” The name originates from the Ottawa tribe’s role as traders among the tribes of the northeast. The Ottawa originally inhabited Manitoulin Island, a small island located in Lake Huron. In the 1740s, the Ottawa moved into northern Ohio to access the rich natural resources of the area. The Ottawa were distantly related to the Delaware tribe and shared many similar customs. The Ottawa were experts at fishing. Fish made up a large part of their diet. They also hunted and farmed for food.

The Ottawa lived in permanent villages. Ottawa villages included waginogan, or wigwams, longhouses, and meeting houses. Hunting parties used tents that could be easily transported from place to place. Like other Ohio tribes, the leader of the tribe was the chief, called a gimaa or ogimaa. Male members of the tribe chose the chief from among the former chief’s male relatives.

title: The Seneca
text:
The Seneca people lived in northeastern and central Ohio. Originally part of the Seneca tribe that inhabited present-day New York, the Ohio Seneca left the larger tribe to form their own tribe in the mid-1700s. This group included members from other tribes, including the Seneca-Cayuga, the Conestoga, the Erie, and other tribes. They established villages along the Sandusky River.

Like many of the tribes in Ohio, the Seneca relied on the natural resources of their environment to meet their needs. They engaged in farming but also hunted and fished for food. The Seneca constructed longhouses, which could house up to 60 members of the tribe. Like the Delaware, the Seneca were a matrilineal tribe.

title: The Shawnee
text:
Some historians and archaeologists believe that the Shawnee are the descendants of the Fort Ancient people. The Shawnee were more nomadic than their neighboring tribes. They followed the migration patterns of animal herds during the winter. Because they were more nomadic, the Shawnee lived in wigiiwa, also called wigwams. Wigwams were small, domed-shaped homes that could be easily transported. They lived in more permanent settlements during the spring and summer.

Shawnee women planted crops in the spring and harvested them in the summer and fall. Men hunted and fished to provide food for the tribe. They were also warriors and defended the tribe. Women wore long skirts and the men wore breechcloths and leggings made from animal skins. The Shawnee were divided into five different groups. These groups were the Chillicothe, Hathawekela, Kispoko, Mekoche, and Pekowi. Each group had its own territory. Each territory had a central town where the tribe lived and held important meetings and ceremonies.

Each group of the Shawnee was led by a king or chief called a hokima. The hokima was in charge of civil matters. A person called a neenawtooma served as the war chief for each group. Women also served as leaders of each Shawnee group. The hokima wiikwes, or “chief women,” were in charge of all agricultural decisions, harvest rituals, and were consulted by the hokima and neenawtooma on matters of peace and war. The Shawnee were a patrilineal society. Members of the tribe belonged to their father’s clan.

title: The Wyandot
text:
The Wyandot tribe, which was originally known as the Wendat, was formed in 1650 when three nations, the Tionontati, Wenrohronon, and Attignawantan, joined together. These tribes originally lived in Canada but moved south to Ohio to escape conflict with other tribes in the area. Men were responsible for hunting and protecting the members of the tribe. Women were responsible for growing, harvesting, and cooking food.

The Wyandot controlled a large portion of northwest Ohio. They had three primary villages that they inhabited on the Scioto River. Each village was surrounded by walls to protect the tribe. The Wyandot lived in longhouses, which were wooden dwellings covered in bark and animal hides. Multiple families lived in each longhouse. Like the Delaware tribe, the Wyandot had a matrilineal society. The Wyandot engaged in trade with tribes in the area, including the Shawnee and the Delaware tribes.

title: Cooperation, Conflict, and Compromise Among the Tribes
text:
The American Indian tribes of Ohio interacted with one another in many different ways. There was cooperation, conflict, and compromise between the tribes. Cooperation is the process of working together to achieve a common goal or resolution. Conflict is a disagreement between groups and individuals. Compromise occurs when multiple parties meet, discuss different solutions, and decide which solution is best as a group. In a compromise, both sides give up something they want in order to reach a solution.

Cooperation

Cooperation came in many forms between the tribes of Ohio. Tribes created agreements and alliances to obtain resources and protect the members of their tribe. An alliance is a relationship in which people, groups, or countries agree to work together. Marriages were arranged to link the tribes and create peaceful alliances. The tribes of Ohio also created verbal treaties to reach agreements. A treaty is a formal agreement between nations. Treaties were often created to form alliances between tribes with a common enemy. For example, the Delaware and Shawnee tribes became allies of one another through a verbal treaty in the 1700s.

Conflict

The Iroquois, who inhabited many areas in what is now the United States, fought with several tribes for control of the land. As a result, the Wyandot and Ottawa left their ancestral homelands and migrated to Ohio. The Wyandot and Seneca tribes were enemies of one another long before the two tribes migrated to Ohio. Hostilities between the tribes began when a Wyandot man wished to marry a woman from the Seneca tribe, but she refused. The tribes went to war against each other for over 100 years over the issue. Both tribes suffered many losses and the Wyandot population was almost completely destroyed. It would take many years for the populations of both tribes to recover. The Shawnee, one of the oldest tribes of Ohio, were forced to move to southern Ohio when the people of the Iroquois tribe claimed the Shawnee ancestral homeland as their own.

Compromise

Tribal leaders often compromised with one another to meet the needs and wants of their people. After more than 100 years of fighting and hostilities, the Seneca agreed to let the Wyandot settle in Ohio in exchange for peaceful relations between the tribes. The Wyandot agreed to let the Delaware tribe settle in eastern Ohio in exchange for goods and a military alliance against the Wyandot’s enemies.

title: Essential Question
text: How do different types of resources affect an economy?

title: Natural Resources
text:
A natural resource is something found in nature that people can use. There are many types of natural resources in the world around us. These include soil, plants, coal, water, natural gas, and even animals. We use natural resources to meet our needs and wants. Sometimes, we use natural resources just as they are. For example, we use water for drinking, cooking, and cleaning. We

also eat fruits and vegetables that grow naturally in our environment. We use some natural resources to make products that make our lives easier.

North America is considered one of the leading producers in the mining and use of coal. Coal mines are found in the Appalachian area of the United States and can be mined either underground or in large open pits. Coal is mostly used as a source of energy when burned. It provides power to heat our homes, schools, and businesses. We use trees to build furniture and houses. In the tropical region of South America, many high-value trees, such as mahogany and rosewood, are used for cabinets and floors. Chile, a country in South America, has tree plantations that give them the opportunity to produce wood chips, plywood, and paper pulp. We also use natural resources to make some of the items we use daily. This includes cell phones, computers, clothing, and even your toothbrush!

Natural resources can be either renewable or nonrenewable. Renewable resources are those that can be renewed, or replaced. Trees are an example of a renewable resource. This is because new trees can be planted to replace those we cut down. Even though renewable resources can be replaced, it’s important to use our resources wisely and not waste them. Nonrenewable resources are resources that cannot be easily replaced. Oil and natural gas are two examples of nonrenewable resources. It took millions of years to form these resources. Once we use them all up, they’re gone forever. It’s important to learn to conserve, protect, and use our natural resources wisely. If we do, there will be enough of them in the future. Conserving our natural resources also helps us protect the environment.

title: Human Resources
text:
Human resources are the people who make up a business’s labor force. They are workers with specific skills. Human resources contribute their skills and ideas. Natural and human resources work together.

North American dry zones, such as the Southwest United States, Northern Mexico, and Prairie Provinces of Canada, along with the Pampas or flat grasslands, showcase how natural and human resources work together. These areas are best for livestock, such as cattle or sheep, due to their large masses of land and the ability of ranchers to move livestock around for grazing or feeding.

Cowboys or workers on the ranches ensure the livestock’s health is taken care of and maintained while herding or moving the livestock to protected areas away from predators or to more favorable lands for grazing. Brazil and the United States are some of the top countries in the world that have beef as one of their top products for sale.

Human resources give a country the capability to produce a product or deliver a service. It takes people to plant and harvest crops, dig ditches, and move water. Human resources are needed to repair cars, design new buildings, or teach a class. The jobs in your community often reflect the natural resources in your environment.

title: Capital Resources
text:
Capital resources are the tools we use to help us make other things. Capital resources include tools, buildings, machinery, or equipment. These items are human-made. This means they do not occur naturally in the environment. They have to be created before they can be used to build other things.

An example of this would be how the process used to make paper uses lots of capital resources. The saws and machines used to cut and deliver the trees are capital resources. The equipment that makes the paper is also a capital resource. The company uses trucks to deliver the finished paper to customers. The trucks, factories, and machines are all capital resources.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
The price of goods and services changes. Most of the time, the price of goods and services depends on supply and demand. Supply is the amount of product that is available. Economists look at several things when they study supply. They look at the product being sold. Next, they make note of who is selling it. Finally, they study the market for the product. Economists study changing prices for a product and how much it costs a company to make it.

Demand is the amount of product people actually want or need. When there is a greater demand for a product than producers can supply, a shortage occurs. A shortage usually means prices go up as people compete to buy a product. When there’s a greater supply of something than a demand for it, it’s called a surplus. A surplus usually means prices go down. Producers lower prices to boost sales.

title: Scarcity
text:
Scarcity is when there is not enough of something. Sometimes, scarcity can be a big problem. If food or water is scarce, it is hard for people to survive. When goods and services become scarce, families have to make choices about how to spend their money to meet their wants and needs.

The scarcity of a major resource can affect an economy. When an area doesn’t get enough rain, it can affect the economy. Without rain, farmers have a harder time growing crops. That means less food is produced for people to eat. Less rain can also affect tourism. People will be less likely to visit lakes and rivers if the water levels are low. As a result, there will be less money coming to gas stations, souvenir stores, and hotels near those bodies of water.

Many power plants depend on water. Less rain makes it harder for those places to produce electricity. Less electricity can cause power bills to go up. When supplies are scarce, people have to make difficult choices. They may have to give up something in order to get whatever is in scarce supply. Every choice has value to each person. The products a person gives up are an opportunity cost.

title: Resources
text:
A resource is material people can use. Things like food, air, and water are resources. Resources help us meet our needs and wants. People use three main types of resources in their daily lives. These are natural, human, and capital resources.

People depend on resources to survive. They need resources to produce goods. If a resource is limited, the production of a good could also become limited. For example, if the weather destroyed a citrus crop used to make orange juice, the cost of orange juice may go up. Also, the product supply for orange juice could be much smaller than usual. It’s important for people and communities to use resources wisely. This way, we make sure there will be enough for us to use in the future.

title: Ashlee's Lexile Measure Test
text: South Dakota has a state seal. A seal has words and pictures. It describes our state. Our state seal has mountains and a river with a boat. It has a farmer and a furnace. Why do you think each part was included?

After the Constitutional Convention, George Washington became the first president of the United States. The new government faced many challenges, including war debt and balancing the demands of manufacturing and agriculture. Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton created a plan to pay off the debt and strengthen the economy by establishing the Bank of the United States and promoting manufacturing. Hamilton's and Thomas Jefferson's differing opinions led to the formation of two political parties, the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans. The Alien and Sedition Acts, passed by Congress, challenged freedom of speech and the press, and were later repealed. In the 1800 election, Thomas Jefferson won over Aaron Burr after Alexander Hamilton endorsed Jefferson, leading to the first peaceful transfer of power. Jefferson later made the largest land purchase in US history.

title: Ryan Hickman
text:
Ryan James Hickman is a third grader who likes to recycle. He is a junior entrepreneur. When Ryan was three years old, he started to recycle. He and his dad took a bag of recyclables to recycle. He earned about five dollars. He has been recycling ever since.

Ryan is now eight. He recycles to help people, plants and animals. His neighbors, friends and family recycle with him. He now has schools and even country clubs that recycle with him. Ryan will go the country clubs and collect bottles. He puts all the bottles into his dads’ truck and brings them home. Then he and his family empty and sorts the bottles. They drive to the recycling center to drop off the bottles.

Ryan has recycled about 270,000 bottles and cans.

title: Water, Population, and Brazil
text:
Located in eastern South America with a border of the Atlantic Ocean and holding about 12 percent of the world’s freshwater resources, Brazil is becoming increasingly aware of the need for water for its country.

Brazil is the seventh-largest country in the world based on its population. São Paulo, its most populated city, has close to 11 million residents. Most of the citizens throughout Brazil live in megacities like São Paulo or Rio de Janeiro. These cities border the Atlantic coast and rely heavily on local river basins instead of the Amazon River. The Amazon River and the Amazon River Basin contain roughly 50 percent of Brazil’s water supply. However, only four percent of Brazil’s population uses the Amazon River. This leads to many water resources being unevenly distributed or given out across the country.

These megacities are now considered to have high water stress. They will be looked at by a variety of organizations to ensure Brazilian citizens will be given the resources to get water into their homes and cities.

title: Why Do Geographers Need Data?
text:
Geographers study the physical world and the people who live in it. One important source of information for geographers is data. Much of what they want to know can be measured. Those measurements can then be used to infer or gather information about the world and its inhabitants.

Data helps provide specific information about geography, such as patterns and trends in the use of water in an area. Geographers can then use the patterns and trends to draw conclusions about the subjects they study.

Geographers gather data in a variety of ways. When studying the physical world, they may rely on remote sensing technologies like global positioning systems (GPS) to gather data. Gathering physical samples also falls under this category. Gathering data when studying human geography can include statistics like population data or resource usage. However, it can also include information like surveying or observing people.

Geographers use other types of data to study the world by creating and analyzing maps, looking at statistics, and examining the collected information. Using geographic information systems (GIS) allows data to reveal interesting and useful relationships between humans and the physical world. Mapping census data using GIS can illuminate population trends and patterns.

Once geographers have gathered the information they need, they can then use their skills and knowledge to infer conclusions about the topic they are studying. This allows them to better understand the physical world and how humans impact and are impacted by it.

title: Population and Census Data
text:
Countries throughout the Western Hemisphere have a variety of ways they track and look at patterns and trends of their country’s population. One tool that helps people chart population growth and decline is the census. A census is a survey that measures how many people are living in a certain area. This type of data is considered a primary source for research.

The U.S. Census is the count of how many people live in the United States. A new census is conducted every 10 years. A list of questions called a survey is sent to every home. If the survey isn’t returned, a census worker visits the home. The survey asks for specific information about the people, such as their age and what they do for work. The U.S. Constitution requires a census. Regions grow or shrink in population, and this requires government officials like the House of Representatives to be changed and adjusted based on the population in an area. People can use census details in many ways, as it is made public. Private sectors or private businesses can make decisions for their companies based on the population size around them.

Canada also has a census, but they collect data for their census every five years from May through July. Their census data is mandated by law through their Constitution Act in 1867 and the Statistics Acts in 1985. This data is broken up into two parts, with 25 percent of Canadian households receiving a long questionnaire form and the rest of Canadian households receiving a short questionnaire. The goal is to provide a “statistical portrait” of the different demographics and social and economic characteristics throughout Canada. The process for data collection is very similar to the United States, as they send out the questionnaire first. If the form is not completed and returned, an official government worker is sent to that home to help the people fill out their survey. Canada uses their data to realign or adjust their boundary lines for electoral districts, help transfer different forms of payments between levels of government, and help plan community services. These services include things like schools or emergency services. They also give private sectors ways to support decisions for their businesses.

Peru, which is located in South America, completes their census data every 10 years, just like the United States. The importance of census data in Peru is to see the changing patterns of population within the urban and rural areas. Peru utilizes the data to look at the basic characteristics of housing and the services the people need. The government creates a database to help with the evaluation and monitoring of its public policies and administration resources for the economy.

title: Organizations for Water Scarcity
text:
Organizations around the world are working to come up with ways to help countries have better resources to provide people with safe and clean drinking water. The United Nations (UN), an organization currently made up of 193 countries, protects human rights and gives assistance to countries in need. The UN has created and set up development goals for the year 2030 to maintain a better future for all. UN members have been working to help address water issues by helping countries figure out ways to access safe drinking water.

Another organization that has helped in the aid of water and ensuring countries have drinking water is WaterAid. Starting in Central and South America in 2011, WaterAid worked to help get water and improved hygiene to different parts of the North Caribbean region. In their 2021 annual report, 2,000 people in Colombia gained access to clean water, with 33 communities in Nicaragua helping to create a platform through the arts and social media on healthy water and hygiene habits.

title: Using Data
text:
A line plot shows the increase or decrease of something over time. An example would be the population in different countries over time.

A bar graph compares different sets of data between different groups. Geographers can use this when they compare the data, such as comparing different city populations in the United States to each other.

A table chart showcases data in columns and rows. This allows geographers to label each of the columns and rows to describe the information they are presenting.

A circle graph is another method used by geographers to display information about a country. Circle graphs show the total number of things counted, while the slices show parts of the total. The larger the slice, the greater the number. The smaller the slice, the smaller the number.

title: Protecting Our Rights
text:
The Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights are all founding documents of the United States of America. These documents were written not only for the people in the past but for us today. The Founders created these documents to explain the rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

Rights are freedoms that every person has. Rights include the privilege to believe, say, and make decisions as an individual in your community, state, or country. In the United States, you have the right to live. You have the freedom to think, speak, and make decisions. You have the freedom to make choices to do the things that make you happy.

These documents also explain the role of our government. Our government is a constitutional republic. A constitutional republic is a state where the chief executive and representatives are elected and the rules are set down in a written constitution. It is designed to protect our rights. The people are the ones who make important decisions. They choose their leaders. People make these decisions by voting. For the government to work, everyone’s voice should be heard. We all have to play our part in making decisions.

title: Monarchies
text: A monarchy is one of the oldest kinds of government. A monarch is a person who is in charge of the government. A monarch’s authority comes from family inheritance. This means the role of the monarch usually stays in the same family when the monarch dies. Monarchs are responsible for the safety, security, and welfare of their people. The people are considered subjects of the monarch, not citizens.

title: In God We Trust
text:
“In God We Trust” is the national motto of the United States. This phrase has been used throughout American history. In 1864, the phrase “In God We Trust” was used during the Civil War on coins to unify the country. Samuel P. Chase was the secretary of the treasury in the 1860s. He received many requests that “In God We Trust '' be added to the country’s two-cent coin. These requests stated that the motto would be a reminder of the country's original desire to be free.

The motto is even found in the national anthem. In the final verse of the song “The Star-Spangled Banner,” written in 1814 by Frances Scott Key, it says: “And this be our motto: In God is our trust.”

Congress adopted the national motto in 1956, and it is still used on our money today.

title: Bald Eagle
text:
The bald eagle is the United States national bird and a symbol of the United States. The bald eagle has been used since ancient times as a symbol of strength. Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, and John Adams were tasked with creating a new symbol for the new nation. Many suggestions were given to the three men for a new design. Congress didn’t like any of their attempts. Charles Thomson was given the task to take all of the ideas and create a symbol. Thomson took the suggestion of an eagle and added it to the design. Congress approved a design for the new seal on June 20, 1782, which included the bald eagle. Since then, the bald eagle has become a symbol of freedom and strength for the United States.

Bald eagles are found only in North America and are free to soar through the skies, which was a great symbol for the United States as a country that had just fought for freedom from England. Today, bald eagles are protected by federal laws. These laws ensure that bald eagles can live safely in the wild.

title: Volunteering
text:
Citizens who want to give something back to the community can volunteer, or donate their time to help others. Many people volunteer because they want to help others in need. There are many ways you can volunteer in your community.

People can volunteer for drives. Different types of drives collect things for people in need. Some volunteers help with community clean ups. Other volunteers serve in community fire departments and neighborhood watch programs. The list of volunteer jobs is very long. If you want to give back to your community, find out about where you could volunteer. Someone will really appreciate your help!

title: Trans-Saharan Caravan Trade
text:
Trade was extremely important during the medieval period, just as it still is today. Caravans from all over northern Africa and the Mediterranean traveled across the Sahara Desert to the city of Timbuktu. Here they traded gold, ivory, salt, dyes, copper, iron, ceramics, gems, grain, glass, weapons, textiles, enslaved people, and more. Different regions had goods to trade with that people from other regions wanted and needed. For example, rock salt was mined in abundance in the Sahara Desert region, but the landscape was so harsh that food could not be grown there. In the grasslands to the south, farming and agriculture thrived, but salt was nowhere to be found. These two areas relied on trade with one another to get the goods they needed.

Trade goods were not the only things that were exchanged, though. Ideas, architecture, art, religion, and more made their way to new places along trans-Saharan trade routes. For example, Arab traders who traveled across the Sahara Desert were among the first to bring Islam to West Africa. Scholars, artists, and architects each made their way to Mali, where they introduced new art styles, architecture, literature, and religious knowledge.

For North African traders, traveling across the Sahara Desert was no easy feat. There were no cars, roads, GPS, gas stations, or cell phones to help people navigate or call for help if they got lost. A journey across the Sahara took between 40 and 60 days. Caravans usually set out in the winter season, since it would be cooler. They traveled in the morning and late afternoon, stopping to rest during the hottest part of the day. Stops had to be made at oases along the way for water. There was always the chance that an oasis had no water or wells had dried up. Venomous snakes, scorpions, bandits, and sandstorms were all hazards of traveling in the desert.

Camels were the main mode of transport across the desert by the fifth century C.E. They were sturdier than horses or donkeys, better built for the desert, could carry more weight, and could go longer without water. Caravans had an average of about 500 camels, but some caravans that traveled once a year could have as many as 12,000 camels.

Experienced trans-Saharan travelers collected and passed down their knowledge on how to travel through and survive in the desert. Exact routes through the desert were carefully mapped and followed to avoid getting lost or missing the much-needed relief of oases along the way. Stars were used to navigate by night, and other methods of navigation were used during the day, such as the scent of the sand and vegetation, mountains on the horizon, wind direction, and more.

Without the knowledge and expertise of these caravan leaders, trans-Saharan trade wouldn’t have been possible. The people and goods they helped bring across the Sahara Desert never would have made it. West Africa would have been a much different place without it.

title: Djenné
text:
In the Middle Ages, rather than traveling all the way from one region to the other, it was common for people to travel to cities and towns at a halfway point to trade for goods. In Mali, cities such as Djenné and Timbuktu served as large and important trade centers for people of the north and south of western Africa. These trading centers were located along the Niger River and trans-Saharan land routes helped them to grow into major trade centers. Wealth and knowledge grew in both cities, and both thrived as destinations for caravans, merchants, and scholars. Both cities were well known as centers of learning and study for Islam.

In the West African kingdom of Mali, the city of Djenné rose to prominence as a wealthy city during the medieval period. Before the city of Djenné, the nearby settlement of Djenné-Djenno was established around the year 250 B.C.E. The settlement rested on a floodplain that was good for farming and agriculture. In addition, Djenné-Djenno also sat at a crossroads of the Niger River and trans-Saharan overland trade routes. This made Djenne-Djenno a hub for trade between the northern desert and southern forests of West Africa. It became such a successful city that its population grew to 20,000 at its peak.

However, by the 800s C.E., Djenné-Djenno began to decline. Eventually, it was replaced by the medieval city of Djenné a mere two miles away. By the 1300s, Djenné-Djenno had been virtually abandoned and Djenné, founded by Muslim traders, had become the new hub for trade and agriculture. Islam had been the main religion in Mali for hundreds of years by this point, and in the 1300s, the people of Djenné built an enormous, mud-brick mosque within the city.

Not many sources survive to tell us what Djenné was like during the medieval period, but oral tradition suggests that it was a thriving and important city in its day. Oral tradition is when people pass on knowledge, beliefs, or history from generation to generation through the spoken word. Many African societies used oral tradition to preserve history. This was the case for the Mali Empire until Islam’s influence led to the creation of written histories, preserved in libraries.

title: Timbuktu
text:
Almost 200 miles to the northeast of Djenné, the city of Timbuktu became the next major hub of trade and learning in medieval West Africa. The city started in the 1100s as a camp for African nomads, or people who traveled from place to place. Like Djenné, Timbuktu was established on a spot where land and river routes crossed. As Mali grew to become a rich African kingdom, Timbuktu became an important city for trade and learning. Timbuktu saw more traffic and wealth than Djenné because its location on multiple trade routes allowed goods to be traded between the east and west, as well as the north and south of northern Africa.

Timbuktu had walls built around it to protect its inhabitants from enemy raids and invasions. Large warehouses were built to store trade goods between destinations, and merchants lived in apartments within the warehouses. An architect from Cairo was even hired to build a large mosque in the city, and a royal palace was also constructed, even though Timbuktu was not the capital of the Mali Empire.

Time and erosion have caused many of the original buildings in both Timbuktu and Djenné to crumble and be lost, but some of the buildings, particularly the mosques, have been preserved or rebuilt by the people living there. Both cities have been listed as UNESCO heritage sites and are world-famous today.

The Mali Empire’s wealthiest ruler, Mansa Musa I, helped make Timbuktu even more prominent by building universities and mosques there. He also brought back books from his travels, recruited learned scholars from places like Egypt and the Middle East, and sent scholars to other countries to acquire more knowledge and return to Mali as teachers. Because of this, many scholars, artists, and members of the Muslim religion were drawn to Timbuktu, making it a major center of trade, culture, and learning.

Timbuktu had several universities with large libraries. Students learned and trained at the universities in Islam. They also studied subjects such as medicine, astrology, history, and more. In addition to Islamic studies, Timbuktu was also famous for its doctors and their knowledge of medicine.

A 19th-century explorer named Félix Dubois described the learning in Timbuktu by writing: “The scholars of Timbuctoo yielded in nothing to the saints and their miracles. During their sojourns in the foreign universities of Fez, Tunis, and Cairo, 'they astounded the most learned men of Islam by their erudition.’” Some scholars who went to Timbuktu hoping to be teachers ended up discovering they still had much to learn.

title: Pilgrimage to Mecca
text:
Look at a map of Saudi Arabia and find the city of Mecca, the birthplace of the Islamic prophet Muhammed. Muslims consider Mecca the holiest city in the Islamic religion. It is in Mecca where Muslims find their most sacred shrine or religious structure. They call the shrine the “Ka’aba,” which is a square building housing a black stone. People also call it the “House of God.” Muslims believe that the biblical prophet Abraham and his son, Ishmael, built the Ka’aba. Wherever a Muslim lives in the world, he or she faces the direction of Mecca and the Ka’aba while they recite their five daily prayers.

All Muslims try to visit the Ka’aba at some time in their lives. Muslims call the holy trip that they take to Mecca a “hajj,” or pilgrimage. Approximately two to three million people complete the hajj each year. The hajj doesn’t stop once a Muslim reaches Mecca, however. Once in the holy city, the hajj lasts for five days, during which each person completes several rituals and ceremonies, such as walking around the Ka’aba seven times, praying and meditating from noon to sunset on Mount Arafat, and making sacrificial offerings.

title: The Malian King Mansa Musa
text:
Sometimes described as the richest man in history, Mansa Musa took the throne of the already thriving Empire of Mali in 1312 C.E. During his reign, Mansa Musa built ancient Mali into one of the richest empires in the world and made Timbuktu a great city of trade and learning.

After assuming the throne, rather than try to rule and control the entire empire directly, Mansa Musa divided the empire into provinces. Then he appointed governors to rule over them. These leaders were responsible for their province and reported back to Mansa Musa.

Mansa Musa strongly believed in education and built schools throughout his empire. He also built libraries and collected books from all over the region. Mansa Musa also built mosques, or places of worship, all over Mali in which he and his people could practice the Islamic faith. As a Muslim, Mansa Musa also went on a pilgrimage, or holy trip, to the Islamic city of Mecca between 1324 and 1325 C.E.

In addition to fulfilling his religious duty by going on pilgrimage, Mansa Musa also wanted to use the journey to put Mali on the map. He did this by displaying his empire’s wealth. Several accounts claim that Mansa Musa took between 8,000 and 60,000 people with him for the 2,700-mile journey. These people included enslaved people, servants, heralds, soldiers, civilians, his wife, and her 500 ladies in waiting. Mansa Musa brought enough provisions to feed and water all of the people and animals in his caravan. His caravan also included between 80 and 100 camels, each of which carried about 300 pounds of gold. Along the way to Mecca, Mansa Musa gave much of the gold away to the poor.

When he stopped in Cairo, Egypt, Mansa Musa and those in his company spent so much gold that the value of gold in Egypt dropped. Because there was so much gold in the market, the price of ordinary goods like bread and milk increased to the point that regular people could not afford them. It took many years after the visit for the value of gold to recover in Egypt.

Few people outside of Africa knew about Mansa Musa when he first became emperor of Mali. However, his pilgrimage to Mecca changed that. Mapmakers in the 1300s added the Kingdom of Mali to their maps. Another result of his travel was that European leaders learned of Mansa Musa and all of the gold. European rulers then became more interested in the African continent (and its gold).

title: The Slave Trade in Medieval Africa
text:
Slavery has existed in Africa since recorded history began. Some of the earliest records describing the capture, sale, and enslavement of people come from ancient Egypt. Before individual land ownership came into practice, wealth and power were determined by how much of a resource or product a person or country owned. Therefore, the more enslaved people a person or country owned to work the land, the more resources could be produced.

Enslaved people in ancient and medieval Africa were most often acquired by one group raiding another and taking people as prisoners of war. These people were then sold into slavery for goods that Arab traders brought with them on trade routes all over Africa. An Arab historian of the ninth century, Al-Ya'qubi, wrote about the slave trade in Africa: "They [the Arabs] export black slaves ... belonging to the tribes of Mira, Zaghawa, Maruwa and other black races who are near to them and whom they capture."

Contemporary explorers and historians, such as Ibn Battuta and al-Idrisi, also described how leaders of tribes and countries carried out raids on neighboring villages and countries to capture people to sell in the slave trade. Al-Idrisi noted: "The people of Lemlem are perpetually being invaded by their neighbors, who take them as slaves ... and carry them off to their own lands to sell them by the dozens to the merchants."

Some trade routes that enslaved people were taken on went to Egypt or Arabia. In these instances, the enslaved people were transported north by boat on the Nile or from ports on the Red Sea. In Southeast Africa, enslaved people were often sold in port cities, where they would then be transported to India.

title: Test
text:
When creating a map of an area, cartographers and geographers often divide places into regions. Regions are areas that are defined by certain characteristics, such as population, geography, economics, government, climate, or other features. Regions can also be organized by imaginary borders and cultural characteristics. This indicates not only a geographic location but also implies certain traditions, beliefs, and manners. Cultural regions include places like the “Deep South,” the Bible Belt, and the Jell-O Belt.

Physical geography is one of the most common ways land is divided into regions. Examples in the U.S. include the Rocky Mountains, the Great Plains, and the Great Lakes. Regions can have political boundaries, such as cities, states, countries, and continents. Regions can also be organized by systems of people, goods, and ideas. Some regions have earned nicknames from their economies, such as the Breadbasket, Silicon Valley, and the Rust Belt.

Regions can also be categorized by historical context. An example of this is the original 13 Colonies. The Colonies were organized into the Northern, Mid-Atlantic, and Southern regions. Regions can also be organized by imaginary borders and cultural characteristics, such as the “Deep South.” This indicates not only a geographic location but also implies certain traditions, beliefs, and manners.

During the early 1800s, the United States was divided into three regions: the North, the South, and the West. In the 1800s, an imaginary line called the Mason-Dixon Line divided the eastern side of the country into the North and the South. The Mason-Dixon Line was measured between 1763-1770 by British surveyors Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon. A surveyor is a person who examines land and makes maps of it.

The Mason-Dixon Line was a man-made line that marked the boundary between slave-holding states and states where enslavement was illegal. States north of the line had a more industrial economy with factories that produced manufactured goods. States south of the line had a more agricultural economy and used the fertile southern soil to grow food and cash crops. Today, the Mason-Dixon Line no longer exists, but the cultural and economic characteristics of each region live on.

The West is a region that was originally defined as everything west of the original 13 Colonies. Before settlers moved out west and began establishing cities and towns, King George III of England made the Proclamation Line of 1763. The proclamation stated that all land west of the Appalachian Mountains belonged to the Indigenous peoples already living there. English colonists were not allowed to settle past that boundary. At that time, land west of the Appalachian Mountains was called the “West” or the “frontier.” This line continued to shift over time as wars and changes in government affected westward expansion.

The “West” or the “American frontier” was commonly what people called the land beyond the westernmost European settlement. Settlement increased dramatically after the Louisiana Purchase nearly doubled the size of the U.S. in 1803, and the starting line for the American West continued to move as settlers expanded across the country. Today, the West is considered to be the states west of the meridian that runs through the middle of the United States.

title: Test 2
text:
When the colonists arrived at Plymouth, they did not have anyone to make the rules for them. There wasn't a government in place. They had to set up their own. Their government did a lot. It set a standard for much that would follow in later American government.

Other colonies had a royal charter or a proprietor. The Plymouth colonists created a self-governing system. They wrote their laws and followed them. Their goal was to make a “government of laws and not of men.” This meant that what mattered most in governing were the laws. Those elected were to enact and enforce the laws.

The early Code of 1636 was like a constitution. It outlined the powers of law makers and the duties of government officers. It also outlined a court system and who had authority to declare war. Early laws in Plymouth were about basic problems like land ownership and crime. As the colony grew, the society's needs grew. The laws began to cover things like highways and bridges, wages, and caring for the poor.

Not every part of the Plymouth colony's government was something later Americans would want to follow. The Puritan laws also covered what leaders considered living “a godly life.” There were laws about everything from drunkenness to swearing. There could even be laws about clothing. Leaders wanted to enforce the order, restraint, and simplicity they valued. One young woman, Mary Downing, wrote to her father about having to remove lace from her clothes. She said, “I wrote my mother for lace not out of any prodigal or proud mind, but … the elders with others entreated me to leave them off, for they gave great offense.”

The leaders did not feel they were forcing others to believe as they did. Instead, they felt they were warning away those who did not live Christianity in their way. Later they would make laws about religion. In 1657, leaders of the Plymouth Colony collected taxes in each town to support a town preacher. The government selected the preacher. People had to pay, whether they belonged to that religion or not. The same year, they passed laws banning citizens from having members of the Quaker religion in their homes. They also outlawed all Quaker meetings in Plymouth.

It was a challenge for the Plymouth leaders to create a new government. Later American leaders would take many good ideas from this early government. They would also learn important lessons about separating church and state.

title: Akramah Writes
text:
There are both positive and negative economic incentives. Positive incentives are gifts or rewards attached to a choice people make. As a third grader, it could be the time you get to play a video game when you finish a task quickly. It could also be a toy you get with a meal.

Businesses offer positive incentives to encourage people to buy their products. These incentives can be discounts or other offers. For example, a grocery store might offer a coupon for a product. The coupon reduces the price people pay for that item. Sometimes, shoppers get a gift for spending a certain amount of money in a store. These incentives encourage people to spend more.

Government also uses positive incentives. For example, in 2008, there was a recession. The economy slowed down. In order to boost the economy, the government gave families a stimulus check. This encouraged families to spend money. Also, in 2009, the government decided that some cars were not good for the environment. Government gave citizens who traded those old cars for new ones part of their money back. This encouraged people to buy new cars that were good for the environment.

Businesses also benefit from government’s positive incentives. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many businesses laid off their workers. This created a problem for the government. In 2020, the government tried to encourage businesses to keep their workers. That is why the Employment Retention Credit was created.

title: Tammy Duckworth, U.S. Senator
text:
Tammy Duckworth is a U.S. senator from Illinois. She is an Iraq War veteran. Tammy is also a Purple Heart recipient. This is an important military award. It is given to members of the armed forces.

Tammy Duckworth served in the Armed Forces for 23 years. She served in Iraq as a Blackhawk helicopter pilot. In 2004, her helicopter was hit by enemy fire. The helicopter crashed. Tammy lost her legs. She also lost partial use of her right arm. The accident, however, did not stop her desire to help others.

In 2016, Tammy Duckworth was elected to the U.S. Senate. Before, she represented her state in the U.S. House of Representatives. She served there for two terms.

In the U.S. House, Tammy represented working families. She worked to find better ways to create jobs for everyone.

In the U.S. Senate, Tammy works on solutions for our country. These include rebuilding the infrastructure of our country. She also works to help her state of Illinois. Tammy wants to protect people in her state from lead poisoning.

Tammy Duckworth has been recognized for her work and service. She shows her love for the people of our country. She continues to dedicate her life to helping others.

title: Ritchie Valens, a Rock Star!
text:
Ritchie Valens was a Mexican-American singer and songwriter. He was born on May 13, 1941. He grew up in Pacoima, California. Ritchie's original name was Richard Stephen Valenzuela.

From a young age, Ritchie loved music. He learned how to play various musical instruments. However, the guitar became his primary instrument. Ritchie was inspired by different types of music. They included Mexican music, R&B, and rock and roll.

At the age of 16, Ritchie joined his first band. It was called The Silhouettes. Together, they performed at local gigs. In one of their shows, Ritchie met a music producer. It was the summer of 1958. The music producer asked Ritchie to audition for him. Next, Ritchie recorded two of his most famous songs. These were “Donna” and “La Bamba.”

In 1959, Ritchie went on a concert tour. He traveled with other musicians around the country. Together, they did the Winter Dance Party Tour. After one of their shows, they had a problem. Their tour bus's heater had broken down. They decided to hire a small plane. The plane would take them to their next show. Sadly, the plane crashed shortly after takeoff. Ritchie Valens and all the passengers died on February 3, 1959.

Ritchie Valens was one of the first Hispanic American rock stars. He received many awards and honors after his death. Ritchie's music has been played all over the world. His music influenced the careers of many artists. It has also inspired many artists to pursue their dreams.

title: Ellen Ochoa, a NASA Astronaut
text:
Ellen Ochoa is a Hispanic American engineer. She grew up in La Mesa, California. From a young age, Ellen enjoyed math and science. While in college, Ellen studied physics and engineering. She also studied electrical engineering. Ellen finished her studies in 1985.

After graduation, Ellen Ochoa applied to work for NASA. NASA stands for National Aeronautics and Space Administration. NASA hired Ellen in 1988. There, she worked as a research engineer. Ellen made important contributions. Next, NASA selected her as an astronaut. Ellen had advanced skills in robotics. She was a valued member of the NASA team. Ellen flew in four space shuttle missions. Ellen has also served at Johnson Space Center. She served as one of their leaders. Ellen retired from NASA in 2018.

Ellen Ochoa continues to serve her country. She works with institutions to promote science and engineering. She has given more than 300 presentations about STEM. STEM stands for science, technology, engineering, and math education. Ellen believes STEM programs can help students in schools. Students can learn about science and engineering. They can learn how to solve problems using their knowledge. Students can become scientists and engineers.

Ellen is the first Hispanic American astronaut. She is an inspiration to young students. Through her work, she showed that anything is possible. When you study and work hard, you can be successful.

title: Marie Curie
text:
Marie Curie loved to learn, even as a little girl. She was a very curious girl. She wanted to be a scientist like her father. When she grew up she studied radioactivity, X-ray machines and magnetism.

Do you see the two words “radio” and “activity” in the word radioactivity? Do you see the word magnet in magnetism?

Marie was friends with the famous inventor, Albert Einstein. In 1911, she was the first female scientist to win the Nobel Prize.

title: Rosa Parks
text:
On Dec. 1, 1955, Rosa Parks was riding on a bus in Alabama when she was asked to give up her seat to a white man. African Americans were only allowed to sit in certain sections of the bus. And if the bus got full, they were to give up their seats to any white person who asked. Rosa was tired, and she believed it wasn't fair for her to be asked to stand so that a white person could sit. Rosa refused to give up her seat. Because of this, Rosa Parks was arrested.

After hearing of her brave actions, the Montgomery Improvement Association, led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., organized a boycott by all African American citizens against the city bus system. To boycott the buses meant that the African American citizens refused to ride the buses until the rules were changed. The boycott lasted 381 days before the Supreme Court ruled that the segregation (keeping African Americans and whites apart) of buses was unconstitutional.

Rosa Parks' act of bravery made others aware of the unfair treatment of African Americans and helped to get these unfair laws changed.

title: Albert Einstein
text:
Albert Einstein is one of the most famous scientists of the last 100 years. You might even have seen his picture on a poster or a T-shirt.

Albert Einstein discovered a lot about light, energy and matter. When Albert was a child, he loved to ask questions. One of the first things he wondered about was energy and how it worked.

title: Jackie Robinson
text: Jackie Robinson was born when African Americans did not have the same rights as other people. He was a great baseball player, but was not allowed to play on the same team as white players. As an adult, he became the first African American man to play professional baseball. Not everyone liked him playing, but he still tried his best. He won an award at the end of his first season with the Brooklyn Dodgers. He was a hero for reminding us that everyone should be allowed to play sports together.

title: Albert Einstein
text:
Little Albert Einstein was very special. Not only did he learn to play the violin before age 5, but he became the most famous scientist of modern time. Chances are that you have seen a picture of Einstein—you know, the happy-looking gentleman with frizzy hair. Perhaps you have even seen his great equation, E=MC2, and wondered what it meant. (Don’t worry. Most adults don’t understand it, either.)

Einstein was not afraid to ask questions. He wondered if Newton was right about space and time. His Theory of Relativity showed that Newton was not completely right about time and space. Basically, the Theory of Relativity showed that time and distance in the universe were different depending on where you stood.

That was just one of his revolutionary ideas that changed modern science. He came up with the idea that photons (particles of light) existed. He created the idea of energy and matter being related (his E=MC2 formula). He developed a system of counting and measuring atoms, a theory that light is both a particle and a wave, and many other great theories. Einstein even answered the question, “Why is the sky blue?”

When did he do all of this? Well, most of his great ideas came while he was working at a patent office in 1905. Einstein’s quest for knowledge about the universe inspired many more scientists to keep trying to answer those questions.

title: George Washington Carver
text:
George was born a slave in 1864 in Diamond Grove, Missouri, and was raised by his owners, Moses and Susan Carver. George's father had died in an accident soon after George was born, and his mother was kidnapped. When the slaves were freed in 1865, the Carvers continued to raise George and care for him. They taught him to read and write. And when he turned 11 years old, they sent him to a school for African American children in Neosho.

After George graduated from college, Booker T. Washington asked George to go to the Tuskegee Institute to teach school. The Tuskegee Institute is an agricultural college (a college that teaches people how to farm and care for animals) for African Americans. George moved to Alabama, where the school was located, and soon became head of the Tuskegee agricultural department.

Around 1914, George began doing research on the peanut. He figured out how to make more than 300 products from the peanut, including a milk substitute, face powder, printer's ink and soap. George Washington Carver is still remembered today for his research on peanuts.

George never married, but spent most of his money trying to help young African American students have the chance to go to school. He is a great example of someone who worked hard and overcame great odds to find success.

title: American Government
text: The United States Constitution establishes the conditions for government. It is the people who give authority to the United States government. The people are to be informed about the people they elect to office. The people are to be involved in letting their representatives know what they want. This is called civic responsibility. The representatives must decide what is good for the freedom and liberty of many people over what is good for a few. This is called common good. In the United States, the government is to work for the common good.

title: Week 5 Framing Question
text: How are fairness and equality different?

title: Essential Question
text: What are the natural resources of Pennsylvania and why are they valuable?

title: Three Branches of Government
text:
The Constitution says that the United States should have three branches, or divisions, of government. Each branch has its own structure. Each branch also has its own leaders and processes. The three branches of government are the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The three branches were designed to balance the power of each branch. This prevents one person or group of people from having all of the power to make decisions.

People in the executive and legislative branches are elected to office for different terms of service. The legislative branch includes the Senate. A senator serves six years. The second part of the legislative branch is the House of Representatives. A representative in the House serves for two years. The executive serves for four years. After each election, there is a peaceful transition to the newly elected members.

Elections are the best way for the people to be actively involved in the governing process. Once elected, the members of the government are to represent the people who elected them.

title: Essential Question
text: How can using a budget help people make responsible economic decisions?

title: Separation of Power
text: The three branches of government have limits on what they can do. This means the legislative, executive, and judicial branches have to work together for the common good. Each can influence laws and actions of the government. No single branch can make an independent decision that would affect the people. This separation of powers provides a means of sharing decision-making called checks and balances.

title: Voting and Elections
text:
In a constitutional republic, the people elect representatives to make decisions for them. The Constitution describes how we elect our leaders and representatives. It also defines their responsibilities.

At the national level, citizens elect the President of the United States. They also elect representatives to serve in the House of Representatives and in the Senate. State and local governments are modeled after the federal government.

Citizens who want to serve in government go through a campaign process. We call people running for office candidates. Each candidate shares what they believe about different issues. Citizens review each candidate carefully. They choose the one who best represents their viewpoints or who they think will do a good job. On election day, citizens vote. The candidate with the most votes wins!

In order for a constitutional republic to work, citizens need to take an active role in making changes in local and national governments. Part of taking an active role means voting for elected officials and on important issues. Voting gives you a voice in government. To vote, citizens must be 18 years old or older. They also need to register, or sign up, to vote. Citizens vote for community, state, and national leaders.

title: Responsibility
text:
In a democratic government, it is the responsibility of the people to obey the laws. If people feel the law is not fair, they can change it through working with government officials. It is the responsibility of the people to have civic awareness.

Adults can be active by voting, running for office, obeying traffic laws, and paying taxes. Kids show their active involvement by respecting others in the community. Showing respect for property is another way to demonstrate civic responsibility.

title: Consequences for Disobedience
text:
There are consequences if the law isn't obeyed. The Constitution limits the actions against a person accused of breaking the law.

An accused person must be tried in a court of law. Twelve people from the community are selected. These people are called jurors. Jurors sit in court and listen to the facts. Lawyers explain how the law may have been broken. Juries decide if the accused is innocent or guilty of breaking the law.

A person returns to the community when found innocent. When guilty, the person has to accept the consequences.

This is an important part of our country's legal system. It can only work properly if responsible citizens participate in the process as jurors.

title: Consensus and Compromise
text: Consensus is when most people in a group have the same opinion or when they agree to the same solution. People often have different opinions about how to solve a problem. It's hard to agree on a solution. When we can’t agree, we have to compromise. When we compromise, we change our thinking about a solution. In a compromise, everyone gives up something to create a solution. When we compromise, we think about the common good, not just about what we want.

title: Engaged Citizens Make a Difference
text: The Constitution guarantees the right of the people to ask the government to change. Many people have protested unfair laws over the history of the country. Engaged citizens can change a law by going through the courts to show the unfairness of a law.

title: This is an article to test uploading audio.
text:
Seneca Oil

Three hundred million years ago, plants and water were trapped under the Allegheny Plateau while the Appalachian Mountains were being formed. Pressure and heat over time created coal, oil, and gas pockets. The oil would seep or leak through the ground along stream banks. This crude oil is golden-brown in color. There is a slight smell to it. As a sticky, gooey liquid, it floats on top of water. The oil could be skimmed or removed from the surface. The Seneca skimmed the oil into containers. The oil was used as a salve. That means it was used an ointment used as medicine. It was also used as a tonic, or healthy drink.

European settlers called the crude oil “Seneca Oil”. Settlers also used the oil as a salve or tonic. The settlers discovered the oil could burn. However, the smoke and obnoxious smell prevented further use as a fuel. The European settlers found the oil to be troublesome.

From the 1830s to the 1850s, many people experimented with Seneca Oil. Samuel Kier discovered the oil could be sued to make different products. It needed to be heated or refined. The most valuable product was kerosene. Kerosene was used in lamps. To make products like kerosene, producers had to find a more oil to meet the demand.

Drilling for Oil

In 1859, Colonel Edwin Drake and a banker, James Townsend, financed a drilling rig. Drake found William Smith, a blacksmith that worked for Samuel Kier. Known as “Uncle Billy”, Smith agreed to work the drilling engine and machinery. Drake was determined to drill for oil. Drake thought that oil had to be below the water in the ground. His plan was to drill past the water level into the oil pocket. Drake drilled a well near Oil Creek in Titusville, Pennsylvania. On Saturday, August 27, 1859, they hit oil. The great oil boom had begun. Within a year, more than 60 wells were drilled at Oil Creek.

The Oil Industry Begins

The area near Titusville and the Allegheny River Valley boomed with oil rigs and drilling crews. New people arrived making claims for oil. Pastures were filled with drilling equipment. Hillsides were covered in drilling huts. Towns were created overnight.

Other businesses were created because of the oil drillers. There were jobs that had never existed before. A refinery was needed to make kerosene. Barrels were needed to store the oil. Wagons and horses were needed for transport. Eventually, a railroad was built. It traveled to the most successful towns. Pipelines were used to transport oil from areas that were unreachable by roads. Iron tank cars were created to transport large quantities of oil.

Millions of dollars were made and lost in the rapidly growing economy. Eventually, one man emerged to create order. John D. Rockefeller organized Standard Oil Company in the 1870s. Standard Oil grew to dominate the oil business for the rest of Rockefeller's long life. Pennsylvania oil would transform the nation. It would keep the nation dependent upon oil for its energy needs.

title: Spread of Religion into Africa
text:
It is against Islamic law to force people to convert to Islam. However, in the medieval era Muslims were encouraged to be missionaries. Islam also spread in other ways, through trade and new exposure through conquest. Islam spread throughout Africa in all of these ways.
