title: Early Indian Cultures
text:
You may remember meeting Little Turtle from the time of the Archaic Indians. This week, we will look at two cultures that began during the Woodland Indian period: the Adena and Hopewell cultures.

Early Woodland Cultures

Have you ever heard anyone say, "Time marches on"? This means time never stops, and things are always changing. The Archaic Indian culture began to change as Little Turtle's children and his children's children found new ways to grow food, build homes, and bury their dead. One culture grew into another.

By 800 B.C.E., a new and more advanced culture called the Adena was living in the southern part of Ohio. They were in the places we now call Kentucky, Indiana, and West Virginia. At first, the Adena lived very much like Little Turtle's people lived. But as time passed, things began to change. They stopped moving around so much and lived in small villages. They grew more crops and found more uses for pottery. Their ideas and creativity were changing their culture.

Cultures Overlap

The Archaic culture started in 8,000 B.C.E. and went on until about 500 B.C.E. However, the Adena culture started about 800 B.C.E. For about 300 years, both cultures were in Ohio at the same time. How is that possible? Well, no one woke up one day and said, "It's 800 B.C.E., let's start a new culture!" Instead, culture usually changes very slowly, and everything doesn't change at once. Little Turtle's great-grandchildren might have found new ways to grow food, communicate, and create art. Slowly these new ideas spread to other people in other places. That's the way culture has grown and changed ever since people first appeared on Earth.

When archaeologists find evidence that a culture has changed in important ways, they give that culture a new name. That doesn't mean things changed everywhere all at once. Usually many of the things that had been going on continued to go on. For example, the Archaic Indians hunted and gathered their food. That continued with the Adena culture. But the Adena learned how to plant gardens as well. Planting gardens meant the Adena could stay in one place longer. They didn't quit making pottery. They just made it differently and found new uses for it. New ideas spread, and cultures grew and changed.

The growth of culture is amazing! As you go through Studies Weekly this year, you will find many examples of how cultures grow and change and how those changes affect the people in Ohio

title: The Archaic Indians
text:
When the ice age ended, the open space that the Paleo-Indians had lived in disappeared. The climate became warmer and more stable, and deciduous trees (trees that lose their leaves in the winter) started to grow. Soon, forests covered Ohio. As the environment changed, so did the culture. The Archaic Indians and their culture descended from the Paleo-Indians. The story below is about Little Turtle, a young member of the Glacial Kame Indians who lived at the end of the Archaic Indian period.

I am Little Turtle. It is summer, so my clan and I live near the big water they call Erie. Many clans have gathered here to hunt the fish that easily feed us all. When the days grow short, my family will travel to our camp in the forest so we can hunt deer and rabbits during the cold times. I have seen 10 winters, so I am old enough for my father to teach me how to use the atlatl. He has made a small one just for me. My atlatl has a hook made of bone from the deer we hunted a moon ago and a wooden shaft and handle so I can sling a spear at our prey. My family laughed at my first efforts. I was so ashamed that I practiced until I could throw the spear a long distance. I have been proud to add two rabbits to our family meal.

Our life in the warm times is good. We gather around the fire at night to share stories of the ancient ones after feasting on fish from the big water. It is said there were giant animals and no forests then. I cannot imagine such a time. The forest gives us all we need: animals, berries, and nuts to help us live through the winter. I feel sorry for my ancestors when I hear these stories.

My brother, who is four winters older than me, has learned how to make an ax from the stone we found in the valley. It is hard stone and good for cutting down trees and digging out the canoes we use to travel to other camps. He hopes to learn how to cut and polish this stone into pieces of art that show our hunters wearing the mask of the wolf. This will show respect to our great hunters. I will learn how to make real masks with the skull of the wolf and bear. I will learn to polish the skulls and make masks the great hunters will use. Maybe one day my brother will use stone to create the image of a hunter who wears a skull mask made by me.

Use any color to circle or highlight three relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that, etc.) in this week’s magazine. Underline the related noun.

title: The Adena Culture
text:
The Adena culture is the group of prehistoric people who lived in southern Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky, and Indiana during the very early Woodland Period, from 800 B.C.E to 1 C.E.

The Adena Culture Begins

The Adena culture began about 800 B.C.E. Their culture changed from hunting and gathering to a more settled way of life that included farming. In fact, they are called Ohio's first farmers. The Archaic Indians were already gathering and eating many of the seeds the Adena would use as crops they could depend upon for food.

The Adena lived in villages near their gardens. They grew sumpweed, goosefoot, knotweed, and maygrass in the wetlands. They also grew squash and sunflowers, just like their ancestors. The Adena are one of only seven groups of people in the world who turned local plants into a food-producing economy. This change would affect many cultures in years to come. The Adena still moved often since they continued to hunt or gather some of their food. This added variety to what they harvested from their gardens. They also traded for copper and shells as their ancestors did. The Adena ground their seeds and cooked them in large pots made of pottery to make something that was much like today's oatmeal.

The Adena people did not bury their dead in Glacial Kames as their Archaic ancestors did. Instead, they built mounds of earth for their dead. The largest Adena mound is the Miamisburg Mound, found in Montgomery County.

Where did the name "Adena" come from?

Adena is not actually the name of this tribe. We don't know what these ancient people actually called themselves. The name “Adena” is given to the people whose culture was different from any other culture in the area. The name actually comes from the name of the land owned by Ohio's sixth governor, Thomas Worthington. His land was known as the Adena Estate. A big mound on the land was called the Adena mound, and since that mound was such a good example of the culture, the name stuck!

Hopewell Culture

Between 100 B.C.E and 500 C.E., a cultural explosion took place. Things changed so much that archaeologists gave the culture a new name: the Hopewell Culture, also called the mound builders. They worked hard building very large mounds. They had to first dig tons of dirt and then carry thousands of baskets of the dirt to the mound. That's the way they built enclosures too. Enclosures are like dirt walls built all the way around a place (often a hill) where they held special ceremonies. The Hopewell are also known for making beautiful works of art from materials brought to Ohio from far-away places such as the Gulf of Mexico and the Rocky Mountains. They developed new styles of stone tools and pottery.

The largest group of enclosures built by the Hopewell culture is in Newark, Ohio. The enclosures are called the Newark Earthworks. This is our official State Prehistoric Monument. In Warren County, you will find the Fort Ancient Earthworks. It is the largest example of a hilltop enclosure. Finally, the largest group of Hopewell mounds is the Mound City group in Chillicothe. These places were not villages. They were special places for ceremonies and rituals, including the burial of honored dead.

Not all mounds were for burial. Some, like the Great Serpent Mound, were made in the shapes of animals. These are called effigy mounds. Mounds were also used as foundations for temples or even as platforms for other mounds. Many archaeologists believe the earthworks were places where different groups would gather with old friends from other groups for celebrations or ceremonies.

The Hopewell Culture Grew and Changed

The Hopewell people lived in small villages in the river valleys of southern Ohio. They grew crops, hunted in the forests, and fished like their Adena ancestors. The Hopewell people were the first people in Ohio to grow maize (corn). They began to use bows and arrows for hunting and in war.

Archaeologists think the Hopewell culture may have come to an end because of wars among the people living in that area. However, they may have also disappeared during epidemics of diseases or a cooling of the climate that made it very hard to grow the crops they needed.

Just like the Adena, the Hopewell culture is named after the person who owned the land where the Hopewell Mound Group was found: Mordecai C. Hopewell.

title: Who Were the Abolitionists?
text:
Many people in America opposed the enslavement of people. Most of the northern states had abolished, or legally ended, slavery by the early 1800s. However, slavery remained legal in all of the southern states.

Many people opposed abolition. They believed people from Africa were not equal to people from Europe. They believed in keeping people enslaved. The pro-slavery group had authority in making laws. Laws were made and enforced to keep Black people enslaved.

Pennsylvania was very active in protesting the laws that kept slavery legal. The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) believed in peace and equality of all people. The Quakers worked to end slavery and free all people. They even petitioned Congress to end slavery in 1790.

Philadelphia became home to the abolitionist movement. People organized and raised awareness of abolition with print, speeches, and actions.

William Lloyd Garrison started an anti-slavery newspaper called the Liberator. He published his beliefs about equality. He wanted African Americans to be granted every liberty and right promised to white Americans. He became a strong spokesperson for abolition.

Other abolitionists were African Americans who had escaped slavery. People like Sojourner Truth, Frederick Douglass, and William Wells Brown gave speeches to large audiences about their lives and experiences. This endangered them because they were exposing their status as runaways. They could have been captured and forced to return to their former lives.

When people disobey a law, there are consequences. Knowingly going against a law in protest is called civil disobedience. The abolitionist movement practiced civil disobedience. Breaking the law can have dangerous consequences. Law-abiding people willingly broke the law to help enslaved men, women, and children to escape to freedom.

title: Culture Clash
text:
In the 1700s, cultures in Ohio were about to collide, with consequences that are still felt today. Usually, one culture grows out of another, with many things staying the same and just a few things changing slowly. What happened in Ohio was something totally different, and it happened all over the country.

As the eastern colonies began to grow and prosper, many American Indians were pushed westward. When the colonists won the Revolutionary War, the American Indians who had fought on the side of the British had to leave the newly formed states. Soon those states got crowded, and settlers started moving west, pushing the American Indians even further west. The settlers had begun a westward movement that would last more than 100 years and would only end when they reached the Pacific Ocean. But for now, let's talk about what happened in Ohio.

Many settlers learned how to farm from the American Indians. They learned how to grow crops like corn, sweet potatoes, and pumpkins. Ohioans still grow and eat many of those same crops. Some Ohio Indian tribes adopted many of the settlers’ ways to try and fit in. Others didn't want to change and fought against it. But it was coming anyway. Like the eagle, peregrine falcon, and bison, the Ohio Indians were about to find their lives changed forever. The European settlers had arrived, and nothing would ever be the same.

title: Week 19 Framing Question
text: What was the experience of African Americans like during the era of enslavement?

title: Shawnee and Miami Indians
text:
The Shawnee

The Shawnee moved to the southern Ohio Valley in the late 1600s because it was a rich hunting ground. The powerful Iroquois drove them out for a short time, but the Shawnee returned. They became great warriors and were feared and respected by other American Indians.

Different Roles for Men and Women

Shawnee men were skilled hunters and warriors. After a hunt, they sat around the fire and had long talks. Women and children enjoyed sitting around the fire with them and listening to stories about all the exciting things they had done.

While the men hunted in the forests and fought in battles, the women of the tribe had a lot of work to do. They built the homes, prepared the meat caught by the men, planted and harvested the crops, and scraped and tanned the animal hides. They used the hides to make clothing, shoes, pouches, knife sheaths, and other things they needed. Women also made blankets and wove baskets. They used clay gathered from creeks to make plates, pots, and cups. It was the women's job to mix herbs as medicine to take care of members of the tribe who got sick. Did you ever hear that blueberry root tea is good for treating the hiccups? That's an old Shawnee cure!

Everyday Life

Shawnee families lived in small, round homes called wigwams made of wood and covered with bark. They built their homes around a large Council House in the plaza for meetings and ceremonies. Fields of corn were planted outside a tall, wooden fence (called a palisade) that helped protect the village from their enemies.

The Shawnee culture revolved around the clans, farming, and war. Ceremonies like the Green Corn Dance celebrated their skill as farmers. They grew squash, maize, sunflowers, and pumpkins in their fields. The women ground corn between two rocks to make corn meal for corn fritters.

The Miami Indians

The Miami Indians moved into the Maumee Valley around 1700. Here they settled around the Great Lakes and the rivers of northern Ohio, where there was rich farmland and good hunting. They became the most powerful tribe in Ohio. The word "Miami" means "mother" in their language.

Different Roles for Men and Women

The men of the Miami tribe were hunters but would also go to war when necessary. Only a man could be a main chief at that time, and being the chief was hereditary. That means when a chief died, his oldest son took his place. The war chief was a different chief, and he was chosen because of his skill.

The women took care of the children, the farming, and the cooking. They also made peace treaties and were in charge of religious festivals. Both men and women told stories, created art and music, and learned about herbs and medicine.

Everyday Life

Miami villages were a lot like the Shawnee villages of the time. Round wigwams were built around a plaza and cornfields surrounded the village. The Miami Indians, like others then in Ohio, made dugout canoes by hollowing out big trees. To travel on land, the Miami used dogs to carry packs or pull a wooden sled called a travois. The Miami people grew corn, beans, and squash and made cornbread, soups, and stews.

Like the Shawnee, they were divided into clans. Members of one clan could not marry a member of the same clan, since they were considered family. The Miami named most clans after an animal, including Wolf, Eagle, Buzzard, and Panther. The Miami loved to play games. Sometimes gambling games were played between different villages. Women sometimes played a gambling game called the "Bowl Game" for days on end!

title: The Underground Railroad
text:
When a person was enslaved for life, the only way for them to gain freedom was through escape. In the North, owning another person was illegal. To an enslaved person, the trip to the North could be as short as 10 miles or as long as 110 miles. They had never seen a map. They only knew that “north” meant freedom. Staying put offered no freedom. Getting caught as a runaway meant severe punishment. The punishment was meant to scare other enslaved people by showing them what would happen if they ran away.

To make the trip north, a runaway needed help. They needed people to guide them across unfamiliar land. There were people along the way who would hide and feed them. Abolitionists knew how to help, even though they knew that helping an enslaved person escape was against the law. The consequences for helping an enslaved person escape were severe. Farms were burned, people were injured, and some were arrested. These consequences did not stop the abolitionists.

A system of secret codes, paths, and hideaways was created. The paths, or tracks, would be hidden from the public eye. There would be people to act as guides along the tracks, like conductors on a railroad. The escaping people were the passengers. They were given food, clothing, and supplies to help them make it to the next part of the trip. The passengers traveled at night. They traveled quietly and as quickly as they could. This is how the Underground Railroad was created and operated.

title: Harriet Tubman
text:
Araminta Harriet Ross was born into slavery in Bucktown, Maryland, in 1820. When she was a child, she was “hired out” to people. The people paid her enslaver for her work. She worked for several very cruel people, who injured her. These injuries bothered her for the rest of her life.

In 1844, she was allowed to marry a free man named John Tubman. When her enslaver died, she knew it was her chance for freedom. She ran north. She had no plan, and the journey was terrifying and difficult. She used different stations on the Underground Railroad. She had no conductor between stations. She traveled alone and made the 90-mile journey to Philadelphia. Harriet Tubman said about realizing she was in Philadelphia:

When I found I had crossed that line, I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees, and over the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaven.

In Philadelphia, she met a man named William Still. He was a clerk and janitor for the Pennsylvania Society for the Abolition of Slavery. He introduced her to many people connected to the Underground Railroad. Tubman didn’t stay in the safety of Philadelphia for long. She became a conductor on the Underground Railroad.

Tubman often made daring trips along the Underground Railroad and helped many people escape from slavery. She was called “Moses” by many for leading people to freedom. She was one of the most successful “conductors” on the Underground Railroad.

title: The Ottawa and Mingo Indians
text:
This week we're looking at more things the historic Ohio Indians had in common and some things that set the Ottawa and Mingo apart.

Ohio: 1750

By 1750, two more bands of American Indians had arrived in Ohio. The Mingo (also called the Ohio Seneca) had been forced out of their New York homelands by English colonists. For a while they lived in Eastern Ohio, around the area we know as Steubenville. Then they moved into Central Ohio and settled along the Scioto River. The Ottawa Indians came from Canada and Michigan, settling in Northern Ohio near Lake Erie. They came to Ohio to be part of the fur trade, first with the French and later with the British.

In the middle of the 18th century, at least six bands of American Indians, including the Shawnee, Miami, Wyandot, Delaware, Mingo, and Ottawa, called Ohio home. They still sometimes moved from place to place to find game or to trade. All of them used canoes to travel on the rivers and streams. They used dogs as pack animals, tying bundles onto their backs or having them pull sleds called travois. Many of the bands, especially those in the northern areas where winters meant deep snow, made snowshoes from curved wood laced with deerskin.

All of the Ohio Indians relied on animal skins, mostly deerskin, to make clothes and shoes. In the winter, many Ohio Indian women made and wore robes of rabbit fur to keep warm. Women and girls also wove baskets and made clay pots for carrying food and water. By this time, all Ohio Indians were getting used to having to pack up and move. Baskets and pots helped them do that quickly. Men made stone points for spears and arrows and large stone blades to serve as knives or be tied to a wooden handle as a tomahawk. For fishing, they used spears, hooks made of bone or bird claws, and nets made of brush.

Ohio Indian children learned to do the things their parents did. Girls worked and learned with the women of the band. Once they were old enough, boys worked and learned with the men. Most boys played lacrosse and enjoyed games of strength and skill. That's how they learned to be hunters and warriors. Girls played with cornhusk dolls and pretended to do the same work their mothers did. As they played, they were really learning how to plant, harvest, cook, and take care of children.

What's the Difference?

Now you know even more things the historic Ohio Indians have in common. What made the Mingo and the Ottawa different? What set them apart from the other tribes in our state?

Let's start with the Ottawa. They were amazing traders. In fact, they could be called the real businesspeople of the Algonquian nations. They traded over long distances, using birchbark canoes and the river systems around the Great Lakes. When they met the first French traders, they knew a good business opportunity when they saw one! The French wanted furs; the Ottawa knew how to get them. In Europe, using beaver furs to make coats, hats, and other clothing was very popular. They couldn't get enough! When British traders came to Ohio, the Ottawa saw a new opportunity. What they didn't realize was that the British didn't just want furs; the British had come to Ohio to stay.

Ottawa men wore very little during the wintertime to prove how tough they were. All men in the tribe were expected to jump into the river or lake for 10 days in a row in the early spring to make them strong and to condition them for hardship. All Ottawa lived by the 21 Precepts, or rules to live by, that date back far into their history.

What about the Mingo? The Mingo were not really just one tribe. They were a group of different Iroquois bands that lived and worked together. The Mingo knew how to steam wood to make curved tools like bows. The men sometimes cut their hair into a Mohawk, but women only cut their hair when someone died. The Mingo sometimes wore painted masks over their faces because they believed the masks would frighten away evil spirits.

The Mingo had a tribal council chosen by the "clan mothers." But the Mingo council always had to answer to the Iroquois Great Council: eight chiefs who looked out for the interest of all Iroquois people. This is similar to our own government. Each state has its own separate government, but the U.S. government looks out for all U.S. citizens and has the final say. The Founding Fathers used the Iroquois system of government as a model when they wrote the Constitution and decided how the new U.S. government would work.

title: Sojourner Truth
text:
In 1791, Isabella Baumfree was born into slavery. A Dutch family in New York owned her. As a woman enslaved by many different owners, Baumfree had a hard life. When her owner would not obey the law that ended slavery in 1827 in New York, she ran away. She was helped by a Quaker family. This family encouraged her to speak about her life as an enslaved woman.

Many people were interested in her story. She was a tall woman with a strong voice. She spoke with energy and confidence. People were inspired by her talks about ending slavery in America. She also began speaking for women to have more rights in the law. Baumfree changed her name in her new life. She became Sojourner Truth. This new name had great meaning. “Sojourner” means “one who journeys (travels), declaring truth to those who would listen.”

Sojourner Truth challenged people’s ideas that women and enslaved people were weak. She demonstrated strength and showed that both causes, the rights of women and the freedom of African Americans, were important.

title: Frederick Douglass
text:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in 1818. His mother was an enslaved woman on a plantation in Maryland. He never knew his father. As a young boy, his enslavers sent him to their relatives in Baltimore. The lady of the house taught him the alphabet and easy words. Teaching enslaved people to read and write was illegal at that time. Despite this, Douglass continued to learn to read in secret.

As a teenager, Douglass was sent to a plantation to work in the fields. Life on the plantation was cruel, and Douglass attempted to run away. He was caught and punished severely. Finally, when he was 20 years old, he successfully ran away and lived freely in Massachusetts. He became involved with an abolitionist group to stop slavery. He continued to educate himself.

Douglass was very good at public speaking. People liked to listen to him, and they were interested in his story. He spoke about the cruelty of slavery. He spoke about ending the practice of keeping people as property.

Douglass became a speaker for the American Anti-Slavery Society. He was such a successful speaker that he became famous. He always spoke for the people who were enslaved, and he worked hard his entire life for African Americans to have equal rights.

title: What is Wampum?
text: When you go to the store to buy something, what do you use? Money, right? American Indians had a kind of money too, but if you saw it, you might think it was just a decoration. Wampum wasn't used as money at first. The word “wampum” actually means "white shell beads." The beads were made from large clamshells. The shells were made into beads that were then turned into belts, necklaces, and other ornaments with beautiful designs. Some designs told of past events of the tribe and were a record of the tribe's history. When the European settlers started to trade with the tribes, wampum became their form of money. It was so beautiful that it became the fashion for European kings and queens to wear. Tribes continued to use wampum for money until after the American Revolution. It is still made today by American Indians who live along the East Coast.

title: Wyandot and Delaware Indians
text:
The American Indians who lived in Ohio during the 18th century had many things in common with their prehistoric ancestors and with each other. But there were some differences, as well.

Imagine that you could go back in time almost 300 years. What would you have seen in Ohio then? All over the state, you would have seen American Indian villages. As you approached a village, the first thing you would have noticed would have been fields where corn and other crops grew. Beyond the fields, you may have seen a palisade, or a tall fence, built around the homes. Can you picture it in your mind? Inside the palisade, you would probably have seen a council house in the middle of a central plaza, with wigwams or longhouses arranged around it. If you looked closely at the buildings, you would see bark or animal hides stretched over wood frames.

As you looked around, you might see men returning from the hunt carrying deer or other small game. Those fields you passed? The women planted all of those crops, and they harvested them when the time was right. They cooked the food for every meal. Corn, beans, and squash, known as the Three Sisters, were the main crops grown in Ohio then. You might have seen Ohio Indian women using the Three Sisters and whatever meat the men had caught to make soups, stews, and cornbread. They may have added some herbs or other plants they gathered from the woodlands, while children played nearby. You may have seen fish drying on a rack and a pile of oyster shells leftover from other meals.

Why Ohio?

The historic Ohio Indians began arriving in our state in the late 1600s. The Miami and Shawnee came to Ohio for the rich farmland. The Wyandot and Delaware came to Ohio not long after the Shawnee and Miami, but they didn't come by choice. The Wyandot (also called the Huron) came from Canada and Michigan, driven south into Ohio by the Iroquois in the early 1700s. They settled in Northern Ohio, from the Great Lakes to the Cuyahoga River Valley. The Delaware Indians called themselves the Lenape or Lenni Lenape ("True People") and lived in the states we know as New Jersey, Delaware, New York, and Pennsylvania. As more settlers came from England, the Delaware had to move west. They ran into the Iroquois, who pushed them into Ohio at about the same time as the Wyandot arrived. Some Delaware settled in Eastern Ohio, along the Muskingum River, while others kept going into the northwestern area, near the Auglaize River.

What's the Difference?

If the Wyandot and Delaware had so much in common, then what was different? For one thing, the Wyandot formed alliances with the Shawnee, who called the Wyandot their uncles. The Delaware were called the Grandfathers by other Algonquin tribes because it is believed that they are one of the oldest tribes of the Algonquin people. (By the way, Algonquin is the name of the people. Algonquian is the name of their language.) The Wyandot nation included 12 family clans, while the Delaware were divided into three: the Turtle, Wolf, and Turkey clans. The Wyandot chief was a man, but the women got to choose which man would be chief. The Delaware chief always came from the Turtle clan and was always a man, but women were sometimes village leaders. The Delaware also had two medicine men. One healed the sick, and the other interpreted dreams.

title: Building a Nation
text:
Imagine that you have wood, nails, and shingles. You have bricks and cement. You even have tools like hammers and saws. What would you build? A house? A school? How about a country? The Founding Fathers didn’t build the United States of America out of bricks and wood, but they did build a new nation. How? Keep reading to find out!

Now imagine that you have land and people. You have homes and businesses and farms. You even have tools like paper and pens. Would you build a country? That’s what the Founding Fathers did!

Have you ever heard of Ben Franklin and Thomas Jefferson? What about George Washington, James Madison, and John Adams? They are some of the men we know today as the Founding Fathers. The Founding Fathers didn’t wake up on July 4, 1776, and say to each other, “Hey! Let’s build the United States of America!” So, how did they build a new nation? And why?

In the 1770s, the Founding Fathers lived in the American colonies. A colony is a place that is governed, or ruled, by a different country. The American colonies belonged to England, and King George was in charge.

When it came to running the colonies, King George only thought about one thing: making money! He needed lots of money to run his country and its colonies. And to get money, King George started asking the colonists to pay taxes. First, he came up with the Stamp Act. The Stamp Act added a tax to everything people in the colonies wrote, including letters, newspapers, and magazines. If they wrote it, King George taxed it. Then he started taxing things like molasses, tea, silk, coffee, and sugar.

The colonists were tired of being bullied by King George. Some of them formed a secret group called the Sons of Liberty. One day, in 1773, the Sons of Liberty dressed as American Indians and boarded a British ship in Boston Harbor. They dumped all of the tea on the ship right into the water! Now that was one big tea party, don’t you think? As a matter of fact, today we call it the Boston Tea Party.

Well, what do you think King George did to get back at the colonists? He bullied them some more. He told the colonists that their leaders weren’t in charge anymore and put his men in charge instead. He sent British soldiers to the colonies. He told the people that they had to feed his soldiers and let them live in their homes.

The colonists had had enough of King George and enough of England. In 1775, the Revolutionary War began. The war lasted eight years. Many soldiers fought and died. Their bravery and sacrifice made it possible for the Founding Fathers to start building our country.

In 1776, Thomas Jefferson took out his pen and paper and started writing. He wrote some very powerful words called the Declaration of Independence. It told the world the colonies were independent and free. It told King George that the colonists were no longer British citizens. The colonists were now Americans.

That’s how it started. The Founding Fathers used paper and pens to write more words. They wrote the Articles of Confederation and then the U.S. Constitution. Those simple tools, paper and pens, helped bring together the land, people, homes, and farms. In the hands of the Founding Fathers, paper and pens built the foundation of a new nation: the United States of America.

title: Independence May be the Only Answer
text:
The tension between Great Britain and the colonies kept growing. The Proclamation of 1763, the Quartering Act, and the Stamp Act had all angered the colonists. They believed Great Britain was not treating them fairly. The massacre in Boston brought the colonists closer together in their disagreements with the king and Parliament of Great Britain.

The Boston Tea Party

After the Boston Massacre, British leaders realized that something must be done to calm down the colonists. Parliament agreed to repeal, or cancel, all of the unpopular taxes the colonists had to pay. All except one, that is. They wanted to show the colonists they were still in control, so they put a tax on their favorite drink: tea. When they heard about the tea tax, many colonists refused to buy tea from Britain. This was bad news for the British East India Company, which made most of its money from tea sales. The company lost money quickly.

To save the company, Parliament passed the Tea Act in May 1773. This act made it nearly impossible for colonists to buy tea from any company other than the British East India Company. Of course, this act made the colonists angrier than ever. The price of tea went down, but they did not like being forced to buy tea from only one company. They were also worried that Great Britain might soon decide to pass other laws that limited where colonists could buy things.

Colonists protested, or spoke out against, the law. In Boston, the Sons of Liberty decided to take action against the British. On the night of December 16, 1773, Samuel Adams led a group of men dressed as American Indians. They stormed three ships sitting in the Boston Harbor. The men dumped 342 crates of tea into the harbor. The tea was ruined, which caused the British East India Company to lose a large amount of money. The colonists called the event “the Boston Tea Party." People in England were shocked at the colonists' behavior, and King George was very angry. Parliament began to think of a way to punish the colonists for dumping the tea.

The Intolerable Acts

Now the British thought most colonists were just troublemakers. The king passed new laws to punish the colonists and keep them under control. These laws were very harsh. Many colonists said they were so bad they could not stand them. They called these harsh new laws the Intolerable Acts. (Intolerable means unacceptable.) The British closed Boston Harbor in March 1774. Ships could not enter or leave Boston until the colonists agreed to pay for the tea that was destroyed. Many people lost their jobs at the harbor. They had a hard time paying for their homes and food. People in the other colonies agreed to help the people of Boston. Many of them sent money, food, and supplies to the city.

First Continental Congress

More and more colonists started thinking it was time to take action against Great Britain. They were tired of taxation without representation and wanted to protect their rights and liberty more than ever. In September 1774, 56 leaders from 12 colonies met in Philadelphia to talk about the problems with Great Britain. (Georgia did not send anyone to the meeting.)

John Adams, Patrick Henry, Samuel Adams, and George Washington were there. Most of the delegates wanted to make a peace agreement with Great Britain. But they also wanted Britain to know that an attack on one colony would be considered an attack on them all. The colonies were making the first step to band together against Great Britain.

The First Attacks: Lexington and Concord

After the First Continental Congress, colonists started organizing and training militia. These small armies of ordinary citizens were ready to take on the British if they attacked. Just after midnight on April 19, 1775, British soldiers marched from Boston to Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. The king had ordered British soldiers to arrest rebel leaders and seize (take away) their weapons. Boston silversmith Paul Revere rode to Lexington with the news that the British Army was on its way. About 60 militiamen faced hundreds of well-trained British soldiers. No one knows for sure who fired the first shot at Lexington, but many have called it "the shot heard 'round the world."

Later that same morning, nearly 1,000 colonial militiamen waited in nearby Concord for the British. At the end of the battle, almost 300 British soldiers had been killed or wounded.

The Second Continental Congress

In May 1775, colony leaders met in Philadelphia again at the Second Continental Congress. Sixty-five delegates acted as the government for the colonies. First, they established a Continental Army. Congress chose George Washington to lead the new army because he was an experienced soldier and a strong leader.

The most difficult decision was whether or not to declare independence from Great Britain. Some Patriots, like John and Samuel Adams, were ready for a fight. Most delegates, though, were still loyal to King George. They hoped the colonies could make peace with Great Britain.

Common Sense

Thomas Paine only lived in the colonies a short time before he knew that freedom from Great Britain was best for America. In January 1776, he wrote a booklet called "Common Sense." In it, he argued that America should rule itself and show the world a better form of government. He said independence was not only the people's right but also their only choice. People everywhere read it and started to lean toward declaring independence. In just a few months, Paine convinced many people that independence may be the only answer.

title: Westward Expansion
text: By the mid-1800s, thousands of Americans had moved westward. Western land was cheap. People needed very little money to build homes and start farms. The rumor that the West was full of possibilities spread through books and newspapers. People from other countries and from the United States wanted the opportunities the American West provided. Not all people in the American West had a positive experience with westward expansion. For many Native American tribes already living in the West, the expansion brought disruption, hardship, and tragedy.

title: Week 17 Framing Question
text: What factors led to the United States’ expansion from coast to coast?

title: Impact on Native American Tribes
text:
Westward expansion had a major impact on Native American tribes. Bison were a main source of food and clothing for the tribes of the Great Plains. European hunters killed many of the bison in America. The Indigenous tribes could no longer maintain their way of life and faced starvation.

Many European settlers wanted to use land for farming, ranching, and mining. Some Native Americans were farmers, but they did not sell their crops for money. Many tribes believed they should not overuse the land. They wanted to preserve it for their children. They left areas of land for nature and animals. European settlers believed that unused land was wasted land. They wanted to take the Native Americans’ land. When many Native American tribes would not willingly leave their land, the United States government forced the tribes to live on reservations.

title: Conflict Between the United States and Indigenous Peoples
text:
U.S. expansion into western territories provided many opportunities for Americans. These opportunities came at the expense of tribes of Indigenous people. Westward expansion led to hostility between settlers and the Indigenous nations. The hostility led to open conflict and war. This was between the U.S. government and many Indigenous tribes. Almost every tribe fought against the United States at some point. The main reason for conflict was land.

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to one of the darkest periods in our nation’s history. From 1830 to 1850, more than 200,000 Indigenous people were forced to leave their homes. At times, they were forced to walk over 1,000 miles from their homelands to Oklahoma Territory or Kansas Territory. The conditions were inhumane, and food was not readily available. The weather was often cold and wet, and there was no shelter. Diseases and exposure killed many people. Many died on the long and arduous journeys that dozens of tribes had to endure. This journey is often called the Trail of Tears.

The survivors of the forced removals had to start new lives in Oklahoma and Kansas. The tribes were given small parcels of lands called allotments. They had to farm and build their homes on these allotments. It was difficult to produce food because the tribes didn’t know how to farm in the new environments. The tribes helped each other as best they could. However, many of the tribes were from different parts of the country and spoke different languages.

title: Oregon, California, and Mormon Trails
text:
The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the United States. When the Corps of Discovery shared what they had discovered, people were excited. People from the eastern states packed their belongings into covered wagons and headed west. They became known as pioneers. Pioneers are people who are the first to do something. Trail companies were formed. They helped the pioneers on their journeys.

Most trail companies started in St. Louis, Missouri. Multiple families joined a trail company to make a wagon train. Many trails were named for where they led. The Sante Fe, Oregon, and California trails were destination trails. The Mormon Trail was named after a religious group that traveled that trail.

Thousands of pioneers made the journey west. Each had their own reasons for the journey. The trails were perilous, with landforms that made travel difficult. The greatest danger was the risk of disease and the lack of fresh water. People did not have the resources to wash their hands or bathe very often. These types of conditions spread diseases that were contagious and deadly. Many pioneers did not live to see their destination.

title: Steam Engine
text:
Science advanced in the 1800s to control steam pressure. This was used to make wheels rotate. The steam was created by burning coal under a boiler of water. The water was heated to boiling, which created steam. The steam pressure was then used to move mechanical parts.

The steam engine was invented in England. Americans imported the first steam engine from England in 1829. This triggered a new industry. Entrepreneurs began experimenting with how the steam engine could be used to make work easier. Many new jobs were created because of the steam engine.

The steam engine was used to create better transportation on water and on land. When this engine was put into a boat, a boat could move through the water without depending on the wind or currents. Boats could travel up to five miles per hour. The steam locomotive could move more cargo and do it faster than horses or oxen could. Transporting goods and people became faster. The dependability of the machines led to predictable schedules for getting goods to market. The northern states used this new technology to increase manufacturing.

title: Essential Question
text: What are human characteristics and how do they differ from place to place?

title: Rural, Suburban, and Urban
text:
People form communities based on how they use the land they live on. Rural communities have large spaces of undeveloped land. This land is used for farms that grow food for the urban and suburban communities. Houses are far apart in rural communities. Businesses are built together in a town. There are not usually many public transportation options. Roads connect goods and people with the towns. In 2020, the U.S. census recorded that about 14 percent of the total population of the United States lived in rural areas.

A suburban community is formed when there are fewer businesses but more people living in one location. Living space on the land has areas with no buildings. These spaces include yards, parks, and open lots or fields. Transportation systems in the suburban community are smaller. Highways connect goods and people to neighborhoods and areas of business. There is some land available for families to have small farms and grow food. Food is brought in to help feed the population in suburban communities.

When many people live in one location, it is known as an urban area. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, an urban area has a population of 50,000 people or more. Urban areas can also be called cities. In cities, buildings for businesses and homes are developed to be close together. Tall buildings with many floors, or stories, are built so many people can live on smaller pieces of land. Transportation in urban areas is organized to move as many people and goods as possible around and in and out of the city. There is less land available to grow food in urban areas. Food for many people has to be brought into the city.

title: Population Density and Distribution
text:
Population size is the number of individuals in a population. Population density is the average number of people living in each square mile. This number is found by dividing the total population by the land area. Population distribution is how people are spread across a specific area. It shows the pattern of where people live.

This population map shows the pattern of human settlement in the United States. It shows the average number of people who live on one square mile of land. The dark red areas of the map show where the largest number of people live, or the most dense populations. The light yellow areas of the map show where fewer people live.

This population map shows the settlement patterns in Ohio. Ohio’s surface area is approximately 44,825 square miles, making it the 34th-largest state in the U.S. in terms of size. title: Rural Communities
text:
Rural areas of the United States are characterized by small populations and large amounts of undeveloped land. In 2020, approximately 46 million people lived in rural communities across the United States. States with the largest rural populations from 2010-2020 included Maine, Vermont, West Virginia, Mississippi, and Montana. Because of the low population and large amounts of undeveloped land, the primary economic activities of rural areas of the United States are agriculture, forestry, and mining.

Most areas of Ohio are considered rural. In 65 of the state’s 88 counties, 90 percent of the land is rural. The most rural of Ohio’s counties is Vinton County. Vinton County, located about 70 miles southeast of Columbus, is the most rural county in Ohio. In 2020, the total population of Vinton County was 12,800. With an area of 415 square miles, the population density of Vinton County is about 31 people per square mile.

title: Suburban Communities
text:
Suburban areas are located close to urban or city areas. Suburban areas are less crowded and are usually quieter than urban areas. There is more space for homes and businesses in suburban communities. People who work in urban areas often live in suburban areas and commute, or travel, to work. Suburban areas are also close enough to major cities for people to take advantage of the amenities a city offers, such as sports teams, universities, museums, and hospitals.

There are thousands of suburban cities and towns in the United States. The largest suburban area in the United States by population is Mesa, Arizona. About 3,636 people live in each square mile of Mesa’s city limits. Mesa is a suburb of Phoenix, Arizona. Phoenix is the capital of Arizona and home to much of the state’s manufacturing, finance, shipping and trade, education, and health service industries. Thousands of people commute daily from Mesa to Phoenix for work and school.

Parma is the largest suburb by population in Ohio. Parma is a suburb of Cleveland, the second-largest city in Ohio. Parma has a population of 79,982. The population density of Parma is about 4,053 people per square mile. Parma shares many of the same economic activities as Cleveland, including manufacturing, health services, trade, and retail.

title: Urban Communities
text:
An urban area is a city with a larger population than the surrounding areas. People often choose to live in urban areas because of the available resources, including jobs, housing, education, healthcare, and industry. There are many urban areas in the United States. The New York metropolitan area is the largest urban area in the United States by population and land area. Metropolitan refers to an area that has at least one urban city. This area encompasses parts of New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut, including New York City. This area is 4,669 square miles and home to over 19 million people. This area is one of the world’s most industrialized areas and is a center of finance, business, and tourism.

The most densely populated urban area in the western United States is Los Angeles and the surrounding area. This includes the cities of Los Angeles, Long Beach, and Anaheim. There are about 7,000 people per square mile that live in the Los Angeles metropolitan area.

The largest urban area in Ohio is Columbus. Columbus is the capital of Ohio and the largest city by population in the state. As of 2021, the population of Columbus was 906,528. With an area of 220 square miles, the population density of Columbus is about 4,116 people per square mile. Columbus is the fastest-growing metropolitan area in the Midwest. The city is home to many businesses, museums, and professional sports teams. It is also the home of Ohio State University, which is the third-largest university in the United States.

title: Transcontinental Railroad
text:
The invention of the steam engine paved the way for the railroad. Most inventions are created to solve a problem. The steam-powered locomotive was created to help transport heavy mining materials from one place to another. The first railways were created in England for the coal mining industry. Locomotive and railway technology came to the United States in the early 1800s.

The first railroads in the U.S. were built in the industrial northeast, in places like Boston and Baltimore. These cities did not have easy access to rivers that could connect them to the interior of the United States. The railroad solved this problem. After railroads were built, cities on the East Coast were now connected to cities across the country, all the way to the Mississippi River.

Most Americans agreed it would be great to have a railroad that stretched from the East Coast to the West Coast, but deciding what route the railroad should take wasn't easy. Finally, it was decided the railroad should follow the old Platte River Road, and President Abraham Lincoln decided that the western track would begin in Omaha, Nebraska.

The job was enormous and very expensive, but railroad workers were able to complete the track in record time. The Union Pacific (from Nebraska, building west) was racing the Central Pacific (from Sacramento, California, building east). Both sides worked very hard, and the entire job was finished in about six years. Omaha became the headquarters of the Union Pacific Railroad, and the population of the city doubled in just one year.

title: Ellis Island Experience
text:
European immigrants entering the United States once had to go to a check-in station in New York. There, they were asked questions to test their knowledge about the United States. They were also asked about their education and work skills. Immigration officers decided if immigrants met the requirements to be let into the U.S. This was where many immigrants started their new lives.

As the number of immigrants grew, the New York station became too small. The station was moved to Ellis Island in 1892. Ellis Island is a small island in New York Harbor. It is named after Samuel Ellis. It was once an oyster-hunting site for Native Americans. It was also a picnic spot for early Dutch settlers.

There were three basic steps to enter the United States through Ellis Islands. First, immigrants had to take their belongings to a baggage room. Next they received two exams. One was to check their general health and the other was to check them for any eye disease. If a serious physical or mental illness was suspected, a chalk letter would be drawn on the back of the immigrant's coat. That person would then have to go through a more thorough exam.

The last step was to answer questions. These questions included the immigrants’ names, occupations, and how much money they had. They were also asked where they were planning to go. If the immigrants passed through these steps successfully, they were allowed to enter the country. The process usually took 3-5 hours.

In 1965, Ellis Island was made a part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument. In 1990, Ellis Island was made into a museum. There, tourists can see documents and artifacts about the old immigration process.

title: Technological Advancements
text:
There were many important inventions during the 18th century. These inventions helped turn the United States from a rural country into an urban one.

Transportation innovations changed the United States. Steam locomotives could travel across the country faster than horses. Railroads played an important role in the westward expansion of the United States. Both people and information could get across the country in a matter of days instead of weeks.

Steam-powered boats could travel up to five miles per hour. Up to 100 passengers could travel at a time. These steam-powered boats also played an important part in the westward expansion.

An important mechanical invention was the cotton gin. This machine separated cotton fibers from the seed. It was invented by Eli Whitney in 1794. It made processing cotton easier, faster, and cheaper. This made it easier to make new clothes.

The earliest methods of long-distance communication took a long time. Then, Morse code was invented. This code could be transmitted by a telegraph. The telegraph was used in the United States for over 100 years.

title: Essential Question
text: What is the type of criteria and data that can describe the characteristics of region(s) in South America?

title: Regions of South America
text:
South America is located in the Southern Hemisphere and is the fourth-largest continent in the world. It extends from the Caribbean Sea in the north to Cape Horn in the south. The Pacific Ocean lies to the west. The Atlantic Ocean borders the continent to the east. South America is divided into three different physical regions: mountains and highlands, river basins, and coastal plains.

South America's geography is influenced by different kinds of physical features. Some examples include the Amazon River, the Andes Mountain Range, and the Brazilian Highlands. The country of Brazil is home to the Amazon River. A great variety of plants, animals, and insects form the wildlife of the Amazon River. The Amazon River is an example of a diverse biome.

A variety of small oceanic islands surround South America, primarily in the southern part of the continent. The bigger and more well-known islands around South America are the Falkland Islands, southwest of Argentina, and the Galapagos Islands, west of Ecuador.

Countries in South America make most of their money by selling goods and natural resources to other countries. Nearly half of the world's coffee comes from the countries of Brazil and Colombia. The United States receives many products from South America. These include coffee, sugar, bananas, fish, beef, lamb, wool, and plastics. These are consumed by communities all around the United States.

title: Characteristics of South America
text:
There are 12 countries in South America and three dependencies. A dependency is a country or province that is under the control of another. South America is the fourth-largest continent and has the fifth-largest population in the world. Currently, it has a population of about 428 million.

The largest country in South America is Brazil. Brazil’s population is about 209 million. Brazil covers more than half of the continent. The smallest country in South America is Suriname. Suriname has one of the smallest populations in the world, with a population of about 563,000.

Paraguay and Bolivia are the only two landlocked countries in South America. A country that is landlocked does not share a border with an ocean and is entirely surrounded by land.

title: Mountains and Highlands
text:
Mountains

The mountain regions of South America contain seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina. These countries have a primary mountain system as part of their physical geography called the Andes. This mountain range is the world’s longest, and it stretches about 5,500 miles from north to south. Many of the peaks are considered volcanic, as it is part of the Circum-Pacific volcanic chain, also known as the Ring of Fire. It stands about 15,000 feet tall, and the area has a variety of earthquakes.

Features that are important to notice in the mountain regions are rift valleys. Rift valleys are valleys created by faults in the land rather than erosion. They form short distances in the land with hot lowlands and snowy mountain peaks. Cordilleras, or groups of mountain ranges, make up the different features of mountains within South America.

Highlands

The north and east in South America house the highlands region of Guiana and Brazil. The Brazilian Highlands, or the Brazilian Plateau, are south of the Amazon River in Brazil and are made up of a variety of low mountains and plateaus, with the average elevation being 3,300 feet. This highland region houses Bandeira Peak, which has an elevation of 9,482 feet and is one of the highest peaks in Brazil.

The Guiana Highlands are at lower elevations, around 1,000 feet or lower, and are divided by marshy depressions. There are a few steep-sided hills that go up to almost 2,000 feet in elevation. This highland region is between the Amazon River and the Orinoco River. This region covers the southern part of Venezuela, French Guiana, Guyana, northern Brazil, and parts of the southeast of Colombia.

title: River Basins
text:
A river basin is a defined area in which all water that falls in that area eventually flows to a single point. That point in a river basin is the mouth of a river, which then flows into a larger body of water like a lake, sea, or ocean. River basins are generally created based on the terrain. Large mountain ranges or other highlands force water to flow in certain directions, influencing the course of rivers and the shape of river basins.

Due to its rough terrain and tall mountain ranges, South America has many river basins. Many of these are smaller river basins existing from the runoff of the Andes Mountains. The river basins throughout South America run east to west and vary from tropical rainforests to grasslands. The three main river basins that are found in South America are the Amazon basin, the Orinoco basin, and the Paraguay-Paraná basin.

The Amazon basin is located in parts of northern and all of central and eastern South America. The Amazon basin covers eight different countries: Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Peru, Suriname, and Venezuela. It takes up about 2.7 million square miles of land and is considered the largest watershed, or river system, in the world.

The Orinoco River is north of the Amazon River and borders the Guiana Highlands. It empties into the Atlantic Ocean out of Venezuela. This river system flows west to northwest and takes up about 80 percent of Venezuela and about 20 percent of Colombia.

The La Plata River basin flows through four different countries; southeastern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. This river basin covers over one million square miles and has a series of waterfalls that extend for 1.7 miles, including Iguazu Falls. This basin is located in the west of the Andes in Bolivia and in the east of the Brazilian Highlands. It has a variety of marshes due to the system of rivers that blend and merge with this basin. The La Plata River basin is also known for its flooding tendencies and creates swamps.

title: Coastal Plains
text:
A plain is a wide, flat area of land. South America has a few different plains that exist near the ocean, known as coastal plains. The coastal plains regions in South America cover the northeastern coast of Brazil on the Atlantic side. A coastal plain is considered a low-lying piece of land next to the ocean that is separated from the rest of the country's landforms, usually by mountains. The Pacific coast of South America has coastal plains in Peru and Chile.

The northeastern coastal plains are extremely dry. Moist sea air is pushed away because of the Brazilian Highlands. The western coastal plains are also extremely dry due to the cold Peruvian air currents that go through the Andes Mountains. This results in thermal inversion in the western coastal plains. This means that a thick layer of clouds sits at a low altitude, trapping cold air.

title: Movement
text:
Movement is the study of how people, resources, and ideas move. People move for different reasons. Sometimes, people choose to move because there are better jobs, more freedom, or different resources in other places. Sometimes, people are forced to move. They may move because of war, natural disasters, or persecution.

Throughout history, people have explored new places for various reasons. They explored to find resources, spread religion, or expand their empire. As exploration increased, human interactions became more frequent. Exploration led to settlements in new places. Movement from one country to another is called immigration.

When people choose to move within the same country, it is called migration. Migration is one way people, ideas, and materials move. Ideas move with people as they travel from place to place. Ideas also move through communication and technology.

Goods are moved from place to place in many ways. Moving goods can be as simple as carrying a basket of peaches to a market or as modern as transporting goods on a jet. When people study movement, they ask questions like “Why and how do people, ideas, and materials move?” and “What is the result of this movement?”

title: Push-Pull Factors
text:
People move from one area to another for many reasons. Geographers call these reasons push factors and pull factors. Push and pull factors help us understand how and why people move. Push factors are conditions that push people from an area. Push factors are usually negative. Push factors include war, natural disasters, and religious persecution.

Pull factors are usually positive conditions that encourage people to settle in a new community. Pull factors include better jobs, more freedom, or different resources. Push-pull factors can be simple or complicated. However, they are always important. They can also be influenced by various factors. These factors are economic, political, and environmental.

People migrate or immigrate to different areas because of push-pull factors. People can migrate or immigrate to new cities, states, and even countries. Movement to and from an area can affect communities. A large increase in population may put a strain on natural resources. However, large amounts of people leaving an area may also put a strain on local businesses. When people migrate or immigrate to a new place, they bring many different cultures together to create a new community.

Many push and pull factors have influenced immigration and migration to and from Ohio. During Ohio’s territorial period and early statehood, thousands of settlers from Pennsylvania, New York, and other northeastern states migrated to Ohio in search of new economic opportunities and land. The Native People tribes that lived in Ohio were eventually pushed out by these new settlers and forced to migrate farther west and into areas of the American South.

During the early and mid-1800s, thousands of German, Irish, and British immigrants left their homelands because of economic and political instability. Many of these immigrants settled in Ohio in search of economic opportunity, land, and better resources. Even today, the influence of these immigrants can be seen in the culture of the state.

title: Historic Immigration and Migration Waves in United States History
text:
Immigration and Migration Timeline

1607: British settlers established Jamestown, Virginia, the first permanent British settlement in what is now the continental United States.

1619: Portuguese traders brought the first group of enslaved Africans to North America, who were purchased and enslaved by colonists in Jamestown. This started the Trans-Atlantic slave trade, which lasted for hundreds of years.

1787: The Congress of the Confederation of the United States passed the Northwest Ordinance. This act created the Northwest Territory. Thousands of Americans migrated to the Northwest Territory from other states to settle.

1841: The first immigrants used the Oregon Trail, established by fur traders, to move west. By 1869, over 400,000 settlers had traveled on the Oregon Trail to settle in the western areas of the United States.

1845-1852: Up to two million Irish immigrants came to the United States during the Irish Potato Famine, which was a widespread failure of the potato crop due to disease.

1848: The California Gold Rush began. Thousands of immigrants from all over the world came to California in search of gold.

1863-1869: The Transcontinental Railroad was constructed and connected the east and west coasts of the United States. Thousands of immigrants, primarily from Ireland and China, immigrated to the United States to work on the railroad.

1882: The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed by Congress. This act prevented Chinese immigrants from settling in the United States until 1943.

1892: The Ellis Island immigration station opened on Ellis Island in New York Harbor. From 1892 to 1954, over 12 million immigrants were processed through Ellis Island.

1910-1970: Between 1910 and 1970, about six million African Americans left the American South and settled in the northeast, midwest, and western United States in search of economic, educational, and equal opportunities. This period was known as the “Great Migration.”

1930-1936: Over 300,000 migrants left their farms and homes in Arkansas, Kansas, Missouri, Nevada, Oklahoma, and Texas in search of economic opportunities in California as a result of the Dust Bowl.

1942: Congress approved the Bracero Program. Under the Bracero Program, Mexican immigrants were permitted to come to the United States to work as farm laborers and on the railroads.

1961: Congress passed the Cuban Refugee Assistance Program. This program provided healthcare, educational services, and employment assistance to Cuban refugees coming to the United States in an effort to escape the communist government of Cuba.

2021: Approximately 46.2 million immigrants lived in the United States.

title: Charting Populations
text:
Many factors have influenced migration patterns to and within the United States. Our nation was built by people who were looking for freedom and a better life. Many immigrants came to the Americas following the Age of Exploration. They created communities that came together to become states and, in time, a new nation.

During the late 1800s, many people immigrated to the United States. They came from all around the world. In Europe and Asia, there was disease, war, and a lack of freedom. Some factors that pushed people from their homes were starvation, unemployment, and fear. Millions crossed the Atlantic Ocean and settled in cities throughout the U.S. They risked their lives and everything they owned to create better lives in the United States. Today, millions of Americans move to and from cities throughout the country in search of better opportunities.

Geographers can chart the population of a city, state, region, country, or continent. They do this to determine migration patterns. They can also predict if the population of a place will change in the future. We can use many tools to determine an area's population and chart its growth or decline. Geographers also study population maps to learn about population. A population map is used to show the overall population distribution within a particular area or region. Most maps use colors or symbols to represent the varying populations. Population maps help the government distribute resources and information to various groups worldwide.

title: Ohio’s Changing Population
text:
Just as place names or artifacts can tell us about the people who inhabited a place, numbers can also tell a story. Look at the charts. They include numbers taken from Ohio census data over a span of 150 years. They show the countries where the largest groups of immigrants to Ohio came from. The state’s rich resources have always pulled people to live in Ohio. Large cities have also provided immigrants with many opportunities for jobs. However, events outside of Ohio and the U.S. also affect immigration trends. These push factors can include famines, wars, and environmental or economic disasters. Having family, friends, or people from their home country in a place can influence where people decide to settle. Familiar people can make it easier to adapt to a new country and language. This can explain why the same countries of origin often appear in the top groups of immigrants to the state.

Look at the charts collected from census data. How many countries were in the top five places of origin? From which country did most immigrants come to Ohio over the 150 years of data collection?

title: History of Ohio

title: Langford Hot Springs
text:
Aleki and his family planned a trip to Langford Hot Springs. When he asked his dad what he should pack, his dad told him to bring a swimsuit. Aleki was expecting it to be warm and sunny! When they arrived, Aleki got out of the car and shivered. This isn’t swimming weather, he thought. His family all headed into a locker room to change into swimsuits. Aleki was not excited about that idea. He decided to trust his parents. He finally dipped his toe in the water. He was surprised that the water was warm, even though it was cold outside. As he sat in the hot spring, he noticed steam all around. He wondered why there was steam. He had only seen steam like that when his family cooked pasta. What caused the steam to form?

title: Tribes of the Southeast
text:
The Southeast region of the U.S. includes land from the Ohio River to the Gulf of Mexico and from Texas to the Atlantic Ocean. The Native Americans who lived in this area had access to excellent soil for growing crops. Many of them were farmers. Corn was an important crop and was traded with other tribes. Southeastern tribes hunted and fished for sources of proteins. The land was also rich in plants that were made into medicines to help heal people. Because this area is a mixture of forests and grasslands, homes ranged from grass huts to wooden houses.

One of the largest groups of the Southeast was the Creek people. Many early Creek tribes built large earthen mounds throughout the region. These mounds were part of large ceremonial complexes. The Creek lived in log cabins made from lumber, mud, and tree bark. Like other tribes, the Creek adapted to their environment and used the resources available where they settled. The Creek were expert farmers and planted crops such as corn, beans, and squash. They also hunted and fished for food.

title: Tribes of the West
text:
Many American Indian tribes lived in the West. The West includes parts of Nevada, Idaho, Oregon, Utah, California, Colorado, Montana, and Wyoming. This area is very diverse, with mountains, rivers, coasts, and deserts.

Tribes relied on the region's abundant resources to establish a way of life. Many western tribes gathered, hunted, and fished for food. Coastal areas and the rivers of the Great Basin provided many fishing opportunities for native peoples. Tribes hunted large animals, such as bison, deer, and elk. They also gathered wild berries and nuts for food.

Many tribes followed large herds of animals and moved throughout the region. They lived in easy-to-move lodge homes, such as tepees or wickiups. A wickiup consisted of a wooden frame covered with woven leaves and brush. Some tribes lived along the Pacific coast.

Tribes of the Western region engaged in trade with one another. The tribes of the Great Basin traded shells, animal hides, furs, clothing, and baskets for other items. They used resources found in their environment for clothing. They traditionally wore furs in colder climates and seasons. In warmer areas and warmer parts of the year, they wore clothing made from bark, grasses, and animal skins.

Like other tribes, tribes of the West have a deep connection with their environment. Sacred sites that are important to the beliefs of the tribes, like mountains, sequoia trees, and rivers, are given special respect.

title: Historical Analysis
text: Many events in history can occur around the same period. The tools and items people used in the past become artifacts we can study. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technology change over time. Artifacts help us understand how people’s lives have changed over time. Historians analyze how much things have changed throughout history. They examine patterns to understand how and why things happened.

title: Traci's Lexile Test
text: The country of Italy was not united during the 1400’s. It was controlled by a variety of city-states or a city that had control of the territory around it politically, economically, and/or culturally. Italy was divided up into 23 city-states that were in the northern or central part of the Italian peninsula; these city-states had populations up to 20,000 people or more. The Italian peninsula is also surrounded by the Mediterranean Sea, and it became a natural place of exchange for the East (Asia) and West (Europe). Northern Italy was controlled by the Kingdom of Naples, previously a very wealthy and prosperous area. However, during the Renaissance period many other countries such as Spain and France, gained control and influenced its economic state that slowly declined. Central Italy was a hub of trade and prosperity during the 1400-1500’s. The Papal States held Rome and the Vatican which was the head of the Catholic Church, and would be a key figure in the Renaissance. Northern Italy held three of the greatest city-states, Florence, Venice and Genoa. These areas held a place of luxury and goods that traveled between Asia and the Middle East.

title: The Ghana Empire
text:
West Africa was home to three medieval civilizations: the Kingdom of Ghana, the Mali Empire, and the Songhai. Although these civilizations were all located in slightly different areas of West Africa, they took advantage of many of the same resources and benefitted from the trade that developed in the area during its earliest periods. The history of these empires can be difficult to study because there are not many written records, as most of the people of these empires belonged to an oral history tradition. Much of our knowledge of Ghana comes from griots, Ghanaian storytellers who pass on the traditions and tales of ancient Ghana through generations.

Ghana was the first of the larger kingdoms to rise in West Africa. Around 300 C.E., the Ghana Empire began, but it rose to prominence in the 700s and was a well-established and powerful empire by 800 C.E. The ancient empire was located a couple of hundred miles away, near a “V” made by the Niger and Senegal rivers. Ghana was located near a third river, the Gambia. This meant Ghana had access to three major rivers: the Gambia, the Senegal, and the Niger. Having so many waterways allowed this empire to flourish in trade and transportation. The medieval empire of Ghana was located in a different place from the modern country of Ghana.

This area has more tropical climates. It also has a rainy season. When you have tropical temperatures and more rainfall, you have a better chance of growing crops and raising animals. Farmers in this region grew millet, rice, and sorghum. Farther south, there was even more rain, and root vegetables grew particularly well. So, the people in the Empire of Ghana chose to settle down rather than live nomadic lifestyles. Nomads are people who frequently move in search of resources, often following migrating animals. Ghanaians learned to farm, grow crops, and raise animals. Staying in one place helped them to develop other economic enterprises.

Ghana was situated between gold mines, south of the empire, and salt deposits, north of the empire. A Ghanaian king saw an opportunity to control the trade route between the gold and salt mines. He ordered his soldiers to guard and protect traders’ caravans for a price. Charging traders for safe passage was one reason Ghana became so wealthy and powerful. Ghanaian kings also extracted tribute from smaller groups that surrounded the empire. Eventually, Ghana’s merchants had so much gold that even their animals wore it as a decoration. Arabs came from the north with salt to trade for gold, ivory, and enslaved people.

Ghana was controlled by kings who listened to the arguments of their people and passed judgment. Ghana’s kings were powerful at home, but they were also powerful in the trade between nations. Ghanaian kings would eventually take over the southern lands where gold was produced. However, competition for control of the gold trade was high. Due to outside pressure and conflict, the Ghana Empire lost power around the 1000s, and after a short stint of Almoravid power, the Mali Empire took over.
