Between the ages of 8 and 14, you will experience changes in your body. This process is called “going through puberty.” Puberty is the process of your body maturing from a child to an adult. One change you may notice is that your sweat will start to have a stronger smell. This is because your body is creating hormones. You will need to start wearing deodorant and pay more attention to personal hygiene as a result.

Many physical changes happen during puberty, some of which are influenced by your genetics. Your genes can influence how tall you get or how much weight you gain during puberty. Everyone develops at different rates. Puberty affects everyone in different ways. Try not to compare yourself to others. As long as you are making healthy choices for your body and your personal hygiene, then your body can be healthy just the way it is.

One result of puberty is the ability to reproduce, meaning to produce offspring. Different body parts and sexual organs perform different functions during the process of reproduction. People with penises and testicles are able to produce sperm. People with vaginas and ovaries are able to produce eggs, which drop about once a month during their menstrual cycle. During a menstrual cycle, the egg drops from one of the ovaries into the uterus. If this person has unprotected sex with someone who produces sperm, their egg can be fertilized by that sperm. If this person does not have unprotected sex with someone who produces sperm, the egg cannot be fertilized and will exit through the vagina in the form of menstrual bleeding. When a person has menstrual bleeding, they can use pads, tampons, or some other method to absorb the blood and avoid illness. If a person with a vagina and ovaries and a person with a penis and testicles have sex, their sperm and egg can combine, creating an embryo, which can become a fetus and grow into a baby.

During puberty, your body grows, and your hormones grow too. You may start to feel attracted to other people. It’s important to weigh the risks before engaging in any type of sexual activity. Sex is a consensual act (agreed upon by all the people involved and by individuals legally old enough to give consent by state law) that can have lasting consequences. Sexually active relationships can be very emotional and can cause physical infections called Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs). Individuals should make sure they are both physically and emotionally prepared when engaging in sexual activity.

Physical preparation for intercourse may include forms of birth control. There are many different forms of birth control, like internal or external condoms. Though they don’t eliminate the risk completely, condoms can decrease the risk of STDs and chances of an individual becoming pregnant.

If an individual is considering becoming sexually active, they should talk to a trusted adult or doctor to make sure they are educated and have access to appropriate care, including birth control. Abstinence means not having sex. Abstinence is the only way to guarantee that a person will not get pregnant. Abstinence also protects against STDs such as HIV and AIDS. STDs can have a variety of negative effects on a person’s health and wellness. They can cause rashes, itchiness in the genital areas, nausea, headaches and fevers. Most STDs can be managed with medication but there are some that have no permanent cure. If a person thinks they may have an STD, they should seek medical attention immediately.

Many things can influence a person’s behavior. Peer pressure, social media and even family all impact a person’s decisions and health. Teens are particularly vulnerable to inaccurate or unrealistic messages about sex and sexual health in the media and, without comprehensive education on the topic, this can lead to higher risks of teen pregnancy or STD transmission. If a person does become pregnant, they should talk to a trusted adult or a doctor right away. Signs of pregnancy include: a missed menstrual cycle (also known as period), nausea, and enlarged or tender breasts. A human baby grows and develops for nine months in the person’s uterus. Young people experiencing teen pregnancy (pregnancy during the teenage years) can receive assistance and discuss options with a medical practitioner. Pregnant individuals may explore options like placing the baby up for adoption, abortion (terminating the pregnancy, which is an option up to a certain point in a pregnancy), or choosing to have and parent the baby. All options involved in teen pregnancy can be life-changing for the teen parents and their families. It’s important to be aware of the risks and how certain consequences can change a person’s life when making choices to be sexually active.

title: Age of Encounters
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa. Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He was sure that he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.”

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures. Columbus became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they learned on the voyage, other explorers followed.

Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim.

Explorers share information that helps others explore. Many followed Columbus’s precedent and shared their new knowledge.

1. Christopher Columbus

Spain paid Christopher Columbus to sail across the Atlantic in 1492. Columbus hoped to reach India by sailing west. Instead, his ships landed in the Caribbean. There, Columbus met the Taíno people. Columbus’s voyage increased Europe’s interest in exploration and led to many other voyages and colonies.

2. John Cabot

Learning from Columbus, John Cabot became interested in finding a shorter route across the ocean. England sponsored Cabot to sail through the North Atlantic in 1497. Cabot thought he had landed in Asia, but it was actually what is now Canada. His voyage proved a northern route to the Americas could work. He met the Eastern Woodland American Indians.

3. Pedro Álvares Cabral

In 1500, Portugal paid for Pedro Cabral to take 13 ships to India for trade. Cabral’s plan was to sail around Africa, but on the way, his ships sailed far into the Atlantic. This misdirection caused Cabral to land on the coast of South America. He met the Tupiniquim people. Cabral and his ships then sailed east across the southern tip of Africa to India.

4. Vasco Núñez de Balboa

In 1513, Spain sponsored an explorer named Vasco Núñez de Balboa. He was the first European to find the Pacific Ocean. Knowledge of the Pacific gave evidence that the land was not the East Indies. This inspired further exploration.

5. Jacques Cartier

France hoped to find a northwest passage to reach the Pacific Ocean through North America. In 1534, France paid for Jacques Cartier to search. Cartier sailed up rivers in what is now Canada. He didn’t find a route to the Pacific, but he did meet the Mi’kmaq people and the powerful Iroquois Confederacy. Cartier’s trips started French trade in North America.

title: Tribal Structures
text:
The Plains tribes organized themselves into bands. Bands were independent groups that came together for specific events like the harvest, hunting, or military action. Some bands were very unified, while others were not. The Cheyenne was composed of 10 distinct bands. They were one of the most unified of the Plains tribes. When there were important decisions to make, the tribe would call a council of peace chiefs. About 44 peace chiefs from the 10 tribes came together and made decisions. Because of the unity that existed between the bands of the Cheyenne, anything that the peace chiefs decided was enforced and obeyed by all 10 tribes.

The Comanche tribe had a republic-like system of governance. Smaller bands of the Comanche had single chiefs, who oversaw band politics and needs. However, band chiefs would come together when they needed to discuss important issues. Most of these issues would have been about war and the defense of Comanche territory. The same basic structure of each band having a chief and a band council being called together for important matters, such as war, existed in other tribes as well. These tribes include the Assiniboine.

title: Economy
text:
For centuries, Native Americans grew crops such as maize (corn), beans, sunflower seeds, and squash. Women were the farmers among the Indigenous groups of the Plains. They practiced intercropping, which is planting different crops together. For example, they planted beans among the corn because beans return nitrogen to the soil, and corn needs nitrogen to grow. In addition to growing crops, women collected wild produce like turnips and chokecherries.

They also hunted bison and other game, such as elk and deer, to eat. Staying close to rivers and streams was vital to the survival of the Indigenous groups of the Plains, so fish were also caught and eaten. One hunting practice that the Plains people used to harvest bison was called a pishkun. The whole community would drive a herd of bison over a steep cliff and then gather the hides and meat to use for all their needs. Often it was the women’s job to skin the animals and cut up the meat. Most of the meat was dried and made into jerky. This meat lasted a long time. Other portions of meat were mixed with fat and berries to make a long-lasting food, called pemmican.

Trade was another economic activity that the Indigenous groups of the Plains engaged in. The most common trade relationship existed between nomadic and sedentary groups. Sedentary groups had goods like corn and squash, while nomadic groups had meat to trade. Nomadic groups also came into contact with other Indigenous groups in a wider range of geographic locations and habitats. Because of this, they became middlemen in continental trade. For example, goods like seashells passed through nomadic Plains tribes and were traded to groups in other areas, who then used them for currency or sacred objects.

title: The Horse Changes the Economy
text:
The Great Plains stretch from Texas to Canada. On the Plains, the summers are hot, and the winters are cold. The nomadic peoples who lived on the Great Plains followed bison herds. When the bison moved, so did the people. They moved their homes and all of their belongings either by themselves or by using dogs to carry cargo. Bison hides were used for shelter and clothing. Bison were also a source of food. Bison meat was ideal for Indigenous peoples because it could be dried and saved for the long, cold winters on the Plains.

When the Spanish first came to the Americas, they brought horses with them from Europe. Some of the horses ran away and lived in the wild. They began to thrive in the grasslands of North America, an ideal habitat for them. During the late 1500s and early 1600s, some Indigenous people began catching wild horses and learning to ride them. Among the first tribes to do so were the Comanche, a Southern Plains tribe.

With horses, nomadic tribes could move and travel a long way to hunt bison. Some tribes that were sedentary changed the way they lived and became nomadic. The arrival of the horse changed the amount of territory that Indigenous tribes could travel through. Because of this territorial expansion, more tribes came into contact with one another. Sometimes this led to conflict on the Plains. The horse trade became a large market among Plains tribes. The Cheyenne were the middlemen in the horse trade. They controlled the trade of horses between the northern and southern tribes.

title: Language
text:
Native American languages were spoken across the Plains region. These Indigenous peoples spoke many languages from many language families, including Algonquian, Siouan, Caddoan, and Uto-Aztecan. The Algonquian languages traveled from eastern areas, and the Uto-Aztecan languages came from the south. Some of the languages and dialects spoken by Indigenous peoples were Arapaho, Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Pawnee, Crow, Comanche, and many more. The Indigenous peoples of the plains also invented a sign language for common trade goods and animals, like bison. This sign language was known throughout the entire range of the Plains region.

The Comanche, a Southern Plains tribe, call themselves Nʉmʉnʉʉ. This means “the people.” The Comanche language is from the Uto-Aztecan family. The Comanche were closely tied to the Shoshone tribe through location, language, and other kinship relationships. Their language was once a dialect of Shoshone. After separating from the Shoshone people and moving to the Southern Plains, their dialect diverged so much that it became its own language.

Like the Comanche, the Arikara are closely related to other tribes. The Arikara language comes from the Caddoan language family. They are a Northern Plains tribe. Their language and the language of the Pawnee, another Northern Plains tribe, are both dialects of the same language. The name Arikara means “horn,” which references the way that members of the tribe used to wear their hair in two pieces, resembling horns.

As early settlers and trappers began interacting with Indigenous people, they began using many of their words to describe plants, animals, and places that they had never seen before. Many of the words and place names we use today come from native languages that have been used for hundreds of years. Some of these words are: caribou, woodchuck, toboggan, pecan, skunk, and moccasin.

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
The Indigenous peoples of the Plains believed that everything had a spirit. Animals, plants, the sun, moon, wind, and many more natural elements each had a spirit. Ceremonies, dances, and prayers were performed to communicate with these spirits. Most Plains tribes believed that these spirits would intervene on their behalf. Some tribes, like the Cheyenne, believed in a supreme spirit, or god, who was more powerful than all others. Other tribes, like the Crow, believed in many spirit gods who each possessed the same amount of power as the others.

Dance is a treasured and sacred tradition for many Indigenous Americans. Styles of dancing have been passed down for hundreds or even thousands of years. Each tribal group has its own styles of dance. Some dances are for family celebrations, like marriages and birthdays. Some dances prepare the tribe for hunting. Dances can show gratitude for the land. Indigenous groups from the Plains frequently used vocals, drums, percussion, and flutes in their music, which accompanied the dance.

One of the oldest dances is the Grass Dance. This dance comes from the tribes of the Northern Great Plains. The Pawnee, Omaha, Winnebago, and Iowa were warrior tribes who danced in this style. The Great Plains were covered in long, tall prairie grass that flowed back and forth like waves in the wind. The Grass Dance is a beautiful, flowing dance. The dancers hop from one foot to the other, following the rhythm of the drum and the singers. Their heads, arms, and shoulders sway back and forth. The tassels on their brightly colored clothing move like grass.

Among many Plains tribes, a naming ceremony was held when a baby was born. In the Cree Tribe, the mother would make a feast. Elders would gather, and the mother would tell the name of the child to an elder. Children were usually named after animals or objects. The elder would hold the newborn in his arms and keep a beat with a drum or rattle. He would sing a song to the spirit of the object or animal that the child was named after. In the Ojibwe tribe, when a child is given a name, it is announced to each of the four directions. Then, everyone gathered at the ceremony repeats the name.

title: Oral Tradition
text: Just like in other cultures, the oral traditions of the Indigenous groups of the Plains tended to deal with lessons that elders wished to pass down to children. They also dealt with religious topics like creation and the advent of important traditions. Many groups believed there was a trickster god named Iktomi. Iktomi was a common spirit-being among many Plains tribes, including many Sioux tribes. They told stories about how Iktomi created the world. In the beginning, no land existed on the Earth. So, Iktomi tricked some animals to try and find land beneath the depths of the sea. Unfortunately, the only animal that made it back to the surface was a muskrat, who was clutching some earth in his hands. Iktomi took the dirt from the muskrat and created land. Iktomi was not a creature that people used to teach morals, but he was a creature that taught about how life can sometimes be unfair or even random.

title: Introduction to the Southeast
text:
The Southeast region of the U.S. includes land from the Ohio River to the Gulf of Mexico and from Texas to the Atlantic Ocean. The Indigenous peoples who lived in this area had access to excellent soil for growing crops. Many of them were farmers. Corn was an important crop and was traded with other tribes. Southeastern tribes hunted and fished for their meat. The land was also rich in plants that were made into medicines to help heal people. Because this area is a mixture of forests and grasslands, homes ranged from grass huts to wooden houses. The Indigenous peoples of this area could meet their needs with the natural resources that were available to them. Because they had access to similar resources, the people of this region had many similarities in how they used those resources.

Southeastern tribes often used the abundant natural resources of the area to build large earthen mounds. Groups like the Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw built elevated mounds of earth for ceremonial and practical purposes. These mounds still dot the landscape throughout the Southeast. Their shelters also used many of the same resources. Some tribes, like the Creek and Cherokee, incorporated the use of sticks and logs from the trees of the area. Most tribes included thatched roofs made of abundant grasses. The Choctaw and Chickasaw would make summer and winter homes with different materials because of the changes in the weather. Winter houses were sturdier log houses with clay walls while the summer houses had thinner walls or sometimes removable walls to allow for a cooling breeze.

The tribes in the Southeast used the environment for their food. The climate and soil of the Southeast made it a perfect place to plant corn, beans, and squash. Every tribe grew corn as the main crop to be eaten directly or used in various recipes and dishes. The Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Creek all grew beans and squash as well. Along with corn, these crops were known as the Three Sisters. The Southeast teemed with animals for the people of the region to hunt. Deer were particularly plentiful. Small animals, like raccoons and squirrels, featured in the diets of the southeastern peoples. The rivers and coastlines of the Southeast provided fish and other food as well.

Despite these similarities, the Indigenous peoples of the Southeast had independent, unique cultures with their own beliefs, languages, tribal structures, economies, and other traditions. While living in the same region and even while coming into contact with one another, they maintained distinct cultures and identities.

title: Week 16 Framing Question
text: What did the indigenous groups of the Southeast have in common culturally and archaeologically?

title: Tribal Structures
text:
The Indigenous peoples of the Southeast organized their social and political lives in a variety of ways. Rather than large, uniform groups, the tribes of the Southeast were usually divided into clans or families. The clans of the Southeast were matrilineal, which means that children were members of the same clan as their mother. These clans were looked at as a family, and many people within each clan were related to one another. Because of this, marriages between people within a clan were usually forbidden. The peoples of the Southeast generally married someone from another clan but still within their tribe.

Each tribe organized its clans in a different way. In some tribes, like the Choctaw, the clans were ways to organize families together in certain locations, like towns or villages. In contrast, Creek, Cherokee, and Chickasaw clans all lived together in their villages, where each clan performed a different function in that society, like hunting, farming, or healing.

The towns and villages were usually the simplest forms of government in the Southeast. Town councils were convened when decisions were to be made. Leaders of the clans would often serve on these councils. It was uncommon to find a single leader in charge of an entire village, much less the whole tribe, especially before the 1500s. When necessary, tribal councils would include individual participants from these town councils.

Within these systems, there were variations. The Creek divided their villages into Red and White, or war and peace. The clans in the Red villages were responsible for protecting the tribe and conducting war, among other things. The clans in the White villages conducted peace talks, integrated the members of tribes that were conquered in war, and had other responsibilities. The Cherokee had similar ideas for war and peace governments, but their Red and White governments resided in the same town and swapped authority depending on whether they were at peace or war.

title: Economy
text:
The tribal economies of the Southeast were reliant primarily upon the natural resources available to the people living there. Acquiring these resources generated the majority of the food and materials the Indigenous peoples of the Southeast used to survive. Farming was a major source of food. Women cultivated the Three Sisters (corn, beans, squash) as well as a variety of other fruits, vegetables, and roots. Corn, in particular, dominated the agricultural output of this region. The men added meat to the tribe’s diet from hunting and fishing. Their economy was considered subsistence, because they farmed and hunted enough food to support themselves but did not usually create or hunt in surplus.

In addition to food, plants and animals provided the materials to create goods and tools. Traditional clothing was usually made from the hides of hunted animals. Deer hide was a common source of clothing for the people of the Southeast. Weapons and tools were crafted from sticks and stones, like flint. Artisans within the various clans used these materials to make baskets, musical instruments, pots, and other items.

Although much of their geography was similar, certain tribes did have access to unique resources that they could trade with the other peoples they were in contact with. Groups in the coastal areas had access to fish, salt, and shells that they could use to make jewelry like necklaces and other implements. They then traded those resources and materials to other people who lacked access to the coastline. In return, there were resources in the interior that they would accept. Certain animal pelts, types of wood, and flint were in high demand in coastal locations. This was the primary trade process. It made less sense for tribes who had access to the same resources to trade with one another.

title: Language
text:
Several groups of Indigenous peoples in the Southeast have languages that belong to the same family, the Muskogean language family. While they are distinct languages, they likely derive from a language spoken by a common ancestor group. Some are so similar, like the Choctaw and Chickasaw languages, that some think of them more as two dialects of the same language. The Creek language is also a member of the Muskogean language family. These languages have lent names to a variety of places in the Southeast. The Chattahoochee River is named after a Creek word meaning “painted rocks.” The root of the Creek word meaning “town” shows up in the name of Florida’s capital city, Tallahassee.

Unlike the Muskogean languages of the Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw, the Cherokee language is a part of the Iroquoian language group. This language family has a relative in the northern region of the United States. This suggests that at one point, the Cherokee people lived closer, or perhaps within, the area of the Great Lakes, where other Iroquoian language speakers lived. In an interesting twist, the word “Cherokee” is from the Creek language.

title: Religion
text:
The Indigenous peoples of the Southeast had diverse yet strong beliefs about religion and spirituality. The religion of these peoples usually included aspects of the natural world, with mythical explanations for natural phenomena, as well as deities, or gods, that inhabit the natural world. Some cultures of the Southeast included the idea of a supreme deity, like the Chickasaw’s Abaꞌ Binniꞌliꞌ, who created life on Earth. The Choctaw had a belief in a similar creator god, who went by several names.

Indigenous religions and mythologies included many stories that explained the world around them. One Choctaw legend is the story of the Unknown Woman who brought corn, the most important crop to the Choctaw, to her people. Several of the Indigenous peoples in the Southeast have deities that represent the thunder and lightning that is common because of the thunderstorms in this area. Some gods take the form of animals, like rabbits and birds. In addition to natural animals and phenomena, legends of the southeastern peoples include mythological beings. The Cherokee mythology has beings made of rocks, small beings, and invisible ones as well.

The nations of the Southeast also participated in traditional ceremonies for a variety of reasons. Some of these ceremonies were unique to the tribe, while others were more widespread. One traditional ceremony that seems to have been common throughout the Southeast is the Green Corn Ceremony. When the corn crop ripened in summer, the peoples of the Southeast would gather for the multi-day ceremony. It was a ceremony of renewal and included feasts, fasts, performances, and the repair and improvement of the village.

title: Archaeology
text:
We have no written language documents from the Indigenous tribes of the Southeast. They did not write down any information that historians can use to learn about these people, their traditions, their culture, and their way of life hundreds of years ago. Modern members of these tribes maintain their oral tradition and continue to ensure that their culture continues on. But we also have archaeological evidence of their lives that they left behind and that archaeologists can use to learn about them.

Throughout the Southeast, archaeologists have investigated the mounds created by the Indigenous peoples of this region. There are mound sites throughout the Southeast, in states like Alabama and Florida. Excavations at these sites have revealed that villages were often erected around these mounds. Archaeologists discover what life in these villages was like by examining the items they find there. Evidence of life in these villages comes in the form of tools, weapons, and other materials that reveal what kinds of things they did and what types of materials they had available to them. The knowledge of trade among the tribes of the Southeast came from the discovery of items far from where they naturally occur, like obsidian tools.

Archaeological evidence of Indigenous peoples is so common in the Southeast that builders are often required to have archaeologists on-site when they start digging the foundations of a new building. The archaeologists are trained to find any evidence of Indigenous life. They can even identify where wooden structures, long rotted away or removed, have changed the color of the soil. These discolorations serve as evidence of a structure and possibly a village site. Combining these findings with traditional knowledge from the descendants of these peoples creates as complete a picture as we can make of people living hundreds or even thousands of years ago.

title: Past, Present, Future
text:
History tells the story of people and events that happened in the past. The things we did before are in the past. The things we are doing now are called the present. The things we will do later are called the future.

Chronological means that we put events in the order they happened. We do this by thinking about what came first, then next, and so on.

Look at the list of items, and think about your day today. Which events have happened or will happen to you today? Organize the events into the correct chronological order for you. What other events could you add?

title: What Are Natural Resources?
text:
A natural resource is something found in nature that people can use. There are many types of natural resources in the world around us. These include soil, plants, coal, water, natural gas, and even animals. We use natural resources to meet our needs and wants. Sometimes, we use natural resources just as they are. For example, we use water to drink and for cooking and cleaning. We also eat fruits and vegetables that grow naturally in our environment.

Sometimes, we use natural resources to make products that make our lives easier. We burn coal and use natural gas to power and heat our homes, schools, and businesses. We use trees to build furniture and houses. Trees are also used to make paper and books. We also use natural resources to make some of the items we use daily. This includes cell phones, computers, clothing, and even your toothbrush!

title: Introduction to Ancient India
text:
India is a modern country located in South Asia. The region is known as a subcontinent, a unique part of the continent of Asia. To the north lies the Indus River Valley. This region became home to the Indus Valley Civilization between 7000 and 600 B.C.E. The valley is bordered by mountains to the north and the Thar Desert to the south. Most importantly, it contained two important rivers, the Indus River and the Saraswati River. The Indus River is an important source of water in the region today. However, the Saraswati River is believed to have dried up almost 6,000 years ago. This is one possible reason for the decline of the civilization. At its height, ancient India was home to more than five million people. This makes it the largest known ancient civilization at the time. In contrast, ancient Egypt had a population of 1.5 million. Mesopotamia only supported a population of 50,000.

Ancient India was a center of trade and innovation. Bronze from regions like Mesopotamia has been uncovered at ancient sites in India. Cotton and clay seals from ancient India have also been found throughout the Middle East and Africa. Cities like Harapa and Mohenjo contained multi-story homes, large bathhouses, and even advanced plumbing, like flush toilets that moved waste using gravity and jars of water.

The Gupta Empire ruled India between 300 and 800 C.E. The empire stretched across northern, central, and parts of southern India between approximately 320 and 550 C.E. The period is noted for its achievements in the arts, architecture, medicine, religion, and philosophy. It is often called the “golden age” of India.

title: Geography of Ancient India
text:
The region of India is known as a subcontinent, or a large, unique landmass part of the larger continent of Asia. What makes the land unique are mountains to the north, separating India from the rest of Asia, and ocean to the east, west, and south. These unique features classify India as a very large peninsula.

India’s name comes from the Indus River. Its floodplain became home to the Indus River Valley civilization. This grew to be the largest civilization of its time because of its access to rivers. Unfortunately, one of the major rivers, the Saraswati River, dried up nearly 6,000 years ago. What remains in this region is now called the Thar Desert. This may have been one reason for the decline of this massive civilization. The Ganges River also plays an important cultural role in India. Many believe the river has religious connections. The river is sometimes called “Mother Ganges.”

In central India lies the Deccan Plateau. A plateau is a large, flat landmass that is high in elevation. This region is rich in minerals and precious metals, like gold and silver. The plateau has been the center of major conflicts, specifically within the Gupta Empire. This is because of those valuable resources.

Various mountain ranges also border the entire subcontinent. The Himalayas and the Eastern and Western Ghats form geographic borders around the region. They also play a major role in the climate of India.

title: Mountains and Monsoons
text:
The Indian subcontinent is home to the largest mountain ranges in the world. The Himalayas are located to the northeast, the Hindu Kush are to the northwest, and the Eastern and Western Ghats are to the south. These ranges form geographic borders around the entire subcontinent. These mountains also help create monsoons that last all year.

The summer monsoon season is a long, wet season. It regularly causes rivers to flood. Winds blow from the southwest in the warmer summer months. Moisture is collected from the ocean, and as the air rises over the Western Ghat Mountains, the moisture cools and condenses into rain, causing long periods of wet weather. Since summer monsoons caused flooding in many of India’s rivers. River valleys tended to have fertile soil, which helped people grow crops like cotton, wheat, and rice.

During cooler months, the winds shift and come in from the northeast. The Himalayas block most of the moisture from reaching the coast, causing periods of dry weather. This is known as the winter monsoon season. The predictable weather pattern between winter and summer likely helped early Indian civilizations grow.

title: Agriculture
text:
India has a rich agricultural history. It includes two stages of development. In the earlier stage, agriculture was just being established near the Indus River Valley. This time is known as the Agricultural Revolution. The environment influenced the emergence of this civilization. Farmers relied on the large rivers and monsoon season for water to grow crops. Barley and wheat were the main crops. Barley is an important grain and a natural sweetener in cooking. Wheat is a grain commonly used in baking bread. There was more than enough water, food, and land to sustain large cities and a flourishing civilization.

The second stage of development includes evidence of another crop: cotton. Cotton was used to make cloth. This cloth became an important cultural connection to society. People in ancient Indian civilizations wore mostly cotton clothing. Traditionally, men wore dhoti. This is a cloth wrapped around the waist and knotted at the back. Women typically wore skirts and a cloth head wrap, intended to keep the sun off. Cotton caught the eye of neighboring civilizations, such as ancient Egypt, China, and Mesopotamia in the Middle East. Trading with these civilizations added additional crops to ancient India, such as rice, pepper, and sugar.

title: Infrastructure
text:
Like the peoples of Mesopotamia and Egypt, the Harappans created irrigation systems. These systems helped make sure that crops got plenty of water and grew quickly. Unlike Mesopotamia and Egypt, the people of the Indus valley also used water for sanitation. They created the first known city sewer systems.

Individual homes got their fresh water from wells. Wastewater flowed into covered drains on the streets. Houses even had toilets that flushed. This was much more high-tech than what later civilizations had in their cities. Even the smallest homes on the outskirts of cities were connected to this system.

Every Harappan city had two main sections. The raised area with public buildings was the citadel. The lower town held all the other buildings. All the streets in these cities formed a grid pattern. The streets ran north to south and east to west. Houses built on street corners had rounded edges. This probably made it easier for carts to turn corners.

Like other ancient cultures, the Harappans built with bricks. Unique to this civilization is the fact that all the bricks were uniform. This means they were the exact same length, width, and height. Researchers think there must have been a central government that decided the best size to make bricks. Doors and windows didn’t open onto main roads. They opened onto smaller, side lanes. This may have been so people couldn’t see inside buildings while they were passing them. Many buildings had a "wind catcher" on the roof. This acted as a sort of cooling system for the building.

title: Transportation in Ancient India
text:
Roads and rivers were the main routes for transportation within the Indian subcontinent. Evidence of dugout canoes for river transportation were found in archaeological digs within the Indus River Valley. As agriculture grew, trade developed across the oceans. Trade took place with Egypt, China, the Middle East, Greece, and Africa. The need for safe, quick, and reliable transportation over the water was necessary.

The earliest mention of an Indian ship is found on an Indus Valley clay seal from about 3000 B.C.E. The ship is shown being elevated at both bow and stern, with a cabin in the center. We also see various paintings and mentions of ships and trade in religious texts. The people of the Indus River Valley even constructed the first tide dock and cargo facility in the world. The docks and cargo facilities held evidence of a vast trading network between the major ancient civilizations of the time.

Once goods were brought to the docks, oxen and carts were necessary to move around the subcontinent. As trade grew, so did access to faster over-the-land transportation like horses and swifter-moving carts. This brought the need for improved roads rather than early trail systems. Recent excavations within the Indus River Valley have found evidence of early roads, carts, and wagons as well as remains of horses, oxen, and elephants that were used to move these goods.

title: Indus Valley Settlements: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
text:
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the two largest cities of the Indus River Valley. The city of Harappa was built on the banks of the Ravi River. Mohenjo-Daro was built further south, up the Indus River. Researchers estimate the population of Harappa was between 23,500 and 35,000 people. Mohenjo-daro probably had between 35,000 and 41,250 people. Both cities were one square mile.

The Indus River Valley civilization was famous for its large, complex cities. Indus River Valley cities were very well-constructed for their time. Each city was very carefully planned. Mohenjo-daro was in the center of the Indus Valley civilization. It had a large public bath. The bath may have been part of the religion, used for cleansing. Or it may have been a pool for swimming.

Harappa sat on the edge of the Indus Valley region. It was a gateway into the culture of the people. It would have been an important place for trade. Archaeologists think these two cities were centers of politics. The Indus River Valley may have been one big empire with two capitals.

title: Specialization and Trade
text:
The people of Ancient India held many types of jobs. Many people were artisans. An artisan is someone whose work requires a specific skill. Artisans often make products by hand. Some artisans from Ancient India made clothing. Some made pottery. Traditional pottery was made on a wheel that spun while the artisan shaped the clay. Others made tools or weapons. With access to rivers and the ocean, shipbuilding was another trade many artisans specialized in.

Farming was another important job in this ancient society. The Indus River provided water and fertile fields to grow crops. Farmers grew mostly wheat and barley. They also grew rye, peas, cotton, and rice. Farmers raised buffaloes and pigs for meat. They also raised horses and camels for transportation.

As society grew, these jobs became very specialized. The need for trade became necessary. Specialization is when people in society focus on one area of expertise. Early people needed to clothe, feed, and entertain themselves. Through specialization, they could trade services and goods to meet their needs. In the early Indus River Valley civilization, the people traded with Egypt, Greece, and the Middle East. In later years, this trade network expanded to China, Japan, and other East Asian countries. This expansion of trade helped grow imports like silk. It also helped Indian farmers and artisans sell their goods to other parts of the known world.

text: Why does planning make cities more efficient? How did the people of Ancient India accomplish this?

title: Bullock Carts and Transportation
text:
As road systems and trade expanded throughout Ancient India, the people also made progress in transportation. They invented the bullock cart. A bullock cart is a cart pulled by oxen or bulls. Bullock carts are still used in rural parts of India. A driver sits at the front of the cart to control the oxen. Goods or passengers sit in the back. There’s no set design for the carts. Some carts have two wheels. Other carts have four wheels. Some carts have covers. Ancient carts were made of wood.

Bullock carts appeared in the Indus Valley between 2600 and 1900 B.C.E. Archaeologists have found drawings and other types of art that show these carts being used in a variety of ways and in lots of different styles. Each cart was made for different needs. Scholars believe the people of Ancient India didn't get the idea for the carts from other people. We have not found evidence of them in other parts of the world until much later in history, so they must have been invented in India. Indian carts also have unique designs specific to each region.

title: Society and Government
text:
The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt, helped scholars understand hieroglyphics because the exact same script was written in Greek. Since Greek was a known language, it helped decode Ancient Egyptian writing. Interpreting the ancient writings of India has been more of a challenge. The system of writing developed in Ancient India is known as Indus script. To date, archaeologists have not found evidence to help decode Indus script, so we are not certain how the government of that civilization functioned. Archaeologists needed to make inferences based on the evidence.

Evidence (What We Know)

Inference (What We Conclude)

The writing system is consistent across the entirety of northern India.

The government likely maintained lots of control and was quite powerful.

Many raw materials, shipyards, and warehouse foundations have been found near water sources.

Ship building and trade with other civilizations must have been important to the economy.

Evidence has been found of goods from Ancient Egypt and the Middle East in the Indus River Valley.

A cultural and economic exchange happened between civilizations because of trade.

Archaeologists have found evidence of ancient universities, like Nalanda and Takshashila, that date back to the Gupta Empire. School is also mentioned in a religious text called the Vedas.

Students were likely taught subjects like religion, writing, astronomy, math, and medicine because of the innovations that we know came from the Indus Valley civilization.

The claim: It can be inferred that society was complex and needed a centrally organized government to keep the empire together. Value was likely placed on the economy, trade, and religion due to the artifacts found throughout the region.

title: The Vedas
text:
Scholars have found a lot of ancient writing to explain the laws of Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt. However, that kind of evidence doesn’t exist to describe the laws of Ancient India. Instead, they rely on Vedas.

The Vedas are some of the earliest known texts in Ancient India. The word “Veda” means “knowledge” in an ancient Sanskrit language. Scholars have made an inference that Ancient Sanskrit is based on Indus Script because of its connection to Ancient India. The Vedas are thought to contain a collection of knowledge used to guide the lives of the people in the region. This collection of text provided many of the rules people lived by. They began as oral traditions, which are stories passed from generation to generation through spoken word.

Between 1500 and 500 B.C.E., the Vedas began to be written down. This era is called the Vedic period. It is known to be a time when many of the rules, art, and literature that influence modern India came from. It is not yet known who wrote the teachings of the Vedas. But some of the earliest known writings in historical collections and museums today were written on clay tablets and palm leaves.

There are four Vedas in total, and each Veda has four parts. These ancient texts include poems, hymns, and teachings that many laws and traditions in India are based on. These ancient texts also formed the basis for a major world religion called Hinduism. The Rig Veda is the earliest of the four Vedas and one of the most important texts in the Hindu tradition. It is a large collection of hymns that help followers understand the nature of Hinduism.

Ever since people have been working together, we’ve been setting rules for ourselves. The earliest human civilizations also had laws that told people how to live their lives. The Vedas help us understand what laws may have been like in Ancient India. Based on the Vedas, religion in India had a lot of influence on every part of life, including government, society, and culture.

title: Caste System
text:
Many ancient civilizations had a firm social order that decided what jobs people did and how they were treated in life. Scholars think that the people of ancient India had a similar social order, based on the way their cities are built. The city of Harappa had walls that separated groups of people. Some archaeologists think this means that the Harappans had a similar caste system to what India had for much of its history.

The caste system is a structure of social ranking. It existed in India for as long as the Harappans existed. The caste system has four main groups. The Brahmins are priests and kings. They are at the top of the order. Under them are the Kshatriyas, who are warriors and nobles. Under that group are the Vaishyas, who are cultivators, artisans, and merchants. The next group is the Shudrà. They’re peasants and workers. Finally, members of the lowest caste are now called Scheduled Castes.

Each caste had its own set of rules to obey. Hindus believed that people who followed all the rules of their caste would be rewarded in their next life through reincarnation.

In modern India, it is illegal to treat people differently because of their caste. Scheduled Castes were oppressed and discriminated against throughout the history of India. Caste-based discrimination is now illegal.

title: Hinduism
text:
Hinduism is one of the largest religions in the world. It began in ancient India.

Hindu people today follow teachings and traditions that reach back thousands of years. Most religions grow out of older religions. Hinduism evolved from Brahmanism. Brahmanism was based on the Vedas. Brahmins were the priests or noble people who used these writings. They prayed for healthy families, good weather, and wealth. The major beliefs and practices of Brahmanism began to mix with the beliefs and practices of the people already living in the Indus valley. This mixture formed the beginning of Hinduism. Like the Brahmins, the Hindus believed in a caste system, which is a social order of people in society. At the center of this system is a belief in reincarnation, or each person being “reborn” over and over again, living a series of lives.

Many historians believe Hinduism is the world’s oldest organized religion. Some Hindus believe their religion never had an origin or beginning. They feel their beliefs are timeless. Hindus have so many different viewpoints that it is considered one of the most tolerant, accepting religions in the world.

title: Buddhism
text:
Buddhism is another of the world’s oldest religions, and it also began in India. Buddhism is sometimes described as a nontheistic religion, or a religion with no specific god. Buddhists do believe in some spiritual or supernatural figures, like devas and ghosts. Buddha, the man who started the religion, is often described as a teacher of both people and gods. His name was Siddhartha Gautama. According to tradition, he was an Indian prince who founded Buddhism. Gautama came to be called Buddha, which means “the enlightened one.” Followers of Buddhism are called Buddhists.

Buddha spent his life traveling through India. He taught others what he had learned about living a peaceful life. Buddha believed one way to understand this was to follow the Noble Eightfold Path. Buddhists are peaceful and believe in respecting nature. Even though Buddhism began in India, the religion has spread throughout the world, especially in countries like China and Japan.

title: Achievements of Ancient India
text:
The term “Golden Age,” is a period of time with great wealth, stability, peace, and innovation. This is exactly how the rule of the Gupta Empire in northern parts of India is seen. Chandragupta II was one of the most influential rulers of the Gupta empire. He ruled between 375 and 415 C.E. This is when the Gupta empire was at its height. This period of time is often referred to as the Golden Age of India. Some achievements of the Gupta include:

Standardized Money

For prosperity in the arts and science, someone needs to fund the work. Typically, wealthy families or governments provide this type of support. Chandragupta II valued this prosperity and helped pay for research, experiments, and artistic projects. Archaeologists have even found coins created by the Gupta government. There is also evidence that these coins were mass-produced and that a complex tax structure on businesses helped support the empire and its people.

Decimal Numeral System

The most important mathematical achievement during the Gupta Empire was the invention of the decimal system, with zero as a value. Due to extensive trade, the Indian numeral system was brought to China and the Middle East. This system helped create many of the mathematical achievements the world has come to discover.

Medicine

It is believed the Gupta Empire had perhaps the best medical system and knowledge in the world. Medical experiments were common. Doctors learned to sterilize wounds and stop infections from happening. The construction of hospitals, production of surgical instruments, invention of medicines, and use of vaccinations were also common. Significant medical achievements included a smallpox vaccine and types of reconstructive surgery.

title: The Proclamation of 1763
text:
The Proclamation of 1763 created a legal boundary between British colonies and American Indian tribes. The proclamation stated that any lands west of the Appalachian Mountains were reserved for American Indian tribes. Lands east of the mountains belonged to the British. The tribes thought they had secured their homelands, but British colonists bitterly criticized the agreement. The colonists stated they needed those lands more than the tribes. The proclamation would be a major grievance the colonists would cite against the British king and be a step towards the colonists claiming their independence from the crown.

In the summer of 1763, the Great Lakes tribes of the Odawa, Ojibway, Shawnee, Miami, Delaware, Seneca, Potawatomi, Sauk, Fox, Huron, and others fought back against the British. The tribes argued that France had no right to give away their lands. The tribes, under an Odawa war chief named Pontiac, planned multiple attacks throughout the Great Lakes on British forts. The tribes were able to take nine of 13 British forts in 1763. The two major forts, Fort Pitt and Fort Detroit, never fell to tribal forces. The tribes’ victories made the British realize the tribes could not be pushed around. Pontiac’s War officially ended in 1764. An agreement had to be made with the tribes in order to have peace.

title: The 72nd Pennsylvania Infantry Regiment
text:
The 72nd Pennsylvania Infantry Regiment was a group of volunteer soldiers who served in the Union Army. Infantry refers to soldiers who are trained to fight on foot. Many of these soldiers were firefighters from Philadelphia. The 72nd was involved in many battles during the Civil War. These included battles in Antietam, the Overland Campaign, and Gettysburg. At Gettysburg, they defended an area known as “the Angle” and helped defeat the Confederate forces there. They also helped stop “Pickett’s Charge,” when the Confederate Army attempted to take Cemetery Hill from Union control. The 72nd's soldiers helped secure the Union Army’s defenses, and the Confederate Army was stopped.

The surviving members of the 72nd Infantry Regiment wanted a monument built to honor and remember their role in the battle. The correct placement of a monument was important to the soldiers who fought there. The former soldiers wanted their monument placed exactly where they fought. Many did not agree with the planned location of their monument. They took the group responsible for placing the monument to court. The case made it all the way to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, the highest court in the state. The former soldiers of the 72nd Infantry won their court battle. Their monument was placed where they wanted it on the battlefield as part of the Gettysburg National Military Park.

title: Renewable Resources
text: Natural resources can be either renewable or nonrenewable. Renewable resources are those that can be replaced. Trees are an example of a renewable resource. New trees can be planted to replace those we cut down. However, renewable resources also need to be used wisely. It takes time to replace them. Some trees, for example, take many years to grow.

title: Nonrenewable Resources
text: Nonrenewable resources are resources that cannot be easily replaced. Oil and natural gas are two examples of nonrenewable resources. It took millions of years to form these resources. Once we use them all up, they are gone forever. It's important to learn to conserve, protect, and use our natural resources wisely. That way, there will be enough for future generations to use. Conserving our natural resources also helps us protect the environment.

title: Mining
text:
Mining means digging into the ground to get useful rocks and minerals. A mineral is a natural resource that forms inside the Earth’s crust. There are many kinds of minerals. Some examples are coal, dolomite, and salt. Diamonds and gold are minerals, too. Limestone and sandstone are rocks. Miners dig tunnels or pits into the earth so they can reach the minerals and rocks.

Then, they use machines and tools to take them out of the ground. People in other industries can use the rocks and minerals to make things. For example, more than 60 minerals are needed to make a single computer. Minerals can also become part of automobiles, jewelry, vitamins, and much more.

title: Manufacturing
text: Manufacturing is the business of creating goods. It often happens in factories. Workers use machines to process natural resources into new products. Most factories use machines to process, or change, resources. One Toledo factory might take trees and turn them into paper. Another factory might use steel, rubber, and glass to make cars. Wool from sheep can be turned into clothing at a factory in Cleveland. A factory in Cincinnati may also make goetta from grains and pork.

title: Agriculture
text: Agriculture is another word for farming. It is about growing crops and raising animals. Farmers need healthy soil, clean water, and good weather. These are natural resources. Farmers grow the plants that we eat, such as corn, wheat, and apples. Farmers also raise animals that give us things like milk and eggs. These goods are considered natural resources as well. They can be sold to grocery stores. They can also be sold to bakeries and restaurants. There, these resources may be used to make other products, such as bread and apple pie.

title: The Middle Passage
text:
In the first 300 years after Columbus reached the Americas, ships that crossed the Atlantic almost always came from Europe. However, most didn’t sail straight from Europe to the Americas. The sea currents and wind directions made sailing south toward Africa easier and faster than sailing directly west across the Atlantic. This route presented opportunities for trade by staying near the continents. European traders found a market with the nations in West Africa.

This voyage from Europe to Africa was called the Outward Passage. Ships carried tools, weapons, cloth, and other goods to Africa. Merchants and soldiers would pressure African leaders to trade those goods for people who had been captured in wars or kidnapped.

These people were imprisoned and held as products to be traded. The European traders did not care about the welfare of the people they considered “cargo.” These men, women, and children were put in dark, dank ships. The living conditions were inhumane. The traders who held them against their will were transporting them to be sold to new enslavers in the West Indies and American colonies. The voyage from Africa to the colonies in the Western Hemisphere was called “the Middle Passage.”

No words can describe the terror and hopelessness felt by the African men, women, and children who experienced the Middle Passage. Nothing can justify the choices the European traders and colonists made in the past to ruin so many lives.

We study history to learn from it. We can learn about the people who experienced the Middle Passage and what they faced.

title: Physical Characteristics
text:
Physical characteristics describe the natural environment of an area. These characteristics include landforms, bodies of water, and climate. Examples of landforms are mountains, plains, valleys, and deltas. Bodies of water include rivers, lakes, and oceans.

Earth’s physical characteristics are shaped over time. Wind, rain, drought, volcanoes, and earthquakes all help shape Earth's surface. Geographers use physical characteristics to describe a place. Physical characteristics make the different places on Earth interesting and unique!

A physical map shows the major physical characteristics of a place. Look at the physical maps of the United States and Ohio. Can you locate the rivers? Can you identify the surrounding oceans?

title: Essential Question
text: What are physical characteristics?

title: Rivers, Lakes, and Oceans
text:
Water is a natural resource. Water can change landforms. The water from different mountain streams connects to form a river. Rivers are flowing bodies of water. This means the water in them moves. Rivers connect to form larger rivers. Rivers usually make routes from the mountains toward lakes or oceans. Lakes are large areas filled with water. They are surrounded by land. Unlike rivers, the water in lakes tends to remain still or move very slowly. Oceans are bodies of salt water. Oceans cover most of the Earth's surface.

The edge of the land beside a stream or river is called a bank, or shore. The edge of the land beside the ocean is called a coast. Coasts are often many miles long. Coasts make up the border between continents and oceans.

title: Plains
text:
A plain is a landform that is mostly flat. It has few or no trees at all. Plains grow a lot of grass. Ice and water often leave soil and rocks on land’s surface. This is what causes plains to form. Lava flow can also deposit soil and rocks to create a plain. This often happens when a volcano erupts.

Ohio used to be covered by a large sheet of ice known as a glacier. As the glacier melted, it left behind a plain. A plain left behind by a melting glacier is called a till plain.

title: Plateaus
text:
The word “plateau” is from an old French word that means level, or flat. It describes a mountain that is flat at its peak. The core of the Earth is very hot. Rocks close to that core are melted. They are called “magma.” Sometimes, magma flows toward the surface of the Earth and pushes it upward. This creates a plateau.

The Allegheny Plateau goes through Ohio and other states.

title: Essential Question
text: Why is it important to use different sources to study the past?

title: Human Characteristics
text: Human characteristics include the number of people who live in a place and their ideas. People make choices about where to live. They use their ideas to build the place. People make choices on how to meet their basic needs. They meet their needs by using the physical features of the place. The way people build their homes is part of the human characteristics of a place. So are the clothes they wear and the foods they eat. A new park in your neighborhood is a human characteristic. Our transportation systems are too. Human characteristics tell us about people and culture.

title: Essential Question
text: What are human characteristics?

title: A Geographer
text:
A geographer thinks about people and how they live and work in their environment. This year, you have studied the importance of location, place, human-environment interaction, and movement in geography. These help us ask and answer important questions about the world and its people. We use them to organize our thinking about the world into spatial terms through different tools. These include maps, globes, graphs, diagrams, aerial and other photographs, and other geographical representations.

You have also learned about the importance of culture. Culture is the beliefs, traditions, and celebrations of a group of people. You have learned about the different characteristics of culture. These are architecture, language, arts and literature, religion and beliefs, celebrations, food, and clothing.

Understanding the importance of location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, and culture will help you to become a responsible global citizen.

title: An Economist
text:
This year you have studied different aspects of economics, just like an economist. An economist studies money and finance. They look at money and production of goods and services in a community. They also look at a community's resources. Economists use the information to make claims about the economy. This helps people make responsible financial choices.

You have learned about economic principles. These are identifying needs and wants, types of resources, various economic activities, production of goods and services, and ways to earn income.
