title: A Problem Solver
text:
Problems are part of our everyday lives. You will face challenges and obstacles throughout your life. Some will be small, while others require more extensive thinking and planning to solve. It is important to remember that all problems have a solution. Being a problem solver requires creative thinking. Creative thinkers are people who are not afraid to try different solutions to solve a problem.

You have the power to overcome obstacles, create solutions to a problem, and make a difference. When you work to solve problems, you can help yourself and others. This can make your life and the lives of others better in many ways. You can make a difference in your family, school, community, and the world. Keep working for the common good, and use the knowledge you learned this year to make a difference!

title: Louisiana’s First Inhabitants
text:
Archaeologists and historians estimate that the first groups of Indigenous people settled in Louisiana around 11,500 B.C.E. Archaeologists and historians refer to these people as the Paleo-Indians. The Paleo-Indians were nomadic and traveled in search of food, shelter, and resources. The Paleo-Indian culture gradually became more advanced over many generations. As the culture became more advanced, different groups, or tribes, formed. Tribes developed their own customs, traditions, language, and government.

Louisiana’s Paleo-Indian period lasted from 11,500 to 8500 B.C.E. and was followed by the Archaic Period. This was the longest of the three prehistoric Indigenous periods in North America and lasted for about 8,000 years. Archaic peoples were less nomadic than their ancestors. They stayed in places longer and used more resources from their environment before moving on to other settlements. The agricultural revolution in North America also encouraged Archaic peoples to stay in settlements longer than their ancestors. Archaic peoples also developed new tools, weapons, and cultural practices that dramatically changed the way they lived.

One of the greatest changes that occurred in Louisiana during the Archaic period was the introduction of mound building. Louisiana is home to the oldest mounds constructed by Indigenous peoples in North America. They range from single mounds to large complexes with multiple mounds. Tribes began to create more permanent settlements near these mound complexes. Archaeologists and historians have learned much about life in Archaic Louisiana by studying these mounds and the artifacts left behind by the people who built and occupied them.

title: Week 24 Framing Question
text: How did values and beliefs shape Louisiana's first societies?

title: Archaic Period
text:
The Archaic period began in North America in 8000 B.C.E. and lasted until 800 B.C.E. Archaeologists divide this period into three smaller subperiods:

Early Archaic period (8000–6000 B.C.E.)

Middle Archaic period (6000–2000 B.C.E.)

Late Archaic period (2000–800 B.C.E.)

This was a period of great change in Louisiana and North America. The environment and geography changed dramatically. As the Ice Age ended, icebergs began to melt, and sea levels rose. The Archaic peoples of Louisiana moved further inland. Environmental changes impacted the wildlife and vegetation in many areas of North America. The Indigenous peoples of the continent adapted to these changes and adopted new techniques for hunting, gathering, and growing food.

New tools and technological innovations were developed during the Archaic period. The Indigenous peoples of North America continued to use the Clovis points developed during the Paleo-Indian period, but they adapted them for short-range throwing and to use with the atlatl. During this period, tribes began to use stone tools not used by their ancestors. They also used stones to grind seeds, grains, and nuts to make flour and eventually bread. Archaeologists have found evidence that the Indigenous peoples of North America began to make and use clay vessels for cooking during the Archaic Period.

The clothing of the Indigenous peoples reflected the environment where they lived. Groups that lived in Louisiana wore lighter clothing made of plant fibers and thinner animal skins, like deer. People living in colder climates made clothing from animal skins that would provide more warmth, such as bison, rabbit, elk, and bear.

Archaic peoples were semi-nomadic. They continued to travel in search of resources but stayed in settlements for longer periods of time than their Paleo-Indian ancestors. Archaic groups continued to utilize natural shelters, such as caves, but they also constructed small, dome-shaped homes. These homes were built using small trees called saplings. The saplings were bent until the poles met at the top. Then, the saplings were tied or fastened together. The frame was then covered with mats woven together from grasses and reeds.

During the late Archaic period, the Indigenous peoples of Louisiana began to make ornamental items that archaeologists believe were used for important occasions or ceremonies. While excavating different sites, archaeologists found beads made from stone, copper, and clay. They have also found many clay and stone figurines carved into the shapes of people and pendants carved to resemble insects, birds, small tools, and geometric shapes. These artifacts are some of the oldest examples of art created by the Archaic peoples of Louisiana.

title: San Patrice Culture
text:
The cultural group that followed the Clovis culture was the San Patrice culture. This culture emerged and flourished during the early Archaic period. As archaeologists began to excavate Archaic Indian sites in northern Louisiana, they uncovered hundreds of spear points that were different from Clovis spear points. Archaeologists quickly realized that this was evidence of a different Archaic culture that inhabited the area. The name “San Patrice'' was given to this culture because the first spear points were found by archaeologists in the San Patrice stream, located south of Shreveport, Louisiana.

The San Patrice people lived near streams and rivers because of the number of valuable resources in the area. They used gravel and stone found in streams and rivers to make tools. Another distinct tool of the San Patrice culture was the Albany side-scraper. This tool was used for carving and cutting. The San Patrice people also created tools from other resources that were readily available in their environment, including animal bones, shells, and wood. These tools were primarily used for hunting.

The San Patrice people were not as nomadic as their ancestors. They moved between a few settlements throughout the year. The primary source of food for the San Patrice culture was hunting and fishing, but they also gathered wild plants, nuts, and berries. Archaeologists have not found evidence of extensive trade in Louisiana during this time. This has led experts to believe that the San Patrice people of Louisiana relied on their environment to meet all of their needs.

title: Evans Culture
text:
Another culture that thrived in Louisiana during the Archaic period was the Evans culture. The Evans culture flourished between 3400 and 2800 B.C.E. The Evans culture lived in settlements in northeastern Louisiana. The San Patrice and Evans cultures are similar, but there are distinct differences between the two. Archaeologists have been able to tell the difference between these two cultures because of the shape of the spear points they carved. San Patrice spear points each had one notch carved into the base to secure it to the handle. The Evans spear points each had two notches carved into both sides of the base to secure the point to the handle.

The Evans culture relied heavily on the rivers, streams, and lakes of Louisiana for food and resources. Archaeologists have found the remains of shellfish, fish, and marine mammals and reptiles at sites where the Evans culture lived. They estimate that fish and shellfish made up about 80 percent of their diets. Archaeologists have also found evidence to show that the people of the Evans culture hunted small mammals and deer for food. They also gathered acorns, nuts, and berries to build their food supply.

The Evans culture was the first group of Indigenous people in North America to construct large earthen mounds. The oldest Evans culture mounds are located in East Baton Rouge Parish. Archaeologists estimate that “Mound A,” located at this site, was built around 5000 B.C.E. Over the years, these mounds have worn away due to erosion or have been demolished to make way for farms, homes, and buildings. Despite the time and the destruction of many mounds, there are still more than 800 mounds throughout Louisiana, many of which were constructed by the Evans culture.

title: Watson Brake
text:
The most well-known of the mounds constructed by members of the Evans culture are the Watson Brake Mounds. Construction of the Watson Brake Mounds began around 3500 B.C.E. They are the oldest earthwork mounds in North America and some of the oldest surviving structures in the world. They are even older than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt and the Great Wall of China!

The Watson Brake Mounds are located in northeastern Louisiana, near present-day Monroe, near the Ouachita River. There are 11 mounds in the complex, ranging from one to 25 feet tall. The mounds were constructed close to each other to form an oval shape and are connected by earthen ridges. To build each mound, the Evans culture gathered stone, gravel, and dirt from the local area. Then, they sculpted the material they collected into mounds or hills. Ridges were constructed of the same material to connect the mounds.

Through excavations of the site, archaeologists have determined that many of the mounds were built in multiple phases over several years. Some of the smaller mounds were built in one phase. Artifacts found at the site prove that the Watson Brake Mounds were occupied year-round. They were used as gathering places and served as a settlement complex for the people of the Evans culture.

Archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of artifacts at the Watson Brake Mounds that provide evidence of what life was like for the people of Evans culture. These artifacts include remains of over 50 plant and animal species that made up the diet of the people who lived there. Archaeologists have also found tools, bone fishhooks, and stone beads. The people of the Watson Brake Mounds were among the first people to make beads in Louisiana. They used these beads for ceremonial purposes and to make jewelry.

Today, archaeologists continue to study the site to learn more about the ancient peoples of Louisiana.

title: Mound Building
text:
During the Archaic period, different cultures across North America constructed thousands of earthen mounds. These mounds served different purposes for various cultures. Some mounds were built for burial purposes. Others were built for ceremonial reasons. Whatever the purpose, earthen mounds are an example of the engineering ability of the ancient peoples of North America.

The Mound Builders, also known as the Mississippians, lived in the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys from about 1000 to 1700 C.E. Also called the Temple Mound Builders or the Mound Builders, no one knows for sure where they came from. This culture received its name from the raised mounds found in the ruins of its ancient cities. One of the largest settlements was found in Illinois. It was called Cahokia. At its peak, the city of Cahokia had a population of between 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. The remnants of Cahokia stand today as the Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site.

The Fort Ancient people of Ohio constructed one of the most well-known mounds in North America. Serpent Mound is located in present-day Adams County, Ohio. A smaller mound was originally constructed by the Adena people about 2,000 years ago but was repaired and enlarged by the Fort Ancient people around 1100 C.E. The mound is over 1,300 feet long and is 20 to 25 feet wide. Archaeologists believe that the mound was constructed to honor the snake, which was an important animal in many native cultures.

Louisiana is home to over 800 archaeological sites with earthen mounds. They are found throughout the state, but the majority are located in northeast Louisiana. The largest of the ancient mounds found in Louisiana is Mound A at Poverty Point in West Carroll Parish. Mound A is over 70 feet tall and 700 feet long! Thousands of people visit the site each year to learn more about the ancient peoples of Louisiana.

title: A Proprietary Charter
text:
A colonial charter could be given to an individual by the monarch. This type of charter was known as a “proprietary charter.” A proprietor is an owner of property. The charter gave a person the rights to land in America. The monarch gave up all ownership or claim to the land. Being the owner of the land, the proprietor could sell or keep any parts of the colony.

The borders laid out in the charter were important because they showed the extent of the land the proprietor owned. When borders were not specific, it led to conflict between colonies.

The proprietor could also decide what type of government would lead the colony. The government had to honor the rights of Englishmen, provide representation for the people, and not go against the king. This meant that the proprietor could be the governor of the colony, or the proprietor could choose someone else to be their representative. The governor would then have a council or legislative body to advise him and report from the people. The authority of the council would depend on whether the proprietor wanted to give them authority.

Taxes in the colonies were set by the charter. In a proprietary colony, certain taxes went to the proprietor. Taxes could only be generated if the land had people. People paid taxes and produced goods and services. Many proprietary colonies gave away land to motivate people to settle and live there.

Some taxes would go to the British government. To attract people to live in America, however, the king also exempted colonists from paying taxes. This meant colonists were not taxed by the British government for a period of years.

The charter also gave the proprietor the choice of who could settle in the colony. William Penn chose to open Pennsylvania to all people, regardless of their religion. The Calverts chose to open Maryland only to people of the Catholic faith. The proprietor determined the businesses, products, and services in their colony.

The colonies that were established by proprietors included New York, New Hampshire, Maryland, North Carolina, New Jersey, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania.

title: A Royal Charter
text:
In a royal charter, the monarch gave themselves a colony. The charter defined the boundaries of the colony that would most benefit the monarch. Sometimes, boundaries overlapped with previous boundaries set by a previous charter. This ultimately led to conflict, which the monarch would resolve.

A royal charter defined the government structure of the colony. The colonists would have the rights of Englishmen and some form of representation to be their voice in the colony. The monarch would appoint a royal governor to be the crown’s representative in the colony. The royal governor would have the authority of the king in the colony. There would be some type of council of men who were elected by the people to give counsel to the royal governor. The royal governor did not have to heed anything the council said. The royal governor could also suspend or dissolve the representative council.

In Virginia, this council was called the House of Burgesses. In the New England Colonies, there were town meetings and town councils.

The monarch could encourage people to live in a royal colony with land giveaways, tax exemptions, and other means to populate the colony to generate goods and services. The monarch determined the religion that would be followed in the colony. As the head of the Anglican Church of England, the monarch would choose the Anglican church to be the official religion of a royal colony. At the beginning, this influenced who came to live in the colonies, but eventually, other protestant religions were tolerated.

Taxes were determined by the monarch. There were rarely individual taxes in a royal colony. The monarch wanted the taxes from the import and export of goods and services. The royal governor would appoint tax collectors and customs house officials as part of his duties.

New York and Georgia began as royal charter colonies. Eventually, the king revoked (took away) many company charters to give royal authority to the colony. This proved to be in the best interest of the monarch.

title: Running for Office
text:
In the United States, voters elect people to represent them in their local, state, and national governments. The people who want to be elected to government positions are called candidates. Candidates need to meet official requirements for the government job, or office, they want. Different offices have different requirements. Here are the requirements for two important government offices:

President of the United States

Citizenship

Born in the United States

Age

At least 35 years old

Residency

Lived in the U.S. for at least 14 years

Governor of Louisiana

Citizenship

U.S. citizen for at least 5 years

Age

At least 25 years old

Residency

Lived in Louisiana for at least seven years

The requirements for the U.S. president are written in the United States Constitution. Requirements for Louisiana governor are written in the Louisiana state constitution. Counties, cities, and towns often have their own candidate requirements.

Before election day, candidates spend a lot of time campaigning. This means they let voters know who they are, what they believe, and what they would like to do if they win the election. They might use signs, flyers, billboards, and commercials to campaign. They also give speeches and often have debates with other candidates. Many candidates choose to run for office as part of a political party. Political parties are groups of people who share similar political values and goals. The United States has many political parties. The two main parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. Candidates can also be independent, which means they don’t have a political party.

After the election is over, candidates learn whether they won or lost. The candidate who wins is responsible for representing their constituents. Constituents are the citizens who live in an election area. Whether a constituent voted for a representative or not, they can petition their elected representative to take action to meet the community’s needs.

title: Civil Rights Activists
text:
Thanks to civil rights activists, African Americans gained more representation in the fields of education, business, and politics. Between the mid-1960s and the early 1970s, schools, offices, and governments began to change from mostly white to multiracial.

Edward Brooke of Massachusetts became the first African American to be elected to the U.S. Senate in more than 85 years. Thurgood Marshall was sworn in as the first African American Supreme Court Justice. Johnny Ford became the first African American mayor of a city with more than 10,000 people.

Many African Americans were also hired as police officers, firefighters, and teachers during the 1960s.

title: The Civil Rights Acts
text:
The Civil Rights Act of 1964

Because of the work of civil rights workers of all races, life was getting better for African Americans. Their actions caused Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964. This made segregation of all public places illegal. It allowed all children, regardless of race, to attend any public school and play in any public park. It meant that African Americans could enter all restaurants through the front doors. They did not have to drink water from different fountains. The law also made it illegal for employers to refuse to hire someone because of their race.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965

The Selma-to-Montgomery March in Alabama drew attention to the need for voting rights. Not long after the march, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act of 1965. This law made it illegal for states to make people take tests or pay poll taxes in order to vote. After the Voting Rights Act, states were still allowed to make up their own rules for voter registration. But those new rules could not take away the rights now guaranteed by the Voting Rights Act.

The Civil Rights Act of 1968

The first Civil Rights Act changed many things. However, African Americans still faced discrimination when they looked for places to live. In 1968, Congress passed a new Civil Rights Act. It was called the Open Housing Act. This law made it illegal for anyone to be denied the right to buy or rent homes because of race. As a result, African Americans could choose to live wherever they wanted to live. Slowly, neighborhoods across America began to be more integrated.

title: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Martin Luther King Jr. was born on Jan. 15, 1929. He followed the examples of his father and grandfather, who were both Baptist pastors. King graduated from high school at age 15. He earned numerous college degrees, including a Ph.D. from Boston University. In 1954, he became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. There, he began organizing and working for the Civil Rights Movement. King soon became recognized nationally as a leader of the movement. He continued his efforts, wrote numerous articles, and led peaceful protests and marches. He gave countless speeches, including his famous “I Have a Dream” speech during the historic March on Washington in 1963. In 1964, King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. On April 4, 1968, he was in Memphis, Tennessee, preparing to lead another protest, when he was assassinated.

title: Ruby Bridges
text:
Ruby Bridges was born in Mississippi in 1954. When she was only six years old, she changed the world. Bridges was an African American girl who integrated an all-white school in New Orleans in 1960. Bridges and other children had to take a test to determine if they could go to the all-white schools. Bridges passed the test. The New Orleans school board delayed her first day of school until November. The white public did not want African American students to go to their schools.

When Bridges tried to go to class, many people tried to keep her out and were yelling at her. Four federal marshals were sent to the school to escort her to class. Once inside, she had her own classroom and teacher. None of the white parents would allow their children to go to the same school as Bridges. A woman named Barbara Henry was the only person who wanted to be her teacher. Henry and Bridges met each school day for the rest of the year.

What does Ruby say about all this today? She says that when she was six, she had no idea why people hated each other. She didn't understand what desegregation was; she just wanted to go to school. Today, she still fights for civil rights.

title: Jackie Robinson
text:
“The right of every American to first-class citizenship is the most important issue of our time.”

- Jackie Robinson

Jackie Robinson grew up with four siblings in Cairo, Georgia. His mother worked hard to provide for their family. Robinson did not have much growing up, but that did not stop him from finishing school and becoming an athlete.

Robinson served in the U.S. Army during WWII. While riding a bus on the military base, he was asked to move to the back of the bus. Robinson refused. The bus driver had Robinson arrested.

When Robinson left the Army, he went back to playing baseball. In the 1940s, baseball teams were segregated. Robinson soon made headlines when he was the first African American player to play on a white team, called the Montreal Royals.

People treated Robinson badly. Some teams even said they would not play against the Royals if he was on their team. Robinson did not let that stop him from playing the game he loved. Soon, he was invited to join the Brooklyn Dodgers. He played for the team for nine years.

When Robinson stopped playing baseball, he continued to work for the rights of African American people. He started the Freedom Bank of Harlem and worked for the NAACP. He wrote articles for local newspapers and gave speeches on equal rights. He never stopped working “for the right of every American to a first-class citizenship.”

“Jackie Robinson made my success possible,” said Martin Luther King Jr. “Without him, I would never have been able to do what I did.”

title: Week 29 Framing Question
text: How did everyday people encourage change?

title: The Cold War and the Space Race
text:
After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union competed for power and influence. Each country wanted to spread its way of doing things to other countries. The United States and the Soviet Union had very different ideas about how a country should work. They disagreed about how the economy and government of a country should work.

Even though these two countries didn't agree, they never actually fought one another. Their conflict became known as the Cold War. This war was “cold” because there was no fighting between soldiers. Instead, the two countries found other ways to challenge and compete with each other.

The countries competed with rocket technology. They developed new rockets. These rockets made it possible to send things and people into space. This competition was known as the “Space Race.” Each country wanted to be the first to send things into space. First, the countries sent satellites into space. Then they sent animals. Finally, they sent people into space.

In the Space Race, the United States focused on putting a person on the moon. The United States created the Gemini missions. These missions were designed to prepare for a manned trip to the moon.

The Soviet Union could not develop a rocket strong enough to reach the moon. The United States was able to create the Saturn V rocket. This rocket was powerful enough to reach the moon. On July 21, 1969, U.S. astronaut Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the moon. The two countries continued to improve their capabilities in space. But putting a man on the moon is the moment when the United States “won” the Space Race.

title: The Space Race Timeline
text:
USSR

Oct. 4, 1957: first artificial satellite (Sputnik 1)

Nov. 3, 1957: First animal on spacecraft (Sputnik 2 with dog Laika)

March 1960: First cosmonauts were selected.

April 12, 1961: first human orbit; Yury Gagarin (Vostok 6)

June 16-19, 1963: first woman in space; Valentina Tereshkova (Vostok 6)

Oct. 12, 1964: first multi-person spacecraft (Voskhod 1)

title: Television and Space Exploration
text:
Before the Cold War, technology was not readily available. In 1950, less than 10 percent of American homes had a television set. By 1955, nearly 70 percent of homes had one. Television made information more available to audiences faster than ever before. The government often used television broadcasts to discuss news from around the world.

Television brought images of world events right into American homes. People were able to see events live, or as they happened. Information was shared. News programs became very popular. People could learn about current events. Television allowed people to watch astronauts land on the moon. Around 600 million people watched this historic event take place.

title: The First Men in Space
text:
On Oct. 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik I. Shortly after, they launched the first human into space. His name was Yuri Gagarin.

When the Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft into orbit, Americans were shocked. The Space Race had just begun, and they were already behind! In 1961, President John F. Kennedy made an announcement. He said that the U.S. planned to land a man on the moon. The Soviet Union responded by being the first to send an animal into space. The race was on!

On Feb. 20, 1962, John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. This was one of the first steps toward landing a man on the moon.

Feb. 20, 2012, was the 50th anniversary of John Glenn’s first orbit. Glenn was honored for his courage to travel into space at Cape Canaveral in Florida.

title: One Small Step for Man ...
text:
In October 1958, the United States formed the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. This program was called NASA for short. It was formed to research and create ways to explore space.

The people at NASA worked hard for 10 years. Their work made it so the United States was ready to send a man to the moon. On July 20, 1969, millions of people turned on their televisions and radios. They watched a special broadcast that changed history. About 240,000 miles from Earth, Neil A. Armstrong prepared to step foot on the moon. Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin watched from inside Apollo 11 while Armstrong slowly moved out of the spaceship.

Armstrong stepped down the exit ladder. He looked through the bubble of his space helmet at the moon’s surface. With one last step, Armstrong pushed off the bottom of the ladder and landed both feet on the moon. He was the first person in history to accomplish this task.

Millions of people around the world watched as Armstrong stepped foot on the moon. Armstrong said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind," as he made his way across the lunar surface.

These missions also served as test runs for the various maneuvers that the spacecraft and astronauts would have to perform during their trip to the moon and back. Orbiting Earth and the moon, as well as reentering the Earth’s atmosphere, had to be performed precisely and accurately.

title: Separate but Equal
text:
In 1896, the U.S. Supreme Court decided that racial segregation was constitutional. Racial segregation was the separation of white Americans and Black Americans in public facilities. The requirement was that the separate facilities had to be of equal quality.

After the Civil War ended, many African Americans lived in very poor conditions. Many African Americans in the South were sharecroppers. Sharecroppers grew crops and gave up part of their crops as rent. Entire families worked to make enough money to meet their basic needs. Many children in these families worked beside their parents. This meant they could not go to school.

During this time, many people, Black and white, worked to make things better for African American children. In the 1930s, a businessman named Julius Rosenwald established a fund. His goal was to improve the education of African Americans. He wanted to build schools in rural areas. Septima Clark, an African American teacher, created Citizenship Schools in 1957. These schools helped African Americans learn to read. Knowing how to read meant that they could qualify to vote. Many southern cities required voters to be able to read.

Efforts to change laws and provide equal opportunities for all students regardless of race continued. In 1954, the Supreme Court heard a case, Brown v. Board of Education. This case led to the desegregation of schools. This decision faced opposition. It would take many years to desegregate schools.

title: Week 28 Framing Question
text: What were some key events in the Civil Rights Movement?

title: Civil Disobedience: Rosa Parks
text:
Rosa Parks was heading home after work in 1955. The African American woman got on a city bus. The public bus had clearly marked seating for white people and African American passengers. Parks sat in the African American section for the ride home. Passengers continued to board the bus. The seats for white people filled up. The bus driver told Parks and three other African American passengers to give their seats to white passengers. Parks refused to give up her seat. She was arrested for refusing the orders of the bus driver. What Parks did was civil disobedience.

Civil disobedience is when a citizen refuses to obey certain laws or commands of a legal authority. When a citizen practices civil disobedience, they accept the consequences. Civil disobedience is used to call attention to a law that many feel is unjust.

In reaction to Rosa Parks's arrest, African Americans in Montgomery, Alabama boycotted the city bus system. The boycott was led by a minister named Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Parks remained a leader in the civil rights struggle. She is remembered as the “mother of the Civil Rights Movement.”

title: Civil Disobedience: Greensboro Sit-In
text:
Five years after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, four African American college students decided to get something to eat. They left their college campus and headed to a lunch counter at a local store in the town of Greensboro, North Carolina. No one paid attention to the young men as they entered the store. It was open to customers of all races. The lunch counter in the store, however, was for white customers only. The four students sat down at the lunch counter. They asked the server to take their order. The other customers were shocked. The server reminded them that the lunch counter was segregated. This meant that African Americans were not allowed to eat there. The students were asked to leave, but they silently remained where they were.

When the store closed for the evening, the Greensboro students left peacefully. The following day, the group of four students brought more people to sit at the lunch counter. The sit-in lasted for many days. Both African Americans and white people participated. Some people even taunted and harassed them. In other cities across the South, thousands of people held the same types of demonstrations. There was a set of rules for those who wanted to participate. They were instructed to follow these instructions exactly:

Do not:

1. Strike back nor curse if abused.

2. Laugh out.

3. Hold conversations with the floor walker [store supervisor].

4. Leave your seat until your leader has given you permission to do so.

5. Block entrances to stores outside nor the aisles inside.

Do:

1. Show yourself friendly and courteous at all times.

2. Sit straight; always face the counter.

3. Report all serious incidents to your leader.

4. Refer information seekers to your leader in a polite manner.

5. Remember the teachings of Jesus Christ, Mahatma Gandhi, and Martin Luther King. Love and nonviolence is the way.

These examples illustrate the force for change that can come from standing up (or sitting in) against injustice.

title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
text:
Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing the bus driver’s request to give up her bus seat to a white person. A prominent African American civil rights leader, E.D. Nixon, decided that Parks should be the central figure of legal action. His goal was to overturn Montgomery’s segregation laws. At the same time, other civil rights leaders decided to attack the laws using different methods.

An African American women's civil rights group called the Women’s Political Council organized a boycott of the bus system. A boycott is a voluntary refusal to buy goods or use services from a specific person or organization. In Montgomery, 75 percent of the city’s bus riders were African American. That was about 40,000 people. On December 5, 1955, all of those people refused to ride the buses. They started a boycott. At the end of the day, civil rights leaders met, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. They decided to continue the boycott until the city met their demands.

With the majority of Montgomery bus riders refusing to board, the bus company began to lose money. The city still wouldn't change the laws. The boycott went on for over a year. Finally, in December 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court supported a lower court’s decision on segregation. The lower court had decided that segregated seating on buses violated the 14th Amendment to the Constitution. Part of the 14th Amendment guarantees equal treatment under the law. The court said that this meant all riders should be treated the same. All seats had to be open to all riders. This was the successful ending to the 381-day boycott.

title: Freedom Riders
text:
The Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) revived the Freedom Riders initiative in 1961. They wanted to test the Supreme Court decision that said segregation in buses was unconstitutional. African American and white riders began their trip in Washington, D.C. They planned to travel through the southern states to New Orleans. African American riders would attempt to use white-only restrooms, lunch counters, and waiting areas along the way.

The ride was fairly uneventful through Virginia and North Carolina. When the riders reached Rock Hill, South Carolina, an African American rider named John Lewis, a white rider named Albert Bigelow, and another African American rider tried to enter a whites-only waiting room. These three were confronted by white people waiting in the terminal and a fight broke out.

As the ride continued, the group split onto two buses, a Trailways bus and a Greyhound bus. When the Greyhound bus arrived in Anniston, Alabama, a mob of white people was waiting at the bus terminal. The driver kept driving past the terminal. The mob followed in cars. The tires on the bus were blown out. When the bus stopped, someone started the bus on fire. The Freedom Riders all escaped, but then they were attacked by the mob. The Trailways bus riders also met with mob violence when they reached Birmingham, Alabama, and again in Montgomery, Alabama.

Photographs of what was happening to the Freedom Riders were printed in newspapers and broadcast on television. The nation’s attention was drawn to what was happening. Pressure from the government and the shocked public resulted in regulations established by the Interstate Commerce Commission to be respected. There were no more segregated facilities in bus terminals.

title: The Mayflower Compact
text:
The Mayflower Compact was only 166 words long, but it is one of the most famous documents from early American history. A compact is an agreement or contract between individuals or groups of people. Why was the Mayflower Compact so important to Plymouth Colony?

The Pilgrims’ ship was supposed to land in the chartered area of Virginia. Instead, the ship landed in a place not legally governed by the Virginia Company. Pilgrim leaders realized that if they didn’t set up some temporary rules, there would be no order, and the colony might fail. The 41 adult male passengers and crew came together and created a set of laws that everyone would agree to obey. All of the men signed the document. Women were not allowed to sign. At the time, only men made the rules in government.

The Mayflower Compact is an example of self-government. Self-government means people work together to pass laws for themselves that benefit all citizens. This is the central idea behind our government today.

The settlers lived up to the Compact, and the colony survived. One year later, a man named John Pierce expanded the Mayflower Compact so the English government would support it. The Mayflower Compact continued to be used to govern Plymouth Colony for more than 70 years.

title: The Kingdom of Songhai
text:
At the height of its power, the Kingdom of Songhai was an empire covering a large swath of land south of the Sahara. Its capital city, Gao, was located on the Niger River. Prior to its rise as an empire, Gao and Songhai were conquered by the Mali king Mansa Musa in the early 1300s. The area remained under the control of the Mali Empire until Mansa Musa’s death.

In 1464, a Songhai leader named Sunni Ali expanded the borders of the kingdom and began taking territory from Mali. Timbuktu, a major center of trade in the region, fell under Songhai control, as did the Niger River. With these victories, Sunni Ali was able to expand his influence along the Niger River valley. Eventually, the Songhai Empire extended from the Sahara in the east to the Atlantic Ocean in the west, making it the largest empire in West Africa before European colonization.

Gao served as the center of political power in the Songhai Empire. For over 100 years, monarchs ruled over the empire from within the walls of Gao. Control of Timbuktu and the Niger River allowed the Songhai to exert their influence throughout the region. Merchants and traders traveled along the river and through Timbuktu with their goods. Songhai warriors traversed the rivers in canoes to capture additional territory.

In 1493, a new king came to power in the Songhai Empire. Muhammad Ture established the Askia dynasty at this time and brought about a thriving period for the kingdom. His successes earned him the name Askia the Great. While early additions to the empire were accomplished through conflict, Muhammad Ture used diplomacy. He is credited with expanding trade beyond the Songhai borders. He also established new schools and grew the impressive university in Timbuktu.

The prosperity of the Songhai Empire was threatened by power struggles from within. Before he could pass his position to one of his sons, one of them took the throne from Muhammad Ture. From there, brothers fought brothers, and rulers were replaced frequently. The instability during this time weakened the Songhai Empire. The internal fighting crippled their control over the kingdoms they had conquered. Eventually, the Songhai Empire was invaded and defeated by forces from Morocco to the north in 1591.

title: Government and Leaders
text:
The Songhai Empire’s government was a monarchy. Kings ruled over the kingdom, and as it expanded, the empire. There were several dynasties during the height of the Songhai Empire as sons took over for their fathers. Power was passed down through the family until a new ruler defeated them and took over. This process is how the Songhai Empire came to be the dominant power in West Africa.

The Songhai Kingdom was established as a monarchy long before it became an empire. Sunni Ali began the Sunni dynasty when he defeated the Mali Empire in battle and expanded the kingdom’s territory. As Sunni Ali conquered neighboring kingdoms, the Songhai Kingdom became an empire, ruling over other people. As its leader, Sunni Ali held absolute power over the empire. When Sunni Ali died, his son took over. The only way to become the leader of the empire was to be the son of the king or to take the throne through force.

Perhaps the greatest ruler of the Songhai Empire was Muhammad Ture. Due to his many accomplishments and the prosperity that the Songhai enjoyed during his reign, he was known as Askia the Great. The word Askia was what rulers of the Songhai Empire became known by, just as other cultures used King or Pharaoh. Ture restructured the Songhai government. He appointed a variety of officials to take care of the many administrative tasks that running the empire required.

title: Trade
text:
The expansion of the Songhai Empire was driven by trade. Goods and resources traveled along the Niger River and overland through cities like Gao and Timbuktu. One of Sunni Ali’s goals in conquering neighboring kingdoms was to control the trade routes and benefit from the great material wealth that was passing through the region. His strong military allowed him to protect his vast trading network.

Natural resources were traded throughout the Songhai Empire and with outside kingdoms. Farmers and fishermen provided food for the region’s inhabitants. Minerals and metals like gold and salt traveled along the trade route within the Songhai Empire and north to the people living north of the Sahara. The gold was mined in West Africa, and the salt came from the Sahara Desert. Other natural resources like copper, iron, and nuts, in addition to crops and fish, were traded within the Songhai Empire and with neighboring kingdoms. Accounts from the time period also mention animal products like cattle, milk, and butter as well.

Artisans and merchants also traded manufactured goods. Items made of ivory, gold, copper, and more were crafted by skilled artisans. Merchants bought and sold these items throughout the region, especially in large cities like Gao and Timbuktu. The safety of these merchants and traders was important to the success of the empire, so a strong military was maintained to provide security along the trade routes.

title: Wars and Invasions
text:
During its reign as the most powerful empire in West Africa, the Songhai Empire engaged in several internal wars and endured invasions. Because the Songhai Empire was a monarchy, the only way to become the leader was to fight the current leader and overthrow him. This happened with relative frequency following the reign of Sunni Ali. His son was quickly challenged and defeated, which led to the rise of Muhammad Ture and the Askia dynasty.

During the Askia dynasty, there continued to be internal unrest and fighting. Ture's sons overthrew him and fought amongst themselves for control of the empire. Brothers killed brothers in the ensuing wars. Periodically, a leader would emerge and guide the empire through a relatively calm period. Soon though, the infighting and rebellions would return. The empire suffered through successful and unsuccessful revolts. This chaotic time eventually led to the weakening of the Songhai Empire.

Focused on protecting their power in Songhai, the leaders were unable to maintain their hold on the outer edges of the empire. With their attention divided, they were unable to defend against an invasion by Moroccan forces in 1591. This defeat signaled the end of the Songhai Empire as the major power in West Africa. Shortly after this loss, European powers like the Dutch and Portuguese gained more influence over the region and eventually began colonizing the area.

title: Other West African Kingdoms
text:
The Songhai Empire brought together many different kingdoms of West Africa under the control of one leader. However, before and after the Songhai Empire, these kingdoms and others existed and thrived in West Africa. Sometimes these kingdoms were a part of the Songhai Empire and other times they maintained their independence.

One was the Benin kingdom of the rainforest, which was famous for its bronze artwork and wooden crafts, like sculptures and masks. When Europeans came to the area, Benin traded with the Portuguese and the Dutch. The kingdom of Benin existed for many years until the British took it over in the 1800s. Today, the Benin people are independent once more and live in the country of Nigeria.

The Yauri Kingdom was also located in Nigeria. The kingdom was supported by the Niger River and the smaller streams that connected to it. The geography of this area is excellent for agriculture. The area’s beneficial geography attracted multiple groups of people that populated the Yauri Kingdom.

The Asante Kingdom in the southern region of West Africa held valuable gold mines. This provided the kingdom with great wealth. The people of the Asante Kingdom were known as the Akan people. The wealth of the Asante Kingdom brought the attention of European countries as the colonization of Africa began. The boundaries of the kingdom were located near where the modern-day country of Ghana is today.

title: Comparing Kingdoms
text:
Despite their common location in West Africa, the kingdoms of this region had many differences. The geography of West Africa is diverse. The various kingdoms had access to different resources and biomes, which influenced their lifestyles, cultures, and economies.

Some kingdoms, like Benin, were located in forested areas. These kingdoms had access to different kinds of woods from many species of trees. Other kingdoms, like the Asante Kingdom, had access to areas with valuable mineral resources, like gold. Still others inhabited areas along the major rivers, like the Niger River. The Songhai used the river to transport goods and move soldiers around the kingdom quickly. The Yauri benefitted from the fertile land provided by the region’s rivers.

West African kingdoms also differed in their traditions and religions. Many practiced traditional customs that had been passed down through the generations. Others adopted customs and religions they came in contact with or that their leaders adopted. Muhammad Ture, leader of the Songhai Kingdom, solidified the Muslim religion in the kingdom. In the Yauri Kingdom, the various ethnic groups adopted Islam, Christianity, or maintained their traditional religious beliefs and practices.

title: The Inca Empire
text:
The Inca Empire was one of the largest empires in the world from around 1400 C.E. until its end in 1533 C.E. The Inca lived in and around the Andes Mountains and called their empire Tahuantinsuyu. This translates to “four quarters,” which is how they divided their government. The empire had a population of 10 million people that spoke 30 different languages.

The expansion of the Inca Empire started slowly, through diplomacy and maintaining good relationships with the people and governments around them. However, when that failed, the Inca went to war. Their empire began to expand rapidly through conquest. To prevent uprisings from occurring among the people they conquered, the Inca relocated them from their homes into new territories that were unfamiliar to them, with foreign languages. This strategy prevented conquered people from organizing uprisings.

Stretching more than 2,500 miles from Santiago, Chile, in the south to Quito, Ecuador, in the north, the Inca Empire was truly massive. Inca engineers solved the problem of communicating over this great distance by creating highways that ran along the tops of the mountains and along the coast. Teams of runners could deliver a message 1,200 miles away in less than a week.

The supreme ruler of the Inca was called the Sapa Inca and lived a life of luxury in a magnificent palace. The Sapa Inca ruled over an extensive political and social system. By the time the empire had reached its peak, the government employed a large group of politicians, which included four governors who ruled over the four quarters, or Tahuantinsuyu.

The Inca borrowed advancements and technologies that had been developed during earlier civilizations, including building pyramids, temples, and elaborate terraced farms. The Inca worshiped several gods, chief among them the sun god. Mummification and sacrifice were important parts of religious worship for the Inca. Inca mathematicians based their calculations on the number 10, including a decimal system.

title: Timeline
text:
1100–1400 C.E.: The Chimú Empire exists in the northern area of Peru.

c. 1100 C.E.: The Inca settle the Cuzco Valley.

1438 C.E.: Pachacuti defeats the Chanca people.

c. 1450 C.E.: Pachacuti begins to build Machu Picchu.

1463 C.E.: The Chimú Empire is conquered by the Inca.

1493 C.E.: Huayna Capac becomes Sapa Inca.

1526 C.E.: Huayna Capac dies and civil war begins between his sons, Atahualpa and Huascar.

1530 C.E.: Atahualpa defeats Huascar.

1531 C.E.: The Spanish, led by Francisco Pizzaro, arrive in the Inca Empire.

1532 C.E.: Atahualpa is captured by the Spanish at Cajamarca.

1533 C.E.: Cuzco, the capital, is captured by the Spanish.

title: Week 17 Framing Question
text: How did the Inca keep such a large empire united?

title: Pachacuti: Founder of the Inca Empire
text:
Pachacuti is considered to be the founder of the Inca Empire. The Inca had been settled in the Cuzco Valley for hundreds of years when a new group, the Chanca, threatened the Incas’ home in Cuzco. Pachacuti’s father, King Viracocha, was losing a long battle. King Viracocha decided to abandon the city with his older son and heir, Urcon. Pachacuti, whose name may be translated as Earth Shaker, knew that most of the people in Cuzco would likely be killed. He refused to leave the city and decided to defend it.

Pachacuti asked the gods for help and then recruited soldiers for the fight. When the battle was over, the Inca had won under Pachacuti’s leadership. Eventually, King Viracocha acknowledged Pachacuti’s victory and leadership. Pachacuti gave himself the title of Sapa Inca, which was the highest position of leadership. He began his conquest of neighboring villages. Pachacuti offered citizenship in the Inca Empire to those who surrendered without resistance. He allowed local leaders to stay in power, but only if they were loyal to him. If people refused, Pachacuti’s soldiers attacked.

Pachacuti’s strong central government was centered in the capital city of Cuzco. He directed everyone in his empire to practice the same religion and learn the same language, Quechua. He had workers build one of the greatest road systems in the world. All the main roads led to the capital city, Cuzco. People who traveled on the Inca roads carried messages and goods across deserts and mountains to all parts of the empire. The Inca built bridges over rivers and gorges. Their common language, religion, and roads all helped unite the people of Pachacuti’s empire.

The empire was supported by farmers who used terraces, irrigation, and fertilizer to grow huge amounts of crops to feed the people. Under Pachacuti’s rule, the Inca built schools and beautiful palaces. In Cuzco, Pachacuti built a massive temple to the sun god, named Inti, the most important god in the religion of the Inca. The temple was filled with gold. It was the belief of the Inca that gold was the sweat of the sun. Gold and silver were not used as money but only for religious purposes. He was also responsible for building the famous city Machu Picchu, which means “Old Mountain” or “Old Peak” in the Quechua language.

title: Conquest
text:
After Pachacuti took over the leadership from his father, King Viracocha, he quickly began to turn the kingdom of the Inca into one of the world’s most powerful empires. Under Pachacuti’s rule, the empire grew throughout the Andes Mountains until it covered much of modern-day Peru, Ecuador, and Chile. At its greatest point in the 1520s, the Inca Empire stretched from present-day Chile to Ecuador.

After defeating the Chanca, Pachacuti moved to conquer the Colla people, who lived in the Lake Titicaca region, which is located on the modern-day border of Peru and Bolivia. Next was Arequipa, to the south of Cuzco. Pachacuti and, eventually, his son, Tupac Yupanqui, would conquer the Chimú Empire and its capital city, Chan Chan. The empire would stretch as far north as Quito and as far south as modern-day Santiago, Chile.

When a group of people resisted the army of Pachacuti, they were treated brutally. However, when they accepted the army of the Inca without resistance, they were treated much more kindly. The people were able to keep their local religion and were often given gifts. The people who were in power were given privileged positions within the empire. In order to keep order in conquered territory, the Inca built administrative or military outposts. Depending on whether or not the conquered people were accepting or rebellious changed the outposts’ purpose from administrative to military.

Sometimes if a rebellion was intense enough, the Inca king himself would come with the military and attempt to squash the rebellion. This happened in the early 1500s when Huayna Capac, the Inca king at the time, traveled to Quito to try and quell the rebellion there. He eventually got sick and died, and his sons began a civil war to see who would become the next Sapa Inca.

title: Political System
text:
The Sapa Inca was the supreme ruler over the empire and its people. The Inca believed that the Sapa Inca was the literal son of the god, Inti. Inti was the sun god. As the son of Inti, the Sapa Inca was believed to be a god. He had special powers that allowed him to intervene with the sun and made him vital to the agricultural harvest. The Sapa Inca hosted daily feasts and was revered as a god, which meant that no one could touch him, and no one could approach him without a gift. The Sapa Inca was also taken care of in the afterlife. When a ruler died, they were mummified and then brought out at public events, all dressed up, to serve as a “consultant” to the current Sapa Inca. Their status as a god made them immortal.

The four quarters of the empire, or Tahuantinsuyu, were administered by four apo. These governors were close relatives of the Sapa Inca. They were the administrators of their quarters, but they also served as advisors to the ultimate ruler, the Sapa Inca. As the empire grew, the four quarters were divided even further into eight provinces. In each of the provinces, administrators existed, usually working out of an administrative or military outpost. One of their main tasks was to keep a census of the people so that they could contribute to the labor tax, called the mit’a.

Cuzco was the capital of the empire. It was a large city with a population of somewhere around 100,000 people. Cuzco was divided into two sections: the hanan, or the upper city, and the hurin, or the lower city. This was a social and political division. Usually the Sapa Inca and his family came from hanan Cuzco.

title: Mit’a System
text:
The economic and tax system that existed in the Inca Empire was unique. Money was not used. Precious metals like gold and silver that were used as coinage and money in other parts of the world were considered to be sacred religious objects among the Inca. Gold was the sweat of the sun god. Silver was considered to be the tears of the moon goddess. Gold and silver were formed into religious objects and placed in temples. People in the Inca Empire did not buy goods but traded with members of their kinship groups, called ayllus, for the goods they needed or wanted.

Since there wasn’t any currency in the empire, the government did not tax people for money. It did not even tax people for their goods. The tax system that existed in the Inca Empire was a labor tax system called the mit’a. The government kept track of all of the people in their empire with an extensive census-taking system. The Inca did not have a written language, but they did have a system of record keeping, called quipus. Quipus were knotted strings tied together. Historians believed that quipus held all kinds of information, including harvests, astronomical observations, important dates, and the census. After each person was counted, they were required to work on behalf of the empire and Sapa Inca.

In the mit’a system, a person could farm, herd llamas, or build a road or a temple. People also offered military service or worked in mining operations. The type of labor you gave depended on where you lived, if you were from a rebellious portion of the empire, and what your social status was. The empire divided all land into thirds. No matter where you lived in the Inca empire, one-third of the land was set apart for the Sapa Inca, one-third was set aside for religion and temples, and the final third was set aside for the people. If your mit’a was offered by farming or herding, you worked on the Sapa Inca’s land or on temple land.

title: The Woodland Period
text:
The Woodland Period lasted from 800 B.C.E. to 1200 C.E. with early, middle, and late subperiods. The Woodland Period marked a shift from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to a more sedentary lifestyle of living and growing crops in one area. The plants they began to grow included crops such as squash, sunflowers, maygrass, and others.

These early farming communities started out small, with no more than two or three family groups. Over time, the communities grew to larger populations. Cultural groups, such as the Adena and Hopewell, began building large earthwork structures for various purposes, such as burials, ceremonies, and homes. Several of the sites where these people lived can still be seen and visited today.

In addition to farming and building earthwork structures, people also began to dabble in creating pottery. Designs and ingredients varied from region to region, but it suggests that American Indian groups were living in more permanent settlements. During the late Woodland period, the atlatl was replaced with the bow and arrow. Large spear points were replaced by stone arrowheads. The bow and arrow made hunting easier, but the new tool also became a weapon of war.

What we know about these ancient peoples is limited to what we can learn from the artifacts they left behind and the structures they built. Large trade networks developed, and culture and language spread in addition to resources between different groups of people.

title: Introduction to Ancient North America
text:
As civilizations rose and fell in the Near East, India, Africa, and the Mediterranean, new cultural groups and civilizations were forming in North America. Beginning around 30,000 B.C.E., groups of people left Asia and migrated to North America, settling in present-day Alaska and Canada. Experts refer to these people as Paleo-Indians. They traveled from place to place in search of food, shelter, and resources. The Paleo-Indian culture gradually became more advanced over many generations. With advancements in their culture, their children's children became separate groups, or tribes. The Paleo-Indian period lasted until approximately 8,500 B.C.E.

The period that followed is often referred to as the Archaic Period. The Archaic people were the direct descendants of the Paleo-Indians, but they were different in many ways. Archaic peoples formed larger groups than their ancestors and created larger settlements. Later, Archaic groups began to farm and grow their own crops during the agricultural revolution in North America.

The Archaic period was followed by the Woodland Period, which began in 800 B.C.E. The Woodland Period lasted until about 1200 C.E. During the Woodland Period, the Indigenous peoples of North America formed larger tribes than those of the Archaic Indians. They began to create more permanent settlements and engaged in widespread agriculture. Hunting became easier with the introduction of the bow and arrow. The Woodland people also engaged in trade to obtain the resources they needed.
