title: Geography of North America
text:
The continent of North America encompasses an area of over nine million square miles. It extends from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Isthmus of Panama in the south. Today, North America is divided into 23 different countries, including the United States, but in ancient times, it was one continuous mass of land.

North America is surrounded by multiple bodies of water. The Atlantic Ocean borders the eastern coast of the continent. The Pacific Ocean borders the west coast of the continent. Several smaller bodies of water also surround North America, including gulfs and bays. One of the largest is the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf of Mexico is a large body of water that feeds into the Atlantic Ocean. It is located between Mexico and the southeastern coast of the United States, bordering several modern-day states, including Louisiana.

The geography and landforms of North America vary greatly throughout the continent. Two major mountain ranges dominate North America. The Appalachian Mountains are located in the eastern part of North America. They extend south from Canada to Georgia. The highest peak is Mount Mitchell at 6,684 feet. The Rocky Mountain range is the biggest mountain range in North America. It begins in Canada and extends through central New Mexico. Many of the peaks are more than 12,000 feet high. Mount Elbert in Colorado is the tallest peak in the range at 14,433 feet.

Rivers have played a vital role in the history, economy, and actions of governments in North America for thousands of years. One of the most important is the Mississippi River. The Mississippi River is the second-longest river in North America. Its name comes from a Chippewa word meaning "Father of Waters." The Mississippi River formed when glaciers melted about 12,000 years ago. The Mississippi River is nearly 2,400 miles long and runs through 10 states before it pours into the Gulf of Mexico. Like the Nile River, the Mississippi River has a large delta where the Mississippi meets the Gulf of Mexico. The river’s delta is a large, swampy area. This area is considered a wetland. Wetlands are areas of land where water covers the soil at varying levels year-round.

Another defining geographic feature of North America is the Yucatán Peninsula. The Yucatán Peninsula is the easternmost region of Mexico. It is surrounded by water on three sides by the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. This area of North America has sandy soil and little surface water. Much of the water in this area is found underground, in natural aquifers. An aquifer is an underground reservoir of fresh water.

title: Migration to the Americas
text:
Before European exploration and colonization, thousands of Indigenous people lived in the Americas and the Caribbean Islands. However, their ancestors were not originally from these regions. Historians, scientists, and archaeologists have developed many theories to explain how Native Americans first arrived in the Western Hemisphere.

For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of the Indigenous peoples who lived in the Americas before exploration and colonization came to America from Siberia, a region in northern Asia. They concluded that these people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska. This land bridge is known as the Bering Strait. From there, they settled in other areas of North America. Eventually, they migrated to Central and South America and the Caribbean Islands.

In recent years, archaeologists in North and South America have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land-bridge travelers. The bones in particular were very different from those linked to the people who crossed the land bridge. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago. This larger group split into smaller tribes about 15,000 years ago. Some traveled south through the Americas.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people in the Americas traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups represent the earliest ancestors of Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

title: North America
text:
The term “Americas” refers to the continents of North and South America. Together, these continents total over 16 million square miles, which is most of the land in the Western Hemisphere. The term “Americas” comes from the name of a 15th century explorer. In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Spain, Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic.

Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an Italian merchant, navigator, and explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim. “America” is a Latinized version of Amerigo’s name.

The inhabitants or groups of people from a specific place are often referred to by the continent where they live or their native continent. For example, people from Europe are often called Europeans. However, this is not the case for the people of the Americas. The term “American” refers to a native or someone who lives in the United States. The term “American” was commonly used during the colonial era to differentiate between English colonists living in the North American colonies and those living in England. This is where the name “the United States of America” originates.

People from other countries in North America are referred to by the country they live in. For example, people from Canada are called Canadians. People who are from Mexico are often referred to as Mexicans. If someone says they are from Latin America, they are referring to Central and South America. This is because the most common languages spoken in these areas are Spanish and Portuguese. These languages are rooted in Latin, which was the language spoken across the Roman Empire.

title: Archaeology in Louisiana
text:
How do we know what life was like thousands of years ago? How do we know anything about their lives? People leave clues that help us understand them long after they are gone. Sometimes, ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind innovations we still use today. Some of these include crops, like corn, and medicines. People left behind objects they made, too. We call this archaeological evidence.

An archaeologist studies things left behind by people who lived a long time ago. Some objects, called artifacts, get covered by earth or water for thousands of years. Archaeologists often recognize patterns. They may see differences between earlier objects and later, more advanced ones. They may find evidence of trade by tracking the movement of similar artifacts. At archaeological sites, or places where there is evidence of past human activity, they also study structures and human-made features. Features like fireplaces or storage pits can also help scientists imagine what daily life in ancient cultures was like.

Archaeologists in Louisiana have learned much about the ancient Indigenous people who once inhabited the area through archeological digs. The largest archeological site in Louisiana is the Poverty Point National Monument, located in Epps, Louisiana. Since 1962, archaeologists have worked tirelessly to excavate the large network of earthen mounds.

Archaeologists at Poverty Point have learned much about the people who lived at the site by studying the artifacts they left behind. Archaeologists have been able to determine that this site was once a center of trade. They have found objects and materials that are not native to the area, including several tons of rocks used to construct the mounds. They estimate that this material was collected from sites almost 1,000 miles from Poverty Point.

title: Artifacts: Learning About Our History
text:
Archaeologists have found thousands of sites in North America where the ancient peoples of the continent once lived. One of the oldest archaeological sites we know of in North America was found in Cactus Hill, Virginia. Here, archaeologists found evidence of a people known to have lived about 14,000 years ago.

As archaeologists dug deeper, layer by layer, into the earth of Cactus Hill, hundreds of artifacts were uncovered. These pointed to another group of people, dating back around 18,000 years. What piece of evidence suggested that a different group of Indigenous peoples had lived there? The tools were not the same as the ones found in the earth above them. That means that 4,000 years earlier, people camped and cooked and fished in the same place as those who came after them.

Archaeologists have found evidence of long-distance trade among the Indigenous peoples of North America. Two thousand years ago, there was a great city of people located in what is now Ohio and Illinois. Archaeologists have studied the remains of the city. The artifacts tell us that Hopewell was a huge metropolis of people, religions, entertainment, and trade. The variety of trade goods was extensive and came from all over the continent.

Another example of trade that archaeologists have found comes from the Hohokam tribe in what is now Arizona, the ancestral home of the Hohokam tribe. During excavations, archaeologists have found bison hides and seashells. Neither resource comes from Arizona. The hides came from tribes on the Plains. Plains tribes often traded bison robes, dried meat, and tallow with other tribes for corn and squash. The shells came from the Mojave tribe in California. By trading with both groups, the Hohokam became middlemen within a larger trade route. Middlemen took goods from one group to another during trade.

title: Geography of Louisiana
text:
The state of Louisiana stretches over 43,000 square miles. It extends from the Gulf of Mexico in the south to the border of Arkansas in the north. The Sabine River creates a border between Louisiana and Texas. Louisiana shares its eastern border with Mississippi. The geography of Louisiana has distinctly different landforms and waterways. These features provide homes for animals and people. They are sources of food and natural resources.

Bayous

Louisiana is home to over three million acres of bayous. A bayou is a creek or swampy area that usually feeds into a larger body of water. The word “bayou” is a Choctaw word that means “small stream.” Bayous near the coast have brackish water. Brackish water is a mixture of fresh and salt water. They are habitats for plants. This includes mosses, trees, and water celery. Bayous have large amounts of wetlands, which is good for the fishing industry. Nearly 75 percent of the fish and shellfish caught in Louisiana come from wetlands. This includes oysters, crabs, and shrimp.

Salt Domes

Another landform found in Louisiana are salt domes. Salt domes take thousands of years to form. As water from the Gulf of Mexico washes ashore and recedes, it leaves behind a large deposit of salt. This salt gathers underground. When this happens, it creates domes. As the domes grow, they push up the rocks to form salt domes.

Many salt domes are located in the southern part of the state. They can be up to five miles wide. Some salt domes are 10,000 feet deep. Salt domes can be useful. Oil and natural gas are found near or in salt domes, and they are mined frequently around the Gulf of Mexico. Five islands in Louisiana were formed because of salt domes, including Avery, Belle Isle, Cote Blanche, Jefferson, and Weeks.

Coastal Wetlands

Louisiana is home to 40 percent of the wetlands found in the continental United States. Wetlands are areas of land where water covers the soil at varying levels year-round. The majority of Louisiana’s wetlands are located in the coastal areas of the state. The water from the Gulf of Mexico drains into these areas. The coastal wetlands are rich in natural resources. They store carbon and help control floods. Coastal wetlands are also sources of fish and shellfish.

The White Lake Wetlands are located near Lafayette. They are home to different species of birds, including the whooping crane and herons. The Terrebonne Basin, located along Terrebonne Bay, encompasses thousands of acres of swamp and marsh areas. The Terrebonne Basin provides many threatened and endangered animals with a safe habitat to live in, including bald eagles, American alligators, West Indian manatees, and slender glass lizards.

Rivers

There are more than 60 rivers in this state. Rivers are important to Louisiana. They carry water to different areas, provide nutrients for wildlife, and help make the soil fertile. A variety of wildlife lives in and along rivers. This includes catfish, turtles, ducks, dragonflies, and beetles. The most important river in the state is the Mississippi River. At over 2,320 miles long, it is the fourth-longest river in the world. The Mississippi River has been a vital trade route and cradle of resources to the people of Louisiana for thousands of years. Many of Louisiana’s rivers feed into the mighty Mississippi, creating an extensive system of navigable waterways across the state.

Plains

A plain is a large area of flat land with few to no trees. The Gulf Coastal Plain extends from Florida to Mexico along the Gulf of Mexico. Part of the Gulf Coastal Plain is located in Louisiana, near the Gulf of Mexico. It is called the East Gulf Coastal Plain. This area is dominated by marshes and wetlands. The Mississippi River Delta is located in the East Gulf Coastal Plain. This area is home to 37 percent of the country’s estuary marshes. An estuary marsh is a wetland area with high levels of salt and brackish water. Estuaries provide a unique environment for wildlife. They also serve as a buffer area from flooding between coastal areas and large bodies of water.

The physical geography and landforms of Louisiana have provided people with resources to meet their wants and needs for thousands of years. The Indigenous peoples of Louisiana relied on the geography of the area to survive.

title: Resources and Climate
text:
A resource is material people can use. Things like food, air, and water are resources. Resources help people meet their needs and wants. People depend on resources to survive. They need resources to produce goods. A natural resource is something found in nature that people can use. There are many types of natural resources. These include soil, plants, coal, water, natural gas, and even animals. People use natural resources to meet their needs and wants.

Ancient Indigenous peoples in North America relied on the land for food. They hunted, gathered, and farmed for food. Many of the foods Indigenous people ate were based on the seasons. Seasonal crops and hunting patterns played a huge role in community activities. Members of each native group worked together to provide food for their communities. Many of the foods that we enjoy today can be traced back to the crops grown by the Indigenous peoples of North America. These include corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, wild rice, squash, and beans.

Indigenous peoples used natural resources from the land to create clothing. Their clothing represented the natural environment in which they lived. It was practical and reflected the climate where they lived. They used animal products, such as fur, feathers, bones, teeth, and claws to make clothing and jewelry. They also used plants like tree bark and various grasses to make woven fabrics. They wore different forms of clothing for different purposes. Many tribes wore decorative headdresses, masks, and clothing for ceremonies and celebrations.

The resources of an area are often determined and affected by climate. Climate is the average weather conditions of a place over an extended period of time. While the weather can change in just a few hours, climate takes hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years to change. Climate includes the average temperatures, precipitation, and wind in an area. Precipitation includes rain, snow, and sleet. There are five climate zones found on Earth. These are tropical, dry, temperate, continental, and polar.

The climate of Louisiana has changed dramatically over time. During the last ice age, the climate of Louisiana was cold and dry. As the ice age ended, the climate began to change. Today, Louisiana has a humid subtropical climate. This means that the area has long, hot summers and short, mild winters. On average, Louisiana receives from 50-70 inches of precipitation per year. The climate of Louisiana has had a profound impact on the way people in the area have met their wants and needs for thousands of years.

title: Nomadic Societies of Louisiana
text:
Archaeologists and historians estimate that the first groups of ancient peoples migrated to Louisiana as early as 11,500 B.C.E. The ancient Indigenous peoples of Louisiana were nomadic. This means that they traveled from place to place, looking for food and resources.

During the last ice age, the climate of North America was very different than it is today. Sea levels were much lower, including sea levels around Louisiana. Scientists and archaeologists estimate that sea levels around Louisiana were 400 feet lower than they are today. These areas were once filled with ancient cypress tree forests. The ancient nomadic peoples of Louisiana hunted and gathered wild plants, nuts, berries, and honey in these forests.

Because they were nomadic, the ancient Indigenous societies of Louisiana did not establish permanent settlements. They lived in shelters that could be easily transported and that were made from the natural resources of their environment. Hunter-gatherer societies often found shelter in natural rock formations, caves, and overhanging cliffs. This nomadic period of life lasted until about 8000 B.C.E., when groups of ancient peoples began to establish semi-permanent settlements.

title: Seasonal Hunting and Gathering
text:
When you look around your community today, it may seem easy to find food. Grocery stores, restaurants, and even some community gardens carry many of the nutritious things we use to feed ourselves. Stores and restaurants supply many different types of food. Through processes established over a long period of time, people now have ways to ship food from all over the world. Finding food wasn’t always as easy as it is today. Thousands of years ago, people only lived off the animals they could hunt and the plants they could gather in the natural world around them. These people were called hunter-gatherers.

Early hunter-gatherer societies were groups of about 10-12 people that belonged to larger bands. A band is a group of people of the same tribe who are closely connected, often by family ties. Together, these groups hunted wild animals, fished, and searched their environment for nuts, berries, and other edible plants to feed themselves and their families. Hunter-gatherers in coastal areas, including Louisiana, gathered shellfish. Hunter-gatherers were nomadic. Once they used up all the natural resources in one place, they had to move on to another location.

Hunter-gatherer groups also followed large herds of animals, which were used for food and resources. Ancient hunter-gatherer groups followed herds of large animals, including mastodons, wooly mammoths, and giant sloths. When the ice age ended about 9,000 years ago, many of the animals these people hunted went extinct. Hunter-gatherers began hunting different, often smaller, animals, such as deer and antelope. Hunter-gatherers in coastal areas also fished and hunted larger marine animals for food.

Hunter-gatherers relied upon seasonal patterns of plant growth and movement of herds. As animals migrated to warmer areas to prepare for the winter, the ancient Indigenous peoples of North America followed the herds for food and resources. Some plants, berries, and nuts only grow at certain times during the year. Hunter-gatherers found different food sources throughout the year based on what was available where they traveled.

title: New Tools and Practices
text:
As the ancient Indigenous peoples of North America began to adapt to the changing climate and availability of resources, they developed new tools and practices to meet their needs and wants. A new culture emerged during this time, called the Clovis culture. Archaeologists have given this name to a group of ancient Indigenous people who lived across North America, including Louisiana, from 9500 to 8800 B.C.E. The name “Clovis” was given to this culture because the first major archaeological discovery and excavation of this culture took place in Clovis, New Mexico.

The spearpoints discovered in Clovis, New Mexico, were different from others previously found by archaeologists. Clovis spear points were carved from soft or brittle stones, such as flint, obsidian, jasper, or chert. Grooves, called flutes, were carved into the base of each spearhead to hold them in place. This was a revolutionary innovation that had never been used before. Archaeologists have studied spearheads and points from other areas of the world that are older than Clovis points. They can find no other points that are the same shape or made of the same materials as Clovis points. This means that Clovis points were invented in North America.

Another important invention created during this time was the atlatl. The atlatl was used to throw spears farther and faster than they could be thrown by hand. It was made of a thin piece of wood with a notch carved into the end. The spear rested on the notch before it was thrown. The atlatl made it easier to hunt and helped ancient Indigenous people obtain the resources they needed more quickly. They also carved various stone tools, designed for scraping and cutting.

title: The Agricultural Revolution in North America
text:
The agricultural revolution, or Neolithic Revolution, began about 12,000 years ago. During this period of human history, people began to make the transition from hunter-gatherers to more settled societies. They began to build more permanent shelters. They settled beside lakes or rivers, where they could fish and plant seeds and roots in the fertile soil. Gradually, they learned how to clear large areas of land and irrigate the fields to water plants. They tended the trees and gathered fruit. They also learned how to domesticate animals and use them for farming or for food.

The agricultural revolution started at different times in various parts of the world. Archaeologists estimate that the agricultural revolution began in North America around 6000 B.C.E. Some of the earliest instances of farming began in Mesoamerica. The first crop that the ancient peoples of Mesoamerica domesticated was maize or corn. Paleo-Indian groups and tribes in areas of what is now the United States obtained maize through trade. They began to grow the crop themselves, along with sunflowers, squash, and beans.

Paleo and Archaic Indian groups in areas of the American southwest began to develop irrigation systems to water their crops, like the systems of irrigation created in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. Tribes that lived in settlements along the Colorado River dug irrigation canals through the deserts of present-day California, Arizona, Nevada, and Utah to water their crops.

As trade became more widespread throughout the continent, agriculture and farming spread to many more areas of North America. Groups of people living in the eastern parts of North America, particularly along the Atlantic seaboard, began farming different crops around 3800 B.C.E., including corn, sunflowers, squash, gourds, and beans. Because of the rich and abundant resources of the natural environment, agriculture did not become a common practice among the Indigenous peoples of Louisiana until around 900 C.E.

title: Settlements
text:
As societies began to engage in agriculture, they also began to build more permanent settlements. Living in a permanent settlement was much different than life in traditional hunter-gatherer societies. It took time and a larger labor force to build homes, clear the land, and grow crops. As people began to build permanent settlements, groups and tribes began to grow larger. As populations grew, more food and resources were available. This meant people could share what they had. Small settlements got bigger and gradually became villages and towns.

Permanent settlements were developed in Louisiana during the Middle Archaic Period, which lasted from 6000 B.C.E. to 2000 B.C.E. Archaeologists believe that the Indigenous peoples of Louisiana began to form permanent settlements at this time because of evidence found in mound complexes throughout the state. Many of the Archaic groups of Louisiana built large earthen mounds for burials, ceremonies, and as gathering places. They built villages around the mounds. Eventually, these mound complexes became a center of trade and a meeting place for multiple groups.

title: A Return to Europe
text:
The Middle Ages were a difficult time for much of the world, especially Europe. Half of Europe’s population had died as a result of the plague. However, the survivors often found themselves living better than they had before. New questions arose about the power of the Catholic church, and people wanted to have more access to knowledge and learning. Soon, Europe’s population began to grow again, creating more demand for goods and services. This caused the economy to grow. Trade within Europe expanded into Southwest and East Asia.

The feudal system ended in Italy, and a new economic system emerged during the Renaissance. Banks began lending money to middle-class merchants, who were once a part of the peasantry in the feudal system. Credit is money that is loaned to someone and must be paid back. Bankers or credit lenders often require the borrower to pay interest. Interest is extra money added to a loan. Usually, it is a percentage of the amount of money borrowed. In the Renaissance, loans on credit allowed people to build businesses and helped towns and cities to grow economically. Interest allowed banks to become wealthier. Italian banks helped finance Europe’s trade and manufacturing by supplying money or credit to merchants. In this new economic system, merchants could stay in one area and employ other people to sell their goods throughout Europe, Southeast Asia, and East Asia. Italian merchants often specialized by only manufacturing and trading one good. This allowed them to focus on making manufacturing efficient and cheaper, which lowers the cost to the consumer. This often increases the number of consumers that a merchant has. Essentially, specialization helped merchants make more money.

title: Italian Geography
text:
The country of Italy was not united during the 1400s. Power on the Italian peninsula was split between various city-states. A city-state is a city that controls the territory around it politically, economically, and often culturally. Northern and central Italy were divided into 23 city-states. These city-states had populations of 20,000 people or more. The Italian peninsula is surrounded by the Mediterranean Sea, and this location allowed it to become a key location for trade between Asia, Africa, and Europe.

Central Italy was a hub of trade and prosperity during the 1400s and 1500s. The Papal States controlled Rome and the Vatican, where the Pope lived as head of the Roman Catholic Church. The Roman Catholic Church would be a key player in the Renaissance. Northern Italy was home to three of the greatest city-states: Florence, Venice, and Genoa. These areas created luxury goods that were traded between East and Southwestern Asia. Southern Italy was controlled by the Kingdom of Naples, a very wealthy and prosperous area. However, during the Renaissance period, many other countries, such as Spain and France, gained control of this region, causing a slow economic decline.

title: Humanism
text:
The Renaissance is known for reintroducing the ideas and knowledge of classical societies to Europe. These classical societies were the ancient civilizations of Greece and Rome. The start of the Renaissance is often thought to coincide with the publication of three Italian authors: Dante, Petrarch, and Giovanni Boccaccio. After the fall of the Byzantine Empire in the mid-1400s, many Greek scholars left Anatolia and brought classical texts to Europe, especially Italy. The arrival of these texts was celebrated by many, especially Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio. Access to these texts allowed these authors to build up their own libraries with classical texts and reintroduced them to many elements of classical thought.

Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio’s writings highlighted the values and ideas of classical society. These authors began a shift in academic thought: that studying classical art, literature, and knowledge would bring wisdom and virtue to their own society. This shift was called humanism, or the philosophy that education should focus on learning from classical art, literature, and science.

The people who subscribed to humanism were called humanists. Humanists believed that the styles of classical thinking that occurred in Rome and Greece would help their city-states have greater success. Humanists promoted education for everyone and believed anyone could gain knowledge through observation and analysis of the natural world. Art appreciation was encouraged by humanists, as was the study of the skill it took to create realistic figures in marble or bronze.

title: The Renaissance
text:
After the devastation of the Black Death, Europe changed. That change would appear as the birth of a new age we call the Renaissance. The Renaissance, which is French for “rebirth,” was a time in which many people began to think and live differently. Rather than focusing mostly on religion, the Renaissance offered people a chance to learn about other sciences and arts.

The Renaissance began in Italy and soon spread throughout Europe. The Renaissance did not start with a single event or even a single year but was a gradual change that occurred over several centuries. Historians generally place the start of the Renaissance in the 14th century, or the 1300s, and believe it lasted until the 17th century, or the 1600s. It slowly emerged as Crusaders returned from Southwestern Asia after visiting cities like Constantinople and Jerusalem. The people in these cities had preserved and translated Greek and Roman works. So, as the crusaders came home to places like Venice, Florence, Milan, and Genoa, they brought new and rediscovered knowledge with them.

Italian explorer Marco Polo traveled to China in the late 1200s and early 1300s. He brought new insights, knowledge, and goods to Italy. All of this new and rediscovered information slowly changed the culture of Italy. Eventually, a focus on humanism and classical learning emerged in Italy. People began relearning Greek methods of cartography and astronomy by reading Greek and Roman texts. Academic debate flourished as people shared intellectual insights after reading these ancient texts. It was during this time that great artists, such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, worked for wealthy families and produced some of the greatest works of art that are still celebrated today.

title: Florence
text:
Many historians point to a small city named Florence, located 170 miles north of Rome, as the birthplace of the Renaissance. With a population of about 90,000 people, Florence differed from other city-states because its people had many more freedoms, including the ability to participate in government. Many of Florence’s residents were quite wealthy from trade. The Arno River flows through Florence, and when the Florentines conquered Pisa, they had direct access to the Mediterranean Sea. Merchants and bankers were now in possession of great amounts of money, and they were looking for ways to spend it.

Florentines began to spend their money on the arts. Eventually, Florence became known as the new Athens, as Greek and Roman plays and other dramatic works were staged across the city. Renaissance directors sometimes adapted the plays to reflect a more current style of speech and dress. These performances led writers to create their own Florentine tragedies and comedies. The city became a destination for philosophers and artists, for it had long welcomed the free exchange of ideas.

Florence also housed many schools, including a university. A large population of Florentine citizens could read, and this attracted many people from rural areas of Italy to move to Florence. Greek architecture saw a revival in Florence. The bell tower of Palazzo Vecchio was the center of Florentine government, commerce, and banking. Commerce is the exchange of goods between two or more groups. Florence’s banks funded many commercial projects, including textile production. Florentine banking became regarded as the best in Europe, and money flowed into the city. Merchants and others soon had a disposable income. A disposable income can be spent on wants, such as luxury goods and the arts.

title: The Medici Family
text:
Florence attracted many wealthy families, and a new middle class emerged in society. This middle class was created by successful merchants, many of whom had started life in the feudalistic lower classes. The Medici family of Florence were members of this new, merchant middle class. Their fortune was made in textile manufacturing. They would soon wield tremendous power in Florence and across the world. The Medici family used their wealth to support the growth of the arts in Florence and eventually all of Europe over their 300-year dynasty in Florence. They used their position to control the government as well as pursue the arts. The Medicis amassed Europe’s largest library.

Cosimo de' Medici was the first in the Medici political dynasty and lived from 1389 to 1464. He is credited with establishing the Medicis as patrons of the arts, giving money to architects and artists, and providing Florence's first public library. Cosimo's grandson, Lorenzo, proved to be an even larger supporter of the arts. He supported up-and-coming artists, such as Botticelli, who is known for his painting The Birth of Venus. He also supported Michelangelo, who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and sculpted a 17-foot-tall marble statue. This sculpture, David, is based on a man from a story in the Bible. In fact, Michelangelo lived in the home of Lorenzo for three years. The Medici family purchased so many pieces of art that Florence quickly attracted artists who were eager to make a name for themselves. Florence had other influential families, including the Borgia family. Another was the Albizzi family, who were once richer and more powerful than the Medici family.

title: City-States
text:
Italy’s many city-states helped the Renaissance flourish in Italy and across Europe. The money that flowed into these city-states fueled the Renaissance. Trade was the main source of money in Italy, but banking and the textile and manufacturing industries also brought capital. Florence’s power in the textile industry was undisputed, but Venice was another city-state that influenced the rise of the Renaissance in Italy.

Venice sits on the coast of the Adriatic Sea. It was built on 118 islands with buildings constructed on wooden pilings. Except for narrow walkways throughout the city, people use boats to travel Venice's 160 canals. Venice linked sea and land trading routes between the Balkan mountains into the Byzantine Empire before it fell. Along with Venice, Genoa was another coastal trading city. However, it was located on the opposite side of the Italian peninsula, on the Ligurian Sea. Venice and Genoa were also banking centers. Their banks funded merchant expeditions across the Mediterranean Sea and into Asia. Genoa and Venice were also centers of shipbuilding and insurance companies because of their vital role as trade centers between Asia and Europe.

Milan was another city-state that grew and reached economic success during the Renaissance. Because Milan is located in the Po Valley, at the base of the Alps, Milan became a trade center, a middle ground between Italy and the rest of Europe. During the Renaissance, Milan was able to control the trade that happened on land between Italy and Europe and specialized in metal goods, such as armor. Milan also has many waterways and lakes that help give it rich soil for agricultural production.

title: Early Exploration
text:
In the 1400s, the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe all had large, growing kingdoms and empires. Rich empires offered patronage to scholars, merchants, and artists. This meant that richer kingdoms paid people to study, explore, or create art, all for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and the exchange of new ideas through trade and exploration. To aid in the trade and exploration of the Renaissance, a skill was revived, called cartography. Cartography is the production of maps and is a combination of science and art. Maps are vital to trade and exploration. During the Renaissance, the Greek scholar Ptolemy’s writings were rediscovered. Ptolemy was the first person to divide the Earth into a series of grids, called latitude and longitude. These lines are very useful in helping sailors, traders, merchants, and navigators determine their exact location and the direction they should travel. Cartographers in the early and late 1400s quickly set out to make maps featuring these grid lines. These maps with latitude and longitude lines would soon become much more vital as trans-Atlantic trade and travel would be undertaken in the late 1400s and early 1500s.

One of Italy’s early explorers was Marco Polo. Polo belonged to a wealthy merchant family from Venice. He went on his first voyage at the age of 17 and met the ruler of China, Kublai Khan. On this voyage, Polo sailed across the Mediterranean Sea to Southwest Asia. The rest of the journey was an overland trail called the Silk Road, through Persia, the Gobi Desert, and Mongolia, ending in China. Polo impressed Kublai Khan with his interest in the different languages, cultures, and customs of the Mongols. Kublai Khan was a Mongol ruler based in China. He allowed Polo to travel throughout the Mongol Empire, and Polo was considered an ambassador for Kublai Khan. Polo saw and wrote about different cultures and customs of many places in Asia, including the different spices, jewels, and people he encountered. After being away from Venice for 24 years, Polo traveled back home. This journey took him two years. He left China, sailed around India, ventured across Arabia, sailed across the Black Sea, and finally crossed the Mediterranean Sea to Venice. Polo went on to inspire other Europeans with his travels by writing about his experiences. His original book was lost. However, it was translated into many different versions and languages. Marco Polo left a legacy that would connect Europe, Southwest Asia, and East Asia.

title: Letters from a Pennsylvania Farmer
text:
While fighting the French and Indian War in North America, Great Britain also fought a war in Europe. Supplying an army costs a lot of money, and during this short time, Great Britain’s national debt doubled. To pay for these wars, Parliament, or the British government, began directly taxing the American colonies for the first time. Throughout the 1760s, Parliament continued to set heavy taxes on the colonies. These new taxes did not sit well with the colonists.

Parliament felt it had the right to tax the American colonists. They were British citizens, and they relied on their government for many things. The purpose of government is to provide safety and security for those in the community from threats outside the community. A government also provides justice and maintains order within the community. Governments should also help the members of the community meet their wants and needs. In order to provide all this for its citizens, a government needs money. It gets this money through taxes. One colonial citizen, John Dickinson, pointed out that the problem was not with taxes. It was setting taxes on people who had no representation in their government.

Dickinson was a lawyer living in Philadelphia during the 1760s. He owned a great deal of land in Pennsylvania and Delaware. When Parliament began setting taxes on the colonies, Dickinson recognized the economic burden. He also saw a problem with how the taxes were set. In order to explain his position, Dickinson created a fictional character who wrote a total of 12 letters. This character simply signed these letters as “a Farmer.” Newspapers published one letter each week, beginning in December 1767. In the letters Dickinson argued that these taxes were unconstitutional by British law. He urged the colonists to unite in opposing them.

Dickinson agreed that governments should be able to set taxes. He was concerned that the people weren’t represented in the government setting the taxes. When Parliament set a tax on the colonists, there were no representatives from the colonies in Parliament. They could not agree to the taxes or how the money was used. As he stated in the seventh letter, “We are taxed without our own consent, given by ourselves, or our representatives.”

After newspapers printed the letters, all 12 were collected and printed in a pamphlet, or little book. People all over the colonies and Great Britain read Letters from a Pennsylvania Farmer. Dickinson’s aim was to defend the British constitution against what he saw as bad laws. He wanted people to reject the bad laws and try to fix things within the current system. Many of the ideas in his letters caught hold among the colonists in ways he didn’t imagine. The power of the printed word caused Dickinson to be known as the “Penman of the Revolution.”

title: Continental Congress Pennsylvania Representatives
text:
As Parliament set taxes on the colonies, conflict between the British government and colonists grew. The colonists knew they needed a plan to deal with this conflict. The colonies needed to work together. They organized a Continental Congress. The colonies sent delegates, or representatives. These representatives debated, or talked about the actions of the colonies. The first Continental Congress was held in Autumn of 1774. The second operated from 1775 until 1781. The third, from 1781 to 1789, was also the country’s first national government. Nine delegates represented Pennsylvania in the Continental Congress.

title: Diplomacy Before War
text:
After the French and Indian War ended, Parliament taxed the colonies to pay for the war. The colonists were upset that their government continued to set new taxes for them. The colonists protested the taxes. In the beginning, representatives in the local government sent letters of protest to the royal colonial governor. The government failed to respond to the colonists' requests. So, the protests became more intense.

Parliament passed more taxes, like the Stamp Act in 1765. In response, the 13 Colonies organized the Stamp Act Congress. Representatives from the colonies asked for representation in Parliament. The Stamp Act was repealed, or reversed by law. However, Parliament ignored the request for representation.

In 1767, Parliament passed more taxes. Each colony responded by boycotting, or not purchasing British goods. Colonial newspapers published Letters from a Pennsylvania Farmer to support the protest. Parliament continued to enforce taxes and strengthened the authority of the king by sending army troops to the colonies.

In 1773, Parliament put a tax on tea. The colonists responded by destroying tea shipments. In response to the tea parties, Parliament passed many restrictions on the colonial government. This took away the representation of the people. More British troops were sent to the colonies.

In 1774, the colonies formed a Continental Congress to meet in Philadelphia. At this point, Congress continued to say the colonists were loyal to the king.

In 1775, in Massachusetts, armed conflict broke out between the colonists and the British army. Many lives were lost. The Continental Congress assembled again. The Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king, declaring loyalty and hoping for peace. In response, King George III rejected the petition and declared the colonies in a state of rebellion.

title: The British Occupy Philadelphia
text:
During autumn of 1777, the British army was determined to capture the patriot capital Philadelphia. Capturing the capital would threaten the safety of the congress. The British government considered each man who had signed the Declaration of Independence a traitor.

The British army left New York City in 265 ships. The ships sailed south and then north into Chesapeake Bay. The soldiers planned to march from Elkton, Maryland, to Philadelphia. The Continental Army met them along the way. General George Washington led the Continental Army against British General William Howe in the Battle of Brandywine Creek. The Continental army was defeated. This left the route to Philadelphia open for the British.

Word of the British approach reached the people of Philadelphia. Congress moved west to York, Pennsylvania. They sent the Liberty Bell north to Allentown so the British Army could not melt it down and use it for ammunition. The Continental Army went through Philadelphia, taking away anything that could be useful to the British Army. They took blankets, animals, firewood, and food, leaving only enough for the people.

On September 26, 1777, General Howe and the British troops paraded into the city. The former head of the Pennsylvania Assembly, Joseph Galloway, welcomed them. The British spent the winter of 1777-1778 in Philadelphia. They were cut off from receiving many supplies. Prices for food skyrocketed for civilians. The army quartered, or housed, the soldiers in private houses. The army commandeered, or took possession of, food from the surrounding farms. Officers held parties throughout the winter.

Meanwhile, General Washington and the Continental Army were less than 20 miles away in a place called Valley Forge.

title: Franklin's News Network
text:
A young Benjamin Franklin formed a printing partnership with Hugh Meredith in Philadelphia. The two had a successful business. Franklin paid his success forward. He brought in apprentices, or students learning a business. The apprentices learned the newspaper and printing business under Franklin’s instruction. Franklin would then sell printing equipment to the graduated apprentices. They would start their own print shops in other towns. Franklin also set up printers in other colonies.

Each print shop would share news stories with the others. Franklin also sent messengers between all the shops regularly. This provided up-to-date information for each newspaper in the network. Information about colonial assemblies and actions of the Continental Congress was shared rapidly.

This was the first formal media network in the colonies. Connecting all the colonies with the same information helped influence public opinion. Colonists shared the desire for representation in Parliament or independence. Franklin’s network played a key role in the revolution.

title: Patriots, Loyalists, and Quakers
text:
Colonists who supported the war for independence were called Patriots. Patriots supported independence in many ways. Many served in the military. Some got involved in government. They often wrote letters and talked with friends. Patriots often boycotted British goods. They supported the Continental soldiers and provided supplies.

James Forten was 10 years old when he heard the Declaration of Independence read out. When he was 15 years old, he joined the Continental Navy. He was captured and held on a prison ship. Forten was a free Black man from Philadelphia. He grew up believing in the freedom and equality of the Revolution. Forten supported the new nation. Many free Black citizens from Pennsylvania were part of the revolution. Some served in the Continental Army and Navy. After the nation won independence, Forten reached out to other veterans and worked to abolish slavery in Pennsylvania.

Some colonists were loyal to the British king and Parliament. They were called Loyalists. At the beginning of the conflict with Parliament, James Galloway was a member of the first Continental Congress. Galloway was speaker of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives in 1766. Galloway debated with patriot John Adams. Galloway presented a “Plan of Union” to keep the colonies under the government of King George III. The Plan of Union was rejected by Congress in a vote, 6-5. Galloway sent a copy of the plan to Benjamin Franklin. Franklin shared it with members of Parliament. No action was taken.

Galloway moved to New York to escape threats against him and his family. Galloway joined the British Army in 1776. He published many writings supporting the Loyalist cause. Galloway moved to Great Britain in 1778, where he lived for the rest of his life.

The Society of Friends, also known as Quakers, believed in nonviolence. The Quakers would not support military actions. When both British and colonial armies came to Pennsylvania, Quakers stayed neutral, or did not choose sides. Quakers refused to pay taxes that would support an army. Paying money to the Continental Congress would support the cause for independence. Paying money to the king would support the cause of the Loyalists. By not making a choice, many Quakers were persecuted by people on both sides.

title: The Voting Record
text:
Thomas Jefferson wrote “Notes of Proceedings in the Continental Congress” to give future generations a record of what happened in Philadelphia in July 1776. These notes are considered a primary document because they were written by a person who experienced the event. Historians use primary documents to connect with the past. Jefferson’s notes give us a glimpse of what was happening in the Continental Congress at a precise moment in history, Independence Day.

July 1, 1776

The consideration of the original motion made by the delegates of Virginia, [independence from Great Britain]… was carried in the affirmative [agreement] by the votes of N. Hampshire, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode island, N. Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, N. Carolina, & Georgia. S. Carolina and Pennsylvania voted against it. Delaware having but two members present, they were divided: the delegates for New York… were [instructed]… to do nothing…

Mr. Rutlege of S. Carolina then requested the determination might be put off to the next day.

July 2, 1776

The Virginia resolution was again brought for consideration… S. Carolina [agreed] in voting for it. In the meantime a third member had come… from the Delaware counties and turned the vote of that colony in favor of the resolution. Members of a different [opinion] attending that morning from Pennsylvania also, their vote was changed, so that the whole 12 colonies, who were authorized to vote gave their voices for it; and within a few days the convention of N. York approved of it… making the vote for independence unanimous.

Congress then considered the declaration wording. They reviewed and made some changes to Thomas Jefferson’s text.

July 3, 1776

The document for the declaration of independence was revised and officially written for presentation to the congress by Mr. Timothy Matlack, a clerk to the congress.

July 4, 1776

The declaration was reported by the committee, agreed to by the house, and signed by every member present.

title: Evidence
text:
Evidence is information that can help you figure out what is true or not. Evidence can be numbers or words. It can describe something. It can measure something. Evidence is collected by observation and answering questions. It is also collected by counting and measuring. Evidence should be organized to make sense. If it isn’t, it is just a jumble of words, numbers, or pictures. The type and how you collect evidence will depend on your investigation. If your evidence is just observations, you can record it in a list or a table. Your evidence may require you to collect measurements. title: Everyday Life
text:
The Incas didn’t use money. They also didn’t use a market economy. This means that they didn’t make their living through buying and selling goods. So, farmers did not own the land they worked. Most of the food they produced belonged to the community. They paid their “taxes” by spending some of their time working on community construction projects, or serving as soldiers, or mining. In return, they were able to share in the resources the community produced. The government would also provide food at the monthly festivals, maintain the roads and aqueducts, and provide pack animals for transportation.

The Inca people had to live up to high standards. The three most important rules were: Do not steal, do not lie, and do not be lazy. There were even government officials who had the job of making sure people’s houses were clean.

Commoners made up about 90 percent of the Inca population. They rarely traveled, except to festivals in the cities. They spent most of their time working. The children of commoners were not educated. They were simply trained to do their job, whether as farmers or artisans. Sometimes, especially talented or beautiful commoner girls would be chosen to work in the cities as spinners or weavers, since textiles were highly valued. Or they would learn about the Inca religion and work in temples.

The upper classes were priests and government officers. Their children were educated for about four years. They would memorize stories from history and religion. They would learn to do government and religious jobs. They might learn to use a quipu, a series of strings with special knots tied in them. Where and how the knots were tied would convey a message.

People in the upper classes could own land and did not have to pay the labor tax. They wore earplugs made of shell or metal in their earlobes. They would put larger and larger earplugs in until sometimes their earlobes stretched all the way down to their shoulders.

title: The Census
text:
The U.S. census is the count of how many people live in the United States. This count is done every 10 years. A list of questions, called a survey, is sent to every home. If the survey isn’t returned, a census worker visits the home. The worker helps the people living there to fill out the survey. The survey asks who is living at the address. It asks for important information about the people.

The census is important. The U.S. Constitution requires a census. The House of Representatives is based on the number of people in a district or region. Regions grow or shrink in population. This causes the number of representatives to be adjusted.

Census information is made public. People can use census details in many ways. Businesses can determine if they should expand or downsize. Social scientists can use the information to learn about people and communities. Individuals can use census data to find ancestors and family members. Population information is available from every census since 1790. The data is considered a primary source for research.

title: Week 18 Framing Question
text: What did the upper and lower classes of Inca society have in common?

title: Terrace Farming
text:
The Andes provided a good ecosystem for farming, but the land was not very flat. Farmers needed to find a way to work the soil on hillsides. They learned to use the terrain and landforms together with the climate and became very skilled farmers. They developed a technique called step, or terrace, farming. They dug out flat patches of land for farming that made the side of the mountain look like a giant staircase. In order to water their crops, engineers and architects built canals and aqueducts. Aqueducts are human-made structures, usually made from stone, that bring water from one place to another. The Inca also used rainfall and river water to supply an irrigation system.

Farming was very important to the Inca, and they used every available bit of earth to grow their crops through terrace farming. The benefit of terracing farmland was twofold: the Inca were able to grow crops on previously unusable steep hillsides, and they were able to save soil and water by reducing the amount of erosion. Erosion is when soil is removed from its original location by wind or water. Terraces prevent soil from moving through either means: wind or water. The Inca incorporated crop rotation to help the soil recover lost nutrients and added fertilizer to boost crop production. Only growing a crop in one field for a few seasons or rotating which crop grew in which field is called crop rotation.

The Inca used llamas to carry supplies and goods. Llamas were also used for moving valuable metal resources from mines to city centers. Most importantly, llamas were used to support the Inca’s main economic source: farming.

title: Societal Structure
text:
All of Inca society organized themselves into family clans called ayllus. Trade and ancestor worship was conducted within the ayllu. Inca society was divided further into four classes. There was only one person in the top class: the Sapa Inca, or the king. The Sapa Inca was considered to be a god and was treated like one. The Sapa Inca was so important that his old clothing, hair, and nail clippings were saved. These items were used to create huacas, a kind of statue that represented the Sapa Inca whenever he could not be somewhere.

The next class down, the royalty class, was made up of people who were related to the founders of the Inca civilizations by blood. They were direct relatives of the Sapa Inca. They lived in luxury and held the highest governmental and religious positions. For example, the Willac Umu was the high priest. The Incas believed he spoke directly with Inti, the sun god. The king’s first wife, called the Coya, also held much power. Political power in the Inca Empire was hereditary. This meant power stayed within the family. So, future kings were selected from this class of people.

However, as the empire grew, there weren’t enough direct relatives of the Sapa Inca to run the high levels of government and religion. So, some people who were not royalty or blood relatives of the Sapa Inca were brought in to help. They were called Inca-by-privilege.

The next class down was the administrative class. It was made up of people who ran the lower levels of government and religion. For example, when the Incas conquered a group of people, they would often leave the people’s ruler in charge, if that ruler would be obedient to Inca rule. These people were called Curacas. Tax collectors were also a part of this class. They made sure that people contributed their share of labor to the community. Record keepers kept track of how much people contributed and where those contributions were stored. The government would use these contributions to feed the upper classes, the army, and the poor and disabled.

The bottom class, the commoners, was made up of artisans, farmers, and herders. The artisans were considered higher-class than farmers and herders. They forged jewelry, wove cloth, and made pottery. Farmers worked on terraced farms: their own, as well as the fields dedicated to the government and religious purposes. They also worked regularly on government projects, such as roads, aqueducts, and food storage buildings. Herders maintained the llama and alpaca herds. These animals were valued as pack animals as well as for their wool, which the Incas made into warm clothing. Warm clothing was necessary in the Andes Mountains because it got very cold during certain times of the year.

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Like many Mesoamerican cultures, the Inca were polytheistic. They worshiped many gods. Some of these gods included Inti, the sun god; Mamaquilla, known as Mother Moon, who was in charge of the calendar; Illapa, who controlled the weather; and Pachamama, the Earth Mother who protected crops. However, the Incas also sometimes worshiped household gods. These gods were often represented with small carved objects resembling crops or animals. As the Inca Empire expanded, the Inca would allow conquered people to keep their local gods, but it was understood that the Inca gods would be the highest gods.

The Inca were very religious. They had religious festivals every month with a five-day feast at the end of the year. The first festival of the year was meant to initiate boys into manhood. The festival held in June focused on the sun god and marked the beginning of the plowing season. Another festival was held during the rainy season (when there was a lot of sickness). The Incas would shake out their clothes and carry ashes out of their cities to drop in a river. Then they would purify themselves by washing in the river. These rituals helped prevent the sicknesses that the rainy season brought.

Some of their festivals involved human sacrifice. The Incas considered it an honor to be sacrificed to the gods. Some of the world’s best-preserved mummies are Inca human sacrifices. The cool, dry climate of the Andes helped to preserve these mummies.

The Sapa Inca was considered a god. When Sapa Inca died, he would be mummified. The mummified bodies of the Sapa Inca would be stored and brought out for important festivals. The Inca believed that the mummies of their kings would give them wisdom through oracles. An oracle was a priest who sought advice from and spoke for the mummified Sapa Inca and other Inca gods.

Ordinary people also created mummies. Whenever a person died, they were brought to the ancestral burial grounds where their body was preserved. Like the Sapa Inca, these mummies were consulted and brought out for festivals, however, this was only done among the family clan, or ayllu. The worst thing that could happen to a person was to have their dead body burned. The Incas believed burning a body would destroy its vital essence and make it difficult for the person to get to the afterlife, which was a paradise.

title: Oral Traditions
text:
Most cultures have an origin story, describing how the Earth was created and how humans populated it. Since the Incas didn’t have a written language, their origin stories are oral stories. They were passed from one person to another for many centuries.

One origin story talks about a god named Viracocha who originally created the world, but it did not have sun, moon, or stars. At first, he sculpted and painted large, strangely shaped giants to populate the Earth. But they were larger than he was. He decided that wouldn’t be a good idea, so he made them his own size. All these people lived in darkness. Viracocha gave them a commandment, but they broke it. So he turned some of them to stone or had the earth swallow them. Then he sent a flood to drown the rest.

Different groups of people who made up the Incan civilization had different stories about how their ancestors were saved from the flood. Some say their ancestors climbed a mountain that floated on the water. Others said that no one escaped the flood and that Viracocha created entirely new people to populate the land. They said that after the flood, Viracocha created the sun, moon, and stars. Then he painted pictures of various groups of people and told his two servants where to go to summon the people. So the servants traveled around, calling people out of the lakes, springs, valleys, caves, trees, and rocks.

These newly created people all spoke one language. As they moved from place to place, they started to change their language, some of them copying the sounds of animals. When they met up again, they could not understand one another. Some of them could no longer recognize Viracocha and tried to kill him. He brought down fire from the sky to protect himself. Soon, he turned the rule of humans over to lesser gods and disappeared.

title: Machu Picchu
text:
Perched high atop a peak in the Andes Mountains sits one of the most amazing human construction projects ever created. It was an Inca city. It was discovered by chance about 100 years ago, but it had been built nearly seven centuries ago. It is called Machu Picchu. In 2007, it was named one of the new Seven Wonders of the World. It sits nearly 8,000 feet above sea level in the mountains of Peru; the historic Inca city of Cusco is the closest major city.

What it was used for is still a topic of discussion. Most historians believe that Machu Picchu was built by the originator of the empire, Pachacuti. Some believe that a population of 300 to 1,000 people lived in the stone buildings, platforms, and plazas there. The people probably survived by farming the hillsides and growing food in terraced gardens. It was a sacred site for the Inca; its buildings also served as observatories for sky-watching. Astronomy was important to the Inca, and Machu Picchu was built to follow the sun.

The stone structures were built so well that they are expected to stand for hundreds of years more. The builders did not use mortar to hold the stones together, yet the stones seem locked in place with no gaps between them; a knife blade and even a needle can’t pass between two locked stones. This design has helped Machu Picchu’s architecture survive many earthquakes. When a building is built with mortar and an earthquake comes, the mortar crumbles and the building collapses. However, with the Inca design, when an earthquake comes, the rocks can move back and forth against each other and settle back into their original places without cracking or crumbling. There were no wheels to help move the stones up the mountain, so the Inca either had to chisel the rock out of the mountain or push the stone up the mountain, using only human power. It is truly an Andean marvel.

title: Data, Data, Everywhere
text:
The census counts people and collects information about each person who is counted.

Let's look at the questions on the 2020 census:

Who lives in the household?

How are they related to each other?

Age, sex, and race?

Own or rent the house?

Phone number?

The census of 1880 had 26 questions. Questions from 1880 asked for the number of people living in the dwelling as well as their ages, sexes, and races. Other questions included whether the people in the dwelling could read and write. They answered what country they were born in. They also wrote their occupations. In 1880, the most populated city was New York City. Ohio was ranked third in population.

The actual counting of people was done by individuals. This process sometimes took years to finish. In 1890, counting everyone was done using an electronic punch card system. A modern computer was first used in 1950. Today, the use of computers makes the census count go faster. Computers also help share the information collected in tables, charts, and maps.

A line graph shows the increase or decrease of something over time.

A bar graph is used to compare things between different groups.

A pie chart in another method of displaying information. A pie chart is round. It represents the total number of things counted. The slices show parts of the totals. The larger the slice, the greater the number. The smaller the slice, the smaller the number.

A map can also display data. A map can represent larger or smaller numbers by using different colors.

A table chart gives data in columns and rows. Each column and row is labeled with the type of information shown.

title: Mesoamerican Civilizations
text:
For thousands of years, different civilizations developed in Mesoamerica. Mesoamerica is another way of saying Central America. Mesoamerican civilizations included the Olmec, the Maya, the Zapotec, and the Toltec Empires. All were located in Mesoamerica, but more particularly, their homelands centered in modern-day Mexico, although some of them spread further.

These civilizations had many characteristics in common. They all built urban centers and used pyramid architecture. Some pyramids were small, and others very large, but all the civilizations used them as places of religious worship. They served other functions in various societies, but the religious performance was a pyramid’s primary function in all of these civilizations.

These cultures interacted with each other, traded with each other, sharing ideas and goods. However, these civilizations would not just influence their contemporaries, or the civilizations that existed at the same time as their own, but would have influence throughout time. In particular, these cultures and civilizations would influence the Aztec Empire. The Aztecs themselves would credit the cultures and civilizations that preceded them with being the origin of many of their political, religious, architectural, and other cultural ideas.

title: Teotihuacán
text:
Teotihuacán was a Mesoamerican city that was inhabited from around 100 B.C.E. to about 650 C.E. In the Nahuatl language, Teotihuacán means “city of the gods.” This meaning was very literal for many of the people who lived in Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs. They believed that the city was where the gods came to Earth and humanity began. The city was ruled by a religious government. At its height, Teotihuacán was home to 125,000–200,000 people.

The city’s structure and design were planned. Down the center of the city was a long street called the “avenue of the dead.” Three large pyramids were located along the “avenue of the dead.” The Pyramid of the Sun was the largest temple, the Pyramid of the Moon stood about 70–80 feet shorter than the Pyramid of the Sun, and another temple was dedicated to the god Quetzalcoatl. Quetzalcoatl means “feathered-serpent” in Nahuatl. In the Maya language, Quetzalcoatl was named Kukulcán. This god would become a major focus of Toltec and Aztec religious practice after the city of Teotihuacán fell.

One of the unique features of Teotihuacán was that its citizens lived in apartment-style buildings. They were only one story high, but they were all connected in the residential part of the city. Teotihuacan was very colorful. All the buildings were painted with murals. Archaeological evidence shows that the Teotihuacános would plaster the walls of the buildings to make them easier to paint. Some of the buildings also had artistic carvings on their walls.

Teotihuacán became the center of religious practice and the economy of much of Mesoamerica during the height of the city’s power. Archaeologists have studied the bones of people who were buried in Teotihuacán and have found that the city was populated with many immigrants. People who had been born in other parts of Mexico or Guatemala left their homes and came to Teotihuacán to live. Some people worked as merchants, others as soldiers. These people probably came to Teotihuacán for a variety of reasons: they might have come because the city was a religious center and religion was very important to the people living in medieval Mesoamerica. Also, people might have come because Teotihuacán was an economic center for agriculture and trade.

About two-thirds of the people living in Teotihuacán worked in the agricultural fields that surrounded the city. Tradesmen in Teotihuacán made ceramics. They also mined and shaped obsidian tools. Obsidian is a type of rock called volcanic glass that is very hard and very sharp. These characteristics make it a useful tool. In addition to its practical value, obsidian also had religious value. The obsidian found in the mines around Teotihuacán was unique because it had a green sheen to it. Green was an important color in many Central American religions because it represented life. So the green obsidian located at Teotihuacán was highly valued by people across Mesoamerica. Traders sold this obsidian abroad, and archaeologists have found it as far as modern-day Guatemala. Obsidian was one of the trade goods that made Teotihuacán such an important economic power.

Eventually, Teotihuacán’s power faded, and the city was abandoned. Some historians think that part of the reason the city fell was because of political unrest. Evidence shows that the citadel, the portion of the city where the religious and political leaders lived, was burned. Because the burning was limited to that portion of the city, historians think that the people revolted against the religious and political powers of the city. This could be one reason that the city was abandoned.

title: Tula or Tollan
text:
The Toltecs lived from about 850 C.E. to about 1150 C.E. It is unclear where the center of their civilization was. However, Aztec records talk about the capital of the Toltecs, named Tollan or Tula, in Central Mexico. Archaeologists have searched the areas of Mexico that the Aztec records identify as the home of the Toltecs, and they think that the capital of the Toltecs might be an archaeological site near the modern-day city of Tula de Allende.

At the height of Tula, the population would have numbered somewhere between 30,000 and 40,000 people. The layout of the city was very similar to Teotihuacán: there was a main avenue down the center of the city. The city had three temples, one dedicated to the sun and another to the moon, but the largest temple was probably dedicated to Quetzalcoatl. The archaeological site also has a palace complex and two ball courts. The ball game was an important cultural feature of many Mesoamerican civilizations. It was played by men and used for many purposes; sometimes the game even determined the outcome of religious, political, and military events. The city, like Teotihuacán, was colorful and highly decorated. Artisans in Tula created sculptures and paintings of pumas, eagles, and jaguars. All these animals had religious meanings. Artisans also used jade and quetzal feathers to create other religious, decorative objects.

Aztec records talk about a “golden age” of the Toltecs and state that the Toltecs claimed to have descended from the people of Teotihuacán. Being descendants of Teotihuacán gave the Toltecs strong ties to the gods because Teotihuacán was the city of the gods. Consequently, the Aztec claim to be descendants of the Toltecs, which also gave them a strong connection to the gods. One of the other cultural features that the Aztecs believe they inherited from the Toltecs was a religious calendar. The calendar used by the Toltecs came in a 52-year cycle and determined sacrifices, feast days, family organization, and many other features of their culture. This calendar cycle would become a defining feature of Aztec culture.

title: Other Mesoamerican Empires
text:
The Olmec

The Olmec lived in the ancient period of Mesoamerica from about 1100 to 800 B.C.E. The name Olmec means “people of the rubber country” in the Nahuatl language. They got this name because extracting latex rubber from Panama rubber trees was one of the economic activities central to Olmec society. The Olmec had large trading networks as well.

The most prominent archaeological feature of the Olmecs are the large stone heads that range from five to 11 feet tall. Many of these stone heads have helmet-like gear on their heads. Archaeologists believe that these represent the heads of Olmec rulers. The Olmec also built cities and large pyramid architecture. Most historians believe that the Olmec are the originators of many features that existed throughout Mesoamerican cultures down to the Aztecs.

The Maya

The Maya culture existed for many centuries in the modern-day areas of Mexico (the Yucatán was one of the strongest Maya areas in the region), Guatemala, and Belize. The Maya built large cities throughout the areas of their dominance. These cities had monumental architectural structures, such as palaces, plazas, ball courts, and pyramids. The height of Maya building power was from about 250 C.E. to 900 C.E. The people spoke many different dialects of the Mayan language, and, depending on the area or city, the Maya displayed different cultural characteristics. The most prominent cities of the Maya were Tikal, located in northern Guatemala, and Chichen Itza, in the Yucatán. Chichén Itzá has a very similar city layout to Teotihuacán and Tula.

The Zapotec Culture

The Zapotec, or Mixtec Culture, like the Maya, existed for many centuries but reached a peak of power and city building from around 300 C.E. to 900 C.E. One of the largest cities built by the Zapotec was Monte Albán. This city is located in the Oaxaca region of modern-day Mexico, in a mountainous area. Monte Albán has shortened pyramids, or pyramids that look like they’ve been cut off at the base. Monte Albán has a great plaza built on the highest hill of the city. Surrounding the plaza were two temples. The city also has a ball court, and archaeologists have discovered around 170 tombs in the city.

title: The Control of Europe
text:
During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, Europeans mainly belonged to one religion: Roman Catholicism. The Pope ruled the Roman Catholic Church from Vatican City. Vatican City is an independent city within Rome, populated by clergy and church employees. The church had religious and political power throughout the continent. It collected taxes and selected and removed kings.

Some Roman Catholic leaders were tremendously wealthy. There were clergy and other individuals who had authority in the church and lived like kings in lavish palaces, surrounded by expensive art. The clergy gave their friends the jobs with the highest pay and benefits, while the church demanded more taxes from the public to support its clergy and the building of opulent churches. The church even offered indulgences in order to raise more money. An indulgence was money paid to the church to receive forgiveness for breaking the laws of the church. Therefore, if you had money, you were able to afford indulgences and forgiveness. Poor people could not afford to pay for indulgences.

The Roman Catholic Church also had an influence on educational institutions throughout Europe. Throughout the Middle Ages and into the Renaissance Europe was an agricultural society. This meant that the majority of the people farmed or worked on the land to pay for their homes and food. Most people could not afford to go to school or even learn to read and write. This cycle continued as families had to keep their children at home to help with the farm work instead of paying to send them to school. This resulted in a low literacy rate. Literacy is the ability to read and write. These things caused some people to question the power of the church. They began to seek change.

title: Week 24 Framing Question
text: How does the Reformation lead to a time of change and challenge for Europe?

title: Timeline
text:
1507 C.E.: Martin Luther becomes a priest in the Roman Catholic Church.

1517 C.E.: Martin Luther writes his 95 Theses.

1521 C.E.: Martin Luther is excommunicated from the Roman Catholic Church.

1522 C.E.: Huldrych Zwingli begins the Reformation movement in Switzerland.

1526 C.E.: Luther and Erasmus begin debating religious topics.
