1534 C.E.: English King Henry VII establishes the Anglican Church.

1536 C.E.: John Calvin publishes Institutes of the Christian Religion.

1545 C.E.: The Pope organizes the Council of Trent.

title: Martin Luther
text:
In 1505, a German law student named Martin Luther decided to change the focus of his studies from law to religion. After his religious studies, he became a monk. Luther decided to earn his doctorate, which is another university degree. This allowed him to become a university professor. As he became more educated about the Church, its rules, and its doctrine, he started questioning its role in society and even some of its teachings. Luther’s questions were the start of the Protestant Reformation. The Protestant Reformation was a religious reform movement that started a new branch of Christianity.

Eventually, Luther wanted to change the way some things were being done in the Roman Catholic Church. He began by trying to change the church from within. He voiced his concerns with the leaders of Roman Catholicism in Germany. Luther objected to the payment of indulgences. He also believed that everyone should be able to read and study the Bible, not just the clergy. At the time, only clergy and highly educated people could read the Bible because it was in Latin. Latin was not spoken by anyone in Europe other than Roman Catholic clergy, because it was the ancient language of the Roman Empire. Eventually, Luther changed this for the German people by translating the Bible into their native tongue. This meant that anyone who could read German could read the Bible.

Armed with a strong determination and considerable knowledge, Luther wrote what is known as the “95 Theses.” Luther wanted to get the attention of Church officials and followers. The common story is that Luther nailed his 95 Theses to the doors of the church in Wittenberg, Germany. His theses were written mostly as questions. His intent was to start a debate about the Church and its methods. A debate did ensue, resulting in Luther being excommunicated, or kicked out of the Catholic church. After being excommunicated, Luther created his own church. Anyone who followed in Luther’s footsteps was called a Protestant.

title: The Printing Press and 95 Theses
text:
Luther’s collection of statements questioning the Church’s practices, known as the “95 Theses,” might not have been so widely read had it not been for the invention of movable type and the printing press, created by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440. Luther worked to challenge the Catholic Church by using Gutenberg’s device to rapidly create copies of the German translation of the Bible to spread to the masses. Historians believe this new technology helped fuel the spark that started the Reformation. By 1517, the pamphlet holding the 95 Theses became a bestselling hit. By 1525, Luther had published over half a million works, allowing him to become a bestselling author and known throughout Europe. This event established the power of the printing press and the importance of books and reading across Europe.

Here are six of Martin Luther’s 95 theses. They focus on Luther’s concerns about indulgences:

33. Men must especially be on guard against those who say that the pope’s pardons are that inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him.

36. Any truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without indulgence letters.

43. Christians are to be taught that he who gives to the poor or lends to the needy does a better deed than he who buys indulgences.

44. Because love grows by works of love, man thereby becomes better. Man does not, however, become better by means of indulgences but is merely freed from penalties.

45. Christians are to be taught that he who sees a needy man and passes him by, yet gives his money for indulgences, does not buy papal indulgences but God’s wrath.

46. Christians are to be taught that the buying of indulgences is a matter of free choice, not commanded.

title: Spreading of the Reformation
text:
Most Europeans were members of the Roman Catholic Church at the beginning of the 16th century, or 1500s, but by the latter part of the century, many different Protestant religions had taken hold of the continent. The Reformation was the beginning of a period of challenge and change in European history.

While the Renaissance was a time of change for the middle and upper classes in Europe, the Reformation was a movement that affected everyone, from the rich to the poor. The working class of Germany was the first people to start asking questions and listening to Martin Luther. This extended to the working class of many other European countries. Then, small towns and territories began questioning the authority of the Roman Catholic Church. People and governments started making their own decisions about who owned the land and how money was going to be spent, essentially taking back land that had belonged to the Roman Catholic Church and no longer paying tithes to the church. This created change not just in religious practice, but in politics and economics.

Eventually, these changes spread across Europe. Many other people and countries throughout Europe decided they wanted to change and challenge the Roman Catholic Church. Looking at the map, what can you infer about the religions and how they spread?

title: Challengers and Division
text:
There were many different reformers who contributed to religious change throughout Europe. Desiderius Erasmus shared many beliefs with Martin Luther, such as humanism and education. He also supported many of the changes that Luther wanted to make within the Roman Catholic Church. However, Erasmus did not agree with Luther on many points of doctrine. Erasmus would stay a Roman Catholic priest his whole life. Erasmus wrote many books and worked to change the views of religion throughout France, England, and the Netherlands.

Huldrych Zwingli brought the Reformation to Switzerland. He was a philosopher and a priest in the Roman Catholic Church. Zwingli was directly influenced by Erasmus and his writings. They both wanted to change the church from the inside. However, Zwingli would later embrace a more radical reform movement. Zwingli, like Luther, objected to the indulgences, along with other church practices.

John Calvin was born in France in 1509. He followed in the footsteps of Luther for a time, but his reform ideas would eventually differ from Luther’s. Calvin spent time in Germany, and as a student, he studied law and religion. He moved to Geneva, Switzerland, and became a religious and political leader. In 1536, Calvin published his own book and ideas about religion in the Institutes of the Christian Religion. He believed that religion was personal and that no church should tell anyone what they could do. His followers spread across France, Switzerland, and North America. The Puritans, who settled the Massachusetts Colony and established Boston, were known as Calvinists because they believed in the ideas that John Calvin wrote about and preached.

England became a key country in the Reformation movement by challenging the Roman Catholic Church. Their church reform began with the king of England, Henry VIII. When Henry’s wife did not have a son who could be heir to the English throne, Henry asked the Pope for a divorce. The Pope did not grant the divorce. Henry did not think anyone should have greater authority in England than the king. If the Pope, or the leader of the Catholic Church, could tell the king what to do, then who was really the authority in England? King Henry VIII decided to use his own power, similar to how the princes of Germany had followed Martin Luther and left the Roman Catholic Church. Henry VIII went on to found his own church, the Church of England, also called the Anglican Church. This move took away the authority, or power of government, of the Roman Catholic Church in England.

title: Counter-Reformation
text:
In 1545, the Roman Catholic Church began a movement called the Counter-Reformation, or a response within the Roman Catholic Church to Martin Luther’s challenges against church doctrine and practice. The Roman Catholic Church soon realized that they were not going to be able to get rid of the Protestant Reformation. They had to determine how they were going to respond to reformers’ questions and concerns. They did this by holding a meeting called the Council of Trent.

At the Council of Trent, different leaders of the Catholic Church came together to review the laws and policies of the church. This council lasted from 1545 to 1563 and was held in three different sessions. Protestants, or people who had left the Roman Catholic Church, were invited to the council, but none came. These sessions confirmed the authority of the Roman Catholic Church, discussed the ideas being challenged by reformers, and established the vision and goals of the Church. The decrees, or decisions made here, ended the sale of indulgences, improved education for the clergy, reaffirmed doctrine about forgiveness, and decreed that the Roman Catholic Church was the only true religion.

Eventually, European countries such as Germany, Netherlands, and Scandinavia became predominantly Protestant, while countries such as Italy, Spain, and France remained Catholic. The Reformation made monarchs (kings and queens) more powerful. The translation of the Bible allowed more people to learn to read, and Protestant leaders encouraged more people to learn to read. At the end of the Reformation, the question was: How did this affect the Roman Catholic Church’s position within Europe and the rest of the world?

title: The Aztec Empire
text:
The Aztec Empire was a tributary empire that began in 1428, located in the Valley of Mexico. Before it was an empire, there were many separate city-states in the Valley. They had been dominated by another tributary empire, ruled by the city of Azcapotzalco. Eventually, three cities would band together and overthrow the authority of Azcapotzalco. The most important city in the Aztec Empire was Tenochtitlan. The people of the city called themselves the Mexica. The Mexica claimed this authority by two means. First, they claimed that the god of war and the sun, Huitzilopochtli, had given them the power to rule by making them successful in war. Second, they claimed to be the direct descendants of the Toltec Empire, the empire that preceded the Aztecs in Central Mexico.

There are various origins stories that the Mexica tell about how they reached the Valley of Mexico. In one account, the Mexica say that they emerged from a place called the “Seven Caves.” It is a common tale among many Mesoamerican cultures that humanity came from caves. The land they lived in after coming out of the caves was covered in thorns and was full of dangerous animals. So, they took a canoe across a lake and began to wander. They followed the priests of the god Huitzilopochtli. The people paused at Culhuacán, one of the last cities of the Toltec. Then they left and wandered even more. Finally, they arrived at Lake Texcoco, where the god Huitzilopochtli told them to build a new city, promising that it would be a mighty city.

title: Week 20 Framing Question
text: How did the Aztec Empire end up controlling so much of Central Mexico?

title: Political Structure
text:
The Aztecs created an empire in Mesoamerica. Before they created their empire, the area was organized around city-states. Each city controlled the area around them. The cities were the main population centers of the Aztec Empire. Very few smaller towns and villages have been discovered from that time. The city-states were the primary political entities in the Aztec Empire. Aztec city-states were called altepetl in the Nahuatl language, which is the language the Aztec people spoke. Each altepetl had a ruler called a tlatoani, which meant “speaker.”

Eventually, three city-states created an alliance amongst themselves and formed the Aztec Empire. In the 1400s, the leaders of the city-states known as the Triple Alliance, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan joined forces, with Tenochtitlan as the capital of the new empire. The empire grew as the Aztecs conquered other city-states, creating a vast political empire in Mexico. When a city-state was conquered, they were required to provide a tribute to the empire. This often came in the form of goods. City-states that paid their tribute were generally left alone.

As the ruler of the most powerful city-state, the tlatoani of Tenochtitlan was the emperor of the entire empire and was known as the Huey tlatoani, or “great speaker.” The new emperor was often chosen from the male relatives of the previous emperor by four nobles who had been related to the previous emperor. Despite this, being related to the previous ruler was not a requirement. The emperor had complete power over the empire but usually left local issues up to the leaders of each city-state. He also depended on a council for advice and support.

The city of Tenochtitlan was split into small administrative units called calpulli. The leaders of the calpulli monitored the population of their district by recording all births and deaths. They also enforced the social rules of the city by punishing ordinary citizens who wore clothing items that were reserved for nobility. Each calpulli ran a warrior school for the boys who lived within their borders. These warrior schools were very important to the people of Tenochtitlan because their Empire was expanded through conquest. Also, order in the Empire was maintained by having the largest, most threatening, and successful warriors in all the surrounding territory.

title: Moctezuma II
text: The last leader of Tenochtitlan and the Aztec Empire was Moctezuma II. Historians know the most about Moctezuma II because he was in power when the Spanish reached Tenochtitlan. Moctezuma had taken over the rule of Tenochtitlan from his uncle, Ahuitzotl. The Empire was the largest it had ever been, stretching into the modern-day countries of Honduras and Nicaragua. However, the Empire and Moctezuma were facing quite a lot of uncertainty. The religious omens were predicting an uncertain future, and the people were becoming restless. Also, Moctezuma’s uncle and many other people in the city had died of unknown diseases. These were most likely European diseases that had reached the Tenochtitlan by way of the Yucatán. Spanish explorers had reached the Yucatán in the early 1500s, bringing germs and bacteria that the Native Americans were not immune to. These Spaniards had been driven out of the Yucatán by the Maya. The uncertainties would be part of the reason that Moctezuma would first let the Spanish enter Tenochtitlan without any resistance.

title: Triple Alliance
text:
The Triple Alliance is the name of the alliance between the city-states of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan. The strength of this alliance allowed them to create the Aztec Empire. The leader of Tenochtitlan, Itzcoatl, formed the alliance to resist the influence of another city-state, Azcapotzalco. As the capital of the Tepanec Empire, Azcapotzalco demanded tribute from the city-states under its control. The Triple Alliance formed during the war against the Tepanec, which eventually ended with the defeat of Azcapotzalco in 1428. At that point, the Triple Alliance became the strongest military force in central Mexico.

The Triple Alliance used their new power in much the same way as previous empires and city-states in the area. Even though they rebelled against expensive tribute payments in their war with the Tepanec, the Aztec implemented the same kind of payments against the city-states they conquered. The difference between Azcapotzalco and the Triple Alliance was the scale at which they expanded. To that point in history, no empire had been able to conquer and extract tribute from as many city-states as the Aztec Empire did.

The expansion of the Triple Alliance was driven by economic concerns. They wanted the tribute that conquered city-states could give them to support their cities. After the Triple Alliance conquered a city, they did not replace existing leaders. If the city paid their tributes to the Triple Alliance, the individual rulers kept their autonomy, or ability to govern without interference from the Triple Alliance. By letting these leaders stay in power, the Aztec Empire was able to avoid much of the internal unrest that other empires have historically encountered.

title: Tenochtitlan
text:
Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire. It was founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. Lake Texcoco was located in the Valley of Mexico and was surrounded by mountains. The cities that were a part of the Triple Alliance were nearby. Texcoco was located to the east of Tenochtitlan, on the eastern border of Lake Texcoco. Tlacopan was located very close to the western side of Tenochtitlan. Historians know much about the capital city because Hernán Cortés and other Spanish conquistadors wrote about the city. Cortés wrote his observations of the city to the king of Spain. In the letter he wrote in 1520, Cortés compares its size to major cities in Spain. The city had wide avenues with bridges over the lake. At this time in its history, Tenochtitlan was a bustling economic center.

Cortés mentions the large markets in the city. There, people bought, sold, and traded all manner of goods. Precious metals like gold, silver, copper, and more were available there, as were animals, including many different kinds of birds, as well as rabbits, deer, and more. The city also had barbers, restaurants, and apothecaries, which are a type of pharmacy where citizens of the city could get medicines. The importance of the Aztec religion was obvious in the grand temples and pyramids located at the center of the city.

Tenochtitlan did not grow into the great city Cortés described overnight. It began as a small city, but around 1470, the tlatoani of Tenochtitlan began to expand the city. The city was laid out on a grid system. It was built like this to reflect the city of Teotihuacán, the city of the gods. At the center of the grid system was a huge religious complex where the two largest temples in the city were located. One was dedicated to the god of war and the sun, Huitzilopochtli. The second was built for the god of rain, Tlaloc. Both temples rose about 200 feet. There were many more temples located throughout the city, including one dedicated to Quetzalcoatl.

Eventually, the island was too small for the expansion of the city, so the inhabitants created human-made islands, called chinampas. The city was built on these islands and new canal systems replaced roads on the outer sections of the city. Great bridges were built to connect these islands to the large island at the center of Tenochtitlan. The city was connected to the mainland by massive causeways, or human-made land bridges, that rose above the water level. The water in the lake was too salty for humans to drink, but there were fresh springs on the island. However, as the city grew, they needed more water than the springs could supply, so they built a stone aqueduct that brought water into the city.

title: Military Conquest
text:
The Aztec Empire was created and expanded through military conquest. The three city-states of the Triple Alliance fought against the Tepanec Empire in order to gain their independence. The war against the Tepanec was characterized by brutal warfare and the destruction of much of their capital city of Azcapotzalco. This freed them from paying tribute and allowed them to expand their influence through their military strength.

The Aztec Empire’s expansion was one of extreme violence. Each new emperor would undertake a war of conquest to expand the empire. The armies of the Aztec Empire were not always successful. They suffered some defeats, but their victories outnumbered their defeats by a large number. Sometimes the people who were conquered were offered as sacrifices. Victories also secured further economic wealth for the Aztec Empire through tribute. A Spanish writer, Diego Durán, described the tribute system, saying that tributes did not just include food or precious metals, but things like scorpions, spiders, feathers, and fish bones. In the city of Tenochtitlan, there were entire warehouses full of tribute goods: clothing, food, tobacco, cacao, and animals.

Not all of the wars fought by the Aztec Empire were clearly for conquest. For decades, they took part in a conflict known as the Flowery Wars. Historical accounts of this conflict differ, as some consider it a failed war of conquest while other interpretations focus on the ceremonial aspects of the war to argue that it was serving a purpose other than conquest. Fighting the kingdoms of Tlaxcala, Cholula, and Huexotzinco, some claim that the Aztec Empire was using the war to give their soldiers practice. The small size of these kingdoms seems to verify this theory. The strength of the Aztec Empire should have been more than enough to defeat the cities they were fighting against. However, these kingdoms claim that they were able to successfully repel these attacks for what they were, attempted conquests.

title: Government in the United States
text:
The government has several purposes. One is to provide safety and security for those in the community from threats outside of the community. Another is to maintain justice and order within the community. A third purpose is to help the members of the community meet their wants and needs. The government of the United States is a constitutional republic.

A constitutional republic is a form of government. It is based on a written document that determines the power and functions of an elected representational government. The written law of the Constitution is enforced by representatives chosen by the people. At every level, the people's consent is what gives the government power to act. This is known as popular sovereignty. A constitutional republic must balance individual rights with the common good. Effective leaders work to meet the needs of citizens and protect their rights.

Americans have different customs, traditions, and ethnic origins. Americans are united by the principles of a constitutional republic. The Constitution states that citizens need to respect individual rights and freedoms. Authority from the people limits the actions of the government, which protects their rights of liberty and freedom. By creating and enforcing laws, citizens can ensure their rights are protected. Respecting the rights of others means that everyone is treated equally. The principles of fairness, equality, and justice have influenced new laws and policies over time at the local, state, and national levels of government.

Fairness, equality, and justice are principles that have influenced government and laws. Fairness is a fundamental American value. Fairness is about making sure that everyone has what they need to be successful. Our government supports fairness by making laws to keep things fair for everyone. All people should be treated fairly.

Equality means that all people are treated the same, regardless of who they are. Our government provides services and protection to all citizens. Justice means that people behave in a way that is fair, equal, and balanced for everyone. Fairness, equality, and justice are democratic values. These values guide our government. They protect the rights of citizens.

According to one of the Founders, John Adams, “Government is instituted for the common good … not for profit, honor, or private interest of any one man, family, or class of men.” The common good is when people think about what is best for everyone. It refers to decisions that benefit most members of a community. Our government supports the common good through laws. If citizens work together toward the common good, freedom and self-government can be successful. Everyone in the community benefits.

Another important facet of the United States government is rule of law. John Adams stated that “the rule of law means a government of laws and not of men.” Rule of law is based on fairness, equality, and justice. It means that the government is accountable to the law. The government can only use its power as defined by laws. There are four important ideas of the rule of law:

Laws have to be adopted and approved through government processes.

Laws have to be clear, and everyone needs to know about them.

Laws are applied equally to all citizens.

When there are disputes about the law, individuals will have representatives who are neutral to deliver the best outcome.

In the United States, we have a federal government that leads our country. The federal government shares its power with state governments. The federal government has the power to:

print money

declare war

build the military

make treaties (agreements with foreign countries)

make and enforce laws for doing business between the states and foreign nations

make laws to enforce the Constitution

State governments control laws within each state. They also have elected officials. The leader of the state is the governor. The governor appoints officials. The governor also signs or vetoes bills passed by the state legislature. The governor serves as the commander-in-chief of the state’s military. Each state has its own constitution. Like the United States Constitution, state constitutions must enforce laws in ways that protect the rights of citizens.

We also have local governments. They lead our towns, cities, and counties. Cities and towns elect leaders called mayors. People also elect city managers, town councils, and county commissioners. These officials address community concerns, help out in the community, and act as a voice for the community. Local governments are in charge of police and fire departments. They also handle public transportation systems, road maintenance, community parks, trash removal, and building codes.

title: Three Branches of Government
text:
To keep any one person or group from having too much power, the Constitution divides the government into three branches. We call this a system of checks and balances. Each branch was designed to address specific issues and concerns. Each branch has its own structure, processes, and leaders. These leaders use different processes as checks to protect individual liberties. Individual liberties are rights that the government cannot take away. For example, the president may veto legislation passed by Congress. A veto can stop a bill from becoming a law, but Congress can override the veto with a two-thirds majority vote. Congress also has checks on the president. For example, the Senate must confirm executive appointments. The courts can check Congress by declaring laws unconstitutional. This basic structure of the national government is also used to guide the development of state and local governments.

The three branches of government are the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The executive branch of government enforces our country’s laws. It is also in charge of the military. The head of the executive branch is the President of the United States. The president is chosen by voters. The president and vice president are elected together for four years. They may serve two terms, for a total of eight years. The president chooses members of the cabinet to advise him or her. Cabinet members are often experts in their fields. They help run the executive branch by leading departments. For example, the Department of Defense is in charge of the military. At the state level, the executive branch includes the governor, departments, and agencies that enforce state laws.

The legislative branch makes the laws and sets taxes. Congress is the legislative branch of our government. It is divided into two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. Two senators are elected from each state. A state’s number of representatives depends on how many people live there. Larger states send more representatives. Smaller states send fewer. Today, there are 100 senators in the Senate and 435 representatives in the House. All of them were elected by the people of their states.

The judicial branch interprets the laws, or decides what they mean. It also determines whether the laws follow the Constitution. The judicial branch is headed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court is made up of judges called justices. They are chosen by the president and voted on by senators. State supreme courts are similar to the U.S. Supreme Court. They decide whether laws go against their state’s constitution. The judicial branch also includes other federal courts and local courts. Local courts decide whether someone is guilty of a crime. The judicial system’s role is to make sure the law is followed and all citizens’ rights are protected.

title: Checks and Balances
text:
The writers of the U.S. Constitution wanted to limit the power of government. That way, they believed the United States would be strong and endure.

Articles I, II, and III of the Constitution separate the government into three branches. This ensures that branches of government share power equally. In order for these branches to work together, the Founders created a system of checks and balances. This means that each branch of the government has to be in agreement with the other two.

Each branch has the power to stop certain actions of another branch. This happens if a branch believes those actions are unconstitutional or not in the best interest of the country. The system of checks and balances helps make sure that no branch of government becomes more powerful than the others.

Congress can pass a law, but the president must approve it. Congress can also override the president's decision to veto, or reject, a law. The Supreme Court has the power to strike down a law that has been approved by both Congress and the president. The Justices must say why they believe the law is unconstitutional. The president appoints justices to the Supreme Court. However, Congress must approve the choices. This system of checks and balances has protected the rights of U.S. citizens.

title: Historical Analysis
text:
Many events in history can occur around the same period. The tools and items people used in the past become artifacts we can study. People, places, ideas, cultures, and technology change over time. Artifacts help us understand how people’s lives have changed over time. Historians analyze how much things have changed throughout history. They examine patterns to understand how and why things happened.

This type of study is called continuity and change. Historians can use this to look for the cause and effects of the change. Understanding cause and effect is an important skill for historians.

When we look at the causes of events in the past, we can learn from them. This will help us make decisions today. The analysis of people and events in history helps guide decisions for the future. We can repeat what they did or make different choices.

title: Social Skills
text: Social means with other people. Skills are things you can do. Social skills are the things you know to do around other people.

title: Poverty Point Culture
text:
Poverty Point is located in northeastern Louisiana and was built over 3,000 years ago. The people who lived there did not leave behind written records, but archaeologists have helped us learn a little bit about what their lives were like.

The people who built and lived at Poverty Point were different from other groups at that time. While they were a hunter-gatherer society, they lived year-round at Poverty Point.

Poverty Point is surrounded by several rivers, including the Mississippi River. Rivers were highways for trade and transportation. The population at the site would have been much larger than was common for that time period. Hundreds of people were living at Poverty Point at its peak.

title: Framing Question Week 25
text: How can archaeological evidence help people learn about the prehistoric peoples of Louisiana?

title: Poverty Point Mounds
text: The mounds and ridges at Poverty Point were constructed sometime between 1700 B.C.E. and 1100 B.C.E. No one knows for certain why the mounds were constructed or what they were used for. Because of the lack of domestic artifacts, many scholars believe that the mounds were only used for ceremonial purposes. For a long time, it was believed that the mounds were used for burials, but no evidence of burials or remains has been found in excavations to support this.

title: Ridges and Plazas
text:
The people who lived at Poverty Point moved an estimated two million cubic yards of earth to build the earthworks found at the site. These people did not have dump trucks or complex machinery to move all of that earth. The mounds and ridges were all built by hand, most likely by moving earth with baskets, around an enormous 43-acre plaza. Archaeological evidence suggests that the people worked to keep to plaza level by regularly filling in depressions and gullies with soil.

Because the people living at Poverty Point didn't leave behind any written records, it's impossible to know for sure why they built the mounds and ridges at the site or what they were used for. There is evidence to support that special ceremonies were held on the mounds and ridges and in the large plaza. Post holes arranged in circles are found on both the ridges and around the plaza. This indicates that structures once stood on these sites.

There are six rows of ridges at Poverty Point that are all C-shaped around the grand plaza. More artifacts, such as ovens, post holes, and daub, have been found on the ridges than anywhere else at Poverty Point. Archaeologists believe that this means people lived and built domestic structures and homes on the ridges.

title: Recording History and Oral Traditions
text:
Many Indigenous tribes of North America didn’t have a written alphabet or use a written system of language. However, this doesn’t mean that they did not keep records of important events and experiences. Oral tradition and storytelling are a large part of the culture of Indigenous peoples. Native peoples of North America used the spoken word to communicate and preserve their history and traditions. Often, their speeches took the form of stories. Many stories explained their beliefs and the creation of the world.

Some stories represented actual events that happened in the tribe’s past. Some represented relationships between families and their ancestors. Other stories are more like religious stories for the tribes. These stories have lessons on how to be a good person and treat everything with respect. Elders often taught these stories to children. Animals, birds, and the environment were often part of these important stories, creating a special bond with the land.

Indigenous peoples also used the resources from their environment to record information. One example is called petroglyphs. A petroglyph is a picture carved into a rock. Petroglyphs represent important cultural beliefs, tribal stories, and significant events. Indigenous peoples living in North America today consider petroglyphs sacred.

Indigenous peoples that lived in coastal areas of North America often used wampum as a form of record keeping. Wampum are small cylinder shaped beads made from shells. They were strung together and worn as jewelry and belts. They were used to record important events, including treaties between tribes. The color and pattern of the beads represented different words and ideas. When woven together, the beads created a complete story or summary of the event.

title: Societies
text:
The community at Poverty Point traded with many different people over long distances. Some of the rocks found at Poverty Point are from 800 miles away. Knowing this, Poverty Point residents would have been able to trade in news, culture, and language, as well as goods from hundreds of miles around.

Nothing is known for certain about the social structure of the Poverty Point people. There is no evidence to indicate that any of the domestic buildings in the community were larger or grander than others. This suggests that people likely lived equally without social hierarchies. The lack of any grand burial sites filled with burial goods in the area also supports the idea that these people did not have kings or a class of nobility.

title: Homes and Clothing
text: The soil at Poverty Point is very poor for preserving organic material. Because of this, very few artifacts of the people who lived there have survived. Almost nothing is known about what kind of clothing they wore, but they most likely made clothing out of animal skins and plant fibers that were native to the area. Homes were most likely constructed on the earthwork ridges around the plaza. The size and placement of post holes found in excavations show that structures were haphazard and constructed as needed, rather than all at once. Each home would have had a framework of post holes, an earthen oven for cooking food in, and the roof and walls may have been constructed of animal skins or plant fibers.

title: Hunting Methods and Food
text:
Poverty Point is surrounded by natural grasslands, rivers, woodlands, and wetlands, which provide for a wide variety of plant and animal life. This means the people of Poverty Point would have had a rich and varied diet.

The people of Poverty Point were hunter-gatherers, or people who hunt and look for food. The people hunted and ate things like fish, frogs, squirrels, turtles, and deer. They gathered nuts, fruits, and other wild foods. Remains of tools were found that showed they used wood and stones to make tools and weapons.

Hunters used weapons with stone tips, such as spears, atlatls, and bows and arrows, to hunt game. It is also likely that they used nets for fishing, attaching special stone weights to the nets to help catch more fish. Fish bones are the most common type of bone found at Poverty Point.

Stone was rare and had to be traded for at Poverty Point. In addition to being used to make tools and weapons, stones were also used for cooking by heating the stones in a fire and then placing them in earth ovens to cook food. Without stone, people packed soil into balls and baked them to make them harden. These were then used in the same way as stones for cooking.

title: Art and Artifacts
text:
Because stone was scarce in the area, the people who lived at Poverty Point traded for stone to make tools and artwork, such as spear points, stone bowls, beads, and figurines. The different types of stone found at the site came from hundreds of miles away, which suggests that Poverty Point was an important hub for trade. Some of the few artifacts left behind that show the artwork created by the Poverty Point inhabitants are stone beads and pendants. These would have been used to make jewelry and decorations. Beads and pendants were sometimes carved with patterns or images of animals, such as birds or turtles.

Other artifacts found include small figurines made of clay or carved out of stone. Many small female-shaped figurines have been found. Some are simply made, while others are more detailed, including hairstyles, clothing, belts, and faces. Many of these figures are missing their heads. It’s unclear if the heads broke off, were removed intentionally, or were made without them. It is also unknown what they were made for. Some ideas of what they were made for include ceremonial purposes, honoring deceased relatives, decoration for homes, or even toys for children.

title: The Persian Wars
text:
Trouble started in Ancient Greece after people moved across the Aegean Sea and set up cities in the Persian Empire (now Türkiye). When the Persians demanded that the Greeks pay taxes, they refused, and the Persians attacked their cities and took control. The Greeks tried to win back their freedom with a revolt, but they failed. The revolt caused the Persian Emperor to send a large army across the sea into Greece. In 490 B.C.E., about 25,000 soldiers and 600 ships landed on the plains of Marathon. Athens gathered an army of 10,000 soldiers who marched to stop them.

Marathon

The Battle at Marathon is one of the most well-known battles of the ancient world. The Athenians were completely outnumbered when the general ordered his soldiers in the middle of the battle to retreat. The Persians thought they were winning and charged ahead. Then, the rest of the Athenian soldiers surrounded the Persian army and won the battle.

After Marathon, the Persian Empire spent the next 10 years gathering a large army. Sparta, Athens, and many other city-states joined together to fight. The Greeks were heavily outnumbered, but they held off the Persian army for three full days before being defeated. After winning, the Persian army marched to Athens and burned down the city. While all this was happening, the Greek navy gathered their ships and the naval leader formed a plan. They sailed into a narrow bay, and when the Persian ships followed them, the Athenians attacked. The Greek ships were shorter than the Persian ships and could move more easily. About 200 Persian warships were destroyed, while the Athenians only lost about 40.

The following year, the Greek army defeated the Persians at the Battle of Plataea. A few weeks later, Persia’s fleet lost another major battle in Mycale. Many smaller battles were fought over the next 30 years. The Greek city-states, led by Athens and Sparta, proved to be a powerful military force. Their fierce determination to win, their heavier armor and spears, and their better knowledge of the land helped them to defeat the mighty Persians.

title: Week 16 Framing Question
text: What are the legacies of Greek Culture? How do they affect us today?

title: The Peloponnesian War
text:
During the Persian Wars, Athens and Sparta were allies. Sparta had a very strong army, and Athens had a very powerful navy that ruled the Mediterranean waters. Both city-states made alliances with the smaller city-states that surrounded them. For a while, Athens and Sparta stayed friends.

Sparta controlled most of the peninsula of Peloponnese, but Athens controlled the wealthy communities on the coasts. Over time, Athens became more and more powerful and tensions began between Athens and Sparta. In 431 B.C.E., after years of trying to keep the peace, war broke out between the two cities.

At first, Athens appeared to be unbeatable. They were wealthy and had a powerful navy. They fought off several attacks from Sparta’s well-trained soldiers. Then the plague, a serious disease, spread among its citizens and weakened Athens’ army.

As the war continued, the two sides traded victories back and forth. At one point, both powers agreed to stop fighting and declare peace, but the agreement didn’t last. Athens grew even weaker when political problems grew within the government. Then a small group of leaders formed an oligarchy and took control of Athens. This small group refused another offer of peace. Finally, a Spartan commander named Lysander was finally able to destroy Athens’ navy. Without ships to bring supplies, Athens fell to the Spartan army. The war lasted for almost 50 years.

title: The Golden Age
text:
After the Persian Wars ended, the Golden Age of Greece began. Athens had been destroyed, but the people returned and began rebuilding the city. Pericles led Athens during the Golden Age. He created a city that was a center of learning, art, and culture. He welcomed people from all over the world to come and share new ideas.

Like many Greek city-states, Athens was built on a high hill. The hill of Athens is called the Acropolis and is fortified by stone walls. It was originally built as a fortress where the people could go when the city was attacked. The people used many of the ruins left from the burning of Athens to build the North Wall of the Acropolis.

The Athenians valued beauty, logic, and order. Art, sculpture, and architecture were very important in their society. Their buildings were unique and featured different types of columns. They created works of art, monuments, and temples to honor their gods. The most famous temple of Ancient Greece is the Parthenon. It was built in the center of the Acropolis and was made to honor the Greek goddess Athena. On the outside, there were 46 columns that were 6 feet in diameter and 34 feet tall. Inside was a large gold and ivory statue of Athena.

The Agora in Athens was a large market and gathering place. It was where leaders came to meet and travelers came to share their goods and information about the world. It was where thinkers like Socrates spent time talking with people and teaching.

Athens is well known for its focus on education and philosophy. The word “philosophy” in Greek means “the love of wisdom.” Athens produced the most famous philosophers of the Golden Age. Ancient Greece had many great thinkers in the areas of math and science. Much of what we learn in math and science classes today comes from the Golden Age of Athens. Even with the emphasis on wisdom and education, girls in classical Athens did not go to school. Their mothers taught them skills so they would know how to run a household and raise children. In comparison to men, women in Athens had very few rights. They rarely owned land or property, and they were unable to vote or participate in government.

title: Socrates
text:
Socrates was a Greek philosopher who lived between 469 and 399 B.C.E. He spent his life searching for knowledge. Socrates was a great thinker even as a boy. It is said that he once told his father that a pitcher was just an arrangement of clay, but that using it is what gave the pitcher beauty. Socrates spent his days at the Agora of Athens, walking among the people, chatting, questioning, and thinking. He wanted to learn from others. People nicknamed Socrates the “Great Questioner” because he said that to learn, one must ask questions—lots of them!

Socrates’ teaching got him into trouble. The Greek government accused him of corrupting young minds and disrespecting religious traditions. They put Socrates on trial, found him guilty, and sentenced him to death. Socrates accepted his sentence because he believed in the idea of trial by jury. Socrates’ most famous student was Plato, who also became a great thinker, philosopher, and teacher.

title: Plato
text:
Plato was a scientist, philosopher, and mathematician who lived between 427 and 347 B.C.E. He was one of Socrates' students and wrote down everything that Socrates taught him. His family was wealthy and well-connected. They may have expected him to find a career in government, but Plato was much more interested in the arts. When he was young he wrote plays and poetry. When Socrates was executed, Plato left Athens and traveled around the Mediterranean region. He studied many subjects including science, math, and philosophy. He visited and wrote about places like Egypt, Rome, and North Africa.

Plato's most famous writing is The Republic. In it, several characters have a discussion about the meaning of justice and how it is related to happiness. It describes an ideal city and the idea that a just government can create happiness. Plato returned to Athens when he was about 40 years old. He started a school called the Academy that taught things like philosophy, astronomy, biology, and mathematics. Plato’s most famous student was Aristotle who studied at the Academy for nearly 20 years.

title: Aristotle
text:
Aristotle was a Greek philosopher who lived between 384 and 322 B.C.E. Aristotle was born in Macedonia. Aristotle’s family believed education was important. His father was the king’s physician. Aristotle probably would have become a doctor if his father hadn’t died when Aristotle was young. As a teenager, Aristotle went to Athens and became a pupil at Plato’s academy. Aristotle is often called the father of science. He was interested in anatomy, astronomy, geography, meteorology, zoology, and much more.

As a teacher, Aristotle also had a very famous student. On his return to Macedonia, he tutored King Philip’s son, Alexander. For seven years, Aristotle worked with Alexander. He taught him much about Greek culture. Alexander grew up to become Alexander the Great, a ruler who expanded Greek influence and changed the course of ancient civilizations. As you can see, Socrates’ influence continued through many generations.

title: Alexander The Great
text:
Whenever a country’s citizens fight among themselves, the country becomes weak. Soldiers die in battle, people neglect their farming, and they are working against each other instead of working together. After the Peloponnesian War, a group of people from the north, the Macedonians, took advantage of the turmoil in Greece. Seeing the weakness of their Greek neighbor, King Philip and his troops conquered all of Greece by 338 B.C.E. Not long after this, Philip died and his young son, Alexander, became king. Alexander’s troops conquered Persia, then Egypt. He went on to build one of the largest empires the world has ever seen. In only 11 years, Alexander conquered all the lands from Egypt to India. But at the Indus River, Alexander’s exhausted soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander was forced to give up and begin the long march back home. Alexander the Great founded nearly 70 cities. He named many of them after himself. It is said he once wept because there were “no more worlds to conquer.”

Thanks to his teacher, Aristotle, Alexander loved Greek culture. Wherever he went, he spread Greek ideas to those he conquered. Historians call this period the Hellenistic Era—a time when many people imitated the Greeks. Hellenistic means “Greek-like.” Grecian-style buildings were popular, as was Greek literature. Alexander also enjoyed learning about the different cultures of the people he conquered. He learned astronomy while in Mesopotamia. In Egypt, he traveled the Nile River exploring the land. Alexander also built museums to display the many artifacts he collected.

As a ruler, he could be ruthless. The people of Thebes thought Alexander was too young and inexperienced, so they rose up against him. Alexander responded swiftly. He burned the city to the ground as a warning to any other city that might act against him. Alexander died of illness when he was 32 years old and his empire soon unraveled. Alexander didn’t have any sons but said on his deathbed that he wanted to leave his empire “to the strongest.” His generals started to argue among themselves as to who should rule. Eventually, the three strongest generals divided the empire into three parts.

Alexander’s Legacy

A legacy is something you leave behind after you die. It doesn’t have to be an object or an artifact; it can be things like knowledge or traditions. Alexander was a skilled soldier. He conquered much of the known world. However, Alexander’s greatest legacy was his sharing of Greek culture. His love of the culture caused him to share the customs, language, writing, literature, and ideas of the Greeks with all he met.

title: Religion
text:
Ancient Greeks were polytheistic. They believed that there were many gods who were involved in all aspects of human life—politics, work, family, art, and war. The Greeks believed gods were responsible for all of nature. They believed their gods looked like people but were taller, more beautiful, and could live forever. They also believed the gods could display anger, jealousy, humor, and other emotions.

The chief of all the Greek gods and goddesses was the mighty Zeus, the sky god who threw lightning bolts. The most important gods and goddesses lived in a palace on Mount Olympus, high in the clouds away from the view of humans. Some other important gods were Hades, the god of the dead; Poseidon, the god of the ocean; and Athena, the goddess of wisdom and art. The Parthenon in Athens was built to honor and worship her.

Many temples and shrines were built throughout the cities so people could come to worship the gods. The Ancient Greeks believed in an afterlife. They believed that the gods would take care of them after they died if they showed them the right love and respect.

The Greeks went to special places called oracles to ask the gods and goddesses for advice and to hear about their future. Greeks built the Oracle of Delphi for the sun god, Apollo. People paid a small fee to ask a question. The answer was usually a riddle, which the questioner had to interpret.

One legend says King Croesus of Lydia asked an oracle if he should go to war against the mighty Persians. The oracle said that if he did, a great kingdom would be destroyed. The king thought it meant he would defeat the Persians. He was wrong. His kingdom was the one destroyed.

title: Mythology
text:
Throughout history, many cultures have developed beliefs that help explain the world around them. The Greeks believed in a large group of gods and goddesses. Myths, or stories, about these powerful beings helped the Greeks understand the world around them. Greek storytellers wrote myths about gods, goddesses, monsters and heroes as a way to explain what they noticed about Earth and the environment. Other stories about the gods explained human behavior. The collection of myths within a culture makes up what is called its mythology.

Zeus was the most powerful, awesome, and frightening god in Greek mythology. He was king over the other gods, and he controlled the sky. Zeus lived on Mount Olympus with all the other gods. Because he controlled the skies, he used thunder and lightning to rule the world. Zeus was believed to be wise, fair, and fun-loving, but he also had a temper. When there was a storm, it was because Zeus was angry.

Poseidon was Zeus’ brother and the god of oceans and other waterways. Statues and paintings of Poseidon often show him carrying a trident and riding through waves in a horse-pulled chariot. A trident is a spear that splits into three points at the end. Greek myths say that when Poseidon got angry, he could shake the Earth with his trident one moment and calm the ocean the next.

Mount Olympus was home to many goddesses as well. Hera was the queen of Olympus and the goddess of marriage and birth. She sat next to her husband, Zeus, on the throne of Olympus. Myths about her say she could often become very jealous. Artemis was the goddess of the moon, forests, and hunting. Hestia was the goddess of homes and families.

The ancient Greeks didn’t just tell stories about their gods. They also told stories about a lot of different creatures, monsters, and heroes. The Greeks used these stories to explain the world and why people behaved the way they did.

title: Cyrus II
text:
Over 2,500 years ago, Persia had its own leadership, but it was not independent. It relied on another group of people, the Medians, for economic, military, and political support. The Median king ruled over Persian leaders and citizens and treated them as inferior. As time passed, Persia and its leaders became powerful enough to form their own empire. One of these leaders was Cyrus II.

Cyrus was born sometime between 600 and 580 B.C.E. Historians aren’t sure where he was born, but they agree it was probably in the Persis area. Today, that area is part of Iran. Some experts think Cyrus was from a royal family, while others believe that he rose from a humble family of herdsmen. Everyone agrees that he rose to power around 559 B.C.E. Cyrus then led a revolt against King Astyages. He defeated the Medians and started the Persian Empire.

Cyrus convinced the Persian citizens to keep fighting with him. His army began to march to nearby countries. Every time Cyrus conquered a new land, Persia's wealth and power grew. By 539 B.C.E., Persia's troops had conquered the neighboring lands of Elam, Lydia, and Babylonia. The most important of these victories was Babylonia, which was a very powerful empire. Luckily for Cyrus, the people of Babylon did not like their king, and they helped the Persians win. Many of these citizens were Jewish people who were forced to stay away from their homes. When Cyrus captured Babylonia, he allowed the Jewish citizens to return to Jerusalem. This helped Cyrus earn a reputation as both a warrior and a liberator.

After conquering so much territory, Cyrus declared himself to be king of the four corners of the world. He was known as a fair, open-minded leader. Cyrus wanted to learn from the people he conquered. He listened to his people and tried to help them. He divided the empire into areas called satrapies. Each satrapy had a governor who was loyal to Cyrus. This meant that the people in each area could keep their culture and traditions. As the Persian Empire expanded and flourished, Cyrus used the empire’s new wealth to build fortresses and cities. One of these new cities was Pasargadae, which became the empire's new capital. His smart leadership earned him the nickname Cyrus the Great.

Cyrus ruled his empire for over 25 years. During his rule, the Cyrus Cylinder was carved. This stone was etched with laws that experts believe may be the first written statement of human rights. Cyrus the Great died in 530 B.C.E. The details of his death aren’t known for certain. Most historians say that he was killed in a battle, while others claim that he died peacefully at home. Even after Cyrus died, his empire continued to grow under the leadership of his son, Cambyses II. Together, Cyrus and Cambyses are known as two of Persia’s greatest leaders. People in Iran still remember him as a hero.

title: The Persian Empire
text:
Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire over 2,500 years ago. Today, we know it as the Persian Empire. Cyrus and the next two leaders, Cambyses II and Darius, helped Persia grow into one of the largest empires the world had ever seen. They took control of most of the lands in western and central Asia and captured Egypt’s capital, Memphis. Darius was able to defend the huge empire, and he soon became known as Darius the Great.

Cyrus and Darius ruled over many different races and countries. The empire covered thousands of miles of territory. There were many different cultures and traditions. The rulers allowed these differences to continue and grow. Darius understood that his people needed to live the way they were used to, but he also knew that his empire would become even more powerful if they were all united. He did this in two ways. First, he used tax money to build a huge network of roads that connected all of the empire’s major cities. These roads allowed government officials and citizens to travel quickly and safely throughout the empire. Messengers on horseback used the roads to bring news and supplies to people. Second, Darius united his kingdom by using a single form of currency, or money. He created a system for making gold and silver coins that could be used all across his empire. The system was a success, and Darius became known as a businessman as well as a kind, smart king.

Darius appointed a governor, to rule over each region or area. They collected taxes and maintained order, but they also reported to Darius’ officials and military leaders. Darius’ reign did have some hard times, however. Not all of the regions liked paying taxes and being controlled and some of them revolted. Darius was forced to use his armies to put down these revolts. Darius died in 486 B.C.E. His son, Xerxes, took control of the empire.

title: The Greek Language
text:
We know so much about the ancient Greeks because they loved to write things down. Around 900 B.C.E., the Greeks developed a writing system. They wrote speeches, books, poems, and information about things like the Olympic games and government. The Athenians especially valued the preservation of history. Even today, you can read the works of an Athenian historian named Herodotus. He became known as the “father of history,” because he documented historical information about the Persian Wars. Another famous historian was Thucydides. In addition to being a general in Athens’ navy, he wrote about the historical events of the Peloponnesian War. Another soldier known for his historical writing is Xenophon. He wrote about war tactics, politics, the general history of Greece, and even horse breeding.

The ancient Greeks developed their writing system after contact with the Phoenicians, who developed the first alphabet. Herodotus called the Greek writing system “phoinikeia grammata,” or Phoenician letters.

In the beginning, the Greeks copied the Phoenician idea of writing from right to left. But they eventually changed to ox-turning. That means they wrote from right to left on one line and then reversed the writing in the next, switching direction when they started each new line. That was pretty confusing, so they dropped the idea eventually. The Greek alphabet changed again after the people came in contact with the Romans.

Many of our English words have Greek origins. For example, the word “panic.” It comes from the name of the Greek god Pan, who lived in the forest. He often shouted loudly to scare away any enemies. We also have some common expressions in English that come from ancient Greek myths. Achilles was a Greek hero. His entire body was indestructible except for one heel. Today we use the expression “Achilles’ heel” to point out a weakness we have. For example, “I'm trying to get good grades in school, but math is my Achilles heel.”

Many prefixes and suffixes also came from Greek to the English language.

-graph, like in paragraph, means to write.

Astro-, like in astronaut, means star.

Bio-, as in biodiversity, means life.

-logy, as in biology, means the study of something.

Micro-, as in microwave, means small.

title: Persephone: a Greek Myth
text:
Why do seasons change and leaves fall off the trees? Why does the sun rise every day and set at night? Why is there an echo in a canyon? These were a few of the many things the ancient Greeks did not understand. They created stories, or myths, about gods and goddesses to help explain things they didn't understand.

One day, a beautiful young woman named Persephone went for a walk. Persephone's mother was Demeter, the goddess of growing things. She stopped to view her mother's beautiful flowers growing in the field. The ground opened up, and a man wearing a black helmet emerged. He was aboard a black chariot pulled by black horses. This man, named Hades, fell in love with Persephone and took her down with him to the land of the dead (which was also called Hades). Persephone became his bride. Hades was the brother of Zeus and god of the underworld. When Demeter could not find her daughter, she was very sad. She learned from Hermes (the messenger god) that her daughter had become queen of the dead. Demeter would never see Persephone again.

In her misery, Demeter stopped growing things. Flowers wilted on their stems, crops stopped growing in fields, and the Earth looked bleak. People went hungry because there wasn't any food. Zeus had to do something. He demanded that his brother return Persephone to Demeter. Zeus made a deal for Persephone to spend part of the year with Hades and part of the year with her mother. When Persephone was home with her mother, Demeter was happy, and crops, flowers, and trees bloomed. When Persephone returned to Hades, Demeter was sad and stopped growing things. Which event in nature did this myth try to explain? If you said the change of seasons, you'd be correct. Look outside your classroom window. Where is Persephone today?

title: Olympic Games Then and Now
text:
The first Olympic Games were held in 776 B.C.E. They were part of a religious ceremony that honored Zeus, the king of the gods. The Greeks sacrificed 100 oxen during the event at the great altar of Zeus. Ox was Zeus’ favorite food. Greek athletes competed in events like running, boxing, discus throwing, javelin throwing, and chariot racing. Athletes who won were given crowns made of olive branches. The games were held every four years. They became so important that the Greeks would stop fighting in wars so that soldiers could compete.

Women were forbidden to attend the events. Historians aren't sure why women couldn't attend the games, but maybe it was because the male athletes participated without wearing any clothing. Some Greek women didn't like that they could not watch or participate in the events, so they formed their own games. Women called their events the Heraea Games, in honor of the queen of all the gods, Hera. Women ran races and winners also received olive wreath crowns.

Today, the Olympics are held biennially, or every two years. The Olympics alternate between summer and winter games. Cities all over the world take turns hosting the events. Not only are both men and women allowed to compete, but athletes with physical or mental disabilities also compete in special events.

title: Introduction to Ancient Greece
text:
As civilizations grew in power in the Ancient Near East and Northern Africa, another society was gaining power and influence along the Mediterranean Sea. This civilization took longer to develop than earlier civilizations like Egypt and China. While people had been living in the area for thousands of years, all the characteristics that made Ancient Greece a true civilization didn’t come together until around 1000 B.C.E.

Greece is located on the Aegean Peninsula, which is a landform surrounded on three sides by water. The Ancient Greeks grew crops, but their economy relied more on their abilities as sailors and their interactions with other cultures, like the Minoans and Mycenaeans.

The ideas and culture of Greek society had an important impact on the ancient world and also on the world we live in today. The ancient Greek civilization started out on a small, mountainous peninsula. It grew and expanded to become one of the most important and influential civilizations in human history.

Famous philosophers like Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle changed the way people think about important topics like how to live good lives. Skilled military leaders like Alexander the Great expanded Greek influence and changed the course of ancient civilizations. Architects like Ictinus left examples of their work. These examples influenced building styles around the world and throughout history. Storytellers like Homer changed the way people shared stories and knowledge. These are just a few examples of the many ancient Greeks whose ideas and actions shaped Greek culture and influenced human history.

title: Framing Question Week 15
text: How did rocky peninsulas, islands, and surrounding seas affect the development of the Ancient Greek Civilization?

title: Timeline of Ancient Greece
text:
The Ancient Greek Civilization in the Mediterranean, c. 1200–323 B.C.E.

c. 6000 B.C.E.

Early settlements and the beginning of agriculture

c. 2000 B.C.E.

Early Greeks begin to settle the Peloponnese.

c. 900 B.C.E.

The city of Sparta is founded.

776 B.C.E.

First Olympic games in honor of the Greek god Zeus

490 B.C.E.

The Greeks fight the invading Persian armies.

431 B.C.E.

The wars between Sparta and Athens begin.

336 B.C.E.

Alexander the Great becomes king of Macedon.

title: Geography of Ancient Greece
text:
Ancient Greece was located on a peninsula that sticks out into the Mediterranean Sea between Europe and Asia. A peninsula is a landform with water on three sides. There are three main bodies of water that touch Greece. They are the Ionian Sea to the west, the Aegean Sea to the east, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. The Mediterranean gave Greece access to much of the ancient world. It stretches from the Atlantic Ocean all the way to the Near East, where Egypt and Mesopotamia were located. The southern section of Greece is another peninsula. It is called the Peloponnesus, or the Peloponnese peninsula. It is connected to the main Greek peninsula by the Isthmus of Corinth, a land bridge.

The Aegean Sea is smaller than the Mediterranean, but many Greek islands are located there. Settlement on the islands of the Aegean Sea goes back beyond ancient Greece. The largest island, Crete, was the home of the Minoans, who lived there for thousands of years.

The geography of Greece is unique compared to other early civilizations. Most of the earliest societies developed around one or more large rivers. These rivers helped civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, and China grow and flourish. Greece has no major rivers and lacks good soil for agriculture. Instead of wide, flat river valleys, the land of Greece is rough and mountainous. Greece's highest peak is Mount Olympus, which is about 9,600 feet tall. There are also many rocky islands along the coastline.

The islands, mountainous terrain, and lack of large rivers kept the Greeks from having a connected population. Geography forced villages, towns, and cities to form independently. In order to support a large population, cities needed to be near one of the rivers or freshwater springs that ran through the mountains. Athens, Olympia, Sparta, and Thebes are just a few of the famous ancient Greek cities.

title: The Sea
text:
The sea was a central component of life in Ancient Greece. The people living both on the peninsula and on the islands used the sea for fishing, transportation, and trade. Because of the many mountains, the people had difficulty traveling on land. They began to spread out among the islands of the sea. There are over 3,000 rocky islands scattered in the Aegean and Ionian Seas. Because of the early troubles with transportation, ancient Greece developed relatively late in history. Other early civilizations in the region, like Egypt and Mesopotamia, had existed for over 1,000 years before the Greek civilization developed.

The people became excellent boat builders and sailors. Transporting people and goods was important because it was difficult for the islands to be self-sufficient. This means they did not have all the food and other resources they needed. So they traded between islands. And because the Aegean Sea was connected to the Mediterranean Sea, sailors could trade with other cultures and then distribute those goods to the many city-states on the main peninsula of Greece and on its islands.

title: The Minoans
text:
The Minoans were the earliest people to live in Greece. They lived on the island of Crete in about 3000 B.C.E. The name “Minoan” comes from a mythical king of Crete, Minos. According to legend, King Minos built a huge labyrinth, a maze-like structure. The Minotaur, a half-human and half-bull monster, lived inside it. The real Minoans were an advanced society. They built large cities, had a central government, and developed a writing system. The Minoan kings lived in decorated palaces, their goldsmiths made detailed jewelry, and their artists created pottery in an amazing variety of forms, colors, and patterns. The Minoans were also excellent sailors and traders. Their routes ran as far as Egypt and Mesopotamia.

Around 1730 B.C.E., much of the island of Crete was destroyed by an earthquake, but the Minoans rebuilt. About 200 years later, the Minoans and their way of life disappeared. Historians believe earthquakes or volcanoes triggered tidal waves that destroyed many of their cities. Nearly all the sites on the island were burned or abandoned, including all of the palaces. The Mycenaeans, who left central Asia and came to Greece around 1900 B.C.E., eventually conquered the island of Crete. Thousands of years later, archaeologist Arthur Evans discovered a palace at Knossos that taught us much about the Minoan culture. The palace had more than 1,500 rooms. It even had plumbing for running water and bathrooms.

title: Trade
text:
Without good soil and wide river valleys, the people of ancient Greece could not grow a surplus of food. So they traded for grain and other crops. As masters of the seas, the ancient Greeks used their extensive coastline and many islands to establish trade routes. Merchant ships were built to carry a large variety of goods, including grains, figs, honey, cheese, tools, pottery, and even animals, like sheep and goats. The trade routes crisscrossed the Mediterranean Sea. The most important routes connected them with river valley civilizations. These were places like Egypt and Mesopotamia, which had excess crops to spare. Importing crops was so important that the ancient Greek governments had officials to make sure that the prices of the crops were fair and the quality was good.

In order to trade for food, the Greeks had to have something of value to offer. Greek ceramics were one major good they exported to other places. Archaeologists have found evidence of the Greek’s extensive trade network throughout the Mediterranean region. Bowls, vases, figurines, and other ceramic works from Greece were found in many areas across the ancient world. Trade in ancient Greece was helping the world’s economy and also enriching the world’s culture. In exchange for these fine works of art, traders brought back not only grains, but gems, ivory, and valuable metals. As trade routes grew, new technologies and ideas also spread.

title: Greek City-States
text:
In Ancient Greece, there were only small pockets of land that could support large populations. Mountains and sea waters isolated them, so the people began to form independent villages and towns. Soon there were organized centers of power, called poleis. These poleis, or city-states, were the community structure of ancient Greece. Each city-state consisted of a city and surrounding countryside, and each had its own laws and government. People didn't consider themselves simply Greek. They were Macedonians, Spartans, Corinthians, or Athenians, each named after their city.

Corinth, Sparta, and Athens

Geography had an impact on how the cultures of the different city-states developed. For example, Corinth was located on a narrow strip of land. So the Corinthians took advantage of their location and established trade routes with the neighboring city-states. Trade became an important part of the city-state economies. Around 600 B.C.E., each city-state began to make its own coins. Greek coins were made of precious metals, and each city-state had its own versions. The coins had illustrations of heroes, gods, and symbols that were important and unique to their city.

The citizens of Sparta weren’t as anxious to trade. Sparta was located inland, away from the sea, so they focused on having the strongest army in Greece. The Spartans were incredibly war-like. They conquered their neighbors and enslaved them. Outsiders were not welcome. To be a Spartan citizen, both parents had to be from Sparta. Spartans did not want wealth because they believed it led to laziness and weakness.

Athens was located by the sea. They created a navy along the waterways of Greece’s coast. The Athenians were more peaceful. They valued education and art. They practiced an early form of democracy, a system of rule where ordinary people had a say in decisions made by the government.

title: Roots of Democracy
text:
At first, most Greek city-states were monarchies. This means they were controlled by one ruler or monarch, usually a king. By about 800 B.C.E., however, things had changed, and most of the laws and government decisions were in the hands of oligarchies. An oligarchy is a small group of wealthy men who shared power and ruled together. Over time, men in some Greek city-states used violence to take over control from the oligarchs. These men claimed that they wanted to make life better for the people, but they were harsh leaders, and most tried to scare the people into accepting their power. We call this kind of leader a tyrant or dictator.

In about 500 B.C.E., a new idea was born in Athens: democracy. It was a way of governing that depended on the power and will of the people. Every two weeks, thousands of citizens would gather to discuss whatever issues had come up. After talking about each issue, the citizens would vote on what they were going to do. This was the first known time in history that citizens were allowed to participate in the government and have a voice in lawmaking. Once decided, both the people and the government had to know and obey the law. This is called rule of law.

One leader, Pericles, understood the importance of rules decided by many people, not just a few. When Pericles was the ruler of Athens, thousands of citizens were part of the law-making group. Yet at that time, not everyone was considered a citizen. Only certain adult men could participate. Women, children, enslaved people, and anyone not born in Athens were not allowed to vote.

The government of the United States is called a democracy. Ancient Greeks had a direct democracy. That means that every eligible citizen had a vote on every issue. The United States has a representative democracy. Our citizens elect leaders to represent them when decisions need to be made. Elected representatives serve us in our hometowns, our states, and in Washington, D.C.

title: Thessalonica
text:
Thessalonica is a city located in northern Greece on the Thermaic Gulf of the Aegean Sea in the Macedonian kingdom. The Aegean Sea directly affects the climate of Thessalonica. Its climate is classified as a Mediterranean climate, bordering on semi-arid. Places with a Mediterranean climate typically have dry summers and mild, wet winters.

Thessalonica was founded in 316 B.C.E. by the Macedonian general Cassander. He named the city after his wife, Thessalonike (Thessalonica is also called Thessalonike). It was built in the middle of a major trade route, which made it very prosperous.

In 168 B.C.E., during the Third Macedonian War between the Roman Republic and several Greek kingdoms, the Roman army defeated the Greek army led by King Perseus. This allowed Rome to take control of Macedon and end its monarchy. Macedon was made into a Roman province in 148 B.C.E., and Thessalonica was made it's capital. Thessalonica was known for being very diverse. It had a large Jewish population who were visited by the Christian missionary Paul in the first century C.E. This made the city quite important in the early spread of Christianity.

When future Roman emperor Galerius defeated the Persian king Narses, he celebrated by building a huge arch in Thessalonica. Carvings on the arch show scenes of Galerius’s victories. When he became the emperor in 305 C.E., he decided to make Thessalonica his home. He built a new hippodrome (a place for horse racing), and a forum (a place for public meetings, courts of law, gladiatorial combat, and open-air markets), to the benefit of the city.

The city remained rich when eastern Rome became the Byzantine Empire. Only the capital of Byzantine, Constantinople, was more important. Thessalonica had so many fortifications constructed for it that it was able to hold off attacks by the Slavs during the sixth and seventh centuries C.E. Thessalonica still exists today as a city in Greece. There are a lot of archaeological remains to see, many of them from the reign of Galerius. You can see the remnants of the hippodrome, Galerius’s triumphal arch, and many other buildings.

title: The Strait of Bosporus
text:
The Bosporus (also spelled Bosphorus) is a strait in present-day Turkey. It is a relatively small physical feature in the region, but it is very important. The Bosporus is a natural waterway that flows for 32 kilometers (about 20 miles) from north to south, and it is 3.7 km (about two miles) wide at its northern entrance.
