title: Queen Aliquippa
text:
Once known as “Logstown,” the city of Aliquippa was named after Queen Aliquippa. Born in the early 1670s, Queen Aliquippa ruled over the Seneca in what is now Greater Pittsburgh. She was a strong leader for the Seneca. At the time, they were the largest of the six Iroquois Nations.

Queen Aliquippa was a great supporter of the British. On several occasions, she met with the young militia officer George Washington. Upon their meeting, Washington presented Aliquippa with gifts as a sign of respect. Her influence within the Seneca nation was powerful. Aliquippa met with all European representatives to keep her people at peace.

In July 1754, Washington and his British troops were defeated by the French at Fort Duquesne. After the battle, Queen Aliquippa met Washington again. She and other pro-British Native Americans moved to a fortified post in Aughwick. Aughwick Creek joined the Juniata River in Huntington County. She died at the post before the end of the year. After her death, her son continued her legacy. He was a Seneca war captain named Newcastle. He too was a peacemaker between the Iroquois and the colonists.

title: Fort Duquesne to Fort Pitt
text:
The three rivers area in western Pennsylvania was important to the European armies. Known as “The Point,” the land had a view of all movement in each direction. The British sent a small army to build a fort at the Forks of the Ohio. However, the French military arrived first. They built Fort Duquesne, named after the governor of New France in Canada.

The British tried to gain control of Fort Duquesne in 1755. They sent their best military commander, General Edward Braddock. Braddock’s army was defeated in battle. The French kept control of the Ohio country until British General John Forbes marched across Pennsylvania. He arrived with a large army. Knowing that Forbes was coming, the French burned the fort. They retreated north.

The Point became Fort Pitt in 1758. The fort was named after the British prime minister, William Pitt. The area around the fort became known as Pittsburgh.

title: Three Nations, One Land
text:
The Iroquois Confederacy
Before the arrival of Europeans, the American continent was home to the great Iroquois Confederacy. A confederacy is a term for many groups coming together. The five nations of the Iroquois Confederacy were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca. The Tuscarora joined later. They became the sixth nation in 1722. The six nations of the confederacy formed a government. Each nation had one vote. The confederacy was used to keep peace and protect themselves from invasion. Each nation maintained its own unique culture and language.

The name the Iroquois Confederacy used for their alliance was "Haudenosaunee." It means "people who build a house." These people’s homelands extended from the Great Lakes to the Mississippi River, over the Appalachian Mountains, and south to Georgia. The confederacy had elaborate trade systems. Waterways were often used to connect and trade with each other. Their alliances with each other and other Native American nations created security and protection for their people.

The French
Into this vast empire of the Iroquois Confederacy came two empires from Europe: the French and British. French explorers began coming to North America in the early 1500s. As they explored, they met many Native American tribes and began to trade with them. At first, it was just for small items. When fur became more popular in Europe, however, the fur trade took off. French traders made alliances with many Native American nations in the Great Lakes region. The French were in the northeast region of the continent in present-day Canada.

The British
Beginning in 1607 with the settlement of Jamestown, Virginia, the British began to establish colonies in North America. It became clear to many early British colonists that they were not prepared to live in North America. They began to trade with Native Americans for food, tools, and animal hides. However, by the 1750s, the Iroquois found the British moving westward into their territory. The British came into the Iroquois land and built permanent trading posts that expanded into settlements for colonists. New British settlements used many natural resources the Iroquois needed for their people. This created a conflict in trading and other relationships with the Iroquois Confederacy.

These three very different nations wanted the same territory in North America. The Iroquois Confederacy was trying to keep control of the land they had lived on for hundreds of years. The British and the French wanted the land for themselves and their interests. The empires were caught in a three-way struggle for power. This power struggle would eventually lead to war.

title: Physical Characteristics
text: Physical characteristics describe the natural environment of an area. Landscapes, plants, climate, and animals are physical characteristics. Bodies of water, including rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans, are also physical characteristics. Landforms are also a physical characteristic of an area. Some examples of landforms are mountains, plains, valleys, and deserts. These characteristics are all connected and help geographers describe different areas on the Earth’s surface. Physical characteristics are what make the Earth interesting and unique! A physical map shows the world's major physical features. Look at the physical map of the United States. Can you locate the rivers? Can you identify the surrounding oceans?

title: The First Emperor
text:
"I found Rome a city of bricks but left it a city of marble." That is how Augustus Caesar described his impact on the Roman Empire. He was the first official emperor of Rome and one of its most powerful leaders. Augustus was named Octavian at birth. He was the grandnephew of Julius Caesar. Caesar later adopted Octavian as his son.

Following Caesar’s death in 44 B.C.E., Rome was facing civil war again. Octavian tried to stabilize Rome and keep control of its growing territory, wealth, and population. He made an alliance with a powerful general named Marc Antony. The two men worked together to fight opponents around the Mediterranean Sea. They won these wars and divided up the land they conquered. Octavian took control of Rome, while Antony went to help Cleopatra, the ruler of Egypt. Over time, Octavian became worried that Antony would betray him, so he attacked Egypt. He destroyed most of Cleopatra’s fleet at the Battle of Actium in 31 B.C.E. With this victory, Octavian became a Roman hero. His name was changed to Augustus to honor him. Augustus Caesar is considered the dividing line between the Roman Republic (which gave most of the power to the voters) and the Roman Empire, which gave the emperor all the power.

Augustus ruled for about 45 years. During that time, the empire grew in importance. Augustus secured the Roman Empire by building a permanent army of about 150,000 men. He also ordered workers to rebuild Rome with beautiful buildings. He made sure the poor were fed and made the Roman tax system fairer. He placed honest people into government office. Augustus also changed the legal system and set up laws for people in the empire who weren’t Roman citizens. The city of Alexandria was the biggest gain from his victory in Egypt. It became one of the richest and most powerful cultural and trade centers in the world.

title: Week 19 Framing Question
text: What were some of the successes and failures of the Roman Empire?

title: Expanding Territory and Trade
text:
At the height of the Empire, the city of Rome was the center of a huge network of trade. Roman roads connected Europe, Greece, Anatolia, Syria, and North Africa. The entire Roman Empire used the same currency, which made trading easy. Resources were brought in from every direction.

Alexandria, in Egypt, was a cultural center. Athens, in Greece, had academies and educational centers. Gaul, the land that later became France, developed close ties with Rome. The Empire expanded north to the island of Britain, where an emperor named Hadrian built a wall to mark the northern boundary of the Empire. Emperor Claudius added the kingdom of Mauritania, which made Rome even richer. Carthage, in North Africa, brought still more to Rome’s wealth. Rome also used trade routes on the ocean to make connections with eastern Asia. Wealthy Romans soon wore jewels from India and clothes made from Chinese silk.

title: Pax Romana
text:
From 27 B.C.E. to 180 C.E., Rome enjoyed a period of peace and prosperity. We call this period the Pax Romana, which is Latin for “Roman peace.” It began when Augustus became the leader of the Roman Empire. The policies he created and the changes he made created a foundation for peace and stability. The citizens were secure and had more rights. The government kept law and order. During the Pax Romana, the Roman Empire reached its peak in terms of land area. Historians estimate that there were over 70 million people living within the Roman Empire.

When Roman emperors conquered new cities, they offered to protect anyone who became a citizen of the wealthy empire. This offer helped them conquer most of the desirable land around them. Rome’s territory to the north stopped at a cold land of forests. Deserts lay to the south and southeast. The ocean was to the west. The Persian Empire was to the east. The Romans' attempts to expand in that direction failed. They could not defeat the Persians, but the two groups still traded goods and shared religious ideas. War and conquest were not the only things that mattered. During these 200 years, Romans achieved much in science, literature, art, and technology. Historians also call this period the Golden Age of Rome.

title: Innovation
text: Rome had advanced technology for its time. It had significant technological features like arches, plumbing, and concrete. We think of those things as common today, but long ago, they were innovative and sophisticated beyond what other cultures and civilizations had. The engineering, roads, bridges, buildings, and art of Rome made it spectacular. Aqueducts brought in fresh water from far away and supplied plumbing water to homes. Imported goods fed millions of people. There were huge buildings for races and games, and there were theaters and public baths. There were courts of law and markets with exotic goods and services and places for people to meet and discuss the issues of the day.

title: Aqueducts
text:
For hundreds of years, Romans used water from the Tiber River or from wells and springs. As Rome grew, however, there was more demand for water, so the Romans began building aqueducts. An aqueduct is a channel that carries water from one place to another. Although the ancient Greeks, Egyptians, and Persians also built aqueducts, the Romans became famous for this feat of engineering.

The word aqueduct comes from two Latin words: “aqua,” meaning “water”; and “ductus,” meaning “to lead.” Long stone channels carried water from streams in nearby mountains and hills into the city to public fountains, public baths, and a few wealthy homes. The first Roman aqueduct was named the Aqua Appia. It carried water over 10 miles from mountain springs into the center of Rome. Much of it was underground. This protected it from enemies who might try to poison the water supply. The aqueducts leaked quite badly and needed lots of maintenance. The channels and tunnels were mostly made of stone, but sometimes the Romans used leather, lead, clay, wood, and other materials for pipes. Eventually, Rome had 11 aqueducts to supply an ever-growing population with clean water. Many of the houses had pipes, which carried water into the home and into underground heating systems. Some of the ancient Roman aqueducts still work today.

The ancient Romans also created innovative systems for dealing with sanitation problems. According to written records, it was common for Romans to throw waste out of windows into the streets. The Romans created a system of large sewers covered by stones. The main function was to move filthy water away from the city, where it affected cleanliness, health, and economic growth. Waste flowed through channels into the main sewage system and then into rivers or streams. These sewers ran throughout the city. Some were connected to private toilets, but they were also used as dumping grounds by people whose homes were not connected to a sewer. There were also large public toilets with room for many people at the same time.

title: Roman Roads
text:
Roman roads crisscrossed the continent and were an important part of the empire’s success. The first major road was completed in 312 B.C.E. It was a supply route between the Republic of Rome and the city of Capua. The road’s length and beautiful construction earned it the nickname “the queen of roads.”

Historians estimate that the Romans built over 55,000 miles of roads over the next several centuries. Every time the Roman army conquered a new region, Roman surveyors, engineers and builders soon arrived. They used the best supplies from local areas to build roads that connected the new land to the capital city of Rome. Many of these roads were even paved.

Roman roads were built in layers to make them strong enough for lots of use and heavy loads. The first layer was gravel, followed by crushed limestone. The road was then paved using neatly ordered blocks of lava rock or iron ore. Builders took the time to make sure the roads were carefully leveled. They even built drainage ditches to protect against erosion during rainy seasons. Each side of the road also had a path for people who were traveling on foot. As Rome grew, the roads they built made it possible to keep track of new lands and control how they developed. Traders and soldiers could travel quickly and safely. Messengers could travel faster, which helped leaders communicate.

title: Roman Art and Architecture
text:
Roman artists and architects created magnificent art and impressive monuments. These works are part of the Romans’ lasting legacy. Greeks styles and techniques had a strong influence on early Roman art. The emperors and wealthy families often paid artists to create works of art. They carved many sculptures, mostly of people. They also created many paintings and mosaics. Artists would paint directly on the walls, not on a canvas. Mosaics could be created on the walls or on the floors.

The Greeks also influenced early Roman architecture, but as the Empire expanded, Roman craftsmen developed new skills and created their own styles. Soon, they were influencing other cultures. The Romans used brick and marble for many of their buildings. Roman architecture is known for arches, domes, amphitheaters, temples, and large apartment buildings.

One of the most important Roman accomplishments in architecture was the arch. A keystone in the center held wedge-shaped blocks together and distributed the weight. This replaced the need for support posts in the middle of large entryways. The arch allowed Roman architects to make larger and larger buildings. Many of them still stand today, thanks not only to the skills of their designers but also to the ingenuity of scientists who developed formulas for cement and concrete. The Romans recognized that building with a quick-drying, liquid material was far easier than trying to build the same features in brick or stone. The use of arches and the development of concrete led to the design of dome ceilings. Many temples, palaces, and baths had domes. These allowed Romans to build large rooms with wide, open spaces and no stone columns or wood supports.

The Colosseum in Rome is a great example of Roman engineering and construction. The Colosseum was a large outdoor stadium that could seat around 50,000 people for various forms of entertainment, such as gladiator games, mock battles, and dramas. The huge Colosseum is freestanding and built with concrete and multiple arches to give it strength. Much of it still stands today, although earthquakes have knocked parts of it down.

title: The End of an Empire
text:
For many centuries, Romans excelled at agriculture, art, architecture, literature, law, philosophy, engineering, martial arts, and war. The Romans were even good at having fun. They attended fancy feasts prepared by master chefs. They enjoyed theater, races, games, and contests.

How could the world’s most powerful empire tumble into ruin? It’s a good question. People living at the time may not have seen it coming, but historians since then have spent hundreds of years trying to understand why the Roman Empire fell. They may not always agree, but after sorting through all the information and evidence available, most have come to the conclusion that there were many important contributing factors. They also agree that it did not happen overnight.

As Roman conquests came to an end, taking treasures from conquered territories stopped. Taxes were not enough to make up the difference. The army no longer enslaved people from conquered countries. Roman society depended greatly on enslaved people to serve not only in homes, but also in the businesses, farms, mines, and mills of the empire. The empire was getting old. The roads were worn by weather and use. Water and sewer systems needed repair. But there were not enough workers or resources. The armies needed new equipment and more soldiers.

For centuries, the city of Rome had been the center of the empire, but now its rulers faced complications. In Europe, there were five major barbarian tribes: the Visigoths, the Saxons, the Huns, the Vandals, and the Franks. All of them wanted to destroy Rome. There were political disagreements, social problems, revolts, and invasions. Running such a large territory and fighting off invaders got harder and harder for one central government to handle. In 286 C.E., the emperor Diocletian decided to make things easier to manage. He divided the empire into two sections, eastern and western. There were now two emperors, one in each half, and they governed independently. At first, their forms of leadership were similar and they enforced some of the same laws. But as time went on, the differences between the two halves grew, especially in religion, language, and culture.

The Western Roman Empire

The new faith of Christianity was spreading. Theodosius I, the emperor who ruled from 379 to 395 C.E., had such a strong Christian faith that he helped spread Christianity throughout the empire until it became the official Roman religion in 380. Conflicts and political troubles weakened the empire from within. The Roman armies were constantly having to beat back attacks from tribes outside its borders. The army started recruiting troops from other countries, but they were undisciplined and not loyal to Rome. By 476, there was not enough support for Rome. In 476 C.E., King Alaric and the Visigoths sacked the city of Rome, and soon after, the entire Western Roman Empire fell.

The Eastern Roman Empire

The governing city of the Eastern Empire was Byzantium, a small city in the Mediterranean region. The city’s location gave the Empire an important position between Europe and Asia. Emperor Constantine I made Byzantium his home and declared it the “new Rome.” The city was renamed Constantinople. Historians refer to this time as the Byzantine Empire. It prospered and flourished for another 1,000 years. Eventually, divisions over opinions and beliefs weakened the Byzantine Empire, and it fell to the Turkish Empire.

title: Famous Romans
text:
Cicero (106–43 B.C.E.)

Cicero was a Roman lawyer who lived in the time of Julius Caesar. He was one of Rome's greatest speakers. Here are some famous quotes from his speeches. What do you think they mean?

Where there is life, there is hope.

He is his own worst enemy.

Not to know what happened before you were born is to remain forever a child.

One does not have to believe everything he hears.

Virgil (70–19 B.C.E.)

Virgil was a famous Roman poet. Virgil's poems told how wonderful it was to live in a time of peace (Pax Romana). In other poems, he wrote about living a simple life and about Italy's beautiful land. Virgil's most famous poem (a long poem called an epic) actually filled 12 books. In the epic Aeneid, Virgil told of Aeneas, a hero who fled from Troy after the Greeks captured it and then traveled to Italy, where he became the ancestor of the Romans. He wrote of the adventures of Aeneas and his people as they traveled across the sea to Rome. Virgil wasn't happy with this work and asked that people burn it after he died. Fortunately for the world, his relatives did not do so!

Hadrian and His Wall (76–138 C.E.)

Historians consider Hadrian one of Rome's Five Good Emperors. As emperor, Hadrian decided not to expand the Roman Empire. In fact, one of the first things Hadrian did was return much of the eastern lands the emperor before him had taken.

A famous wall bears Hadrian's name. While visiting Great Britain in 122 C.E., Hadrian ordered that workers build a wall. He wanted this wall to be the boundary for the end of the Roman Empire. The wall ran about 74 miles along northern England. It took workers seven years to build and was eight feet thick. They built many forts along the wall as watchtowers to keep an eye out for the Picts, their enemies in the north. The workers built a large ditch, said to be as tall as three men, in front and behind the wall. After the Roman soldiers left Great Britain in 410 C.E., the wall eventually fell into disrepair, but much of it still exists.

title: Barbarians at the Border
text:
The term “barbarian” is not new, and it is not usually meant as a compliment. For centuries, people have used it as a way to describe or judge someone who is different from them. Those who use the term often do not personally know the people they are describing. They usually assume the people they’re describing are uncivilized, vulgar, evil, or somehow just not as valuable. Where does the word come from? Who were the first people to use the term, and whom were they talking about?

The word “barbarian” comes from the Greek root word “barbarous,” which means “babbler.” The Greeks were the first to use the term, and they used it to refer to anyone who could not speak or understand their language. At the time, that was a pretty large group of people. Ancient Greeks may have used the term “barbarian” to refer to Egyptians, Persians, Indians, Celts, Germans, Phoenicians, Etruscans, Macedonians, Carthaginians, Vikings, and Goths. Later, Romans used the term to describe all foreign, non-Roman people. It was used to describe the tribes or nations they wished to conquer, along with those they hoped to defend against. As it turned out, they sometimes had good reason to be worried. When groups of so-called barbarians united and took up arms against the Romans, the groups were a powerful force and eventually contributed to the fall of the Roman Empire.

Today, people often use the word “barbarian” to refer to someone who has uncivilized behavior or who behaves in a cruel or inhumane way. When used carefully and knowledgeably, it can be a powerful descriptor. When used carelessly, the word is only hurtful and can be harmful to relationships.

title: The Strait of Bosporus
text:
The Bosporus (also spelled Bosphorus) is a strait in present-day Turkey. It is a relatively small physical feature in the region, but it is very important. The Bosporus is a natural waterway that flows for 32 km (about 20 miles) from north to south, and it is 3.7 km (about two miles) wide at the northern entrance. At its narrowest point, the strait is only 750 meters across. What makes such a small body of water so important? Not only does the Bosporus connect the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, but it also separates Asian Turkey from European Turkey. It is a continental boundary between Asia and Europe. It is one of only two passages between the Black and Mediterranean Seas. Civilizations throughout the centuries have relied on the passage to build strong trading economies.

If traders could use the strait, armies and navies could as well. Many emperors built castles or fortifications on the European side to defend the city of Constantinople from invaders. Today, the city is known as Istanbul. The Bosporus continued to attract interest from governments and generals as the world went to war in the 20th century, too.

Today, the Bosporus is a very busy place. On its southern end, it is bordered on both shores by the bustling city of Istanbul. It is the main waterway for ships that transport fuel to European countries from Russia and western Asia. Around 48,000 ships make their way through the strait each year, including several thousand oil tankers. The tankers and trading vessels share the channel with a rich population of tourists and fish. Several species of fish use the Bosporus as a seasonal migration route from the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. Shores on both sides are lined with resorts and villages. Cross a bridge and enjoy your vacation on another continent!

title: Introduction to Mesoamerica
text:
The Americas were home to many different cultures, possibly as early as 20,000 B.C.E. Mesoamerica saw many vibrant and innovative societies. This area is located in the center of North and South America. The term “Mesoamerica” is used to describe a historical region that includes parts of present-day Central Mexico, Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, El Salvador, and Guatemala. The term was first used by anthropologist Paul Kirchoff in 1943 to distinguish the people of this region from other regions of the Americas.

For thousands of years, Mesoamerica was home to several cultures, including the Olmec, Maya, and Aztec. Each had its own unique practices, customs, and traditions. These early inhabitants of Mesoamerica gradually developed complex and sophisticated societies. They made great cities, built monumental buildings, and created beautiful works of art. These groups left a lasting legacy that continues to be studied and admired today.

The oldest of these cultures is the Olmec. It emerged around 1500–1400 B.C.E. in the Gulf Coast region. The Olmec culture flourished for hundreds of years in southern Mexico.

The Maya were one of the largest and most advanced early civilizations of Mesoamerica. The Maya civilization extended from the tip of the Yucatán Peninsula to the Pacific Ocean. The modern countries of Guatemala and Belize, as well as parts of Mexico and Honduras, were part of the Mayas' large territory. The Maya civilization is known for its complex hieroglyphic writing system and its advanced calendar. The Maya people were skilled builders and artists. They left behind a rich legacy of pyramids, temples, and monuments.

The Aztec Empire encompassed much of Central Mexico, west of the Maya. The Aztec was the most recent of the three major civilizations of Mesoamerica. The Aztecs were skilled warriors and traders. They expanded their empire through a combination of alliances and conquests.

text: How did geographic factors affect the early people of Mesoamerica?

title: Geography of Mesoamerica
text:
The physical characteristics of Mesoamerica vary greatly throughout the regions, making it an incredibly unique area of North America. The region of Mesoamerica is bordered by many major bodies of water, including the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean Sea.

Mesoamerica is also home to many important rivers. The longest is the Usumacinta River, which runs from Guatemala and through southeastern Mexico before emptying into the Gulf of Mexico. The Yucatán Peninsula is a large piece of land that sticks out into the Caribbean Sea. Although many rivers flow through Mesoamerica, the northern part of the Yucatán Peninsula has almost no above-ground waterways. The fresh water supplied to this area comes from underground aquifers accessible through sinkholes, openings, or natural wells in the bedrock, called cenotes.

One of the most distinguishing physical characteristics of Mesoamerica is its mountains. The main mountain range of Mesoamerica is the Sierra Madre range. The Sierra Madre range not only includes mountains but also over 80 active volcanoes. The largest peak in the Sierra Madre range is a dormant, or inactive, volcano called Pico de Orizaba, located in Mexico. It stands well over 18,000 feet tall.

Rainforests cover much of the landscape of Mesoamerica. Mesoamerica is home to the second-largest tropical rainforest in the Americas, after the Amazon Rainforest in South America. The Maya Forest covers an area of millions of acres that stretches across southeastern Mexico, northern Guatemala, and Belize.

title: Resources
text:
The region of Mesoamerica is rich in natural resources. For thousands of years, early societies relied solely on the resources of the natural environment to meet their needs and wants. Like other nomadic cultures, the people of Ancient Mesoamerica hunted and gathered for food before widespread agriculture became a common practice. Mesoamerica was home to thousands of plants and animals native to the region. The people of the region relied on these animals and plants for food, clothing, and tools. The Olmec, Maya, and Aztec hunted many different types of animals, including deer, armadillos, tapirs, peccaries, monkeys, guinea pigs, and iguanas. Animals were also hunted to make other goods. Animal furs, feathers, and hides were used to make clothing and other goods. The furs of jaguars, cougars, jaguarundis, margays, ocelots, and oncillas were considered luxury items because of their unique coats and connections to Mesoamerican cultural beliefs and creation myths.

Groups that lived in the coastal areas of Mesoamerica also hunted marine mammals and reptiles, such as manatees and turtles. They fished and gathered shellfish, including lobster, shrimp, and conch. Mesoamerica is also home to thousands of native plants that produce fruits, vegetables, nuts, and berries. The people of Mesoamerica gathered plants, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and berries to increase their food supply, including avocados, papaya, guava, and cacao beans. Plant fibers, such as cotton, yucca, and agave, were gathered to make textiles, like clothing.

title: Trade
text:
The people of Mesoamerica also tapped into the rich resources found in the mountainous areas of the region. Gold, silver, and obsidian were mined and used to make goods. Obsidian is incredibly strong and makes an ideal material for tools. It was also believed to have spiritual properties and was used for ceremonial purposes. The Maya also mined other valuable resources, such as jade and limestone.

The vast natural resources of the region led to extensive trade networks. Trade was an important part of life in ancient Mesoamerica and helped civilizations to thrive and grow. Archaeologists have found significant evidence that the peoples of Mesoamerica were involved in short- and long-distance trade. Researchers believe they traded natural resources and the goods they produced with other cultures in the region as well as tribes in North and South America. They traded everyday items like food, clothing, and tools. Aztec merchants throughout Mesoamerica also traded luxury items, such as quetzal feathers, jade, and cocoa beans. For centuries, the Aztec and Maya civilizations dominated the obsidian trade.

These early societies used a system of standardized weights and measures to make trade easier. Like many early civilizations, the Maya mostly bartered, trading items they had for things they needed and wanted. They may also have used cacao beans as a form of money. A new study suggests that chocolate became a little like coins and was used to pay workers and to buy things at the marketplace.

title: Life in the Rainforest
text:
The Maya civilization stretched from the lowlands of the Yucatán Peninsula to the highlands along the Pacific Ocean. The geography of the Maya Lowlands is very different from the geography of the rest of the region. Unlike the mountainous and dry areas of the highlands, the Maya Lowlands is covered with dense tropical rainforests. This region of Mesoamerica was not an easy place to live. The thick tropical rainforests were not easy to navigate and travel through. There are very few navigable rivers, lakes, or other sources of freshwater in the Maya Lowlands.

One of the most impressive things about the Maya was their ability to build a great civilization in a tropical rainforest climate. They collected water from underground cenotes to supply fresh water to the city. They adapted their crops and agricultural ways to marshlands. They took advantage of the variety of plants and animals in the rainforest, using them for food, medicine, and other purposes. They built sturdy homes that could withstand the climate.

Despite the challenges posed by this region, the Maya still thrived in this environment. One of their largest cities was located in dense rainforests. Chichén Itzá was founded around 400 C.E. and grew into one of the most important cities of the Maya civilization. The people of Chichén Itzá used abundant sources of stone to construct large temples, plazas, homes, and courts for recreational purposes.

title: The Agricultural Revolution in Mesoamerica
text:
Mesoamerica is considered the cradle of the Agricultural Revolution in North America. Archaeologists estimate that the Agricultural Revolution began in Mesoamerica around 6000 B.C.E. It began in Central Mexico in the lush river valleys of the region. Because it is close to rivers, the soil of Central Mexico is very fertile and there is a consistent source of fresh water for plants.

The first crop to be domesticated and cultivated by the people of Mesoamerica was teosinte. Teosinte was an early form of maize that is native to Mesoamerica. At first, the early people of the region gathered teosinte to supplement their diet. Then, they began to clear small areas of land and plant crops. Over time, the Mesoamericans began to cultivate certain strains, or types, of teosinte, which developed into maize and eventually the modern form of corn that people eat today. The people used the same methods to cultivate other native plants, including beans and squash.

As trade became more widespread throughout the continent, agriculture and farming spread to other areas of Mesoamerica, and new plants were domesticated. The people of the Yucatán Peninsula began to engage in agriculture around 2500 B.C.E. They cut back and used burning techniques to clear areas of the dense forest. They also constructed raised fields in the swampy areas of the lowlands and built irrigation canals to carry water from underground cenotes to the fields.

The ancestors of the Maya who inhabited the mountainous areas of the region dug out flat patches of land for farming that made the side of the mountain look like a giant staircase. This technique is called step, or terrace, farming. In order to water their crops, engineers and architects built canals and aqueducts. The ancient people of the area also used rainfall and river water to supply an irrigation system. They used crop rotation to help the soil recover lost nutrients and added fertilizer to boost crop production.

As agriculture became more widespread, the Indigenous people of Mesoamerica began to domesticate other native plants. Fruit was an important part of the Indigenous diet. Domestication of guava, papaya, avocado, banana, and breadnut trees made access to these fruits much easier. The Indigenous Mesoamericans also domesticated various vegetables and other plants, including black and red beans, pumpkins, peppers, sunflowers, tomatoes, tobacco, oregano, vanilla, and agave. One of the most valuable domesticated plants was the cacao tree. Cacao beans became a highly desired trade item, were served at royal feasts, and were even used as currency. The people of Mesoamerica also domesticated wild animals during this time. The first animals to be domesticated in Mesoamerica were turkeys and dogs

.

title: Mesoamerican Groups
text:
Many experts estimate that people have lived in Mesoamerica for over 12,000 years. New evidence and research have led some archaeologists and historians to believe that people could have lived in Mesoamerica as early as 20,000 B.C.E. Despite these differing theories, experts agree that people have inhabited this region for thousands of years. The early people of Mesoamerica were nomadic hunter-gatherers. Over time, the groups of hunter-gatherers began to build permanent settlements, form tribes, and eventually establish large societies. While the Maya dominated much of the region, other cultures also lived and thrived in Mesoamerica.

The Olmec

The Olmec were the first large culture, or organized group of people, in the area. They are considered to be the "mother culture" of Mesoamerica because many later groups, such as the Maya and the Aztec, developed from the cultural traditions of the Olmec. The name “Olmec” means “people of the rubber country” in the Nahuatl language. They were given this name because they inhabited areas of Mesoamerica that had an abundant supply of rubber trees. Extracting and using latex rubber from rubber trees was common among the Olmec.

The Olmec were the first people to build pyramids in ancient Mesoamerica. Their largest pyramid was over 100 feet tall. The most famous archaeological feature of the Olmec is the large stone heads that range from five to 11 feet tall. They are carved from single blocks of stone. Many of these stone heads have war-like helmets on their heads. Archaeologists believe that these represent the heads of Olmec rulers.

The Zapotec Culture

The Zapotec, or Mixtec culture, like the Maya, existed for many centuries but reached a peak of power and city building from around 300 C.E. to 900 C.E. One of the largest cities built by the Zapotec is now known as Monte Albán. This city is located in the Oaxaca region of modern-day Mexico, in a mountainous area. Monte Albán has shortened pyramids or pyramids that look like they’ve been cut off at the base. It also has a great plaza built on the highest hill in the city. Surrounding the plaza were two temples. The city also has a ball court, and archaeologists have discovered around 170 tombs in the city.

Teotihuacanos

Around 100 B.C.E., another civilization flourished in what is now central Mexico. The city was begun by a group of people known as the Teotihuacanos, but it was later occupied by other cultures, mainly the Aztecs. There is still much that we don’t know about the Teotihuacanos. The civilization did not leave a written language and much of its history has been lost to time. Based on archaeological evidence and the accounts of later cultures, we know that the Teotihuacanos were skilled architects and engineers. They built many impressive structures, such as the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, and the Avenue of the Dead.

title: Week 28 Framing Question
text: What factors shaped the lives of the Maya people?

title: The Maya Civilization
text:
The Maya Civilization lasted for over 2,000 years. It covered parts of what are now Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Belize. The Yucatán was the heart of the Maya civilization for hundreds of years. The Maya were advanced mathematicians and agriculturalists. They knew how to rotate crops to keep farm soil from being overused. They used math to create complex architecture and accurate calendars. The Maya had a written hieroglyphic language and a sophisticated government system. This civilization existed between many independent city-states. Trade existed between the city-states. However, each settlement tended to manage its own people.

The height of the Maya building power happened from about 250 to 900 C.E. The Maya built large cities throughout their territories. These cities had monumental architectural structures, such as palaces, plazas, and pyramids. The people spoke many different dialects of the Mayan language, and, depending on the area or city, they had different cultural characteristics. The most prominent cities of the Maya were Tikal, located in what is now northern Guatemala, and Chichén Itzá, in the Yucatán.

Archeologists often divide Maya culture into multiple time periods. The Classic Period, from 250 to 900 C.E., is considered the golden age of the Maya city-states. During each period of its history, the culture, government, traditions, and economy of the Maya civilization adapted and evolved.

title: Society
text:
The Maya culture began with small farming villages. As agriculture and trade spread, the people began to build more permanent settlements. This required a larger workforce to build homes, clear the land, and grow crops. As populations grew, more food and resources were available. Small Maya settlements grew and gradually became towns and cities.

The great civilization of the Maya emerged around 200 B.C.E. Cities had hundreds of homes and dozens of pyramids. They were constructed around a large central plaza, which served as a meeting area. As the civilization expanded, the rulers divided the territory into individual political states. At the height of the Maya civilization, there were 18 separate states. These states each had smaller towns and villages, all of which were governed by a capital city.

The Maya had a hierarchical society. People had different positions in society based on their job, rank, and birth. The highest class was the nobility. This included the ruler, government and military officials, and priests. The ruler, also called halach uinic, which means “true man,” was the highest member of the nobility. The ruler had total power. He was assisted by advisors and governors. Leadership positions were passed down through family lines. Members of the nobility usually lived in the central areas of Maya cities.

The next level of Maya society was the artisans and merchants. Artisans produced luxury goods, painted, and made sculptures. Merchants traveled the land to sell and import items. Near the bottom of the social hierarchy were the commoners, including farmers, servants, and laborers. Commoners were forbidden from wearing clothing reserved for the nobility and could not buy luxury items, but they could advance to a higher rank in society through military service. Enslaved people and their children were at the very bottom of the social hierarchy. Enslavement was a form of punishment for committing a crime or failing to pay debts. Captives from wars were also enslaved and forced to work as laborers.

title: Daily Life
text:
Daily life and activities often revolved around families. The center of much of Maya society was the family and the home. For most Maya, a home consisted of several buildings. The main house was the area where families gathered together, ate, slept, and worked. Smaller buildings were built near the main house. These buildings often had a kitchen, storerooms, and workshops. Some homes even had a steam or bath house.

Most women and girls were responsible for keeping house and cooking. They were also responsible for raising children, making pottery, and weaving cloth. Men were responsible for supporting their families. Many homes also had their own small farms and gardens. Men worked these family farms and gardens. They also hunted and fished. Boys learned how to take care of their families from their fathers and other male relatives.

Nobles had an easy life and freedom to do activities they enjoyed. Noblemen had duties related to their position in government or the military. Children from noble families received a formal education. They learned mathematics, astronomy, medicine, religion, and other subjects.

The social hierarchy also influenced daily activities. The lives of commoners and enslaved people were very different from the other classes. Their activities revolved around hard work. They worked in agriculture or as laborers in the cities. Their children learned the same skills and often worked alongside their parents from a young age.

All levels of society participated in special events, such as blessings, coming-of-age celebrations, and marriage ceremonies. Archaeologists continue to find evidence to support theories about the Mesoamerican lifestyle, social structure, culture, and religion. They have found remains of large stone ball courts in cities such as Chichén Itzá, Cerros, , Palenque, and Copán. In these courts, teams of two or three players would attempt to get a very hard rubber ball through a stone ring that stood 27 feet above the ground. They couldn’t use their hands. Spectators would come and watch the ballgame at the arena, much like modern sporting events today. Historians believe the game played on these courts was more than a sport. It was also a religious ceremony.

title: Beliefs
text:
Like many ancient civilizations, the Maya were polytheistic. Many of their gods and goddesses were associated with nature or important aspects of Maya life. For example, Itzam Ná is the Maya god of creation, while Hun H'unahpu is the god of maize.

The Maya believed that the world was divided into three separate realms: the Earth, the Celestial Realm, and the Underworld. They believed that the Earth rested on the back of a turtle or caiman floating in the sea between the Celestial Realm and the Underworld. The Maya religion divided the Earth into four separate quadrants that corresponded to the four cardinal directions. At the center of the Earth was the cosmic tree, which represented life.

Specific symbols represented different beliefs of the Maya. One of the most powerful symbols of the Maya culture was the jaguar. The jaguar is native to Mesoamerica, and the Maya believed it symbolized strength, bravery, and ferocity. Jaguars were also believed to be the gods of the Underworld and were the rulers of day and night. Maya warriors would wear jaguar skulls into battle as a symbol of their bravery and strength.

Maya priests communicated with the gods and shared their wisdom with the people. Priests were in charge of many aspects of Maya life, including rituals, ceremonies, calculating time, medicine, and recording important events. Much of what we know about the Maya religion comes from a book called the Popol Vuh. The Popol Vuh was written in the 1500s by Francisco Ximenez, a Spanish friar who observed the religious practices of the Maya.

title: Conflict
text:
Although the Maya shared cultural customs, beliefs, and traditions, conflict still existed between political leaders and the various city-states. Conflict in the Maya civilization often stemmed from environmental, political, and social changes. One of the greatest examples of conflict occurred because of a natural disaster in the region.

Between 600 and 1000 C.E., a series of severe droughts impacted Mesoamerica. These repeated droughts caused water levels in human-made reservoirs and natural cenotes to drop. The lack of fresh water caused a decline in agriculture. As agriculture declined, food sources became more scarce. The people needed to place blame on someone for the terrible conditions they faced.

The Maya believed that the ruler and priests were in direct communication with the gods. The people believed that these droughts occurred because their rulers and priests refused to ask the gods of rain to lift the drought. Rulers of various city-states fought for power. They promised that they would ask for the rains to return if they were given more power. City-states formed alliances to overthrow other city-states. Archaeologists have found evidence of competition, war, and alliances by studying stone monuments from this time. Many stone monuments were created to record the events that occurred during this time in Maya history.

title: End of the Maya Civilization
text:
The mighty Maya civilization eventually fell like many ancient civilizations across the world. There have been many different theories and claims made by historians to explain the fall of the Maya civilization. The most common theories for the decline of the Maya civilization are drought, overpopulation, and warfare. Despite these differing theories, experts agree that the decline or end of the Maya civilization occurred between 800 and 1000 C.E.

One of the most common theories to explain the decline is drought. One of the main causes of the drought was a lack of rainfall in the region. Another source of the drought was large-scale deforestation and the clearing of land for farms. This agricultural practice led to a lack of moisture in the ground and soil. This caused underground sources of water to decrease. Droughts led to a decline in crops and sources of food.

Another theory that explains the decline in the Maya civilization is overpopulation. Archaeological evidence suggests that tens of thousands of people lived in and around each of the large cities in the Maya Lowlands. The large population put a strain on the already-limited resources of the region. As a result, thousands of people left the large cities and migrated to less populated areas of the Maya Highlands.

Both drought and overpopulation led to conflict and warfare. About 90 percent of the population of the Maya Lowlands were farmers. The farmers blamed their rulers for the lack of rain. They believed their rulers did not ask the gods for rain or that the gods were displeased with the nobility. This led to conflict between the social classes. Some members of the nobility wanted to take power for themselves and overthrow the rulers. As war and conflict increased, more people abandoned the cities.

By 950 C.E., the once-thriving cities of the Maya Lowlands were abandoned, but the Maya did not disappear completely. New settlements and sprawling cities were constructed in the Maya Highlands. The Maya civilization did not officially end until 1524 C.E. when Spanish explorers and soldiers defeated the Quiche Maya at the Battle of Utatlan. Many of the descendants of the Maya who remained in Mesoamerica through Spanish exploration and colonization still live in the area today.

title: The Inca
text:
The Inca Empire was one of the largest civilizations in the world from around 1400 C.E. until its end in 1533 C.E. The Inca lived in South America, in and around the Andes Mountains. Stretching more than 2,500 miles from Santiago, Chile, in the south to Quito, Ecuador, in the north, the Inca Empire was truly massive. It was called Tahuantinsuyu, which translates to “four quarters.” This is how the empire was divided by the government. The empire had a population of 10 million people that spoke 30 different languages.

The climate of the Andes Mountains was ideal for farming, but the land was not very flat. Farmers needed to find a way to work the soil on hillsides. They learned to use the terrain and landforms together with the climate and became very skilled farmers. They developed a technique called step, or terrace, farming. They dug out flat patches of land for farming that made the side of the mountain look like a giant staircase.

In order to water their crops, engineers and architects built canals and aqueducts. Aqueducts are human-made structures, usually made from stone, that bring water from one place to another. The Inca relied on rivers that flowed through the Andes Mountains. Many of these rivers flow out of the mountains and empty into the mighty Amazon River. The Inca also used rainfall and river water to supply an irrigation system.

title: Teotihuacán
text:
The city of Teotihuacán was the political and cultural center of Central Mexico. With over 25,000 people living there, it was home to religious temples that still stand today. Carefully planned and beautifully created, the archaeological remains of the city are still studied for the information they can reveal about the people that lived there from some time around the 2nd century BCE until it began to decline in the mid-7th century. The ruins of Teotihuacán represent one of the largest, most advanced cities of its time in central Mexico.

Teotihuacán featured well-planned streets arranged in a grid pattern with its main street running north to south and cross streets running east and west. It was not a city that developed randomly as it grew. Instead, it clearly demonstrates that influential people in their society took time to figure out the best way to lay out the city. The city planners even rerouted the San Juan River that ran through the city. The residents of Teotihuacán lived in apartment-style buildings, including some with more than one story. Many of the features of the city influenced the later cultures in the area, including the Maya and Aztecs. People from around the region came to the city to trade and pay tribute.

Despite the great thought and effort that went into the construction of Teotihuacán, not much is known about the people who lived there and constructed the great ancient city. Because of this, its name is lost to history. The word “Teotihuacán” comes from the Aztec name for the place where the gods were created. Given the massive step pyramid temples found there, the name makes sense. Teotihuacán served a particular religious purpose for its citizens. The construction of these geometrically precise structures reveals the advanced knowledge of the people who built them. Many of the temples still stand, including the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, and the Temple of Quetzalcoatl.

title: Mexica Culture
text:
The Aztec were a group of warriors that settled in the land that is now called Mexico during the 13th century. They fought wars with other groups in Mexico until they controlled most of what is now modern-day Central America. The Aztec called themselves the Mexica people. Mexica culture was greatly influenced by the Mesoamerican cultures before it. The Mexica inherited many cultural features from the Toltec and Teotihuacanos. Like the Maya and Toltec who came before them, they built spectacular cities. The layout of their capital city, Tenochtitlan, was inherited from Teotihuacán.

Tenochtitlan was built over Lake Texcoco. It became their most important city-state and the center of the powerful Aztec Empire. A city-state is a city that operates as an independent country and often controls the territory around it politically, economically, and culturally. The city-state structure originally came from the Maya.

The Mexica people themselves credited the Teotihuacanos and Toltecs as the originators of many of their cultural characteristics, including religious practices and authority. Like the Teotihuacanos and the Toltecs, the Aztec played the ball game and built fields and courts to play it. From the Toltecs, the Mexica copied the cyclical calendar and many other features in their art.

However, one of the most important cultural features that influenced the Mexica’s daily life, as well as their celebrations, was war. The Aztec Empire gained control of its large territory through war. War had political and economic motivations, but preparing for war, going to war, and giving thanks for victory required rituals, sacrifices, and celebrations. These were often undertaken at the temple of the god of war and were huge elements of Mexica culture. As the Aztec conquered the people around them, the Mexica culture affected the cultures of the other city-states controlled by the Aztec Empire.

title: Week 21 Framing Question
text: Which cultural characteristic of the Aztec Empire had the most influence on the daily lives of the Mexica people?

title: Language
text:
The Mexica people spoke Nahuatl. This language was a part of the Uto-Aztecan language family. It was related to other Central American languages, as well as some North American languages, like Comanche, Shoshone, Ute, and Hopi. The Mexica believed their language was sacred. They believed words had power, especially when it came to communicating with the gods. The Mexica thought that those who spoke different languages were lesser than them, especially because they could not communicate with the gods the way that the Mexica could.

The Nahuatl language has been preserved orally, meaning that there are still people who speak Nahuatl today. However, at the time of the Aztec Empire, the Nahuatl language did not have a written alphabet. About 30 years after the Aztec Empire was conquered by the Spanish, a Roman Catholic missionary and Franciscan friar named Bernardino de Sahagún wrote down the Nahuatl language using Spanish letters. He recorded Nahuatl vocabulary and collected information about Mexica culture from the former nobility of Tenochtitlan. He compiled all of this information into a book called the General History of the Things of New Spain, also called the Florentine Codex because the original manuscript is kept in Florence, Italy.

There are a few other Nahuatl manuscripts that were written by Spaniards and some that were written by native peoples. One was written by another missionary, a Dominican friar named Diego Durán. It holds valuable information about the rise of the Aztec Empire. Another writer named Fernando de Alva Cortés Ixtlilxóchitl was the grandson of the tlatoani of Texcoco. However, he writes mostly about Texcoco and the Chichimeca ethnic group. In many historians’ opinions, the best record of the Nahuatl language and culture of the Mexica is contained in Sahagún’s book, General History of the Things of New Spain.

title: Aztec Gods
text:
The Mexica were polytheistic, meaning they believed in many gods. At the center of the city of Tenochtitlan were two temples. The first temple was dedicated to the god of war and the sun, Huitzilopochtli. In Nahuatl, the name Huitzilopochtli literally means “hummingbird from the left/south.” In oral histories about the god Huitizilopochtli, he usually takes the form of a hummingbird. Huitzilopochtli was also the god who had led the Mexica to their city, Tenochtitlan, in the form of a hummingbird. The god of war, just like his temple, was central to the culture of Tenochtitlan and the Mexica. War was how they gained and maintained their empire. The second temple was dedicated to Tlaloc, the god of rain and agriculture. Rain and agriculture were also central to the lives of the Mexica. Without rain and a good harvest, the city and its people would not survive.

The god Quetzalcoatl also had a temple near the center of the city. Among the Mexica, Quetzalcoatl was the god of the wind, and he was closely associated with priests and priestly knowledge. Priests were very important figures among the Mexica. They kept the calendar, interpreted the gods’ desires, and performed rituals and sacrifices.

The Aztec calendar was copied from the Toltec calendar and was cyclical. The Mexica believed that every 52 years, the calendar started over. They also believed that the calendar worked in cycles of prosperity and decline. In the calendar, each day was named, and each god was in charge of certain days. Children born in Tenochtitlan were partly named after their day sign.

The supreme god among the Mexica was Tezcatlipoca. This name literally translates to “smoking mirror.” Tezcatlipoca determined human destinies. He was everywhere and all-powerful. The Mexica did not believe in benign or benevolent gods. They believed that gods did not care very much about humans or their problems. The gods demanded sacrifice and would only be urged to intervene for humans after suffering.

title: Rituals, Feasts, and Festivals
text:
Because priests were in charge of keeping the Aztec calendar, they were often at the center of important events, such as feasts and festivals. However, rituals, feasts, and festivals were not just important for priests. Every person spent much of their time engaged in these activities. One historian of the Aztec Empire lists over 19 festivals celebrated throughout the year in the Aztec calendar. There were also sacred, ritual actions that took place outside of these festivals. These rituals were connected to many aspects of ordinary life, such as marriage, births, the harvest, and war.

Each calpulli, or neighborhood, had women healers and midwives. Midwives are women who help pregnant women during the births of their children. These healers and midwives were very important to the Mexica people and were celebrated during the Festival of Ochpaniztli in the month of September. These women also helped perform rituals for the Mexica. When a new baby was born, the midwife and priest performed a ritual to give the baby its day sign from the Aztec calendar. Other ritual activities included all the family and neighbors of the new baby bringing gifts to the home. If the baby was a boy, the neighborhood boys announced the birth of the new warrior by shouting the baby’s name through the calpulli.

One other important aspect of ritual life among the Aztec was sacrifice. Sacrifices were performed almost daily. Almost all sacrifices offered by the Mexica were human sacrifices. Special sacrifices were offered when a new tlatoani was installed. When a new temple or other building was finished, sacrifices were offered to dedicate the building. Whenever a major war was won, sacrifices were offered to Huitzilopochtli, the god of war, to thank him for their success. Rituals, feasts, festivals, and sacrifices were all significant aspects of the lives of the Mexica people.

title: Art and Architecture
text:
The city of Tenochtitlan was modeled after the holy city of Teotihuacán. Tenochtitlan was a city of palaces and temples. The temples were painted red and blue while the palace was painted white. Bernal Díaz, a Spanish conquistador, described the architecture of the city like this:

And when we saw all those cities and villages built in the water, and other great towns on dry land, and that straight and level causeway leading to [Tenochtitlán], we were astounded. These great towns and [temples] and buildings rising from the water, all made of stone, seemed like an enchanted vision.

… The sight of the palaces in which they lodged us! They were very spacious and well built, of magnificent stone, cedar wood, and the wood of other sweet-smelling trees, with great rooms and courts, which were a wonderful sight, and all covered with awnings of woven cotton.

The art created by the Mexica had similar themes as the civilizations before the Aztec. They carved, painted, and sculpted all kinds of art. Animals were common themes in Aztec art. Jaguars and eagles were used quite often. They also sculpted snakes, complete with intricate scales and fangs. Sculptures often represented the gods. They were treated as holy, adorned with jewels and precious metals. They were also fed because the Mexica believed them to be alive.

One of the most unique forms of art created by the Mexica was their featherworks. Feathers were highly prized among the people of Tenochtitlan. The book General History of the Things of New Spain claims that the Aztec even waged war to gain access to more beautiful and exotic feathers. The most treasured feather of all was the tail feather of the quetzal, which shines iridescent black and green. Featherworkers used these to create magnificent clothing and other artwork.

title: Agriculture
text:
It’s true that the Mexica were great warriors, but few people know that they were also great farmers. About one-fourth of the population of Tenochtitlan worked as farmers. Aztec agriculture was very successful for two reasons: first, the chinampas system; and second, crop rotation. Chinampas are human-made islands where the Mexica planted their crops. They were often called floating gardens because the way they were constructed made it seem like they could float. Farming in the middle of the lake was necessary because the marshy banks of Lake Texcoco, which surround Tenochtitlán, were poor for farming. Crop rotation means changing what crops are grown in an area based on what nutrients they take from or give to the soil. For example, planting beans gives nitrogen to the soil, and planting corn takes nitrogen from the soil. These are great plants to cultivate together or one after the other.

Chinampas are long, rectangular plots of land built above the water level. Builders used a type of fencing to create a plot of land and filled it with soil and decaying plants. Once one was completed, they would start building a neighboring one, leaving a narrow canal between them. An extensive drainage system was maintained to keep the crops moist and to allow floodwaters to drain away.

Another important Aztec farming technique was the use of fertilizer to add nutrients to the soil. They used sludge taken from the extensive sewage system around their cities. Unfortunately, they had no large animals to pull plows or move large loads to clear land for planting. People had to do this themselves.

With effective irrigation, fertilizer, and crop rotation, the chinampas were so effective that in some years, they could cultivate up to seven yields. That means that they harvested each chinampa around seven times a year. The Aztec produced enough food to support a very large population in the city of Tenochtitlan. At its height, the city had between 200,000 and 400,000 people. Some of the crops the Aztec grew would be sold at markets or exchanged as part of a trade.

title: Economy
text:
There were many products that could not be grown in Tenochtitlan. However, for an empire as large as the Aztec, they could also rely on products and crops grown outside of their cities. The cotton that the Mexica used in clothing, blankets, and armor couldn’t grow in the highlands of Tenochtitlan. Cacao beans, one of the most valuable products in the Aztec Empire, didn’t grow in the region of Tenochtitlan either. They traded for these goods, or extracted tribute from groups that grew them.

Trade extended throughout the Aztec Empire, and the leaders of the Triple Alliance regulated it. Regional markets sold everyday goods: cloth, knives, medicine, produce, pottery, and gems. There was no currency in the Aztec Empire, so goods were bartered. Government officials were always nearby, not only to make sure the prices were fair but also to take their share of the goods through tribute. Crops, goods, or cacao beans were taken from all the merchants. A vast marketplace drew thousands of shoppers and vendors each day.

Long-distance traders known as pochteca were both a source of goods and a source of information for the officials of the Aztec Empire. These traders would travel great distances over land to acquire goods for the nobility of the Empire. These goods could have included special feathers or precious gems. While they were traveling, they would share information from different parts of the empire and even act as spies.

In addition to government officials and pochteca, the Mexica had a diverse economy. People worked as priests, goldsmiths, and feather workers. There were also midwives, teachers, and farmers. People even worked as sanitation specialists, taking canoes that operated as latrines to the chinampas or the shore of Lake Texcoco.

title: Scientific Revolution
text:
For hundreds of years, the Roman Catholic Church controlled much of what people knew about science and how they could pursue new scientific knowledge. When people didn't understand or lacked knowledge about something, it was common practice to look back at the writings of classical scholars like Aristotle, Plato, and Ptolemy. This often led to dead ends because classical writers did not study every subject. People were not free to explore or learn anything new. In fact, there were laws that prevented people from exploring and making new scientific discoveries. The fear among church and government leaders was that they would lose power if the common people gained their own knowledge and could challenge their authority and teachings.

In the 15th and 16th centuries, things began to change. The printing press allowed people to share ideas and knowledge faster and more efficiently than ever before. More and more people began to learn how to read, which meant more and more people had access to knowledge. They could participate in debates and discussions about important topics.

Eventually, laws were relaxed and then repealed, allowing people to pursue knowledge and learn freely. Doctors and scientists now had more freedom to learn about human anatomy, which led to major advances in medicine. Engineers and inventors were able to study and improve upon past ideas to create new inventions and engineering feats that changed the world. Astronomers and physicists made new discoveries about the universe and its workings that changed the way people saw the world around them forever. This time period received the name the Scientific Revolution, and it was a revolutionary time to be alive.

title: Week 25 Framing Question
text: How did the scientists during this period challenge accepted beliefs?

title: Innovations
text:
The Scientific Revolution was an era of new inventions and improvements in technology. Great minds all over Europe often made the same discoveries, but independently. Because of this, it is often difficult to determine who was the first to come up with a new invention. It is likely that many of the inventions created during the Scientific Revolution were the result of research, experimentation, and work done by multiple people. There are many examples of different inventions and innovations that scientists made during this time, but there are two inventions that have lasted into the 21st century: microscopes and telescopes.

In the late 16th century, Zacharias Janssen of the Netherlands created the first microscope. Janssen worked in his father’s business making spectacles, or eyeglasses. This gave Janssen the knowledge and skill needed to make glass lenses with different magnifications. He used these lenses to create the first microscope. This microscope was essentially a metal tube with special glass lenses on each end that made small objects look bigger, making it easier to study them.

Around the same time in the Netherlands, another spectacle maker named Hans Lippershey was also experimenting with lenses. He is often credited with making the first functional telescope. While Janssen's invention was used to look at things that were very small, Lippershey's invention was used to look at things that were far away.

Galileo Galilei did not invent the microscope or the telescope. Instead, his innovative idea was to improve upon the original design of the telescope and use the microscope for scientific study. The telescope he built had a strong enough magnification for him to study the surface of the moon. With the microscope, he studied tiny forms of life, such as flies, fleas, and moths.

Years after Galileo’s death, Sir Isaac Newton further improved upon these previous designs of the telescope and created the first reflecting telescope in 1667. The reflecting telescope uses two mirrors, one curved and one flat. This design created a clearer image for the viewer.

Today, innovations have made telescopes see farther and more accurately than ever before. Telescopes continue to help us study and learn about space and other planets. Improvements have also been made to microscopes that allow us to see objects thousands of times larger than their original size. Microscopes help scientists and doctors to study microscopic organisms like bacteria and viruses in order to treat diseases.

title: Different Theories
text:
Many brilliant minds were at work during the Scientific Revolution. New scientific discoveries and theories were being formed and shared all over Europe. For example, in the medical field, a man named William Harvey spent a lot of time studying the circulatory system of the human body. He discovered that the heart worked like a pump and was responsible for moving blood around the body.

Astronomers Nicolaus Copernicus and Galileo Galilei both thought that planets revolved in a perfect circle around the sun. However, mathematical equations showed that this could not be the case. The mystery of planetary orbits remained unanswered until Johannes Kepler came along. Kepler studied the planet Mars for many years. Using mathematical equations, he discovered that the orbit of Mars was not a circle, as previously thought, but an ellipse, or oval. Kepler then concluded that planets move in ellipses around the sun. This became known as Kepler’s First Law of Planetary Motion.

The scientific method that we use today was also a product of the Scientific Revolution. Many people could be credited with creating the scientific method, but René Descartes wrote a book called Discourse that described four steps for making a scientific inquiry. These steps included: 1) question anything that isn't supported with evidence, 2) divide problems into their smallest parts, 3) solve problems starting from the simplest to the most complex, and 4) check your work. These steps are the basis for the scientific method we still use today. The list of different theories that were both posed and proven throughout the Scientific Revolution goes on and on. Just like scientists of old, great minds continue to form and test new theories today.

title: Nicolaus Copernicus
text:
Nicolaus Copernicus was still in his 20s when he first calculated that our planetary system was heliocentric, or that the sun is the center of the solar system and all other planets revolve around it. He also theorized that the Earth rotated daily on its own axis in addition to revolving around the sun. Telescopes had yet to be invented, so Copernicus made his calculations based on what he could see in the sky with the naked eye.

Prior to his work, people believed that the universe was geocentric, or that the Earth is the center of the universe and the other planets orbit around it. This theory had been established by ancient scientists, including Greek astronomers Ptolemy and Aristotle. The Roman Catholic Church believed that the Bible supported this theory and accepted it as God's divine design of the universe. Any ideas that differed from this theory were seen as heresy and a challenge against God's design. Teaching anything other than geocentrism was a punishable offense by the church.

Copernicus only shared his work with close friends and fellow scholars at first. Some encouraged him to publish his work for others to study, despite the criticism he might face. His ideas were revolutionary and went against years of established teachings. Understandably, he faced great opposition, especially from the Roman Catholic Church. When his book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was eventually published, he dedicated it to the pope and explained his reasons for publishing it. He died shortly after its publication. Although geocentrism continued to be accepted for many years after he published his book, Copernicus’s theories and work were later proven correct many years after his death by Galileo Galilei.

title: Galileo Galilei
text:
Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who made important discoveries about our universe. Galileo heard about instruments made by Dutch spectacle makers that could help a person see things that were far away or magnify things that were very small. After hearing about these inventions, Galileo set out to build his own. The first telescope he built made objects appear three times larger. Although this wasn’t much by modern standards, his patrons were very excited by the invention and raised their salaries for it. As he refined his design and made improvements, Galileo created a telescope with 30 times magnification.

Galileo used his telescope to study astronomy. With it, he discovered that the surface of the moon had mountains and craters. Everyone had thought the surface of the moon was perfectly smooth before this. He was also able to determine that multiple moons orbited Jupiter. He suggested that if these moons revolved around Jupiter and not the Earth, then the Earth couldn't be the center of the universe, just as Copernicus had theorized.

Unlike Copernicus, Galileo published and distributed his findings almost as soon as he discovered them. It was around this time that Copernicus’s book and his theories were officially condemned by the Roman Catholic Church. In spite of this, Galileo published his book Dialogue which confirmed Copernicus’ theory. Even though he could prove that the universe had a heliocentric system, Galileo was arrested and tried in a church court. The Church wanted Galileo to withdraw his scientific statements because they went against the church’s teachings. Faced with execution, Galileo agreed to withdraw his statements. He was then placed under house arrest for the rest of his life and forbidden to write or talk about heliocentrism ever again.

Although his discoveries were never officially accepted in his lifetime, we know today that Galileo’s findings proved that our universe is heliocentric. Galileo is remembered as one who contributed greatly to science and learning.

title: Sir Isaac Newton
text:
Sir Isaac Newton is remembered as one of the most brilliant minds of the Scientific Revolution. He was able to prove mathematically how gravity works. He also theorized the three laws of motion.

Although it was already understood that gravity was the force that pulls objects toward the Earth, Newton made the connection between Earth’s gravitational pull and its orbit. One legend claims that he came up with his gravitational theory when he saw an apple fall from a tree to the ground. Whether or not the apple legend is true, Newton spent close to 20 years studying gravity. Thanks to the work of men like Copernicus and Galileo, he understood that the Earth orbited the sun each year and that it rotated 360 degrees on its own axis each day. However, he concluded that the same gravitational force that made objects fall toward the Earth was what kept Earth and the moon in orbit. Not only did Newton make this connection, but he also worked out mathematical equations that supported his theory.

Newton studied many scientific subjects, but he is especially well-known for his contributions to the field of physics. In 1687, Newton published a work called Principia. In it, he listed his three laws of motion. These were:

Objects at rest stay at rest unless acted upon. Objects in motion stay in motion unless acted upon.

The acceleration of an object depends on two things: first, the mass of the object, and second, the amount of force applied.

Every action always has an opposite and equal reaction.

Newton’s work had a huge impact on the field of physics, and his work was universally accepted within 50 years. Other minds have since expanded upon his work and improved his calculations. However, Newton’s ideas are still considered some of the greatest works of scientific and abstract thinking ever produced.

title: Discovery and Navigation
text:
During the Renaissance, trade became very important to the economy of Europe. The coastal city-states of Genoa and Venice had the funds to produce well-made ships. Many of the people living in these places became sailors and started traveling the Mediterranean Sea. As trade increased, a desire to trade with Eastern Asia also increased. However, for many centuries the only way to get goods from Eastern Asia was through the traders of Southwest Asia.

The Asian traders of the Southwest knew the trade routes of the Silk Road. They also studied the currents and winds of the Arabian Sea that could take their ships to India and China.
