When these traders sold Eastern Asian goods to European traders, they increased the price to compensate for the money they spent on trading expeditions. European governments began to put more money into developing the tools, gathering supplies, and finding the people who could find new trade routes to Eastern Asia. They wanted to cut out the traders of Southwest Asia to decrease the price of goods and increase their own profit.

Historians call this time period the Age of Exploration. Europeans eventually found ways to reach Eastern Asia. While on a quest to find a western route to Eastern Asia, Christopher Columbus encountered the Americas. These explorations in Asia and the Americas would have both positive and negative results for the people living in this time period and well beyond.

Because of exploration, Europeans enjoyed new foods such as sugar, lemons, tobacco, chocolate, potatoes, and turkey. Some of these were from Asia; others were from the Americas. Many Europeans gained wealth, knowledge, and resources from the new lands that their explorers journeyed to.

However, the Age of Exploration also led to conflict and other negative outcomes. Conflicts developed over land and resources. European, Asian, and African diseases were introduced to the Americas by European explorers. These diseases killed many Indigenous people because they didn't have immunity against these illnesses. Entire groups of people disappeared, along with their cultures, knowledge, and histories.

Europeans began claiming territory in the Americas and Asia as colonies. However, a worker deficit was created when nearly one-third of the European population died from the Black Death and the Indigenous population was decimated by new diseases. To make up for this lack of workers, especially in their new colonies, Europeans began enslaving people. Later, Christian missionaries came to these colonies. Sometimes, they forced their religion upon enslaved and Indigenous people.

title: Week 26 Framing Question
text: How did the Portuguese help to instigate the age of exploration?

title: Timeline
text:
1418–1487 C.E.: Prince Henry the Navigator begins sponsoring Portuguese voyages to Madeira, the Azores, Cape Verde, Congo, and many other places.

1488 C.E.: Bartolomeu Dias makes it around the Cape of Good Hope.

1492 C.E.: Christopher Columbus, sponsored by Spain, reaches the Americas.

1497 C.E.: John Cabot, sponsored by England, explores Newfoundland.

1497–1498 C.E.: Vasco da Gama reaches India and sets up trade for Portugal.

1499 C.E.: An Italian explorer, Amerigo Vespucci, reaches the mouth of the Amazon River.

1519–1521 C.E.: Ferdinand Magellan rounds the southern tip of the American continent and begins a voyage around the entire globe. He dies in battle.

1522 C.E.: Juan Sebastian Elcano finishes Magellan’s circumnavigation of the globe.

1534 C.E.: Jacques Cartier, sponsored by France, explores the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

1539–1543 C.E.: Hernando de Soto, a Spaniard, explores North America, including the Appalachian Mountains and the Mississippi River.

1607 C.E.: Henry Hudson, sponsored by England, sails up the Hudson River.

title: Henry the Navigator
text:
Prince Henry was the son of King John I of Portugal. He helped fund and sponsor Portuguese explorers in the early to mid-1400s. Henry was not the heir to the throne because he had older brothers. Because Henry would not inherit land or a title, he decided he would have to win them through war and conquest. With the help of his father, the king, Henry captured the North African town of Ceuta in 1415. This successful conquest led to two things: Henry’s father gave him land and titles in Portugal, and he became the head of a Roman Catholic organization in Portugal, called the Order of Christ.

When Henry became the head of the Order of Christ, he gained access to a lot of money. Henry used his money to sponsor exploratory voyages. He sponsored voyages to the south of Portugal, along the African coast. He hoped to gain access to the gold trade and the slave trade. He also hoped to establish Portuguese colonies that could increase his personal wealth and the wealth of Portugal.

It took many years, but eventually, Henry’s sponsorship paid off. In 1441, a ship brought back both gold and enslaved people from the coast of West Africa. In 1448, the Portuguese built a fort on Arguin Island. They hoped this fort would help facilitate trade, especially the trade of enslaved people. When Henry’s nephew, Alfonso, became king in 1438, he gave Henry exclusive rights to send ships along the coast of Africa.

One of the most significant enterprises that Henry sponsored was in Madeira, an island about 600 miles southwest of Portugal. The Portuguese discovered that sugarcane grew well in Madeira. Henry helped bring enslaved people to Madeira to work in the sugarcane fields. Because Henry didn’t pay laborers and because sugar was becoming popular in Europe, the sugar plantations of Madeira became a very lucrative venture for Henry and Portugal.

title: Portuguese Exploration
text:
Bartolomeu Dias

Bartolomeu Dias was chosen by King John II of Portugal to find the southern limit of the African continent. The king wanted Portuguese explorers to find the southern edge of Africa because it would bring the country one step closer to making contact with East Asia.

Dias set out with three ships in 1486 or 1487; the exact date is unknown. He and his crew passed every known landmark that former Portuguese explorers had chronicled. Most sailors rarely left sight of the shore, but Dias and his crew had to sail away from the coast because of the storms and high winds. They did not want to get shipwrecked on the coastal reef. Because Dias sailed out of sight of the shore, he did not see the Cape of Good Hope when the ship passed it.

The Dias expedition made it to the Great Fish, or Groot-Vis, River. This is located on the eastern side of modern-day South Africa. Dias rightfully believed that as their ships had turned northward, they had made it to the eastern side of the African continent. After reaching the Groot-Vis River, the expedition turned around and arrived back in Portugal in 1488.

Vasco da Gama

Vasco da Gama was the third son of a minor nobleman in Portugal. In 1492, he earned a name for himself by seizing French vessels that had violated Portuguese shipping rights. After this successful mission, the king chose da Gama to lead an expedition to East Asia and set up trade between Portugal and Asia.

In July 1497, da Gama set out with four ships. By January 1498, they had reached Mozambique, an island off of the eastern coast of Africa. The da Gama expedition spent an extended period of time there resting and recovering from scurvy. Scurvy is a disease that sailors often developed from not getting enough vitamin C. Sailors got this disease from not having enough fresh fruits or vegetables on their ships.

The trade routes, currents, and winds on the eastern side of Africa had been known and traveled for hundreds of years by Muslim traders. The Portuguese used this knowledge to reach India in May 1498. The expedition had achieved its goal. Da Gama returned to Portugal but later returned to India on two more voyages.

title: The Caravel
text:
During the Age of Exploration, a new type of ship revolutionized sea travel. It was called the caravel. The caravel was probably developed by the Portuguese. It became very popular among Portuguese sailors who explored the coast of Africa. The caravel had a shallow keel. It was also smaller, lighter, and easier to navigate than older boats. The caravel’s lighter weight and smaller design also made it faster. Though caravels were small, they had thick planking and could carry a lot of goods or people.

Most ships only had one kind of sail, but caravels were equipped to use both square and triangular sails. Triangular sails allowed caravels to sail into the wind. They did this by using a method called tacking, which looks like zig-zagging. The square sails were used when sailing with the wind. Square sails made boats very fast. The caravel allowed explorers to sail along shorelines as well as in open water.

Two of Christopher Columbus' ships, the Pinta and Niña, were caravels. Explorers such as Bartolomeu Diaz and Vasco da Gama also chose to sail caravels. Another feature that made the caravel so popular among explorers was that it required fewer men to operate it. With fewer crew members, labor was cheaper and there was more space left for cargo.

The caravel could hold about 130 tons of supplies and still operate with a small crew. With a length of only 65 feet, the caravel could sail upriver in more shallow waters without a problem. Easy to maneuver and lighter than other ships of the time, the caravel was the ship that helped make the Age of Exploration successful.

title: Tools of Exploration
text:
There were many tools that made European exploration possible. Funds, like those that Prince Henry the Navigator provided, were vital to exploration. The caravel also made traveling on the open ocean possible. However, other tools were crucial to the Age of Exploration.

Cartographic Improvements

Maps and, more specifically, accurate maps were not very common in the Middle Ages. Prior to the printing press, all maps were hand-drawn, which made them very difficult to create. During the Renaissance, cartography took on new importance. The Greek scholar Ptolemy studied cartography and developed a series of grids called latitude and longitude. These could be used to help travelers determine their exact location. Latitude and longitude lines were tools used by Renaissance-era cartographers to create better maps.

As European explorers traveled to new areas of the world, they made maps to chronicle where they had been, to stake claims for their governments, and to help others to travel back to these destinations. In 1569, Gerardus Mercator innovated cartography even further by creating a map that flattened out the globe. The longitude and latitude lines on these maps were straight. This flat map was a tool that allowed sailors to plot their destinations on fixed lines. It made traveling across oceans easier.

Astrolabe

For hundreds of years, people have looked at objects in the night sky to help keep track of where they were. Looking at the night sky and knowing where the stars are helps a person on the ground know which direction to travel. For example, the North Star will tell you which direction is north, no matter where you are. Once explorers know which way is north, they can use other scientific tools to pinpoint their location, chart their courses, and sail all the way around the world.

One of the most important tools navigators used was the astrolabe. Sailors used astrolabes to travel across wide-open seas by measuring the latitude of a ship at sea. Using the sun during the day and the North Star at night, sailors would point the indicator on the astrolabe at their chosen celestial object (the sun or the North Star). Then, they would read the dial to determine their latitude. They compared their measurements to a table of latitudes that told them where they were.

Sextant

Sextants, like astrolabes, measure angles to determine the latitude of a ship. However, they also measure longitude. Using mirrors, sextants measure the reflection of the sun with that of the horizon. That measurement is matched with the measurements on a table, which identifies a location. Knowing both longitude and latitude gives them an exact location. Sextants are still used by sailors today.

Compass

One of the earliest navigational tools was the magnetic compass. It was first invented in China over 1,000 years ago. Europeans learned about the compass from the Arabs, who had originally learned of this invention from the Chinese in about 1000 or 1100 C.E. To use the first compasses, sailors rubbed an iron needle on a rock called a lodestone. The needle became magnetized. Then they stuck the needle into a piece of straw or something else that would float and put it in a cup of water. The needle would always point north. The compass did not pinpoint location, but it helped sailors know which direction they were traveling.

title: Primary Source: The Columbus Expedition
text:
This is a selection of entries translated from the journal, or diary, of Christopher Columbus.

Monday, 6 August. The rudder of the caravel Pinta became [loose], and Martin Alonso Pinzon, who was in command, believed or suspected that it was by a contrivance of Gomes Rascon and Cristóbal Quintero, to whom the caravel belonged, for they dreaded to go on that voyage. The Admiral says that, before they sailed, these men had been displaying a certain backwardness, so to speak. The Admiral was much disturbed at not being able to help the said caravel without danger, and he says that he was eased of some anxiety when he reflected that Martin Alonso Pinzon was a man of energy and ingenuity. They made, during the day and night, 29 leagues.

Sunday, 9 September. The day the Admiral made 19 leagues, he arranged to reckon less than the number run because if the voyage was of long duration, the people would not be so terrified and disheartened. In the night he made 120 miles, at the rate of 12 miles an hour, which are 30 leagues. The sailors steered badly, letting the ship fall off to N.E., and even more, respecting which the Admiral complained many times.

Friday, 21 September. Most of the day was calm, and later there was a little wind. During the day and night, they did not make good more than 13 leagues. At dawn, they saw so much weed that the seas appeared to be covered with it, and it came from the west.… The sea was very smooth, like a river, and the air was the best in the world. They saw a whale, which is a sign that they were near land because they always keep near the shore.

title: Travel and Technology
text:
The arts and education weren’t the only beneficiaries of the Renaissance. Exploration began in earnest, and explorers needed new technology if they were to willingly travel out of sight of land for weeks or even months at a time.

Not all sailors were educated. The invention of the traverse board made it easy for any sailor to help keep track of the ship’s direction using a series of pegs on strings placed into holes on a wooden compass rose.

Another invention, called the cross-staff, measured the height of the sun in the sky, creating an angle that gave sailors their latitude. To protect the sailors' eyesight, the backstaff was invented so navigators could use the shadow cast by the sun to find their location.

The lead line was used to determine the depth of the water; a hollowed base of the lead bulb would also pull up a bit of the soil from the bottom to let the captain know what was down there.

One of the inventions that helped sailors is still around today: the anemometer, which measures wind speed. Ships moved at the mercy of the wind, so it was important to be able to calculate the wind speed.

Finally, the hourglass proved to be a very useful tool; it enabled ships’ crews to work on timed shifts.

title: Chart a Course
text:
Before the invention of maritime navigation tools, most sailors relied on stars to chart their courses. Brighter stars were grouped together into constellations that were easier to recognize. The hemisphere a person was in also determined which constellations they could see at night. The location of each constellation in the sky also depended on the time of night as the Earth rotated. In the Northern Hemisphere, sailors relied heavily on Polaris or the North Star. Polaris doesn’t move much, even as the Earth rotates, so it gave sailors a fixed point from which to find other constellations and chart their courses.

Look at the table of constellations.

On the star chart, find these constellations from the table and connect the dots to match.

title: Motivations of Exploration
text:
Before the land that covers the Earth had been fully explored and charted, those who chose to venture out into unfamiliar areas had a variety of motivations for doing so. There was much to be gained by sailing or hiking into the unknown, though as it turned out, the areas they ventured into were hardly unknown to the people who were already living there.

Early explorers were the ones who began to work toward completing the world map, surveying distant shorelines and pushing inland, encountering new terrain, and establishing civilizations. These new places provided many different opportunities for explorers and the countries that sponsored their voyages.

Some explorers were driven by the quest for riches and resources. The mystery of unknown lands held the promise of gold for many at a time when knowledge of the world was limited. By this time, Europe’s resources and lands were thoroughly claimed by governments and leaders. European explorers saw the resources and land of unknown places as an opportunity to get rich. Kings and queens in Europe funded these explorers, hoping they would return with gold and other riches. The kingdom and the explorers would share the money and glory that came from their expeditions. Some kingdoms and explorers were successful, while others were not, but the allure of gold and fame was often too tempting to resist.

As explorers charted the areas of the world they had no knowledge of, they encountered the civilizations and peoples already living there. This offered a new motivation for exploration. European religious leaders believed these people needed to convert to Christianity. Missionaries traveled to these lands to convince or, in some cases, force the local populations to abandon their traditional beliefs and adopt Christianity. Like those venturing for wealth, the religious missionaries had varying levels of success.

European countries began to claim these lands and settle them with their own citizens. In this way, countries like Spain, England, France, Belgium, and others began building empires. Each distant land they took control of became a colony in their overseas empire. Countries with large empires and many colonies benefited from the natural resources and labor the local populations provided. These empires continued to explore, which expanded their trading networks. As these empires grew, a new motivation emerged: competition between European countries. European countries fought to create the largest empire, with the widest trading network to become the most powerful empire.

Whether it was the quest for gold and fame, the motivation to spread their religion, or the competition to be the most powerful empire, European exploration left a permanent mark on the world today. It changed the fate of people around the world, brought new goods to far-flung markets, and altered the physical and political landscape forever.

title: Week 27 Framing Question
text: Which motivation of exploration had the most impact on the explorers of England, France, and Spain?

title: England: Henry Hudson
text:
Before the North American continent was mapped, people thought it might be possible to sail west from Europe all the way to Asia. This would have allowed goods to travel much easier between the continents and would have been a major advantage for countries like England. In an effort to compete with the expanding Spanish and Portuguese empires, a British trading company, the Muscovy Company, sent explorer Henry Hudson to see if he could find a water route through North America to Asia. This mythical route became known as the Northwest Passage.

Hudson made his first voyage in 1607, traveling north into the Arctic Ocean, thinking that a water route through the far northern parts of North America would allow him to reach Asia. This first attempt failed when sea ice blocked his way. Another trip in 1608 ended similarly.

Having failed the Muscovy Company, Hudson was hired by the Dutch East India Company for another attempt at finding the Northwest Passage. This time, he navigated further south and entered a river in modern-day New York. He traveled up this river for over 100 miles but found no pathway to Asia. This river is now known as the Hudson River, named after Henry Hudson. On his final trip in 1610, he again sailed inland but was trapped by ice. His men, unhappy with his failures and the terrible conditions, turned on Hudson. They set him adrift in a small boat, and he disappeared from the historical record.

title: France: Jacques Cartier
text:
Other countries were exploring and acquiring wealth through resources and trade. France did not want to be left behind. French king Francis I decided to send explorer Jacques Cartier to search for gold and the Northwest Passage. If they could find gold and a path to Asia, they could become richer and more powerful than other countries in Europe.

Cartier left France in 1534 for North America. He arrived on the east coast of what is now Canada. In fact, the name “Canada” comes from Cartier, who took it from a word the native people he encountered used to refer to their village. He charted the coast and the Gulf of St. Lawrence while meeting with native peoples and made efforts to learn their language. He did not find gold or passages to the Pacific, but he did hear of a mythical land of gold from the people there.

On Cartier’s second voyage, the local people told him more stories of riches, which motivated him to continue searching. Despite his efforts, he never found the sources of these riches. A final voyage in 1540 led to the discovery of what he thought was gold and diamonds. These turned out to be fool’s gold and quartz instead. Although he never found riches or passage to Asia, he is credited with establishing French influence in the area, which eventually led to French settlement and colonization.

title: Spain: Christopher Columbus
text:
In the earliest years of European exploration, there was no specific knowledge of the American continents. Europeans knew the Earth was round, but the land to the west was mythical at this point. There were stories, but no one knew for sure what lay in that direction. Knowing that the Earth was round, some thought that sailing in that direction would eventually lead to Asia. The sailor who accomplished this feat would create a new, lucrative trade route, benefiting himself and his country.

In 1492, Italian explorer Christopher Columbus convinced Spanish rulers King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella to sponsor a voyage west, in hopes of finding a route to Asia. His three ships, Niña, Pinta, and Santa María, made the journey in just a few weeks. However, instead of arriving in Asia, he sighted islands that are likely part of what we now know as the Bahamas, in the Caribbean Sea. He visited several islands during this time and returned with reports of the islands and the people living there. Columbus thought he had arrived in Asia. However, he revealed the location of the Americas to European explorers, which opened them up for exploration.

His accomplishments earned him three more trips to the newly revealed lands. In these later voyages, Columbus brought people with him. These people were colonists. They settled in the Americas. Columbus was made the governor of the island of Hispaniola, where the modern-day countries of Haiti and the Dominican Republic are. His time as governor was unsuccessful, and he was removed by the Spanish rulers and returned to Spain to live out the rest of his life.

title: Spain: Hernando de Soto
text:
Hernando de Soto spent much of his life exploring and conquering lands in South, Central, and North America. He made his first voyage as a teenager to Central America as part of the expedition of Pedro Árias Dávila in 1514. De Soto became rich during his time in Central America as he conquered lands that are now a part of Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Honduras.

Following his exploits in Central America, Hernando de Soto traveled with the expedition of Francisco Pizarro to Peru in South America. The home of the Inca civilization had few answers for Spain’s weapons and the illnesses brought from Europe. Diseases they had never encountered were especially deadly. De Soto took part in conquering the Incas and gained massive wealth in the process. Returning to Spain, de Soto was soon given permission to explore a new land, known as La Florida.

De Soto traveled to Cuba to begin his expedition. Landing near what is now Tampa Bay in 1539, de Soto began an overland exploration, the first Europeans to do so in that area. His travels took him and his men as far north as the current state of Tennessee and as far west as the Mississippi River, where they became the first Europeans to cross the mighty river. De Soto’s expedition often clashed with the native peoples of these areas, but they continued their trek through present-day Arkansas. De Soto’s expedition provided Europeans with the first major account of the interior of North America. However, de Soto would not survive the voyage. He fell ill and died in 1542 after three years of exploration.

title: Spain: Ferdinand Magellan
text:
Once Europeans proved they could navigate across oceans and around continents to reach lands and markets far away, they began pushing the boundaries of how far they could go. Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan was one of them. He believed that experienced sailors could travel around the Americas and reach Asia. The adventure of sailing around the world, a process called circumnavigation, was too tempting to resist.

Sponsored by King Charles I of Spain, Magellan left on his voyage in 1519. Sailing southwest, Magellan and his men navigated south along the coast of the modern countries of Brazil and Argentina. The conditions were difficult, and the climate became more extreme as they traveled south. Their knowledge of the South American coastline was incomplete, but Magellan was searching for a way to get from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. They eventually sailed far enough south to round the tip of South America, passing through a passage now known as the Straits of Magellan, and into the Pacific Ocean.

Magellan and the first men to make the voyage from the Atlantic to the Pacific continued on their way to Asia. The long trip across the world’s largest ocean was difficult for Magellan and his men. Throughout the trip, Magellan dealt with unrest and even a mutiny by his sailors. They arrived at the island now known as Guam in 1521 with almost no supplies or food. They were able to get food from the island and continue their attempt to sail all the way around the world. They arrived in the Philippines, where Magellan tried to convert locals to Christianity. When they refused, he attacked them. Magellan died in the battle. Men from his expedition would continue on and eventually complete the circumnavigation without him, arriving back in Spain in 1522.

title: Spain: Amerigo Vespucci
text:
Although the lands encountered by European explorers were already inhabited, the explorers often came up with names for these locations independent of what the local people called them. Sometimes the explorers would alter a word or name from the local language. Other times they would name a place after someone famous, like the Philippines, which Magellan named after the Spanish King Philip II. One explorer even lent his own name to the massive continents of North and South America. His name was Amerigo Vespucci.

Vespucci was involved in exploration from the very beginning. He helped organize and supply Christopher Columbus’s famous 1492 voyage. When Columbus returned with a lot of information about what he saw but no real wealth or riches, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain decided to send another team to continue exploring in 1499. Vespucci went along for the ride, contributing his knowledge of navigation to the endeavor.

Vespucci used his knowledge of astronomy to chart the new constellations during the voyage to South America. He took detailed notes about the trip, including the mouth of the Amazon River and the climate, ecosystems, and people he encountered. He returned to Spain with his observations. His writings caught the attention of the rulers of Portugal, who sent him out on another voyage because they did not want to fall behind Spain in exploring these new lands. As he mapped more of the South American coast, he was convinced that he had found a new continent, not just another part of Asia. Vespucci’s voyages became well-known and a mapmaker in Germany named the new continents “America” after Vespucci’s first name, Amerigo.

title: Map Activity
text:
Ocean travel during the medieval era required the use of ships and sails. Many advancements made sailing quicker and easier. However, captains were still at the mercy of the wind. Take a look at the two maps. Notice that the maps are of the same part of the Indian Ocean.

Air currents and even ocean currents act as conveyor belts on our planet. In the area of the Indian Ocean, these air currents, which make sailing feasible, shift greatly twice during the year. Each map shows different wind and current directions.

Arab traders knew that during the summer monsoon season, they could easily travel to the port city of Calicut. They would have to wait to return. As the ocean cooled, it helped shift the winds in a nearly opposite direction. The best time to sail from Calicut back toward the Arabian Peninsula and Africa was early spring or early fall. Any other time, the weather would be too dangerous to sail.

title: African and Asian Explorers
text:
While European exploration is often focused on in relation to North and South America, people around the world were interested in finding new trade routes and discovering lands of riches. Explorers from Asia and Africa were also venturing out to distant places, expanding their knowledge and connecting themselves with the wider world.

Admiral Zheng He of China undertook seven different expeditions from the waters of China, all the way to the coast of Africa. He set off on his first voyage in 1405 with over 200 boats. He traveled to what is now Vietnam as well as the islands of Southeast Asia and all the way to India. His goal was to promote Chinese diplomacy and make trade connections. His future voyages were similar and eventually created a strong trade network in the region.

The Muslim explorer Abu Abdullah Muhammad Ibn Battuta, known as Ibn Battuta, ventured throughout the Middle East. He first made a pilgrimage from his home in Morocco to Mecca in what is now Saudi Arabia in 1326. From there, he extended his travels to central Asia and places we know today as Turkey and Azerbaijan. He even went as far as India and spent almost a decade there. During his travels, he recorded things he saw. His account is the most comprehensive historians have of the Islamic world at that time.

The business of overseas travel and exploration was a diverse one. Even when most of the captains and explorers whose names ended up in the historical record were from Europe, many of the men who ventured across the oceans were from all over the world. An enslaved man known as Estevanico from North Africa accompanied several explorers on their voyages to North America. Many others, both enslaved and free, participated in the exploration of the Americas.

title: Empires of the Americas Before European Exploration
text:
Ancient civilizations in the Western Hemisphere are often grouped into three time frames. These time frames are the pre-classic, the classic, and the post-classic eras. These eras cover the period of time from around 2000 B.C.E. until the Spanish conquest during the 1500s C.E. The Maya, Aztec, and Inca are just a few of the many complex societies that existed in the early Americas.

The Maya

The classic period saw the rise of the Maya culture. This civilization began long ago, when a large migrating group arrived in Central America. Thousands of years ago, the people became agricultural and built settlements in what is now southern Mexico, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, and the Yucatán Peninsula. The Maya built huge cities with pyramids marking sacred sites. They developed astronomy, complex mathematics, and a perfected calendar. However, they slowly declined in numbers and strength until the civilization mysteriously collapsed in the early 1500s. The Maya did not vanish, though. Today, there are still Maya people. Many keep traditions passed down from their ancestors.

The Aztec

To the north of the Maya, another civilization formed. They were called the Aztec. They also began as a hunter-gatherer tribe. Around 1300 C.E., they arrived in what is now south-central Mexico. When they saw an eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake, they took it as a sign to settle there. Though the land was swampy, the Aztec drained it and built islands. There, they planted crops and built the foundations of their capital city, Tenochtitlán. Through careful agricultural practices and a strong military tradition, the Aztec were able to quickly build their empire. They constructed many cities with artistic and religious centers and markets. The Aztec enjoyed their greatest power during the post-classic period. Long after the empire fell, Aztec influence can still be seen in the cultures of Mexico and the United States.

The Inca

Far south of the Aztec people, in what is now Peru, there lived a small mountain tribe called the Inca. The Inca Empire was also on the rise in the post-classic era. During the 1400s C.E., the Incas’ expansion of roads and expertly built bridges led to growth. They added other peoples to their empire through gifts or military force. This small farming tribe rose to great power, conquering land as far as modern-day Ecuador, Chile, and Belize. Their empire spread to the Pacific Ocean and grew to about 10 million people. Although the Inca Empire no longer exists, their advances in farming and medicine still influence life today.

title: Week 28 Framing Question
text: What were the consequences of Spanish exploration for the Aztec and Inca Empires?

title: Spanish Exploration
text:
During the 15th century C.E., the whole world was on the move. In the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, empires were growing. Rich leaders served as patrons, meaning they could pay, or sponsor, people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. In 1490, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella became the rulers of Spain. In 1492, Spain had just won a war with the last Muslim kingdom in Spain. They also signed a document that required all Jews to either leave the kingdom of Spain or convert to Roman Catholicism. These two actions allowed Ferdinand and Isabella to take the property of Jews and Muslims in Spain, which made them rich enough to be patrons. Ferdinand and Isabella wanted to sponsor voyages to find new trade routes to supply more income for the kingdom.

An entrepreneur named Christopher Columbus had an unusual idea. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean to find a new trade route to India. Columbus needed a wealthy patron to sponsor his voyage. Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand agreed to be patrons for Columbus. They paid for supplies, three ships, and the crew needed for the voyage. Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. He did not make it to India. However, he did encounter the Americas.

After his first expedition, Columbus brought gold and evidence of his trip back to Europe and shared his findings. Columbus took four voyages to the Americas. Many Spanish explorers followed Columbus’s route and traveled to the Americas. These explorers sought land, riches, and glory. Some of them found it, but many others did not.

Columbus’s journey also led to changes in government, knowledge, and trade all across Europe. Powerful rulers sent explorers to expand their empires. From the late 1400s to the mid-1700s, the rulers of Spain, Portugal, France, England, Denmark, Russia, and the Netherlands fought to create colonies and dominate trade worldwide.

title: Spanish Conquest and Conquistadors
text:
Why is Spanish the official language of Mexico and many Central and South American countries? It’s because the Spanish conquered those countries hundreds of years ago. “Conquistador” means “conqueror” in Spanish. Conquistadors were Spanish explorers who attacked and defeated the native peoples living in the Americas. The conquistadors stole from the native people, destroyed their cities, and claimed lands for Spain and for themselves. The time in which the conquistadors lived and conquered was called the Spanish Conquest. It began with Columbus’s voyage in 1492. After this time, the Spanish sent many conquistadors to the Americas.

The first Spanish contact with what is now Mexico happened in 1517. It was in this year that a conquistador named Francisco Hernández de Córdoba sailed through the Caribbean Sea and landed his ship on the Yucatán Peninsula in modern-day Mexico. After landing on the Yucatán Peninsula, he and his men continued to explore and sailed up into the Gulf of Mexico.

Córdoba and his men made contact with the Maya. Some of their interactions were peaceful. However, some of their interactions were violent, and a battle between the conquistadors and the Maya ensued. Half of Córdoba’s men were killed, and he was badly wounded. He escaped on his ship and later died of his wounds. Although this trip was considered unsuccessful, other conquistadors followed.

A later expedition by conquistador Juan de Grijalva helped the Spanish determine that Mexico was not an island, but part of a continent. That expedition also painted a picture for the Spanish of a land dominated by a powerful people, the Aztec, who had made many enemies in the people they conquered. After receiving this information, the Spanish decided to send a larger expedition, led by conquistador Hernán Cortés. This expedition would forever change the lives of the Aztecs.

title: Conquest of the Aztec Empire
text:
The Aztecs once controlled a far-reaching empire. Their rule stretched from modern-day central Mexico to Guatemala and from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. The Aztec Empire was centered in three main cities: Texcoco, Tlacopan, and the capital city Tenochtitlán. In Tenochtitlán, the Aztecs created their grandest city, and in its center, they constructed a nearly 200-foot-tall pyramid called Templo Mayor. Some 200,000 people lived in this great city on the shore of Lake Texcoco.

In 1518, when the Aztec Empire was at its height and under the rule of Moctezuma II, the Spanish were sending conquistadors in search of gold. One particular conquistador played a huge role in the history of the Aztec Empire. His name was Hernán Cortés.

Cortés helped the Spanish conquer Cuba. He was then put in charge of a mission to Mexico. His instructions were to trade with the Aztec in Tenochtitlán. However, Cortés was interested in conquering and conquest, not trade. He decided to march to Tenochtitlán to take over. Cortés brought about 600 men with him. However, his force grew as he marched to Tenochtitlán. He and his men fought and made allies with Indigenous people who did not like the Aztec.

When Cortés, his force, and their allies arrived in Tenochtitlán, he met with the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II. Some historians think that the Aztec leader believed Cortés to be the return of an Aztec god and not the conquistador he actually was. The meeting was initially peaceful. However, conflicts over religion and power arose between the Spanish and the Aztec. Cortés took the Aztec king hostage. Cortés now controlled the powerful Aztec Empire.

However, the Spanish had gotten word that Cortés had disobeyed their instructions to trade. They sent a force to Mexico to arrest Cortés. Cortés had to leave some of his men in charge of the city to go fight this force. Cortés was able to win the battle. However, he returned to Tenochtitlán and found fierce fighting between the Aztec and the men he had left in charge. Many Aztec, including King Moctezuma II, and many Spanish soldiers and their allies had been killed. The Spanish were eventually driven out of Tenochtitlán by the Aztec.

However, Cortés and the Spanish didn’t give up. They retreated to nearby cities and conquered or made alliances with the Indigenous people against the Aztec. At the same time, a smallpox epidemic broke out among the Aztec in Tenochtitlán. The Spanish had unknowingly brought diseases with them from Europe that the Aztec had no immunity to. Many Aztec, including their new emperor, died in this epidemic.

In 1521, Cortés and his allies launched a final attack on Tenochtitlán. The city was conquered by the Spanish for the last time, and the Aztec Empire fell. Many of the surviving Aztecs were enslaved. The Spanish built Mexico City atop the ruins of Tenochtitlán. Today, visitors to Mexico City can still see the Aztec ruins, including Templo Mayor, being excavated.

title: Conquest of the Inca Empire
text:
Conquistador Francisco Pizarro first traveled to the Americas just 10 years after Columbus’s voyage and was involved in several conquests. Inspired by stories of great wealth, Pizarro traveled south along the coast in search of wealthy civilizations. Pizarro and a group of men traveled to a part of South America known to the Spanish as “Peru.” When talking about the prospects of this expedition, Pizarro said, “There lies Peru with its riches; Here, Panama and its poverty. Choose, each man, what best becomes a brave Castilian.”

When Pizarro and his men arrived in Peru, they encountered the Inca Empire and its riches. Pizarro decided to take possession of the Incas’ wealth. However, before he could attack, he had to sail all the way back to Spain to get the support of Spanish Emperor Charles V. It helped that conquistador Hernán Cortés had recently returned to Europe with examples of great wealth obtained through his conquests. Charles V agreed to Pizarro’s plan, and the conquistador sailed again for the Americas in 1530.

The timing of Pizarro’s second arrival was fortunate for the Spanish and catastrophic for the Incas. When Pizarro again entered Peru, the Incas were in the midst of a civil war. In 1528, the Inca ruler, Huayna Capac, had died without deciding which of his sons would take his throne. A civil war broke out between Huayna Capac’s two sons, Atahualpa and Huascar. This weakened the Inca Empire. Another thing that had weakened the Inca Empire was disease. When the Spanish first arrived in the Americas, they brought with them diseases that the Indigenous people had never encountered. With no immunity, sickness and death ravaged the population. In fact, historians believe that Huayna Capac died of a foreign disease, possibly smallpox.

Pizarro’s return also coincided with the victory of Atahualpa over Huascar. When he met up with Pizarro, Atahualpa did not think he could be defeated by Pizarro’s small army of 180 men. However, Pizarro set a trap and, using superior weapons, quickly took over Atahualpa’s forces. The Inca offered a ransom for Atahualpa’s release and provided Pizarro with 24 tons of gold and silver. Pizarro accepted the ransom but then killed Atahualpa anyway. Pizarro then conquered the Inca capital of Cusco in 1533, which ended the Inca Empire.

title: The Effects of Conquest
text:
Soon after the conquest of the great civilizations of the Americas, Spanish settlers began immigrating to the land in large numbers. Native languages, art, customs, and traditions mixed with Spanish culture. Most of the surviving Aztec, Inca, and Maya were converted to Christianity by choice or by force. Many of the native religions were almost forgotten.

The settlers also brought new diseases with them. Smallpox, measles, and influenza spread quickly. Within 100 years, these diseases wiped out a large percentage of the Maya, Inca, and Aztec peoples. Thousands more were killed in battle. The few who survived were often enslaved and forced to work in mines or on large farms. In Mesoamerica, this system of forced labor was called the encomienda system. In South America, another system of forced labor was called the mita system.

However, the Maya, Inca, and Aztec peoples survived. Descendants of the Maya, Inca, and Aztec still live in and near the places where their ancient civilizations began. Today, nearly 10 million Maya live in Central America, and there are many small villages in Peru where only Quechua (the Inca language) is still spoken. Tens of thousands of Mexican people can trace their family lines back to the ancient Aztec people. The Spanish Conquest did not completely destroy the culture or the spirit of these ancient civilizations.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
In 1494, one man who had sailed across the Atlantic Ocean returned home with all sorts of wild stories. He described the new world he had seen, full of strange plants, animals, and foods. He talked about the people he had met there. This man was not Christopher Columbus or a member of his crew. He was a Taíno from the Bahamas whom Columbus had captured and taken back to Spain. We don’t know his real name, but Columbus gave him the name Diego Colón.

After returning home, Colón told his friends and family about Spain. He described “the great cities and fortresses and churches” and “the people and horses and animals.” He saw strange “lands and food ... and bullfighting.” All were new to him, just like Indigenous peoples and their homelands were new to Europeans. As people traveled between the continents, they were exchanging ideas about technology, religion, and ways of life.

As European explorers reached different parts of North America, people from different groups, like the Iroquois and Patuxet, were brought across the ocean and saw Europe. People in the Americas and in Europe were not just curious about each other. As soon as they met, many saw new opportunities to meet their economic wants and needs. The people on the two sides of the Atlantic quickly exchanged goods, people, plants, animals, and diseases.

This exchange between the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia is called the Columbian Exchange. A historian named Alfred Crosby named the exchange after Christopher Columbus. The Columbian Exchange had a huge impact on life for people all around the world.

title: Week 29 Framing Question
text: Which item of exchange had the most impact on the Americas? On Europe?

title: Plants
text:
Many plants from the Americas also had a big impact on Europe, Africa, and Asia. American plants, such as potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, tobacco, beans, cacao, and corn, changed how people ate.

In Europe, people did not eat corn; it was mainly grown to feed livestock. Potatoes, however, became a very popular crop for people. Potatoes can grow in all kinds of soil, and they are also full of vitamins and nutrients. Potatoes helped feed Europe's population better than other crops that had been grown previously, which led to better health and an increase in population. Potatoes also store well, and sailors could take potatoes on their ships. The potatoes’ vitamins would prevent them from getting scurvy.

Tobacco was first brought back to Europe by the Spanish. The Spanish experimented with the plant until they produced a variety of it that had a much better flavor than the original. The Spanish didn't share their secret recipe with the rest of Europe, which created a monopoly on their tobacco. However, the English were eventually able to obtain some Spanish tobacco seeds and plant their own crops in Jamestown Colony. Tobacco became a massive cash crop industry as a result.

Cacao was another plant that explorers brought back home with them. Cacao was mixed with water by native peoples to make a bitter drink. Europeans added sugar and vanilla to it, making it into a sweet food. That is what we call chocolate today.

Another substance that has its origins in American plants is rubber. The rubber tree was native to Mesoamerica; its sap has latex and rubber in it. The Olmec, the Maya, and the Aztec used the sap to create rubber balls for the ball game that they played. The sap was also used to make things like tile waterproof. Columbus brought rubber to Spain and eventually, it became an important cash crop.

The people of the Americas were also introduced to new crops and plants. European settlers brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, bananas, grapes, wheat, cotton, and even honeybees with them to the Americas. Several of the plants introduced to the Americas grew well in the soils and climates there. In particular, sugarcane, wheat, and cotton did very well in warmer climates. Europeans began growing them on large plantations, which required them to clear large pieces of land. This destroyed local vegetation, and it disrupted the natural habitats of local wildlife.

title: Animals
text:
In the Americas, people domesticated very few animals. Llamas, alpacas, and guinea pigs were tamed and used for work and food. However, Europeans, Asians, and Africans domesticated many animals. Domesticated animals like horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs changed economic life in the Americas. These farm animals became new food sources. Pigs eat just about anything and reproduce quickly, which made them a great resource for meat in the Americas. Cattle were used to plow fields and also provided meat and dairy products.

Horses had existed in the Americas anciently, but by the medieval and early modern eras, they had gone extinct. When they were reintroduced, horses quickly became popular among the people of the Americas, who used them in their everyday lives. They used horses for transportation and work. Horses also became a valuable trade resource. Horses changed the way tribes like the Sioux and the Comanche hunted and traveled. Riding horses was a much faster form of transportation than following bison herds on foot. Descendants of these horses are still found on the East Coast and in the western lands of the United States.

New animals also caused problems, however. The introduction of certain domesticated animals in the Americas caused an imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation were left with nothing to eat.

title: Technology
text:
After new animals were brought to the Americas, people adopted new ways of doing work. Although native peoples of the Americas farmed and grew crops, they did not practice large-scale agriculture the way Europeans did. Europeans brought new technologies with them, such as the metal plow, which was pulled by a horse, ox, or cow. This made it easier to plow fields quickly. Indigenous peoples could plant more crops and bring in bigger harvests.

Europeans used horses, cattle, and oxen to plow fields, pull wagons, and transport people. Over time, the Indigenous peoples of the Americas began to use these animals for the same purposes. They developed a special connection with horses, in particular. Europeans also introduced ways to use wheels on carts, for making pottery, and to move water. Archaeologists and historians have evidence that native peoples used wheels on toys, but before the Columbian Exchange, they did not use the wheel as a tool.

Silk was an important textile (cloth) in China. It is derived from worms that live on mulberry bushes. Spanish colonists brought mulberry bushes and silkworms to Mexico in the early 1500s. Textile (cloth) makers from Europe showed Indigenous peoples how to spin wool, dye cloth, and weave. By the late 1500s, dozens of textile workshops employed native peoples, especially in Mexico.

Another technology Europeans brought with them were tools and utensils made of metal. Indigenous peoples used stone or flint to make their weapons and tools. Metal axes, swords, hammers, and eating utensils like forks and knives became popular trade items.

Europeans also brought guns and cannons with them. Over time, Indigenous peoples traded their goods for muskets and rifles. This exchange was particularly widespread in North America, where many tribes traded beaver pelts for muskets and rifles. This began to change the way Indigenous people hunted and fought in battles.

title: Ideas
text:
Like the Europeans, the people of the Americas had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had their own governments and religions. Tolerance between the Native American and European cultures could have expanded the positive exchanges. However, the Europeans were not often tolerant of the differences they encountered. They believed the peoples of the Americas were inferior because their ways were different. Intolerance caused conflict and the captivity and deaths of many Indigenous American people.

The Indigenous peoples of the Americas used the natural resources in their environment to build homes and make clothing and tools. The type of clothing, homes, and tools they made were different from the Europeans. Europeans believed that their own way of life was better and that they needed to change how Indigenous people lived and worked. The Spanish enforced these changes by making laws that privileged people who wore Spanish clothing, practiced Christianity, and spoke Spanish.

Native peoples of the Americas also practiced polytheism or the worship of more than one god. The Europeans were Catholics and only worshiped one god. They believed it was their duty to convert native peoples to Christianity. Christian missionaries crossed the Atlantic to preach to the Indigenous peoples. Some native peoples converted to Christianity willingly, but many others resisted. They didn’t want to give up their beliefs and their ways of life. This often led to conflict and fighting between the two groups.

There were, however, some Indigenous ideas that Europeans used or even exploited. For example, quinine was a type of medicine created by the people of the Inca Empire. It was made from the bark of the cinchona tree. This medicine could actually be used to combat malaria, a disease prevalent in Africa. Another example from the Inca is the mit'a system. This was a labor tax system created and used by the Inca government. When the conquistadors took over the Empire of the Incas, they used this labor system to force native people to work in Spanish silver mines.

title: Diseases
text:
The most deadly exchange that happened as a result of the Columbian Exchange was unintentional. The Europeans brought diseases with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. Some of these diseases were related to being exposed to the domesticated animals Europeans worked with and ate. For example, chickenpox is a disease that is thought to have originated in chickens, but because Europeans lived in such close proximity to their animals and because they ate chicken, this disease transferred to humans. After long and repeated exposure to these diseases, Europeans and their ancestors had developed immunities to them.

The people of the Americas, on the other hand, had never been exposed to such deadly germs. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of diseases were easily transported by unsuspecting Europeans. This all happened at a time before people understood how diseases spread. It was also long before antibiotics and other life-saving medicines had been discovered. Nowadays, there are vaccines that prevent diseases such as chickenpox and measles. Native peoples of the Americas had neither vaccines nor previous exposure. The results were deadly.

Native peoples’ immune systems were completely unable to fight off the new European diseases. Historians estimate that disease killed between 80–90 percent of the native population of the Americas within 150 years. In some cases, entire populations of Indigenous people died.

title: Lasting Effects
text:
Some of the lasting effects of the Columbian Exchange can still be seen in the world today. Animals and foods from both sides spread all over the world. New crops allowed farmers on both sides of the Atlantic to plant and harvest more food than ever before. Diets became more varied the world over.

There were many lasting effects of the Columbian exchange. Some were positive, but many were negative. One of the most enduring changes brought by the Columbian Exchange was not goods, animals, plants, or diseases, but the transfer of people. Columbus brought sugarcane to Hispaniola in 1493. Sugarcane grew well in the Americas and sold well in Europe. As sugar plantations sprang up and grew, the demand for labor increased. At first, Europeans paid or enslaved native peoples to work on the plantations. As the demand for labor increased, Europeans turned to the African slave trade.

People seeking new opportunities began crossing the Atlantic Ocean with the hope of making their fortune by farming land in the Americas. More and more people began immigrating to the Americas. Colonies began to develop. Some colonies failed after a few years, but many others were successful. Towns like Jamestown, Virginia; St. Augustine, Florida; and Plymouth, Massachusetts, that are still around today started out as European colonies.

Although there were many positive and negative consequences to the Columbian Exchange, it was undoubtedly one of the biggest events in history that forever changed the world.

title: The Qin and Han Dynasties
text:
One era of time in China is known as Imperial China. The word “imperial” comes from “empire.” An empire is a large group of countries, territories, or people that are ruled by a single person or government. Another characteristic of an empire is the focus on conquering more and more territory to expand its borders. The goal of imperial rule is economic and political control.

The first example of this in China was the Qin Dynasty in 221 B.C.E. Before the Qin Dynasty, the Zhou dynasty had broken apart. The kingdom had grown so large that it was divided into smaller separate states. There were different rulers in different parts of the country and the states were constantly at war with each other. The wars lasted more than 200 years. This is called the Warring States Period. During these wars, one particular state gained control over other states. It was the state of Qin. The leader was King Ying Zheng. He was a skilled warrior and very good at strategy. He was able to defeat the other armies and expand his territory. The Qin became the rulers over all the other kingdoms.

After the wars ended, King Yin Zheng took all of the small, individual states and united them, making them into one large region. He established the Qin Dynasty, claimed the Mandate of Heaven, and declared himself emperor. He was the first Chinese king with the title of emperor. The Qin dynasty did not last very long. After Qin Shi Huang died, another dynasty took over the empire. This was the Han dynasty. The Han made China even bigger by taking control of more land in the south and east. The Han dynasty lasted almost 400 years. It was a peaceful time for most of the people who lived in China. It was a time of innovation and growth. China became one of the great civilizations in the world during this time. The Qin and Han dynasties laid the foundation for China as we know it today. They created a common identity for all the people who lived in the empire.

title: Week 20 Framing Question
text: How did different leaders affect China’s development and contribute to its success?

title: Timeline of Imperial China
text:
The Qin and Han Dynasties in Imperial China, c. 221 B.C.E.–220 C.E

230 B.C.E.

King Ying Zheng of Qin defeats the other warring states.

221 B.C.E.

King Zheng claims the Mandate of Heaven and becomes Emperor Qin Shi Huang.

221 B.C.E.

Work begins on the Northern Frontier Wall.

210 B.C.E.

First Emperor of China Shi Huang dies.

202 B.C.E.

The Han dynasty begins a time of prosperity and growth for China.

141 B.C.E.

Emperor Wu extends the empire through military conquests.

c. 100 B.C.E.

The Han dynasty opens the “Silk Road.”

title: Emperor Qin
text:
Once King Ying Zheng had declared himself the emperor of China, he took the name Qin Shi Huang. He then set about creating a central government and unifying his empire. As an emperor, Qin had great power and complete control. Anyone who disagreed with him was punished. He made many changes to protect his empire and unify it into one country.

To keep other families from becoming too powerful, he took their lands away. He made all his citizens use the same writing system, money, weights, and measures. He did not want his people to waste time. He did not allow farmers to get an education. They had to focus on growing food and making silk. Qin Shi Huang burned any books he thought were useless. He also created a spy system, so that people would watch each other and report disobedience. Emperor Qin believed the country needed better protection, so he put people to work building a wall on the northern border.

Emperor Qin had planned for his son to take over the empire one day. But when Qin died, a peasant named Liu Bang began a revolt against the government. Many others joined in the revolt, and it was successful. Liu Bang became the new emperor. He called his dynasty the Han Dynasty.

title: Soldiers Made of Clay
text:
In 1974, local people were digging wells near the city of Xi’an, China. They found pieces of a terracotta statue deep underground. Terracotta is a type of clay. Archaeologists began an excavation. They discovered a statue of a life-size man dressed as a soldier. They kept digging. They found statues of more men. There were also statues of horses. The statues were standing in rows, like an army of soldiers. No two soldiers were exactly alike. They all had different facial expressions, clothing, and hairstyles. In the end, there were almost 8,000 statues of men and horses. Swords and chariots were also buried with the sculptures.

Scientists studied the statues. They learned that the terracotta soldiers were made for the tomb of Emperor Qin Shi Huang. The emperor believed that the army of statues would protect his tomb. The discovery of the Terracotta Warriors was an important event in the field of archaeology. Today, visitors can explore the site, see the warriors up close, and learn more about their history and significance.

title: Unifying China
text:
During the Qin and Han dynasties, China was bigger than before. There were many people spread across lots of territories. China’s rulers had to think of new ways to organize and unify the country.

Emperor Qin divided the empire into provinces. Each had two government officials in charge of it. The provinces were divided into smaller districts. Each district also had two people in charge of it. Districts were divided into even smaller units, with each unit reporting to the one above it. This system allowed the emperor to keep order and control over a vast and diverse empire. It became a model for future Chinese dynasties.

The Han Dynasty started a series of changes that strengthened the central government and improved the lives of the common people. The Han emperors established a strong military, which helped keep the country secure. As they conquered neighboring countries they united them with China. This made the country stronger and more powerful. The Han rulers also improved the roads and river systems making it easier for the people of China to trade and do business with each other.

The unification of ancient China was a very important time in Chinese history. It allowed the Chinese to develop their own culture and way of life, and to make important advances in art, science, and technology. It was hard to keep a large country together. Over time, disagreements and struggles for power began to rise. After 400 years, the Han empire split into three different kingdoms. The Han dynasty ended in 220 CE. Later in China’s history, other dynasties worked to reunite the country.

title: The Han Dynasty
text:
The Han dynasty lasted from about 202 BC to 220 AD. It is known for its great economic, cultural, and political achievements. Liu Bang, also known as Emperor Gaozu, made many changes that improved the lives of the people and encouraged innovation and growth. He was followed by a series of rulers who continued to expand and strengthen the empire. The Han dynasty had a total of 14 rulers.

During the Han Dynasty, Buddhism was introduced to China. Buddhist monks from India traveled to China along the Silk Road. Before this, most Chinese followed the ideas of Confucianism and Taoism. To help the people understand Buddhist concepts, the monks borrowed ideas from Daoism. At first, the ideas and practices spread mostly to the common people. Over time, Buddhism became a very influential religion in the lives of the Chinese, from the common people to the emperor himself.

The Han dynasty is known today as the golden age of Chinese history. A golden age is a time of growth and creativity. Many great achievements of China started during the Han dynasty.

The Han leaders promoted education and the arts and encouraged the study of subjects such as history and science. The people created many works of art and literature. Inventions from this time period include the magnetic compass, paper, the seismograph, and fireworks.

title: Xianyang and Chang’an
text:
Xianyang and Chang’an were the capital cities of the Qin and Han dynasties. They were two of the biggest cities in the ancient world. Roads went out to every part of the empire from Xianyang. The city was next to the Wei River which gave the people of Xianyang fresh water and good soil for growing crops.

Emperor Qin moved thousands of families to Xianyang. These families became the workers to build Qin’s palaces. They also built canals. The canals made travel easier and helped transport goods and people throughout the empire,

When the Han dynasty took power, the emperors liked having the capital near the Wei River. It was a good central location for running the empire. However, they wanted to build their own city. The new city was across the Wei River. It was just a few miles away from Xianyang. The Han capital was called Chang’an. Like Emperor Qin, the Han emperors forced thousands of families to move to the new capital. The families built magnificent palaces for the ruling family.

The Han leaders increased trade with other countries. China became famous in Asia and Europe for the valuable things it traded. Chang’an was a strong and prosperous city at the start of the trade routes that stretched from China to Europe.

title: Emperor Wu and Confucianism
text:
Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty had one of the longest reigns in Chinese history. He ruled from 141 BCE to 87 BCE. He was emperor for 54 years. During Wu’s reign, China had more contact with other countries. Emperor Wu also encouraged artists to write music and poetry. He wanted China to make beautiful things.

Emperor Wu made the Chinese government stronger. One way he did this was by promoting the teachings of Confucius. Confucius lived hundreds of years before Wu. There were many wars during the life of Confucius. Confucius tried to create peace in China. He taught that people should be respectful and kind to each other. Emperor Wu believed in these ideas and this helped make him a popular ruler.

Emperor Wu believed that Confucianism would help keep order in society. He made Confucianism the official religion of China. More than 2,000 years later, Confucianism is still an important part of Chinese culture.

title: Great Structures of Imperial China
text:
In ancient times, the Chinese built two of the biggest construction projects in the world. The Grand Canal helped the Chinese travel, communicate, and move goods within the country. The Great Wall helped defend the country from invasions.

The Grand Canal

Using boats and rivers, a society can transport people and goods quickly from one place to another. The Chinese people had learned early how to travel on rivers. They also learned how to make canals. A canal is an artificial river. The Chinese dug canals to connect the natural rivers. That way, they could travel even longer distances on the water.

The first canal in China was built around 500 BCE. For thousands of years, the Chinese added to and enlarged the canal system. Today, the Grand Canal in China is a massive waterway that stretches more than a thousand miles. It connects the Yellow River in the north to the Yangtze River in the south. The Grand Canal is considered a great achievement in engineering. In one part of the Grand Canal, ships come from the ocean to pick up and deliver goods. The canal is a very important part of China's history that is still used today.

The Great Wall

The Great Wall is one of the most famous structures in China. It was originally started to protect China against invaders from lands to the north. The earliest sections of the wall were built during the Warring States period. During the Qin dynasty, many sections were connected. Over the centuries more sections were added, expanded, and strengthened. The Great Wall was built using a variety of materials, including earth, stone, and brick. It is more than 13,000 miles long! In most places, it is about 25 feet high and about 20 feet wide. It is the longest structure in the world.

For many years, the Great Wall helped the Chinese fight wars. It was also a good way to move people and supplies around the empire. Today it is one of the most amazing structures in the world. People from all over the world go to China just to walk along the Great Wall.

title: Gifts of Ancient China
text:
Do you enjoy fireworks? Have you ever played with a yo-yo? We can thank the Chinese for these inventions. Have you read a book or written on a piece of paper today? The Chinese were the first to invent paper and printing. Do you use a toothbrush? Scientists believe they were invented in China. Do you like playing soccer? The Chinese started playing a game just like soccer thousands of years ago.

The Chinese gave the world many other gifts. Paper money, eyeglasses, umbrellas, and waterproof clothing were all Chinese inventions. The ancient Chinese were the first to use coal for heating. They invented the harness and stirrups for horses. The Chinese figured out how to make cloth from the cocoons of silkworms. They used kites as a form of communication. The Chinese made the first magnetic compasses using lodestone. Some researchers believe the Chinese made the first windmills. There is much we can learn about Ancient China from the creativity and innovation of the early Chinese people.

title: Framing Question Week 21
text: What contributions have the Chinese made to our lives today?

title: Silk
text:
People in China learned how to make silk about 5000 years ago. Silk is a strong thread that can be made into soft, shiny material for clothing and decoration. Silk can even be used to make fishing lines, musical instrument strings, and paper.

Silk comes from the cocoons of silkworms. To make silk, people have to carefully unravel the cocoons. The Chinese figured out how to make high-quality clothing, wall hangings, and even tents using silk. For the best silk, silkworms must grow at just the right temperature and without loud noises. The process is so complicated that at first silk was worn only by the emperor and people close to him. In ancient times, only the Chinese knew how to make silk. This process was carefully guarded by the Chinese government. Anyone caught trying to take silkworm eggs or cocoons out of the country would be punished.

People in other parts of the world wanted silk. Because only the Chinese could make it, it became very valuable. It was the most expensive thing that China traded. Routes were created for traders to travel between Europe and China. These routes became known as the Silk Road.

title: The Silk Road
text:
During the Han dynasty, China became stronger and richer. Han emperors wanted to open trade with other societies. The Chinese had been isolated for hundreds of years, and now they wanted to learn about other places and cultures. In 130 B.C.E., the Han emperor started sending traders to travel west of China. That was the beginning of the Silk Road.

The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of paths and routes that traders used to move goods between the different regions of Asia, Europe, and Africa. The routes changed over time, but the area they covered was over 4,000 miles long. It was the longest trading route in the world. The Silk Road passed through deserts and mountains. There were cities and towns along the way. There were also robbers. To protect themselves, traders traveled in groups called caravans.

Many things were traded along the Silk Road. Silk was the most valuable thing that the Chinese made. Other valuable things from China were porcelain, spices, tea, and precious stones. Most people who traded along the Silk Road did not travel down the entire road. Goods were often passed from one group of traders to another.

Stories, beliefs, and ideas were also traded along the Silk Road. cities began to rise along the trade routes. These cities were full of people from different cultures. They interacted with each other using different languages and writing systems. They taught each other new ways to create goods, art, and architecture. They shared new ideas about religion and government. Researchers estimate that the Silk Road was used for more than 1,000 years. During all those years it played a critical role in trade and cultural exchange between the different civilizations.

title: Porcelain
text:
About 30,000 years ago people figured out how to make pots out of clay. They started with wet clay, so they could form the shape they wanted. After the pot was formed and the clay dried, they baked it in a fire. After baking, the clay was hard and kept its shape, even when it got wet. This is called ceramics.

Around 3,500 years ago, people in China discovered how to make a new kind of ceramic. We call it porcelain. It became one of the most valuable inventions in Chinese history. To make porcelain, people use a special kind of clay called kaolin. When the porcelain was finished, it was harder than other ceramics. It had a smooth, shiny surface which was easier to paint with fine designs or scenes.

People in Europe saw porcelain for the first time around 1300 CE. They tried to make porcelain, but they did not know how. Just like silk, the secret of porcelain-making was carefully guarded by the Chinese. For thousands of years, only they knew how to make porcelain. Other civilizations were willing to trade many valuable things to get porcelain from China.

Today, many people in the United States have porcelain in their homes. Small statues, dinner plates, and tea sets can all be made of porcelain. Sometimes we say that things made of porcelain are made of “china.” That’s how famous porcelain from China became.

title: Paper Making
text:
Historians believe the Chinese were the first to create paper. Before the invention of paper, people used materials such as clay tablets, papyrus, and fabric to write down and record information. However, these materials were expensive and difficult to produce. In China, bamboo was often used for writing, but it was bulky and heavy.

Around 105 C.E., a man named Ts'ai Lun discovered something else that could be used for writing. He developed a method of making paper using a mixture of tree bark, plant fibers, and old rags. After soaking the materials in water, he ground them into a pulp and then pressed them into flat sheets. This process was much easier and cheaper than the previous methods, and it began to spread to other parts of the world. People experimented with other materials. Vegetable fiber, fishing nets, rice straws, and bamboo canes were also used to make paper. Today, paper is an essential part of our daily lives and is used for many purposes.

title: Woodblock Printing
text:
For thousands of years, most things were made one at a time. If people wanted more than one copy of a document or record, it had to be written by hand. It was a slow process. It took years to make many copies of the same book. That all changed when the Chinese invented printing.

Around 700 C.E., the Chinese began to use ink, paper, and wood for printing. Using carving tools, an engraver would carve characters or pictures on a block of wood. Then they would spread a thin layer of ink across the carved surface of the block. When the wood block was pressed onto a piece of paper, the ink printed the characters onto the paper. Then they could just apply more ink and use the same block to make more copies.

Woodblock printing made it possible to get information to more people. The Chinese printed books about farming and medicine. They printed calendars and beautiful pictures. They printed receipts for business deals and tax payments. Woodblock printing was an important technological advancement. It allowed for the mass production of books, religious texts, and other written works. It also played an important role in the spread of knowledge and ideas throughout the world.

title: Weights and Measures
text:
When Qin Shi Huang became the emperor of China and began to unite all the states, people were using many different ways to measure and weigh things. Often, these were based on the physical characteristics of common objects, like the length of a foot or the weight of a grain of rice. But people’s feet are different sizes and not every grain of rice weighs the same. With different systems, it was difficult for people to compare the value of their goods and services. The people needed measurements that everyone used so they could trade with each other. The rulers wanted a more uniform system so they could collect the same taxes from everyone. The creation of standards for weight and measurement was an important step in the development of ancient China. With shared standards, the country was more united.

One of the most important units of length in ancient China was the chi, which was a little more than a foot. The chi was divided into 10 smaller units called cun, and those were divided into 10 fen. This system allowed for very precise measurements. Weight was typically measured using the jin, which was equal to 1.10 pounds. The jin was divided into 10 liang, and each liang was divided into 10 qian.

title: The Magnetic Compass
text:
When you want to get somewhere, it’s useful to know which direction you are headed. Finding the right directions when you travel is called navigation. People in ancient China invented an important tool for navigation: the compass.

A compass is made of a special magnetic rock called a lodestone. If you suspend a lodestone from a string, it uses Earth's magnetic field to turn and point north. The Chinese figured out how to attach a lodestone to a plate so the lodestone could spin. They could move the plate in any direction, and the lodestone would always point to the north. Early Chinese compasses were made in the shape of a spoon. The thick part of the spoon pointed north. The thin part pointed south.

At first, the Ancient Chinese people did not use compasses for travel. Instead, they believed that compasses helped them make wise decisions. They used compasses to decide where to build a house or where to bury their relatives. Later, they learned to use compasses for navigation.
