title: War Ends! Pennsylvania Becomes a State
text:
The War of Independence ended in 1781. Great Britain agreed the colonies could be free and independent states. That meant the Continental Congress had to become a national government. Members of the Continental Congress feared a government with too much authority. So, they made a confederation, or an alliance of states. The delegates of each new state signed the Articles of Confederation.

The government under the Articles of Confederation had little authority. Individual states had more authority than the national government. Taxation authority was in the states. Military actions were controlled by each state. Trade with foreign governments was controlled by each state. The states were not known for working together for the common good. The new nation was in danger of collapse.

Between May and September of 1787, delegates from the 13 states met in Philadelphia. The delegates debated the Articles of Confederation. They decided to write a new constitution that would remove authority from the states.

The constitution would create a strong national government. There were many debates and many compromises between the men who wrote the constitution. When it was finished, the people of each state had to ratify, or vote to approve, it. The majority of people in nine of the 13 states needed to approve the new government. This would mean that “we the people” were in support of a strong central government and less power in the states. The new constitution framed a government with separate, balanced authority. The government was a constitutional republic. Its central idea was representing the people and having rule of law for all.

Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution on December 7, 1787. Five days later, on December 12, 1787, Pennsylvania ratified the Constitution. One delegate, James Wilson, led the way for its ratification. In a speech, he stated, “Regarding [the Constitution], then, in every point of view … I am bold to assert that it is the best form of government which has ever been offered to the world.”

It was only 12 weeks after the Constitution was framed that Pennsylvania ratified it. Some states took two years. Ratifying early sent a message to the other states that Pennsylvania wanted a federal government. This was Pennsylvania’s commitment to the union of the states.

In 1788, New Hampshire was the ninth state to ratify the Constitution. The Constitution became the supreme law of the land. Elections for the new government were set for Monday, December 15, 1788, to Saturday, January 10, 1789. The new legislative, executive, and judicial branches would begin officially on March 4, 1789. On this day, George Washington was inaugurated as the country’s first president.

title: Essential Question
text: How did events in Pennsylvania support the establishment of the new nation of the United States of America?

title: Gradual Abolition Act of 1780
text:
The American colonies in North America needed large numbers of workers. To get these workers, the colonists enslaved African people. Throughout the 1700s, the Pennsylvania Assembly tried to discourage slavery. They taxed slavery to discourage people from being enslavers. In 1775, the Pennsylvania Abolition Society was formed. Abolition means to end the practice of something, like slavery.

In 1780, Pennsylvania became the first colony to try to abolish slavery. The Pennsylvania Assembly passed the Gradual Abolition Act of 1780. This Act did not free enslaved people immediately. It freed them over time. It was the first law of its kind in the colonies. The Act stated “that all persons … who shall be born within the state from and after the passing of this act, shall not be deemed and considered as servants for life or slaves.” Anyone born in Pennsylvania from 1780 on was born free.

Many other Northern states followed Pennsylvania’s lead. By 1784, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island had also passed complete or gradual abolition laws.

title: The Whiskey Rebellion
text:
After the American War for Independence, the government followed the laws set out in the Articles of Confederation. One of the difficulties with these articles was that Congress could not collect taxes. Money for the government came from the states. This changed with the new Constitution of 1787. A strong central government had the authority to make and collect taxes.

Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton introduced a new tax to pay the war debt. This was a tax on distilled spirits, or alcohol. Distilled spirits are drinks for adults that have been processed from rye, wheat, or corn. The population in the coastal cities had a market for distilled spirits made in the region west of the Appalachian Mountains.

Farmers knew it was easier to transport liquids to market by horse and wagon than it was to take bushels of solid grain or corn. Getting goods to market was important for the economy and welfare of the farmers. The new tax was on the drinks, not the grains the farmers grew. It was not welcomed. The farmers did not want to pay the tax since they only distilled the grains into the liquid spirits to make them easier for transport. The main markets for the drinks were over in the eastern cities. The new federal government demanded payment in cash. Cash money was not available in the rural west. Bartering with goods and services was the means of paying debt. People who did not pay the tax had to appear in federal court 300 miles away in Philadelphia.

For a while, the Pennsylvania farmers refused to pay the tax with no consequences. A local farmer named Albert Gallatin wanted to go through legal channels to change the tax. Gallatin led a group to ask for repeal of the law through the courts. Other farmers thought the process was too slow. Tensions and conflict increased between tax collectors and farmers. Tax collectors began to demand payment. As a result, tax collectors met with violence from the farmers. Using his authority as president, George Washington issued a proclamation to the farmers to stop the violence and obey the law. Small changes in the law were made, but none satisfied the Pennsylvania farmers.

In 1794, there was violence against regional tax collector John Neville. In response, President Washington met with state governor, Thomas Mifflin. Washington issued a proclamation calling on the protesters “to disperse and retire peaceably to their [homes].” The actions of the protesters “amount to treason, being … acts of levying war against the United States; the said persons having on the sixteenth and Seventeenth of July last past proceeded in arms (on the second day amounting to several hundreds) to the house of John Neville Inspector of the Revenue for the fourth survey of the District of Pennsylvania.”

The proclamation said, “it shall be lawful for the President of the United States to call forth the militia of such State to suppress such combinations and to cause the laws to be duly executed."

Over 10,000 militia formed in Harrisburg. Washington, and Alexander Hamilton led them west in October 1794. About 150 protesters were arrested. Most were released due to lack of evidence. Two were convicted of treason but pardoned, or released with no penalty.

The protest against the distilled spirit tax became known as the Whiskey Rebellion. It is the only time a serving president of the United States led a militia into action. Washington’s actions strengthened the federal government’s authority to enforce laws. Future presidents would use Washington’s actions as an example of using federal militia to enforce laws of the federal government.

title: The War of 1812 and the Battle of Lake Erie
text:
The United States went to war again with Britain from 1812 to 1814. One reason for this new war was because Britain and France were already at war. Britain did not want the U.S. to trade with France. The British also supported Native Americans who resisted U.S. settlers moving into their lands. This created conflict between native peoples and U.S. settlers. It also led to trade issues. Goods from Philadelphia were blocked. France and other nations were unable to buy these goods.

Throughout the war, there were several important battles. At first, the war did not go well for the U.S. However, the Battle of Lake Erie changed that for the Americans. At this time, the British Navy had around 500 vessels, or ships. The United States only had 17 vessels. In February 1813, Oliver Perry was put in charge of the naval force on Lake Erie. It was important to succeed here to protect the Northwest Territory. The U.S. also wanted to cut off a British supply route.

On September 10, 1813, Perry unrolled a flag on his ship, the flagship Lawrence. This flag said, “Don’t Give Up the Ship!”, a phrase that many recognize today. Unfortunately, the Lawrence could not resist all the British attacks. Perry then had to take his flag and put it on the flagship Niagara. The British were eventually forced to surrender. After the battle, Perry sent a message to Major General William Henry Harrison that said, “We have met the enemy and they are ours.” This win led the U.S. to have more success on land and control of the territory.

title: Richard Allen
text:
Richard Allen was an enslaved man living in Delaware. He spent five years working and saving to buy his freedom. He then moved to Pennsylvania. He wanted to live somewhere that supported the abolition of slavery. In 1786, he became a preacher for St. George’s Methodist Church in Philadelphia. Allen was only allowed to preach to a segregated audience. Segregation is keeping people apart based on race, class, or another social grouping. This led Allen and other church members to leave the church.

In 1787, Allen and a man named Absalom Jones formed the Free African Society (FAS) in Philadelphia. They created the FAS to help freedom seekers escape from slavery. They provided money and support to people who were starting new lives.

The FAS decided to create a new church. They founded the Mother Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME) church in 1794. In this church, African Americans could worship without being segregated. Allen's ordination, or becoming an official minister, was in 1799. He was the first African American to be ordained as a Methodist Episcopal minister.

The Bethel AME church has a long history of providing help to others. Throughout the early 1800s, Allen and his wife, Sarah Bass, helped freedom seekers build new lives.

title: Albert Gallatin
text:
Albert Gallatin was a quiet, well-educated man from Switzerland. He came to Fayette County, Pennsylvania, in 1780. Gallatin built a large estate, Friendship Hill, in what is now the Uniontown area. The people of Fayette County elected Gallatin to represent them in ratifying the Constitution. They also elected him to represent them to the House of Representatives. It was Gallatin who established the Congressional Ways and Means Committee. The purpose of this committee is to set taxes and government spending. It also aims to openly disclose how the government uses money.

Gallatin was appointed secretary of the treasury by President Thomas Jefferson in 1801. It was Gallatin who arranged for the financing for the Louisiana Purchase. He strongly supported the use of government money for improvements to roads, canals, and ports. Gallatin was secretary of the treasury for 14 years. After serving as a diplomat, he retired to New York. James Madison wrote to Jefferson in 1796, “Gallatin is a real treasure. He is sound in his principles, accurate in his calculations and indefatigable [tireless] in his researches.” Gallatin is credited today with providing stability in the early finances of the country.

title: Pittsburgh: From Fort to City
text:
Pittsburgh’s location and geography made it a perfect place for trade and transportation. Pittsburgh is located in southwest Pennsylvania. It sits where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio River. Long before European explorers and immigrants settled Pittsburgh, the Shawnee and Leni Lenape lived on that land. European explorers and traders were attracted to the area's location and resources. They established forts and settlements there. Due to its location where three rivers meet, Pittsburgh grew as a center for trade and transportation. Pittsburgh could control river traffic to the American West. After the American Revolution, the village of Pittsburgh grew. The town became a possession of Pennsylvania in 1785. Many people used Pittsburgh as a launching point to explore and settle the Northwest territory. Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery stopped in Pittsburgh to get supplies for their journey west in 1804. After the War of 1812, the population of Pittsburgh qualified it to become a city.

November 25, 1758

General Forbes leads British forces to the area. They arrive to find the French Fort Duquesne destroyed. It is said that Forbes referred to this area as “Pittsburgh” even before they arrived.

December 1758

Colonel Mercer builds a new fort in the place of Fort Duquesne. It is called Mercer’s Fort.

Spring 1759

Civilians arrive with pack horses and goods. Many decide to stay and build small homes on the flat ground.

Summer 1759

Plans begin to build Fort Pitt. Two new towns spring up around the fort: Lower Town and Upper Town.

July 1760

One hundred and forty-nine civilians are recorded to be living in Pittsburgh.

Spring 1763

Residents take cover in Fort Pitt during Pontiac’s War. This was an uprising of Native Americans against British forts and settlements, including Fort Pitt.

1764

John Campbell lays out a new town for the reopening of the fur trade at Fort Pitt.

May 1765

Leni Lanape, Shawnee, Mingo, and Seneca hunters come back for the fur trade. Pittsburgh becomes a base for the new trade in the Illinois Country, far to the west.

1772

The British Army receives orders to evacuate Fort Pitt. It is sold to two local residents.

Fall 1774

Pittsburgh serves as a site for Virginians to fight against the Shawnee.

1784

Heirs to William Penn convince officers at Fort Pitt to sell lots of land in the area that is now downtown Pittsburgh.

August 31, 1803

Meriweather Lewis and William Clark, hired by President Thomas Jefferson, leave on a westward expedition from Pittsburgh.

1816

The city of Pittsburgh is incorporated. When a city is incorporated, it receives a charter from the state allowing it to have its own elected officials and rules. Ebenezer Denny becomes the city's first mayor.

title: Ebenezer Denny
text:
The first mayor of the city of Pittsburgh was Ebenezer Denny. Ebenezer was born in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, in 1761. Early in his life, he became involved with the military. At the age of 13, he was a dispatch rider who took messages to Fort Pitt. This was a very dangerous job. He did this to help with his family’s income.

During the American War for Independence, Denny led the Pennsylvania Regiment. He was in Yorktown, Virginia, when the British were forced to surrender. He had taken the Pennsylvania Regiment to help reinforce the French in Virginia. In his military journal, Denny wrote, “Joined by the last of the troops from the eastward. French encamped a few miles on the right; busy in getting cannon and military stores from on board the vessels.”

After earning the rank of major and serving in the army for 15 years, Denny retired. He then moved to the area near Fort Pitt. In 1797, Denny began his political career as a county commissioner. When the city of Pittsburgh was officially established in 1816, Denny was chosen to be the first mayor. After serving for two years, he decided not to serve a second term.

title: Essential Question
text: How has transportation helped us move people and goods?

title: What Is Transportation?
text: Transportation is how a person or a thing gets from one place to another. Movement has always been important for people to meet their wants and needs. People have consistently looked for better and more convenient ways to travel. Better ways of transportation increased interdependence and economic growth. A key piece of technology for transportation is the wheel. This simple shape has had many innovations over the years. The wheel is attached in different ways to a box to carry goods or people. Yet the wheel is still round and is important for travel.

title: Moving People on Land
text:
Carriages and coaches were what people used for transport before the 20th century. They were boxes designed for comfort with cushioned seats. They also had four wheels. The carriage was pulled by one or two horses. The coach was built for longer distances. It was bigger and more sturdy. A larger team of horses pulled a coach.

Innovators took the design of the box on four wheels and created an automobile. Automobiles became more comfortable for people to use. The motors became more powerful and increased the automobiles’ speed. Speed is important to move people quickly from one place to another.

Automobiles were adjusted to meet the needs of growing cities. The box and wheels became longer and wider. It was a form of transportation called a bus. Factories began to manufacture buses.

Automobiles and buses allowed trade to expand. Roads and highways were built as these means of transport improved and their speeds increased. Greater use of highways changed the landscape. The engines from the automobiles and buses caused air pollution.

title: Transportation on Land
text:
A covered wagon was four feet wide and nine feet long. It was used for carrying possessions, not for people to ride in. A full wagon needed 4–6 horses to pull it. Two oxen could also be used. The wheels were made from wood with iron rims. There were no roads, just open ground. The rough travel often broke the wheels.

Trucks evolved from wagons. Trucks came in all shapes and sizes and had motors. However, they all had four wheels. If heavier loads were needed, additional wheels were added to help move the trucks. The wheels were covered with thick rubber tires. Tires made riding in the truck much easier. Tires also helped protect the load from damage. Today, trucks with 18 wheels use highways to transport the heavy loads they carry.

The railroad was developed to move more products over great distances. A train has an engine that pulls many attached cars, or boxes on wheels. The wheels on the train were made to sit on rails of steel. One train can move tons of goods and thousands of products across the country.

A trolley was designed from a train. It is designed to move people. The wheels of the trolley usually run on a track of two steel rails. Trolleys are powered by electricity. The electricity runs along an overhead wire to the trolley.

title: Transportation in Air
text:
The Wright brothers flew the first airplane in 1903. They designed the plane by studying birds in flight. Scientists had done many studies on air currents and wind. Air travel is possible because of science. An airplane uses air to move. However, it also has wheels to help it land and take off. Airplanes move people and goods across continents and oceans.

Today, air transportation does not just use airplanes. Drones are also used for delivering packages. These small, robotic vehicles use propellers to fly. Drones use data input from computers to fly.

title: Transportation in Your Community
text:
The articles this week have been about transportation. As transportation across the country has grown, it has left its mark on towns, cities, and the land. There are many large airports with long runways. Train tracks and stations crisscross the country. There are interstate highways with many lanes to allow for speedy, long-distance travel. There are bridges, tunnels, and parking lots across the land. Small roads connect rural towns and neighborhoods.

What types of transportation are in your community? What is the same across each type of transportation?

title: Movement of People, Products, and Ideas
text:
Look at the following scenarios. For each scenario, discuss how you could transport the people, goods, or ideas.

You listed a pair of shoes for sale online. Someone in New York bought the shoes. How could you transport the shoes to New York?

Your grandmother lives in Mexico. You want to visit your grandmother for the holidays. How could you travel to Mexico?

You need to go grocery shopping for the week. How could you get to the store and back with your groceries?

You have some homework due for your class. The homework is at your house. How could you transport your homework to your teacher?

A company mined a lot of coal. You need coal to heat your home this winter. How could you transport the coal from the mine to your home?

You want to go to the movies. How could you travel to the nearest movie theater?

You bought a new model airplane from Canada. The instructions were not in the package. The company said they will send you a new set of instructions. How could they transport the instructions to you?

title: Transportation on Water
text:
People have traveled over water for thousands of years. They used to travel in canoes. Canoes could go long distances on rivers and streams.

A ferry is a flat platform that carries cars and wagons across a river. It is used where there is no bridge. There were many ferries before bridges and highways were built.

Ships were created to carry large cargo across the ocean. Early ships used sails. The sails caught the wind and pushed the ship through water. Innovators changed the ship’s design. The design allowed ships to move easily through the ocean. A clipper ship carried goods and passengers faster than ever before.

Later, motors were attached to ships. A motor could move the ship through the ocean without needing the wind. Ocean travel became much faster and more dependable. Today, some ships are so big they are like floating cities.

title: Essential Question
text: What makes a culture unique?

title: What Is Culture?
text: Culture is the beliefs, traditions, and celebrations of a group of people. There are many characteristics of culture. Architecture, arts, literature, music, and language are some. Religion, clothing, and food are others. Culture reflects a group’s way of life. It includes things they produce and use. It also includes the skills and traditions passed down to younger generations. People use resources around them to meet their needs. Local plant and animal resources are used to make food, clothing, and shelter. A group’s culture develops using these resources.

title: Architecture
text: Architecture is the style and design of a building. We can learn about a culture when we look at its architecture. Look at the images. Compare the design and structure of the buildings. What resources did the people have access to? What beliefs might be important to these cultures? What skills did the builders have?

title: Language
text: Language is an important part of culture. When people move, they bring their languages with them. For example, explorers from Spain traveled around the world. Now, people speak Spanish all over the world. Many early immigrants to the United States spoke English. American Indians all over the country now speak English as well as their native languages. In early Ohio history, many German Americans came from Pennsylvania and Germany. Some people in Ohio still speak German. The movement of language impacts culture.

title: Fine Arts and Literature
text: Sculptures, photographs, and paintings show the art of a culture. We can learn about different cultures when we study their art. Artists draw what they see around them. These images include people, traditions, and celebrations. Literature comes from stories people share. Reading, telling, and listening to stories are ways that people share their ideas and beliefs. These shared stories become part of their culture.

title: Celebrations
text: One way people express culture is through celebrations. Geography influences how people celebrate and what the celebration is about. Some cultures celebrate the seasons. Other cultures celebrate planting and harvesting crops. As people move from place to place, they bring their cultures and celebrations with them.

title: Food
text: The food people eat often comes from the resources around them. For example, in countries near the ocean, people eat a lot of seafood. People have also developed skills to preserve and prepare local food. These skills are part of their food culture. For example, most cultures have developed a typical bread using local grain. French baguettes and Indian naan are examples. So are Ethiopian injera and German rye bread.

title: Clothing
text: Environments people live in affect the way they dress. People in hot climates wear lightweight clothing to keep cool. People in colder climates wear heavy clothing to keep warm. The material of clothing reflects local resources. Grasses, palm fronds, pigskin, and cloth made from natural fibers are some things people use. Dye for cloth can be made from local plants. Traditional or ceremonial clothing is often very well made and decorated. It reflects the traditional skills of the people.

title: Claire and Miguel's Mini Golf Course
text:
Golf Course Engineers

Claire and Miguel want to be great mini golfers. They practice together. They learn how to make the golf balls move in different ways. They each use 10 hits to get their ball into the hole. To improve, they need to move the ball with fewer hits. Can you design a course that will help them?

My Observations

My Questions

In response to the damage of the tea cargo in Boston, Parliament created the Intolerable Acts, also called the Coercive Acts. These were designed by King George III to punish Massachusetts for the tea party and their continued resistance to his actions and his government. The following was directed at Massachusetts:

Boston Port Act (June 1, 1774): closed off the port of Boston, eliminating commerce and trade in the city.

Administration of Justice Act (May 20, 1774): granted a change of location to Great Britain or a British Colony in the event of a jury trial.

Massachusetts Government Act (May 20, 1774): repealed the colony’s charter and created an unprecedented amount of royal control.

Quartering Act (June 2, 1774): allowed new royal governor General Thomas Gage to house British soldiers in private homes, inns, and other buildings without permission from colonists.

Quebec Act (June 22, 1774): designated the western region north of the Ohio River as part of Quebec and made Roman Catholicism the established religion of Quebec; this upset colonial Protestants.

Each colonial legislature called for a meeting of representatives. This was called the First Continental Congress. Representatives gathered in Carpenters Hall in Philadelphia on Sept. 5, 1774. Twelve of the 13 colonies sent delegates.

The first order of business was to write a petition to King George to remove the recent Acts applied to Massachusetts. Each colony had protested the Tea Act in some manner, but Massachusetts was receiving the punishment. The delegates at the congress knew the king could do the same to each of their colonies at any time.

The delegates continued to prepare. They agreed that if the offending Acts of Parliament were not repealed, the colonies would boycott British goods. The congress also recommended that each colony continue to defy Parliament and the king. They also recommended that each colony prepare a militia and to begin gathering supplies.

The delegates of the congress sent their petition to King George through Benjamin Franklin, who was in London as an agent for the Pennsylvania colony. At the end of the congressional session in October 1774, the members agreed to meet in a second continental congress the following May, in 1775.

title: Tchefuncte Culture
text:
The Tchefuncte people lived on the northern shore of Lake Pontchartrain, near present-day Mandeville. The Tchefuncte hunted, gathered, and planted small gardens to obtain food. Primary sources of protein for the Tchefuncte included clams, raccoons, alligators, fish, bears, and deer. They used traps and nets to catch fish and marine birds. They gathered various nuts and fruits including acorns, hickory nuts, grapes, plums, and persimmons. The Tchefuncte also planted small gardens to supplement their diet.

The people of the Tchefuncte culture are best known for the pottery they left behind. Unlike their neighbors at Poverty Point, the Tchefuncte culture was very involved in creating decorated pottery. The pottery was poorly made because the pottery makers never included a temper in the clay they used. A temper is an ingredient that helps the clay harden better, such as ground-up shells, bones, sand, or even moss. Because of this, their pottery broke more easily with use and during the firing process. The pottery was highly decorated with lines, dots, and patterns from textured cloth pressed into the clay.

Other artifacts found at Tchefuncte sites include things like tools made of bone, shell, and stone. Most burials that have been found were buried under shell middens, or refuse heaps. Based on the remains found in these burials, burying the dead with grave offerings and burial goods seems to have not been practiced by the Tchefuncte.

title: Marksville Culture
text:
The Marksville site was used during the Middle Woodland period from 1 C.E. to 400 C.E. At its peak, Marksville covered an area of 60 acres. The people who lived at Marksville constructed earthworks including mounds, rings, and a c-shaped ridge around the site. Six earthen mounds and a ring-shaped earthwork are found within the ridge and one large ring and two smaller rings outside of the c-shaped ridge.

The Marksville people borrowed and adopted many parts of the Hopewell culture, which is evident in the artifacts and structures they left behind. The designs found on Marksville pottery are almost identical to those found on Hopewell pottery. Archaeologists believe that the people of Marksville adopted many styles and customs from the Hopewell culture. The ring-shaped structures at Marksville are not found at any other Hopewell sites, so the rings may have been built and used for a purpose unique to the Marksville people. However, the mounds at Marksville form geometric patterns like those at Hopewell sites.

After many excavations, archaeologists have determined that some of the mounds at the Marksville site were burial mounds. Several graves have been found in these mounds. It is believed that those who were buried in the mound were important people in the community. This theory is supported by the fact that archaeologists have found important items in the burial mounds, such as copper, pearl, shell, and stone jewelry, as well as pottery, stone points, precious stones, and shells.

No homes or domestic structures have been found at Marksville, so it is believed that the site was only used for ceremonial purposes.

Archaeological evidence also shows that the Marksville people did not rely on trade to meet their wants and needs but instead relied on their local resources. They made tools and pottery from stone and clay within their own environment. They also enjoyed a variety of foods found within their local environment. They hunted animals like deer, rabbits, birds, and turtles; fished and gathered freshwater clams; and they also collected wild plants, nuts, and fruits. They also stored food for long periods of time in woven baskets and clay pots.

title: Baytown Culture
text:
The term “Baytown culture” refers to the Indigenous peoples who lived in northern Louisiana and parts of Mississippi, Arkansas, and Tennessee during the late Woodland period. The culture of the Baytown people was similar to the culture of other late Woodland tribes and people. They engaged in agriculture and grew different types of grasses, sunflowers, herbs, gourds, and squash.

The Baytown people also gathered nuts and wild fruits, which were a large part of their diets. They used bows and arrows to hunt deer, squirrels, raccoons, turkeys, and pigeons. The Baytown people relied on the resources from the rivers, lakes, and streams of the region. They fished and trapped aquatic reptiles and mammals for food and other resources.

Little is known about the homes and settlements of the Baytown culture. Archaeologists have found the remains of very few structures at different sites. It is unclear if the artifacts and remains of structures that they found were homes. Archeologists do believe that the Baytown people lived in small settlements with few homes.

Like the Tchefuncte and Marksville cultures, the Baytown people made and used pottery for cooking and storing food. Archaeologists have found remnants of Baytown pottery at various sites in the Southeast. The style of pottery and patterns they used for decoration are similar to pottery styles and patterns found at other sites not associated with the Baytown culture. This demonstrates evidence of communication and shared ideas between tribes across the Southeast.

Despite these similarities, cultures and groups in Louisiana became increasingly different and adopted their own cultural practices, government structures, and traditions. The Baytown people engaged in more wide-spread trade with neighboring cultures. During the late Baytown period, the Baytown people began to use different materials to decorate pottery, including paints made from natural resources.

Archaeologists believe that the Baytown culture was divided into individual tribes led by a tribal leader. Leaders were chosen by the members of the tribe because of their achievements, but they worked with all members of the tribes to make decisions. Members of the various tribes met at mound sites and held large feasts and civic ceremonies.

title: Troyville Earthworks
text:
The Baytown people constructed earthwork mounds like many of the cultural groups that came before them. The largest complex of mounds in Louisiana constructed during the Baytown period was located near present-day Jonesville. This complex is called the Troyville earthworks. These mounds were constructed between 400 and 700 C.E. Archaeologists estimate that there may have been as many as 13 mounds at this site during the height of the Baytown culture.

Many of the mounds at the Troyville complex were destroyed during the late 1800s and early 1900s. Earth from the largest mound was used to fill in the land during road and bridge construction during the 1930s. Before their destruction, the mounds were a popular tourist attraction. In 1882, author Mark Twain visited the site. He wrote:

Troy, or a portion of it, is situated on and around three large Indian mounds, circular in shape, which rise above the present water about twelve feet. They are about 150 feet in diameter, and are about two hundred yards apart. The houses are all built between these mounds, and hence are all flooded to a depth of eighteen inches on their floors. These elevations, built by the aborigines, hundreds of years ago, are the only points of refuge for miles…

Through excavations and the accounts of people who visited the site, archaeologists have been able to determine how the largest mound was constructed. Mound 5, also called the Great Mound, had three tiers or levels. The tiers were constructed at different times. When all three tiers were completed, the total height of the mound was about 80 feet, making it one of the largest earthen mounds constructed by Indigenous peoples in North America.

Archaeologists have also been able to determine that some of the mounds at the Troyville site were burial mounds, but it is unclear if the site was a permanent settlement. The other mounds were used for public ceremonies.

title: Coles Creek Culture
text:
The Coles Creek culture was one of the largest late Woodland period cultures that inhabited Louisiana. The Coles Creek people established settlements throughout the Lower Mississippi River Valley. The Coles Creek culture shared many customs and practices with other Woodland cultures in Louisiana and the southeast, but the Coles Creek people adopted new innovations and practices that developed during this time across North America.

Like their predecessors, the Coles Creek people hunted, fished, gathered, and grew their own food. Tribal locations played a large role in the diets of the Coles Creek people. Tribes that lived inland relied more on hunting and gathering food. Tribes that lived in coastal areas or near water sources were experts at catching and trapping fish, shellfish, and marine mammals and reptiles. Many of the Coles Creek tribes also grew corn, squash, gourds, and sunflowers. All tribes gathered wild fruit, plants, nuts, and berries.

Unlike the Baytown culture, the chosen leader of Coles Creek tribes had more control and made the decisions for the members of the tribe. They also developed different types of pottery. The pottery made by the Coles Creek people was more durable and thicker than the pottery made by other Woodland cultures. They also used different patterns to decorate the pottery they created.

The most visible difference between the Coles Creek culture and other Woodland cultures was the type of earthen mounds they constructed. Coles Creek mounds closely resembled a plateau, with sloping sides and a flat top. Homes were constructed on some of these flat-topped mounds. Archaeologists believe that the leaders of the tribes lived in these homes. Other Coles Creek mounds served as the site where ceremonies took place. All important ceremonies took place at these mound complexes.

Early Coles Creek sites traditionally had three mounds built around a plaza. Permanent settlements were built around the site. As the population of the culture grew, more mounds were constructed at various sites. Settlements were built near the ceremonial mounds. The largest of the Coles Creek culture mounds are located in the Lower Mississippi River Valley. Archaeologists have also found smaller Coles Creek culture mounds in the coastal areas of Louisiana.

title: Bringing New Life to Ancient Civilizations
text:
Many ancient civilizations were famous for their technological advancements. Early societies were constantly seeking new ways to improve their tools and weapons, cultivate crops, and build structures and cities. In some cases, they developed new technology through their own ingenuity. In other cases, they learned from neighboring cultures and adapted existing technologies to meet their needs. Over time, the ability to innovate and develop new technology allowed ancient civilizations to thrive and expand, laying the foundation for today's world.

Today, technology is something we all rely on. It touches every aspect of our lives and rules the modern world. Archaeologists have always been quick to use the latest technologies to help them do their jobs. In the 1940s, radiocarbon dating, or measuring the amount of a specific carbon in an object to determine its age, changed the field of archaeology.

Archaeologists are now using a wide range of rapidly advancing technology. These high-tech inventions help us uncover ancient secrets and learn more about the cultures and civilizations of the past. From aerial photography and remote sensing to 3D modeling and virtual reality, technology is playing an increasingly important role in archaeology. It is helping archaeologists to map sites in greater detail, understand artifacts and remains better, and to share their findings with more people.

title: Framing Question Week 30
text: How does today's technology help us learn about ancient civilizations of the past?

title: Magnetometry in Egypt
text:
Magnetometry is a technology that helps archaeologists find things that are hidden underground. Objects within the ground cause small differences in Earth’s magnetic field. Using special tools, scientists measure the magnetic properties of the ground and then create maps from the data. These maps help archaeologists “see” what type of objects lay buried on a site and their exact locations without even having to dig.

In Egypt, magnetometry has been used to study a number of ancient sites. In Saqqara, an ancient Egyptian city located near Cairo, measurements from magnetometry revealed underground structures. They were identified as walls and foundations. The site was then excavated. Archaeologists found a series of previously unknown tombs that date back to the Old Kingdom period of Egypt. The tombs contained a wealth of artifacts that helped us learn more about the lives of the ancient Egyptians who were buried there.

In addition to these new discoveries, magnetometry has also been used to study the layout and construction of already-known archaeological sites in Egypt. In 2018, a team of archaeologists used magnetometry to survey the area around the pyramids of Giza. This led to the discovery of several structures that were previously unknown, including a cemetery for the workers who built the pyramids.

Another example is in Luxor, Egypt. Researchers using magnetometry have found a hidden extension of the Karnak temple. They believe that the temple contains buried sections on its northern and eastern sides.

title: A Political Scientist
text:
A political scientist is someone who thinks about how a government works. This year, you have learned many things about the United States government. You have learned that the United States is a constitutional republic made up of three branches that share power equally. This means people elect leaders who represent them in the government. The purpose of the United States government is to protect citizens' rights and promote the common good. The government works because it receives the power to act from its citizens.

The values of our nation are defined in legal, political, and historical documents. Documents written during our nation’s history are visible outcomes of rules and laws. They protect citizens' rights. Our country’s important documents include the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, and the Declaration of Independence.

title: LiDAR in Central America
text:
LiDAR is a remote sensing technology that uses lasers to create detailed maps of the surface of the Earth. It works by emitting pulses of laser light and measuring the time it takes for them to bounce back. This information is used to create a high-resolution 3D map of the terrain. LiDAR is currently being used by archaeologists to uncover hidden Maya ruins.

The Maya people built thousands of elaborate temples, pyramids, and other structures. When the civilization collapsed, they were abandoned. Now, they are overgrown by the jungle, making them difficult to locate and study. One of the key advantages of LiDAR is its ability to penetrate dense vegetation, such as the jungle in Central America. Planes can fly above the trees and use LiIDAR to create detailed maps of the ground below. This has allowed archaeologists to identify many previously unknown Maya ruins, including entire cities.

One example of this is the Petén region of Guatemala, which was explored using LiDAR in 2016. Working with the data, researchers were able to create 3D models of the landscape in areas that would be extremely difficult to access by vehicle or on foot. The researchers used a series of filters to help them identify the features picked up by LiDAR. They then created detailed 3D maps that can help them understand the layout and function of the Maya cities, as well as how they were built and how they changed over time.

In the Petén region, over 50,000 structures were revealed with LiDAR, including temples, pyramids, and causeways, or raised roads. Many of the structures discovered were platforms for houses. This was a crucial new piece of information. Before the Petén LiDAR project, experts thought that during the Mayan Classical period, about 1–2 million people lived in the central lowlands. Based on the new data, experts think the area may have had up to 11 million people.

title: Virtual Reality in Copán
text:
Virtual reality is opening up new and exciting ways for researchers to study the ancient Maya civilization. VR (virtual reality) technology is being used to explore the ancient ruins of Copán, located in what is now Honduras. This site was once the center of a powerful Maya kingdom. It is known for its impressive ruins and intricate sculptures.

LiDAR images have allowed scientists to create detailed 3D models of the site. Combining 3D mapping with VR technology allows archaeologists to explore the site virtually. Wearing a VR headset, they immerse themselves in the ruins of Copán. This gives them a better sense of the scale and complexity of the site. They can also interact with the ruins in ways that would not be possible in real life, such as by walking through structures that have since collapsed.

One of the key benefits of using VR to explore Copán is that it allows researchers to study the site without having to physically be there. This is particularly important because of the challenges of working at the actual site. Copán is located in a remote area. VR allows researchers to return again and again to the virtual site. This gives researchers the time they need to make more precise and accurate observations. They don’t have to travel, worry about the weather or the time of day, or get insect bites.

Another advantage of using VR to explore Copán is that archaeologists can share their findings with a wider audience. With VR, people who are not able to travel to Copán can still experience the site and learn about its history and significance. This is helping more people take interest in the site, which raises awareness about the importance of preserving ancient ruins like Copán. It also helps to prevent damage to the site while still making it accessible to researchers and the public.

title: New Technology at Poverty Point
text:
The Poverty Point Mounds are a series of earthworks built by an ancient culture in what is now northeastern Louisiana. In recent years, technology has given us new insights into the mounds and the people who built them. The previous maps and images of the area were made by tracing aerial photography, photographs usually taken from a plane. Now, archaeologists are using ground-penetrating radar, LiDAR, and other sophisticated surveying techniques. Lasers have produced more precise, detailed measurements. Radar has found objects we can’t see with our eyes.

New maps and models made with this technology show that the mounds are not symmetrical. This led researchers to change their belief that the Indigenous people had a master plan for the mounds before they began building. Another surprising discovery made using technology is a complex network of large wooden poles and posts under the mounds and under the plaza. Today, these posts are buried under dirt and completely invisible at the ground level, but long ago, they must have been a visible and central part of life at Poverty Point. Although we don’t know their exact purpose, this discovery is evidence of advanced engineering. It even suggests that the mounds were part of a much more complex settlement than researchers realized before.

Traditional archaeological excavation is a time-consuming task. Magnetometers and ground-penetrating radars speed things up, but collecting and interpreting the data can still take time. As technology advances and improves, larger areas can be studied more easily, and results are quicker. Most importantly, the new tools allow us to explore using methods that don’t destroy the site and often don’t even disturb the land. Digging into the ground can cause damage to the site and its structures. If not done carefully, it can destroy artifacts and structures. Excavation can cause environmental damage to the site and disturb the local ecosystem. New technology is playing an important role in protecting and preserving archaeological finds.

title: Luminescence in the Arabian Desert
text:
Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) is a dating technique that can be used to determine the age of sediment or artifacts found at a dig site. It measures the amount of light given off by an object. This light emission is known as luminescence.

This is how it works. Minerals can store energy from the environment around them. Sunlight allows all of this energy to escape. When minerals are buried, the energy builds up over time. To find the age of an artifact, scientists place a sample into a machine called a luminescence reader. The machine shines a special light on the sample. The energy from the sample is released as luminescence. The amount of luminescence is measured and used to calculate how long ago the minerals were last exposed to sunlight, or in other words, how long the artifact has been buried.

OSL dating is a useful tool for dating samples that are hundreds of thousands of years old. It was used to date the oldest known human remains in Australia. It is also being used to date sediment along the banks of the Yellow River in China. Recently, OSL dating led researchers to change their estimates and dates for human migration out of Africa. Using OSL, the researchers found that stone artifacts uncovered in the Arabian desert are about 106,000 years old. That means that humans left Africa much earlier than we previously thought. The research also showed that they probably left in many waves of migration, not just one large event.

title: Underwater Marvels in the Mediterranean
text:
Sunken Cities

Ocean robots, also known as autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), are used to explore the depths of the ocean. These robots are able to navigate in environments that are difficult for humans. Archaeologists used AUVs to explore the lost city of Thonis-Heracleion which was discovered off the coast of Egypt. This city was once a major port and center of trade in the ancient world, but it had disappeared completely under the Mediterranean Sea and was buried by layers of sand and silt for over 1,200 years. A team of underwater archaeologists found the remains and, with the help of sonar, ocean robots, and giant underwater vacuum hoses, rescued many artifacts.

Archaeologists had to depend on modern technology to explore the underwater site. The waters are murky, and it is hard to see anything, especially after storms when the water is all mixed up with floating sand and mud. Ocean robots explored the city and collected data to create detailed 3D maps of the city. The biggest items pulled from the waters were the giant statues, over 16 feet tall, of a king and queen. The large objects were the easiest to locate in the murky waters, but smaller items were also found, including goblets, figurines, and coins.

Ancient Shipwrecks

AUVs can give researchers detailed 3D maps of the seafloor and anything on it, such as a submerged ship. The data can even be used to show how the shipwreck might have occurred.

The Antikythera shipwreck was discovered off the coast of the island of Antikythera. It is a Greek trading ship from over 2,000 years ago. The most famous artifact from the wreck was a mechanism with a system of gears and dials that were used to track the movements of the sun, moon, and planets.

The artifacts recovered from the Antikythera wreck make it one of the most important finds in modern archaeology. But despite that, the wreck site has remained largely unexplored. This is mostly because the wreck is too deep for SCUBA divers and too shallow to use a human-occupied submersible. The site is also near steep underwater cliffs, and the wreck lies at an angle that makes it hard for an AUV to access.

Underwater Suits
Recently, archaeologists have been testing what may be the next big thing in underwater archaeology. The exosuit is a wearable, full-body diving suit that is designed to help divers work in deeper waters and for longer periods of time than they would be able to with regular diving gear. The suit has a life support system that provides the diver with a supply of air. It allows the diver to move freely and perform a variety of tasks underwater. It allows divers to be 1,000 feet down underwater for up to 50 hours. This makes it an ideal tool to safely explore shipwrecks and other submerged sites in greater detail. The exosuit is being used to help uncover more secrets from the Antikythera shipwreck.

title: The Research Process
text:
Use the compelling question "What causes people to change where they live?" or create one of your own. Follow the inquiry process:

Ask a compelling question.

What do I want to know about this?

What do I already know? / What evidence do I already have?

What else do I need to find out?

Make a claim.

What is a possible answer?

What supporting question will help me focus my research?

Search for answers. / Experiment.

What kinds of resources will help me find answers?

Where can I find the resources?

How do I know the information is credible?

Interpret the information.

How does this information relate to my compelling question?

Which parts help answer my question?

Which parts do not support

my question?

Does it create other questions?

Present your conclusions.

Summarize my information. / What is the main idea?

What is the answer to my compelling question?

Does it support my claim or not?

title: Framing Question Week 32
text: How does practicing the research process help you learn?

title: Make a Claim
text:
What is your initial claim to your compelling question?

Compelling question:

title: Present a Counterclaim
text:
During the research process, we create claims, but a good research project looks at multiple perspectives. As a researcher, you should look for any claim from an opposite or contrasting viewpoint. This is called a counterclaim. Take a look at the evidence you’ve gathered and find an idea or argument that contrasts with your claim. This is part of the reflection process. Then use your evidence to argue against that claim. Presenting a counterclaim showing you know what someone else might say about your topic, can make your claim stronger and your evidence clearer.

Present a counterclaim!

While some researchers say … I claim …

It’s easy to think … but when you look at the facts …

Others may say that … but I argue …

A common argument against this position is … but …

title: Identify the Right Evidence
text:
Conduct a close read for each source, and take notes (annotate). Then, think about what connections you can make between your sources (corroborate). What do you notice about your sources? What connections can you make?

Corroboration

What other evidence do you need to support your claim? What is missing?

title: Present Your Conclusions
text:
What is the answer to your compelling question? Does it support your hypothesis or not? Summarize the information. How will you present your conclusion?

What is the main idea? What is the supporting evidence?

If your compelling question is a problem, what solution do you recommend? Write it down!

What is your counterclaim? Write it down. Does this change your claim?

How are you going to use the knowledge you gained from your research?

title: Enduring Changes
text:
European exploration dramatically changed the world in many ways. First, the Columbian Exchange changed the way that people lived on every continent. These changes affected the economies, political structures, and cultures of many people. One example of cultural change can be seen in the cuisine of every continent. Corn is native to the Americas, but it traveled to Africa and became a staple crop for many groups of people there. Rice is native to Asia, but can you imagine Mexican or Brazilian food without rice? Tomatoes are native to the Americas, but can you imagine Italian food without them? Traditional dishes and many other aspects of culture changed everywhere as plants, food, animals, ideas, and technologies were exchanged between Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

The most significant changes came to the Americas. Disease, colonization, the plantation system, and the slave trade changed the demographics, or population structure, of the Americas. Disease decimated the Indigenous population in the Americas. Many people died. Colonization brought settlers, mostly of European descent to the Americas in search of land, riches, and opportunities that they could not find in Europe.

As settlers came to the Americas, they also brought their ideas. A large group of Spanish settlers were Roman Catholic missionaries, priests, and friars. They were motivated to spread their religion and convert the Indigenous people of the Americas. Christianity would affect the culture, economics, and government of the Americas.

Colonization also brought changes to the American economy. The encomienda system and the plantation system used native people as enslaved laborers. In addition to dying of disease, Indigenous people also died in the harsh environment of the encomienda and plantation systems. The transatlantic slave trade would grow to support these systems. Enslaved Africans were sold and forced to work in the Americas.

title: Week 30 Framing Question
text: How did the colonization of the Americas lead to the mission system, the encomienda system, and the transatlantic slave trade?

title: Spanish Colonization
text:
The first Spanish colonists were mostly men. They came to the colonies to be conquistadors, hoping to gain land and wealth by conquest. The first Spanish settlements were on an island that Columbus named Hispañola. This Island is located in the Caribbean and is the home of the modern-day countries of Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The native people from the island were called the Taíno, and they called their island home Quisqueya.

Because the Taíno were the first Indigenous Americans to have Europeans live in constant, close proximity, they suffered terribly from the diseases that the Spanish brought. The first Spanish colonists also forced the Taíno people to work for them in the encomienda system. Spanish writer Bartolomé de las Casas lived in Hispañola in the first wave of colonization. He estimated that 80–90 percent of the Taíno people died within the first 50 years of Spanish colonization.

Early Spanish colonization focused on the areas of major conquest: the Caribbean, the Aztec Empire, and the Inca Empire. The Caribbean islands that were conquered by the Spanish were often called the West Indies because Columbus mistakenly thought he had reached islands on the outskirts of India. The former Aztec Empire was called New Spain by the Spanish conquistadors. The Spanish would call the area of the Inca Empire Peru. This name most likely came into being when the Spanish misunderstood a Quechua word.

During much of the Spanish colonial period, only men migrated to the area. They often had relationships with and married native women. Because of these relationships, the population of the Spanish colonies grew to be mostly people of mixed Spanish and Indigenous heritage.

The Spanish colonies would eventually extend into Florida and the Southwestern portion of the modern-day United States. Spanish colonies also spread throughout all of Central America and everywhere in South America, except for Brazil. The Portuguese claimed Brazil as their own colony.

title: Encomienda System
text:
Many types of labor systems existed in the Spanish colonies. The first and most devastating was called the encomienda system. To understand the encomienda system, it must first be understood that when the conquistadors arrived in the Americas, they claimed all the land for their king and queen. Because of this, the Spanish believed that all the land in the Americas belonged to their kingdom.

In the encomienda system, the Spanish crown would give a portion of land to a specific person. This land was usually given as a reward to a conquistador, a nobleman, or a military leader. According to Spanish law, this person now owned the land, and it was called an encomienda. The person who owned the encomienda was also in charge of all of the people living on the land. This included any Indigenous people who had lived and worked on the land for hundreds or even thousands of years. Many encomienda owners used the native people as free laborers because they believed that was their right to do so as the encomienda owner.

A missionary named Bartolomé de las Casas lobbied the Spanish crown and wrote a book advocating for the end of the encomienda system. He believed that the native people were being used unfairly. He gave evidence that the native people were dying because of the encomienda. He won his case against the encomienda system, and the system was ended. However, it was replaced with other economic systems, called the repartimiento and the hacienda.

The repartimiento is often associated with mining precious metals. Although the Spanish conquistadors did not find gold in the Americas, they did find silver. There were many silver mines in the Spanish colonies, but the two most productive were Zacatecas and Potosí. According to the repartimiento, the overseers of the mine could force Indigenous people to work in the mine for a period of time.

In the hacienda system, the labor of Indigenous people was not regulated by a single encomienda owner but by the crown itself. The crown still required native people to work, often for free. The hacienda system was usually a large agricultural estate. Similar to the plantation, the hacienda focused on producing cash crops. Maize, wheat, and sugar were all items produced in the Spanish hacienda system. Labor was obtained through many means: forced labor, slavery, debt bondage, and sometimes wage labor. However, all labor was regulated by the crown.

title: Christianity: Mission System
text:
One of the groups that came to the Spanish colonies was Christian missionaries. Their goal was to convert the Indigenous population of the Americas. One way that missionaries tried to convert native people was by building missions. Missions focused on converting, educating, and eventually transforming the natives’ way of life to follow European, Christian standards. A group in the Catholic church known as the Franciscans was largely responsible for the missions.

Missions were more than buildings. They included land for ranching and farming, running water, and a forest to provide wood for building, cooking, and heating. Around each mission, the Spanish built presidios or armed settlements. So, in addition to being places of work and worship, they were also meant to be Spanish strongholds on the colonial frontier.

Many Native Americans were forced to relocate to missions. At the missions, they were educated but also forced to work. If they tried to leave, they were forcibly brought back. Because of the mission system, many native cultures were completely lost. Many lives were lost as well because of their close, constant contact with Europeans and their diseases.

Missions stretched across North America and even into South America. Florida saw the first North American missions in 1573. Dozens more were built along the coastlines and remained until the English began moving into Florida. After El Paso was established, a mission was built to convert the Manso and other local tribes. Eventually, missions spread north into New Mexico.

In California, Franciscan friar Junípero Serra was asked to start missions for two purposes. One was to baptize American Indians into the Catholic faith. The other was to have a permanent Spanish presence in California to keep the Russians from claiming it. Eventually, California was home to 21 missions. The first mission in California was San Diego de Alcala, and that is where we get the name of the city San Diego. Santa Barbara, Santa Cruz, San Jose, Santa Clara, and San Francisco de Asis all shared their names with the cities that were built around them.

The Spanish sought to convert the native people of Central and South America, too. Jesuit missions were built in Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Bolivia in the early 17th century.

title: Sugar
text:
After the Crusades, Europe began trading with Asia for sugar. People in Europe loved the taste of sugar and paid high prices for it. Sugar is produced from sugarcane. Sugarcane needs a warm environment to grow. It also needs lots of rain or good irrigation. Europe did not have the right climate to grow sugar, so they had to trade for it.

This changed when Portugal claimed islands off the coast of Africa. These islands included the Azores and Madeira. They had a suitable climate for growing sugarcane. Beginning in 1445, the Azores rapidly filled with colonists. They developed a rich sugar-producing colony. The sugar was exported to European markets. The Portuguese also established trading posts along the west coast of Africa.

These trading posts were to trade Portuguese goods with African traders. Men, women, and children were captured by the African traders and sold to the Portuguese as enslaved people. The enslaved captives were taken to sugar plantations on the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

When European explorers came to the Americas, they also found a warm, wet climate where sugar could grow. Sugarcane grew especially well on islands in the Caribbean Sea. European colonists realized sugar could become a cash crop. A cash crop is a crop people grow to sell and make money rather than to use it themselves. This led to large areas of land being used to grow only one kind of cash crop. These large farms became known as plantations.

It took hard work to grow and harvest sugarcane. Sugarcane doesn’t produce seeds. Someone had to cut hard stalks into pieces by hand and then plant them. It was also difficult to get soft sugar out of the tough stalks. During a harvest, sugar had to be extracted and processed very quickly; otherwise, it would go rancid. Sugar mills ran 24 hours a day during the sugar harvest.

Plantation owners looked for ways to get free labor to plant, harvest, and process the sugar. They began enslaving the Indigenous people of those lands, taking away their freedom and forcing them to do the work. When many of the native people died from diseases or risked punishment to escape, plantation owners turned to the slave trade from Africa. Enslaved Africans were sold to plantation owners and forced to work in harsh conditions without pay or freedom. In Europe, sugar became easier to buy as the supply increased. European plantation owners became very wealthy at the expense of enslaved people.

title: The Transatlantic Slave Trade
text:
Many colonies in the Americas produced cash crops like sugar and tobacco. Growing these crops was hard work. From the 1500s to the 1800s, most of this work was done by enslaved men, women, and children. They were forced to work without being allowed to choose where or how to live. The majority of enslaved people were brought to the Americas from Africa in what is known as the transatlantic slave trade. This trade was facilitated by Portuguese traders who had established trading posts along the coast of Africa.

Ships that crossed the Atlantic almost always came from Europe. Most didn’t sail straight from Europe to the Americas, though, because there was less cargo from Europe to sell in America than cargo from America to sell in Europe. Ship owners could make more money if the ships stopped in Africa first. This voyage from Europe to Africa was called the Outward Passage. Ships carried tools, weapons, and cloth to Africa. Merchants and soldiers would pressure African leaders to trade those goods for people who had been captured in wars or kidnapped. The first recorded ship carrying 200 enslaved African people sailed to the Caribbean in 1525. They were sold into a lifetime of slavery, to work on sugar plantations.

People had been enslaved in Europe and Africa before, but this slave trade was different. People who were enslaved in Europe or Africa might be treated as equals; they might be freed, or they might even escape and be able to return home. For people sent to the Americas, there was almost no chance of equality, freedom, or escape. Over three centuries, millions of enslaved people from Africa were brought by ship to the Americas. The voyage from Africa to the Americas was called the Middle Passage. The conditions of the Middle Passage were horrific.

When ships reached the Americas, enslaved people were inspected as property and sold at auction. If a person had any friends or family on the ship, they were often separated. Enslaved people might be able to stay in one place after arrival, but they might also be sold and separated from family members and friends again and again. Some enslaved people managed to escape and live among the native peoples of the Americas or other places where they could be free. Most did not escape.

title: Life of an Enslaved Person
text:
Life among enslaved people varied from person to person. However, they did share some common experiences. Most enslaved people were from different tribes or parts of Africa. They could not communicate with each other, especially after just arriving in the Americas. Plantation owners also did not want enslaved people to learn to speak a common language because they did not want them to speak out against slavery. Information about the slave trade mostly comes from ship and court records, but a few people who had been enslaved learned to speak, read, and write in European languages. Some of them wrote their stories.

Olaudah Equiano was just 11 years old when he was enslaved in what is now Nigeria. He wrote about his experiences and the experiences of the enslaved people he knew. About his own experience arriving in the Americas, Equiano said:

I now totally lost the small remains of comfort I had enjoyed in conversing with my countrymen; the women too, who used to wash and take care of me, were all gone different ways, and I never saw one of them afterwards.… I was a few weeks weeding grass, and gathering stones in a plantation; and at last all my companions were distributed different ways, and only myself was left. I was now exceedingly miserable, and thought myself worse off than any of the rest of my companions.… I had no person to speak to that I could understand. In this state I was constantly grieving and pining, and wishing for death rather than any thing else.

The life of an enslaved person was full of work, hardship, and turmoil. For example, enslaved people who worked on a sugar plantation worked almost 24 hours a day during harvest. Since the climate that sugar was grown in had a constant growing season, harvest amounted to about half of the year. Harvesting and processing sugar was hard and dangerous work. The sugarcane had to be cut, crushed, boiled, purified, and separated into white and brown sugar. After harvest, they still worked long hours, without freedom or reward. This is just some of the work that an enslaved person might do.

People have always looked up at the night sky and wondered what was out there. The theories are endless. Even today, you will hear about aliens and spacecraft. title: Connections to the Past
text:
As you read about ancient civilizations this year, you’ve been told how important it is to learn about the past. Still, there might have been times when you thought it didn’t have much to do with your life today. But if you look closely, you can see that in many ways, the past really is your present. How? Let’s take a quick look at your day.

As you start out your day, do you check to see what time it is? The idea of dividing the day into smaller units of time, such as hours and minutes, started with the ancient people of Mesopotamia. Do you know what day of the week it is? Well, think of the people of Mesopotamia again. They established a seven-day week, and then the ancient Romans named the days.

How did you get to school today? The earliest known wheels were invented by the ancient Sumerians and later adopted by the ancient Egyptians, who used them on chariots. How about the streets you travel to get to school? The people in the ancient Indus Valley were the first to use a city plan of laying out streets and lanes in a grid to make them easier to navigate.

At school, do you use paper and books? The ancient Chinese invented paper by pressing a wet pulp into thin sheets. This method has been refined but is still used today. The Chinese also used wood blocks and ink to invent a form of printing that was used to make the first books.

How about your lunch? Corn and beans were first domesticated in Mesoamerica, and the ancient people of India were the first to refine sugar. Did you wash your hands with soap? The ancient Phoenicians invented the original bar of soap, using goat fat and wood ash. Is music an important part of your day? The ancient Greeks developed a system that uses letters and symbols to represent musical notes. This system was added to by the Romans to show rhythm and tempo.

Where do you go during recess? The ancient Romans were among the first to use concrete. Do you play sports and games? A game played by kicking a leather ball through an opening in a net was popular during the Han dynasty and is considered to be the oldest known ball game in the world.

After school, do you spend time on your phone or computer? Wait a minute! Modern devices can't be connected to ancient times, can they? Actually, many historians trace computer technology back to a mechanical calculator developed by the ancient Greeks more than 2,000 years ago. Even with the many advances in technology since then, the basic principles of computation that were developed by these civilizations continue to be used in modern computers. Making connections between the past and the present can help you better understand both the world you live in now and the events and experiences that have shaped it.
