title: Vocational and Trade Schools
text:
In 1970, the Pennsylvania legislature passed House Bill 1942. Funding for trade schools and classes was made available through this bill. Students could take shop classes at public school. These classes focused on things like woodworking, auto mechanics, or welding. Students could also take home economics classes in school. These classes focused on areas like cooking, sewing, and child care. After graduating high school, students could expand their learning. They could attend higher education vocational schools.

A vocational school is a school where people learn how to do a job that requires specialized skills. At vocational schools, students can get specific training in auto mechanics, agriculture, technology, welding, construction, and more. These types of schools offer an opportunity for a student to specialize in one area. In some cases, they offer certification programs if that might be required in an industry. Some of Pennsylvania's fastest-growing industries are manufacturing, technology, and agriculture. Vocational schools are an important support to those growing industries.

Today, Pennsylvania has an initiative called PAsmart. PAsmart helps students and workers develop skills necessary for success in a modern economy. The program focuses on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

title: Political Leaders of Pennsylvania
text:
In the United States, the military is controlled by the civilian, elected representatives of the people. It is the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives that provide supplies and funds for the military. The generals of the U.S. Army are also appointed by the Congress. The president of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the military. This means that the military follows the directions of the elected government and does not operate independently. The following men were active in the government during the Civil War. Through their leadership and service, they assisted the military in preserving the union and emancipating enslaved people.

James Buchanan

Born and raised in Pennsylvania, James Buchanan served five terms in the U.S. House of Representatives. He then served in the Senate for 10 years. He was elected the 15th president of the United States in 1856. Much of his presidency was spent trying to prevent a civil war from breaking out between the North and the South.

Buchanan was opposed to secession. He believed that the government could find compromises to make everyone happy. Unfortunately, he was unsuccessful in preventing war. Within one month after he left office, South Carolina seceded from the Union. The Civil War began.

Andrew Gregg Curtin

Andrew Curtin is best remembered for his role as Pennsylvania’s governor during the Civil War. Curtin was a fierce supporter of the Union. He supported them even when many felt the war was going poorly for the North. To boost morale, Curtin organized a conference for northern state governors. It was called "The Loyal War Governors' Conference." There, he gave speeches and encouraged other northern governors and state leaders to support the war effort and Lincoln's administration.

Curtin further supported the war effort by making resources from Pennsylvania available to the Union army. After the war, he set up a system of schools for children who were orphaned by the war.

Simon Cameron

Simon Cameron was a successful newspaperman. He invested in many different businesses, including railroads. This wealth brought him influence in government. Cameron was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1845 to fill the vacancy, or empty seat, of the new president, James Buchanan. Cameron was one of the first supporters of the new Republican political party in 1860. Cameron spent time campaigning for the new Republican presidential candidate, Abraham Lincoln. It was Cameron’s influence that helped Lincoln win the Pennsylvania votes. Lincoln appointed Cameron secretary of war in his new administration. Political rivals accused Cameron of being dishonest with government funds. Cameron was replaced as secretary of war. Cameron went on to serve in government in other ways. In 1867, Cameron returned to the Senate, representing Pennsylvania for another 10 years.

Thaddeus Stevens

After graduating from Dartmouth College, Thaddeus Stevens moved to Pennsylvania to practice law. As a lawyer, he represented diverse clients, including many members of minority groups. Stevens worked to establish equality for all people. He became an active abolitionist and advocated against slavery.

In 1848, Stevens was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. Stevens became a founder of the Republican party. During the Civil War, Stevens worked with President Lincoln to support the military, save the union, and emancipate all enslaved people.

In 1865, the 13th Amendment, abolishing slavery, was proposed in the House of Representatives. Stevens worked tirelessly to get the votes to send the amendment to the Senate. The 13th Amendment was approved and ratified in 1865.

Stevens also worked to draft the 14th and 15th Amendments to ensure that formerly enslaved people would become citizens and could vote.

title: Union Military Leaders from Pennsylvania
text:
Pennsylvania produced a number of Union military leaders during the Civil War. These men fought to preserve the Union and win freedom for all people to enjoy.

George Meade

George Meade is remembered as the general who led the Union army at the Battle of Gettysburg. Gettysburg was one of the bloodiest battles of the Civil War. Meade started his military career in the Civil War as a volunteer for the Union army. He led several divisions of soldiers in various battles. He was promoted to commander of the Army of the Potomac. This army met and fought against Confederate General Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. Meade led his army to a Union victory in the battle. He continued to command Union troops for the rest of the war. He helped secure the Confederate surrender that ended the Civil War.

John Frederick Hartranft

John Frederick Hartranft experienced failure as a leader early in his military career. Rather than give up, he learned from his mistakes. He found success commanding the 51st Pennsylvania Volunteers. When the soldiers of the 51st were reaching the end of their enlistments, Hartranft gave a speech that inspired many to reenlist and fight for the Union's cause. Hartranft fought in 23 battles. He was finally promoted to general in March 1865. After the war, Hantraft eventually became the governor of Pennsylvania. He served two terms in that office.

John Fulton Reynolds

John Fulton Reynolds trained and led troops in many battles and conflicts throughout his military career. Before the Civil War, he was an instructor at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. After the war began, Reynolds served in the Union army as a military governor. He was a commander of several different divisions. At the Second Battle of Manassas, Reynolds led his men in a counterattack. It allowed the rest of the Union army to retreat. He also fought in the battle of Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville. While leading his men in the Battle of Gettysburg, Reynolds was killed in action on the battlefield.

James Addams Beaver

Before he entered military service, James Addams Beaver was a practicing lawyer in Pennsylvania. He entered the army in 1861, shortly after the Civil War broke out. Beaver's largest role during the Civil War was when he was assigned to command the 148th Regiment, Pennsylvania Volunteers. During his service with this unit, Beaver was wounded four times. One of these wounds led to the loss of his right leg. Beaver was transported home to recover from his wounds. In recognition of his service, President Lincoln promoted Beaver to brigadier general. Beaver was elected governor of Pennsylvania in 1886.

Strong Vincent

When the Civil War broke out, Strong Vincent enlisted to serve in the Union army. He joined on the same day he got married. Vincent believed that the Union was fighting for good reasons. In a letter to his young bride, he wrote: "If I fall, remember you have given your husband to the most righteous cause that ever widowed a woman." While fighting in the Battle of Gettysburg, Vincent was charged with holding the Union line at a strategic point known as Little Round Top. Vincent fought with his men. He held the Union position at Little Round Top but was wounded in the battle. Five days later, he died of his wound.

Montgomery Meigs

Montgomery Meigs was a master of order and organization. He used his skills during his long military career to feed, clothe, and house over a million soldiers. Meigs was known for combing through military budgets and supplies and eliminating wasteful expenses. He ensured that soldiers were provided for.

Meigs was very good with money. He was trusted with spending over a billion dollars from the public treasury to pay for military needs. He did not participate in much of the fighting during the Civil War. However, he helped to ensure that other leaders had what they needed to carry out their orders.

Meigs also oversaw the building of warehouses, officers' quarters, and cemeteries, including Arlington Cemetery. Thousands of Civil War soldiers were buried there. After the war, Meigs went on to oversee many public projects. These projects included the building of the Washington Aqueduct, the U.S. Capitol Building, and the Pension Building. Meigs left his mark on Washington, D.C., and our nation. He's remembered for the integrity and competency with which he fulfilled his responsibilities. He is also remembered for his contributions to the public buildings that we still use today.

Winfield Scott Hancock

Although he fought in some of the most intense battles of the Civil War, Winfield Scott Hancock is best remembered for his leadership during the Battle of Gettysburg. His leadership, tactics in battle, and courage earned him the respect of his men and the thanks of the U.S. Congress. He was wounded during the Battle of Gettysburg. He never fully recovered.

He continued to serve on the front lines, however, until the end of 1864. Complications from his wound forced him to leave the field. He took on work behind the lines until the end of the war. After the war, he continued to serve in various military assignments. His roles included overseeing the Reconstruction of the South. He was well-liked by the public. He even ran for president in 1880. Although he was not elected, Hancock spent the rest of his life serving as the commander of the Division of the Atlantic.

title: Copperheads
text:
During the Civil War, "Copperheads" were a group of Democrats from the North who were opposed to the war. The name was given to them by political opponents because of the copper coins they wore as badges to identify themselves. They were also called the "Peace Democrats."

Copperheads believed that war and bloodshed could be avoided through peaceful debate, diplomacy, and negotiation. They believed that violence was unnecessary. They criticized Abraham Lincoln and his policies.

They protested the war by participating in politics, resisting military drafts, and trying to persuade Union soldiers to desert. Some groups talked of violent resistance, but any plans that were made were either stopped or not carried out. Because of their anti-war stance, many Copperheads were suspected of being disloyal to the Union. Some were even accused of treason for their actions. Some Copperhead leaders were arrested and kept in military prisons for months at a time.

In politics, the Copperheads worked to get Lincoln and his cabinet removed from office. They tried to put a new president into power. The Copperheads organized a democratic convention in 1864. They chose George B. McClellan for their presidential candidate. This proved to be the undoing of their cause. McClellan denounced the peace platform they wanted him to use. Their influence was further weakened after bloody battles such as Gettysburg and Vicksburg. Eventually, the Copperhead party’s popularity declined until it died out altogether.

title: Confederate John C. Pemberton
text:
Not all Pennsylvanians chose to fight for the Union during the Civil War. Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton was born and raised in Pennsylvania. However, he made the decision to fight for the Confederates despite his northern roots.

Pemberton had married a woman from Virginia, one of the Confederate states. He also spent years of his military service in the southern states before the Civil War. Because of this, Pemberton grew to love the South. He felt loyal to it.

As a graduate of West Point Military Academy, Pemberton was highly valued. After the war began, he became a lieutenant general in the Confederate Army. He was assigned to hold the city of Vicksburg and the Mississippi River. Vicksburg was an important strategic site in the South. It helped control the Mississippi River. If the Union captured Vicksburg, it would cut the Confederate states in two. That would give the Union control of the river.

Pemberton did his utmost to defend the city. He had his men construct forts and earthworks around the main roads leading into Vicksburg. Canons and munitions were stationed along the earthworks to defend the city. For nearly two months, Pemberton and his men withstood the assaults of the Union army led by General Grant. They were able to maintain Confederate control of Vicksburg. However, after 47 days under siege, Pemberton was forced to surrender to General Grant.

After this defeat, Pemberton resigned his commission as lieutenant general. Instead, he chose to serve as a lieutenant colonel of artillery until the end of the war.

title: Confederate Josiah Gorgas
text:
Born in Pennsylvania and raised in New York state, Josiah Gorgas grew up and attended West Point Military Academy. He graduated sixth in his class of 52. He spent the next 20 years serving in various military positions in the North and South.

While serving in Mobile, Alabama, he met and then married the daughter of a former Alabama governor. This relationship and the family ties that came with it had an influence on Gorgas's politics and values. He became very loyal to the South.

Gorgas had been frustrated and dissatisfied with his military career for years. When the Civil War started, he quickly resigned his commission from the U.S. Army. He offered his services to the Confederate army. It was not an easy decision. He became permanently estranged from his own family in Pennsylvania.

His first position with the Confederacy was chief of ordnance. His first task involved keeping Confederate troops supplied with weapons and munitions. Gorgas took an inventory of the small arms and cannons available to southern soldiers. He found their supplies woefully lacking. Many of the cannons were very old or unusable. The army needed weapons, but the South was a heavily agricultural society. Factories and manufacturing were very limited. To address this problem, Gorgas began importing goods from Europe.

However, this was not sustainable. Gorgas worked to build factories and increase the South's capacity to produce their own weapons and munitions. He created other programs to arm soldiers. Those included mining for materials; melting down existing metals, such as church bells and plows; and searching old battlefields for weapons and munitions. The weapons they found could be repaired and used. Although Confederate soldiers were poorly supplied with food and adequate clothing, they were well-supplied with muskets, powder, and ammunition.

After the war, Gorgas invested in producing goods made of iron. He purchased the Brierfield Iron Works. He ran the ironworks for a couple of years before financial problems forced him to sell it. For the remainder of his life, he worked at the University of the South in Tennessee and the University of Alabama.

title: Women from Pennsylvania During the Civil War
text:
Although only a few made it to the front lines, women also played important roles during the Civil War. Women sewed and knitted clothing for soldiers to wear. They mailed goods to soldiers. Women also ran farms and businesses while the men were away fighting.

Mary Hazlehurst Ashhurst
Mary Hazlehurst Ashhurst made an important contribution simply by writing down her everyday experiences during the war. Thanks to people like her, we have primary accounts of what life was like during the Civil War.

Ashhurst lived in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, during the war. She described her fears of the Confederates invading Philadelphia. She wrote a detailed account of the Battle of Gettysburg, as reported in the newspapers.

Anna Maria Ross
Born and raised in Philadelphia, Anna Maria Ross volunteered as a nurse when the Civil War started. She was put in charge of the Cooper Shop Hospital. It was built beside the Cooper Shop Volunteer Refreshment Saloon. The saloon was one of Philadelphia's busiest stops for soldiers. They could stop by, rest, and get something to eat or drink on their travels.

The hospital provided medical care for wounded soldiers. Ross served as the lady principal. She managed the nursing staff in addition to working shifts, day and night, to care for patients. Ross became known as “the Soldier’s Friend.”

In addition to caring for soldiers in the hospital, Ross also created a fundraiser to pay for a "Soldier's Home" for Civil War veterans. She went door to door collecting donations, which she used to help open the Soldier's Home.

Mary Morris Husband
Mary Morris Husband was 35 when the Civil War began. She was married and had two sons. When both of her sons decided to enlist and fight for the Union, Husband decided to support the cause as well. She offered her services as a nurse. She began volunteering in a Philadelphia hospital sometime between 1861 and 1862. She dressed wounds, made beds, cooked meals, and helped make wounded soldiers more comfortable.

Husband spent about a year at the hospital before she decided to start working for hospital transports. They treated and transported wounded soldiers from the battlefield. She became Lady Superintendent of one of the transports that moved to and from New York. Husband was so well-liked that many soldiers called her "mother."

Husband traveled wherever she was needed. She went from hospitals to army divisions to army camps. She treated soldiers from the bloody battles of Antietam, Chancellorsville, and Gettysburg. She spent the rest of the war traveling with hospital transport divisions and providing care wherever she was needed.

title: Essential Question
text: How does industry influence communities?

title: Essential Question
text: How can people spend or save money they earn?

title: Types of Economic Activities
text:
Agriculture is the business of growing crops and raising animals. Fruits, vegetables, flowers, and cotton are agricultural products. Dairy farming and beekeeping are agricultural businesses. Natural resources are important to agriculture.

Manufacturing is using raw materials to make products or goods to sell. Cars, computers, and toys are all manufactured products.

Research and development is about creating new services or products. It can also be about improving existing services or products.

Healthcare is a service industry. It includes all the goods and services used to treat people who are sick.

Tourism is providing goods and services to travelers. Some places have tourist attractions based on unique physical characteristics in their area, such as oceans, mountains, and national parks. Other tourist attractions, like theme parks, are human-made. Tourism strengthens the economies of cities, states, and countries.

title: Entrepreneurs
text:
An entrepreneur is someone who comes up with an idea and then uses this idea to start a business. Entrepreneurs are people who have a vision about something new or helpful they can offer their community. They combine the natural, human, and capital resources in an area to produce goods and services. They make decisions about what to produce based on the needs and wants of people in their area.

Entrepreneurs have many reasons for wanting to start their own businesses. Some entrepreneurs want to build something of their own. Others feel they can make a lot of money working for themselves. Others have a solution to solve a problem. There are big opportunities and risks involved in being an entrepreneur. Successful entrepreneurs often have a great impact on their communities.

title: Entrepreneurs in My Community
text:
Find out about an entrepreneur. Answer the following research questions about them and their business.

How did they come up with the idea?

What were the needs or wants they were serving?

What is their reason for starting their own business?

What were the risks or difficulties they faced?

How did they find their market?

What influence have they had on their community?

title: The Road to Civil War
text:
The Constitution defined how the states interacted with the federal government. Each state had its own constitution and laws. The concept behind the United States was about the individual states working together “to form a more perfect union.”

Not all states were united on issues, however. Legalized slavery was always a topic of conflict. It existed in every colony and every state. Many people wanted to end slavery. Laws were passed in the northern states to abolish it. Others believed the economy needed enslaved people for labor. The conflict continued for decades. It was a conflict Congress tried to resolve through compromise and cooperation.

In 1820, 1850, and 1854, the federal government tried to legislate compromises to stop the enslavement of people. The laws limited the number of states that could have legalized slavery. Another law prohibited any talk of abolition in Congress. Eventually, Congress compromised. They let the people living in new states make the decision about abolition or slavery. None of the compromises were compatible with the founding idea that "all men are created equal."

The compromises failed, and so did the communication. The conflict escalated to physical violence. The states in the South felt all they could do was leave the Union. South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee seceded. To secede means to separate or break away. The 11 states formed a new government called the Confederate States of America.

The remaining states said the Union could not be dissolved or broken. To defend their beliefs, each side entered into war. This has been called the Civil War, the War to Preserve the Union, and the War between the North and the South. The term civil war is used when citizens of the same country fight each other.

Pennsylvania had been a leader in the abolition movement. Pennsylvania was one of the first states to raise militia to fight to preserve the Union. The industries of iron, lumber, coal, and railroads in Pennsylvania supported the military with supplies and materials. The people of Pennsylvania responded to the call to defend the Union. It had been founded in their own city of Philadelphia. Each community in Pennsylvania responded in some way to this terrible time in American history.

title: Essential Question
text: What contributions from Pennsylvania helped save the Union?

title: Military Response to Secession: Regiments in Pennsylvania
text:
After the surrender of Fort Sumter in April 1861, President Lincoln called for volunteers to defend the Union. Volunteers enlisted to serve and fight for the Union. After New York, Pennsylvania recruited the most soldiers in the Civil War. The state mustered, or assembled, more than 200 regiments. There were 215 infantry regiments and 22 cavalry regiments. Ten of the infantry regiments were composed of African Americans. There were also additional reserve and artillery regiments.

A regiment is a group of approximately 1,000 soldiers. Ten companies made up a regiment. A company was formed from men enlisting, or agreeing to fight for a set period of time. Men from the same communities were known to enlist together in the same companies. Many men brought their own equipment for cooking and a supply of food.

Following are some of the most notable regiments organized in the state.

42nd Regiment: The Bucktails
The 42nd Pennsylvania Volunteer Infantry were famously known as the Bucktails. They were called Bucktails for the buck, or deer, tails they wore in their caps. Recruitment for this regiment was done by Thomas L. Kane. Kane was an abolitionist, lawyer, and businessman from McKean County. Volunteers for the Bucktails were mostly mountain men. They were skilled marksmen. The Bucktails are remembered most for their actions at the Battles of Antietam and Gettysburg.

72nd Regiment: Baxter's Fire Zouaves
The 72nd Regiment was originally organized in Pennsylvania as the Third California Regiment. This regiment was part of the Philadelphia Brigade. They were known as the Zouaves for their uniforms. They wore blue baggy pants, short jackets with red trim, white gaiters, and a turban. This regiment was mustered by Edward D. Baker, a Congressman and friend of Lincoln. Most of the men recruited to this regiment were firefighters from Philadelphia. They were known for their physical feats of strength and acrobatics. The 72nd Zouaves fought in the Battle of Gettysburg. They defended against Pickett's Charge and marched in pursuit of General Lee afterward.

105th Regiment: The Wildcats
Amor McKnight, a lawyer from Brookville, Pennsylvania, organized the Wildcat Regiment. The name comes from the congressional district in Jefferson, Clearfield, and Clarion Counties. The men of the regiment came from this region. They organized in Pittsburgh before marching to Washington, D.C. The Wildcats supported the defenses in Washington, D.C. They also fought in the Battles of Gettysburg and Appomatox.

Every county in Pennsylvania erected a monument to the men who served in the Pennsylvania regiments. These monuments can still be seen today.

title: Phenomenon
text: Each American who uses a reusable water bottle can keep an average of 156 plastic bottles a year out of the land, ocean, and air.

title: The Loyal Governor's War Conference in Altoona
text:
In 1862, the governor of Pennsylvania, Andrew Gregg Curtin, decided to organize a war conference. Delegates from the loyal Union states met there. He selected the Logan House Hotel in Altoona to meet. Located in central Pennsylvania, it was a strategic choice. It was close to the Midwest and New England. The delegates could easily travel to Altoona via the Pennsylvania Railroad.

Gathering representatives from all the states that were loyal to the Union created a show of support. Thirteen governors and state delegates met Sept. 24–25, 1862. The talk at the conference was about the necessity and purpose of the war. At the end of the conference, each loyal state voted to support President Abraham Lincoln and his actions to save the Union.

And we pledge without hesitation, to the President of the United States, the most loyal and cordial support, hereafter, as heretofore, in the exercise of the functions of his great office.…

We hail with heartfelt gratitude and encouraged hope the proclamation of the President, issued on the twenty-second instant, declaring emancipated from their bondage all persons held to service or labor as [enslaved persons] in the rebel States …

Lincoln had proposed an emancipation of all enslaved people in the disloyal states. With the vote of support from the governors, the Emancipation Proclamation was signed on January 1, 1863. All enslaved people "shall be then … and forever free."

title: African Americans in the War
text:
At the beginning of the Civil War, many free Black people stepped forward to fight for the Union army. At first, many were turned away. Eventually the United States government recognized that more soldiers were needed. On January 1, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation. The proclamation established freedom for enslaved African Americans living in Confederate states. It also made it legal for African Americans to serve in the army.

Citizens of Philadelphia worked together with the government to recruit Black soldiers. The citizens and government of Pennsylvania eventually established Camp William Penn. Camp William Penn was the first camp created specifically to train Black soldiers. It was officially opened on June 26, 1863, in Cheltenham Township, Pennsylvania. Many Black soldiers rushed to sign up. Before the end of July, three regiments of Black soldiers had volunteered.

In total, 11 regiments of Black soldiers volunteered. They were trained in Camp William Penn. They were called the Third, Sixth, Eighth, 22nd, 24th, 25th, 32nd, 41st, 43rd, 45th, and 127th U.S. Colored Regiments. They made significant contributions in many battles of the Civil War.

There were also many Black women who worked for the military. They served as cooks, spies, nurses, laundresses, and scouts.

The many contributions of the African American population helped preserve the union. It also established their future involvement in the United States military.

title: A Soldier's Life
text:
Many soldiers fought and gave their lives during the Civil War. The soldiers' lives were hard. Using information from the following primary sources, discuss what life was like for soldiers during the Civil War.

Susie King Taylor, a Black woman who worked with one of the African American regiments
We had fresh beef once in a while, and we would have soup, and the vegetables they put in this soup were dried and pressed.… Salt beef was our stand-by. Sometimes the men would have what we called slap-jacks. This was flour, made into bread and spread thin on the bottom of the mess-pan to cook. Each man had one of them, with a pint of tea, for his supper, or a pint of tea and five or six hard-tack.

Captain James Wren, PA 48th
August 12, 1862
Camp Front of Fredericksburg
We left camp this evening at 6 PM. We started the march and continued it until 3 in the morning of the 13th and took no nap until 6 AM … started again on the march and marched all day until the evening of the 13th and put up for the night … resumed our march again at reveille, which was at 4 AM of the 14th and reached the railroad station at 11 AM of the 14th. During the night, it rained very, very heavy and having no tents, it was rather disagreeable.

Samuel R. Watkins, Company H, 1st Tennessee Infantry Regiment
A long line of box cars was drawn up at Camp Cheatham one morning in July, the bugle sounded to strike tents and to place everything on board the cars…. Every soldier had enough blankets, shirts, pants and old boots to last a year.… In addition, every one of us had his gun, cartridge-box, knapsack and three days rations, a pistol on each side and a long Bowie knife.… We got in and on top of the box cars, the whistle sounded, and amid the waving of hats, handkerchiefs and flags, we bid a long farewell … to old Camp Cheatham.”

... I cannot remember of ever experiencing a harder or more fatiguing march. It seemed that mountain was piled up mountain. No sooner would we arrive at a place that seemed to be the top than another view of a higher, and yet higher mountain would rise before us. From the foot to the top of the mountain the soldiers line the road, broken down and exhausted. First one blanket was thrown away, and then another; now and then a good pair of pants, old boots and shoes, Sunday hats, pistols and Bowie knives strewed the road. Old bottles, jugs and various and sundry articles were lying pell-mell everywhere.

title: Women in the Allegheny Arsenal
text:
The Civil War was a difficult time for everybody. It was especially difficult for poor families. With their fathers, husbands, brothers, and sons gone, many women struggled to provide for their families. They desperately needed work.

The Allegheny Arsenal was a supply and manufacturing center in Lawrenceville, Pennsylvania. During the war, the number of employees at the center increased from 300 to about 1,100. The workers made ammunition for the troops. The arsenal provided work for many women and young girls. Some were as young as 14. They worked for 12 hours a day, six days a week. Each working day, they made about 128,000 cartridges. The workers earned between 50 cents and $1.10 a day. It was a dangerous job because they worked with gunpowder, which is explosive. On September 17, 1862, there was an explosion at the arsenal. Seventy-eight people were killed, many of them women and young girls. The loss of life was tragic. The explosion indicated that more safety measures needed to be enforced to protect the workers.

title: Pennsylvania's Industrial Response to Civil War
text:
Pennsylvania has significant sources of raw materials. These natural resources were already being developed by industries before the Civil War. Being an established industrial center allowed Pennsylvania to make a vital contribution to the Union Army.

Lumber was used to make wagons, wheels, and boxes to transport goods and ammunition. Vast amounts of iron and steel were used in ships, trains, large artillery guns, and other machinery. Coal was used to power machines. Pennsylvania’s large industries had factories. They made products with these resources before the war began. There were large shipyards already building ships. There were other transportation systems, like railroads, waterways, and roads, set up to move the products.

Pennsylvania had a large number of smaller manufacturers too. They made different kinds of products across the state. They shifted quickly to support the war effort. They produced steel swords, rifles, pistols, tools, and camp implements. Some made tents, blankets, uniforms, and other items. Pennsylvania farmers also supplied significant quantities of flour, meat, and other foodstuffs for the troops.

All these factors meant that Pennsylvania was an essential economic support to the federal armies.

title: Role of Government in Economics
text:
The government's main economic role is to use money and funds to provide services to citizens. We use government goods and services every day. An example is the school you attend, if it's a public school. The road you took to school is another example. The government provides these goods and services. People who work pay a part of their income to the federal government in the form of taxes. When you buy something, you pay a little more than the price tag says. This is because you're also paying a small tax, called a sales tax. Sales tax helps the government provide goods and services to everyone.

Many of the goods and services the government provides are known as public services. An example of this is going to your community library. It doesn't cost you any money to borrow books or other materials from your local library. The government provides this public service to the community through money collected from taxes. Other public services provided by the government include the police, fire and water departments, parks, and public health departments.

Businesses people own are considered private enterprises. What are some private businesses in your area? Think about the restaurants, stores, and gas stations you visit.

title: Farm to Market
text:
The food grown on farms is transported to urban and suburban markets. The system of highways, seaports, and airports creates the routes from farm to market. Consumers purchase products from all over the world.

Producers send products all over the world. This great system, or network, of producers and consumers is called interdependence. Each depends on the other for success. Sometimes, this is also called a supply chain. We will be learning about interdependence using apples, a natural resource.

title: Essential Question
text: How are goods and services connected throughout communities?

title: Production: How Are Apples Grown?
text:
Some parts of the United States are very good for growing apples. Ohio is ranked ninth in apple production in the United States. Apples grow best in climates where winter is cold and summers are warm. To produce a good crop, most apple trees need about 1,000 hours of chilling time. Chilling time means the weather is above freezing but below 45 degrees Fahrenheit (45° F).

Apple trees grow in orchards, or land where fruit and nut trees grow. In order to plant an orchard, an apple producer needs plenty of open land with good soil. They also need access to lots of fresh water.

The apple producer cares for the trees. They make sure the trees stay healthy by getting enough water and sunlight. In spring, they also make sure the flowering apple trees are pollinated. Pollination is necessary for producing fruit. Bees are the best natural pollinators. Some apple orchards have their own beehives. Many apple producers rent hives from beekeepers.

In the United States, apples usually begin to ripen in July. Different types of apples become ripe at different times. People can harvest fresh apples throughout the fall. Producers often harvest apples by hand instead of using machines. The people who do the work of picking apples are human resources. Human resources refers to all the people who work for a company or organization.

title: Surplus
text: Surplus is when the supply of a good or service is more than the demand. For example, there could be more shorts in winter than people need or want. A surplus often makes prices go down. This is good for consumers. It is bad for producers. Producers can have a hard time making enough money when there is a surplus.

title: Scarcity
text: Scarcity is when there is more demand for something than there is a supply. It is not having enough of something people want or need. Scarcity usually makes prices go up. When goods and services become scarce, their cost increases. Families have to choose how to spend their money carefully. They have to decide what they need most. Sometimes scarcity can be a big problem. If food or water is scarce, it can be hard for people to live.

title: Supply and Demand
text:
The price of a good or service depends on two things. First, it depends on how much of the good there is for people to buy. That is called supply. Next, it depends on how many people want to buy it. That is called demand. When the supply is low and the demand is high, the price goes up. When the supply is high and the demand is low, the price goes down.

When the newest smartphones come out, many people want to buy them. There is a large demand. Prices are high. At clearance sales, stores want to get rid of products that have not sold. In this case, there is a larger supply. Stores lower the prices to try and increase demand and sell their products.

title: What Would Happen?
text:
Look at the information and images. Is this an example of scarcity or surplus? Is the demand high or low? What would happen to the price in this situation?

There has been bad weather in Ohio. The corn harvest was not good.

The store has lots of Easter candy in stock. Easter is over.

A famous singer is giving a concert in Cincinnati. She will only be there for one night. Everybody wants to go to the concert.

title: Supply and Demand in Ohio
text:
Snow can be a lot of fun. However, every winter in Ohio, there are snowstorms. A snowstorm is heavy snow with a lot of wind. A bad snowstorm can disrupt people’s lives. It can break the supply of goods and services.

Look at the list of situations that could happen after a snowstorm. Discuss what the economic impact might be for each situation. Think about demand, supply, surplus, and scarcity. For example, snowstorms bring a lot of snow. This could create a demand for snow shovels or snow blowers. The supply may not meet the demand.

Snowstorms cause a lot of snow to accumulate. Many snow plow drivers are needed to clear away the snow.

People who are traveling, especially by plane, often get stuck.

A storm can cause a lot of damage. It can be very difficult to find material and workers to do the repairs. Cleaning up and repairing damage can take a long time.

If the roads are bad, people can’t get to work. Trucks can’t deliver supplies, like groceries.

Farm livestock and produce can be lost.

Sometimes trees and power lines come down and homes and businesses lose electricity. Emergency services could be overloaded.

title: What is Cultural Diffusion?
text:
“Culture makes people understand each other better. And if they understand each other better ... it is easier to overcome economic and political barriers ... People have to understand that their neighbors are not different even if they have a different religion, or a different sociological background.” - Paulo Coelho

Culture is one way that people can share their values, beliefs, and origins. Culture is the common characteristics between a group of people that relate to a similar place of birth, including language, religion, food, art, music, literature, or social behaviors. Culture allows societies to be vibrant and broadens opportunities to enhance learning and understand history.

Cultures can spread. When people move, they take their culture with them. Cultures can change. Change happens when one culture meets another culture and they exchange ideas. Elements of two different cultures can even combine to create new traditions and customs.

Cultural diffusion is the spread of traditions, ideas, and items, like food, music, tools, and technologies, from one group to another. In early civilizations, cultural diffusion happened when different groups interacted through trade, migration, or conflict. When people traveled and interacted with others whose lives differed from their own, they learned about the ways of other people. Often, they would share or adopt these new traditions. As people traded outside of their own community, they learned about new skills and methods of making things. In ancient times, handicrafts, arts, and even styles of architecture passed from one society to another. Wars also created change. When one group conquered another, they would often force a new way of life on the people they defeated.

title: Comparing Western Hemisphere Cultures
text:
We can compare cultures by looking at the elements of culture and cultural diffusion. The environment and natural resources help to shape culture. History has also affected and shaped the cultures of different regions. The Western Hemisphere has many different cultures that have spread across the hemisphere. Indigenous communities had their own unique cultures when European settlers arrived in the Americas. As the Europeans from various countries came over, they, too, had their own unique cultures. As different cultures blended, they began to evolve into the cultures we are familiar with today.

People have come to the Western Hemisphere from other parts of the world. The world is constantly changing and intertwining on a global scale. Working to study and understand cultures allows people to work together as a community and learn about the diversity of the world.

The cultures of Indigenous people greatly influenced the cultures we know today. Indigenous ideas and values can be found in the art, music, and everyday lives of people everywhere. Many of the foods grown in the Americas were cultivated by ancient civilizations and have remained a part of the American diet. Even some holidays and festivals can be traced back to Indigenous traditions.

Since the arrival of the first settlers, millions more have migrated to the United States. They, too, have influenced our culture. People from Africa, Asia, and various parts of Europe have come, and all have contributed to the present culture. To this day, Scandinavian culture can be found in the names of towns all over the midwestern United States. There are French-speaking communities in New England and Louisiana. In the Southwestern states, we find examples of beautiful Spanish architecture.

People take pride in their cultures. The United States has many cultures that exist and blend together. This is one thing that makes our country such a unique and diverse place to live.

One way to compare cultures is by asking questions. For

example, what kinds of houses do people build? What languages do they speak? What festivals do they have? What is the most common food that people eat? Answers to these questions can tell us a lot about a culture and its people. This allows us to compare and contrast the similarities and differences.

title: Architecture
text:
Architecture also shows a range of cultural influences. Architecture and culture go hand in hand, it plays a part in the identity of the community and is the messenger of the environment, history, and economics. The environment of a region plays a crucial role in the culture of why and how architecture is built. Many European influences affected how architecture was constructed throughout many cities and towns in the Western Hemisphere.

Within North America, early colonial buildings in Virginia were built in a Georgian style. This style has brick walls and white wood. In Florida and the Southwest, stucco buildings with tile roofs show the influence of Spain. The “conch” style includes wrought-iron balconies. These are popular in New Orleans, Louisiana. A new architectural style in the southwestern United States and Mexico grew from two traditions. The Pueblo built homes of adobe. Adobe is made from clay bricks dried in the sun. The Pueblo homes also included wooden ceiling beams. The Spanish adopted this style for many buildings.

One style of home in Mexico is the hacienda. Haciendas are often built with stone and concrete. Haciendas have high ceilings, wide windows, and rounded archways. They also have open-air courtyards in the center. The courtyard in the center is often planted with trees and other flowers and greenery. These plants help cool the area and make the courtyard a lovely place. All these features help keep the house cool.

There is a lot of variety in Canadian architecture today. It is important for Canadian architecture to be able to handle the cold and snow. The roofs are often steep. This allows snow to slide off the roofs more easily. Smaller, cottage-style homes are also common, especially farther north. A smaller space is easier to keep warm in the cold. Often, traditional homes in Canada will have some type of cover over the front door to shield it from rain and snow. There are a lot of forests in Canada, so many homes are built and decorated with wood.

In marshy areas or areas close to the sea, flooding can occur. So some people build their homes on stilts or with a washout floor. In case of flooding, the water would flow under or through the lower level of their homes. The main rooms they live in would not be flooded.

Traditions of ancient Greece and Rome also have had an impact on architecture. The columns and carvings of ancient buildings gave rise to a style called the federal style. This is the preferred style for government buildings in Washington, D.C., and state capitals. It is also often used for government buildings in Latin America.

title: Arts
text:
Born in 1907 in Mexico to a German father and mother of Spanish and Mexican descent, Frida Kahlo had a unique cultural heritage that would influence the artwork she would become so famous for. When she was 18 years old, Frida was in a terrible bus accident that caused her many injuries. While bedridden for three months, Frida took up painting while she recovered. Her mother bought her a special easel and set up a mirror above her bed so she could see herself and paint self-portraits. She was inspired by the styles of several Renaissance artists. Frida embraced her Mexican heritage, which manifested itself in her artwork. Her paintings were deeply expressive and portrayed a unique view of her life and mixed cultural identity.

She also suffered many health ailments and pain from her injuries throughout her life. Many of her paintings reflected the physical and emotional pain she experienced. Frida traveled to America and France in her lifetime, where her artwork was displayed and sold at exhibitions. She died at 47 of health complications. The legacy of her artwork and her life has grown since her death, and she stands today as one of the greatest artists in the Western Hemisphere.

Have you ever heard of the painter and TV sensation, Bob Ross? He was a very popular American artist back in the 80s and 90s. Surprisingly enough, he didn’t get into painting until later in his life. For the first 20 years of his life, he served in the military. It was actually while he was in the army that he really discovered his love of painting after attending a painting class. At first, he painted for pleasure and as a way to make extra money. But when he started making more money from painting than from the army, he decided to leave the service and devote all of his time to painting. Bob Ross eventually started a TV show in 1983 called The Joy of Painting. The show ran for 11 years, and it reached millions of viewers all over the world. Viewers loved Bob’s cheerful attitude and intimate approach to addressing his audience. His frequent use of phrases like “happy little trees” endeared him to his fans. Although Bob died of lymphoma in 1995, the influence of his joyful approach to painting is still seen in popular media, even today.

title: Music
text:
Jazz is a style of music. It started developing in the early 1900s in African American communities and southern cities of the U.S. Jazz really became popular with both African American and white audiences in the 1920s and 1930s. It combines the styles of African and European music to create something unique and American. Jazz is easy to recognize by its rhythms, improvised (made-up) melodies, and unusual harmonies. Famous African American jazz musicians include Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Ella Fitzgerald, Charlie Parker, Wynton Marsalis, and Sarah Vaughan. Research one or more of these famous musicians and learn how they developed their musical techniques. Or, search for a jazz station on your local radio or on the internet.

Born to poor, working-class parents in Mississippi, Elvis Presley grew up in a religious setting. The southern gospel choir at the church he attended was one of the earliest influences on his musical style, as well as the blues clubs he frequented in his youth. Elvis pursued a music career early in his life and gained public attention with his controversial dancing style and his mixing of African American and white music styles. It wasn’t just his mixing of different cultural styles that drew attention to his music, though. Elvis wasn’t afraid to be himself and create a style all his own. In addition to changing the face of American pop culture as we knew it, he also opened the door and paved the way for rock ‘n’ roll as we know it today, which earned him the title of “The King of Rock ‘n’ Roll” or simply “The King.” In addition to his music, Elvis also acted in numerous Hollywood films in his lifetime, which added to his fame and popularity. Although he died young at 42 from heart failure, The King remains a legend and lives on as an example of one who truly lived the American dream.

title: North American Food
text:
Food is an important element of culture. In most places, what people eat is based on what is around them. People who live near the ocean tend to eat more fish than people living inland. The climate also dictates what grows well. This explains why people in different parts of the world eat differently. People in Asia eat a lot of rice and fish, for example. Europeans eat more wheat and potatoes. People in different parts of the world also flavor their foods with different spices.

The foods found in North America come from all over the world. They were introduced by early European settlers, American Indians, and immigrants from other countries. These food dishes can generally fall into six different categories: Native American foods, hybrid dishes, ethnic blends, regional specialties, generic traditions, and manufactured goods.

Native American foods had a variety of different types of vegetables, grains, mammals, nuts, and fish. This came based on each tribe's region, religious observances, cooking techniques, and customs. The “Three Sisters,” maize (corn), squash, and beans, were the primary ingredients in the Indigenous population’s diet.

Hybrid dishes were based on European recipes using the ingredients that can be found throughout North America. An example of this would be cornbread.

Ethnic blend food was created by different cultures settling together in one region and creating a dish with a mix of foods.

Regional specialties look at the variety of North American regions and the type of dishes that each region focuses on.

Generic traditional foods and manufactured goods can be linked back to European recipes and foods. These foods are mass-produced for stores. Examples of this are canned tomato soup or different boxed pastas.

Many of the food groups and diverse dishes that come out of North America revolve around the mixing of cultures and the appreciation for different foods in different regions.

title: South American Food
text:
Jean Francois Revel once wrote, “There is no history of cuisine that is not also a history of prevailing appetite, habits, and taste.” What could he have meant when we wrote this quote?

Revel went around the world reading and studying cookbooks. This gave him insight into the daily lives of people and their cultures through their food.

The different regions of South America bring different flavors to their cuisine. The Amazon basin area has a variety of fresh fish and tropical fruits. The many areas on the coast of the Pacific Ocean have seafood as their main dishes, such as king crab, lobster, or tuna. These areas create a dish called ceviche, which is taking raw fish and curing or marinating it in citrus juices, such as lemon or lime, and adding spices to the mixture.

Many countries, such as Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela, have resource-rich areas where they can grow quinoa, beans, and rice and raise cattle and sheep. Shredded beef is served across the continent in a variety of different food options, such as arepas or empanadas. Peruvian cuisine focuses on their traditional Incan culture by making churrasco, which is grilling meat in the open air.

Many countries within the Andes mountain range have staple foods that have created historical, economic, cultural, and nutritional importance for those countries. Peruvian farmers have harvested about 3,000 types of potatoes, making Peru the original home for the potato. Potatoes are considered a must-have staple food within South American countries, due to their nutritional success. Potatoes are also cold resistant; this is due to the cold climate within the Andes Mountains and potatoes being grown under the ground. There are different types of ways that potatoes are classified based on the way that the potato is cooked. Ch’iri papa is a popular way that cooks use a more bitter potato; cooks will take the potato, leave it outside overnight to freeze, and then fill it with cheese and steam it in the morning.

A delicacy, and one of the oldest traditions in Venezuela, is the dish called a “hallaca,” pronounced as “ah-ya-ka.” This dish is a showcase of many cultures that came together. Many of the ingredients can be traced back to Europe, such as raisins, nuts, and olives, along with the native ingredient of corn meal and the African ingredient of smoked plantain leaves used for the wrapping.

Historically, at Christmas time, wealthy families in Venezuela and other South American countries prepared large meals and banquets. Their leftovers were sent to the enslaved people to eat. The enslaved people wrapped the leftovers in cornmeal and cooked them in the plantain leaves around their homes. The modern-day hallaca is made of meat (pork, chicken, or beef), olives, raisins, a stewed mix of different vegetables, and placed into a smoked plantain leaf. They are then left in the fridge or freezer overnight. Hallacas require organization and planning, as they take many days to prepare and usually involve the whole family to help make. Each hallaca is different, and each one can taste different based on how it is made and which region it was made in.

South American cuisine has a rich history based on the regions throughout the continent, along with cultural customs that date back to when the Europeans first came to South America.

title: What Is Data?
text:
Experts in a wide variety of jobs and professions use data to understand what they are studying. They also use data to help others understand their research. Data is information gathered from different sources to support a claim. Any type of information that can be analyzed, including facts, numbers, observations, and measurements, is considered data.

Geographers, historians, archaeologists, political scientists, and economists analyze data to understand what they are researching. They also create data so others can understand their research. Much of what they want to know can be measured. Those measurements can then be used to infer or gather information about the world and its inhabitants.

Data helps provide specific information about geography, such as patterns and trends in the use of water in an area. Geographers can then use the patterns and trends to draw conclusions about the subjects they study. Geographers use other types of data to study the world by creating and analyzing maps, looking at statistics, and examining the collected information.

Historians use data to understand the past. Historians gather information from primary sources, including letters, newspapers, government documents, diaries, interviews, oral histories, and other credible resources, to obtain data about people, places, and events that they are researching. Historians use data they obtain from sources to support claims they develop during their research. They often publish this data so others can learn about the topics they have researched.

An archaeologist studies things left behind by people who lived a long time ago. Some objects, called artifacts, get covered by earth or water for thousands of years. Archaeologists often recognize patterns. They may see differences between earlier objects and later, more advanced ones. They may find evidence of trade by tracking the movement of similar artifacts.

Like geographers, historians, and archaeologists, political scientists also use data. They use reliable data to understand the actions of the government, study elections, and help community leaders make laws for their people. Economists study the relationship between resources and production in a community, state, or country. They use data to make claims about the economy to help people make financial choices.

Geographers use many tools to understand the data that they gather. These include different types of charts and graphs.

A line plot shows the increase or decrease of something over time. Data is displayed as a set of data points, called markers. Markers on a line plot are connected by a continuous line.

A circle graph is another method of displaying information. A circle graph is round. It represents the total number of things counted. The slices show parts of the total. The larger the slice, the greater the number. The smaller the slice, the smaller the number.

title: Types of Data
text:
Archaeological Data

Archaeologists use different types of data to learn about people, places, and events. Archaeologists primarily use material data in their research. Material data includes artifacts and physical items found during excavations, including jewelry, pottery, tools, weapons, clothing, building materials, and human and animal remains. They also use soil samples to determine when and how a site was formed, different materials buried at the site, and how the site was buried.

Archaeologists use data and evidence called “features” to reconstruct the past. The term “features” refers to evidence of activity that cannot be transported to another place, like an artifact. Features include structural remains of buildings, holes dug for specific purposes, earthworks or mounds, irrigation canals, soil stains, and burned soil.

Time-series data is collected after multiple observations or during multiple periods of time. It can also include multiple subjects that are observed.

Economic Data

Economists use two main types of data, called cross-sectional data and time series data. Cross-sectional data is collected when economists collect observations on a single economic organization or a single period of time. An example of cross-sectional data that an economist may use or collect is information about the income of people in a given area. An economist may also use data to research the output of businesses in a specific year.

Geographic Data

Geographers gather data in a variety of ways. When studying the physical world, they may rely on remote sensing technologies like global positioning systems (GPS) to gather data. Gathering physical samples also falls under this category. Gathering data when studying human geography can include statistics like population data or resource usage. However, it can also include information like surveying or observing people. Geographers use other types of data to study the world by creating and analyzing maps, looking at statistics, and examining the collected information.

Historical Data

Historians use different types of data to understand the past. They obtain data from many different types of primary sources. One of the most valuable types of data that historians use is census data. A census is an official count of the population in an area. The census also includes different demographics of a population, including age, gender, race, ethnicity, occupation, and education level.

Political Data

Political scientists use different types of data when researching the actions of the government, studying elections, and helping community leaders make laws for their people. The most common form of data used by political scientists is public opinion polls and surveys. A public opinion poll is a survey designed to measure the views of the public on a specific topic or group of topics.

title: The U.S. Census
text:
One tool that helps people chart population growth and decline in the United States is the census. The U.S. census is the count of how many people live in the United States. It is conducted every 10 years. A list of questions called a “survey” is sent to every home. If the survey isn’t returned, a census worker visits the home. The worker helps the people living there to fill out the survey. The survey asks who is living at the address. It also asks for important information about the people, such as their age and what they do for work.

The U.S. Constitution requires a census. The House of Representatives is based on the number of people in a district or region. Regions grow or shrink in population. This causes the number of representatives to be adjusted. Census information is made public. People can use census details in many ways. Businesses can determine if they should expand or downsize. Social scientists can use the information to learn about people and communities. Individuals can use census data to find ancestors and family members. Population information is available from every census since 1790. The data is considered a primary source for research.

title: Age of Encounters
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa. Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He believed he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.”

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures and became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they learned on the voyage, other explorers followed. Columbus opened a new door of adventure. Many followed and shared their new knowledge.

Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America,” a Latin version of Amerigo, in honor of this claim.

1. Christopher Columbus

Spain paid Christopher Columbus to sail across the Atlantic in 1492. Columbus hoped to reach India by sailing west. Instead, his ships landed in the Caribbean. There, Columbus met the Taíno people. Columbus’s voyage increased Europe’s interest in exploration and led to many other voyages and colonies.

2. John Cabot

Learning from Columbus, John Cabot became interested in finding a shorter route across the ocean. England sponsored Cabot to sail through the North Atlantic in 1497. Cabot thought he had landed in Asia, but it was actually what is now Canada. His voyage proved a northern route to the Americas could work. He met the Eastern Woodland Native Peoples.

3. Jacques Cartier

France hoped to find a northwest passage to reach the Pacific Ocean through North America. In 1534, France paid for Jacques Cartier to search. Cartier sailed up rivers in what is now Canada. He didn’t find a route to the Pacific, but he did meet the Mi’kmaq people and the powerful Iroquois Confederacy. Cartier’s trips started French trade in North America.

4. Samuel de Champlain

In 1609, Samuel de Champlain explored the northeastern part of North America and brought settlers to Quebec, Canada. Quebec is one of the oldest cities of European origin in Canada and is still one of the largest cities by population in the country. Champlain traded furs with the Huron tribe and allied with them against the Iroquois. He sailed through the Great Lakes and discovered Lake Champlain. Champlain was also a gifted cartographer and writer. The maps he created and the chronicles of his travels were studied and used by other explorers in North America.

5. Rene-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle

In 1682, Rene-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle sailed the length of a waterway that cut through the center of North America. This waterway was the Mississippi River. He claimed the territory along the Mississippi River for France and named it Louisiana after King Louis XIV of France. He also explored the Great Lakes. La Salle established trading posts along the Mississippi River. As a result of his efforts, France became very wealthy through the fur trade in North America.

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
The people of the Americas met their wants and needs using resources from the land around them. They had vibrant societies and extensive trade networks. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had different forms of government and religion. They fed their families by hunting animals and gathering berries, nuts, and fruits. They cultivated crops of corn, squash, beans, tomatoes, potatoes, and some grains. They created tools from the resources around them. They traveled by walking or using boats on the waterways.

The Europeans used natural resources to create manufactured goods. Like American Indians, they also had vibrant societies and extensive trade networks. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had their own forms of government and religion. They fed their families by farming and going to markets. The Europeans domesticated animals to keep on their farms. This meant they didn’t have to hunt for food. They had horses to help with the work on farms and at the markets. They cultivated grain crops of wheat, oats, and barley. The Europeans developed different modes of transportation. They used wagons and carts on land and ships on the sea. They manufactured goods out of metal and wood. They used many of their resources to help them explore new places across the ocean.

When these two societies met, there were intentional and unintentional consequences. The two groups traded ideas for the design of tools and transportation. The Europeans brought domesticated animals, such as pigs, chickens, and horses, with them on their ships. The people of the Americas gave them plants, food, and precious metals. Sign language and gestures were used to help the two cultures communicate with each other.

Tolerance of differences between the two cultures could have expanded the positive exchanges. However, the Europeans were not tolerant of the differences they encountered. They believed the peoples of the Americas were inferior because their ways were different. Intolerance caused conflict and the captivity and deaths of many Indigenous people.

The introduction of domesticated animals in the Americas caused imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation had nothing to eat.

The horse was a new animal to the Americas. The horse quickly became popular, and the people of the Americas began using them in their everyday lives. They used horses for transportation and work. Horses became a valuable trade resource. The horses quickly multiplied. Descendents of these horses are still found on the east coast and in the western lands of the United States.

The most deadly exchange was unintentional. The Europeans brought diseases with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. The people of the Americas had never been exposed to such deadly germs. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of disease were easily transported by unsuspecting people. Historians estimate that disease killed 90 percent of the native population within 150 years.
