Rich deposits of iron ore are found in Pennsylvania. Iron ore is a mineral. It is similar to a rock. Iron ore can be mined and processed to create goods. Iron ore needs to be processed. To do that, small chunks of iron ore are placed in a special oven called a furnace. Furnaces use fuel called "coke". Coke is made from coal. It burns at a high temperature. The iron ore melts in the furnace. It makes a molten, or hot, liquid. The molten iron can be poured into molds. This type of iron is known as “pig iron.” Pig iron can be melted, or fired, again. When it's melted again, it can be placed into larger molds for fencing, pipes, or rods.

Pig iron was used by blacksmiths. A blacksmith is a person who makes and repairs objects out of iron. The pig iron would be heated in a fire until red hot. Then, the hot iron would be shaped. Blacksmiths use hammers to shape it. They pound the hot iron on anvils. Blacksmiths shaped iron for wagon wheels, hinges for doors, horse shoes, tools for farmers, and more.

Iron furnaces were built across Pennsylvania. Places with an iron furnace often included the word “forge” or “furnace” in their name. Some of these places include Valley Forge, Greenwood Furnace, Hopewell Furnace, Helen Furnace, and Old Furnace.

Pig iron was brittle. That means it could crack and break. It couldn’t be made into large iron pieces. Through innovation, a new process was created to strengthen the finished iron. Small amounts of limestone were added to the coke and ore mixture. The limestone helped to burn impurities, or non-ore material, from the iron. This created stronger iron. The stronger iron could be used for larger objects.

Creating Steel
In 1856, Henry Bessemer discovered that piping oxygen into the furnace increased the temperature. The high temperature burned more impurities out of the ore. This process created a strong iron called steel. The Bessemer process made steel that was stronger and unbreakable. The steel could be formed into large beams or long, squared pieces. Steel was used to create the frame or structure of buildings. These buildings could be taller and larger than buildings framed with wood. Steel beams could be used to make bridges over wide rivers. Construction in America increased with the use of steel.

As construction increased, more steel was needed. Steel production had to increase too. Larger furnaces were built. When many furnaces were built in one location, it became known as a steel mill. Many workers were needed to run the mills. Immigrants from Europe came to fill the positions.

Open hearth furnaces were used to make large quantities of steel. Open hearth furnaces had openings for the fire at floor level. They were open in order to add fuel. It would take six hours to melt the iron and remove the impurities. In 1900, there were 16 open hearth furnaces at the Homestead Steel Mill in Pittsburgh. The furnaces heated the iron ore to nearly 3000 degrees Fahrenheit. Each furnace would create 40 tons of molten steel every six hours.

Change in America
Pittsburgh, Sharon, Johnstown, and Bethlehem all had steel mills. Because of the steel industry, other businesses grew too. There were many jobs available in many businesses. This caused even more immigration from Europe. The increase in immigration created more demand for housing, food, and supplies.

During World War II, the steel industry created supplies and materials for the military. Tanks, vehicles, ships, and equipment were made from Pennsylvania steel. This supply helped achieve victory for the Allies.

Steel was key to changing America’s way of living, doing business, and using natural resources. All of it was centered in Pennsylvania.

title: Primary Source: "Conservation as a National Duty"
text:
On May 13, 1908 President Theodore Roosevelt gave this speech at a governor’s conference about the conservation of natural resources. He advocated for the country to preserve its natural resources. The image is from a report of the governor’s conference. The text is in the public domain and excerpts from the speech are contained below the image.

Governors of the several States; and Gentlemen:

…This Conference on the conservation of natural resources is in effect a meeting of the representatives of all the people of the United States called to consider the weightiest problem now before the Nation; and the occasion for the meeting lies in the fact that the natural resources of our country are in danger of exhaustion if we permit the old wasteful methods of exploiting them longer to continue.

With the rise of peoples from savagery to civilization, and with the consequent growth in the extent and variety of the needs of the average man, there comes a steadily increasing growth of the amount demanded by this average man from the actual resources of the country. And yet, rather curiously, at the same time that there comes that increase in what the average man demands from the resources, he is apt to grow to lose the sense of his dependence upon nature. He lives in big cities. He deals in industries that do not bring him in close touch with nature. He does not realize the demands he is making upon nature. For instance, he finds, as he has found before in many parts of this country, that it is cheaper to build his house of concrete than of wood, learning in this way only that he has allowed the woods to become exhausted. That is happening, as you know, in parts of this country at this very time.

…peoples generally, concern themselves only with superficial natural resources; with those which they obtain from the actual surface of the ground. As peoples become a little less primitive, their industries, although in a rude manner, are extended to resources below the surface; then, with what we call civilization and the extension of knowledge, more resources come into use, industries are multiplied, and foresight begins to become a necessary and prominent factor in life. Crops are cultivated; animals are domesticated; and metals are mastered.

We can not do any of these things without foresight, and we can not, when the nation becomes fully civilized and very rich, continue to be civilized and rich unless the nation shows more foresight than we are showing at this moment as a nation. [Applause]

Every step of the progress of mankind is marked by the discovery and use of natural resources previously unused. Without such progressive knowledge and utilization of natural resources population could not grow, nor industries multiply, nor the hidden wealth of the earth be developed for the benefit of mankind.

…Since the days when the Constitution was adopted, steam and electricity have revolutionized the industrial world. Nowhere has the revolution been so great as in our own country. The discovery and utilization of mineral fuels and alloys have given us the lead over all other nations in the production of steel. The discovery and utilization of coal and iron have given us our railways, and have led to such industrial development as has never before been seen. The vast wealth of lumber in our forests, the riches of our soils and mines, the discovery of gold and mineral oils, combined with the efficiency of our transportation, have made the conditions of our life unparalleled in comfort and convenience.

…We can, moreover, add enormous tracts of the most valuable possible agricultural land to the national domain by irrigation in the arid and semi-arid regions, and by drainage of great tracts of swamp land in the humid regions. We can enormously increase our transportation facilities by the canalization of our rivers so as to complete a great system of waterways on the Pacific, Atlantic, and Gulf coasts and in the Mississippi Valley, from the Great Plains to the Alleghenies, and from the northern lakes to the mouth of the mighty Father of Waters. But all these various uses of our natural resources are so closely connected that they should be coordinated, and should be treated as part of one coherent plan and not in haphazard and piecemeal fashion.

It is largely because of this that I appointed the Waterways Commission last year, and that I sought to perpetuate its work. There are members of the coordinate branch present. The reason this meeting takes place is because we had that waterways commission last year. I had to prosecute the work by myself. I have asked Congress to pass a bill giving some small sum of money for the perpetuation of that Commission. If Congress does not act, I will perpetuate the Commission anyway, [Great applause] but of course it is a great deal better that Congress should act; [Applause] it enables the work to be more effectively done. I hope there will be action. But the Commission will go ahead.

…I wish to take this opportunity to express in heartiest fashion my acknowledgment to all the members of the Commission. At great personal sacrifice of time and effort they have rendered a service to the public for which we can not be too grateful. Especial credit is due to the initiative, the energy, the devotion to duty, and the farsightedness of Gifford Pinchot, [Great applause] to whom we owe so much of the progress we have already made in handling this matter of the coordination and conservation of natural resources. If it had not been for him this convention neither would nor could have been called.

We are coming to recognize as never before the right of the Nation to guard its own future in the essential matter of natural resources. In the past we have admitted the right of the individual to injure the future of the Republic for his own present profit. In fact there has been a good deal of a demand for unrestricted individualism, for the right of the individual to injure the future of all of us for his own temporary and immediate profit. The time has come for a change. As a people we have the right and the duty, second to none other but the right and duty of obeying the moral law, of requiring and doing justice, to protect ourselves and our children against the wasteful development of our natural resources, whether that waste is caused by the actual destruction of such resources or by making them impossible of development hereafter.

…So this Nation as a whole should earnestly desire and strive to leave to the next generation the national honor unstained and the national resources unexhausted. There are signs that both the Nation and the States are waking to a realization of this great truth–On March 10, 1908, the Supreme Court of Maine rendered an exceedingly important judicial decision. This opinion was rendered in response to questions as to the right of the Legislature to restrict the cutting of trees on private land for the prevention of droughts and floods, the preservation of the natural water supply, and the prevention of the erosion of such lands, and the consequent filling up of rivers, ponds, and lakes. The forests and water power of Maine constitute the larger part of her wealth and form the basis of her industrial life, and the question submitted by the Maine Senate to the Supreme Court and the answer of the Supreme Court alike bear testimony to the wisdom of the people of Maine, and clearly define a policy of conservation of natural resources, the adoption of which is of vital importance not merely to Maine but to the whole country. [Applause]

Such a policy will preserve soil, forests, water power as a heritage for the children and the children’s children of the men and women of this generation; for any enactment that provides for the wise utilization of the forests, whether in public or private ownership, and for the conservation of the water resources of the country, must necessarily be legislation that will promote both private and public welfare; for flood prevention, water-power development, preservation of the soil, and improvement of navigable rivers are all promoted by such a policy of forest conservation.

…This public interest is omnipresent wherever there is a State, and grows more pressing as population grows.

…Finally, let us remember that the conservation of our natural resources, though the gravest problem of today, is yet but part of another and greater problem to which this Nation is not yet awake, but to which it will awake in time, and with which it must hereafter grapple if it is to live–the problem of national efficiency, the patriotic duty of insuring the safety and continuance of the Nation. [Applause.] When the People of the United States consciously undertake to raise themselves as citizens, and the Nation and the States in their several spheres, to the highest pitch of excellence in private, State, and national life, and to do this because it is the first of all the duties of true patriotism, then and not till then the future of this Nation, in quality and in time, will be assured. [Great applause]

title: Primary Source: "I Have a Dream"
text:
During 1963, more than 250,000 people marched on Washington for jobs and freedom. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his now-famous speech, “I Have a Dream” at the end of the March on Washington. The image is a picture of Dr. King giving his speech at the Lincoln Memorial. Excerpts from Dr. King’s “I Have a Dream” speech follow the image.

...Now is the time to make real the promises of democracy. Now is the time to rise from the dark and desolate valley of segregation to the sunlit path of racial justice. Now is the time to lift our nation from the quick sands of racial injustice to the solid rock of brotherhood. Now is the time to make justice a reality for all of God's children.

...No, no, we are not satisfied, and we will not be satisfied until justice rolls down like waters, and righteousness like a mighty stream.

I am not unmindful that some of you have come here out of great trials and tribulations. Some of you have come fresh from narrow jail cells. Some of you have come from areas where your quest for freedom left you battered by the storms of persecution and staggered by the winds of police brutality. You have been the veterans of creative suffering. Continue to work with the faith that unearned suffering is redemptive. Go back to Mississippi, go back to Alabama, go back to South Carolina, go back to Georgia, go back to Louisiana, go back to the slums and ghettos of our Northern cities, knowing that somehow this situation can and will be changed.

Let us not wallow in the valley of despair, I say to you today, my friends.

So even though we face the difficulties of today and tomorrow, I still have a dream. It is a dream deeply rooted in the American dream. I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.

I have a dream that one day on the red hills of Georgia, the sons of former slaves and the sons of former slave owners will be able to sit down together at the table of brotherhood.

I have a dream that one day even the state of Mississippi, a state sweltering with the heat of injustice, sweltering with the heat of oppression will be transformed into an oasis of freedom and justice.

I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream today.

I have a dream that one day down in Alabama with its vicious racists, with its governor having his lips dripping with the words of interposition and nullification, one day right down in Alabama little Black boys and Black girls will be able to join hands with little white boys and white girls as sisters and brothers. I have a dream today.

I have a dream that one day every valley shall be exalted, every hill and mountain shall be made low, the rough places will be made plain, and the crooked places will be made straight, and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.

This is our hope. This is the faith that I go back to the South with. With this faith, we will be able to hew out of the mountain of despair a stone of hope. With this faith we will be able to transform the jangling discords of our nation into a beautiful symphony of brotherhood. With this faith we will be able to work together, to pray together, to struggle together, to go to jail together, to stand up for freedom together, knowing that we will be free one day.

This will be the day when all of God's children will be able to sing with new meaning: My country, 'tis of thee, sweet land of liberty, of thee I sing. Land where my fathers died, land of the pilgrims' pride, from every mountainside, let freedom ring.

And if America is to be a great nation, this must become true. And so let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York. Let freedom ring from the heightening Alleghenies of Pennsylvania. Let freedom ring from the snowcapped Rockies of Colorado. Let freedom ring from the curvaceous slopes of California. But not only that, let freedom ring from Stone Mountain of Georgia. Let freedom ring from Lookout Mountain of Tennessee. Let freedom ring from every hill and molehill of Mississippi. From every mountainside, let freedom ring.

And when this happens, and when we allow freedom ring, when we let it ring from every village and every hamlet, from every state and every city, we will be able to speed up that day when all of God's children, Black men and white men, Jews and Gentiles, Protestants and Catholics, will be able to join hands and sing in the words of the old...spiritual: Free at last. Free at last. Thank God almighty, we are free at last.

title: Life in the Steel Mills
text:
In Carnegie's Homestead Steel Mill in Pittsburgh, there were 16 open-hearth furnaces. The furnaces would heat the iron ore to nearly 3000 degrees Fahrenheit. This extreme heat would burn off the impurities of the iron ore. This would create 40 tons of molten steel every six hours. The men worked in 12-hour shifts.

Hamlin Garland, a reporter for McClure's Magazine, a popular magazine in 1894, wrote this about the sights and sounds of the steel mill:

“We entered the yard through the fence ... We were in the yard of the ‘finished beams.’ On every side lay thousands of tons of iron.

"Farther on was heard the crashing thunder of falling iron plates, the hoarse coughing of great engines, and the hissing of steam. Suddenly through the gloom I caught sight of the mighty up-soaring of saffron [orange-yellow] and sapphire [blue] flame, which marked the draft of the furnace of the Bessemer steel plant far down toward the water. It was a magnificent contrast to the dusky purple of the great smoky roofs below. The great building which we entered first was a beam mill, ‘One of the finest in the world’, my guide said. It was an immense shed, open at the sides, and filled with a mixed and intricate mass of huge machinery. On every side tumultuous [loud, intense] action seemed to make every inch of ground dangerous. Savage little engines went rattly about among piles of great beams. Dimly on my left were huge engines, moving with thunderous pounding ...

"I was looking at this beautiful light when my guide pulled me suddenly behind some shelter. The furious scream of a saw broke forth—a saw that melted its way through a beam of solid iron with deafening outcry, producing a gigantic glowing wheel of spattering sparks of golden fire. While it lasted, all else was hid from sight. ‘That's the saw which cuts the beams of iron into lengths as ordered,’ my guide said, and we hurried past.

"Everywhere in this pandemoniac [wild and disorderly] shed was the thunder of reversing engines, the crash of falling iron, the rumbling growl of rollers, the howl of horrible saws, the deafening hiss of escaping steam, the wild vague shouts of workmen ...

"We moved toward the mouths of the pits, where a group of men stood with long shovels and bars in their hands. They were touched with orange light, which rose out of the pits. The pits looked like wells or cisterns of white-hot metal. The men signaled a boy, and the huge covers, which hung on wheels, were moved to allow them to peer in at the metal. They threw up their elbows before their eyes, to shield their faces from the heat, while they studied the ingots [blocks of metal shaped like a brick] within.

" 'How long do you work ?' I asked of a young man who stood at the furnace near me. 'Twelve hours,' he replied. 'I go on at six and off at six.'

“ 'For how much pay?'

" 'Two dollars and a quarter [a day, 19 cents an hour, $500 a year].'

" 'Most of the men get under two dollars per day.'

" 'And it is twelve hours' work without stop?'

" 'You bet!' ”

title: Conflict in the Mills
text:
The Homestead Steel Mill in Pittsburgh was a high-producing mill in 1892. It was owned by Andrew Carnegie. He had hired Henry C. Frick to manage the operations. Frick was also in charge of sales. Under Frick, management sought higher profits. That meant they needed to sell the product for more than it cost to produce.

Inside the mill, conditions for many of the workers were dangerous. Shifts were 12 hours long. During that time, workers were exposed to intense heat from the open-hearth furnaces. Those who worked in dangerous conditions were usually given higher wages than those in safer areas.

To get better conditions, the workers created a union. Representatives from the union would negotiate with Frick and his management team. The union was called the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers.

In June 1892, Frick cut the wages of the workers in the Homestead Mill. Carnegie had given him the authority to do it. The workers decided to strike. That meant they stopped working in protest to management’s actions. On June 29, Frick closed the mill. He locked out 3,800 workers. Frick then hired other workers to replace the ones on strike. On July 1, The strikers seized the mill. They prevented entry to the new workers.

Frick said that the mill was private property belonging to Carnegie. The workers had no legal right to prevent entry into the mill. Frick called on law enforcement to disperse or break up the crowd of strikers. Law enforcement was stopped by the group of striking workers.

Frick then hired a private security company. It was called the Pinkerton National Detective Agency. The Pinkertons had previously broken up strikes in coal mines. On July 6, 1892, 300 armed Pinkerton guards and the striking workers had a violent confrontation. It lasted more than 10 hours. The confrontation resulted in injuries and deaths.

At the request of Frick, 8,500 National Guard forces came to Homestead. They gained control of the mill. The strike was over. Frick said, “Under no circumstances will we have any further dealing with the Amalgamated Association as an organization. This is final.”

In 1892, the Carnegie Steel company made $4.5 million in profit.

The steel mills had no union organization for almost 40 years until after World War I.

title: Essential Question
text: What are ways businesses influence change in communities?

title: Andrew Carnegie
text:
Andrew Carnegie was born in 1835. As a child, he came to America from Scotland. He began working with telegraph and railroad companies. Carnegie realized railroads needed stronger iron for tracks. He invested in the steel industry. His first steel mill was the Edgar Thomson Works in Braddock, Pennsylvania. It opened in 1875. The first order from this mill was for 2,000 steel rails. They were used for the Pennsylvania railroad.

With the help of his business partners, Carnegie bought more steel mills. On July 1, 1892, he formed the Carnegie Steel Company. The company's headquarters were in Pittsburgh. Carnegie created an industrial center there. The mills used local sources of iron ore, coke, and limestone. The local river and train transportation were used for shipping. Carnegie bought and built companies to control each part of the steel-making process. He also advertised for workers in Europe. This brought labor to his factories. With a combination of low worker wages, control of resources, and efficient production, the Carnegie Steel Company became highly profitable.

Carnegie gave himself a personal salary of $25 million during the 1890’s. By 1900, Carnegie Steel Company was making $40 million in profit. In 1901, Carnegie turned 65 years old. He sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan for $480 million.

After the sale, Carnegie was the richest man in the world. He became known as a philanthropist. A philanthropist is someone who donates money to causes. Carnegie's money helped build libraries, universities, concert halls, and science research centers.

title: Primary Source: The Code of Hammurabi
text:
Hammurabi, King of the Babylonians, ordered the laws of his Kingdom to be written down. Around 1780 B.C.E., the laws were written on a large stone so that everyone could see it. This image shows a close-up of the cuneiform writing on the original stele.

If he satisfy the elders to impose a fine of grain or money, he shall receive the fine that the action produces.

If any one steal cattle or sheep, or an ass, or a pig or a goat, if it belong to a god or to the court, the thief shall pay thirtyfold therefore; if they belonged to a freed man of the king he shall pay tenfold...

If the witnesses be not at hand, then shall the judge set a limit, at the expiration of six months. If his witnesses have not appeared within the six months, he is an evil-doer, and shall bear the fine of the pending case.

If a chieftain or man be caught in the misfortune of the king (captured in battle), and if his fields and garden be given to another and he take possession, if he return and reaches his place, his field and garden shall be returned to him, he shall take it over again.

If any one deliver silver, gold, or anything else to another for safe keeping, before a witness, but he deny it, he shall be brought before a judge, and all that he has denied he shall pay in full.

If an artisan has undertaken to rear a child and teaches him his craft, he can not be demanded back. If he has not taught him his craft, this adopted son may return to his father's house.

title: The Steelers
text:
The work in the steel mills made men there physically strong. They weren't unlike the steel they were producing. The long hours of physical work created a unique culture in Pittsburgh. The closeness of the community and the families were forged in the heat of the furnaces. Each worker looked out for the other. Together they accomplished their tasks and returned home to their families. This became the tradition of steel workers.

In the 1930’s, Art Rooney founded a football team. The majority of steel workers didn’t work on Sundays. The law was changed to allow for sporting events on Sundays. That way, steel workers could enjoy the sport. Rooney asked the people of Pittsburgh for suggestions on a team name. Rooney chose the name he thought best identified the region. He chose “Steelers.”

The name honors the people and the industry that helped shape America. The Steeler football team has a reputation for hard-work. They take pride in taking no shortcuts to be champions. The team, the city, and the fans are all identified with steel and what that means to them.

title: Decline of Steel in Pennsylvania
text:
Being the center of steel production came with consequences for Pennsylvania. The great furnaces created a black smoke that hung in the air. The rivers were filled with waste from the mills and towns. Acquiring the resources of coal and coke caused acid drainage into the soil and waterways. The natural resources and environment of Pennsylvania suffered.

Those who were not associated with the steel industry were inflicted with poor air quality and unclean water. Unclean water from Pittsburgh entered the Ohio River. That water flowed into the Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico. Pittsburgh's steel industry had effects thousands of miles away.

The steel industry increased safety requirements for workers. This caused slower production. Wages increased for workers too. Their work was dangerous and difficult. They wanted pay that reflected the risk. In 1959, the steel workers went on strike. Steel companies were trying to reduce the number of workers to make steel. Having fewer workers made the work even more dangerous.

The 119-day strike had little effect on buyers. They went to steel companies in other countries. The steel from foreign countries was lower in price. It cost less to make steel in other countries. Wages for workers, transportation for delivery, and cost of materials were all lower.

In the 1970’s the cost of fuel increased. Shortages made fuel difficult to purchase. The transportation and delivery costs of steel increased greatly. The cost of producing large quantities of steel became unprofitable. No one in the market could afford the price. When the cost to produce a good becomes greater than consumers will pay, the product doesn’t sell. With no sales, companies can't function. Employees aren't paid. Supplies aren't purchased. Eventually, mills closed and hundreds of workers were unemployed.

The high unemployment changed the community. There weren't enough positions for the amount of workers. People needed to find other jobs. It wasn't easy to receive new training in another trade. Many unemployed steelworkers moved to other cities to find work. Some were fortunate enough to start their own businesses.

Steel is still made in Pennsylvania. The number of workers is much lower than after World War II. Steel from Pennsylvania is used in many industries today. Steel is used in energy, construction, transportation, and appliance industries. Steel changed America in the 19th century. It continues to change America today.

title: Primary Source: The Epic of Gilgamesh
text:
The Epic of Gilgamesh is a very long, or epic, poem written in the Akkadian language on 12 stone tablets. It is one of the first known pieces of literature. The image is of one of the tablets containing a part of the epic of Gilgamesh. An excerpt from the beginning of the poem follows the image.

I will proclaim to the world the deeds of Gilgamesh. This was the man to whom all things were known; this

was the king who knew the countries of the world. He was wise, he saw mysteries and knew secret things, he

brought us a tale of the days before the flood. He went on a long journey, was weary, worn-out with labor,

returning he rested, he engraved on a stone the whole story.

When the gods created Gilgamesh they gave him a perfect body. Shamash the glorious sun endowed him with

beauty, Adad the god of the storm endowed him with courage, the great gods made his beauty perfect, surpassing all

others, terrifying like a great wild bull. Two thirds they made him god and one third man.

title: Primary Source: Book of the Dead
text: The Book of the Dead was an ancient Egyptian text that was placed in most, if not all, tombs. The book was filled with directions, spells, and other information that would help the dead person make it to the afterlife. The image is one section of a papyrus scroll of the Book of the Dead. A transcript of the Book of the Dead is difficult to create because it contained pictures with meaning, which cannot be directly translated, as well as hieroglyphics with meaning, which can be translated.

title: Primary Source: Analects of Confucius
text:
Confucius was a philosopher during a period of war in China. Many of Confucius’ sayings and philosophies were written down for others to learn from and compiled in a book called Analects of Confucius. The first image is from one Chinese version of the Analects of Confucius. The second image is an English translations of the first book of the Analects of Confucius.

Book I

1.1 The Master said: To study and at due times practice what one has studied, is this not a pleasure? When friends come from distant places, is this not joy? To remain unsoured when his talents are unrecognized, is this not a junzi?

1.3 The Master said: Those of crafty words and ingratiating expression are rarely ren.

1.5 The Master said: To guide a state great enough to possess a thousand war chariots: be attentive to affairs and trustworthy; regulate expenditures and treat persons as valuable; employ the people according to the proper season.

1.6 The Master said: A young man should be filial within his home and respectful of elders when outside, should be careful and trustworthy, broadly caring of people at large, and should cleave to those who are ren. If he has energy left over, he may study the refinements of culture (wen).

1.9 Master said: Devote care to life’s end and pursue respect for the distant dead; in this way, the virtue of the people will return to fullness.

Notes

1.1 ‘The Master’ refers to Confucius: Kongzi, or ‘Master Kong.’

Junzi: Originally ‘a prince’; used by the Analects to denote an ideal moral actor. The term is sometimes rendered ‘gentleman,’ but has a more emphatic moral sense, and is left untranslated here. At times it merely denotes a ruler.

1.3 Ren: The key moral term in the Analects. Rendered as ‘humanity,’ ‘goodness,’ etc., its rich meaning is a mystery to many in the text and defies translation.

1.5 In Classical China, the size of feudal states was often expressed in terms of chariot forces. ‘One thousand chariots’ denotes a mid-size state.

1.6 ‘Refinements of culture’ translates the term wen, which is a key term in the Analects. Its basic sense is ‘pattern,’ and it is applied in a variety of important ways.

title: European Empires of North America
text:
British Empire

During the Age of Exploration, the British government hoped to gain a foothold in North America to obtain land and new resources. British settlers established the first permanent English settlement in North America in 1607 at Jamestown, Virginia. By 1630, Virginia's economy was booming, and by 1640, farmers were exporting over 1.5 million pounds of tobacco to England each year. The success of the Virginia colony encouraged the British government to expand their empire in North America.

In 1620, a group of 102 settlers sailed for North America on a ship called the Mayflower. Today, we call these settlers the Pilgrims. The Mayflower encountered some terrible weather. Storms drove the ship off of its course. When the ship reached land on Nov. 11, 1620, the Pilgrims were much farther north than they intended to go. The Mayflower landed at Cape Cod in Massachusetts. This area of New England was known for great fishing, mild summers, and long, hard winters of snow and cold temperatures. This new settlement became known as Plymouth Colony.

Between 1620 and 1733, the British established 11 more colonies along the Atlantic seaboard. By 1750, the population of the British colonies in North America exceeded one million people. British colonists tapped into the raw materials of the content and engaged in agriculture to produce crops in order to send the materials to England. These materials were used to produce goods that were then sent to the colonies for purchase.

French Empire

The French hoped to have the same success in the Americas as other Europeans. In 1608, French explorer Samuel de Champlain explored the Great Lakes region and established Quebec. Quebec was the first permanent French settlement in North America. It was not until 1634 that the French gained a foothold in what is now the United States. French explorer Jean Nicolet established the settlement of La Baye des Puants. Today, it is called Green Bay, Wisconsin.

In 1701, Antonie de la Cadillac, a French commander, established Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit along the Detroit River. Cadillac picked this area because it would help the French to keep the British from using the Great Lakes to come into Michigan. A settlement was built and eventually became the town of Detroit.

Another important French settlement established at this time was New Orleans. New Orleans was founded in 1718. Because of its location at the mouth of the Mississippi River and its proximity to the Gulf of Mexico, New Orleans quickly became an important port and center for trade. The port of New Orleans took sugarcane and cotton grown in the fertile delta of the Mississippi and shipped it upriver to trading posts in the north. New Orleans’s proximity to island colonies in the Caribbean was another factor that made it an important center for trade.

Spanish Empire

For hundreds of years, the Spanish empire in North America extended from present-day Florida, along the Gulf of Mexico and through present-day Texas. From there, it reached all the way to the Pacific Ocean. In 1565, Don Pedro Menéndez de Avilés sailed to Florida with over 2,000 people, including priests, soldiers, sailors, and their families. They landed along the east coast of Florida and established the city of St. Augustine, the first permanent European settlement in the continental United States.

With a permanent settlement established in Florida, Spain moved to colonize other areas of its vast empire. In 1598, Spain chose Juan de Oñate to lead an expedition through the Southwest. Oñate was the first to claim land for Spain and establish European settlements in the region. He named the new land New Mexico. He established the first Spanish capital in the Southwest and named it San Juan de Los Caballeros. The Spanish met with resistance from the Southwest tribes. The governor moved the capital to Santa Fe because San Juan was vulnerable to attacks. This makes Santa Fe the oldest capital in the continental United States.

title: Control of Ohio
text:
England and France spent much of the 1600s carving up the North American continent into colonies to obtain resources and gain power. England and France both claimed the area they called the Ohio Country. However, this land was already home to hundreds of Native People tribes. The competition over land and resources caused cooperation and conflict between European colonists and Native People in the region.

Beaver Wars

During the colonial era, one of the most valuable resources in Ohio was beavers. Beaver pelts were used to make luxury items, including hats, muffs, and trimming for suits, dresses, coats, and collars. Native People tribes fought for control over the Ohio Country to gain access to the beaver fur trade. The Iroquois Confederacy, a powerful empire made up of the Mohawk, Onondaga, Seneca, Oneida, Cayuga, and Tuscarora tribes, pushed other tribes out of the area to gain control of the beaver fur trade.

Between 1640 and 1701, several wars were fought between the Iroquois Confederacy, the tribes of Ohio and the Great Lake region, and their British and French allies for control of the area. The Treaty of Grande Paix of Montréal, also called the Great Peace Montréal Treaty, ended the Beaver Wars in 1701. Delegates representing England, France, and 39 different Native People nations met in Montréal, Canada, to draft and sign the treaty. The treaty created peace among the tribes in Ohio and the Great Lakes region that lasted for nearly 60 years.

Building of Forts and Trading Posts

During the 17th and 18th centuries, the French and British established multiple forts and trading posts in Ohio. Forts were often constructed near settlements and trading posts to protect the colonists and economic activities in the area. European settlement in Ohio ultimately led to conflict between the French, British, and the tribes of Ohio.

title: The Ohio Company
text:
The charter of Virginia showed that Virginia's borders stretched all the way to the Pacific Ocean, including present-day Ohio. British officials felt that the land was meant for settlers to live there and use the rich resources. In 1748, wealthy colonists in Virginia created the Ohio Company. The Ohio Company bought land in the Ohio Country from King George II. This gave them the legal basis to sell land to settlers at a higher price. This process is called land speculation. Through this process, members of the Ohio Company hoped to become very wealthy.

Royal Lieutenant Governor Dinwiddie of Virginia was an officer in the Ohio Company. Members of prominent Virginia families, including the family of future president George Washington, invested in the Ohio Company. In 1749, King George II and the British Parliament gave 500,000 acres of land in the Ohio Country, between the Kanawha and Monongahela Rivers, to the Ohio Company. In exchange for the land, Parliament required the Ohio Company to settle the area with no fewer than 100 families. Parliament also required the Ohio Company to build a fort to protect the region.

The British were not the only empire to claim the territory. Two other empires claimed the same land: the Iroquois Confederacy and the French. If the French gained full control of the Ohio Country, the Ohio Company could not sell any land. They would lose all their investments. No one would be wealthy. It was very important to the British for the French to be forced out of the Ohio Country. Tensions between the empires eventually turned into war in 1754.

title: Christopher Gist
text:
One of the earliest Americans to explore and chronicle his travels through the Ohio Country was Christopher Gist. Gist was an accomplished surveyor and frontiersman. Because of his talents and skill, Gist was selected by the Ohio Company of Virginia to survey the area between present-day Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Louisville, Kentucky. At the time, this area was considered part of the Ohio Country.

Gist traveled to Ohio in 1750 to survey the territory. In addition to surveying the area, Gist also created maps of the territory and kept a detailed account of his journey. Gist was the first person to create a detailed account of the geography, resources, and people of southern Ohio. He wrote:

Crossed the little Miamee River, and altering our Course We went S W 25 M to the Big Miamee River, opposite the Twigtwee Town. All the way from the Shannoah Town to this Place is rich, fine and level and well timbered with large Walnut, Ash, Sugar Trees, Cherry Trees. It is well watered with a great number of little streams or rivulets, and full of beautiful natural meadows, covered with wild rye, Blue Grass, and clover, and abounds with turkeys, deer, and elks and most sorts of game particularly buffaloes …

After his first trip, the Ohio Company commissioned Gist to explore other areas of the Ohio Country. On this second trip, during the winter of 1751–1752, Gist explored areas of the territory that are now located in present-day West Virginia. He surveyed the land and kept a detailed account of his travels. Cartographers used his accounts to make maps of the territory.

title: George Croghan
text:
George Croghan was an important figure in the development of the Ohio Country. Croghan immigrated to Pennsylvania in 1741. During his time in Pennsylvania, Croghan became an experienced trader, trapper, and hunter. Croghan’s success as a trapper and trader was a result of his close relationships with Native People tribes in Pennsylvania and the Ohio Country. He learned several native languages and customs and respected the traditions of the tribes. Because of his respect and willingness to learn from the tribes, Croghan was permitted to establish trading posts in Native People villages throughout Pennsylvania and the Ohio Country.

Croghan was the first person of European descent to establish a trading post near present-day Cleveland. This trading post was located near Lake Erie near the mouth of the Cuyahoga River. The location was strategically important because the Cuyahoga connects to many other rivers, lakes, and streams, connecting many areas across the region. Croghan expanded his trading empire by establishing trading posts in Wyandot and Miami villages in Ohio. Croghan also worked closely with the Ohio Company of Virginia as a land agent.

text: As more settlers immigrated and migrated to the colonies in the Northeast, several Native People tribes were forced from their ancestral homelands. Many of these tribes, including the Delaware, Seneca, and Shawnee, migrated to and settled in Ohio. Analyze the map to learn more about the migration of native tribes to Ohio.

title: Primary Source: The Writing of Master Han Fei
text:
The writings of Han Fei, called the Han Feizi, are a selection of essays about government power, and practices, as well as economics. Han Fei’s essays take the legal theories that were written before him and analyze them. This image is from a transcription of some of the Han Feizi.

Selections from the Han Feizi: Chapter 49, “The Five Vermin”

When Yao ruled the world, he left the thatch of his roof untrimmed, and the raw timber of his beams was left unplanned. He ate coarse millet and a soup of greens, wore deerskin in the winter days and rough fiber robes in summer. Even a lowly gatekeeper was no worse clothed and provided for than he. When Yu ruled the world, he took plow and spade in hand to lead his people, working until there was no more down on his thighs or hair on his shins. Even the toil of a slave taken prisoner in the wars was no bitterer than his. Therefore those men in ancient times who abdicated and relinquished the rule of the world were, in a manner of speaking, merely forsaking the life of a gatekeeper and escaping from the toil of a slave. Therefore they thought little of handing over the rule of the world to someone else. Nowadays, however, the magistrate of a district dies and his sons and grandsons are able to go riding about in carriages for generations after. There people prize such offices. In the matter of relinquishing things, people thought nothing of stepping down from the position of Son of Heaven in ancient times, yet they are very reluctant to give up the post of district magistrate today; this is because of the difference in the actual benefits received.

title: Fur Trade and Dependency
text:
The Native Peoples of the Americas had developed many innovative technologies prior to making contact with European settlers. For centuries, Native People had been using scrapers, needles, and utensils made of bone to prepare hides for clothing and bedding. Clay pots were made and used for cooking. When Europeans arrived in the Americas, they brought manufactured goods that changed the lifestyles of the Native Peoples.

European trade with Native Peoples began as early as the mid-1500s. French explorers traded for furs to take back to Europe. Furs, animal pelts, and leather were used in European fashion and business. Leather was used to make aprons for blacksmiths, bakers, and construction workers. Fur was used for warmth in clothing. Some animal pelts became a fashion trend for the wealthy. This put a high market value on certain furs.

The trade in furs, pelts, and leather from America became a very profitable European business. The Native People could provide this resource easily. The Europeans offered manufactured goods in exchange. Metal utensils, cookware, and tools became popular with the tribes of North America. They gladly traded animal pelts for these products that made everyday life easier. The Europeans brought ready-made clothing, jewelry, and luxury items. This was convenient and labor-saving for the Native People. The Europeans also brought a new weapon: the musket, with gunpowder and lead balls for ammunition. This new technology changed the balance of dependency in the tribal nations.

The trade for European manufactured goods changed the way of life for the Native People. Their wants and needs for living changed. The European traders made a substantial profit from these trades. In trading muskets, the Europeans knew the Native Peoples could not make their own gunpowder or lead for ammunition. When people keep trading to acquire the same items, it's called trade dependency.

The French and the British had a trade dependency with the Native People. Each wanted the same items in every trade. The French and the British had different methods of trading. The French went to meet the Native Peoples in their villages or special meeting places. The French respected the tribes as trade partners. French traders frequently lived in the Native Peoples villages, married, and had families.

The British trade strategy forced the Native People to come to them. The British built permanent trading posts, which frequently became settlements, farms, and homes. When colonists settled an area, the game, or animals that were hunted, left the area. Game was a resource for the tribes to trade. The British could still trade with the settlers. However, as the game became scarce, the Native People had less and less to trade.

The French competed with the British to trade the most furs, pelts, and leather. As European demand for pelts, furs, and leather increased, the demand for trade with the Native People increased. Simultaneously, as the demand for European manufactured goods, including muskets, gunpowder, and ammunition increased, the demand for trade with the British increased. This trading relationship was profitable for both groups for a short period of time. However, as game decreased, the Native Peoples' ability to trade also decreased, and they became more dependent on the British.

title: Alliances with Native People
text:
The British, French, Native Peoples, and colonists made four important agreements during and after the French and Indian War.

From July 4-10, 1754, delegates from seven colonies and the Iroquois Confederacy met in Albany, New York. A trading and peace treaty was the main purpose of the congress.

The Albany Plan of Union

The delegates also met with each other during this time. How were they going to manage if there was a French invasion? The Albany Plan of Union was proposed by Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Hutchinson. They suggested colonial governments choose members of a “Grand Council,” according to population. The British government would select a “President General.” The council and the president would address Native People trade, border disputes, and collecting taxes.

King George II and the colonial legislatures rejected the Albany Plan of Union. The king thought this gave authority to the colonies. The colonies felt it gave authority to the British government.

The Treaty of Easton

The Treaty of Easton was a 1758 agreement between the British government and the many Native People tribes of the Iroquois Confederacy. These tribes were located in eastern Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey. Under this agreement, the members of the Iroquois Confederacy present at Easton agreed to fight as British allies in return for rights to hunting grounds.

In the treaty, the Lenape tribe sold all claims to the area called New Jersey for the sum of 1,000 Spanish dollars. The treaty also agreed there would be no British settlement west of the Allegheny Mountains. The treaty was signed in Easton, Pennsylvania. It helped the British in the war.

The Treaty of Paris of 1763

The Treaty of Paris of 1763 officially ended the French and Indian War in America. France agreed to give New France (what is now eastern Canada), the Ohio Country, and the Mississippi River to the British. The British government then agreed to grant officers and soldiers land in the Ohio Country, west of the Appalachian Mountains. One of these officers was George Washington. Many companies also bought land, hoping to sell it to new settlers.

The Proclamation of 1763

Native Peoples had not given up their claims. By treaty, they still had legal claim to the land. The Proclamation of 1763 was given by the new British king, George III. He decreed that all land west of the Appalachian Mountains was reserved for the Native Peoples. No settlement would be permitted. It was the first act of King George III to affect all 13 colonies.

Colonists were upset about losing the freedom to move west. Native Peoples were angry because settlers defied the Proclamation of 1763 and moved into the Ohio Country anyway. Without an agreement all groups would follow, conflict in the western frontier increased.

title: Consequences of the French and Indian War
text:
France

The French gave up all of their land in North America east of the Mississippi River.

France retained New Orleans.

The British government promised to allow all French citizens to practice Catholicism.

French ships continued to fish off the coast of Newfoundland.

French-speaking Catholics (Acadians) were forced by the British to leave Acadia (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island); of 14,100 Acadians in the region, 11,500 were displaced.

France no longer had to pay to maintain a military presence in Canada.

Great Britain

The British gained all territory east of the Mississippi River.

The British gained Florida.

Plans to give the British government more control over the colonies were set in motion.

The military was left with little respect for the colonial militias.

Great Britain authorized a permanent army of 10,000 Regulars to stay in America to enforce the proclamation line.

Subjects were guaranteed free rights of navigation on the Mississippi River and through the port of New Orleans.

The British government was left with a large debt from war costs.

The terms of trade with the Native Peoples were changed by limiting the goods available for trade.

Native Peoples

The Proclamation of 1763 tried to keep colonists out of Native Peoples lands in the Ohio Country.

The tribes who allied with the French lost a trading partner and French protection.

The tribes who allied with the British won continued British alliances.

The tribes could no longer go back and forth between the French and British.

The terms for trading changed now that the Native People could only deal with the British; the British limited available goods for trade.

Colonists

French invasion in the colonies was no longer a threat.

Colonial interests no longer aligned with British interests for the future of the colonies.

The Proclamation of 1763 prohibited expansion and settlement across the Appalachian Mountains.

The militia had little respect for the British military.

The colonists became united against a common foe and were more powerful.

The Proclamation of 1763 prohibited the colonies from issuing any more land grants; only representatives of the king could negotiate land purchases.

Britain expected the colonies to pay the debt from the war.

text: What were the consequences of Great Britain controlling the Mississippi?

title: Primary Source: Pericles Funeral Oration
text:
In 431 B.C.E. Pericles gave a funeral speech for all of the soldiers who died in the Peloponnesian War. His speech focused on Athenian democracy and achievements. Historians believe the speech was recorded and rewritten by Thucydides, a Greek historian. The image is a painting of Pericles Funeral Oration by Phillipp Foltz, done in 1852. Since this speech was written in ancient Greek, there are many different translations. The text below is an excerpt from a translation of Pericles’ speech.

...I shall begin with our ancestors: it is both just and proper that they should have the honour of the first mention on an occasion like the present. They dwelt in the country without break in the succession from generation to generation, and handed it down free to the present time by their valour. And if our more remote ancestors deserve praise, much more do our own fathers, who added to their inheritance the empire which we now possess, and spared no pains to be able to leave their acquisitions to us of the present generation. Lastly, there are few parts of our dominions that have not been augmented by those of us here, who are still more or less in the vigour of life; while the mother country has been furnished by us with everything that can enable her to depend on her own resources whether for war or for peace. That part of our history which tells of the military achievements which gave us our several possessions, or of the ready valour with which either we or our fathers stemmed the tide of Hellenic or foreign aggression, is a theme too familiar to my hearers for me to dilate on, and I shall therefore pass it by. But what was the road by which we reached our position, what the form of government under which our greatness grew, what the national habits out of which it sprang; these are questions which I may try to solve before I proceed to my panegyric upon these men; since I think this to be a subject upon which on the present occasion a speaker may properly dwell, and to which the whole assemblage, whether citizens or foreigners, may listen with advantage.

Our constitution does not copy the laws of neighbouring states; we are rather a pattern to others than imitators ourselves. Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy. If we look to the laws, they afford equal justice to all in their private differences; if no social standing, advancement in public life falls to reputation for capacity, class considerations not being allowed to interfere with merit; nor again does poverty bar the way, if a man is able to serve the state, he is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition. The freedom which we enjoy in our government extends also to our ordinary life. There, far from exercising a jealous surveillance over each other, we do not feel called upon to be angry with our neighbour for doing what he likes, or even to indulge in those injurious looks which cannot fail to be offensive, although they inflict no positive penalty. But all this ease in our private relations does not make us lawless as citizens. Against this fear is our chief safeguard, teaching us to obey the magistrates and the laws, particularly such as regard the protection of the injured, whether they are actually on the statute book, or belong to that code which, although unwritten, yet cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace...

title: Primary Source: The Death of Socrates
text: “The Death of Socrates” was painted in 1787 C.E. by Jacques Louis David. David modeled the painting after Plato’s account of Socrates’ death. Socrates refused to deny his beliefs and was convicted of impiety by an Athenian court, then executed.

title: Primary Source: Augustus of Primaporta
text: In 1863, archeologists found a statue of Augustus Caesar at the Villa of Livia in Prima Porta. This was the home of Augustus’ wife. The statue was carved some time in the first century C.E.

title: What Is Light?
text:
Directions: Record your observations of the jump rope demonstration in the box below.

Light is ____________. Remember, energy is the ability to cause change. When you walk into a dark room and turn on a light, what you see changes. Light energy takes the form of waves. There are many forms of energy, but not all are visible. Visible light includes all of the colors that we can see. Each color has a different wavelength. Red is the longest wavelength, and violet is the shortest. The order of the colors from long to short is the same order as the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Remember, the shorter the wavelength, the more energy there is in the wave, so cool colors like blue, indigo, and violet have more energy than warm colors like red, orange, and yellow. We can see color because of the light that is absorbed into each object. For example, if your water bottle is red, all the colors except red are being absorbed into the bottle while red light is being reflected back to your eye, so that is the color you see. Have you ever heard someone say you shouldn’t wear a dark shirt on a hot day? This is because all the colors are being absorbed into the black shirt.

Why do you think wearing black would make you feel warmer on a hot day?

title: Primary Source: The Rock Edicts of Ashoka
text:
People consistently inhabited the subcontinent for thousands of years. After Persian invaded the Indus River Valley Civilization and before the Gupta empire, the Mauryan Empire existed in modern-day India from 322 B.C.E. to 184 B.C.E. The third ruler of the Mauryan Empire was named Ashoka. Ashoka had inscriptions written on over 30 stone pillars throughout modern-day India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. The inscriptions contained edicts declaring reforms to the kingdom. These reforms were composed by King Ashoka and were based on the principles of Buddhism. The image shows a fallen rock edict and the transcription follows. The transcription comes from the First Major Rock Edict.

First Major Rock Edict

The Beloved of the Gods, Piyadassi the king, has had this inscription on Dhamma engraved. Here, no living thing having been killed, is to be sacrificed; nor is the holding of a festival permitted. For the Beloved of the Gods, the king Piyadassi, sees much evil in festivals, though there are some of which the Beloved of the Gods, the king Piyadassi, approves.

Formerly in the kitchens of the Beloved of the Gods, the king Piyadassi, many hundreds of thousands of living animals were killed daily for meat. But now, at the time of writing this inscription on Dhamma, only three animals are killed, two peacocks and a deer, and the deer not invariably. Even these three animal will not be killed in future.

title: Primary Source: Popul Vuh
text:
The Quiche or K’iche’ people were part of the Maya Civilization. A Spanish Dominican friar, Francisco Ximénez, wrote down two mythologies of the Maya people, one was a creation myth, and one about twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué. In one column of Ximénez’s manuscript the mythology is written in Quiche and on the other side is a Spanish translation.

Chapter One of the Popol Vuh

This is the account of how all was in suspense, all calm, in silence; all motionless, still, and the expanse of the sky was empty. This is the first account, the first narrative. There was neither man, nor animal, birds, fish, crabs, trees, stones, caves, ravines, grasses, nor forests; there was only the sky.

The surface of the earth had not appeared. There was only the calm sea and the great expanse of the sky.

There was nothing brought together, nothing which could make a noise, nor anything which might move, or tremble, or could make noise in the sky. There was nothing standing; only the calm water, the placid sea, alone and tranquil. Nothing existed.

There was only immobility and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the creator, the Maker, Tepeu, Gucumatz, the Forefathers, were in the water surrounded with light. They were hidden under green and blue feathers, and were therefore called Gucumatz. By nature they were great sages and great thinkers. In this manner the sky existed and also the Heart of Heaven, which is the name of God and thus He is called.

Then came the word. Tepeu and Gucumatz came together in the darkness, in the night, and Tepeu and Gucumatz talked together. They talked then, discussing and deliberating; they agreed, they united their words and their thoughts.

Then while they meditated, it became clear to them that when dawn would break, man must appear. Then they planned the creation, and the growth of the trees and the thickets and the birth of life and the creation of man. Thus it was arranged in the darkness and in the night by the Heart of Heaven who is called Huracán.

The first is called Caculhá Huracán. The second is Chipi-Caculhá. The third is Raxa-Caculhá. And these three are the Heart of Heaven. Then Tepeu and Gucumatz came together; then they conferred about life and light, what they would do so that there would be light and dawn, who it would be who would provide food and sustenance.

Thus let it be done! Let the emptiness be filled! Let the water recede and make a void, let the earth appear and become solid; let it be done. Thus they spoke. Let there be light, let there be dawn in the sky and on the earth! There shall be neither glory nor grandeur in our creation and formation until the human being is made, man is formed. So they spoke.

Then the earth was created by them. So it was, in truth, that they created the earth. Earth! they said, and instantly it was made.

Like the mist, like a cloud, and like a cloud of dust was the creation, when the mountains appeared from the water; and instantly the mountains grew. Only by a miracle, only by magic art were the mountains and valleys formed; and instantly the groves of cypresses and pines put forth shoots together on the surface of the earth.

And thus Gucumatz was filled with joy, and exclaimed: “Your coming has been fruitful, Heart of Heaven; and you, Huracán, and you, Chipi-Caculhá, Raxa-Caculhá!”

“Our work, our creation shall be finished,” they answered.

First the earth was formed, the mountains and the valleys; the currents of water were divided, the rivulets were running freely between the hills, and the water was separated when the high mountains appeared.

Thus was the earth created, when it was formed by the Heart of Heaven, the Heart of Earth, as they are called who first made it fruitful, when the sky was in suspense, and the earth was submerged in the water.

So it was that they made perfect the work, when they did it after thinking and meditating upon it.

title: Primary Source: "Duties of the Coloni"
text:
Louis the Pious, the son of Charlemagne, was emperor of the Holy Roman Empire. He wrote about the economic responsibilities of coloni, also called serfs. This is a translation and transcription of the “Duties of the Coloni.”

C.13. As to the coloni, they either serve as serfs of the Church or make some kind of fixed payment: this is the agrarian tax according to the opinion of the steward. The steward sees to it that each gives according to what he has; out of thirty muids he gives three muids, and each pays pascuarium according to the custom of the district. He is to plough, sow, enclose, harvest, haul, and put away the crops from the regular enclosures---which are four ten-foot measuring rods in width and forty in length. He is to enclose, reap, gather, and put away one arpent in meadow. Every colonus ought to collect and put away corn to the value of a triens for seed. He is to plant, enclose, dig up, extend, prune, and collect the harvest of the vineyards. They each pay ten bundles of flax. Four hens they must pay also. They give palfreys or go where they are ordered. They do carriage service with a cart up to fifty leagues; to go further is not expected. They are assigned to the demesne houses, haylofts, farms; they have a reasonable amount of land for earning the tax, and when necessary they pay it in a lump sum.

title: The Actions of Parliament and Colonial Responses
text:
From 1764 to 1770, interactions between Parliament and the American colonists created various levels of conflict. Parliament felt it was within its right to tax the colonists based on the cost of keeping them safe during the French and Indian War. The colonists felt differently. Some colonists felt they should pay the various taxes. Others felt that the taxes and Parliament's actions weren't fair. Many colonists did not believe that Parliament treated the colonists as British citizens.

The charters of the colonies were important for providing colonists with the rights of British citizens. However, the colonies had no one to represent them in Parliament.

The Prime Minister and members of Parliament argued that the colonies had representative governments in each colony. They argued that this meant the rights of colonists were being fulfilled. This became the dividing principle. Colonists wanted to have direct representation where decisions were made and taxes were created and levied. The members of Parliament claimed the colonies did not need representation in Parliament. Parliament represented all British citizens.

“No taxation without representation!” became the repetitive answer from the colonists to each of Parliament's actions.

Communication between all the groups (Parliament, King George, colonial legislatures, and the people) began openly. As the decade and actions of Parliament continued, communication from all parties broke down. This began a cycle of decreased communication and conflict. As communication decreased, conflict increased.

1763

Action: Proclamation of 1763: Restricts settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains

Response: Colonists who fought in the French and Indian War for lands are angered.

April 5, 1764

Action: Sugar Act 1764, or American Revenue Act 1764: Makes trading for molasses and sugar more difficult. Taxes are also placed on several foreign goods.

Response: First colonial disagreement with Parliament is published.

1765

Action: Stamp Act: A tax on all paper documents. This is the first internal tax placed directly on American colonists by Parliament.

Response: Massachusetts urges colonies to boycott British goods.

March 24, 1765

Action: Quartering Act: Forces colonial authorities to provide food and lodging for British troops

Response: Sons of Liberty organize

June-July 1767

Action: Townshend Revenue Acts: New York Restraining Act, Customs Service Reform, and Townshend Duty Act. Tax placed on paint, paper, glass, lead, and tea imported into the colonies.

Response: Colonists begin boycotting British goods.

1768-1769

Action: Massachusetts Assembly suspended for refusing to cancel boycotts and the Virginia House of Burgesses closed as punishment for Virginia Resolves opposing British policy

Response: Unrest and mob violence break out and boycotts spread to more colonies.

March 5, 1770

Action: Boston Massacre: Colonist civilians are shot and killed by British soldiers.

Response: Colonists are outraged.

Dec. 16, 1773

Action: Parliament passes a tax on tea.

Response: Members of the Sons of Liberty protest the tax by throwing tea into Boston Harbor.

1774

Action: Parliament passes the Intolerable Acts to punish the colonists of Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party.

Response: Representatives from 12 of the colonies gather in Carpenters Hall in Philadelphia to write a petition to King George to remove the recent Acts applied to Massachusetts.

August 1774

Action: British Regulars seize gunpowder from the powder house in Charlestown, Massachusetts.

Response: Patriots establish an alarm system in case the British move again to take stores of gunpowder. Those who respond become known as Minutemen.

title: Major Battles and Events of the American Revolution
text:
No one is quite sure which side fired that first “shot heard ‘round the world” on April 19, 1775. After the fateful battles at Lexington and Concord, both sides knew they couldn’t back down. The war had begun. There were many battles in the American Revolution. The following were major turning points for the outcome of the war.

June 16, 1776:

British Regulars defeated American Patriots at the Battle of Bunker Hill, which was the first major battle of the American Revolution.

December 1776 to January 1777:

Forces under the command of General George Washington crossed the Delaware River to face British Regulars and their allies. The battles of Trenton and Princeton were fought in New Jersey, resulting in the first major Continental victory.

October 1777:

Patriot forces surrounded British troops near Saratoga, New York, and won a decisive victory. This victory helped persuade the French to join the Patriot cause.

December 1777 to March 1778:

Washington and the Continental Army wintered at Valley Forge near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This was a difficult time for the Continental Army. They were undersupplied. Almost 2,000 soldiers died from disease, while many others deserted and went home. Washington and his foreign allies worked hard to turn the ragtag Continental forces into a professional army before the spring of 1778.

June 1779:

Spain joined the American Revolution, creating an alliance with the American colonists and the French. In exchange for their support, the Spanish hoped to regain control of Florida and other colonies that they lost as a result of the Seven Years’ War.

September 1780:

Patriot forces defeated British and Loyalist troops at Kings Mountain near the border of North and South Carolina. The American victory forced British troops to retreat into South Carolina and prevented them from advancing farther north into Virginia. The Battle of Kings Mountain was a major turning point in the southern colonies.

May 1781:

Spanish forces under the command of Bernardo de Gálvez captured Pensacola and drove the British out of the territory.

title: Defining Timelines
text:
A timeline is a list of events in chronological order. It starts with the earliest event and ends with the most recent event. Throughout history, different societies have used different timelines to mark events and organize information. These timelines are called calendars.

For example, the Egyptians organized time based on the lives of the pharaohs. A new calendar would begin once a new pharaoh took the throne. The Maya in the ancient Americas developed three different calendars. One tracked the dates of religious festivals. Another calendar followed the seasons. A third calendar, called the Long Count calendar, measured history over hundreds of years.

In western society, we mark time using a calendar based on the life of Jesus of Nazareth. The year 1 is the year Jesus was believed to have been born. The years following Jesus’s birth use the abbreviation A.D. (Anno Domini or “in the year of our Lord”) or C.E. (Common Era). For example, the Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776 A.D. or 1776 C.E. The Cleveland Cavaliers basketball team won the championship in 2016 A.D. or 2016 C.E. Events before 1 A.D. or 1 C.E. are marked by different abbreviations: B.C. (Before the birth of Christ) or B.C.E. (Before Common Era). When the timeline extends backward, larger numbers mean the event is older.

For example, the pyramids of Giza were built a long time ago, around 2550-4490 B.C. or 2550-2490 B.C.E. The Roman Empire was established much sooner, in 27 B.C. or 27 B.C.E. Often, when historians are referring to events and people before 1 A.D., they use the word “ancient” to describe them.

Timelines can also identify when historical events happened and how long they lasted. For example, the mound building Adena people lived in the Ohio River valley from 1000 B.C.E. to 200 C.E.

title: Moving Forward
text:
People use calendars to measure time. We also use calendars to organize time. We know that one week is seven days. We know that most months last 30 or 31 days. February is the exception, with only 28 days. This pattern results in one year lasting 365 days.

Calendars help us communicate with each other and keep track of when gatherings, celebrations, elections, and holidays occur during the year. Calendars and timelines provide the world with a clear understanding of how we all measure time. They help us know when something is coming up or has already happened.

Time can be organized into larger units as well. For example, 10 years is equal to one decade, and 10 decades is equal to one century. When we talk about history, some events and movements span multiple years. This is why it is helpful to use larger units to measure time. For example, the land in Ohio was part of the Northwest Territory for just over one and a half decades. It took 16 years for Ohio to gain statehood.

title: Going back into Timelines
text:
Today, most people in the world follow the Gregorian calendar. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the calendar in 1582. The calendar is named after him. Why do you think the Gregorian calendar is used throughout the world?

At the time of the Roman Empire, many different calendars existed. The Roman emperors wanted a single method for measuring time. Julius Caesar reformed Rome’s original calendar. The new calendar was known as the Julian calendar. It established a 12-month year. It organized days into groups of 30 or 31 within each month. The exception was February, the shortest month, with 28 days.

The Julian calendar was a solar calendar. However, as years passed, Christianity gained popularity in the Roman Empire. Many Christian festivals and ceremonies followed a lunar calendar system. This was important in determining the dates of important holidays.

In the sixth century, a monk changed the Julian calendar. It happened when Pope John I asked this monk to calculate the dates of Easter over one hundred years. The monk, Dionysius Exiguus, created a new system for organizing time. He divided time around the life of Jesus of Nazareth. All the years before Jesus was born were labeled B.C., meaning before the birth of Christ. All years after Jesus’ birth were labeled A.D., meaning Anno Domini or “in the year of our Lord.” The year A.D. 1 immediately follows year 1 B.C. This system made Christian timelines more organized. However, nearly three centuries passed before most Europeans began using this way of measuring the passage of time.

Hundreds of years passed. The Julian calendar became the standard. But in the 1500s, many people complained the calendar was inaccurate. These people pointed to agriculture as evidence.

If the calendar were accurate, farmers should plant on the same day each year. But the calendar had gradually come to have farmers planting earlier almost every single year. The calendar appeared to be out of sync with the actual seasons. Many farmers complained to their governments. Another pope looked to solve the problem.

Pope Gregory XIII had his scientists look at the calendar. They said it was off by as much as 11 minutes a year. That doesn’t sound like much, but multiply 11 minutes by 1,000 years. That shows the calendar can be off by seven or eight days! This was the problem that farmers were complaining about.

So, Pope Gregory’s scientists changed the calendar system, and the new calendar was introduced in 1582. The new system corrected the 11-minute difference. The result was the Gregorian calendar.

The Gregorian calendar also changed how leap years were treated. A leap year has one more day than a common year. That extra day is usually added to February. Adding this day every four years allows the calendar to stay in sync with the solar year. A true solar year is about 365.24 days. So, leap years have the following rules:

Is the year divisible by four? If yes, it is likely a leap year.

Is the year also divisible by 100? If yes, it is likely not a leap year.

Is the year also divisible by 400? If yes, it is absolutely a leap year.

This keeps the Gregorian calendar in sync with Earth’s orbit around the sun. It’s nearly perfect, but the Gregorian calendar is about 26 seconds off every year. So, by the year 4909, the Gregorian calendar will be one day ahead of a true solar year.

title: Calendars and Timelines Today
text:
Time can be measured on calendars and represent years, decades, and centuries. To determine historical context and organize their thinking, historians use timelines. A timeline is a list of events in chronological order, or in the order that they happened. It starts with the earliest event and ends with the last event included.

When we use chronological thinking, we measure the passage of time and label it. When historians study events and people in the past, they often think about what was happening in the world at that same time. This allows them to provide context to an event or a person’s life.

Historians also ask questions when examining sources to determine historical context. Where did the source come from? Who is the author? Who created it? Why was it created? How was it created?
