The physical environment of an area includes its landforms, natural resources, climate, and weather. People depend on the environment to meet their needs. The natural features and resources available in an area provide materials, food, and clothing for the people living there.

When people migrate or immigrate to a new place, they generally settle in areas where resources are easily accessible. Early settlers formed towns and cities near bodies of water to meet their basic human needs. These places provided a source of clean water for drinking and growing crops. They also provided waterways used for transportation and trade. Many of the plants and animals needed for food also lived near the water. Materials from these plants and animals were also used to make clothes and build homes.

As more and more people settle in an area, they form communities to meet their needs. They open shops, start schools, and build public meeting places. Many small communities eventually grow into larger cities. New forms of technology such as the railroad, cars, improved roadways, and air travel made it easier for people to move to new places. People also develop economic activities based on the resources available in their environment. These include things such as agriculture, fishing, manufacturing, and tourism.

The physical environment and economic activities of an area determine if people live in rural, urban, or suburban areas. An urban area is a city with a larger population than the surrounding areas. People often choose to live in these areas because of the jobs and industry available there.

Suburban areas are near urban or city areas. Suburbs may be quieter than city homes, but they are close enough to enjoy city advantages such as sports teams, universities, museums, and hospitals. There is more space for homes and businesses in suburban communities. Suburban areas are less crowded than urban areas.

Rural areas have smaller populations and use more land for agriculture or farming. Rural areas also have businesses, shopping, education, and entertainment, but the majority of land is used for growing food and producing other things that we need. These products are shipped to urban areas around the nation.

title: Keep Your Promises
text: Have you ever broken a promise? How did it feel? How does it feel to keep your promises? Being dependable means keeping your promises. You can choose to be dependable.

title: Differences of Opinion
text: Look around your classroom. Is everyone the same? Each person in your class is different. They have their own ideas and opinions. Sometimes we agree with our classmates on an idea or an opinion. Sometimes we might disagree. When we have a disagreement, it can cause a conflict.

title: Location
text:
The term location refers to a particular place. It answers the question, “Where is something located?” We describe location in relative and absolute terms.

Relative location tells us where something is in relation to something else. We describe where something is using relative location when we describe what is close, near, above, or below.

Look at the political map of the world. Locate North America. What oceans are around North America? What continent is located south of North America? Where is North America located in relation to the North Pole or the South Pole? We can describe North America’s relative location by answering some of these questions.

The absolute location of a place is its exact location. We describe where something is using absolute location when we use a coordinate grid. We can find the absolute location on a map by using vertical and horizontal lines. Cartographers use these lines to make finding a location easier. Cartographers are people who create maps.

title: 2. Think of Possible Solutions
text: Brainstorming means thinking about different solutions. Brainstorming gives you time to find solutions. You can ask others to collaborate with you.

title: Some Things Are Out of Your Control
text: There are some things you cannot control, like due dates and homework. But there are also things you can control! You can choose what to do first. You can choose to put your best effort into all of your work.

title: Understanding Perspective
text:
Perspective is how you see a situation. It is your point of view. Everyone has different perspectives because we all have different experiences.

Jolie and Beau have only played soccer once. Jolie’s first time playing soccer was a blast. She played with all her good friends. She even scored a goal!

Beau’s first time playing soccer was hard. He had a hard time kicking the ball. He didn’t know anyone on the team.

Jolie and Beau have different perspectives about soccer because they had different experiences.

title: Choosing Your Attitude
text:
Attitude is how you feel toward something or someone. You can choose your attitude. No matter what is happening around you, you can choose the attitude you have. If someone is unkind to you, you can choose the attitude you have toward them. You can still choose to have a positive attitude. Your attitude can affect the choices you make.

Jolie says she loves soccer. She wants to play it every day from now on.

Beau says he dislikes soccer. He never wants to play it again.

Why do they have these attitudes?

Could they choose to have different attitudes? Yes! Even though Beau did not have a good experience playing soccer, he could choose to have a positive attitude. He could say, “I did not have fun the first time I played, but I bet if I practice, I can get better and enjoy it.”

title: The Power of Gratitude
text:
What do you say when someone gives you a gift? What do you say when someone does you a favor? You say, "Thank you!" Saying "thank you" is a great way to show gratitude. Being grateful means being thankful. You can have a grateful attitude about your life. When hard things happen, think about all the good things in your life. You have friends, and you have talents. Having a grateful attitude can help you feel happier.

What are you grateful for? Draw a picture.

How does being grateful make you feel? Color in the emotion you feel when you choose to be grateful.

Beau and Jolie both felt grateful they were on a soccer team. They said "thank you" to the coach for teaching them new skills. They both said "thank you" to their parents for signing them up and taking them to practices.

title: Focus on the Positive
text:
What do you think it means to “look on the bright side”? Focusing on the good things in your life can help you make good and healthy choices. Focusing on the positive is called being optimistic. It can help motivate you to make healthy choices. Your positive thoughts and words can spread to the people around you. You can help make your home and your classroom a positive place by focusing on good things.

After the second game, Beau was upset he didn’t score a goal. Jolie scored two goals. Beau watched Jolie say something nice to another player about how hard they worked. Jolie told Beau he did a good job blocking a goal. Beau started thinking about how he blocked a goal. Instead of feeling sad that he didn’t score two goals, Beau was happy because he was proud of blocking a goal.

title: Let Go of the Negative
text:
Imagine you are carrying a backpack full of big rocks. You are walking up a hill. How do you feel? Are you tired? Is it fun to walk up a hill with a backpack full of rocks?

Holding on to negative things in your life is not good for you. These negative things can be holding grudges against people or choosing not to forget bad things that have happened to you. When you hold on to negative things, it is like carrying around a backpack full of rocks. The backpack of rocks does not help you; it only makes your walk harder. Guess what? You can choose to put it down. You do not have to carry all those negative things around! You can choose to let go of hard things. This can be a powerful strategy to cope with fear, stress, anger, and grief. There are many things you can do to put the heavy things down. You can write about them, talk about them, or even draw or sing about them.

One day at practice, Jolie accidentally kicked a ball right at Beau. It hit him in the face. Beau cried. His nose hurt. Jolie apologized, but Beau’s nose still hurt. After practice, Jolie apologized again, and Beau forgave Jolie. Beau didn’t want to be upset with Jolie. Beau and Jolie played together again at the next soccer practice. Jolie was careful not to kick the ball at Beau’s face again.

title: The Emotion of Grief
text: People feel many different emotions each day. Different situations cause different emotions. Going to a birthday party might make you feel happy. Losing a competition might make you feel disappointed. Grief is a very strong emotion that is usually experienced when you lose someone or something very important to you. Grief is extreme sadness. Some people have already experienced grief. Some people may not have felt grief in their life yet. Grief can be hard to get through, but with the right tools, you can manage grief.

title: The Grieving Process
text:
A process is a group of steps that helps you get from one place to the next. The process of grief starts with a sad event, such as the death of a loved one, getting diagnosed with an illness, or losing a limb. The process may happen in different orders and take different amounts of time. These are the steps for the process of grief:

Denial

Anger

Bargaining

Depression

Acceptance

title: Understanding the Steps of Grief
text:
If you experience grief, you may feel some of these things. People may spend different amounts of time in each step or none at all. You can allow yourself to feel each feeling.

Denial is not believing that something has happened. Louis felt denial when he was first told his mom had cancer. Louis said to himself, “This can’t be happening.”

Anger is feeling mad. You may feel mad at the situation you are in. You may feel mad at a specific person. Tewili was angry at her dad because he died.

Bargaining is trying to fix your problem. You may say things like, “I would do anything to fix this.” The issues that cause grief usually are not fixable. Guermo wanted to trade his toys for his goldfish to come back to life.

Depression is a feeling of extreme sadness. Experiencing depression might make you feel like you don’t want to see people or like you don’t want to have fun. Depression can feel dark and lonely. Juanita asked for help after feeling depressed about moving to a new town.

Acceptance is when you come to accept or be okay with what has happened. It may take time to make it to this phase, but when you reach acceptance, you will be able to move on and feel happy again. Indie accepted that her grandpa passed away six months ago. She visits his grave and writes in her journal about the good memories she has of him.

title: Talk Through Your Feelings
text: One of the most important things you can do when you are processing your grief is talk about it. You can talk through each phase of your grief. You can talk to friends or family you trust about your denial, anger, depression, or any other emotion you are feeling as you work through your grief. Talking about your emotions can help you understand them and release them. Your family and peers can help you stay healthy and positive as you work through your grief. Family and friends can encourage you to shower, eat, and sleep to take care of your physical well-being while grieving.

title: Healthy Ways to Grieve
text:
Behaviors to avoid (stay away from) when you are experiencing grief include:

Violence

Isolating yourself (being alone)

Holding your feelings inside

Healthy coping strategies to try include:

Communicating your feelings through art, writing, or music

Talking to someone you trust

Exercising

Focusing on the positive

Asking for help

title: Essential Question
text: Why are multiple perspectives of an event important?

title: What Is a Citizen?
text: A citizen is someone who is part of a group. You are a citizen of the country you live in. You are a citizen of your community. You are a citizen of this classroom and your family. As a citizen, you have rights and responsibilities.

title: Your Rights as a Citizen
text:
As a citizen, you have certain rights. A right is something you are entitled to, meaning that no one is allowed to take it away from you. As humans, we are citizens of the world. Everyone has the same rights. Everyone has the right to freedom and safety.

In the United States, when a citizen turns 18, they have the right to vote for leaders of the country. As a citizen of this classroom, you have the right to an education and access to class resources. You have the right to be treated with respect and equality, no matter your race, religion, or opinions.

title: Your Responsibilities as a Citizen
text:
Citizens have responsibilities, which means you have responsibilities. A responsibility is something a person is expected to do. A good citizen is expected to help make the world around them a better place. Taking care of your environment is an important part of being a good citizen. Don’t forget to encourage your peers to take care of the environment too! Here are a few things you can do to be a good citizen:

Report bullying. Tell a teacher or parent if you notice bullying online or if you see inappropriate (questionable) things.

Help reduce pollution. Conserve energy at home. Turn the lights off when you leave a room. Recycle when you can. Remember to recycle plastic items, and try not to be wasteful.

Pick up your trash. Clean up after yourself. Only use what you need.

Follow rules. Did you know that part of being a good citizen is following rules? For example, good citizens follow the rules when they play sports or other games. They do their best to follow the rules in school and at home.

Encourage others to take care of themselves and the environment.

title: Celebrate Diversity
text: Have you ever heard the word “diversity”? Diversity means differences between people. Diversity is important because you can usually learn more from someone who is different from you. Diversity also allows you to see that there are many right ways to think and live. Your way is not the only right way. Each person is different. Each family is different. Families help individuals learn about what is right and wrong. Families help set boundaries and limits, like rules. Some families have two parents; others have one. Some families have lots of kids, and some have none. Some families play lots of sports, while others play lots of music. Families like different kinds of food and different clothes. No matter what your family likes, your family can be a great place to practice being a good citizen. You can practice respecting everyone, no matter how they look, sound, or act.

title: Great Citizens from History
text:
Good citizens can change the world! Many good citizens have changed the world. Let’s talk about some of these important citizens.

Amelia Earhart was the first female pilot to fly a plane across the Atlantic Ocean. She was a good citizen because she supported equal rights for women. She showed through her actions that women had the right to go after their dreams. Working hard and reaching big goals is part of being a good citizen. You can be a good citizen by doing your part and always trying to be your best self!

Anne Sullivan was a gifted teacher. She taught Hellen Keller, who was blind and deaf. Anne Sullivan was a good citizen because she respected people with different abilities, including the deaf and blind. She went to school, then used her knowledge and talents to make the world around her a better place. You can be a good citizen by sharing the talents you have with others.

Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States. Even the president is a citizen! He was a good citizen because he fought for the rights of others. He helped end slavery in the United States and fought for the rights of African Americans. You can be a good citizen by using your voice to stand up for equal rights for everyone.

Frederick Douglass was an American social reformer, orator, writer, and statesman. A formerly enslaved individual, he became a leader of the abolitionist movement. He promoted the idea that formerly enslaved people had the right to function as independent American citizens. You can be a good citizen by standing up for what you know is right.

title: Communication Connects You
text:
Communication skills are important for your health and wellness. Strong communication skills help you take care of your body and your mind. Verbal and nonverbal communication will help you share your thoughts so you can take care of yourself.

Communication helps you manage your well-being by helping you connect with others. You can form friendships. You can build relationships. Talk to others about shared experiences or shared goals. You can talk to coaches, teachers, and doctors about ways to improve your health or take care of your body. Teachers and counselors can help you excel academically and mentally. You can make your needs known in a variety of (or many different) healthy ways.

title: Verbal and Nonverbal Communication
text:
There are things you can do to communicate verbally and nonverbally. Verbal communication is sharing your ideas through words and sign language. Nonverbal communication is sharing thoughts and ideas through facial expressions and body language.

“Stop!” is verbal communication. It tells others you need them to stop what they are doing. Putting your hand out in front of you is nonverbal communication that also communicates that you want someone to stop what they are doing.

title: Assertive Communication
text:
The way you act and the words you say are messages you send to others. Even the face you make after something gross happens communicates with others. You are in charge of what messages you send to others. Being assertive means being able to stand up for your needs or rights and the needs or rights of others in a calm way. Assertive communication is a way to send true messages that do not hurt others.

Assertive Communication Sort

Mark the communication that is assertive.

Your shoes are weird.

I need to take a break.

I don’t know.

title: Communication with Others
text:
Your social wellness can be impacted by your communication with others. Since you are constantly sending messages with your words, body language, and facial expressions, be aware of what messages you want to send. Family members, caregivers, and trusted adults are a part of your life. You choose how you want to communicate with others and which messages you want to send.

Who are the people in your life that you enjoy talking with and why?

What topics of conversation are important to you?

title: Opinions and Facts
text: Opinions are what you believe about information. “Saturday is the best day of the week!” is an opinion. Facts contain accurate information about various topics. “There are seven days in a week” is a fact. You can have opinions about all kinds of things. One of the most important things to learn about is how to take care of your health and wellness. You can study accurate information about health issues in books, on the internet, or in real life experiences. You will form opinions about what you learn based on what you experience. When you learn new things, you can express your opinions and share what you are learning about health and wellness with others.

title: Digital Communication Plan
text:
Communication online can be exciting. There are many people to talk to. There are many different apps and websites available to help people connect virtually. Social media can be a powerful tool to encourage, inspire, and share true information. The internet can also cause harm. In any virtual environment, individuals can share their opinions about any topic in the world. To take charge of your health and wellness, it is important to learn to evaluate the sources of information that you subscribe to. Be smart as you analyze information from sources online.

Think about:

the sources that portray accurate information

how your time online makes you feel physically and mentally

how you respond to the content you subscribe to

As you communicate online, make sure you have a plan to:

Share true information.

Respect the feelings and rights of others.

Be wise about what information you share with people you do not know. Do not share personal information, like your address, with people you do not know!

Communicating only or mostly online can affect your relationships negatively. Be sure to set healthy limits for your screen time and try to have more real-life communication and experiences.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
As European explorers reached different parts of North America, people from different groups, like the Iroquois and Patuxet, were brought across the ocean and saw Europe. People in the Americas and in Europe were not just curious about each other. As soon as they met, many saw new opportunities to meet their economic wants and needs. The people on the two sides of the Atlantic quickly exchanged goods, people, plants, animals and diseases.

This exchange between the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia is called the Columbian Exchange. It is named after Christopher Columbus. The Columbian Exchange had a huge impact on life for people all around the world.

Animals like horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs changed economic life in the Americas. Farm animals became new food sources. Horses changed the way tribes like the Sioux and the Comanche hunted and traveled. Riding horses was a much faster form of transportation than following bison herds on foot.

Many plants from the Americas also had a big impact on Europe, Africa, and Asia. American plants like potatoes, tomatoes, and corn changed how people ate. European settlers brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, bananas, and even honeybees with them to the Americas. Sugarcane grew well in the Americas and sold well in Europe. On both sides of the Atlantic, new plants on farms and in settlements often spread and changed even what grew in the wild. The world was truly never the same because of the Columbian Exchange.

title: Effects of European Exploration
text:
The people of the Americas met their wants and needs using resources from the land around them. They had vibrant societies and extensive trade networks. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had different forms of government and religion. They hunted and gathered berries, nuts, and fruits to meet their basic needs. They cultivated crops of corn, squash, beans, tomatoes, potatoes, and some grains. They created tools from the resources around them. They traveled by walking or using boats on the waterways.

The Europeans used natural resources to create manufactured goods. They had their own forms of government and religion. They fed their families by farming and going to markets. The Europeans domesticated animals to keep on their farms. This meant they didn’t have to hunt for food. They had horses to help with the work on farms and at the markets. They cultivated grain crops of wheat, oats, and barley. The Europeans developed different modes of transportation. They used wagons and carts on land and ships on the sea.

When these two societies met, there were intentional and unintentional consequences. The two groups traded ideas for the design of tools and transportation. The Europeans brought domesticated animals, such as pigs, chickens, and horses, with them on their ships. The people of the Americas gave them plants, food, and precious metals. Sign language and gestures were used to help the two cultures communicate with each other.

Tolerance of differences between the two cultures could have expanded the positive exchanges. However, the Europeans were not tolerant of the differences they encountered. They believed the peoples of the Americas were inferior because their ways were different. Intolerance caused conflict and the captivity and deaths of many Native People. The introduction of domesticated animals in the Americas caused imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation had nothing to eat.

The most deadly exchange was unintentional. The Europeans brought diseases with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. The people of the Americas had never been exposed to such deadly germs. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of disease were easily transported by unsuspecting people. Historians estimate that disease killed 90 percent of the native population within 150 years.

title: Natalia's Quest for Information
text: Natalia is in third grade, just like you! She was assigned to do a research project on her favorite animal, which is penguins. She is very excited about this project. Where should she turn for information? She decides to use the internet. The internet is full of great information that can help you learn and grow.

title: Natalia Gets Help
text:
The next day at school, Natalia told her teacher, Ms. Johnson, what happened while she was researching. Natalia told Ms. J that it made her nervous. Ms. J reviewed the school internet use rules and policies with Natalia. Natalia asked if Ms. J knew of a way to stay away from or avoid situations like this next time. Ms. J told Natalia that school computers have protections set up so that those kinds of messages will not appear. Ms. J also helped Natalia by giving her a list of safe and approved websites to use to research her topic in the future. Ms. J reminded Natalia that it is important to make smart choices when using the internet so she can be safe.

Ms. J's Reminders:

Never share personal information with someone online.

Don’t communicate with someone you do not know.

Do not click on links to random websites.

Ask a trusted adult for help if you feel unsafe or uncomfortable.

title: Smart Choices = Healthy Choices
text: You will have many different experiences while using the internet. It can be an amazing tool! Natalia was able to learn so much about penguins and create an amazing presentation. If you follow school and home rules and safety guidelines when you use the computer, you can have positive experiences. Let’s practice some safe choices!

title: Physical Benefits
text: When you participate in different physical activities, your body learns and practices new ways to move. For example, if you are learning to play basketball, you will learn to dribble a ball and shoot a basket. If you are learning to dance, you learn various positions and movement sequences. A sequence is an order in which events are done. As you practice, your body develops more control, or the ability to decide and execute a movement. Practice also helps with stability, which is the ability to hold still, and balance, which is the ability to distribute weight evenly to perform the movements.

title: Emotional Benefits
text: In a bad mood? Move your body! Exercising every day can improve your mood. When you exercise, the hormones in your body change. Physical activity helps your brain produce feel-good hormones that help you feel happier and less stressed. Movement and activity can also help you regulate your emotions. Regulating emotions means being able to feel and deal with your emotions in a healthy way. You can often release many of your negative emotions, like stress, frustration, or even sadness, when you get your heart rate up through physical activity.

title: Growth Mindset
text:
Are you taller than you were when you were two years old? ________

Do you know more than you did in school last year? _______

You have grown! You can grow physically, mentally, emotionally, socially, and academically. Believing that you can grow and learn new things is having a growth mindset. If you have a growth mindset, you believe that if you work hard, you can reach any goal. When you believe you can grow, you may be more willing to try new things and set big goals.

title: Fixed Mindset
text:
“This is too hard for me.”

“I don’t know how to do that. I can’t.”

“I could never do something that difficult.”

These are all things that a person with a fixed mindset might say or think. A fixed mindset means believing that you cannot learn or get better at things.

How do you think a fixed mindset affects a person’s ability to learn something new? _________________________________________________________________________

What could happen if you have a fixed mindset?

_________________________________________________________________________

title: F.A.I.L. = First Attempt In Learning
text: When you have a growth mindset, you learn from your mistakes. You recognize that you did something wrong and figure out how you can do it better next time. For example, you may get a math problem wrong. Does that mean you are bad at math? No! It just means you learned a way not to do it. Now, you can ask questions and learn how to do it correctly next time. If you have a growth mindset, mistakes don’t need to make you sad or frustrated. Instead, you can look at them as opportunities to learn and grow.

title: Work Hard!
text:
Cameron has a goal to climb a mountain, but he doesn’t believe he can do it. Should he even try?

A fixed mindset can convince you that it isn’t worth trying new things because you might fail. Fixed mindset thinking can persuade you to give up or not start. Cameron may not feel very motivated to work toward his goals if he doesn't believe he can accomplish them.

Working hard helps you use growth mindset thinking. When you work on a problem, you can figure it out. Cameron can make it to the top of the mountain hike if he believes he can and if he works hard. You can reach any goal through hard work when you have a growth mindset.

title: Opportunity Cost
text: People make choices on how to spend their money. Sometimes we want more than one thing at a time. This means we have to make a choice. We have to decide what to keep and what to give up. Opportunity cost is the value of what you give up when you make a choice. Imagine you have $20. Your friends want to go see the new movie, but there is also a book you would like to buy. Before you can make a choice, you need to find out how expensive each option is. You might ask a friend or family member for advice. If you are patient, the price may drop in a few weeks. It might be a good idea to wait for that to happen. Whichever you choose, you also have to think about the opportunity cost. It can be a hard choice!

title: What Is Fear?
text:
Different situations and experiences can cause different emotions. Fear is the emotion of feeling threatened or in danger.

Some fears are because of a bad experience.

A person who has been stung by a bee might feel afraid when they see a bee.

Fear can be a good thing. It can warn you if you are in danger.

A person can have fears because of things they don’t know.

A child walking home alone in the dark might feel afraid and feel the need to call someone to pick them up.

A person may be afraid of the dentist because so many people say it is horrible. But have you actually ever had a bad experience with the dentist?

When you are afraid of something, ask, “Why am I afraid of this thing?” Maybe you don’t need to be afraid at all!

title: Molly’s Fear
text: Molly is in third grade, just like you! She is having a special visitor in her class today. The visitor works at the zoo and is bringing reptiles to show to the class, including three snakes. Molly is very afraid of snakes. When she sees snakes, she feels fear.

title: Effects of Molly’s Fear
text:
When someone is sad, they may cry or wear a frowny face. When someone is happy, they may laugh or smile.

What does fear look like? Everyone shows fear differently. Some people might cry or tremble (shake) or scream. Other people might run away or hide. Other people stay silent when they feel afraid.

When Molly saw the snake, she felt afraid. She started biting her nails and breathing quickly.

title: Molly Manages Her Fears
text:
Coping means doing something to make you feel better. There are many ways to cope with fear.

Molly chose to close her eyes and think about puppies. She loves puppies. They always help her feel happy and calm. Molly chose a healthy way to cope with her fear.

There are many healthy things you can do to cope with fears. Here a few you can try when you feel afraid:

Think of something you enjoy (like Molly did).

Recite poetry or music lyrics that help you feel better.

Take deep, slow breaths.

Write or draw about your feelings.

Talk to someone about how you feel.

Sing a song.

Draw a picture of what you like to do to help you feel better when you feel afraid.

title: Molly Asks for Help
text:
Thinking about puppies made Molly feel a little better. But then she opened her eyes and the zoo worker brought out another snake. Molly felt very afraid and overwhelmed. She decided to ask her teacher for help. She said, “Excuse me, Mr. Taylor. This snake is making me very nervous. Can I wait outside of the room until the snakes are put away?” Her teacher said, “Of course. I will come and get you when we are done with the snakes.”

How do you think Molly handled her fear? When she asked for help, she was calm and clear about what she needed. She got the help she needed.

title: Write Your Own Story
text: Create a comic strip on a separate sheet of paper to tell the story of someone handling their fear in a healthy way, like Molly did.

title: What Did You Learn?
text: On a separate sheet of paper, write or draw what you have learned about fear and coping with fear.

title: Stress Is …
text:
Stress is a feeling. Many things can cause stress. Many things can relieve (lessen) stressful feelings. Stress can come because of …

Problems with friends

Having a lot to do

Arguments with family members

Stress usually happens when you feel overwhelmed or under pressure. Not all stress is bad. Some stress is good for you! It can motivate you to work hard and solve problems.

title: Good Stress
text:
Jackson is stressed. He feels stressed because he has a long to-do list. He needs to clean his room, take out the trash, do his homework, write a thank-you note, and help make dinner.

Can Jackson get all these things done? Yes! The stress Jackson is feeling is healthy. It is eustress. Eustress is stress that helps you get things done and work hard.

title: Bad Stress
text: When you feel too much stress, it may become distress. Distress is stress that affects you negatively. You may feel distress when you have experiences that leave you feeling overwhelmed, hopeless, or like everything is out of your control. Things like arguments, illnesses, or big changes can cause distress. Distress can make you feel sad, frustrated, or even scared. It can make it hard for you to focus in school. It can even make you feel physically sick with a headache or stomach ache. If you are experiencing distress, you may have a hard time sleeping or eating. There are things you can do to reduce distress.

title: Jackson Feels Distress
text:
Jackson worked hard and got everything on his list done. Way to go, Jackson!

The next day, Jackson experienced stress again, but it was different. He had another busy day planned. But his healthy stress turned to distress when Jackson's mom told him she could not drive him to school today. He would have to take the bus, and he hated riding the bus.

Jackson's stress turned to distress again when he realized he had studied the wrong topic for his science test and was not prepared.

These experiences caused Jackson distress. He cried and did not want to stay at school or do his chores or play with friends. He was overwhelmed.

title: Handling Eustress
text: If you are feeling eustress (good stress), the best way to handle it is by getting things done! What did Jackson do when he had his big to-do list? He started working on it! Being positive and productive is a good way to deal with eustress.

title: Handling Distress
text:
If you are feeling distress, you can try some of these things to help you feel better:

Figure out what exactly is causing the distress.

Tell someone how you are feeling.

Ask for help to solve the problem .

Distract yourself from the thing causing distress. You could try:

singing

dancing

coloring

writing

exercising

Recite poetry or listen to music that helps you get motivated or feel calm.

Ask a parent or guardian to tell you a story about a time they felt stressed and how they handled it.

Take deep breaths. Try stretching or doing yoga.

Spend time in places and with people you are comfortable with, where you feel safe (that could even be your school or a public library).

title: Essential Question
text: What were the cultural customs of ancient civilizations in the Americas?

title: Ancient Civilizations in the Americas
text:
Before European exploration and colonization, thousands of Native People lived in the Americas and the Caribbean Islands. However, their ancestors were not originally from these regions. Historians, scientists, and archaeologists have developed many theories to explain how the Native People first arrived in the Western Hemisphere.

For many years, researchers believed that the ancient ancestors of the Native Peoples came to America from Siberia, a region in northern Asia. They concluded that these people arrived about 12,000 years ago by hiking across a narrow strip of land that once bridged Asia and Alaska. This land bridge is known as the Bering Strait. From there, they settled in other areas of North America. Eventually, they migrated to Central and South America and the Caribbean Islands.

In recent years, however, archaeologists in North and South America have discovered ancient tools, weapons, campsites, and skeletons that are even older than artifacts from the land-bridge travelers. The bones, in particular, were very different from those linked to the people who crossed the land bridge. This new research suggests that a large group of migrants crossed the Bering Strait as early as 30,000 years ago. This larger group split into smaller tribes about 15,000 years ago. Some traveled south through the Americas.

Other researchers have proposed that the first people in the Americas traveled here by boat from southern Asia, Australia, India, Japan, or even Europe, arriving long before the land-bridge travelers. These people may have later died out. However, they also could have joined the Siberian tribes who migrated from Asia to Alaska via the Bering Strait. Combined, these groups could represent the Native Peoples’ earliest ancestors.

This week, you will be learning about some of the ancient civilizations of the Western Hemisphere. Each of these civilizations had unique and distinct ways of life. Each had different types of economies, governments, and social and cultural practices. As you study each civilization, take notice of the similarities and differences between each group.

Aztec

The Aztec arrived in Mesoamerica around 1200 C.E. They built their capital city, Tenochtitlán, on artificial islands in the middle of Lake Texcoco. They had a sophisticated agricultural system that utilized irrigation and “floating gardens.” This allowed them to grow much of their own food. The Aztec also formed political alliances with two neighboring tribes that helped to expand their empire. Today, the capital city of Tenochtitlán has become what is now Mexico City, Mexico.

Maya

The Maya Empire lasted for nearly 3,000 years, from 1800 B.C.E. to about 900 C.E. The empire covered parts of what are now Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Belize. The Maya were advanced mathematicians and agriculturalists. They knew how to rotate crops to keep farm soil from being overused. They used math to create complex architecture and accurate calendars. The Maya had a written hieroglyphic language and a sophisticated government system. This civilization existed between many independent city-states. Trade existed between the city-states. However, each settlement tended to manage its own people.

Mississippians

The Mississippians, also known as the Mound Builders, lived in the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys from about 1000 to 1700 C.E. This culture received its name from the raised mounds found in the ruins of its ancient cities. The Mound Builders settled in places all over the eastern half of the U.S. Not much is known about the purpose of the mounds they built. Some researchers believe they could have housed a settlement’s rulers. The mounds were also likely a central location for Mississippian settlements.

Inca

The Inca Empire was one of the largest empires in the world from around 1400 C.E. until its end in 1533 C.E. The Inca lived in and around the Andes Mountains and called their empire Tahuantinsuyu. This translates to “four quarters,” which is how they divided their government. The empire had a population of 10 million people that spoke 30 different languages.

title: Aztec
text:
The Aztec Empire grew rapidly through the 14th century. Its people conquered neighboring peoples and built impressive, thriving cities. At its peak, the Aztec Empire had a population of around five or six million, including conquered peoples. Tenochtítlan, the capital city of the Aztec Empire, had a population of over 140,000, making it the most densely populated city to ever exist in Mesoamerica.

Aztec society was incredibly advanced for its time. The Aztec government was a monarchy, ruled by a monarch known as an emperor. The emperor worked with a council of four advisors to make all decisions for the empire. The empire was organized into provinces, which were required to pay a tribute, or tax, to the emperor, depending on each province’s production. The Aztec government had many of the same systems and leadership roles that we have in our own society today. These included legal courts, a military, governors, tax collectors, postal and messenger services, and more.

The Aztec had a social hierarchy in which individuals were identified as nobles, commoners, serfs, or enslaved people. The noble class was made up of government and military leaders, priests, and lords. The king held the highest rank in the nobility. Commoners were farmers and artisans. Serfs and enslaved people were the lowest-ranking people in the Aztec social structure. Even though there were four main rankings in the Aztec social hierarchy, everyone in Aztec society who wasn’t in the noble class was considered a commoner.

Aztec agriculture was advanced and very successful because the Aztec were both farm laborers and experts in seeding and crop rotation. The Aztec were the first Mesoamerican group to extensively use chinampas, which look like gardens floating on water. This type of farming was necessary because they decided to build the great city of Tenochtitlán on a marshy island in the middle of Lake Texcoco.

Some of the crops the Aztec grew were sold at markets or exchanged as part of a trade. An empire as large as the Aztec Empire also relied on products and crops grown outside of their area. The cotton they used in clothing, blankets, and armor couldn’t grow in the highlands. It would have been acquired from tribes they had conquered farther south. Cacao beans, their primary source of currency, didn’t grow in the region and needed to be acquired through trade.

Regional markets sold everyday goods: cloth, knives, medicine, produce, pottery, and gems. Government officials were on hand, not only to make sure the prices were fair but also to take their share of taxes. Crops, goods, or cacao beans were taken from all the merchants. A vast marketplace drew thousands of vendors and consumers each day.

Long-distance traders known as “pochteca” were both a source of goods and a source of information. These traders traveled great distances over land to acquire goods for the nobility. This could have included special feathers or precious gems. While they were traveling, they shared information from different parts of the empire and even acted as spies. These spies helped the Aztec learn about their enemies’ defenses and made them easier to defeat.

title: Maya
text:
Some of the Maya’s great temples, pyramids, palaces, and residences still stand today, buried deep in the jungle. Historians have determined that the earliest Maya villages appeared around 2000 B.C.E. The Maya started out as farmers, but 2,000 years later, they were creating pyramids and making advancements in mathematics.

A class system existed in the Maya Empire. The ruler was at the top, had total power, and often had the duties of a religious leader or priest. Governors from four royal families controlled the land. Below the governors was the educated class, consisting of artists and architects. Near the bottom were the plebeians, including farmers, merchants, and laborers. Enslaved people and war captives were at the very bottom.

The Maya had a legal system, which included a system for determining guilt, wooden cages to hold prisoners, and fines. At the height of Maya culture, the Maya had 18 separate states. These states each had smaller towns and villages, all of which were governed by a capital city. Half of the states were ruled by a single ruler, while the other half were governed by a council of members of the nobility. Leadership positions were passed down through family lines, or a member of the nobility was elected by the council and religious leaders.

Maya cities included hundreds of homes and dozens of stepped pyramids. It took great engineering skill and mathematical knowledge to construct these well-built cities, the ruins of which have lasted millennia.

The Maya were very advanced in math. While we are comfortable using a base-10 system of mathematics, the Maya used a base-5 or base-20 system. Instead of numerals, they used three symbols: zero: a shell shape; one: a dot; and five: a short line or bar. Armed with this knowledge and no instruments, they made extremely accurate observations of the stars. For example, we know a year has 365 and one-quarter days; the Maya measured it to 365.242 days. We know it takes 29.53059 days for the moon to orbit the Earth; the Maya measured it as 29.5308.

The Maya grew many crops and even domesticated animals, such as dogs and turkeys. They were great hunters and enjoyed deer, armadillos, wild pigs, rabbits, and monkeys. The deadly jaguar was very important to the Maya culture, and a jaguar pelt worn by a ruler was seen as a very high honor.

title: Inca
text:
The expansion of the Inca Empire started slowly around 1400 C.E., through diplomacy and maintaining good relationships with the people and governments around it. However, when that failed, the Inca went to war. Their empire began to expand rapidly through conquest. To prevent uprisings from occurring, the Inca relocated the people they conquered to new territories that were unfamiliar and had foreign languages. This strategy prevented conquered people from organizing uprisings.

Stretching more than 2,500 miles from Santiago, Chile, in the south, to Quito, Ecuador, in the north, the Inca Empire was massive. Inca engineers solved the problem of communicating over this great distance by creating highways that ran along the tops of the mountains and along the coast. Teams of relay runners could deliver a message 1,200 miles away in less than a week.

The supreme ruler of the Inca was called the Sapa Inca and lived a life of luxury in a magnificent palace. The Sapa Inca ruled over an extensive political and social system. By the time the empire had reached its peak, the government employed a large group of politicians. This included four governors who ruled over the four quarters of the empire, or Tahuantinsuyu.

The Inca borrowed advancements and technologies that had been developed during earlier civilizations, including building pyramids, temples, and elaborate, terraced farms. The Inca worshiped several gods, the chief among them being the sun god. Inca mathematicians based their calculations on the number 10, including a decimal system.

The government kept track of all of the people in their empire with an extensive census-taking system. The Inca did not have a written language, but they did have a system of record-keeping using quipus. Quipus were knotted strings tied together. Historians believe that quipus held all kinds of information, including harvests, astronomical observations, important dates, and the census. After each person was counted, they were required to work on behalf of the empire and Sapa Inca.

In the mit’a system, or the tax system, in the Inca Empire, a person could farm, herd llamas, or build a road or a temple. People also offered military service or worked in mining operations. The type of labor you gave depended on where you lived, whether you were from a rebellious portion of the empire, and what your social status was. The empire divided all land into thirds. No matter where you lived in the Inca Empire, one-third of the land was set apart for the Sapa Inca, one-third was set aside for religious sites and temples, and the final third was set aside for the people. If your mit’a was offered by farming or herding, you worked on the Sapa Inca’s land or on temple land.

By 1528 C.E., the Inca Empire had seen its collapse due to disease, invasion, and rebellion. The impact and achievements of the Inca still survives, thanks to written accounts, artifacts, buildings, and roads that are still present. Around eight million people today still speak the ancient Inca language of Quechua.

title: Mississippians
text:
Around 1000 C.E., a people known as the Mississippians occupied much of the southeast region of the North American continent. Also called the Temple Mound Builders or the Mound Builders, no one knows for sure where they came from. They learned to work the land well enough to stay in one place and earned their nickname from the massive mounds they built within their villages.

The Mississippians are believed to have been organized into social orders or governments that included chiefs, warriors, workers, and even artists. Early accounts from Spanish explorers in the area describe powerful chiefs who lived in villages with large, earthen mounds and wooden defenses around the village perimeters.

Larger settlements extended rule over smaller villages. These smaller settlements existed on the borders of large trading centers. Less powerful chiefs paid tribute to the chiefs of the larger settlements. One of the largest settlements was found in Illinois. Today, the site of this settlement is called Cahokia. The remnants of Cahokia stand today as the Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site.

Mississippian burial practices also suggest that they adhered to a social hierarchy. Poorer people were buried with basic tools or nothing at all. Those with wealth or more social standing were buried with rarer treasures, such as ornaments made of copper or shells. Burial mounds sometimes marked the resting places of families of higher rank.

Not only did the Mississippians have sophisticated social structures, but they were also noted for their advanced knowledge of agriculture. Corn was an important food source that encouraged year-round settlements and population growth. The Mississippians built their large villages in the floodplains of large rivers. The floodplains offered rich, well-drained soil that was good for growing corn, squash, and beans. Nearby fish and waterfowl were also readily available in these locations. Deer, raccoons, and turkey remained important sources of food, too.

What they couldn’t grow or make themselves, the Mississippians traded for. Goods moved all across the continent through extensive trade networks. Archaeologists have found late Mississippian artifacts hundreds of miles away from the villages where they started.

The Mississippian people had a variety of different technological advancements, which allowed them to build some of their mounds as large as the Egyptian pyramids. Additionally, they did this without horses, oxen, or even wheels. This is impressive, given the time period. The Mississippian people had excellent engineers.

title: Lives of Native Peoples of North America
text:
For thousands of years, before European exploration of the Americas, people called these continents home. These first peoples were very diverse. They had many names that identified their communities. These communities were called tribes.

Today, the Native Peoples of North America are often called Native Americans, American Indians, Native Hawaiians, or Native Alaskans. Each tribe has its own unique customs and culture. These tribes lived, moved, and called the Americas home long before Europeans arrived.

Each tribe or nation had a different way of life. Still, cultures that had developed by the 1400s shared many similarities.

Each tribe had a sophisticated society of families, markets, and governments. They had celebrations and remembrance ceremonies. Oral histories of heroes and times gone by were in each tribe. Trade and communication were established to meet their wants and needs. Safety and security were part of each community. Entertainment and work were mixed into their days. All the things that mark a vibrant society in any time period were present in the tribes of North America.

title: Archaeology: How Do We Know?
text:
There is no cell phone footage. There are no documentaries. There's not even a photograph to prove that people have been living in the Americas for thousands of years before European explorers arrived.

How do we know that people were here for so long? How do we know anything about their lives?

People leave clues that help us understand them long after they are gone. Sometimes, ancient peoples left clues about how they saw the world in stories passed down to their descendants. They also left behind innovations we still use today. Some of these include crops, like corn, and medicines. People left behind objects they made, too. We call these objects archaeological evidence.

An archaeologist studies things left behind by people who lived a long time ago. Some objects, called artifacts, get covered by earth or water for thousands of years. Many become fragile. To avoid damaging them, archaeologists rarely use their hands to observe artifacts. Instead, they use dry brushes and other tools to clean them. This helps make sure that they won’t remove things like leftover paint and food from the artifacts. For example, stone tools that archaeologists find can reveal traces of foods that Native Peoples ate.

Archaeologists often recognize patterns. They may see differences between earlier objects and later, more advanced ones. They may find evidence of trade by tracking the movement of similar artifacts. For example, Knife River flint comes from what is now North Dakota. Artifacts made from this flint have been found throughout the western United States. They have also shown up as far east as Ohio and Pennsylvania. This evidence suggests that Native Peoples traded the flint all across the country.

However, archaeologists don’t only study objects. At archaeological sites, or places where there is evidence of past human activity, they also study structures and human-made features. Structures like Native Peoples’ homes can suggest whether a certain group had more of a close-knit community or a complex, sprawling society. Features like fireplaces or storage pits can also help scientists imagine what daily life in ancient cultures was like.

Archaeologists study these artifacts carefully. It’s important to show respect to people from the past and their descendants. Sometimes, when archaeologists dig, they unearth sensitive things. They may find places where people are buried. Some people think burials should be examined for evidence. Others think they should be left alone. New technology has helped archaeologists with this problem. Today, they can often scan areas without digging. Not having to dig allows them to show more respect for burial places.

When combined with other forms of evidence, artifacts can tell a story.

One of the oldest archaeological sites we know of in North America was found in Cactus Hill, Virginia. Here, archaeologists found evidence of a people known to have lived about 14,000 years ago.

As archaeologists dug deeper, layer by layer, into the earth of Cactus Hill, other artifacts were uncovered. These pointed to another group of people dating back around 18,000 years. What piece of evidence suggested that a different group of Native Peoples had lived there? The tools were not the same as the ones found in the earth above them.

That means that 4,000 years earlier, people camped, cooked, and fished in the same place as those who came after them.

Archaeology has proven that the early peoples who lived in the Americas were skilled. They built complex societies, traded goods with other ancient peoples, and had vibrant, sophisticated societies in America for thousands of years.

title: Trade Routes in the Western Hemisphere
text:
The best way to learn about the trade routes and sites within the Western Hemisphere is to study the findings at archaeological sites. The development of trade routes on waterways was tricky for areas in the Aztec and Inca empires, as they were based more inland. The different native tribes within North America used waterways and other types of routes to help guide their economies and enhance their trading.

Trade Routes in North America

For thousands of years, Native Peoples operated huge trade networks to get what they needed from other people in the Americas. For example, people in what is now North Dakota quarried a hard stone called flint near Knife River. The stone was so valuable in ancient times that 4,000 years ago, it was being traded for in places far from the quarry. Copper and obsidian have also been discovered far from their natural locations. This proves a trade network existed.

Another example of trade comes from the Hohokam tribe in what is now Arizona. The Hohokam traded bison hides for seashells. Neither resource comes from Arizona. The hides came from tribes on the Plains. Plains tribes often traded bison robes, dried meat, and tallow with other tribes for corn and squash. The seashells came from the Mojave tribe in California. By trading with both groups, the Hohokam became middlemen within a larger trade network. Middlemen took goods from one group to another in trade.

Rivers were extremely important when native people needed to travel. Many traveled by canoe on major rivers like the Mississippi, Ohio, Columbia, and Missouri. Some canoes could haul thousands of pounds of goods for trade. Rivers were the “highways” for tribes. If rivers were the highways, paths were like the smaller “roads” we use today. Paths crossed all over North America.

Native Peoples made and named other paths. One well-known route stretched from the forests by Lake Erie to the South Carolina coast. This trail, called the Trading Path, appeared on maps in the 1700s. Parts of it are still marked today.

Trade was very important to tribes and civilizations throughout the Western Hemisphere. They exchanged food, goods, and information. Some trade locations were more permanent, while others moved where the people went.

One example of a permanent trade location is the straits of Mackinac. The straits of Mackinac are where Lakes Michigan and Huron meet. This area in the Great Lakes attracted tribes from all over the eastern woodlands to trade. The Odawa and Chippewa had villages at Mackinac and conducted the trade.

Trade Routes in Mesoamerica and South America

Archaeologists have found significant evidence that the peoples of Mesoamerica were involved in short- and long-distance trade. Researchers believe they traded natural resources and the goods they produced with other cultures in the region, as well as tribes in North and South America. They traded everyday items like food, clothing, and tools. Aztec merchants throughout Mesoamerica also traded luxury items, such as quetzal feathers, jade, and cocoa beans. For centuries, the Aztec and Maya civilizations dominated the obsidian trade.

The Aztec, Maya, and Inca focused mainly on long-distance trading. The Aztec had people called pochteca. The pochteca were the long-distance professional traders for the empire. They ensured that many luxury and exotic items came from other regions into the capital city of Tenochtitlán. The pochteca kept their trade routes secret.

Researchers and archaeologists have looked into the trade routes of the Maya but found that there is little to no information to learn from. What we do know is that there were markets that were placed within most of the Mayan cities. The Mayan also had an extensive trade route that took place along the Gulf Coast and the river routes. These routes were managed by canoes and other types of seagoing vessels that could hold heavier types of items.

The Inca Empire, located within the Andes Mountains, used a road system to help transport their goods across the empire. With around 25,000 miles of roads, the main road ran north to south. It was connected by two main highways. One ran along the coast, and the other moved into the highlands. These highways then led to secondary roads that led into different parts of the empire and kept the cities connected. The use of llama caravans and porters was crucial to the trade network. The many rivers and the different heights of the mountains and ravines did not stop the Inca from building their roads. Instead, they engineered and built suspension bridges that allowed them to move goods and people across the difficult terrain.

title: Trade Goods
text:
Two thousand years ago, there was a great city of people located in what is now Ohio and Illinois. Modern scientists have studied the remains of the city. The artifacts tell us that Hopewell was a huge metropolis of people, religions, entertainment, and trade. The variety of trade goods was extensive and came from all over the continent. There, archaeologists have recovered ocean shells from the Gulf of Mexico. There is evidence of pigments, which were minerals and soil from the southwest used in paints. The paints were used on pottery, hides, and body decorations.

There was also evidence of mica. Mica is a mineral that is reflective and can be cut into thin sheets. Mica crystals are used in paints, pottery, and decoration. The Appalachian Mountains on the east coast of North America have deposits of mica.

The Appalachian Mountains in Pennsylvania and New York also have large pockets of limestone. Limestone is easily ground down and can be white in color. The white powder of limestone was used in the production of a variety of goods. Limestone can be easily obtained from open pits on the sides of mountains.

Ornaments, jewelry, utensils, and everyday items were also found in the archaeological digs of Hopewell. These items provide evidence to the modern world that a vibrant and extensive trade network was in place in the Americas by the time of the Hopewell city.

The different civilizations within Mesoamerica and South America also tapped into the rich resources found in the mountainous areas of the region. Gold, silver, and obsidian were mined and used to make goods. Obsidian is incredibly strong and is an ideal material for making tools. It was also believed to have spiritual properties and was used for ceremonial purposes.

Researchers have been able to link different obsidian items back to the Maya and the areas where it was formed. The Maya also mined other valuable resources, such as jade and limestone. The Maya had large marketplaces in certain cities that most likely sold or traded food items. This has been determined with technology and soil research in the area.

The Maya were not the only ones who traded food. The Aztec pochtecas traded and sold fish, maize (corn), chile, and cotton. The Aztec were also known for trading exotic or luxury goods. Scarlet macaw and quetzal birds were seen in places as far away as New Mexico and Arizona.

Trade extended throughout the Aztec Empire, and the leaders regulated it. The Aztec also relied on trading for products and crops grown outside of their cities. The cotton that the Mexica used in clothing, blankets, and armor couldn’t grow in the highlands of Tenochtitlán. Cacao beans, one of the most valuable products in the Aztec Empire, didn’t grow in the region of Tenochtitlán either. They traded for these goods or collected tribute from groups that grew them.

The Inca civilization, with its network of roads, was very similar to the Mesoamerican civilizations regarding the different goods they traded across the empire and continent. Talented farmers in the Inca Empire also used terraced farming. Their region included mountains and small plots of sloped land. The Inca learned to dig and reshape the land into leveled steps. This created more space at higher altitudes for farming. The Inca Empire contained several climate zones. Despite the variance in conditions, the Inca grew not only maize (corn) and beans, but dozens of other crops. The Inca also practiced crop rotation and used irrigation to support their crops. Agriculture became a key good that was traded across the Western Hemisphere.

The vast natural resources of the region led to extensive trade networks. Trade was an important part of life in the ancient Americas and helped civilizations to thrive and grow.

title: Trade, Barter, and Money
text:
How people use resources to meet their wants and needs is the basis for economics. There are goods and services needed or wanted in a community. Meeting the wants and needs of the community is considered a trade network.

The Native Peoples of North America used many different resources to meet their wants and needs. We see this in how the homes and shelters of the tribes varied depending on what natural resources were around them in the environment. Tribes on the coast did not have the same resources as the people of the Great Plains. The same is true about their daily lives and their art. To meet their wants and needs, people traded.

One tribe might have a good year farming and raising maize. Another tribe’s crops might be destroyed in a weather disaster. The extra maize of the first tribe would be needed in the second tribe. To acquire the maize, the second tribe would offer the first tribe another resource they had plenty of, such as furs or tools.

Tribes in a local region offered common items for trade. What was common in one geographic region could be highly valued in different geographic regions. For coastal tribes, dentalium seashells were common. However, inland tribes who had never been to the ocean found these seashells to be a high-value trade item.

Sometimes, a tribe sent representatives out to communicate and make connections with other tribes. Sometimes, the traders were welcomed with music and celebration. A market would be opened for goods to be shown. This gave families and individuals opportunities to make a trade on their own. This is called bartering. Each trader had to negotiate for a satisfactory trade. The trade depended on how much one of the traders wanted or needed a good or service. If every family had sufficient furs for the winter, they wouldn’t look to trade for furs. However, if there was a scarcity of an item, trade values would go up in that good, and more goods would be required to make a satisfactory deal.

The people of Mesoamerica and South America also had a system they used to make trade easier. They used a system of standardized weights and measures. Like many early civilizations, the Maya mostly bartered, trading items they had for things they needed and wanted. They did not have a particular kind of money or currency. They did try to use different types of valuable items, such as salt, obsidian, or gold, as a type of currency. They may also have used cacao beans as a form of money. A new study suggests that cacao beans became a little like coins and were used to pay wages and to buy things at the marketplace.

There was no currency in the Aztec Empire, so goods were bartered. Government officials were always nearby, not only to make sure the prices were fair but also to take their share of the goods through tribute.

The economic and tax system that existed in the Inca Empire was unique. Money was not used. Precious metals like gold and silver that were used as coinage and money in other parts of the world were considered to be sacred religious objects among the Inca. People in the Inca Empire did not buy goods but traded with members of their kinship groups, called ayllus, for the goods they needed or wanted. Since there wasn’t any currency in the empire, the government did not tax people for money. It did not even tax people for their goods. The tax system that existed in the Inca Empire was a labor tax system called the mit’a.

title: Trade Routes Impact Today
text:
We still use a lot of ancient trails and trade routes in North America today. Many major city roads and U.S. highways follow the same paths Native Peoples used thousands of years ago. For example, Interstate 94 (I-94) between Chicago and Detroit is on top of an old path native peoples used 11,000 years ago. Another example is Interstate 75 (I-75) from Michigan to Florida. This is also on top of an old native path. The original name for this route was “the Great Path.”

Look at the map and identify the trade corridors or pathways used today that are the same as the paths that Native Peoples used thousands of years ago.

title: Part 2: Recognizing Anxiety
text:
Annie Ant: So, what does anxiety look like? How can I tell when I am feeling anxious or if someone around me is feeling anxious?

Aldo Ant: Let’s explore together! Here are a few things that can happen in your body that let you know you may be feeling anxious.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your head!

Anxiety can cause headaches.

Anxiety can cause negative thinking, like, “This is going to turn out badly,” “I can’t do this,” or, “No one will like me.”

Anxiety can make it harder to focus and concentrate on other things.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your face!

When a person is feeling anxiety, they will probably not be smiling. They may be crying or have a frustrated look on their face.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your shoulders!

Anxiety can cause tension or tightness in your muscles.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your heart!

Anxiety can make your heart beat faster than normal.

Anxiety can make you feel a lot of emotions, like worry, anger, or stress.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your hands!

Anxiety may cause sweaty hands or trembling (shaky) hands.

Dr. Ant: Everyone point to your stomach!

Anxiety can give you a stomachache.

Anxiety can change your appetite (how hungry you are). Food might not sound good to you.

So, Annie, as you can see, anxiety can look different for everyone! Some people might only experience a few of these symptoms. Other people may experience many of them.

title: The World Before the Age of Exploration
text:
In the 1400s, the whole world was on the move. Empires were growing in the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe. Rich empires served as patrons, meaning they could pay people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and exchanges of ideas through trade routes. A trade route is an area used by merchants for economic purposes.

In the Americas, new empires were rising. Near the Great Lakes, the Iroquois Confederacy was gaining more control over trade. Trade was expanding throughout the continent, including what is now Mexico and South America. In Central America, the Aztec Empire was expanding. Aztec rulers were patrons of many great poets. In South America, the Inca Empire was expanding. Inca rulers were patrons of inventors who developed new technologies for farming, medicine, and bridge-building. The empire used this new knowledge to increase trade and exchange ideas.

Across the Atlantic Ocean, in Africa, the Songhai Empire was growing. Trade across the Sahara in salt and gold made the empire wealthy. Songhai leaders became patrons of education. Under the Songhai, thousands of scholars and students gathered to study at the famous libraries in the city of Timbuktu.

In the 1400s, most of the world’s population lived in Asia. China and India had the world’s largest trading economies. Spices, silks, gold, and other goods were traded all the way to Europe. In the 1400s, the Ottoman Empire was rising between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans soon gained control of trade connections between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans were responsible for stopping trade to Europe.

For merchants in Europe, losing control of trade with Asia was hard. The countries of Portugal and Spain, however, saw an opportunity. These countries looked for new routes across the sea to Asia. Patrons from Portugal hoped to make money from trade in Africa and find a way to sail around Africa to Asia.

By 1490, Ferdinand and Isabella were the king and queen of Spain. Spain had just ended a religious war persecuting non-Christians called the Spanish Reconquista. They had taken property from Jews and Muslims in Spain, which made them wealthy enough to be important patrons. Ferdinand and Isabella wanted new trade routes and income. They just needed the right idea to pay for and the right person to try it.

An entrepreneur named Christopher Columbus had an unusual idea. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean and reach India. Columbus was looking for a patron. He went to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand in Spain. Isabella and Ferdinand agreed to be patrons for Columbus. They paid for three ships Columbus could use. They also paid for the tools and crew needed for the voyage. Columbus made an agreement with Ferdinand and Isabella. The agreement described what both Spain and Columbus would receive if his journey was successful. This agreement clarified that Spain and Columbus would share the profits from any cargo he brought back.

Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. His journey would launch the biggest changes in government, knowledge, and trade the world had ever seen.

What was Europe like before westward expansion? Highlight or underline evidence in the article to answer the question.

Instructions:

Create your friction ramp.

Secure the bubble wrap to the front face of the cardboard cereal box with duct tape. Make sure to line the bubble wrap up with the long left edge of the box.

Using the duct tape, secure the piece of felt next to the bubble wrap.

Make sure the bubble wrap and felt are touching. This will leave you with a section of cardboard that is 2.5 inches wide.

Now you have three different mini ramps (one each of bubble wrap, felt, and cardboard) for the car to slide down.

Elevate one end of your friction ramp so that it has a slope. Use books to build a tower that can support your friction ramp. The book tower should be between four and six inches tall.

Test the toy car on the bubble wrap ramp.

Place the toy car at the top of the bubble wrap ramp.

Start the stopwatch as soon as you let go of the toy car.

Stop the stopwatch when the car reaches the bottom of the bubble wrap ramp.

Record the time in seconds on your investigation chart.

Repeat this to complete three trials, all on the bubble wrap. Record each time (in seconds) on the investigation chart.
