title: Academic Coping Strategies
text:
Speaking, reading, and writing are academic skills that help you share what you have learned. If you are going through something hard, you can write about your feelings and your experience in a journal. You can write a letter to yourself or to someone else. You can write poetry. You can write or draw representations of your feelings. Sometimes writing about your feelings can be easier than talking about them. Reading can also help you. You can read happy books to distract yourself from challenges or find solutions. You can read books about people who feel the same way you do to learn how to handle your challenges.

Academic coping strategies are skills that you use to share what you have learned. These coping strategies help you overcome stressors to your academic well-being. If you need to present in class, you can overcome nerves by preparing and practicing what you need to present. If you have a big test coming up, you can use academic coping strategies to help you reduce (lower) your stress levels.

Mnemonic devices

Help you remember small chunks of information

ROY G BIV is an example of a mnemonic device used to remember the order of the colors of the rainbow.

Positive self-talk

Helps you to stay confident

“I can do hard things” is an example of positive self-talk.

Deep breathing

Helps you activate your parasympathetic nervous system (the rest and digest system); this strategy simulates relaxation and helps your body get more oxygen and slow down your heart rate.

Breathe in for four counts and out for four counts.

Creating artistic projects or playing a musical instrument

Accesses the right brain and involves creativity in overcoming stressful feelings; music has a powerful ability to connect to a person’s emotions.

Paint a picture of yourself presenting successfully.

Playing a musical instrument can improve feelings of self-confidence and allow you to communicate with others (through the music) the way they feel.

Reciting poetry

Poetry can boost a person’s mood and improve their mindset or attitude when they are trying to overcome stressful feelings. Memorizing poetry can help you have access to the calming effect as well as positive messages contained in the poetry.

Memorize a poem about the weather, colors, or about someone overcoming something challenging. (This also strengthens short-term memory muscles.)

title: Problem-Based vs. Emotion-Based Coping Strategies
text:
We learned about many different coping strategies that you can use when you are not feeling calm or happy.

All these coping strategies can be split into two categories: problem-based strategies and emotion-based strategies.

Problem-based strategies are things you can do that would fix the problem.

Emotion-based strategies are things you can do that may not change the situation but will help you feel better.

title: What Is Motivation?
text: Motivation is what makes you want to do something. Everyone is motivated by different things. Motivation can help you build the courage to try new things. Working hard to reach a goal is impacted by the motivation you have for accomplishing it.

title: Rules
text:
Rules are instructions that tell people what they can or can't do. They help protect our rights. Rules help us know what is expected in our community. Rules help us live together and treat each other respectfully. They help everyone live together peacefully and fairly.

We can make choices about our actions. Our actions show respect. We can choose to follow the rules. If we choose not to follow the rules, there are consequences.

title: Rules at School
text: Rules at school are important. They help us show respect to all the people at school. Many rules are posted where everyone can see them. The principal and teachers make some of the rules. State leaders also make some of the rules. School rules teach us how to work together. We follow school rules when we treat school property with care. We follow the rules when we show respect for our teachers. We follow school rules when we treat library books respectfully and treat each other fairly.

title: Rules in the Classroom
text: Rules in classrooms are often made by the students and their teachers. Rules help us have order. They help us avoid conflict. Rules help us know the fair way to treat each other. This makes learning safe and fun. Class rules might include how we take care of our belongings. Another rule could be that we raise our hands to speak. Following the rules helps us work together happily and safely. Following the rules in our classroom shows respect for our teacher, ourselves, and our classmates.

title: Laws
text: Laws are rules that are written and approved by people in authority. Like rules, laws describe how people are expected to behave. There are consequences for not following them. Laws apply to everyone in a community. Local, state, and national governments create the laws. These laws protect the rights of people. Laws promote order and security in the community. They help resolve conflicts and promote the common good.

title: Laws in the City
text: Cities and towns have laws. Laws are made to help the city run well. They also keep people safe. For example, most cities have laws about not littering. These laws keep our cities clean and orderly. Some cities have leash laws for dogs. These are safety laws. Other cities require helmets when you ride your bike. When you ride your bicycle safely, you are obeying the laws of your city. When you don't obey the law, you might get a ticket.

title: Laws of the Country
text: The Constitution is the law of the United States. Laws make the country strong. Laws must agree with the Constitution. Every community has laws. If someone chooses not to obey the laws, there are consequences. A consequence is something that happens after making a choice and taking action. Consequences can be positive or negative. There are people in the community who help us obey the laws. Parents help us obey the rules at home. Teachers help us obey the rules in the classroom. The principal is responsible for helping us obey the school rules. The police are responsible for helping us obey the laws of our community.

title: Essential Question
text: What are rules and laws?

title: Government: What Is It, and What Does It Do?
text:
We need rules in school. Rules help us work together in an orderly way. Following the rules helps us manage problems and be safe. Our communities need the same things. Governments were created to perform these functions or tasks. A government is a group of citizens who lead a community. The officials make decisions according to the laws of the country.

The Constitution lists the laws for the United States. The people vote for officials to represent them in government. The people agree to abide by the decisions of their representatives. This agreement is called consent of the governed. The people’s consent is what gives the government power to act. The idea of consent of the governed comes from the Declaration of Independence.

The function of government is to serve the needs of the people in a community. Governments create laws, which help provide order. They protect people and their property. The United States government provides safety and security for the people of the country. It also maintains justice and order. It protects people and their property. The government also provides services.

title: No Motivation? Try Discipline!
text:
There will be times in your life when you do not feel motivated to do the right thing. You might not want to get things done. What do you do when this happens? What can you do when you are not motivated?

Try discipline! Discipline is training yourself to do something, even when you don’t want to. Discipline can help you make responsible and healthy choices when you don’t feel motivated. Here are some examples of students like you using discipline to make healthy choices when they weren’t feeling motivated:

Phirun chose to brush his teeth before bed, even though he was so tired and wanted to go to sleep.

Natalia chose to eat her vegetables first, even though she wanted to skip straight to her burger instead.

Pamela did not want to do her homework, but she chose to do her homework before she played with friends.

Have you ever had an experience like these?

title: What Is Resilience?
text: Resilience means not giving up when things get hard. Everyone goes through hard things. You can be resilient at school, at home, and in relationships. You can even be resilient in your own mind. You can choose healthy thoughts and self-talk. When you are resilient, you choose to overcome, or get through, hard things. You make healthy choices no matter what challenges you face. Being resilient is a healthy choice. You can choose to be resilient.

title: Resilient Emotions
text:
Emotional resilience means overcoming sadness, anger, or other negative emotions. It is normal to feel sad, mad, or anxious. But you get to choose how you respond to those feelings.

Here are a few things you can do to build your emotional resilience:

Recognize your emotions.

Accept your emotions.

Look for the positive.

Make a plan to improve your emotions.

Take a break, do something you love, talk to someone, or practice deep breathing.

You do not always need to be happy, but you can choose to be resilient when you feel negative emotions.

title: Resilient Social Skills
text: Social resilience means being able to be yourself no matter what is going on around you. It means bouncing back quickly when other people are not kind to you. Other people may not always choose to do or say healthy or positive things. You can be resilient by doing what you know is right and what you know is respectful. You can stand up for what you believe and refuse negative peer pressure. Another way you can be socially resilient is by adapting to change. Schedules, plans, or friends might change. But you can be resilient by adapting quickly and keeping a positive attitude.

title: Resilient Mind
text: Mental resilience means being resilient in your mind. When you are mentally resilient, you practice keeping positive thoughts about yourself. You don’t assume that other people are thinking negatively about you. With mental resilience, you can set goals and achieve them. You can have a positive mentality when you face challenges. When challenges arise, you tell yourself, “I can do this!”

title: Resilient Body
text:
Physical resilience is pushing through pain and discomfort in a healthy way. Can you think of situations you might need to be physically resilient? You can be physically resilient when you are exercising. You can run fast or push your body to build muscle or new physical skills. Physical resilience is healthily pushing your body to improve, even when it is tired and sweating. It is important to be physically resilient when you are sick. What does that look like?

Taking medicine, if necessary

Drinking water

Getting enough rest

Actively taking care of your body builds physical resilience.

title: Resourcefulness
text: You do not need to be resilient alone. You can use your resources. A resource is a tool, or something you can use to help you. Your resources might include: parents, siblings, teachers, coaches, books, the internet, or friends. All of these resources can help you be resilient. When you face any kind of challenge, you can consider the resources you have available to you. Resources can help you bounce back and grow during challenges. If you are going through a challenge right now, what resources can you turn to for help?

title: Communicate
text:
In class, Elias sees people speaking and listening to each other. He knows both are important social skills.

Communicating includes speaking and listening. Speaking helps other people get to know you. Speaking helps you say what you need. It helps you stay safe, happy, and healthy. Elias wants to practice speaking clearly and kindly. Elias decides that he will:

share his ideas

share his feelings

stand up for himself and others

explain and defend his personal boundaries

express his needs and wants

Elias also knows that listening will help him be a good friend. Elias decides to pay close attention when his teacher, grandpa, or friends are talking to him. He finds that when he listens carefully, they are happier, and he understands them better.

title: Standing Up for Yourself and Others
text:
Being assertive means standing up for yourself. If someone is doing or saying something you dislike, you can say, “Please don’t do that. It makes me feel sad.” If someone asks you to do something you are not comfortable with, you can be assertive and say, “No. I do not feel comfortable with that.”

You can be assertive by standing up to others when people are being unkind. If you see someone bullying another person, you can be assertive and say, “Please stop. Let’s treat each other with kindness.”

When you are assertive, you can help keep yourself and others safe.

title: Asking for What You Need
text:
You can use assertiveness to ask for what you need. When you are assertive, you know that what you need matters. You have the right to ask someone for help.

You might need help with homework or resolving a conflict with a friend.

You can confidently ask for help when you need it. When you are assertive, other people can know what you need.

title: You Matter!
text: Your thoughts matter. Your ideas matter. Your wants and needs matter. Being assertive helps you communicate that you matter. Train your inner voice to be a source of inspiration and encouragement to you. If you hear, see, or feel discouragement from external sources (other people, media, etc.), remember that you matter. Assertiveness helps you care for your emotional and mental well-being.

title: Help Others Be Assertive
text:
You can help your friends and family be assertive by asking them what they think. Give other people the chance to share their thoughts. Value the opinions of others.

If you and your friends are trying to decide what game to play, you can be assertive by saying what you’d like to do. You can help your friends be assertive by asking, “What game would you like to play?” and then working together to make a plan that works for everyone.

title: Trustworthy
text:
Good friends encourage one another to be honest and trustworthy. Honesty is telling the truth. Being honest is a healthy behavior. Being trustworthy means telling the truth over time. Trust is built over time. Every time you tell the truth, you become more trustworthy. People can trust you more. Being trustworthy helps you build positive relationships. Being honest and trustworthy can help you feel good about yourself.

When someone chooses not to be honest, it can be hard for people to trust them. Dishonesty (not telling the truth) can damage relationships. It is hard to trust someone who isn't honest. Lying can cause your health and wellness to suffer socially and emotionally.

title: Recognize and Fix Mistakes
text:
You can do your best to be trustworthy and dependable. Sometimes, when you are doing your best, you might make mistakes. Everyone makes mistakes sometimes. When you make a mistake like forgetting to take care of a responsibility, you can learn and make things right. You can:

Recognize your mistake.

Apologize to anyone you hurt.

Do your best to fix it by being honest and working hard in the future.

title: Goals
text: A goal is something you really want to do. What is your goal? Make a plan. Do your best.

title: What Are Your Choices?
text: You can choose what to say. You can choose how to act. You have many choices every day.

title: Did It Work?
text: Did your choice work? Was it helpful? What would you change?

title: Communicate
text: Communication can be words. It is talking and writing. It is listening and reading.

title: Words Communicate
text: Speaking communicates ideas. Signing communicates ideas. Speaking and signing use words to communicate.

title: Different Languages
text:
Families communicate in different ways. Some use different languages, like:

Spanish

French

German

Do you know someone who uses a different language than you?

¡Hola!

title: Communicate Without Words
text: How do you know a friend is happy? Friends smile at you.

title: How Else Can We Communicate?
text: You can write. You can tell stories. You can share pictures. All of these communicate!

title: Rights of Citizens
text:
Rights are freedoms that every person has as a citizen of a community, state, or country. Citizens of the United States have the right to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” This means that you have a right to be alive. Liberty means you are free to think, speak, and make decisions. Happiness means that you can create happiness in your life by doing what you like to do. These rights are protected and written in important documents.

The Declaration of Independence is an example of an important document in the United States. This document was written by Thomas Jefferson in 1776. It established the United States as an independent nation away from Great Britain. This meant the United States would have their own government.

The Declaration of Independence explains the rights of people. That is where the right to "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” is written. These rights are very important. The new United States government would be founded on these principles.

title: Rules Online
text: Rules for the internet are good to have. They help you make good choices.

title: What NOT To Share
text: Your name is personal. Your phone number is personal. Do not share personal information online.

title: What Is a Stranger?
text: Strangers are people you do not know. Most people online are strangers to you.

title: Good Character
text: Character is how you act and speak. You can show good character online by using kind words.

title: Speak Up!
text: If you see a problem online, say something. You can talk to an adult. You can get help.

title: Coping Strategies
text:
Changes in your life can be hard. You can do things to help you feel better about change. These things are called coping strategies.

Coping Strategies:

Take deep breaths.

Sing or hum one of your favorite songs.

Go for a walk and enjoy the sunshine.

Do a silly dance.

Paint a picture or draw.

Talk with someone you trust.

title: The Constitution
text:
The Constitution of the United States is the law of the country. It provides the structure of the government. The Constitution protects our natural rights and defines our civil rights. These rights include the right to live, to be free, and to create opportunities to be happy. We all have the right to be treated equally. Tribal nations, states, and cities have constitutions as well.

The Constitution defines the power of the government. It ensures that no branch has too much power. It also limits how much the government can be in our lives. The Constitution checks the balance of power so that the power remains with the people. The preamble defines the responsibilities of the citizen in the government.

title: The Bill of Rights
text:
The Bill of Rights is the first 10 amendments, or changes, to the Constitution. It was created to limit how the government can control our lives. It protects the basic rights of the people. It explains our rights as citizens.

You have rights in school because of the Bill of Rights. For example, you have the right to free speech. This means you can say what you think. It is important to be respectful when you say what you think. You have the right to be treated fairly, no matter what color your skin is or where you are from.

title: The First Amendment
text: The First Amendment is part of the Bill of Rights. It identifies and protects five important rights of citizens. It protects freedom of religion. It protects freedom of speech and press. It protects the right to assemble and petition the government.

title: The Government Provides Services
text:
Governments in the United States provide services to help meet the wants and needs of the public. Government services help provide order and keep us safe. They create opportunities in the community for work. These services support our health. Governments use tax money to provide these services. There are many examples of government services.

Schools: Governments use tax money to help provide schools with buildings, classroom furniture, and playground equipment.

Public Libraries: Governments pay for libraries. Libraries provide books and research services. They also provide educational and entertainment resources.

Recreation: Governments provide places of recreation. They provide public parks, playgrounds, and sports fields.

Fire Department: The fire department is an important government service that protects communities. Firefighters protect life, property, and the environment.

Police: The police department helps fight crime. Sometimes, police officers patrol neighborhoods. They make sure drivers are obeying traffic laws.

Public Sanitation: The government cleans and maintains roads. This government service keeps us safe. Trash pick-up and street sweeping are government cleaning services. Governments pay to help keep our public places clean.

title: The Government Provides Security
text: A function of government is to protect its citizens. Governments create laws that protect people and their property. They also provide services to help do this. Fire departments are government services. If your house catches fire, the fire department will help you. The police department helps provide security. The military is a part of our government. It protects the security of the country.

title: The Government Creates Laws
text:
The purpose of the United States government is to promote the common good. The common good means working to create laws and rules that benefit everyone.

The United States government makes laws that guarantee and protect the rights of people. For example, it is against the law to steal. This law protects people's property. Laws and rules also provide safety and security. For example, it is against the law to injure another person on purpose. This law keeps people safe.

Laws in the United States provide equality for all people. The government is responsible for making sure all people are treated fairly under these laws. For example, it is against the law to treat a person unfairly because of the color of their skin. This law helps everyone to be treated equally.

Government laws apply to everyone in the community. The government has the power to enforce laws, or make sure people follow them. Holding people and the government responsible for their actions is important.

title: The Government Establishes Order
text: The laws the government creates help us work together in an orderly way. Imagine if there were no traffic laws. How would we drive on the roads? Laws help establish the way that we do things in our community. In the United States, everyone has to obey the same laws. The laws apply to everyone equally. Laws are written down so everyone knows what they are.

title: Essential Question
text: What rights do members of a community have?

title: Essential Question
text: How does the government help your community?

title: America Coast to Coast
text:
The Louisiana Purchase doubled the geographic size of the United States. The Corps of Discovery shared their findings. People were excited to go west. People from the eastern states packed their belongings into covered wagons and headed west. They became known as pioneers. Pioneers are people who are among the first to do something. Trail companies were formed to assist the pioneers’ journey. The routes they took were the centuries-old American Indian trading routes. American Indians sometimes served as guides for the pioneers.

The majority of trail companies started the journey in St. Louis, Missouri. Multiple families joined a trail company to form a wagon train. Traveling together was necessary when crossing 2,000 miles. Many trails were named for the destination. The Sante Fe, Oregon, and California trails were destination trails. The Mormon Trail was named after a religious group that traveled that trail. These people were often called Mormons during that time, but are now called by the name the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. They, like others, migrated west because of various push-pull factors. Some traveled west to explore the land and its resources. Others moved west for religious freedom and opportunity.

Thousands of pioneers made the journey west. Each had their own reasons for the journey. The trail was perilous with landforms that made travel difficult. The greatest danger was the risk of disease and the lack of fresh water. People did not have the resources to wash their hands or bathe very often. These types of conditions spread diseases that were contagious and deadly. Many pioneers did not live to see their destination.

In 1848, the reason to move west changed for many people. Gold was found at Sutter’s Mill in California territory. This discovery created a rush of people from all over the world coming to California to strike it rich. Most of the gold miners were men. Women stayed home to take care of families, farms, and businesses while their husbands tried to find a fortune. The men soon learned mining wasn’t easy. They moved rock, dug dirt, and stood in cold mountain streams. Military governor Colonel Richard B. Mason wrote a report to President Polk about the gold fields. Two miners on Weber Creek gathered $17,000 in gold in seven days; six miners with 50 American Indians took out 273 pounds of gold. The real profit in the gold rush was in the sale of equipment. Sam Brannan's merchandise store near the mines earned $36,000 in sales in just 10 weeks. Supply and demand controlled prices and profits at the California gold mines.

The United States borders now extended from sea to shining sea. Thomas Jefferson’s vision was complete. The American people felt entitled and privileged to settle this vast country. Over the next 50 years, movement and settlement of the frontier expanded.

title: Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way by Emanuel Leutze
text:
Emanuel Leutze was a German-born artist who came to America as a child in 1825. He is best known for his painting “George Washington Crossing the Delaware.” In 1861, Leutze was commissioned, or paid to paint, by the U.S. Congress. The 20- by 30-foot mural he painted is in the stairway of the House of Representatives in the Capitol building in Washington, D.C. Look at the painting and answer the questions.

What would you title the picture?

Who is represented in the mural?

Is there anything or anyone in this picture that reminds you of anything in your life?

What do you think the light is in the left corner of the painting?

title: Solving Problems
text:
No two people are exactly the same. We each have different beliefs and experiences. Sometimes people and communities experience conflict because of their differences. Conflict is a disagreement between individuals or groups. Conflict can happen between two people. It can also happen between nations. Although it can be difficult, overcoming conflict is possible.

In order to resolve conflict, it helps to follow a conflict resolution process. This helps us to solve the problem step by step. Each step requires us to take action or make a decision. Some problems affect many people. Good solutions consider everyone involved, not just one person or group. We need to follow this idea when we are solving our own problems. When we work together, we can find solutions to many types of problems.

title: Essential Question
text: How can people solve problems?

title: Consensus and Compromise
text:
Consensus and compromise are two possible ways to find a solution. Consensus is when most people in a group have the same opinion or agree to the same solution. However, consensus isn’t always possible. People often have different opinions about how to solve a problem. It can be hard to reach consensus on a solution.

When everyone doesn’t agree, we can try to compromise. Compromise is when each party is willing to give up part of what they want to create a solution that everyone will accept. When we compromise, we are thinking about the common good. The decisions are based on what is best for everyone, not just on what one group wants.

title: Conflict Resolution
text:
There is a process we can use to resolve conflicts. The process has several steps.

First, we need to clearly identify the problem. This may mean gathering information that identifies the cause of the problem. This way, we can clearly state what the problem is.

Next, we need to think about solutions. There are many ways to solve a problem. It helps to make a list of possible solutions.

Looking at the advantages and disadvantages of each solution is important. For example, which solution costs less and would last longer? Which solution promotes the common good? We need to discuss these options with everyone involved. We often try to choose the solution that most people agree with. It is not always easy for everyone to agree on a single solution.

Once we pick a solution, we implement it. Some solutions may need money or help from experts. Experts can tell us how much money is needed. They can also show us the right way to implement the solution.

After we try a solution, we evaluate the results. To evaluate means to see how well the solution has worked. If the solution worked, is there anything we could do to improve it? If the solution hasn’t worked, we consider why. Once we know why it didn’t work, we can try again to fix it. Evaluating a solution can also mean collecting more data and starting the process again.

title: Practice Solving a Problem
text:
Jack found some beans that he believed were magical. He decided to plant them, even though his mother disagreed. The next morning, Jack woke up to a beanstalk that reached all the way to the clouds. It was enormous! Jack decided to explore the beanstalk. He climbed and climbed until he reached the top. On top of the clouds, he found a castle that was large enough to be home to a giant. He explored the clouds around the castle and found a golden goose that seemed to lay golden eggs. He decided to go back down to the ground to show the goose to his mother.

On his way back to the beanstalk, Jack felt the clouds begin to shake under his feet. He slowly turned around and saw the giant that lived in the huge castle. Before the giant noticed him, Jack scurried down the beanstalk with the goose. He ran back home, yelling, “There is a giant on the beanstalk!” All the townspeople, who had been confused about the beanstalk to begin with, were startled by the news. They decided to call a town meeting. They requested that Jack come to the meeting to explain what was happening.

When Jack arrived, the town began to discuss the dangers that this beanstalk had created for the community. What if it fell? How many resources was it taking from the town? Worst of all, what if the giant came down and attacked the town to get his golden goose back? Jack realized he had made a mistake by planting this beanstalk.

What should the town do to handle the situation of the beanstalk? How should it be removed without the giant coming down? Should the goose be returned? Should Jack get in trouble?

Gather information and clearly identify the problem: What is the problem? Why is the problem happening? What do you already know about the problem? What else should you find out?

List possible solutions: What are possible solutions to the problem?

Consider each option and choose a solution: What are the advantages and disadvantages of each solution? Which solution promotes the common good?

Implement a solution: How can we make the solution happen? Do we need help from experts?

Evaluate your efforts: How did the solution work? How could we improve the solution in the future?

title: Daily Life on the Trail
text:
Records and journals from 1820 to 1860 estimate 40,000 children walked across the United States during westward expansion. The trip took about five months if the weather was good for travel. Many pioneers joined a wagon trail company. The company provided a guide and map for the 2,000-mile journey.

Children had responsibilities with their families for meals and travel. To pass the time, many people told stories. The tall tale was developed on the overland trails. Tall tales were stories that were exaggerated and humorous in the telling. Children heard the stories of Paul Bunyan, Pecos Bill, John Henry, and Casey Jones. Spelling Bees became fun wagon train competitions with children and adults competing. Playing music on the fiddle was a part of the evening traditions. Men competed with complicated music to gain the prize of “best fiddler.” The hardships of the trail were immense. Lack of fresh water and food were common. Disease and injuries were part of the journey. Still, men, women, and children pushed on to find new homes and new opportunities.

James Bryant

Born: 1857; Died: 1937

Mother kept a small sack always in one corner of the wagon box; it was my duty to keep this filled with buffalo chips [dried buffalo droppings] for fuel, unless we chanced to find wood or timber; later it was sagebrush that we used. Whenever we came to a stream of water, there was always one of the men ready to ride his saddle horse into the river, if his horse had to swim he would return as soon as possible, but if man and horse could wade [walk] all of the way across, the company was allowed to march on through. If he had to swim we then made camp, sometimes for ten days, making rafts or floats to enable everything to be taken over to the opposite side.

Mary Jane Mount (Tanner)

Born: 1837; Died: 1890

Mother drove the team the rest of the way … Many times the bushes caught her dress, and she had no choice but to rush on, leaving it in pieces behind her. I wonder if those coming after her knew what those tattered rags meant.

Agnes Caldwell (Southworth)

Born: 1847; Died: 1924

Frequently it would be stormy so that a fire could not be built; then mother would allow each of us to have a piece of cold dried meat on a piece of bread. As food became more and more scarce [limited] and the weather colder, she would stew a little of this meat and make a delicious gravy over it. I guess the reason it tasted so good is that we were allowed only a small portion at each meal.

Rachel Emma Wooley Simmons

Born: 1836; Died: 1926

Independence Rock is the highest point on the prairie. It stands as tall as a twelve-story building. Pioneers knew this marked their half way point in their journey west. Thousands of people carved their names into the rock as proof they had made it that far.

We heard so much of Independence Rock long before we got there. They said we should have a dance on top of it, as we had many a dance while on the plains. We thought it would be so nice, but when we got there, the company was so small it was given up ... It is an immense [huge] rock with holes and crevices [cracks] where the water is dripping cool and sparkling. We saw a great many names of persons that had been cut in the rock, but we were so disappointed in not having a dance.

title: Conflict and Compromise at the Convention
text:
One of the greatest challenges faced at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 was dividing the power between state and federal government. Some delegates wanted a strong central government that had more power over the people and states. They were called Federalists. Other delegates favored a weaker federal government that gave more power to the states and the people. They were called Anti-Federalists. Both sides wrote essays that argued their points. These became known as the Federalist Papers and Anti-Federalist Papers. During the convention, several plans were presented to help balance the power of the new government.

The Virginia Plan

James Madison, a delegate from Virginia, presented the Virginia Plan. This plan gave Congress more power over the states and also provided for an executive branch of national government. This branch would carry out the laws passed by Congress. The plan also included a judicial branch to interpret, or explain, the laws. However, negotiations began to get sticky when the smaller states learned that states with larger populations would have more representatives in Congress than the smaller states.

The New Jersey Plan

William Paterson, a delegate from New Jersey, proposed a different plan. The New Jersey Plan said that each state, no matter its size, would have the same number of representatives in Congress. The large states didn’t agree with this idea. They felt that because they had more people, they should also have more say in running the nation.

The Great Compromise

Roger Sherman of Connecticut came up with an idea that bridged ideas from both plans. He proposed that Congress be made up of two parts, called houses. In the Senate, each state would have two senators, giving both large states and small states equal power. In the House of Representatives, the number of representatives would be determined by population. The larger the state, the more representatives it would have. Both sides agreed to the Great Compromise.

Slavery

The economy of the South relied on enslaved people to keep farms and plantations running. Many delegates of the North wanted to outlaw the slave trade, but delegates of the South disagreed. A compromise was finally reached. The slave trade would be allowed to go on for another 20 years and then be outlawed in 1808.

The North and South also disagreed over how to count the enslaved people when figuring out the population of each state. Population determined how many representatives each state had in Congress and affected collecting taxes. Finally, the Three-Fifths Compromise was agreed upon. Three out of every five, or three-fifths, of the enslaved people would be counted in the population. This ensured that state populations wouldn’t be too high in slave states. From their perspective, the issue of slavery was considered solved, at least for the time being.

Status of Native American Nations

During the Articles of Confederation, each state interacted with various Native American nations. Some states treated the Native Americans fairly. Other states did not. James Madison proposed that Congress be given the power to manage all interactions with the Native Americans, whether they lived within the boundaries of a state or not. This would bring consistency to actions for all tribal nations through the federal government. The final wording of the Constitution said that Congress had power “to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes.”

Individual Rights

Some delegates wanted to add a bill of rights to the Constitution to protect important individual rights. Others felt that since most states had their own bills of rights, this was unnecessary. Thirty-nine of the 55 delegates signed their names to the Constitution without a formal bill of rights on Sept. 17, 1787. Failing to add a bill of rights would prove to be a mistake that had to be corrected in the near future.

title: George Washington
text:
George Washington is often called the Father of Our Country. He was an active member of his community and nation. He served as the leader of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. He inspired the colonial soldiers to be brave and have faith in themselves. Washington led the new United States to victory over Great Britain. People trusted him and believed in him as a leader. He believed that governments should listen to the opinions of the people. Washington served bravely in the war with the other Patriots. Following the Revolutionary War, he left the army and returned to his farm in Virginia to live as a normal citizen.

In 1787, Washington was elected as chairman of the Constitutional Convention. He believed that the new nation could not and would not survive without a strong central government, national freedoms, and the protection of individual liberties. He worked with the other members of the convention to create a document that reflected their ideas for a new government. He believed so strongly in the principles and values outlined in the new Constitution that he was willing to sign it.

In 1789, George Washington became the first president of the United States. Washington tried to get the country's finances in order with the help of Alexander Hamilton, the new secretary of the treasury. He appointed Henry Knox his secretary of war. Knox advised the president on military matters and on relations with American Indians. He worked to create strong alliances with foreign nations. During his first term, Washington toured the United States and learned that most Americans supported their new government leaders. He hoped that the new United States would expand its territory west of the Mississippi River during his presidency.

He served two terms as president and refused to run for a third because he believed that one man should not hold that much power for that long. He set the standards for those that followed in his footsteps. Today, you can find his portrait on the dollar bill and quarter.

title: Alexander Hamilton
text:
At the age of 16, Alexander Hamilton enrolled at King’s College in New York. In 1774, he wrote an article that supported American independence. He then left King’s College to join the Revolutionary War. His bravery and courageous actions caught the eye of George Washington. He served as Washington’s right-hand man for the remainder of the war. After the war, Hamilton returned to his studies and became a lawyer.

In 1787, he was elected as a New York delegate for the Constitutional Convention. Hamilton did everything he could to make the Constitution become the supreme law of the land. He believed in the principles outlined in the Constitution and was willing to sign the important document. He helped write the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution and the new United States Government. In 1789, he became George Washington’s Secretary of the Treasury. As Secretary of the Treasury, he established the money system we still use today.

In 1795, he returned to New York to practice law. He also founded the Bank of New York, which is still in existence today. Today, you can see Hamilton on the 10 dollar bill.

title: Benjamin Franklin
text:
Benjamin Franklin was a talented inventor, scientist, diplomat, and writer. He was highly respected and admired in colonial America. Before working to create the new United States, he owned a newspaper company in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Franklin also served as a member of the Pennsylvania Assembly. He worked to make sure the colonists were treated fairly and had the same rights as all British citizens.

In 1775, he served as a representative of Pennsylvania at the Second Continental Congress. Benjamin Franklin brought consensus and compromise as he helped Thomas Jefferson write the Declaration of Independence.

During the Revolutionary War, he worked tirelessly as an ambassador in France. In 1785, he returned to the United States to serve his country. He served as a member of the Constitutional Convention in 1787. Franklin provided his wisdom and expertise to settle arguments and create compromise among the delegates. His ideas for government were the model for the House of Representatives and the Senate. He signed the Constitution in 1787. Benjamin Franklin signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

title: George Mason
text:
George Mason was a neighbor and friend of George Washington. Although he preferred life in Virginia to politics, Mason made very important contributions to our government. While at the Constitutional Convention, he faithfully attended sessions and spoke up on every topic of importance.

In the 1770s, before he attended the Second Continental Congress, Mason wrote the Virginia Declaration of Rights. This document described the rights of people. It influenced the content of the Declaration of Independence.

When the Constitution was being written, Mason was concerned that a list of guaranteed rights was not included in the new document. Mason was an anti-federalist. He was worried about the new government having too much power over the states. When the delegates voted to accept the new Constitution without a bill of rights, Mason refused to sign. He argued that the states should not ratify the new document unless amendments were included to protect individual rights. After ratification, a bill of rights based on the one suggested by Mason was added to the Constitution, protecting the rights of all Americans. This is the same Bill of Rights we have today.

title: Elbridge Gerry
text:
Elbridge Gerry came from a large Massachusetts family of 11 children. He grew up watching his father serve as an important leader in the community. As a young man, Gerry attended Harvard University. The more he learned, the more he felt that the colonists were justified in resisting unfair rules placed upon them by the British government. Gerry served in several local government positions after graduating. He was chosen to serve as a delegate of Massachusetts at the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

As an anti-federalist, Gerry was concerned about the proposed document of the Constitution. He saw several issues that he believed would make the federal government too powerful. He refused to sign the document unless several amendments were added. These amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

After the Constitution was ratified, Gerry was elected to serve in the House of Representatives in the new Congress. He later went on to serve as vice president to James Madison from 1812 until his death in 1814.

title: James Madison
text:
James Madison is known as the “Father of the Constitution.” Many of the ideas in the Constitution were Madison’s original ideas about the rights and freedoms that individuals should have. Our rights and responsibilities are defined and protected in the Constitution, thanks, in large part, to Madison. He was a very active delegate at the Constitutional Convention. He took notes, kept records, and made more than 150 speeches. When the Constitution was complete, James Madison knew it would take hard work to convince all the states to ratify it. He worked with John Jay and Alexander Hamilton to write the Federalist Papers, which were a series of essays that supported the new government. Madison wrote 29 of the 85 essays. Virginia was one of the last states to ratify the Constitution, and James Madison’s essays helped get the final votes.

Madison and the other Federalists worked hard to maintain the system of checks and balances among the three branches of government and protect the rights of citizens. In 1789, he was elected to the Virginia Assembly and worked to create religious freedom in his home state. He served as Secretary of State during Thomas Jefferson’s presidency. In 1808, he was elected as the fourth president of the United States.

title: Thomas Jefferson
text:
Thomas Jefferson studied many subjects including science, architecture, law, music, history, languages, astronomy, and mathematics. He believed that everyone was entitled to an education and that everyone had the ability to learn. Jefferson was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence. He was one of the first Americans to express the idea that all people are born with certain rights that should never be taken away. He felt that the only way to achieve this goal was to create a new, independent nation. His ideas of “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” would later influence the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.

During the American Revolution, he served as the governor of Virginia. He worked to create an alliance with France. He also worked very closely with fellow founding father James Madison to create religious freedom and equality in Virginia. Following the American Revolution, he served as the ambassador to France. He helped establish a trading relationship between the two countries.

Although he was not present at the Constitutional Convention, he believed very strongly in the Constitution. He agreed that any power not given to the federal government belonged to the states or to the people. He returned to the United States to serve as George Washington’s first Secretary of State. He served as John Adams's vice president until he was elected president of the United States in 1800.

During his presidency, the United States more than doubled in size through the Louisiana Purchase. He also worked very hard to keep the United States from war with France and England. Following his presidency, he founded the University of Virginia and sold his personal book collection. This later became the Library of Congress.

title: Essential Question
text: How did the Constitutional Convention attempt to balance the interests of all of the states?

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
In 1494, one man who had sailed across the Atlantic Ocean returned home with all sorts of wild stories. He described the new world he had seen, full of strange plants, animals, and foods. He talked about the people he had met there. This man was not Christopher Columbus or a member of his crew. He was a Taíno man from the Bahamas whom Columbus had captured and taken back to Spain. We don’t know his real name, but Columbus gave him the name Diego Colón.

After returning home, Colón told his friends and family about Spain. He described “the great cities and fortresses and churches” and “the people and horses and animals.” He saw strange “lands and food ... and bullfighting.” All were new to him, just like Indigenous peoples and their homelands were new to Europeans. As people traveled between the continents, they were exchanging ideas about technology, religion, and ways of life.

As European explorers reached different parts of North America, people from different groups, like the Iroquois and Patuxet, were brought across the ocean and saw Europe. People in the Americas and in Europe were not just curious about each other. As soon as they met, many saw new opportunities to meet their economic wants and needs. The people on the two sides of the Atlantic quickly exchanged goods, people, plants, animals, and diseases.

This exchange between the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia is called the Columbian Exchange. A historian named Alfred Crosby named the exchange after Christopher Columbus. The Columbian Exchange had a huge impact on life for people all around the world.

title: Plants
text:
Many plants from the Americas also had a big impact on Europe, Africa, and Asia. American plants, such as potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, tobacco, beans, cacao, and corn, changed how people ate.

In Europe, people did not eat corn; it was mainly grown to feed livestock. Potatoes, however, became a very popular crop for people. Potatoes can grow in all kinds of soil, and they are also full of vitamins and nutrients. Potatoes helped feed Europe's population better than other crops that had been grown previously, which led to better health and an increase in population. Potatoes also store well, and sailors could take potatoes on their ships. The potatoes’ vitamins would prevent them from getting scurvy.

Tobacco was first brought back to Europe by the Spanish. The Spanish experimented with the plant until they produced a variety of it that had a much better flavor than the original. The Spanish didn't share their secret recipe with the rest of Europe, which created a monopoly on their tobacco. However, the English were eventually able to obtain some Spanish tobacco seeds and plant their own crops in Jamestown Colony. Tobacco became a massive cash crop industry as a result.

Cacao was another plant that explorers brought back home with them. Cacao was mixed with water by native peoples to make a bitter drink. Europeans added sugar and vanilla to it, making it into a sweet food. That is what we call chocolate today.

Another substance that has its origins in American plants is rubber. The rubber tree was native to Mesoamerica; its sap has latex and rubber in it. The Olmec, the Maya, and the Aztec used the sap to create rubber balls for the ball game that they played. The sap was also used to make things like tile waterproof. Columbus brought rubber to Spain, and eventually, it became an important cash crop.

The people of the Americas were also introduced to new crops and plants. European settlers brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, bananas, grapes, wheat, cotton, and even honeybees with them to the Americas. Several of the plants introduced to the Americas grew well in the soils and climates there. In particular, sugarcane, wheat, and cotton did very well in warmer climates. Europeans began growing them on large plantations, which required them to clear large pieces of land. This destroyed local vegetation, and it disrupted the natural habitats of local wildlife.

title: Animals
text:
In the Americas, people domesticated very few animals. Llamas, alpacas, and guinea pigs were tamed and used for work and food. However, Europeans, Asians, and Africans domesticated many animals. Domesticated animals like horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs changed economic life in the Americas. These farm animals became new food sources. Pigs eat just about anything and reproduce quickly, which made them a great resource for meat in the Americas. Cattle were used to plow fields and also provided meat and dairy products.

Horses had existed in the Americas in ancient times, but by the medieval and early modern eras, they had gone extinct. When they were reintroduced, horses quickly became popular among the Indigenous people of the Americas, who used them in their everyday lives. They used horses for transportation and work. Horses also became a valuable trade resource. Horses changed the way tribes like the Sioux and the Comanche hunted and traveled. Riding horses was a much faster form of transportation than following bison herds on foot. Descendants of these horses are still found on the East Coast and in the western lands of the United States.

New animals also caused problems, however. The introduction of certain domesticated animals in the Americas caused an imbalance in the ecosystem. Pigs were turned loose to forage in the forests. The pigs multiplied until there were so many that they depleted the vegetation. Other animals that depended on the same vegetation were left with nothing to eat.

title: Technology
text:
After new animals were brought to the Americas, people adopted new ways of doing work. Although Native Peoples of the Americas farmed and grew crops, they did not practice large-scale agriculture the way Europeans did. Europeans brought new technologies with them, such as the metal plow, which was pulled by a horse, ox, or cow. This made it easier to plow fields quickly. Indigenous peoples could plant more crops and bring in bigger harvests.

Europeans used horses, cattle, and oxen to plow fields, pull wagons, and transport people. Over time, the Native Peoples of the Americas began to use these animals for the same purposes. They developed a special connection with horses in particular. Europeans also introduced ways to use wheels on carts, for making pottery, and to move water. Archaeologists and historians have evidence that native peoples used wheels on toys, but before the Columbian Exchange, they did not use the wheel as a tool.

Silk was an important textile (cloth) in China. It is derived from worms that live on mulberry bushes. Spanish colonists brought mulberry bushes and silkworms to Mexico in the early 1500s. Textile (cloth) makers from Europe showed Native Peoples how to spin wool, dye cloth, and weave. By the late 1500s, dozens of textile workshops employed native peoples, especially in Mexico.

Another technology Europeans brought with them were tools and utensils made of metal. Native Peoples used stone or flint to make their weapons and tools. Metal axes, swords, hammers, and eating utensils like forks and knives became popular trade items.

Europeans also brought guns and cannons with them. Over time, Native Peoples traded their goods for muskets and rifles. This exchange was particularly widespread in North America, where many tribes traded beaver pelts for muskets and rifles. This began to change the way Native Peoples hunted and fought in battles.

title: Ideas
text:
Like the Europeans, the people of the Americas had vibrant societies and extensive trade routes. They had art, history, and protection for their communities. They had their own governments and religions. Tolerance between the Native American and European cultures could have expanded the positive exchanges. However, the Europeans were not often tolerant of the differences they encountered. They believed the peoples of the Americas were inferior because their ways were different. Intolerance caused conflict and the captivity and deaths of many Native Peoples.

The Native Peoples of the Americas used the natural resources in their environment to build homes and make clothing and tools. The type of clothing, homes, and tools they made were different from the Europeans. Europeans believed that their own way of life was better and that they needed to change how Native Peoples lived and worked. The Spanish enforced these changes by making laws that privileged people who wore Spanish clothing, practiced Christianity, and spoke Spanish.

Native Peoples of the Americas also practiced polytheism, or the worship of more than one god. The Europeans were Catholics and only worshiped one god. They believed it was their duty to convert native peoples to Christianity. Christian missionaries crossed the Atlantic Ocean to preach to the Indigenous peoples. Some native peoples converted to Christianity willingly, but many others resisted. They didn’t want to give up their beliefs and their ways of life. This often led to conflict and fighting between the two groups.

There were, however, some Indigenous ideas that Europeans used or even exploited. For example, quinine was a type of medicine created by the people of the Inca Empire. It was made from the bark of the cinchona tree. This medicine could actually be used to combat malaria, a disease prevalent in Africa. Another example from the Inca is the mit’a system. This was a labor tax system created and used by the Inca government. When the conquistadors took over the Inca Empire, they used this labor system to force native people to work in Spanish silver mines.

title: Diseases
text:
The most deadly exchange that happened as a result of the Columbian Exchange was unintentional. The Europeans brought diseases with them. They had developed immunity to many bacteria and viruses over the centuries. Some of these diseases were related to being exposed to the domesticated animals that Europeans worked with and ate. For example, chickenpox is a disease that is thought to have originated in chickens, but because Europeans lived in such close proximity to their animals and because they ate chicken, this disease transferred to humans. After long and repeated exposure to these diseases, Europeans and their ancestors had developed immunities to them.

The people of the Americas, on the other hand, had never been exposed to such deadly germs. Smallpox, tuberculosis, influenza, and other strains of disease were easily transported by unsuspecting Europeans. This all happened at a time before people understood how diseases spread. It was also long before antibiotics and other life-saving medicines had been discovered. Nowadays, there are vaccines that prevent diseases such as chickenpox and measles. Native Peoples of the Americas had neither vaccines nor previous exposure. The results were deadly.

Native Peoples’ immune systems were completely unable to fight off the new European diseases. Historians estimate that disease killed between 80 and 90 percent of the native population of the Americas within 150 years. In some cases, entire populations of Indigenous people died.

title: Lasting Effects
text:
Some of the lasting effects of the Columbian Exchange can still be seen in the world today. Animals and foods from both sides of the Exchange spread all over the world. New crops allowed farmers on both sides of the Atlantic to plant and harvest more food than ever before. All over the world, people’s diets became more varied.

There were many lasting effects of the Columbian Exchange. Some were positive, but many were negative. One of the most enduring changes brought by the Columbian Exchange was not goods, animals, plants, or diseases, but the transfer of people. Columbus brought sugarcane to Hispaniola in 1493. Sugarcane grew well in the Americas and sold well in Europe. As sugar plantations sprang up and grew, the demand for labor increased. At first, Europeans paid or enslaved native peoples to work on the plantations. As the demand for labor increased, however, Europeans turned to the African slave trade.

People seeking new opportunities began crossing the Atlantic Ocean with the hope of making their fortune by farming land in the Americas. More and more people began immigrating to the Americas. Colonies began to develop. Some colonies failed after a few years, but many others were successful. Towns like Jamestown, Virginia; St. Augustine, Florida; and Plymouth, Massachusetts, that are still around today started out as European colonies.

Although there were many positive and negative consequences of the Columbian Exchange, it was undoubtedly one of the biggest events in history that forever changed the world.

title: Change
text: Change is when things become different. Change can happen every day. Big and small things can all change. Every living thing grows and changes during its life.

title: Weather
text:
How the air feels outside is called weather. The weather can change. Sometimes it rains. Other times it is sunny. Windy weather is good for flying a kite. Snowy weather is good for building a snowman.

What is the weather today?

title: Seasons
text:
Seasons are times of the year when the weather changes in big ways.

Winter is the season when it snows. In the winter, it can get very cold.

Spring brings new buds growing on trees. The weather warms from winter. Flowers begin to grow. Sometimes spring has a lot of rain.

Summer is the time of year that it is warmest. Usually, the weather in summer is sunny and warm.

Fall weather cools off and prepares the earth for winter. Plants get less sunlight, so the leaves on trees turn from green to yellow, orange, or red.

title: Growth
text: All living things grow. You grow. Your body is changing every day. How much taller are you today than you were a year ago? You can help your body grow. Eat healthy foods. Drink enough water.

title: Favorites
text: Your choices affect your health and wellness. What are your favorite foods? What are your favorite ways to move? Do you have a favorite toy or game?

title: Skills
text: You learn new skills every day. Can you tie your shoes? Can you write your name? Can you read? What skills will you learn next? As you learn new skills, your abilities change and you grow.

title: Responsibilities
text: Responsibilities are duties or jobs a person has. Responsibilities help people stay healthy. Family members and community members have responsibilities.

title: Families
text: Each person in a family is a family member. Every family is different. Each family member is different. Each family member has responsibilities.

title: Communities
text: Communities are made up of many different people. Each person in a community is a community member. Community members have a responsibility to encourage one another to make healthy choices.

title: Everyone Has Responsibilities
text: Responsibilities can be different in different places. At home, family members have responsibilities to take care of their home and belongings. At school, students and teachers have responsibilities to learn and grow. No matter where we are, we are all responsible for our choices and actions.

title: Managing Time
text: Make choices about how you spend your time. Choose to do your jobs. Choose to take care of your responsibilities. Choose to encourage others to take care of their responsibilities too.

title: Choices
text: Every day you make choices. You choose what you like. You choose what you don’t like. It is healthy to think about your choices.

title: Consequences
text:
Choices have consequences. Consequences are things that happen because of your choices.

If you …

… pop a balloon, it will make a loud sound.

… choose to wear a helmet, your brain will be protected while you ride a bike.

… choose not to tie your shoes, you might trip.

… jump in a puddle, your feet will be wet.

title: Warnings
text: Some choices have serious consequences. Warnings help you avoid negative consequences. Warnings help you know if a choice is dangerous.

title: Healthy or Unhealthy?
text: Some choices are healthy. Some choices are unhealthy.

title: I Need Assistance, Please
text: Everyone needs help sometimes. If you don’t know what choice to make, you can ask for assistance, or help. Ask a doctor. Ask a dentist. Ask your parent or guardian.

title: Growth Mindset
text: Growing means getting bigger or better. Having a growth mindset means believing that you can learn and get better.

title: What Grows?
text:
Organisms grow. Plants grow. Animals grow.

You grow. Your body grows. Your brain grows.

Draw three pictures of a flower as it grows.

title: Fixed Mindset
text: Fixed means stuck. If you have a fixed mindset, you think you are stuck. You believe you can’t grow. Thinking this way doesn’t help you learn or grow.

title: Growing from Mistakes
text: Accept mistakes. Learn from mistakes. Mistakes help you learn what doesn’t work. After a mistake, try something new.

title: Growing with Hard Work
text: You can grow when you work hard. Effort helps you feel confident. Learning new skills helps you grow. Trying after mistakes helps you learn how to keep going.

title: Changing a Fixed Mindset to a Growth Mindset
text:
If you feel stuck with a fixed mindset, you can change it. You can choose to have a growth mindset. Practice thinking about how you can grow. Say …

I LEARNED!

I CAN!

I WILL!

title: Spending
text:
It is necessary for people to spend some of their income on items or services that they need and items or services that they want. Needing something and wanting something are two different things. For example, if the wheel on your bicycle breaks, and you rely on your bicycle for transportation, you need to repair or replace it. You may want to replace it with the most expensive wheel that is made of the coolest materials, but doing so may not be the best way to spend your money. Spending all of your money on all of the items you want might mean that you will not have money left to pay for other items or services that you need. Decisions about how you spend your money are very important ones to make.

When people decide to buy an item or service, there are many ways to do so. If they have the cash, a person can exchange that cash for the item or service. People can also use credit or a loan to buy goods or services. Credit or a loan is when someone borrows money to make a purchase and then pays it back over time. When you borrow money through a loan or credit, you must pay back that money with interest (the fee you pay for borrowing the money). Sometimes, it is necessary to buy goods or services this way. For example, not everybody has enough cash to buy a house or a car.

Borrowing money from a bank is the most common way for people to buy property or housing. By doing this, you can receive something of value now and pay for it over time. In the example of buying a house, it might take a person 15 to 30 years to pay back that loan. Even though that might seem like a really long time to pay back a loan, buying a house or property is an investment. An investment is something that a person buys now with the aim of gaining more money from their purchase in the future.

An important part of making wise decisions about spending is to create a spending plan. By creating a spending plan, you can make sure that you have money for the items or services you need and save money for the items you want. A spending plan is an important tool to help you plan for the future.

title: Debt
text:
When someone borrows money from a bank, that money must be paid back. An interest fee is charged for borrowing the money. Debt is money that one person owes another. Individuals, businesses, and governments can have debt. Many people go into debt to pay for a house, a car, or college. If people aren’t careful with their money, they can also go into debt for everyday items. This includes clothes, entertainment, and food.

One way to stay out of debt is to save money for large purchases. Also, try not to spend more than you earn. To get rid of debt, begin paying it off a little at a time until the debt is gone.

title: Donating
text:
Whether spending, saving, or investing your money, your decisions should be based on good information and advice. This article is about another way that a person can “spend” their money: donating to a charity. A charity is an organization that is set up to help people in need. Donating is giving money, goods, or services to a charity to help others and expecting nothing in return.

For example, a person might donate money to an organization that provides food or shelter for people in need, and that money will help to buy food or items that people need to survive. They might also donate goods and items that they no longer need or use so that others in need might be able to use them.

Another thing that people might donate is their time. For example, a person might volunteer to participate in a park cleanup or help at a local food bank. While they will not receive income for their work, they are helping the organization do their part to make their community a better place. People must make good decisions about where to donate their money, time, or goods. Just like a person should research the best products to buy or the best way to save their money, you have to make sure that the charity you are donating to has a good reputation for helping the community.

Donating money to help others is an important act of community service and could be a part of a person’s spending or savings plan. Just like you can invest in property or a business with the expectation that your investment will grow in value in the future, when you donate your money, time, or goods to a charity, you are investing in something that will help other people get what they need to have a better future.

title: Architecture in Pennsylvania
text:
Architecture is the art of designing and constructing structures and buildings. Architecture can help historians and archaeologists understand the past and how people lived. Certain types of architecture can also help date buildings to a certain time period. Building materials and architectural styles reflect the resources available and the culture of the builders. Pennsylvania has many examples of different architectural styles that span over hundreds of years. This week will look at different buildings and styles of architecture found in Pennsylvania and how each came to be.

Because of the large number of Europeans who immigrated to Pennsylvania over the centuries, European styles had the greatest impact on Pennsylvania architecture. Swedish and German settlers built log cabins in their own distinct styles. The oldest building in Pennsylvania is the Lower Swedish Cabin, found in Drexel Hill. It was built around 1640 by Swedish immigrants and used as a trading post with the local Native American tribes. Its construction is a simple, two-story log cabin. It still stands today and is open for tours.

British immigrants brought Georgian architecture from England. This style includes pillars and domes. It is commonly seen in state government and public buildings. Some examples include the 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, the Pennsylvania State Capitol, and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The rural regions of Pennsylvania have more traditional styles of architecture. The urban areas have newer, more modern architectural styles in addition to older, traditional styles. In Philadelphia, you can find the older brick-style buildings, such as Independence Hall, just a few blocks away from more European designs, such as City Hall.

title: Essential Question
text: How does architecture reflect the natural resources and culture of a place?

title: Architecture Reflects Culture
text:
Culture is the way a society or a community lives. Culture is expressed in clothing, beliefs, art, language, and music. One of the ways people express and preserve their culture is through architecture. Buildings provide shelter and space for people to accomplish their daily activities. They are also places where people can gather for celebrations, government functions, and education. When you look closely at a building, you may be able to tell what traditions were important to the people who lived there.

When European explorers and settlers came to the Americas, they brought their architecture, or building style, with them. They also blended their knowledge with what they learned from native peoples. The state capitol building in Harrisburg has many beautiful artwork depictions of the people, their beliefs, and their culture at the time the building was created and dedicated.

We can learn about a culture's beliefs when we look at its architecture. Stained glass windows are an example of a building's architecture expressing culture. These types of windows let light into a room and provide some privacy at the same time. The windows’ images often tell a cultural story or illustrate an important event.

When different cultures come together in an area, they combine architectural elements and building materials to create new architectural styles.

title: Covered Bridges
text:
Covered bridges have been built all over the world for hundreds of years, particularly in forested areas. Forests usually have many waterways that make it difficult to travel from one place to another. This creates the need for bridges. In times past, bridges were usually built of wood because wood is easy to build with and readily available. However, wood wears out faster when it is exposed to elements such as wind, rain, and snow. So, walls and roofs were built to protect the wooden bridges.

When European immigrants came to America in the 19th century, they brought the skills and knowledge to build covered bridges with them. Though many eastern states still have some of these wooden covered bridges today, most seem to have been built in Pennsylvania. It is estimated that Pennsylvania once had up to 1,500 covered bridges.

As building materials and technology improved, covered bridges fell out of use. Stone, steel, and concrete bridges are stronger and more resistant to the elements. However, many of the architectural designs used to create the wooden bridges of the past are used to construct the steel bridges of today. Hundreds of covered wooden bridges remain a part of Pennsylvania's heritage and history.

title: Skyscrapers and Skylines
text:
If you go to a big city, you will hear lots of noise made by traffic and large groups of people. You will see these groups of people coming and going as they visit stores and shops. The other things that let you know you are in a big city are the buildings. Concrete, steel, and iron are used in city architecture.

Businesses need enough room to meet their needs. But big cities don’t have a lot of land for new businesses to build on. So, instead of creating buildings that are short, flat, and take up lots of land, businesses in cities will construct buildings that are tall and take up less land. These types of buildings are called skyscrapers. When you look up at a skyscraper, it looks like it’s touching the sky. This type of building usually has more than 40 floors and hundreds of people working or living there. The Comcast Tower is the tallest skyscraper in Philadelphia. It has 58 floors.

When a city builds skyscrapers around other buildings, the outline along the top of these buildings against the sky is called a skyline. A skyline is created by the patterns and order of the buildings. A skyline is easiest to see from a distance. Cities like Pittsburgh can be identified by their skylines because of the unique shapes the buildings create.

title: What Is a Constitution?
text:
A constitution is a written document that outlines the basic principles and laws of a nation, state, or group of people. Constitutions also outline the structure, powers, and duties of the government and guarantee certain rights to people in it. The United States has a constitution that established the national government. The U.S. Constitution is almost 250 years old.

Each state in the United States also has a constitution that is modeled after the U.S. Constitution. The U.S. and state constitutions can be altered, or changed, to meet the needs of the people currently living in the United States and the individual states. Changing and updating a constitution to meet the needs of people today happens through an amendment to the constitution. An amendment to a constitution happens through a legal process that requires elected officials and citizens to vote on the proposed changes.

State constitutions are important because they define the rights and responsibilities of citizens who live in that state, as well as set up the state government structures. Each state has unique needs, strengths, and ideals, and a state’s constitution reflects them. Like the U.S. Constitution, each state’s constitution establishes a written contract between the government and the people.

title: Fallingwater
text:
One of the most famous houses in the world is an example of how to combine nature and architecture. Fallingwater is a house designed and built in the 1930s by architect Frank Lloyd Wright. His idea was to use “organic architecture.” Organic architecture mixes human-made structures with nature. Wright designed the house to be a shelter but also to blend in or become a part of nature.

The Fallingwater house was built over a waterfall. You can access the river through a hatch inside the house. The casement windows open to the outside when you turn a crank. This lets the natural light, air, and sounds of nature into the house. Nature is right outside the door.

The inside of the house has large, open rooms. Large terraces can be found on several sides of the house. The fireplace was built around natural rock structures. The stone for parts of the house came from a nearby quarry. This helps to keep the feel of nature consistent throughout the house. If natural material was not available for parts of the house, Wright used concrete, steel, and glass.

However, you can’t see the waterfall from anywhere inside the house. You must hike about 10 minutes away to see it as it comes out from under the house.
