The house was originally built for the Kaufmann family. Edgar Jonas Kaufmann was the owner of Kaufmann’s, a chain of department stores. The house is now open to tourists who want to see for themselves how architecture and nature can work together.

title: Barns and Hex Signs
text:
A barn is a structure where architecture meets agriculture. The style and design of a barn can tell you as much about a culture as the houses. People and cultures create houses or other structures to provide protection and comfort. A barn provides safety and protection for animals and farm equipment.

When the Pennsylvania Dutch settled in Pennsylvania, they brought their knowledge and customs of farming and construction with them. One of their customs was to build a cantilever edge on one side of a barn. A cantilever is created when a large beam is extended beyond the edge of a building. A cantilever edge provides an open space underneath the outside edge of the building and adds extra floor space inside the building. No supporting columns or beams hold up the cantilever.

Barns were also often built into the side of a hill so that there was easy access for animals and machinery on the second floor. This type of barn created extra space for animals, grain storage, and farm equipment.

Pennsylvania barns are often decorated or painted with barn stars. Some cultures call them “hexes.” They are an artistic tradition passed down for centuries among the Pennsylvania Dutch. The patterns of the stars vary. Some stars have six points while others have 12. They are large paintings that can be seen from across a field.

title: The Constitution of the United States of America
text:
The Constitution consists of the preamble, seven articles, and 27 amendments. The preamble explains the purpose of the document. The seven articles lay out the three branches of government and the rules for each branch. The 27 amendments guarantee the rights of the people. The amendments have been added as the nation has grown. The amendments give clarity and specific rules to the government.

Article 1: The Legislative Branch

“All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”

Section 1 grants Congress the power to make laws in two organized parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Section 2: The House of Representatives is defined. The election of members is every two years. Each member must be at least 25 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least seven years.

The number of representatives will be determined by the population “... of free persons, including those bound to Service for a term of years [indentured] and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of other persons.” The country will be counted every 10 years in a census. If there is a vacancy from any state, the executive branch will call for an election. The House of Representatives will have the sole power of impeachment (to challenge and investigate a member of government).

Section 3: The Senate is defined. Each state will have two elected senators to Congress for a six-year term. Each senator must be at least 30 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least nine years. The vice president of the executive branch will be president of the Senate. The vice president may only vote to break a tie. The Senate will also elect a president to serve in the absence of the vice president. The Senate will have the sole power to try all impeachments. Impeachment will not extend to more than a removal from office in the government.

Section 4: Congress will meet at least once every year on the first Monday in December.

The remaining six sections define the rules and responsibilities of each group in the system of checks and balances. They help to keep power distributed across the branches of government. There are clear directions on what Congress is forbidden to do. Only Congress can raise and spend money. Congress is responsible for the Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, and Coast Guard. The representatives of the people are in charge of the military. The final section closes with powers forbidden to the states.

Article 2: The Executive Branch

“The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America. He shall hold his Office during the Term of four Years, and, together with the Vice President, chosen for the same Term.”

Section 1: A person who is a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for 14 years can work for the executive office. Once elected, the president shall take the following oath or affirmation: "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the Office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my Ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States."

Section 2: Sets up the president as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. It further defines the powers within the office for hiring people for government posts with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Section 3: The president is required to give information on the state of the Union to Congress.

Section 4: "The President, Vice President, and all civil Officers of the United States shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors."

Article 3: The Judicial Branch

“The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.”

As established under Article 2, the president will nominate a judge for the judicial branch. The nominee must then be confirmed through the Senate.

Section 2: The office of the judiciary will extend to all cases of law arising under the Constitution. It also covers the laws of the United States and all controversies between the state, citizens and states, and citizens and citizens.

Section 3: Treason against the United States is defined. Treason is giving aid and comfort to enemies or waging war against the United States.

title: Relations of the States to Each Other
text:
“The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.”

Article 4 establishes relations between the states. It also defines the state's relations with the federal government.

Section 1: All legal documents in one state must be accepted by the other states.

Section 2: Criminals must be returned to their state of citizenship by state law enforcement agencies. Any person held to service or labor who escapes to another state will be delivered to the person who claims their labor.

Section 3: Admission of new states to the Union is held in Congress. Congress can change any state boundaries when deemed necessary. State constitutions are to be a representative democracy like the federal government. The states will be protected by the national government against invasion or violence within the state.

title: Amending the Constitution
text:
“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution.”

Article 5: Unique to the United States government, this article defines the process for changing the Constitution. Other governments have to create an entirely new government or Constitution. This was usually done through much conflict.

Any amendments to the Constitution must have the people involved in writing, reviewing, and ratification. Since 1789, 33 amendments have been introduced over the years, but only 27 have been ratified.

One amendment that failed to be ratified was the “Titles of nobility.” This amendment would have taken U.S. citizenship from any American who accepted a title of nobility from a foreign country.

The last amendment that was introduced was in 1985. The District of Columbia would have been treated as a state. The ratification period ended without the required votes for passage.

title: The Supreme Law of the Land
text:
Article 6: This article provided for the peaceful transfer of power from the Articles of Confederation to the new federal government.

The new government honored all debts and contracts made by the Confederation Congress. This also established the Constitution as the “Supreme Law of the Land.” No state law could go against the Constitution. This article established the strong federal government wanted by the Federalists. There were still many parts of the country that supported states' rights. All disagreements went to the Supreme Court to be resolved.

“The Senators and Representatives ... and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.”

title: Ratification Process
text:
The final article of the Constitution defines the process for ratification.

Nine of the 13 states had to vote to approve the Constitution to create the new government. Each state held conventions where each part of the document was discussed. The Federalists and Anti-federalists practiced civil discourse. Civil discourse is when each side tries to persuade people to their views and beliefs in a respectful and open manner. There was concern about the absence of a bill of rights to protect individual rights. Compromises and promises were made to get the Constitution ratified by nine states.

The states and the dates of ratification are listed here, in order of ratification:

Delaware: Dec. 7, 1787

Pennsylvania: Dec. 12, 1787

New Jersey: Dec. 18, 1787

Georgia: Jan. 2, 1788

Connecticut: Jan. 9, 1788

Massachusetts: Feb. 6, 1788

Maryland: April 28, 1788

South Carolina: May 23, 1788

New Hampshire: June 21, 1788

title: Being Informed
text:
It is the responsibility of citizens to be engaged and to learn about what is happening in their community, state, the nation, and the world. This means understanding social, political, cultural, and environmental issues. There are different ways to stay informed. One way is to read and watch the news. There are different news sources available. You can read newspapers and magazines. The news is also available in print and on the internet.

The best way to stay informed is to research a topic. You can investigate issues to learn more about them. You can explore many sources and opinions to better understand the issue. Staying informed also means choosing news sources carefully. Make sure to choose sources that are credible, or reliable. That way, you know the information is correct. You can also talk to an expert to help you understand a topic more clearly.

Staying informed is a very important responsibility for all citizens, especially when it comes to voting. Citizens must be informed on the opinions of candidates and how they will address community issues. Then, citizens can make the best decision when voting in local, state, or national elections.

title: Serving on a Jury
text:
One responsibility U.S. citizens have is to serve on a jury when they are summoned. Juries are important because they help decide if someone who has been accused of a crime is guilty of breaking the law. This is an important part of our country’s legal system. It can only work properly if responsible citizens participate in the process. People who are at least 18 years old are sometimes called to jury duty. A jury is a group of six to 12 people chosen to help decide a court case. In the United States, you are guaranteed a “jury of your peers.” This means that the jury will be made up of citizens just like you.

If you are selected to serve on a jury, you will participate in hearing the court case. Sometimes, this might only be a few days, but in some rare cases, they can go on for months. After everyone has heard both sides of the issue, the jury deliberates, or discusses what they saw and heard, to make a decision. Jury members should use reason and logic when making their decision. In a criminal court, a jury must reach a unanimous decision. This means that all jurors agree on the verdict, or outcome. Juries must deliberate until they reach a unanimous decision. If they cannot, the case may have to start all over with another trial and a different jury. It is very important to take being on a jury very seriously.

title: What Is Fear?
text: Are you scared of anything? Fear is what you feel when you are scared of something or someone. Fear is a normal emotion. It is okay to feel afraid.

title: Fear of Mistakes
text:
Have you ever felt afraid of making a mistake? Everyone is learning. Everyone makes mistakes. You can choose to do things even if you might mess up.

Miguel was afraid to share his answer to the math problem with the class. He was afraid his answer might be wrong. He didn’t want to mess up in front of all his friends. What do you think he should do?

title: Fear of Danger
text: Fear can be a warning of danger. If you feel afraid, you can ask, “Am I in danger?” If the answer is “yes,” you should listen to your fear. Make choices that protect your body. Wear a helmet. Use sunscreen. Wear a seatbelt. Use the crosswalk.

title: Coping with Fear
text:
When you feel afraid, there are things you can do to feel better.

Spend time with your friends or family.

Think about things that make you happy.

Make smart and safe choices.

title: Talking About Fear
text: Talking about your fears can help you feel better. Tell your fear to someone you trust. When you feel afraid, you can say how you feel. You can tell someone what you need and want.

title: Fear of New Things
text:
Trying new things can be scary. Trying new things can help you learn. You can choose to try new things even if you feel afraid.

Draw a picture of something new you would like to try.

title: Anxiety
text: Anxiety is a feeling. Anxiety is similar to stress, worry, and fear. It is normal to feel anxiety sometimes.

title: Stories of Anxiety
text:
Gina has a dance recital in a few days. She feels anxious. She hasn’t learned all the dance steps yet.

Aleki is afraid of the dark. He feels anxious about going to bed.

Miguel is joining a new baseball team. His first practice is tomorrow. He feels anxious about meeting new people.

title: What Can Anxiety Look Like?
text:
Gina had an upset stomach every time she thought about her dance performance.

Aleki couldn’t stop crying.

Miguel felt frustrated and had a headache.

Did Gina, Aleki, and MIguel feel anxiety in the same way?

title: Working Through Anxiety
text:
The kids weren’t going to let their anxious feelings ruin their days.

Gina asked her brother to help her practice her steps.

Aleki chose to close his eyes. He thought of all the things he was grateful for before bedtime.

Miguel went to practice early to talk to his coach about his feelings. He said, “I am feeling anxious about meeting new people.” His coach said they would do some get-to-know-you games before practice.

title: Drawing, Talking, and Moving
text:
These friends beat their anxiety by taking action.

Talking about your anxiety can help. You can talk to your family. You can talk to friends.

Moving your body can help with anxious feelings. Jump up and down. Spin around. Run in a circle.

Draw a picture of how you can beat anxious feelings.

title: Hiro's Bad Day
text: Hiro was having a bad day. He was sad. Nothing was going right. He stubbed his toe getting out of bed. He dropped his toothbrush on the ground. The cereal was all gone when he went to eat breakfast.

title: Make It a Great Day!
text: As he grabbed his backpack for school, Hiro saw the sign on the front door. The sign said, "Make it a great day!" Hiro's mom put the sign there when his sister Marta had a really bad day. Hiro thought about the sign while he walked to the bus.

title: Breathe and Count
text: The other kids at the bus stop were already in line when Hiro got there. Hiro quickly got in line. He felt really mad about being last in line for the bus. He decided to take a deep breath and count to five. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Ah, that felt better. Even though he was last, he was okay. He thought, "Make it a great day!"

title: Ask for Help
text: When Hiro got to school, he realized he forgot his homework. It was still on the counter at home. He felt worried. He almost started to cry. But he thought about the sign on the door: "Make it a great day!" He decided to explain what happened to his teacher. Hiro's teacher listened. She suggested Hiro call home and have his mom email a picture of the homework.

title: Use Resources
text: Hiro worked hard in classes that morning. His stomach growled. Hiro was really hungry. He only had a banana for breakfast. He remembered that his mom put a small snack in his bag. Hiro opened his bag and there was a granola bar. It wasn't his favorite, but it would definitely help him feel better. At recess, he ate the bar and thought, "Make it a great day!"

title: Mom Is Proud
text: After school, Hiro's mom asked how his day was. Hiro told his mom that his day was great! He explained all the things that went wrong. But then he told her that he was able to do things that helped. Hiro's mom complimented him. She said, "Nice job using all of those coping strategies today! I am proud of you."

title: Coping Strategies
text:
When you have a bad day, you can also use coping strategies. Coping strategies are tools to help you calm down. Hiro used some coping strategies to help him have a great day.

Hiro:

took a breath and counted to five.

asked for help and problem-solved.

used resources to help him with his hunger.

title: Motivation
text:
Motivation is what makes you want to do something.

What motivates you to eat? It might be hunger, or it might be your love of food. What motivates you to sleep? Feeling tired could motivate you to get good sleep.

There are different things that can motivate you!

title: What Do You Love?
text:
The things you enjoy can motivate you. If you enjoy soccer, you might feel motivated to practice or play on a team. If you love having a clean bedroom, you might feel motivated to make your bed and pick up your clothes.

Draw a picture of something you love to do.

Draw a picture of something that makes you happy.

title: Hard Work
text: Even if you are not naturally good at something, you can work hard to get better. You can work every day to reach your goals.

title: Good Goals
text:
A goal is something you make a plan to accomplish.

Healthy goals are good. They can help motivate you. When you have good goals, you will feel motivated to work hard to accomplish them.

title: Rewards
text:
A reward is something you receive for doing something.

When you work hard in school, you get good grades.

When you win a competition, you might get a trophy.

When you work at a job, you get paid money.

Highlight the reward in each sentence.

title: Teamwork
text: Teamwork means working together with others. Other people can motivate you to work hard. Other people can motivate you to make healthy choices. Other people can motivate you to try new things. You can help motivate other people too!

title: Resilience
text: Resilience means doing things even though they are hard. You can be resilient when you have hard times.

title: Emotional Resilience
text: You can be emotionally resilient. Emotional resilience is when you pay attention to your emotions. It is when you make healthy choices when hard things happen. You can be emotionally resilient when you are sad or mad.

title: Social Resilience
text: Social resilience is choosing how you treat others, no matter what people around you are doing. You can be socially resilient.

title: Mental Resilience
text: Mental resilience means taking care of your thoughts. You can be mentally resilient by accepting change and thinking healthy thoughts.

title: Physical Resilience
text: Physical resilience is taking care of your body. You can exercise. You can rest when you feel sick. You can eat healthy foods and drink water.

title: Become Resourceful
text: You do not need to be resilient alone. Use resources to help you. You can ask for help.

title: Become Responsible
text: Being responsible is when you do your job. Being responsible will help you be resilient.

title: Become Brave
text: Being brave can help you be resilient. When you are brave, you can face scary or new things. You can be brave.

title: Face the Problem
text:
One way of lowering stress is to face the problem. See if you can change it. Here are some ideas:

Make a to-do list so you don’t forget things.

Chunk the task into smaller parts.

Do things one step at a time.

Ask for help.

title: Relax
text:
Relaxation is a great coping strategy. Our emotions can feel big. It can be hard to think. Give yourself a few moments to quiet your thoughts. Think about what to do.

You can push pause and breathe. You can count to 10. You can listen to music or nature sounds.

title: Move! Move! Move!
text: Move your body! Moving helps you feel better. Moving is a great way to get rid of extra energy. It makes your brain feel better, too!

title: Think About the Good
text: Think about good things in your life. It can change your point of view. You can focus on the positive. Then, when you feel calm, you can look at the problem in a new way.

title: What Is a Team?
text:
What is a team? A team is a group of people working on something together.

Which picture does not show a team?

title: The Butterfly Team
text:
Working with teams can help you do big things.

Claire, Gina, and Steven are on the butterfly team. They need to create a poster about butterflies. The poster must have pictures and facts about butterflies.

Do you think it would be easier to create a butterfly poster alone or with a team?

title: Everyone Can Help!
text:
Each team member has different talents and knowledge. Each member of a team can help with different things.

Claire is a great artist. She will do the butterfly drawings.

Gina’s strength is reading. She will read about butterflies and say what to write on the poster.

Steven has good handwriting. He will write the information about the butterflies.

You can learn from your team members.

title: Using Kind Words
text:
You can be a good team member by the way you talk. You can use kind words. You can share your ideas. Tell each other how you feel. Tell each other what you need.

If Gina has an idea, what should she say?

“I know best. Do what I say.” OR “I have an idea. What do you think?”

title: Listen, Listen
text:
Good team members try to be good listeners. You can listen to your teammates’ ideas. Being a good listener can help keep you and your team happy and safe. Should Claire and Steven listen to Gina’s idea?

YES or NO

title: Positivity Is Power
text:
If you want to be a powerful team member, be positive. Being positive means having a good attitude about people and ideas. It means supporting your team members.

Positivity sounds like …

“Great job on that!”

“I know we can do this!”

“Thank you for your hard work!”

Positivity looks like …

Smiling

High-fives

Doing your part

title: What Is Honesty?
text: Your health is affected by your choices. You can choose to be honest. Honesty means telling the truth. Saying you are cold when you are cold is being honest. Saying you are cold when you are hot is not being honest.

title: Honesty Builds Relationships
text: Healthy relationships need honesty. Honesty helps you make good choices. People can trust you if you are honest.

title: Lying Hurts
text: Lying can cause harm. Lying is when you do not tell the truth or hide the truth. Stealing is taking things that do not belong to you. Stealing is lying. Lying can harm relationships. Lying can put you in danger. How can you be honest about what you need? What is the honest thing to do in this situation?

title: Honesty Helps
text:
All people have basic needs. One basic need is to feel connected. Telling the truth helps you build relationships.

Choose the sentence that is not true.

Bananas are always blue.

Butterflies used to be caterpillars.

Physical activity helps your brain.

title: Goals Are Healthy
text: A goal is something you want to do. People set goals to learn and do new things. Setting goals is a healthy thing to do. You can set a goal.

title: Healthy Goals
text:
It is important to set all kinds of goals. Hygiene is how you keep your body clean. Hygiene goals help you keep your body healthy.

What are your hygiene goals?

Washing your hands:

Brushing your teeth:

Showering:

title: How to Make a Goal
text:
You can set goals by doing these three things:

Think of what you want to do.

Make a plan.

Do it.

title: Think
text:
Sally wants to make a goal to take care of her body. She thinks about it. Sally decides her goal is to have no cavities at her next dentist visit.

Think of how you would like to take care of your body. Here are some ideas:

Brush your teeth.

Eat healthy food.

Exercise daily.

Shower daily.

What is your goal for taking care of your body? Write it down.

title: Plan
text:
Sally has a goal to have no cavities at her next dentist appointment. Sally makes a plan.

Earn enough money to buy her own special toothbrush.

Brush her teeth twice a day every day for the next month.

You can make a plan for how you will reach your goal. You can practice. You can ask others for help.

Write your plan below.

title: Do
text:
Sally follows her plan. She buys a special toothbrush. She brushes her teeth twice a day.

You can follow your plan. You can do a little bit each day. Don't give up. Goals help you grow. You can reach your goal.

Write one thing you will do today to work toward your goal.

title: Reflect and Celebrate
text: When you reach your goal, you can celebrate. You can tell people. Reaching your goal can help you feel happy.

title: What Is Assertiveness?
text: Assertiveness is confidence in what you say and do. It is a way of talking and acting.

title: Being Assertive Matters Because ...
text: Assertiveness helps you meet your needs. When you are assertive, you ask for what you need. You need food. You need water. You need clothes and education.

title: When I Am Assertive, I ...
text:
Say what I think

Ask for what I need

Know that I matter

Stand up for myself

Stand up for others

title: When I Am NOT Assertive, I ...
text:
Yell

Say, “I don’t care” or “I don’t know”

Don’t share my thoughts or ideas

Don’t listen to others

title: Levels of Government
text:
The United States has a national government that leads the country. Tribal nations have their own governments as well. There are state governments that lead individual states. There are also local governments that lead smaller areas. In Ohio, local governments lead cities and municipalities, townships, and special districts.

Governments at all levels promote order and security and protect the rights of individuals. Local, state, and national government officials are elected by vote. People who vote consent, or agree, to be represented. This consent gives each level of government the authority to make and enforce laws for the benefit of the community.

In addition, governments provide public services. These services promote the health and well-being of the communities they serve. Each level of government has its own responsibilities when it comes to the services they provide. Sometimes the levels of government share these responsibilities.

title: State Government
text:
Ohio’s state government has three branches that are elected by Ohio’s voters. There is an executive, a legislative, and a judicial branch. The three branches balance and check each other. This ensures that no one branch has more power than the others.

The executive branch administers Ohio’s laws. The governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general are members of the executive branch. The governor is the leader of the executive branch. It is the governor who signs bills into law. They may also reject bills by veto. It is also the responsibility of the governor to appoint judges.

The legislative branch makes Ohio’s laws. They can also change laws that already exist. The house of representatives and the senate make up the legislative branch. Together, they are called the General Assembly.

The judicial branch decides what laws mean. It decides whether laws go against the state's constitution. The judicial branch also decides how to apply the laws, and which consequences apply to people who break laws. Judges and justices make up the judicial branch. The state Supreme Court is the highest court in the state.

title: Unique Perspectives
text: Every person is different. Every family is different. Every person is unique, or one of a kind. Perspective is the unique way you see things.

title: Local Government
text:
Local means belonging to a particular area or neighborhood. Local governments lead cities, municipalities, townships, and special districts. The structures of local governments can be different, depending on the community. However, they all make laws for their area. They set consequences for breaking each law and enforce them. Local governments also provide services for the people.

Local governments in Ohio often have three branches too. A city or municipality often has a city council, a mayor or city manager, an attorney, and an auditor. The city council or city commission is the legislative branch. The mayor, the city manager, and the city auditor are the executive branch. The city attorney represents the judicial branch.

title: Essential Question
text: How are local governments organized in Ohio?

title: County Government
text:
The Ohio state government provides services for the people. It does this through county governments. The General Assembly runs these county governments. Ohio has 88 counties. The state administers and enforces state laws through elected and appointed officials at the county level.

County officials collect taxes, assess property, and record public documents. It is also the responsibility of county officials to conduct elections and issue licenses. In addition, they provide parks, libraries, and emergency management. They provide public assistance and hospitals as well.

title: City and Municipal Governments
text:
A municipality is a city or village that has a formal charter from the state. Municipalities are made up of cities and villages. Municipalities and cities in Ohio can choose their own type of government. Some municipalities are run by a city council and a mayor, who are elected by the people. Others are run by a mayor, city council, city attorney, and city auditor. They are all elected by the voters of the area. In other cities, the voters elect members of the city commission. The city commission then appoints a city manager. The elected officials work with appointed officials, departments, and agencies to run the city.

City and municipal governments make and enforce city codes. They also create and run parks and recreation services. They are responsible for police and fire departments, housing services, and emergency medical services. Municipal courts, transportation services, and street maintenance, including street signs, are also run by city and municipal governments. Trash and snow removal are also part of their responsibilities.

title: Townships
text:
Township government is the oldest form of government established by settlers. Ohio has 1,308 townships. Townspeople elect three trustees and a finance officer to run a township. They serve a four-year term. They are often helped by a township administrator, who is an appointed official. Other community members are elected to part-time positions.

Township governments provide services like road maintenance and cemetery management. They also provide police and fire protection. In addition, they provide emergency medical services and waste disposal services. Township governments are also responsible for community centers and enforcement of building codes. They take care of street lighting and youth programs as well.

West Chester is the largest township in Ohio. About 62,000 people live there. The smallest township in Ohio is Manchester. Only 54 residents were counted there in 2020.

title: Local Government in My Community
text:
Do some research to find out about your local government. Find answers to the following questions.

Where do you live?

What type of local government exists in your community?

What is the structure of your local government?

Who are the leaders?

What services does the local government provide for your community?

title: Calm or Conflict?
text:
These two bees are the same. These two bees are different.

Differences between people make the world a beautiful place. Sometimes different perspectives can create conflict or disagreement.

title: Conflict Can Be Resolved
text:
Most conflicts can be resolved or fixed. Some ideas can help resolve conflict.

Count to 10 to calm down.

Say what the problem is.

Apologize.

Find a solution.

title: You Can Refuse
text: Some conflicts can cause harm. If you see a situation that could hurt someone, you can refuse, or say “no” to it. You can say “Stop!” You can talk about something else. You can walk away.

title: Think About Your Actions
text:
Thinking critically means making choices that will keep you healthy. A choice is the act of selecting an option. Consequences are the results of your choices. All choices have consequences. Think about your options. Think about what is healthy.

Cameron is growing up. He wants to make wise choices. He wants to be healthy.

“Mom,” Cameron said, “will you see how tall I am?”

“Sure,” his mom said. “Let’s measure you.”

She made a mark on the wall.

“I’m taller!” Cameron said. He knew he was growing up.

He could ride his bike all on his own.

He helped clean the dishes after meals.

He even played soccer on his team at school.

Cameron felt proud of all he was doing.

title: The Northwest Ordinance
text:
When the new United States government signed the Treaty of Paris with Great Britain in 1783, they gained more than just the land within the 13 American Colonies. They also received a large area of land west of the colonies that came to be known as the Northwest Territory. The question of what was to happen with this unorganized territory was one of the first major issues faced by the new country. The answers to this question would impact all future U.S. land claims and territories.

Each new state wanted to gain as much land as they could for themselves, and Virginia was moving aggressively to claim as much of the Northwest Territory as they could. Small eastern states like Connecticut and Rhode Island had no realistic claim to the territory because they were separated from it by other states.

Because of this, they opposed the enlargement of states like Virginia. Giving those states more land would make them more powerful in the new national government. As a democracy, the states with more land and more people would have a larger say in how the country was run.

To further complicate issues of land in the West, soldiers from the Continental Army were given pieces of land for their service during the Revolutionary War. Those former soldiers and other settlers moving west began claiming land for themselves. Some argued that they had bought the land from Native Peoples, while others simply chose an empty piece of land upon which to build their homestead. This led to arguments and disputes over land ownership.

To solve these problems, Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The Ordinance laid out the process by which the Northwest Territory, and all future territories, would be admitted as states to the country. It also ensured that each new state would be equal to all other states, which is not something that was guaranteed before the ordinance was passed.

Each territory would have a governor and other government officials appointed by the U.S. Congress. Once 5,000 free men were living in a territory, it would need to have an elected legislative body. Finally, once the population reached 60,000 people and a state constitution had been drafted, the territory could apply for statehood. The ordinance also outlawed slavery in any newly created territory. This would have major consequences, as there was increased conflict over the issue of slavery between the states into the 1800s. The ordinance also encouraged territories to establish a system of education, guaranteed trials by a jury, and encouraged fair treatment of Native Peoples who lived in the Northwest Territory.

However, the specific question of what to do with the Northwest Territory remained. Using the guidance of the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, Congress eventually annexed Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota into the United States from the land that originally made up the Northwest Territory.

title: Essential Question
text: How did the Northwest Ordinance impact Ohio?

title: Ohio Company of Associates
text:
The Ohio Company of Associates was a land speculation company founded in 1786. The company was created by prominent businessmen from Massachusetts to buy land in the Northwest Territory, The members of the company sent a petition to Congress to purchase large amounts of land in the Northwest Territory. The Ohio Company of Associates petitioned Congress to purchase 1.5 million acres in present-day southeastern Ohio, along the banks of the Ohio River.

After several negotiations, Congress approved the Ohio Company of Associates’s petition to purchase land in Ohio. In addition to the 1.5 million acres purchased, Congress granted the Ohio Company of Associates 100,000 additional acres to create a buffer zone between settlements and the frontier. The members of the Ohio Company of Associates agreed to set aside land in each settlement for schools, churches, and government purposes. They also agreed to set aside land for two universities.

In 1788, the Ohio Company of Associates chose General Rufus Putnam to establish a settlement in Ohio. Putnam established the first permanent non-native people settlement west of the Allegheny Mountains. Putnam chose a site along the Ohio River for the settlement. This would give the settlers access to resources and a way to travel. Settlers traveled with Putnam to establish the settlement. They named the settlement Marietta. Settlers in Marietta built homes, cleared fields for farms, and constructed a fort to defend the settlement. By 1800, 321 settlers lived in the small frontier town.

The Ohio Company of Associates was also responsible for establishing Ohio University. Located in Athens, Ohio University is the first and oldest public university in the state. Construction of the university began in 1804 and took four years to complete. When it opened in 1808, Ohio University only had three students and one professor. Today, Ohio University offers more than 250 degree programs, and over 28,000 students attend the university each year.

title: Marietta: Ohio's First Permanent Settlement
text:
Marietta was the first permanent American settlement in Ohio. The city was established in 1788 by settlers sent by the Ohio Company of Associates. The town was originally named Adelphia, but it was changed to Marietta in honor of Queen Marie Antoinette of France. The original settlers were from different areas of New England. They hoped to create a town similar to those in New England with a school, church, businesses, streets, and common areas.

The early settlers of Marietta established farms and grew a variety of different crops, including apples. Access to the Ohio River allowed settlers to grow and water their crops easily. Marietta’s location also made it a center of trade for people traveling along the Ohio River. The town also became a center for shipbuilding because of its large forests and access to lumber. A fort named Campus Martius was constructed to protect the settlers and town.

By the 1840s, Marietta had over 20 stores and businesses, multiple churches, two public libraries, and a college. The town grew steadily and was home to over 5,000 people in the 1880s. In 2020, the population totaled 13,147. Today, Marietta is a popular tourist destination for history and nature lovers.

title: Conflict in the Northwest Territory
text:
During this time, relations between the Native People tribes and settlers in the Northwest Territory were not peaceful. Thousands of settlers migrated and immigrated to Ohio following the passage of the Northwest Ordinance. American and European settlers cleared the land and built farms and communities across Ohio. Many of these areas were the traditional hunting grounds for tribes of the Northwest Territory. As more settlers came to the territory, animals were pushed out of their natural habitats. This greatly impacted hunting, trapping, and trade for the tribes of the territory.

The tribes of the Northwest Territory were forced to compete with settlers for valuable natural resources. Some tribes were even forced off of their lands. Hostilities between the tribes and settlers became more frequent. As communication between the tribes and settlers decreased, conflict increased.

The violence turned into an open war in 1790 in the Northwest Territory. The Odawa, Shawnee, Ojibway, Potawatomi, Delaware, Miami, and other tribes banded together to fight for possession of their ancestral homelands. This conflict was called the Northwest War, or Little Turtle’s War, after the Miami war chief. President George Washington ordered troops to be sent to the Northwest Territory to protect settlers and stop the conflict.

During the first year of the war, the United States suffered two great defeats in 1790 and 1791. American soldiers were not prepared for the conflict they faced in the Northwest Territory. They did not have the proper training or equipment. The tribes of the territory were experts on the geography and physical characteristics of the area. They used this knowledge to defeat the American soldiers.

The U.S. Army lost over 2,000 soldiers during the first two years of the war.

A turning point in the conflict between the Native Peoples and settlers of the Northwest Territory took place after the Battle of Fallen Timbers. General Anthony Wayne and his men defeated the Shawnee tribe led by Blue Jacket. The Native Peoples knew a change was needed. It was time to seek peace.

The war finally ended with the signing of the Treaty of Greenville in 1795. Boundaries between tribes and settlers were established with this treaty. However, within a few years, American settlers stopped honoring the treaty, and they moved onto tribal lands. This led to more conflict between Native Peoples and white settlers.

title: The Enabling Act
text:
In the late 1790s, conflict arose between rival political parties in the Northwest Territory that had a big impact on Ohio. These rival political parties were the Democratic-Republicans and the Federalists. The governor of the Northwest Territory, Arthur St. Clair, was a member of the Federalist party. St. Clair wanted the Federalist party to remain in control of the territory and did not want Ohio to become a state.

St. Clair wanted the western border of Ohio to be at the Scioto River. He knew it would be difficult to get the required settlers for statehood in such a small area. To keep his job as the governor and maintain power, St. Clair convinced the territory’s legislature to pass the Division Act of 1801. This act placed the western border of Ohio at the Scioto River. If the U.S. Congress approved the Division Act, it would have been a long time before Ohio could have applied for statehood.

President Thomas Jefferson and the Democratic-Republican party were not happy with St. Clair and his plan. The Democratic-Republicans wanted Ohio to become a state as soon as possible. The Democratic-Republicans believed in strong state governments over the federal government. They hoped that if Ohio became a state, they could be elected into power over the Federalists.

Congress did not approve St. Clair’s Division Act. President Jefferson asked Congress to pass the Enabling Act on April 30, 1802. The primary purpose of the act was to set Ohio’s boundaries to the current boundaries that it has today. Because Ohio was so close to having the required 60,000 people to become a state, the Enabling Act also set Ohio’s constitutional convention for November 1802. The act even explained how delegates would be elected to the constitutional convention. The Enabling Act of 1802 put the territory of Ohio on the path to statehood.

title: How Does a Territory Become a State?
text:
What did it take for a territory to become a state? One of the biggest factors was people settling in the territory. Settlers moving to the territory meant there were towns. A town meant there was trade and markets. Trade and markets meant there was money to be made. Being a state was a chance for people to be successful and get rich. It was a chain of causes and effects.

When people build a town, they have wants and needs. Some of these wants and needs are homes, livestock, wagons, and land. Businesses are created to meet these wants and needs. Businesses create jobs. Jobs are work that give earnings to people. If there are more jobs, more people can make earnings. The chance to have more earnings brings more people. More people creates more wants and needs. Providing goods and services to people can create wealth. This is an example of an interdependence web. As unclaimed land, or land that was taken from the Indigenous population, was settled, this interdependence web grew larger. Some of the people in that web were able to become wealthy.

Many other people wanted the chance to become wealthy. They wanted the unassigned lands. At the same time, the United States government wanted the country to extend from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. Having people move into the Great Plains to create towns was an important step to make that happen. The people of a territory wanted it to happen, too. If a territory could become a state, more opportunities were available. A new state would need a government. New laws that guided the growth of the businesses and towns would also be established. Most importantly, the new state would be connected to the government in Washington, D.C. This meant that the new state could receive money and programs to help the new citizens and towns.

There was a special procedure for a territory to become a state. First, the territory had to have a total population of at least 60,000 people. The people of the territory had to vote to notify the U.S. Congress that they wanted to become a state. Then, the territorial representatives drafted a constitution modeled on the U.S. Constitution and sent it to Congress. Once the document was done, Congress would then decide if they would vote on statehood. Sometimes Congress chose not to vote at all. Because of this, some U.S. territories retained that status for many years or never became states.

title: Ohio's First State Constitution
text:
By 1802, the territory of Ohio had completed the first two steps to become a state. The next step was to draft a constitution. In November 1802, delegates met in the capital of the territory, Chillicothe, to write a constitution. Most of the delegates at the convention were Democratic-Republicans. Like the Anti-Federalists, Democratic-Republicans wanted a small central government with limited powers. Delegates who opposed the Democratic-Republicans were members of the Federalist party. Members of the Federalist party wanted a strong central government that had more power over the people and states.

During the convention, there was conflict between the opposing political parties. Because the majority of delegates were Democratic-Republicans, the constitution reflected more of their beliefs for government. Ohio’s first state constitution divided the government into three branches (legislative, executive, and judicial) but gave the majority of the power to the legislative branch. The constitution also guaranteed the right to vote for white men who paid taxes, set the governor's term to two years, listed the rights of Ohioans, and made slavery illegal in the state.

The delegates to the Ohio constitutional convention completed the constitution in December 1802. The constitution was taken to Washington, D.C., to be approved by Congress. On Feb. 19, 1803, Congress approved the constitution and Ohio became the 17th state on March 1, 1803. Ohio’s first state constitution was the law of the state until a new constitution was drafted in 1851.

text: Make sure you use Cmd+Shift+V when pasting text. Revise any bolded vocab text and rebold if needed.

title: What Does It Mean to Be Mindful?
text:
Mindfulness means being present in the present. What does that mean?

The first “present” in the sentence is talking about where you are. If you are present, you are here. Think about when the teacher is calling the roll when school starts. They call each student’s name and the student says, “Here!” or “Present!”

Being present isn’t only about where your body is. It’s also about where your mind is. Being present means you are listening to what is being said and you are aware of your surroundings instead of daydreaming about a vacation or yummy food.

The second “present” refers to the current moment. The present is in between the past and the future. It is right now. Practicing mindfulness means you are focusing on wherever you are, whatever you are doing, and whoever you are with in a moment.

Do you practice mindfulness already? Or is it something you need to work on?

title: The Present Is a Present
text:
The present is a present. What does this mean?

The first “present” is talking about time again. The second “present” is another word for “gift.” In other words, the current moment you are living is a gift. That’s why mindfulness is important. Mindfulness helps you be aware of and enjoy each moment you live.

Some people are stuck living in the past. They choose to constantly think and talk about things that have already happened. The past is important and should never be forgotten, but your life is happening right now. You have choices to make right now. You have people to care for right now. You have experiences and adventures to have right now.

The opposite can also be true. Some people are only focused on the future. They wish time away because they want to be older or taller or able to drive. Those days will come. The future will come. You could regret not enjoying the phase you are in right now.

You might miss your todays if you are always focused on your yesterdays and tomorrows. Enjoy your present!

title: Teamwork = Collaboration
text: Teamwork means working with others to accomplish something great. When you create a project with your classmates, that is teamwork. When you build something with your siblings or friends, that is teamwork. When you play a sport with team members, that is teamwork. Another word for teamwork is collaboration. When you work as a team, you are collaborating!

title: Everyone Has Strengths
text:
Strengths are things you are good at. Everyone has strengths. That means that everyone can help a team in different ways.

In a musical band, one person might be a really good singer. The band also needs someone who is good at playing the drums. It would be good to have someone who could play the guitar too. All of the strengths of the individuals in the band come together to make awesome music.

You can work with people who have different strengths to do great things!

title: Benefits of Practicing Mindfulness
text:
Will practicing mindfulness really help you? Yes. There are so many benefits to practicing mindfulness. It can help you mentally, emotionally, socially, and academically.

Practicing mindfulness can lower your stress. Often, people will be stressed about something that they said or did in the past. Mindfulness teaches you not to focus on the past. Instead, focus on where you are at the moment. Practicing mindfulness also takes care of any stress about the future. When you are practicing mindfulness, you are not thinking about tomorrow or any other day in the future. You are thinking about your now. This increases your ability to focus.

When you put away all thoughts and worries that are not applicable to your current moment, you will find it’s much easier to focus on whatever you are doing. This will be especially helpful to you at school. Practicing mindfulness can help improve your academic performance. You will be able to focus more on your teacher’s lessons and on the assignments you are completing.

What are the social benefits of practicing mindfulness? Being mindful can help you be more aware and thoughtful of other people’s needs and feelings. Being mindful can help you be more aware of how your words and actions affect those around you. Other people will enjoy spending time with you. In addition, practicing mindfulness can help you avoid regret. When you are mindful in the moment, you take the time to make thoughtful decisions. You can be aware of yourself and others. You can think through actions and potential consequences before making a choice. Practicing mindfulness can help you avoid health risks because your decision-making ability will be clear and you will be able to say, “No” to anything that would be bad for you, like gossiping, bullying, drugs, or alcohol.

title: Mindfulness and Emotions
text:
Put your hand over your heart. Close your eyes and do a quick self-check to see what emotions you are feeling at this moment. Are you feeling bored, anxious, angry, happy, excited, or stressed? Maybe something else?

Practicing mindfulness helps you be aware of your emotions. It is important to be aware of your emotions because it helps you learn how things and people make you feel. It can also help you communicate your emotions and needs better. If you don’t know what emotion you are experiencing, it may be difficult for someone to help you.

Being aware of when you are experiencing a positive emotion is also very important. Sometimes it is easier to recognize the negative emotions you experience because they may feel big or loud. Practice mindfulness to make sure you notice when you feel happy, calm, or optimistic too. These emotions should be enjoyed!

When you recognize that you are experiencing a challenging emotion, like anger, practicing mindfulness can help you stay calm and choose to have self-control. If you notice you are feeling angry, you can use these mindfulness strategies to calm down and express yourself:

Notice your breathing and slow it down.

Figure out why you feel the way you do.

Look around you and point out things you like.

Remember that you are safe.

Finally, use calm words to express your feelings.

title: Being a Good Team Member
text:
You can be a good team member when you …

listen

do your part

share your ideas

stay positive

Can you think of anything else that can help you be a good team member?

title: Who Uses Teamwork?
text: Teamwork and collaboration are important in many places. Scientists, doctors, historians, teachers, and students all use teamwork. Adults collaborate every day, just like you. They collaborate at their jobs. They collaborate with your teachers. They collaborate with their friends. They collaborate with other adults in the community. You collaborate with your classmates and teammates. You collaborate with your family and friends. You can use teamwork to solve problems. You can use teamwork to make a positive influence in your community.

title: Ways to Practice Mindfulness
text:
There is not just one way to practice mindfulness. There are many. Everyone can find mindfulness practices that work for them. Circle any of the following strategies that you think you would enjoy or you would like to try:

Soup breathing: Hold your hands in front of you and imagine holding a bowl of warm, delicious soup. Breathe in to smell the “soup.” Exhale to cool off the “soup.” Repeat as many times as needed.

Mindful eating: Choose to savor and notice each bite of your food when you eat. What does it taste like? How does it feel? Do you like it?

Relax your muscles: Lay on the floor and, starting with the top of your head, relax each body part and each muscle in your body, working down to your feet.

Nature walk: Walk outside and observe everything around you.

Journaling: Journaling can help you be mindful of your feelings. You can write everything you are feeling and experiencing.

Coloring: Take time to relax and focus on a small, calm task, like coloring.

Heartbeat: Put your hand on your heart and feel it beat. Remember that you are living and breathing in that moment.

Five senses exercise: Notice five things: one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, one thing you can taste, one thing you can smell, and one thing you can touch.You can practice mindfulness with any activity that helps you be present at the moment. Can you think of any other activities or exercises that help you stay present?

title: Mindfulness Obstacles
text:
While there are many benefits of and strategies to practice mindfulness, there are also some things that can hinder (block) your mindfulness. The main thief of mindfulness is technology: specifically, social media. The time you spend on social media is time spent focused on people you are not with and sometimes on people you don't even know. Social media is not necessarily bad, but your time on it should be limited so you can maximize your mindfulness throughout your day. You can be mindful about your social media usage by setting a time limit.

Another hindrance to mindfulness is comparing yourself to others. Do you ever do that? It is easy to do, but focusing on other people and what they have is not mindfulness.

Social media makes it even easier to compare yourself to others. On social media, you usually see the best side of other people. It makes others seem perfect even though they are not. If you find yourself constantly comparing yourself to other people around you or on social media, refocus your energy and thoughts on you and your strengths.

What do you want to focus on?

What do you love about yourself?

Are you doing something that you enjoy right now?

What are you grateful for?

title: What Causes Grief?
text: Grief is an emotion that is similar to sadness but stronger. The most common cause of grief is the death of a friend or loved one. Other situations can create grief, such as the loss of a friend, experiencing a divorce, losing a limb, or receiving a life-changing medical diagnosis. Grief is a powerful emotion that everyone experiences differently. Some people work through their grief quickly and alone. Others may need months and help from friends and family to heal. Grief is a normal emotion to experience. It is normal to experience grief after a devastating change. But there is hope! If you or someone you know is experiencing grief, know that it is evidence of a valuable relationship, and you do not need to go through grief alone. You can manage feelings of grief in healthy ways, and it can strengthen you for future challenges.

title: Stages of Grief
text:
There are five stages of grief that people usually experience as they work through their feelings. Each person may spend a different amount of time in each of these stages and may even experience them in a different order.

Denial: This is when people have difficulty accepting what has happened. They may say things like “This isn’t real” or “I don’t believe this.” Denial is your brain’s way of trying to protect you.

Anger: Next, people may feel angry about what has happened. They might look for someone to blame. They may say things like “Why is this happening to me?” or “This isn’t fair!”

Bargaining: In this stage, people look for ways to change the situation or look for any source of hope. They may promise to be a better person if the challenge can be taken away, or they may look for a cure for a family member’s illness. They may say things like “I will do anything!”

Depression: This stage can be challenging, but it is also very important. A person will start to come to terms with the reality of the situation. They may feel overwhelmed or deep sadness. The intensity of the emotions may negatively affect decision-making and cause a person to make choices that are not helpful to their health.

Acceptance: Eventually, people choose to accept their loss. They are able to make plans for their future and look forward.

If you are working through your own grief, pay close attention to how, when, or if you experience each of these stages. Do your best to identify which stage you are in at any given time, and be patient with yourself as you work through your emotions.

title: Talking Through Your Grief
text:
It can help you work through grief to make sure you are communicating well with others as you do so. When you have deep feelings of loss, it can help to talk with someone about your feelings. When you do this, here are some things you can remember:

Your thoughts and feelings are valid.

You can say what you need to say.

Talk to someone you trust.

It can be helpful to talk to someone who has had a similar experience.

If someone experiencing grief wants to talk to you about their feelings, do your best to listen. Ask someone else for assistance if you do not know how best to help. When you listen to someone sharing their grief, here are a few things you can try to remember:

Validate their feelings.

Don’t judge them.

Avoid telling them what to do; they usually just need to talk.

You can offer them a hug or a high five.

Say things like “I am so sorry you are going through that,” “Would you like some company?” or “I am here for you and anything you need.”

title: Sympathy and Grief
text:
Sympathy is feeling generous toward someone who is experiencing a challenge in their life. If you have sympathy for someone, you allow their emotions to affect yours. When you have sympathy, you show understanding and patience. For example, if you know your friend’s mom was just diagnosed with cancer, you will probably feel sympathetic toward your friend because you care and you know they love their mom. Sympathy is an important emotion. It helps us care for those around us.

You can show sympathy to someone feeling grief by:

offering a hug

being patient

sending a note

sharing a toy

giving a gift

listening

title: Empathy and Grief
text:
Have you ever broken a bone? __________

Have you ever been stung by a bee? __________

Have you ever lost a pet? __________

Underline any of the questions you responded “yes” to. You can demonstrate empathy for people when you have experienced similar things. Empathy helps you understand another person more deeply because you listen without judgment. When you see someone go through something you have been through yourself, you can show empathy. If you have gone through something hard and have experienced grief in your life, keep an eye out for others who are currently feeling grief. You can be a positive influence for them. Encourage your peers who are feeling grief to continue to make healthy choices such as getting enough sleep, eating healthy foods, and doing their best to take care of themselves. You can listen without judgment and try to understand their perspective while offering support.

title: Coping Strategies for Grief
text:
Grief can feel overwhelming. Sometimes when people experience loss, grief, trauma, or emotional distress, it can be difficult to make healthy choices. Some people may make choices that harm their health and well-being. It is important to develop and practice healthy coping strategies. Coping strategies can help you make healthy choices when you feel big emotions.

When a person experiences grief, they can use some of these coping strategies to help make healthy choices in response to their emotions:

talk to someone they trust

listen to calming music

drink water

keep a journal

write a letter to the person they lost

title: What Is Confidence?
text:
Confidence is when someone knows or believes they can do something. Confidence is knowing that you are enough. Confidence is also being willing to accept that you can grow. Sometimes people mistake confidence for pride or arrogance (someone thinking they are more important than others or have more valuable abilities than others). As you increase in confidence, it is important to also remember to stay humble. Being humble means recognizing that you can always learn something new. It also means you are willing to ask others for help when you need it or share your talents when you can.

Confidence IS NOT …

comparing yourself to others.

thinking you are perfect.

thinking you know everything.

thinking you are better than other people.

bragging about yourself.

never feeling nervous or afraid.

Confidence IS …

believing in yourself.

speaking kindly to and about yourself.

trying new or hard things even when you are nervous.

celebrating your accomplishments without making someone else feel less important.

sharing your talents and abilities with others.

taking responsibility for your behavior and actions.

title: Collect Confidence
text:
Why is it important to have confidence? Having confidence can give you the courage and the power to try new things and set goals that stretch you to accomplish more. Having confidence helps you believe that you can do anything you work hard for. Many people are not held back by their opportunities or abilities, but rather, they are held back by their thinking.

Believing you can do something is half of the battle toward doing something hard. Many coaches and teachers tell their students that they are not allowed to say “I can’t.” Why? Telling yourself that you cannot do something can create a metaphorical stop sign in your brain. Confidence in yourself is what can break down that mental block. You can build confidence. If you don’t feel confident, don’t worry! Confidence is a choice, and you can learn to choose to be confident. You can choose today to believe in yourself. You can choose today to say “I can” instead of “I can’t.”

title: Steps to Build Confidence
text:
There are steps you can take to help you build confidence. For some people, confidence comes more naturally, but for others, it takes more work. Regardless of where you are with your confidence, here are four things you can do to increase your feelings of confidence in yourself:

Use positive self-talk and affirmations.

Surround yourself with people who build you and others up.

Build others up.

Do things you enjoy and are good at, and practice skills you want to improve.

title: 1. Positive Talk
text:
The way you talk about yourself and to yourself is very important. You can build or destroy confidence with the words you use to talk about yourself. Sometimes even if you don’t feel confident, you can act confident until you really feel it. Have you ever heard the phrase, “fake it ‘til you make it”? “Fake it ‘til you make it” means to do your very best and be open to learning more until you’ve got it. Using confident language can help you build confidence when you don’t feel confident yet. You can say things like:

“I can do this!”

“I am a kind friend.”

“I can get good grades if I work hard.”

Comments like these are also called positive affirmations. These positive statements can help you have a positive attitude and believe in yourself.

title: 2. Positive People
text: What happens to a white flower in water with food coloring? The white petals absorb the coloring in the water. People are very similar. When you spend time with others, you soak up some of the characteristics and mannerisms of the people you are around. Throughout your day, you interact with lots of people at home, at school, and at your extracurricular activities (activities after school like sports or music lessons). All of those people send you messages: digital messages on a phone or tablet, verbal messages in person when you talk with them, nonverbal messages through body language and facial expressions, or written messages through notes or letters. Choosing to spend time with people who build you up with encouragement is a great way to increase your confidence. You cannot control what other people say and do, but you can control who you spend your time with. When you surround yourself with people who boost your confidence, you create standards of respect and kindness. If someone is always tearing you down and making you doubt yourself, it may be healthy to choose to spend less time with that person. If someone is encouraging you to do things that are harmful for your health, you can say “no” and choose to spend less time with that person. Surround yourself with people who help you feel happy and healthy.

title: 3. Build Others Up
text: Just like surrounding yourself with uplifting people can build your confidence, building up those around you can boost your confidence as well. When you choose to be a kind, positive person that other people will want to be around, you can feel good about the way you are treating others. You can feel confident that you are meeting your social responsibilities by being a positive influence on others. You can choose to be a positive person and influence your peers by encouraging them to make choices that support long-term health and well-being. Choose a day to be your “building up others day.” Give compliments, kind words, and service. Notice other people’s strengths and point them out. Pay attention to the way you feel when you are building others up instead of tearing them down.

title: What Is Conflict?
text: A conflict is a disagreement. Conflict can happen between any two people. Enemies have conflicts, but best friends can too. Everyone has different opinions and ideas. Learning to deal with conflict in a positive way is a healthy practice. If conflict is not resolved, it can lead to unhealthy and unhelpful behaviors like yelling, name-calling, or violence. Conflict can make people feel sad, but learning to resolve conflict can improve your health and wellness.

title: Causes of Conflict
text:
Any difference of opinion can cause conflict. Conflict can also begin in many ways, including when someone is unkind.

Some conflicts are small. A small conflict could be:

a disagreement with a sibling over what is for dinner

two students arguing over a seat at school

Other disagreements can be large, like:

individuals arguing over their beliefs

countries arguing over land or resources

title: Exploring Solutions
text:
There are healthy solutions to most conflicts. A solution is something that can help those involved in the conflict. When you disagree with someone, you can brainstorm solutions.

Healthy solutions include:

Compromise: finding an option that is in the middle

Apology: saying “sorry” for mistakes or disrespectful behavior

Agree to disagree: Sometimes, people can be okay having different opinions or ideas.

Unhealthy solutions include:

Yelling

Calling names

Any kind of violence

Choosing peaceful solutions to resolve conflict can help you avoid and reduce risks to your health.

title: Resolving Conflict
text:
Resolving conflict means fixing the problem. Conflict resolution comes through good communication. You can talk to the person you disagree with. You can find a way for both of you to be happy. The best way to handle conflict is by using calm and respectful words.

There may be situations of conflict that you cannot solve on your own. You can ask a trusted adult for help. You can say, “My friend and I can’t agree. Can you help us find a solution?”

After doing your best to resolve a conflict, you can ask yourself, “Is the problem resolved?” or “Are things better for both of us now?” If not, you can try something else.

title: Learning from Conflict
text:
Children have conflicts. Adults have conflicts too. Adults have disagreements with friends, coworkers, bosses, and even strangers. Knowing how to resolve conflict in calm and respectful ways is an important skill. You will use this skill throughout your life. When you experience conflict, you can learn and grow. Having the skills to resolve conflict with others can help you. You can have happier and healthier relationships and feelings. Resolving conflicts with friends and family can make your relationships even stronger. When you are able to resolve conflicts with others, you learn that it is okay to have different opinions.

title: Why Should We Set Goals?
text: A goal is something that you want to accomplish, so you create a plan to accomplish it. Setting goals is a healthy behavior because it helps you grow. Setting goals shows that you believe in yourself. You can set goals to help you progress in every area of your life.

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Goals
text:
There are different types of goals:

Short-term goals can be accomplished quickly. You might be able to reach a short-term goal the same day you set it.

Example: Ramon set a goal to eat all his vegetables at dinner tonight.

Long-term goals take more time to reach. These goals may take weeks, months, or even years to accomplish.

Example: Julietta set a goal to get straight A's during her whole third grade year.

title: Who Can Help You with Your Goals?
text:
Some goals may be difficult to reach on your own. People around you can help. Family members, friends, teachers, coaches, and counselors can all help you reach your goals. You might need help reaching a fitness or health goal. You might ask for help from a coach, teammates, parents, or guardians. You might need help with an emotional goal. You might ask a counselor, teacher, or friends for help. Teachers are great helpers for academic or mental goals.

Pay attention to how the people around you make you feel. Do your friends help you reach your goals? Do your best to spend time with people who build your confidence and support your goals.

title: Support Others in Their Goals
text: You can support other people with their goals. If your friends or family members have goals, you can ask them, “What can I do to help you reach this goal?” You can be a positive influence for others. You can help others know that they can accomplish big goals.

title: Engineering Design Scenario
text: Natalia, Cameron, and Jackson are stuck inside on a rainy day. They decide that they want to have a car race, but they do not have any cars. They look around and find some materials in the house that they could use to build cars. They decide to build cars and race them using only what they have available to them!

title: Celebrations and Beliefs
text:
There are many different characteristics of culture. Architecture, fine arts, literature, music, and language are all part of culture. Religion, clothing, and food are also part of culture. Culture is how a group of people act and what they believe.

One way people show their culture is through their celebrations. They celebrate things that are important to them. Most families in America celebrate Christmas with gifts and Christmas trees. Religion is another part of culture and celebrations, like Christmas. Religion is a system of beliefs. Many celebrations and traditions come from a group's beliefs or religion. These celebrations can influence culture. Some cultures celebrate the seasons. Others celebrate special events or people. One special event that is celebrated across the nation is New Year’s Day. On this day, we start a new calendar year. We celebrate the year we’ve lived and the new year in front of us.

title: Inauguration Day
text:
Inauguration Day is the day when the newly elected president of the United States is sworn into office. An election for a new president happens every four years. After the election, on January 20, the person who won the election is sworn in as president. When the elected president is sworn in, they repeat an oath, or promise, as the new leader of the country:

"I do solemnly swear that I will faithfully execute the office of president of the United States and will, to the best of my ability, preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States."

After the person who has been elected is sworn in, they can begin their duties as president of the United States. Many people visit Washington, D.C., on inauguration day to be a part of history as a new president takes office.

title: Christopher Columbus
text:
In the late 1400s, countries on Europe’s Atlantic coast were competing with each other for wealth and power. Portugal was the leader in exploration. In 1488, a ship from Portugal sailed to the southern tip of Africa. Then, in 1492, Spain paid for Christopher Columbus to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus studied everything that was available. He was sure that he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.”

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe. He shared his adventures. Columbus became famous in Europe. Once Columbus and his crew shared what they learned on the voyage, other explorers followed.

Portugal, England, and France sent explorers across the Atlantic. Many early explorers believed they had reached Asia. In 1503, an explorer named Amerigo Vespucci became convinced that the land they were exploring was really another continent. Amerigo Vespucci claimed it was a “new world.” People later called the land “America” in honor of this claim.

Explorers share information that helps others explore. Columbus opened a new door of adventure. Many followed and shared their new knowledge.

title: Phenomenon Comic
text: Phenomenon: Raccoons put their hands in water before they eat.

title: Everyone Has Strengths
text: Everyone is important. Everyone has different strengths. Strengths are things you are good at.

title: What Is Empathy?
text: Empathy is trying to understand someone’s situation or feelings as if you were the person experiencing them. When you have empathy for other people, you put yourself in their shoes and try to see things from their perspective. It is easiest to have empathy for other people when you have been through similar situations. But you can use your mind and your heart to imagine how someone else might feel, even if you haven’t been through the same thing. You can draw on similar experiences, and you can show empathy for any person who is different from you. You can be a better friend when you are empathetic toward others.

title: What Does Empathy Feel Like?
text:
Empathy feels like kindness, patience, understanding, and compassion. An empathetic person does not judge others. An empathetic person is accepting of everyone’s differences in thoughts, opinions, and actions. An empathetic person is a good listener who says things like:

“I can imagine why you feel that way.”

“I’m sorry this happened to you.”

“Your feelings are valid.”

Empathy is not comparing your experiences with someone else’s. An empathetic person does not say things like:

“I’m sorry that happened to you, but this happened to me.”

“That is sad, but at least _______ didn’t happen to you.”

Empathy feels like you care about others. You can practice demonstrating empathy by being a good listener and trying to feel what the other person is feeling.
