title: Set Your Own Standards
text: Your brain is sensitive to everything you read and see. It remembers what you hear and do. Your brain remembers what you see and hear on the internet. You can set guidelines for how much time you spend on the computer. You can be smart about which sites you visit. Spending time online can improve or harm your well-being.

title: Protect Private Information
text: Your name and your birthday are personal information. Your address and phone number are also personal. This information belongs to you and is considered private. Private information shouldn't be shared online.

title: Respect on the Internet
text: Your character is the way you choose to treat others. Your digital character is how you choose to treat others online. It is important to choose your digital words and actions carefully. You should not do things online that could harm others. You can show positive digital character traits when using the internet.

title: Online Problem-Solving
text: Sometimes, you may have problems while online. You may see conduct online that makes you uncomfortable. Conduct is what people say and do. There are things you can do to protect your well-being. You can turn the computer off or delete the app. You can block a sender and report the conduct. When you see uncomfortable things online, you should say something right away. You should talk to an adult you trust.

title: How Can I Grow?
text:
A growth mindset is a way of thinking that helps you accept growth and change. It helps you grow and develop.

Imagine a small plant. If the plant is watered and given the right amount of sunlight, it will grow and develop. The roots will search for food and nutrients to help the plant grow and flourish. Your brain is similar to a plant.

You have neurons, or nerve cells, in your brain that act like the roots of a tree. They use information, experience, and nutrients to help you get smarter and more talented. The neurons create connections and cultivate your brainpower. These connections help you remember the information you have learned and the skills you gained.

title: Stuck in a Fixed Mindset
text:
Understanding the difference between a growth mindset and a fixed mindset helps us develop our growth mindset. People with a fixed mindset believe that intelligence and talent cannot be changed.

Imagine a rock. If you plant the rock in the ground and water it, it will not be able to grow. The rock is an example of a fixed mindset. It will never change.

Often, fearing failure or avoiding new challenges is evidence, or a sign, of having a fixed mindset. You might be experiencing a fixed mindset if you find yourself thinking things like:

I am not good at this.

I am not smart.

title: Growing with Effort and Grit
text:
Effort is a huge part of cultivating a growth mindset. Effort means giving your best attempt at doing, learning, or practicing something. With effort, it's possible to increase knowledge, talents, and skills, even when it is challenging.

Putting in the effort, despite how difficult a challenge might be, is known as having grit. Grit means sticking with something even when it is hard. Grit and effort help create a growth mindset because they help you try again.

title: Growing with Mistakes
text:
Failure can be hard. Remember that failing is a normal part of development. Failure helps us learn and grow. Making mistakes can be frustrating, but you can learn from your mistakes.

Think of a plant with beautiful roots. A mistake is like a root that accidentally grows toward the soil's surface. It can dry up because it does not have enough water or has too much sunlight. The plant will send other roots down deep in the soil so it can get the water it needs to keep growing. The resilient plant learns from its mistakes and looks for other ways to succeed.

title: Growing with Words
text:
Your brain will believe what you say and think. It is important to pay close attention to your thoughts. There are times you might notice negative thoughts. These might include "I can't do this," "I am not good at this," or "This is too hard." When this happens, try adding the simple word yet. You can change your thoughts to be more like this:

"I can't do this, yet!"

"I am not good at this, yet!

Changing the way you think, like adding the word "yet," helps you gain confidence. It will help you develop your growth mindset.

title: How Does a Growth Mindset Help Me?
text:
Your well-being is impacted by your efforts to develop a growth mindset. The more you are open to changing the way you think, the more you will improve your well-being.

Impact to Physical Well-Being

A growth mindset helps you learn new skills like running, playing a game, painting a picture, or playing an instrument.

Impact to Mental Well-Being

A growth mindset helps you think about learning in a different way. When you change your thinking, you increase the amount of things you can learn.

Impact to Social Well-Being

A growth mindset helps you recognize that mistakes and disagreements are a normal part of friendships and relationships.

Impact to Academic Well-Being

A growth mindset allows you to focus on new concepts and opportunities at school, not on your failures or bad grades.

Impact to Emotional Well-Being

A growth mindset can help you identify, label, and communicate your emotions. Remember to be patient and have empathy with others' emotions. This helps you to be more forgiving with yourself and your emotions.

title: Fear: A Natural Alarm System
text: Fear is like your body’s alarm system. It is an emotion that warns you about a threat. A threat is something dangerous or scary about to happen. Usually fear is helpful because it can protect you. Fear causes your brain to send signals to your body. The signals prepare your body to respond to the threat.

title: Learning to Deal With Fear
text:
Coping strategies are helpful ways of dealing with our emotions. Coping strategies are skills you can develop. These skills give you and your brain something to do when you feel different emotions. They can help you deal with fear positively.

When you feel fear, you can use some of these coping strategies:

Exercise.

Find humor in your situation.

Create something.

Journal: List things you’re good at. List things you are grateful for.

title: Afraid of What You Don't Know?
text: Some people feel fear when they do not have enough information. For example, someone might feel afraid of the ocean because they do not know what is in it or how to swim. Fear of the unknown is normal. A little bit of fear will help you make wise choices. If you let fear take over, however, it can stop or slow your growth. When you feel afraid, use coping strategies to help you.

title: Afraid of Messing Up or Missing Out?
text:
Making mistakes is a part of life. Sometimes our fear of making mistakes leaves us stuck between two types of fear: fear of messing up and fear of missing out.

Fear of Messing Up

Fear of Missing Out

What do we call it?

FOMU

FOMO

What does it mean?

You don’t try something new because you are afraid of messing up.

You feel that you are missing out on something exciting happening elsewhere.

What to remember?

Making mistakes is a part of creating a growth mindset. Everybody makes mistakes.

Focus on the good you are getting from the choice you made.

What coping strategy can help?

title: Afraid of Starting?
text: Sometimes people feel overwhelmed when they are starting something new. It can be hard to know where to begin. Some people don't like starting new things. They are afraid of making mistakes. Making mistakes helps you learn. You can break the task into smaller parts. You can then choose one to help you get started.

title: Afraid of Success?
text: Wanting to be successful is normal. A fear of success can come from not knowing what will happen after your success. You might feel guilty because you succeeded. When you experience success, you can overcome the fear. You can show empathy to others who are struggling. You can mentor or help them. You can encourage them.

title: Cotton Gin
text:
Eli Whitney invented a machine that simplified the work of removing cotton seeds from harvested cotton. The southern plantations grew cotton using the work of enslaved people. One enslaved worker could only remove seeds from about one pound of cotton a day. At this speed, farmers did not make much money from cotton. Then Whitney built the cotton gin. The gin was a large wooden box with a crank on the side. The machine could separate the seeds from cotton quickly. It could process 50 pounds of cotton a day. This meant more cotton could be grown, harvested, and sold. The cotton industry expanded. Plantations grew. The new territories in the West could grow cotton. With the rise in cotton production, more workers were needed. Therefore, the need for enslaved people to work the plantations grew.

The southern states were invested in agriculture and the plantation system of using enslaved people for labor. The economic growth in both regions would be a cause of conflict over the first 50 years of the 1800s.

title: Not All Stress Is Bad
text: Did you know that stress can be good? Think of how you feel during a tied game with seconds left to score. That’s good stress! Good stress can make you want to work hard and do great things. It can give you a push to study for a test, practice a presentation, or learn something new. Good stress can be good for your well-being. Bad stress weighs you down instead of helping you work hard. Bad stress can pop up when you feel afraid or overwhelmed. It can make you feel sick, and it also makes it hard to do your best.

title: Stronger with Stress
text: Feeling stress is normal. It is your body and mind telling you that something needs to change. Stress can even be good for your well-being because it can help you learn how to overcome hard things. Dr. Daniela Kaufer studies what stress does to your brain. She’s learned that a little bit of stress can help you pay attention, act wisely, and think clearly. This means a little bit of stress can be good! Remembering this will help you see stress as a chance to learn and grow.

title: What Message Is Your Stress Sending You?
text:
Your stress is sending you a message. It might make you want to do your best or make a good change in your life. Or it might make you feel confused, frustrated, angry, or sad. Like other feelings, stress can tell us to act — but it might also mean we need to stop and think. What is our stress trying to teach us?

When you feel stress, ask yourself:

Is this good stress?

What can this stress help me do?

How will I act?

title: Where Is Your Stress Coming From?
text:
Imagine you’re riding your bike but the tire is flat. It has a leak! You can fix it, but first, you need to find the source of the leak. It’s the same with stress. Finding the source of your stress can help you decide what to do so you can keep going.

These questions can help you find the source of stress:

What is causing me to feel stressed?

Can these feelings help me in any way?

title: Anxious Feelings
text:
Have you ever dreamed about missing a test or making a big mistake? Did you wake up feeling scared? Feeling afraid of something that hasn’t happened yet is called anxiety. Sometimes it’s easy to tell why you’re feeling anxious. Other times, you might feel scared without knowing why.

When you feel anxious, ask yourself: What am I afraid of? For example, if you are anxious about running in a race, you might be afraid of tripping. But what will happen if you trip? You might get hurt. Now that you know you’re afraid of getting hurt, you can start to understand your anxiety.

title: Anxiety in the Body
text:
When you're in danger, your brain releases natural chemicals. These chemicals give you energy and tell your body to get ready to fight or run away. This is called the fight or flight response. Feeling anxious can turn on the fight or flight response, too. However, if you’re not fighting or trying to run away, those chemicals can make you really uncomfortable. You might feel:

Sweaty hands

Pounding heart

Stomachache

Tense muscles

Fast breathing

Headache

title: Anxious Feelings Are Normal
text: Anxiety is part of being alive. It helped our ancestors stay safe by warning them of danger. It also helps you remember to stay safe by looking both ways before you cross the street. But sometimes, your brain can’t tell the difference between a real danger and a math test. Sometimes we have to tell our brains that we aren’t in real danger. Use your growth mindset to help you.

title: Calm Anxiety by Being Present
text:
One way to calm your anxiety is to focus on the present. Don’t think about what might happen in the future. Try this:

Close your eyes.

Take a deep breath.

Think of one thing you can hear right now.

Think of one thing you can smell.

Think of one thing you can taste.

Think of one thing you can feel.

Focus on the feeling of your chair.

Focus on the feeling of your feet in your shoes.

Pay attention to your heartbeat.

Keep breathing deeply.

Do this as often as you need to.

title: More Tools for Calming Anxious Feelings
text:
Strategies are plans that help you do something. Here are a few ideas you can use to create your own strategy for calming anxiety:

Talk to a trusted adult.

Write five things you are grateful for.

Get enough sleep.

Do jumping jacks.

Practice a talent.

Listen to calming music.

Make a list of strategies that work for you. Put it in a place where you can read it when you feel anxious. Ask for help, and talk to your doctor if you feel worried all the time and none of your strategies help.

title: Managing Emotions
text: A coping strategy is something you can use to help you manage your emotions. These strategies can be positive or negative. Negative coping strategies don’t really help you long-term. They may even cause more trouble! Positive coping strategies can help you learn to accept your emotions and face challenges.

title: Problem-Based and Emotion-Based Strategies
text:
Problem-based strategies help us change the problem that is causing our negative emotions.

Asking for support

Making a checklist

Creating a schedule to manage time

Emotion-based strategies help us change our negative feelings into positive ones. Then, we can respond in a helpful way.

Writing down feelings

Exercising

Practicing mindfulness

title: Not Too Hot, Not Too Cold
text: What happens when you start to feel overwhelmed? Do you have a hot reaction and explode with anger or frustration? Do you have a cold reaction and shut down, feeling hopeless or powerless? Coping strategies can help you avoid both of these reactions. Then you can choose to respond to problems in a way that is helpful and productive.

title: Be Prepared
text: Think of coping strategies like a tool kit. You need different tools to help with different things. Try many different coping strategies and find more than one that works for you. Write them down so you can remember them. You can also write down new coping strategies that you want to try out. Keep your list somewhere that is easy to find when you’re overwhelmed.

title: Wanting to vs. Choosing to
text:
Motivation is what you feel when you want to accomplish something. You might feel motivated when something is important to you. You might also feel motivated if you enjoy the task at hand.

Sometimes it can be hard to feel motivated. The task might not be fun or may be difficult. When this happens, you can use discipline. Discipline is choosing to get something done even when you don’t feel motivated.

Motivation and discipline are both important. They can help you reach your goals and become the best version of you!

title: What Motivates You?
text:
Intrinsic motivation means you want to do something because it seems fun or interesting. Can you think of something you like to do because it is fun?

Extrinsic motivation means you do it because of something else. For example, you might be motivated by a due date or a reward. Can you think of something you do because of a due date?

title: What Are Your Talents and Strengths?
text:
When someone is naturally good at something, we call that a talent. One talent is being able to quickly see something good in a hard situation. With a lot of practice, you can turn that talent into a strength. A strength is something you can do really well, over and over again. An example is seeing positive things all around you and helping others stay positive, too.

What are some of your talents?

How can you use motivation, discipline, and perseverance to turn them into strengths?

title: Resilient in Hard Times
text:
Resilience is the ability to push through hard things. Sometimes things happen around us that we can’t control. Being resilient is being able to stay positive when things change unexpectedly. It’s a skill that we learn and practice and it can make us stronger. Resilience is sometimes referred to as grit.

Imagine a rubber band. When you stretch a rubber band, it gets longer. Stretching it changes its shape. After you let go, the rubber band bounces back to its normal shape. It can still hold things together. The rubber band shows resilience.

title: Resilient in Relationships
text:
You can be resilient in your relationships with friends and family. This is called social resilience. You can be socially resilient when you …

Be yourself

Stand up for what you believe in

Resolve conflict with friends

Apologize when you make mistakes

Forgive others

You can have strong friendships when you are resilient.

title: Resilient with Your Feelings
text:
Our emotions change every day. This is not a bad thing. Learning to regulate our emotions builds emotional resilience.

It is important to understand and share how we feel. This helps us manage how we respond to our feelings. It will also help us build empathy.

title: Resilient in Your Mind
text: Mental resilience is being in charge of your thoughts. It is motivating yourself to do hard things. Mental resilience helps you learn new skills. It also helps you get over the negative effects of difficult experiences. Your ability to be strong and confident is mental resilience. You must have confidence in yourself. You should feel confident in providing ideas. You share these ideas with your class, family, or team.

title: A Resilient Body
text:
Physical resilience is helping your body do hard things. When you get injured, your body needs time to heal. If you break your arm, you need physical resilience to heal. If you use hearing aids to hear better or glasses to see better, you are being resilient.

Every person's body can be resilient. Some people have physical differences that impact the way they do things. They are physically resilient because they do things even when it is different or harder for them.

Everyone needs physical resilience at different times in their lives. When we push through physically hard things, we train our bodies. We can respond positively when things are challenging.

title: Use Your Resources
text:
There will be times in your life when you need to be resourceful. Being resourceful means working hard to achieve a goal. Being resourceful means finding a way to use the resources around you to create a solution. You are always searching for ways to achieve your goals.

You can:

Ask for help

Think outside the box

Work together with others

Use available resources

Consider all options

title: Take Responsibility
text: Part of being resilient is being responsible. Everyone is responsible for things in their daily lives. You have responsibilities at home, at school, or on teams. Knowing what you must do helps you achieve your goals. When you act in a responsible way, you build resilience. You know what needs to be done. More importantly, you do it! Being responsible helps you learn that you can count on yourself. You follow through on what you need to do. You can depend on yourself to do what is needed.

title: Courage to Do Hard Things
text: Having courage means being brave. It means facing hard things. It doesn’t mean doing dangerous things. Having courage and being brave help you be more resilient. You do things that stretch your skills. As you stretch, you can make great things happen for yourself. You can grow each day.

title: Lexington and Concord
text:
After the powder alarm of 1774, tensions were high in Massachusetts. The Patriots and the British Regulars continued to clash. Then, in February 1775, General Gage and the British Regulars became the government and law enforcers in the colony.

By April 18, 1775, the Patriot militia in the town of Concord, Massachusetts, had gathered a large supply of munitions. Eighteen miles away in Boston, General Gage was informed of this supply.

The Sons of Liberty heard about the orders. Patriots Paul Revere and William Dawes spent the night riding the 18 miles to Lexington and Concord, giving the alarm: “The Regulars are out.” The Minutemen answered the alarm.

British Colonel Francis Smith and the British Regulars arrived in Lexington early in the morning on their way to Concord. The British troops continued to Concord. The British soldiers went into every home, looting and looking for the supplies. The Patriot militia was waiting for them by the North Bridge on the road out of town.

The British Regulars fired their weapons into the militia on the other side of the bridge. The Patriots returned fire, killing three British soldiers. As the British left Concord to return to Boston, the Patriot militia had grown to include over 2,000 men. They followed the British, firing on them from houses, stone walls, and trees. The British returned fire when they could, killing a total of 95 Patriots. The British had killed or wounded 273 people by the time they reached Boston.

The actions at Lexington and Concord in April of 1775 set off a chain of events that changed the world. These actions became known as “the shot heard ‘round the world.”

title: Continental Congress
text:
The Continental Congress gathered once again in the summer of 1775. It was only weeks after the battles in Lexington and Concord. They didn’t know if the British military might enter the Pennsylvania State House and arrest each man for treason. They were preparing for war. John Hancock was elected the president of Congress to keep the order of business and assign committees. The next year was filled with several key events that ultimately led to the official break between the American colonies and the British government.

June 17, 1775: Inexperienced colonial soldiers held off hardened British veterans for more than two hours at Breed's Hill. Although eventually forced to abandon their position, including the high ground of Bunker Hill, the Patriots showed that they were not intimidated by the British Army. The Continental Congress responded by appointing George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.

July 5, 1775: The Continental Congress approved the Olive Branch Petition as a last appeal to King George III to avoid going to war with Britain. In the petition, the colonists pledged their loyalty to the king and claimed their rights as British citizens. The king responded by declaring that the colonies were in a state of rebellion.

Dec. 1775: Congress created a navy and named Esek Hopkins commodore of the new American Navy. Soon after, Congress authorized privateering and issued rules for dealing with enemy vessels and plunder. In response, the British Parliament banned trade with the colonies and authorized the seizure of colonial vessels on Dec. 23.

April 6, 1776: Congress responded to Parliament's actions by opening American ports to all foreign ships except British vessels.

May 1776: Congress learned that the king had negotiated treaties with German states to hire mercenaries to fight in America against the colonists. This showed them that the king was preparing for a fight.

June 8, 1776: Virginian Richard Henry Lee offered a resolution from the Virginia House of Burgesses stating that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.” John Hancock appointed a committee of five men to draft a document of independence.

June 28, 1776: The Committee of Five presented their draft of a declaration of independence to send to King George. The members of Congress edited and revised the wording. Then the delegates sent messengers back to their home colonies to ask for advice. They needed to know how their colonies wanted them to vote on declaring independence.

title: Skills to Be Social
text: Social skills are communication skills. We use these skills whenever we interact with each other. Using positive social skills helps you create and maintain friendships. We build our friendships when we remember our manners, share, and show respect. You can feel confident in your ability to communicate. People like to spend time with others who have positive social skills.

title: Skills of Communication
text: Positive communication and interactions are important. Communication skills are skills you can learn and practice. These are some communication skills you can develop:

title: Skills of Respect
text:
Everyone deserves respect, including you! Being respectful helps you be a good friend. You can show respect to friends, family, and even strangers by:

Accepting differences

Recognizing cultural differences

Sharing and taking turns

Working together

Being kind

Being patient

title: Skills of Participation
text: Participation helps you improve your social skills. You are participating when you are part of a team or group. Being willing to join a group takes courage. Your ideas have value. Use your communication skills to share your ideas with the group. You can participate in classroom discussions and try new things. Participating with others helps build your confidence. Participation lets others know you are willing to try.

title: Skills of Conflict Resolution
text:
Conflict is a disagreement between individuals or groups. Conflict can happen between individuals, in small groups, and even in large groups. Resolving conflict is a social skill that everyone needs. When conflicts arise, there are questions you can ask. These questions will help you think about the steps you can take to resolve conflict:

What is the problem?

What caused the problem?

What solutions could help?

Which possible solution should I try?

Do I need any help?

title: Skills of Cooperation and Compromise
text: It helps to be adaptable when working and playing with others. Being adaptable means you are willing to change your plan to work with others. It means cooperating and compromising when needed. Cooperating is working together to get something done. Sometimes, when adapting, you have to look at different solutions. Then, you find a compromise that others can agree on. Compromise is when people give up something so everyone can agree on a solution.

title: Skill of Taking Initiative
text: Taking initiative is doing things without being asked. You look around your environment and take action to take care of a need. Look for ways to take initiative. Pick up trash around your playground. Put something away even if you weren’t the person who left it out. Help someone, even when you are not asked to. When you take initiative, it communicates to those around you that you care.

title: Brain and Body Connection
text: All day and night, your brain tells your muscles how to move. But did you know that the way you move influences your brain? Everything you eat, drink, and do affects the way your brain functions. This includes the types of food you eat, how much water you drink, and how much you sleep. It also includes your physical activity. When you make healthy choices about what you eat and drink and how you move, your brain and body get stronger.

title: Physical Activity Helps Your Brain
text:
Here are some of the ways physical activity can help you:

Improved learning and memory

Faster decision-making

Healthier brain cells

Improved mood

Better focus

Less stress

title: Move Safely
text:
Don’t forget to keep your body safe during physical activity by making smart choices. You can use proper equipment during activities to protect your body. You can memorize safety procedures in case of emergencies to protect your body.

When you ride a bike, what choices can you make to protect your body? ______________________

When you are planning to spend all day playing outside in the sun, what choices can you make to protect your body? ___________________________________________________________________________

If there is a fire at school, what choice can you make to protect your body?

Circle the things that are made to protect your body:

title: Move Mindfully
text:
Practicing mindfulness when you exercise can help lower your stress and anxiety even more. You get a rush of feel-good chemicals, but that’s not all. Mindfully focusing on your activities can help pull you out of your worries by focusing your brain power on the movements your body is making.

Focus on the sensations in your body. How does the air feel against your hands? How does your breathing feel? What do you feel when your shoe hits the floor? Pay attention to the sights and sounds, too. Enjoy the moment. Remember that as you move your body, you are helping your brain grow.

title: Get Moving!
text:
Your body is one of a kind, which means you have your own unique needs and abilities. Find the physical activity that works for you! You are responsible for moving your body every day. Aim for around 60 minutes of activity per day, but any amount of physical activity is better than none.

Here are just a few ideas:

Play tag with your friends.

Invent a new game that gets you moving.

Learn jump-rope tricks.

Play in a swimming pool.

Turn on some music and dance.

What can you do if you need ideas for safe and helpful ways to move your body?

title: Who Were Abolitionists?
text:
Many people in America opposed the enslavement of people. Most of the northern states had abolished, or legally ended, slavery by the early 1800s. However, it remained legal in all of the southern states. People who openly opposed slavery were known as abolitionists. They worked toward freeing all people. People organized and raised awareness of abolition in print, in speeches, and through their actions.

Abolitionists also helped enslaved people escape to freedom. Many enslaved people wanted to go North, where slavery was illegal. Escaping from slavery was different, depending on how close to the north a person was. If a person was close to the border with the north, it could be a quicker journey than a person escaping from the Deep South. Regardless, in order to gain freedom, enslaved people needed to escape to the North.

To make the trip north, those escaping needed help. Safe locations were necessary for rest, food, and direction. Abolitionists knew how to help, even though they knew that helping an enslaved person escape was against the law. The consequences for helping an enslaved person escape were severe. Farms were burned, people were killed, and some were arrested. These consequences did not stop abolitionists.

A system of secret codes, paths, and hideaways was created, known as the “Underground Railroad.” The paths, known as “tracks,” were hidden from the public eye. There were people who acted as guides, like “conductors” on a railroad. There were hiding places, or “railroad stations.” The “passengers” (enslaved people seeking freedom) were met in secret by a conductor, who would guide them to the next station. At the station, they were given food, clothing, and supplies for the next part of the trip. The passengers traveled at night. They traveled quietly and as quickly as they could. They would often look for hidden codes along the path as markers to locate the next station.

There were many routes on the Underground Railroad. The routes went to many different cities in the North and eventually to Canada. Enslaved people risked their lives to be free. Many brave people helped them reach freedom.

title: Another Word for "Teamwork"
text: Collaboration is working with others to get something done. Working as a team can help you problem-solve and see things from a different perspective. You can get more done in a shorter amount of time by working together. Working with others can improve your relationships and social connections. Collaboration is a life skill that will help you.

title: Listen to Each Other
text:
Being a good listener is an important part of successful collaboration. Listening carefully to everyone’s ideas (including your own) will help people feel safe and included. Listening to team members will make it easier to solve problems and get things done. Here are some ideas to try that can help you improve your listening skills:

Put away distractions.

Give your attention to the speaker.

Do not interrupt.

Repeat what has been said to check for understanding.

Ask questions to clarify.

title: Use Your Strengths
text: In a team, every single job is important. Everyone on the team has unique strengths. Collaborating means finding a way to use the strengths of each team member. You can accomplish and do some incredible things when you work with others!

title: Known Stops on the Underground Railroad in Pennsylvania
text:
F. Julius LeMoyne House

Washington, PA

The LeMoyne House was built in 1812. It was a center of abolitionist activity and a station on the Underground Railroad. Dr. F. Julius LeMoyne was born in Washington, Pennsylvania, and studied medicine at the Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. In 1834, LeMoyne joined the Washington Anti-Slavery Society and was a regional agent. Washington, Pennsylvania, sits just to the southwest of Pittsburgh.

John Graff House

Blairsville

John Graff was a conductor on the Underground Railroad. At his home in Blairsville, Graff constructed a tunnel near the Conemaugh River shore to his carriage house for freedom seekers to use. In the carriage house, he built a small hidden room where those escaping slavery could eat, rest and bathe before continuing further north. Blairsville had a strong community of abolitionists. Many people seeking freedom found support in this community. Today, the Underground Railroad History Museum is located in Blairsville at the former Second Baptist Church.

Bethel AME Zion Church

Reading

During the years leading up to the Civil War, the congregation of Bethel AME church was very active in the Underground Railroad. Its members often harbored people escaping slavery. Jacob Ross, one of the founding members of the church, found support in the local community. He was a formerly enslaved man from Virginia who decided to settle in Reading and help others escape to freedom.

Oakdale

Chadds Ford

Oakdale

Photograph courtesy of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission.

Oakdale was built in 1840 by Isaac and Dinah Mendenhall, two leading abolitionists who helped to form the Society of Progressive Friends. Oakdale was the first stop north of the Delaware line on the Underground Railroad. The Mendenhalls built a concealed square-shaped room between a walk-in fireplace and carriage house that helped conceal those escaping slavery.

White Horse Farm

Phoenixville

White Horse Farm was the home of abolitionist Elijah Pennypacker. It operated as a depot on the Underground Railroad. He became a leader of Pennsylvania's abolitionist cause. In 1840, he opened his home as a major stop on the Underground Railroad. Hundreds of people escaping slavery were kept safe in this home. No person was ever apprehended while in his care.

Johnson House

Philadelphia

The Johnson House was one of the key sites of the anti-slavery movement in Philadelphia. Many Johnson family members were members of abolitionist groups and became involved in the Underground Railroad. The home, along with the nearby homes of relatives, protected people escaping slavery as a station on the Underground Railroad.

title: Showing Respect Makes Strong Teams
text:
Respect is treating others how you like to be treated.

Do you like when people speak to you with kindness? Do you like when people let you share your ideas? Of course! That is respect, and that is how you can treat others. Collaborating is more enjoyable when everyone in the group is respectful to each other.

If you are ever wondering how to be respectful, you can ask yourself, “How would I want to be treated in this situation?”

title: Support and Encourage Others
text: When working on something new, it won't always go perfectly. Accidents or mistakes are going to happen. Supporting your team when working together is important. Building others up will make you and your team stronger. Encourage others. Help them feel good about their efforts and contributions. Doing this will make your team stronger.

title: Own Your Mistakes
text: Sometimes when things go wrong, people want to blame others. You can choose how you respond when you or others make mistakes. Collaborating means taking responsibility when you make mistakes. Collaborating also means encouraging others positively when they make mistakes.

title: Heroes of the Underground Railroad
text:
Many brave people were involved in the Underground Railroad. Men and women from many communities and cultures came together. Their efforts supported people escaping slavery and seeking freedom. They supported each other in unique ways. Thaddeus Stevens, William Still, and Harriet Tubman were some of the abolitionists who worked for this cause.

Thaddeus Stevens

Thaddeus Stevens was a politician who served in both the Pennsylvania State Congress and the United States Congress. He fought for the rights of Native Americans, women, and those who were enslaved. Recent research has found that Stevens was actively involved in the Underground Railroad. A cistern, or well, was found next to his home in Lancaster. This cistern may have been used to hide freedom seekers from bounty hunters. Stevens was even known to have hired and managed a group of spies to watch for bounty hunters looking for those who were escaping. While a member of the United States Congress, Stevens helped to draft an early version of the 13th Amendment and fought for laws in education and voting rights throughout his entire career.

“No government can be free that does not allow all its citizens to participate in the formation and execution of her laws.” - Thaddeus Stevens

William Still

Known as the “father of the Underground Railroad,” William Still worked to free nearly 800 freedom seekers. He was born free in New Jersey in 1821. In Philadelphia, Still worked as a janitor and clerk for the Pennsylvania Society for the Abolition of Slavery. Through this work, he met people who escaped slavery on the Underground Railroad and began working with the network. He recorded the names of people who escaped and encouraged them to change their names to protect themselves. Due to his records, enslaved people were able to reunite with their families. Ultimately, his detailed notes have helped us learn a lot about the Underground Railroad.

“It was my good fortune to lend a helping hand to the weary travelers flying from the land of bondage.” - William Still

Harriet Tubman

Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Harriet Ross in Maryland in 1820. When the man who enslaved her died in 1849, she took the opportunity to run away. Harriet Tubman ran north and discovered the Underground Railroad on her journey. She arrived in Philadelphia, but she did not stay long. Instead, Tubman returned for her family members and others. She helped them escape slavery. Tubman made many trips along the Underground Railroad, becoming one of its most successful “conductors.” Throughout her life, she used what little money or resources she had to help formerly enslaved people find food, homes, and work.

“I had crossed the line. I was free; but there was no one to welcome me to the land of freedom. I was a stranger in a strange land; and my home after all, was down in Maryland; because my father, my mother, my brothers, and sisters, and friends were there. But I was free, and they should be free.” - Harriet Tubman

title: Talk About Trust
text: Trust is the belief that you can rely on something or someone. Think about the sun. You trust that even on stormy days, the sun is there, behind the clouds. It’s dependable. This means it acts the way it is supposed to. You expect the sun to rise, and it always does! When you trust a person, you can expect them to be honest because they are dependable in their actions.

title: Examining Charles T. Webber's, The Underground Railroad
text:
Born in 1814 in Germany, Theodore Kaufmann studied painting in several large cities. He left for the United States in 1850. He was first exposed to slavery In the U.S. and became an abolitionist. When the Civil War broke out, Kaufmann fought for the Union Army. During that time, he witnessed enslaved people coming to Union encampments and gaining their freedom. His painting, On to Liberty, became a symbol of why he fought against slavery. Kaufmann died in 1896.

Use the table of questions to study the painting.

Describe what you see. What are 10 things you see in the painting?

What do you notice first?

What people and objects are shown?

How are they arranged?

What is the physical setting?

Why do you think this image was made?

Who do you think was the audience for this image?

What can you learn from examining this image?

title: Essential Question
text: How is the Underground Railroad in Pennsylvania evidence of civil disobedience?

title: Becoming Trustworthy
text:
You trust that the sun will come up tomorrow because you have seen it come up every day of your life. The ways you speak and act can help other people learn to trust you. If you say you will do something, do you do it? Trust is built over time.

To build trust, you can:

Speak kindly about everyone

Be honest (even if you might get in trouble)

Keep your promises

Treat others with respect

title: Being Dependable
text:
What would happen if you promised your friend you'd help them with a project, but you didn’t keep that promise? Do you think they would trust you to help them again? How would you feel?

It’s difficult to trust someone who doesn’t keep their promises. To be dependable, do what you say you will do. Being dependable doesn’t mean you have to do everything anyone asks you to do, but it does mean honoring your commitments.

title: Step #1: Identify the Conflict
text:
The first step to resolving any conflict is to identify the conflict. Conflict happens when people do not agree. People in healthy relationships disagree sometimes. Trying to work through differences is healthy. People in healthy relationships can admit that there is a conflict. Identifying the conflict means seeing there is a problem and being willing to work to find a solution.

Everyone has different perspectives, so you can talk to those involved to understand other points of view. Ask questions. Try not to be defensive, and be willing to look at all options. If a friend is doing something that bothers you, you can explain that there’s a problem.

Pay attention to your communication style, and do your best to identify the conflict in a respectful way that invites others involved to help find a solution.

title: Step #2: Identify the Cause
text: When conflict happens, it’s important to figure out how it was caused. Some causes of conflict are easy to solve. Sometimes a conflict comes from a misunderstanding. Sometimes the cause is more difficult to discover. Identifying a conflict requires you to think about words that you said or things that you did.

title: Step #3: Identify Possible Solutions
text:
After you have identified the conflict and the cause, you can start thinking of solutions. Solutions are things that could help everyone involved feel better about the conflict. People in healthy relationships can be open to suggestions because they trust one another. Some solutions may include saying, “I’m sorry,” or making amends, like paying to fix something or correcting a behavior.

As you look for solutions, consider all of the possibilities. Sometimes a silly suggestion will work. Sometimes the solution needs to be more serious.

Everyone needs help finding solutions, so working together will help. You can ask an adult, change your activity, or push pause and count to 10.

title: Step #4: Try to Solve the Problem
text: Decide which of the suggested solutions is best, then put it into action. Be confident in your decision. Trying out what you have decided to do to solve the problem is an important step.

title: Step #5: Ask Experts to Consult
text:
You can reach out to experts for help. They can assist you when you get stuck resolving a conflict. Other people can help you see things a little bit differently. Don't be afraid to ask for advice when solving a problem. Others may have already solved the same problem and might be able to give you the answer you’re looking for.

Who are some people you might consider reaching out to?

title: Organizing Your Time
text:
A schedule is a plan of things to do and when to do them. For example, your schedule might include things like when to leave for school and when to start your homework. Creating a schedule can help you make sure you get things done on time.

A routine is a set of actions you repeat often. For example, you might wash your face and brush your teeth every night before bed. Routines help you remember to do things and remind you what happens next.

title: The External Structures of Animals
text:
Animal Structures

Animals have different ________ structures that help them move, live, and meet their needs.

Move:

Eat:

Meet needs:

title: Priorities
text:
When you have a lot to do, it can feel overwhelming. Prioritizing your responsibilities means deciding which task is most important and needs to be done first. Prioritizing helps reduce stress.

Write a list of things you need to do.

Decide what is most important.

Write the number one next to it.

Continue until you’ve numbered everything on the list.

Rewrite your list in order of importance.

Start getting things done!

title: Making Lists
text:
You can prioritize when you create to-do lists. When you are trying to decide the order of your tasks, you should think about a few things:

Does the item have a deadline? When?

How much time will each item take?

How important is each item?

Does the order matter? (Sometimes one thing must happen before another can.)

title: Procrastination Problems
text:
Procrastination is putting off doing something that should get done. For example, waiting to do your homework until the day it is due is procrastination. When you procrastinate, you have to hurry and can’t give your best effort. You might even run out of time. Procrastination can cause stress and make your well-being feel out of balance.

When you want to procrastinate, ask yourself:

Why am I avoiding this?

Am I afraid it will be difficult?

Do I know where to start?

What is one thing I can do to start the task?

title: Have a Good Attitude
text:
When you start out with a positive attitude, it’s easier to get things done. Instead of procrastinating something, try thinking about how good you will feel when it’s done!

Being positive means seeing the good that can come from difficult situations. It’s great for your well-being!

Tips for staying positive:

Practice being positive every day.

Keep a gratitude journal.

Surround yourself with positive friends.

title: Tips for When Motivation Is Low
text:
If your motivation starts to disappear, here are some tips to help you get it back:

Take a break. Try again when you feel calm.

Remember why you are doing this. Think about what really matters to you.

Break tasks up into smaller steps. Take them one at a time.

Make it fun! How can you reward yourself? What’s a fun way to track your progress? Be creative!

Circle your favorite tips.

title: Test
text: The economy of the South relied on enslaved people to keep farms and plantations running. Many delegates of the North wanted to outlaw the slave trade, but delegates of the South disagreed. A compromise was finally reached. The slave trade would be allowed to go on for another 20 years and then be outlawed in 1808.

title: Why Do Humans Communicate?
text:
While human communication is by far the most complicated, other animals have also found ways to communicate with each other. For example, if baby gorillas need something, they cry and scream to get their mothers’ attention. As gorillas grow older, they use grunts and other similar sounds to get each other’s attention, make their location known, or have social interactions. They communicate most as they travel. They even use facial expressions and body poses to express themselves.

Another interesting example of animal communication is that of whales. Whales use sounds to communicate with each other and hunt. Male humpback whales sing a 30-minute song and can repeat it for hours. Marine biologists aren't sure why humpback whales sing. Some think it's to find a mate and others think the whales sing to socialize with each other. Killer whales also have interesting communication. Each pod (family or group) of killer whales has a slightly different language. They communicate with clicks, whistles, and calls.

Just like these animals, humans communicate for many reasons and in many different ways.

Here are a few of the main reasons humans communicate:

to express needs or wants

to entertain

to educate or relay information

to connect with others

to express feelings

Have you ever communicated for any of these reasons?

title: Phenomenon Comic
text: Phenomenon: While talking over video chat, Gina, Claire, and Miguel notice that the weather in Crystal Beach and Amarillo, Texas, is different.

title: Communicating Through Words
text:
The primary, or main, way people communicate is through words. This is called verbal communication. Verbal communication includes talking and sign language. When you are choosing which words to use to express yourself, take a few things into consideration, such as:

Who are you talking to?

What is your relationship with that person?

Where are you?

What is the situation? Is there any danger?

These factors will affect how loud, how fast, and how casually you speak. If you are talking to your grandmother at a funeral, you will speak more quietly and respectfully so she can understand you. If you are at a birthday party talking to your best friend, you might speak in a loud and excited voice. If you are at a friend’s house and are uncomfortable when they offer you drugs, you can assertively say, “No,” and leave. If you ever feel pressured to do something you are uncomfortable with or you know is unhealthy, like drinking alcohol, taking drugs, or participating in gang activity, it is important that you use your verbal communication skills to help others know where you stand. In different situations, your verbal communication will look and sound different.

title: Communicating Through Actions
text:
Have you ever heard the phrase “actions speak louder than words”? What do you think that means? Do you think this statement is true?

You communicate through your actions every day, even when you don’t realize it. Take a moment to notice how you are sitting right now as you read this article or listen to it being read to you. Are you leaning back in your chair with your arms folded? You might be showing that you are disinterested. Are you laying your head on the table? You may be communicating that you are tired or bored. Maybe you are sitting up straight, on the edge of your seat. You may be communicating that you are engaged and interested. Your facial expressions, body language, and actions are all ways that you communicate. Be aware of how you look on the outside. Sometimes people’s outward behaviors do not match what they feel or think. Check in with yourself often to make sure you are communicating what you want through your facial expressions, body language, and actions.

title: Essential Question
text: What was the historical and modern effect of iron and steel on Pennsylvania?

title: Communicating Through Images
text:
Social media is a great example of how people communicate through images. People post pictures of what they are doing and things that are important to them. People who post many pictures of their family could be communicating that their family is their priority. Other people may have food or fitness blogs or video channels. You can assume that food or fitness is important to them.

Using images can also be a great tool when you are trying to communicate with someone who speaks a different language than you. Pictures can help clarify and explain.

Images and pictures are a fast way to communicate. There are pictures all around us that send us messages. When you drive, there are street signs with images that tell you that there is a crosswalk, that two lanes merge, or that there is a sharp turn coming up. These images quickly communicate important information to help keep you safe.

title: Communicating with Kindness
text: Even when you feel upset, you can communicate with kindness and respect. You can express your ideas and opinions verbally, nonverbally, through writing, or through images. You can do it without calling names or being unkind. You can use your communication skills to show respect to people who are different from you. You can use your communication skills to stand up for others or give people compliments. How you communicate will affect who wants to spend time with you and who wants to be around you. Another way to communicate with kindness is by being a good listener. A good listener shows through their facial expressions and body language that they are listening and care about what is being said. Good listeners make eye contact and do not interrupt. Are you a good listener? What could you do to become a better listener?

title: Physical and Economic Regions of the United States
text:
When creating a map of an area, cartographers and geographers often divide places into regions. Regions are areas that are defined by certain characteristics, such as population, geography, economics, government, climate, or other features. Regions can also be organized by imaginary borders and cultural characteristics. This indicates not only a geographic location but also implies certain traditions, beliefs, and manners. Cultural regions include places like the “Deep South” and the Bible Belt.

Physical geography is one of the most common ways land is divided into regions. Examples in the U.S. include the Rocky Mountains, the Great Plains, and the Great Lakes. Regions can have political boundaries, such as cities, states, countries, and continents. Originally, Native Americans divided the regions by systems of people, trade, and ideas. After colonization, some regions earned nicknames from their economies, such as the Breadbasket, Silicon Valley, and the Rust Belt.

Regions can also be categorized by historical context. An example of this is the original 13 Colonies. The Colonies were organized into the Northern, Mid-Atlantic, and Southern regions.

During the early 1800s, the United States was divided into three regions: the North, the South, and the West. In the 1800s, an imaginary line called the Mason-Dixon Line divided the eastern side of the country into the North and the South. The Mason-Dixon Line was measured between 1763 and 1770 by British surveyors Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon. A surveyor is a person who examines and makes maps of land.

The Mason-Dixon Line was a human-made line that marked the boundary between slave-holding states and states where slavery was illegal. States north of the line had a more industrial economy with factories that produced manufactured goods. States south of the line had a more agricultural economy and used the fertile southern soil to grow food and cash crops. Today, the Mason-Dixon Line no longer exists, but the cultural and economic characteristics of each region live on.

The West is a region that was originally defined as everything west of the original 13 Colonies. Before settlers moved west and began establishing cities and towns, King George III of England made the Proclamation Line of 1763. The proclamation stated that all land west of the Appalachian Mountains belonged to the Indigenous peoples already living there. English colonists were not allowed to settle past that boundary. At that time, land west of the Appalachian Mountains was called the “West” or the “frontier.” This line continued to shift over time as wars and changes in government affected westward expansion.

The “West” or the “American frontier” was commonly what people called the land beyond the westernmost European settlement. Settlement increased dramatically after the Louisiana Purchase nearly doubled the size of the U.S. in 1803, and the starting line for the American West continued to move as settlers expanded across the country. Today, the West is considered to be the states west of the meridian that runs through the middle of the United States.

title: Essential Question
text: How did the regions of the United States differ physically and economically during the early 1800s?

title: The North
text:
Before the Industrial Revolution began in America, most manufacturers were still using the cottage industry. The cottage industry was when people made products by hand in their own homes or small shops. Most skilled workers specialized in a specific trade, such as carpentry, tailoring, metalworking, and others. This began to change as the demand for goods rose. Factories and machinery began to be built that made production faster and easier.

More workers were needed in the factories. More and more people from Europe began to immigrate to the United States, looking for work in the factories. Production grew, and industry really took off in the North. As more and more people came to the U.S., more canals, roads, and railroads were built to accommodate shipping and transportation. Shipping ports on the East Coast were used to ship goods all over the world. This led to more trade, more money, and more industrial expansion.

Wealth began to change as well. Before the Industrial Revolution, having wealth was almost exclusively tied to owning land. Industry began to change that. As manufacturing and production grew, people could become wealthy by starting businesses and producing and selling goods. In the early 1800s, the North was a place full of opportunities and possibilities for the common working person.

title: The South
text:
Unlike the industrialized North, the South’s economy relied heavily on agriculture. While the North had factories and busy cities, the South was mostly made up of sprawling plantations. States in the South had warm summers and mild winters, which was ideal for large-scale agriculture. The best way to make money in agriculture was to grow cash crops, or crops that could be grown in large quantities and sold for a profit. In the early 19th century, those crops included things like cotton, indigo, rice, and sugar.

However, the more of a crop a plantation grew, the more workers were needed to plant, tend, harvest, and process the crops. Rather than pay a wage to hired workers, plantation owners relied on the slave trade for labor. Enslaved people were purchased and then forced to work on the plantations for most or all of their lives without pay. As plantations expanded to make more money, more and more enslaved people were purchased to work the land.

title: Population of the Northern Region
text: In the 1800s, the North and South were very different places to live. A manufacturing economy along with a large population of immigrants caused a growth in urban development in the North.

title: Population of the South Region
text: Because most people in the South lived and worked on farms and plantations, the population of the South was considered rural. Compare the population charts of the North and South. Based on what you have learned about each region, why do you think the populations of the North and South both grew so quickly?

title: The West
text:
In the early 1800s, the West was made up of the states of the Northwest Territory, Missouri, and the rest of the land gained in the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The Northwest states included Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. The rest of the unsettled land was called several names, including the American Frontier, the Wild West, and the West. The western region of the United States was still considered wild in the early 19th century because it remained largely unsettled by white Americans. Before the California Gold Rush in the 1850s, most people who moved west crossed the Louisiana Territory to settle on large farms in Texas or made their way to cities like San Francisco, California.

The states of the West were generally more rural with smaller farms owned and run by families. Most people living in the western region were subsistence farmers, or farmers who lived off of their own land by producing what they needed for themselves. Small but growing cities and towns also dotted the landscape. The bigger cities on the edge of the frontier, such as St. Louis, Missouri, were sometimes called gateways to the West. This was because settlers who wanted to cross the frontier often started their journey in one of these cities. There, they could prepare, pick up supplies, hire a guide, or join a group to travel with to their destination.

During the early 1800s, most people in Ohio earned their living as farmers. As the population grew, early industries began to take shape. Factories produced goods. The factories created new jobs. The new jobs gave people a new way to earn a living. Most of the first factories were part of the agriculture industry. For example, in 1815, Bezaleel Wells started a wool mill in Steubenville. The wool came from the sheep farmers raised. Wells produced cloth from the wool that was used to make clothes.

In 1818, Elisha Mills opened a pork packing plant in Cincinnati. His workers put pork with salt and water into barrels. The brine kept the meat from going bad. Other pork packing plants opened up in the years to follow. Farm machines, such as metal plows, were also made in Ohio factories.

Many cities were built near rivers. The rivers helped new industries grow. Goods were loaded on steamships and sent downriver to be sold. The more factories were built, the more steamboats were needed. Boat-building companies sprang up. Mills to turn wood into lumber also opened.

Settling a new area took time and perseverance. Unlike stepping off a ship in New York and immediately starting work in a factory, settlers who moved west had to cut down trees, plow fields, build their own houses, and make whatever they needed that they couldn't buy in the nearest town or city. For many, the risk and the work was worth the reward of owning land and having the freedom and independence to work it.

title: Population of the Western Region
text: Unlike the North and the South, the West’s population grew much more slowly in the early 1800s. Look at the graphs for North and South population growth and compare them to this graph. How big of a difference is there in growth? Why do you think this was the case?

title: Setting Goals Can Change Your Life
text: A goal is something you work toward. Goals are usually new things or hard things that you want to learn or do. You usually make a plan to reach a goal. They can help you learn and grow. They help you gain new skills and abilities. You can set goals in every area of your life, including school, your hobbies, and your relationships.

title: How to Set Goals
text:
The next time you want to set a goal, try this! Make your goal a S.M.A.R.T. goal! What does that mean? A S.M.A.R.T. goal is:

Specific

Measurable

Attainable

Realistic

Timely

It should be clear what you want to achieve and how you will achieve it.

You must be able to measure your growth.

It should be challenging but possible to reach.

It should be a goal that makes sense and will help your life.

You must have a timeline to follow or a deadline.

Tanya’s Goal: Get a good grade in math.

Is Tanya’s goal specific? _______

Is Tanya’s goal measurable? __________

Is Tanya’s goals attainable? ________

Is Tanya’s goal realistic? ________

Is Tanya’s goal timely? _________

With a partner, rewrite Tanya’s goal to make it a S.M.A.R.T. goal:

title: Every Step Counts
text: Some goals can feel big and overwhelming. If that happens, don’t think of it as just one big goal. Instead, think of it as many small goals, like steps on a ladder. You just have to take one step at a time. Each small step gets you closer to your goal.

title: Keep Moving Forward
text:
There are two things you can do to keep moving toward your goal: be consistent and be persistent.

When you are consistent, it means you stick to your plan. For example, if you want to learn to play an instrument and you plan to practice for one hour every day, you stick to the schedule every day.

When you are persistent, it means you don’t give up, even when something is difficult. Stay focused, and don’t let yourself get distracted!

title: Take a Look in the Mirror
text:
As you work toward your goals, take time to examine the progress you’ve made. This is called self-reflection.

Self-reflection should be positive and encouraging. Think about where you started with your goal. Celebrate what’s going well, and change the things that aren’t working.

How am I feeling?

What progress have I made on my goals today?

Are there any parts of my plan that I’m avoiding or ignoring?

What can I do differently?

title: Progress Is Not Perfection
text:
As you work toward your goal, you might fall short in some areas. That means you set a good goal! It means you are challenging yourself to do things you have never done before. When you fall short, try to figure out what went wrong.

Was the goal too lofty?

Did you need a smaller milestone goal to help you along the way?

After you think about your progress, you can adjust your plans to help you be more successful. Progress is all about moving toward the end goal. Even small steps are progress. Reflecting on outcomes and adjusting your plan can help you continue toward successfully meeting your goal.

title: You Can Do Anything!
text: If you want to achieve your goals, you need to believe you can do it! Use positive self-talk and choose to have an “I can” attitude. Write your S.M.A.R.T. goal down and put it somewhere you will see it often. Remind yourself about the power of YET! Write positive quotes and hang them up as reminders. Keep telling yourself, “I’ve got this!”

title: How Can I Make Good Choices?
text:
You make lots of choices every day. The decisions you make about your health, the way you treat others, and the words you use are very important. Other decisions you make in your life may be easier to make.

How can you make good decisions? Try these steps:

Define the problem.

Brainstorm possible solutions.

Evaluate your options.

Decide.

Reflect.

title: Understand the Choice You Need to Make
text:
A road map for defining a problem is to observe, infer, and ask questions.

Observe what is going on around you. Think about the problem.

Infer, or make your best guess, about what the problem is, based on what you see and hear.

Ask questions to find out as much information as possible about the choice you need to make.

Margot has been feeling tired and sluggish but isn’t sure why. She asked herself, “Am I getting enough sleep?” The answer was yes.

“Am I eating enough vegetables, grains, and protein?” The answer was no. She had been eating more sweets than usual.

“Am I drinking enough water?” The answer was no. She kept forgetting to drink water.

“Am I moving my body each day?” The answer was no. She was sitting on the couch for hours each day, reading her favorite book. She forgot to get up and move.

title: Railroad - An Engineering Miracle
text:
Building railroads is not easy. Civil engineers have to think creatively when they tackle the problem of how to build a railroad line across a difficult stretch of land.

In 1880, the city of Buffalo, New York, used about three million tons of coal a year. The New York, Lake Erie, and Western Railroad and Coal Company wanted to find a fast way to transport Pennsylvania’s coal to Buffalo. However, standing in the way was the Kinzua Valley. The valley was a rugged place and hard to build a railroad through. Thomas Kane, president of the company, decided to build the railroad line over the valley instead.

He hired Octave Chanute to design a trestle bridge over the Kinzua Valley. A trestle bridge is a bridge that is supported all the way along its length by frames anchored to the ground.

First, they built stone foundations to anchor each of the trestles. Some of the foundations started at 35 feet below the ground and reached up to 16 feet above the ground. Then they built the trestles. The trestles were A-shaped supports made of wrought iron. The builders used more than three million pounds of iron to make them. The railroad tracks were then built, using the trestles for support. When the bridge was completed in 1882, it was 301 feet high. That’s as tall as a 21-story building. It was the tallest railroad bridge in the world. The bridge was 2,052 feet long. Almost seven football fields, end to end, would fit on the bridge.

Nonetheless, after only 18 years, the newer trains were too heavy for the bridge. It had to be rebuilt. This time, it was built with steel trestles, which were much stronger. When it was completed, the new bridge weighed twice as much as the old one. The bridge was well-built. However, the winds in Kinzua Valley were so strong that trains were only allowed to travel at five miles per hour over the bridge.

The Kinzua Bridge stood for 121 years. It was used for freight and passenger trains. It was also a tourist attraction. The bridge was made into a state park in 1963. People came from all over to ride on one of the tallest bridges in the world and to see its amazing view of the valley. In 2002, however, a tornado passed through the valley and tore 11 of the 20 trestles down. The bridge collapsed. The remaining portion of the bridge has been made into a skywalk with a glass floor at the end. People can still experience this trestle bridge.

text: What effect does transportation have on trade?

title: Come Up with Options
text:
After you have identified the choice you need to make, you can brainstorm possible solutions. Brainstorming means thinking about your options without having to make a choice yet. It is thinking about any type of outcome and consequence imaginable, even if it seems silly. You can use resources to help you come up with healthy and safe ideas.

Be smart about the resources you turn to. Social media may give you false or unrealistic information. Talking to peers and family members you trust may be a better option to help you brainstorm healthy and safe options.

After thinking about her problem, Margot needed to come up with ideas that could help her have more energy and feel better. She decided to brainstorm with her mom and brother. They came up with these ideas:

Join a dance class.

Play basketball every day for 30 minutes.

Do 100 jumping jacks each day.

Go on walks with friends.

Drink a full water bottle each day.

Eat a vegetable with at least one meal each day.

Drink water at every meal.

Only eat green foods.

Eat seven carrots every day.

text:
