Use your finger to trace a railroad route. Start at a location near your community. Where does the route go?

How is it connected to a larger network of railroads? Explain how these connections would impact a community.

title: World War II
text:
Worldwide conflict erupted in the 20th century. The leadership of some countries tried to control the government, people, and resources of other countries. The first of these was the First World War, or World War I. It was also called the Great War because it was thought that it would be the war to end all wars. World War I involved over 30 nations between 1914-1918. Many of the nations were located in Europe. The United States became involved in the conflict as well. In 1939 a second war began. It involved even more countries from around the world. World War II lasted until 1945.

During World War II, an alliance was formed between Germany, Italy, and Japan. They were known as the Axis powers. The Axis Powers were authoritarian governments. They demanded strict obedience to the government. The Axis governments persecuted minority populations. They used military strength to invade and control countries in Europe, Southeast Asia, and Africa. The Axis powers were aggressive. They provoked war to gain control of natural and industrial resources.

The countries who joined forces to fight against the Axis powers were called “the Allies.” Great Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union wanted to stop the Axis' aggressive actions. World War II was fought in Europe, Africa, and the South Pacific. There were land, air, and sea battles.

Men and Women from each nation became involved in the war. Men served in the Army, Navy, and Marines. The Air Force was part of the Army at this time. Women were also permitted to enlist in the armed forces for the first time. As in other wars, women were allowed to serve as nurses. However, they were also able to serve as mechanics, pilots, and clerks. Women worked in factories building military equipment and resources for the war effort.

The war was fought with new technology in Radio Detection and Ranging (RADAR). It's a system that uses radio waves to find the position of objects that can’t be seen. This helped during air battles. RADAR helped determine when and where planes were approaching. It also improved meteorology, or predicting the weather using science.

Computers were first used to break military codes and secret messages. Rockets were developed along with the fuel to launch them. The new rocket technology would eventually send humans to the moon. Improvements in food preservation made feeding the armed services easier and healthier. There were also great improvements in medical treatment for victims of war. Blood transfusions, greater surgical tools, and medicines like antibiotics increased the survival of the wounded.

The atomic age began in World War II. It began with the development of controlling and creating atomic energy. The first atomic bomb was dropped by the United States on Hiroshima, a city in Japan. A second bombing on Nagasaki, Japan, ended the war. The Axis Powers were defeated. The Allies hoped to establish peace in the world.

title: The Greatest Resource
text:
During World War II, citizens in the United States helped with the war effort. That included Pennsylvania. From volunteering to serve, to taking over jobs, to planting “victory gardens,” citizens rose to the occasion. Because of the people, including those from Pennsylvania, the United States helped win the war.

The 28th Infantry Division
Many Pennsylvanians volunteered to serve in World War II. Members of the 28th Infantry Division began preparing for war in February 1941. The first action this unit saw was during the D-Day operation. It took place in Normandy, France in 1944. These men were the first Americans to enter Germany. They had fought through France and Belgium to get there. The 28th led the way in important battles, like the Battle of the Bulge. These important battles helped the Allies defeat the Axis Powers. The 28th Infantry had a shoulder sleeve patch with a red keystone. This symbolized their history with Pennsylvania. They were first commanded by Major General Edward Martin from Waynesburg, PA. Martin became governor of Pennsylvania in 1943-47. He also served as a United States Senator from 1947-1959. Martin had served in Europe during World War I. He earned medals for bravery and heroism in combat. As governor, he worked closely with the Roosevelt administration to use Pennsylvania industries to support the war effort.

G. Raymond Rettew
Many people were wounded during World War II. Medics needed a way to treat infections. Penicillin, an antibiotic that kills bacteria, was used. It was first introduced in 1928. However, more needed to be produced. G. Raymond Rettew from Chester County found a way to mass produce penicillin for the troops. In September 2002, a historical marker was built in West Chester to honor Rettew's contributions. The marker reads, “In 1943, with Wyeth Laboratories, his lab ... made and sent more penicillin to the Armed Forces than any other lab in the world, saving countless lives on the Battlefields of World War II.”

Women in Pennsylvania
Over 22,000 Pennsylvanian women joined the Armed Forces during World War II. More than 1 million others joined the workforce. Men, the traditional factory workers, had been enlisted. However, the factories still needed workers. Women were finally allowed to take those jobs. Previously, only men had been allowed to do them. The factories produced supplies needed for the war effort. This included tanks, battleships, ammunition, and weapons.

Helen Richey
Helen Richey was an aviator from McKeesport, Pennsylvania. In 1940, Richey became the first woman licensed to be an aviation instructor. During the war, Richey joined the British Air Transport Auxiliary. In England, she delivered the newest technology from factories to military bases. When the United States entered the war, Richey joined the Women’s Air Service Pilots (WASP). She was stationed in Texas. Like in England, she made deliveries from factories to bases.

title: The Horseshoe Curve
text:
In the 1800s, Pittsburgh was considered the gateway to the American West. As people and goods began traveling west, a big obstacle kept them from making the trip easily. It was the Allegheny Mountains. On horseback, it took a month to cross the mountains. The Pennsylvania Railroad built the Main Line of Public Works to try and solve this problem. This was a series of railroads, canals, and inclined planes called the Portage Railroad.

The creation of the Portage Railroad cut the time it took to cross the mountain from one month to four and a half days. In the winter, however, the canals froze and couldn’t be used. Those living on the east side of the Allegheny Mountains in Pennsylvania wanted a railroad line that would go all the way from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. The main problem was finding a route over the mountains that wasn’t too steep for trains.

Chief engineer John Edgar Thomson, was given the task. He had to create a set of tracks that would get the train through the mountain gaps of the Allegheny. Thomson hired Herman Haupt to help him plan for the tracks to enter a valley west of Altoona. The plan was that instead of going straight up the side of the mountain, the train would slowly climb along the side of the mountains until it reached the top. Then, it would make a large, U-shaped turn that looked like a horseshoe. This allowed the train to reach the high point of the mountain. Then, it traveled along the top edge of the ridge until it made its way back down the mountain to the valley on the other side.

About 450 Irish workers built the Horseshoe Curve. They did it all by hand, using picks, shovels, hand drills, and black powder. They had to cut train-sized shelves through solid rock. This new, all-rail route cut travel from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh down to about 15 hours. The Horseshoe Curve was so successful that three more tracks were soon added to it. Other places have created their own types of curves to solve similar problems. In 1967, the National Park Service made Horseshoe Curve a National Historic Landmark. Horseshoe Curve is still an essential part of railroad transportation today.

The completion of this track and the engineering of the Horseshoe Curve opened the way westward.

title: Jeeps
text:
The Jeep was created for the use of the United States military in World War II. It was designed by the American Bantam Car Company of Butler, Pennsylvania. They were originally called Bantam Reconnaissance Cars (BRC).

By 1940, Nazi Germany was quickly taking over much of Europe. The Nazis had a vehicle that was lightweight, fast, and all-terrain. It was designed to travel over all types of ground. The United States military knew that it needed a similar type of vehicle. The government asked over 100 companies to try to create one. They only had 49 days to make a prototype, or model. After that, they would need to make 75 vehicles a day.

Only two companies submitted plans. One of them was the American Bantam Car Company. Bantam was able to finish its prototype within 45 days. However, Bantam could not produce enough vehicles. The Army gave Bantam’s plans to other companies to meet the demand. Bantam worked with the Army to produce 2,675 of these vehicles.

BRC’s were called "general purpose vehicles." The soldiers shortened it to “geep.” The name evolved to be “Jeep.” This vehicle had four-wheel drive and had high clearance for rough terrain. It was designed for function in a war zone, not comfort. Repair parts for damaged vehicles could be taken from other Jeeps by anyone without special skills. The Jeep became known as the vehicle that won the war for the Allies.

title: John Edgar Thomson
text:
At the age of 19, John Edgar Thomson started his career as a civil engineer by working as a rodman. He helped the survey crew measure the path for the Philadelphia and Columbia Railroad. He worked his way up over the next few years. Thomson became the head of an engineering division for the Camden & Amboy Railroad.

At age 26, he was hired as the chief engineer of the Georgia Railroad. He led the building of a 173-mile railroad line from Augusta to what is now Atlanta. When it was completed, it was the longest railroad in the world. A town in Georgia was named in Thomson’s honor. The Pennsylvania Railroad then made Thomson its chief engineer. He helped design the railroad line that went from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. He designed the famous Horseshoe Curve that helped trains cross the Allegheny Mountains.

His next accomplishment was to become the president of the Pennsylvania Railroad. As president, he expanded the railroad from 250 miles of track to more than 6,000 miles, connecting many cities to each other. The Pennsylvania Railroad became the wealthiest and most influential railroad in America. It got so big that Thomson designed a management system to help his 400 employees work and communicate effectively. It is called the line and staff system. Another change that Thomson brought to the Pennsylvania railroad was the use of coal to power the engines instead of wood. Much of the coal that was used was mined in Pennsylvania.

Thomson’s “sober, technical, methodical and non-ideological personality had an important influence on the Pennsylvania Railroad. During his presidency, the railroad was on the cutting edge of technological innovations.”

title: Building America's Train Cars
text:
If someone shipped something by train between the late 1800s and the early 1900s in the United States, there was a good chance that the train car was made in Pennsylvania.

Pennsylvania was home to many rolling stock manufacturers. Rolling stock is what passenger or freight railway cars are called. In 1838, America’s first sleeping car was built in Philadelphia for the Cumberland Valley Railroad.

The Standard Steel Car Company was started by John Hansen and “Diamond” Jim Brady. They bought several different properties in Butler, Pennsylvania, including an old pickle factory. The company became the largest company under one giant roof. The business of creating steel cars grew quickly. The growth of the company created the need for employees to have a place to live and buy the things they needed. This created a new city in the area around the company.

In 1929, Hansen passed away. The Standard Steel Car Company merged with the Pullman Car Company. The Pullman-Standard Steel Car Company was formed. The company continued to grow and develop. The Pullman Car Company became the standard in luxury train travel.

title: George Marshall
text:
George Marshall was a general from Uniontown, PA. His life was one of constant service. In 1902, he joined the U.S. Army. He rose through the ranks.

He served as the Army Chief of Staff during World War II. In 1942, Marshall became a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. This group was created to work more closely with the British military. During this post, he helped develop battle plans that led to Allied victories. President Truman described him as the “architect of victory” in World War II. Even the former Prime Minister of Britain, Winston Churchill, called him the “true organizer of victory.” After the war, Marshall went on to serve at a post in China.

His greatest contribution may be the “Marshall Plan.” He developed the plan in 1947 while he was serving as the Secretary of State. He first explained it during a speech at Harvard University. He proposed that the United States should provide money to European countries. It would be used to help them rebuild after the war.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the Economic Recovery Act of 1948, which became known as the Marshall Plan. Between 1948 and 1951, the United States provided economic assistance to European nations. Not only did it help the economies of these European nations, but also America’s. The Marshall Plan created a standard for the United States to provide help to other countries.

Marshall also helped create NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization). NATO is a military alliance between European and North American nations. It is still very important today. He was later appointed Secretary of Defense. Marshall is also the only general to win a Nobel Peace Prize.

title: Food for the Troops (Hershey for Morale)
text:
In 1937, U.S. Army Captain Paul Logan wanted a new food ration for troops. Rations are a source of food for soldiers in war. Logan wanted something lightweight that could be used in emergencies or long deployments. He went to the Hershey Chocolate Corporation to help.

The Army had very specific requirements for this new ration bar. It needed to be four ounces, be a high energy food, and not melt in high temperatures. Logan also said he didn't want them to taste very good. He worried if they tasted too good, the troops might eat them before an actual emergency. He specified that the rations should taste “a little better than a boiled potato.”

Hershey Chocolate Company took the challenge. They created a new chocolate bar. It became known as the Field Ration D bar.

Hershey produced around 100,000 Field Ration D bars. Once it passed tests in places like the Philippines, Hawaii, and Antarctica, the Army wanted more. The Hershey Chocolate Company produced hundreds of millions of Field Ration D bars by the end of 1945. The company also produced other ration bars for the Army. One was the Tropical Bar. According to Samuel Hinkle, the chief chemist, “We came out with a Tropical bar, a bar that would withstand the heat of the tropics and the cold of the Arctic, and we made hundreds of millions of those bars.”

These ration bars went beyond just feeding the troops. They also started to help boost the morale, or confidence, of the troops. General George Marshall talked about this. As American troops pushed across Europe, Marshall ordered that some of the ration bars be sent to the frontlines. He knew that having access to items like soda and chocolate bars improved the morale of the troops. "Many of our people forget the importance of little things to morale …." As Marshall ordered these items to the troops, he said, "the men think if there is candy up forward, things can't be so bad."

title: Builders of the Railroad
text:
While Pennsylvania’s early railroad lines were being built, immigrants from Ireland were coming to the United States to escape a famine. They were eager to work but didn’t have many industrial skills. Many were looking for ways to meet their needs. The jobs they found were often as laborers for railroad construction. Later, African Americans and immigrants from Italy and Eastern Europe did the manual labor. The workers had to build the railroad almost entirely by hand. They had to cut down trees, remove or cut through boulders, and level the ground. There wasn’t any heavy machinery to help them move large boulders or lay the track, mile after mile. Immigrants were an essential part of building the railroad across Pennsylvania and the continent.

To lay track, crews loaded up carts pulled by horses or mules with ties and rails. At the end of the track, two men would unload one tie at a time. The ties weighed between 100 and 200 pounds. They laid the ties down as far as they could until they ran out. Next, a group of men would take a rail and lay it down across the ties. The rails weighed more than 900 pounds each.

In order to make a tunnel through a mountain, workers had to drive spikes, fill the holes with explosive black powder, and blast through the rock inch by inch. Often, the workers were only able to carve tunnels into the mountains at a foot per day. They also had to build bridges to cross waterways or canyons as they laid out the track. Handcarts were used to collect and move the dirt and rocks as workers moved along. Without heavy machinery to help, building railroads required lifting and moving of heavy materials.

The workers had to live in temporary camps. The camps were often cramped and dirty. When a disease infected one worker, it would spread quickly to many more. Death from accidents, disease, and exposure to the elements was common. The workers were not paid much. Sometimes they received only 25 cents a day.

title: Railroading Language
text:
Railroads made tracks all over the United States. They also left their tracks all over the English language. People use railroad terms without even knowing it!

For example, to baseball fans, the phrase “double header” means two games played in a row. But it started as a term to describe when two engines are pulling a train.

Have you ever jumped on “the bandwagon”? This often means joining a popular group or cause. A bandwagon was the railroad car that workers got paid from. So, of course, everyone wanted to jump on it.

Has someone who is proud of you ever told you that you “made the grade”? That term doesn’t refer to grades at school. It came from railroads. A grade is how steep a hill is. If an engine was able to pull a train up a steep incline, it had “made the grade.”

After venting to a friend about something that had made you angry, you may say, “Thanks for letting me blow off steam.” This actually compares you to a locomotive. When the pressure inside the steam boiler got too high, the engineer would let some of it out. Thus, they were “blowing off steam.”

You may also have wondered which side was the “wrong side of the tracks.” It was the side that smoke from the locomotive blew toward. People with more resources had the means to live on the side where the smoke didn’t blow. Those with fewer resources lived on the “wrong side.”

Of course, there are a lot of tracks and rails in the English language: “You’re getting off track.” “I got sidetracked.” “That conversation got derailed.” “My life has gone off the rails.” “Let’s put that on the fast track.” “You’re right on track!”

We could keep going. However, we’ve reached “the end of the line.”

title: Decisions in Action
text:
After going through the decision-making process, you can make a decision. Move forward with your decision with confidence. You have done your research and decided what to do.

Margot decided to join a dance class, drink a full water bottle each day, and eat vegetables with at least one meal each day.

title: Coming Home from War
text:
World War II ended in 1945. Millions of American soldiers and sailors returned home. They returned to a community that had jobs and new opportunities. Marriage and birth rates boomed as life continued after the war. This increased birth rate was called “the Baby Boom.” The growing families needed homes. However, there weren't enough affordable homes available for all the new families.

The government passed legislation called The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944. It was commonly called the G.I. Bill. It was meant to help the veterans returning to civilian life. One feature of the G.I. Bill was low-cost mortgage loans for homes.

A real estate company owned by William Levitt built housing communities in several cities in the United States. The houses were meant to help the veterans. They were affordable and convenient for families. They had planned neighborhoods with playgrounds and parks. The houses were small with large front and back yards. The newest in home technology developed during the war was included. Natural gas and electricity replaced coal and wood as fuel. The first Levittown was in New York. The second was in Levittown, Pennsylvania in Bucks County. Located outside of urban Philadelphia, the planned towns became known as suburbs.

Other changes were happening too. Automobiles became more affordable. Schools became organized by grade levels with extracurricular sports and activities.

After the war, the United States continued to provide resources for rebuilding Europe and Southeast Asia. The prosperous, or wealthy, economy gave opportunities for families to have higher incomes. The extra money meant families could go out to dinner, have new appliances, or buy a new thing called a television.

Many Americans were happy. Music reflected their attitudes with the new "Rock and Roll." The Philadelphia region became a center for this new music. “Bandstand“ highlighted teenagers dancing and enjoying the upbeat music.

The time after the war was good for many Americans. However, it also became clear that not all Americans were being treated fairly. African Americans and other minority groups were not always given equal opportunities. The Civil Rights Movement grew in protest to this inequality.

title: Reflect on Your Decision
text:
After making a decision, stop and ask yourself how it went. This is called reflection. Reflection is a great tool. Reflection can help you think about your own actions and words and make the best possible decisions for yourself.

Consider a decision you have made recently, and practice reflection:

What outcomes did I get?

How did my choice affect others?

Is there something I can learn from this?

How will I approach this type of decision in the future?

title: Short- and Long-Term Changes
text:
There are different types of changes that happen in your daily life. These include short-term changes and long-term changes. Each of these changes can be small or big.

Short-term changes affect a small amount of time. These changes are not permanent. Temporary changes may include having a babysitter, a birthday party getting canceled, or even breaking a bone.

Long-term changes change your daily life permanently. These changes may begin as temporary changes but can become permanent. Long-term changes may take more time to develop. Parents getting a divorce, a new sibling being born, or learning a new skill are examples of long-term changes.

title: Choose How You Will React to Change
text:
Every change is different. You get to choose how you will react to each one. You can choose to look at the positive, or you can choose to look at the negative. You can find good things about most changes, even hard and sad ones.

You can take time to choose how you want to react. Try asking yourself these questions when you experience a change:

What change has occurred?

How do I feel?

What are the facts?

How can I have a positive attitude about this change?

What will I do? (Make sure that whatever you do is healthy and safe for you and others.)

title: Dealing with Feelings After Change
text: Your brain has a lot of power! When changes occur, you can teach yourself how to respond to them. You can look for healthy ways to express your feelings and emotions. It is okay to allow yourself to experience emotions when changes occur. When changes are too big for you to understand on your own, you can ask for and accept help from others.

title: Changing to Fit Changes
text: Did you know that living things naturally adapt to fit in their environment? You can adapt too! When you choose to put a coat on when it is snowing, you are adapting. When you choose to make a peanut butter sandwich because you are out of turkey, you are adapting. Adapting means changing to fit a situation better. If there is a change around you, you can choose to adapt and change to make that change work for you.

title: Use Strategies When Changes Are Stressing You Out
text:
Some changes can be hard to deal with by yourself. You can use coping strategies to help you through them. Pick a few of these strategies to use when you feel stressed or overwhelmed about changes:

Take slow, deep breaths to calm down your heart and mind.

Sing or listen to one of your favorite songs.

Move your body for 10 minutes.

Spend time outside.

Write about your feelings.

Talk to someone you trust.

title: How Can Critical Thinking Help You?
text: It is fun to ask questions and gather information. Critical thinking is a skill that helps you make healthy decisions. It helps you form opinions. It helps you keep your well-being balanced. Thinking critically helps you understand your likes and dislikes so that you can form opinions.

title: Gather Information with Research
text: An important part of critical thinking is doing your research. Nothing is more powerful than what you see or feel. When you use research to explore the world around you, you gather information and research. Ask questions to help you understand what is going on and why. Consider the source of the information you gather. Is it reliable? Can you trust the information?

title: Form Your Own Opinions
text: Your opinions are what you think or how you feel about something. You can form opinions based on what you believe. You may form an opinion based on the way you feel about what you hear or see. Sometimes opinions are shaped by what others say. It is also important to consider facts and knowledge. Use inquiry and research to decide what your own opinions are.

title: Pressure from Others
text: The people around you influence your life and your choices, even if you don’t realize it. When other people try to make you think or act a certain way, that is called peer pressure. Peer pressure is not always bad. Some people will encourage you to make safe and positive choices. Other times, your peers may pressure you in a negative way. No matter what, you should think for yourself. Form your own opinions and stick to what you believe in. This will help you avoid negative peer pressure.

title: The Yorktown Siege
text:
The last battle between the British and the Americans in the colonies was the Battle of Yorktown. This battle was a siege. A siege is when an army surrounds its enemy. During the Siege of Yorktown, the question was how long the British army could last without getting fresh supplies. They could only defend their position in Yorktown and hope that help would come to break the siege. Despite their resistance, the Americans and French won this battle.

Near the end of the war, a few important things happened. The American soldiers in the South were led by Nathanael Greene. Greene used small forces that could move quickly. His tactics forced the British to spread out their forces, which weakened the army. British General Cornwallis decided to go to Virginia. He planned to get more troops from England. In May 1781, he led 7,000 British troops out of North Carolina.

General Sir Henry Clinton ordered Cornwallis to Yorktown, Virginia. Cornwallis thought this was a bad idea. Yorktown was on the ocean and could be attacked by French ships. Still, the British moved to Yorktown and set up defenses there. They waited for more soldiers to come by ship. On Oct. 17, the British sent a large fleet with 7,000 soldiers to rescue Cornwallis. The fleet ended up being too late to help. Meanwhile, French ships moved toward the Chesapeake Bay, where Yorktown was. They blocked supply lines by sea during the Siege of Yorktown.

At this time, General George Washington was marching south toward Virginia. On Sept. 5, the French defeated Admiral Thomas Graves in the Battle of the Chesapeake. French ships stayed near Yorktown in the Chesapeake Bay. George Washington saw an opportunity. He sent 4,500 troops, led by Marquis de Lafayette, to Yorktown to prevent the British army from leaving. Washington then sent other troops to join the French fleet in the Chesapeake Bay. Blocking the Chesapeake Bay meant nearby British ships were unable to send soldiers to aid Cornwallis. Some of the French boats took Washington and his troops to Williamsburg, Virginia. From there, they moved toward Yorktown.

When Washington arrived at Yorktown, he began a siege on Sept. 28 that lasted for 11 days. The British suffered many losses. They began running low on food and were greatly outnumbered. General Cornwallis had no choice but to end the battle. He sent Brig. General Charles O'Hara to negotiate terms of surrender. Cornwallis claimed he was too sick to attend. Some historians think he was embarrassed. The terms of surrender were written down. They were called the Articles of Capitulation, and they were signed on Oct. 19, 1781.

title: Two Is Better than One
text: Collaboration is the process of two or more people working together to complete a task or achieve a common goal. Working together as a team can help you problem-solve. It can help you see things from a different perspective and get more done in a shorter amount of time. When you work together with others, you can improve relationships and social connections. Collaboration is a life skill that will help you in your career, home life, and extracurricular activities. Many things you do require the ability to work together with others. If you can learn how to collaborate effectively, you will achieve great things.

title: Why Does Listening Matter?
text:
When collaborating, one of the most important skills you can develop is being a good listener. Sometimes listening is hard. You can be distracted by other things going on around you. You can be thinking about what you want to say and miss what the speaker is saying. Becoming a good listener will make you a better student and a better friend.

Listening skills are a big part of life. This important skill can be practiced and learned. Try these ideas to help you practice listening:

Put away distractions so you can focus on who is talking.

Direct your attention to the speaker.

Do not interrupt. Allow the person speaking to finish before saying something yourself.

Check your understanding by repeating what has been said.

Ask questions to clarify what has been said.

title: Why Should I Follow Through?
text: Part of collaborating with others is choosing to be reliable. Being reliable means you follow through and do what you say you are going to do. When you commit to your team members, they are relying on you to do your part. Be someone who they can rely on. Completing your schoolwork on time is being reliable. Part of being reliable is being realistic and responsible about what you are able to do with your time and resources. Communicate openly and honestly to help set achievable expectations.

title: How Can My Strengths Help?
text: When working with a team, it is important to recognize that every single job is important. When you put all those jobs together, you can accomplish some amazing things. The best way is to pay attention to everyone’s unique strengths and figure out a way to use those strengths. Everyone has a unique contribution that they can make, including you! That is the amazing part of collaboration. Working and collaborating effectively with others will provide opportunities for you to accomplish some incredible things.

title: What Does Respect Look Like?
text:
When working with others, respect is an important aspect to consider. Respect is treating others how you want to be treated. Respect includes listening to others’ ideas and letting everyone express their opinions. Respect involves kindness and finding ways to be helpful.

Here are a few ideas to help you demonstrate respect:

Be sensitive to other people’s feelings.

Don’t insult people or make fun of them.

Be considerate of people’s likes and dislikes.

Don’t mock or tease people.

Don’t pressure someone to do something they don’t want to do.

title: What Can I Control?
text:
When working with others, it is important to remember that some things are not in your control. You can choose to focus on what falls in your circle of control.

CIRCLE OF CONCERN (no control)

The circle of concern represents things you have no control over.

This includes what other people say and do.

CIRCLE OF INFLUENCE

The circle of influence includes those things that you can say or do to try to improve your circle of no control.

These include complimenting someone, serving others, standing up for someone being bullied, or influencing someone in some way.

CIRCLE OF CONTROL

The circle of control includes the things you do have control over.

This includes your actions, words, behavior, effort, choices, ideas, and attitude.

title: How Can I Build Others Up?
text:
Building others up will make you and your team stronger. Encourage others and help them feel good about their efforts and contributions. It will make you stronger when you build others up.

You can build up your team by:

Saying things like: “You can do this!” “You are smart!” “Keep going!”

Celebrating the success of others: “Way to go!” “That looks amazing!”

Showing gratitude: “I’m so grateful you are part of this team.” “We are lucky to have you!”

Always saying kind things about your teammates to others: “I love working with my teammates.”

title: Why Is It Important to Take Responsibility?
text:
People make mistakes. Each person can learn and grow from mistakes and improve because of them. You don’t need to feel embarrassed about making a mistake because everyone does. It’s part of learning. By taking responsibility and action to fix or improve it, you show your team, friends, and classmates that you are someone they can trust to make things right.

If someone on your team makes a mistake, it is important to encourage them to fix it and move on. There is no need to tear someone down or make them feel bad. Be willing to help solve the problem to make it right. Always speak kindly to others. Be a collaborator who is willing to take responsibility, make things right, and jump in and help.

title: Be Assertive Because You Matter
text:
You are a very important person. No one has the same qualities as you. You have so much goodness to share with the world. You matter to the people around you. You matter to your family, friends, peers, teachers, and more. There are many skills you can develop that will help you share your goodness with others, and assertiveness is one of those important skills.

Assertiveness is part of communicating. Being assertive is speaking up for yourself in a way that is honest and respectful. Assertive people feel confident enough to take risks. They are willing to make mistakes and learn from them.

Being assertive is letting people know your real thoughts and opinions and being clear about what you want. One important part of being assertive is remembering to listen to what others are saying. Assertive people care about themselves and about others.

title: Upstanders Are Assertive
text:
An upstander is someone who recognizes when something is wrong and acts to make it right. An upstander is assertive and respectful.

You can be an upstander by speaking up when someone is being bullied. Speaking up when you see bullying is being assertive with your communication. You can say something to the person being bullied. You can also say something to a trusted adult to get some help if you aren't sure what to do next. Being assertive about what you see happening can help you be an upstander. Communicate honestly and respectfully about what is going on because everyone matters, just like you matter.

title: Be Flexible
text: Sometimes plans change. Some things are out of your control. Accidents, surprise assemblies, or illnesses can cause unexpected changes in how you use your time. Having a schedule and a routine can help reduce stress. These can help you get things done. When unexpected things change your schedule or routine, being flexible helps you continue to feel good and make healthy choices. Being flexible means being able to change and adapt without breaking. You can practice being flexible when your plans are changed by staying calm and thinking positively. You can think, “Today is not going to look the way I thought it would, but I can still have a good day.”

title: Trust the Sun
text:
Trust is the belief that you can rely on someone or something. Think about the sun. You trust that even on stormy days, the sun is behind the clouds. It’s dependable. You don’t have to question whether the sun will be there. You expect it to rise, and it always does!

When you trust a person, you can expect them to be honest because they are dependable in their actions.

You can be like the sun by being honest and dependable.

title: You Can Be Dependable
text:
If your neighbor trusts you to walk their dog after school and you don’t show up, do you think they’ll trust you to help them again? It’s hard to trust someone who is unreliable. Being unreliable means not doing what you say you will do. It is the opposite of being dependable. When someone is unreliable, you can’t be sure of how they will act.

Being dependable doesn’t mean you have to do everything anyone asks you to do. But it does mean honoring your commitments, so think before you promise something. Make commitments you know you can keep.

title: You Can Be Trustworthy
text: Trust doesn’t happen automatically. It’s built little by little through words and actions. People will choose to trust you based on the things you say and do. If you say you will do something, do you do it? Are you honest, even if it might get you into trouble? You can build trust by showing those around you that they can rely on you to tell the truth, keep your promises, and treat others with respect.

title: You Can Learn from Your Mistakes
text:
Making mistakes is a normal part of growth and development. You might make a mistake that causes someone to lose their trust in you. Usually, you can build that trust back by changing your words or actions and by being dependable. Here are some ways you can start rebuilding trust:

Accept responsibility for your mistake. Don’t make excuses.

Apologize.

Avoid making the same mistake again.

Don’t give up! Keep being dependable and honest.

title: You Can Forgive Yourself
text:
When you make mistakes, like not following through on commitments, others may not feel like they can trust you. You may feel disappointed in or frustrated with yourself. It’s normal to feel that way. Those uncomfortable feelings help us change and grow. If you get stuck in those feelings, though, it can be difficult to learn from your mistakes. Reflecting can help.

Reflecting on your behavior can help you forgive yourself. Forgiving yourself means letting go of negative feelings so you can move forward. It doesn’t mean you erase the past and pretend you never made a mistake. It also doesn’t mean you beat yourself up for making a mistake. Forgiving yourself means that you consider the impact of your actions and then think about what you will do differently the next time. You can choose to use your empathy and growth mindset to make changes and create a happier future.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
text:
The Declaration of Independence says that every person has the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. In 1948, the United Nations wrote another document, called the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. They decided to write this document after World War II, a time when the rights of millions of people had been taken away. It was signed by 48 nations and is considered a standard for the world. There are 30 human rights listed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Here are some of them:

Article 1: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

Article 3: Everyone has the right to life, liberty, and security of person.

Article 4: No one shall be held in slavery or servitude; slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms.

Article 17: 1. Everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others. 2. No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his property.

title: Making Elections Possible
text:
Having an election does not just require voters and candidates but also many volunteers. Election volunteers can run polling stations, help count votes, and do many other jobs. Everyone involved in an election uses technology to help them complete their role.

Media plays a large role in voting, campaigning, and elections. In addition to voters being able to learn about candidates from flyers, commercials, or speeches, voters can also learn about candidates on social media or websites. Often, election volunteers will keep these media platforms up-to-date.

When candidates have been elected and take office, they will communicate with their constituents, or the people they represent. They usually do this through social media, email, and websites.

title: Helping Wisconsin's Environment
text:
People and communities can have an impact on their environment. Some of the positive ways to do this are by cleaning up litter, protecting endangered species, planting trees, and growing your own plants and vegetables. Other things that can have a positive impact on the environment are conserving water and electricity, using reusable water bottles, and buying locally grown food. People can work together to protect natural resources and have a positive impact on the environment.

Various efforts have been made to conserve resources and protect the environment in Wisconsin. The Nature Conservancy is an organization that is dedicated to protecting the lakes, rivers, forests and prairies of the state. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources has programs that promote clean air initiatives, drinking water conservation, and the development of cleaner energy sources. Some of Wisconsin’s cleaner energy sources are wind farms. These wind farms generate electricity for Wisconsonites to use.

title: Goals to Grow
text:
A goal is something you want to accomplish, so you make a plan to help you to achieve it. Setting a goal is a fun way to progress, learn, and grow in a direction that matters to you. Goals help you thrive. They make life exciting, and they give you something to look forward to and celebrate. Setting goals can help you achieve incredible things!

Brainstorm different goals you would like to set in each area of your health and wellness.

title: Make Sure Your Goals Are S.M.A.R.T.
text:
Set goals the S.M.A.R.T. way!

Specific: What do you want to accomplish? Good goals are specific, which means they are focused, clear, and defined.

Measurable: How will you know when you’ve achieved it? You must be able to measure your progress—and celebrate it!

Attainable: Is the goal challenging but possible to reach? Attainable means it can be achieved.

Realistic: Is this goal important enough for you to spend time on it? Choose goals that help you thrive.

Timely: How long do you have to complete your goal? Make sure every goal has a deadline so you’re motivated to keep going.

title: Two Keys to Success
text:
It can be difficult to see your progress when you are working on a goal, especially if your goal seems far away. There are things you can do to keep moving toward your goal. To make progress, you should be consistent and persistent.

When you are consistent, it means you stick to your plan. For example, if you want to learn to play an instrument and plan to practice for one hour every day, you stick to the schedule.

When you are persistent, it means you don’t give up, even when something is difficult. Review your plan to see if you need changes. Accept the challenge, and keep moving forward. Stay focused on your final goal, and believe in yourself!

title: Port Ulao, Wisconsin
text:
In 1847, a man named James T. Gifford built a 1,000-foot pier on the shore of Lake Michigan. It was just east of the town of Grafton. He named the pier Port Ulao. The farmers around Port Ulao started cutting down trees and clearing the land for agriculture. They sold the wood from the trees to Gifford. He sold the wood to the steamship captains on Lake Michigan. The captains used the wood to power their ships. A fishing station was soon added to the pier. Fishers could pay to clean and smoke their fish there. Eventually, a train station and feed mill were built at Port Ulao.

Port Ulao was quite successful for a while. However, as time went on, the forests near Port Ulao were cut down. This made wood more expensive. Then, technology advanced and steamships no longer used wood for fuel. Port Ulao’s staple resource was no longer needed. Port Ulao survived for a while because of its train station, but without a profitable resource, it began to decline. Eventually, it disappeared.

title: Set Mini Goals to Reach Your Big Goals
text:
Sometimes a big goal might feel overwhelming. If that happens, don’t think of it as just one big goal. Instead, think of it as many small goals, like steps on a ladder. You just have to take one step at a time, and as you do, you’ll get closer and closer to the top. Making small goals also makes it easier to track your progress and celebrate the amazing things you’ve done!

So when you create a big S.M.A.R.T. goal, think of the steps you’ll need to take to get there. Then, set your smaller goals that will take you higher and higher up that ladder. Make sure they’re S.M.A.R.T., too!

title: Check In on Yourself
text:
Another important part of making goals is self-reflection. This means taking time to look at how you’re doing and examine the progress you’ve made.

Self-reflection should be positive and encouraging. Don’t think of it as punishment for mistakes or missteps. Think of it as a chance to celebrate what’s going well and change the things that aren’t working. For example, you can add more small goals if you need more steps in your ladder.

As you work toward your goals, ask yourself:

How am I feeling?

What progress have I made on my goals today?

Are there any parts of my plan that I’m avoiding or ignoring?

What can I do differently?

title: Mistakes Are Part of Progress
text: You don’t have to be perfect in order to make progress. In fact, mistakes can teach you a lot! You can learn from what worked, what didn’t work, and what could have gone better. Then you can adjust your goals and change your plans if you need to. A mistake might be the best thing that could happen.

title: Henry "Hank" Aaron
text:
When Henry Aaron was 13 years old, Jackie Robinson became the first African American to play in Major League Baseball (MLB). This inspired Aaron. After years of work and practice, he began playing professional baseball with the Indianapolis Clowns 1952 and then with the Milwaukee Braves in 1954. Both the Braves and Aaron moved to Atlanta in 1966. Aaron played his final two seasons, from 1974 to 1976, with the Milwaukee Brewers.

Aaron was a great baseball player. He broke many MLB records. Aaron also endured racism during his career. In 1974, Aaron was about to break Babe Ruth’s home run record. Some people were angry about this, but Aaron was not discouraged. He broke the home run record in 1974 and then surpassed it.

Aaron helped break down barriers for African Americans in many ways. He supported the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. When Aaron asked a friend if he should join the Civil Rights March on Washington in 1963, his friend replied that Aaron was contributing to the Civil Rights Movement by playing baseball and breaking down barriers for other African Americans.

title: Vel Phillips
text: Vel Phillips was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. When she won a speech contest in high school, she was awarded a scholarship to her choice of colleges. She chose to attend Howard University. When Phillips graduated, she returned to Milwaukee and joined the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). While at a NAACP dinner, she met Dale Phillips. They got married and then attended the University of Wisconsin Law School together. She and her husband experienced housing discrimination in Wisconsin. They and many other African Americans experienced discrimination and segregation throughout their lives. In 1956, Phillips ran for Milwaukee City Council and won. While on the city council, Phillips worked to outlaw housing discrimination. Later, Phillips was a Milwaukee County judge. She ran for Wisconsin Secretary of State in 1978 and won. She was the first African American and first woman to be a city council member, judge, and secretary of state.

title: Tell Yourself You Can!
text:
“Whether you think you can or you think you can’t, you’re right.” – Henry Ford

If you want to achieve your goals, you need to believe you can do it! Use positive self-talk and choose to have an “I can” attitude instead of “I can’t.” Write your S.M.A.R.T. goal down and put it somewhere you can see it often. When you look at it, remind yourself that you can achieve it. If you want, you can write positive phrases around your goal as reminders. Remember the power of the word “yet.” Even if you fall short of your goals, adjust and keep going. Keep telling yourself, “I can!”

title: Specialization in Wisconsin
text:
The natural resources available in an area influence what type of products people make or specialize in. For example, Wisconsin has a lot of land to raise animals and grow animal feed on. So, many people raise cows. The type of human-made resources available in an area also influence what products people make or specialize in. Wisconsin has a lot of manufacturing plants. With so many cows and manufacturing plants, a lot of people specialize in making cheese.

Making Cheese

Rearing: Farmers raise and feed dairy cows.

Harvesting: The cows are milked by machine.

Storing: The milk is stored in a large, clean, refrigerated tank at the farm.

Transportation: The milk is pumped into large, refrigerated trucks for transport to the processing factory.

Processing: The milk is heated to kill germs and then cooled. Special ingredients called a starter and rennet are added to the milk to create cheese curds. The curds are heated, and the extra moisture is drained. Salt is added.

Packaging: The cheese curds are formed into blocks and packaged.

Shipping: The cheese is shipped to stores in refrigerated trucks.

Selling: The packaged cheese is displayed in refrigerators at the store. Customers buy the cheese.

title: Geographic Tools
text:
Geographers study the Earth. They ask questions about the physical features of the planet. They also ask questions about how people affect and are affected by their environment. Geographers use many tools and types of information to answer their questions, including maps, images, and data.

Previously, you learned how maps and globes show where features, such as bodies of water, mountains, or countries, are located. You also learned that thematic maps can display information, such as population data or the physical features of a place. This week, you will learn about other geographic tools, including satellite images, aerial photographs, and informational charts. You will learn about the purpose of these tools and how they help geographers and ordinary people answer questions and make decisions.

title: Satellites
text: Satellites are objects that orbit, or move in a circle, around a planet. Earth has one natural satellite: the moon. Earth also has thousands of human-made satellites. The first human-made satellite was sent into orbit by the Soviet Union in 1957. It was called Sputnik 1. It sent a radio signal back to Earth. Modern satellites do many things. They take pictures of planets and other objects in space. Satellites also transmit TV or cell phone signals. There is a group of satellites called the Global Positioning System, or GPS.

title: Satellite Images
text:
The human-made satellites that orbit the Earth take many different types of images of our planet. Some of them are photographic images, but many are not. Satellites also use radio signals, ultraviolet light, and infrared to create images and gather information. Satellite images can show many different aspects of the Earth, from the density of a forest to the movement of a hurricane.

Satellite images are used for many purposes, such as creating accurate maps. However, one of their main purposes is to track changes on the Earth over time. Scientists can use satellite images to help make decisions that will conserve water or other resources.

Meteorologists, or weather forecasters, can use satellite data to help predict the weather.

title: Aerial Photographs
text:
When photographs are taken from the air, it’s called aerial photography. Some of the first aerial photographs were taken by cameras attached to balloons or kites. Soon, cameras were also attached to parachutes and pigeons.

Eventually, airplanes would dominate aerial photography. As both aviation and photography improved, photographs could be taken from greater heights. Drones are now one of the most widely used means of taking aerial photographs.

Aerial photographs have most often been used for military purposes, for example, to get information about battlefields or enemy encampments. But aerial photographs can be used for a variety of purposes. They can track changes to environments over time.

They can be used for urban planning and conservation.

title: Charts and Data
text:
Wisconsin has a continental, or temperate, climate. This means it has warm summers and cold winters. Climate is the average weather conditions of a place over an extended period of time. Scientists use many criteria to classify the climate of a region.

The most important criteria are precipitation, vegetation, seasons, and temperature. The first graph shows the average temperature of Wisconsin for each month of the year. The second graph shows two countries with the same climate classification as Wisconsin. There are two other countries on the graph with climates that are different from Wisconsin. What similarities and differences do you see between these countries and Wisconsin?

title: Why Are You Scared?
text: You can think about your feelings. Try to understand why you feel scared.

title: Fear of Danger
text: It is normal to be afraid of getting hurt. Rules keep you safe so you don’t have to be afraid. When you follow the rules, you don’t need to fear.

title: Let It Be Written
text:
Writing systems are one of the most important pieces of human invention. Some say they are as important as the invention of the wheel. Writing systems make it easier for people to communicate. The use of writing systems varied between Indigenous American peoples. The Maya created an elaborate writing system based on hieroglyphs, or picture-based symbols. The system is considered by archaeologists to be the most sophisticated system ever developed in Mesoamerica. It took several researchers to decode the language. Decoding the language allowed people to learn more about the ancient Maya. Most books written in Maya hieroglyphs have not survived. Only three or four books have been found. They are named after the cities they are kept in. These books are called “codices” and are one of the most important sources of information about the Maya.

The Aztec also used a picture-based writing system. Only nobles and priests learned to read and write using this system. The Aztec empire needed accurate records. They used the system to track taxes and record events that occurred during the year. It was also important to track family histories. Much of what we know about the Aztec today comes from the written records they left behind. It takes many years of study to understand the symbols, though. It is very hard to know every symbol’s exact meaning.

The Inca in Peru had no written alphabet. Instead, they kept records by tying knots into strings. The way a knot was tied or its position in a sequence of knots communicated meaning. This is how the Inca kept records throughout their empire. No matter where information came from, it could be read. The Inca knot-record system was called “quipu.”

The Mississippian Mound Builders had no writing system that we can identify. This leaves many questions about these ancient American Indians. How did they communicate with each other? Did they keep records, like the Inca or Aztec? How could they build such large structures without a writing system? A lack of written history shrouds the Mississippian people in mystery.

title: Changes All Around
text:
Change happens when something around you becomes different in some way. Changes can be big, like getting a new pet. Changes can be small, like getting new shoes. Change happens to everyone. You get to choose how you react to change. Dealing with changes in a positive way helps keep your well-being in balance.

People become used to changes that occur every day. Changes that happen daily become part of your daily routines. Routines involve changes you can expect to happen. When changes happen that you are not used to or are not part of your normal routines, you get to decide if they impact your life positively or negatively.

What if your teacher decides to move around the desks in your classroom? This changes your normal routine. Your desk is now in a different place. You get to choose how you will react to this change.

Replacing the sugar in a cookie recipe with salt will probably not make the cookies taste better. It will make the cookies salty, so they will not taste delicious. This is an example of your brain interpreting this change as a negative change. What if instead of substituting salt, you just changed the amount of each ingredient by doubling it? This would result in more cookies, and you may interpret this as a positive change.

title: Temporary and Permanent Changes
text:
Short-term and long-term changes can vary. They can be small things, big things, things that happen in the world, things that happen around you, or things that happen inside your body and brain. Learning how to deal with change in a positive way will help you maintain a balanced well-being over time.

Short-term changes, or temporary changes, are interruptions to your routines. Temporary changes may include getting a low score on a test, having a substitute teacher for the day, or having family members visit.

Long-term changes happen over time and become part of your daily life and routines. These may begin as temporary changes but can become permanent. Long-term changes take more time to develop. Puberty is an example of a long-term change.

title: Change Causes Emotions
text:
Change impacts your emotions. When something changes, we react differently. We might be happy with the change, or we might not be happy with the change. You can look for healthy ways to express your feelings and emotions. It is helpful to allow yourself to experience emotions when changes occur. When changes occur, you can teach yourself how to respond.

Changes don’t always happen one at a time. Some days, you will experience many different changes. These different experiences can cause you to feel many emotions at once. Sometimes, this can cause you to act in a way that is different from your normal behavior. It is normal to feel overwhelmed when big, long-term changes occur in your life. When changes are too big for you to understand on your own, you can ask for and accept help from others.

title: Choosing How to Respond to Change
text:
There are many different things that can change. As a result, there are different ways you can choose to respond to change. A response to change can be appropriate as long as you are not hurting yourself, others, or the things around you.

Follow this process to respond to change appropriately:

Observe the situation.

Consider your feelings (self-reflection).

Evaluate the facts.

Ask yourself: "Is this change happening to me or for me?"

When you believe a change happens to you, you may experience anger, sadness, or frustration. You may feel like the change has power over your emotions.

When you believe a change happens for you, you can still experience anger, sadness, and frustration. However, you can identify, label, and communicate your emotions. This helps you manage your response to the change.

Decide how you will respond.

title: Internal and External Control
text:
When you experience change, you can choose to see the change in two ways. First, you can view it as happening to you. Second, you can view the change as happening for you. You can ask yourself how you will respond.

A person with an internal locus of control believes they are responsible for the choices they make. They believe that their actions impact the outcomes and rewards they earn. With an internal locus of control, you focus on a solution and allow change to take place while you manage your emotions and behaviors.

A person with an external locus of control believes that things happen to them, whether good or bad. They believe they have little or no control over what happens in their life. When a person has an external locus of control, they might complain, get upset, or argue because they feel like there is no control.

title: The Decision-Making Process
text:
You make lots of decisions and choices every single day. You decide what to eat, what music to listen to, and what your attitude will be. Many decisions you make are not of great importance. However, the decisions you make about your health, the way you interact with others, and moral decisions are very important. Every decision you make has consequences. Your decisions can lead to positive or negative consequences.

Positive consequences might help you feel good about yourself, feel confident, and build your relationships with others.

Negative consequences might cause harm to your physical health, distract you from your goals, or cause damage in your relationships with others.

When you encounter a problem, you get to make decisions. You can define your problem. Think about what the problem looks like.

Each problem you encounter can be solved. When you think about a problem you are trying to solve, think about the decisions that need to be made, observe what is happening, and then move forward.
