text: How has water shaped the physical and human characteristics of the regions of Wisconsin?

title: Week 13 Inquiry Question
text: How were the tribes of Wisconsin similar to each other and how were they different from each other?

title: Ojibwe
text:
The Ojibwe are sometimes called the Chippewa, which comes from a European pronunciation of the Ojibwe name. According to tradition, the Ojibwe moved west from the eastern part of the North American continent because one of their leaders received a prophecy. He was told that white people would take their land, so they should move west in search of a place where food grew on water. The Ojibwe found this food, wild rice, in the area surrounding the Great Lakes, including Chequamegon Bay in Wisconsin. The Ojibwe was one of three tribes that belonged to the Anishinaabe, or the Three Fires Confederacy. The other two tribes were the Odawa and the Potawatomi.

The Ojibwe are patrilineal, which means they trace family relationships through their fathers. There are many different clans among members of the Ojibwe, including the Crane, Loon, Eagle, Bear, Marten, Lynx, Bullhead, Sucker, and Turtle clans. Each clan fulfills different responsibilities in their band. Historically, the Crane clan were the speakers and leaders of the tribal band, and members of the Bear clan were warriors.

In the past, the Ojibwe migrated with the seasons and traveled in bands. The bands separated into smaller family groups in the fall and winter because it was easier to feed smaller groups of people in those difficult months. The Ojibwe harvested wild rice and tapped maple trees for sugar. They also hunted game and planted gardens near rivers. Today, the Ojibwe still engage in traditional hunting and gathering activities. They also participate in many more economic enterprises.

The Ojibwe were heavily involved in the fur trade and allied with the Huron and French in the 17th and 18th centuries. In the mid-1800s, the United States government tried to forcibly remove the Ojibwe from their homes and into Minnesota. This was a violation of many of the previous treaties between the Ojibwe and the U.S. government. The Ojibwe resisted removal, and Chief Kechewaishke, sometimes called Chief Buffalo, made a journey to Washington, D.C., where he petitioned the president to stop the forced removal of his people. He succeeded. A new treaty was signed in 1854, which created four Ojibwe Reservations: the Red Cliff, the Band River, the Lac Courte Oreilles, and Lac du Flambeau.

Historically, there were 15 Ojibwe bands. Today there are many more. There are six bands in the state of Wisconsin: the Red Cliff Band, the Bad River Band, the Lac Courte Oreilles Band, the Lac du Flambeau Band, the St. Croix Band, and the Sakoagan (or Mole Lake) Band.

title: Week 14 Inquiry Question
text: What natural resource is the most significant among the Ojibwe bands?

title: Red Cliff Band
text:
The Red Cliff Band currently occupies the northern shore of the Bayfield Peninsula. It has close access to Madeline Island, which is the spiritual and economic center of the Ojibwe bands who make their home around Lake Superior. Madeline Island is one of the Apostle Islands. This area was a crossroads throughout history. It was one of the places where the French built a fur trading fort. The Ojibwe worked with the French traders.

The Red Cliff Band Reservation was created in 1854 after Chief Buffalo met with the president of the United States and negotiated for the Ojibwe to remain on their land. The Red Cliff Band has direct heritage to Chief Buffalo. While the Red Cliff Band stayed in the area around Madeline Island, the Bad River Band moved to Chequamegon Bay and the valley of the Bad River.

Today, the Red Cliff Band has a government that consists of a nine-member council. The Red Cliff Band is named for the unique red color of the rocks on their reservation. According to tribal elders Andrew Gokee and Marvin DeFoe, using sustainable practices and conserving natural resources is an Ojibwe way of life. It is something that the modern Red Cliff Band is trying to exemplify and teach. One way the Red Cliff Band has done this is by creating the first Tribal National Park, called Frog Bay Tribal National Park. By creating Frog Bay, the Red Cliff Band hopes to teach and preserve the cultural and spiritual importance of Lake Superior.

title: Bad River Band
text:
The Bad River Band originally came from the area of La Pointe on Madeline Island. They left Madeline Island and made their reservation near the Bad River, on the shores of Lake Superior. The Red Cliff Band was mostly made up of people who had converted to Christianity, and they stayed near Madeline Island. The Bad River Band, on the other hand, was mostly made up of people who still practiced their traditional religion, called Midewiwin. In the Ojibwe language, the Bad River is actually called Mashkiiziibii, which means Medicine River. Medicine is a word in Ojibwe that describes healing. Healing was achieved through many means, including spiritual ceremonies and herbal remedies.

The Bad River Band Reservation, like the Red Cliff Band Reservation, was created by the Treaty of La Pointe in 1854. The Reservation sits in a valley, surrounded by highlands on the west, south, and east sides. On the north side is Lake Superior. All the rivers in the reservation flow north to Lake Superior.

Traditionally, bands of the Ojibwe tribe were led by a chief who made decisions with the consensus of the members of the band. This position was hereditary. Today, the Bad River Band is led by a Tribal Council with seven elected officials: a tribal chairman, a vice chairman, a secretary, a treasurer, two senior council members, and one junior council member.

title: Lac Courte Oreilles Band
text:
The Lac Courte Oreilles Band of Ojibwe call themselves Odaawaa Zaaga’iganiign, which means the People of Odawa Lake. “Lac Courte Oreilles” means “Lake Short Ears” in French. There are two traditional stories that explain the origins of both the Ojibwe and French names. Tribal member and former Tribal Chairman Rick St. Germaine tells the oral history of how the land of Lac Courte Oreilles began as Odawa land. The Odawa used to clip the bottoms of their ears. When the French met the Odawa, they described them as people with short ears who lived near a lake. The reason the Ojibwe call themselves the people of Odawa Lake is because they moved to this place after the Odawa left. St. Germain describes a group of Ojibwe from the Bear clan traveling to the area, but as they left, their leader had a dream that this place was sacred and would become important Ojibwe land.

Historically, the Ojibwe had a lot of conflict with the Dakota Sioux tribe, which lived south of Lac Courte Oreilles. Eventually, the conflict between the Ojibwe and Dakota forced the Dakota to move west. The Treaty of La Pointe of 1854 created the Lac Courte Oreilles Reservation. It is located in Sawyer County and has more than 15 lakes as well as many rivers. Reservation land is mostly forested.

Some members of the band live on the reservation. Others live on tribal trust land in Burnette and Washburn Counties. Some live in urban centers. The current Lac Courte Oreilles Band government has a seven-member tribal council.

title: Lac du Flambeau Band
text:
The Lac du Flambeau Band of Ojibwe’s reservation is located in the southwestern portion of Vilas County and the southeastern side of Iron County. The band calls itself Waaswaaganing, meaning “The People of the Torch.” The land has 260 lakes and 65 miles of rivers and streams. Strawberry Island is considered the heart of the Lac du Flambeau Band of Ojibwe’s land. It is called the “Place of the Little People” in Ojibwe and means that this island is a place where spirits gather. Strawberry Island is also the site of the last battle between the Ojibwe and the Lakota Sioux.

As with the Red Cliff, Bad River, and Lac Courte Oreilles Bands, the Lac du Flambeau Reservation was created in the 1854 Treaty of La Pointe. However, the Lac Courte Oreilles Band had moved from Madeline Island more than 100 years before the treaty. In 1745, the Lac Courte Oreilles Band was led by Chief Keeshkemun to search for land. They decided to make this area their new home when they saw a crane resting on a rock on the lakeshore. Because the Crane was their clan animal, this was a sign from the Creator that this was their new home.

The name “Lac du Flambeau” is a French phrase that means “Lake of Torches” or “Lake of Flames.” The French gave the band this name because it was and still is a common practice to spearfish on the lake at night by torchlight. There have been controversies, even lawsuits, between sport fishermen and the Lac du Flambeau over spearfishing rights. However, the Lac du Flambeau are a sovereign nation and can regulate the laws on their land. The Lac du Flambeau are committed to conserving the wildlife and natural resources on their land.

title: St. Croix Band
text:
The St. Croix Band of Ojibwe does not reside on a single piece of land. There are 11 communities of the St. Croix Band in various Wisconsin counties. The five major cities of the St. Croix Band are Sand Lake, Danbury, Round Lake, Maple Plain, and Gaslyn. The headquarters of the St. Croix Band is located in Big Sand Lake.

The St. Croix Band moved from Madeline Island around 1700. At that time, the Ojibwe were very involved in the fur trade with the French. Members of the Marten clan moved to a place where the St. Croix River meets four other rivers. At this place, they would have access to beaver pelts and easy travel to the French fort on Madeline Island. The St. Croix Band is named after the St. Croix River.

Unlike the Red Cliff, Bad River, Lac Courte Oreilles, and Lac du Flambeau Bands, the St. Croix lost their federal recognition as an independent nation in 1854. It is not clear how this happened. Either the St. Croix did not send a representative to sign the Treaty of La Pointe or the representative might have signed under the Lac Courte Oreille Band. Without a clear signature for the St. Croix, the federal government took away their recognition. In 1934, the U.S. government passed something called the “Indian Reorganization Act.” Under this new law, the St. Croix became federally recognized and organized the St. Croix Band’s Reservation.

title: Sokaogon Chippewa, Mole Lake Band
text:
The Sokaogon Chippewa, or Mole Lake Band, of Ojibwe left Madeline Island and moved to the area of Mole Lake sometime in the 1700s. The band calls themselves Sokaogon, which means “post in the lake.” The name comes from a petrified tree in Post Lake. The post has spiritual significance for the Sokaogon. Another significant place to the Sokaogon is Mole Lake. This area is full of wild rice beds. This food was vital to the Ojibwe people. The Sokaogon fought the Dakota Sioux over this area and its wild rice. It was a devastating battle, and the Sokaogon won. Today, there is a historical marker that describes the Mole Lake Battle.

The Sokaogon, like the St. Croix, were not included in the La Pointe Treaty of 1854. The Sokaogon did not send a representative to Madeline Island. But the next year, Chief Migiizi signed a different treaty guaranteeing the Sokaogon Band’s independence. However, the agent who had the treaty signed by President Franklin Pierce drowned in Lake Superior, and the documents were lost. The Sokaogon lost their federal recognition.

After a lot of work and hardship, Chief Willard Ackley received federal recognition and reservation status for the Sokaogon in 1937. Ackley was the last hereditary chief of the Sokaogon. He was born on the shores of Bishop Lake in 1889. Ackley’s nephew Fred said this about his uncle: “He was chosen by the people the old way — he came to us down through heaven, through the sky, and was put here as [chief].” Today, the Ojibwe celebrate Ackley for his determination to get federal recognition and also for his knowledge of his people’s customs. He passed down knowledge of plant medicines, birchbark craft, and many other traditions.

title: Managing Time
text:
“Tick tock, tick tock.” “Hurry up!” “Don’t be late!” Have you ever heard these phrases? Look around the room. How many clocks do you see? ________ Why is it so important for us to always know the time?

The first clock ever invented didn’t actually look like a clock. It was called a sundial. It was created thousands of years ago and kept track of time by measuring the shadow of the sun. Clocks are one of the oldest inventions in the world.

Keeping track of time has always been important for people. Although clocks were not accessible to everyone for many years, they were usually found on towers, churches, or other important buildings. Nowadays, most people have direct access to multiple clocks at any time of the day.

Time helps us know how to manage our days in order to get things done. It helps us coordinate with each other. Time allows us to organize our days and create patterns and routines. Managing your time helps you make healthy decisions and removes barriers to practicing healthy habits. Why do you think keeping track of time is important for you?

title: What Are Your Priorities?
text:
A priority is something important to you that you make time for. You can choose what things are your priorities, then make sure you have time in your day for those things. Some of your priorities might be fun things, like reading or spending time with friends. It is also good to prioritize things that will help you grow. Things like doing your homework or completing chores should also be high on your list of priorities. People will know they can depend on you when you manage your time wisely and take care of all of your responsibilities.

Your family culture might affect what your priorities are. In some family cultures, dinner is a very important time, and everyone works together to help prepare the food and then eats together. Physical activity is an important priority in some families. In other homes, families value family time together. What influences what is important to you? Analyze how your home, school, and community impact your personal practices and behaviors. You may use more of your time for high priorities. List some of your priorities and analyze why they are priorities to you:

______________________________

______________________________

______________________________

______________________________

______________________________

______________________________

Keep in mind that your priorities will probably change as you move through different life stages and as you gain new abilities and responsibilities. Choose the things that are high on your list of priorities right now.

title: Avoid Procrastination
text:
Natalia needed to clean her room. Her dad had already asked her to clean it … twice. She was about to start cleaning when she saw her favorite comic book under the bed. She hadn’t read it in forever. So she sat down and read for 10 minutes. Now, it was time to get to work. She stood up to start folding some of her clothes when she found a candy bar in one of her pants pockets. Yum! She paused and enjoyed her candy. Okay, now she decided to wipe off her dresser—wait. What was that? It was a fidget spinner! Natalia loved fidget spinners. She began to play with it for just a few minutes before she got back to cleaning her room.

What word could you use to describe this situation? It is procrastination. It is getting distracted or putting off something you need or want to do. Everyone procrastinates sometimes. However, procrastination is the opposite of productivity. Procrastinating prevents you from getting what you need to do done. Cleaning her room should have taken Natalia five minutes. Instead, she chose to procrastinate, so it took much longer than it needed to. When you avoid procrastination and focus on your priorities, you can get things done efficiently (using resources like time wisely) and then have time for more fun things later. Here are a few things you can do to avoid procrastination and be efficient:

Make a to-do list, then follow it.

Set a timer.

Count down from three, then do your task.

Try these suggestions when you are tempted to procrastinate. Think about how you will feel after you have completed your task. There are some responsibilities that should not be procrastinated.

title: Schedules
text:
A schedule is a plan for your day. Some people have very detailed schedules, with every minute of their day planned out and written down. Other people have simple, flexible schedules in their heads that tell them a few things they should get done that day. Everyone is different, and everyone has different schedules. No matter what kind of planner you are, using a schedule is a great way to make your priorities clear and avoid procrastination.

There are many ways to create a schedule. You can figure out what works best for you. You can write it down in a physical planner that has space to write your to-do tasks next to every time of the day. You could use a phone or a computer to create a simple to-do list. You may need to coordinate your schedule with other people’s schedules, like your friends or family members. You can ask your parents when dinner will be and write it down.

On your schedule, you can include important responsibilities like chores or homework. You can also schedule play or relaxing time because that can be important too. Having a schedule for your day can help you feel in control and productive. It can help you feel confident as you check things off your list and see all that you accomplish in a day. Give scheduling a try, and see how it makes you feel.

title: How Will You Use Your Time?
text:
There are 24 hours in a day. That’s 1,440 minutes! When you wake up each morning, you get to choose how you will use all those minutes: who you will see, what you will wear, and what you will get done. Everyone has different priorities and enjoys different things. You are in charge of your day, and you are ultimately in charge of choosing what to fill it with. When you choose what activities to fill your day with, ask yourself, “Will this help me grow, or is this wasting my time?” You can choose to spend your time doing things that will teach you or help you become a kinder person. If you consider whether an activity will help you grow, you may find yourself trying new things or doing things you don't think are fun but know are important. You can choose to spend time reading, even if it is not your favorite thing to do, because you know it will help you become a better reader and may even help you enjoy reading more. You can clean and get chores done because you know you will feel accomplished afterward. As you choose how to use your time, always ask, “Will this help me grow, or is this a time waster?”

Are there any time wasters you would like to stop doing? _________________________

title: Choose to Be Flexible
text:
There will be some days where you have a plan and a schedule but nothing gets done. Some days, your schedule just won’t be kept. You might get sick or be late to school, or your homework could take longer than you thought it would. Sometimes things won’t go as you planned. That’s okay!

When there are unexpected changes to your day, you can take a deep breath and make a new plan. Your day can still be a success. If someone is running late or forgets about plans you made with them, you can be patient and adjust your expectations. You can make every day a great day by choosing how you respond.

title: Shelley-Test
text:
Designing a roadway is a difficult process. Highway engineers make sure the roads we travel on are designed, planned, and built to be safe for passengers and vehicles. A few responsibilities in this career include planning the precise routes of roadways and determining the number of lanes needed in an area. They also map traffic patterns to ensure they flow safely. To make these decisions, highway engineers conduct tests and studies that provide valuable information for saving lives.

Another important role of a highway engineer is ensuring that runaway truck ramps are placed in the proper locations and built to handle the massive size and weight of runaway trucks. These ramps can also be used by any vehicle with failing brakes traveling down a steep roadway. To provide the best results, highway engineers carefully consider all the options and potential scenarios. They are always looking for ways to improve existing designs and make runaway truck ramps more effective.

title: Katie-Test
text:
Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland in 1847. He stopped going to school at age 15. He moved around a lot as he got older. He ended up teaching at a school for deaf children in Boston, MA.

Bell was inspired by his students to develop different ways to communicate. In I876, he invented the “electrical speech machine.” This is what he called the first telephone.

He learned that human speech traveled in sound waves. He created technology to send sound waves through wires. He made a telephone device. The first words he sent with the device were “Mr. Watson, come here. I need you.”

Bell also helped create other inventions. He helped create the air conditioner. He helped create technology for airplanes. He even helped invent the metal detector.

Bell’s inventions and knowledge were important to the science and engineering fields. He used his curiosity and determination to help our society. Our lives are much more comfortable with his inventions. Bell’s discoveries and solutions to problems have made lasting impacts on science and society.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 7
text:
You can plan and conduct a descriptive investigation to explore the patterns of forces. Select a topic to study. In this example, we shall pick friction. Next decide how you will investigate friction. Friction is a contact force. This means objects must be touching for there to be friction. Select something that you can observe where one object touches another. For this example, we’ll pick a textbook on the floor. In order to explore patterns, you will need to conduct an investigation using more than one condition. In our investigation, our first condition will be to measure the effect of carpet friction on the movement of a textbook. We will compare this with the effect of friction on the movement of the same textbook on a hard floor. We have planned our two tests with only one thing that changes. So, we can conduct an investigation that will study patterns of forces.

When you design your investigation, you will have to plan a few more things. First, you will need to decide how to move the textbook across the floor. You will also need to decide how far you will move it. Lastly, you will need to measure the amount of force needed to move the textbook.

In this investigation, we will tie a string around the textbook. Then, form a loop at the end of the string. Next, we’ll attach a spring scale to the loop. We will pull the textbook using the spring scale. The spring scale will give us a measurement of force to move the textbook. Next, we will decide the distance to move the textbook. In this case, let’s move the textbook one meter. Find your two surfaces, carpet and a hard floor. Pick one of the surfaces. Place the meter stick next to the bottom edge of the textbook. Pull the textbook one meter in a constant, steady motion. While pulling, read the number on the spring scale and record it. Repeat the same steps several times to get a consistent reading from the scale. Repeat the exact same steps on the other surface. Record the number on the spring scale. Repeat as before to get a consistent reading from the scale. Compare your results to observe a pattern between the two surfaces. A higher number on the spring scale means more force is needed to move the object. This means the force of friction is greater. Based on your data, you may be able to conclude that carpeted surfaces create more friction than hard surfaces.

The last bell rang.

“It is raining outside, and I have to walk home," Aleki said. "And I didn’t pack a rain jacket today.”

“Looks like you need to run home,” said Natalia. “Too bad we’re going in opposite directions.”

Twelve minutes later, Aleki opened his front door. He was huffing and puffing.

“Aleki, are you okay?” his mom asked.

“I ran home so I wouldn’t get so wet,” he said. “My school supply box opened when I was running! Everything that was in the box fell out and got wet!”

Aleki pulled off his sopping wet backpack and opened it. Stuck together in a big messy clump were his magnetic tiles, staples, pencil lead, binder clips, paper clips, and art scissors.

“How am I ever going to get these apart?” Aleki sighed. He shook the items, trying to separate them.

“Let’s start by putting these back into your supply box,” Aleki’s mom said. She took out wet crayons, erasers, markers, and highlighters from the bottom of his backpack.

Why did some of Aleki’s school supplies stick together? These items were magnetic. Magnetic items are attracted to or repelled by other magnetic items. We can observe if an item is magnetic. We can place a magnet near it. If the item is repelled or attracted to the magnet, it is magnetic. Items that have no reaction to a magnet are not magnetic.

Matter can be classified based on whether it is magnetic. This can prevent items from sticking together, like the school supplies in Aleki’s bag. For example, a toolbox often has drawers and compartments. This keeps magnetic items separated. Tools, nails, screws, and magnets all have their own place. Keeping them organized makes them easy to find and easy to use!

title: Rural, Suburban, and Urban
text:
In general, there are three types of communities: rural, suburban, and urban. Rural communities have large spaces of undeveloped land. This land is used for farms that grow food for urban and suburban areas. Houses are far apart in rural communities. Businesses are built together in a town. There are few public transportation options. Roads connect goods and people with the towns. In 2020, the U.S. Census recorded that about 14 percent of the population in the United States lived in rural areas.

A suburban community is formed when a few businesses and people live in one location. Suburban houses and businesses are built closer together than in rural areas. Instead of farms, the empty spaces are yards, parks, and open lots or fields. Transportation systems in suburban communities are small. Highways connect suburban areas to goods, businesses, houses, and cities. There is some land available for families to grow food on small farms. However, most of the food is brought in from rural areas to help feed suburban communities.

When many people live in one location, it is known as an urban area. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, an urban area has a population of 50,000 people or more. Urban areas are also called cities. In cities, businesses and homes are very close together. Tall buildings with many floors, or stories, are built so that many people can live on smaller pieces of land. Transportation in urban areas is organized to move as many people and goods as possible in and out of the city. There is almost no land available to grow food in urban areas. Most food has to be brought into the city from rural areas.

Many cities in the United States started as rural settlements. New York City is an example of a rural settlement that grew to be a city. For thousands of years, Algonquian tribes inhabited the area. The first European explorer arrived in present-day New York City in 1524. The Spanish, French, English, and Dutch explored the area for 100 years before the first European settlement was established by Dutch fur traders in 1624.

In 1625, Dutch settlers from the Netherlands established a colony that they called New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island, where the Lenape people lived. This settlement eventually became New York City. The Dutch settled in this area because of its proximity to a deepwater port along the Hudson River. They built trading posts, a fort, and various mills near the Hudson River. This allowed the settlers to easily access trading posts, defend their settlement, and use the river to power their mills. Today, New York City is the largest city in the United States. More than eight million people live there.

Milwaukee is another example of a rural settlement that grew into a large city. Like New York City, the area of modern-day Milwaukee was inhabited by Native Americans for thousands of years. The first European to record visiting Milwaukee was a French Jesuit missionary named Jacques Marquette in 1674.

In 1795, a French trader named Jacques Vieau built a post on the eastern bank of the Milwaukee River. When he died, he gave the land to his son-in-law, Solomon Juneau, who began building a town. Two other towns were established on the western and southern sides of Milwaukee. The towns were combined to form Milwaukee in January 1846.

Milwaukee sits on the western shores of Lake Michigan at the confluence of three rivers: the Milwaukee, the Menomonee, and Kinnickinnic. These waterways made it easy for immigrants to travel to Milwaukee in the 1800s. Milwaukee’s waterways helped it become a center for the manufacturing and shipping industries. The city has more than half a million residents.

title: Norman Borlaug
text:
Norman Borlaug was born near Cresco, Iowa, in 1914 to a family of farmers. Growing up on a farm in a rural part of the country gave Borlaug a start in his career. He studied forestry at the University of Minnesota while working for the U.S. Forestry Service. Following his work there, he returned to the University of Minnesota to earn a master's degree and a doctorate in plant pathology.

He used his knowledge and education to work on developing new wheat plants. He was able to develop a version of wheat that had several advantages over previous versions. His wheat was more resistant to disease, which meant that more of the crop would survive to produce food. His wheat also yielded more wheat per acre. By this time in the 1960s, it was obvious to him that his new wheat plant had a chance to help ease world hunger.

Borlaug traveled the world, sharing and spreading his new wheat plant. People in countries throughout South America, Africa, and Asia were able to plant this wheat, which provided them with more food. For his contribution to helping ease world hunger, Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. He continued in his work, identifying new dangers to wheat production worldwide and offering solutions until he died in 2009.

title: Immigrants
text:
The United States has a long history of immigration. People from around the world came to take advantage of the opportunities our country provided. Immigrant communities developed across the country. As people from other countries and cultures arrived in the United States, they contributed to the success of their immigrant communities, as well as to the country.

Immigrants have historically come to the U.S. for better opportunities in education and work. Many have successfully obtained a higher education or found success in a field of work they might not have had the opportunity to pursue in their home country.

Immigrant communities have also contributed to the growth of the country. During the late 1800s, immigrants from China, Ireland, and other countries were the main workers for the Transcontinental Railroad. This was the first railroad to cross the entire country. The completion of this railroad allowed goods and people to make the trip from coast to coast faster than ever, which improved the economy of the country.

American culture has been influenced by immigrants as well. Many musical composers and artists during the 1900s were immigrants or children of immigrants. Irving Berlin, born in Russia, wrote “God Bless America,” among many other well-known songs. Immigrants have shared their unique perspectives through song, dance, theater, art, music, movies, and more, all of which have influenced American culture.

title: The Underground Railroad
text:
Before the Civil War, slavery was legal in the southern United States. During this period, there were enslaved people who found opportunities to escape their enslavers by making the dangerous journey to northern, free states, including Wisconsin. The network of abolitionists and routes that helped enslaved people gain freedom was called the Underground Railroad. Abolitionists were people who opposed slavery.

The Underground Railroad became even more important after the Fugitive Slave Act was passed in 1850. This law required enslaved people who had escaped to a free state to be sent back to their enslavers. Because of this law, those who were escaping slavery had to journey not just to free states in the north but out of the country. Most of the time, they escaped to Canada.

Wisconsin was a free state that bordered Canada. This made Racine, Waukesha, Milton, and Milwaukee strategic cities on the Underground Railroad. Because the Underground Railroad was a secret operation, there are only a few records of the people who traveled on it. Caroline Quarlls is the first recorded freedom seeker to come through Wisconsin. She escaped her enslaver in St. Louis. She traveled up the Mississippi River and sought refuge in Racine, Milwaukee, and Waukesha during August 1842. Eventually, she fled east around Lake Michigan, made it to Detroit, and went on to Canada.

Another successful freedom seeker was Joshua Glover. Glover escaped his enslaver in Missouri. He got to Milwaukee but was then arrested because of the Fugitive Slave Act. However, many abolitionist citizens in Milwaukee stormed the prison and helped Glover escape. He fled to Waukesha and took refuge there until he boarded a steamship in Racine that took him to Canada.

title: Ojibwe Code Talkers
text:
Code talkers were Native Americans who used their native languages to send secret communications on the battlefields of World War I and World War II. There were code talkers from more than 40 Native nations. These pioneering code talkers were from the Choctaw, Eastern Band Cherokee, and Ho-Chunk Nations. Ironically, the U.S. government had forced many children from Native American nations to attend English-speaking schools, where they were often punished for talking in their native languages. However, the ability of Indigenous groups to speak in their native tongues would win battles and save lives during World War I and II.

Normal military codes took hours to send and decode because they were based on complex mathematical formulas. The code talkers created their own codes, which only took 1-2 minutes to send and decode. Most Indigenous languages did not have words for military terms, so code talkers used everyday words to represent military tools. For example, the Comanche used the word “turtle” to mean “tank.” The Navajo used the word “potato” to represent the term “grenade.”

Members of the Ojibwe Bands from Wisconsin were recruited by the U.S. Army from 1940 to 1941. The codes the Ojibwe created used colors to indicate different Army divisions: blue meant infantry, yellow meant cavalry, and red meant artillery.

The military did not want the secret of Native code talkers to be revealed in case they were needed in another war. So, most code talkers were not allowed to talk about their role in either World War. This ended in 1968 when the role of code talkers was declassified. Code talkers have been honored by their own nations for many years, and the U.S. government has also recognized their major contributions. They saved thousands of lives and made a significant difference on many battlefields.

title: Harley-Davidson
text:
The Harley-Davidson Motor Company was founded in 1903 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The company was started by two friends: William Harley and Arthur Davidson. They were interested in building a motorized bicycle. They started out with a bicycle frame and a very small engine. The motorbike did not work very well or for very long. Arthur’s brother Walter came from Kansas to help improve the motorbike. Finally, a third Davidson brother joined them and helped create the bike’s second prototype. On September 8, 1904, the Harley-Davidson company competed in a motorcycle race at the Wisconsin State Fairgrounds.

The Harley-Davidson Company’s motorcycles were used in World War I and II. It was the largest motorcycle manufacturer from the 1920s to the 1950s. Harley-Davidson started in a shed in the back of Davidson’s Milwaukee home. Today, the company’s headquarters sit in the same place, just in a larger building.

title: Green Bay Packers
text:
The Green Bay Packers are an American football team that was organized August 11, 1919. The team got its name from its original sponsor, the Indian Packing Company. The founders of the team, Curly Lambeau and George Whitney Calhoun, recruited players from Green Bay’s high schools. They began to play against local and regional teams. In 1921, they joined the American Professional Football Association, the precursor to the National Football League (NFL).

One of the most important members of the Green Bay Packers was Vince Lombardi. He was the team’s coach from 1959 to 1967. With Lombardi as coach, the team won five national titles, including Super Bowls® I and II. Lombardi was one of the NFL’s greatest coaches. Today, the team that wins the NFL championship game wins the Lombardi Trophy.

As of 2022, the Green Bay Packers team holds the record for the most NFL championships and the most wins in NFL history.

Patterns

title: Energy and Matter and Stability and Change
text:
Energy and Matter

Everything on Earth is made up of matter. Chairs are made of matter. So is water. Energy creates change. Heat is energy. Sound and light are energy, too.

Stability and Change

title: TEKS Explained - Standard 6A
text:
Matter has physical properties. Texture, flexibility, and temperature are properties. Texture is how something feels when you touch it. Flexibility is how well matter bends. Temperature is how hot or cold something is. You observe and measure these physical properties. Observations and measurements help you classify matter by texture, flexibility, and temperature.

Classify the following materials: yarn, a cotton ball, a craft stick, and a pencil. First, observe the object’s physical properties. Then, classify them based on similar properties. Start by touching each object to decide its texture. Classify the yarn and cotton ball as soft and fuzzy. Classify the craft stick and pencil as hard and smooth. Next, decide the object’s flexibility. Try bending them. Classify the yarn and cotton ball as flexible. The craft stick and pencil are not flexible.

Classify the following objects by temperature: ice cubes, fire, hot chocolate, and ice cream. To classify them, use what you already know about the object. Classify ice cubes and ice cream as cold. Classify fire and hot chocolate as hot.

Matter can be solid or liquid. A solid keeps its shape. Pencils and books are solid. A liquid takes the shape of its container. Water is liquid. When you put water into a cup, the water takes the cup’s shape. To identify if a material is solid or liquid, think about its shape and if it changes. Is a computer solid or liquid? It keeps its shape. It’s solid. Is milk solid or liquid? Milk does not keep its shape. Its shape changes when you pour it into a cup.

title: TEKS Explained - Standard 6B
text:
Conducting investigations is a great way to explore and explain how physical properties can be changed.

For this investigation, you will change an object's shape by folding and cutting. Fold a piece of paper in half. Draw half of a heart along the folded side. Cut along your drawing. Open your paper. It’s not a rectangle anymore. You now have a heart shape. You used folding and cutting to change the paper’s physical properties.

For this investigation, you need a piece of wood. You can sand a piece of wood to make it smooth. Ask an adult to help you. Rub sandpaper back and forth on the wood. This makes the wood smooth. You used sanding to change the wood’s physical properties. Now, it is smoother. But it’s still wood!

Gather a few tools to change the properties of wax. Ask an adult to help you. Use a dull knife to cut the ends off your wax. This makes your block smaller. Put the wax in a pan. Slowly, soften the wax on a stove. Wait until it’s cool but soft. Then, use your hands to mold the wax into the shape of a bowl. Next, place your wax in a freezer. Your wax will get very cold and stay in its new shape. You used cutting, melting, freezing, and molding to change its properties. But it’s still wax!

title: TEKS Explained - Standard 7B
text:
Pushes and pulls can have different strengths. They can be strong. They can be weak. They can change an object’s motion, which is how the object moves.

Make a plan to investigate how the strengths of pushes and pulls change an object’s motion. Think about the objects you’ll use. What can you push and pull easily? How about a toy car? What will you use to push the object? How about your hand? Your plan can be to push and pull the car with your hand. Your plan can be to push and pull the car with different strengths.

Conduct an investigation using a toy car and your hand. Your investigation will demonstrate the strength of pushes and pulls on an object's motion. First, use your hand to push the car softly. This is a weak push. With a weak push, how far did the car move in front of you? It did not travel a great distance. Now, give the car a strong push with your hand. How far did it move in front of you? The car moved farther than it did with a weak push. It went a greater distance. Next, investigate strong and weak pulls. Put the car next to you. Pull it backward with weak strength. The car does not move far behind you. Put the car next to you again. Give it a strong pull backward. The car moves farther behind you.

title: TEKS Explained - Standard 6C
text:
You can demonstrate how to combine and reassemble small units by building using snap cubes. The snap cubes are your units. Use the snap cubes to make objects. First, combine the snap cubes to make a chair. The chair is your object. Its purpose is for sitting. Now, take the chair apart. Reassemble the snap cubes. Make a new object: a bed. The bed has a new purpose. The bed’s purpose is for sleeping.

Sometimes you need different materials for building certain objects. Wood, paper, clay, and glass are materials. Different materials have different physical properties. To make a kite, you need a material that the wind can lift. That means the material’s weight needs to be light. Paper is not heavy. Paper is light. Use paper to make your kite. Choosing the right material for what you want to make is important.

title: TEKS Explained - Standard 7A
text:
Objects come in contact with one another every day. Objects touch or collide. When objects touch or collide, they push on each other. For example, your finger is an object. A button is another object. You can touch your finger to the button. This touch is a push. Your finger pushes the button. When you push the button, it moves. Here is another example. A baseball and a bat are objects. The bat collides with the ball. When they collide, they push on each other. The bat pushes the baseball away!

When objects touch or collide, they may change shape. They can bend, stretch, squish, or more. The strength of the collision can make one, or even both, of the objects change shape. A clay ball is an object. Your finger is another object. Push your finger into the clay ball. The ball will change shape. It squishes. The touch of one object forces the other object to change shape. Did you know that even a baseball changes shape when hit by a bat? It compresses! This means it gets squeezed, or pressed, kind of like t

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 8A
text:
Many things cause vibrations. Vibrations are when an object moves quickly back and forth. Objects make vibrations in different ways. Hitting a baseball causes vibrations. Slamming a door causes vibrations. Sounds from objects also cause vibrations.

To demonstrate that vibrations can be caused by different things, including sound, use a bowl, cling wrap, rice, and a drum. Place the cling wrap over the bowl. Make sure it is very tight. If needed, hold it in place with a rubber band. You have created a drum. Put a few pieces of rice on top of the cling wrap. Now, hit the drum many times with your hand. Watch the rice as you hit the drum. The sound from the drum makes the rice vibrate.

Sound is vibrating matter. Sound vibrations move through the air. Many things make sounds with their vibrations. For example, people talk. This is a sound. That means that people make sound vibrations. Talking creates sound vibrations that move through the air. We are able to hear them. Drums are an instrument that makes sound vibrations. Trains make sound vibrations, too.

To demonstrate that sound is made by vibrating matter, use a rubber band and a cup. Place the rubber around the top and bottom of your cup. The rubber band should be over the cup’s opening. Next, use your finger to pluck the rubber band over the top of the cup. This is similar to plucking a guitar string. Plucking the string causes vibrations. You are able to see the string move quickly back and forth. This demonstrates how vibrations are caused by various things. Also, you will hear a sound from your string and cup. This is sound vibrations reaching your ears.

title: What Is a Monopoly?
text:
A monopoly is when one proprietor controls an entire industry and its resources so that no other business can enter the market. A monopoly has no competition. Without competition, the monopoly does not need to improve products or keep the price of their product affordable. The consumer then has little to no choice in the marketplace.

Carnegie Steel is an early example of a monopoly. Andrew Carnegie started this company in the 1870s. Over the years, Carnegie managed to gain ownership of each resource necessary to make and ship steel. For instance, since making steel requires iron ore, Carnegie opened the Scotia Iron Mines in the Mesabi mountain range of northeastern Minnesota. The steel production process also requires anthracite coal, found in the Appalachian Mountains. Carnegie became a partner in the Monastery Coke Works and Larimer Coke Works in order to control the price he had to pay for coal. Next, Carnegie bought a controlling interest in the Pittsburgh Limestone Company to control the price he paid for the last raw material used in steel production. Carnegie began to purchase and build railroad lines to transport all of these resources to his steel mills in Pittsburgh. He eventually controlled each railroad track that entered or left Pittsburgh.

If a competitor wanted to start a steel mill, Carnegie would increase the price of materials to the competitor and prohibit the growth of competition. Carnegie Steel was a monopoly, and Carnegie himself became an extremely wealthy man. The profits of his monopoly continued to climb, and by 1900, Andrew Carnegie was the richest man in the world.

Carnegie and other captains of industry created a bustling economic system that the world had never seen before. Because these proprietors sold products at inexpensive prices, industry grew, cities expanded, and people traveled easily from coast to coast. Communication became faster and more convenient.

The wealth that these men accumulated also made them powerful and gave them control over world economics. They could create or destroy businesses. They did not want competition and would ruin any business that challenged them. Many entrepreneurs and companies experienced these unrelenting business tactics. To many people, they were not captains of industry but robber barons who exploited workers and were ruthless in business.

title: Philanthropy
text:
“The man who dies rich dies disgraced.” -Andrew Carnegie

Unlike any other mogul of his time, Carnegie systematically began to give his wealth away. The act of giving money to worthy causes is known as philanthropy. Carnegie’s philanthropic efforts started a trend among the wealthy in the United States. There was an intense competitiveness among American business tycoons. This competitiveness extended to their work in philanthropy. Each magnate wanted to outdo the others in their philanthropic works.

Carnegie provided funds for 1,600 libraries to be built among various communities in the U.S. In 1889, Carnegie published a list of philanthropic endeavors that he would focus on:

1. Universities

2. Free libraries

3. Hospitals

4. Parks

5. Concert halls

6. Swimming baths

7. Church buildings

There are buildings that exist today because of Carnegie’s philanthropy. His love of music inspired him to donate pipe organs to over 4,000 churches in the United States.

John D. Rockefeller preferred to make large donations to institutions that he believed had great promise. “The best philanthropy,” he wrote, “is constantly in search of finalities — a search for a cause, an attempt to cure evils at their source.” Early in his philanthropy, Rockefeller supported the Baptist church, missionaries, and relief workers. He also had an interest in higher education for African Americans. In 1882, he began supporting the Spellman School, a school for African American women. He also gave money to the Tuskegee Institute and Morehouse College, both African American schools. Rockefeller donated $600,000 to start the University of Chicago in 1890. Over the rest of his life, he would give $35 million to this university.

Rockefeller also concentrated his philanthropic efforts on medical research. He established the first biomedical institute in the U.S. Rockefeller Medical Research Institute is still one of the United States’ leading research facilities today. This research facility has employed 24 Nobel Prize winners. Rockefeller’s charitable work did not stop when he died. He created ongoing foundations that continue to help the world.

J.P. Morgan was one of the wealthiest business tycoons. He devoted his wealth to a few favored causes. Morgan was a patron of the fine arts. By purchasing original art from artists, he enabled them to make a living and devote their time to creating more art. He donated his extensive art collection to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Morgan also donated money to help pay the museum’s staff. Morgan’s donations of money and art helped the Metropolitan Museum of Art become one of the finest museums in the world.

Morgan also had a lifelong interest in natural science and was a patron of the American Museum of Natural History for 44 years. He contributed artifacts from around the world to the museum's collections. Morgan was also interested in the Episcopal Church. His donations supported cleric salaries and the construction of St. John the Divine Cathedral in New York City.

title: Leaving Europe
text:
As the United States went through the Civil War and its aftermath, European countries were also engaged in conflict. During the 1860s and 1870s, many people in Europe were clashing with aggressive government authorities. Some governments in Europe were becoming antagonistic towards certain religious, linguistic, and ethnic groups. Jewish people, Slavic-speaking people from Eastern Europe, and other groups were subjected to targeted discrimination.

The problems facing European countries extended beyond discrimination. Many battles took place on civilian soil. Farms were ruined and much of the labor force was serving in the military. Consequently, there was a scarcity of food. Governments raised taxes to pay for their armies. However, because of the destruction of so many farms, most civilians had no income to pay taxes. The people and communities of Europe suffered greatly.

Discrimination, war, famine, and destruction of property were all reasons that people decided to leave Europe. These are called push factors.

At the same time in the United States, Andrew Carnegie, John D. Rockefeller, Cornelius Vanderbilt, and others were building railroads and factories. They needed a large labor force. News of economic opportunities in America reached many communities in Europe. Europeans began to move to the United States in search of these opportunities. The factors that attract people to a region or country are known as pull factors.

These push and pull factors inspired Europeans to move to the United States. Ships left for America every day from every seaport in Europe. The ships needed deep water ports for docking because they were extremely large. New York City was the most popular destination.

Passage to America was a specialty of many steamships. A typical steamship could transport over 1,500 passengers in a week across the Atlantic. The steamship companies kept excellent records of who sailed with them.

There were three levels, or classes, of tickets. The price was dependent on the services offered. A first-class ticket offered private rooms and all your food and beverages. First-class passengers had access to fresh air on the decks throughout the day. The bedrooms, the dining rooms, and entertainment rooms in first-class were elegant and heated.

Second-class passengers paid for smaller cabins and limited eating and deck access. Third-class tickets were the least expensive and what most passengers bought. This class was also called “steerage.” Third-class passengers had large open dormitory sleeping arrangements with no privacy and no heat. Food was provided, but passengers had to bring their own plates and utensils. Water was provided from a common barrel. Access to the decks for fresh air was restricted.

A steerage ticket price was between $25 and $50 in the 1890s. This would be more than half of what most people earned in a year. Often passengers had to sell everything they owned to pay for the ticket. If they could not sell their belongings, they gave them away or abandoned them, bringing only what they could carry.

The decision to immigrate involved careful planning, since its effects were life-changing. After all, people were making the choice to leave everything they knew behind for the possibilities of America.

title: Who Came to America?
text:
Millions of immigrants came to the United States during the 1880s and 1890s. With such great numbers, U.S. ports were places of confusion. People crowded the piers to welcome passengers. Passengers disembarked with luggage and possessions in tow.

When immigrants came to the United States, they had to go through an entry process with government agents. To reduce confusion at the port and control the entry of new people into the country, Ellis Island Immigration Station was built in 1892. Third-class passengers were taken by ferry from the ship to Ellis Island. Immigration department staff would receive the ship’s manifest, or list of people onboard the ship, and then they would question each steerage passenger. First- and second-class passengers were processed on the ship and then free to go to port.

Ellis Island is in New York Harbor, close to the island that houses the Statue of Liberty. If an immigrant sailed into New York Harbor, the statue was their first view and Ellis Island was often the first piece of the United States they set foot on.

On Ellis Island, third-class passengers waited three to five hours to be seen and questioned by staff. Their names were checked against their ship’s manifest at each point in the interview process. Many different languages were heard in the station. Quick medical exams were done on each person. The staff did not always understand the language of the people they met, but sometimes there were interpreters available to assist them. Once processed, families and individuals were free to start their lives in the United States.

title: The Johnstown Flood
text:
On May 31, 1889, a devastating flood hit the town of Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The combination of geography, weather, economics, and social factors created a disastrous event that killed 2,209 people.

Social Factors

The South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club was an exclusive vacation spot for many of Pittsburgh’s wealthiest industrialists and bankers. There were 61 members of the club, including Andrew Carnegie, Andrew Mellon, Henry Clay Frick, Daniel Morrell, and Philander Knox. An earthfill, or dirt dam, on the Conemaugh River made a lake two miles long and one mile wide. Club members stocked the lake with expensive and rare fish.

The dam was built in the 1840s for the Pennsylvania canal transportation system. Starting in the 1850s, the dam was poorly maintained. The Club also modified the dam to make room for a road and put a fish screen in the spillway. These developments are believed to have further weakened the dam’s structural integrity.

Economic Factors

The South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club existed for industrialists to escape the pollution of the large steel mills in Pittsburgh, mostly during the summer. Much of its workforce came from Johnstown. Their wages were low, and their hours were inconsistent. Engineers and many local workers over the years warned the club members that the dam needed maintenance and repairs, yet no one took action.

Cambria Iron Works employed 7,000 local and immigrant workers for the city of Johnstown. They had no organized union. The company rented houses to its employees, which were built close together between the mills. Workers bought necessities at the company department store. Wages were typical for the time. People earned just enough to live on, but rarely saved any money.

Geographic Factors

Johnstown was located in the narrow valley at the confluence of the Conemaugh River and Stony Creek. A confluence is the point where two rivers meet. This particular confluence was located in the Allegheny Highlands of the Appalachian Mountains, 14 miles south of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club.

Rainfall was high in the Allegheny Mountains. By May 31, 1889, after two days of constant rain, Johnstown had accumulated 6 to 10 inches of rain. The Conemaugh and Stony Creek were overflowing. Most of the streets in Johnstown were under one to two feet of water.

The Facts

The constant rain had saturated the earth of the South Fork Dam as the water in the lake kept rising. The dam was weakened from years without maintenance. Workers from Johnstown tried to reinforce the dam, but it was not enough. At 3:00 in the afternoon, the dam began to collapse and the lake was released into the valley below.

A telegram came into Johnstown from the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club warning that the town was in danger. Train whistles sounded, warning people of the coming flood. People ran to reach higher ground. Many survived, but others were caught in the wall of water that came down from the dam. The buildings in Johnstown were wiped out in the flood.

Aftermath

The American Red Cross came to help with disaster relief in Johnstown. The South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club was eventually disbanded. The club never claimed any responsibility for the catastrophe, though some members sent support for rebuilding and relief for the people of Johnstown. The people of Johnstown rebuilt their city. Today, there is a national memorial to the victims of the May 31, 1889 disaster.

title: Using Data from History
text:
A census is a count of all the people who live in an area. According to the United States Constitution, the country must conduct a census every 10 years. This is important, because each state’s allotment of seats or members in the House of Representatives is based on their population. However, members of the Constitutional Convention in 1787 had differing ideas about how to count the population.

The controversy focused on how enslaved people should be counted in the census. A higher population would mean more members in the House of Representatives. More members would mean more votes, which would mean controlling legislation. Because of this connection between population and control, enslavers wanted enslaved people included in the census count. However, the enslavers also believed that the Black individuals they held in forced labor were property, like tools or farm animals. People and property were two different things. The enslavers could not have people for representation and property for their labor.

The Constitutional Convention delegates who represented the enslavers compromised. They agreed that for the census, enslaved people would be counted as three-fifths of a person. This meant that a group of 25 enslaved individuals would be marked in the census as only 15 people. Free Black individuals were counted as a whole person. American Indians were not counted at all.

After the ratification of the 14th Amendment in 1868, anyone born in the United States could be considered citizens under the law. Each individual was counted for representation.

The United States Census became more detailed over time. After the 1890 census, the Census Bureau released the Statistical Atlas of the United States. This is a book of charts, graphs, and numbers of the census information. This atlas gives an accurate view of the demographics of the nation. Census data is extremely valuable in the study of history. Building skills in analysis and critical thinking for data is necessary for historical perspective.

Using Charts for Learning

Charts and graphs are visual representations of numbers. They contain a lot of information organized concisely. Maps express information about a geographic region. Maps, charts, and graphs all help readers quickly understand a large amount of data.

Using a Chart to Find Information

1. Look for the title of the chart. What is it showing?

2. On the chart, look for the labels on the sides. What do the vertical lines (going top to bottom) and the horizontal lines (going side to side) represent? These labels tell you what is being measured.

3. On the map, look at the bar graph. What data is represented on the graph?

4. Put all the details together to understand the information.

5. Ask questions. Is there a pattern? Is there growth or decline? What could have caused the changes over time? Do you need more information to fully understand the chart or map?

6. How can you use this information to better understand the subject?

7. Communicate the questions.

8. Communicate the answers.

9. Continue until questions are answered.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 8B
text: There are different levels of sound. Sounds can be loud or soft. Sounds can be low or high. We use different levels of sound every day. Can you think of a very loud sound? A fire alarm is a loud sound. It’s important that alarms are loud because we use them to alert people. For example, fire alarms are used to alert people of danger. Another loud sound is an alarm clock. They alert people to wake up in the morning. Can you think of a soft sound? Soft sounds are quiet. A whisper is a soft sound. We use it to talk quietly. Another soft sound is the hum of a refrigerator. We want this sound to be quiet because refrigerators are on all day. We do not want them to disturb us. As you can see, we use many levels of sound! We use them every day, and we use them for different reasons.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 8C
text:
People communicate every day. Often, people need to communicate over a distance. They need devices to communicate over a distance. Phones, microphones, and loudspeakers are devices that help people communicate.

To design a device to communicate over a distance, use two cups and a string. Design them to use like a phone. One person will talk into one cup, and another person can listen with the other cup. The string will connect both cups.

To build this device, poke a hole in the bottom of both cups. Pull the string through one cup’s hole. Tie a knot. Now, take the other end of the string. Pull it through the other cup’s hole. Tie a knot. The bottoms of both cups are connected by a string. You have built your communication device! Now, stand as far away from a partner as the string allows. Put one cup up to your mouth. Have your partner put the other cup to their ear. Keep the string tight. Quietly talk into the cup. Your partner will hear you because your voice, sound, travels through the connecting string. You can use your device to more easily communicate over a distance.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 9A
text:
The sun, moon, and Earth are all in space. People live on the Earth, so when we look up into the sky, we see the sun and the moon. The sun, Earth, and moon all interact.

The sun is a star, and it is the closest one to Earth. The sun is very important to Earth. It provides Earth with light and heat. The sun produces bright light. Light from the sun is called sunlight. Sunlight shines on Earth’s surface. Sunlight helps people and animals see. It helps plants grow. The sun also provides Earth with heat. When sunlight shines on Earth, its surface heats up. The heat helps people, plants, and animals survive.

Close your eyes and picture the moon. What do you see? Usually, people picture a big, glowing object in the night sky. But did you know the moon is not actually glowing? The moon does not make its own light. The moon reflects the sun’s light. The sun’s light shines on the moon’s surface. The moon’s surface reflects, or bounces back, the light. When this happens, the moon looks like it's glowing. However, people are seeing the reflection of the sun’s light.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 9B
text:
Go outside at different times of the day, and observe the objects in the sky. During the daytime, you see the sun, clouds, and birds. Sometimes, you can see the moon during the daytime. Next, go outside during the nighttime to observe objects in the sky. You can see the moon and many stars.

Objects in the sky can be very far away. They are more visible when you use a tool to observe them rather than just using your eyes. A telescope is a tool that helps people study the sky. With a telescope, objects are more visible. Compare what the moon looks like using a telescope and not using a telescope. Without a telescope, the moon might look like a flat, glowing object. You may see some darker lines. Now, look at it using a telescope. How is it different? The moon is more visible. It appears bigger and clearer. Its appearance is more detailed, too. You can see craters on the moon!

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 10A
text:
Wind and water are constantly moving. When wind and water move, they make other things move, too. Wind and water can move particles of soil and rock. Particles are tiny pieces. Wind and water move the particles across Earth’s surface.

Soil is the top layer of the Earth’s surface. When the wind blows, it picks up dry particles of soil. The wind’s gusts carry the soil particles across Earth’s surface. We know this as dust. To investigate how wind moves soil particles, use a baking pan, soil, and a hair dryer. Put the soil in the baking pan. Turn the hair dryer on, and aim it toward the soil. The air from the hair dryer picks up the top layer of soil particles. It carries them across the baking pan. It deposits them on the other side.

Wind also moves rock particles. The wind picks them up, and carries them across Earth’s surface. To investigate, repeat the wind investigation. This time, use sand. Remember, sand is made of weathered rock particles. Place the sand in the baking pan. Turn the hair dryer on and aim it at the sand. The top layer of sand is picked up and moved across the baking pan. The particles are deposited in a mound on the other side of the pan. It takes a stronger wind to move rock particles. Sand dunes are evidence of wind-blown sand.

Water moves both soil and rock particles across Earth’s surface. Rain, streams, and oceans are examples of water on Earth. When water moves over Earth’s surface, it picks up the soil and rock particles. Then, the water carries both particles from one place to another. To investigate how water moves soil and rock particles, use a baking pan, soil, rocks, and a watering can. Place the soil in a layer in the baking pan. Add rocks on top. Prop up one end of the baking pan with a book. Now, on the higher side of the baking pan, slowly pour water out of the watering can. You’ll see the water pick up soil particles and carry them across the baking pan. Slowly add more water until you see the water pick up the rocks and move them. River deltas are evidence of the movement of rock and soil particles by water.

As you can see, wind and water are always moving particles on Earth!

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 10B
text:
Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. People measure temperatures with a tool called a thermometer. The weather can be hot or cold. To measure the temperatures of weather, place a thermometer outside. We record temperatures using degrees on a Fahrenheit or Celsius scale. Record the temperatures each day by writing it down on a sheet of paper. After a week or month, use your data to create a graph. Make a bar graph that shows each day’s temperature. Use your bar graph to notice any patterns with the temperatures.

Precipitation is water that falls from clouds in the sky to the ground. There are different forms, or types, of precipitation. Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are all types of precipitation. They are forms of water that fall from clouds. People measure rainfall using a tool called a rain gauge. A rain gauge collects rain like a cup. Numbers on the rain gauge’s side show the amount of rainfall. This amount is the measurement. Precipitation may be measured in inches or centimeters. Record the amount of precipitation by writing down the number on a piece of paper. After a week or month, create a bar graph to show the data. Use your bar graph to notice any patterns in precipitation.

As you can see, temperature and precipitation are important parts of weather! It’s fun to measure, record, and graph them, and then look for patterns!

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 10C
text:
Weather can be severe. This means the weather is extremely bad and serious. Hurricanes, tornadoes, and floods are types of severe weather events. Different regions have different types of severe weather. In some regions, certain events are more likely to happen than others.

Hurricanes are most likely to form in regions with warm ocean water. Areas near the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean are most likely to experience hurricanes. To investigate hurricanes, you need a few things. Get a large bowl, cornstarch, blue food coloring, gravel, sand, and a wooden spoon. Place the gravel and sand in your bowl. Fill the rest of the bowl with water. Then, stir the cornstarch into the water. Stir until the water looks milky. Wait for the water to stop moving. Now, add blue food coloring to it. Slowly stir the food coloring with the spoon. You’ll see the food coloring move in a circular motion. This is how a hurricane forms and moves.

Tornadoes form over land. Their energy comes from large, severe thunderstorms. Tornadoes form in regions that have strong thunderstorms. Tornado Alley is a region that experiences a lot of tornadoes. To investigate tornadoes, you need a jar, water, liquid soap, and vinegar. Fill the jar three-fourths of the way with water. Put three squirts of liquid soap inside the jar. Add one tablespoon of vinegar. Close the jar tightly. Move the jar in a swirling motion. Look inside and you’ll see a funnel shape. This resembles a tornado. This investigation shows what a tornado looks like and how it moves.

Floods can happen anywhere. They are most likely to occur in areas near water, like coastal areas or rivers. To investigate floods, you need a toy house, toy trees, gravel, sand, newspaper, water, and a stream table. Make balls of newspaper. Use them to line half of the stream table’s bottom. Press sand and gravel on top of the newspaper. Make a slope by piling the sand and gravel higher at the stream table’s end. Put houses at the slope’s top. Put trees at the slope’s bottom. Add water to the empty half of the stream table until the water floods the land. In your investigation, water covers the trees and reaches the houses. You’ve shown the effects of floods.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 11A
text:
A natural resource is a resource found in nature. Water, air, plants, and animals are natural resources. They’re found all over Earth. For example, water exists in many places, like oceans and rivers. That means, water is a natural resource. It occurs in nature.

A human-made resource is a resource that a human makes. Resources like rubber, plastic, and paper are human-made. Processes are used to make human-made resources. For example, people use a process to create paper from wood. Since paper is created through a process, it’s a human-made resource.

Take a look around you. Try to tell between natural and human-made resources.Think to yourself if the resource happens naturally, or if humans made it. Trees are a resource people use for wood. Trees grow in nature. Are trees a natural resource or a human-made resource? They are a natural resource. A plastic water bottle is a resource. It’s a human-made resource. Plastic doesn’t occur in nature. Humans use a process to create the plastic that is used to make your water bottle. As you can see, these types of resources are everywhere. It's important to distinguish one from the other.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 11B
text:
When humans use materials, they impact Earth. Human impact can be limited by making choices. One choice is to conserve materials. When you conserve something, you use it carefully. Humans conserve by reducing, reusing, and recycling. Reducing means using less of something. You do not use a lot of it. Using less limits your impact on Earth. It causes less pollution. It also saves natural resources. Reusing means using something more than once. This is important because you stop materials from piling up in landfills. Also, fewer resources are needed to create new materials.

Humans have another choice to limit their impact on Earth. This is to properly dispose of used materials. This means you get rid of them the right way. It’s important to properly dispose of materials like paper, plastic, and metal. Recycling can be used to dispose of these materials. Recycling means turning used materials into something new. Old paper can be made into new paper. Old plastic can be made into mats and rugs. Old metal can be made into cans.

There are many ways human impact on Earth can be limited. We just need to make choices to conserve. We need to properly dispose of materials.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 12A
text:
Environments have physical characteristics. They support the plants and animals that live there. Physical characteristics include light and warmth. They include rocks, soil, and water. Plants and animals need specific physical characteristics in their environment. They need them to survive.

A rainforest has many important physical characteristics that support the plants and animals living there. Rainforests get a lot of sunlight. The sunlight helps the plant species grow. The trees in the rainforest are tall and thin to reach the sunlight. They have wide, green leaves to collect sunlight to make their own food. The trees provide animals with food and homes. The sunlight also warms the rainforest. The warm temperature helps the plant and animal species survive. Lastly, rainforests get a lot of rain! Water helps the plants grow. The animals living in the rainforest drink the water. The water keeps their bodies hydrated. The environment’s physical characteristics are very important to the plants and animals living there.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 12B
text:
Ecosystems have plants and animals in them. Food chains help us see which plants and animals depend on each other. They show us the plants and animals that get eaten.

Food chains start with energy from the sun. Plants depend on the sun. Plants are called producers. Plants use sunlight to produce, or make, their own food. Producers are very important in food chains. Animals eat producers. Without producers, the animals would not have a food source. They would not have a way to get their energy. In a food chain, animals are called consumers. Consumers can eat producers, but sometimes they eat other animals. All consumers depend on living things for food.

When creating food chains, first identify the producers and consumers. To identify producers, look for the plants. To identify the consumers, look for the animals that eat plants. Also, look for the animals that eat other animals. Use arrows in your food chain to demonstrate how animals depend on living things.

Create a food chain with the following living things: wild berry plants, grasshoppers, rats, red foxes, and coyotes. The wild berry plants are producers. Grasshoppers eat wild berry plants, so you draw an arrow from the wild berry plant to the grasshoppers. You’ve shown that grasshoppers depend on wild berry plants. Continue creating your food chain. Draw an arrow from the grasshoppers to the rats. Then, draw an arrow from the rats to the red foxes. Finally, draw an arrow from the red foxes to the coyotes. You’ve demonstrated which living things depend on other living things for food.

title: TEKS Explained: Standard 12C
text:
Plants need help to move their pollen and seeds to make new plants. They depend on other living things, wind, or water for help.

Pollen moves from one plant to another to produce new plants. Seeds are also important because they grow into new plants. Wind can knock pollen and seeds loose, and carry them in gusts. Similarly, water moves pollen and seeds. Water carries them in its currents. Wind and water help pollen transfer to other plants. They help seeds move to new areas.

Animals are a big help with pollination. When animals drink nectar, the plant’s pollen sticks to the animals. Then, the animal moves to a new plant. When they move, they carry the pollen with them. The pollen transports from one plant to the next. Animals also help move seeds. Seeds get stuck to animals’ fur or feathers, and move along with the animal.

To demonstrate how living things, wind, and water move pollen you need: two flower cutouts, cheese puffs, and small candy pieces. First, mix the cheese puffs and candy together. Then, put one flower on a desk. Put half the cheese puffs and candy in the middle of the flower. Put the other flower on a different desk. Put the rest of the cheese puffs and candy in the middle of that flower. Wash your hands. Make sure all the powder from the cheese puff is washed off. The candy represents the nectar animals eat. The cheese puffs represent pollen. Now, use your hand to collect candy from the first flower. Look at your hand. You’ll see powder from the cheese puffs has stuck to it! Now, go to the next flower. Grab the candy from that flower. Some powder from your hand moves onto that flower. You’ve demonstrated how living things move pollen from one flower to another.

To demonstrate how plants need things to move their seeds make a model. Use a cotton ball, feathers, straws, and glue to make a model of a dandelion seed.
