Now, you can compare the properties of the substances after they are combined. You’ll notice the properties have changes in the solution. The salt is fully dissolved, which makes the salt participles impossible to see. You can no longer identify its properties like you could prior to mixing. Water is still liquid, but may now appear cloudy.

It’s important to know that matter is conserved in solutions. It is not gained, and it is not lost. You can demonstrate this by measuring and recording the mass of both the salt and the water prior to mixing them together. Once you combine them, you can find the mass of the saltwater solution. You’ll see their combined mass will be equal to the individual masses. This confirms that matter stayed the same in the solution, despite any physical changes to the substances. You’ve demonstrated that the amount of matter in your solution did not change, it was conserved.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 6D
text:
There are three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas. All three common states of matter are made up of particles. Particles are too small to be seen, but it’s important to know that everything is made of them! Particles are constantly moving, but they move differently depending on the state of matter.

In solids, the particles are so close together that they cannot move past one another easily. Solid particles are arranged in a fixed pattern, which is why solids keep their shape. To illustrate particles in solid matter, you can first draw a cube. A cube is solid. Next, you can draw little circles to represent particles. Inside your cube, draw a layer of little circles (particles). Make sure each circle is touching. On top of that layer, draw another layer of little circles, exactly like the one below it. This is a fixed pattern! Keep drawing layers of circles until your entire cube is filled with particles. You’ve illustrated particles in solid matter.

In liquids, the particles are close together, but have the ability to easily slide past each other. Although the particles can move freely, they are still linked to one another. To illustrate particles in liquid matter, first draw a container. Then, add a line to represent water. In the part of your container that represents water, draw your circular particles. Since particles in liquids move freely, they do not need to follow a set pattern, or layers, like the solid particles. You simply must have the particles touching to show that they are linked. Be sure your particles fill the liquid portion of your container.

Lastly, in gases, the particles are far apart and can move around freely. They are not constantly touching like solids and liquids. How do we know that air particles exist if we can’t see them? Filling a transparent balloon with air is a perfect example. Air is a gas, so its particles move about freely. As air fills the balloon, the balloon expands. Even though you cannot see anything inside the balloon, it maintains its new, inflated shape. To illustrate gas particles, first draw the balloon. Then, draw circles inside the balloon to represent particles. The circles do not need to touch. They do not need to follow a pattern. They move around freely.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 7A
text:
When we talk about forces, we generally categorize them as equal and unequal forces. Both equal and unequal forces act on objects. Remember, forces are pushes and pulls. When pushes and pulls act on an object, they cause patterns of motion, and the transfer of energy. Energy transfer occurs when the energy of one object affects another object. It’s important to know that energy is not gained or lost, but transferred between objects.

When equal forces act in opposite directions, there is no change in motion or position. Neither force is stronger than the other, which causes them to cancel their effects. You can investigate equal forces by playing a game of tug-of-war. Create two tug-of-war teams with the same amount of players and strength. Each of the two teams holds opposite ends of a rope. Then, both teams start to pull the rope with the same amount of force. In this investigation, you may see that the forces from both teams are equal and acting in opposite directions. The amount of energy transferred between the teams pulling the ropes is the same in both directions. You know the forces are equal because the tug-of-war teams don’t move — they stay in their position. Also, the rope doesn’t move in one direction or the other.

With unequal forces, one force is stronger than the other. Unequal forces cause a change in motion or position. You can investigate unequal forces by playing another game of tug-of-war. This time, make sure one team has more players and strength than the other team. Now, when both teams pull the rope, the side with more players will be pulling with greater force. The transfer of energy is not the same on both sides. One side is transferring more energy, or pulling with greater strength, than the other side. This creates an unequal force. How do you know the forces are unequal? In this investigation, the tug-of-war rope and team will move, and its position will change. It will move in the direction of the stronger tug-of-war team.

This pattern of motion or non-motion can be predicted when we investigate equal and unequal forces.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 7B
text:
Forces can affect objects. They set objects into motion, and affect the object’s speed. It’s exciting to design investigations that test the effects of forces on objects in a system. To do this, you can design an investigation using a toy car and a ramp. You can use your hand as the force in this investigation by using your hand to push the toy car. The toy car, ramp, and your hand make a system. They work together to perform a task, which, in this case, is to test how the car moves.

One thing you can choose to do is to design your investigation to calculate measurements, like distance and time. For example, you can test how different strengths of forces affect the distance the toy car moves beyond the ramp. Or, you can test how different strengths of forces affect the amount of time the car rolls after you push it.

To carry out your investigation, you’ll want to first create a ramp. What materials do you want to use in your design? Think about materials that will help your car move. For instance, you want your ramp to be smooth rather than bumpy. Next, you want to make sure your ramp is angled so the car can move down it. You can use objects to prop one side of the ramp up. Next, you’ll want to decide how many times you will test your investigation. It’s important you test more than one time to make sure your findings are consistent! As you test your design, collect your data. Measure how far the car moves with lighter or stronger pushes, or measure the time the car continues rolling with lighter and stronger pushes. After you test, you’ll discover through your investigation that pushing the car harder with your hand increases the force on it. The car will move faster and farther. When a smaller amount of force is applied, the car will move slower and won’t travel as far.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 8A
text:
Energy transformation includes a change of one form of energy into potentially multiple forms. Different forms of energy include chemical energy, electrical energy, and light energy. Energy does not disappear, even when it transforms from one form to another. It is simply changing its form.

You can use a flashlight to investigate the transformation of energy in systems. Flashlights are a system with a two-stage energy transformation. It’s important to know that batteries contain stored chemical energy. To start your investigation, remove the batteries from the flashlight. What do you think will happen when you turn the flashlight on? The flashlight does not light up. When batteries are not in a system, the chemical energy inside of them does not transform into electrical energy. There are no energy transformations in your flashlight system.

Now continue your investigation and place the batteries in the flashlight. Turn the flashlight on. Do you see a difference in the flashlight system? Yes, you will see the flashlight’s light bulb lights up! How do you think this investigation shows multiple energy transformations? When the flashlight is in use, the chemical energy in the battery transforms into electrical energy. This shows the first energy transformation — chemical energy transforms into electrical energy. Then, the electrical energy moves through the flashlight’s closed path. As it interacts with the lightbulb, the electrical energy transforms into light energy. Light energy is the energy we can see in this flashlight system. The electrical energy to light energy was the second energy transformation. Now you’ve investigated energy transformation! You’ll notice energy transforms in many of the systems we use each day.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 8B
text:
It’s important to identify the requirements for a functioning, or working, electrical circuit. For a circuit to be complete, it requires a closed path. The closed path must contain a power source, an energy pathway, and an energy receiver called a load. These parts must be connected for the electrical energy to continue to flow throughout the circuit. The power source in an electrical circuit can be a battery or an electrical outlet. The energy pathway usually consists of metal wires, which are a great tool for connecting pieces of the circuit. Common examples of energy receivers are lightbulbs, motors, fans, and buzzers. When these three components are connected correctly, the electrical circuit functions properly.

When in a complete circuit, electrical energy can be transformed into motion, light, sound, or thermal energy. You can demonstrate this by building a simple circuit with a battery, wires, and a lightbulb. The battery is the power source. It contains chemical energy. The load is the lightbulb. You can use wires to connect the battery to the lightbulb. You do this by touching one wire to the top of the battery and the side of the light bulb’s base. Then, touch a second wire to the bottom of the battery and the bottom of the light bulb’s base. You can use electrical tape to hold the wires to the battery. When the parts of the circuit are connected, the circuit is closed. Chemical energy transforms into electrical energy, then into light energy. How can you observe this in the lightbulb? The light bulb lights up! That’s evidence of light energy. Using the same circuit, you can show the transformation of electrical energy into thermal energy. If you were to carefully touch the light bulb, it would feel hot. The light bulb heated, which shows evidence of thermal energy. You can demonstrate the transformation of electrical energy into motion energy using the same circuit. Replace the lightbulb with a small fan. The fan moves once the circuit is complete, showing evidence of motion energy. As you can see, energy transformations are everywhere!

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 8C
text:
Light energy travels in a straight line, a lot of them! Once light is produced, it continues in straight lines until it comes in contact with something else. When light comes in contact with something, it can be reflected, refracted, or absorbed.

You can demonstrate how light travels in a straight line by using three CDs, clothespins, and a candle. Clip the clothespins to the bottom of the CDs, to create a base that helps the CDs stand straight up. Next, in a straight line, place each CD a few inches apart on a table, checking that their holes line up. Then, place your candle at the opposite end of the table. Line up its wick with the CDs’ holes. Light your candle, go to the table’s opposite end, and look through the first CD's hole. You’ll be able to see the candle’s flame through all three holes! This demonstrates how light travels in a straight line because it’s shining through the three CDs three holes.

Reflection occurs when the light bounces off of an object. Smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors, smooth water surfaces, and metal are great at reflecting light, but they aren’t the only reflective surfaces. To demonstrate light being reflected, you need a flashlight and a mirror. Turn the flashlight on, and shine it on the mirror. Now, look behind you. You’ll see the light from the flashlight because the light has bounced off the mirror.

Refraction happens when the light bends, or changes direction, after passing through a substance. It’s easy to observe refraction using a transparent substance, like water, glass, or plastic. You can demonstrate how light is refracted by placing a straw into a glass of water. The part of the straw extending outward from the water’s surface looks straight. However, when you observe the straw beneath the water’s surface, the straw will look bent.

Lastly, light can be absorbed. This means an object can soak up light. To demonstrate light absorption, you need a flashlight and a book. First, turn on the flashlight. Place it on a table facing a wall. You can see the light on the wall. Next, place the book in front of the flashlight’s light. When the light hits the book, you can see the light on the book. You can’t see the flashlight’s light on the wall anymore. The book is absorbing the light.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 9
text:
Earth rotates, or spins, on its axis. Earth’s axis is an imaginary line that runs through Earth’s center from pole to pole. Earth rotates counterclockwise. Earth’s rotation causes two things to happen: the day and night cycle, and the appearance of the Sun moving across the sky, resulting in changes in shadows.

You can set up your own demonstration to show that Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours. All you need is a styrofoam ball, a stick, a marker, a flashlight, and a timer. First, carefully poke your stick through one end of the ball. Push it through the center of the ball until it exits the ball’s opposite side. The stick represents Earth’s axis, and the ball represents Earth. Next, use your marker to draw a dot on one side of the ball. Turn the flashlight on, and set it on a table. Start by facing the dot toward the flashlight, which represents the Sun. Now it is daytime. Start your timer for 24 seconds to represent 24 hours. Now, slowly rotate the ball (which is Earth) counterclockwise. Different sides of the ball face the flashlight (which is the Sun) as the dot slowly faces away. After 12 seconds, the dot faces entirely away from the flashlight. Now it is nighttime. Keep on rotating! After 24 seconds (which represents 24 hours), the dot faces the flashlight once again. You’ve demonstrated that it takes Earth 24 hours to rotate on its axis one full time.

Earth’s rotation is why we have a day and night cycle. As Earth rotates, different sides face the Sun. When a side faces toward the Sun, it experiences daytime. At the same moment, the opposite side of Earth is facing away from the Sun. That side experiences nighttime. As Earth continues to rotate, the sides facing toward and away from the Sun continue to change. The side experiencing daytime rotates away from the Sun. Then, they experience nighttime. After approximately 24 hours, the process starts again, giving us 24 hours in a day.

Earth’s rotation makes it look like the Sun is moving. In fact, the Sun isn’t moving. It’s Earth that moves! When Earth spins on its axis, it changes the position of the Sun in the sky. This creates the patterns we observe in shadow positions. A shadow occurs when an object blocks the Sun’s light. Shadows take the shape of the object. The Sun’s position in the sky creates patterns in shadows that we can predict. When the Sun is to the left of an object, the shadow is cast to the right of the object. Similarly, if the Sun is in front of an object, the shadow is cast behind it. Additionally, the Sun’s position affects how short and long shadows appear. When the Sun is high, the shadows are short because the Sun is directly overhead. Shadows are long when the Sun is low because the light is at an angle.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 10A
text:
Every day, the Sun and ocean interact in the water cycle. As the Sun heats the ocean’s surface, the water absorbs heat energy. This causes ocean water to evaporate. When it evaporates, it rises into the atmosphere as water vapor, which is a gas. Once in the atmosphere, the water vapor cools. Then, the gas condenses into clouds and becomes liquid again. This step is called condensation. Wind causes clouds to move all over Earth. Then, the water returns to Earth’s surface as precipitation. Types of precipitation include rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Sometimes, this water even returns to the ocean! The water cycle continues when, once again, the Sun heats Earth’s surface and causes evaporation.

When the Sun and ocean interact in the water cycle, they affect the weather. Both the Sun and ocean contribute to cloud formation, storms, and rainfall. Remember, the Sun evaporates ocean water, which condenses into clouds holding precipitation. When the wind moves the clouds all over Earth, it moves the precipitation in the clouds, too. When these clouds travel to surrounding areas, it affects the weather in that location. For example, clouds that form over the ocean often hold a lot of rain. When the rain clouds move to another area, that area eventually experiences heavy rain. The clouds created in the water cycle also affect an area’s temperature. The Sun’s light shines and warms Earth’s surface. Clouds can trap heat to warm the Earth and reflect sunlight to cool the Earth. The water cycle can affect other types of weather, such as storms, cloud coverage, and air pressure. As you can see, when the Sun and ocean interact in the water cycle, they directly affect the weather!

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 10B
text:
The formation of sedimentary rocks is a very long process. It can take thousands, or even millions, of years! Sedimentary rocks form on Earth’s surface through weathering, erosion, and deposition. To start, weathering breaks down large rocks into small pieces, such as sand and pebbles. The weathered rock pieces become part of sediment. Sediment is a solid material made up of weathered rocks, minerals, and the remains of plants and animals. Then, erosion carries the sediment, along with other minerals, and deposits them in a new location. Over time, layers of sediment build up on top of one another. As they build up, their weight causes the layers of sediment to compress and harden into sedimentary rocks.

The formation of fossil fuels is another long process that occurs with the formation of sedimentary rocks. Fossil fuels are natural substances that form from the remains of buried organisms like plants and animals. The dead plants and animals settled into the ground and decompose. Then, they were covered by sediment and compressed along with the layer of sedimentary rock. Eventually, the remains of the plants and animals changed into fossil fuels through heat and pressure. Now, fossil fuels are buried beneath the many layers of sediment.

The processes of sedimentary rock and fossil fuels formation are slow and difficult to see in the natural world. Therefore, a model can help us demonstrate the concepts. Start with gathering four colored clays — red, blue, black, and green. Break the red, blue, and green colored clays into tiny pieces – this models weathering! Next, you need one cup. Place the red pieces of clay into the cup. Then, place the blue pieces of clay onto the red layer. Now, take your black clay. Roll a few balls of black clay, and place them on top of the red layer. These represent organisms that have died, which become fossil fuels. The black clay models how organisms become buried under layers of sediment, and results in fossil fuels forming along with sedimentary rocks. Lastly, place the green clay pieces on top. Firmly press the layers with your fingers. The layers need to be compact to represent the compressed, hardened layers of sediment buildup. Now, flip your cup upside down and carefully pop the layers out. The clay layers stick together. You’ll see you’ve made a sedimentary rock model! You can see three, distinct colored layers of clay. If you break the model in half, you’ll see the black clay (or fossil fuels) between the second and third layers. From the pressure of you flattening the layers, the fossil fuels will be embedded in between layers.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 10C
text:
Earth’s surface is constantly changing. Water, wind, and ice are elements that change Earth’s surface. They assist in the formation of many landforms, including deltas, canyons, and sand dunes.

Deltas are wetlands formed at a river’s mouth, which is the river’s end. Deltas are often triangular in shape, or in the shape of a fan, and they are flat. As water flows in rivers, it carries sediment in its currents. Sediment includes gravel, sand, and clay. Deltas form when the river slows at its mouth and deposits the sediment. There, in the slower moving water, sediment settles and collects. This becomes a new landform – a delta.

You can model how a delta forms by using a baking pan, one pound of sand, a cup, and water. Place the sand in the upper half of the baking pan. Press it lightly so it’s flat, and then create a slope leading into the bottom half of the pan. Leave enough space for the delta to form in the tray’s bottom half. Next, slowly pour water from your cup onto the sand. The water will run down the sand and begin to fan out. You’ll see a delta begin to form in the pan’s bottom half! You’ve modeled changing Earth’s surface by using water to form a delta.

Canyons are deep, narrow cuts in rock. They have steep sides, and rivers often run through the middle of them. Canyons form as water pressure repeatedly cuts through the rock, weathering and eroding pieces until the landform develops. Water can seep into the rock’s surface. It freezes in the cracks and expands. The ice acts as a wedge, and forces pieces of rock to break apart. This causes huge chunks of rock to break off of the canyon’s sides. Wind also contributes to the formation of canyons. High winds move through the canyon, which shape and smooth its sides.

You can model how a canyon forms by using sand, gravel, clay, soil, a baking pan, a watering can, and water. Spread the sand, gravel, clay, and soil in individual layers in the baking pan. After each layer, press it firmly with your hands before adding a new layer on top. These represent the rock layers on Earth. Next, use your finger to draw a curved line in the top layer. Your line should go from one end of the baking pan to the other end. This represents the river running through the rock. Next, pour water from your watering can into your river. Start with a little bit of water, and then increase the amount. You’ll see layers of rock wash away, and a canyon starting to form! You’ve modeled changing the Earth’s surface by using water to form a canyon.

Sand dunes are hills of sand along a beach or desert. They form when the wind carries sediment into a sheltered area and deposits it. The sand accumulates into a mound. Once the mound is formed, the sand continues to collect. Water assists in forming sand dunes along a beach. The ocean carries sediment onto the coast and deposits it into the existing mound. Wind can also move sand from the beach onto the dune. Due to how easily sand moves, dunes are always changing their shapes and heights!

You can model how a sand dune forms by using a deep container, a pound of dry sand, and a blow dryer. Start by placing the sand into the bottom of the container. Next, turn the blow dryer on a low setting. Carefully use it to blow “wind” across the sand’s surface. Watch as the sand begins to accumulate into a mound at the opposite end of the container! You’ve modeled changing the Earth’s surface by using wind to form a sand dune!

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 11
text:
Using natural resources impacts the environment. It’s important to develop solutions that minimize the environmental impact of the use of natural resources. A solution means you are solving a problem. Conservation, recycling, and the proper disposal of materials are peoples’ solutions to minimizing environmental impact.

You can design your own solution to minimize environmental impact! Water is a natural resource that is limited. Therefore, it’s important that people conserve water. However, people need to continue to use water. For example, in the spring and summer, people often plant gardens in their yards or communities. People need to water their gardens to help their fruits and vegetables grow. What solution can you design to conserve water, but also still be able to water a garden? Your solution needs to allow you to collect water and store it to use at a later time.

First, think about how you use water each day. Is there any leftover water you can collect? We have leftover water from when we make food, like when we boil potatoes or pasta, or steam vegetables. Next, think about other ways you have access to water. When it rains, we have access to rainwater that we can collect. Finally, think about how you can store the water until you use it to water the garden’s plants. You can design a container to hold water you collect. You can reuse a clean plastic jug from a gallon of milk. If you cut the top of the jug off, you can place it outside to collect rainwater. Whenever you have leftover water from cooking, you can add the water to your rainwater collection. You can use the collected water to water the garden! Now, you’ll use less water from a hose. You’ve designed a solution to conserve water!

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 12A
text:
In a healthy ecosystem, a variety of organisms survive by interacting with living and nonliving factors. Biotic factors are living factors in an ecosystem. They include plants, animals, and bacteria. These are the producers, consumers, and decomposers that cycle matter and energy throughout the ecosystem. The cycle of matter and energy helps the organisms live and grow, and the ecosystem stays healthy. Abiotic factors are the nonliving factors in an ecosystem. Abiotic factors include sunlight, water, air, temperature, and soil. These nonliving factors are necessary for biotic organisms to survive. For example, they provide the oxygen to breathe. They provide the water to drink and grow plants. They include the necessary temperature for species to thrive.

Let’s study a healthy Texas ecosystem. If you go outside, you can find a grassy field. If you’re able to stay and observe your surroundings, you’ll see many things! You’ll see both biotic and abiotic factors. These factors are around you each day, and now you can observe how they interact.

First, observe the biotic factors, which are the plants and animals around you. On the ground, you may observe plants that include flowers and grasses. You may observe rabbits and lizards, too! In the air, you’ll see bugs, bees, and birds, like hawks. Now that you’ve identified the biotic factors, you can observe how they interact to survive. Remember, living things rely on one another for food and energy. In the grassy field, you can observe a rabbit eating grass. The bees may be buzzing from flower to flower, eating pollen. There are many dependencies in the grassy field’s ecosystem. You might not see them today, but the hawks depend on rabbits for food, and the lizards depend on bugs. When organisms eat properly, they stay healthy, continue to grow, and produce offspring.

Next, study the abiotic factors in the grassy field. You can observe sunlight, rocks, and water. You can’t see oxygen, but you know it’s there because you’re breathing. You can feel it fill your lungs. Now, let’s observe and describe how the biotic factors interact with these abiotic factors to survive. When you see sunlight shining on the grass, you’re seeing how the Sun provides grasses (the producers) with the energy needed to make their own food. If you watch the animals carefully, you’ll see they are breathing. They are breathing in the air around them. If you are able to find any streams or puddles in the field, you may observe animals drinking water from them. Oxygen and water help the animals stay healthy. These organisms will appear energetic and strong.

As you can see, in all healthy ecosystems, you can observe and describe how various organisms survive by interacting with biotic and abiotic factors.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 12B
text:
In order to predict changes in a food web, you’ll need to first look at the cycling of matter and the flow of energy. Consider the following food web in a pond ecosystem: the Sun, algae, flies, frogs, herons, and bacteria. Algae are producers. Flies, frogs, and herons are consumers. Bacteria are decomposers. The Sun’s light transfers energy to the algae. Algae use sunlight, and matter from the air and water to produce their own food. When flies consume algae, energy and matter transfer from the algae to the flies. Next, the flies are food for frogs. Flies contain energy, that, when eaten, transfers to the bodies of frogs. The matter from the flies helps the frogs physically grow and repair their bodies. Similarly, frogs are food for herons. When herons eat frogs, they receive energy and matter. Finally, when living plants and animals die, their remains become energy and matter for bacteria and new plant growth.

Now, let’s predict what will happen in the food web if there are changes in the pond ecosystem. Sometimes in an ecosystem, the population of a producer, consumer, or decomposer can change. A population can increase or decrease. Let’s pretend the population of flies decreases. We will predict how this change affects the cycling of matter and the flow of energy. First, remember that frogs eat flies. A decrease in the fly population means there will be less food for the frogs. Now, what do you predict will happen to the cycling of matter in the food web? Most likely, with less food, there is less matter available to help the frogs grow and repair their bodies. The frogs may not appear as healthy. They could get sick and die. If the frogs begin to die, the herons will begin to lose their food source. What do you think will happen to the herons? With less food, there is less matter available to help the herons grow and stay healthy. When the flies are removed, they also affect the flow of energy. What do you predict will happen to the food web’s flow of energy? When flies are moved, there is less energy available for the frogs and herons. There are no flies to provide the frogs with energy. In turn, this decreases the amount of energy available to the herons because they eat the frogs. As you can see, if you first study the cycling of matter and the flow of energy in a food web, you’ll be able to predict how changes in the ecosystem will affect it!

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 12C
text:
A healthy ecosystem has many different types of organisms living in it! We call the living organisms in an ecosystem the biotic factors. A healthy ecosystem needs nonliving factors, called abiotic factors, too. Sunlight, air, water, and temperature are abiotic factors. You can describe an ecosystem as healthy when it’s able to support the range of biotic factors living in it. That means a healthy ecosystem can provide plants and animals with food, water, shelter, and air. In a healthy ecosystem, the biotic factors will live, grow, and reproduce. Sometimes, human activities affect a healthy ecosystem. Human activities can be harmful, or they can be beneficial.

Human activity has been harmful to healthy ecosystems in many ways. Pollution, deforestation, overhunting and overfishing, and introducing invasive species to habitats are all harmful human activities. Human activity can be described as harmful when it hurts the organisms living there by destroying the resources needed for shelter, water, and food. Harmful activity can cause a population to decrease, which negatively impacts food webs. Let’s look at an example of human activity, and describe how it hurts an ecosystem. Zebra mussels, which are small, striped, freshwater mussels, are an invasive species in Texas’s lakes. Humans accidentally brought zebra mussels to North America. Now, zebra mussels harm native mussel species by over-eating their common food source. This leaves less food for native mussels so their numbers decrease.

Human activity can be beneficial to ecosystems, too. Humans work hard to help struggling species, plant and grow more plants, reduce human waste, and preserve habitats. Human activity can be described as beneficial when the ecosystem continues to thrive. The plants and animals living there grow, live, and reproduce. Here is a real-world example of beneficial human activity. Currently, humans are trying to protect and preserve coastal ecosystems. They are strengthening sand dunes and planting seagrass. This will protect the plants and animals living along the coast from the wind and ocean waves. Humans are removing invasive plants from sand dunes, and planting native ones to provide food and shelter for living organisms. Providing food will help the organisms stay healthy, live, and grow. Shelter ensures the organisms have a safe place to live and raise their young.

When humans help take care of an ecosystem's biotic and abiotic factors, the ecosystem continues to thrive and stay healthy. The next time you head outside, think about your actions. Are you harming or helping the ecosystem?

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 13A
text:
A structure is something that’s made up of parts. Its function is what the structure does. Structures can be internal or external. Internal structures are structures on the organism’s inside, like the heart and lungs. External structures are structures on the outside of the organism, and include things like eyes, claws, and tails. Sometimes structures are common, like a heart or brain. Other times, structures are unique to the organism, like flamingos' long legs. Structures and functions are necessary for survival. For example, they help the organism find food and water, or they help the organism hide from danger.

Different species are able to survive in the same environment due to their unique structures and functions. Elephants and lions are organisms that survive in the same environment. Their environment is open land with plants, different animal species, and watering holes. You can analyze the elephant’s structures and functions to see how it survives in its environment. A trunk is an important elephant structure. The trunk has several functions that provide the elephant with nutrients. It helps the elephant breathe air and drink water. The trunk helps the elephant grab food and bring the food to its mouth. Another structure is the elephant’s ears. They are able to funnel in sound waves and hear any nearby predators. They also help the elephant stay cool on hot days. Now, analyze the lion’s structures and functions. Lions have structures that help them obtain nutrients. Lions have powerful leg muscles, which allow them to sprint and capture prey. Lions’ claws function as a way for them to catch, grip, and tear their food. Lions have ears that rotate. This allows them to hear prey from all sides. Even though elephants and lions have different structures and functions, they can both survive in the same environment.

title: TEKs Explained - Standard 13B
text:
Behavior in organisms can be either instinctual or learned. Both types of behavior are key to increasing the organism’s chances of survival.

Instinctual behavioral traits are inherited from past generations. These traits do not need to be taught to an organism. This means instinctual behavioral traits happen automatically – they are not learned. Hibernating, walking, taking care of offspring, and building nests are examples of instinctual behaviors. These instinctual behaviors provide the organism with food and energy, ensure the offspring can live and grow, and provide shelter from danger. All are essential to the organism's survival. A great example of an instinctual behavior trait is when turtle hatchlings return to the sea. The mother lays eggs in the sand, and leaves them to develop and hatch on their own. This means there is no parent to teach the turtle hatchlings once they're born. Once the babies hatch, it is instinctual for them to return to the sea as a large group. This increases the chance that they’ll survive waiting predators.

Learned behavioral traits are behaviors learned through experience. This means an organism’s experiences change how the organism acts. Sometimes offspring learn these survival skills by watching their parents. Avoiding danger, finding food, and communicating are behavioral traits organisms can learn from their parents, and increase their chances of survival. A great example of a learned behavioral trait is orca whales hunting in packs. Orcas teach their young how to hunt along with the pack to increase the chances of catching prey. In fact, orcas have been known to catch and release seals as a way for their young to practice catching seals. As you can see, orca hunting is not entirely instinctual. The young experience hunting in packs and learn through observing their parents. These learned behaviors help the orcas survive.

title: Economic Expansion
text:
When the Spanish-American War ended, the United States became the new power in the Pacific Ocean. The United States gained control over Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippine Islands, and Guam. Shortly afterward, the United States also gained Hawaii, Wake Island, American Samoa, and the Panama Canal Zone. It was believed that the addition of these territories would give America access to many new markets.

However, some Americans warned that colonialism would cause the country many problems that would cost lives and a lot of money. Other critics referred back to the Constitution, which did not mention gaining colonies. Still others predicted that the United States would be dragged into wars with other powers, especially European powers. These European powers were stronger and already better established in the area than the United States was.

After some debate, President McKinley finally decided to make the Philippines an American colony. Many Americans felt that the Philippines and Guam could be used as gateways to new markets, especially China. Merchants hoped to gain a bigger piece of the rich Chinese market. Missionaries hoped to spread Christianity to the Far East.

However, China presented a new problem for the United States. Other major European powers were already dividing the land into areas they each controlled. Britain had control of Hong Kong. Portugal claimed Macao. Russia seized Port Arthus. Japan claimed Taiwan. Germany claimed the port of Kiaochow. These claims made it difficult for the United States to trade with China.

Something needed to change so that the United States could trade with China. Finally, U.S. Secretary of State John Hay stepped forward with a plan. He wrote letters to the European powers and proposed his plan, which he called the “Open Door” policy. His policy said that all countries, including America, had equal rights to trade with China.

title: The Panama Canal
text:
Completed in 1914, the Panama Canal symbolized U.S. technological advancement and economic power at that time.

Having a water passage for ships to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean was not a new idea. Upon discovery of the isthmus, ideas of a passage were discussed but never attempted until the 1880s. The French had started trying to build the canal in the 1880s, but failed to complete it. They abandoned the zone in 1889.

The building of the canal was considered a very important event in foreign policy at the time. Both the U.S. and the British wanted to find a way to ship goods quickly and cheaply between the Atlantic and Pacific Coasts. In 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt was able to purchase the Panama Zone that the French had once occupied. He helped Panama secede (break away) from Colombia. This established a bond between the two countries. It eventually allowed the U.S. to successfully gain the canal zone through an agreement with Panama’s government.

In 1903, the United States was granted access to the canal region. Construction began at once. The canal was made as a system of dams and locks. Locks open and close to allow the controlled passage of boats and ships. Locks allow the water levels to be raised and lowered over the physical features of the land.

The project was finished in 1914. Theodore Roosevelt considered the canal a symbol of American strength and success.

title: Engineering Design Scenario
text: Natalia loves art. She keeps forgetting to bring her fancy drawing pencils to school. She doesn’t want to put them in her backpack because they might break, but she keeps leaving them on the table.

title: Daily Life in the Early Colonies
text:
What was daily life like for the people of British Colonial America? As the colonies were getting started, daily life was very hard. People had to figure out how to survive.

Early colonial farmers woke up early, ate, and started their work in the fields. The work they did depended on the season. In the spring, they would plow and plant the fields. They worked with their hands or with the help of an ox or horse. During fall, they harvested their crops. Year-round, they tended the fields, took care of livestock, chopped wood, fixed fences, and made house repairs.

Tradesmen worked long hours in villages. Depending on their trade, they had different tasks. For instance, blacksmiths spent their days making tools like axes and hammers for fellow tradesmen and average citizens. Most tradesmen trained apprentices as well.

Since there weren’t many women in the colonies, they often had more significant roles than in Europe. Without a strong and productive wife, a family would struggle to survive. Daily, women were responsible for raising their children, preparing meals, making and washing clothes, preserving food for winter, and fetching water.

Children worked and had no time to play. By the age of three or four, they had to get up early and work alongside their parents. Boys often helped their fathers with work on the farm as well as with hunting and fishing. Girls, on the other hand, usually helped their mothers and learned housekeeping skills.

Indentured servants worked on farms and large plantations. It was hard work to use the hoe, scythe, ax, and plow to cultivate and harvest crops. These people had very little freedom. Nearly every aspect of their lives was strictly controlled by the people who indentured them.

Enslaved Africans were forced to work in the fields or the home of their enslavers. Once someone was enslaved, they were enslaved for life. They had no rights and were often mistreated.

title: The Workforce in the Colonies
text:
As the colonial charters said, profit was necessary for the colony to survive. Even if plantations were large, there were few workers to manage them. Over time, the introduction of new people and economic systems supplied the colonies with a stable workforce. This workforce included families, indentured servants, free men, apprentices, women, and enslaved people.

Families were often the first source of labor that the colonists had. All members of a family were expected to contribute to their homes, farms, small businesses, or a combination. Learning business, farming, or a craftsman’s trade was typically passed from father to son.

Indentured servants were men and women whose journey from England to the colonies was paid for by another person. In exchange, they signed a contract with that person that required them to work on farms or in households for a certain number of years. Protected by the law, this contract of indenture was a legal and binding agreement. Once their debt of passage (about $2,500 today) had been repaid, the contract was complete. Then, the servant was free to live and work in the colonies. Sometimes, they would receive land, money, weapons, clothes, or food upon the contract’s completion.

Free white men in America were no longer bound by the restricted social class system of England. In England, men from lower-class families had few opportunities to advance in society. In America, new laws favored ambitious men who worked and contributed to the success of the colony. These men, according to the charter, could own land. With that land, a man could become a farmer, a merchant, or join another profession. Land ownership also meant new rights and privileges, like voting, for these men.

Apprentices were another common labor source in America. Often, orphans or younger sons of large families were contracted to master craftsmen for years to learn a specific trade. These contracts were drawn up, signed before the courts, entered into a deed book, and considered binding. As part of the contract, an apprentice agreed to work for a master craftsman or tradesman without pay. Masters were obligated to provide basic education (reading, writing, and arithmetic), room and board, and sometimes tools or clothes upon completion of the apprenticeship.

Enslaved people were kept in bondage and forced to work on farms and later on plantations. Enslaved people came from Africa, where they were captured and sold into slavery. Under the law, these people were considered property. They had no freedom or rights. These people were enslaved for life. Any children they had were also enslaved. When indentured servitude became unsustainable, many landowners looked to enslaved Africans as a profitable labor source.

title: Cycle of Debt
text:
There are factors that determine the price of a commodity or product. Some of these factors include the cost of production, the quality of the product, and how many products will be available in the future. The most critical factor is demand, or the desire people have to buy a product. If there is no demand, it doesn’t matter how much of a product there is or what it costs. If no one wants it, it won’t sell.

In Great Britain, there were large companies that bought and sold one valuable product: tobacco. These companies were called brokerages. Only brokerages could buy American tobacco. Tobacco farmers worked with brokerage firms to get the tobacco from the plantation to Great Britain. The broker would decide how much the plantation owner’s tobacco was worth.

In the 17th century, no direct payment was involved. The brokerage house worked like its own bank. The plantation owner would be given credit for the value of the tobacco. This amount of credit was recorded by the brokerage house.

Manufactured goods had to be purchased from Great Britain and shipped to the colonies. If there was anything the plantation owner and his family wanted to buy from Great Britain, they made a list and gave it to the broker. The broker purchased the items using the credit from that year’s tobacco sales.

The owner had to trust the broker with these purchases. There were no prices on the list, so the owner didn’t know how much each item would cost. The broker would purchase only the best for his client. Most of the time, the cost of the items was more than the owner had in his account. The broker promised that the planter could pay off the rest when he returned with the next year’s crop. The plantation owner would then be in debt to the broker. This process often repeated the next year. So, the plantation owner would always be in debt to the broker. It was extremely difficult to reverse this cycle.

title: Life of Enslaved Africans
text:
The life of a person who was enslaved changed little from day to day. Enslaved people were considered property by the people who enslaved them. They were clothed, fed, and sheltered by what the enslaver wanted to provide. The workday was structured by the enslaver.

There were public consequences for outward defiance. This was done to create fear within the enslaved people so they did not want to rebel against their enslavers. Sometimes, enslaved people fought back and rebelled against their enslavers and living conditions. This caused enslavers to fear future rebellion. It also proved that enslaved Africans not only desired their freedom but were willing to risk their lives to get it back.

There were many other ways that enslaved adults and children resisted their enslavers and their situation. Some resisted by breaking tools used for cultivating cash crops. Others planned and escaped from the enslavers. Escape was very dangerous. If successful, there was freedom. If unsuccessful, there was extreme punishment. The enslavers tried to control everything.

The enslaved men, women, and children who were working on the plantations had been taken from their homes and families in Africa. They were bought and sold as property to people in a strange new land. Everything in their lives was turned upside down. They were forced to work in an unfamiliar environment with unfamiliar people. They had to learn how to use unfamiliar tools, grow new crops, and learn a new language. Sometimes, they also had to adjust to a different climate.

In addition to all the loss and change they experienced, enslaved people also knew they would never see their homes again. The one thing the enslavers could not take from the enslaved people was their memories. They kept the celebrations and traditions of their communities and cultures alive. They remembered the stories, songs, and skills they learned in Africa. Enslavers tried to stop the African people from expressing their cultural identities. Despite these efforts, the enslaved Africans continued to preserve their memories and culture. These were things no enslaver could ever take from them.

title: The Gilded Age
text:
The period of time between the 1860s and the early 1900s is sometimes known as the “Gilded Age.” The name came from Mark Twain’s book, The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today. When an item is gilded, it is usually made of an inexpensive but durable material and covered with gold. It appears shiny on the outside, but it is not really valuable. Likewise, the Gilded Age may have appeared industrious and profitable, but underneath, it wasn’t shiny. It was corrupt and represented suffering for many people.

During the Gilded Age, the United States was experiencing significant economic growth through the expansion of railroads and factories. Factory owners became rich by selling products at high prices and paying workers cheaply. Businesses grew and expanded into monopolies within the oil, coal, steel, and railroad industries. These industries were led by prominent business leaders like Andrew Carnegie (U.S. Steel), John D. Rockefeller (Standard Oil Company), Leland Stanford (Central Pacific Railroad), and John Osgood (Colorado Fuel and Oil).

These men controlled the markets for these industries and used their wealth to buy votes and political favors. These businessmen were called “robber barons.” They got this name from the ruthless and corrupt practices they used in running their businesses and in taking over smaller companies. Without laws in place to prevent rich men from forming monopolies and gaining power, they could do whatever they wanted. They lived lavish and expensive lifestyles. Meanwhile, workers struggled to feed themselves and their families.

The groups most affected by the widespread corruption of government and big businesses were factory workers, women, and children. As railroads stretched across the nation, people traveled more and relocated to find jobs in factories. Their working conditions were harsh and unsanitary. Their hours were long. The average factory worker worked ten hours or more per day, six days a week. Factories were unsafe and filled with dangerous machinery. Workers were often injured in factory accidents. They were also prone to developing diseases from the unhealthy atmosphere inside the factories.

The coal mining industry was also dangerous. Workers experienced injuries, coal-induced health hazards, and even death. Female workers were paid half as much as the men. Children as young as five years old worked alongside their parents in the mines and factories. Eventually, workers began to join together and form unions, or workers’ groups, to protest harsh working conditions. Because of these conditions, the Gilded Age also represented a time where the labor movement in the U.S. was gaining momentum.

Newspapers and magazines became more prevalent during the Gilded Age. Public information was reaching more people than ever before. Journalists like Ida Tarbell investigated and exposed corruption among industrialists and politicians. These journalists were called “muckrakers.” They helped in the effort to end corporate monopolies. Muckrakers also exposed other issues, such as how foods were processed. The issues made public by muckrakers and other writers led to legislation to make life in America safer.

With the growth of industry during this time, cities grew. Urbanization brought changes in technology and engineering advancements. For example, the Pennsylvania Railroad built two tunnels under the Hudson River to bring railroad service to Manhattan. Before the tunnels were built, all rail lines ended at the Hudson River. To get to Manhattan (which is an island), people had to take ferries across the river. This could be dangerous during storms and in the winter. With the Hudson River train tunnels, transportation in New York became safer.

The skyscraper was another engineering marvel of the time. The Home Insurance Building in Chicago, Illinois, was completed in 1885. It was considered the first skyscraper in the world. It had ten stories. With the building of skyscrapers came other technologies, such as the escalator and electric elevator.

The Gilded Age had two sides. One was the glittering gold of industrial growth and wealth. The other was the difficulty and danger of labor and poverty. It was also a time of progressivism and social reform that expanded the influence of the U.S. government in the lives and business of its citizens.

title: The Progressive Movement
text:
While the Gilded Age boosted the U.S. economy, the quality of life for most Americans declined. Workers living in northeastern cities worked long hours for little pay. Often, work was dangerous and work environments unhealthy. Change was hard when industrial leaders bribed politicians to ignore workers’ rights in favor of personal profit.

The Progressive Movement

To combat the corruption of the Gilded Age, the Progressive Movement emerged. The Progressive Movement was a period of reformation. It debated the responsibility of the government to improve citizens’ living and working conditions while eliminating corruption. The Progressive Movement cut across party lines. It was bipartisan. Both Republicans and Democrats worked together. They believed their changes would create a better America that would be more prosperous, democratic, and moral. Their goals included:

Right to safe food

Rights of workers (an eight-hour day, safe working conditions, and a voice at work)

Rights of women and children (right to vote and elimination of child labor)

Controlling big business (elimination of trusts and monopolies)

Ending political corruption

Overall moral reform

Women

Women became an important force for change during the Progressive Movement. Many women's organizations lobbied and protested until there was equality for women in the workplace. The right to vote in 1920 grew out of their hard work.

Muckrakers

Muckrakers were another important part of the Progressive Movement. Muckrakers were investigative journalists, scholars, preachers, and novelists who exposed unfair and unsafe practices. They wrote pieces about political corruption and unsanitary food processing plants. They also wrote about the mistreatment of laborers. When the general public read about these conditions, they pressed Congress and the White House even harder to legislate changes.

Roosevelt, Taft, and Wilson

The Progressive Movement finally gained a powerful executive and leader when Theodore Roosevelt won the White House in 1901. From 1901 to 1909, Roosevelt used his theme of a Square Deal to fulfill most of his promises. These presidential actions delighted the Progressives. From 1909 to 1913, William Howard Taft continued the Progressive agenda. From 1913 to 1921, Woodrow Wilson vowed to give America a "New Freedom." Wilson's Progressive goals were just getting started when World War I interrupted the course of progressive change.

Each of these presidents had to wrestle with the same problem: What role should America's government play in the new industrial age?

Should it let competition prosper by enforcing the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 and break up the large trusts and monopolies?

Should it create laws to break up some monopolies while protecting others?

They decided on the second option. Their actions furthered the Progressive Movement.

title: President Woodrow Wilson
text:
Woodrow Wilson, the 28th President of the United States, served from 1913 to 1921. While he is primarily known for his role during World War I, he was also a major reformer during the Progressive Movement. He recognized how industrial and governmental corruption was spreading, and he was determined to end the suffering of the poor.

Woodrow Wilson was born in Virginia. He worked there as a teacher and public official. He even had the nickname "Schoolmaster in Politics." Wilson graduated in 1879 from the College of New Jersey, which was later renamed Princeton. He served as president of Princeton University from 1902 to 1910, when he became the state governor. His work in New Jersey later helped him win the presidential election.

As president of Princeton, Wilson fought for educational reform. As governor of New Jersey, he worked for industrial and government reform. He wanted to regulate political campaigns and utility rates. He also wanted workers to receive a fair wage. As U.S. president, he wanted to reform government policies. He guided America through World War I and promoted an international peace organization called the League of Nations. His work with the league helped him win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1920. Wilson died in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 3, 1924.

title: Ida Tarbell and the Muckrakers
text:
Muckrakers were the investigative journalists of the Progressive Era. They were writers, reporters, and photojournalists who went deeper than the surface-level facts of an issue to find out what was really going on. They investigated and exposed corruption in government and business. Ida Tarbell was one of the best muckrakers. She pioneered investigative journalism.

When Tarbell was 14 years old, her father had a small, successful oil refining business. He and his partner would process crude oil into a purer form that could be used in engines. Then, they shipped it to customers using railroad lines. Standard Oil Company was a large oil company owned by John D. Rockefeller. His company formed secret partnerships with railroads to raise the shipping prices they charged. The railroads also gave rebates, or money back, to Standard Oil when they used their railroads to ship their oil. Many of the small companies couldn’t afford to pay the higher costs. When they struggled, Rockefeller offered to buy their businesses. Most of them sold, but Tarbell’s father wouldn’t sell. His company ended up in deep debt. He eventually had to mortgage the family’s house to pay the debts. This made Tarbell angry. She vowed that if she ever got the chance, she would fight injustices like this.

Ida Tarbell decided to become a writer when she was in college. After college, she was hired to write for a magazine called McClures. She wrote a series of articles about the French general Napoleon. She wrote another series about Abraham Lincoln. Her articles were so popular that subscriptions to the magazine doubled. In 1900, she saw her chance to fulfill her promise to fight for justice. Tarbell took on John D. Rockefeller and his Standard Oil Company.

Tarbell began to dig into the practices of Standard Oil and how they ran their business. She wrote a 19-part series and a book. Both were called The History of the Standard Oil Company. The series of articles confirmed what many people had suspected for a long time. Her work uncovered patterns of deceit and corruption. She exposed efforts by Rockefeller to take complete control of the oil industry and its supply and distribution chains.

The information Tarbell published led to the breakup of Standard Oil’s monopoly of the oil industry. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the company had violated the Sherman Antitrust Act. Standard Oil Company was divided into a number of smaller companies, which included Exxon and Chevron. These companies still supply oil and gasoline today. Rockefeller told his advisers not to comment publicly on any of Tarbell’s accusations, referring to her as, “that poisonous woman.” Tarbell’s courage and persistence resulted in justice. It was too late for her father, but her actions helped many other small businesses survive.

title: Europe in 1914
text:
During the late 1800s and early 1900s, many European nations were competing against each other for business, trade, and expansion opportunities. Jealousy and fear spread through Europe. Many nations started to form alliances (partnerships that join together for a common cause) to protect themselves. Germany formed the Triple Alliance with Austria-Hungary and Italy. Great Britain, France, and Russia opposed the Triple Alliance and created the Triple Entente. The two alliances protected their own interests and promised that if one member of the alliance was attacked, the others would join the fight. As the countries began to strengthen their borders with troops and supplies, tensions grew.

On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, who was the heir to Austria's throne, visited Bosnia with his wife. They stopped in Sarajevo. Suddenly, gunshots rang out, and Ferdinand and his wife were dead. They had been assassinated by a young member of a Serbian terrorist group called the Black Hand.

The Austrian government blamed the Serbian government for the attack. A month later, Austria-Hungary declared war against Serbia. This triggered the alliances into action to protect each other. Nations began to declare war. Russia mobilized against Austria. Germany declared war on Russia. When Germany marched through Belgium, Great Britain declared war on Germany. Once the war began, the Triple Entente became the Allies, and the Triple Alliance became the Central Powers. By Christmas of 1914, England, France, and the other Allies were bitterly fighting the Central Powers of Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire.

The United States was not yet in the war, but that was about to change. The sinking of the British passenger ship, the Lusitania, and other acts brought the war to the United States in 1917.

title: The Lusitania and the Zimmermann Telegram
text:
Two events affected America’s policy of isolationism regarding the war in Europe. Many Americans were immigrants who had loyalties on both sides of the fighting in Europe. They had no desire to join in this conflict between their homelands. Others thought that it was a war among European countries that did not concern the United States. Within two years, however, the United States became convinced that they had to join World War I.

The Lusitania was built in 1906 as a transatlantic passenger ship. After WWI began, the Lusitania was modified to carry weapons and war supplies across the Atlantic. The Germans knew this. As a warning, they published newspaper ads reminding passengers that Germany and Great Britain were at war. The ads warned that ships sailing through waters around the British Isles could be attacked. These warnings were ignored.

On May 7, 1915, a German submarine called a U-boat shot a torpedo at the Lusitania. The ship sank completely within 20 minutes. The attack resulted in the deaths of 1,195 passengers, including 123 Americans. Because American citizens had been killed, the attack strained relations between the U.S. and Germany. Many Americans also began to view Germany negatively and to justify war.

The second major event that convinced the U.S. to join WWI was the Zimmermann Telegram. The Zimmermann Telegram was a coded message sent from German government minister Arthur Zimmermann to Mexico. The telegram stated that in the event of the U.S. entering the war on the side of the Allies (Russia, France, and Great Britain), Germany would provide weapons and funding for Mexico to attack the U.S. to regain Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The telegram was intercepted and decoded by the British. President Woodrow Wilson was informed of the contents.

President Wilson had won his recent election promising no U.S. involvement in WWI. However, the Zimmermann Telegram, along with the sinking of the Lusitania, convinced Wilson of the aggressive intentions of Germany. The U.S. declared war on Germany in April 1917, and the U.S. actively entered World War I. Eventually, more than four million Americans would actively participate in the war, with 116,000 soldiers losing their lives in battle. The rallying cry that inspired men to join the fight and drove the troops during battle was, “Remember the Lusitania!”

title: Life in America in Wartime
text:
Because of the United States’ previous position of isolationism, there was not much public support for the war. To increase support, posters began to appear that touched on themes like patriotism and civic duty. The posters emphasized the connection between U.S. democracy and the democracies of the Allied countries. The government sold war bonds and stamps to raise money for war expenses.

As soon as Congress declared war, attitudes began to change. More than 1.3 million men and 20,000 women enlisted in the Armed Services. The government also instituted the Selective Service Act of 1917. This act reintroduced military conscription, also known as the draft. The military didn’t want to rely solely on volunteers to fill the ranks. The draft was well-received. The number of people dodging military service was low.

Because most American men were overseas fighting in the war, women worked in factories. In many states, these factories changed their production to materials needed for war, such as guns, ammunition, and medicine. Wartime demands also supported the textile and agriculture industries. The need for uniforms, tents, and other materials made from textiles sent the price of cotton soaring.

Troops also needed food and supplies, so farmers grew more food. To ensure there was enough food for the troops, committees provided instructions on how to plant and grow “liberty gardens." They also instructed people how to can and preserve foods.

Women joined groups such as the American Red Cross and the YWCA. These and other groups launched fundraisers for the war effort. Later, suffragists argued that their patriotic efforts during the war meant they should get the right to vote. This argument was successful. Soon after the war, government leaders approved the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote.

Everyone in the United States had a role to play in World War I. Life changed dramatically.

title: Juneteenth
text: Juneteenth is the country’s newest holiday. It is known as Freedom Day. It celebrates the day all enslaved people in America were freed.

title: Effects of the Treaty of Versailles on Germany
text:
The Treaty of Versailles was meant to establish peace between the Allied European countries and Germany. However, some of the Allied leaders harbored resentment toward Germany because of the war. Both French and British leaders thought Germany should pay their governments’ war costs. Georges Clemenceau, the French prime minister, wanted to ensure that Germany was incapable of becoming powerful in the future. Others felt differently. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson desired world peace and complete military withdrawal on behalf of all parties. His Fourteen Points plan and League of Nations advocated for lesser punishments for Germany.

Unlike Woodrow Wilson’s forgiving proposal, the Treaty of Versailles took harsh actions against Germany. The main requirements of the treaty were:

1. Germany was forced to surrender 10 percent of its territory and all of its overseas possessions.

2. Germany was ordered to demilitarize. Its navy and army would be severely limited, and the country was forbidden to maintain an air force.

3. The treaty required that Kaiser Wilhelm II and other Axis leaders be tried for war crimes.

4. Germany was forced to accept full responsibility for starting the war.

5. Germany was ordered to pay enormous reparations to cover Allied losses.

The German people felt betrayed by their government leaders who signed the treaty. The treaty’s terms added to the effects of economic depression in Germany and the world. The resulting anger and economic hardships led to the rise of radical right-wing political groups in Germany. One of these groups was the National Socialist Workers’ Party, or the Nazis. The stage was being set for Adolf Hitler’s meteoric rise to power just 13 years later.

title: America’s Postwar Prosperity
text:
With the end of World War I, the United States entered the 1920s, which was an exciting, energetic period in American history. It was an age of prosperity and wealth for the nation. From 1921 to 1929, the average income per person rose from $522 to $716 a year. Americans had more disposable income. Disposable income is extra money that can be saved, invested, or spent for pleasure. Americans also had shorter work hours. This meant they had more time for entertainment.

During the 1920s, petroleum and electricity became widely available. They powered machines in factories and tractors on farms. Over 200 electric companies brought affordable power to more than 30 states. By 1920, most homes in the United States had electricity.

Henry Ford’s assembly line process in factories decreased production costs and made it more efficient to mass produce automobiles. This made car ownership possible for many people. Other factories had adopted this method of production, so relatively inexpensive goods were readily available to consumers. Consumers were buying these products, including radios, beauty products, frozen foods, watches, clothing, and more. Homemakers were also enjoying new labor-saving devices like electric irons, toasters, washing machines, and refrigerators.

Throughout the war years, people had sacrificed. During the 1920s, Americans could begin consuming products in mass. New technologies made previously expensive items available to the middle class. For instance, people who could not afford expensive fabrics could now buy artificial, or synthetic, fabrics such as rayon. Synthetic materials replaced costly wood or metal in many products. This drove prices down. New machines turned out products faster and cheaper. This too caused prices to fall. The cost of a tire, for example, dropped from $30 in 1914 to $15 in 1929.

Even those who did not see a rise in their incomes could join the buying spree. The increasing availability and use of credit put manufactured goods within the purchasing reach of more people. Of course, the credit wasn’t free money. Credit is a type of loan with interest. Interest is a percentage that is charged for borrowing money. For example, if someone borrowed $100 and the lender charged an interest rate of five percent, the customer would be expected to pay back the $100 plus $5 for interest, or $105 total. Lenders were making a good profit funding the American desire for a higher standard of living.

Consumers could also make use of another new financing option: installment buying. A family could buy its first radio and pay for it over time in small monthly payments rather than all at once. Installment loans included interest too. However, the introduction of credit and installment buying came at a cost. Overbuying without having enough money sometimes led people into debt.

Although for most people the “roaring” 1920s meant new opportunities, some groups suffered dearly during this time. Economic hardships for farmers and discrimination against African Americans challenged the otherwise prosperous times. Changes for both the better and the worse were at hand in America.

title: The Decade That Roared
text:
The decade of the 1920s was dubbed “The Jazz Age” by one of its most prominent authors, F. Scott Fitzgerald. This time period later came to be known as the Roaring Twenties. It was a decade of dramatic change in America, with economic and cultural developments.

In general, the economic climate of the U.S. during the 1920s was prosperous. The nation’s total wealth doubled at the time. Consumers had more money. Improved industrial processes like the assembly line lowered prices. People could spend more freely on new, cheaper products, and there were many to choose from.

The increasing availability of electricity sparked many new inventions for the home. Previously, people had to take soiled rugs outside and beat the dirt out. New vacuum cleaners removed the dirt from rugs inside the house. Electric refrigerators kept food cold consistently. Before, people used ice boxes, which needed a continuous supply of ice to keep food cold. Electric washing machines did the laundry, freeing people from hours of work. Electric razors gave men a smooth shave, unlike a traditional straight razor, which often cut their faces.

The affordability of the automobile and more leisure time gave people opportunities to travel for pleasure. The first motor hotel opened in San Diego, California, in 1925. One year later, Route 66, a major U.S. highway, opened. The highway stretched from Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California. This new major road made travel much more convenient for people all across the country.

With more leisure time, people sought out different ways to entertain themselves. One of the most popular sources of entertainment came from the radio. More than 12 million households had radios in the 1920s. Families gathered around them for news and entertainment. By 1923, there were 500 radio stations broadcasting in the United States. Advertising on the radio and in magazines encouraged consumers to purchase products nationwide.

New kinds of music, dance, and clothing spread quickly. Jazz, a new style of music, spread from New Orleans to the north and became very popular. New dances like the Charleston were faster and more energetic than styles of the past.

Talking pictures (movies) also premiered. One year later, the first animated cartoon debuted. By the end of the decade, three-quarters of Americans attended the movies every week.

People’s appearances even changed. After receiving the right to vote in the 19th Amendment in 1920, women felt more free to make clothing choices. The flapper fashion was especially popular. To look like “flappers,” women would wear knee-length skirts, get bobbed (shorter) haircuts, and use makeup.

Instead of making clothing by hand, factory-made clothing could be purchased. Clothing was sold “off the rack” in department stores and clothing shops. Other new personal goods were also available, like mouthwash, deodorant, and hair dye.

American citizens were making history during the 1920s. Adventurers like Amelia Earhart and Charles Lindbergh thrilled the world with their daring airplane flights across oceans. In 1923, archeologist Howard Carter discovered the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh, King Tutankhamun. Egyptian-inspired fashions and decor became very popular.

In 1924, American athletes competed in the first Winter Olympics, which were held in France. In 1928, scientist Alexander Fleming discovered the miracle drug, penicillin. This first antibiotic drug changed the world of modern medicine.

These dramatic changes in American economics and culture truly earned this decade its reputation as the decade that roared.

title: Charleston and the Charleston
text:
A new dance craze spread through the country in the 1920s. It was considered scandalous at the time, but it became an iconic image of the era. Young people flapped their arms, kicked up their heels, and let loose as they danced the Charleston.

The origins of the dance can be traced back to the city of Charleston, South Carolina. It is thought to be based on an African American dance called the Juba, which was brought to America by enslaved people. Versions of the dance came north with African Americans during the Great Migration.

In 1923, a dance based on the movements of the Juba was included in a Broadway musical called Runnin’ Wild. Audiences went wild for the new dance called the Charleston. It entered everyday American culture. Josephine Baker, a famous African American dancer, performed her very energetic version of the Charleston as part of a show in Paris. Her popular performances helped make the new dance famous in Europe as well.

title: Anna May Wong
text:
Anna May Wong was a famous Chinese American actress. She was the first Chinese American movie star.

Anna May Wong was born on Jan. 3, 1905, in Los Angeles, California. Her given name was Wong Liu Tsong. It means “Frosted Yellow Willows.” As she grew up, her family called her a more English-sounding name, Anna May.

Anna May’s family immigrated to America from Taishan, China. Her grandfather, Leung Chew Wong, moved to America in 1853. Gold was discovered in Michigan Bluffs, California, in 1848. Leung moved there and set up two stores in the 1850s. He earned money by selling products to miners. Anna May’s father, Sam Sing Wong, was born in Michigan Bluffs in 1858. Sadly, Leung died soon after Sam was born. Sam married a woman named Gon Toy Lee. Together, they opened a laundry store on North Figueroa Street in Los Angeles. They had eight children. Anna May was their second child.

Around 1910, all the big movie companies moved from New York to California. Anna May loved to visit the sets where movies were being filmed. She loved the movies so much that she even skipped school and used her lunch money to go see movies. When she was nine years old, she decided she wanted to be a movie star. She even came up with her own stage name. She joined her Chinese and English names to form Anna May Wong.

When she was 14 years old, she finally got her first role in a movie. She was an extra in a movie called The Red Lantern. Anna May continued playing extras in movies while she went to school. She had a busy childhood. She went to school, worked in her family’s laundry, and studied Chinese. Eventually, in 1921, she decided to quit school and become a full-time actress.

Anna May wanted to play the big roles in new movies. However, the large movie companies wouldn’t let her. They only wanted her to play small roles that made fun of her people and culture. This upset Anna May. She decided to open her own movie company in March 1924. She wanted to make movies the way she would like to. Unfortunately, she had to close her company. Her business partner was caught breaking the law.
