Anna May decided she didn’t want to work in America anymore. She experienced discrimination because she was Chinese. American movie companies also didn’t let her play big roles. In 1928, she moved to Europe, where she starred in lots of movies and plays.

Finally, in the 1930s, American movie companies began allowing Anna May to star in big roles. However, they still made her act in ways that didn’t honestly represent her culture. In 1932, she appeared in her most famous film, Shanghai Express. Despite her success, movie companies still refused to give her big roles in new movies. One day, she auditioned to play a Chinese woman in a movie. The role was given to an actress who wasn’t even Asian! This made Anna May very sad. She took a year-long trip to China to visit her family, who had moved back to Taishan in 1934. It was her grandfather’s hometown. She wanted to understand her culture and study Chinese theatre. She wanted to be able to play Chinese roles better.

After her trip, Anna May did not get much work. She mostly starred in smaller films. People were not interested in the kinds of characters she played anymore. However, she eventually became the first Asian American to lead a U.S. television show, called The Gallery of Madame Liu-Tsong.

On Feb. 3, 1961, Anna May passed away. Her acting career was so influential that awards for Asian American Arts and Fashion were named after her. Her appearance in films that many Americans watched helped them to learn that Chinese American citizens were just as American as anyone else.

title: The History of Juneteenth
text:
Juneteenth is short for “June 19th.” On this day in 1865, enslaved people learned that they were free. It has been celebrated in many African American communities ever since.

In 1863, President Lincoln signed an important document. It was called the Emancipation Proclamation. This document freed enslaved people in the U.S. On June 19, 1865, the news of emancipation finally reached Galveston, Texas. This day became known as “Juneteenth.” In 2021, the president of the United States made Juneteenth a national holiday.

title: The Revolution’s Many Participants
text:
The United States has always been made up of diverse groups of people. Even at the time of the Revolution and the country’s founding, people with all different backgrounds and experiences joined the cause.

Native Americans

Most Native Americans tried to stay out of the war. Native Americans did not want colonists moving west. The British promised Native Americans that they would keep colonists out of the west. The British talked the Cherokee into fighting the Patriots. This was called the Cherokee Campaign of 1776. The Cherokee lost to the Patriots. As a result, the Cherokee had to leave many towns and were forced to move west.

The Oneida Nation sided with the colonial army when the Revolutionary War began. Other nations of the Iroquois Confederation remained allied with the British. The Oneida provided the colonial army with information, soldiers, scouts, and spies and aided troops in various ways. The division of loyalty within the Iroquois Confederacy caused conflict, and it eventually fell apart.

Each Native American tribe tried to gain an advantage with each side. If the British won, the tribes who were their allies would have a chance of getting their lands returned to them. Other tribes wanted to side with the Americans to gain an advantage in trade and power after the war.

Black People

During the American Revolution, thousands of free and enslaved Black people supported the Patriot cause. By the end of the war, between 5,000 and 8,000 Black people served on the battlefield or in non-combatant roles. Non-combatant roles meant working in the military encampments as cooks, wagon drivers, and craftsmen. In February 1778, Rhode Island voted to officially enlist enslaved people in the military. At its peak, this regiment had 600 Black members.

Hundreds of free and enslaved Black men served in the navy. They worked as boat pilots, gunners, sailors, and privateers. Privateers were individuals commissioned by the Continental Congress to attack and take supplies from British ships. Some enslaved Black men earned their freedom through their service in the Continental Army and Navy. Unfortunately, many Black men remained enslaved after the war, despite their contributions.

The British army encouraged enslaved people to leave their Patriot enslavers. Lord Dunmore, the Royal Governor of Virginia, issued a proclamation in 1775. Only enslaved people who escaped from Patriot enslavers would be freed if they joined the British. Any enslaved people who escaped from Loyalists would be returned to their enslavers.

Women

Women were vital to the war effort across the colonies. They weren’t allowed to participate in the military, but they found other ways to be Patriots. Many women supported the war effort by organizing fundraisers to provide supplies to the troops. They made clothing for soldiers, worked in the military camps, and tended to wounded soldiers. The women had to find ways to make do when war prevented supplies from getting to market. Women kept farms active while men were at war. Women found iron that could be melted to make musket balls. Women also acted as servants to British officers and spied on them.

The most important job of the women focused on the future. The women educated their children to be independent and educated communities on being a republic. Mercy Otis Warren recorded the actions of the Patriot cause for future generations. Her view of independence inspired many to build the country. The women of the Revolution knew the war could be won. It was up to future generations to uphold that victory.

title: The Harlem Renaissance
text:
The period of time known as the Harlem Renaissance was a golden age for social and artistic expression that began in African American communities. The Harlem Renaissance movement focused on the beauty, strength, and talent of African Americans. Jazz music, realistic literature, colorful poetry, and abstract art created during this period influenced American culture for years to come.

From the 1910s to the mid-1930s, this artistic movement began to change stereotypes. It impacted how other people viewed African Americans and their contributions. It also encouraged African Americans to explore and deepen their relationship to their heritage.

This blossoming of African American artistic culture was not limited to Harlem, but Harlem was at its core. Beginning with the Great Migration, African Americans moved to big city neighborhoods, especially in New York. One of the biggest and most important African American neighborhoods was Harlem. The Harlem neighborhood bustled with African Americans. Many of them owned businesses. These included publishers, newspapers, music companies, theaters, and nightclubs. When the Harlem Renaissance developed, artists had plenty of places to share their creativity.

One of the most popular developments during the Harlem Renaissance was jazz. Jazz is a style of music that originated in New Orleans in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It is a mix of African American musical traditions. Jazz has a lot of rhythm and expresses many different emotions. After World War I, there was a new appreciation for what many today consider “America’s classical music." Some of the most famous jazz musicians of the time were Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, and Dizzy Gillespie. Many famous jazz musicians performed at a distinguished ballroom in Harlem called the Cotton Club.

Sometimes called the “Queen of the Renaissance,” Zora Neale Hurston was a prominent African American writer and anthropologist. She was college-educated and spent a lot of time collecting oral histories and folklore. She also wrote stories and plays that portrayed and celebrated the lives of everyday African American people.

Another talented performer of the Harlem Renaissance was Josephine Baker. She was born into a very poor family in St. Louis, Missouri. When she was eight years old, she started cleaning houses for wealthy white people to help support her family. When she was 13 years old, she left home and became a waitress. At the same time, she discovered her love for dancing, a career she pursued with incredible success. She performed in America and in Europe. She even became the most popular and highly paid performer in Europe.

Another major figure of the Harlem Renaissance was Aaron Douglas. He moved to Harlem in 1925 and started illustrating for two important magazines in the movement, The Crisis and Opportunity. Instead of painting traditional landscapes, he created modern, geometric pieces. His paintings often portrayed important themes regarding African Americans and their lives. He was especially inspired by their struggle for political and creative freedom.

The Harlem Renaissance was named after the intellectual and artistic period of rebirth called the Renaissance. African American musicians, dancers, writers, and artists thrived in the creative climate of Harlem. They embraced their heritage and created a new culture for themselves.

title: Mary McLeod Bethune
text:
Mary McLeod Bethune was born on July 10, 1875, in Mayesville, South Carolina. Her mother and father had both been enslaved, but they were freed at the end of the Civil War. Bethune was the 15th of 17 children. Some of her siblings had been sold to other slave owners, but her parents kept track of them. They eventually got all of their children back after the Civil War ended.

For most of her early childhood, Bethune worked on her parents’ farm for 12 hours a day, almost every day. When she was 11 years old, she entered her first school. She loved learning and decided she would dedicate her life to helping other African Americans learn too. Although the war was over, some white people still didn’t want African Americans to get an education. Bethune was determined to change that.

All her life, Mary McLeod Bethune worked to end discrimination. She wrote many magazine and newspaper articles. She also founded the National Council of Negro Women in 1935. By 1955, more than 800,000 women belonged to her organization.

Impressed with her efforts, President Franklin Roosevelt made Bethune a special assistant to the Secretary of War during World War II. She became very good friends with First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt.

In 1904, Bethune moved to Daytona Beach, Florida, and opened her own school. She called her school the Daytona Literary and Industrial School for Training Negro Girls. It started with only six students. Five were girls, and one was Bethune's son.

However, Bethune and her students couldn't afford to buy many school supplies. They used crates for desks, charcoal for pencils, and crushed berries for ink. To get money for the school, Mary and her students baked pies and made ice cream to sell to local workers. Despite its modest beginnings, the school grew.

In 1923, the school started admitting African American boys, as well as more girls. When that happened, Mary changed the name of the school to Bethune-Cookman Collegiate Institute. Today, it serves as a university.

After Mary died in 1955, people continued to remember her contributions. In 1985, she was recognized as one of the most important African American women in the history of our country. The U.S. Postal Service issued a stamp with her picture on it, and a statue of Mary was placed in a park in Washington, D.C.

Mary McLeod Bethune was an extremely accomplished and revered woman. At a time when it was almost impossible for an African American woman to get an education, Bethune got one. At a time when others were trying to stop African American children from going to school, she taught them herself. At a time when discrimination was everywhere, she fought to end it.

title: The Great Migration
text:
Six million African Americans left the rural South between 1916 and 1970. In this movement called the Great Migration, African Americans hoped to escape Southern poverty, racism, and violence. They wanted to find a better life.

During World War l, American farms and factories had increased the production and shipping of goods to supply U.S. allies. The military needed engines, ships, and weapons to fight the war. As production increased, so did the need for workers. Companies began to recruit African Americans to move north and fill those jobs. By 1919, an estimated one million African Americans had left the South and moved to the North.

African Americans also moved to the North to escape racial violence and discrimination in the South. Jim Crow laws inhibited the growth of African Americans as equal citizens. Their voting rights were restricted with new laws, and many experienced intimidation and violence. They couldn’t find houses or jobs due to unfair procedures. African American children were placed in separate, inferior schools. For all of these reasons and more, African American families were attracted to the North.

Many African Americans migrated to large industrial cities like New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Detroit. Men quickly found jobs in places such as factories, slaughterhouses, and metal workshops. They were often hard, dangerous jobs that no one else wanted to do. Women had a harder time finding jobs. There was more competition for traditional jobs open to women like housekeeping.

Finding housing in the North also presented a problem. By this time, the U.S. Supreme Court had declared that racially based housing restrictions were unconstitutional. To get around this ruling, many neighborhood residents agreed on their own neighborhood rules. These rules often kept homeowners from selling or renting their homes to African Americans. In other areas, landlords rented to white Americans for a regular price and raised the rent for homes and apartments for African Americans.

As a result, many African Americans created their own cities within cities. The Harlem area of New York City was an example. Previously designated as a white residential area, by the 1920s, more than 200,000 African Americans formed their own community in Harlem. Their settlement and activity in this area eventually led to the Harlem Renaissance.

At the beginning of the Great Migration, 90 percent of African Americans lived in the South. By its end in the 1970s, 47 percent of African Americans lived in the Northern and Western United States.

title: The NAACP
text:
During the first half of the twentieth century, African Americans yearned for the day when their children could attend good schools with new equipment and textbooks. They wanted to take their children to the city park, to the swimming pool, and to the corner store for ice cream sodas. They wanted better jobs and homes with indoor plumbing. They wanted the same opportunities and the same rights as white citizens.

African American community leaders encouraged their fellow citizens to be proud of their cultural achievements. However, they also dreamed of a better future. They talked about how to bring about change. They realized they would have more influence if they organized themselves and worked as a group.

In response, the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) held a meeting in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1947. The purpose of the meeting was to recruit members who would dedicate themselves to the fight for civil rights. Among the people who attended the meeting that day were Rosa Parks, Johnnie Carr, and E.D. Nixon.

Founding members included suffragists, social workers, journalists, labor reformers, and other activists. The founding charter championed equal rights and eliminating racial prejudice. It also advocated for African American voting rights, legal justice, education, and employment opportunities.

The NAACP has been defending the rights of African Americans for over 100 years. The NAACP is still true to its original commitment to champion equal rights and advance the cause of justice.

title: The Jazz Age
text:
The African Americans who gathered in America’s big cities also introduced the world to a new style of music: jazz. It is believed that jazz music originated in New Orleans, Louisiana, early in the 20th century. Traditional African American sounds and rhythms mixed with sounds and rhythms of other cultures, and jazz was born.

Jazz is very personal. Many jazz bands create the music as they play, which is a style called improvisation. Also, the style of a song changes depending on the musician who’s playing it. The song’s rhythm and patterns are interpreted by each performer. The same tune can be played by three different musicians, and it will sound different each time. There are also different types of jazz music. These include traditional jazz, swing, bebop, and cool jazz.

Trumpet player and singer Louis Armstrong was one of the most famous jazz musicians. Nicknamed “Satchmo,” he created a new style of trumpet playing that brought people out of their seats and onto the dance floor. Some other famous American jazz musicians include Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Ella Fitzgerald, Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, and Sarah Vaughan. White Americans, as well as African Americans, soon had a taste for jazz. Young women called “flappers” flocked to nightclubs to dance to the beat.

At first, jazz music was mostly played to accompany dancing. After a few early recordings were made available, jazz spread widely. The style continued to evolve. This evolution was made possible by the many brilliant musicians of the era that took this style of music and made it their own. Jazz trumpet players and band leaders impressed both black and white audiences with their brilliant and masterful performances.

Over time, jazz became popular all over the world. It even opened the door to the pop and rock styles of music today.

title: The Stock Market Crash
text:
October 29, 1929, is often called “Black Tuesday.” On that day, billions of American dollars were lost, wiping out the fortunes of thousands of investors. The stock market had crashed. To understand this disaster, you need to understand what the stock market is and how it works.

Imagine that a company is growing and decides it wants to expand. To do so, it needs to hire more employees and buy new machinery. The company can’t afford to do this on its own, so it goes public. That means the company offers the public a chance to buy stock. Buying stock means investing money in the company. These investments pay for the company to expand. In return, when the company is successful and makes a profit, that profit is then shared with its investors. Each share pays a dividend, or a portion of the company’s profits. The higher the dividend, the more valuable the stock. However, if the company doesn’t do well and it loses money, its value goes down. In that case, the company doesn’t have the extra money to pay dividends to its investors. It also means the stock decreases in value. If investors try to sell the stock, they will not get as much money back as they paid. The system set up to keep track of the buying and selling of stock is called the stock market.

With the economy rapidly growing in the 1920s, many people thought they could make money by investing in new and expanding companies. Many investors couldn’t afford to purchase the stock they wanted, so they borrowed money from banks. When the value of the stocks increased, they could pay the bank back and still have money left. They made a profit.

This system worked well until the months leading up to Black Tuesday. Many factories had produced too many goods. People weren’t buying them because they already had what they needed. Factories slowed down and cut back on production. They didn’t need as many workers, so people lost their jobs. When people didn’t have jobs, they couldn’t afford to buy things, so the companies slowed down even more. The stock that people had purchased lost its value. Everyone wanted to sell their stock quickly before it lost any more of its value. People began to panic and rush to sell their stock. That caused values to drop even more until stocks became worthless. The resulting stock market crash paved the way for an extreme economic recession in the 1930s called the Great Depression.

title: The Great Economic Depression
text:
Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, was the end of a successful and hopeful time in the United States. During the 1920s, millions of people had purchased shares of stock, or partial ownership of companies. Stock prices continued to rise. People borrowed more and more money from banks to buy more shares. On Black Tuesday, the prices of stocks fell sharply until the shares were worth nothing. Many people lost everything they owned that day. The stock market had crashed, and the U.S. economy crashed along with it.

The stock market crash was only the beginning of tough times for the country. Many banks lost money too. People worried that the money they had in banks might not be safe, and they rushed to the banks to withdraw their funds. This rush was called a bank run. Because banks had borrowed money and invested it too, they didn’t have enough money to pay everyone. Some people who went to withdraw their money found there was no money left. When the banks were out of money, they closed their doors. Some of the banks began to go out of business completely.

Banks tried to get back the money that they had let people borrow. Sometimes, the banks took people’s homes and farms when their loans weren’t paid. People were left homeless. Without their farms, they had no way to make money.

Businesses were also affected by the economic hard time. Some businesses lost a lot of money in the stock market crash. Many of them had to cut back employees’ hours and reduce their pay. Many people lost their jobs altogether when businesses closed.

Farmers in America had already been suffering economically since the end of World War I. During the war years, Europe needed food and was willing to pay high prices for it. Farmers made profits, and many of them expanded their farms by purchasing new equipment. The farmers borrowed money from banks to help pay for the land and machinery. Then the war ended, and prices for crops dropped. Farmers could not pay back the money they had borrowed from the banks. Many farmers lost their land, and the unpaid loans contributed to the failure of some banks by 1929.

Within a few years, millions of Americans were out of work. Some of these people traveled on railroads from town to town, looking for new jobs. Farmers who had lost their land traveled all over the country to find work on other people’s farms. Some businesses had more than 1,000 people applying for a single job opening.

Though the Great Depression started in the United States, it quickly became a worldwide problem. After World War I, the United States helped many European countries pay their debts. When the American economy failed, there was no money to send to foreign countries. As a result, the western European countries fell into a period of economic depression too. Great Britain and Germany were hit the hardest.

The Great Depression lasted more than a decade. Unfortunately, it took another war to bring prosperity back to the U.S.

title: Banking Reforms
text:
On March 6, 1933, barely 36 hours after taking the oath of office as President of the United States, Franklin D. Roosevelt issued Proclamation 2039. The proclamation called for a “banking holiday.” All banks were ordered to close for a week. This would give the president and Congress time to come up with a plan to restore the public’s confidence in the banking system.

The plan that the president presented and Congress passed was called the Banking Act of 1933. The act had two purposes. One was to regulate banking procedures. The other was to ensure the safety of customers’ deposits. The act gave the president the power to reopen healthy banks and provide assistance to failing banks. The act also restricted banks from making risky investments like those that led to the failures of the Great Depression. Lastly, the act created the FDIC, or Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. This organization ensured that if a bank failed in the future, customers’ deposits at the time would be refunded up to $2,500. The FDIC is still regulating banks and ensuring the safety of deposits today.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
text:
America’s 32nd president, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, is often referred to by his initials, FDR. He was elected president in the middle of the Great Depression and served as president through the majority of World War II. The country looked to him to do what was necessary to bring it out of that devastating era.

Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born in 1882 in Hyde Park, New York. His father, James Roosevelt, was the vice president of the Delaware and Hudson Railway. His fifth cousin was President Theodore Roosevelt. He went to Harvard University, followed by Columbia Law School.

In 1905, Roosevelt married Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin. Franklin and Eleanor had common interests. They both felt a commitment to help others. The Roosevelts had six children. They loved doing fun things with their children, who they called "the chicks." In 1921, Roosevelt fell out of a friend's boat and into freezing water. After the accident, he thought he had caught a cold. However, his condition worsened, and Roosevelt was diagnosed with polio. The disease slowly took away his ability to walk, and he spent much of his later life in a wheelchair. Roosevelt developed the Warm Springs George Foundation to do research on polio and help people who were suffering from the disease.

Roosevelt entered the world of politics. He was elected as a New York state senator in 1910. He became the Democratic Party’s nominee to become the vice president of the United States in 1920. FDR became the governor of New York in 1928.

In 1933, Roosevelt was elected as president of the United States. It was the beginning of a dozen years in the White House. Roosevelt was elected to four terms as president, more terms than anyone had ever served before. He is the only U.S. President to serve more than two terms. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution now limits a president to only two terms.

As president, Franklin D. Roosevelt faced many challenges. One was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. Roosevelt’s New Deal was his plan to develop programs that would help the unemployed, those who had lost farms and homes. It also provided economic stimulus to help agriculture and business recover from the economic depression.

Later, Roosevelt would lead the United States through World War II. He looked forward to peace, but he didn’t live to see it. The president died on April 12, 1945, before peace was declared. News of his death spread quickly. Millions of people mourned.

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
text:
President Franklin Delano Roosevelt led the United States during some of its greatest challenges: the Great Depression and World War II. He never let being confined to a wheelchair keep him from reaching his goals. In one famous speech, Roosevelt told Americans, "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself." Certainly Roosevelt believed this, and he lived his life as proof the statement was true in his own heart. His courage and leadership earned him the respect of people around the world. He is considered by many to be one of the greatest U.S. presidents.

Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born in 1882 in Hyde Park, New York. His father, James Roosevelt, was the vice president of the Delaware and Hudson Railway. His mother raised young Roosevelt with loving firmness, and her direction continued even after he was grown. After Roosevelt was married with children of his own, his mother would remind him to put on his rubber shoes before going outside in the rain.

During this period of time, many young men attended boarding schools. When he was 14, Roosevelt enrolled in the Groton School in Groton, Massachusetts. It was here he became interested in public service and helping those less fortunate. After graduating, he attended Harvard University.

In 1905, Roosevelt married Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin. Franklin and Eleanor had common interests. They both felt a commitment to help others. The Roosevelts had six children. They loved doing fun things with their children, who they called "the chicks." In 1921, Roosevelt fell out of a friend's boat and into freezing water. After the accident, he thought he had caught a cold. However, his condition worsened, and Roosevelt was diagnosed with polio. The disease slowly took away his ability to walk, and he spent much of his later life in a wheelchair. Roosevelt developed the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation to do research on polio and help people who were suffering from the disease.

In 1933, the United States was in the middle of the Great Depression. Businesses had closed. Many workers lost their jobs. Banks failed. Those that didn’t fail needed loans repaid by farmers and homeowners. People who were unable to repay their debts had their farms and homes taken away. Most people had very little hope that things would get better. In that same year, Roosevelt was sworn in as the new president of the United States. He brought hope and inspiration with him. It was the beginning of a dozen years in the White House. Roosevelt was elected to four terms as president, more terms than anyone had ever served before. He is the only U.S. president to serve more than two terms. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution now limits a president to only two terms.

As president, Franklin D. Roosevelt faced many challenges. One was finding a way to bring the country out of the Great Depression. Roosevelt’s New Deal was his plan to develop programs that would help the poor and the elderly. The plan also helped farmers, created jobs, and changed America.

People all over the nation started feeling hopeful. They had confidence that President Roosevelt was leading the country in the right direction. Through it all, cheerfulness and optimism characterized Roosevelt. He tried to encourage the nation through a series of nationally broadcast radio talks called "fireside chats."

On April 12, 1945, just a few months after beginning his fourth term as President, Roosevelt suddenly fell over in his chair while an artist painted his portrait. "I have a terrific headache," he said. Those were his last words. He died a few hours later. News of his death spread quickly. Millions of people mourned.

title: The Alphabet of the New Deal
text:
The New Deal was the title President Franklin Delano Roosevelt gave to the expansive new plan he and his advisors introduced to bring prosperity back to America. The New Deal created many new government agencies. At the time, people called them the “alphabet agencies.” Here is a list of the major elements of the New Deal. The chart shows the alphabet acronym for each agency and its purpose. Using the “New Deal Agencies” word bank, match the names of the agencies to their acronyms and write them in the correct spaces.

title: The Russian Revolution of 1917
text:
For hundreds of years, life in Russia had gone on much the same, one generation after another. The country was ruled by a royal family called the Romanovs. The emperor was called the “czar.” Besides the czar’s family, there were also other royals and people of high rank, birth, and wealth. These people lived lives of comfort and ease, hardly aware of the struggles of others in their country. There was a tiny middle class of merchants, bankers, and other professionals who made a good living. A slightly larger working class of artisans, soldiers, or sailors managed well enough. However, the largest class of people by far was the poor. Most of the people in Russia were farmers, who usually worked on other people’s lands and lived in extreme poverty.

Around the turn of the twentieth century, technology in farming and industry in Russia was far behind other European countries. Finally, between 1890 and 1910, the Second Industrial Revolution reached Russia. Millions of people began moving to cities for jobs, nearly doubling the populations of major cities. The cities became severely overcrowded. Living conditions were terrible. At the same time, Russia was involved in several expensive wars, which resulted in food shortages for common people.

In 1905, people were angry and held large public protests against the czar. It was their first revolution. The czar’s troops were sent out, and they killed many unarmed protesters. Czar Nicholas II promised reforms. One change was the Russian Duma, a representative governing body who would approve new legislation. It was a hopeful step, but World War I broke out before other reforms could be made.

German allies had declared war on Serbia, a Russian ally, so Russia was pulled into the war. German forces were far superior to the Russian army. Russia had more casualties than any other country in the war. The limited food and fuel available in Russia went to the soldiers at the front.

In 1915, the czar headed to the front to join his troops in the war. While he was gone, his wife, Empress Alexandra, began replacing government officials. A man named Rasputin became her closest advisor. He was disliked by many of the Russian nobles. These nobles suspected him of having too much influence over the empress. They plotted against Rasputin and succeeded in murdering him.

The czar then dissolved the Russian Duma. This action, on top of the Russian people’s desperate living conditions, caused many to lose faith in the royal government. Radical groups emerged and began to rally the people against the czar. Poor people began street riots demanding bread. Factory workers walked out on their jobs and went on strike.

Army troops were called out by the government to put a stop to the riots. Many demonstrators were killed, but the protests continued. A number of the troops began to feel sympathetic toward the demonstrators’ cause. At this point, the czar abdicated (resigned his throne and power), and a new, temporary government took over.

The most powerful rebel party, the Bolshevik Party, was led by Vladimir Lenin. He guided the Bolsheviks as they took over the temporary government. They set up a new government led by soldiers, workers, and the poor. Lenin became the head of the dictatorship they put in place. He put into place a new system of government called “communism.”

There were many people in Russia who either still supported the czar or strongly opposed the communist philosophy. These people formed an army called the White Army. They fought against the Red Army formed by the Bolsheviks and their supporters. The Red Army kidnapped and murdered the czar and his family. At that point, the White Army became discouraged, and the Bolsheviks took complete control of the country. They changed the name of the country to the Soviet Union. The first communist government had officially been established.

title: The Communist Government of the Soviet Union
text:
For centuries, Russia had been ruled by a monarch called the czar. “Czar” is the Russian word for caesar, the title of ancient Roman emperors. In 1917, the monarchy in Russia was overthrown by the Bolshevik Party, led by soldiers, workers, and the poor. Their aim was to form a society where no individuals owned land or factories. No small group of wealthy nobles would profit off the hard labor of the poor. There would be no upper or lower class in society. Everyone would have equal social standing. The government would own everything, and everyone would share the wealth. This form of government is called communism.

Communism began as a reaction to capitalism. Capitalism is an economic and political system in which a country’s trade and industry are owned privately. Communists believed that capitalism created too big of a difference between the rich and the poor. Those aligned with communism believed that if the government controlled resources and spread them equally among citizens, life would be more fair.

Unlike capitalism, under a communist system, all businesses and property such as homes, land, and money are owned and controlled by the government. The government then shares everything with the citizens. For many years, communism was a leading form of government for many of the countries in Europe, Asia, South America, and Africa. In the 1900s, communism grew, and certain groups took advantage of its influence to gain power.

After the Russian Revolution in 1917, more republics were added to the country. Eventually, the whole region was unified into the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, or USSR. Joseph Stalin was the communist leader of the USSR, or Soviet Union, from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953. Stalin wanted the Soviet Union to overcome its problems and become a world power. He took farmland from the poor and put it under government control. He also set and reached many goals for mining and manufacturing. Stalin’s efforts made the Soviet Union an impressive industrial nation. Under Joseph Stalin, communism continued to extend from the Soviet Union across much of Eastern Europe.

Stalin seemed to accomplish much for his country as the leader of the Soviet Union. His methods did not consider the needs of the people he ruled over, though. As a dictator, meaning a government leader with absolute power, Stalin was in a position to do whatever he wanted without being questioned. There was no system in place in the government to check his power. The citizens of his country and the other government officials feared him.

Stalin, a communist dictator, and Hitler, a Nazi dictator from Germany, disagreed on many things, but they signed an agreement in 1939 that said their nations would never attack each other. Just two years later, however, Hitler broke the agreement by attacking Russia. As a result, Stalin joined the Allies in the fight against Germany during World War II.

title: Appeasement in France and England
text:
A policy of appeasement means that countries give in to some of another country’s demands in order to avoid conflict. This was the British government’s policy toward Germany in the 1930s. It had been less than 20 years since the end of World War I by the time the Nazis rose to power in 1933. Britain didn’t want to get involved in another war.

The prime minister of Great Britain at this time was Neville Chamberlain. He supported the British agenda to appease Germany in order to avoid war. He was opposed by another British government leader named Winston Churchill. Churchill warned the government that Hitler was dangerous and could not be trusted. He was ignored.

In 1938, Adolf Hitler, Benito Mussolini, Neville Chamberlain, and French Prime Minister Édouard Daladier, met in Munich, Germany. They discussed Germany’s plans. Hitler said he wanted to take back the Sudetenland, an area in Czechoslovakia where three million ethnic Germans lived. The leaders in attendance agreed to this plan when they signed the Munich Agreement. Chamberlain thought this concession would appease Hitler and avoid war.

However, Chamberlain's appeasement plan did not bring peace. Germany quickly moved into Czechoslovakia and took over the entire country. Then they moved to invade Poland in 1939. This left Great Britain and France no choice. They had to declare war to stop German advancement in Europe.

title: American Neutrality
text:
After World War I ended, the U.S. vowed to stay out of all future wars. During the 1930s, the U.S. Congress passed a series of laws called the Neutrality Acts. These laws stated that the United States would not get involved in or take sides on any conflicts between foreign nations. It would remain neutral.

First Neutrality Act

In 1935, Congress proclaimed that the U.S. could not export any weapons, ammunition or “implements of war” to belligerent (warring) nations. Americans were also warned that if they sailed on a belligerent’s ship, they did so at their own risk.

Neutrality Act of 1936

This law renewed the First Neutrality Act for another 14 months and said that no loans or credit could be offered to belligerent nations.

Neutrality Act of 1937

This act renewed the previous neutrality acts and made it illegal for any U.S. ships to carry military equipment to belligerent nations. Citizens could no longer sail on belligerents' ships. It also gave the president the power to sell supplies (but not weapons and ammunition) to belligerent nations, as long as they paid for these items at the time of purchase.

Neutrality Act of 1939

By this time, Germany was at war with Great Britain and France. Congress passed a law stating that the U.S. could sell weapons, ammunition and other military supplies to belligerent nations. Again, nations had to pay for supplies at the time of purchase.

Lend-Lease Act of 1941

This law marked the end of U.S. Neutrality Acts. It allowed the U.S. to lend, sell or give war supplies to its allies. President Roosevelt could now offer our foreign friends more than just a few kind words. He could, and did, send them money, weapons, vehicles, and after the attack on Pearl Harbor, U.S. troops.

title: Pearl Harbor and Entry into the War
text:
December 7, 1941, was another sleepy Sunday across America. Families were coming home from morning church services. Others were settling down after brunch with the Sunday paper. Still others were simply enjoying their Sunday, listening to music on the radio.

However, far away to the west, a completely different kind of morning was breaking over Hawaii. Across the sea, low on the horizon, a strange formation had gathered in the morning sky. As it approached, people watched from a distance. They thought it was a squadron of U.S. B-17 planes returning from a training mission. The planes’ real purpose wouldn’t become clear until the planes were right on top of them and bombs started dropping.

Pearl Harbor in Hawaii was the home of America's largest naval base in the Pacific region. At this time, nearly every ship of the U.S. Pacific Fleet was docked at Ford Island in the harbor. At 7:55 a.m. in Pearl Harbor, hundreds of Japanese airplanes attacked American ships and aircraft.

Immediately, alarms sounded all over Hawaii. A message went out, "Air raid on Pearl Harbor. This is not a drill."

Japanese fighter planes, torpedo bombers, and dive bombers took only 1 hour and 55 minutes to empty their bombs and bullets. Thousands of American sailors, soldiers, and marines were killed, as were many civilians working at the base. More than another thousand people were wounded.

In addition to the loss of life, there was loss and destruction of equipment at the base. Several of the U.S.’s large battleships were sunk or severely damaged. Many smaller ships met the same fate. Hundreds of navy and army planes on the ground were damaged or destroyed. Many of the docks, repair facilities, hangars, and runways were damaged or destroyed. The devastation of the port facilities, the highways and service connections kept rescue and recovery vehicles from aiding the wounded. When word of the attack reached the mainland United States, panic, disbelief and anger spread from coast to coast. Along the western coastal cities, people feared a direct attack of Japanese military from the sea. Instead of a day of rest, that Sunday became a dark day of worry. The event would propel the United States into the world conflict.

Many people questioned if the United States should have seen the attack possibility before it happened. Since the island of Japan lacked the natural resources to increase its economy, it had launched an attack on China in the 1930s to expand. After that attack, the United States had placed trade restrictions on Japan. The restrictions were a way to try to peacefully prevent ongoing Japanese expansion. Japan realized the United States could also be a military threat to their efforts to expand control in the Pacific Ocean. The many small islands in the southwest Pacific Ocean gave Japan a place to protect their interests and keep foreign military from their country. Japan occupied the Marshall Islands located between the Philippines and Hawaii. It was a next step for the Japanese military to take the offensive to disable the U.S. naval military force in Hawaii.

On Monday, Dec. 8, 1941, the day after the attacks, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt gave one of the most famous speeches in American history. In a joint session of Congress, he called December 7, “a day that will live in infamy.” In the speech, Roosevelt officially asked Congress for a declaration of war on Japan.

The power to declare war is assigned to Congress in the U.S. Constitution. The Senate voted 82 to 0 in favor of declaring war. The House voted in favor 388 to 1. This authorized “the President… to employ the entire naval and military forces of the United States and the resources of the government to carry on war against the Imperial Government of Japan, and, to bring the conflict to a successful termination, all of the resources of the country are hereby pledged by Congress of the United States.”

On December 11, 1941, Congress also declared war on the Axis Powers of Germany and Italy in response to Adolf Hitler declaring war on the United States. The Axis Powers had a pact with Japan to be their allies. The United States was now fully involved in the worldwide conflict. The isolation of the previous decade was gone.

title: Allied Forces in the European Theater
text:
The 133rd Infantry Regiment of the 34th Division of the U.S. Army was the first army unit sent to the European Theater after America entered the war. They arrived in Belfast, Ireland, late in January of 1942. Thousands of soldiers, support people, equipment and supplies followed for the next three years.

A “theater of operations” is the military term referring to land and sea areas to be invaded or defended. America would fight in three theaters of operations in the war: the European Theater, the Mediterranean Theater and the Pacific Theater. American troops entering the European Theater joined Britain and their other ally, the Soviet Union. Together the three nations formed the core of the Allied powers.

British and American forces trained together to become an invasion force. The Russians engaged the Nazis on their shared border. Their goal was to defeat the Axis Powers and to free the occupied countries under Nazi German control.

General Dwight Eisenhower was named Supreme Commander of Allied Expeditionary Forces in Europe. Eisenhower and his team of generals studied maps of Europe. The geography would determine the plan for defeating the Axis Powers.

Every military force needs to have a continual supply of ammunition, transportation, food and medical supplies. This would be kept at bases close to the troops. To free Europe, Eisenhower’s team chose to start in Italy. The base for supplies would have to be across the Mediterranean Sea in Nazi-occupied north Africa. Operation Torch was in 1942-43. The Allied Forces gained control of northern Africa in May 1943.

With supply bases in place, the allied invasion of Italy began in July 1943. Troops landed in Sicily, Italy. The Allies forced the German and Italian troops to evacuate Sicily and move for the Italian mainland. After losing Sicily to the Allies, the Italians lost confidence in their dictator, Benito Mussolini, and He was forced out of office. The Allies gained control of Italy in September 1943. This eliminated one of the Axis powers and left Nazi Germany on their own in Europe.

Nazi Germany was now fighting in three fronts of military conflict. The Allies were in the east, the south and the northwest. This meant the supply bases for the troops were not close to the fighting. U.S. and British airplanes began strategic bombing raids. They targeted German factories, highways, and important industrial cities. Soviet troops were battling German forces on the Eastern Front. Ultimately, both allied lines were working to squeeze Germany into a position where surrender was the only option.

The first day of a military operation is called “departed date” (D-Day). June 6, 1944, became D-Day for Operation Overlord on the beaches of Normandy in Northern France. American and British troops created the largest invasion assembled in history. A force of 156,000 men crossed the English Channel, stormed the beaches and caused the Nazi army to retreat.

Russia was advancing on Nazi Germany’s eastern front. The Nazi troops pulled back to protect the capital. Nazi troops were being separated from supplies. The end of the war was near. In May 1945, Russian, American and British troops met in Berlin and accepted surrender from the remaining Nazi leadership.

title: Segregation in the Military
text:
The world came together to fight for freedom from controlling governments of Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Imperial Japan. As the Allies worked together towards this freedom, there were imbalances in freedom in their own countries. The United States was legally denying civil rights to African Americans at home and in the military.

African Americans who enlisted in the armed services were segregated from white American units. African Americans were consistently given non-combat assignments in food service, maintenance of equipment and supply lines to combat units. There were segregated barracks, hospitals and cafeterias. The role of the African American units was vital to the war effort and necessary for victory. However, few were included in combat ready units.

In 1944, the “Red Ball Express” was a military unit of African Americans. The Red Ball Express delivered vital supplies of gasoline, ammunition and medical equipment to the Third Army. The Third Army was trying to bring relief to Allied troops in northern France at the Battle of the Bulge. The Red Ball Express drove up to 400 miles on narrow roads in all weather conditions night or day. Crossing German military lines, the brave men kept the Third Army tank battalion moving to victory.

title: Allied Forces in the Pacific Theater
text:
After December 7, 1941, the Japanese Military was able to capture many islands in the Pacific Ocean. Japanese troops controlled many of these islands during the course of the war. The Japanese military also went northwest to the Aleutian Islands west of Alaska.

The geography determined the Allies would need specific strategies in the Pacific. The goal was to have Allied Forces close to the Japanese capital. The Allies could then invade and cause the government to surrender. The plan would involve multiple land, sea and air assaults.

Leapfrogging, also known as island hopping, was a strategy where the Allies bypassed certain islands heavily defended by the enemy. The Allies attacked and seized less-protected islands. This action made it more difficult for the Japanese to move between the islands. Difficulty in travel meant that supplies for the Japanese military would be interrupted. This allowed Allied Forces to gain advantage over the Japanese. The Allies also weren’t spending time, resources and human life to capture every Japanese-held island.

Choosing which islands to occupy was also a strategy used by the Allies. A captured island could then be used as a base for supplies and equipment. Gradually the Allies were making their way to be geographically closer to the Japanese mainland for air assaults.

There were three sizes of airplanes used in the war. The largest was the B-29 “flying superfortress” that was capable of long flight bombing missions. Gaining islands that could be used for building airfields was critical in reaching victory. Iwo Jima was one critical island in creating a chain of airfields. Japanese forces held the small island. Enemy air fighters from Iwo Jima were causing problems for Allied ships and airplanes.

United States Marines invaded Iwo Jima in February, 1945. The battle raged for 36 days with the Marines being victorious. Under Allied control, Iwo Jima became the link to the last and largest battle.

“Operation Iceberg” was the largest water, land and air invasion in the Pacific Theater. The fighting for Okinawa was the fiercest of the war. Okinawa was the last island needed to put aircraft and ships close to the Japanese homeland. It would be a B-29 named the Enola Gay that would deliver the secret weapon of the “Manhatten Project," the world’s first atomic bomb.

On July 29, 1945, the Allies demanded surrender of the Japanese government. The Japanese refused. The next day, President Harry S. Truman authorized the use of the atomic bomb on Japanese cities.

On the morning of August 6, 1945, the city of Hiroshima, Japan, was destroyed in the first atomic blast. Still, the Japanese government would not surrender. On August 8, the city of Nagasaki became the second target of an atomic weapon. The Japanese government asked for terms of surrender.

World War II ended with the Japanese surrender to Allied Forces on August 15, 1945.

title: The 761 Tank Battalion
text:
The 761 Tank Battalion was part of General George Patton’s Third Army. This unit was the first African American military division to be in combat in Europe, 1944. The Third Army was racing across France, liberating towns from Nazi control. There were 30 African American officers, six white officers and 676 enlisted men. The battalion wore a panther patch on their uniforms. The men of the “black panthers” were a fearsome fighting unit. They earned eleven Silver Stars, 69 Bronze Stars and 300 Purple Hearts. These medals are awarded for valor in combat.

In 1997, President Bill Clinton awarded the Medal of Honor to seven members of the 761 Tank Battalion. At the ceremony, Clinton said, “Now and forever, the truth will be known about these African Americans who gave so much that the rest of us might be free.”

title: The History of Juneteenth
text:
Juneteenth is short for “June 19th.” On this day in 1865, enslaved people learned that they were free. It has been celebrated in many African American communities ever since.

In 1863, President Lincoln signed an important document. It was called the Emancipation Proclamation. This document freed enslaved people in the U.S. On June 19, 1865, the news of emancipation finally reached Galveston, Texas. This day became known as “Juneteenth.” In 2021, the president of the United States made Juneteenth a national holiday.

title: The Tuskegee Airmen
text:
From the segregated military of World War II rose a group of very intelligent and successful African American men. The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American military pilots in America. The first group of men began training at the Tuskegee Army Airfield in Alabama. Nearly 15,000 pilots, navigators, and bomber crew members were eventually trained.

Approximately 450 men became pilots to serve overseas. These men distinguished themselves by flying over 1,500 missions. They earned 96 Distinguished Flying Cross medals for achievement in battle.

The Airmen successfully escorted bombers into enemy territory. Their smaller planes could guard the larger bombers with mobility, speed and accuracy. They were in demand for their services by the allied bomber units. Their record of success was unmatched by any other unit.

The Tuskegee Airmen are continually honored for courage and skills. Today they are recognized as being instrumental in breaking segregation in the military.

title: Technology of World War II
text:
During World War II,there were great advancements in medicine, technology, and equipment. Improving these three areas saved many soldiers’ lives. The improvements influenced civilian and military life in the years ahead.

Medicine - New techniques in blood transfusions and surgical tools saved many lives. The commercial production of antibiotics (Penicillin) by the Allies enabled more soldiers to heal and spend less time in hospitals. Penicillin remains a critical form of treatment for bacterial infections.

Navigation - Scientists from Great Britain and the United States worked together to perfect Radio Detection And Ranging (RADAR). They used newly discovered short range “microwaves” to detect positioning of objects too far away to be seen by the eye. By using radar and mapping positions using the longitude and latitude coordinates, accuracy in combat increased. This technology eventually developed into the global positioning system (GPS) we use today in cars and smartphones.

Equipment - Moving soldiers on the battlefield from one place to another required a form of transportation. The Army requested a general purpose vehicle that was lightweight and four-wheel drive for all terrain types. The result was the Jeep. This small vehicle was the worker of the war. The jeep was used by commanders to lead their troops and as ambulance units for wounded soldiers. This piece of equipment was vital to the war effort.

Rockets - The V-2 rocket was developed by Nazi Germany. This destructive weapon could travel long distances with accuracy. The V-2 could destroy multiple buildings. Allied Forces secretly sent teams into Nazi Germany to seize the plans and overtake manufacturing of the rocket. Over 100 key rocket personnel surrendered to the Allies. They then proceeded to assist the Allies in creating rockets to use against the Axis Powers. Rocket technology was used in the “Manhattan Project,” which would develop the atomic bomb.

title: Life in the Middle Passage
text:
In the first 300 years after Columbus reached the Americas, ships that crossed the Atlantic almost always came from Europe. However, most didn’t sail straight from Europe to the Americas. The sea currents and wind directions made sailing south toward Africa easier and faster than sailing directly west across the Atlantic. This route presented opportunities for trade by staying near the continents. European traders found a market with the nations in West Africa.

This voyage from Europe to Africa was called the Outward Passage. Ships carried tools, weapons, cloth, and other goods to Africa. Merchants and soldiers would pressure African leaders to trade those goods for people who had been captured in wars or kidnapped.

People were imprisoned and held as products to be traded. The European traders treated the enslaved people on their ships as 'cargo.' The men were kept below deck. They were held with leg irons so they could not move. The area was so short, the men could only crouch or lie down. The women and children were usually held on deck. There was not much sanitation. The odor of these ships could be smelled for miles. Since the ships were so dirty and the people so close together, disease spread easily. Until the 1750s, one in five Africans died on these ships. The traders who held the Africans against their will were transporting them to be sold in the West Indies and American colonies. The voyage from Africa to the colonies in the Western Hemisphere was called “the Middle Passage.”

title: Tribal Government
text:
One of the defining principles of government in the United States is the division of power between multiple branches and levels of government. There are many levels of government in the United States, including tribal, state, and local.

There are approximately five million people in the United States who are of Native American descent. These people belong to hundreds of tribes across the country. Many Native American nations in the United States have their own tribal governments. This means they have their own sovereignty. Sovereignty is an inherent right to self-govern. Tribal governments within the United States follow laws created by the federal government and the U.S. Constitution. However, when Native Americans are on tribal lands, they are subject to the laws of their tribal nation.

The federal government has a duty to protect the rights of Native American tribes. In the U.S., Indigenous tribes are often called “nations within a nation.” They can receive federal designation from the United States government. Federally recognized tribes have an official relationship with the U.S. government. They have certain rights, responsibilities, and powers. They are able to access some benefits, services, and protections from the U.S. government.

There are 574 federally recognized tribes in the United States. Members of these tribes are the descendants of the ancient peoples that lived in North America for thousands of years. Each of the federally recognized tribes of the United States has its own reservation. A reservation is an area of land designated to a tribe or tribes by the United States government.

Tribes that are not federally recognized could be one day. They can petition the Bureau of Indian Affairs to receive federal recognition. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is a government agency that establishes which groups are federally recognized and which are not.

The largest federally recognized tribe in the United States is the Cherokee Nation. The Cherokee Nation, whose central tribal government is located in Oklahoma, is made up of over 800,000 members. The Oneida Nation is the largest federally recognized tribe in Wisconsin. The Oneida tribe has over 16,000 registered members. The smallest federally recognized tribe is the St. Croix Band of Ojibwe with a little more than 1,000 members.

The 12 tribes that live in Wisconsin all set up their governments differently. Many tribes elect officials who serve on a council. The council usually rules by majority. Tribal councils make laws for their tribal nations. They write their own constitutions and have their own court systems. The Ho-Chunk have a much more complex government with a general council, a legislature, an executive branch, and a judiciary branch. All of these branches of the Ho-Chunk government have their own powers and responsibilities. Tribal governments tax their people, too. They use the money to pay for police services, education, and healthcare. They also decide how to spend money on roads, public water, and electricity.

title: State Government
text:
Each of our 50 states has a state government. State governments are modeled after the federal government and consist of executive, legislative, and judicial branches. All state governments are led by the executive branch. The executive branch is responsible for signing bills into law, appointing judges, proposing the state budget, organization of the state militia, and overseeing all agencies that work within the government.

The executive branch is led by the governor of the state. The governor is elected by the people. Of the 50 states in the country, 28 states limit a governor’s term in office to two consecutive, or back-to-back, terms. Thirteen states do not have a term limit for the governor, including Wisconsin. The remaining states have varying term limits.

Most states also have a lieutenant governor, a secretary of state, and an attorney general. These make up the executive branch and are elected by the people and serve varying terms. The lieutenant governor assists the governor in matters of state and fulfills the responsibilities of the governor if they are unable to do so. The secretary of state is responsible for elections, record keeping, and safeguarding the state archives. The attorney general is the head of law enforcement for the state. In Wisconsin, the executive branch has a lieutenant governor, a secretary of state, an attorney general, and two more elected officials: the state treasurer and the state superintendent of public instruction. The treasurer is in charge of state finances, and the state superintendent oversees public education.

The legislative branch is responsible for creating state laws. All states, except for Nebraska, have a legislative branch made up of two houses. This is known as a bicameral legislature. The larger of the two houses is often called the House of Representatives, but it is also called the House of Delegates, or the State Assembly. The smaller of the two houses is called the Senate. In Wisconsin, the lower house is called the Assembly, and the upper house is called the Senate.

The state’s judicial branch is led by the state supreme court. State supreme courts are responsible for correcting or definitively ruling on decisions that have been made in lower courts. The justices ensure that the correct procedures were followed. If problems or disagreements cannot be resolved within the state, cases can be taken to the U.S. Supreme Court.

title: State Constitutions
text:
Just like the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions guarantee and protect citizens' basic rights. State constitutions list the rules for state government. They also explain how a state can make laws. State constitutions describe how the state government divides and shares power with counties and cities.

State constitutions can change over time. These changes are called amendments. Lawmakers and voters can work together to amend the existing state constitution to meet the needs of citizens. To amend means to change or add to. Citizens can vote to amend their state constitution.

title: Tribal, State, and Local Courts
text:
The purpose of local, state, and tribal courts is to interpret laws and settle conflicts. How does the court system work? First, citizens bring their problems to state trial courts. Members of Native American tribes often bring their issues and legal matters to tribal courts first. State trial courts are located in the county you live in. Tribal courts are located on Native American reservations. The judges in the trial and tribal courts listen to the problem, or case, and both sides of the story. They think about the evidence that each side presented and then make a decision based on what they heard. Judges' decisions solve conflicts and provide consequences for those people who break the law.

If a person does not agree with the trial or tribal court's decision, they can file an appeal. This appeal goes to the Court of Appeals at the state level. Sometimes, the Court of Appeals keeps the trial court's decision. Other times, they overturn the original outcome. If a person is still unhappy after the Court of Appeals' decision, they can apply to take their case to the state supreme court.

State supreme courts vary in the number of judges, or justices, that they have. They make decisions on cases and solve problems that people bring before them. The state supreme courts take cases that have first gone through the trial courts and Court of Appeals. Justices decide cases in two ways: by opinion or by order. In both types of cases, the judges must meet to analyze the case and determine the verdict.

If a case cannot be resolved by the state courts, it can be elevated to the Supreme Court of the United States. The U.S. Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It upholds and interprets the laws of the Constitution. It also ensures that the rights of all Americans are protected. Currently, the Supreme Court is made up of nine judges. Supreme Court justices work together to determine the outcome of important court cases. The Supreme Court reviews thousands of cases each year.

title: Food, Livestock, and Plants
text: Native Americans taught Europeans about corn and potatoes. Corn became a very useful crop for European immigrants. It was easy to grow. Their livestock could also eat it. European immigrants brought wheat and other grains to Native Americans. They exchanged these for corn and potatoes. Europeans also brought pigs, sheep, and cattle. They brought chickens and horses, too. Horses made hunting and traveling easier for Native Americans.

title: Tools and Items
text: European immigrants brought some new items to the Native Americans. These were things like different cloths, metal pots, knives, and sewing needles. Native Americans traded furs, pelts, and works of art with Europeans for these items. The items created some new ways of doing things for both groups. Native Americans made some new types of clothes with the new cloth.

title: Disease
text: European immigrants brought new diseases to the Americas. Native Americans were not used to these diseases. As a result, many of them died.

title: Beliefs
text: Native Americans had very different beliefs from Europeans. Many tribes believed that everything in their environment was connected and should be treated with respect. European immigrants did not always share this belief. Many immigrants believed the land and animals were there to be used. These and other differences in beliefs led to conflicts. Many European immigrants thought it was their duty to convert Native Americans to Christianity. European immigrants wanted all people to believe like they did. They tried to change the beliefs, traditions, and customs of Native Americans. Some Native Americans were forced to abandon their cultural traditions and beliefs to adopt Christian beliefs. Tribal members were forbidden to speak their own language, wear traditional clothing, or practice cultural customs that had existed for thousands of years.

title: Land
text: Over the years, more and more immigrants came to America. They wanted land for farming and creating towns. Some immigrants traded for the land. Some took the land from Native Americans by force. The Native Americans did not want to give up their land easily. In many cases, Native Americans were forced to move from land that had been their home for many generations.

title: History of Juneteenth
text:
Juneteenth is short for “June 19th.” On this day in 1865, enslaved people learned that they were free. It has been celebrated in many African American communities ever since.

In 1863, President Lincoln signed an important document. It was called the Emancipation Proclamation. This document freed enslaved people in the U.S. On June 19, 1865, the news of emancipation finally reached Galveston, Texas. This day became known as “Juneteenth.” In 2021, the president of the United States made Juneteenth a national holiday.

title: Daily Life in the Early Colonies
text:
What was daily life like for the people of British Colonial America? As the colonies were getting started, daily life was very hard. People had to figure out how to survive.

Early colonial farmers woke up early, ate, and started their work in the fields. The work they did depended on the season. In the spring, they would plow and plant the fields. They worked with their hands or with the help of an ox or horse. During fall, they harvested their crops. Year-round, they tended the fields, took care of livestock, chopped wood, fixed fences, and made house repairs.

Tradesmen worked long hours in villages. Depending on their trade, they had different tasks. For instance, blacksmiths spent their days making tools like axes and hammers for fellow tradesmen and average citizens. Most tradesmen trained apprentices as well.

Since there weren’t many women in the colonies, they often had more significant roles than in Europe. Without a strong and productive wife, a family would struggle to survive. Daily, women were responsible for raising their children, preparing meals, making and washing clothes, preserving food for winter, and fetching water.

Children worked and had no time to play. By the age of three or four, they had to get up early and work alongside their parents. Boys often helped their fathers with work on the farm as well as with hunting and fishing. Girls, on the other hand, usually helped their mothers and learned housekeeping skills.

Indentured servants worked on farms and large plantations. It was hard work to use the hoe, scythe, ax, and plow to cultivate and harvest crops. These people had very little freedom. Nearly every aspect of their lives was strictly controlled by the people who indentured them.

Enslaved Africans were forced to work in the fields or the home of their enslavers. Once someone was enslaved, they were enslaved for life. They had no rights and were often mistreated.

title: The Workforce in the Colonies
text:
As the colonial charters said, profit was necessary for the colony to survive. Even if plantations were large, there were few workers to manage them. Over time, the introduction of new people and economic systems supplied the colonies with a stable workforce. This workforce included families, indentured servants, free men, apprentices, women, and enslaved people.

Families were often the first source of labor that the colonists had. All members of a family were expected to contribute to their homes, farms, small businesses, or a combination. Learning business, farming, or a craftsman’s trade was typically passed from father to son.

Indentured servants were men and women whose journey from England to the colonies was paid for by another person. In exchange, they signed a contract with that person that required them to work on farms or in households for a certain number of years. Protected by the law, this contract of indenture was a legal and binding agreement. Once their debt of passage (about $2,500 today) had been repaid, the contract was complete. Then, the servant was free to live and work in the colonies. Sometimes, they would receive land, money, weapons, clothes, or food upon the contract’s completion.

Free white men in America were no longer bound by the restricted social class system of England. In England, men from lower-class families had few opportunities to advance in society. In America, new laws favored ambitious men who worked and contributed to the success of the colony. These men, according to the charter, could own land. With that land, a man could become a farmer, a merchant, or join another profession. Land ownership also meant new rights and privileges, like voting, for these men.

Apprentices were another common labor source in America. Often, orphans or younger sons of large families were contracted to master craftsmen for years to learn a specific trade. These contracts were drawn up, signed before the courts, entered into a deed book, and considered binding. As part of the contract, an apprentice agreed to work for a master craftsman or tradesman without pay. Masters were obligated to provide basic education (reading, writing, and arithmetic), room and board, and sometimes tools or clothes upon completion of the apprenticeship.

Enslaved people were kept in bondage and forced to work on farms and later on plantations. Enslaved people came from Africa, where they were captured and sold into slavery. Under the law, these people were considered property. They had no freedom or rights. These people were enslaved for life. Any children they had were also enslaved. When indentured servitude became unsustainable, many landowners looked to enslaved Africans as a profitable labor source.

title: Native American Lands
text:
Native Americans had great respect for Earth and all life on it. They used the land they lived on in many different ways. Some farmed the land. They stayed near the same location for a growing season that was three to four months long. Some hunted game in the forests and the waterways. They used each part of an animal to meet their needs for clothing, tools, weapons, utensils, and bedding. They also gathered wild fruits, nuts, and berries. The fruit was dried and preserved to eat in the winter. The land provided for their wants and needs.

These resources were sometimes used by multiple groups at the same time. The Native American nations would create alliances over the resources and the land. Other times, Native Americans defended the lands to protect their access to these resources. However, the Native Americans believed land could not be owned. They had no units of measurement for measuring land. For Native Americans, land use was shared or fought over, but the land itself was never owned.

The Europeans wanted the land for their farms and domesticated animals. More importantly, they wanted to use the resources for economic gain. The Europeans had a system of measurement for land. Surveying created boundaries. These lines could be marked clearly so everyone could know and respect the ownership.

When Europeans came to America, they brought the idea of land ownership with them. Native Americans frequently negotiated and traded the same area of land to many different Europeans, just as they did with fellow Native Americans. This caused considerable confusion. Europeans thought they were buying rights to own the land. Native Americans thought the Europeans were paying for the right to use the land. They considered the negotiated cost a “user's fee.” This fee would give the colonists access to the land for hunting, fishing, and using some of the resources. It was not for ownership. This misunderstanding often led to Native Americans being brought into the colonial courts on charges of breaking a negotiated contract.

Not every colonist or colonial government negotiated or traded with Native Americans for the land. There were many instances of colonial governments selling land to new settlers that had not been negotiated for with the local Native American nations.

All Native American land was acquired by Europeans through negotiation, trade, or force. These opposing views of how to use the land brought each side to various levels of conflict from court testimony to bloodshed and war.

title: Distribution of Land in the Colonies
text:
During the colonial era, colonists saw the land as readily available for free, white men. In England, the monarch decided who owned property. When colonists sailed to America, they hoped to seize opportunities that came along with land ownership. If they owned land, these men could vote and hold government offices.

In the New England Colonies, early colonists received 50 acres of land. They took the greatest risks to be there, so this land was meant as a reward. Families obtained land if they promised to farm and improve the property. The land was surveyed, and then land deeds were processed by the royal governor’s office. These deeds were sometimes recorded in the colony’s government records.

In the Middle Colonies, proprietors could sell or gift land to others. The proprietor determined the price, and the measurement of the land was recorded in the proprietor’s office. Individuals could then resell part or all of the land. This was one way people could speculate, or purchase large tracts of land and then resell them in smaller parts for profit.

In the Southern Colonies, the headright system was established by the governor and the colonial government. The government gave 50 acres of land to adult men. They were also given 50 acres for each person who worked for them. A clerk in the governor’s office recorded land measurements and transfers. Large land ownership became known as a plantation.

title: Mercantilism
text:
The American colonies were chartered to trade with England. Colonists sent raw materials to England. These raw materials would be used in England to make manufactured goods that would be exported to the English colonies. This economic system is called mercantilism. In the mercantile system, governments want to increase exports, or what they sell to other countries. They also want to decrease imports, or what they buy from other countries. That keeps more money flowing into their economies. When a country sells more than it buys, it has a favorable balance of trade.
