Mercantilism in the colonies meant that the colonies could not sell their raw materials to anyone but the English. They were not allowed to import anything except from England. This guaranteed only English goods were sold in the colonies. To keep this balance, England also charged tariffs. A tariff is a tax on goods coming from another country. Tariffs were added to the cost of the goods. This made the goods more expensive.

Each colony in America had a deep-water seaport. Large ships crisscrossed the Atlantic with goods to and from these ports from all over the world. A port was essential to the economy in each colony. Each port had a royal customs office at the docks. This office checked and taxed all cargo being brought on or off ships. This ensured the royal customs officer knew exactly what was being shipped. This also guaranteed the royal customs officer knew where the ships were going.

England created rules to make sure they would have a favorable trade balance. These rules were called the Navigation Acts. They required:

Only England or English colonial ships could carry cargo between England and the colonies.

Certain goods, including tobacco, rice, and furs, couldn’t be shipped to foreign nations unless they went through England or Scotland first. The English government would pay bounties, or rewards, to Americans who produced certain raw goods while raising tariffs on the same goods produced in other countries.

American colonists would not compete with English manufacturers in large-scale manufacturing.

This favorable trade balance created a network of trade routes between England, Africa, and America and the West Indies. It was referred to as triangular trade because there were three connecting routes. Each part of the triangular route had a name. The voyage from Europe to Africa was called the Outward Passage. Ships carried manufactured goods for trade in Africa. Enslavers traded human beings for these manufactured goods. The enslavers captured men, women, and children. They were then sold to become enslaved workers for the colonies. The Middle Passage, as it was called, went from Africa to the West Indies and American colonies. The Inward Passage then shipped raw materials to England.

In the triangular trade system, as in the Columbian Exchange, England benefited greatly from the natural resources of America. Each section of the colonies had specialized goods they provided in this trade triangle. The geographic location, the climate, and the population of the colony determined what goods it produced. American colonies built economies based on supply and demand. This system was regulated by the government to make sure England made a large profit. The mercantile system made many colonists in the Americas and investors in England rich. It was the drive for wealth that created mercantilism. Merchants involved in the triangle trade pursued wealth. They gained wealth by neglecting the well-being of indentured servants and enslaved people.

title: Cycle of Debt
text:
There are factors that determine the price of a commodity or product. Some of these factors include the cost of production, the quality of the product, and how many products will be available in the future. The most critical factor is demand, or the desire people have to buy a product. If there is no demand, it doesn’t matter how much of a product there is or what it costs. If no one wants it, it won’t sell.

In Great Britain, there were large companies that bought and sold one valuable product: tobacco. These companies were called brokerages. Only brokerages could buy American tobacco. Tobacco farmers worked with brokerage firms to get the tobacco from the plantation to Great Britain. The broker would decide how much the plantation owner’s tobacco was worth.

In the 17th century, no direct payment was involved. The brokerage house worked like its own bank. The plantation owner would be given credit for the value of the tobacco. This amount of credit was recorded by the brokerage house.

Manufactured goods had to be purchased from Great Britain and shipped to the colonies. If there was anything the plantation owner and his family wanted to buy from Great Britain, they made a list and gave it to the broker. The broker purchased the items using the credit from that year’s tobacco sales.

The owner had to trust the broker with these purchases. There were no prices on the list, so the owner didn’t know how much each item would cost. The broker would purchase only the best for his client. Most of the time, the cost of the items was more than the owner had in his account. The broker promised that the planter could pay off the rest when he returned with the next year’s crop. The plantation owner would then be in debt to the broker. This process often repeated the next year. So, the plantation owner would always be in debt to the broker. It was extremely difficult to reverse this cycle.

title: Daily Life in the Colonies
text:
Life in the early 1700s was very different from when the colonies were first established. There was a greater trade balance. This meant more manufactured goods were available from England, like paper, sugar, and tea. Colonists could trade for or buy things. They didn’t have to make everything themselves.

Every city had a newspaper, which included news, weather, opinions, and advertisements. Even though most people could read, they often gathered at a local meeting house to hear the news read out loud.

Farmers sold their produce at markets. Families in the city would have a kitchen garden. They would still go to the market to purchase or trade with items such as meat, vegetables, and preserved fruit. Much of the preparation was done before foods arrived in city kitchens. This eased the workload of women and children.

Colonists’ daily diets included dried or salted meat and corn mush or bread. Meals might include a stew or pie filled with meat and vegetables in gravy. The drink of choice was apple cider. People rarely drank water because it was not clean. People living in cities often got sick from bad water.

Craftsmen took in apprentices to teach them a trade. These boys acted as servants in a craftsman’s household and shop. They ran errands, tended fires, cleaned, and learned the trade. Blacksmiths, silversmiths, glassworkers, and printers were all open for apprenticeships.

Boys had two shirts, one for work and one for church. Socks were mended until they couldn’t be mended anymore. Women and girls usually had only one dress and a few aprons. Aprons protected their dresses for church on Sundays. When children outgrew their clothing, they passed it down to their siblings.

Shoes were individually made by village shoemakers to a general size. There were no right or left shoes. They did not fit well and had to be tied or buckled to stay on. Only the very wealthy could have shoes made to fit their feet.

The average lifespan of a colonist in the 1700s depended on their work situation, their wealth, and luck. Poor and enslaved people died young from disease, accidents, or being overworked. Those who had easier work could expect a longer life. Although life had gotten better since the early days of colonization, it still wasn't easy. Every day presented its own difficulties.

title: Games, Science, Technology, and Travel During Colonial Times
text:
You might think living in the 1700s was boring. There were no computers or televisions or even places to get a soda. If you wanted to go somewhere, you couldn’t jump into the family car and head out. How did children in the 1700s travel? What games did they play? What were technology and science like?

The most common way to travel in the 1700s, although not the fastest, was on foot. Some people had a wagon or horse and buggy, while some rode on horseback. To get from one country to another across the ocean, people traveled by ship. A trip from England to America took about six to eight weeks each way. Most children worked at home to help their families survive. Sometimes, they worked for other people to learn a trade or earn extra money. When they had time to play, children played games like tag or hide-and-seek, jumped rope, or played marbles.

Communication technology wasn’t very developed in the 1700s. If a person needed to talk to someone in another town, they couldn’t call them on the phone or send them a message online. The telephone wasn’t invented until 1876, and the first home computer wasn’t invented until 1975. People in the colonies communicated by talking face-to-face or by writing letters. A letter could take weeks to arrive after it was sent. Before there was an official postal service, letters and packages were usually carried by someone who was traveling to another destination. Letters and packages were easily lost because of this, and sometimes, they never made it to their destinations.

In the 1700s, people knew electricity existed, but they didn’t understand it. Benjamin Franklin was one of the first people to understand electricity and how it affected the world around him. Franklin was always conducting science experiments. He believed lightning might be the same thing as electricity, and he was right. He was mostly right about the Aurora Borealis, which is another name for the Northern Lights. Franklin was convinced that the colors in the sky were caused by electrical charges in the air.

title: Japanese American Internment Camps
text:
After the attack on Pearl Harbor and the United States entered the war, there was great suspicion and anger in the general public against Japanese Americans. Bias and prejudice against people from Asia grew rapidly. The concern was loyalty to the United States or Imperial Japan.

Public concerns for national security made it to Congress. Congress reacted by activating the U.S. Army in the West Coast. The entire West Coast was declared a military area. Ten weeks after the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066.

Executive Order 9066 gave the military broad power. People who the military thought to be suspicious in loyalty to America were targeted. An area 50 to 60 mile wide in the coastal area from Washington state to California was put in military jurisdiction. The area also extended inland into southern Arizona. The order authorized the forced removal of citizens, mostly Japanese Americans, to concentration camps. These camps were quickly organized and governed by the military. This order also applied to smaller groups of U.S. residents who were of German and Italian descent. However, it was tens of thousands of Japanese Americans who lost liberty, freedom and property as a result of the order.

Japanese Americans and their families were given very short notice to sell or store their homes, possessions, and businesses. They could only take what they could carry. Then, men, women and children of all ages were transported and incarcerated in detention centers.

From the detention centers, the people were transferred to concentration camps located in seven states. Camps were often on remote and barren sites inland, such as Manzanar in eastern California and Topaz in the desert of central Utah. These concentration camps were built quickly and with poor materials. When the first people reached Topaz, the buildings weren’t finished. The newly arrived residents had to finish their own barracks.

The area was divided into 42 blocks. A block was designed for 250 people. Each block had 12 barrack buildings. Every block also had a cafeteria, a laundry room, toilets, baths and showers, and a recreation hall. Recreation halls sometimes served as stores, libraries, and churches.

Each barrack in Topaz was 120 feet long by 20 feet wide. The barrack was divided into six different sized rooms. Each family was assigned to one of the rooms. The size of the room depended on the size of the family. The rooms only held army-style cots with bedding. There was no running water or indoor plumbing. Each room had a coal stove to provide heat. The people forced to live there often used scrap wood and wooden packing crates to build tables, chairs, and other furniture.

The entire area was fenced to keep all people inside the concentration camp. There was no freedom of movement, no liberty of choice, and few rights were respected. More than 120,000 Americans were incarcerated. The concentration camps were used until Imperial Japan surrendered to the Allied Forces in August of 1945.

title: Fred Korematsu
text:
Fred Korematsu was 23 years old when Executive Order 9066 was given. Japanese Americans were to be incarcerated in guarded concentration camps. Korematsu refused to go. He was arrested and convicted for this action. Korematsu was forced to live at the Tanforan “Assembly Center” in California. This was a former horse racing track converted quickly to be housing for Japanese Americans. Korematsu and his family were then forced to move to Topaz, Utah.

Korematsu and others believed the incarcerations were unconstitutional. He appealed his case through the court system to the Supreme Court in Washington D.C. In 1944, the Supreme Court ruled incarcerations of Japanese Americans during war was justified as a “military necessity”.

In 1980, President Jimmy Carter appointed a special commission to review the facts of incarceration for Japanese Americans. This commission concluded the decision to forcibly relocate American citizens occurred because of prejudice, fear, and poor political leadership. It discovered evidence supporting freedom for Japanese Americans that was not presented to the courts.

In 1983, Korematsu’s conviction was overturned. The government offered Korematsu a pardon. Korematsu responded that he was not interested in a pardon from the government. The government should be seeking a pardon from him and the others who were wronged.

title: Daniel Inouye
text:
Daniel Inouye was from Hawaii. His ancestors were Japanese. After the bombing of Pearl Harbor, Inouye wanted to enlist in the U.S. Army. He was denied because he was a Japanese American. President Roosevelt was convinced to create a segregated military unit of Japanese Americans to fight in Europe. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team was created in 1943.

Inouye was finally permitted to enlist and became part of the 442nd. He led many combat missions in Italy against the Nazi troops. During combat in his last mission, Inouye’s right arm was severely wounded. In spite of his own wounds, Inouye continued to lead his men to safety.

For his many actions in combat, Inouye was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross, the Bronze Star and the Purple Heart with Cluster. The cluster of oak leaves on the award indicate the soldier was wounded in different battles.

After the war, he practiced law in his native Hawaii. Inouye was active in the process of gaining statehood for Hawaii in the late 1950’s. When Hawaii became the 50th state, Inouye was one of the first representatives to the U.S. Congress. In 1962, he won election to the U.S. Senate. He served in the Senate for 50 years.

In 1992, President Bill Clinton honored Inouye with a Congressional Medal of Honor for his courage during the war. In 2012, President Barack Obama gave Inouye the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He is the only senator to receive both medals.

title: The 442nd Regimental Combat Team
text:
Executive Order 9066 forced removal of Japanese Americans to concentration camps. The same order created military units for Japanese Americans. Over 2,800 men were recruited from the concentration camps. Sons of Japanese Americans became the 442 Regimental Combat Team. The 442nd fought in the European theater. They fought in Italy, France and Germany. The 442nd became a highly decorated unit for courage, bravery and action. “Go for Broke” was the motto of this combat troop.

The 442nd was awarded eight Presidential Unit Citations, with five being earned in one month. Twenty one members were awarded Medals of Honor. During the war, 9,486 Purple Hearts were earned by this combat unit.

Asian Americans had to wait until 2000 to be awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor. In a White House ceremony President Bill Clinton gave recognition to 23 individuals and thousands of others who served America in World War II. It was in the 1990s that the Army investigated how dozens of Japanese American and Pacific Islander soldiers were denied awards because of bias and prejudice of the 1940s.

title: Discrimination Against Jews in Nazi Germany, 1933-1945
text:
After World War I, the nations of the world did their best to recover. It was a time of change in Europe where the fighting occurred. Governments vowed to make sure a war of this size would never happen again. When there has been much tragedy, expense and loss, people try to find reasons to explain how such things happened. The people of Germany were stunned they surrendered. The returning soldiers were trying to make sense of their service to Kaiser Wilhelm. The Kaiser was removed and went into retirement. New leaders emerged. One man became very popular because he wanted to place blame for the war, not rebuild and change because of the war. Adolf Hitler and the National Socialist German Workers’ Party, known as the Nazi Party, were loud in placing blame for Germany’s post-war situation. They verbally attacked minorities. They targeted anyone who was not of German heritage. Hitler gained more and more popularity. He lashed out at old hatreds and misbeliefs against Jews. This specific population became the focus of prejudice, bias and bigotry by the Nazi Party.

The Nazi’s gradually stripped rights from German citizens because they were Jewish. The legalized discrimination began slowly and gained acceptance by communities of people who were not Jews.

The following is a timeline of the legalization of segregation, exclusion and persecution of the Jews by the Nazi government.

1933

The Nazi government organized a boycott, (not making purchases) of Jewish shops and businesses.

Books by Jewish authors were destroyed in large public bonfires.

Jewish civil servants, lawyers and teachers were fired from jobs. Jewish doctors and dentists were only permitted to see Jewish patients.

Jews were not allowed to own farms. Property ownership was legally restricted.

1934

Jewish shops were marked with a yellow star on the front entrance.

Jews had to sit on separate seats on buses and trains. Many city councils banned them from public spaces.

Jews had to wear a yellow star on their outer clothing to identify themselves as Jews.

1935

The Nazi government passed a series of discriminatory laws.

These laws removed Jews of German citizenship. Without citizenship the Jews were not protected by the laws.

They could not obtain a passport to leave Germany to live in another country.

The Nazi government forbade marriage between Jews and Germans

The Nazi government removed all the civil and political rights of the Jews. No voting, holding public office, being in law enforcement or being a member of the courts. Jews could not be members of a jury.

Jews were not allowed in the army.

1936

Nazi Germany hosted the 1936 Olympics. The eyes of the world were on Hitler and the government. There was no visible public persecution of Jews in Berlin during the Olympics but it continued in other areas.

1938

Jews were ordered to register all wealth and property.

They could no longer practice as doctors or lawyers, and Jewish businessmen could not have Aryan clients.

Jews were forced to change their middle names: males would be known as Israel, females as Sarah.

Jewish children were forbidden to go to school and universities.

Kristallnacht - 9 November (The Night of Broken Glass). The Nazi government organized attacks on Jewish homes, businesses and synagogues in retaliation for the assassination of the German ambassador to France by a young man who was Jewish. During Kristallnacht, 400 synagogues and 7,500 shops were destroyed. Jews were then made to clear up the destruction and pay a fine to the government. The remaining Jewish property was then confiscated. Jews were forced into ghettos, areas in a city that have few resources and many people living in poor conditions.

1939

The Nazis, who had been encouraging Jews to emigrate from 1933 onwards, now started “forced” emigration. 150,000 Jews were deported, but they had to pay a large “tax” before they could leave.

In March, there were mass arrests. 30,000 Jews were sent to concentration camps.

1940-1945

6 million Jews were murdered in the concentration camps. This became known as the Holocaust.

Quote: "Some of the people disapproved, but their disapproval was only silence." - kurt messerschmidt, jewish survivor

title: Women at Work
text:
In the decade before World War II, more American women joined the workforce than ever before. The economic difficulties of the Great Depression made it a necessity for most of them. Traditionally, if women worked outside their homes they worked in fields such as nursing and teaching. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, many things changed in the country, including the workforce. Women started working in a variety of jobs that had not been open to them before.

When the United States entered World War II, changes happened fast. The nation needed its factories to produce goods for the war effort. Almost overnight, automobile and appliance factories became airplane and weapons factories. New factories were also built to produce the materials that the U.S. needed.

There was one major problem, though. Most of the men went off to war. Suddenly, there were not enough workers to run the factories. This was not the type of work women traditionally did in the workforce. There was a shortage of workers, though, and all at once women were needed to work in factories.

In 1942, a song called "Rosie the Riveter" became popular and provided the nickname for female workers. A riveter is a worker who joins pieces of metal together with short metal fasteners. The image of Rosie the Riveter, a woman rolling up her sleeves and doing "men's work" in a factory, was everywhere. She appeared on an iconic poster in her red bandana and overalls, proudly declaring, “We Can Do It.” Billboards and magazines carried advertisements using Rosie's picture. The advertisements convinced women to go to work. Rosie represented a new, independent, confident woman who could do whatever needed to support the war effort. The government hoped to convince women that taking a job was not a choice. It was their duty as U.S. citizens.

During World War II, many women went to work for wartime industries. Women worked in shipyards, steel mills, foundries, lumber mills, warehouses, offices, hospitals, and day care centers. They were welders, drafters, truck drivers, riveters, and more. More than 6 million women across America left their chores and family-rearing at home to join the workforce.

The aviation industry hired the most women. More than 300,000 women worked on building bombers and transport planes. Second to aviation, the munitions industry recruited women to work in factories. They made weapons, shells, and bullets, among other equipment for the war.

Women’s opportunities were expanding. Their challenges increased as well. Mothers faced balancing childcare and work. Working long shifts of labor-intensive actions left the workers tired. The women then had to go home to work to care for their families. Fathers, husbands, brothers, and uncles were gone. It was not an easy time for families in America.

Not all women found equal treatment at work. There was discrimination against African American women. They were often rejected by employers in favor of white applicants. When they did get a job, they got paid less than white workers for doing the same work. In general, women received much less pay than men did. Then, when men returned from the war, women were pressured to give their jobs back to the men and return home.

title: Women Airforce Service Pilots Program (WASP)
text:
During World War II, women in America stepped into the workforce in jobs that used to be for men only. Women built military equipment in factories. Delivery of this equipment also became a job for women. The Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASP) was a civilian organization formed to help with these deliveries. Women who could pilot planes joined to do this critical work. Being a female pilot was unique, but not unknown. Since the early days of aviation female pilots such as Amelia Earhart took to the skies. When America needed them, many women stepped forward to follow Earhart’s adventurous spirit.

The WASP members did more than deliver airplanes to military bases from the factory. They towed targets behind their planes in the air for troops to practice with live anti-aircraft guns. They transported cargo across the country and across the oceans. Each woman pilot doing this work freed a male pilot for military service.

Gwendolyne Cowart was a WASP member from South Carolina. The Atlanta Constitution newspaper declared Cowart was the, “youngest girl in the South to get a commercial flying license.” In 1940, Cowart made news for landing a plane in a cow pasture when it ran out of fuel. Cowart transported P-38s and P-47s. These small planes were used in both the European and Pacific theaters. They often escorted larger bombers. When asked about the plane's performance, Cowart said, “You know, you can pick up a nice 350 miles an hour in those ships.”

The WASPs provided a vital service to the war effort. They logged over 60 million miles in the air. Before the organization disbanded, 38 women lost their lives in aircraft related accidents. In 1977, the WASPs were granted veterans’ status. This meant they were officially recognized as vital to the war and the Armed Services. In 2009, WASPs were awarded the Congressional Gold Medal.

title: Berlin Before and After
text:
After the D-Day Invasion at Normandy on June 6, 1944, the Allied military focused on reaching Berlin. This was the capital of Nazi Germany. The French, English, and Americans approached Berlin from the west. The Russians approached from the east. It was a race to see who would get there first. It was spring as the troops battled their way through the countryside. Farms, equipment, and villages were destroyed by the fighting. No new crops were planted.

German soldiers surrendered to the Allied troops as they closed in on the city. By late April, 1945, Hitler and many of his staff were dead. Berlin was left with few defenses. The Russians were the first to reach the government buildings in Berlin. On June 5, 1945, one year after D-Day, the military leaders of the Allies met in Berlin. They signed the Berlin Declaration. This proclaimed the unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany and made the Allies the governing authority there.

Before the war, Berlin had been a vibrant, world-class city. Berlin hosted the 1936 Olympic games. Visitors from around the world came. Everyone admired the architecture and high-quality businesses of Berlin. Sounds of the city were clamorous. Back then, the streets were filled with traffic. Busses and trains routinely came in and out of the city. The air filled with music from restaurants and clubs, along with people delivering and selling goods and services. Busy factories added to the hum of the vibrant city.

In June of 1945, the city was silent. There were few buildings left standing from the relentless Allied bombings. The crowds of people were gone. There were a few survivors from the bombings. The only food available was through the Allied troops' supplies. This helped the Allied troops know who was in the city when they came for food. Soldiers and their equipment were everywhere. Where there used to be cars, there were now armored tanks. There was no free movement. No one could be out on the streets without official purpose. Many people were arrested and investigated for their participation in the war. Berlin was now an occupied, defeated city under military rule.

title: The Ohio and Erie Canal
text:
In the early 1800s, most of the land west of the original 13 British colonies was still considered the frontier. There were very few established settlements and towns. Most people who lived in the West were farmers and frontiersmen. The federal government and merchants encouraged settlers to settle in the West. Movement of people brings about the exchange of ideas. It also creates the demand for better technology to make that movement easier. Once in a new place, people still have wants and needs. Communities create markets. New markets increase demand for products. Demand for products increases the need for transportation. Increased transportation keeps people in communities more connected. This growth cycle was happening in America from 1800 to 1860.

Waterways in America were the highways for moving people and goods. New York City merchants wanted goods from the western frontier. Connecting the Hudson River to Lake Erie became a goal for the state of New York. The Erie Canal was the first publicly funded project. A canal is a large channel dug in the earth that is filled with water for boats to use. The New York government used tax money to pay workers to dig the canal. From 1817 to 1825, thousands of workers used shovels and carts to dig 363 miles of canal. From Albany, New York, to Buffalo, New York, the canal was the longest human-made waterway in North America. Use of the canal for transporting goods to market made New York City’s harbor the nation's busiest harbor.

Ohio settlers and merchants wanted to connect the frontier to markets in the east through the Erie Canal. In 1825, plans were created to connect the Cuyahoga and Ohio Rivers to Lake Erie, which would link Ohio to the Erie Canal. Landowners in the Cuyahoga River Valley offered land to the state government to construct the canal. It took workers seven years to dig the 308-mile-long canal from Portsmouth, a small settlement on the Ohio River, to Lake Erie.

The Ohio and Erie Canal was completed in 1832. The Ohio and Erie Canal greatly decreased the travel time between Cincinnati and Cleveland. A trip that once took weeks was shortened to just days because of the canal. Businesses began to profit from the construction of the canal, too. Shipping records show that before the completion of the canal, merchants in Cleveland sent about 1,000 barrels of flour to Buffalo, New York. After the completion of the canal, merchants were able to ship nearly 250,000 barrels of flour to Buffalo. Goods were then shipped to larger markets, including Philadelphia, New York City, Boston, and Europe.

Many cities in Ohio profited from and grew rapidly as a result of the Ohio and Erie Canal. One of these cities was Cleveland. Before the opening of the canal, the population of Cleveland was 1,075. By 1840, the population grew to 6,071, making it the 45th-largest city in the United States. By 1850, the population more than doubled, reaching 17,034. Akron also grew quickly following the completion of the Ohio and Erie Canal. In 1830, Akron’s population was 910. By 1850, the population grew to 3,266.

Because of the success of the Ohio and Erie Canal, more canals were constructed in Ohio to link western settlements to the Ohio River and Lake Erie. The Ohio and Erie Canal linked Ohio and its resources to the United States and the world.

title: Yalta Conference and the Big Three
text:
The three largest members of the Allied Powers were Great Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States. They were known as “The Big Three.” Winston Churchill was Prime Minister of Great Britain. Franklin Roosevelt was President of the United States. Joseph Stalin was Premier of the Soviet Union.

Great Britain and the United States were governments based in democracy. Citizens had their individual rights and private property protected from government control. The Soviet Union's government was based in Communism. Citizens there had no private property. Property was held by the government. Each citizen worked and was paid by the government. The more property the government held, the more resources and the more wealthy a nation could become.

Great Britain and the United States were allies before and during the first world war. The Soviet Union was a new government in 1922 and not supportive of democracy. Despite their differences, all three countries recognized they had to work together during World War II. Hitler’s Nazi government in Germany was a threat to them all.

The Big Three worked together, but there was great mistrust among them. In February, 1945, the three leaders met at Yalta, Ukraine, Soviet Union. The intent of the meeting was to create a plan for Europe after the war was over. The memory of the Treaty of Versailles after World War I was fresh in their minds. The consequences of that treaty was one of the main reasons for the rise of the Nazi government. They knew they needed to be careful in how they planned.

Each country had an agenda to accomplish. Roosevelt wanted Stalin to support the United States’ planned invasion of Japan in the Pacific Theater. Churchill wanted to establish democracy in the countries controlled by the Nazis. Stalin wanted to expand Soviet influence into the Nazi-occupied countries. He wanted to protect the Soviet Union from any future aggression from a newly democratic Europe.

The Big Three negotiated and strategized to get what each wanted. By the end of the Yalta Conference, they reached agreement.

These were some of the points of agreement:

They would accept only unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany.

France would be included in the peace process once the French government was restored.

Berlin would be divided into military regions.

The defeated Germany would not be permitted to have a military of any kind.

Any remainders of the Nazi government would be eliminated.

Stalin would pledge that Poland could hold free elections.

Stalin would commit to enter the war against the Empire of Japan after the war in Europe was over.

Nazi war criminals were to be found, arrested, and tried in a court of law.

There were great hopes for a bright future at the end of the Yalta Conference as the leaders returned to their homes. Within eight weeks of the conference, President Roosevelt died and a new leader came to the world stage. Harry S. Truman became the 33rd President of the United States. Only time would determine if the future was as bright as everyone had hoped.

title: Displaced Persons
text:
From 1939 to 1945 Europe was a place of constant war. In war, people move from places of danger to places they think will be safe. In constant war, there are few places that can be safe. Thousands of people fled their homes in search of safety from all armies.

People were also forced to leave their homes by the Nazi government. Many families remained separated for years. Nazis had seized and never returned their property. Survivors of the Holocaust Jewish concentration camps were malnourished and traumatized by the actions of the Nazis.

Millions of people needed food, shelter, and medical care. The survivors needed more than their physical needs to be taken care of, though. They needed help with their emotional suffering too. They needed to find lost family members and loved ones. They needed help adjusting to being a survivor when so many had died. The military forces from France, Great Britain, United States, and the Soviet Union were the authorities to provide these services.

The Allies created Displaced Persons camps to care for those uprooted by the war. The new camps were crude in their structures of tents and plywood housing. There was no privacy, no indoor toilets or cafeterias. There were many people and not enough supplies for everyone. Water for drinking, cooking, and bathing had to be trucked to the camps. Supplies came in slowly.

Some had survived the war but did not survive the transition to peace.

title: Demilitarization of Germany
text:
Great Britain, United States and Soviet Union leaders met at Yalta, Ukraine, in 1945 to plan for postwar Europe. Containing and disarming the Nazi military was necessary. As an army surrenders, there are procedures to follow for safety. The new authorities have to keep careful records of all these procedures. They have to demobilize the defeated armed services and disable their equipment. Besides defeating the military, authorities have to dismantle the country’s war industry and factories. All symbols of the former government, such as Nazi flags, need removal too. The Allies shared these responsibilities in Germany.

According to agreements made at Yalta, Germany was divided into sections and territories. The capital, Berlin, was also divided into military sections. The Soviet Union was to manage eastern Germany and eastern sections of Berlin. France, Great Britain, and the United States managed the north, west, and south sections of the country and Berlin.

The Soviet Union pursued an active dismantling of all factories and industrial complexes. This action provided no future means of work for the German citizens in the Soviet-managed area. The other Allies restructured industries for consumer use. This would give work in the future for the German citizens.

By 1948, the western territories under the control of the French, English and Americans were beginning to recover. The foundations for democracy were forming. The western Allies gave economic aid and helped the people move toward being self-sufficient. The Soviet-controlled territory in the east got pulled into communist rule. The government owned the property. The people had to work for the government, not for themselves. There was a split forming in the four allies. It was splitting Germany into two, creating East and West Germany.

The Allies pressured the Soviet Union to change communist policies for Germany. The Soviets responded with restricted access in and out of Berlin. Suddenly, millions of people who were rebuilding Berlin had no access to food, medical help, or fuel. West Berlin became isolated. The Soviets thought this would make the Allies abandon the city. The Allies brought supplies in by airplane. The Berlin airlift continued for over a year. In 1949, the Soviets reopened supply routes to Berlin.

title: Berlin Airlift and the Candy Bomber
text:
After the Soviet Union restricted all vehicles in and out of Berlin in 1948, the Allies began to drop supplies by air. Giant cargo planes were loaded with food and other goods. The planes flew over the occupied zone through open air channels. As they flew over Berlin, they dropped their cargo. This operation was known as the “Berlin Airlift.”

While the airlifts were going on, one cargo pilot discovered a very special mission of his own. U.S. Air Force pilot Gail Halvorsen was at a Berlin airfield when he met some German children. In Europe, children knew American soldiers had chocolate bars and chewing gum. Children often asked the soldiers to share their rationed sweets.

However, this group of children just watched him in silence. Halvorsen offered the group two sticks of gum. He watched as the children carefully broke the gum into small pieces so each child could have a taste.

The children’s reaction to his small gift touched Halvorsen. He promised to drop candy to them on his next flight. “Watch for me, I’ll wiggle the wings,” he told them. He asked other pilots to donate their rations of gum and candy. As his plane flew over the group of waiting children, he “wiggled” the wings. The crew dropped candy and gum attached to small, white handkerchief parachutes. This continued every day. Soon, newspapers learned what Halvorsen was doing. They printed his story. People in the U.S. began to flood Halvorsen with candy donations.

The American people opened their hearts to the children of Germany. The harshness of the war was being forgotten in the smiles of the children of Berlin.

Japan's government has played a crucial role in shaping the standard of living for its citizens. This has been accomplished through a combination of economic policies, healthcare initiatives, education, and social services. It is also accomplished through infrastructure development, environmental sustainability, cultural support, and work-life balance efforts. These approaches have contributed to Japan's reputation as a country with a high standard of living and a strong commitment to the well-being of its people.

The Japanese government has implemented a range of economic policies to promote growth and stability. Key initiatives include investments in infrastructure and technological innovation. Others include support for vital industries like automotive and electronics. These policies have helped create a robust job market and a strong economy. This has boosted the standard of living for many Japanese citizens. The government provides an extensive social safety net. This safety net includes unemployment benefits, pensions, and support for populations such as the elderly and disabled. These social services contribute to a sense of security and stability among citizens.

Japan also has a universal healthcare system that provides access to high-quality medical services for all residents. The government regulates healthcare costs. It also ensures that citizens receive timely and affordable medical care. This commitment to healthcare contributes to longer life expectancies and overall well-being.

Japan places a strong emphasis on education. Mandatory free schooling is available up to the lower secondary level. This focus on education has led to a highly skilled and literate workforce. The government also invests in research and development. This fosters innovation and technological advancements that benefit society as a whole.

Japan also invests in advanced infrastructure. Advancements include efficient public transportation systems, well-maintained roads, and modern urban planning. These investments enhance the overall quality of life. Investing in transportation reduces commute times, improves access, and ensures safety during the travel of daily life. The Japanese government has also implemented environmental policies that address issues like pollution and natural resource conservation. These efforts aim to create a clean and sustainable living environment. This is done in an effort to positively impact the health and well-being of citizens.

The Japanese government promotes cultural activities and heritage preservation. This contributes to a sense of national identity and pride. Cultural initiatives enhance the quality of life. They also provide opportunities for artistic expression, community engagement, and cultural enrichment. The government has encouraged a better work-life balance. One way it has done this is by implementing policies like "Premium Friday." Premium Friday encourages companies to allow employees to leave work early on the last Friday of the month. These efforts promote well-being and family life.

title: The Allies Rebuild Europe: Potsdam Conference and the Marshall Plan
text:
With the unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany, the task of caring for the people of Europe fell to the Allied Powers. The Big Three, Great Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States led the planning for post-war Europe. After their first meeting in Yalta in February 1945, it was time for these leaders to gather again. A conference in Potsdam, Germany, began on July 17, 1945 and lasted over two weeks.

By summer of 1945, there was new leadership in two of the Allied Powers. United States President Franklin Roosevelt died in April, 1945. Harry Truman became the new executive. Winston Churchill had lost his position in the election of July, 1945. The new Prime Minister Clement Attlee attended the conference with the outgoing Churchill. Joseph Stalin remained the Premier of the Soviet Union.

The Allies were a mixture of democracies and communist-based governments. Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union was a strong advocate for communist principles. In communism, the government owns all property and the people share in the benefits according to government policies.

When the Big Three met at Potsdam, Germany in 1945, there were many agreements reached to finalize the war and build the peace. They created a Council of Foreign Ministers to manage the peace treaties. The council would help the new governments to establish peaceful relations with other countries. It would also assist the new governments to join the new United Nations.

The war destroyed the economy of each country in Europe. The currency from Nazi Germany was worthless. Factories were in ruins. Transportation for goods and services was disrupted. Agriculture was inadequate for supplying enough food. For a strong future, the economies of the nations had to be addressed. U.S. Secretary of State George Marshall designed the “European Recovery Plan.” It is more commonly called “The Marshall Plan.” This was a four-year plan to reconstruct cities, industries, highways and railroads. The plan would also establish trade between the European countries with the world. The Marshall Plan was rooted in capitalism, meaning private ownership of businesses and free trade. The Soviet Union’s communist government did not support capitalism.

The Marshall Plan provided over $15 billion to war-torn countries of western Europe. The military territories that were assigned at the Yalta Conference and strengthened at the Potsdam Conference were the recipients of the funds. The Soviet Union declined any participation in the Marshall Plan. This decision would have great impact in the countries within the Soviet Union’s district.

In 1952, the Marshall Plan concluded. Western Europe’s economy was stronger than pre-war levels, both in manufacturing and trade.

title: Europe’s Political Boundaries Before and After the War
text:
The First Look at the Map

Look at the title and the shapes on the map. Does the map look familiar? Is this a place you recognize from memory? Is this place new and unfamiliar?

Locate the compass rose to determine what the orientation (position in space) is.

Look at the scale. Is this a map for accuracy or illustration?

Look for general features on the map, such as geographic landforms, human characteristics, or political boundaries.

Next, generate questions from your first scan concerning what you want to learn from the map.

The Second Look at the Map

This time, look for details that can answer the questions from your first look. Take note of details, such as geographic features, the names of places, the distance between locations, coloring or symbols, and others. Answer the questions you asked after the first look. Do the answers from the first round of questions create more questions?

The Third Look at the Map

Focus on specific details to answer questions. To help focus, block sections with your hand or a paper. This will give your eyes just one place to look. Then move to another section and do the same.

Start comparing what you are finding with what you already know. How is this information the same? How is this information different from what you know?

Take time to answer the questions while you compare the two maps. Share what you have learned from the map, either with a friend or in a writing assignment.

Use the process for each map. Then, compare and contrast how they are the same and different. Reflect and share what you have observed from studying the maps.

title: The World Working Together
text:
The world had been at war twice in the first half of the 20th century. The League of Nations formed after the first war. The United States did not participate in the League of Nations. At the end of the second war, the United States emerged as a military giant and one of the wealthiest nations in the world. The war allies of the United States were thriving in the post-war world.

The Allied Powers stood in a position to work together for world peace. They followed the spirit of the League of Nations. Dissolving that league, they began a new world peace organization. The United Nations was created in 1945. The United Nations charter is the document that defines and governs the nations who join. The charter is considered an international treaty. A treaty is a legal agreement between governments.

The United Nations charter states in Article 1:

“The Purposes of the United Nations are: 1. To maintain international peace and security, and to that end: to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace ... and to bring about by peaceful means ... with the principles of justice and international law, adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach of the peace.

2. To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, and to take other appropriate measures to strengthen universal peace …”

title: The Creation of Israel
text:
The millions of people displaced by war and the Holocaust and the systemic persecution of Jews by the Nazi government became some of the first items the new United Nations addressed. There were survivors of the Holocaust with no families, no property, and no resources for change.

There were world governments discussing various plans to assist the needs of the survivors. There were religious and private organizations contributing ideas from all over the world. The survivors were left with nothing; no home, no property, no citizenship, and no country after the Holocaust. These factors influenced and impacted the complications of the plans at every level.

It is difficult to simplify decisions that would impact millions of lives. The United Nations took many ideas from governments and organizations. From these ideas they created Resolution 181.

On November 29, 1947, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181. This is also known as the Partition Resolution. Great Britain had been governing the area known as Palestine in the Middle East since World War I. The British were withdrawing from the region. The Partition Resolution proposed that the region be split to include a place for Jews and a place for Palestinians.

The nation of Israel was created as a Jewish state, a place where Jewish victims of the Holocaust and worldwide persecution could live. The geographic region had historical significance for thousands of years to the Jews. Jewish leaders celebrated the nation of Israel as a great achievement. The reaction was the direct opposite for the Palestinian Arabs who lived there. Groups of Palestine residents argued they were in the majority and should have more input into governing. Great conflict began and continues today in the region.

Nearly 200 nations are members of the United Nations. Over 160 of these governments recognize the nation of Israel. The state of Palestine has also been recognized by 138 countries. The separation of this geography into two political states is a concern still brought before the United Nations today.

title: NATO The North Atlantic Treaty Organization
text:
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was another treaty created to support the United Nations. NATO is made up of governments from both North America and Europe. Its purpose is to guard freedom and the safety of each of its members through military and political cooperation.

The NATO charter states that, “The Parties to this Treaty reaffirm their faith in the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations and their desire to live in peace with all peoples and all governments.”

By cooperating together, each of these nations, “seek to promote stability and well-being in the North Atlantic area.”

By joining the organization, nations commit that, “They are resolved to unite their efforts for collective defence and for the preservation of peace and security.”

The charter continues to instruct NATO members, “to settle any international dispute in which they may be involved by peaceful means ... refrain in their international relations from the threat or use of force in any manner inconsistent with the purposes of the United Nations."

NATO members “... will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions.” The treaty also encourages members to find ways to encourage peace through policy: “They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.”

NATO continues its work in the 21st century.

title: Winston Churchill and the Iron Curtain
text:
Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill delivered a speech in a small college in President Harry Truman’s home state of Missouri. President Truman attended the speech. Churchill used this opportunity to speak to the world about current happenings and their impact on the future.

The following are excerpts from his speech, “Sinews of Peace.”

It is also an honour, perhaps almost unique, for a private visitor to be introduced to an academic audience by the President of the United States. ... Let me, however, make it clear that I have no official mission or status of any kind, and that I speak only for myself. There is nothing here but what you see.

The United States stands at this time at the pinnacle of world power. It is a solemn moment for the American Democracy. For with primacy in power is also joined an awe inspiring accountability to the future.

... Our supreme task and duty is to guard the homes of the common people from the horrors and miseries of another war. ...

A shadow has fallen upon the scenes so lately lighted by the Allied victory. Nobody knows what Soviet Russia and its Communist international organisation intends to do in the immediate future, ... I have a strong admiration and regard for the valiant Russian people and for my wartime comrade, Marshal Stalin. ... We understand the Russian need to be secure on her western frontiers by the removal of all possibility of German aggression. We welcome Russia to her rightful place among the leading nations of the world. We welcome her flag upon the seas. Above all, we welcome constant, frequent and growing contacts between the Russian people and our own people on both sides of the Atlantic. It is my duty however, for I am sure you would wish me to state the facts as I see them to you, to place before you certain facts about the present position in Europe.

From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent. Behind that line lie all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe. ... all these famous cities and the populations around them lie in what I must call the Soviet sphere, and all are subject in one form or another, not only to Soviet influence but... to control from Moscow. ... The Communist parties, which were very small in all these Eastern States of Europe, have been raised to pre-eminence [superiority] ... and are seeking everywhere to obtain totalitarian control.

Police governments are prevailing in nearly every case, ... there is no true democracy.

... From what I have seen of our Russian friends and Allies during the war, I am convinced that there is nothing they admire so much as strength, and there is nothing for which they have less respect than for weakness, especially military weakness.

If we adhere faithfully to the Charter of the United Nations and walk forward in ... strength seeking no one’s land or treasure, seeking to lay no arbitrary control upon the thoughts of men; ... the high-roads of the future will be clear, not only for us but for all, not only for our time, but for a century to come.

title: The Men Come Home
text:
After World War II, millions of American soldiers returned home. Men and women were ready to pick up where they left off when the nation entered the war on Dec. 8, 1941. Americans began working to make their lives better than ever.

The country had changed dramatically in four years. War efforts brought many technological changes as well as advances in medicine and communication. During the war, special medicines called antibiotics were discovered. Medicines like penicillin helped the body fight bacterial infections. These new medicines saved millions of lives. Also, new medical procedures that were developed in war could save lives on the home front.

Perhaps the greatest change for many of the returning soldiers was that they returned to a nation that had pulled itself out of the Great Depression. When they got home, the soldiers found jobs and other opportunities. Some soldiers returned to the jobs they had before the war. Many chose to start their families. Marriage and birth rates in the country soared. The increased birth rate was called the Baby Boom. For these new families, finding housing was extremely important.

For the men returning to civilian life from the military, the government passed legislation to provide assistance. The G.I. Bill allowed veterans, or those who had served in the Armed Forces, to borrow money to buy homes. However, there weren't enough homes available for all the new families. A real estate company owned by William Levitt worked to build housing communities in several cities in the United States. These communities were called Levittowns. The first one was on Long Island in New York. The houses in Levittowns were affordable and convenient for new families. The developments were built close to cities in the surrounding countryside. Americans flocked to these housing developments. The new communities were called suburbs. They were planned communities and offered families a different kind of life than before the war.

Families in Levittowns settled down into their daily routines. The men worked while many women returned home to take care of the children. Some of the women decided to continue working outside of their homes. Money was no longer as scarce as it had been in the Great Depression. Now, families had money to spend on new, exciting things like store-bought clothing, dinners at restaurants, and appliances and furniture for their homes.

Extra money meant most families also owned automobiles. War technology had been used to make military vehicles like jeeps. Now, this technology was used to make cars look sleeker and move faster. Some of them even had air conditioning and radios. The automobile industry grew quickly.

People describe the time immediately after World War II as a time when life was better for Americans. This was true for many people. However, it was also a time when it became clear that not all Americans were being treated fairly. African Americans and other minorities (smaller groups of people differing in race, religion, language, or politics) were not always given equal opportunities. The country continued to strive for equality and freedom.

title: Interstate Highways & Suburbanization
text:
In 1919, Dwight D. Eisenhower was part of the military's first automobile caravan. It took them 62 days to get from Washington, D.C. to San Francisco because the roads weren't in good condition. When Eisenhower toured Germany after the war, he saw how well the Autobahn (German highways) had survived the bombs. They were made of strong materials like concrete and asphalt.

He saw the benefit of the U.S. having good roads like those in Germany. He convinced Congress that interstate highways would let the military get wherever they were needed quickly. The roads could also be used to evacuate people from the cities in case of emergencies. As a result, Congress passed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956. Under this law, any highway paid for by the government became an interstate highway.

States were responsible for the location and construction of the roads. Congress authorized a gasoline tax to help pay for the system. These taxes collected from American citizens raised 90 percent of the construction costs. State governments picked up the rest of the costs.

The Interstate Highway System Law required at least two lanes in each direction. The roads had to handle car speeds up to 70 miles per hour. They would not have any intersections or traffic lights. Instead, cars would enter the highway on long entrance ramps. This gave them enough room to reach the high speeds of other cars on the highway, so they could get on the highway without slowing down traffic. Likewise, when a car left the highway, it would now use an exit ramp so that cars could leave the highway without slowing down. This long off-ramp is called a controlled-access road. Planners gave north and south roads a two-digit odd number, while east and west roads had a two-digit even number. Beltways, which wrap around a city or region, had three numbers. The last two numbers matched the connecting main interstate.

The 46,000 miles of the Interstate Highway System took nearly three decades to complete. With these new roads constructed, American families of the 1950s began exploring the country. New highways and reliable automobiles made cross-country trips fast and easy. Families were now able to explore scenic wonderlands all across the nation. Prior to the war, Americans had only read about them. The interstate system also spawned new businesses. Roadside gas stations, motels, and restaurants popped up along the roads. Food, mail, consumer goods, and fresh produce could be transported faster. Billboards lined the roads, advertising nearly everything.

With access to these new roads, more and more families started to migrate to suburbs. Many people were attracted to the suburbs to raise their families in less crowded neighborhoods. Economic growth and the G.I. Bill allowed many more people to buy houses. By the end of the 1950s, more people owned their homes rather than renting them. However, living in suburban homes meant that people lived farther from work, shops, and other places they needed to go. Cars were necessary to live in the suburbs. Parents had to drive miles to work in many cases. Now that suburbs were the most popular place to live, many families were facing this situation. Urban workers who moved to the suburbs moved even farther away from their factories and offices. Reliance on cars also increased smog and traffic congestion. Fewer people used trains and buses.

Most importantly, America became a mobile society. People could go wherever they wanted whenever they wanted. Americans now had a sense of independence they had never known.

title: Development of the Middle Class
text:
Due to the security and prosperity of the 1950s, many Americans entered into a large middle class. The term “middle class” was used to describe a new postwar social class. They weren’t considered in poverty, yet they weren’t wealthy. They were in the middle.

Getting a higher education after high school was expensive. Few families could afford to send sons and daughters to get a four-year degree. After the war, veterans could use the G.I. Bill to get an education and find good job opportunities. Educational opportunities enabled more people to become professional businessmen, lawyers, or doctors. Many jobs in the fields of technology and business hadn’t even existed before the war. These jobs required highly skilled workers and paid very well. There was also more independence and choice in employment opportunities. The new middle class enjoyed a high level of economic security that had not been possible for many people in the past.

Many of the members of this new class were also starting families. Their steady incomes and affordable G.I. Bill loans allowed middle-class families to buy suburban homes and cars. By 1960, 60 percent of Americans owned their own homes rather than renting them. By 1950, one in every three women were in the workforce as well. With both husbands and wives working, the basic expenses of living could be met. This gave families extra money. This extra money was used to buy things for the home, recreation equipment, and conveniences like going to restaurants.

title: The G.I. Bill
text:
As the U.S. entered World War II, government leaders made a plan to care for returning soldiers. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944. However, most people called this act the G.I. Bill. After the war, veterans found themselves in new and different lives. The G.I. Bill made low interest loans available, which returning soldiers could use to buy a home or car, or pay for college. There were also funds to cover tuition and expenses for college or trade schools. With this plan in place, veterans were able to ease back into civilian life without worrying about finding a job immediately. They were able to make the transition from soldier to civilian more smoothly by taking classes and preparing themselves to work at stable, higher-paying jobs.

When government officials first began writing the G.I. Bill, they didn't expect that nearly 8 million members of the military would take advantage of the education benefits. Veterans studied hard and earned their degrees. They contributed to their local economies by buying goods and services from nearby businesses. They secured higher-paying jobs and paid taxes. Some opened their own businesses and hired others to work for them. They bought new cars and built houses filled with the newest inventions of the 1950s and 1960s.

Soon, the nation's economy was growing dramatically. Houses, highways and technology were creating an industry that needed more workers. The G.I. Bill helped many veterans gain financial stability.

However, African American veterans were not given the same opportunities in the G.I. Bill that their white comrades were given; banks, new housing, and new jobs were not centered in African American communities. The benefits were available in the legislation, but were not available in real life.

title: African American Soldiers Return
text:
In 1948, President Harry Truman signed Executive Order 9981. The order required every branch of the military to be open to all races, even during peacetime. This order ended segregation in the military. There would be no separate battalions for African Americans or Japanese Americans. All soldiers, sailors, and marines would train and live together.

This was a landmark decision. Many states had laws which legally prohibited such actions as using the same facilities. This was frequently seen in the southern states that had been part of the Confederacy of the Civil War. However, this also happened in America’s large cities such as New York, Chicago, San Francisco, and Seattle. Legal segregation of separate but equal was in each city's laws.

Housing loans that were provided in the G.I. Bill were denied to African American veterans. The loan was available on paper. In practice, personal prejudice and bias of bankers, real estate developers and investors kept non-white applicants from being accepted. The same bias and prejudice was evident in all other aspects of the G.I. Bill. Non-white veterans were unable to access the same opportunities as other veterans.

Organizations such as the NAACP gained membership to advocate for civil rights. Veterans came home and went on to play key roles in civil rights organizations. Hosea Williams was wounded in battle with General Patton’s Third Army. Medgar Evers, a veteran of the Red Ball Express, became a well-known activist for civil rights. Each veteran had gained experience which would help in their future fight for civil rights.

title: Life in the '50s
text:
As more and more people moved to the suburbs in the 1950s and 1960s, these areas quickly became self-contained. People didn't need to go to the city for entertainment and shopping anymore. These conveniences were often right around the corner.

Fast Food

The fast food industry grew out of post-war prosperity and changing consumer lifestyles during the 1950s and 1960s. Clever businessmen saw the potential of offering quick and inexpensive food to consumers. With families to feed, this idea appealed to many Americans. An increase in driving also influenced the growth of fast food. Sometimes, people wanted to eat a quick meal in their cars or grab something fast and cheap on their way home. Either way, fast food was often the solution.

In 1948, the first McDonald’s restaurant was opened in California by two brothers, Dick and Maurice McDonald. It was equipped with a “Speedee Service System.” This was an extremely efficient process for making three items: hamburgers, french fries, and milkshakes. This system had the customer coming to a window to place and pick up their order. This was a revolutionary concept in food service. By the early 1950s, their success had led to eight more McDonald’s restaurants in California.

In 1958, Ray Kroc, a wealthy businessman, helped the brothers establish McDonald’s restaurants outside of California. Three years later, Kroc bought the company. Inspired by McDonald’s success, many other companies got into the fast food business during the 1950s and 1960s.

Rock ‘n’ Roll

Rock and roll became the most popular music genre of the 1950s, especially among teenagers. This genre was born out of traditional African American R&B (rhythm and blues) and gospel music. However, the earliest African American rock and roll artists weren’t well-received due to racial discrimination. For this reason, many record producers in the 1950s tried to find a white performer to capture the African American sound. In 1954, Sam Phillips, a record producer in Tennessee, discovered Elvis Presley. Presley produced the sounds from rhythm and blues. The public went wild for the amazing sounds that came from a white singer. As rock and roll achieved public acceptance, some African American performers began to enjoy broad success as well. Artists like Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, and Little Richard were especially popular. However, white middle-class adults and churches often condemned rock and roll as tasteless. Still, teenagers in the 1950s and 1960s couldn’t get enough of it.

Drive-In Movies

In May of 1933, an auto parts salesman named Richard Hollingshead received a patent on a new outdoor movie theater. Less than a month later, he opened the first drive-in called Park-In Theaters in Camden, New Jersey. He charged 25 cents per car and 25 cents per person, but no group paid more than one dollar in total. His invention was a hit. When Hollingshead’s patent was overturned in 1949, anyone was allowed to copy his idea. Drive-in theaters started showing up everywhere.

The popularity of the drive-in hit its peak in the 1950s and 1960s. About 5,000 drive-in theaters operated across the nation. For many families living in suburbs, drive-ins were entertaining weekend retreats. The drive-in soon became a symbol of American culture of the time.

title: Television
text:
The 1950s were times of economic prosperity which allowed for the development of new industries and technologies. These technological changes brought convenience and comfort to many American homes. Arguably, the most significant and impactful innovation of all was the television.

During the postwar years, families with young children were more likely to spend their time at home. This created the perfect opportunity to introduce the television. People who already loved the radio could now see their favorite programs as well as hear them. Television also made it possible for news to be filmed and broadcast. As a result, many rushed to buy TV sets. Between 1950 and 1960, nearly 15 million TV sets were sold. Popular programs included I Love Lucy, Leave It to Beaver, and Father Knows Best. Children also loved shows like Davy Crocket and Roy Rogers. These programs portrayed simple, happy family life in the postwar decades. The shows contained stereotypes of suburban life and the white families who lived there.

However, when television became popular in the 1950s, not everyone was happy about it. Many people cautioned that the television would keep children watching programs for hours. They feared children would give up reading books, practicing music, or playing in the sunshine. Some critics considered the potentially damaging effects of fictional stories being believed as reality. Advertisers flooded television with messages that made smoking tobacco look harmless. Despite its critics, televisions were in family rooms all over America in the 1950s and 1960s.

title: Tribes of the Northwest
text:
Northwest peoples lived in a land full of plants, fish, and wild animals. Tribes such as the Tlingit, Haida, and Puyallup had very distinct cultures. They ate bear, elk, and deer. They fished in the rivers for salmon and captured whales and sea lions from the ocean. People used the land and resources around them to build their homes. Clothing was made from local materials, like woven grass and animal skins.

Tribes of the Northwest, like the Suquamish people, lived in shelters called longhouses during the fall and winter. During the spring and summer, they lived in portable shelters like tepees. Tepees are tall, cone-shaped houses made of stretched animal hides or woven plant fibers over a frame of wooden poles. Tepees were especially useful when hunting game because they could be set up and taken down quickly.

The tribes traveled frequently throughout the year, harvesting and securing food. They were very skilled at using natural resources to meet their needs.

The ocean, mountains, and land all are part of the history and traditions of these tribes. A unique tradition of the Northwest tribes is the building of totem poles. Totem poles help tell the tribes’ histories and stories.

title: Korea Splits
text:
The Korean people have a rich history and heritage. Their country was created when three kingdoms were united on the Korean peninsula in 918 A.D. The country has not had a peaceful history. It has been invaded by their neighbors the Mongols, the Manchurians, the Russians, and the Japanese.

In the early 20th century, war over Korea’s land and resources resulted in the Russo-Japanese War. Russia had no warm water ports to use in the winter when its existing ports were frozen. Czar Nicholas II, the Russian emperor, decided Korea would meet this need and attempted to capture the peninsula. The Japanese feared Russian expansion into the Pacific and declared war on Russia. In the end, a treaty was signed that left Korea vulnerable to a Japanese takeover.

The Korean Peninsula was invaded and taken over by Japan in 1910. The Japanese occupied Korea until 1945. The occupation was brutal. To maintain control of the Korean people, it became illegal to speak Korean in any public place. Everyone was forced to learn the Japanese language. People were required to change their Korean names into Japanese names. The Japanese also made it illegal to teach Korean history in schools. Multitudes of historical books and documents relating to the history of Korea were burned. Land was taken from Korean farmers and given to Japanese farmers who immigrated to Korea. Koreans were forced to work in Japan. Korean soldiers were required to fight against the American allies in World War II.

The war ended in the Pacific Theater in September of 1945 when the Allies defeated the Japanese. At the Yalta Conference in February of 1945, The Big Three Allied Powers decided that the Japanese would leave the Korean Peninsula. Korea would be temporarily divided into occupation zones like what had been done in Europe. The Soviet Union would occupy the land north of the 38th parallel, or the 38 degree latitude line. The land south of the 38th parallel would be occupied by the American military.

Over the next few years, Korean communists and Korean nationalists fought for political control of the country. A civil war resulted. The U.S. tried to negotiate with the Soviets on a plan to reunify the north and south, but the Soviets refused. In 1948, the U.S. reacted by setting up a democratic government in the South. The South Koreans elected Syngman Rhee as their president. In response, the Soviets set up a communist government in the north. They made a loyal Korean communist, Kim Il Sung, the leader. After elections in the south, the Soviets announced they would not support Rhee. They declared that Kim Il Sung was the true leader of all of Korea. The population of Korea could not agree.

Supported by the Soviet Union, the North Koreans invaded South Korea in 1950. They attempted to unite the two Koreas under communism. The new United Nations Organization became involved to secure peace. This became known as a police action, which technically was not a war. There were no declarations of war by any government. Through the United Nations, many countries became involved in the actions to stop communism. Active military movements ended in a mutual cease-fire in 1953. The cease-fire agreement created a buffer zone between north and south. The demilitarized zone separated the peninsula. They remain separated in the 21st century.

North Korea has become a very isolated country. The government controls movement into and out of the country. The communist government controls information to the people and the world. Some people have managed to escape, and they report that most North Koreans live in poverty.

South Korea continues to be supported by U.S. troops, who maintain several military bases there. The country has developed strong economic policies that produce and export many products throughout the world. Many Koreans still hope to unify the country one day.

title: Containment of Communism: the Domino Effect
text:
During the Cold War, the term “domino effect” was used to describe the spread of communism. If a person takes a set of dominoes and stands them on end in a row, then pushes the first one over, it topples into the second one. The second domino topples into the third, and so on. If the action is not stopped, the entire row of dominoes will fall. The free countries of the world feared the domino effect of communism. If the communists were able to take control of one country, then subsequent countries would fall to communist rule like dominoes.

The domino theory became reality on a summer day in June of 1950. On that day, 75,000 soldiers from the North Korea People’s Army crossed the 38th parallel from North Korea into South Korea. Historians consider this the first military action of the Cold War between the world’s superpowers, the Soviet Union and the United States.

At the end of World War II in 1945, Korea had been split into two countries in the north and south. The Soviets, under Joseph Stalin’s leadership, installed a Korean communist dictator to govern North Korea. Stalin followed with military support of the new government. On the other side of the border, American troops were in South Korea supporting its democratic government and rebuilding the country. There had been skirmishes along the border since the division of the country. Both sides wanted to unite the country, but they had very different political systems in mind.

When the North Korean troops crossed over the border, it shocked American officials. They saw this invasion as a step by the Soviets to spread communism throughout the world. The U.S. felt they had to intervene. The United Nations recommended that the U.S. use military force to “contain” the communist expansion.
