title: The History of Pennsylvania Oil Industry
text:
Pennsylvania has abundant deposits of oil and gas deposits under the Allegheny Plateau. Native Americans were the first people to use the oil and gas deposits that seeped to the surface. The Seneca tribe collected the the oil and stored it in containers. The oil was used for medicinal purposes. As a result, early European settlers called the oil collected by the Native Americans "Seneca Oil."

At first, European settlers did not see the need for oil. The settlers needed salt to preserve food. Iron tools were made that could drill into the ground for “salt wells”. However in Pennsylvania, the oil created a problem. James Kennedy was a salt well worker near Tarentum, PA, "[The oil] had never been seen in salt wells, and they were afraid that it might ruin the salt works... It just came right up and out of the ground along with the salt water as it was pumped by the engine. It got to be a nuisance, for we were after salt water then, and didn't want anything else."

Samuel Kier took the oil from his salt wells and started selling it as “Kier’s Petroleum, or Rock Oil” cure-all tonic. It took a group of rowdy young men to show that the oil could be ignited and burn for a long time. This caused many eager entrepreneurs or business person to experiment with the crude oil. Through experimentation it was found that refining or heating the oil could change it. This removed some of the disagreeable smell. It also allowed the oil to burn more controllably and brighter. Further experimentation proved that a substance called kerosene could be produced. Kerosene could be used in lamps to light the darkness. However, the oil was still a by-product of salt wells.

Colonel Edwin Drake teamed up with James Townsend, a banker to finance a drilling rig, in 1859. On Saturday, August 27, 1859, Drake and Townsend struck oil near Titusville, Pennsylvania. The great oil boom had begun. The area near Titusville boomed with oil rigs and drilling crews. Farmers pastures were filled with drilling rigs. Towns were created overnight with people coming and making a claim for oil. There were few rules and no laws in these new towns. People would destroy other drillers equipment. Fire was the greatest danger that would destroy an entire drilling town.

Many other businesses were created because of the oil drillers. A refinery was needed to make kerosene. Barrels were needed to store the oil. Wagons and horses were needed for transport. Eventually, a railroad was built to the most successful towns. Pipelines were used to transport oil from areas unreachable by roads. Iron tank cars were created to transport large quantities of oil.

From this rapidly growing economy millions of dollars was made and lost. Eventually, one man emerged to create order in this chaos. John D. Rockefeller organized Standard Oil in the 1870’s and grew to dominate the oil business for the rest of his long life. Pennsylvania oil would transform the nation to become dependent upon oil for its energy needs.

title: Interest
text:
Did you know that you can earn income by lending someone some of your money? Interest is another form of income that people might earn. Sometimes, people need to borrow money in order to buy things they need or want. They may borrow money from a bank, a company, or another person, who is often called a lender. The loan, or money borrowed, must be paid back to the lender within a certain amount of time.

The person borrowing money has to pay interest on the loan. Interest is the amount of money a lender or financial institution receives for lending out money. For example, if a person borrows $100 from a bank, the bank will charge interest on that loan. When that person pays back the loan, they will have to pay $100 plus the interest charged. You might be wondering where banks get the money that they loan to people and business. That money can come from you. If you have a bank account that earns interest, the bank pays you to allow them to use your money.

title: Midwest
text:
The Midwestern states are different from the rest of the nation. They feature fertile soil, big rivers, and thousands of lakes. The Midwestern region contains 12 states. Half of these states border the Great Lakes. These states are Minnesota, Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, and Ohio. States that don't border the Great Lakes are North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri, and Iowa.

The Great Lakes are an important physical feature of the Midwest. The term “great” is no exaggeration. They are so big that at their widest points, you cannot see the other side. Lakes Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, and Superior hold more than 80 percent of the fresh water in the United States. The Great Lakes provide drinking water for 48 million Americans and Canadians. They have a big impact on the economy of the Midwest. More than $50 billion is spent on recreation at the Great Lakes each year. Fishing and boating are two of the biggest activities. It is estimated that over one million jobs are connected to the Great Lakes.

Many of the states in this region have rich, fertile soil. Where does it come from? The rivers provide it. Three of the largest rivers in the U.S. cross the Midwest. The Missouri, the Mississippi, and the Ohio rivers help drain the lands. Regular flooding deposits nutrients into the soil. Parts of the region get heavy rainfall in the spring and summer. These rivers carry that water away. Unfortunately, annual flooding can cause major issues for people who live in those areas. Both the Missouri and the Ohio are tributaries of the Mississippi. This means they flow into the Mississippi. The Mississippi eventually flows south into the Gulf of Mexico.

Part of the Midwest region is very hilly. South Dakota’s Black Hills feature the rugged Badlands National Park. Rolling hills can be found in many states. Some of these are the remains of glaciers. As glaciers inched forward thousands of years ago, they left their mark on much of the Midwest. Flat land can make for good farming, but the landscape also produces lots of wind. Many states have fields of wind turbines that produce electricity as they spin. Other types of wind common to the Midwest are not so helpful. Tornadoes are a dangerous menace across the Midwest. They have been known to strike in nearly every state. Tornadoes seem to occur frequently in this region during May and June.

title: Southeast
text:
The Southeast region has 12 states. The inner southeast states are Arkansas, Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia. Eight southeastern states border either the Atlantic Ocean or the Gulf of Mexico. The states that border the Gulf of Mexico are Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana. The states that border the Atlantic Ocean are Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida.

Water is a great resource for both work and play in the Southeast. Fishing and visiting the beach are very popular activities. Florida borders both the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. Its beaches are world-famous. North Carolina’s beaches are historic. The Wright Brothers flew the world’s first airplane at Kitty Hawk on North Carolina’s Outer Banks.

Agriculture is a major industry in the Southeast. This region has mild winters and hot, humid summers. This makes the Southeast an ideal spot to grow crops. The Southeast has long been known for growing cotton. Did you know the nation’s peanut supply comes from the Southeast? Georgia farmers produce nearly half of all peanuts grown in the U.S. The area has hundreds of thousands of acres of mostly flat land dedicated to growing cotton and peanuts. Other important crops are corn, sorghum, and citrus crops, like oranges and grapefruit.

Many businesses have opened up in this part of the country. Why here? People like to live in places with good weather that offer many things to do. Automobile manufacturing is an important industry in the Southeast. Eleven different car companies have factories in the region. They have thousands of people working for them. All those people build more than one million cars each year. Other big employers with headquarters in the region are banks, beverage companies, and retail stores.

title: Southwest
text:
The states that belong to the Southwest region are Arizona, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas. This region uses its natural resources to make products and provide services. Mining and oil drilling are very important. Texas and Oklahoma produce much of the nation’s oil. The Southwest is also rich in minerals, such as coal, copper, and silver. Mining and oil companies provide jobs for workers in this region. These companies also sell their products to other companies throughout the nation and the world.

Most of the land in the Southwest is too dry to grow crops naturally. There are some areas that receive enough rainfall water. However, others use irrigation ditches and canals. This helps to bring water in from other places to grow crops. The Southwest grows many crops. These include cotton, lettuce, melons, grapefruit, onions, nuts, hay, and more. These crops are shipped across the nation and the world. This brings millions of dollars into the Southwest’s economy. Ranchers here also raise dairy and beef cattle, pigs, sheep, and chickens. If you eat brown shrimp, chances are they were caught along the Texas coast!

Tourism brings millions of dollars into the economy of the Southwest. Tourists from colder climates enjoy visiting these states during the winter months. When it is cold and snowy back home, it is often warm and pleasant in the Southwest. Visitors come to the Southwest to see Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona and Carlsbad Caverns National Park in New Mexico. These locations and many others bring money into the economy. They also provide jobs for people in the area.

title: Human-Environment Interaction
text:
An important theme of geography is human-environment interaction. Humans have basic needs. We need food, clothing, and a place to live. The physical environment, including landforms, climate, and weather, influences where people settle, their jobs, and their lifestyles.

If you live on the beach, your environment includes the ocean, the fish, the trees, and the wind. We rely on resources in our environment to meet our needs. People who live near the ocean often eat fish. They use the wind to power sailboats. They use wood from trees to build homes to protect themselves from stormy weather. People usually choose to live close to resources that help them meet their basic needs.

title: Draw, Label, and Write
text:
Illustrate the landforms and natural features discussed in the articles. Use the information you learned this week about landforms and natural features to help you.

Choose one of the claims you made in the Shaping California graphic organizer. Write a paragraph that explains your illustration. Be sure to include the names of the natural features that you drew in your illustration. (mountain, valley, biomes)

title: Trade Routes, Water, and Transportation
text:
For thousands of years, people in communities produced most of the things that they needed. Later, as civilizations expanded, people learned that they could specialize in one thing and then trade with others. Soon, trading became so common that some people did nothing but conduct trade. These people were called merchants.

In the 1400s, the whole world was on the move. In the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, empires were growing. Rich empires served as patrons. This meant they could pay people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and exchanges of ideas through trade routes.

A trade route is an area used by merchants for economic purposes. The voyages of Christopher Columbus and other explorers opened trade routes between the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere. Many explorers hoped to find a waterway across North America to increase trade between Europe and Asia. They were not successful. However, they did discover many resources and new sources of trade across the continent.

Accessible waterways made European colonization of the Americas possible. Access to water also greatly influenced where people settled. Many of the first colonies in North America were located near bodies of water. Fresh water provided settlers with many of the resources they required to meet their basic needs. Eventually, waterways became the primary mode of transportation for the colonists in North America and greatly influenced trade. Today, waterways still play a vital role in trading operations across the United States and the world.

Early settlers used waterways for trade and transportation. However, they also utilized trade routes developed by American Indian tribes in North America. For thousands of years, American Indians operated huge trade networks to get what they needed from other people in the Americas. We still use a lot of native trails and trade routes. Many major city roads, railroad lines, and interstate systems follow the same paths American Indians took thousands of years ago.

Advances in transportation also played a significant role in settlement. For thousands of years, traveling by boat was much easier and more reliable than traveling overland. New forms of technology increased settlement in many areas of the United States. Covered wagons, such as the Conestoga and prairie schooners, made transportation easier in the 19th century, but overland journeys continued to be long and dangerous.

The invention of the steam engine revolutionized transportation and trade. The steam engine was used to create better transportation on water and on land. When this engine was put into a boat, it could move through the water without depending on the wind or currents. The steam locomotive could move more cargo and do it faster than horses or oxen could. Transporting goods and people became faster.

The steam engine led to large networks of railroads that stretched from coast to coast. The completion of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869 made transportation and trade even easier. This railroad connected economic centers on the East Coast with new markets along the West Coast. Thousands of settlers took advantage of the possibilities opened up to them by the Transcontinental Railroad.

The construction of new railroads across the country greatly increased trade and transportation. New towns and cities developed as a result of the railroad. The invention of the automobile in the late 1800s increased trade and made transportation even easier. This technology required new and more reliable roads. Highways were constructed across states. Eventually, the interstate highway system connected many of these highways.

Trade and transportation have changed drastically from the time of European exploration to the present.

title: The Constitution of the United States of America
text:
The Constitution consists of the preamble, seven articles, and 27 amendments. The preamble explains the purpose of the document. The seven articles lay out the three branches of government and the rules for each branch. The 27 amendments guarantee the rights of the people. The amendments have been added as the nation has grown. The amendments give clarity and specific rules to the government.

Article 1: The Legislative Branch

“All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”

Section 1: Grants Congress the power to make laws in two organized parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Section 2: The House of Representatives is defined. The election of members is every two years. Each member must be at least 25 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least seven years.

The number of representatives will be determined by the population “... of free persons, including those bound to Service for a term of years [indentured] and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of other persons.” The country will be counted every 10 years in a census. If there is a vacancy from any state, the executive branch will call for an election. The House of Representatives will have the sole power of impeachment (to challenge and investigate a member of government).

Section 3: The Senate is defined. Each state will have two elected senators to Congress for a six-year term. Each senator must be at least 30 years old and a citizen of the United States for at least nine years. The vice president of the executive branch will be president of the Senate. The vice president may only vote to break a tie. The Senate will also elect a president to serve in the absence of the vice president. The Senate will have the sole power to try all impeachments. Impeachment will not extend to more than a removal from office in the government.

Section 4: Congress will meet at least once every year on the first Monday in December.

The remaining six sections define the rules and responsibilities of each group in the system of checks and balances. They help to keep power distributed across the branches of government. There are clear directions on what Congress is forbidden to do. Only Congress can raise and spend money. Congress is responsible for the Army, Navy, Marines, Air Force, and Coast Guard. The representatives of the people are in charge of the military. The final section closes with powers forbidden to the states.

Article 2: The Executive Branch

“The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America. He shall hold his Office during the Term of four Years, and, together with the Vice President, chosen for the same Term.”

Section 1: A person who is a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for 14 years can work for the executive office. Once elected, the president shall take the following oath or affirmation: "I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the Office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my Ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States."

Section 2: Sets up the president as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces. It further defines the powers within the office for hiring people for government posts with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Section 3: The president is required to give information on the state of the Union to Congress.

Section 4: "The President, Vice President, and all civil Officers of the United States shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors."

Article 3: The Judicial Branch

“The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.”

As established under Article 2, the president will nominate a judge for the judicial branch. The nominee must then be confirmed through the Senate.

Section 2: The office of the judiciary will extend to all cases of law arising under the Constitution. It also covers the laws of the United States and all controversies between the state, citizens and states, and citizens and citizens.

Section 3: Treason against the United States is defined. Treason is giving aid and comfort to enemies or waging war against the United States.

title: Relations of the States to Each Other
text:
“The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.”

Article 4: Establishes relations between the states. It also defines the state's relations with the federal government.

Section 1: All legal documents in one state must be accepted by the other states.

Section 2: Criminals must be returned to their state of citizenship by state law enforcement agencies. Any person held to service or labor who escapes to another state will be delivered to the person who claims their labor.

Section 3: Admission of new states to the Union is held in Congress. Congress can change any state boundaries when deemed necessary. State constitutions are to be a representative democracy like the federal government. The states will be protected by the national government against invasion or violence within the state.

title: The History of Electricity at the White House
text:
The White House was originally constructed in 1792 to serve as the home of the president of the United States. The White House has gone through extensive changes during its over 200-year history. One of the greatest changes was the energy source that powered one of the most important buildings in the United States. The first sources of energy used in the White House were candles and eventually oil lamps. That all changed with the introduction of electricity in 1891.

Sept. 14, 1891: Electricity was first installed in the White House. At this time, many people were afraid that they would be electrocuted by the electric surge of energy running through their homes and businesses. President Benjamin Harrison and his wife, Caroline were no exception. They feared that they would be electrocuted by this new source of energy and refused to touch the light switches themselves.

1926: During the presidency of Calvin Coolidge, the first electric refrigerator was installed in the White House.

1933: Air conditioning was installed in the private rooms of the White House during Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s first term in office.

1948-1952: The White House underwent a major renovation. New electrical systems were installed throughout and updated fixtures and features were added.

1979: Energy production moved toward conservation with the installation of solar panels on the roof of the west wing. The solar panels were installed to heat the water in the White House staff cafeteria and dining area.

1993: Upon moving into the White House, President Bill Clinton attempted to conserve energy through various projects. Energy-efficient windows were installed; a new air conditioning system replaced the old, ineffective system; and all the lightbulbs were replaced with energy-efficient bulbs.

2003: Toward the end of his first term in office, President George W. Bush installed the first solar electric system in the White House, which included 167 solar panels on the roof of the maintenance facility to power the building. Solar systems were also installed to heat the water for the White House pool and spa.

2008: The famous lantern on the White House portico was updated and new light-emitting diode (LED) lights were installed. LED light bulbs use 75 percent less energy and last 25 times longer than incandescent light bulbs.

2014: Solar panels were installed on the main building of the White House during President Barack Obama’s second term in office, providing 6.3 kilowatts of solar energy. This is enough energy to power a 2,000 square-foot home.

title: Thinking About Myself
text:
To gain a sense of self is to look within and understand yourself. Using inquiry is a great way to learn more about yourself. Write your answers to the following questions on the figure:

Who am I?

Who do I want to be?

What are my strengths? What am I good at?

What are my weaknesses? What do I want to work on?

What do I like?

What do I dislike?

Try saying this in your mind:

I LOVE WHO I AM!

When you know who you are and what you like, you develop self-awareness! Looking deeper is called research. When you add research to your sense of self, you can explore new information to make the best choices possible.

title: Framing Question
text: What are some celebrations that represent your traditions?

title: Holidays and Celebrations
text: Every country has holidays. Every country has celebrations. We celebrate people. We celebrate important events. We celebrate time passing.

title: Mardi Gras
text: Mardi Gras is celebrated in Louisiana. It is also celebrated in other states. There are parades. It takes place on a Tuesday in February or March. This holiday happens the day before Lent starts.

title: Juneteenth
text: Juneteenth is a short way of saying "June nineteenth." It is a day for people to celebrate freedom. It is a day to celebrate African American history and culture. In 2021, it became an official national holiday.

title: Columbus Day
text: In October, we celebrate Columbus Day. Christopher Columbus was an explorer. He lived over 500 years ago. He sailed across the Atlantic Ocean. He explored the Americas.

title: Thanksgiving
text: We celebrate Thanksgiving in November. We are thankful for what we have.

title: Christmas Day
text: Christmas Day is on December 25. People often give each other presents. They decorate trees. They decorate their homes. People celebrate with their family and friends.

title: New Year’s Day
text: Many countries celebrate the New Year. We celebrate the start of a new year. We think about how we want to be better.

title: Independence Day
text: Many countries celebrate their independence. They each celebrate the day they became a country.

title: Framing Question
text: How do people interact with their environment?

title: People and the Environment
text: People change things around them. They make changes to meet their needs. This is human-environment interaction.

title: Places to Enjoy
text: Humans can build places to have fun. Playgrounds and parks are fun. They are human characteristics.

title: Urban Community
text: You can live in an urban community. It is a big city. It has many houses. It has tall apartments. Many people live there.

title: Suburban Community
text: You can live in a suburban community. It is near a big city. It has houses. It has apartments. They are not as tall as city buildings.

title: Rural Community
text: You can live in a rural community. It is not a big city. It has houses. It has farms, too.

title: Resources
text: Resources are things we use to make what we need. Resources also help us have what we want.

title: Natural Resources
text: Natural resources come from nature. Plants and animals are natural resources. Air and water are natural resources.

title: Jefferson Becomes President
text:
The election of Thomas Jefferson in 1800 was the first peaceful transfer of power for the United States. There were many disagreements over the presidency between the two major political parties, the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans, or Anti-Federalists. After many weeks, both sides came to a compromise and Jefferson was elected president. Jefferson was a firm believer in the tenets of the Constitution. He wished to strengthen these principles through his presidency. His first goal as president was to create peaceful cooperation between the Federalists and the Democratic Republicans. This was not an easy task. In many ways, it wasn't successful because both groups had opposing beliefs and ideas.

Jefferson also had to attend to U.S. foreign policy issues. Foreign policy is how one country interacts with other countries. During his second term, Washington signed a Proclamation of Neutrality that prevented the United States from entering foreign conflicts. Jefferson agreed that the United States should remain neutral and not enter foreign wars. France and Great Britain were at war with one another. The United States refused to enter the conflict.

Jefferson and his cabinet hoped to maintain a friendship with both countries. This angered Great Britain. The British Navy blockaded European ports. This affected American trade immensely. The British also seized American goods and forced American sailors to work on British vessels. In response, Jefferson asked Congress to expand the U.S. Navy and restrict the import of goods from Great Britain.

Jefferson served a second term as president from 1804 to 1808. Hostilities between France and Great Britain continued, as did their issues with U.S. neutrality. Both countries attacked American ships and seized their cargo. Jefferson encouraged Congress to act. In 1807, the government passed the Embargo Act. An embargo is an order to stop ships from delivering goods. The law stated that goods couldn't be shipped to any foreign port.

The United States hoped that both France and Great Britain would be devastated without American supplies. Unfortunately, the Embargo Act backfired. Great Britain and France survived without U.S. goods. The U.S. economy, on the other hand, suffered greatly due to the act, angering American citizens. President Jefferson repealed the Embargo Act before leaving office in March of 1809.

title: Ethnic and Racial Relations
text:
During the early 1900s, racial and ethnic conflict grew in the United States. During the early years of the century, immigration to the United States increased. More people from other countries were arriving, looking for new opportunities. These immigrants were changing the demographics of the country. In addition to these new citizens, there was a large Black population still struggling against mistreatment and a lack of equality and opportunities. As the 1900s progressed, conflict continued around racial and ethnic relations in the United States.

Roosevelt faced many of these ethnic and racial issues during his presidency. In an effort to identify and address issues specific to Black Americans, he created what was known as the Black Cabinet. A president’s cabinet is a group of people who advise the president and lead various governmental departments. Roosevelt’s Black Cabinet was a group of African American leaders who were brought together to advocate for the needs of Black people in the country. This group included important figures like Mary McLeod Bethune and other African American government officials.

When the government passed policies and made efforts to try and help people recover from the Great Depression, the Black Cabinet advocated for assistance to be given to the African American community as well. Before this, African Americans were often intentionally or accidentally excluded from benefiting from these programs. They also lacked access to educational opportunities and voting. In addition to these issues, segregation was still enforced in many parts of the country, which legally excluded African Americans from certain public and private places.

Through the efforts of Black Cabinet members, government employment programs that helped people get work were opened to African Americans when they might otherwise have been excluded. Despite some successes, Black Cabinet members faced conflict when attempting to accomplish their goals. Exclusion and inequality continued for African Americans in the United States.

Another racial and ethinc issue arose for Roosevelt during the days and months following the Japanese attack on American naval and air bases in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. This attack brought the United States into World War II. During the wave of immigration in the 1900s, thousands of Japanese citizens came to the United States, with many earning citizenship or having children who became citizens.

Although there was no evidence that people of Japanese descent were untrustworthy, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 3066, an order that forced the removal of people of Japanese descent from Pacific Coast states like California, Oregon, and Washington. It did not matter if they were born in Japan or the United States or whether they were citizens or not. The U.S. Army set up camps in remote western states like Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming. Over 120,000 people were held against their will in these camps.

title: Europeans Came to North America
text:
Many European explorers came to North America on boats. These ships landed in natural harbors on the East and West Coasts. On the East Coast, many of the explorers were from France, England, the Netherlands, and Spain. Spanish explorers also traveled along the west coast. Some explorers came by land. They traveled north from what is now Mexico or south from what is now Canada.

People from all over the world came to North America. They wanted to settle on land where Indigenous tribes were already living. There was great conflict over the land and the right to live there. The newcomers brought diseases that infected the Native Americans. It is thought that up to 90 percent of Native Americans in some areas died from such diseases. Weakened and outnumbered, the Indigenous peoples had their land taken by the new settlers.

title: Goods and Services
text:
People use resources to produce goods and services to provide for their needs and wants. Goods are things made for people to buy and use. Goods include food, furniture, and houses. Services are work that a person does for someone else. Services are actions like cutting hair, repairing cars, and teaching.

In the United States, there are private and public goods and services. Private goods and services are provided by businesses. You buy them, and then you own them. Private goods include things like clothing, cars, and toys.

Public goods and services are paid for by taxes, not individuals. They are shared by the community. Schools, police stations, and public transportation are public goods. Another example is your public library. The items at the library belong to the community. It doesn't cost you money to borrow things from your local library. The government provides this service to the community through money collected from taxes.

title: Capital Resources
text: Capital resources are the tools that help us make other things. These items are human-made. This means they do not occur naturally in the environment. They need to be created before they can be used. Capital resources include tools, buildings, or machines. Machines like lawn mowers or ovens are capital resources. Buildings like factories and warehouses are other examples.

title: Acadians
text: Long ago, many people came to Louisiana from Canada. They were called Acadians. They built new homes. They settled new towns. Some Acadians became farmers. Some hunted and fished.

title: Framing Question
text: How do individuals and groups contribute to a culture?

title: Africans
text: Many people came to Louisiana from Africa. They brought their traditions with them. They brought their cuisine. They brought their languages. They shared their culture with others.

title: Canary Islanders
text: Hundreds of years ago, another group came to Louisiana. They were from the Canary Islands. They crossed the ocean on boats. Their relatives still live in Louisiana. They celebrate their culture every year.

title: French
text: Louisiana used to be ruled by France. France is a country in Europe. The king of France sent people to create new towns. Settlers sailed to Louisiana in ships. Many town and street names are French. Many people in Louisiana speak French today.

title: Germans
text: German settlers first came to Louisiana hundreds of years ago. Germany is a country near France. Settlers brought music with them. They brought food they liked to eat. They made buildings that looked like buildings in Germany.

title: Haitians
text: Haiti is an island in the Caribbean Sea. Haiti was once part of France. Many people left Haiti and came to Louisiana. They brought their customs and traditions with them. People still move from Haiti to Louisiana today.

title: Native Americans
text: Native Americans have lived in Louisiana for thousands of years. They built settlements across the state. They grew crops. They hunted and fished for food. Many landforms and towns still have Native American names. Town names like “Natchitoches” and “Houma” come from Native American languages.

title: Asian Americans
text: Many Asian Americans live in Louisiana. They came from countries all over Asia. Some settlers came from the Philippines. They brought their culture and traditions. They built a town near New Orleans. It was the first Asian settlement in North America.

title: Spanish
text: Spain once owned parts of North America. Spanish settlers came to Louisiana. They built large farms. They raised cattle. Some places in Louisiana have Spanish names. “Capitan Parish” comes from the Spanish word for "captain." Galvez, Louisiana was named for a famous Spanish general.

title: What If You Lose Motivation?
text:
What if your motivation fades?

Choose your favorite ideas to help you get it back:

Take a break. Try again when you feel calm.

Remember why you are doing this. What really matters to you?

Break tasks up into smaller steps. Take them one at a time.

Make it fun! Can you make a game out of it? Can you listen to music? Be creative!

title: Celebrations and Holidays
text:
Every country has holidays and celebrations. Holidays celebrate important events. They celebrate time passing. They celebrate people.

The United States has patriotic holidays, too. These holidays honor important people. They honor events in our history.

title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
text: Martin Luther King Jr. believed all people should have the same rights. He worked hard. He shared his beliefs. He taught us to respect all people.

title: Independence Day
text: July 4 is Independence Day. It celebrates the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Families and friends watch fireworks. Communities have parades.

title: Washington's Birthday
text: George Washington was the first president of the United States. We celebrate his birthday in February. It has been a national holiday for over 100 years. We can celebrate Washington by learning about him. We can learn about things he did for our country.

title: Memorial Day
text: Many people have died serving our country. We remember them on Memorial Day. Memorial Day is in May.

title: Labor Day
text: Workers have made our country strong. We celebrate them on Labor Day. Labor Day is in September.

title: Veterans Day
text: Veterans Day is on November 11. It is a day for honoring people in the military. We honor people who served in the past. We also honor people who are serving now.

title: Thanksgiving
text: We celebrate Thanksgiving in November. On Thanksgiving, we can be grateful for the things that we have.

title: Treatment of Diverse Groups in the Colonies
text:
As the colonies grew, they attracted people from all over Europe. Early colonists sailed from England, Ireland, and Scotland. Over time, more traveled from the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Sweden. Thousands of immigrants journeyed to the Americas seeking new opportunities. People came from diverse cultures with different backgrounds and belief systems. Jewish people settled mainly in port cities like New Amsterdam (now, New York City) or Newport, Rhode Island. They were especially attracted to colonies founded on religious freedom. Some colonies, like Georgia, had charters that promised religious liberty to all people. Not all migrants were welcomed into the colonies or treated fairly, though. The poor and the powerless were often mistreated in the colonies, just as they had been in England.

Women were expected to follow strict guidelines of behavior. These guidelines restricted women to certain roles. They were expected to perform household chores like cooking, cleaning, and laundry. Women could wash other people’s laundry to earn money or food. They could also be midwives, who deliver babies, because these jobs were considered suitable for women. Women couldn’t have any rights unless they were married or had a male guardian.

A lot of people died of disease or starvation in the early colonies. Parents lost children, and children lost parents. Orphaned children often became servants for other families so they could survive. They had few rights until they married.

Most colonists didn’t trust people who were not residents. The law was not kind to a person without a home. Strangers were treated with suspicion. A person who could not pay their way or was deep in debt would be imprisoned until the debt could be paid.

English colonial leaders never accepted American Indians as citizens in their towns. American Indians were not seen as equals to white European settlers. Some were even enslaved by the colonists.

Most African Americans in the colonies were enslaved people. A few were born free, bought their freedom, or were set free by their enslavers. African Americans were rarely accepted by white colonists.

title: Mardi Gras
text: Mardi Gras is a special holiday in Louisiana. People celebrate with music. They celebrate with food. There are many traditions. A community in North Louisiana has a special parade. Their parade has a royal court of pets. In southwestern Louisiana, people dress in colorful costumes. They gather ingredients to make gumbo.

title: Columbus Day
text: Columbus Day is the second Monday of October. It celebrates Christopher Columbus. He was an explorer. Over 500 years ago, he sailed across the Atlantic Ocean. He explored the Americas.

title: Inauguration Day
text: People elect a president of the United States every four years. Inauguration Day is January 20, after the election. This is the day the elected person becomes president. They are "sworn in." This means they repeat an oath, or promise.

title: Christmas Day
text: Christmas Day is celebrated on December 25th. People often celebrate with family and friends. Many people give each other presents. They put up decorations, like Christmas trees and lights.

title: The Anishinaabe or Chippewa
text:
Michigan is home to several tribes of the Chippewa (Ojibwe) people. The Chippewa people are part of the 12 federally-acknowledged American Indian tribes in Michigan. Some groups of the Chippewa have schools that teach children about their tribe’s culture. They also teach children how to use natural resources responsibly. Tribal nations have departments that help them get the most out of their natural resources. The native people believe that anything they take from nature must be returned to it.

The Chippewa use land to build museums and parks. These help to keep their culture alive. Members of the community and tourists visit these museums and parks for recreation, where they can learn about the Chippewa people.

Today, members of the Chippewa tribes work as scientists, professors, and doctors. Others serve in the military. Many also own their own businesses. Some are teachers, nurses, and factory workers, too. There are also those who work in farming, fishing, and hunting.

Today, the Chippewa have diverse beliefs. Many have added ideas from other religions into their traditional practices. They celebrate their traditional festivals together. One type of traditional festival is called a powwow. The powwows in Michigan are open to the public. Look for one to join and celebrate with the Chippewa Tribe.

title: Oceans and Coasts
text:
Water is a natural resource. Water can change landforms. The water from different mountain streams connects to form a river. Rivers connect to form larger rivers. Rivers make routes to lakes and oceans. Oceans are bodies of saltwater. Oceans cover most of the Earth's surface.

The edge of the land beside a stream or river is called a bank or shore. The edge of the land beside the ocean is called a coast. Coasts are many miles long. Coasts make up the border between continents and oceans.

title: Urban Communities
text: People form communities based on how they use the land. When many people want to live in one location, the land is known as an urban area. Urban areas can also be called cities. In cities, buildings for business and homes are developed to be close together. Tall buildings with many floors, or stories, are built so many people can live on smaller pieces of land. Transportation in urban areas is organized to move as many people and goods as possible in and out of the city. There is less land available to grow food in urban areas. Food for many people has to be brought into the city.

title: Framing Question
text: Why do we celebrate patriotic holidays?

title: Inauguration Day
text: Inauguration Day is an important day. It is celebrated every four years. It happens in January. It is a ceremony to celebrate the new president of the United States.

title: Pontiac
text:
Pontiac was a Native People chief of the Ottawa tribe. Ottawa comes from the Algonquin word "Adawe" meaning "to trade.” Their name originates from their role as traders even before they met the French. Pontiac saw how trading with the Europeans made his people dependent on European goods. He urged his people to go back to the Ottawa heritage of living off the land.

When the French left after the French and Indian War, Pontiac knew his people had lost their protection against the British. He worried that the Ottawa would lose their culture and their land to these enemies.

Pontiac spoke to the Wyandot, Shawnee, Seneca, and other Native American nations. He said they should unite against the British. Many listened. Warfare began, and many died fighting for western lands. This three-year war was known as “Pontiac's Rebellion.”

In the end, the Native Peoples couldn’t win against the British military. There were no weapons or ammunition coming from their French allies. Pontiac negotiated with the British to bring no more conflict to the frontier. Pontiac spent the remainder of his life with his family near the Maumee River in what became Indiana and Ohio.

title: Taxes and Tyranny
text:
Colonists in America and the British Parliament were in a constant struggle over taxes in the 1770s. The Townshend Acts, passed in 1767, put taxes on many household items, such as paint, glass, and tea. Colonists didn’t want to pay taxes on items sold by the British. They decided to boycott them, or refuse to buy them. The boycott of British goods by the colonists ended up being very effective. The Townshend Acts were repealed, or reversed, in 1773. Parliament still insisted they had the privilege of taxing the colonies, though. To make this point, Parliament passed the Tea Act and continued to tax tea for the colonists.

The boycott of British goods hurt the profits of many companies. One company, the East India Company, had influence with the British government. The company’s directors convinced Parliament to help them out with the Tea Tax of 1773. This act taxed tea but also supported the East India Company. Parliament and the king said that the East India Company was the only company that could import tea to the colonies. This created a monopoly, meaning no one else was selling the same product.

Before the Tea Act was passed, tea was imported to America by individual merchants. Chests of tea were auctioned to merchants in London. The auctions were open to all businessmen, who bought the tea at competitive prices. The merchants paid the tax and included the tax in the price they charged for the tea.

The Tea Act took away all competitive buying from merchants. It meant that all the profits made from the tea would be given to the East India Company and their chosen agents in the colonies.

Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Charleston were selected as places for the delivery of the tea. The royal governors of the colonies selected the agents who would purchase and resell the tea. Governors selected friends and men loyal to the king to be tea agents. Colonists were angry. They saw this tax as a way for people loyal to the king to get rich and make the colonists pay for it.

The ships with the cargo of tea chests were scheduled to arrive in the colonies in November 1773. Everyone was making plans: Parliament, the East India Company, tea agents, and the Sons of Liberty. A tea storm was brewing.

title: The Intolerable Acts
text:
In response to the damage of the tea cargo in Boston, Parliament created the Coercive Acts. These acts were designed by King George III to punish Massachusetts colonists for the tea party and their continued resistance to his actions and his government. Because of this, the acts also became known as the “Intolerable Acts.”

The following was directed at Massachusetts:

Boston Port Act (June 1, 1774): closed off the port of Boston, eliminating commerce and trade in the city.

Administration of Justice Act (May 20, 1774): granted a change of location to Great Britain or a British Colony in the event of a jury trial.

Massachusetts Government Act (May 20, 1774): repealed the colony’s charter and created an unprecedented amount of royal control.

Quartering Act (June 2, 1774): allowed new royal governor General Thomas Gage to house British soldiers in private homes, inns, and other buildings without permission from colonists.

Quebec Act (June 22, 1774): designated the western region north of the Ohio River as part of Quebec and made Roman Catholicism the established religion of Quebec; this upset colonial Protestants.

Each colonial legislature called for a meeting of representatives. This was called the First Continental Congress. Representatives gathered in Carpenters' Hall in Philadelphia on Sept. 5, 1774. Twelve of the 13 colonies sent delegates.

The first order of business was to write a petition to King George to remove the recent Acts applied to Massachusetts. Each colony had protested the Tea Act in some manner, but Massachusetts was receiving the punishment. The delegates at the congress knew the king could do the same to each of their colonies at any time.

The delegates continued to prepare. They agreed that if the offending Acts of Parliament were not repealed, the colonies would boycott British goods. The congress also recommended that each colony continue to defy Parliament and the king. They also recommended that each colony prepare a militia of Patriots and to begin gathering supplies for them.

The delegates of the congress sent their petition to King George through Benjamin Franklin, who was in London as an agent for the Pennsylvania colony.

At the end of the congressional session in October 1774, the members agreed to meet in a second continental congress the following May, in 1775.

title: Louis Armstrong
text: Louis Armstrong was born in New Orleans. He was a famous jazz musician. He helped make jazz music popular all over the world. He helped other people be treated fairly.

title: Data, Data, Everywhere
text:
The census counts people and collects information about each person who is counted.

Let's look at the questions on the 2020 Census:

Who lives in the household?

How are they related to each other?

What is the age, sex, and race of all those living in the household?

Do those living in the household own or rent the house?

What is the phone number?

The Census of 1880 had 26 questions. Questions from 1880 asked for the number of people living in the dwelling as well as their ages, sexes, and races. Other questions included whether the people in the dwelling could read and write. Those living in the dwelling also answered what country they were born in. They also wrote their occupations. In 1880, the most populated city was New York City. Milwaukee was ranked no. 19 in population.

The actual counting of people was done by individuals. This process sometimes took years to finish. In 1890, counting everyone was done using an electronic punch card system. A modern computer was first used in 1950. Today, the use of computers makes the census count go faster. Computers also help share the information collected by creating tables, charts, and maps.

A line graph shows the increase or decrease of something over time.

A bar graph is used to compare things between different groups.

A pie chart is another method of displaying information. A pie chart is round. It represents the total number of things counted. The slices show parts of the totals. The larger the slice, the greater the number. The smaller the slice, the smaller the number.

A map can also display data. A map can represent larger or smaller numbers by using different colors.

A table chart gives data in columns and rows. Each column and row is labeled with the type of information shown.

title: Tribal Government
text:
One of the defining principles of government in the United States is the division of power between multiple branches and levels of government. There are many levels of government in the United States, including tribal, state, and local governments.

There are approximately five million people in the United States who are of Native American descent. These people belong to hundreds of tribes across the country. Many Native American nations in the United States have their own tribal governments. This means they have their own sovereignty. Sovereignty is an inherent right to self-govern. Tribal governments within the United States follow laws created by the federal government and the U.S. Constitution. However, when Native Americans are on tribal lands, they are subject to the laws of their tribal nation.

The federal government has a duty to protect the rights of Native American tribes. Tribes are often called "nations within a nation." Tribes can receive federal designation from the United States government. Federally recognized tribes have an official relationship with the U.S. government. They have certain rights, responsibilities, and powers. They are able to access some benefits, services, and protections from the U.S. government.

There are 574 federally recognized tribes in the United States. Members of these tribes are the descendants of the ancient tribes that have lived in North America for thousands of years. Each of the federally recognized tribes of the United States has its own reservation. A reservation is an area of land designated to a tribe or tribes by the United States government.

Tribes that are not federally recognized could be one day. They can petition the Bureau of Indian Affairs to receive federal recognition. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is a government agency that establishes which tribes are federally recognized and which are not.

The largest federally recognized tribe in the United States is the Cherokee tribe. The Cherokee tribe, whose central tribal government is located in Oklahoma, is made up of over 800,000 members. The Navajo tribe is the second-largest federally recognized tribe in the United States, with over 300,000 members. The smallest federally recognized tribe in the United States is the Augustine Band of Cahuilla Indians. Located in southern California, the Augustine Band of Cahuilla Indians tribe includes 3,000 registered members.

Tribal governments are led by Native American chiefs. Tribal councils make laws for their tribal nations. They write their own constitutions and have their own court systems. Tribal governments tax their people, too. They use the money to pay for police officers, education, and healthcare for the people. They also decide how to spend money on roads, public water, and electricity.

title: Essential Question
text: What are the purposes, structures, and functions of tribal, state, and local governments?

title: State Government
text:
Each of our 50 states has a state government. State governments are modeled after the federal government and consist of an executive, legislative, and judicial branch. All state governments are led by the executive branch. The executive branch is responsible for signing bills into law, appointing judges, proposing the state budget, organization of the state militia, and overseeing all agencies that work within the government.

The executive branch is led by the governor of the state. The governor is elected by the people. Of the 50 states in the country, 28 states limit a governor’s term in office to two consecutive, or back-to-back, terms. Thirteen states do not have a term limit for the governor, while the remaining states have varying term limits.

Most states also have a lieutenant governor, a secretary of state, and an attorney general. These make up the executive branch and are elected by the people and serve varying terms. The lieutenant governor assists the governor in matters of state and fulfills the responsibilities of the governor if they are unable to do so. The secretary of state is responsible for elections, record keeping, and safeguarding the state archives. The attorney general is the head of law enforcement for the state.

The legislative branch is responsible for creating state laws. All states, except for Nebraska, have a legislative branch made up of two houses. This is known as a bicameral legislature. Nebraska has a unicameral legislature. This means that the legislative branch of Nebraska has only one house. The larger of the two houses is often called the House of Representatives, but it is also called the House of Delegates or the State Assembly. The smaller of the two houses is called the Senate.

The state’s judicial branch is led by the state supreme court. State supreme courts are responsible for correcting or definitively ruling on decisions that have been made in lower courts. The justices ensure that the correct procedures were followed. If problems or disagreements cannot be resolved within the state, cases can be taken to the U.S. Supreme Court.

title: State Constitutions
text:
Just like the U.S. Constitution, state constitutions guarantee and protect citizens' basic rights. State constitutions list the rules for state government. They also explain how a state can make laws. State constitutions describe how the state government divides and shares power with counties and cities.

State constitutions can change over time. These changes are called amendments. Lawmakers and voters can work together to amend the existing state constitution to meet the needs of citizens. To amend means to change or add to. Citizens can vote to amend their state constitution.

title: Local Government
text:
A local government is a government that serves the people of a town, city, or county. There are several types of local government structures in the United States. The most common types of local government structures are county governments, municipal governments, and special districts.

County governments are responsible for assisting the state government in meeting the needs of those who live within the county’s boundaries. County governments are run by a board of supervisors. Members of the board of supervisors are elected by the people who live in their county. County governments are usually responsible for keeping records. This means that counties keep track of births, deaths, marriages, and business licenses. County governments are also in charge of voting, vehicle registration, and collecting taxes on land and property. Many counties also offer health and welfare services, like nursing care, immunization, and child care classes. Some counties also run the public library system.

Municipal governments are responsible for the health, welfare, and safety of people in a town, city, village, or borough. Municipal governments are run by elected officials, including a mayor or city manager, city council, or board of directors. These local leaders help make good decisions for the people who live in a city or town.

Special districts are created by a state to serve a specific purpose. Special districts usually serve a single purpose. School districts are a type of special district. School districts are responsible for the education of the students who live within the district. School districts are run by a school superintendent, along with a board of education. A school superintendent is a professional teacher or school administrator who is hired to lead the school district. The superintendent works with the school board to make decisions about how the schools in the district should run.

title: Tribal, State, and Local Courts
text:
The purpose of local, state, and tribal courts is to interpret laws and settle conflicts. How does the court system work? First, citizens bring their problems to state trial courts. Members of Native American tribes often bring their issues and legal matters to tribal courts first. State trial courts are located in the county you live in. Tribal courts are located on Native American reservations. The judges in the trial and tribal courts listen to the problem, or case, and both sides of the story. They think about the evidence that each side presented and then make a decision based on what they heard. Judges' decisions solve conflicts and provide consequences for those people who break the law.

If a person does not agree with the trial or tribal court's decision, they can file an appeal. This appeal goes to the Court of Appeals at the state level. Sometimes, the Court of Appeals keeps the trial court's decision. Other times, they overturn the original outcome. If a person is still unhappy after the Court of Appeals' decision, they can apply to take their case to the state supreme court.

State supreme courts vary in the number of judges, or justices, that they have. They make decisions on cases and solve problems that people bring before them. The state supreme courts take cases that have first gone through the trial courts and Court of Appeals. Justices decide cases in two ways: by opinion or by order. In both types of cases, the judges must meet to analyze the case and determine the verdict.

If a case cannot be resolved by the state courts, it can be elevated to the Supreme Court of the United States. The U.S. Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It upholds and interprets the laws of the Constitution. It also ensures that the rights of all Americans are protected. Currently, the Supreme Court is made up of nine judges. Supreme Court justices work together to determine the outcome of important court cases. The Supreme Court reviews thousands of cases each year.

title: Movement
text:
Movement is a concept that influences geography and history. People, resources, ideas, and goods move around the world for different reasons. Resources and goods often move for economic reasons. Resources and goods are traded across communities, states, nations, and even the world. People move because of the choices that they make. Sometimes, people choose to move to find better jobs, more freedom, or new and different resources. People can also be forced to move. They might be forced to move because of conflict, natural disasters, or persecution. Ideas usually move with people. When people move, they bring their ideas, culture, and customs with them. Sometimes people visit a new place temporarily and take new ideas back to their homes. Movement can also create conflict. Sometimes when people move, clashes of culture, people, and ideas happen.

The motivations that cause people to move are called push and pull factors. Push factors are things that cause people to leave an area. Push factors are usually negative things, such as conflict, drought, or economic depression. Pull factors are things that cause people to come to an area. Pull factors are usually positive motivators, including economic opportunity or safety. When people are pushed from an area or pulled to a new region, the result is change. Populations grow or shrink. Cultures are reshaped to accommodate new people and ideas. Economies are transformed by new resources and materials. Can you think of more changes that take place when goods, people, or ideas move?

title: Week 30 Inquiry Question
text: What factors have most often influenced movement throughout history?

title: Community Growth
text:
The city of Madison, Wisconsin, has had a unique history of movement. The area around Madison was inhabited by Native Americans for thousands of years. The most recent Indigenous group to live in the area was the Ho-Chunk. The Ho-Chunk people built effigy mounds all around the area. They were most likely drawn to the area because of its close proximity to the Great Lakes. In fact, the area is called Taychopera, which means “land of the four lakes” in Ho-Chunk. The Ho-Chunk were forced to leave the area because of conflicts with other Indigenous groups and white settlers.

The land around Madison was bought by a man named James Duane Doty in 1829. When Wisconsin became a territory of the United States in 1836, a temporary territorial capital was established at Belmont. One of the first missions of the territorial government was to find a permanent place for the capital. Doty immediately began lobbying that Madison become the new capital. Surprisingly, the city of Madison did not yet exist, and no one lived there. Doty offered bison robes and discounts on land sales for legislators. He hoped to persuade government officials to choose Madison as the new capital. The potential city’s central location was a feature that made it appealing to legislators. Madison was situated between Milwaukee, Prairie du Chien, Green Bay, and the lead mines in the southwestern part of the state. Eventually the territorial legislature chose Madison as the site for the new capital.

While Madison was being built, the capital was moved to Burlington for a time. Eventually, people began moving to Madison. No one lived in Madison before the legislature voted to make Madison the capital. In 1846, when Wisconsin became a state, Madison had 626 residents. The state charter set aside land and funding for a state university. In 1849, the University of Wisconsin–Madison was established. By 1856, Madison had grown to a city of 6,863 people. According to the 2020 census, Madison currently has 269,840 residents.

Push Factors

Pull Factors

Indigenous groups were forced to leave because of conflict.

Legislators had to move away from old capitals: Belmont and Burlington.

Access to water: Lakes Mendota, Monona, Kegonsa, Waubesa, and Wingra

Ho-Chunk visited effigy mounds.

Push Factors

Many Native Americans in the 1830s and beyond were forced to move away from their homelands by the United States government. This included many tribes that lived in the area of Wisconsin, including the Ho-Chunk, Sauk, Fox, and Menominee.

In the late 1840s, many German revolutions had failed in Europe. Germans left their homelands for several reasons, including because their land had been destroyed by war, because the government was unstable, or because they had become political enemies of the government.

Many people were experiencing persecution for their religion. Many Quakers and Haugeans emigrated from Norway to escape religious persecution.

Soil in Europe was often overworked and less fertile. Land was also expensive and was often closed off by elite land owners, especially in places such as England.

Drought, famine, and natural disasters also spurred emigration. In Ireland, the potato crop, which the working class depended on for food, was infected with a disease. This caused a famine that lasted from 1845 to 1852. During that time, more than one million people emigrated from Ireland.

Pull Factors

The discovery of lead in the southwestern portion of Wisconsin during the 1820s brought people to work in the new industry. Expert miners from Cornwall County in England settled in Wisconsin to take part in lead mining.

In 1832, the Erie Canal, which connected the Hudson River system to the Great Lakes, was completed. This made travel easier from the East Coast to the interior of the United States. Also in the 1830s, the federal government had broken down most Native American resistance to white settlement and began selling land in Wisconsin to white settlers. These factors combined and caused many people to come to Wisconsin to buy land.

Many immigrants settled in Wisconsin to join their family members. Some immigrants also came to Wisconsin because they heard about large communities of people with similar cultural and language backgrounds to their own.

The resources drew people to Wisconsin and created new economic opportunities. People used resources and their own expertise to develop new industries in the area. Germans used the factory infrastructure in Milwaukee to develop the brewing industry in Wisconsin. Scandinavians from Norway and Sweden often worked in logging, taking advantage of Wisconsin’s large forests. Other immigrants brought skills and knowledge in dairy farming and cheese making to Wisconsin’s fertile farmland.

title: The Great Migration
text:
The push and pull factors that influence individuals’ movement are unique to every individual. However, historians look for patterns of movement between people and time periods. One example of this in United States history is the Great Migration. Six million African Americans left the rural South between 1916 and 1970. This movement was called the Great Migration. African Americans hoped to escape Southern poverty, racism, and violence. They wanted to find better lives.

During World War l, American farms and factories had increased the production and shipping of goods to supply U.S. allies. The military needed engines, ships, and weapons to fight the war. As production increased, so did the need for workers. Companies began to recruit African Americans to move north and fill those jobs. By 1919, an estimated one million African Americans had left the South and moved to the North.

Segregation laws in the South inhibited the growth of African Americans as equal citizens. New laws restricted their voting rights, and many experienced intimidation and violence. They couldn’t find houses or jobs because of unfair procedures. African American children were placed in separate, inferior schools. For these reasons and more, African American families were attracted to the North.

Many African Americans migrated to large industrial cities, including New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Detroit. Men quickly found jobs in factories, slaughterhouses, and metal workshops. These were often hard, dangerous jobs that no one else wanted. Women had a harder time finding jobs. There was more competition for traditional jobs open to women, such as housekeeping.

Finding houses in the North also presented a problem. By this time, the U.S. Supreme Court had declared that racially based housing restrictions were unconstitutional. To get around this ruling, however, many neighborhood residents agreed on their own neighborhood rules. These rules often kept homeowners from selling or renting their homes to African Americans. In other areas, landlords rented to white Americans for a regular price and raised the rent for African Americans moving into similar homes and apartments.

As a result, many African Americans created their own cities within cities. The Harlem area of New York was an example. Previously designated as a white residential area, Harlem was home to more than 200,000 African Americans by the 1920s. Their settlement and activity in this area eventually led to the Harlem Renaissance.

At the beginning of the Great Migration, 90 percent of African Americans lived in the South. By the end of the movement in the 1970s, 47 percent of African Americans lived in the northern and western United States.

title: Technology and Global Movement
text:
Most travel technologies, such as wagons, canals, and railroads, made movement easier within a limited area. For example, by the late 1800s, railroads connected most of North America. However, railroads were not built across large bodies of water. They were not often built from one continent to another either. This limited global travel. If people wanted to travel from one continent to another, they had to travel on ships. Although steam-powered boats or ships were more efficient than sailboats, it still took a considerable amount of time to travel across large bodies of water. Even with significant technological improvements, movement was still limited. The most restrictions on movement were on global movement.

The Airplane

In 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright built an airplane and completed the world’s first flight. The airplane only flew for three seconds, but the two brothers continued to improve their airplanes. Soon the planes were able to fly for much longer periods of time. In 1919, only 16 years after the Wright brothers’ first successful flight, a plane called NC4 crossed the Atlantic Ocean.

The world’s first airplanes could only carry one person. Soon two people, both aviators, could fly a plane, but they flew in open air. Eventually people developed airplanes that had the capacity to carry nonessential people who were protected from the elements. After World War II, air travel became more common for ordinary people. With the invention of the jet engine, airplanes became bigger, faster, and more fuel efficient. With more people paying for less fuel, air travel costs decreased, and more people could afford to fly on airplanes.

Air Travel Today

Today, more than 45,000 flights take off every day in the United States. Globally, there are more than 100,000 flights per day. Some of these flights move cargo and goods. Some are military flights. However, the vast majority are passenger flights. Air travel allows people to move across oceans and continents in only a matter of hours. The increase of technology has changed the frequency and capacity for people, goods, and ideas to move across the globe.

title: Working to Solve Problems
text:
Issues in a community can impact the daily lives of citizens. Common community issues in many areas of the United States include transportation, water quality, access to clean water, funding education, and rising taxes. Citizens can work with their local, state, and federal leaders to solve problems that impact their community by attending meetings and contacting their representatives to make sure their opinions and ideas are heard.

One way that we can solve problems is by engaging in civil discourse. Civil discourse helps people have conversations about their community in a way that is respectful of other people’s opinions and points of view. You practice civil discourse when you talk in appropriate ways with other people to build understanding about an issue or problem. Although there are people with different opinions, practicing civil discourse reminds us to treat others with respect.

Steps that people can use to work together to solve problems in their community:

State the problem in a way that everyone can understand.

Identify potential causes for the problem.

Reach out to experts to brainstorm possible solutions. Some experts may include teachers, parents, and community helpers.

Suggest solutions to address the problem and create a plan.

Attempt to solve the problem.

Reflect on the plan and make changes if needed.

Through practicing civil discourse and community problem solving, citizens and elected leaders can work together to overcome issues in their community, state, and country.

title: Domestic Instability
text:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt faced domestic issues that caused conflict in the United States during his presidency. Domestic problems occur within a country, and the ones Roosevelt faced mainly affected Americans during this time. The biggest domestic challenge during his presidency was the Great Depression. This was a devastating economic collapse that created major domestic issues and led to conflicts and cooperation over potential solutions.

Beginning in the late 1920s, before Roosevelt became president, the U.S. economy suffered major problems. Many people lost massive amounts of money when the stock market crashed on Oct. 29, 1929. These economic problems led to people spending less money. With people spending less, companies began losing money and cutting jobs, putting many people out of work. With the unemployment rate climbing, fewer people had money to spend, which caused companies to make even less money and cut more jobs. These events led to the Great Depression.

By the time Roosevelt became president, around 13 million people were out of work, and banks were no longer operating. During the Great Depression, thousands of Americans rushed to take their money out of the banks. When the banks did not have enough money on hand to give to their customers, they had to close. The people who were unable to get their money back lost that money. Roosevelt was responsible for leading a country where one in every four workers had no job and many people had recently lost their life savings in the “run on the banks.”

Some of the major political conflicts Roosevelt faced came from his effort to solve the economic issues of the Great Depression. Labor organizations made up of worker groups had certain needs and demands. Business owners and other capitalists had different desires. Political opponents thought Roosevelt’s solutions were straying too far away from the ideals of capitalism. Others thought his solutions did not go far enough to help people who needed help most.

Other domestic issues impacted the country during Roosevelt’s presidency. The country was seeing more immigrants arriving from different countries. New groups of people arriving in the United States found a country struggling with racial and social issues. As president, Roosevelt was the leader of the entire country, and he was faced with uniting an increasingly diverse population. He faced conflict from different groups based on decisions he made in an effort to solve or help reduce racial and social issues. Various racial and social groups benefited from policies Roosevelt created, even as other groups suffered.

title: The Battle of Fort McHenry
text:
In August 1814, the British controlled Chesapeake Bay. That same year, they invaded the new American capital, Washington, D.C. They burned the Capitol building and the White House. First Lady Dolly Madison managed to save the portrait of George Washington and a few other items before leaving. The destruction of Washington, D.C., lasted 26 hours.

Following the attack on the nation’s capital, British naval forces entered Baltimore Harbor to attack Fort McHenry. That night, Francis Scott Key, an American lawyer, was helping to negotiate a prisoner's release. He watched the battle from a British warship. The British bombarded the fort with cannons throughout the night. The American flag over Fort McHenry never fell, though. This signaled an American victory. Key was so inspired watching the battle that he wrote his thoughts as he watched the flag.

“Oh, say can you see by the dawn's early light

What so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming?

Whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight,

O'er the ramparts we watched were so gallantly streaming?

And the rocket's red glare, the bombs bursting in air,

Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there.

Oh, say does that star-spangled banner yet wave

O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave?”

Key’s words would later be set to music and become the national anthem of the United States in 1931.
