text: How did geography and the government impact Quebec's Independence Movement?

title: Citizen Participation
text:
The main feature of a democracy is that citizens participate in the government. In a parliamentary democracy, citizens have specific ways of participating. All Canadian citizens are eligible to vote once they turn 18 years old. Every vote counts equally. It doesn't matter who the person is. Citizens also participate in the government by running for and holding government office.

The person who receives the most votes is the winner of a Canadian election. This is different in some democracies that require the winner to have earned at least 50 percent of the vote. An election winner in Canada could be elected with less than 50 percent of the vote. They simply need more votes than the other candidates running against them. Elections are held to fill all the government offices in each level of the Canadian government. All Canadian citizens can vote in federal elections. At lower levels, only citizens of a given province or territory can vote in those elections. This way, the leaders are elected by the people they will be representing in government.

In addition to voting and serving in office, the Constitution of Canada ensures other ways for citizens to participate. Citizens have the freedom to speak out for or against their government. They can also peacefully assemble for protests. The government cannot interfere with or punish Canadian citizens for exercising their right to speak out against or protest government officials or actions. However, Canadian citizens must remain nonviolent while exercising these rights.

title: Roles and Responsibilities of the Government
text:
The Constitution of Canada details the roles and responsibilities of the Canadian government. Each level of government, from the federal government to the local level, has different roles and responsibilities based on who they represent. The federal government represents all Canadians. Its roles and responsibilities center around the interests of every person in the country. Provincial and territorial governments represent the population of those provinces and territories. Their roles and responsibilities are limited to just those populations.

The federal government is responsible for issues that affect the entire country. It is at this level that Canadian law is debated and created. Issues of national security are also the responsibility of the federal government. The Canadian armed forces, including the army, navy, and air force, are a part of this level of government. Policies and decisions regarding immigration and trade are also generally part of the federal government.

Provincial and territorial governments are only responsible for issues that affect their province or territory. Provincial governments operate schools and hospitals. There is no federal Department of Education in Canada. The federal government has some involvement in the healthcare system. It helps fund provincial healthcare services, enforces safety regulations when appropriate, and provides or assures access to healthcare for certain groups of people. Many times, provincial and territorial governments share the same issues. Because of this, provincial and territorial governments often share resources and work together to develop solutions to problems.

Municipal governments are responsible for the welfare and care of people within their municipality. They provide services to the local community. These services include waste management, water services, transportation, fire and police services, and recreation. Municipal governments also supply funds for public libraries and community centers. Elected officials at all levels of Canada’s government work together to ensure that the needs of people are met at the community, provincial, territorial, and federal levels.

title: Conclude and Connect
text:
The government of Canada is the result of major historical events that led to the creation of the country. Formed as part of the British Empire, the parliamentary government closely resembles the British system. As governments progressed and changed, greater emphasis was placed on the rights and freedom of citizens. In Canada, these were written into the Constitution. They became a guarantee for current and future generations. The parliamentary government of Canada is a form of democracy. It is meant to provide citizens with the right to direct government actions through participation in the government.

Free and fair elections allow Canadian citizens to vote for their representatives. The Constitution of Canada guarantees the right to vote, among many others. It also ensures that citizens are given specific freedoms common in democracies around the world. These include the freedom of speech and religion. The government of Canada represents people of many different origins, races, and ethnicities. A history of interactions between Native people and immigrants led to conflict and created the Canada of today. The rights and freedoms guaranteed in the Constitution are for all Canadian citizens.

title: Indigenous Peoples of Canada
text:
Before European exploration of the Western Hemisphere, people lived in Canada for thousands of years. The descendants of these first peoples still live in Canada today. The Canadian Constitution recognizes three major Indigenous groups: First Nations People, Inuit, and Métis. Each group developed their own governments, languages, and cultural practices. They preserved their history and traditions. They passed them to the future generations. According to the 2021 Canadian census, more than 1.8 million people in Canada identify as Indigenous.

Many historians believe that the Inuit were the first people to settle in Canada. Fifty-three Inuit communities are spread across four different regions. Most are located in the northern part of Canada. In 2021, a little over 70,000 people in Canada identified as Inuit or were of Inuit descent. The Inuit language is called Inuktitut. About half speak Inuktitut, but many also speak English. Inuktitut is spoken throughout Canada. Different dialects are spoken in different regions of the country.

The Métis are the descendants of Indigenous Canadians and European settlers, or Euro-Canadians. As the Métis population grew, smaller tribes and subgroups formed. The Métis combined their Indigenous and European traditions, beliefs, and languages. This created new cultural customs. In 2021, over 624,000 Canadians identified as Métis.

The early First Nations People lived in six geographical regions in Canada. These groups and tribes are often referred to by the region they lived in. Woodland First Nations lived in the eastern dense forests. The Iroquoian First Nations lived in the fertile areas of southeastern Canada. The Plains First Nations tribes lived throughout the grasslands and large prairies. The Plateau First Nations lived in the northern semi-desert, high mountains, and forests. The tribes of the Pacific Coast First Nations lived along the coast of the Pacific Ocean. The First Nations of the Mackenzie and Yukon River regions lived in the dark forest, swamps, and barren land of the river’s basins.

Québec is one of the provinces within Canada. It has three main groups of Indigenous peoples. They have lived there for hundreds of years. These groups traditionally lived in specific geographic regions in and around Québec.

The Subarctic Indigenous peoples lived throughout central Canada. The area they lived in stretched from the Bering Sea to Newfoundland. Their primary languages broke off from the Algonquian and the Iroquois language groups. However, different groups also developed dialects influenced by the Cree language.

The Arctic Indigenous peoples are also referred to as the Inuit. Historically, they lived primarily in the northern part of Canada. They had little contact with European explorers. They were isolated due to their geographical region.

The descendants of the early groups of the Eastern Woodlands Indigenous peoples have lived along the St. Lawrence River in southern Québec for hundreds of years. This area's two prominent language and cultural groups are Algonquian and Iroquois. They had the most contact with European explorers. This was due to the extensive fur trade in southern Canada and the St. Lawrence River area. There was a need for fur, goods, and finding different trade routes between Asia and Europe. Countries like France and Britain were led to look at Canada economically for their futures.

title: Essential Question
text: How did geography and the government impact Quebec’s independence movement?

title: European Exploration and Colonization
text:
During the Middle Ages, trade became very important to the economy of Europe. The coastal Italian city-states of Genoa and Venice were major ports. They had the funds and resources to produce ships that could travel long distances. Many people living in these places became sailors. They started traveling throughout the Mediterranean Sea. As trade increased, a desire to trade with East Asia also increased. A demand was created for spices and goods found in East Asia. However, for many centuries, the only way to get those goods was through Ottoman traders of Southwest Asia. Ottoman traders knew the Silk Road trade routes. They also knew the currents and winds of the Arabian Sea that could take ships to India and China.

The traders who sold East Asian goods to European merchants charged high prices. That was to compensate for the money they spent on trading expeditions. In the mid-1400s, the Ottoman Empire stopped all trade with China. It cut off European access to goods from East Asia. This forced European governments to put more resources into finding new trade routes to East Asia. They put money into developing tools, gathering supplies, and sending explorers out.

Historians call this period of time the Age of Exploration. Europeans eventually found other ways to reach East Asia. While searching for a western route, Christopher Columbus encountered the Americas. These explorations in Asia and the Americas would have positive and negative consequences for the Indigenous peoples during that period and beyond.

As a result of exploration, Europeans were introduced to new foods. Sugar, lemons, tobacco, chocolate, potatoes, and turkey were some of these foods that came from Asia and the Americas. Many Europeans gained wealth, knowledge, and resources from the new lands that their explorers journeyed to. However, the Age of Exploration also led to conflict and other negative outcomes. Europeans began claiming territory in the Americas and Asia as colonies. The act of colonization, or taking over an area of land for their own, became common practice. Conflicts developed over land and resources.

European, Asian, and African diseases were introduced to the Americas by European explorers. Indigenous peoples did not have immunity to these diseases. As a result, many tribes and groups, along with their cultures, knowledge, and histories, disappeared. Archaeologists and historians are working to learn more about these groups and record their histories and stories.

title: Founding of Québec
text:
French colonization of the Western Hemisphere began in 1523. France wanted to colonize areas of the Western Hemisphere, as many other European countries had already done. France colonized based on its standards of government and religion. This meant that the government was run as an absolute monarchy. France mostly followed the Catholic religion. The people believed that the French monarch was given the power to rule the country by the divine right of God. This led to the government and the Catholic Church acting as one political unit for the country. Additionally, the French wanted to open new trade centers and use the natural resources in conquered areas for the benefit of France.

French explorers focused their attention on present-day Canada and New England. They set up trading posts and colonies along rivers and at the mouths of bays. They used the area's rich resources to produce goods, which were sent back to France. Eventually, these sites were abandoned, and the colonists returned to France. The French realized they had to create a permanent foothold in North America to continue the trade networks they had established.

In 1608, Samuel de Champlain was sent to Canada to establish a colony and find a route to Asia. As he did this, he had the opportunity to observe and describe many of the areas of present-day Nova Scotia and the Saint Lawrence Gulf and River. He wrote in his journal:

Their settled habitation, the till-age and the beautiful trees, gave me the impression that the air there is milder and better than that where we passed the winter, and than that of other places on the coast. The forests in the interior are very light, but, nevertheless, consist of oaks, beeches, ashes and young elms. In wet places there are a great many willows.

As Champlain moved inland, he looked for a location that would be good for trade and settlement. He found an ideal site and noted it in his journal:

… on that river, at which place I had all the goods unloaded, with the men, laborers and artisans, to go up the river to find a place convenient and suitable for a settlement. When I had found the narrowest place in the river, which the natives call Quebec.

Once Québec was founded, Champlain turned his attention to the continent's interior, hoping to discover more territory to colonize. This led him to the Great Lakes Region and led many other explorers on unofficial expeditions to those areas. Champlain established another trading post south of Québec along the St. Lawrence River. Over time, this trading post grew into the city of Montréal.

For many years, Québec and Montréal served as the major trade centers in New France. The fur trade became the primary economic activity in the mid-1700s. The colonists sent fur pelts back to France to supply hat and clothing companies. The Métis played a crucial role in the fur trade, as they were skilled hunters and trappers in the region. By the end of the 1700s, trade became the primary economic activity for the Métis. The Métis worked alongside three major fur companies: the Hudson Bay Company, the North West Company, and the American Fur Company. This allowed them to make the maximum profit they could by selling to the highest bidder. In 1821, the Hudson Bay and North West Company merger created a monopoly in the fur trade. This reduced the profits of the Métis because there was not as much competition.

This type of trade allowed for the increased use of the waterways throughout Canada. Many roads were not yet built for trade and transportation. Communities were connected through the extensive waterways across the country. Voyageurs, or boatmen, were important to the fur trade system. At the start of the fur trade, the voyageurs were French Canadian, Iroquois, and Algonquin. After the fur companies merged, the Métis became the primary voyageurs for the fur trade. This tradition of fur trapping eventually extended to the prairie provinces of Canada.

The struggle to control land and the need to expand past areas that had been discovered became France’s primary goal for Canada. Explorers, frontiersmen, and merchants hoped to profit from Canada’s vast resources. Some explorers hoped to make scientific discoveries. Others looked for adventure in the forests and wilderness of Canada.

The economy of Canada changed in many ways during the mid-1800s. By the 1870s, the fur trade was coming to an end. Settlers began to trade with the Inuit in the Arctic areas. Fur farming became a new economic activity. The history of the fur trade is a crucial part of the Canadian economy. It was also one of the primary reasons for exploration. Today, many Canadians still celebrate this tradition. The Métis hold an annual celebration to honor their culture and history called “King Trapper” events.

title: Québec's Independence Movement
text:
Canada’s history as an area of exploration, colonization, and economic activity has led it to be a country of change. A drastic change for the Canadians occurred after the Seven Years’ War, as it was called in Europe. In North America, the war was called the French and Indian War. It ended in 1763. This conflict was fought between France, Great Britain, French and British colonies in the Americas, and their Native American allies. This conflict centered around control of land throughout North America.

The Seven Years' War

May 28, 1754: French Ambassador Joseph Coulon de Jumonville is killed.

1755: Braddock's defeat at Fort Duquesne

1756: The French take Fort Oswego.

1757: Battle at Fort William Henry

1757: American colonists refuse to serve under a British officer.

1758: Louisbourg and Fort Duquesne are captured by the British.

1759: Battle of Québec

1760: Iroquois join British-American Alliance.

1760: The French surrender Montréal.

1763: The Treaty of Paris ends the war.

With the signing of the Treaty of Paris in 1763, France lost control of the resources and government in Canada to the British. However, this treaty did allow for the freedom of religion in Canada. It meant that French Canadians could continue to practice Catholicism.

After the Seven Years’ War, there were many other conflicts, such as the American Revolution and the French Revolution. These all took place after the colonization of Canada. These conflicts were actually beneficial for French Canadians. European governments were too distracted by other conflicts to pay close attention to the French Canadians.

The Start of the Québec Independence Movement

1774: The Québec Act allows for the French language to be used throughout the courts and to be part of French civil law.

1791: Canada is broken up into two provinces: Upper Canada (English-speaking) and Lower Canada (French-speaking).

1791: The Act of 1791 gives French Canadians access to be sitting members of their government, regardless of their religion. It also gives French Canadians the right to practice Roman Catholicism.

1792: Lower Canada starts building their first parliament.

1826: The Patriote Party is formed.

November 1837: First Lower Canada Rebellion

November 1838: Second Lower Canada Rebellion

1840: The Act of Union is created and signed, uniting Upper and Lower Canada together as one country.

The division of English- and French-speaking citizens of Canada led to a need for structure. Dividing Canada into Upper and Lower provinces allowed for more equality and freedom of religion and language. This gave Great Britain a group of colonists who were loyal to the British crown. This loyalty was especially important during times of conflict. However, as time passed, English Canadians wanted more freedoms, as their French Canadian counterparts were receiving more freedoms.

In 1792, there were few English-speaking Canadians. The French Canadians called for all elections, documents, and court proceedings to be held in French. The opposing English-speaking members of the parliament objected. They announced that all elections, documents, and legal proceedings should take place “in the language of the empire to which we have the happiness to belong.” They felt that matters should be conducted in English in British colonies. They also felt that people should speak English as their first language. This was the start of many years of frustration, conflict, and fighting among the assembly and members.

Another distraction from Canada came when the War of 1812 broke out. The War of 1812 was a conflict between the newly-formed United States and Great Britain. The French Canadian middle class now controlled the parliament in Lower Canada. This eventually led to a nationalist movement throughout Canada. Little focus was given to Canada from Great Britain. The French Canadians wanted to create a distinct French cultural identity throughout Lower Canada, particularly Québec.

To achieve this, the Patriote Party was formed. The Patriote Party was organized in 1826 by Louis-Joseph Papineau. He sought to challenge the power or authority of the Legislative Council within the Assembly. The bourgeoisie, aristocracy, and colonial administration controlled the Legislative Council. The Legislative Council had the most power. The party's goal was to work on the region's economic development. The party looked at who was running the country based on their socioeconomic status to determine the influence that individuals had. The Patriote Party also focused on the agricultural production of the country rather than commercial businesses.

This division in the country led to rebellions in Lower Canada in 1837. The Patriote Party clashed with the British soldiers in Canada in November 1837 and then again in November 1838. These conflicts led to a British victory over the Patriote Party. As a result of these rebellions, the Canadian government passed the Act of Union in 1840. Under this act, Lower and Upper Canada were united. They became the Province of Canada as a whole. This was the start of a responsible government in Canada. This meant the people held the government responsible, not the British crown.

It was not until the 1950s and 1960s that the nationalist movement reemerged. This movement was called the Quiet Revolution. The goal of the movement was to create separatism throughout Canada, particularly in Québec. The idea of separatism is based on advocacy to separate from a larger political unit or from colonial oppression. As this movement began to resurface, so did many political parties surrounding the idea. By 1968, multiple political parties merged to form the Parti Québécois (PQ). Led by René Lévesque, the Parti Québécois advocated for Québec to become politically independent but stay connected to Canada economically. As in the past, they wanted to keep a French-Canadian culture intact throughout Québec.

The Parti Québécois was elected into the Assembly with a 41 percent popular vote and 71 seats. The PQ’s first goal was to move toward independence for Québec. To do this, the PQ created a referendum, or vote, for the people of Québec to decide if they wanted to become their own independent country from Canada. The referendum was rejected by the majority of voters in Québec. However, this did not stop the PQ. They were reelected in 1981.

In 1980, the Prime Minister of Canada worked to remove British powers in Canada by renewing and revising the Canadian Constitution. As a promise to the people of Québec, the Prime Minister agreed to transfer the authority to the Canadian Parliament. He also promised to create a new constitution called the Charter of Rights and Freedom. This was enacted in 1982 with the Constitution Act. The Constitution still applied to the province of Québec. However, the PQ did not sign the act, which began the downfall of the party.

During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the PQ regrouped and declared they would work harder for an independent Québec. About 65 percent of Québec’s population supported the movement, but support declined to 40 percent after 1994. In October 1995, a second referendum was created to support the sovereignty, or independence, of Québec. If approved, the referendum would create an economic partnership between English Canada and Québec. The referendum was rejected. Many people felt that independence for Québec was lost.

title: Conclude and Connect
text:
The pursuit of independence did not leave the people of Québec. In 1998, the Prime Minister created the office of Intergovernmental Affairs. The purpose of this office was to analyze Québec’s independence movement and develop solutions. He created a two-part approach. The first was to showcase and characterize Québec as its own distinct society. The second was not to allow Québec to separate from Canada or the Canadian Constitution legally. Québec’s government did not accept the second approach.

On Aug. 20, 1998, the Canadian courts ruled on Québec’s separation from Canada. They ruled that Québec could not legally separate unless it had a clear majority of its population that voted in favor of the motion. If that were the case, then the provinces of Canada and the federal government would negotiate the terms of separation together. Representatives of Québec accepted this ruling. This ruling was considered a victory for both sides. This was a profound time in Canadian history. The government developed a clear plan for an area to separate from their country peacefully and organized.

Canada has become a country that honors and showcases its history. Each province and Indigenous population has its own stories, legends, and culture. These cultural experiences create the cultural identity of the country. European exploration and colonization influenced the political and social wants and needs of the country. European exploration and colonization also caused many conflicts between the major powers of Europe. French colonization of Canada gave the country a distinct cultural identity for French Canadians. The movement to keep and increase their French language and culture influenced the decisions and development of the Québec independence movement.

title: Introduction
text:
The term “Latin America” does not refer to a single location. It is a region that includes 21 very diverse countries and territories. This region is divided into three subregions: Central America, South America, and the Caribbean nations. The geography of Latin America varies, from moist tropical beaches to rugged mountains thousands of feet high to deserts so dry that rainfall has rarely been recorded.

The region of Latin America begins in Mexico and Central America. Central America is to the south of Mexico. It is made up of seven countries, including Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. Central America is connected to South America by the isthmus of Panama. An isthmus is a narrow strip of land bordered by large bodies of water on both sides.

South America is located in the Southern Hemisphere. It is the fourth largest continent in the world. It extends from the Caribbean Sea to Cape Horn. South America is bordered by the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Atlantic Ocean to the east.

The Caribbean Islands are primarily located between North America and South America. They are a massive archipelago surrounded by the Caribbean Sea to the south, the Gulf of Mexico to the west, and the Atlantic Ocean to the north. Archipelago means group of islands. The Caribbean has over 700 islands. These islands are organized into 30 territories, dependencies, and sovereign countries. A dependency is a country or province that is under the control of another.

title: Essential Question
text: How does location impact a region's cultural, social, and economic development?

title: Bodies of Water
text:
The Amazon River

The Amazon River dominates South America's northern and central parts. Although it mostly runs through Brazil, its tributaries and watershed extend into Suriname, Guyana, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. Its watershed, the area of land where precipitation eventually makes its way to the river, is the largest of any river system in the world. The Amazon River also moves more water than any other river in the world.

The Caribbean Sea

The Caribbean Sea is a tropical sea that is located in the Western Hemisphere. It is considered one of the largest saltwater seas and covers about 1,063,000 square miles. The Caribbean Sea is surrounded by South America to the south, Mexico to the west, Central America to the southwest, and the Antilles to the northeast.

The Gulf of Mexico

A gulf is a deep inlet of water that connects coastal areas to a larger body of water, such as a sea or ocean. The Gulf of Mexico is located between Florida and Mexico. It covers about half a million square miles of water. The Gulf of Mexico shares a border with five states in the United States and also with Mexico. It shares borders with many islands in the Caribbean as well. It has 33 major tributaries, or rivers, that flow into it. The Rio Bravo in Mexico is one.

The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans

The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans are located on the east and west sides of Latin America respectively. The Pacific Ocean creates a coastline across many countries, including Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Chile. The Atlantic Ocean borders many countries in Latin America to the east. It creates a coastline for Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, the Falkland Islands, French Guiana, Guyana, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands, Suriname, Uruguay, Venezuela, Belize, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, and Panama. The Atlantic Ocean also surrounds the Caribbean Islands that lie outside of the Caribbean Sea.

The Panama Canal

The Panama Canal is located in Central America. The canal, which stretches across the country of Panama, connects the Pacific Ocean to the Caribbean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. Ships used to sail all the way around South America to travel from one ocean to the other. The Panama Canal allows ships to travel more quickly from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. It was completed in 1914 by the United States.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: Latin America is one of the most diverse geographic regions in the world. Latin America stretches from Mexico to Cape Horn in Argentina, including most of the Western Hemisphere countries. A vast amount of mountain ranges creates different climates throughout the regions. South America is home to one of the largest river systems in the world: the Amazon River and its main tributaries. The geography of Latin America has a profound impact on all human activity in the region. The actions of governments and the economic activities of the region are strongly influenced by the natural environment of Latin America.

title: Essential Question
text: How does location impact a region's cultural, social, and economic development?

title: Natural Resources
text:
Cuba

Cuba’s climate and geography create an environment where many resources occur naturally and are found in abundance. Many mineral resources are found in Cuba. Cuba’s leading mineral resources are nickel and cobalt. Cuba is consistently among the world's top nickel and cobalt exporters. Cuba also has large deposits of oil and natural gas. Cuban refineries process oil and natural gas. This is used to power machinery in factories and is exported to other countries.

Other major natural resources in Cuba are forests. Cuba’s natural hardwood forests support a thriving forestry industry in the country. Lumber mills harvest and process various species of hardwood trees, including ebony, mahogany, cider, and pine trees. Cuban lumber is shipped to markets around the Western Hemisphere to build furniture and homes and produce paper.

Arable land is one of the most important natural resources in Cuba. Arable land is land that can be cultivated and used for agricultural purposes. The primary crop grown and harvested in Cuba is sugarcane. Sugarcane was brought to Cuba in the late 1500s by Spanish explorers. Cuba’s tropical climate and fertile soil allow sugarcane to grow easily. Cuban farmers also grow large quantities of tobacco, citrus fruits, cotton, rice, and bananas. Arable land also allows farmers to raise livestock, including pigs, poultry, and cattle.

Water is also an important natural resource in Cuba. Cuba is an island nation surrounded by the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean Sea, and the Atlantic Ocean. Because of its proximity to large bodies of water, Cuba has easy access to marine resources. Cuba’s commercial fishing industry is a major part of Cuba’s economy. Cuban seafood is shipped to international markets across the globe.

Brazil

Brazil has the world’s fifth-largest economy. This is largely due to the country's variety and abundance of natural resources. Brazil is rich in mineral and agricultural resources. Mining is a major industry throughout Brazil. Large deposits of gold, iron ore, nickel, aluminum, and manganese are found in the Espinhaço Mountains and the Amazon River Basin.

Agriculture is one of the largest economic activities in the country because of the climate and fertile soil. Brazil is the fourth-largest producer of agricultural products in the world. Brazil’s major crops and agricultural exports include coffee, soybeans, citrus fruit, and sugarcane. Brazil also has one of the world's largest cattle and poultry industries.

Large deposits of oil and natural gas are found throughout Brazil. Large deposits of natural gas are found in the coastal regions of Brazil and offshore. Some of the oil Brazil produces is processed, while some is left in its raw form. Refined oil is sent to markets globally, making Brazil the 12th-largest producer and exporter of oil in the world.

Forests are another vital natural resource in Brazil. Brazil is home to five different types of forests, covering almost half of the country's total land area. The largest of these forests is the Amazon Rainforest. The Amazon Rainforest is the largest rainforest in the world. It covers about 2.3 million square miles of Brazil’s total land area. Brazil’s forests are home to many different types of trees. The country’s lumber industry relies on the abundance and variety of trees found in Brazil’s forests.

Water is one of the most important natural resources in Brazil. The Amazon River is Brazil's longest river and the second-longest in the world. The Amazon River has over 1,000 tributaries that flow through Brazil and other areas of South America. The Amazon River and its tributaries provide fresh water for millions of people and make it possible for agricultural production to flourish in Brazil.

Mexico

Like Brazil and Cuba, Mexico’s economy relies heavily on the country's natural resources. Many industries in Mexico depend on these resources. Mining is one of the largest economic activities in the country. People have mined in Mexico for thousands of years. Mexico is one of the world's leading producers of gold, silver, copper, lead, and zinc. Other minerals found in Mexico include iron, coal, manganese, and mercury. All are of vital importance to Mexico’s economy. Oil and natural gas are also mined throughout Mexico.

Mexico’s climate and geography are ideal for agricultural production. Many of Mexico's native crops and plant species have become popular around the world through centuries of trade. Avocados, corn, tomatoes, chili peppers, chia seeds, agave, cocoa beans, vanilla, squash, and sweet potatoes are native crops that are still grown and harvested in Mexico. Today, Mexico is the world’s largest producer of avocados. Mexican farmers have diversified their crops over the years. Cotton, wheat, strawberries, pineapples, mangoes, papayas, rice, and peanuts also grow well in Mexico's varying climates and geographical regions.

Mexico is a peninsula bordered by three very distinct bodies of water: the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean Sea. This means that marine resources are found in abundance in the waters around the country. The fishing and seafood industries are among the leading economic industries in Mexico. Mexican seafood is exported to markets around the world.

title: Distribution of Natural Resources
text:
Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico are rich in natural resources. The availability and distribution of natural resources depend on an area's climate and geography. Mountainous areas generally have larger deposits of mineral resources than areas at lower elevations. Areas with sandy or rocky soil are not ideal for growing a variety of crops. Additionally, some crops do not grow well in tropical climates and require a temperate climate. Brazil and Mexico's climates and geography vary throughout each country, so more natural resources are available in these countries. Cuba’s climate and geography are not as diverse as Mexico's or Brazil’s. This impacts the distribution of natural resources.

Many of the largest cities in Latin American countries, including Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico, are located on or near ancient settlements. The Indigenous peoples of Latin America chose where to settle based on the availability of natural resources. Large quantities of natural resources are still found near these cities. As a result, many of Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico’s most populous cities are found near sites of ancient settlement.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The environment of Latin America is one of the most diverse in the world. The region’s physical characteristics, geography, and climate allow many resources to occur naturally and in great quantities. The abundance, diversity, and availability of natural resources in Latin America make the region one of the largest exporters of goods in the world. Natural resources have played an important role in Latin America's settlement and government decisions. Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico's economies depend on natural resources. Humans have learned to adapt to and modify the environment of Latin America to meet their needs and wants. However, this often comes at a price. Human-environment interaction has profoundly impacted the physical environments of Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico. In recent years, efforts have been made to reduce the impact of humans on the environment across Latin America.

title: Essential Question
text: What factors impact the governments and economic systems of Latin America?

title: Roles and Responsibilities of Government
text:
In a republic like Mexico, the government's main role is to represent and serve the interest of its citizens. The federal government in Mexico sets policies and operates governmental programs that affect the entire country. The executive branch, with the president as its head, is responsible for leading the Mexican military forces. Leading the country means that pursuing and signing foreign treaties is also a responsibility of the president. The president also has the privilege of introducing laws to the legislature to be passed. In Mexico, many laws begin with a presidential suggestion.

The president of Mexico appoints members to a cabinet. The cabinet provides advice and assistance in running the government. It also operates a collection of offices that deal with a variety of issues through policies and programs. Cabinet leaders are known as secretaries. The titles of these secretaries indicate what part of the government they are responsible for. These include the education, energy, health, and foreign affairs secretaries.

The federal legislature of Mexico has a host of responsibilities and powers. This group of elected representatives passes laws. These laws address specific issues throughout Mexico. These representatives are also responsible for the country’s federal budget. This includes enacting and collecting taxes. Congress also has the ability to oversee the executive branch. This is done by reviewing presidential decisions on foreign treaties and maintaining the power to declare war.

According to the federal government system, each state operates its own independent government with similar roles and responsibilities within that state. The state government imposes taxes, operates a state budget, and passes legislation. Most services fall to the local or municipal governments at the city level. Garbage collection, public safety, parks, and other local concerns are the responsibility of the municipal government. Much of their funding comes from the federal and, to a lesser extent, state levels.

title: Factors of Economic Growth
text:
Mexico’s economy continues to grow slowly but steadily. The country’s rate of growth is affected by many factors. These are the same factors that influence all economies. Investments in human capital, as well as capital goods, can spur economic growth. Improving the education and capabilities of a country’s population can lead to increased economic productivity. More money invested in capital goods, like factories, machinery, and other equipment, can also make an economy more productive.

One way to measure the potential productivity of the population is its literacy rate. Generally, this is the percentage of the population, aged 15 and up, that can read and write. The higher the literacy rate, the more people in a country can read and write. People who can read and write can perform more complex job responsibilities. They are also generally more productive from an economic perspective than those who cannot. The literacy rate in Mexico has been steadily increasing. This has led to a more educated and productive workforce. Recent investments in public education have led to increased literacy rates in Mexico, which have led to more positive economic outcomes as well.

The many free trade agreements Mexico is a part of, like NAFTA and the USMCA, encourage local and foreign investments in capital goods. Companies build and invest in new and more advanced factories, technology, and machinery. Agreements make trade easier between countries. Because of this, companies are incentivized to spend more money to make their factories and workers more productive. Building better and more efficient factories is one way to do this.

The free market also encourages entrepreneurship. This can stimulate economic growth. Government policies that support and encourage entrepreneurs to take risks and start businesses can put people to work and strengthen the economy. Recently, the Mexican government has focused on supporting small and medium-sized businesses. This has led to an increase in the employment rate and economic development. Despite this, more work is needed to protect business owners and increase economic productivity.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The Mexican government and economy encourage citizen participation and freedom. Their federal presidential republic guarantees that citizens are involved in the government. They do this by choosing and serving as representatives. Political freedom carries over into their economy as well. While officially considered a mixed market economy, Mexico emphasizes free market policies and pursuits. The government has recently pursued policies and decisions to create a more educated and entrepreneurial population. This has contributed to political and economic growth and freedom.

title: Government of Cuba
text:
Cuba is one of the few countries in the world, and the only one outside of Asia, to have a government designed around the communist ideology. The Cuban Communist Party took control of the government in 1959. It runs the government with no other political parties to serve as opposition or alternatives. Although the country's official name is the Republic of Cuba, the government lacks the features of a true republic.

The National Assembly of People’s Power is the principal legislative body in Cuba. Elections are held to determine who will serve in this organization. However, everyone running for office is from the Cuban Communist Party. Local committees and labor unions choose the nominees rather than the voters. In addition, there are exactly as many nominees as there are positions in the National Assembly. This means that while elections technically occur, the results are predetermined. Voters have no direct choice in who their representatives in the National Assembly will be through the voting process. In the 2023 election, 470 people ran for the 470 positions in the National Assembly. Members of this body serve for five-year terms.

Although the government has the traditional three branches of government, the legislative branch has most of the influence on the government. As the main component of Cuba’s legislative branch, the National Assembly elects the country’s president. They also appoint judges to the People’s Supreme Court, the highest court in the judicial branch of the country’s government. When the National Assembly is out of session, a smaller group, called the Council of Ministers, assumes legislative control. All of this is generally controlled by the Cuban Communist Party.

title: Essential Questions
text: What factors impact the governments and economic systems of Latin America?

title: Citizen Participation
text:
The greatest opportunity for citizen participation in the government comes at the local level in Cuba. Cuban citizens have universal voting rights for all those aged 16 and over. Voting in Cuba is not restricted based on any criteria except age. In municipal elections, citizens are able to vote for representatives. Those representatives then serve in local assemblies. Usually, there are anywhere from two to eight nominees for voters to choose from in municipal elections.

At the higher levels of government, citizens are still able to vote. However, their votes do not determine who is elected. At those levels, there are as many nominees as there are open positions. That means that the election of those people is merely a formality. Voters are given no actual choices between candidates. Unlike democracies around the world, the Cuban government forbids open dissent and criticism of the government. Although the Cuban constitution guarantees the right of the people to assemble, that freedom does not extend to protests against the government or the Communist Party.

title: Roles and Responsibilities of Government
text:
The Cuban government takes on many roles and responsibilities. Often, in democratic capitalist countries around the world, those are met by private industries and companies. Communist countries like Cuba assume major responsibilities in providing education, health care, and other services to their citizens. Cuban citizens receive free education and medical care. It is subsidized or paid for by the government. As a result, the government is responsible for ensuring that the services provided to its citizens are of good quality. Private schools and health care facilities are technically illegal in Cuba. There are certain exceptions. However, citizens often cannot choose an alternative if the government-provided service is low-quality.

The Cuban government dominates life in Cuba. Because everything in a communist country is owned by the government, all property is the responsibility of the government. Recently, there have been changes to the constitution to allow for the ownership of private property. The change has relieved the government of some responsibilities. It has also loosened restrictions on certain freedoms of the Cuban people.

The government of Cuba also assumes many of the roles that can be found in democratic governments. The National Assembly, as the legislative branch of the government, is the lawmaking body. They can pass new laws as well as modify or repeal current laws. The National Assembly also sets the national budget and foreign policies. The People’s Supreme Court serves as the highest judicial court in the country. The president is the leader of the executive branch. The president serves as the leader of the country’s armed forces.

title: Economic System in Cuba
text:
The reach of Cuba's communist government extends to the country's economic system. A communist economy is a form of a command economy. Ownership and most other economic decisions are controlled and directed by the government. Historically, the Cuban government dominated the economy. Almost all economic activity came from state-owned companies and enterprises. In the last few decades, Cuba has developed into more of a mixed command economy. A greater portion of Cuba’s GDP comes from private companies and activities than had been allowed previously. However, most workers are still employed by the government.

As a result of tight government control, entrepreneurship has generally been rare and even illegal in Cuba. Recent reforms have loosened economic restrictions. A small but growing number of small business owners are contributing to the Cuban economy. Private property ownership restrictions have been relaxed as well. Citizens are able to own and sell cars and other consumer products. Tourism to the Caribbean island is also a significant portion of the country’s economy. Issues that could disrupt the tourism industry, including travel restrictions and safety concerns, have the potential to negatively affect the tourism industry. Any disruption in tourism has an impact on the overall economy of Cuba.

Despite the recent reforms to incorporate more capitalist policies and economic freedom, Cuba still has one of the least free economies in the world. The government takes a major role in planning and operating the country’s economy. Cuba is dependent on other communist countries for support. In the past, Cuba has benefitted from cheap oil imports from Venezuela, which also has a mixed command economy. As a result, a weakening Venezuelan economy has hurt the Cuban economy.

title: Conclude and Connect
text:
As a communist country centered around a mixed command economy, Cuba’s government and economy are closely linked. The Cuban Communist Party controls most aspects of the government and economy. Elections do occur, but all elected representatives are from the communist political party. No opposition parties are allowed. Citizens are given choices for representatives at lower levels within the government. However, in the upper levels of the government, election results are already decided. No actual choices are available.

This lack of choice and freedom in Cuba also extends to the economy. The Cuban government runs a mixed command economy. It limits the ownership of private property and businesses. State-owned businesses dominate the country’s economy. The government also provides services like education and health care to the population. Private companies that could provide these services are not allowed. The modern global economic environment has forced Cuba to relax some of its economic directives. The change allows for the ownership of some private property and the ownership and operation of certain private businesses. Relationships with other countries have a major influence on Cuba’s economy, both positively and negatively.

title: Government of Brazil
text:
Brazil is the fifth-largest country in the world by land area. Governing a country that size presents major problems that would be difficult for a single government to solve. As a result, Brazil has developed a federal presidential republic that organizes the country into 26 smaller states. These states are led by a federal government with a president and other representatives. These leaders are voted into office by Brazilian citizens. The idea with this system is that the government can be more responsive to the needs of its citizens, even as they are spread across long distances. Even with this system of government, the large size of Brazil, and the challenges created by its geography, present unique challenges for its people and government.

Brazil’s official name is the Federative Republic of Brazil. The federal government is organized into the executive, legislative, and judicial branches in order to ensure the separation of powers. This is meant to ensure that any single person or group is unable to amass too much power and influence. These branches of the federal government are responsible for policies and programs that impact the entire country. The president, as the leader of the executive branch, is elected to four-year terms. Presidents have the ability to be re-elected one time. Like other presidents in federal republics, the president of Brazil serves as the leader of the country’s armed forces. They also appoint officials as leaders of various cabinet positions to help them lead the country.

The Brazilian legislative branch is called the Congresso Nacional, or National Congress. It is bicameral, which means it is divided into two houses. The smaller house is also the upper house. It is known as the Senado Federal or Federal Senate. It has 81 members: three representatives from each state and three from the federal district. The lower house, known as the Câmara dos Deputados (or Chamber of Deputies), is larger. It has 513 representatives. The number of representatives from each state is determined by its population. States with larger populations have more representatives in the Chamber of Deputies. States with smaller populations have fewer representatives. In a republic, these officials are elected by the citizens to serve as their representatives in the government.

The legislative and executive branches of the government work together to appoint judges to the Supremo Tribunal Federal, or Supreme Federal Court. The 11 judges on this court serve until the mandatory retirement age of 75 years old. When a position becomes available through retirement, the president can appoint a new judge to the court. The Federal Senate must then approve that choice. Like other federal judiciaries, the Supreme Federal Court of Brazil judges the constitutionality of laws and interprets them when questions arise.

Brazilian state governments are organized in a very similar way to the federal government. They are led by a governor as head of the executive branch, and each has a legislature. State governments are responsible for governing their state and addressing issues at the state level. There are state-level courts as well. In practice, certain parts of Brazil are remote due to the size of the country and the thick vegetation of the rainforest. This makes it difficult for the state and federal governments to provide the necessary services to all Brazilians.

title: Essential Question
text: What factors impact the governments and economic systems of Latin America?

title: Citizen Participation
text:
As a republic, citizen participation is a significant factor in a healthy, functioning government. There have been several different governments in Brazil’s history. Each has had varying levels of participation guaranteed to the citizens. The most recent major change was the change from a military dictatorship to the current republic in the 1980s. The current constitution has many similarities to other republics around the world. Brazilian citizens are guaranteed certain rights and freedoms like freedom of speech and religion.

Because elections are such an important part of a republic, voting in Brazil is compulsory for citizens between the ages of 18 and 70 years old. Making voting mandatory means that more people vote. The idea for this is that the results of those elections will more closely reflect the will of the people. In addition to the required voting ages, voting between the ages of 16 to 18 or over 70 is voluntary. Presidential elections are held every four years. Elections for the legislative branch occur at the same time. However, because those representatives serve eight-year terms, not all positions are up for election at the same time.

The Brazilian constitution protects the rights of its citizens to assemble peacefully. This includes addressing and protesting government actions. Like other republics, this form of citizen participation is protected. However, despite these protections, protests have been broken up, and protesters have been arrested by police and military forces. Protests have become increasingly common. As a result, the Supreme Federal Court suspended the right to protest in Brazil.

title: Roles and Responsibilities of Government
text:
The organization of Brazil’s government is similar to other federal presidential republics, and the roles and responsibilities of the government are, therefore, similar as well. The three branches of the federal government serve unique roles in running the country and checking the power of the other branches. The executive branch, with the president as the leader, runs the government and the military. The legislative branch is the law-making body. Made up of representatives elected by the people, they pass new laws. They can also modify or remove laws. The judicial branch is the courts, which interpret laws and, if a law is challenged, determine if it is constitutional. Within the functions of these branches, there are ways that each one can check the power of the others. The president can veto laws passed by the legislative branch. The legislative branch can choose not to approve the judges appointed to the Supreme Federal Court by the president. The judicial branch can declare laws passed by the legislative branch as unconstitutional.

The federal government has several responsibilities to the country and its people. Ensuring the safety of people and property through military and police organizations is the responsibility of the president as head of the executive branch. Setting the national budget is also a responsibility of the federal government. Pursuing and maintaining international relationships is another. This includes economic relationships and treaties. As part of funding the government, the federal government has the ability to collect taxes. The federal government also plays a part in national education efforts and supports scientific research and development for the good of the country. States and municipalities retain responsibilities and roles that are not officially given to the federal government by the Constitution. These include more regional or local issues, like transportation, and services like urban planning and garbage pickup.

title: Factors of Economic Growth
text:
Brazil has a wealth of natural resources to contribute to its economic growth. Its human capital is just as important to its growth and success. Educational reforms have been focused on improving early childhood education. This has resulted in improving literacy rates. Despite this, as much as six percent of the adult population in Brazil cannot read. Further improvements to literacy rates in the country can lead to increased economic production and growth. Brazil’s population is also affected by illegal activity and government corruption. These issues limit the ability of private companies and businesses to flourish. Solving these problems would improve the economic outlook of Brazil's private business owners and entrepreneurs.

Some state-owned companies believe that the government should invest in these companies through capital goods like factories, refineries, and machinery. Doing so would boost economic growth, which it has done in the past. Infrastructure is another area in which the government could also invest to increase economic growth. Improvements in roads and other services would allow the large country to be more closely connected. It would also allow for the movement of goods and resources within the country.

title: Conclude and Connect
text:
Brazil has been a republic since the 1980s. However, it also has a history of dictatorships and strong central governments. This means that its economy is a truly mixed economy. Many large, state-owned businesses dominate the energy and natural resource industries. There is also a robust private sector that is vulnerable to instability. This is brought on by illegal activity and government corruption. The government is a republic whose elections see high turnout due to compulsory voting. This is intended to lead to the successful representation of the population. However, due to political instability, the country has not benefited from sustained government efforts to spur economic growth.

Brazil is dependent on its vast natural resources. Investment in infrastructure and capital goods like machinery and technology could help improve the rate of economic growth moving forward. Improvements in infrastructure can help Brazil solve one of its largest problems: the large size and difficult geography of the country. Efforts to support Brazil’s human capital through educational reforms have shown improvement in literacy rates. However, there is still room for improvement in the lives of its people and the economy of the country.

title: Trade in Latin America
text:
Like Australia and Canada, trade is one of Latin America's most important economic activities. Many economies in Latin America, including Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico, rely on importing and exporting goods and services to markets around the world. Latin American imports and exports are directly impacted by the natural resources available in the country. Some natural resources are only found in Latin America. Access to specific natural resources allows producers in Latin America to specialize in specific products and markets. This also allows for the specialization of trade.

Unlike Australia and Canada, trade in many Latin American countries is hindered by the country's government structure. Brazil and Mexico both have a mixed economy. This type of economy is similar to the economic structure of Canada and Australia. It allows for the specialization of trade. Mexico and Brazil’s mixed economy encourages trade while still protecting the rights of consumers and producers. Voluntary trade is also a key component of both economies and allows specialization to occur.

Cuba’s economy is very different from the economies of Brazil and Mexico. Cuba has a planned socialist economy. This economic system was implemented during the regime of communist leader Fidel Castro, which began in 1959. In a planned socialist economy, the state or government owns all economic resources. It also determines all production and distribution of goods and restricts private ownership of capital. This economic system has profoundly impacted trade and other economic factors in Cuba for over 60 years. It continues to influence the country’s economy today.

title: Essential Question
text: What factors impact the governments and economic systems of Latin America?

title: Currencies
text:
Trade in and out of Latin America is dependent on many factors. One factor is the exchange of currency. This can be a difficult task because there are 38 different currencies used throughout Latin America. Many countries use the U.S. dollar as their primary currency. Others have their own currencies.

The primary currency used in Brazil is the Brazilian real. Brazil’s currency consists of seven denominations of paper bills and six coins. The paper bills range from 2 to 200 reals. The Brazilian real is the national currency of the country. However, there are over 80 coins that have been minted by banks around the country to stimulate local economies. While exchange rates vary and change constantly, one Brazilian real is usually worth about 20 cents in U.S. dollars.

In Mexico, the national currency is the Mexican peso. Mexico’s currency consists of six paper bills, ranging from 20 to 1,000 pesos, and seven coins. The exchange rate between the Mexican peso and the U.S. dollar averages one peso for every 50 cents.

The national currency of Cuba is the Cuban peso. There are 10 different Cuban paper pesos, also called banknotes. These range from one to 1,000 pesos. Cuban currency also includes seven coins, called centavos and pesos. One Cuban peso often averages around .042 U.S. dollars.

title: Barriers to Trade
text:
Brazil

Like Australia and Canada, Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico experience barriers that impact international trade.

Producers and consumers in Brazil face different barriers to international trade. Like other countries throughout the world, trade in Brazil is hindered by tariff and non-tariff barriers on imports, exports, and services. Brazil’s government imposes various import taxes, tariffs, and fees. Companies are required to pay an import duty fee, merchandise and service circulation tax, and an industrialized product tax. Brazil’s industrialized product tax can be as high as 15 percent. The merchandise and service circulation tax ranges from 17 to 19 percent on imports. Most Brazilian exports are exempt from taxes and fees.

Brazil’s government also imposes various non-tariff trade barriers on imports. These barriers make it difficult for many countries to import goods and services into the country. They include certifications that are hard to get. They also include labeling and authorization requirements. There are also restrictions that prohibit importing certain goods. The Brazilian government recently encouraged consumers to buy goods and services produced in Brazil. The government of Brazil also puts trade quotas, or limits, on the specific types and amounts of imports from particular countries.

Cuba

Cuba imposes tariff barriers that have an impact on trade. However, the largest barriers to trade are non-tariff barriers. Government restrictions and regulations have hindered trade with Cuba since Castro’s communist regime took over the government in 1959. The government restricted trade with many countries, including the United States. Before the Cuban Revolution, many U.S.-owned companies had manufacturing plants and factories in Cuba. After Castro and his government took control of the country, they seized U.S.-owned companies, factories, and production facilities.

As a result, the U.S. government placed a trade embargo on Cuba in 1960. An embargo is a ban on trade or other commercial activity issued by one country against another country. This embargo prohibited the exportation of goods to Cuba from the United States, except for food and medicine. In 1962, the embargo was placed on all exports. This was because of growing hostilities between the Cuban and U.S. governments. In recent years, the United States has reinstated some diplomatic relations with Cuba, but the trade embargo remains largely in effect.

Mexico

Mexico imposes various tariff barriers on its imports. Import taxes and tariff rates vary based on the types of products that are imported. Agricultural products are usually charged a higher tax rate. Non-agricultural products are charged a lower tax rate. Mexico also imposes a specific tax on the sale of foreign goods, products, and services. This tax is called the value-added tax (VAT). It averages about 16 percent of the total bill of sale.

Non-tariff barriers are also obstacles to trade in Mexico. Non-tariff barriers include licensing requirements and restrictions, product bans, safety regulations, and customs procedures. Technical requirements also create non-tariff barriers. These include labeling and packaging requirements, ingredients, weight and size of goods, testing, and certification processes.

title: Imports and Exports
text:
International trade is an important part of the economic development in many Latin American countries. Latin Americans rely on imports and exports to meet their needs and wants. Many goods cannot be produced in countries in Latin America. This is because some natural resources are not available or are difficult to obtain. Because the climate across Latin America is largely tropical, many goods cannot be produced there. Many countries can only obtain the goods and services they need through trade.

This is dependent upon the volume and type of natural resources available in the area. Many fruits, vegetables, and nuts are native to Central and South America. Cashews, Brazil nuts, papayas, pineapples, avocados, potatoes, corn, and tomatoes are native species of Latin America that still thrive in the region today.
