title: United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)
text: Mexico has many free trade agreements in place. They are meant to facilitate international trade more efficiently and effectively. One of the most profitable trade agreements in effect is the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). This agreement facilitates free trade between Mexico, Canada, and the United States. As a result of this agreement, Canada has become Mexico’s fifth-largest trading partner, and the United States has become Mexico’s largest trading partner. Around 78 percent of all of Mexico’s exports are sent to the United States. The USMCA allows Mexico to create new jobs, promote investments and trade, and prevent economic inequality between regions in the country.

title: Conclude and Connect
text:
Economies throughout Latin America have changed in many ways throughout its history. Despite these changes, trade has remained a constant and important part of the region’s economy. Many factors impact trade. One of the biggest factors that impact trade is the government. Government actions and policies can encourage or hinder trade. This has occurred across Latin America throughout history.

Latin America’s economic history is deeply rooted in trade. Its current economic infrastructures and trade patterns can be traced back to European exploration of the region. Exploration of Latin America began as a result of the need to discover and establish new trade routes. What started as a means to discover a new trade route to Asia began many years of colonization of Latin America and led to the establishment of some of the largest empires in the world. The lasting impact of the exploration and colonization of Latin America can still be seen today in the economy.

title: Indigenous Populations of Latin America
text:
Latin America has been home to many cultures, empires, and people throughout history. Historians and archeologists estimate that people have inhabited Latin America since 20,000 B.C.E. The early people of Latin America were nomadic hunter-gatherers. Over time, the groups of hunter-gatherers began to build permanent settlements. They formed tribes and eventually established large societies. Many societies built great cities. They constructed monumental buildings and created beautiful works of art. These cultures left a lasting legacy that continues to be studied and admired today. Among the largest societies of Latin America were the Olmec, the Maya, the Aztecs, the Incas, and the Taíno people.

The Olmec

The Olmec, Maya, and Aztec civilizations dominated Central America. The Olmec were the first large culture, or organized group of people, in the area. They are considered to be the "mother culture" of Central America. Many later groups, such as the Maya and the Aztecs, developed from the cultural traditions of the Olmec.

The Olmec were the first people to build pyramids in ancient Mesoamerica. Their largest pyramid was over 100 feet tall. The most famous archaeological feature of the Olmec is the large stone heads that range from five to 11 feet tall. They are carved from single blocks of stone. Many of these stone heads have war-like helmets on their heads. Archaeologists believe that these represent the heads of Olmec rulers.

The Maya

The Maya Empire lasted for nearly 3,000 years, from 1800 B.C.E. to about 900 C.E. The empire covered parts of what are now Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Belize. The Maya were advanced mathematicians and agriculturalists. They knew how to rotate crops to keep farm soil from being overused. They used math to create complex architecture and accurate calendars.

The Maya had a written hieroglyphic language and a sophisticated government system. This civilization existed between many independent city-states. Trade existed between the city-states. However, each settlement tended to manage its own people.

The Aztec

The Aztecs settled in Central America around 1200 C.E. They built their capital city, Tenochtitlán, on artificial islands in the middle of Lake Texcoco. They had an advanced agricultural system. It used irrigation and “floating gardens” that allowed them to grow much of their own food. The Aztecs also formed political alliances with two neighboring tribes. Those alliances helped to expand their empire. Today, the capital city of Tenochtitlán has become what is now Mexico City, Mexico.

The Aztec empire grew rapidly through the 14th century. Its people conquered neighboring peoples and built impressive, thriving cities. At its peak, the Aztec empire had a population of around five or six million, including conquered peoples. Tenochtitlán, the capital city of the Aztec empire, had a population of over 140,000. It was the most densely populated city to ever exist in Central America.

The Inca

The Inca Empire was one of the largest empires in the world from around 1400 C.E. until its end in 1533 C.E. The Inca lived in and around the Andes Mountains. They called their empire Tahuantinsuyu. This translates to “four quarters,” which is how they divided their government. The empire had a population of 10 million people that spoke 30 different languages.

Stretching more than 2,500 miles from Santiago, Chile, in the south to Quito, Ecuador, in the north, the Inca Empire was truly massive. The Inca borrowed advancements and technologies that had been developed during earlier civilizations. They built pyramids, temples, and elaborate terraced farms. The Inca worshiped several gods. The sun god was chief among them. Mummification and sacrifice were important parts of religious worship for the Inca. Inca mathematicians based their calculations on the number 10, including a decimal system.

The Taíno

The Taíno people were one of the largest tribes in the Caribbean for more than 2,000 years before European colonization of Latin America. The Taíno were descendants of the Arawak people of South America. They shared many cultural similarities with their ancestors. The Taíno inhabited the islands throughout the Greater Antilles. That included modern-day Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic.

Taíno society was divided into different kingdoms. Each kingdom was ruled by a hierarchy of leaders called caciques. Men and women served as caciques in the various kingdoms. The Taíno lived in settlements ranging from a few families to thousands of inhabitants. The Taíno were skilled farmers, hunters, and sailors. They constructed large canoes to travel between the various islands of the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean.

title: Essential Question
text: What factors and events have impacted the people and culture of Latin America?

title: Spanish Exploration and Colonization
text:
During the 15th century, the whole world was on the move. The empires in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas were growing. Rich empires served as patrons, meaning they could pay people to study, explore, or create art for the glory of the empire. This patronage led to new advances in knowledge and exchanges of ideas through trade routes. In the 1400s, most of the world’s people lived in Asia. China and India had the world’s largest economies because of their trading. Spices, silks, gold, and other goods were traded all the way to Europe. At this time, the Ottoman Empire was rising between Asia and Europe. The Ottomans gained control of trade connections between the two continents and stopped trade with Europe.

For merchants in Europe, losing control of trade with Asia was hard. The government of Spain, however, used this situation as an opportunity to find and create new sources of trade. In 1490, Ferdinand and Isabella became the king and queen of Spain. Spain had just ended a religious war persecuting non-Christians. They had taken property from Jews and Muslims in Spain, which made them rich enough to be important patrons. Ferdinand and Isabella wanted new trade routes and income. They just needed the right idea to pay for and the right person to try it. An entrepreneur named Christopher Columbus had an unusual idea. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach India and create a new trade route.

Columbus needed a wealthy patron to finance his voyage. Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand agreed to be patrons of Columbus. They paid for tools, three ships, and the crew needed for the voyage. Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. He was sure that he could reach India by sailing west. No one in Europe at the time knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India. When Columbus landed, he thought he had reached India. It is believed he called the people he met “Indians” due to his misconception.

Columbus brought evidence of his trip back to Europe and shared his adventures. Columbus’s journey launched the biggest changes in government, knowledge, and trade the world had ever seen. Powerful rulers sent explorers to expand their empires. Many Spanish explorers followed Columbus’s example and set sail for the Americas. Most of the early Spanish explorers that sailed to the Americas focused their attention on exploring Latin America. One of the primary goals of Spanish exploration was to establish permanent colonies in the Americas. For nearly 300 years, Spanish settlers established new colonies through Spain’s vast empire in the Americas.

Timeline of Spanish Exploration and Colonization of Latin America

1492: Christopher Columbus reaches the Caribbean, exploring multiple islands. He claims the land for Spain.

1493: Columbus claims the island of Puerto Rico for Spain and names it San Juan Bautista.

1496: The first Spanish colony in the Americas is established at Santo Domingo, Hispaniola (now the Dominican Republic).

1508: Juan Ponce de León establishes the first European settlement in Puerto Rico, which he names Caparra. Eventually, the city is renamed San Juan.

1515: Spanish explorer Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar conquers Cuba and settlers establish the city of Havana.

1519: Hernán Cortés conquers what is now central and southern Mexico, establishing the Spanish colony of New Spain.

1533: Francisco Pizarro overthrows the Inca empire in Peru and claims the territory for Spain.

1537–1543: Spanish conquistadors explore present-day Colombia and Venezuela. They establish the New Kingdom of Grenada.

1541: Pedro de Valdivia establishes the first European settlement in Chile.

1541: Spanish explorers establish the city of Asunción, Paraguay, in Central America.

title: Portuguese Exploration and Colonization
text:
The Portuguese began to explore other areas of the world in the late 1400s. They concentrated their initial efforts on Africa. The Portuguese wanted to establish trade with Africa and find a way to sail around Africa to reach Asia. Prince Henry the Navigator was a Portuguese duke. Although he was called “the Navigator,” he never went to sea. He did, however, control a large amount of money for an organization called the “Order of Christ.” This organization brought navigators and geographers together. They planned expeditions to unexplored regions along the Atlantic coast, south of Portugal.

The Portuguese government hired a sea captain named Bartolomeu Perestrello and his ship for their expeditions. The early voyages sent Perestrello to the mid-Atlantic islands, such as Madeira and the Azores. These explorations were followed by routes along the west coast of Africa. As a result of their exploration, the Portuguese began to colonize new areas.

Beginning in 1445, the Azores rapidly filled with colonists. They developed a rich sugar-producing colony. The sugar was exported to European markets. The Portuguese also established trading posts along the west coast of Africa. In 1488, the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias reached the southern tip of Africa. He was the first European to ever do so. He entered the Indian Ocean and paved the way for others. Portuguese explorers followed Spain’s example and expanded their efforts to Latin America.

Timeline of Portuguese Exploration and Colonization of Latin America

1500: Pedro Álvares Cabral lands in Brazil and claims the land for Portugal.

1502: Portuguese explorers establish the first European settlement in Brazil north of present-day Rio de Janeiro. Within a few years, the settlement is abandoned.

1519–1522: Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan becomes the first person to circumnavigate (sail completely around) the globe.

1532: Portuguese settlers establish São Vicente, the first permanent settlement in Brazil.

1533–1539: Portuguese explorers and settlers establish Pernambuco and Rio. During this time, sugar plantations are established at Sâo Vicente, Pernambuco, and Rio.

1549: Brazil becomes a crown colony of Portugal, making it a vital part of the vast Portuguese empire.

title: Influence on Religion, Language, and Culture
text:
Religion

Religion was one of the primary motivations for the Spanish and Portuguese exploration of Latin America. During the Age of Exploration, the governments of Spain and Portugal were strongly intertwined with the Roman Catholic Church. The Catholic Church influenced many of the decisions of the Spanish and Portuguese governments. It also helped finance expeditions to the Americas. Because of this, many explorers were tasked with converting the people they conquered to Christianity.

As the Spanish and Portuguese expanded their empires throughout Latin America, explorers and settlers brought their religious beliefs and customs with them. They also converted millions of Indigenous people to Catholicism. Sometimes they converted by choice; other times, the colonizers used force. Regardless, Catholicism became the predominant religion of Latin America. It remains so to this day.

Language

In addition to their religious beliefs and customs, explorers and settlers brought their languages. While Spain and Portugal were the primary countries who established colonies in Latin America, they were not the only countries to do so during the Age of Exploration. This is part of the reason that so many languages are spoken in Latin America.

Spanish is the predominant language spoken throughout Latin America. Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Puerto Rico, and many countries in South America were once Spanish colonies. Today, Mexico is the largest Spanish-speaking country in the world. Roughly 60 percent of Latin America’s total population speaks Spanish.

Great Britain also had colonies in the Caribbean. These include Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Dominica, Bahamas, Barbados, and the British Leeward and Windward Islands. These islands were traditionally referred to as the West Indies. English continues to be one of the predominant languages in this region of the Caribbean.

Martinique was the first French colony in the Caribbean. The French also conquered the Caribbean islands of Saint Christopher (now called Saint Kitts) Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy, Grenada, Saint Martin, Tortuga, and the western half of Hispaniola, which is now called Haiti. French is still spoken and is one of the primary languages of these island nations.

Dutch explorers led expeditions throughout Latin America in the 1500s. They did not establish any formal colonies. However, they did manage to settle on Surinam, parts of Saint Martin, and the Guyanas. Dutch is still spoken by small pockets of the population in these areas.

Brazil is the only Latin American country where the primary language is Portuguese. Brazilian Portuguese is still similar to European Portuguese. However, it has many differences as well. Brazilian Portuguese has been influenced by other European languages, native South American languages, and languages brought to Latin America by enslaved Africans.

Culture

Latin America has been a melting pot of cultures since European exploration. As different groups of people came together, new cultures formed. Over time, European and African settlers and Indigenous people shared their cultural customs with each other. Many people in Latin America are of mixed European, African, and Indigenous descent.

The largest ethnicity in South America is the mestizo culture. The term “mestizo” comes from the Spanish word for mixed. People who identify as mestizo are a mixture of Indigenous, African, and European ethnicities. Overall, about 34 percent of Latin America’s population identifies ethnically as mestizo. This is not a new concept for Latin Americans. The Spanish colonial caste, a social class system, determined the position of mestizo people within Latin American society. During the 20th century, many Latin American governments adopted a social system called mestizaje. This social system identified all citizens of different countries as mestizo in order to create racial equality.

title: The Middle Passage
text:
As the Portuguese explored the western coast of Africa, they established trading posts. These trading posts were used to trade Portuguese goods to traders in Africa. Over time, African merchants began to trade enslaved people in exchange for goods. By the mid-1550s, 10 percent of Portugal’s population was enslaved men, women, and children. This early trade by Portuguese ships established the system of bringing enslaved people across the Atlantic. The first recorded ship carrying 200 enslaved people sailed to the Caribbean in 1525.

In the 300 years following Columbus's journey to the Americas, almost all ships that crossed the Atlantic came from Europe. However, most ships didn’t sail straight from Europe to the Americas. The sea currents and wind directions made sailing south toward Africa easier and faster. This route presented opportunities for trade by staying near the continents.

This voyage from Europe to Africa was called the Outward Passage. Ships carried tools, weapons, cloth, and other goods to Africa. Merchants and soldiers pressured African leaders to trade European goods for people who had been captured in wars or kidnapped. Enslaved men, women, and children were put in dark, dank ships. The traders who held the Africans against their will transported them across the Atlantic. They were sold to enslavers in the West Indies and American colonies. The voyage from Africa to the colonies in the Western Hemisphere was called “the Middle Passage.”

title: Sugar Production in Latin America
text:
In the 1400s, Europe traded with Asia for sugar. People loved the taste of sugar and paid high prices for it. Sugar is produced from sugarcane. Sugarcane needs a warm environment to grow. It also needs lots of rain or good irrigation. When European explorers arrived in Latin America, they found a warm, wet climate where sugar could grow easily. Sugarcane grew especially well on islands in the Caribbean Sea. European colonists realized sugar could become a cash crop. A cash crop is a crop people grow to sell and make money. This led to large areas of land being used to grow only one kind of cash crop. These large farms became known as plantations.

It took hard work to grow and harvest sugarcane. Sugarcane doesn’t produce seeds. Someone had to cut hard stalks in pieces by hand and then plant them. It was also difficult to get soft sugar out of the tough stalks. As plantation owners earned more money from sugar, they looked for ways to get cheap labor to plant, harvest, and process the sugar. They began enslaving native people, taking away their freedom and forcing them to do the work. When many died or escaped, plantation owners turned to the slave trade from Africa.

Once the sugarcane was harvested, it was processed and shaped into blocks. The blocks of sugar were then packed into barrels and shipped to Europe and eventually North America. As production increased and became more readily available, sugar went from being a luxury item to a staple in most homes. Sugar production continues to be a vital part of the economy for many countries in Latin America.

title: Effects of Colonization on Latin America
text:
Beliefs

Before European exploration of the Americas, Native Americans had very different beliefs from Europeans. Many Europeans wanted Native Americans to convert to Christianity. Some Native Americans chose to convert. Others did not. These differences in beliefs often led to conflicts between Native American tribes and European settlers.

Disease

Europeans unknowingly brought many diseases with them to the Americas. These diseases included smallpox, measles, and influenza. These diseases were very contagious and often deadly. The Indigenous population of the Americas had no immunity to these diseases. They spread very quickly and easily in Indigenous communities. Millions of Indigenous people died from these diseases. These diseases had a devastating impact on Native American tribes.

African Enslavement

As European colonization of the Americas began to spread, the demand for labor increased. European enslavers and traders from Portugal, France, England, and the Netherlands bought enslaved people from Africa. Enslavers, traders, and merchants packed their ships with enslaved people. They then made the dangerous journey across the Atlantic Ocean to sell the enslaved people in the Americas.

Wealthy businessmen took advantage of the slave trade to increase their wealth. Cash crops like sugarcane, tobacco, and cotton all required a great amount of work to grow.

The life of a person who was enslaved changed little from day to day. They were clothed, fed, and sheltered with whatever the enslaver wanted to provide. The workday was structured by the enslaver.

Enslaved people were taken from their homes, families, cultures, and everything they had known. Everything in their lives was turned upside down. They were forced to work in an unfamiliar environment with unfamiliar people. They had to learn how to use unfamiliar tools, grow new crops, and learn a new language.

The one thing the enslavers could not take from the enslaved people was their memories. They kept the celebrations and traditions of their communities and cultures alive. They remembered the stories, songs, and skills they learned in Africa. Enslavers tried to stop the African people from expressing their cultural identities. The enslaved Africans continued to preserve their memories and culture despite these efforts.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The history of Latin America has been greatly influenced by Indigenous peoples for thousands of years. During the Age of Exploration, European and African cultural influences were introduced. Many new customs and traditions were created. Some of the new cultural customs were positive. Many others had a negative impact on the Indigenous peoples of Latin America and the enslaved Africans that were brought to the region through the Atlantic slave trade. The culture and history of Latin America have often been characterized by the themes of conflict and change. These themes continued through the 20th and 21st centuries.

title: History of Cuba
text:
Cuba is surrounded by the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico. Florida is located to the north. Jamaica and the Cayman Islands are found to the south. Hispaniola is to the east. Mexico is located just west of Cuba. This prime location opens Cuba up to many trade opportunities.

In 1492, Cuba was claimed by Christopher Columbus and officially became a colony of Spain. This marks only the start of Cuba being transferred back and forth between many international empires. The timeline describes the events in Cuba between the founding of the country and the start of the Cuban Revolution. How do these events lead to Cubans wanting independence?

1511: Diego Velazquez is appointed the first governor of Cuba by the Spanish government.

1514: Havana is founded.

1537: The French occupy Havana.

1662: The British capture Cuba.

1670: The British leave Cuba.

1748: The British gain a victory over Spain during the Battle of Havana.

1762: The British attack Havana as part of the Seven Years’ War.

1763: The British transfer Cuba back to Spain.

1868: Cuba’s first war of independence from Spain begins.

1895: The second war for independence against Spain begins.

1898: The Spanish-American War begins, culminating in the transfer of Cuba to the United States.

1899: U.S. Secretary of War William Howard Taft becomes the provisional governor of Cuba. He creates a provisional government and works to establish Guantanamo Bay as a naval base.

1902: Cuba becomes independent and holds its first elections. However, the United States still has protection rights on Cuba and can intervene.

1906: The first president of Cuba resigns. The United States comes back to Cuba to occupy it for the second time.

1909: The United States leaves Cuba. The second Cuban president is elected by the people.

1924: Gerardo Machado takes over Cuba and creates a dictatorship.

1925: The Socialist Party is formed in Cuba, leading to the basis for the Communist Party.

1933: Gerardo Machado is overthrown in a rebellion led by Fulgencio Batista.

1934: The United States is no longer involved in Cuba’s internal issues, however, it works to favor the tariffs and sugar quotas for Cuba.

1952: Fulgencio Batista creates a corrupt and powerful regime.

1953: Fidel Castro leads an unsuccessful attempt to take power away from Fulgencio Batista.

1959: The Cuban Revolution begins.

The United States had worked alongside Cuba as an aid within their economic boundaries. The United States worked to build and increase the economic system in Cuba. They also tried to help and guide the political situation. The United States had great economic success within Cuba during the 1950s.

During that time, the United States helped to provide 90 percent of telephone and electric services. They helped provide 50 percent of public service railways.
