Thousands of jobs are also supported by film productions. In addition to its economic benefits, the film industry has also helped to promote Georgia as a tourist destination. Many visitors come to Georgia to see the locations featured in their favorite movies and television shows. Georgia has capitalized on this interest by promoting film-related tourism.

Tourism and the film industry have had a significant impact on Georgia's economy and reputation. Millions of people from around the world visit Georgia each year. They enjoy a vast diversity of landscapes and historical and cultural attractions. The revenue generated from their visits benefits the state and its residents.

title: Port of Savannah: Gateway to the World
text:
The Port of Savannah is a major gateway for international trade. A port is a town or an area of land where ships are loaded or unloaded. A port is also an area where ships may be protected from storms and other bad weather. Many goods shipped in and out of the United States pass through Savannah. As a result, the Port of Savannah is one of the busiest and fastest-growing ports in the United States.

In Georgia’s early colonial years, Savannah was a key port. The city's location led to its growth as a trading hub. It had the advantage of being near the Savannah River and the Atlantic Ocean. The Savannah River's size and depth made it possible for larger sailing ships to dock there. Various agricultural products were shipped from the port. Indigo, rice, and cotton were some of the major exports.

Savannah's port continued to thrive in the years leading up to the American Civil War. The city became an important shipping center for the cotton trade. Cotton produced in the surrounding region was transported to the port. From there, it was exported to European and Northern United States markets.

The Port of Savannah also played a vital role during the American Civil War. In 1864, General William T. Sherman captured the city of Savannah. This secured a critical supply line for the Union Army in the South. After the war, Savannah's port played a role in the Reconstruction era. The city worked to rebuild its economy and infrastructure.

In the 20th century, the Port of Savannah continued to grow, change, and modernize. Over the years, various improvements were made to the port's infrastructure. These improvements included dredging, or cleaning up the bottom of the river, to increase the depth of the river channel. The construction of larger container terminals allowed for an increase in shipping traffic. As a result of the improvements, the Port of Savannah has experienced significant growth and expansion in recent decades. This expansion has had a significant impact on Georgia's economy. The increased traffic through the port has created new job opportunities. It has also boosted economic activity throughout the state. In 2020, the port handled over 4.6 million TEUs (20-foot equivalent units) of cargo. A TEU is the size of a standard shipping container. It's 20 feet long by eight feet wide by eight feet tall. As a result, the Port of Savannah is among the top U.S. ports based on the amount of cargo that passes through its waters.

The Port of Savannah's expansion has positively affected other industries in Georgia. Many businesses have set up operations in the state to take advantage of the port's access to global markets. This has led to new job opportunities and economic growth. On a global level, the expansion of the Port of Savannah has also helped to position the United States as a significant player in international trade. The port's strategic location on the East Coast of the United States allows it to serve as a key gateway for goods from Asia and Europe.

title: The Intolerable Acts
text:
In response to the damage of the tea cargo in Boston, Parliament created the Coercive Acts. These acts were designed by King George III to punish Massachusetts colonists for the tea party and their continued resistance to his actions and his government. Because of this, the acts also became known as the “Intolerable Acts.”

The following was directed at Massachusetts:

Boston Port Act (June 1, 1774): closed off the port of Boston, eliminating commerce and trade in the city.

Administration of Justice Act (May 20, 1774): granted a change of location to Great Britain or a British Colony in the event of a jury trial.

Massachusetts Government Act (May 20, 1774): repealed the colony’s charter and created an unprecedented amount of royal control.

Quartering Act (June 2, 1774): allowed new royal governor General Thomas Gage to house British soldiers in private homes, inns, and other buildings without permission from colonists.

Quebec Act (June 22, 1774): designated the western region north of the Ohio River as part of Quebec and made Roman Catholicism the established religion of Quebec; this upset colonial Protestants.

Each colonial legislature called for a meeting of representatives. This was called the First Continental Congress. Representatives gathered in Carpenters' Hall in Philadelphia on Sept. 5, 1774. Twelve of the 13 colonies sent delegates.

The first order of business was to write a petition to King George to remove the recent Acts applied to Massachusetts. Each colony had protested the Tea Act in some manner, but Massachusetts was receiving the punishment. The delegates at the congress knew the king could do the same to each of their colonies at any time.

The delegates continued to prepare. They agreed that if the offending Acts of Parliament were not repealed, the colonies would boycott British goods. The congress also recommended that each colony continue to defy Parliament and the king. They also recommended that each colony prepare a militia of Patriots and begin gathering supplies for them.

The delegates of the congress sent their petition to King George through Benjamin Franklin, who was in London as an agent for the Pennsylvania colony.

At the end of the congressional session in October 1774, the members agreed to meet in a second continental congress the

following May, in 1775.

title: Everyday Life
text:
The Incas didn’t use money. They also didn’t use a market economy. This means that they didn’t make their living through buying and selling goods. So, farmers did not own the land they worked. Most of the food they produced belonged to the community. They paid their “taxes” by spending some of their time working on community construction projects, or serving as soldiers, or mining.

In return, they were able to share in the resources the community produced. The government would also provide food at the monthly festivals, maintain the roads and aqueducts, and provide pack animals for transportation. The Inca people had to live up to high standards. The three most important rules were: Do not steal, do not lie, and do not be lazy. There were even government officials who had the job of making sure people’s houses were clean.

Commoners made up about 90 percent of the Inca population. They rarely traveled, except to festivals in the cities. They spent most of their time working. The children of commoners were not educated. They were simply trained to do their job, whether as farmers or artisans. Sometimes, especially talented or beautiful commoner girls would be chosen to work in the cities as spinners or weavers, since textiles were highly valued. Or they would learn about the Incareligion and work in temples.

The upper classes were priests and government officers. Their children were educated for about four years. They would memorize stories from history and religion. They would learn to do government and religious jobs. They might learn to use a quipu, a series of strings with special knots tied in them. Where and how the knots were tied would convey a message.

People in the upper classes could own land and did not have to pay the labor tax. They wore earplugs made of shell or metal in their earlobes. They would put larger and larger earplugs in until sometimes their earlobes stretched all the way down to their shoulders.

title: Terrace Farming
text:
The Andes provided a good ecosystem for farming, but the land was

not very flat. Farmers needed to find a way to work the soil on hillsides.

They learned to use the terrain and landforms together with the

climate and became very skilled farmers. They developed a technique

called step, or terrace, farming. They dug out flat patches of land for

farming that made the side of the mountain look like a giant staircase.

In order to water their crops, engineers and architects built canals and

aqueducts. Aqueducts are human-made structures, usually made from

stone, that bring water from one place to

another. The Inca also used rainfall and

river water to supply an irrigation system.

Farming was very important to the

Inca, and they used every available bit

of earth to grow their crops through

terrace farming. The benefit of terracing

farmland was twofold: the Inca were able

to grow crops on previously unusable

steep hillsides, and they were able to save

soil and water by reducing the amount of

erosion. Erosion is when soil is removed

from its original location by wind or water.

Terraces prevent soil from moving through

either means: wind or water. The Inca

incorporated crop rotation to help the

soil recover lost nutrients and added

fertilizer to boost crop production.

Only growing a crop in one field for

a few seasons or rotating which

crop grew in which field is called

crop rotation.

The Inca used llamas to carry

supplies and goods. Llamas were

also used for moving valuable metal

resources from mines to city centers.

Most importantly, llamas were used to

support the Inca’s main economic

source, farming.

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Like many Mesoamerican cultures, the Inca

were polytheistic. They worshiped many gods.

Some of these gods included Inti, the sun god;

Mamaquilla, known as Mother Moon, who was

in charge of the calendar; Illapa, who controlled

the weather; and Pachamama, the Earth Mother

who protected crops. However, the Incas also

sometimes worshiped household gods. These

gods were often represented with small carved

objects resembling crops or animals. As the

Inca Empire expanded, the Inca would allow

conquered people to keep their local gods, but it

was understood that the Inca gods would be the

highest gods.

The Inca were very religious. They had

religious festivals every month with a five-day

feast at the end of the year. The first festival

of the year was meant to initiate boys into

manhood. The festival held in June focused

on the sun god and marked the beginning

of the plowing season. Another festival was

held during the rainy season (when there

was a lot of sickness). The Incas would

shake out their clothes and carry ashes out

of their cities to drop in a river. Then they

would purify themselves by washing in

the river. These rituals helped prevent the

sicknesses that the rainy season brought.

Some of their festivals involved human

sacrifice. The Incas considered it an honor

to be sacrificed to the gods. Some of the

world’s best-preserved mummies are

Inca human sacrifices. The cool, dry

climate of the Andes helped to preserve

these mummies.

The Sapa Inca was considered a

god. When Sapa Inca died, he would be

mummified. The mummified bodies of the

Sapa Inca would be stored and brought

out for important festivals. The Inca

believed that the mummies of their kings

would give them wisdom through oracles.

An oracle was a priest who sought advice

All of Inca society organized themselves

into family clans called ayllus. Trade and

ancestor worship was conducted within

the ayllu. Inca society was divided further

into four classes. There was only one

person in the top class: the Sapa Inca, or

the king. The Sapa Inca was considered

to be a god and was treated like one. The

Sapa Inca was so important that his old

clothing, hair, and nail clippings were

saved. These items were used to create

huacas, a kind of statue that represented

the Sapa Inca whenever he could not

be somewhere.

The next class down, the royalty class,

was made up of people who were related

to the founders of the Inca civilizations

by blood. They were direct relatives of the

Sapa Inca. They lived in luxury and held

the highest governmental and religious

positions. For example, the Willac Umu

was the high priest. The Incas believed he

spoke directly with Inti, the sun god. The

king’s first wife, called the Coya, also held

much power. Political power in the Inca

Empire was hereditary. This meant power

stayed within the family. So, future kings

were selected from this class of people.

However, as the empire grew, there

weren’t enough direct relatives of the

Sapa Inca to run the high levels of

government and religion. So, some

people who were not royalty or

blood relatives of the Sapa Inca were

brought in to help. They were called

Inca-by-privilege.

The next class down was the

administrative class. It was made up

of people who ran the lower levels of

government and religion. For example,

when the Incas conquered a group

of people, they would often leave the

people’s ruler in charge, if that ruler would

be obedient to Inca rule. These people

were called Curacas. Tax collectors were

also a part of this class. They made sure

that people contributed their share of

labor to the community. Record keepers

kept track of how much people contributed

and where those contributions were

stored. The government would use these

contributions to feed the upper classes,

the army, and the poor and disabled.

The bottom class, the commoners, was

made up of artisans, farmers, and herders.

The artisans were considered higher-class

than farmers and herders. They forged

jewelry, wove cloth, and made pottery.

Farmers worked on terraced farms: their

own, as well as the fields dedicated to

the government and religious purposes.

They also worked regularly on government

projects, such as roads, aqueducts, and

food storage buildings. Herders

maintained the llama and

alpaca herds. These animals

were valued as pack animals

as well as for their wool,

which the Incas made into

warm clothing. Warm clothing

was necessary in the Andes

Mountains because it got very

cold during certain times of

the year.

Ordinary people also created

mummies. Whenever a person died,

burial grounds where their body was

mummies were consulted and brought

out for festivals, however, this was only

done among the family clan, or ayllu.

The worst thing that could happen to

burned. The Incas believed burning a

body would destroy its vital essence and

make it difficult for the person to get to

the afterlife, which was a paradise.

title: Oral Traditions
text:
Most cultures have an origin story, describing

how the Earth was created and how humans

populated it. Since the Incas didn’t have a

written language, their origin stories are

oral stories. They were passed from one

person to another for many centuries.

One origin story talks about a god named

Viracocha who originally created the world,

but it did not have sun, moon, or stars. At first,

he sculpted and painted large, strangely shaped

giants to populate the Earth. But they were larger

than he was. He decided that wouldn’t be a good

idea, so he made them his own size. All these people

lived in darkness. Viracocha gave them a commandment,

but they broke it. So he turned some of them to stone or had

the earth swallow them. Then he sent a flood to drown the rest.

Different groups of people who made up the Incan civilization had different stories

about how their ancestors were saved from the flood. Some say their ancestors climbed a

mountain that floated on the water. Others said that no one escaped the flood and that

Viracocha created entirely new people to populate the land. They said that after the flood,

Viracocha created the sun, moon, and stars. Then he painted pictures of various groups

of people and told his two servants where to go to summon the people. So the servants

traveled around, calling people out of the lakes, springs, valleys, caves, trees, and rocks.

These newly created people all spoke one language. As they moved from place to

place, they started to change their language, some of them copying the sounds of

animals. When they met up again, they could not understand one another. Some of

them could no longer recognize Viracocha and tried to kill him. He brought down fire

from the sky to protect himself. Soon, he turned the rule of humans over to lesser gods

and disappeared.

title: Machu Picchu
text:
Perched high atop a peak in the Andes Mountains

sits one of the most amazing human construction

projects ever created. It was an Inca city. It was

discovered by chance about 100 years ago, but it

had been built nearly seven centuries ago. It is called

Machu Picchu. In 2007, it was named one of the new

Seven Wonders of the World. It sits nearly 8,000 feet

above sea level in the mountains of Peru; the historic

Inca city of Cusco is the closest major city.

What it was used for is still a topic of discussion.

Most historians believe that Machu Picchu was built by

the originator of the empire, Pachacuti. Some believe

that a population of 300 to 1,000 people lived in the

stone buildings, platforms, and plazas there. The

people probably survived by farming the hillsides and

growing food in terraced gardens. It was a sacred site

for the Inca; its buildings also served as observatories

for sky-watching. Astronomy was important to the

Inca, and Machu Picchu was built to follow the sun.

The stone structures were built so well that they

are expected to stand for hundreds of years more.

The builders did not use mortar to hold the stones

together, yet the stones seem locked in place with no

gaps between them; a knife blade and even a needle

can’t pass between two locked stones. This design

has helped Machu Picchu’s architecture survive many

earthquakes. When a building is built with mortar and

an earthquake comes, the mortar crumbles and the

building collapses. However, with the Inca design,

when an earthquake comes, the rocks can move back

and forth against each other and settle back into

their original places without cracking or crumbling.

There were no wheels to help move the stones up the

mountain, so the Inca either had to chisel the rock out

of the mountain or push the stone up the mountain,

using only human power. It is truly an Andean marvel.

title: Culture
text: Each society has a unique and distinct culture that has developed over time. Culture is composed of various characteristics that make up a society’s way of life. Many factors contribute to the characteristics of a culture. These things develop naturally over time. Traditions and customs can be influenced by climate and geography. The resources available in a certain area will determine what people eat, do, and create. Religion spreads and changes as people travel and share their beliefs. Each culture has developed a way of governing its society, which may differ from the governments of other cultures. Cultures change and develop as societies develop over hundreds or even thousands of years. Traditions, customs, and religions change and alter through interactions with other cultures or the effects of time.

title: Governance
text:
In every society, there is the question of who should be in charge. How will the people choose a leader? Should it be one person or many people? How much power should that person or those people have? The connecting theme of governance has been a question for every society. Simple societies, like the earliest ones in human history, likely found simple answers to those questions. They might have been ruled by one leader who had all the power.

As societies became more complex, governments became more complex. Over time, large countries formed. One person or group couldn't keep up with all of the government's needs, especially over long distances. Governments began to develop complex bureaucracies with different levels staffed by officials who took on various roles and responsibilities. A country like the United States has different government levels and branches. Each city, country, and state has its own government.

title: How the War Was Fought in the South
text:
In the summer of 1778, the British soldiers realized that they were not winning the war in the Northern and Middle Colonies. So, they turned their attention to the Southern Colonies. Many southern colonists remained loyal to the soldiers and provided additional support to them. The British military was confident that it could defeat the Patriot forces in the south.

Fighting in the Southern Colonies was different from fighting in the Northern or Middle Colonies. The weather, land, and plants were different. The southern states were also less populated.

The geography of the Southern Colonies had wide, rolling hills and open fields. There were large areas of thick woodlands, and there were also great areas of marshland. The natural features of the South were spread farther apart than features found in the close terrain of the Appalachian Mountains. Movement was easy in the fields, but the marshes and swamps were more difficult to navigate. The woodlands were so thick that wagons couldn’t travel through them.

The Southern Colonies had a large number of Loyalists in each colony. The British army appealed to their loyalty and asked the Loyalists to share information about their Patriot neighbors. This created a great amount of tension between neighbors and friends. Friendships were questioned, and in the name of the king, some friendships ended.

The Patriot forces were usually outnumbered by the British forces. The British forces were also better trained, so the Patriot forces had to find other ways to win.

Typical battles during the Revolution required two armies to face each other in an open field. However, the Patriot forces learned another strategy from the American Indians. A small group of Patriots would hide in the underbrush and launch a surprise attack on the larger British army. Then, the Patriots would run back into the forest and marshland, letting the British soldiers chase them. They weakened the British army this way. Patriot soldiers also attacked British supply lines, which made it hard for the British soldiers to receive the food and support they needed.

British generals felt the American Patriots were not honorable in the way they fought. However, the Americans were fighting for independence. They believed they had to use the strategies that would help them win.

title: The Yorktown Siege
text:
The last battle between the British and the Americans in the colonies was the Battle of Yorktown. This battle was a siege. A siege is when an army surrounds its enemy. Successful sieges cut off supplies, which makes it hard for the enemy to keep fighting. During the Siege of Yorktown, the question was how long the British army could last without getting fresh supplies. The army could only defend its position in Yorktown and hope that help would come to break the siege. Despite the British resistance, the Americans and French won this battle.

Near the end of the war, a few important things happened. The American soldiers in the South were led by Nathanael Greene, who used smaller forces to move quickly. Although he was ultimately defeated, his tactics weakened British forces and were key to British General Charles Cornwallis’s decision to leave North Carolina.

Cornwallis set up defenses at Yorktown, Virginia, and waited for reinforcements to arrive by ship. However, French forces blocked supply lines to Cornwallis and his troops; the French military also defeated Admiral Thomas Graves in the Battle of the Chesapeake. General George Washington saw an opportunity and sent 4,500 troops to Yorktown to prevent the British army from leaving. Washington also sent troops to join the French fleet in the Chesapeake Bay. Blocking the Chesapeake Bay meant nearby British ships were unable to send soldiers to aid Cornwallis. Trapped on the Yorktown Peninsula and Gloucester Point, Cornwallis was surrounded.

When Washington arrived at Yorktown, he began a siege on Sept. 28, 1781, that lasted for 11 days. The British forces suffered many losses. They began running low on food and were greatly outnumbered. General Cornwallis had no choice but to end the battle. He sent Brig. General Charles O'Hara to negotiate terms of surrender. Cornwallis claimed he was too sick to attend. Some historians think he was embarrassed. The terms of surrender were written down. They were called the Articles of Capitulation, and they were signed on Oct. 19, 1781.

After the Americans and their allies won at Yorktown, fighting in the colonies came to an end. Battles at sea between the French, British, and American privateers continued for some time, though. Peace talks began in 1782, and finally, the Treaty of Paris officially ended the Revolutionary War in September 1783.

title: The Inquiry Process
text:
Use the compelling question "How did geography, climate, and proximity to water affect the lives of the Indigenous peoples of North America?" Follow the inquiry process.

Ask a compelling question.

What do I want to know about this?

What do I already know? What evidence do I already have?

What else do I need to find out?

Make a claim.

What is a possible answer?

What supporting questions will help me focus my research?

Search for answers. Experiment.

What kinds of resources will help me find answers?

Where can I find the resources?

How do I know the information is credible?

How does this information relate to my compelling question?

Which parts help answer my question?

Which parts do not support my question?

Does it create other questions?

Present your conclusions.

Summarize my information. What is the main idea?

What is the answer to my compelling question?

Does it support my claim or not?

title: Climate
text:
Climate is a major factor in where people choose to live in Australia. Perth and other cities in the temperate zone of southwestern Australia experience mild winters with above-average rainfall and dry, hot summers. At times, arctic winds cause cold fronts to move through the region. The temperate zone of eastern Australia has a mild climate. Still, the region’s major cities experience very different weather patterns throughout the year. On average, Brisbane receives less rainfall than Melbourne and Sydney. The weather is less predictable in Melbourne than in the other areas of the temperate zone.

Cities in Australia’s tropical climate area experience wet and dry seasons. This is the only area of Australia that has a wet season and a dry season. The wet season occurs from November to April, characterized by heavy rains, high humidity, and thunderstorms. The dry season occurs from May to October. The dry season brings warmer temperatures and sunny days. There is little humidity and cooler temperatures at night.

Although there are areas that receive large amounts of rainfall annually, Australia is the driest inhabited continent on Earth. Roughly 70 percent of Australia is located in a dry climate zone. This area is a desert. It is often called the Australian Outback. The Outback is hot and dry for most of the year. Temperatures average around 84°F. However, temperatures as high as 122°F have been recorded in the Outback. Areas of the Outback can also experience freezing temperatures at night. The Outback has few water sources and rainfall is very sporadic or infrequent.

An area's climate often determines the houses people live in, the type of clothing they wear, and the food they eat. In Australia, the homes people live in reflect the climate. Some areas of Australia experience temperatures that exceed 110 degrees. In the opal mining town of Coober Pedy, which has a dry climate area, a large part of the city was built underground to stay cool. In places near the coast, some people have built houses on stilts. This allows the sea breeze to cool the houses naturally.

Population data demonstrates that cities in temperate climates, where the weather is more mild, have a larger population than cities with a tropical climate. The table provides data about the most densely populated cities in each of Australia's climate areas. The least densely populated cities in Australia have a dry climate. The harsh elements of a dry climate make it more difficult for people to settle in this region of Australia.

title: Distribution of Natural Resources
text:
The availability of natural resources has and continues to have a profound impact on patterns of settlements across Australia. An area's climate determines the available resources. That impacts where people settle. People need natural resources to meet their needs and wants. Areas with a dry or desert climate, like the Australian Outback, have fewer natural resources available. Cities like Melbourne, Darwin, and Sydney have access to marine natural resources. These include different bodies of fresh and salt water, seafood, and marine plants. These resources are not easily accessible in the Outback.

Settlers also developed economic activities based on the resources available in their environment. Australia's physical environment and natural resources determine the economic activities of an area. Farming and raising sheep and cattle became one of the primary economic industries in coastal areas. This is due to better soil and access to water in these regions. As people moved further inland, they had to engage in different economic activities. A lack of water and drier soil was not good for agricultural production and raising livestock. Settlers realized that regions of Australia with a dry climate were home to large mineral deposits. As a result, the mining industry became a major economic activity in Australia.

Because Australia is an arid country, there are many dams and reservoirs. A dam is a barrier that stops or restricts water flow. A reservoir is a lake that is created when humans build a dam. When people build dams and reservoirs, they store fresh water for future use. Dams are also used for hydroelectric power, flood control, and irrigation.

Irrigation canals and systems also provide water to the driest parts of Australia. Irrigation is a system that supplies water to crops, often through pipes. Some dams transport their stored water directly to these pipes to support local farmers. This method is beneficial in regions that receive very little precipitation. Approximately 90 percent of the water used by Australia's farms comes from irrigation canals.

title: Kentucky’s Road to Statehood
text:
When the Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776, the Commonwealth of Virginia covered a huge area that includes what is now the states of Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky. The area we now know as Kentucky was made into a county at that time. European settlers were living in the area. The number of settlers increased when Virginia started giving land in Kentucky County to people who had served as soldiers in the Revolutionary War. As more settlers arrived, the area was divided into nine counties and called the District of Kentucky.

However, the District of Kentucky was far away from the capital of Virginia. This meant that it was hard to reach the government. In addition, Virginians didn’t want people who lived in Kentucky to trade with nearby New Orleans, and Kentuckians wanted to change that. The settler population soon became big enough that the District of Kentucky asked the Continental Congress to make it a state under the Articles of Confederation in 1784. But the Constitution would soon be ratified and replace the Articles of Confederation. In 1788, Congress said it would make Kentucky a state but that it would have to wait until it could be made a state under the Constitution.

Kentucky became the 15th state in the United States on June 1, 1792. It was the first state west of the Appalachian Mountains.

title: Kentucky’s Constitution
text:
Before Kentucky could become a state, it had to have a constitution. This process was started in 1784, when Kentucky’s first constitutional convention was held. But it took 10 more constitutional conventions over the next eight years to finish it in 1792. It was considered an experimental constitution.

The constitution was reevaluated and changed in 1799. For example, in the 1792 constitution, the governor, senators, and representatives were elected by an electoral college. The 1799 constitution had these offices be elected by the people. In 1850, even more changes were made. Now all state offices were elected by the people.

Unlike the previous three constitutions, the 1891 constitution begins with a bill of rights and says that the state government can’t infringe on these rights.

To guard against transgression of the high powers which we have delegated, we declare that everything in this Bill of Rights is excepted out of the general powers of government, and shall forever remain inviolate; and all laws contrary thereto, or contrary to this Constitution, shall be void.

The next section of the constitution sets out how the government will be structured. It also provides a way to amend the constitution. The 1891 constitution is the one Kentucky uses today.

title: International Leaders
text:
Sitting Bull

Born in 1831 in South Dakota, Sitting Bull was a spiritual and political leader for his people, the Hunkpapa Lakota. It was difficult being a Plains Indian during Sitting Bull’s lifetime. White settlers were taking over their land. Food was scarce because most of the bison had been killed. When the U.S. government offered Sitting Bull a treaty, he would not sign it. “I do not propose to sell any part of my country,” he said. Through his leadership, he helped his people defend their land.

Nelson Mandela

Nelson Mandela lived in South Africa, where the government discriminated against Black people. He studied law and helped start South Africa’s first Black law practice. Government officials sent him to prison for almost 26 years for opposing its discriminatory policies. Four years after he was freed, he was elected the first Black president of South Africa. His government had both Black and white members.

Ellen Johnson Sirleaf

Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was elected president of Liberia, Africa, in 2006; she served as president until 2018. Early in her life, she went to the United States, where she studied economics and public administration. She became the minister of finance in Liberia, but her honesty about the country’s spending led to her imprisonment. After she was released, she spent many years living outside Liberia. When she returned, she ran for president and won. She received a Nobel Prize for promoting women’s roles in peacekeeping.

Angela Merkel

In 2005, Angela Merkel was the first woman to be elected chancellor of Germany. She grew up in communist East Germany. While in school, she won prizes for her accomplishments in mathematics and Russian. Later, she earned a PhD in quantum chemistry. When communism was overturned in East Germany, Merkel became a politician. After serving in a variety of government positions, she was elected as chancellor and kept the office for four terms.

title: Protecting Human Rights
text: There are leaders, businesses, and organizations around the world that work to protect human rights. They provide help to people and countries in need. They provide safe places for people to live, good drinking water, food, and supplies.

title: World Conflict
text:
Conflicts can arise between nations. These conflicts might be about borders. They could be about the use of land or resources. Conflicts may be about different political ideals. Nations have to work together to solve problems. When they agree on a solution, they sign treaties. Treaties are formal agreements that show the responsibilities of each side.

Sometimes nations of the world need help to solve their problems. Outside governments sometimes help negotiate solutions. Organizations can also help. The United Nations is a global organization that works to resolve conflicts between nations around the world.

The United Nations has 193 member countries. Its purpose is to increase cooperation and maintain peace in the world. It is important for people from many different countries to work together to solve the world's challenges.

Government and private organizations like the American Red Cross, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and the World Health Organization (WHO) offer help when conflict creates emergencies.

title: Civic Responsibility
text:
A civic responsibility is something that citizens are expected to do in their community. All citizens are expected to make choices for the common good. Members of a community are expected to obey laws. We are all expected to work to improve our communities.

Some civic responsibilities are enforced. This means that there are consequences if we do not follow them. Obeying the law and serving on a jury are enforced, or required, responsibilities. A jury is a group of citizens who are selected to decide a court case.

We vote to elect public officials. However, voting is not enforced. It is by choice. Volunteering is also by choice. It helps the community and people in need. Serving in the military or holding a public office are also things citizens can choose to do to help their community. Other countries have different rules about civic responsibility.

title: Compelling Question
text: How do citizens participate in government?

title: Voting
text: In the United States, voting is a right. When citizens turn 18 years old, they can vote. Voting is the way we choose our leaders. Voting gives people a chance to make their voices heard. Voters have the responsibility to learn about issues and the people they are voting for. If we don't have all the facts, we may find out later that we voted for something we didn't want. Voting is an important civic responsibility in our system of government. In some countries, people are not allowed to vote. In other countries, such as Austria, Chile, and Singapore, people are required by law to vote.

title: Volunteering
text:
Citizens who want to give something back to the community can volunteer, or donate their time to help others. Many people volunteer because they want to help others in need. There are many ways you can volunteer in your community and around the world. Opportunities to volunteer around the world include everything from drives to collect supplies to skilled doctors and teachers volunteering their time.

People can volunteer for drives. Different types of drives collect things for people in need. Some volunteers help with community cleanups. Other volunteers serve in community fire departments and neighborhood watch programs. The list of volunteer jobs is very long. You can even volunteer to help people in other countries. If you want to give back to your community and the world, find out where you could volunteer. Someone will really appreciate your help!

title: Serving in the Military
text:
Some people in the United States choose to be participating citizens by joining the military. A military is a group of people who are given power to defend a country. People choose to serve in the military in different ways. Some military members help when there is a natural disaster. Other military members fight in combat to protect their country. We honor military members who choose to serve our country on special holidays, such as Veterans Day.

In some countries, such as Finland, all males are required to serve in the army for a set time. In other countries, such as Israel, everyone 18 years of age or older must serve in the military, with a few exceptions.

title: Running for Political Office
text:
In countries that use democratic processes, citizens interested in serving in the government participate in a campaign process. People who want to be elected are called candidates. Candidates need to meet official requirements for the government job, or office, they want. Before Election Day, candidates spend a lot of time campaigning. This means they let voters know who they are and what they believe about different issues. They talk about what they would like to do if they win the election. They might use signs, flyers, billboards, and commercials to campaign. They also give speeches and often have debates with other candidates.

Citizens study each candidate carefully. They vote for the person who best represents their viewpoints. The candidate with the most votes wins. Candidates can vote for leaders of their community, state, or country.

Not all countries use democratic processes. Some countries are run by dictatorships or monarchies that do not use elections.

title: Paying Taxes
text:
Taxes are money people pay to the government. The laws of Kentucky and the United States say that citizens must pay taxes. There are many types of taxes. When we purchase an item at a store, we pay a sales tax. People who have jobs pay income taxes. Citizens who own land or buildings pay property taxes.

Tax money is used for many things. Taxes pay government workers. Taxes also help pay for services such as libraries, trash pickup, and police and fire departments. Schools use tax money to buy books and supplies. Tax money also helps repair school buildings and pay teachers and staff. Many other parts of a community, including roads and parks, also rely on tax money. Responsible citizens obey the law and pay their taxes. The money from taxes helps make our communities better.

Taxes and what they are spent on differ from country to country. Some countries, such as Sweden, have high income taxes and use those taxes to pay for state-funded health care and higher education.

title: International Space Station
text:
Every 90 minutes, the International Space Station orbits the Earth. That means it travels approximately five miles per second, or faster than 300 miles a minute or 175,000 miles per hour.

How did such an amazing machine get made? It was through international cooperation.

Both Russia and the United States had put space stations into orbit during the 1970s. In 1984, President Ronald Reagan challenged NASA to develop a manned space station within a decade. In the following years, NASA began working with Japan, Canada, and several European countries, collectively called the European Space Agency (ESA), on the project. In 1993, Russia joined in. That’s why it is called the International Space Station.

The station has been built piece by piece. Each piece is called a module. Russia uses six of the station’s modules. The United States, Japan, Canada, and the ESA use the other 10 modules. It took a lot of negotiation and organization to fund, construct, and maintain the space station. Countries coordinate the space they use in the space station based on how much they contributed to the project and other arrangements they make.

The first long-term crew arrived at the space station in 2000. Humans have lived in the space station ever since. There are usually seven crew members on board. They do experiments, take astronomical observations, and repair the station. One astronaut stayed on the ISS for almost a year.

title: How Leaders Were Chosen Throughout History
text:
Since monarchy was the most common form of government until the 20th century, most new leaders of countries were chosen from the ruling families. Often the eldest son of the king would inherit the throne when his father died. In the ancient Roman Empire, the emperor was chosen by the senate from members of the ruling family. Sometimes rivalries between royal siblings would lead to civil war.

Kings and queens would choose secondary leaders to run various branches of the government. These secondary leaders were from the upper class. These leaders would choose people to do the day-to-day work of running the government.

Though ancient Greece had a form of democracy, only upper-class males could vote. It was not until the 20th century that many countries started using democracy as part of the way they choose leaders. Democratic elements are largely used on the continents of North and South America, Europe, and Australia.

title: International Alliances
text:
When different groups or organizations work together, it’s called an alliance. Around the 15th century, Native Americans living in what is now the northeastern part of the United States made an alliance called the Iroquois Confederacy. The alliance originally brought together five tribes. The tribes agreed to help each other if one of them was ever attacked.

After World War II, many European and North American countries wanted to protect themselves from other countries, so they formed the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). The countries promised to help defend each other if one of the alliance countries was attacked.

At about the same time, the United Nations (UN) was started. The organization had 51 countries at the beginning. It now has almost 200. Some of its goals are to “maintain international peace and security” and “achieve international cooperation.”

title: Incentives and Opportunity Costs
text:
Every business has goals. Owners of businesses must make decisions about how to meet their goals. When making decisions, business owners often use two economic ideas for guidance: incentives and opportunity costs.

Incentives are opportunities to succeed or gain a reward. Business owners can use incentives to help them succeed. When business leaders keep track of their goals, they feel more motivated to achieve those goals. Keeping track of their success is an incentive. When customers of a business are offered an incentive, they might feel motivated to buy something. An example of an incentive is a lower price.

Businesses can’t always control everything. Business owners have to think about opportunity costs and incentives. Opportunity costs mean that when you spend money or time on one thing, you are passing up an opportunity to do something else. If you have a small amount of money, you might have to choose between doing two fun things with it. You don’t have enough money to do both things. Business owners have the same problem. They have to make choices about how to spend their time and money. They think about the opportunity costs. They think about what they might be giving up.

title: Types of Government
text:
A government is a group of people who lead a community. Government can be at the level of a city, a state, or a nation. Countries around the world have governments.

The government of any country has authority, or the right to make laws and then enforce those laws to make sure that people follow them. For example, many governments raise taxes, or collect money from citizens, so that the government has money to provide services.

The services that governments provide are important in a community. These services include things such as education, healthcare, roads and buildings, safety, and setting up rules for the economy.

Many governments also protect the country. Often, a country’s military is run by the government. The military protects the country and helps its citizens feel safe. Often government officials also work with the governments of other countries to solve problems.

While all governments have some type of power, not all governments work the same way. There are many types of governments in the world. Three government types are democracy, monarchy, and dictatorship. As we look at these three types of governments, pay special attention to the services provided by each government. Also, pay attention to the role of citizens in each type of government.

title: Compelling Question
text: How does the type of government affect the people who live in the country?

title: Democracy
text:
Direct Democracy

The first democracy was established in 508–507 B.C.E. in Athens, Greece. The ancient Greeks had a government of the people. When decisions were being made, each male who was not enslaved could vote. This type of government was called a direct democracy, meaning “ruled by the people.” There were three branches of the ancient Athenian government. One branch wrote the laws. Another branch was a council of representatives. The third branch was a court of justice with a jury to decide cases.

The founders of the United States used parts of Athenian democracy while setting up our government. Many countries in the world use some elements of democracy. But they practice democracy in different ways.

Representative Democracy

In a representative democracy, leaders are elected by the people. These leaders represent the people and make the laws. If the people agree with the laws, they may elect the leaders again. If the people don’t agree with the laws, they may elect different leaders.

To be good citizens in a representative democracy, people must be informed about the issues. They must gather facts and study different perspectives. Then they can vote for the best leaders.

Government services in a representative democracy are based on the needs of the citizens. The government often focuses on safety, healthcare, recreation, and education. Democratic governments often allow people to own private property. People can do what they want with their property as long as they are not breaking the law.

title: The Articles of Confederation
text:
The members of the Constitutional Convention studied several types of government as they tried to decide on the rules needed to run the government of the United States of America. Greece and Rome were some of the ancient civilizations that the convention members studied. They read about how to give people a voice in decisions through the principles of democracy.

These leaders read about how to use the ideas of a republic because they knew that there were too many people to have each person vote on each decision. Electing representatives helps the work of the government to get done without taking too much time.

Another important model the convention members looked at was a confederation. Many of the delegates had worked with the Iroquois Confederation over the years. The words of Canasatego, leader of the Onondaga Nation, were wise:

We heartily recommend Union and a Good Agreement between you our Brethren. Our wise Forefathers established Union and Amity [friendship] between the Five Nations; this has made us formidable [mighty], this has given us great weight and Authority with our Neighboring Nations. We are a Powerful confederacy, and by your observing the same Methods our wise Forefathers have taken, you will acquire fresh Strength and Power.

The convention members used these models as well as important ideas from philosophers and mixed them together to create the government that still runs the United States today. That is why the United States is called a democratic republic.

title: Monarchy
text:
In a monarchy, the country is ruled by a king or queen. Usually, the role of king or a queen is passed down to a child of the current king or queen.

Kings and queens are known as monarchs. Absolute monarchs make the laws. They also appoint other leaders to run the government. Most citizens in an absolute monarchy have no voice in the government. Only the leaders can affect the government. Private property may or may not be respected by a monarchy.

Some countries, like the United Kingdom, Japan, and Spain, have constitutional monarchies, in which the king or queen shares power with other government leaders, such as a prime minister. The monarch may have to obey the country’s constitution. The monarch’s role may be as a symbol of unity for the country.

Monarchy is an old government system. Ancient Egyptians, Mesopotamians, and Incas used it. The English population of North America was ruled by monarchs until the American Revolution. Monarchy was the most common government in the world until the 20th century. There are still many countries that have a monarch, but now they are often only part of the government. There are currently only a few countries in the world that are absolute monarchies.

title: Authoritarian/Dictatorship
text:
A dictatorship usually starts when a leader takes over a government by force or is voted into office and then takes more power. A dictator has all control over laws. However, a dictator still appoints lower leaders to help run the government. Sometimes these lower leaders try to overthrow the dictator so they can be dictators instead.

A dictatorship usually does not respect private property. All the land belongs to the dictator. The role of the citizens in a dictatorship is to obey the dictator. They have no voice in the government. However, they may try to have a revolution. Since the government is headed by one person, the concerns of the government will be whatever the concerns of the dictator are.

title: World Communities
text:
Sometimes people from all around the world unite to form a community. They often do this to help others.

For example, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has about 20,000 staff members in more than 100 countries. The organization got its start in 1863. During its first 150 years, ICRC members helped people who were victims of war and violence. Prisoners of war during World War I and World War II often received Red Cross packages, which contained food and personal items. Today, the ICRC is an emergency response organization that aids in times of both violence and natural disaster.

Another community that has members from all over the world is Doctors Without Borders. It was created by doctors and journalists in France. They provide medical aid in war zones. They speak out about the bad things they see so that those things can be stopped in the future. Doctors Without Borders has more than 63,000 staff providing medical assistance and consultations in more than 70 countries every year.

title: People Who Made a Positive Impact on Kentucky
text:
Sophia Alcorn

In 1909, Sophia Alcorn started teaching at the Kentucky School for the Deaf. She had a student named Oma Simpson who couldn’t see or hear. Alcorn developed a way to teach Oma. Oma would place her fingers on Alcorn’s cheek and neck. When Alcorn spoke, Oma could feel the vibration of her teacher’s vocal cords and the movement of her lips. Oma learned words this way and was the first deafblind person to be educated through speech. She learned history, knitting, and typing. Alcorn called this kind of communication the Tadoma Method.

Stephen Bishop

The greatest modern explorer of Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave system was Stephen Bishop. Since Bishop was enslaved, he didn’t have a formal education. But he taught himself geology and how to read and write. The Mammoth Cave is the longest cave system in the world, and Bishop was stationed there as a guide. It had been used by Native Americans, but Bishop and a visitor were the first people to explore past a part called the Bottomless Pit. He was among the first to explore parts of the cave beyond that. He drew a map of the cave network from memory. The map was published and used by explorers for the next 40 years.

Mae Street Kidd

Mae Street Kidd was born in 1904. She had a Black mother and a white father. Many laws in the South discriminated against Black people at that time. Since Kidd had light skin, she was sometimes discriminated against and sometimes wasn’t. She joined a Black-owned insurance company and became one of its top sellers; she also served with the Red Cross in Europe during World War II. After she retired, she ran for a seat on the Kentucky General Assembly and won. She helped sponsor the Kentucky Fair Housing Act, which provided low-income housing. She also sponsored the resolution that led Kentucky to ratify the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments in 1976. These amendments abolished slavery, made Black people citizens, and gave African Americans the right to vote. The amendments had been passed by the federal government in the mid-1800s, but Kentucky had never ratified them.

Abraham Lincoln

One of the most visited national monuments in Washington, D.C., is the Lincoln Memorial. It was built to honor Kentucky-born Abraham Lincoln. Since he worked on his family’s farm, he only had 12 months of official schooling. So he taught himself. He became a lawyer, a state legislator, and a member of the U.S. Congress before being elected the 16th president of the United States. The Civil War broke out shortly after he became president in 1861. Lincoln worked throughout the war to keep the nation together and abolish slavery. He is considered by many scholars to be the greatest president in U.S. history.
