title: Families Change Over Time
text: Families change over time. Our families grow. They get bigger as people and pets join our family.

James Oglethorpe’s plan to create a colony in North America for Britain’s poor was approved. The Charter of 1732 established the Georgia Colony. Georgia was the first new colony established in North America in over 50 years. It was the last established of the original 13 American colonies. Georgia’s colonial charter was written as a trustee colony. A group of 21 British trustees was appointed to govern Georgia. A trustee is a person who has the authority to make decisions for another person or group of people. As a trustee colony, the people selected as trustees could not profit or personally benefit from the decisions they made. Instead, the trustees were entrusted to act and make laws that would benefit the people for whom they were responsible. The trustee’s motto was Non sibi sed aliis, which means “Not for self, but for others." Georgia was the only one of the 13 original colonies established as a trustee colony.

According to the Charter of 1732, Georgia Colony was created for three purposes: philanthropy, economics, and defense. Philanthropy is a word that refers to an activity designed to help the poor or others who are less fortunate. Through his efforts, James Oglethorpe was able to help improve the lives of many of Britain’s poor. With hard work, colonists could improve their lives in Georgia. Their efforts would also benefit the British Empire economically. Georgia Colony could grow and produce items that could not be grown or produced in England. Additionally, the colony's location became a way to keep the Spanish away from South Carolina.

The board of trustees changed Oglethorpe's original plan for the colony. Instead of allowing people from debtors' prisons to move to Georgia, only the “deserving poor” were invited to move to the colony. The trustees selected individuals based on the skills and benefits they would bring to the colony. Those who could not pay their way to the colony would have their way paid for by the group of trustees.

Three thousand people emigrated to the new colony of Georgia. Two thousand had their passage paid for by the trustees. Due to the colonists' low social and economic status in Britain, the trustees did not think colonists could govern themselves or make their own laws. While they were given supplies and land, the colonists had to follow strict guidelines and rules in return. Colonists were encouraged to grow certain crops on their land. These crops included grapes, rice, indigo, silk, and, eventually, tobacco. These crops would ensure that Britain had a supply of goods to sell throughout the world. Alcohol, such as rum, was not allowed in the colony. However, the trustees felt the new colony could also be a new source of wine to sell in Europe. Wine was not considered "alcohol" like rum and was allowed. All colonists were required to set aside land to plant mulberry trees to feed silkworms. Silk was in high demand by Europe's upper classes, but Britain did not have the right climate for raising silkworms. By requiring Georgia’s colonists to raise silkworms, the British Empire was guaranteed a steady supply of silk.

Colonists were also given land but were not allowed to sell it. Inheritance laws were written so that land could only be passed down to males in the family. These laws kept colonists from selling their land and moving from the colony. The trustees believed that the colonists should work the land themselves. They were also wary of other colonies, such as South Carolina, where enslaved people outnumbered British colonists. Because of this, laws were written that did not allow enslaved people to be purchased and used for labor in Georgia. Given the extreme poverty in Britain and the land and opportunities available in Georgia, many colonists agreed to the trustees' rules.

title: President Andrew Jackson
text:
Andrew Jackson became the seventh president of the United States in 1829. He had a background that was very different from previous United States presidents. He was born in 1767 on the American frontier before the start of the American Revolutionary War. As a young man, Jackson and his brother Robert served in the Revolutionary War. They were too young to join the army, but they served as messengers and scouts for the Continental Army. After he and his brother were captured by the British, both boys contracted smallpox. Unfortunately, Jackson’s brother died from the disease shortly after. Jackson blamed the loss of his brother on the mistreatment they suffered after being captured. This and other events led Jackson to develop both a lifelong prejudice against the British and a passion for United States military service and politics.

Growing up, Jackson had little formal education. His father died before he was born, and his mother died during the Revolutionary War. Jackson later attended school sporadically but eventually became a self-taught lawyer in Tennessee. As his law practice grew, he purchased a plantation near Nashville, Tennessee, called the Hermitage. Jackson purchased over 100 enslaved people to grow, pick, and clean cotton on his plantation.

However, Jackson’s passion for military service never left him. In 1802, he served in the Tennessee militia as a major general. In this role, he led 2,500 United States troops against American Indians in the Creek War. The Battle of Horseshoe Bend ended with a United States victory and the defeat of the Muscogee (Creek). Jackson was also able to fight against his former enemies, the British. In the War of 1812, Jackson organized a military victory against the British in the Battle of New Orleans. This battle made him a nationally recognized hero.

In 1815, the Treaty of Ghent ended fighting between Great Britain and the U.S. In 1818, Jackson next led United States troops against the Seminole people in Spanish Florida. On top of capturing the Spanish fort of St. Marks and taking over the town of Pensacola, he also fought against the Seminole people. The Seminole were rumored to be hiding runaway enslaved people. While there, Jackson captured, tried, and executed two British citizens, whom he charged with helping the Seminole and runaway enslaved people. Jackson's actions in Florida created an international incident between the United States and the British and Spanish. Despite this, Jackson was absolved of any wrongdoing.

Following the battles, Jackson was part of the U.S. negotiations with the many American Indian people, including the Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Cherokee. Through a series of treaties following the military campaigns, millions of acres of land in Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and West Tennessee were surrendered to the ownership of the United States government. Jackson then turned his attention from the military to politics.

When Spain ceded Florida to the U.S., President Monroe appointed Jackson as governor of Florida. Jackson's background and notoriety from the military made him a very popular politician. Jackson supported a popular ideal of the time that all American Indians should be removed from their lands in the South. This forced removal relocated all American Indians from the South to another territory. Jackson was not the first to have this idea. President James Monroe had suggested the same idea in 1818, urging for either the assimilation of American Indian people into “white culture,” or their forced removal from areas where American citizens wanted to settle.

In 1823, Vice President John C. Calhoun (under John Quincy Adams and Andrew Jackson) suggested the removal and relocation of the American Indians to territories west of the Mississippi River. More and more American citizens desired land in the South. Because of this, the idea became more popular with voters throughout the United States.

title: Essential Question
text: How did significant factors contribute to Georgia's growth between 1789-1840?

title: American Indian Resistance to Forced Removal
text:
Chief John Ross led the Cherokee people as president of the Cherokee National Council from 1819–1826. During this time of his leadership, the Cherokee people adopted many of the American ways of living. In the early 1800s, settlements of Cherokee farms were located on over 43,000 miles of land. As this had been the home of the people for centuries, many Cherokee resisted and rejected the idea of being relocated away from their ancestral lands. In 1827, with Ross on the Cherokee Council, the Cherokee of Georgia created a constitutional government. The seat of the government was established in New Echota, Georgia, the Cherokee capital. This establishment of their constitutional system was meant to show that they were a sovereign nation. A sovereign nation is independent and not under the rule of any other country. The Cherokee wanted to show the governments of both Georgia and the United States that, because of their status as a sovereign nation, they could not be removed from their lands. The sovereign nation status of the Cherokee was immediately challenged by the Georgia state government.

Not all American Indians resisted relocation or the sale of their lands. William McIntosh was the chief of the Lower Creeks in the early 1800s. McIntosh was a controversial leader. Many Muscogee (Creek) people did not fully trust him, as he had sided with the United States in the Creek War. He also called for the “civilization” of American Indian people by adopting European culture. McIntosh had also been known to accept bribes in exchange for land. He approached two land agents sent from the United States government to negotiate Muscogee (Creek) removal from lands that are today part of Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi. Called the Treaty of Indians Springs, McIntosh agreed to give away all Muscogee (Creek) rights to the land in exchange for $400,000. Half of the money was paid directly to McIntosh and two others. The Creek National Council found out about the deal, and McIntosh and his two co-conspirators were killed under Muscogee (Creek) law. The Creek National Council sent a delegation to negotiate a new treaty, as the one brokered by McIntosh was based on bribery and fraud. A new treaty was created. However, the Muscogee (Creek) still lost their rights to their ancestral lands in the end.

title: Indian Removal Act 1830
text:
Andrew Jackson entered the race for president of the United States in 1824. While he lost the election through his defeat in the Electoral College, he won the popular vote. He ran again for president and won in 1828.

Jackson was determined to remove American Indians from all United States lands and relocate them to the Oklahoma Territory. In 1829, Jackson outlined a plan for Indian removal from Georgia, Mississippi, and Alabama in his first message to Congress. Jackson stated in his first inaugural address:

It will be my sincere and constant desire to observe toward the Indian tribes within our limits a just and liberal policy, and to give that humane and considerate attention to their rights and their wants which is consistent with the habits of our Government and the feelings of our people.

On May 26, 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. The act called for the removal of all American Indians from the southern states to be relocated to new territories in modern-day Oklahoma and Nebraska. President Jackson signed the bill into law two days later.

Chief John Ross and many Cherokee had served with Andrew Jackson in the Creek Wars. Ross personally wrote direct letters to President Jackson. In his letters, he pleaded for his and the Cherokee people’s right to stay on their lands. Jackson did not respond to Ross and ignored his communications.

Some American Indian people left voluntarily to avoid further conflicts. This included some Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole, and Cherokee people. Many decided to stay and fight the removal in court and through physical resistance.

title: Worcester v. Georgia
text:
Samuel Worcester was a Christian missionary who lived and worked in Georgia in the 19th century. Worcester lived with, worked with, and advised the Cherokee people in 1830. Worcester and a group of other missionaries also served as advisors to Chief John Ross and the Cherokee government. They advised Ross and the Cherokee on their legal and political rights. This helped the Cherokee fight the state of Georgia’s attempts to take control of their lands and people. In 1831, the Georgia government passed a law forbidding white people from living on Cherokee land without obtaining an official license and swearing an oath of loyalty to the state. Worcester and his fellow missionaries did not have an official license. They were arrested and put on trial for not obtaining a license and not taking the oath of allegiance to Georgia. The missionaries were found guilty of breaking Georgia law. They were sentenced to four years of hard labor at the prison in Milledgeville, Georgia.

Worcester appealed his conviction. The Worcester v. Georgia case went before the United States Supreme Court. The Supreme Court agreed that the Cherokee were independent and sovereign. Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in the majority opinion of the court that the Cherokee people were “distinct, independent political communities retaining their original natural rights.” Chief Justice Marshall criticized the laws of Georgia. He ruled that they could not impose law on the Cherokee in their own sovereign territory.

The favorable ruling of Worcester v. Georgia did not change much for either the Cherokee or Worcester and his fellow missionaries. Georgia state officials refused to release the missionaries. Instead, they ignored the ruling from the United States Supreme Court. The state continued to regulate Cherokee lands and persecute those who did not follow Georgia laws. President Andrew Jackson refused to enforce the ruling of the Supreme Court as well.

In Jackson’s 1833 Address to Congress, he said:

[That tribes] can not exist surrounded by our settlements and in continual contact with our citizens is certain… they must necessarily yield to the force of circumstances and ere long disappear.

In 1835, a small group of Cherokee, led by John Ridge, met with United States government representatives. The Cherokee negotiation group did not include Chief John Ross. The group falsely claimed that they represented the over 16,000 Cherokee people of Georgia. The group negotiated and signed the Treaty of New Echota. This treaty with the United States government gave up the Cherokee people’s claim to over seven million acres of their homeland in Georgia. In exchange, the Cherokee negotiators were granted $5 million and land in modern-day Oklahoma.

After learning of the treaty, Chief Ross and other leaders of the Cherokee appealed to Congress that the treaty was not valid. It wasn’t negotiated by the Cherokee leadership. A recorded 3,352 Cherokee signed a petition against the ratification of the treaty. However, the United States Congress still ratified the treaty in 1836. This sealed the fate of the Cherokee. The Cherokee became the last of the American Indian people in the South to be removed from their ancestral lands.

title: The Trail of Tears
text:
One by one, American Indian tribes were removed forcibly from their lands. This was done under the orders and supervision of the United States Army. American Indian people were required to relocate to the “Indian Territory.” This territory is in what is now the state of Oklahoma. The journey began by walking to one of three “round-up camps.” These camps were little more than open areas surrounded by stockade fencing. People were forced to walk hundreds of miles from these locations, carrying what they could. Thousands of American Indians died on the journey from illness, disease, exhaustion, and lack of food.

Many Cherokee continued to resist the forced relocation from their homes in Georgia. However, by 1838, the United States government authorized the removal of the Cherokee through military force. The United States Army went onto Cherokee lands. Under the threat of violence, they forcibly removed Cherokee people from their homes. By the summer of 1838, over 12,000 Cherokee people were placed in stockade internment camps in Tennessee. From October 1838 to March 1839, most of the Cherokee were forced to walk over 800 miles through wintery conditions to the Oklahoma Territory. The trip was long and difficult. It was especially difficult for the very young and the elderly, who suffered the highest number of deaths. U.S. government records documented less than 1,000 Cherokee deaths on the journey to the Indian Territory, but oral tradition suggests that as many as 4,000 Cherokee perished over the course of their forced removal. The forced removal from their homes, the harsh conditions, the loss of life, and other factors led to this journey later being called "The Trail of Tears."

Although the Cherokees’ journey became known as the “Trail of Tears,” many other American Indian peoples traveled on the same routes when they were removed to the Indian Territory. It is estimated that from 1831 through 1838, over 100,000 American Indians from many different tribes were removed from their homes in the southern United States.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: By the end of Andrew Jackson’s presidency, the United States government had negotiated approximately 70 removal treaties. The treaties led to the removal of nearly 50,000 American Indians. These people were relocated to Indian Territory in modern-day Oklahoma. Their removal opened up 25 million acres of land to American settlement and agriculture. The increase in agriculture and farming led to the expansion of slavery in the southern states. In 1987, U.S. Congress designated the Trail of Tears as a National Historic Trail. In 2009, the original trail was surveyed and expanded, almost doubling in size, to include newly documented routes and sites used during the removal.

title: The Industrial Revolution
text:
As American Indians, such as the Cherokee, were forcibly removed from their homes and land in Georgia, major changes were coming to the state. Many of these changes were also happening in other parts of the country and the world. Inventions and innovation were changing both how products were made and how they were sold. This time of invention and innovation was called the Industrial Revolution.

The first “Industrial Revolution” began in Great Britain in around the 1750s. Machine manufacturing was introduced. Society began to shift from handcrafts and physical labor to manufactured products. These machines increased productivity for new goods and services to be created and sold. Industry refers to how items are manufactured or produced and later sold. Prior to the Industrial Revolution, industry was mainly based locally. Goods and services were usually produced by hand and in smaller quantities. This is often called a cottage industry.

The rapid change to industrialization came to the United States through the introduction of new ideas and working methods, such as the factory system. The introduction of metals such as iron and steel had a huge impact on tools and machines. It allowed for new designs and inventions. Some of these inventions include large items, such as the spinning jenny and power loom, which changed the way that cotton and wool were spun into cloth and woven into fabric. Suddenly, wool and cotton could be spun quickly into thread. The thread could then be woven into fabric. The textile industry expanded quickly in the North, where access to streams and other water sources to power and cool the machines was plentiful.

title: Essential Question
text: How did significant factors contribute to Georgia's growth between 1789 and 1840?

title: Samuel Slater: Father of the American Factory System
text:
Samuel Slater was born in 1768 in Derbyshire, England. He was the youngest of five sons. After finishing school, Slater went to work in a water-powered textile mill. Textile is another word for cloth or fabric that is woven together. Water sources from streams or dams would turn water wheels. This moved the mechanical parts of machines housed in factories. Being near water sources for energy was essential for the machines to be powered.

In the late 1700s, people of different classes, backgrounds, and education had more opportunities in the United States than in Great Britain and Europe. As a member of a British lower class, Slater realized that he would have more opportunities to build a mill in the United States. In 1789, Slater boarded a ship for New York. He had to travel secretly, as textile workers were forbidden to leave England. It was feared that they would take the secrets of their industry with them. This would provide competition with the mills in Great Britain. Slater had secretly memorized how the machines in the textile mills worked. Soon after he arrived in the United States, Slater convinced investors to help him build the first American textile mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. By 1791, Slater’s waterwheel was working to power the mill, and raw materials like cotton were being spun into thread.

title: Rise of Industry in the North
text:
Now that Slater had his factory, he needed to have people to work in it. During the turn of the century, Slater also invented the “Rhode Island System of Manufacturing.” He would employ entire families in the mills, even children as young as seven years old. This system was common in British factories. It soon became very popular in the mills in the North. Small villages began to form near the factories and mills. Families that couldn’t afford land to farm went to work in the factories and mills. They often settled in the villages nearby. These villages were often called “mill towns.”

The mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, proved to be so successful that by 1807, 13 more mills had been built in the North. In 1807, President Thomas Jefferson enacted an embargo, or official ban, on importing British goods. This was an attempt by the United States to stay neutral in conflicts in Europe, especially between Great Britain and France. While this was an unpopular act, it created more opportunities to build mills in the United States. By 1812, the textile industry had taken hold in the northern United States. Seventy-eight more mills were built in the North. The American textile business was booming. However, not all of the mills and factories were located in the North. Though the majority of the factories were located in the northern states, by 1820, there were textile mills and factories located in Virginia and Kentucky.

title: The Cotton Gin Changed the South Forever
text:
As Samuel Slater was arriving in Rhode Island, another man was making his way to Georgia. Eli Whitney, a recent graduate from Yale University, was unemployed. He began to look for work as a tutor. He came to Georgia in 1792 to work for the Greene family. Whitney had been friends with both General Nathaniel Greene and his wife, Catherine. The Greene family had six children, and Catherine had recently been widowed. She asked Whitney to come to their plantation, called Mulberry Grove, and help tutor her children. A plantation is an agricultural estate usually worked by laborers who live on the estate. In the South at this time, plantation labor mainly consisted of enslaved people who were considered the property of the plantation owners. While at the Mulberry Grove Plantation, Catherine explained to Whitney that there was a large demand for cotton in the textile mills, however, she could not afford to grow and sell it. Cleaning the seeds from short-staple cotton was time-consuming and difficult to do. The amount of time it took to clean the cotton to prepare it for sale did not make it a profitable crop.

Whitney took the problem of efficiently removing seeds from cotton as a challenge. In 1793, he created a gin (short for "engine") to clean the cotton. The simple machine could be turned by hand or a crank attached to an animal. Later, the gin would use a steam engine. Raw cotton could be placed inside the gin. As the handle was turned, the cotton would be pulled through the machine by multiple hooks, or teeth, separating the fibers. The fibers would be pulled through "ribs," which were too narrow for the seeds. The loose seeds would then fall to the floor or be collected in a mesh net.

The cotton gin, as it came to be known, could clean up to 50 pounds of cotton in a day when hand-cranked by two people. This was a vast improvement. Previously, it took one person 10 hours to clean one pound of cotton by hand. Whitney officially patented his design in 1794 and started his own cotton gin production company. As more people saw the design, they began to create their own version of the cotton gin. Cotton became a crop that could not only be grown in abundance but could also be easily cleaned. This made cotton extremely valuable. Demand for clean, cheap cotton in both the northern states and Great Britain led to large profits for planters throughout the South. By the mid-1800s, cotton became the United States’ number one sales export to the northern textile mills. The number of plantations growing and selling cotton skyrocketed, as did the demand for enslaved people to work in the fields. The Lower Piedmont region was known to have nutrient-rich land suitable for growing cotton. This caused a larger concentration of cotton plantations in the region.

title: King Cotton and Slavery
text:
As cotton became more valuable, so did the land it could be grown on. Georgians were eager to remove anyone who was living on land that could be used to grow the valuable crop. In the early 1800s, the Cherokee people were forcibly removed from their homes in Georgia. The land they had been living on was made available for cotton to be planted. More plantations and fields meant there was a need for more labor. Like other crops grown in the South, such as rice, indigo, and tobacco, southern farmers relied on enslaved people for that labor. This demand led to a direct increase in the amount of enslaved people exploited by Georgian planters. Enslaved people were purchased to work in the fields. They were also used to clean and prepare the cotton for sale.

Enslaved people were purchased and forced to work as another person’s property. This, of course, was happening in a country that had recently declared “All men [were] created equal.” The increase in enslaved people can be correlated with the invention of the cotton gin, the increase in cotton sales, and the increase in cotton plantations throughout Georgia. In 1790, there were 29,264 enslaved people recorded in Georgia. By 1810, the number of enslaved people in Georgia was 105,218. Just before the American Civil War in 1860, the number of people enslaved in Georgia had grown to 462,198. Enslaved people made up approximately 44 percent of the state's total population at the time. Due to the huge profits and the impact cotton had on the economy and society, the cotton industry there was often referred to as “King Cotton.”

title: Transportation Revolution
text: As more and more cotton was being grown in the South, finding ways to transport it for sale led to further innovation. Transportation to the North was often difficult without reliable roads. Moving large amounts of cotton to the coast for ocean transport was costly. New methods of transportation were being developed throughout the world at this time. These new innovations in transportation would not only transport goods but also people and ideas. Innovations in transportation would revolutionize how people would travel and lead them to consider their place in the United States.

title: Roads and Canals
text:
Over hundreds of years, Indigenous peoples had created many travel and hunting routes throughout the vast wilderness in North America. European settlers later adapted many of these routes into more permanent roads for travel and trade. Prior to the Industrial Revolution, roads in the United States had been built to carry mail and travelers. These roads were often poorly maintained outside of major cities or towns. This began to change in 1794.

The first toll road was built in Pennsylvania between Lancaster and Philadelphia. Built by a private company, the road had nine “tolls,” or fees, where travelers were charged to use the road. The road was managed and covered with crushed rocks, or gravel, for maintenance. The road was a success. Soon, toll roads were being built across the states. They were called turnpikes because the roads were blocked by a pike or long stick until the fee was paid. Important roads, such as the Cumberland Road, stretched over 600 miles, from Maryland to Illinois. Roads made it possible to traverse areas of land that were previously inaccessible by wagon. This opened up the possibility for people to move further west. By the 1820s, thousands of miles of roads had been built, connecting communities and providing access to land and resources.

Canals also became an important means of transportation in the 1800s. A canal was a human-made waterway that was used to transport people and goods across long distances. The largest canal in the United States was the Erie Canal. It took eight years to engineer and construct the 363-mile-long canal from 1817 to 1825. The waterway measured four feet in depth and 40 feet wide. This canal connected Buffalo, near Lake Erie, to Albany, New York. This was significant as Albany is located on the Hudson River, which flows directly to New York City Harbor.

The canal was constructed using both man and animal power to clear natural obstacles and dig the canal. Large trees, boulders, and other landscape features had to be removed to dig the canal. The canal was a huge success and made transportation and trade in the Northern United States easier and cheaper. As trade through the Hudson River grew, New York City also became an important port. Soon, New York City became the center of trade and finance in the North. Canals grew in popularity and were soon a major source of transportation across the Northern United States where waterways could be connected. By 1840, more than 3,000 miles of canals had been dug, connecting rivers and waterways across the North and Midwest. They remained a valuable part of transportation through the late 1800s, when they would be replaced by a new technology, the railroad locomotive.

title: Steam Engines, Railroads, and Steamboats
text:
The first steam engine was invented in Great Britain in 1712 by Thomas Newcomen. It was designed and mainly used to pump water out of coal mine shafts. In the late 1700s, Scottish engineer James Watt adapted the steam engine. He updated the design to make it useful in other industries. His new steam engine was soon in demand. It was used in various flour mills and in the production of paper, iron, and textiles.

The demand for steam-powered engines was not limited to industry, however. The idea of using the steam engine in transportation was also being explored by inventors. They adapted the steam engine for boats, which changed water transportation. The steam-powered boat was successfully introduced into America’s rivers in 1807 with the launching of the Clermont. The Clermont was a paddle-wheel steamboat. It moved at unheard-of speeds for the time: five miles an hour! The first journey of the Clermont took the boat up the Hudson River from New York City to Albany, New York. Steamboats could transport large amounts of goods and people. They soon became popular on major rivers across the United States. They became very popular on large rivers such as the Mississippi. The width of the river allowed for two-way boat traffic. Travel and trade by paddle boat became very common by the mid-1800s.

Boats were not the only area of transportation where steam engines were being used. In 1802, British inventor Richard Tevithick used Watts' designs to power the first locomotive on rails with steam engines. On Feb. 21, 1804, he recorded that he had completed the first trial of his engine. The engine had successfully "carry'd ten tons of Iron, five wagons, and 70 Men … above 9 miles … in 4 hours and 5 Mints." As the age of locomotive trains began, improvements were made to the original designs. The invention of the rail locomotive at first only provided transportation between waterways. Trains soon became a more reliable form of transportation. Winter weather made water transportation difficult or impossible. Trains, however, were largely unaffected. At first, railroad companies often did not use a standardized system of rails for the tracks. As train wheels are fixed and need tracks to move, the lack of standardized track size was a huge issue. Each railroad could only travel on the tracks that had been placed by that company. Standardization was introduced to the American railroad companies. By the Civil War, most trains in America were standardized and could run on any track.

As the demand for more locomotive train transportation grew, so did the demand for iron, steel, and wood. To lay railroad track, the ground would be leveled and covered with gravel. Wood "ties" were then laid down on the ground. Wood was the perfect material as it is strong, yet flexible. Finally, the iron tracks would be secured on top of the ties. The trains were most often powered by wood or coal. The materials were burned, which created steam, which was used to move the heavy train engines. Their fixed wheels traveled quickly on the track.

The locomotive industry took hold in the United States. By 1861, over 22,000 miles of train track had been built in the Northern states, and over 9,000 miles in the South. Railroad hubs in the South were built in Atlanta, Georgia; Chattanooga, Tennessee; and Richmond, Virginia. Southern states embraced the railroad as a way to transport crops, such as cotton, to the North or to the coast for trade. However, due to the South’s agrarian, or farming-based, way of life, the number of train tracks was less than half of what was laid in the North. The amount of rail lines would later play a large factor in the Civil War that was looming in the not-so-distant future.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The first Industrial Revolution, which lasted from the late 1700s to the mid-1800s, was a time of great innovation. Changes came with travel using water and roads via stagecoach. However, by 1869, the Transcontinental Railroad connected North America's east and west coasts. Locomotive travel times were cut by up to 90 percent. People began to flood across the country. They moved to the West to settle and look for new opportunities. As innovations in industrial technology, travel, and transportation were taking place, a growing sense of divide in the regions of the United States was deepening. Sectionalism, also known as regionalism, was seen as loyalty to a person’s state or region that they lived in. This could come from the point of view of a region's perceived culture, values, politics, and economies. The rise of factories in the North and cotton fields and plantations in the South only deepened the social tensions between the two regions. The American Civil War would eventually stem from these divisions.

title: Suburban Communities
text: A suburban community is formed in areas outside of a city. Suburbs have fewer businesses and people living in one location. There are fewer developed areas with tall buildings. Living spaces have open areas with no buildings. These spaces are yards, parks, and open lots or fields. Transportation systems in the suburban community are smaller. Highways transport goods and people to business and residential areas. There is some land available for families to have small farms and grow food. Food is brought in to help feed the population in the suburban community.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
In 1494, one man who had sailed across the Atlantic Ocean returned home with unbelievable stories. He described the places he had seen, full of strange plants, animals, and foods. He talked about the people he had met there. This man was not Christopher Columbus or a member of his crew. He was a Taíno from the Bahamas that Columbus had captured and brought to Spain. His real name has been lost to history, but Columbus called him Diego Colón.

After returning home, the man called Colón told his friends and family about Spain. He described “the great cities and fortresses and churches” and “the people and horses and animals.” He saw strange “lands and food ... and bullfighting.” All were new to him, just like native peoples and their homelands were new to Europeans. As people traveled between the continents, they exchanged ideas about technology, religion, and ways of life.

As European explorers reached different parts of Latin America, people from different groups were brought across the ocean and saw Europe. People in the Americas and in Europe were not just curious about each other. Many saw new opportunities to meet their economic wants and needs as soon as they met. The people on the two sides of the Atlantic quickly exchanged goods, people, plants, animals, and diseases.

This exchange between the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia is called the Columbian Exchange. It is named after Christopher Columbus. The Columbian Exchange had a huge impact on life for people all around the world. Without it, Italy would never have invented pizza, and Ireland would never have grown potatoes. Indigenous people would never have ridden on horseback. Animals like horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs changed economic life in the Americas. Farm animals became new food sources. Horses changed the way tribes hunted and traveled. Riding horses was a much faster form of transportation than traveling on foot.

European settlers also brought sugarcane, olives, citrus, bananas, and even honeybees with them. Columbus brought sugarcane to Hispaniola in 1493. Sugarcane grew well in the Americas and sold well in Europe. Many plants from the Americas also greatly impacted Europe, Africa, and Asia. American plants like potatoes, tomatoes, and corn changed how people ate. On both sides of the Atlantic, new farm and settlement plants often spread. This even changed what grew in the wild. The world was truly never the same because of the Columbian Exchange.

title: Edenton Tea Party
text:
In 1827, a naval officer was at a shop far from his home in North Carolina. He saw a drawing that interested him. It was from a London newspaper published in 1775. The drawing was making fun of people who participated in an event from the American Revolution. At the bottom of the drawing were the words “A Society of Patriotic Ladies at Edenton in North Carolina.” The officer had never heard of this event. He purchased the drawing.

When he returned home, he shared the drawing with his friends and family. No one knew what it was about. There was nothing written about it in North Carolina history. They looked for answers. Eventually, they pieced together the details of an important event that had happened more than 50 years earlier: the Edenton Tea Party.

Drinking tea was an important tradition for English colonists. Before the American Revolution, the British government imposed taxes on tea. This upset the colonists. Citizens in Boston expressed their displeasure by dumping hundreds of chests of tea in the harbor.

Edenton was the capital of the Province of North Carolina at the time. It was an important trading port. As a sign of support for the Boston Tea Party, 51 women in Edenton agreed to stop using British tea and cloth. In 1774, the women wrote a resolve, signed it, and sent it to England. This was one of the first political acts by women in the colonies. Historians believe Penelope Barker played a key role in the Edenton Tea Party. Her husband, Thomas Barker, was treasurer of the Province of North Carolina.

Today, a cannon from the Revolutionary era sits in front of the Chowan County Courthouse. There is a teapot mounted to the cannon in memory of this early example of activism by women.

title: Theodore Roosevelt
text:
Theodore Roosevelt

October 27, 1858 – January 6, 1919

Theodore Roosevelt was a sickly and nervous little boy. He had asthma attacks and couldn’t breathe very well. The doctors gave him treatments, but nothing worked. Theodore’s family called him Teedie. He loved nature and the outdoors. He loved to read. He read books about explorers and adventurers in the West. He wanted to be like them. He thought he was too sickly to become that kind of hero.

One day, a doctor told Theodore’s parents that his chest was too small for his lungs to grow. Theodore’s father told Theodore that “without the help of the body, the mind cannot go as far as it should.” His father encouraged him to exercise. Theodore exercised hard every day. He still wasn’t strong. He decided to learn how to box. Boxers didn’t wear gloves in those days. They got hurt in the ring. Theodore kept boxing anyway. He entered a boxing tournament and won.

Theodore’s mother taught her children at home. When Theodore was eighteen, he left for Harvard University to study biology. He joined the rowing team. He also continued to box. After the death of his father, Theodore began studying history and government. He wanted to be a public servant to honor his father.

Theodore said that he believed in working hard to reach a goal. His body was strong because he exercised every day. He went on hunting trips to the American West. He lived the life he had read about as a child.

After he graduated from Harvard, Theodore entered public service. He was elected as a New York state senator. Then, he became the New York City police commissioner. He was in charge of all the police in New York City. He served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. He fought in the Spanish American War. Theodore earned the Medal of Honor for bravery.

Theodore became the governor of New York. Then he became vice president of the United States. President McKinley was shot and killed. Theodore then became president. President Roosevelt fought for all Americans to have a square deal. He wanted everyone to have an equal chance to succeed. He led legislation to make sure big businesses treated their workers fairly. He began the Food and Drug Administration to inspect meat and drugs would be safe for people to consume. He protected the environment. He created Yellowstone National Park. The first of many national parks.

President Roosevelt also worked hard to make the United States a world power. He managed the building of the Panama Canal. It was a man-made canal that became a shortcut for ships carrying goods around the world. He helped end a war between Russia and Japan. Theodore earned the Nobel Peace Prize doing it.

Theodore Roosevelt was considered to be one of the best U.S. presidents. Partly because of his hard work, our nation is strong. Our land is cared for in national parks. Americans are also more safe and free at home and in the world because of President Roosevelt.

Theodore Roosevelt died in 1919. His image is carved into the granite at Mt. Rushmore to honor his work for America.

Fun Facts

Theodore Roosevelt was the youngest president in the history of the United States. He was 42 when he became president.

Theodore Roosevelt was an author and historian. He wrote 35 books about politics, ships, and hunting.

The teddy bear was invented in honor of President Theodore Roosevelt.

Quotes

“Nothing in this world is worth having or worth doing unless it means effort, pain, difficulty.”

“We must show, not merely in great crises, but in the everyday affairs of life, the qualities of practical intelligence, of courage, of hardihood, and endurance, and above all the power of devotion to a lofty ideal, which made great the men who founded this Republic in the days of Washington, which made great the men who preserved this Republic in the days of Abraham Lincoln.”

title: The Common Good
text: The United States Constitution establishes the conditions for government. According to the Constitution, people give authority, or power, to the government by electing representatives. A representative is someone who makes choices and acts for other people. The representatives must choose what is good for the freedom and liberty of many people instead of what is good for a few. This is called common good. In a democratic community, citizens behave in a way that supports the common good. In the United States, the government works for the common good through policies and laws.

title: Natural and Human Characteristics
text:
All maps have a purpose. They have different types of information. The information can be divided into two big categories: natural characteristics and human characteristics.

Natural characteristics are things like physical landforms and bodies of water. They are things that are naturally part of the land.

Human characteristics are a result of people’s ideas, choices, and actions on the land. Political characteristics are things like county, state, and country boundaries. Cultural characteristics relate to things people make and do. They include houses, bridges, factories, buildings, and parks.

title: Historical Maps
text:
Most historical maps were made long ago. They are records of the past. They can show us what life and places were like in the past. They can also show us how places have changed over time.

Study the maps. How did Savannah change over time?

title: Political Map
text: A political map shows how places are divided by people. The United States is divided into 50 states. Five states share a border with Georgia. Georgia is divided into 159 counties. Political maps often show capital cities.

title: Physical Map
text: Physical maps show landforms and bodies of water. Georgia has mountains, plateaus, hills, and plains. There are also reservoirs, lakes, and rivers. The area near the Atlantic Ocean has wetlands.

title: Population Map
text:

Use the Georgia population map and the legend/key to answer the following questions.

Questions

2. What color on the map shows you where the most people live?

title: Resource Map
text:
A resource is something that people can use. Resources help us meet our needs. Many resources come from nature. We call them natural resources. Things like soil, trees, and minerals are natural resources.

Georgia has almost eight million acres of prime farmland. This means that Georgia has good soil. It also has a long growing season and enough moisture to grow many crops.

More than 60 percent of Georgia is covered by forests. Trees in these forests produce many different things. Christmas trees, resin, medicines, and timber are some of these things.

Kaolin is another important resource in Georgia. It is a type of clay made mainly of minerals. Kaolin is used in products like paper, paint, and ceramics.

title: Bartering
text:
Bartering means trading goods or services for goods or services. Before people used money, they bartered for goods or services. Farmers could trade a chicken or two for sugar, bread, or a cooking pot. Even today, people might receive food as payment for working on a farm.

But, bartering has problems.

Imagine having a cow you want to trade. Is it easy to get a cow into a store to trade it for a bike? Some things are hard to carry or travel with.

What if the bicycle store doesn’t want your cow? You have to find someone who wants what you have in order to make a trade.

What if you want to barter your cow’s milk? You can only trade with someone who lives close to you because milk is perishable. Something perishable goes bad quickly.

Bartering also makes it difficult to decide how much something is worth. How many bikes is a cow worth? How many bottles of milk does a pizza cost?

title: What Is Money?
text:
Eventually, communities began using mediums of exchange. This meant that people could use other items to buy goods or services. Some of these items were shells, salt, or pieces of precious metal. Gold and silver soon became the most acceptable mediums of exchange. They were rare so they were valuable. Mediums of exchange needed to be easy to carry, so precious metals began to be made into coins. Gold, silver, and bronze were made into coins. So were copper and iron.

The word “money” began to be used to describe all mediums of exchange. Now, most people use money to buy the things they want. There are two main categories of money. One is physical money. This is paper or coins. Paper and coins are also called cash.

The other is digital money. Digital money is not physical. It is money that can be transferred online. It allows people to pay for goods and services with a card. A debit or credit card represents a lot of paper and coins.

title: Characteristics of Money
text:
There are some qualities that money must have to be a good medium of exchange.

It must be portable. That means it is easy to travel with it.

It must be durable. This means it is strong and will last a long time.

Money has to be divisible. This means it can be divided to pay for things that cost different amounts.

Money needs to be recognizable. This means everyone must recognize it is money.

Money must also be acceptable. This means that it must be accepted by everyone. You must be able to use it to pay the government and others.

Many countries today have their own money, or currency. The United States uses dollars and cents. Mexico uses pesos and centavos. Some countries share the same currency. Most countries that are part of the European Union use the Euro.

Using money is a lot easier than bartering. We can buy items almost anywhere in the world because we use money.

title: Trade
text:
The word “trade” has more than one meaning. Exchanging goods or services is one meaning of trade. In economics, trade is also the buying and selling of goods between communities.

Trade depends on imports and exports. Imports are goods that are brought in from another country or state. Exports are goods that are sent out of a state or country to be sold.

Most states and countries don’t make everything their citizens need or want. Each place has its own resources. Sometimes states and countries have to buy things from other places. Some states and countries have oil and coal. Others have fish, fruits, and vegetables.

People around the world depend on each other. The United States does not produce everything Americans need or want. The United States trades with other countries. We import and export goods.

title: annette test
text:
Have you ever laid down in the grass and observed the night sky? If you have, you probably noticed many of the objects that are visible to us, including the moon and stars. Looking up to observe the moon, stars, and other objects at night is known as stargazing.

When stargazing, we are able to locate the positions of constellations. Although some stars are visible in the sky, others are too small or far away to be seen with the naked eye. The closest star to Earth, other than the sun, is about 4.24 light-years away. Despite being that close, it is too faint for our eyes to pick up.

To help with this problem, scientists use telescopes. A telescope is a tool that astronomers use to help them see objects that are very small or far away. Telescopes work by using mirrors to focus light from the night sky. The bigger the mirror, the farther or dimmer the objects that the telescope can detect.

Telescopes allow astronomers to view constellations throughout the year. Not only can they see the star patterns within the constellations, but they can also study how the constellations move throughout the year. This helps them explain the seasonal pattern that constellations follow.

Tools, such as telescopes, are important to astronomers because they make it easier to explore the universe. Telescopes aren’t just reserved for astronomers though. We can also use telescopes when stargazing to see more stars and other objects. Next time you have the opportunity, be sure to take a peek through one to experience the night sky like never before!

title: The Oregon Trail
text:
Oregon Country, which included the modern-day states of Oregon, Washington, and part of Idaho, was a disputed piece of land in North America for many decades. Many American Indians lived in and claimed the land as their home, but European countries and the newly created United States believed their claims on the land were legitimate.

In the early 1800s, the land was particularly disputed between Great Britain and the United States. Britain believed its claims extended well back into the earliest years of exploration, and the U.S. believed it had claimed the territory during Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery expedition to the Pacific Ocean. Finally, after years of tension, the United States and Great Britain signed a treaty that established the 49th parallel as the border between British territorial claims in the north (now Canada) and the United States. The treaty was signed in 1846 and meant that the Oregon Country was now part of the United States.

Pioneers began traveling to Oregon even before the U.S. and Great Britain had resolved their contest for the land. Pioneers went to claim cheap land and find economic opportunity in the Oregon Country. The path that they took to Oregon was called the Oregon Trail. The entire Oregon Trail covers about 2,000 miles. It took 4–6 months to reach the end of the trail. Many settlers did not survive the journey. An estimated 20,000 people died on the Oregon Trail. They died from sickness, accidents, lack of food, lack of shelter, and exhaustion. Despite the hardships of the trail, thousands of pioneers completed the journey and settled in the American West.

title: Essential Question
text: How do you choose between needs and wants?

A government does many things. The government provides safety and security for those in the community from threats outside of the community. The government maintains justice and order within the community. The government helps members of the community meet their wants and needs. The government of the United States is a constitutional republic.

A constitutional republic is a form of government based on a written document. That document determines the power and functions of an elected representational government. The written law of the constitution is enforced by representatives chosen by the people. At every level, the people's consent is what gives the government power to act. This is known as popular sovereignty. A constitutional republic must balance individual rights with the common good. Effective leaders work to meet the needs of citizens and protect their rights.

Americans have different customs, traditions, and ethnic origins. Americans are united by the principles of a constitutional republic. The U.S. Constitution states that citizens need to respect individual rights and freedoms. Authority from the people limits the actions of the government, which protects their rights of liberty and freedom. By creating and enforcing laws, citizens can ensure their rights are protected. Respecting the rights of others means that everyone is treated equally. The principles of fairness, equality, and justice have influenced new laws and policies over time at the local, state, and national levels of government.

Fairness, equality, and justice are principles that have influenced government and laws. Fairness is a fundamental American value. Fairness is making sure that everyone has what they need to be successful. Our government supports fairness by making laws to keep things fair for everyone. All people should be treated equally.

Equality means that all people are treated the same, regardless of who they are. Our government provides services and protection to all citizens. Justice means that people behave in a way that is fair, equal, and balanced for everyone. Fairness, equality, and justice are democratic values. These values guide our government. They protect the rights of citizens.

According to one of the Founders, John Adams, “Government is instituted for the common good … not for profit, honor, or private interest of any one man, family, or class of men.” The common good is when people think about what is best for everyone. It refers to decisions that benefit most members of a community. Our government supports the common good through laws. If citizens work together toward the common good, freedom and self-government can be successful. Everyone in the community benefits.

Another important facet of the United States government is rule of law. John Adams stated that “The rule of law means a government of laws and not of men.” Rule of law is based on fairness, equality, and justice. It means that the government is accountable to the law. The government can only use its power as defined by laws. There are four important ideas with the rule of law:

Laws have to be adopted and approved through government processes.

Laws have to be clear, and everyone needs to know about them.

Laws are applied equally for all citizens.

When there are disputes about the law, individuals will have representatives who are neutral to deliver the best outcome.

In the United States, we have a federal government that leads our country. The federal government shares its power with state governments. The federal government has the power to:

print money

declare war

build the military

make treaties (agreements with foreign countries)

make and enforce laws for doing business between the states and foreign nations

make laws to enforce the Constitution

State governments control laws within each state. They also have elected officials. The leader of the state is the governor. The governor appoints officials and signs or vetoes bills passed by the state legislature. The governor is also the commander-in-chief of the state’s military. Each state has its own constitution. Like the United States Constitution, state constitutions must enforce laws in ways that protect the rights of citizens.

We also have local governments. They lead our towns, cities, and counties. Cities and towns elect leaders called mayors. People also elect city managers, town councils, and county commissioners. These officials address community concerns, help out in the community, and act as a voice to the community. Local governments are in charge of police and fire departments, public transportation systems, road maintenance, community parks, trash removal, and building codes.

title: Spending, Saving, and Investing
text:
When you earn money, you have the choice to save or spend your income. People should spend part of their income on goods and services to meet their basic needs. These include housing, electricity, food, water, clothing, transportation, and medical necessities. After paying for your weekly, monthly, or yearly needs, you must decide what to do with your remaining income. You can spend it on things you want or save it for the future. Many people spend too much income on their wants. This may not leave enough money to pay for things they need.

Saving money is very important. People save money to buy things in the future. Many families save money to buy a car or a house. Some families save money for a vacation. The more something costs, the more money you have to save. People can save money in many ways. You can place your money into a savings account at a bank. You can also compare prices on items you buy and use coupons to save on your purchases. It's important to make good choices with your money to plan for your future.

If people invest some of the money they've saved, they can earn even more money for emergencies or later use. To make an investment means to purchase something with the hope that it will make more money in the future. People can invest in businesses, raw materials, goods, and services to earn additional funds.

When someone invests money, they usually buy an asset, like stock in a company. If that company does well, the stock is worth more. The more money someone puts into stocks, the more money can grow. Stocks can be a little risky. If the business fails, the stocks are lost. It is important to research and choose stocks that will grow. Over time, many businesses do well. People who invest can earn a lot of money.

title: “The Rabbit in the Moon”
text:
Long ago, Jade Emperor, the ruler of heaven, needed help. He disguised himself as a poor old man and went down to Earth.

He begged for food from the animals. The monkey brought fruit from the trees. The fox brought fish from the river.

title: Midwest: Physical Characteristics
text:
The Midwest region has 12 states. The land in these states is mostly flat. In other parts of the Midwest, there are rolling hills, high mountains, and deep valleys. Some states in the Midwest have rivers as their borders, including the Mississippi River. Six of the 12 states fall within the Great Lakes area.

The Midwest has a humid continental climate. In summer, it gets hot and humid. In winter, it can get very cold. There is a large difference between the temperatures in summer and winter.

Prairie grasses cover the region. This flat grassland is called the Great Plains. The grasslands make the soil fertile, or good for growing crops. Blueberries, corn, and asparagus grow well in the Midwest.

Animals that live here include bison, prairie dogs, and black bears.

title: Essential Question
text: What are physical and man-made characteristics?

title: Midwest: Man-Made Characteristics
text:
The population of the Midwest is about 68 million. The Chippewa, Lakota, and Blackfoot were some of the Native American tribes living in this region before Europeans arrived.

The Midwest is known for some of the finest architecture in the United States. Many of the architects who created these structures were from Europe. The buildings often show the style of their architects’ home countries.

Since the land is fertile, many people farm in the region. Farmers grow wheat, soybeans, and corn. Ranchers raise hogs and dairy cows. The Midwest is one of the most important areas of agricultural production in the world. The area is also home to many manufacturing industries. Many vehicles and machines are made in the Midwest.

title: Southwest: Physical Characteristics
text:
The Southwest region includes four states. The Gulf of Mexico and 10 rivers are the main bodies of water in the region. The area also has a few lakes. Landforms in the Southwest include high mountains, plateaus, valleys, and seven barrier islands. The southern portion of the Continental Divide runs through New Mexico. The region is also home to the Grand Canyon.

Both dry and tropical areas are in the region. Rainfall is mostly seasonal. In summer, only the tropical areas receive rainfall. Other areas receive most of their rainfall during the winter.

Trees, such as blue palo verde, Texas ebony, Arizona cypress, and white oak, grow in the region. Cotton, lettuce, melons, and grapefruit are crops that grow well in the Southwest.

Swift foxes, black-tailed prairie dogs, and Texas horned lizards are some of the animals found in the Southwest.

title: Southwest: Man-Made Characteristics
text:
There are more than 42 million people living in the Southwest region. Indigenous peoples who live in the Southwest have influenced the culture of the region. These people include the Navajo, Hopi, Pueblo, and Apache. The stone and mud homes and the food eaten in the region show this cultural influence. This influence can also be heard in the names of cities and towns in the Southwest.

Coal, oil, and natural gas abound in the region. Agriculture and mining are also big industries in the area. Oil, however, is the most important industry. There is also a growing aerospace manufacturing industry.

title: Northwest: Physical Characteristics
text:
There are three states in the Northwest region. All three states have beaches along the Pacific Ocean. The area also has many rivers, lakes, and waterfalls.

Mountains and valleys also cover the region. Some of the mountains are volcanoes.

This region has temperate and polar climates. The temperate areas have redwood, Douglas fir, and western hemlock trees. The polar areas have lichens, mosses, and sedges.

Polar bears, walruses, cougars, black bears, grizzly bears, wolves, and moose can all be found in the Northwest region.

title: Northwest: Man-Made Characteristics
text:
Many different Indigenous peoples lived in the Northwest before Europeans came. More than 68 million people now live in this region. The Pacific coast provides fresh seafood. Forests provide wood for homes and furniture.

Grapes, apples, and potatoes grow well in the Northwest. Oil, coal, and natural gas are important resources. Gold and zinc can also be found in this region. The region is also known for dams that provide water and electricity.

Agriculture, mining, and logging are big industries in the region. Manufacturing and healthcare provide jobs, too. Tourism is also a big business in the area. People travel to the Northwest to ski, climb rocks, and observe wildlife.

title: The West: Physical Characteristics
text:
Eight states make up the West region of the United States. The area is beautiful and diverse. Because it is close to the Pacific Ocean, there are many islands and coastlines. The region also has numerous rivers and waterfalls. The area features lakes, hot springs, and geysers, too. The West is home to mountain ranges, valleys, and canyons.

The West has dry, temperate, and tropical climate areas. Joshua trees and cacti grow in the dry areas. The temperate areas feature redwood, Douglas fir, and different kinds of juniper trees. Coconuts, pineapples, and sugarcane are plentiful in the tropical areas of the region.

Animals in the region include elk, wolves, and bighorn sheep. There are also bison, rattlesnakes, and horned lizards. Marine life can be found in the coastal areas.

title: The West: Man-Made Characteristics
text:
The population of the West is about 58 million people. European settlers moved to the area in large numbers, looking for gold and land. Many American Indians lost their homes when the Europeans came. Copper, coal, oil, and natural gas are still found in the area. The region is also famous for potatoes, pineapples, almonds, and grapes.

A transcontinental railroad was connected in this region. The Union Pacific Railroad was built from the west, and the Central Pacific Railroad was built from the east. The two trains met at Promontory Summit in Utah.

Forestry, fishing, and ranching are big industries in the region. Entertainment and mining are also important in the area. Amusement parks, ski resorts, and national parks attract a lot of tourists. The region’s islands also provide a tropical getaway.

title: New Year’s Day
text: New Year’s Day is a national holiday. It is celebrated on January 1. We celebrate the beginning of a new year.

John Adams was born in Massachusetts in 1735. Although raised in a farming family, he had a passion for the law and a strong desire to contribute to the growing movement for American independence. Adams attended Harvard College (now Harvard University), located in Cambridge, Massachusetts, to pursue a career as a lawyer. In his early career, Adams actively sought out legal cases that championed colonial rights and challenged British authority. A pivotal moment in Adams' early legal career came in 1770, following the Boston Massacre. Despite his American patriotism, Adams upheld his commitment to justice and agreed to defend the British soldiers accused of firing into a crowd and killing Boston colonists. This decision demonstrated Adams' belief in the importance of fair trials and the rule of law, even when it conflicted with his personal beliefs. As tensions with Britain continued to increase, Adams' principles and powerful oratory (speaking) skills pushed him to the forefront of the independence movement. Adams established himself as a vocal and influential advocate for American independence.

In 1774, John Adams was elected to the First Continental Congress. It was during the meetings that he gave impassioned speeches, and he became a leading voice for stronger resistance against British tyranny. Adams initially supported the effort to seek peace with King George III before the war. However, he was also a strong advocate for independence and ultimately favored a break with Britain. Adams played a crucial role as part of the committee that was chosen to draft the Declaration of Independence in 1776. While Jefferson is known as the primary author, Adams used his legal and political knowledge to help shape the document's arguments.

During the Revolutionary War, Adams served Congress by being a part of numerous committees, showcasing his dedication and leadership. He also played a crucial role as a diplomat, traveling to France and the Netherlands to secure vital loans, military aid, and diplomatic recognition for the fledgling United States. His biggest domestic job was helping to support the Continental Army through his involvement on the Board of War and Ordnance. It was here he worked closely with General Washington during the years of fighting.

After the war, Adams' reputation for intelligence and patriotism led him to become the first Vice President under President George Washington. He served two terms as Vice President from 1789 to 1797. In 1796 Washington declined a third term as President. Adams ran for president as the Federalist candidate. He faced a fierce challenge from Thomas Jefferson, his friend-turned-rival, representing the Democratic-Republican Party. Both the political parties engaged in harsh attacks and smear campaigns against each other. The Federalists accused Jefferson of being an atheist (not believing in God) and a radical politician who would bring about anarchy. Anarchy is a situation where there is no government or laws, which can lead to chaos and disorder. The Democratic-Republicans accused Adams of wanting to be a king and of trying to destroy the ideals that America had fought for in the Revolution.

In the end, Adams narrowly won the election. He secured 71 electoral votes to Jefferson's 68. He became the second president of the United States, taking office in 1797. As the runner up in the election, Jefferson became Adams’ Vice President.

title: Dropping the Bomb: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
text:
On July 29, 1945, Japan refused to surrender following the demand to do so by the Allies at the Potsdam Conference. The next day, President Truman decided to authorize the atom bomb to be dropped on Hiroshima. It was dropped on Aug. 6, 1945.

The bomb blast killed 86 percent of the people within a half-mile of ground zero. It wounded another 10 percent in that circle. Between 1/2 and 1 1/2 miles from ground zero, 27 percent of the people were killed instantly and another 37 percent were wounded. When there is an atomic blast, it creates radioactive dust called fallout. This fallout comes back down to the ground as radiation-contaminated rain. The fallout from the Hiroshima blast affected an area 12-15 miles from ground zero. Much more was carried by winds around the area. Fallout causes radiation sickness and death. The sickness can last from a few hours to several decades. It killed and sickened many more people. Some people got terrible burns and others got different kinds of cancer.

When the Japanese still did not surrender after that bombing, the president authorized another bombing on Nagasaki. After that, Japan surrendered.

Was President Truman justified in using the nuclear bomb? Why do you think no nuclear bombs have ever been used since the two in Japan in 1945? What do you think the president discussed with his advisers before authorizing the use of the bombs?

title: The CCC and Georgia
text:
When Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected president, he started something called the New Deal. This was a plan to provide jobs for people all over the United States. Many jobs were available to the citizens of Georgia. These jobs helped people survive through this difficult time.

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was a New Deal program. It was established on March 31, 1933. It provided jobs for millions of single young men between the ages of 18 and 25. The CCC worked in Georgia to help conserve, or save, the state’s natural resources. They constructed almost 500,000 erosion-controlled dams, ran over 3,600 miles of telephone lines, and planted more than 22 million trees across the state.

One anonymous CCC enrollee wrote a poem about their work: “All over this country, the work we did with our hands, our minds, and our bodies, still stands today as a monument.… We put our mark on this land and that mark will be seen for many years to come.”

One great legacy, or long-lasting impact, left by the CCC in Georgia was its state parks, national forests, and national parks. The Corps established 12 state parks, including the A. H. Stephens, F. D. Roosevelt, Fort Mountain, and Kolomoki Mounds. During these projects, workers created lakes, ponds, cabins, lodges, and trails. They also set up group camps at some parks with the help of the Works Progress Administration (WPA).

The programs of the New Deal helped improve Georgia and provided jobs for many of its citizens. However, some Georgians still struggled. It wasn’t until war hit in the 1940s that hard times changed in the United States.

title: Becoming a Citizen
text:
A citizen is an official member of a country, state, or community. If you were born in the United States, you are a U.S. citizen. If your parents are U.S. citizens, you can become a citizen no matter where you were born. People who are born outside of the United States can choose to become a U.S. citizen. If you choose to become a citizen of the United States, the government requires specific things.

To become a citizen, you must be at least 18 years old and have lived in the United States for at least five years. You must be loyal and be willing to pledge allegiance to the United States. To pledge allegiance means to take an oath of loyalty.

You must also have a basic understanding of U.S. history, the U.S. government, and the U.S. Constitution. In addition, you must be able to speak, read, and write English.

The process of becoming a citizen has three steps. First, you must file an application. This includes being fingerprinted, taking photographs, and providing legal documents. You must also pay a fee to submit your documents.

The next step is to take the naturalization exam. This exam has two parts. It has an English test as well as a U.S. history and government exam.

The last step is to appear in court. You must go before a judge and ask to become a U.S. citizen. The judge listens to your reasons for wanting to become a citizen. Then, the judge will make a final decision. Once you are made a citizen, you have all the rights and duties of any other U.S. citizen.

title: Works Progress Administration (WPA)
text: The Works Progress Administration (WPA) was a large effort that began in 1935. The WPA employed men, women, and even some youth. This program impacted almost every community because it hired millions of people at the same time. They built new bridges, parks, public buildings, and schools in their communities. They even constructed stadiums, swimming pools, and golf courses. The goal of the WPA was to provide every family that experienced long-term job loss with work. Many of the improvements made through the WPA are still being used and appreciated today.

title: Essential Question
text: What are the rights of U.S. citizens?

title: Rights of Citizens
text:
People have many different rights. These include unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights. Rights have different functions. Unalienable rights, also called natural rights, are rights that people are born with that cannot be taken away. The Declaration of Independence defines these rights as the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

Civil rights protect people from the actions of government, organizations, or other people. The United States government, organizations, and other people cannot prohibit the rights of citizens to:

vote

a fair trial by jury

government services

due process of the law (legal actions or proceedings that must be followed)

serve in the military

serve in public office

equality through the law

assemble or petition the government

freedom of speech

freedom of religion

freedom of the press

Political rights allow people to participate freely in government. People can protect their civil rights through political rights. These rights are defined in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights at the federal level. They are defined at the state level in state constitutions. Examples of political rights include:

voting

serving on a jury

holding political office

attending a protest

petitioning the government through action and/or speech

supporting a social or political issue

expressing an idea in speech and the press

joining a political party

equal accessing of public services

Economic rights are financial choices and privileges that individuals may select without government interference. These rights enable people to make use of civil and political rights. Economic rights include the right to:

own property

change employment

operate a business

join a labor union

access polling places

meet basic wants and needs

have multiple economic opportunities

not have to pay fees and taxes based on race, gender, ethnicity, religion, or sexual orientation

title: Americans with Disabilities Act
text:
One law that protects the unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights of people living in the United States is the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Congress passed the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990. Its purpose is to “prohibit discrimination against people with disabilities in several areas, including employment, transportation, public accommodations, communications and access to state and local government programs and services.”

The Americans with Disabilities Act is divided into five titles, or sections. Each title has a specific purpose.

Title I: Protects against discrimination in the workplace and ensures that people with disabilities receive appropriate accommodations in their workplace

Title II: Ensures access to services, facilities, and transportation provided by local and state governments

Title III: Prohibits discrimination in public places and requires that people with disabilities receive appropriate access to facilities

Title IV: Requires telecommunications companies to provide equal services to people with disabilities

Title V: Defines various types of disabilities and prevents retaliation by employers, organizations, and other people, etc., against individuals who enforce their rights under the act

By protecting unalienable, civil, political, and economic rights, governments can ensure that all citizens have the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. These rights also ensure that governments cannot interfere with the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

title: Legislation that Protects the Rights of Citizens
text:
Throughout the country’s history, the federal government has passed many laws and constitutional amendments to extend, strengthen, and protect the rights of citizens.

Amendment or Legislation

Year Passed

Purpose
