Cotton crops were a crucial source of income for many farmers. The boll weevil laid its eggs in the cotton plants. After the larvae hatched, they would eat the plant. In around 1915, the insects spread from Texas across the southern states, bringing devastation to cotton crops along the way. By 1923, the boll weevil had destroyed over half of the cotton plants in Georgia. A drought in 1925 dried up many water sources in Georgia. This double devastation of the boll weevil and drought forced many Georgian farmers to leave to find new opportunities in the North or the West.

title: Language
text:
The tribes of the Northeast spoke different languages and dialects. A dialect is a way of pronouncing and speaking a language. A dialect is often unique to an area or community. For example, Lenape is an Algonquian language. However, the Lenape people spoke different dialects of the language.

The Algonquian language family connects many tribal languages. These languages are all across the eastern and middle parts of North America. A language family is a group of languages that share a common ancestor or parent language. Among the Lenape, there were three dialects: Munsee, Unami, and Unalachtigo.

The Powhatan and Potawatomi also spoke dialects of the Algonquian language. The Powhatan language was related to the Munsee, Unami, and Unalachtigo dialects. Potawatomi is closely related to other Algonquian languages spoken by the Ojibwe, Cree, and Shawnee.

American Indians who lived in present-day Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Rhode Island spoke many different languages. The Wampanoag lived in present-day Massachusetts. They and other tribes in the area spoke the Massachusett language. This language was first spoken by the Massachusett tribe. This tribe is where the name of the state comes from.

title: Oral Traditions
text:
Passing knowledge, beliefs, and history from generation to generation by word of mouth is called oral tradition. Older people in Indigenous groups often told stories to the younger members. Many stories explained beliefs about creation. They also explained other beliefs, traditions, and historical events. Sometimes, as the stories got passed down, different versions of the story or folktale were created. Two Lenni Lenape stories about creation were recorded by Europeans in the 1600s and 1700s.

The first story says that a woman fell down from the heavens. As she fell, she continued to float in the air, searching for a place to rest. She couldn’t find one. Finally, some sea creatures decided to help her. A large tortoise came to the surface of the sea. It let the woman rest on its back. The dirt, plants, and shells of the sea gathered around the turtle. This mass grew until it became the Earth. This became the home of the Lenape people.

The second story says that a turtle came up to the surface from the deep part of the ocean. As the water drained from the turtle’s back, a tree began to grow. The tree’s roots sent out two sprouts. One sprout grew into a man. The second sprout grew into a woman. These were the first ancestors of the Lenape people. In both versions of the story, the turtle represents Earth. The turtle was a very important and respected symbol among the Lenape people.

title: Religion
text:
Many American Indian tribes of the Northeast held deep religious beliefs. Most of these religious beliefs were influenced by the natural world. The Lenape believed in a creator god called Kishelëmukong. They also believed in other gods or spirits, called manëtu or manitou. Most animals, plants, and some objects are thought to have manitou. For example, there are manitou called "pethakhuweyok," or “the thunder beings.” The winds of the four cardinal directions are also considered manitou. They are called Grandfather of the North, Grandfather of the East, Grandfather of the West, and Grandmother of the South.

The Illiniwek of Illinois were also very religious. They believed in a Master of Life. They believed in individual spirits. They prayed to these spirits for help. They had religious traditions and ceremonies for weddings and burials. These ceremonies often involved gifts. The Illiniwek did not value personal wealth. A person who could give away possessions earned great respect. When a person died, the Illiniwek buried them with gifts of things they might need in the afterlife.

An important leader of the Kickapoo tribe of the Great Lakes was the shaman. A shaman communicated with the spirit world. They also predicted the future and cured the sick for the band. Sometimes, a shaman had more power than a chief. The Kickapoo believed in a Great Manitou in the spirit world who ruled over everything. Lesser manitous were in fire, the sky, the moon, the stars, the four winds, and Grandmother Earth. Wisaka was Great Manitou’s son. He created the Earth and everything in it. The Kickapoo performed many ceremonies, such as the Bison Dance. This ceremony asked for protection and a successful hunt.

title: American Indian Life Today: The Northeast
text:
Thousands of American Indians still live in the Northeast today. Today, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, and Vermont have the largest American Indian populations in the region. The tribes of the Northeast continue to share their culture, history, and traditions with younger members of their tribes and communities.

Many American Indian artists share their history and culture. They do this through their works of art. Mary Leaf was a member of the Akwesasne Mohawk Nation. She was a famous basket maker. She taught others the traditional way to make baskets. Her baskets are on display in many museums. This includes the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C. Maude Kegg was a member of the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe of Minnesota. She was a famous storyteller. Kegg was also a very talented artist. She used beadwork to tell stories. Her stories taught people about Ojibwe culture.

In Massachusetts, members of the Patuxet and Wampanoag tribes continue to preserve and share their history. Some do this at the Plimoth Patuxet Museums. Visitors can learn about Patuxet and Wampanoag. They can learn about their history, beliefs, and tribal life. Visitors can learn about their interactions with English settlers. Members of the tribes give demonstrations about the Patuxet and Wampanoag.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The Great Depression was a time of significant economic downturns. It affected many people's lives in the United States. However, a series of government programs, called the New Deal, was initiated by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. These programs were aimed at helping those struggling during the Great Depression. The New Deal was intended to provide relief to farmers, financial support for the unemployed, and initiatives to rebuild the economy. While these initiatives would not happen overnight, the New Deal marked a turning point. The United States began to recover from the devastating effects of the Great Depression.

title: Essential Question
text: How did major events of the 20th century affect Georgia?

title: Freedom of Religion
text:
Founder James Madison said the issue with religious beliefs is that people usually cannot agree on them. Religion can bring people together. It can also drive people apart. People often feel strongly about their religious beliefs. This can make freedom of religion messy.

Conflict happens when people believe their views should control how others live their lives. Some people have used freedom of religion to discriminate against others who do not share their beliefs. Discrimination is treating people unfairly because of their race, gender, age, or any other reason.

Why is freedom of religion important?

The Puritans and other religious groups came to the American colonies to escape religious persecution. Persecution is treating people unfairly based on what they believe or do not believe. The Puritans formed communities where everyone shared the same beliefs. When religious leaders didn’t like someone’s ideas, they would banish, or permanently send away, that person from the colony. They also passed strict laws about how to practice religion. This shows how the people who were persecuted could also persecute others.

The Founders decided that freedom of religion was an important principle. This right is protected in the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Indiana State Constitution has four sections about religious freedom.

Section 2: All [people] shall be secured in the natural right to worship Almighty God, according to the dictates of their own consciences. People have the freedom to worship in the way that feels right.

Section 3: No law shall … control the free exercise and enjoyment of religious opinions, or interfere with the rights of conscience. Laws cannot control the practice of religion.

Section 4: No preference shall be given, by law, to any creed, religious society, or mode of worship; and no [person] shall be compelled to attend, erect, or support any place of worship, or to maintain any ministry. The government cannot give preference to any religion. No one will be forced to practice religion.

Section 5: No religious test shall be required [for a person to qualify] for any office of trust or profit. Government workers are not required to meet any religious qualifications.

title: Great Britain in the 1700s
text:
Great Britain in the early 1700s was an economically prosperous empire. It was also considered one of the strongest empires in Europe. The country was primarily united under one religion: the Church of England. It was also united primarily through one language: English. Socially, however, Britain was divided in many ways. The British government was in control of Wales, Ireland, and Scotland at this time. These lands were located near England. Wales and Scotland were absorbed into the empire of Great Britain by 1707. Most people in Wales, Ireland, and Scotland did not speak English or follow the Church of England. Many people living in these lands were Catholic. In addition, many Scottish people kept their cultural practices, which were different from those of the British.

British society was partitioned, or divided into different sections, during this time. On one end of British society was the extremely wealthy class. This small percentage of the British population owned most of Britain’s wealth. On the other end of society were Britain’s extremely poor. These people worked hard but did not own land and had little income. There was little opportunity in Britain for people to change their social or economic status. In 1709, British writer Daniel Defoe wrote about seven different categories of British society:

The great, who live profusely.

The rich, who live plentifully.

The middle sort, who live well.

The working trades, who labour hard, but feel no want.

The country people, farmers, etc., who fare indifferently.

The poor, who fare hard.

The miserable, that really pinch and suffer want.

Some of the British wanted to find a way to improve the lives of the poor because society was so economically divided. Others believed that moving the lower classes out would improve society in Britain. Newly colonized lands in North America provided a perfect opportunity for both groups to pursue options for dealing with the poorest people in Britain.

title: Essential Question
text: Did the Georgia colony fulfill the vision of James Oglethorpe and the British trustees?

title: Spanish Threat from the South
text: The Spanish explored the Carolina territory and established settlements in the region in the 1500s. By 1587, however, the Spanish had abandoned their settlements in the area and moved south to La Florida. The West Indies and South America provided Spain with gold and other valuable resources. The Spanish still claimed the Carolina region as part of the Spanish Empire. However, the British Empire felt that the Carolina territory belonged to them. Due to these conflicting claims, British settlements in South Carolina were under constant threat of attack by the Spanish. By the 1700s, war between Spain and Britain threatened to disrupt South Carolina’s rice and indigo production. This would weaken the British Empire’s power in Europe. Britain had to find a way to protect South Carolina from the threat of Spanish attack.

title: Georgia: A Buffer Colony
text:
James Oglethorpe was a social reformer in Britain and a member of British Parliament. When he was 33 years old, one of Oglethorpe's closest friends was put in prison for being unable to repay his debts. This punishment was common for people who could not pay back their debts in Britain at that time. While in prison, Oglethorpe’s friend caught smallpox and died from the disease. Oglethorpe felt that the debtors' prison system was unjust. He began to investigate the British prisons and the struggles the poor faced. Being a member of Parliament, Oglethorpe proposed establishing a colony in America. This new colony would be a place where Britain’s poorer citizens could move and start new lives. He believed this plan would solve Britain’s social and economic problems. Oglethorpe believed that opportunities in this new colony would help the poorest people become productive members of British society. He called this new colony Georgia in honor of King George II.

Additionally, this colony would protect the colony of South Carolina. The land that would become the Georgia Colony was located between South Carolina and La Florida. The Georgia Colony would be the perfect buffer, or protection, for South Carolina against Spanish attacks.

title: Trustee Era: Charter of 1732
text:
James Oglethorpe’s plan to create a colony in North America for Britain’s poor population was approved. The Charter of 1732 established the Georgia Colony. Georgia was the first new colony established in North America in over 50 years. It was the last of the original 13 American Colonies to be established. Georgia’s colonial charter was written as a trustee colony. A group of 21 British trustees was appointed to govern Georgia. A trustee is a person who has the authority to make decisions for another person or group of people. As a trustee colony, the people selected as trustees could not profit or personally benefit from the decisions they made. Instead, the trustees were entrusted to act and make laws that would benefit the people for whom they were responsible. The trustee’s motto was "Non sibi sed aliis," which means “Not for self, but for others." Georgia was the only one of the 13 original colonies established as a trustee colony.

According to the Charter of 1732, the Georgia Colony was created for three purposes: philanthropy, economics, and defense. Philanthropy is a word that refers to an activity designed to help the poor or others who are less fortunate. Through his efforts, Oglethorpe was able to help improve the lives of many of Britain’s poor people. With hard work, colonists could improve their lives in Georgia. Their efforts would also benefit the British Empire economically. The Georgia Colony could grow and produce items that could not be grown or produced in England. Additionally, the colony's location became a way to keep the Spanish away from South Carolina.

The board of trustees changed Oglethorpe's original plan for the colony. Instead of allowing people from debtors' prisons to move to Georgia, only the “deserving poor” were invited to move to the colony. The trustees selected individuals based on the skills and benefits they would bring to the colony. Those who could not pay their way to the colony would have their way paid for by the group of trustees.

Three thousand people emigrated to the new colony of Georgia. Two thousand had their passage paid for by the trustees. Due to the colonists' low social and economic status in Britain, the trustees did not think the colonists could govern themselves or make their own laws. While they were given supplies and land, the colonists had to follow strict guidelines and rules in return. Colonists were encouraged to grow certain crops on their land. These crops included grapes, rice, indigo, silk, and, eventually, tobacco. These crops would ensure that Britain had a supply of goods to sell throughout the world. Alcohol, such as rum, was not allowed in the colony. However, the trustees felt the new colony could also be a new source of wine to sell in Europe. Wine was not considered "alcohol" like rum and was allowed. All colonists were required to set aside land to plant mulberry trees to feed silkworms. Silk was in high demand by Europe's upper classes, but Britain did not have the right climate for raising silkworms. By requiring Georgia’s colonists to raise silkworms, the British Empire was guaranteed a steady supply of silk.

Colonists were also given land but were not allowed to sell it. Inheritance laws were written so that land could only be passed down to male members of families. These laws kept colonists from selling their land and moving from the colony. The trustees believed that the colonists should work the land themselves. They were also wary of other colonies, such as South Carolina, where enslaved people outnumbered British colonists. Because of this, laws were written that did not allow enslaved people to be purchased and used for labor in Georgia.

Given the extreme poverty in Britain and the land and opportunities available in Georgia, many colonists agreed to the trustees' rules.

title: The Yamacraw Nation and Savannah
text:
The early 1700s brought unrest between the British and American Indian groups in southeast South Carolina. As more British colonists settled in Yamasee Territory, conflicts over fur trading and control of the land grew. For these reasons, the Yamasee War was fought between the British and Yamasee from 1715 to 1717.

The British victory led to the loss of power and land for many American Indian nations. This devastating loss led many Yamasee to leave the region. Some Yamasee joined the Muscogee (Creek) people. Others ventured farther south to join the Seminole in La Florida. Some remaining Yamasee joined together with other American Indians to form new nations. This was the case for the Yamacraw.

The Yamacraw tribe was founded by leader Tomochichi in 1728. It was made up of some 200 people from the Yamasee and Lower Creek tribes. Tomochichi and the newly formed Yamacraw established themselves on the banks of the Savannah River. Tomochichi and the Yamacraw believed that this area was the resting place of their ancestors. It was also located on a major waterway, making trade between the Yamacraw and the British easier to access.

title: Oglethorpe in Georgia
text:
In November 1732, James Oglethorpe and a group of British colonists set sail on the ship the Anne. Oglethorpe, as a trustee, could not own land or profit in any way from the new colony of Georgia. He joined the first colonists on the two-month journey to Georgia to help establish the colony. Upon reaching North America, the Anne landed briefly in Charleston, South Carolina, to resupply. Next, the Anne sailed farther south to Point Royal, South Carolina. Oglethorpe left the colonists in Point Royal. From there, he and several men went to search for a potential settlement site in Georgia. They found a potential settlement area on the southern side of the Savannah River. This place was called the Yamacraw Bluffs. Being located near the river was important to colonists. The river served as an access point for trade. Nearness to water also provided water to grow crops. It also made transportation easier.

It was on the Yamacraw Bluffs that Oglethorpe and his settlement scouts first met Tomochichi and the Yamacraw people. Tomochichi and his people had met British settlers previously while in South Carolina. Tomochichi and the Yamacraw met Oglethorpe and his group with caution. When Oglethorpe encountered Tomochichi and his followers, he quickly enlisted the help of local interpreter Mary Musgrove.

Musgrove's mother was Muscogee (Creek), and her father was a British settler in South Carolina. Born in 1700, Musgrove grew up spending time in both Muscogee (Creek) villages and South Carolina British settlements. She was considered a member of both societies. She spoke both Muskogee and English fluently. After she married, Musgrove and her husband set up a trading post near the Savannah River. It was here that James Oglethorpe first met Mary and hired her to be his interpreter.

Musgrove became Oglethorpe’s primary interpreter for 10 years, from 1733 to 1743. During that time, she was instrumental in keeping the peace and negotiating treaties between the Yamacraw, other American Indian nations, and incoming British settlers. Musgrove played a key role in the creation of the colony of Georgia.

Over time, Oglethorpe and Tomochichi developed mutual respect and admiration for each other as leaders. In 1736, Tomochichi and his wife, Senauki, traveled to Britain as American Indian goodwill ambassadors for the new colony of Georgia. They, along with their nephew Toonahowi and six other Yamacraw, met with the king and queen of Great Britain. They also met with members of the British Parliament. Their diplomatic mission was to ensure fair trade with the British and establish peaceful relationships. The Yamacraw were treated as honored guests in Britain. Tomochichi later indicated that he felt assured that his people would be better protected under the British in the region.

title: Establishment of Savannah
text:
With Mary Musgrove as their interpreter, Tomochichi and Oglethorpe established a friendly, working relationship. Oglethorpe and the settlers were allowed to clear away trees in order to establish a permanent settlement. Oglethorpe and settler William Bull designed the layout of Savannah in a series of grids. This layout included wide streets and public park spaces, known as squares. Originally, 24 squares were located throughout the settlement. Today, 22 of the 24 original squares are still in use. Oglethorpe helped other groups of people arriving in the new colony. He helped them develop and plan towns with similar grid formats and layouts.

Oglethorpe and Tomochichi developed a deep understanding of each other as leaders of their own nations. Tomochichi helped the colonists lay out roads south from Savannah to New Inverness. He also helped Oglethorpe determine the colony's southern border. He was also instrumental in helping Oglethorpe maintain peaceful relationships with other American Indian nations in the region.

Tomochichi died at the age of approximately 90 years old in 1739. Oglethorpe arranged a British military funeral for his friend. The funeral was planned to honor their friendship and the immense contribution Tomochichi made to the peaceful British colonization of Georgia. Oglethorpe, British settlers, and members of the Yamacraw nation all paid tribute to Tomochichi at his funeral service.

title: Introduction to the Plains
text:
The Indigenous peoples of the Plains region lived on the large grasslands of the Great Plains. A plain is a large area of flat, grassy land with few to no trees. The Great Plains region is a large area east of the Rocky Mountains. It is very flat. It extends from Mexico to Canada and eastward to Illinois. For many years, hundreds of tribes lived in this region. Historians often divide these tribes into two groups: the Northern Plains tribes and the Southern Plains tribes. Tribes of the Northern Plains included the Assiniboine or Plains Cree, Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Crow, Dakota Sioux, Mandan, and Osage. Tribes that lived in the Southern Plains included the Apache, Arapaho, Comanche, Kiowa, Pawnee, and Wichita.

The plains of North America are ideal for farming. They're also ideal for hunting animals that graze for food. For centuries, the American Indian tribes who lived in the Great Plains were hunter-gatherers and farmers. Hunter-gatherer tribes moved with the animals they hunted. Their main source of food was bison. They used every part of the bison to meet their needs. Bison hides were used to make tepees, clothing, containers, and blankets.

The American Indians who lived a hunter-gatherer lifestyle had to move around a lot. Their houses needed to go with them. So, they often lived in tepees. Tepees were made of tall, thin logs. The logs were set up vertically and leaned against each other. Animal hides covered the logs to make large, cone-shaped shelters. Tribes moved throughout the Plains region. They settled in areas near water sources.

Some tribes farmed. These tribes didn’t move around much. Some groups lived in more permanent villages. These villages had homes that couldn’t be transported like tepees could.

Many tribes farmed in this region. This included the Wichita and the Caddo. They grew corn, pumpkins, beans, and squash. They also hunted deer, antelope, bear, and bison.

Many tribes in this region built earth lodges to live in. Earth lodges were built close to forests and wooded areas. They were constructed from a few supporting logs attached to beams on top. Then, smaller logs branched out from them like the sun’s rays. All of it was covered with thick layers of dirt and grass. A hole was left in the top to allow smoke from the cooking fire to escape. Earth lodges used materials on the Great Plains to make houses that could stay warm during the cold, windy winters. Dozens of people could live in a single earth lodge.

title: Essential Question
text: How were the tribes of the Plains similar? How were they different?

title: Government Structures
text:
The Plains tribes organized themselves into bands. A band was an independent group. Bands came together for specific events, like the harvest, hunting, or military action. Some bands were more unified than others. The Cheyenne were composed of 10 different bands. They were one of the most unified of the Plains tribes. When there were important decisions to make, the tribe called a council of peace chiefs. About 44 peace chiefs from the 10 tribes came together and made decisions. Anything that the Cheyenne peace chiefs decided was respected and obeyed by all 10 tribes.

The Comanche tribe had a different type of government. Smaller bands of the Comanche had single chiefs. The chiefs were responsible for making decisions. They were also supposed to help people meet their needs. At times, band chiefs came together when they needed to discuss important issues. Most of these issues would have been about war and protecting the Comanche territory. Each band chief worked with a group called a council. Members of the band council helped the band chief make decisions. Other tribes of the Plains region had this type of government. These included the Assiniboine and the Sioux tribes.

title: Clothing
text:
The tribes of the Plains relied on natural resources for clothing. Plains tribes traditionally made clothing from animal hides. They used the hides of deer, bison, and elk. Clothing varied from the Northern Plains to the Southern Plains.

Areas of the Northern Plains are often colder than areas of the Southern Plains. Tribes that lived in the Northern Plains wore more clothing year-round. Men and boys wore shirts, breechcloths, leggings, moccasins, and robes. These were usually made from bison hides. Women and girls of the Northern Plains wore long-sleeved shirts, skirts, leggings, robes, and moccasins. Tribes of the Southern Plains wore similar clothing. However, they only added leggings and robes when it got cold.

Many tribes in the Plains added decorations to their clothing. Decorations included fringe, porcupine quills, shells, and feathers. Clothing was often painted with symbols that were important to each tribe. Most tribes of the Plains region wore jewelry and armbands. These were often made of natural materials. Tribes across the Plains also wore headdresses. These were worn during important ceremonies and times of war. They were often made of feathers, animal hides, and other natural materials.

title: Language
text:
Many American Indian languages were once spoken across the Plains region. These languages came from different language families. These included Algonquian, Siouan, Caddoan, and Uto-Aztecan. The Algonquian languages traveled from eastern areas to the plains. The Uto-Aztecan languages came from the south. Some of the languages and dialects of the Plains were Arapaho, Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Pawnee, Crow, Comanche, and many more. The tribes of the Plains also invented a common sign language. Signs for common trade goods and animals were understood by all. This sign language was known throughout the entire range of the Plains region.

The Comanche, a Southern Plains tribe, call themselves Numunuu. This means “the people.” The Comanche language is from the Uto-Aztecan family. The Comanche were closely tied to the Shoshone tribe. They were connected through location, language, and other family relationships. Their language was once a dialect of Shoshone. After separating from the Shoshone people and moving to the Southern Plains, they created their own language.

Like the Comanche, the Arikara are closely related to other tribes. The Arikara language comes from the Caddoan language family. They are a Northern Plains tribe. Their language and the language of the Pawnee are both dialects of the same language. The name "Arikara" means “horn.” Members of the tribe used to wear their hair in two pieces, resembling horns.

Early settlers and trappers began interacting with the American Indian tribes of the Plains. They began using many of their words to describe plants, animals, and places that they had never seen before. Many of the words and place names we use today come from Indigenous languages that have been used for hundreds of years. Some of these words are “caribou,” “woodchuck,” “toboggan,” “pecan,” “skunk,” and “moccasin.”

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Beliefs

The American Indians of the Plains believed that everything had a spirit. Animals, plants, the sun, moon, wind, and other natural elements each had a spirit. Ceremonies, dances, and prayers were performed to communicate with these spirits. Some tribes, like the Cheyenne, believed in a supreme spirit, or god, who was more powerful than all others. Other tribes, like the Crow, believed in many spirit gods who each had the same amount of power as the others.

Ceremonies

Dance is a treasured and sacred tradition for many tribes of the Plains. Styles of dancing have been passed down for hundreds or even thousands of years. Each tribal group has its own style of dance. Some dances are for family celebrations, like marriages and birthdays. Some dances prepare the tribe for hunting. Dances can show gratitude for the land. American Indian groups from the Plains frequently used vocals, drums, percussion, and flutes in their music. This music accompanied the dances.

One of the oldest dances is the Grass Dance. This dance comes from the tribes of the Northern Great Plains. The Pawnee, Omaha, Winnebago, and Iowa were warrior tribes. They danced in this style. The Great Plains were covered in long, tall prairie grass. It flowed back and forth like waves in the wind. The Grass Dance is a beautiful, flowing dance. The dancers hop from one foot to the other. They follow the rhythm of the drum and the singers. Their heads, arms, and shoulders sway back and forth. The tassels on their brightly colored clothing move like grass.

Among many Plains tribes, a naming ceremony was held when a baby was born. In the Cree Tribe, the mother made a feast. Elders gathered, and the mother told the name of the child to an elder. Children were usually named after animals or objects. The elder held the newborn in his arms and kept a beat with a drum or rattle. He sang a song to the spirit of the object or animal that the child was named after.

title: Oral Tradition
text:
The oral traditions of the American Indians of the Plains tended to deal with lessons that elders wished to pass down to children. They also dealt with religious topics. These topics included things like creation and the start of important traditions.

Many groups believed there was a trickster god named Iktomi. Iktomi was a common spirit-being among many Plains tribes. This included many Sioux tribes. They told stories about how Iktomi created the world. In the beginning, no land existed on the Earth. So, Iktomi tricked some animals to try and find land beneath the depths of the sea.

Unfortunately, the only animal that made it back to the surface was a muskrat. He was clutching some earth in his hands. Iktomi took the dirt from the muskrat and created land. Iktomi was not a creature that people used to teach morals. He was a creature that taught about how life can sometimes be unfair or even random.

title: American Indian Life Today: The Plains
text:
Thousands of American Indians still live in the Plains region today. Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and South Dakota have the largest American Indian populations in the region.

The Sioux Nation is the largest tribe of the Plains region. Today, there are over 170,000 members who belong to the different bands of the Sioux Nation. The Lakota tribe is the largest of the Sioux bands. It has about 100,000 members. Many members of the Sioux have contributed to life in the United States. Ed McGaa was a member of the Oglala Lakota. He served in the U.S. Marines during the Korean War. After leaving the military, McGaa became an author. He wrote many books about American Indian life. Gregory “Pappy” Boyington was a member of the Brulé Sioux tribe. He was a pilot during World War II. He received many medals for his service, courage, and bravery.

Members of Plains tribes have preserved their history and traditions through art. Richard Aitson was a member of the Kiowa and Kiowa Apache tribes. He was a famous artist and writer. He was well-known for his beadwork. Aitson helped to preserve Kiowa and Kiowa Apache history and culture. Diane O’Leary was a member of the Comanche tribe. She was a very talented artist. Her paintings focus on American Indian life. O’Leary’s paintings can be found in museums and art galleries around the world.

title: Introduction to the Environment in Africa
text: Africa is a continent rich in natural beauty and resources. However, Africa also faces significant environmental challenges. These challenges affect both the people living there and the natural environment. The continent faces three important issues: water pollution and unequal access to clean water, deforestation, and desertification. These challenges can arise from both human activities and natural occurrences. However, these challenges also provide an opportunity for people to understand their impact and work toward finding sustainable solutions.

title: Essential Question
text: What effect do Africa’s geography and environment have on the way people live and work?

title: Water Pollution and Unequal Access to Water
text:
Water is a vital natural resource. It sustains life on Earth. Unequal access to clean water is a major issue in Africa. Many people, especially those living in rural areas or impoverished communities, struggle to find clean water sources. This lack of access to water resources can impact people’s health, education, and overall quality of life. Water pollution is a growing concern in many African countries. Pollution occurs when harmful substances enter lakes, rivers, or groundwater. This pollution makes the water unsafe for humans to drink or use for cooking. It may harm animal life and impact agriculture as well. There are many causes of water pollution in African countries. Common sources of pollution are industrial waste, sewage, and agricultural chemicals.

One barrier to equal access to clean water is a lack of infrastructure, or systems, for getting water. This can be especially true in rural areas. Limited water supply systems and poor sanitation facilities make accessing safe water sources challenging for some communities. In many rural regions, girls are responsible for walking long distances daily to community wells, where they collect water for their families. They must carry the water back to their homes in pails or buckets. In some rural areas, 74 percent of girls and women were responsible for the daily water supply for their families. This responsibility impacts their ability to attend school or gain employment.

Agriculture plays a crucial role in Africa's economy. However, farmers struggle to irrigate or water their crops without reliable access to clean water. There is also concern about providing enough water for livestock. Lack of access to clean water can result in reducing the quantity and quality of food available for trade.

Access to water can also impact industries across the continent of Africa. Industries require clean water for manufacturing, processing, and cooling machinery. Unequal access to clean water can impact the production of goods. This can lead to an overall reduced productivity. Without water, industries may face difficulties in meeting production targets. This difficulty can result in lower profits, as well as impact employment opportunities and the overall economic growth of a country.

Many African governments and international organizations are working to improve water infrastructure. Improvements are being made by building new wells and water treatment facilities. Water conservation practices are also being taught and encouraged. These practices include reducing water waste, raising awareness about water pollution, and encouraging responsible water use. Educating communities about proper sanitation practices, promoting handwashing, and building sanitation facilities have also been a way to combat water pollution and promote hygienic practices that can lead to better health.

title: African Rainforests
text: Over 50 percent of the land on the continent of Africa is made up of grasslands and forests. Twenty-six percent of that is classified as forest. The continent is home to over 42 billion trees. The world’s second-largest rainforest, the Congo Basin, is located in the sub-Saharan region of Africa. Located in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), this rainforest is an important part of the Earth’s ecosystem. Rainforests produce approximately 20 percent of the world's oxygen. The trees in the rainforest also use and store large amounts of carbon. Trees cycle through photosynthesis, using sunlight to help store carbon dioxide and produce oxygen. This cycle is important to maintain healthy forests and ecosystems and combat changes in climate.

title: Deforestation
text:
Deforestation is the term that refers to the clearing, removal, or destruction of forests. Trees play a crucial role in our environment. They provide oxygen, absorb carbon dioxide, and support ecosystems for many different species of plants and animals. However, deforestation has become a significant problem in Africa due to activities like logging, farming, and the expansion of cities. Responsible logging practices can be environmentally sustainable. However, excessive and illegal logging practices have had severe consequences. Valuable trees, like ebony and mahogany, have been cut down without proper replanting efforts. Agriculture is necessary to provide food to the growing populations in Africa. However, slash-and-burn techniques to clear forests for farming expansion have led to deforestation. Slash-and-burn refers to the practice of clearing land by cutting and burning trees. This technique produces harmful smoke and gases and leads to soil erosion. The expansion of cities is due to many African countries’ rapid population growth and the need for more housing, industries, and infrastructure. As cities grow, trees are cut down to make way for roads, buildings, and other developments.

When forests are cleared, the habitats of various wildlife species are disrupted. This can lead to a loss of biodiversity. Biodiversity is the variety of life in the world or in a particular habitat or ecosystem. Deforestation also contributes to a change in weather patterns. This change happens as there are fewer trees with the ability to absorb carbon dioxide. Carbon scientists have identified carbon dioxide as one of the greenhouse gases responsible for global warming. Greenhouse gases are gases in Earth's atmosphere. They let sunlight pass through the atmosphere, but they prevent the heat that the sunlight brings from leaving the atmosphere.

Deforestation is also a cause of poor soil in many regions of Africa. Soil plays a vital role in supporting plant growth, providing nutrients, and ensuring food security. Food security is having reliable access to a sufficient quantity of affordable, nutritious food. Poor soil is another factor contributing to environmental concerns on the continent of Africa. There are many causes of poor soil quality in Africa. Along with deforestation, other causes include overplanting and overfarming. Soil management is very important in agricultural practices for maintaining the health of the soil. Overplanting leads to the reduction of nutrients available to grow healthy crops. It can also lead to the erosion of topsoil. Erosion is when wind or water wash away the fertile layer of soil, leaving poor soil that is unsuitable for growing crops.

Deforestation through cutting down trees without planting new ones disrupts the natural cycle of soil nutrient replenishment. Trees help retain moisture, prevent erosion, and provide organic matter that enriches the soil. Changing weather patterns, such as increased droughts or heavy rainfall, also affect soil moisture and fertility. Extreme weather events can also lead to soil erosion and the loss of topsoil.

title: Desertification
text:
Desertification is the process by which agricultural land is transformed into a dry desert. This occurrence is due to many factors. These factors include climate change, overgrazing of livestock, and unsustainable farming practices. African countries like Niger (Nai-jer) and Sudan face desertification challenges. Desertification can lead to soil erosion and loss of vegetation. These, in turn, lead to a loss in agricultural products. Lack of resources to grow food can lead to the displacement of people. Populations leave as they search for better living conditions. It also increases food insecurity as farming becomes increasingly difficult in these arid regions. Arid regions receive little precipitation: less than 10 inches, or 25 centimeters, of rain annually.

These challenges threaten the agricultural productivity and livelihoods of local communities. One region of Africa that is particularly at risk for desertification is the Sahel region. This region is approximately 3,000 miles long and crosses 10 African countries. It faces frequent droughts and soil erosion. These challenges have led people to migrate as they search for better farmland.

There are effective strategies and initiatives that can help restore and protect the land from further erosion and deforestation. Afforestation and reforestation are the deliberate planting of trees on land dedicated to forestry. Combining trees with sustainable agricultural practices can help combat desertification. They also promote sustainable land use. Planting rows of trees or shrubs around fields acts as a windbreak. Windbreaks reduce soil erosion and protect crops from strong gusts of wind. The shrubs and forests also serve as habitat for wildlife.

Soil conservation and water management are other ways to combat desertification. Some soil management techniques include adding mulch and cover crops. Cover crops are an added layer of organic material, like straw or leaves, applied to the soil surface. This process helps hold in moisture, reduce water evaporation, and improve soil nutrients. It can also help reduce insects and pests that may attack crops. Planting cover crops between growing seasons also helps protect the soil from erosion. It maintains nutrients for future crops.

title: Introduction to the Southwest
text:
The landscape of the Southwest varies. There are deserts, mountains, valleys, plateaus, and coastal areas. Indigenous peoples, such as the Apache, Chumash, Halchidhoma, Hopi, Mojave, Navajo, Paiute, Pueblo, Quechan, and Salinan, lived in this area. These groups found different ways to use the resources in their environment. People on the coast fished for food. People who lived in the plateau areas used acorns for food. They also hunted for antelope, rabbits, and deer.

These people used the resources around them to build their homes. Many tribes in this region lived in homes built of dried clay called adobe. Adobe is a mixture of water, clay, and straw baked into bricks. Some tribes built adobe homes into the rock cliffs in the area.

Other tribes built hogans. These were made of wood and packed dirt. Some tribes built dwellings into the sides of large rock formations. They did this for protection. Other tribes lived in coastal areas, like the Chumash and Salinan. They built rectangular homes made from tree posts. They covered these homes in bundles of marsh grasses. This created the roof and walls. Some tribes lived in the deserts, valleys, and mountains of Utah, Colorado, Nevada, and Idaho. They moved throughout the year. They constructed tepees from wooden poles. They covered these with bison hides.

The tribes of the Southwest also farmed the land. Water can be a scarce resource in the Southwest. Southwest tribes were very resourceful. They found ways to irrigate farmland. They brought the water from one place to where it was needed. They gathered water from rivers. They also used underground water sources to grow crops. They grew many crops, like corn, pumpkins, beans, and squash. They also grew melons and other types of fruit. After contact with European explorers and settlers, some tribes raised cattle, sheep, and horses. The Hopi, who lived in Arizona, were one of the most skilled tribes at raising livestock.

title: Essential Question
text: How were the tribes of the Southwest similar? How were they different?

title: Government Structures
text:
Each tribe in the Southwest region had its own unique tribal structure. The chief of the Chumash tribe was often the richest person in the tribe. Chumash women could also serve as chiefs. This was unlike many tribes in the Southwest region.

The Mojave tribe was organized into clans. The chief of the whole tribe was known as the "aha macav pina ta’ahon." The title was passed from father to son. The chief was advised by leaders from the other clans. Together, the chief and his advisors made all of the decisions for the tribe.

Salinan tribal groups selected their own leaders to represent their interests. Tribal leaders were chosen by the tribe for their bravery. The leader of the tribe served as an advisor for his people. He worked with a council of elders to make decisions about social, economic, and political matters. Every adult member of the tribe was allowed to express their opinions on tribal matters.

The Shoshone tribe was divided into different bands. The bands lived in different areas of the Shoshone territory. The traditional bands of the Shoshone include the Eastern Shoshone, Northern Shoshone, and Western Shoshone. Each band was divided into smaller tribes. Chiefs of each band were chosen by the members of the tribe. Chiefs were often chosen because of their success in war or other abilities they had.

The Ute lived in bands made up of related family groups. Each band had a chief. The chief was more like the leader of a family. The chief made key decisions for the band. Neighboring bands and groups joined together to conduct ceremonies, celebrations, and large hunts.

title: Clothing
text:
The tribes of the Southwest relied on natural resources for clothing. Unlike many tribes in the Southwest and other regions, the Hopi and Pueblo made clothing from cloth. Yarn was made from cotton and other plant fibers. Dyes were made from clay and different plants to dye the yarn. The yarn was woven into cloth. The cloth was then made into different pieces of clothing. The Hopi and Pueblo also made clothing from deerskin.

The Halchidhoma and Quechan people made clothing from animal skins, bark, and desert plants. They used feathers to decorate their clothing. Jewelry was made from shells and stones. They also made sandals from deerskin. The sandals protected their feet from the hot desert sand.

The Chumash people used natural resources to meet their wants and needs. They created clothing from deerskins and plant fibers. The chief of the tribe often wore a bearskin cape. For special celebrations, members of the tribe wore body paint. They also wore headdresses and skirts made of feathers. The Chumash also used shells to decorate their clothing and make beads for jewelry.

title: Conclude and Connect
text: The environmental challenges facing an entire continent affect everyone. They influence the economic and political decisions leaders make for their countries. However, they also provide opportunities for human ingenuity and invention. One strategy to reduce desertification is the “Great Green Wall.” This involves planting trees across 4,500 feet of the Sahel region. The concept is that it will help reduce desertification, create jobs, and provide better food security. An additional benefit is the idea that this will help to encourage people to return to the region. Many have previously migrated. The Great Green Wall project began in 2007. More than 12 million trees have been planted since then. It is estimated that over 37 million acres of land have been restored through this project.

title: Language
text:
Many American Indian languages were once spoken across the Southwest region. These languages came from different language families. The largest language family in the Southwest was the Uto-Aztecan language family. It includes 30 different languages. The Uto-Aztecan language family extended from Montana to Mexico.

The Uto-Aztecan language family was historically divided into seven different dialects. The largest was the Numic dialect. The Numic dialect was spoken by tribes in modern-day California, Colorado, Idaho, Nevada, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming. The languages of the Chemehuevi, Paiute, Ute, and Shoshone belong to the Numic dialect.

The Hopi language also belongs to the Uto-Aztecan language family. The term "Hopi" comes from the word “Hopituh-Shi-Nu-Mu,” which means “peaceful people” or “people who live in the correct way.” The Hopi language is divided into different dialects. Today, about 5,000 people speak the various Hopi dialects.

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Beliefs

The Navajo divide the world into two groups: the Earth People and the Holy People. The Earth people are the Navajo, who live on Earth. The Navajo believe that the Holy People control their lives. The Holy People are the gods and powerful spirit beings. They travel on the wind, sunbeams, rainbows, and thunder. Every act of the Navajo people's holidays is an attempt to please the Holy People. Navajo ceremonies are performed to prevent or cure diseases.

The religion of the Pueblo people is called Kachin or Katsina. The Pueblo believe in a supreme being or god. They also believe in hundreds of spirits that can communicate with the supreme being. The Pueblo create Kachina dolls to represent the spirits. Kachina represent element spirits, like the sun, moon, stars, and animals.

Ceremonies

Members of the Chumash tribes gather together for ceremonial dances to honor animal spirits. The most important of these ceremonies is the Swordfish Dance. The Chumash believe the swordfish was the chief of all sea creatures. It provided food for the tribe. In return, they offer the swordfish food, beads, and other gifts.

The Halchidhoma, Mojave, Quechan, and Salinan people do not hold ceremonial dances like the Chumash. Instead, they celebrate through singing. Each song tells a different story. Songs are often associated with the creation myths of the tribes. Some songs are sung by the whole tribe. Others can only be sung by a shaman or leaders of the tribe.

The most important ceremony for the Ute tribe is the Bear Dance. The Bear Dance honors the spirit of the bear. The Ute believe that a connection to the spirit of the bear makes them stronger. The Bear Dance is performed after the first thunderstorm in the spring. The ceremony lasts for four days.

title: Oral Traditions
text:
Storytelling has always been an important part of the culture of the tribes of the Southwest. The purpose of many stories was to explain the beliefs of the tribe. Other stories were used to teach children about nature.

The Chumash have passed down stories orally for hundreds of years. This was because the Chumash did not have a written language. To explain sunrise and sunset, the Chumash believed that the sun carried a torch across the sky to light the world. When his journey was over, the sun blew out his torch. The sparks from the torch created the stars in the night sky.

The Apache believe that Fox brought fire to Earth. Fox learned to fly with the geese. He visited the village of the fireflies. He took part of their fire and gave it to the hawks and cranes. The birds spread the fire throughout the land and brought fire to the Earth.

Each tribe also has their own creation beliefs. The Salinan tribe believe that Earth was created by three animal creators: the eagle, coyote, and kingfisher. The Chemehuevi tribe believe Earth was created by two spirits: Coyote and his elder brother Puma. Some Shoshone tribes believe that people were created by the great coyote spirit. The coyote spirit is part of many Shoshone stories.

title: American Indian Life Today: The Southwest
text:
Thousands of American Indians still live in the Southwest region today. Arizona, California, Nevada, and New Mexico have the largest American Indian populations in the Southwest.

Each year, the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians holds an annual powwow. The powwow takes place every year in Santa Ynez, California. Members of the tribe gather to perform traditional songs and dances. Chumash and other tribal artists display their art, jewelry, pottery, and many other items. This powwow is open to the public. Visitors can learn about the customs and histories of different tribes.

The Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians has a 31,500-acre reservation. It is located in Palm Springs, California. The tribe has over 500 registered members. It also has its own tribal council. Council members are elected by voting members of the tribe. The tribe supports many charities in the Palm Springs area. The tribe has contributed millions of dollars to schools, libraries, youth groups, and healthcare organizations throughout the Coachella Valley.

The Navajo Nation extends over 27,000 square miles. Its reservation covers about 14 million acres. This is about the size of the state of West Virginia. It spans across parts of three states: Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. In 2010, the reservation was home to about 175,000 members of the Navajo Nation.

One of the most famous contributions of the Navajo nation occurred during World War II. During World War II, secret American codes were being broken. Codes were used to send messages during battles. When the codes were broken, battles were lost. A man named Philip Johnston had an idea to fix this. He thought the Navajo language could be used to create new military codes.

The Navajo language is very complex. Very few non-Navajo people knew how to speak it at the time. The U.S. military liked this idea. Navajo soldiers were trained as "Code Talkers." They created a code using their language. The code was unbreakable. This code guided and protected American troops. The Navajo Code Talkers contributed much to the country and helped win the war.

title: Cooperation Between American Indians and Europeans
text:
In the 1600s, when Europeans first came to stay in North America, thousands of American Indians already lived in the New England area. They outnumbered the Europeans. The Dutch, French, and English settlers came with different goals. The Dutch were mainly interested in trading with the Indigenous peoples of North America. They weren’t interested in expanding their territory. The French wanted to establish political and trade alliances with the American Indians. The English wanted to establish permanent settlements in North America.

The Europeans and American Indians had different languages and cultures. They frequently misunderstood each other. These differences sometimes led to conflict. Other times, they were able to overcome their communication and cultural barriers to cooperate. They did this mainly through trade.

At first, the Europeans just wanted food so they could survive. American Indians traded with the new settlers. They taught settlers techniques for farming in North America. Successful crops were harvested and gave life to colonial settlements. In the beginning, there was an exchange of cultures, goods, and services between many of the tribes and the colonists.

The Native Americans wanted cloth, tools, iron pots, and glass beads. Most importantly, they wanted firearms. European trade items made life very different for the tribes. Daily life, diets, and the dynamic of power changed. Cooperation between the two cultures was balanced. Each group used the other to improve their lives.

Trade between Europeans and American Indians began with European traders arriving in the Americas. They traded with local American Indians and then departed again for Europe. Then, things began to change. Different European countries began to compete with one another for control of trade and territory in the Americas. In 1614, the Dutch established settlements on the east coast of what is now the state of New York. They established the colony of New Netherland. They named their two main settlements "New Amsterdam" (now New York City) and Fort Orange (now Albany). These permanent settlements gave the Dutch a geographic advantage when trading with local Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois tribes in the New England area. The Dutch were mainly interested in the fur trade.

Native Americans were eager to provide furs and pelts for trade. However, they wanted to trade for items and materials they couldn't get from their own environment. These items included things like muskets, cloth, needles, and thread. They also wanted metal objects, like axes, knives, and cooking and eating utensils. The Dutch even began importing conch shells from the Caribbean. They would carve the shells into images and figures that appealed to the local Haudenosaunee tribes. The Dutch used these items specifically in the fur trade.

Fort Orange became the main center of the Dutch fur trade. The more furs the Dutch traded for, the more scarce game became in the New York area. Indigenous peoples began to hunt farther inland. Eventually, they encroached on other tribes’ territories. The English eventually took over New Netherland. They renamed it New York and expelled the Dutch from their colony. Although the Dutch were forced from their colony, the fur trade continued long after their departure until it came to an end in the 1700s.

The French had working relationships with the Huron, Montagnais, and Algonquins in the Great Lakes area. Relatively few French people settled in the Americas. There was less cause for conflict in the area known as New France.

English colonies were expanding every year. They wanted larger areas of land for farming and raising domesticated animals. This altered the area the American Indians could use for living. The many tribes of the Northeast joined with the French to keep the English off their lands.

English traders set up credit systems with the American Indians. They would give the American Indians goods before a hunt. Then, the tribes would pay them back with furs and food. Europeans wanted so many furs that the land became overhunted. This meant American Indians had to hunt in other tribes’ territories for food. This action sometimes sparked conflict.

Sometimes, American Indians could not pay back their debts to the traders. Some of them would sell their people’s lands to the traders. The land, however, wasn’t theirs to sell. It belonged to the tribe. Conflicts between and within tribes began to develop. Conflicts between the French and English were arising as well. With tensions rising, it was only a matter of time before violence erupted.

title: Essential Question
text: How did life change for Native Americans as a result of the arrival and settlement of European conflicts?
