title: Freedom of Education
text:
The 1816 Indiana State Constitution promised the state would provide free public schools. These schools would be “equally open to all.” The government wanted to open schools “as soon as circumstances will permit.” With the population growing quickly, people were more concerned with growing food and building houses.

Churches ran private schools that cost money. Most people couldn’t afford to send their children to these schools. For all children to receive an education, the state needed to provide it. It took time for Indiana to build its school system. The biggest problem was money.

Here is a timeline of Indiana’s public school development:

1824: The School Law is passed. It requires all men to help build the local school building one day a week. There isn’t enough money to hire teachers.

1833: The law is revised to let voters decide if they want to fund a school. Many vote to not fund schools, so many areas have no schools.

1835–1837: The law is revised so women could teach, but there is no money to pay them.

1843–1847: Teachers form groups to demand reform in funding education.

1849: Taxes are set up to fund public schools.

1851: Indiana’s new constitution sets up a permanent fund for state schools.

1877: The Indiana Act is passed, requiring school districts to educate Black children.

In about 60 years, Indiana established free public education for most children. Native American children attended boarding schools run by religious groups. These schools were funded by churches, private citizens, and the federal government. Native American children were not included in Indiana’s public school system.

Why is the right to a free public education so important?

Providing education is part of democracy. Being educated opens opportunities. It helps society function.

Literacy, or the ability to read and write, is important. People gain information by reading and writing. Being literate helps people communicate. Learning math helps students recognize patterns. It helps people learn to think through problems. Learning to think critically helps students make important decisions.

When learning is restricted, or only allowed for certain people, that creates an unequal society. Having the right to a free public education gives everyone basic tools.

title: Physical Characteristics of Indiana
text:
Physical characteristics describe the natural environment of an area. Landscapes, plants, climate, and animals are physical characteristics. Bodies of water, including rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans, are physical characteristics. Landforms are also physical characteristics of an area. Some examples of landforms are mountains, plains, valleys, and deserts. These characteristics are all connected to help geographers describe different areas on the Earth’s surface. Physical characteristics are what make the Earth interesting and unique.

A physical map shows the major physical features of a place. Look at the physical map of Indiana. Can you locate the rivers? Can you identify a lake?

title: Essential Question
text: What natural resources are available in Indiana?

title: Introduction to the Northwest
text:
The Northwest region extends from northern California along the Pacific Coast all the way to Alaska. Indigenous peoples in the Northwest lived in a land full of plants, fish, and wild animals. Tribes such as the Chinook, Tlingit, Haida, Salish, Yurok, Quileute, Suquamish, and Puyallup had very distinct cultures. They ate bear, elk, and deer. They fished in the rivers for salmon. They captured whales and sea lions from the ocean.

People used the land and resources around them to build homes. Tribes of the Northwest lived in shelters called longhouses during the fall and winter. The Suquamish people were one such group. During the spring and summer, they lived in portable shelters. These homes were especially useful when hunting game. They could be set up and taken down quickly.

Some tribes, like the Yurok, used redwood and cedar trees to create their homes. They cut the trees into boards. These were used to build walls and a pitched, or raised, roof. Each home was given a specific name. This name lasted through multiple generations. Each Yurok village also had a sweathouse. There, the men met and held purification rituals before ceremonies and hunting trips.

Many Northwest tribes were also skilled basket weavers. They used natural plant fibers, such as tree roots, marsh grasses, and leaves. These were used to create detailed patterns in their baskets. Baskets had many purposes. They were used to gather and store food. They were also an important trade item for many tribes in the Northwest.

Tribes traveled frequently throughout the year. They harvested and secured food. Most tribes of the Northwest were also skilled canoe builders. They used canoes to travel and fish. They were skilled at using natural resources to meet their needs. The ocean, mountains, and land are all part of the history and traditions of these tribes.

title: Essential Question
text: How were the tribes of the Northwest similar? How were they different?

title: Landforms and Bodies of Water
text:
The United States is a diverse country. There are many unique characteristics. They impact the way people live and interact with their environment. Landforms and bodies of water help mold the country into its unique shape. Landforms are natural features that make up the Earth’s surface. Bodies of water include lakes, rivers, and oceans.

Indiana has its own unique landscape. The landscape is divided into three regions, which have different characteristics. These regions are the Northern Lakes and Moraines, the Central Till Plain, and the Southern Lowlands. These regions have diverse landforms and bodies of water.

The Great Lakes Plains region is very flat. Glaciers moved across the area long ago, creating lakes and moraines. A moraine is material, usually rock and sediment, left behind from a glacier. Lake Wawasee, the largest natural lake in Indiana, is located in this region. Sand dunes rise along the shoreline of Lake Michigan in the region.

The Central Till Plain region has primarily low, rolling hills, and shallow valleys. A plain is a large area of flat land with few to no trees. There are many farmlands in the region. The landforms and soil make it an ideal place for farming. The state’s highest point, Hoosier Hill, is located in central Indiana. It rises 1,257 feet in the air. That is as tall as the Empire State Building!

The Southern Hills and Lowlands are a mixture of forest and hilly areas. There is also farmland. The region has numerous caves. These caves contain limestone, which is used to build structures all over the United States. The Wabash, White, and Ohio Rivers meet toward the southernmost part of the state. A river is a large, flowing body of water that moves across the land. This makes it a perfect place for many plants, animals, and people to live.

title: Government Structures
text:
Tribal governments varied throughout the Northwest region, but they shared some similarities. The people of the Northwest belonged to different tribes. Tribes were made up of related family groups. Most tribes in this region included social classes. This means that a tribe was divided into different groups. Groups were based on social and economic factors.

Social classes in Northwest tribes were determined by wealth. Wealthier members of the tribe belonged to the noble class. Members of the noble class led the tribe. They made decisions for all members of the tribe. They also shared their wealth with other members of the tribe through gift-giving. The Chinook, Yurok, and other tribes were governed by the wealthiest men in the village and their immediate families.

The Tlingit and Haida were divided into two groups, known as moieties. A moiety is a small group that belongs to a larger clan or tribe. Moieties were named after different animals. The animal became the symbol of the moiety. Because the Tlingit and Haida were closely related, they had the same moieties. These moieties were called the Eagle and the Raven. People belonged to the same moiety as their mothers.

Most tribes of the Northwest also had a shaman who helped guide the tribe. Shamans inherited their position from a family member. They would often advise the chief or leader of the tribe.

title: Clothing
text:
Clothing varied throughout the Northwest region. However, all clothing was made from natural resources.

Most Yurok clothing was made from deerskin. This is similar to other tribes that lived in the Northwest. They used the deerskins to make shirts, pants, leggings, skirts, and shoes. Skirts were sometimes made from maple tree bark.

In the colder months, Yurok men and women wore capes. These were made from deerskins or smaller animal skins pieced together. Wealthier members of the tribe decorated their clothing. They used valuable items, such as shells and pieces of obsidian.

The working dress of most men along the coast was similar. It was often a breechcloth of hide. This could be tucked through the legs and into the back of the belt during work. For warmth, a cloak or vest of fur was added.

Some tribes in the Northwest have been skilled weavers for hundreds of years. The Salish, Tillamook, and Kalapuya tribes are some examples. They combined plant fibers with the wool of mountain goats to create yarn. Yarn was used to make clothing and blankets. Blankets were highly prized and traded widely throughout the Northwest.

title: Language
text:
Several groups of American Indians in the Northwest have similar languages. These languages often belong to the same family. Each language is a dialect of a few language families of the Northwest. Most in the Northwest belong to the Salishan, Wakashan, and Athabaskan language families.

The Salishan language family includes 19 different languages. These were spoken by tribes in northern Washington and southern Canada. The dialects spoken by the Puyallup tribe also come from Salishan.

The Wakashan language family has seven different languages. Each has multiple dialects. These were traditionally spoken by tribes that lived in the coastal areas of southern Canada and northern Washington.

Athabaskan was the largest language family in the Northwest. It was divided into multiple groups. Many tribes spoke Athabaskan dialects. Some are still spoken in the Northwest today.

Most Athabaskan languages are spoken by tribes in the Northwest and parts of Canada. However, some dialects are also spoken in the Southwest. This is because some of the tribe members migrated to the Southwest many years ago. They brought their languages with them.

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Beliefs

American Indian tribal beliefs are often rooted in nature. Tribes used these beliefs and legends to explain the world around them. Many tribes in the Northwest share similar beliefs with one another. Some beliefs are very specific to one tribe.

The Yurok believe that redwood trees are sacred. They also believe they are the guardians of sacred places. The Quileute tribe believes that all animals are sacred. They believe animals were sent to the tribe by the spirit world to help them survive. The Tlingit tribe believe that Kah-shu-gooh-yah, a sacred being, controls the sun, moon, and stars and all of their functions. The Salish people believe that each person has their own guardian spirit that guides them through life.

Ceremonies

One of the most important ceremonies for Northwest tribes was the potlatch. A potlatch was a large feast given by a wealthy member of the tribe. At the end of the feast, the host gave expensive gifts to those who came. Some gifts included canoes, mats, and blankets. Others included jewelry, baskets, carved wooden boxes, dishes, and food. It took years to prepare for a potlatch. They lasted for days at a time.

The most important guests received the most expensive gifts. Each gift the host gave away had to be matched by the person who received it. This was how wealthy members of the tribes increased their wealth. A person who couldn’t return the favor at their own potlatch was looked down on.

title: Traditions
text:
Tribes of the Northwest have practiced different traditions for thousands of years. Many of these traditions are still practiced today. A unique tradition of the Northwest tribes is the building of totem poles. Totem poles help document the histories and stories of a tribe. Totem poles were also used to symbolize family crests. They also served as ornamental house posts, entryways for dwellings, memorials, and grave markers for the dead.

Most totem poles are between nine and 60 feet tall. Tribes traditionally carved them from cedar trees. Cedar trees are found in many areas of the Northwest. They are easy to carve. They are also resistant to rot. This means that they are almost completely waterproof. Designs were carved into the tree to represent important symbols. The designs were then painted. Totem poles are still constructed today. They honor the traditions and history of many tribes.

Storytelling is an important tradition for many tribes of the Northwest. Many tribal stories explain religious topics, like creation. Others explain the start of important traditions. The Chinook believe that humans were created by the mighty thunderbird. The Haida believe that their ancestral homeland was created by the raven. They gave the raven the name Yáahl. Yáahl grew bored of being surrounded by only water, so he created land. The Squamish believe their tribe was created by a great creator. The creator gave the first Squamish a salmon trap, an adze (a tool similar to an ax), and a wife.

title: American Indian Life Today: The Northwest
text:
Thousands of American Indians still live in the Northwest region today. Today, Alaska has the largest American Indian population in the Northwest. Many of the descendants of these tribes still live along Canada’s Pacific coast, too.

Over 50 Northwest tribes are federally recognized by the United States government. This means they are sovereign nations. They have their own constitutions. They have independent governments. The tribes hold their own elections. Tribes also work with the U.S. and state governments. They work to meet the needs and wants of their people. Tribes also have their own reservations. A reservation is an area of land designated to a tribe or tribes by the U.S. government.

Many members of Northwest tribes have shared their history and culture through their works of art. Boeda Strand was a very famous basket maker. She was a member of the Snohomish tribe. She taught Indigenous people the traditional methods of basket weaving. Robert James Schoppert was a member of the Tlingit tribe. He was a successful woodcarver, painter, and author. His work highlighted the traditions of Northwest tribes. Many of his works are still on display. They can be found in schools, art galleries, and museums around the United States.

Northwest tribes work to preserve and share the traditions and history of their ancestors. Many tribes continue to practice the art of canoe making. They share this art with members of the public. In Seattle, Washington, the city government has worked with members of the Salish tribe to build a facility for traditional canoe building. When complete, the Northwest Native Canoe Center will serve as a place to create, store, and launch traditional canoes. It will also be a center of education. Visitors will be able to learn about the tribes of the area.

title: Introduction of the Arctic
text:
Arctic Indigenous peoples lived in parts of northern Canada, Alaska, and Greenland. The Inuit, Cree, Dene, Athabascan, and Aleut are examples of Arctic tribes. The people of the Canadian Arctic are known as the Inuit. Inuit means “the people.” About 50,000 Inuit live in northern Canada today. This region is known as Inuit Nunaat, meaning “Inuit homeland.”

The land of the Arctic region remains frozen most of the year. In the past, food in the Arctic was not available in large amounts year-round. The native peoples who lived in this region had a very special understanding of how to get food. The climate was cold and harsh. The Inuit could not farm like tribes in other regions. Hunting provided the majority of food for Arctic tribes. Tribes also fished and gathered plants and shellfish for food. Meat was the main staple in Arctic tribe diets. Arctic tribes traveled great distances to hunt animals like seals and caribou. Men were responsible for hunting game.

Arctic tribes were also experts at fishing. Women and children also gathered seaweed, sculpins, and clams to eat. Plants are not abundant in the Arctic. However, they do exist. Wild plants, berries, and roots were gathered in the spring and summer. These were stored for the winter. Many people gathered when a large animal, like a whale, was caught. They used all parts of the animal and its resources. When food was scarce, communities organized into small units to share food.

Different shelters were used depending on the time of year. People lived in tents made of animal skins. They also built underground dwellings made of wood or bone. Igloos were usually only temporary shelters. Igloos were built near hunting grounds during the winter months. Many Arctic tribes, like the Inuit, used dogs for transportation. For fishing, however, they made wood-carved kayaks. They also traveled on sleds and toboggans. The Arctic peoples adapted to their environment. They used natural resources for survival and trade. They thrived in all seasons.

title: Essential Question
text: How were the tribes of the Arctic similar? How were they different?

title: Government Structure
text:
Most Arctic tribes did not have a formally organized government in communities. However, there were elders, leaders, and shamans. They helped keep the peace. They settled arguments and created a united way of life. For most of the year, people lived in small groups that worked together equally. Smaller bands gathered in the winter in large bands to share resources and decisions.

There were also oral laws. Oral laws were spoken laws. These laws involved things like respecting wildlife and the environment. They also included avoiding selfishness and fighting. The Inuit believed that breaking these laws would lead to bad consequences. These could be things like bad winter storms, illness, or famine.

If a person caused an issue or broke one of the laws, they had to meet with the elders of the community to discuss their behavior. The elders encouraged them to change and be better. If the person did not change, the same process was repeated. This was done until either the person changed their behavior or faced severe consequences. Love, patience, understanding, and talking peacefully were important tools used to maintain peace and solve problems.

title: Clothing
text:
The tribes of the Arctic were the only tribes in North America that did not use deer or bison hides, plant fibers, and cloth to make clothing. Instead, they used the available resources of the Arctic for clothing. The climate of the Arctic is cold year-round. The clothing of Arctic tribes did not change throughout the year.

Caribou furs and hides were the most commonly used resource for clothing. Other furs and pelts were also used to make clothing. These included fox, wolf, and polar bear furs and pelts. Seal hides were very valuable. This was because they were waterproof. Feathers were sometimes used to decorate clothing.

Arctic clothing for men and women often included long, hooded coats called parkas; pants; and mittens. People wore many layers of clothing. This was to protect themselves from the harsh natural elements. Children often wore a jumpsuit made from caribou fur to keep warm. Thick socks and boots were also worn. They protected people's feet from the Arctic cold and snow. Arctic tribes also made goggles from animal bones and antlers. These goggles protected their eyes from the glare of the sun on the snow and ice.

title: Language
text:
Hundreds of languages have been spoken by the tribes of the Arctic for many years. In western Canada and Alaska, most languages belong to the Na-Dené language family. Na-Dené is the largest language family in the Arctic region. It includes nearly 50 different languages. This language family is divided into three smaller groups: Haida, Athapascan, and Tlingit.

Languages spoken in areas of eastern Canada belong to the Algonquian language family. These languages are closely related to those spoken by tribes in the Northeast region. About 175,000 people speak Algonquian languages in Canada today. Languages spoken in the most northern areas of the Arctic region belong to the Inuit-Yupik-Unangan. This is also called the Eskimo-Aleut language family.

There are 20 dialects of Inuit-Yupik-Unangan that are still spoken today. Over 60,000 people speak these 20 dialects. The largest dialect of the Inuit-Yupik-Unangan language family is Inuktitut. About 40,000 people in northern Canada speak Inuktitut dialects.

title: Weather
text:
Weather is what is happening outside your window right now. Is it hot, cold, wet, dry, calm, stormy, clear, cloudy, or windy? Whatever it is, that is the weather! The weather can also change. Our lives can be affected by the weather. The weather can affect what we wear and what we do. Weather is the short-term atmospheric conditions in a specific location.

When discussing the weather, three primary factors should be considered. These factors are temperature, precipitation, and wind. Temperature is the measurement of how hot or cold something is. A thermometer is a tool used to measure temperature.

Precipitation is water that falls from clouds. It comes in the form of rain, snow, sleet, or hail. The form it takes depends on the temperature. If it’s fairly warm outside and it starts to precipitate, it will rain. If it’s cold outside, it can snow.

Wind is moving air. You can measure the speed of wind and the direction it is moving. Wind direction is measured using the directions north, south, east, and west. Wind speed is measured using an anemometer and recorded by measuring where the wind blows from, not where the wind blows toward. It is recorded as miles per hour.

In Indiana, the weather is mild. That means it is comfortable almost year-round. The summers are warm, humid, and partly cloudy. The winters are freezing, snowy, and mostly cloudy.

What type of weather have you seen in your part of the state?

title: Beliefs and Ceremonies
text:
Beliefs

The beliefs of the tribes of the Arctic are closely connected to the natural world around them. Many beliefs centered on opposites in nature. This included light and dark, water and land, and bad weather and good weather. Many activities and beliefs were connected to the sun, moon, and stars.

Cree beliefs focus on the connection between people and nature. The Inuit believe that all living creatures have a soul. Proper respect had to be shown to the land and animals. If not, a person or community would face negative consequences. The Athabaskans of Alaska pleased the spirits of the natural world through singing and dancing.

Ceremonies

One tradition shared among different tribes in the Arctic is throat singing. The Inuit tribe uses throat singing in many ceremonies. Throat singing is practiced and performed by Iniut women. Throat singing was traditionally used to sing children to sleep or as a game. Some throat singers also incorporate special dances with their singing.

One of the most important ceremonies of the Cree people is the Sun Dance. It is also called the Thirst Dance. The Sun Dance is performed each summer. This ceremony was often performed to ask the spirits for help. Another important ceremony for the Cree is called the Walking Out Ceremony. This ceremony is to officially welcome children into the tribe. Drum dances are also important parts of many ceremonies. Drum dances are often performed to ask the tribal shaman for help. Sometimes drum dances are performed to entertain the tribe.

title: Oral Traditions
text:
Storytelling is one of the most important traditions for Arctic tribes. Stories and folktales are passed down from one generation to the next. Stories shared by the tribes of the Arctic are often used to teach important lessons. They are also used to explain things that happen in the environment, or natural phenomena. Other stories are used to explain the creation of the world and people.

The Kaska Dene people believe that the land on Earth was created by a bird named Diver. Long ago, the Earth was completely covered in water. Beaver, Muskrat, and the many birds of the Earth wanted to reach the land below the water. They dove under the water many times to reach the land. However, they were not successful. One day, a bird called Diver volunteered to bring the land to the surface of the water. He dove under the water’s surface. He swam for six days. Diver was able to bring pieces of the land back with him in his claws. Beaver, Muskrat, and the other animals gathered the soil and dirt from Diver’s claws. By doing this, they created the land.

One of the most famous and well-known stories among Inuit tribes is the story of the sea goddess. She is called by many different names. However, the story of the sea goddess is the same among the many Inuit tribes. Long ago, a young girl fell into the ocean. She sank to the bottom of the ocean. However, she did not die. She became a powerful spirit and the mother of all sea creatures. The Inuit offer prayers and gifts to her in exchange for food and easy travel on the seas and oceans.

title: American Indian Life Today: The Arctic
text:
The descendants of the ancient Arctic tribes still live in the Arctic region of North America. Today, this region is home to thousands of American Indians. In the northernmost areas of the Arctic region, most of the population belongs to one or more Arctic tribes. Over 20 percent of Alaska’s population belongs to Arctic tribes.

One of the most famous Inuit artists of the 20th century was Kenojuak Ashevak. She was born in a remote Inuit village in northwestern Canada. She began her career by drawing. She soon became a skilled painter and sculptor. Ashevak’s works focus on Inuit life and legends. Many of her drawings have been used on Canadian coins and stamps.

Markoosie Patsauq was a famous Inuit author. In 1969, he wrote the book Harpoon of the Hunter. The book is about a young Inuit boy on an important journey to find a wounded polar bear. Patsauq’s book was the first book published in the Inuktitut language. The book has been translated into many languages. People around the world can enjoy his work.

title: Natural Resources
text:
A natural resource is something found in nature that people can use. There are many types of natural resources in the world around us. These include soil, plants, coal, water, natural gas, and even animals. We use natural resources to meet our needs and wants. Sometimes, we use natural resources just as they are. For example, we use water to drink and for cooking and cleaning. We also eat fruits and vegetables that grow naturally in our environment.

We use some natural resources to make products that make our lives easier. We burn coal and use natural gas to power and heat our homes, schools, and businesses. We use trees to build furniture and houses. Trees are also used to make paper and books. We also use natural resources to make some of the items we use daily. This includes cell phones, computers, clothing, and even your toothbrush!

Natural resources can be either renewable or nonrenewable. Renewable resources are those that can be renewed, or replaced in a couple of decades. Trees are an example of a renewable resource. New trees can be planted to replace those we cut down. Nonrenewable resources are resources that cannot be easily replaced. Oil and natural gas are two examples of nonrenewable resources. Once we use them all up, they will not be replaced for millions of years.

Indiana has many natural resources. Gas, oil, and coal are all natural resources found in the state. Indiana produces over 36 million tons of coal each year. This helps provide electricity to the whole state. Some other natural resources are sand, gravel, and limestone. Sand and gravel are mined to build roads, bridges, buildings, and other structures.

title: Spanish Exploration of North America
text:
The world changed in many ways during the 1400s. Asia was the center of trade. People in Europe wanted goods from Asia. Many countries fought over these resources and ways to reach them. Countries in Europe looked for new routes across the sea to Asia.

King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain wanted to find new trade routes to Asia. They were willing to pay someone to find these new routes. An entrepreneur named Christopher Columbus had an unusual idea. He hoped to sail west across the Atlantic Ocean and reach India. Columbus was looking for a patron. He went to Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand in Spain.

Isabella and Ferdinand agreed to be Columbus’s patrons. This means that they agreed to pay for his trip. They paid for three ships, tools, and a crew for the voyage. Columbus made an agreement with Ferdinand and Isabella. Columbus, Ferdinand, and Isabella agreed to share whatever he brought back to Spain. Columbus set sail from Spain in 1492. His journey launched the biggest changes in government, knowledge, and trade the world had ever seen.

In time, more explorers were sent by the Spanish government to explore other areas of the world. Spain’s primary motivations for exploration were the three G’s: God, gold, and glory. The Spanish government and explorers wanted to spread their religious beliefs to the Americas. The Catholic Church worked with the Spanish government to send missionaries to the Americas. They also gave them funds to construct missions across the Americas. The purpose of the missions was to convert American Indians to Christianity.

Spanish explorers also searched for gold, minerals, and other valuable resources. They hoped to take the resources back to Spain and use them to make valuable goods. These goods were traded and sold across the world. Spanish explorers also wanted to obtain glory for themselves and for Spain. As a result, Spain claimed land across North, Central, and South America.

title: Essential Question
text: Why did the Spanish explore and colonize North America?

title: Christopher Columbus
text:
Christopher Columbus was an Italian explorer. Spain paid Columbus to sail across the Atlantic Ocean. Columbus sailed from Spain in 1492. He was sure that he could reach India by sailing west. But an unknown obstacle stood in his way. At the time, no one in Europe knew there were continents between the Atlantic Ocean and India.

On October 12, 1492, Columbus landed on the island of Guanahani. He renamed the island San Salvador. When Columbus landed in the Caribbean, he thought he had reached India. He called the people he met “Indians.” On his expedition, Columbus explored other islands in the Caribbean. He explored the islands of Cuba and Hispaniola. He found many resources and encountered different American Indian tribes. Columbus also claimed all of the islands and land he explored for Spain.

Columbus's journey took seven months. When he returned, he reported to the king and queen. He brought back riches and resources. Ferdinand and Isabella were pleased. They learned about Columbus’s adventures and discoveries. Secretly, the two had believed Columbus wouldn't return. Now they hoped to use the information Columbus had brought back to make Spain richer and more powerful.

After his first voyage, Columbus went on more expeditions to the Americas. The Spanish government sent Columbus back to create colonies, or settlements. This is called colonization. He was also asked to find a passage to Asia. On these expeditions, Columbus explored Central and South America. He determined that there was no passage to Asia. He discovered that the continents of North and South America were much bigger than Europeans knew.

title: Climate
text:
What’s the difference between weather and climate? Weather is what is happening outside right now. Climate is the pattern of weather conditions in an area over a long period of time. The climate takes hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years to change. We know about the climate of Indiana because climatologists, or scientists who study the climate, have been recording climate conditions for many years.

There are five main climate zones found on the Earth. They are tropical, dry, temperate, continental, and polar. Tropical climates are hot, wet, and humid. Dry climates are hot with little precipitation. Temperate climates have warm summers and cold winters. Continental climates are dry, with very hot summers and very cold winters. Polar climates are cold and dry.

Indiana has a temperate climate. That means that the summers are warm and the winters are cold. Overall, the climate is generally comfortable most of the year. The warmest months are from May to September. The average temperature in those months is around 74°F. On average, the people in Indiana enjoy about 186 sunny days each year. This is a little lower than the national average of 202 sunny days.

Rainfall happens year-round, although it rains more in the spring and early summer. Indiana gets about 43 inches of rain each year. This is more than the national average of 28 inches a year. This rainfall helps nourish the crops grown in Indiana.

Indiana’s coldest months are from December to March. During these months, the average temperature is around 46°F. Winter temperatures can go into the low 20s or lower. Indiana averages 22 inches of snowfall per year. The snowy period of the year is typically from November to April, with February being the snowiest month.

title: Juan Ponce de León
text:
The first European explorer to reach the continental, or continuous, United States was Juan Ponce de León. Ponce de León was a Spanish conquistador. “Conquistador” means “one who conquers.” This title was given to Spanish soldiers. These soldiers explored, conquered, and settled lands around the world. Ponce de León sailed with Columbus on his second voyage to the Americas. This was before he explored the continental United States. He was also the first European explorer to explore Puerto Rico. He claimed it for Spain.

In 1513, Ponce de León went on an expedition through the Bahamas. He hoped to find the fabled Fountain of Youth. He also wanted to find rich natural resources and new lands to colonize. In March 1513, Ponce de León and his crew landed on the east coast of Florida. He thought that he had discovered a new island in the Bahamas. He had actually landed near present-day St. Augustine.

Ponce de León named the area “La Florida.” This was in honor of a Spanish celebration, the “Feast of the Flowers.” It was also because the area was covered in flowers. He returned to Florida in 1521. He wanted to create the first European settlement in the area. The settlement quickly failed. This was due to hostilities between the settlers and the Calusa tribe. Ponce de León was wounded by an arrow. He died not long after.

title: Vasco Núñez de Balboa
text:
Vasco Núñez de Balboa was another Spanish conquistador. He made a name for himself in the Americas. In 1501, Balboa went on his first expedition to the Americas. He sailed with explorer Don Rodrigo de Bastidas to South America. They explored present-day Venezuela and Colombia. Then they sailed to the Caribbean.

In 1510, Balboa joined Martin de Enciso’s expedition to South America. They looked for treasure along the way. Balboa helped set up a new settlement in present-day Panama. It was called Darién. It is the oldest permanent settlement in Central America. Balboa was selected as the leader of the settlement, but he wished to continue exploring in search of gold and other riches.

Balboa heard rumors about a large sea. It was supposed to be located to the west of Central and South America. He wanted to see if the rumors were true. In 1513, he led an expedition to find the rumored ocean. Balboa and his men walked through the thick jungles of Panama. It took them 24 days to reach the ocean. Balboa was the first European to reach the Pacific Ocean. Spain rewarded his efforts. He was made the governor of the provinces of Panama and Coiba.

title: Hernando de Soto
text:
Hernando de Soto was a Spanish explorer and politician. De Soto went on his first expedition of the Americas when he was a teenager. He helped other Spanish explorers conquer parts of Central and South America. He also made a lot of money on these expeditions. He used this wealth to become an important member of the government.

In 1536, King Charles V of Spain appointed de Soto as the governor of Cuba. The king ordered de Soto to lead an expedition through present-day Florida. De Soto set sail from Cuba. He landed near present-day Tampa on May 25, 1539. De Soto and his army marched north from Tampa. They explored areas that were previously unexplored by other European explorers. They explored much of the peninsula of Florida. They traveled north into the panhandle. Then, they traveled farther north into present-day Georgia.

De Soto and his army also explored other places. They explored present-day South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama before crossing the Mississippi River. In 1542, De Soto got sick and died. Members of his expedition marched south. They eventually reached Spanish settlements in Mexico. There, they shared their experiences with other explorers.

title: Conflict and Cooperation: Spanish Explorers and American Indians
text:
Thousands of American Indian tribes once lived in North, South, and Central America. This was before Spanish explorers reached the Americas. The meeting of these two groups was sometimes good, but at other times, conflict occurred. The Spanish and American Indians had different languages and cultures. These differences often led to misunderstandings. These differences sometimes led to conflict. Other times, they were able to work together. They did this mainly through trade.

Christopher Columbus was the first Spanish explorer to encounter American Indians. Columbus and his crew met the Taíno, Arawak, and Lucayan tribes of the Caribbean. Columbus and his men did not create a good relationship with the tribes that they met. They forced the American Indians to give them resources. They also enslaved a large number of American Indians and forced them to travel with the expedition.

Most of the encounters between early explorers and American Indians were hostile. Spanish explorers hoped to take control of all land and resources. They also wanted the American Indians they met to become Christians. Many American Indian tribes of the Southeast did not like this. They refused to give up their resources, cultures, and traditions. Spanish explorers also unknowingly spread European diseases to the tribes of the Americas. As a result, thousands of American Indians became sick. Most died from these diseases.

The Spanish government also gave the explorers orders to treat the American Indians fairly. Several explorers did not listen to these orders, including Juan Ponce de León and Hernando de Soto. In return, many tribes refused to meet with the Spanish. American Indians often attacked Spanish expeditions. Vasco Núñez de Balboa also had a bad relationship with the American Indian tribes he encountered in present-day Panama. He forced American Indians to farm and build the settlement of Darién.

However, some Spanish settlers argued that they should be kinder and work with the American Indians they met. Bartolomé de las Casas was a Spanish priest. He traveled with Spanish explorers to the Americas. He tried to convince the Spanish explorers and settlers to treat American Indians with kindness and respect. De las Casas encouraged the Spanish government to make changes. He encouraged the government to create laws to protect American Indians in the Americas.

title: Essential Question
text: How did the U.S. get involved in World War I?

title: Alliances with American Indians
text:
The British, French, American Indians, and colonists made four important agreements during and after the French and Indian War.

From July 4–10, 1754, delegates from seven colonies and the Iroquois Confederacy met in Albany, New York. A trading and peace treaty was the main purpose of the Congress.

The Albany Plan of Union

The delegates also met with each other during this time. How were they going to manage if there was a French invasion? The Albany Plan of Union was proposed by Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Hutchinson. They suggested colonial governments choose members of a “Grand Council.” Members would be chosen according to population. The British government would select a “President General.” The council and the president would address trade with American Indians. They would also address border disputes and the collection of taxes.

King George II and the colonial legislatures rejected the plan. The king thought this gave authority to the colonies. The colonies felt it gave authority to the British government.

The Treaty of Easton

The Treaty of Easton was a 1758 agreement. It was between the British government and the many tribes of the Iroquois Confederacy. These tribes were located in eastern Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey. Under this agreement, the members of the Iroquois Confederacy present at Easton agreed to fight as British allies. In return, they would be granted rights to hunting grounds.

In the treaty, the Lenape tribe sold all claims to the area called New Jersey. In return, they received the sum of 1,000 Spanish dollars. The treaty also agreed there would be no British settlement west of the Allegheny Mountains. The treaty was signed in Easton, Pennsylvania. It helped the British in the war.

The Treaty of Paris of 1763

The Treaty of Paris of 1763 officially ended the French and Indian War in America. France agreed to give New France (what is now eastern Canada) to the British. The French also ceded the Ohio Country and the Mississippi River. The British government then agreed to grant officers and soldiers land in the Ohio Country, west of the Appalachian Mountains. One of these officers was George Washington. Many companies also bought the land. They hoped to sell it to new settlers.

The Proclamation of 1763

American Indians had not given up their claims. By treaty, they still had a legal claim to the land. The Proclamation of 1763 was given by the new British king, George III. He decreed that all land west of the Appalachian Mountains was reserved for the Native Americans. No settlement would be permitted. It was the first act of King George III to affect all 13 colonies.

Colonists were upset about losing the freedom to move west. American Indians were angry because settlers defied the decree and moved into the Ohio Country anyway. Without an agreement all groups would follow, conflict in the western frontier increased.

title: Essential Question
text: What were the consequences of Great Britain controlling the Mississippi River?

title: English Exploration of North America
text:
Spain was not the only country to explore the Americas during the Age of Exploration. England also sent explorers to the Americas. Tales of Columbus’s journey and his success reached England. English explorers hoped to have the same success as Columbus. English merchants also wanted to compete with Spanish and Portuguese merchants in European markets.

In 1496, King Henry VII of England agreed to sponsor the first English exploration of North America. Henry agreed to sponsor Italian explorer John Cabot. He gave Cabot five ships. He gave Cabot permission to investigate areas unknown to other European explorers. Henry did not know if Cabot’s voyage was going to be successful. He took the risk anyway. His risk paid off. Cabot returned with news of new land. He also brought resources back with him. This was the start of the English exploration of the Americas.

English explorers focused their attention on exploring North America. This is because Spain and Portugal had already claimed much of the land in Central and South America. Between 1497 and 1607, several English explorers journeyed to North America. They traveled throughout the continent. They learned as much as they could. They learned about the people and resources of North America. Their research encouraged English settlement in North America. In fewer than 100 years, England’s primary goal for exploration changed to creating colonies in North America.

title: Essential Question
text: Why did the English explore and colonize North America?

title: John Cabot
text:
John Cabot was inspired by Columbus. He became interested in finding a shorter route across the ocean. In 1484, Cabot traveled to England to find funds for his own expedition. After many years, Cabot convinced King Henry VIII of England to pay for his expedition.

In 1497, Cabot sailed across the North Atlantic. Cabot thought he had landed in Asia. He actually landed in present-day Newfoundland. Newfoundland is a large island off the coast of Canada. Cabot did not find a route to Asia. But his voyage proved that a northern route to the Americas could work. He brought back information about the people and resources of North America.

King Henry VII agreed to pay for Cabot to go on another expedition in 1498. Cabot’s goal was to explore more of Newfoundland. He also wanted to explore areas west of Newfoundland. Unfortunately, Cabot and his crew never returned to England. Many people believe that his ship was wrecked or sunk in the dangerous waters of the North Atlantic.

title: Sir Francis Drake
text:
Sir Francis Drake was one of the most famous English explorers of the Age of Exploration. He was also the first English explorer to sail around the world. Drake began his naval career when he was young. He became the captain of his own ship at the age of 20. For many years, he sailed around the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. He fought against the Spanish navy. He captured treasure from Spanish ships.

Drake returned to England in 1573. He did not stay long. Queen Elizabeth I asked Drake to sail to North America. She asked him to find a route to Asia. She also gave him a special license to be a privateer. A privateer was a person who was given permission to attack enemy ships and take treasure.

Drake hoped to find the fabled Northwest Passage. Many explorers believed this passage connected the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. In 1577, Drake left England. He sailed across the Atlantic and followed the coast of South America. It took a year for him to reach the southern tip of South America.

Drake and his crew sailed through the Drake Passage. The Drake Passage connects the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. He sailed along the west coast of South America and Mexico before reaching North America. In 1579, he landed near present-day San Francisco, California. Drake claimed the land for England. From there, he sailed across the Pacific Ocean. He eventually reached the Cape of Good Hope in Africa. After three years of traveling, Drake returned to England with riches and spices. He became an English hero, and many explorers tried to follow in his footsteps.

title: Henry Hudson
text:
Henry Hudson was an English sea captain. He was also an explorer who started off as a failure. He sailed on two voyages for England. He wanted to find a northern water route to the rich spice trade in Asia. On both voyages, the icy northern seas blocked his way. He returned home defeated. That didn’t stop him.

In 1609, Hudson and his crew sailed west across the Atlantic Ocean. This time, he sailed for a Dutch company called the Dutch East India Company. He traveled along the east coast of North America. He traveled from Newfoundland to the settlement at Jamestown, Virginia. Hudson did not stay in Jamestown for long. He sailed north from the settlement along the coast.

After a short time, Hudson and his crew landed in present-day New York on the island of Manhattan. He sailed inland up a wide river and explored the surrounding valley. Several landmarks in North America were named in honor of his exploration. These include Hudson Bay, the Hudson River, and the Hudson Valley. Hudson sailed along the Hudson River. He determined that it did not reach the Pacific Ocean. He returned to Europe, but he was not done exploring.

Hudson was sent on one more expedition in 1610 to find a northern route to Asia. They were unable to go far because of the icy waters and large sheets of ice. Hudson’s crew was not willing to continue. They forced Hudson and other crew members to leave the ship. Historians do not know what happened to Hudson after his last expedition. He is remembered for his exploration of North America.

title: Bartholomew Gosnold
text:
One of the most successful English explorers during the Age of Exploration was Bartholomew Gosnold. Gosnold was an early supporter of English exploration and colonization in North America. He helped find funds for explorers. Later, he asked the English government for permission to explore North America. In 1602, Queen Elizabeth I gave Gosnold permission to sail to North America. However, he had to find the funds for ships, supplies, and a crew on his own.

After finding the funds, Gosnold sailed to North America. He hoped to establish a colony south of Newfoundland. Gosnold and his crew landed in present-day Maine in May 1602. He sailed down the coast. He reached a large bay surrounded on three sides by water. He named the bay Cape Cod. This was because of the large amounts of cod fish in the bay.

Gosnold explored many areas around Cape Cod. He also established a settlement on the Elizabeth Islands. The settlement did not last long. Gosnold returned to England. He did not give up his dream of exploring North America. He helped create the Virginia Company to establish a colony in Virginia. In 1607, Gosnold and other members of the Virginia Company sailed to Virginia to establish the Jamestown Colony. He helped create the town and fort.

title: Conflict and Cooperation: English Explorers and American Indians
text:
English explorers encountered many different American Indian tribes in North America. Some of their interactions created cooperation. Other interactions created conflict. In 1585, explorers and settlers established a colony at Roanoke in present-day North Carolina. At first, the colonists and American Indians of the area were friendly with one another. They traded goods and shared resources. Over time, however, the colonists took too many resources from the American Indians. This created conflict. The colony at Roanoke was abandoned after just a few years.

Henry Hudson was the first English explorer to meet the American Indian tribes of coastal New York and New Jersey. Hudson and his crew traded with the tribes they met. They gave the tribes tools, clothing, and beads. They received furs, bread, corn, meat, and oysters in exchange. Unfortunately, Hudson’s crew thought the American Indians would steal from their ship. Hudson's crew refused to continue trading. This led to fighting between Hudson’s crew and the American Indians in the area.

The first known meeting between English-speaking explorers and the American Indians of the West took place in 1579. It was between Sir Francis Drake and the Coastal Miwok of California. Members of the tribe welcomed Drake and his men. Members of the neighboring Coastal Miwok tribes also visited Drake’s camp. Drake and his crew left to continue on their journey up the coast. The Coastal Miwok were upset by their departure. The English and Coastal Miwok were curious about one another. The customs and traditions of each group were foreign to the other. They did not speak the same language or look like one another. But they created respect between them.

title: French Exploration
text:
Like the Spanish and English, France sent explorers to the Americas during the Age of Exploration.

France wanted to colonize areas of the Americas, like other European countries. France’s main goals for exploration were to spread the Catholic religion and create new trade routes.

The French government and explorers wanted to spread their religious beliefs to the Americas. The Catholic Church worked with the French government to send missionaries to the Americas. They also gave them funds to construct missions across the Americas. The purpose of the missions was to convert American Indians to Christianity.

The French also wanted to find new resources. They hoped to use the resources of the Americas to make goods. French explorers also wanted to find and create new trade routes. The French also wanted to open new trade centers. The first French explorer to explore North America was Jacques Cartier. His journey encouraged other explorers to leave France and explore North America.

At first, French explorers focused their attention on present-day Canada and New England. The early French explorers arrived in the area. They didn't find any gold or silver there. However, they did find something of great value: furs! Wealthy French men and women loved to wear fancy clothing and hats made from the furs of beaver, mink, and otter. These furs and skins were widely available in North America. French explorers quickly established trade networks with many North American Indian tribes.

French explorers set up trading posts and colonies along rivers and at the mouths of bays. They used the area’s rich resources to produce goods. The goods were sent back to France. Many of these early sites were not successful. The settlers abandoned them and returned to France. The French realized they had to create a permanent foothold in North America to continue the trade networks they had established.

title: Essential Question
text: Why did the French explore and colonize North America?

title: Natural Hazards
text:
People move to and live in areas that meet their needs. However, many places around the world also have hazards, or dangers. The environment can cause natural hazards. A natural hazard is a dangerous event in nature. Some examples of natural hazards are hurricanes, tornadoes, wildfires, and earthquakes.

People have to think about the hazards of an area when they choose a place to settle. These hazards can be dangerous and cause massive amounts of damage. Hazards can affect homes, schools, industries, and the natural environment. There are many natural hazards that affect people in Indiana. These are tornadoes, earthquakes, floods, drought, and blizzards.

Tornadoes

A tornado is a devastating storm with high winds that usually form over land. Tornadoes form very quickly. Sometimes, they give only a few minutes of warning before they strike. Indiana is located in an area of the United States called “Tornado Alley.” This region spans the Great Plains, from Texas through North Dakota. Indiana has an average of 22 tornadoes a year. Three tornadoes happened on April 3, 1974, in southern Indiana. They crossed six counties, leaving lots of damage behind.

Earthquakes

An earthquake is a natural event in which the ground beneath the surface of the Earth shifts, causing waves of movement and shaking on the surface. Rocks and soil vibrate in response to the movement. The movement of the waves through the land causes buildings and roads to vibrate and shake. In the United States, most earthquakes happen along the fault lines in California, Oregon, and Washington. However, earthquakes can happen anywhere. Although they are rare, earthquakes do impact central Indiana. Recent earthquakes were felt in April 2008 and December 2010.

Floods

A flood is an event in which water rises in an area and has no place to go. Floods are caused by many different factors. Some of these are heavy rain, hurricanes, rapidly thawing snow, ice jams, and broken dams or levees. Floods can happen over a few hours, days, or weeks. One of Indiana’s most devastating floods happened in June 2008. The city of Columbus was completely flooded in a day. It ruined nine percent of farmland.

Droughts

People use surface water and groundwater to meet their wants and needs. If there isn’t much snow or rain, the groundwater can be diminished. This means it is used up and not replaced. A drought is a long period of time when an area receives less than average precipitation. This creates a shortage of water, which can lead to problems. Droughts affect people, animals, plants, and even the soil. Indiana experienced its last drought in 2012. Indianapolis set a record for only receiving 0.09 inches of precipitation in 47 days.

Blizzards

Blizzards are snow storms with high winds of at least 35 miles an hour. Blizzards limit people’s vision, restrict travel, and freeze animals and crops. The upper Midwest and the Great Plains experience blizzards often. Indiana was devastated by a blizzard in January 1978. Some areas were covered in over three feet of snow!

No matter the natural hazard, it is important to be prepared. You should always have a safety plan in place. Having an emergency kit assembled will help you to deal with natural hazards that you may encounter.

title: Jacques Cartier
text:
In 1534, King Francis I of France sent sailor Jacques Cartier to find a direct water route to Asia. There was no such water passage for anyone to find. Instead, Cartier was the first European to explore Newfoundland in Canada. He was also the first to explore the St. Lawrence River and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. He claimed all of the lands he explored for France. The St. Lawrence River flowed past a large hill that Cartier named Mont Real, which is French for "King's Mountain." It's now the city of Montreal.

Cartier named the lands that he explored “Canada.” Historians believe that the name “Canada” comes from the Huron-Iroquois word “kanata.” “Kanata” means “settlement” or “village.” Cartier learned the word from members of the Huron and Iroquois tribes. Cartier returned to France, but the king was not impressed with his tales of exploration. The king had hoped that Cartier would bring back riches and valuable resources, but he was not successful.

In 1541, Francis I ordered Cartier to return to Canada to help establish a permanent French settlement. Settlers tried establishing a colony near present-day Quebec City, but it failed. The settlers didn't get along with the native peoples of the area. Also, they couldn't stand the harsh winters. France didn't send another explorer to that region for 70 years. Cartier returned to France with barrels of what he thought were gold and diamonds, but he was wrong. He actually collected quartz crystals and a mineral called “fool’s gold.” After this, Cartier’s exploration career ended.

title: Samuel de Champlain
text:
Samuel de Champlain was a French explorer and mapmaker. He took several voyages to the Americas with other explorers before leading his first expedition. In 1608, Champlain was sent to Canada to establish a colony and find a route to Asia. On his expedition, he had the opportunity to observe and describe many of the areas of present-day Nova Scotia and the St. Lawrence Gulf and River.

As Champlain moved inland, he looked for a location that would be good for trade and settlement. He chose a site near the St. Lawrence River and Gulf. This area was called “kebec” by the American Indians of the region. He named the settlement Québec City. Champlain helped the settlers build a fort and a small town before he continued exploring the area.

Once Québec City was founded, Champlain traveled west. He hoped to discover more resources and areas to colonize. He explored the Great Lakes. Champlain established a new trading post south of Québec City along the St. Lawrence River. This trading post was near Cartier’s failed settlement. Over time, this trading post grew into the city of Montreal. In addition to being the first to explore areas of Canada, Champlain also created maps of the area. His maps were used by other explorers and settlers who came to the area.

title: Louis Jolliet
text:
One of the most successful French explorers of the 1600s was Louis Jolliet. Jolliet was one of the first French explorers born in Canada. Before becoming an explorer, he was a merchant. He bought and sold goods to settlers in Canada. He was not happy with his life as a merchant and trader. He wanted to do something more exciting.

In 1673, Jolliet partnered with a French priest named Jacques Marquette. Together, they traveled down the Mississippi River. They hoped to reach the mouth, or end, of the Mississippi River. Jolliet and Marquette learned a lot about the areas along the Mississippi River. They learned much from the American Indian tribes they met. They also traded with the tribes of the area.

Jolliet and Marquette traveled as far south as present-day Arkansas. They returned to Canada. They shared what they had learned with other explorers and merchants. Jolliet continued to explore areas of Canada. He explored the coast of Labrador and the Hudson Bay. He also explored many rivers in eastern Canada. He shared his experiences with other explorers. Jolliet’s experiences helped people settle in other areas of Canada.
